en: An Introduction to Master Han’s *Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
When Master Han showered the Dharma upon the world, even a single word that fell upon paper spread to the four quarters without waiting for legs.
His prolific writings have not been equaled since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; both the ignorant and the wise are well aware of this. (Sheng) Not.
This must be discussed in detail. (Voice: I was born at a time when a Great Master appeared in the world; yet, unfortunately, I became mired in worldly affairs.
My study of the Way was delayed, so that though I finally possessed ears and eyes, I was unable to hear or see [the truth].

When I finally began to feel regret and awakening, I was able to read the writings of our Great Master, but my karmic conditions were exhausted and my time had run out before the Master could dwell among humans again. Now, his...
The Elder remarked that two superior men had arrived here during the final days of the month. Among them was my friend Mr.
Cheng Zhongyan, with whom I first began my travels. After wandering for several days, I inquired in detail about the Master’s lifelong conduct and all matters concerning his pen and tongue;
thus, I was able to see the draft of the *Huayan Gangyao* (Essentials of the Avatamsaka Sutra), which the Master had personally annotated and revised by hand.
My friend has presented me with his examination of the Master’s original works and various miscellaneous writings that have not yet been published for the world.

As I read them, my heart was moved with profound sorrow. I reflect that we have never known these great matters from our youth, nor have we sought to enter the Master’s hall to behold his countenance.
Now, without intending it, I suddenly encounter the traces of his own hand—his ink-stained manuscripts—as if I were face-to-face with the Master himself.
Master, you have traveled throughout the great mountains, rivers, capitals, and major cities of the South and North seas, preaching the Dharma;
there are very few places you have not reached. Yet, you alone have never once set foot in our Xin’an.
Now, that you have arrived here with this unfashioned Great Dharma, which moreover bears the traces of your own handiwork—is this not the work of Heaven? (Shēng) Zhī.
It has been only a few years since this great undertaking began; thus, it has not yet been possible to read the Master’s works in their entirety.

However, looking back, the Master has already provided extensive commentaries on the greatest and most essential of the various sutras. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* alone remains unannotated, and I have resolved to complete it without delay.
It is most fitting that this be done with the utmost urgency. It should be completed by Cheng of Xin’an.

As the Master perceived that his worldly lifespan was nearing its end, he strove with solemn diligence day and night to hasten the completion of this work; for the Buddha’s mandate, the Master’s mandate, and the mandate of all living beings, rest entirely within it.
These two eminent men were of extraordinary and profound character, truly not unworthy of being descendants of the Dharma King. This is solely due to the Great Master...

The posthumous writings have not yet been carved, and I find no rest; this matter is particularly urgent. As soon as we began discussing the carving of the blocks, Master Cheng Ziwen took it upon himself to oversee the transcription.
All disciples of the Buddha should arrive in succession, lest some remain unaware of this.
Humbly drafted by his disciple Jinsheng of Haiyang,
as a preface to the *Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra is the Dharma-gate of the ultimate, perfect, and sudden *dhāraṇī*, which manifests the inherently wondrous adornment of cause and effect according to the measure of the Dharmadhātu, as proclaimed by Vairocana Buddha.
Its text is vast and its meaning is rich; its phenomena are profound and its principle is mysterious.
To summarize its essentials, it does not transcend the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). These four dharma-realms are: first, the realm of principle (*li*);...

The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is the realm. Because within the dharma of true nature there is fundamentally no such thing as the names and concepts of "sentient beings" or "Buddhas," how could there be images of self and other?
All worldly and world-transcending dharmas, as well as the causes and conditions of defilement and purity, are in their very essence entirely empty, ultimately pure, and inconceivable;
this is called the Dharma-realm of Principle (*li-fajie*). Second is the Dharma-realm of Phenomena (*shi-fajie*). This realm is precisely the Dharma-realm of Principle. Upon reaching...

Empty yet spiritual, pure to the ultimate degree and thus wondrous; unmoving in its original nature, it manifests according to karma. Suddenly transforming into the two divisions of appearance and perception, it illusorily opens the two paths of delusion and enlightenment.
Sentient and insentient beings, the holy and the mundane, the primary and the secondary—blazing with their similarities and differences, all that exists is ultimately inconceivable.
This is called the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Third is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

This is the realm (*dhātu*). Thus, there is no phenomenon outside of principle, and no principle outside of phenomena. Principle does not reject phenomena; bondage and liberation are distinct and clear.
Phenomena do not reject principle; arising and ceasing are quiescent. Though the waves and billows are myriad, they fully manifest the substance of water;

though the nature of water is of a single flavor, it universally displays the ripples. Emptiness and existence are applied together; essence and characteristics are non-dual. This is inconceivable. This is called...

This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai fa-jie*). Fourth is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai fa-jie*).
When these three realms are combined, they perfectly enter into the one true reality. Since principle and phenomena do not contradict one another, they are inherently unobstructed.

By entering phenomena into principle, principle is inexhaustible and phenomena are likewise inexhaustible; by subsuming phenomena within principle, principle is without distinction and phenomena are likewise without distinction.
Marvelous! By raising a single thought, the three periods of time are perfectly illuminated; by blowing upon a single hair, the ten directions are vividly manifested.
Within the fundamental reality (the "correct") lies the dependent world: within a single pore are immeasurable and boundless worlds. Within the dependent world lies the fundamental reality:
within a single atom are infinite and inexhaustible Tathāgatas. One and many are mutually fused; extension and contraction are sovereign and free. This is inconceivable. This is...

This refers to the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*). Thus, all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—whether form or mind—do not transcend these four types of Dharma-realms.
Furthermore, these four realms are nothing other than the single mind; apart from the mind, there is no phenomenon that can be spoken of.
This mind, too, is but a provisional designation; it cannot be described in words and is inconceivable. It is the one true Great Dharma.

It is the realm (*dhātu*). The Tathāgata has realized the nature of this dharma-realm, manifested the characteristics of this dharma-realm, expanded the measure of this dharma-realm, emitted the light of this dharma-realm, gathered the capacities of this dharma-realm, revealed the assemblies of this dharma-realm, exhausted the principles of this dharma-realm, and expounded the sūtras of this dharma-realm.
This sūtra has a single name yet comprises three sections; as its chapters, verses, and content are extensive, the number of fascicles is particularly numerous.
It was difficult for humans to preserve this secret treasury; the Dragon Palace had long guarded it in mystery.

During the period when the Semblance Dharma dwells in the world, the Great Master Nāgārjuna exhaustively mastered all the precious scriptures of the world. While searching for treasures within the ocean, he encountered these wondrous sūtras, the unsurpassed True Vehicle.

Alas, that the Great Dharma was not heard! How could one have perceived the manifestations of one’s own mind? Had the Perfect Teaching not been realized, how could the radiance of the *dharmatā* have been revealed?

By focusing my spirit upon the profound records, I attained the beginning and end of the lower sections; exerting all my strength in its proclamation, I expanded the knowledge and vision of those of superior faculties.
First it was disseminated in Khotan, and subsequently transmitted and expounded in China. Since this scripture first appeared...

Regarding other countries, it is only here in this land that Zen teachers—drawing from both the monastic and lay communities, the enlightened and the wise—have manifested unimpeded eloquence and attained teacherless wisdom.
With their powerful faculties and great functions, they discourse vertically and horizontally, moving freely and without fear between birth-and-death and nirvana.
Standing atop the crown of Vairocana, transcending the eon of Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, from antiquity to the present, it is beyond all calculation.
Is it not the case that all have emerged from the transformative teaching of this sutra?

Or, whether through other scriptures or the conditions of teachers and friends, if one attains realization of one's own nature through a single moment of resonance, one must still receive certification from this sutra before being able to propagate [the Dharma].

The self-nature is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed. Thus, the ancients said: "There is nothing that does not emerge from this Dharma-realm; there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.
Is it not for this reason? From ancient times to the present, people have derived great utility and attained great mastery through this sutra.
One cannot fail to know the origin of this sutra; one cannot fail to know that which was bestowed by the Great Master Nāgārjuna.

Regarding the commentaries and treatises on this sutra, there have been masters of the lineage throughout the generations; yet, it is only the Great Master Qingliang who alone transcends all previous works.
Contemplating the essence of the Dharma-realm, this commentary opens and synthesizes the sūtra. It is truly the response-body of Mañjuśrī and the universal illumination of Vairocana.
Through the six aspects and ten mysteries, its profound purport is revealed; through the five periods and four divisions, its complete text is gathered.

Dividing the chapters and clarifying the meanings is like the bright moon shining upon a clear sky; revealing the essential principles sentence by sentence is like the ocean-seal reflecting the celestial bodies.

In principle, nothing is left unprepared; in practice, nothing is left incomplete. Thus, the commentaries and sub-commentaries may truly be said to form a harmonious union with the sūtra, like the relationship between sovereign and minister.

Since these commentaries first appeared, from the Tang dynasty through to the Ming, they have been expounded in every generation without fail. Even during the reign of our current dynasty’s Shenzong, they were lectured upon year after year until the sessions could no longer continue.
Alas, for the past twenty years, we have heard nothing regarding the investigation of the meaning of these commentaries.

In this profound essence of the Way, both people and things have diminished; body and mind are equally frail and weak. When examining affairs, they seem easy, yet one fears the difficulties of the Way.
Regardless of whether one is a layperson or a monk, all are robbed by the prevailing climate of the times.

Even among the clergy who serve as masters of seats, regarding the Sūtras or the Śāstras, most are unwilling to seek them deeply; whether it be a single phrase or a single passage, they follow only what is superficial.

They consider it fastidious, regarding it as simple and clear; conversely, they treat the ancient commentaries as迂談 (迂談: far-fetched talk) and take the colloquialisms of the current age as the most essential and wondrous.
Consequently, at recent Dharma assemblies, there is a preference for pointing out the literal text, while formal exegesis gradually becomes superficial.
As a result, the ancient commentaries and sub-commentaries are on the verge of being lost, causing the ocean of the Tathāgata’s single-character Dharma-gate to... [be obscured].

Though the ink remains, the sutra scrolls have not been fully preserved; the Dharma-realm is encompassed without remainder, yet it remains as if entirely unheard of—how much less can one grasp its true meaning?
That the transmission of the Dharma has reached this state is truly to be lamented. Indeed, the commentaries of the ancients all flowed forth from wisdom.
Sometimes the general meaning is presented in outline; sometimes the fine details are analyzed with precision. There are direct expositions and indirect elucidations;

comprehensive clarifications and supportive illuminations; specific citations and anticipatory divisions. Turning in circles to enter the subtle, the methods of opening and closing vary. Alas! Many scholars today possess broad knowledge yet shallow understanding;
consequently, when they encounter the commentaries of the ancients, they deem the realms of wisdom to be fragmented and disjointed.
Furthermore, at this time, the habitual tendencies of narrow-minded pride increase and deepen day by day, while frivolous and shallow views become increasingly tainted and thickened.
Consequently, regarding this very scripture, many turn back upon reaching its shores;

it is not only that ancient commentaries are shunned for their complexity and left unexamined, but there are even those who toy with *nidānas* as the ultimate vehicle of the *zong*, disparaging the Tripitaka teachings as mere dregs and textual words, constantly shaking their heads in disregard.

They cover their ears and refuse to hear. How is it that they pursue the branches while forgetting the root, identifying with the tributaries while losing sight of the source, and falling into such inversion?
By what cause might they be awakened? When perverse winds blow wildly, a single period of time is difficult to turn back. My late master, Hamsan, relied upon the great vow of the Dharma-dhātu.
Manifesting his birth at this juncture, he deeply lamented the temporal obscurations. He focused his attention on the Great Sūtra and allowed his mind to roam through the ancient commentaries.

Extracting the governing principles and grasping the essentials, he resolved the meanings and divided the text. Within three years, the general purport of the entire sūtra was clear from beginning to end;

furthermore, regarding points in the commentaries that had not yet been fully developed, he provided supplementary explanations. Thus, he gathered all interpretations within the span of his fingers and palms, and peered into the Dharma-realm from the tip of a single hair.

The single nature is perfectly luminous and entirely without obstruction. This *Essential Outline* (*Gangyao*) is composed so that students may, by means of the outline, access the extensive commentaries;

through the commentaries, enter the sutras; and through the sutras, realize their own nature. It is intended to cause those with narrow and inferior habits to gradually approach the truth while distancing themselves from delusion, and to lead them ever deeper into the vast and sublime realm.
This is the purpose for which this *Essential Outline* was written. Thus it is said. Qing... [text ends].
The Great Master Liang was the meritorious minister of this fundamental scripture, and my late teacher, Hanshan, was the guiding master of its commentaries and sub-commentaries.
On the very day he was about to set down his brush after completing his work, Caoxi made an earnest request; out of a sense of righteousness, I could not decline.
This work is appropriate for such conduct. Consequently, the origins and transmission of this commentary have not been recorded; its general outline lacks a title from beginning to end.
Furthermore, as my late teacher passed away at Caoxi before completing it, this particular case study has resulted in an incomplete tradition.

Fortunately, through the diligent efforts of Master Yi (Yìgōng), a member of the Dharma lineage, funds were raised and the carvers of Xīn'ān completed the woodblock printing. Alas, Master Yi also passed away while still burdened by his labors.

This, too, does not yet suffice to request a preface for the Great Dharma. In the spring of the Dingchou year, while I was at Mount Kuang’s Fayun Hermitage on account of performing the memorial rites for my late teacher, I obtained this newly carved edition;
it was as if I had recovered a long-lost treasure. As each dharma manifests before me, its utility is inexhaustible.
Therefore, I have exhausted these humble words to serve as a proclamation for future generations. Thus it is said.
On the Buddha’s Birthday in the fourth month of the year Dingshou of the Chongzhen era,
the dharma-heir Guanheng burned incense and inscribed this at the Venerable’s Quarters of Fayun Chan Temple on Wuru Peak.
Essential Summary of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Hanshan at Fayun Monastery on Mount Kuang in Ming China, who has organized and categorized the sections and chapters of this sutra according to the *Xiyuji*.
According to the *Xiyuji*, it is said that there are three versions: the superior version contains thirteen thousand great chiliocosms.
The verses number as many as the atoms in a world-system (*dhātu*), and the chapters (*parivarta*) number as many as the atoms in a single four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*).

The middle-length version consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters. The abbreviated version contains one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.
When the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna entered the Dragon Palace, he beheld both the superior and middle versions; these are beyond the mental capacity of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Nengchi (Aśvaghoṣa) subsequently recorded the lower version for circulation among humanity. What has been transmitted to this region today consists of eighty fascicles and thirty-nine chapters;
because the arrival of the scripture was incomplete, what is currently practiced is but an abridged version. Nevertheless, this scripture is my...

When Vairocana Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment, he expounded [the teaching] in accordance with his true nature at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), speaking it all at once and pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Therefore, the number of sections varies according to the differences in what is seen and heard.
Now, there are seven locations where this sūtra was preached, nine assemblies, and thirty-nine chapters. As for the meaning elucidated therein:
It encompasses the four dharma realms and subsumes the causes and effects of the five periods and six positions.

Master Qingliang’s commentary structures and explains the entire sutra through the fourfold division of faith-understanding, practice, and realization. It consists of seven locations, nine assemblies, and thirty-nine chapters.
In the first assembly at the site of enlightenment, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva expounded the Dharma-gate of the causes and effects of the primary and secondary [aspects] of Vairocana Tathāgata.
From the first fascicle to the eleventh fascicle, there are six chapters of the sutra. As for these six chapters:
(The Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Sovereign; The Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata; The Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra;
The Chapter on the Formation of the World; The Chapter on the Flower Treasury World; The Chapter on Vairocana).

The second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*). Therein, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva expounded the Dharma-gates of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and other teachings.
This comprises six fascicles from the twelfth to the fifteenth, containing six chapters. As for these six chapters:
(The Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata; The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths; The Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance; The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Wisdom;
The Chapter on Pure Conduct; The Chapter on Worthy Leader).
The third assembly was held in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace. Therein, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati expounded the Dharma-gates such as the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
This comprises six chapters of the sūtra, from fascicle sixteen to fascicle eighteen. As for these six chapters:
(Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter on the Ten Abodes; Chapter on Holy Conduct;
Chapter on the Merit of the First Resolve for Enlightenment; Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma).
The fourth assembly was held in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. Therein, the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha expounded the Dharma-gates such as the Ten Practices.
This comprises four chapters of scripture from fascicle nineteen to fascicle twenty-one. As for these four chapters:
(Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of Yāma; Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Palace of Yāma; Chapter on the Ten Practices;
Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries).
From the fifth assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja expounds the Dharma gates such as the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Self-...
From fascicle twenty-two to fascicle thirty-three, there are three sections of sutra. As for these three sections:
(1) "The Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," (2) "The Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," and (3) "The Chapter on the Ten Dedications."
The sixth assembly was held in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Therein, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*).
This spans from fascicle thirty-four to fascicle thirty-nine, comprising one single chapter of the sutra;
that chapter being the "Chapter on the Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*).

In the seventh assembly, the Hall of Universal Radiance, Vairocana Tathāgata taught Dharma-gates numbering in the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), as well as the merits of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks and light rays.
Furthermore, Samantabhadra and other bodhisattvas taught the ten great samādhis and other gates to the Dharma of Equal Enlightenment.
This section spans from fascicle forty to fascicle fifty-two. Together—
The Eleven Chapters of the Sūtra. As for the eleven chapters:

(1) "The Chapter on the Ten Samādhis Spoken by Samantabhadra," (2) "The Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," (3) "The Chapter on the Ten Endurances," (4) "The Chapter on the Incalculable [Aeon] Spoken by the Buddha," (5) "The Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata Spoken by Cittarāja Bodhisattva," and (6) "The Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas."

The preceding clarifies the causes of differentiation: the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Inconceivable Dharma" spoken by the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, and the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies" spoken by Samantabhadra.
The following clarifies the fruits of differentiation: the "Chapter on the Merits of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks" spoken by the Buddha.
[Finally,] the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" spoken by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra clarifies equality.
Because it explains the Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata, it clarifies the fruit of equality;
from the second assembly above down to this point, it has once again clarified the cause and fruit of the six stages.
The eighty-third assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance, where Samantabhadra Bodhisattva expounded the Dharma-door of Transcending the World.
This spans from fascicle fifty-three to fascicle fifty-nine, comprising one single chapter of the sutra. As for this "one chapter":
(These two [chapters] from the "Chapter on Transcending the World" universally clarify the cause and effect across the six stages.
In the ninth assembly at Jetavana, there are two assemblies: the primary and the secondary.
First, Vairocana Tathāgata emits light and manifests signs to answer the thoughts and requests of the bodhisattvas; this constitutes the primary assembly. Next, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...
Emerging from the Well-Situated Pavilion, he went among humans to awaken six thousand bhikṣus and directed Sudhana to visit the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

These constitute the final assembly, collectively forming the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*), which spans from the sixtieth to the eightieth fascicle as a single chapter. Regarding this single chapter:
(That is, the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter; these three [chapters] clarify the cause and effect of the six stages throughout.
Regarding the division of the eighty-fascicle scripture into five cycles and four sections:
first is the cycle of the cause and effect of faith (*śraddhā*). This refers to the section that cites the fruit to encourage the joyful arising of faith; namely, the First Assembly.
In the *Bodhimaṇḍa*, the *Vairocana-āśraya-samyak-phala-vipāka-dharmaparyāya* is taught, spanning from the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers" to the "Chapter on Vairocana.

These six chapters of the sūtra extol the inconceivable fruits of the Tathāgata’s two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—thereby exhorting sentient beings of great resolve to give rise to aspiration and engender pure faith. [The preceding section concludes.]
The five preceding chapters reveal the merit of the fruit—the reliance (the environment) and the supported (the body)—of Vairocana; the final chapter clarifies the Buddha’s original cause.
Therefore, this is called the "Section on the Completeness of the Cause and Effect of What is Trusted," and it is also named the "Section on Exalting the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith."
Second, the section on the "Pervasive Cause and Effect of Distinctions" is also called the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding.

It begins from the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsagṛha*), where it teaches the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), ten abidings (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Then, following the reassembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance, it continues through the ten concentrations (*samādhi*) up to the "Chapter on the Abodes of All Bodhisattvas. Together, these comprise twenty chapters.
The six chapters of the sutra clarify the perfection of the causes of differentiation.

The subsequent three chapters—the "Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha" chapter, the "Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" chapter, and the "Virtues of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks" chapter—clarify the fulfillment of the fruits of differentiation.
The six chapters from the "Ten Samādhis" onward clarify Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), while the final three chapters clarify Sublime Enlightenment (pratyekabuddha-bodhi).

Regarding the third point, the "completeness of the equality of cause and effect": this refers to the two chapters of the sutra—the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" and the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata"—which clarify the equality of cause and effect.
In the former, the "Practices of Samantabhadra," it is shown that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition.
Next, the appearance of the Tathāgata clarifies that the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause; because cause and fruit are non-dual, it is called "Equivalence.
Together with the preceding two cycles of differentiation, this is collectively titled the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding."

Regarding the fourth section, "The Completion of the Cause and Effect of Accomplishing Practice," it is also titled "The Section on Entrusting the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct.

This refers to the teaching of the *Lokottara-dharma* (Dharma Transcending the World) across eight assemblies and three sessions in the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantābhāsa-maṇḍala*). Thus, the cause and effect of accomplishing practice are completed:
as the clouds of universal wisdom give rise to two hundred questions, the vase of Samantabhadra pours forth two thousand responses, comprehensively clarifying the cause and effect of the six stages.

From fascicle fifty-three to fifty-nine, there is one continuous sutra. The first part generally elucidates the causes of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), while the latter part elucidates the fruit of the eight aspects (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
The causes of the five stages consist of the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), direction (*pratipatti*), ground (*bhūmi*), and equal enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
The fruit of the eight phases consists of descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing Māra and attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and entering Nirvāṇa.
These are based upon the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu*. As one advances in cultivation to perfect these practices, the stages interpenetrate one another;
because each single stage is fully endowed with all stages, the names of the individual stages are set aside, and only the perfectly interfused practice is elucidated. Therefore, it is so named.
Entrusting oneself to the Dharma for further cultivation.
Regarding the "Section on the Completion of the Causes and Effects of the Fivefold Realization," it is also called the "Section on Achieving Virtue through Realization by Relying on Persons.

This refers to the teaching of the *Dharmadhātu-praveśa-dharmaparyāya* (The Dharma-Gate of Entering the Dharma Realm) in the ninth assembly at the Jetavana Grove, which consists of thirty chapters requested by the Bodhisattvas.

Question: He inquired about the matters within the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition. Because the ocean of fruition transcends all words, the Tathāgata responded by manifesting signs and further emitted light to receive him.
Within that light, he clearly beheld all that he had asked, causing him to realize it through direct manifestation;
this constitutes the primary assembly. Next, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Pavilion of Excellent Abiding and gradually proceeded toward the human realm.
In the interim, before the Great Stūpa, six thousand bhikṣus were made to realize the fruit instantaneously.
Next, he directed Sudhana to travel southward to visit fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); these are collectively termed the "Final Assembly.

Furthermore, at the very end, Sudhana beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and entered into a single pore of Samantabhadra’s body, thereby instantaneously perfecting the fruits of kalpas of cultivation. Thus, the first thirty [chapters]...

The eighth chapter merely summarizes the causes and effects of the six stages, causing one to give rise to faith and develop understanding, so that by relying upon it, one initiates practice and cultivation;
only upon reaching this point does one truly enter realization. Therefore, it is called the "Section on Entering Realization and Accomplishing Virtue Based on the Person.
If there were no actual realization, then the preceding stages of understanding and practice would all be in vain; thus, the work concludes with realization.
However, this preceding eighty-fascicle scripture is divided into thirty-nine chapters (*pāda*). These many chapters are subsumed within the five cycles and four sections (*catur-bhāga*).

This work merely divides the text into chapters to provide a detailed commentary on the scriptural passages. The meanings elucidated by those passages consist of the four dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Ancient masters interpreted the scriptures using the six characteristics (*ṣaḷ-lakṣaṇa*) and the ten layers of the gate of mystery (*daśavidha-gūḍha-dvāra*) to encompass the entirety [of the teaching].

Regarding the meaning of the "sections" (*bu*): the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) are: first, the dharma-realm of principle; second, the dharma-realm of phenomena; third, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;

and fourth, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. As for the six characteristics (*liuxiang*), they are: totality and particularity, sameness and difference, formation and disintegration.

It is through these six characteristics being simultaneous that the ten layers of the profound gateways (*xuanyuanmen*) are established, thereby manifesting the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
The Ten Mysterious Gates are: 1. The Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment (like a single drop of ocean water containing the flavor of all rivers); 2.

The Gate of Unimpeded Sovereignty over the Broad and the Narrow (a one-foot mirror manifesting a thousand layers of reflections); 3. The Gate of the Interpenetration of the One and the Many without Confusion (a thousand lamps in a single room, each light merging with every other);
4. The Gate of the Sovereign Identity of All Dharmas (like gold and its color, which are inseparable); 5. The Gate of Secret Concealment and Manifestation...

The Gate of the Subtle Interpenetration and Stable Establishment (*Sūkṣma-anyonyānugama-vyavasthāna-mukha*). (Like a crystal vase containing many mustard seeds. 3. The Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net (*Indrajāla-gocara-mukha*).
(Ten mirrors reflecting each other; images appear in infinite layers. 4. The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena (*Vastu-niśraya-dharma-pratibodhana-mukha*).

(Setting up an image and raising an arm; everything the eye touches is the Way. 5. The Gate of the Formation of Distinct Dharmas Through Temporal Separation (*Adhvavyavaccheda-dharmavaiśeṣya-siddhi-mukha*). (A dream of a single night soars through a hundred years. 6. The Gate of the Sovereign... [text fragment]
This accompanies the Gate of Perfect Interfusion and Endowment (wherein all the stars bow toward the North Star).
Because these six aspects and ten mysteries are simultaneously and fully present, the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*) is established.

Therefore, whenever a single phenomenon, a single action, or a single dharma is cited in the sutras, it necessarily encompasses the meaning of these six aspects and ten mysteries to manifest the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm. However, this is extensive...

The Great Unbounded Principle is subsumed within the gate of the Dharma-realm contemplation (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*). It is gathered back into the single mind, wherein every thought-moment is fully complete;

only thus does one accord with this school, which stands far beyond all other teachings. Therefore, these wondrous practices of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) multiply by a factor of ten thousand times a hundred million between day and eon, as detailed in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.

The items listed above constitute the general purport of the entire sutra. Anyone who recites this sutra must first understand its sections and chapters and become thoroughly proficient in the contemplation of its principles;
only then, when facing the text, will they be able to enter the boundless Dharma-realm in every thought-moment.

Because the scriptural text is vast and its encompassed meanings are boundless, commentators have divided it into five sections and four parts so that the meanings may find their proper place and the reader may naturally attain realization upon encountering the text.
This is the general outline of the structural analysis. As for the underlying principles, each chapter has its own specific direction and purpose.
Next, I shall explain the title.
The title, *The Great Vaipulya Buddha-Flower Adornment Sūtra* (*Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*), is established based on person, dharma, metaphor, cause, and result.

The three characters "Great," "Vaipulya" (Widely Extensive), and "Broad" refer to the Dharma; they represent the entire substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), encompassing its essence, characteristics, and functions.
Because of its great significance, the Buddha is the person who is able to realize it; the three greatnesses of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are the dharmas that are realized.

The flower serves as a metaphor for the cause cultivated within the nature of the dharma-realm; "adornment" refers to the adornment of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) to achieve the fruit of the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Regarding the "three greatnesses": "great" refers to the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*). By citing the dharma-realm itself, it is shown to be vertically exhaustive throughout the three periods of time.
It extends horizontally throughout the ten directions, vast and all-encompassing; great without exterior, it takes the measure of the ultimate *dharmadhātu* and is conventionally termed "Great.
Thus it is said to be "expansive, inclusive, and boundless. "Directions" (*fang*) refers to characteristics (*xiang*), which are like phenomena (*fa*).
Since the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is originally without characteristics, it now manifests its entire substance as the phenomenal characteristics of the ten *dharmadhātus*. All sentient beings...

Sentient beings possess this Dharma-nature which maintains the tracks [of reality] and enables the arising of understanding; therefore, it is said that they "sustain themselves by means of the True Dharma.

This means that within the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), there is not a single phenomenon with characteristics that is not fully present; thus, these characteristics are also "great. "Vast" refers to the greatness of function;
this means that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* possesses great functional power, as it is able to transform and give rise to the functions of the ten dharma-realms. Therefore...

It is said that [the Dharma-body] accords with its essence and is all-pervasive. If there are sentient beings who can awaken to this essence, they immediately possess the function of transforming the mundane into the sacred;
thus, the function is also great. By means of these three greatnesses, the true source of the single Dharma-realm is encompassed in its entirety.
Because one awakens to this fundamental source, one is called a Buddha; thus it is said that one awakens to this profound mystery. "Buddha" means awakening.

Since the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is also termed the *vimala-dharmakāya*, yet it must rely upon the adornment of myriad practices (*sāhasra-pratipatti*) to become the *saṃbhogakāya*, it is designated as the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Because one cultivates the causes by means of this, the flower serves as a metaphor for the merit of the myriad practices; regarding the word "flower," it necessarily...
There is a fruit. "Adornment" (*yan*) refers to embellishment; it means to adorn the essence of the fruit, the Dharma-body, with the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices.
This is because it constitutes the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogabuddha*). "Adornment" also means to refine the Dharma to form a person. One who now preaches this sutra is precisely the Reward Buddha.
At the first assembly at the site of enlightenment, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva served as the presiding host. He expounded the teaching on the manifestation of the fruit (*phala*).
This consists of six chapters of sutra, categorized into four sections; specifically, this is the section titled "Manifesting the Fruit and Encouraging Joyful Faith."
Chapter One of One: The Sublime Array of the World Lords (*Lokendra-vyūha*).

This clarifies the exhortation to aspire by citing the fruit [of Buddhahood]. There are six chapters in this scripture, which are divided into ten sections: 1. The Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching (the first chapter);
2. The Section on the Joint Request of the Great Assembly; 3. The Section on the Gathering of the Multitude through the Light from the Face; 4. The Section on the [Light from the] Ūrṇā-kośa...
1. The Section on Manifesting the Dharma; 2. The Section on the Emission of Light from Between the Eyebrows—these two are in the second chapter.
3. The Section on Samādhi of Samantabhadra; 4. The Section on the Shared Empowerment of All Buddhas; 5. The Section on the Dharma Lord Arising from Concentration; 6.

The Section on the Great Assembly’s Repeated Request—these five are in the third chapter. 7. The Section on the Correct Exposition of the Ocean of Dharma—this is contained within the final three chapters.
Regarding the phrase "The Sublime Array of the World’s Sovereigns" (*Lokendra-vyuha*): "World" (*loka*) refers to the three worlds:

the world of the Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened Ones (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*), the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*). "Sovereign" (*indra*) refers to the Buddha as the sovereign of the world of the Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened Ones;

the Bodhisattvas and the various devas of the desire realm as the sovereigns of the receptacle world; and the various classes of spirits as the sovereigns of the world of sentient beings. "Array" (*vyūha*) refers to the... [Vairocana].
When Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment, his primary retributive fruit-body was adorned with marks and embellishments as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field;
now, dwelling amidst the ocean-like assembly at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he serves as the adornment for two kinds of worlds.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas and the various devas and celestial kings serve as his retinue, thereby adorning the Lord Buddha.
The ground, the diamond-jewel trees, and so forth, serve as the adornment of his environment.
Thus, the threefold world—comprising both the primary and secondary retributions—adorns one another; therefore, it is called "wondrous adornment."
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the forest retreat, having newly attained perfect enlightenment.
That ground was firm, composed of vajra, and adorned with exquisite jewel wheels and various precious flowers.
Adorned with pure maṇi jewels, the infinite oceans of all forms and appearances manifest therein.
Maṇi banners constantly emit radiance and perpetually produce sublime sounds. Nets of various jewels and garlands of exquisite fragrant flowers hang down, draped all around.
The sovereign maṇi-jewel king manifested with sovereign mastery, raining down inexhaustible jewels and various wondrous flowers that were scattered across the ground.
Rows of jewel-trees stood in formation, their branches and leaves lush and radiant. Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the adornments of this site of enlightenment were reflected therein.
That Bodhi tree was lofty, eminent, and extraordinary; its body was of diamond and its trunk was of lapis lazuli.
Various exquisite jewels formed its branches, while precious leaves spread out in lush profusion, casting a shade like clouds.

Jeweled flowers of diverse colors were distributed across the boughs, their reflections shimmering; furthermore, *maṇi* gems served as its fruit, radiating luster and emitting flames, interspersed among the blossoms.
Those trees were perfectly circular and all emitted brilliant light. From within that light, mani-jewels rained down.
Inside those mani-jewels were various bodhisattvas; like a mass of clouds, they appeared simultaneously. This was further due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
That Bodhi tree constantly emits sublime sounds, expounding various dharmas without end or limit.
The palaces and towers where the Tathāgata dwells are vast, magnificent, and beautiful, pervading the ten directions, and are composed of mani jewels of manifold colors.
It was adorned with various kinds of precious flowers. All the ornaments emitted flowing light like clouds, which gathered from between the palaces to form banners.
Boundless assemblies of bodhisattvas at sites of enlightenment gathered there.
It possessed a net made of the sovereign maṇi-jewel-king of inconceivable sounds that manifests the radiance of all Buddhas—the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
The power of spiritual penetrations causes all realms to emerge from within it. The dwellings and houses where all sentient beings reside all manifest their reflections therein.
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Buddhas' spiritual powers, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment.
Its lion throne is lofty, vast, and exquisitely beautiful; its dais is made of mani jewels, and its lattice-work is formed of lotus flowers.
Its wheels were made of pure, wondrous jewels; its necklaces were fashioned from flowers of various colors.
Its halls, pavilions, towers, galleries, steps, and windows—indeed, all manner of objects and forms—were fully adorned. Precious trees with branches and fruits were arranged in rows all around.

Clouds of mani-jewel light illuminate one another. The King of Jewels manifested by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the wondrous gems within the topknots of all Bodhisattvas all emit radiance, coming to shine with brilliant clarity. Furthermore, they are sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas.
He expounded the vast realm of the Tathāgata; his sublime voice resounded afar, reaching everywhere.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this seat, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena; his wisdom entered the three periods of time, being entirely equal.
His body fills all worlds; his voice universally accords with the lands of the ten directions.

Just as empty space contains all images yet makes no distinctions among any objects, and just as empty space pervades everything and enters equally into all lands, so too does his body constantly sit pervasively within all sites of enlightenment amidst the assemblies of bodhisattvas.

His majestic radiance blazes forth like the rising sun illuminating the world. Having completely purified the great ocean of all merits cultivated throughout the three periods of time, he constantly manifests birth in the lands of all Buddhas.
His boundless forms and perfect light pervade the entire dharma-realm without distinction, expounding all dharmas like the spreading of a great cloud from every single tip of a pore.
They are able to contain all worlds without obstruction; each manifests immeasurable powers of supernatural penetration to teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings.
Their bodies pervade the ten directions without coming or going, and their wisdom enters into all phenomena.
He realized the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena. Within that radiance, he beheld every supernatural transformation of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
All the inconceivable adornments of all Buddha-lands throughout all inconceivable eons were made manifest.
He was surrounded by a multitude of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds. Their names were as follows: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [and so forth].

their eye of wisdom is clear and penetrating, observing the three periods of time with equanimity. They are endowed with the purity of all samādhis; their eloquence is as vast and inexhaustible as the ocean.
Possessing the Buddha’s merits, they are majestic and venerable; knowing the faculties of sentient beings, they transform and subdue them according to what is appropriate. They enter...
The wisdom of the treasury of the dharma-realm is without distinction; it realizes the profound and vast liberation of the Buddhas.
It is able to enter each stage according to skillful means, sustained by the ocean of all vows, and remains ever conjoined with wisdom until the end of the future.
It thoroughly understands the rare, vast, and secret realm of all Buddhas, and is well-versed in the equal dharma of all Buddhas. Thus it is said.
They tread upon the Tathāgata’s Ground of Universal Radiance and enter the ocean-gates of immeasurable samādhis.
In all places, they manifest bodies in accordance with the needs of beings; their worldly conduct is entirely identical to that of others.

They possess vast dhāraṇīs that gather the ocean of all dharmas, and through skillful eloquence, they turn the non-retrogressive wheel. The great ocean of the merits of all Tathāgatas enters into their very bodies. One.
I shall go to all lands where all Buddhas reside, in accordance with my vows. Having already made offerings to all Buddhas throughout boundless eons, I shall remain joyful and tireless.
Wherever any Tathāgata attains Bodhi, I shall always be present therein, drawing near and never abandoning them.
Constantly employing the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows that I have attained, I shall cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the body of wisdom.
Having thus accomplished such immeasurable merits, there were furthermore as many Vajradharas as there are atoms in a Buddha-world.
They were as follows: the Vajradhara of Wondrous Color Nārāyaṇa, and the Vajradhara of the Swift Banner of the Solar Disk.

he enters the inconceivable realm of liberation and abides amidst assemblies with a particularly outstanding majestic light;

From "Thus have I heard" down to "the assembly gathered like an ocean of clouds" constitutes the common introduction (*nidāna*). This provides the causal conditions for this Dharma assembly.
Within it, the six factors of accomplishment are constantly mentioned: namely, faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly.
When these six are complete, the conditions for the Dharma arise. Furthermore, these are words of the Buddha’s final charge found throughout all sutras; therefore, they are called "common."
Preface. This sutra has six matters which, if aligned with the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), are utterly distinct from other sutras.
If one says, "Thus have I heard," it means that Mañjuśrī and Ānanda, by virtue of their Dharma-realm wisdom, universally hear the universal Dharma of the Dharma-realm.
"I" refers to the true self of the non-self Dharmakāya; "hearing" refers to the true hearing that enters the Dharma-realm. "At one time" refers to Vairocana...
At the time of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, there was neither past nor present; it was a time of equality regarding kalpas and moments of thought.
As for the place, it was the Bodhimaṇḍa, the dwelling place of the wisdom of self-awakening.
As for the assembly, it was the assembly manifested by the Sāgaramudrā-samādhi. These six aspects are all described in terms of the Dharma. That ground is as firm as adamant.
This is the adamantine ground of the mind (*vajracittabhūmi*). Next, the superior and wondrous jewel wheels and so forth manifest the adornments of the stages of realization (*bhūmi*).
The Bodhi tree and so forth constitute the adornments of the tree of awakening; the abodes of the Tathāgatas and so forth constitute the adornments of the palace.
The lion thrones and so forth constitute the adornment of the seat; these are all adornments of the secondary retribution (*niṣyanda-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Abiding upon this throne, he attains supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), thereby fully accomplishing the adornment of the Teacher’s body, which pervades all worlds.

This is what is meant by "the ten bodies pervading" and "the three karmas universally encompassing," which clearly manifests the adornment of primary retribution (*vipāka-adhiṣṭhāna*). Because the primary and secondary retributions mutually adorn one another, it is called "wondrous adornment. Next—
He was surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds; this constitutes the adornment of the retinue, as well as the mutual adornment of the principal and the associates.
This ocean-like assembly of beings consists of two categories: those born together with him and those born separately from him.

The bodhisattvas constitute the group born together, while the various devas, celestial kings, and others constitute the group born separately. Of these, the bodhisattvas form a single, unified assembly. It is said:

"Those born together" refers to Bodhisattvas who equally attain the Dharma-nature body, as they are all born from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and manifest in the uniform form of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, "equal" means that this applies to all stages. There are thirty-nine assemblies of various celestial kings and others.
"Those born separately" refers to those of diverse classes who manifest in the forms of various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This is because of the nature of the case. Furthermore, it is for the sake of the distinct virtues of the *dharmadhātu*.

Moreover, there are forty-two assemblies, consisting of the assembly flowing forth from within the lion throne and the assembly emerging from between the eyebrows. These forty assemblies are assigned to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of holiness (*daśārya*).
The assembly on the lion throne corresponds to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); the assembly emerging from between the eyebrows corresponds to Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha*).
These collectively correspond to the forty-two stages, each attaining the dharma-gate of a single stage, thereby collectively adorning the resultant essence of Vairocana.

Thus, they constitute the adornment of the retinue and the adornment of the companions, as they assist and support the transformation of the Dharma. Together, they form the "Sublime Adornment. Once the assembly of Bodhisattvas had gathered, he then uttered this praise:
"Virtue-Cloud," and so forth, all arise from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness; therefore, they constitute the assembly of those born together [with the Buddha].
Next, there are vajra-wielding spirits (vajrapāṇi) as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-world, continuing down to the Great Sovereign Heavenly King of the Ocean of Wondrous Flames.
These constitute the assembly of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), totaling thirty-nine groups. Each of these celestial kings and deities—

Ten sections are taken to symbolize inexhaustibility; each begins with ten to collectively embody a single virtue. The complete assembly of the ocean-like multitude constitutes the general introduction.

titled "The Ocean-like Assembly Praises His Virtue."
The assembly above gathers like a sea of clouds. This section below constitutes the specific introduction explaining the causes and conditions for the manifestation of this sutra.
Thus, the various heavenly kings each praise one liberation of the Buddha.

While the preceding section takes ten people collectively possessing a single virtue as the general principle, this section below clarifies the specific meaning by showing each individual possessing one liberation; thus, the general and the specific are perfectly integrated.
Together they form a single resultant body of Vairocana, and also manifest the resultant virtue of wondrous adornment; therefore, this applies throughout the entire chapter.

Regarding the assembly listed therein, it begins with the Bodhisattvas and ends with the Celestial King Wondrous Flame-Ocean (*Sudharmasāgara*). Furthermore, the current praise of virtues proceeds from the final one, Wondrous Flame-Ocean, back to the beginning of the Bodhisattvas.
This is to symbolize that the general and the specific, the beginning and the end, together perfectly complete a single resultant body.
Therefore, the various deva-kings each spoke verses of praise. Furthermore, the meaning of the sūtra is self-evident according to the dharma-gates realized by each;
this extends from the Arising from the Ocean of Wondrous Flames up to the Moon Deva-son.

At that time, the ocean-like assembly at the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment had already gathered like clouds; beings of infinite categories surrounded and filled the space, each with distinct forms, colors, and retinues.
From whichever direction they had come, they drew near to the World-Honored One and gazed upon him with single-minded devotion.
This entire assembly has already abandoned all defilements of the mind and their residual habitual tendencies;
having shattered the mountain of heavy obstructions, they perceive the Buddha without hindrance.

All of them were once gathered by Vairocana Tathāgata through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as he practiced the bodhisattva path throughout oceans of kalpas, and each planted roots of goodness in the presence of every Buddha.
At the stage of the faculties, they have all been well-guided through various skillful means, taught, and brought to maturity, establishing them upon the path to omniscience.
Having planted immeasurable roots of goodness and acquired great merit, they have all entered the ocean of skillful means and vows.
Their practiced conduct is fully pure, and they are already well-able to emerge upon the path of renunciation, constantly beholding the Buddha with clear vision.

He illuminated and understood. By the power of resolute conviction, he entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits and attained the gates of liberation and the playful mastery of supernatural powers of all Buddhas.

That is to say: the Great Sovereign Heavenly King of the Ocean of Wondrous Flames attained the gate of liberation through the power of skillful means for the tranquility of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space;
the Heavenly King of Light with Sovereign Renown attained universal observation...

The Celestial King Great Wisdom Delightful to Behold attained the liberation door of the ocean of wisdom that directly perceives the true nature of all dharmas. The Immovable...
The Celestial King Sovereign of Light attained the liberation door of the great skillful means concentration that bestows boundless peace and happiness upon sentient beings.
The Celestial King Eye of Sublime Adornment attained the liberation door that causes one to contemplate the dharma of tranquility, thereby extinguishing all darkness of ignorance and fear.
The Celestial King Light of Skillful Contemplation attained the liberation door of skillfully entering boundless realms without giving rise to any thoughts regarding the karma of existence.
The Celestial King Great Wisdom of Delight attained the liberation door of traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to preach the Dharma while remaining unmoving and without dependence.
The Celestial King Banner Adorned with Universal Sound attained entry into the Buddha’s silence...
The liberation door of the universal manifestation of light within the realm of tranquility;
and the liberation door of the Heavenly King Renowned Light of Excellent Diligence, who dwells in the state realized by himself while taking infinite and vast realms as his object of focus.
