Having attained such immeasurable light of wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mahātejas, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke these verses:
"Having heard the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma, I have attained the light of wisdom; by this, I behold the World-Honored One."
All deeds performed in the past, In every place of birth, The distinctions of names and bodies,
And the offerings made to the Buddhas— All this I see clearly. I have served all the Buddhas of the past,
Practicing for immeasurable eons To purify and adorn the oceans of lands.
They relinquish their own bodies, vast and boundless; they cultivate the most supreme practices to purify the oceans of all buddha-fields.
Giving away their ears, noses, heads, hands, feet, and even their various palaces in measureless quantities, they purify the oceans of all buddha-fields, being able to do so in each and every field.
For inconceivable billions of eons, they have practiced the conduct of enlightenment;
By the power of Samantabhadra’s great vows, throughout the oceans of all Buddha-realms, They cultivate immeasurable practices to adorn and purify the oceans of lands.
Just as by the light of the sun one is able to see the solar disk itself, So too do they perceive the source of their own practice.
By means of the light of the Buddha’s wisdom, I behold the path traversed by the Buddhas;
I contemplate the oceans of Buddha-fields, pure and of great radiance, where enlightenment is realized in tranquility pervading the entire realm of phenomena.
Just as the World-Honored One has done, I shall extensively purify the oceans of fields through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.

At the time when he was practicing the conduct of enlightenment, that Tathāgata descended and extensively expounded the Dharma-gate known as the *Sūtra on the Universal Collection of the Sovereign Dharmas of All Buddhas of the Three Times*.
This is the dharma personally realized by that Buddha; therefore, Mahāteja...
Upon hearing this Dharma, the Bodhisattva immediately attained the light of wisdom of twelve kinds of samādhi.

Having received these benefits through that great majestic radiance, he further spoke verses in praise. The preceding section describes the attainment of benefits upon hearing the Dharma; the prose section clarifies the attainment of the Dharma itself.
There are ten verses in this hymn:

"O Sons of the Buddha! At that time, because the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Light had seen, served, and made offerings to the Buddha Sumeru-Vijaya-Cloud of All Merit Mountains, his mind attained realization in the presence of the Tathāgata, and he manifested [this] for all the worlds."
It reveals the ocean of the Tathāgata’s past practices; it displays the skillful means of the Bodhisattva’s past conduct; it displays the ocean of all Buddhas’ merits;
it displays the pure wisdom that universally enters all dharma realms;

it displays the sovereign power of attaining Buddhahood within all sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it displays the non-differentiated wisdom of the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses; it displays the universal...
He manifested the body of a Tathāgata; he displayed inconceivable Buddha-miracles; he displayed the adornment of immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands;
and he displayed all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

He caused sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within Mount Sumeru to resolve upon the bodhicitta, and he caused sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field to achieve the purity of a Tathāgata.
Purifying the Buddha-land. At that time, the Buddha Meruśikharabhadrajyotismegha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Mahātejaḥprabha:
"Excellent, Mahātejaḥprabha! Treasury of merit, of vast renown, For the sake of benefiting sentient beings..."
Having set out upon the path to enlightenment, you have obtained the light of wisdom;
Filling the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), your merit and wisdom are both vast. You shall attain the ocean of profound knowledge.
Practicing within a single buddha-field for as many eons as there are atoms in a field, Just as you see me now, you shall obtain such wisdom.
Those of inferior practice cannot understand this skillful means;
Only those who have attained the power of great diligence can purify the oceans of buddha-fields. Within each and every atom, they must practice for immeasurable eons;
Only such persons can achieve the adornment of all buddha-fields For the sake of every single sentient being.
Cycling through oceans of kalpas in saṃsāra, may your mind never grow weary;
May you become a World-Leader, making offerings to each and every Buddha until the very end of the future;
With a mind free from even momentary fatigue or aversion, may you attain the Unsurpassed Way. May all Buddhas of the three times together fulfill your vow.
Within all the assemblies of Buddhas, your body dwells therein;
All Tathāgatas possess boundless vows, And you, a master of great wisdom who has attained thorough penetration, Are able to know this skillful means.
O Great Radiance, you have made offerings to me; Therefore, you have obtained great majestic power, Causing sentient beings as numerous as motes of dust...

Maturing [beings] toward enlightenment, Practicing all the conduct of Samantabhadra, The Bodhisattva of Great Renown adorns oceans of Buddha-fields, Pervading the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
[This section below clarifies that after attaining realization through majestic light, he performs the work of transforming sentient beings; this is the first period.]
The following section clarifies the transformation and awakening of others by displaying ten kinds of Dharma gates to benefit many sentient beings.

Next, at the point where it says, "At that time, beneath the mountain of all merits," it indicates that the Tathāgata also spoke verses of praise to encourage [the Prince] regarding his majestic light and the great fruit he was to achieve;
these consist of eleven verses. Above this, the Crown Prince Mahātejas first encountered one...
The account of the Buddha Sarvaguṇaparvata is now complete.
O Sons of the Buddha, you should know that within that Great Adornment Eon (Mahāvyūha-kalpa), there were as many intermediate eons (antarakalpa) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
The human lifespan there is two small kalpas. O Sons of the Buddha, the lifespan of that Buddha Supreme Cloud of All Merit Sumeru is five billion years.
These two lines from another sutra clarify the meeting with the second Buddha by Wei-guang; therefore, this serves as a conclusion to the preceding account of his birth.
The subsequent passage provides a general explanation of the kalpa-lifespan to clarify the duration of the minor and major kalpas; this is intended to manifest the appearance of many Buddhas.

Regarding the mention of human lifespan and the Buddha’s lifespan: because the Buddha’s lifespan was brief while human lifespan was long, he was able to serve three Buddhas throughout his single lifetime by means of his majestic radiance.

After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Paramita-Sunetra-Vyūha-Rāja, who likewise attained perfect enlightenment within that same Great Forest of Maṇi Flower Branches. At that time, the youth Mahātejaḥprabha...

Beholding that Tathāgata’s attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment and his manifestation of supernormal powers, he immediately attained the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi called the "Gate of the Boundless Ocean-Treasury.
He immediately attained the dhāraṇī called the "Dharma Abyss of Great Intellectual Power.

He immediately attained great loving-kindness called "Universally Following Sentient Beings for Their Taming and Deliverance. He immediately attained great compassion called the "Cloud Enveloping All Realms."
He immediately attained great joy, named "The Power-Treasury of the Ocean of Merits of All Buddhas.

He immediately attained great equanimity, named "The Pure Equality of the Space of Dharmatā. He immediately attained the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), named "The Pure Body of the Dharmadhātu, Naturally Free from Defilement.
He immediately attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), named "Unobstructed Light Manifesting Universally. He immediately attained eloquence (*pratibhāna*), named...
He skillfully entered the profound abyss free from defilement and immediately attained the light of wisdom called "The Pure Treasury of All Buddha-Dharmas.
In this way, he thoroughly mastered ten thousand such Dharma-gates. At that time, the youth Great Splendor, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, spoke these verses for his retinue:
Within inconceivable billions of kalpas, it is rare to encounter a world-guiding, enlightened teacher.
The sentient beings of this land possess much merit and benefit, for they have now beheld the Second Buddha.
The Buddha’s body universally radiates great light; its physical marks are boundless and utterly pure.
Like clouds filling all lands, the light of the Buddha’s merit is praised everywhere;

wherever it shines, all rejoice. The suffering of sentient beings is entirely extinguished, and each is led to give rise to a heart of reverence and compassion. This is the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
They emit clouds of inconceivable transformations and radiate nets of light in immeasurable colors, filling all lands throughout the ten directions;
these are manifested through the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
From every single pore, clouds of light appear, pervading the entirety of space and emitting great sounds.
There is no realm of darkness that is not illuminated; The manifold sufferings of the hells are all extinguished.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous voice pervades the ten directions, Fully manifesting every possible sound and speech.
In accordance with the power of the past virtues of sentient beings, This is the miraculous application of the Great Teacher.
Within immeasurable and boundless great oceans, the Buddhas appear therein all at once;
they universally turn the inexhaustible, wondrous wheel of Dharma, subduing all sentient beings.
The Buddha’s power of spiritual transformations is limitless, appearing within every single realm.
The Sugata possesses such unimpeded wisdom; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he has attained perfect enlightenment.
You all should give rise to a heart of joy, leaping with delight and profound reverence.
I shall go there together with you, so that when you behold the Tathāgata, all suffering will be extinguished.
"Generating the mind [of awakening] and dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi, with compassionate thoughts for all sentient beings,
may we all abide in the vast vows of Samantabhadra, and like the Dharma King, attain sovereign mastery— O sons of the Buddhas!
When the youth Mahāteja uttered these verses, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, his voice was unimpeded.
All worlds heard it, and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, Prince Mahātejas, surrounded before and behind by his parents, his retinue, and an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of beings,
with jeweled canopies like clouds covering the entirety of space, proceeded together to the Pāramitā-sudarśana [Bodhisattva].

They went to the presence of the Tathāgata King of Adornments. That Buddha was preaching for them the *Sūtra on the Adornment of the Pure Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm*, with as many *sūtras* as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds serving as its retinue.
When that great assembly had heard this sūtra, they attained pure wisdom called "Entry into All Pure Expedients" and attained the stage of "Stainless Radiance."
The wheel of the perfection of wisdom is named "Manifestation Adorned by the Love and Delight of All Worlds.
The wheel of the expansion of practice is named "Pure Vision of Boundless Radiance Universally Entering All Buddha-lands.
The wheel of the progression toward practice is named "Luminous Banner of Clouds of Stainless Merit. The wheel of entry into realization is named "Ocean of All Dharmas."
The vast radiance is named the Adornment of Great Wisdom, as it attains the practice of ever-deepening dedication.

The ocean of wisdom of consecration is named the Supreme Vision of Effortless Cultivation. The manifestation of great luminosity is named the Pervasive Illumination of the Reflected Light of the Tathāgata’s Ocean of Merits.
The pure wisdom born of the power of vows is named Faith in Immeasurable Vow-Power.
The Commentary on the Treasury. At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Light:

“Excellent, O ocean of merit and wisdom! Having resolved your mind to advance toward great enlightenment, You shall attain the inconceivable state of Buddhahood, Universally serving as a refuge for all sentient beings.”
You have already been born into the great ocean of wisdom, And are fully able to comprehend all phenomena;
Now, by means of inconceivable and wondrous skillful methods, Enter the inexhaustible sphere of the Buddha’s conduct.
Having beheld the clouds of merit of all Buddhas, You have entered the ground of inexhaustible wisdom.
The great one of renowned fame shall fulfill the ocean of skillful means of all the pāramitās;
having attained the gate of dhāraṇī of skillful means as well as the gate of inexhaustible eloquence,
he shall cultivate all manner of practices and vows, and shall realize peerless, great wisdom.
You have already given birth to the ocean of all vows; you have already entered the ocean of samādhis.
You shall possess various great supernormal powers and the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha.
Having reached the ultimate limit of the inconceivable Dharma-realm, your vast and profound mind is already purified.
Universally beholding all Buddhas of the ten directions, And the oceans of lands adorned and free from defilement—
You have already entered my bodhisattva conduct, The ocean of skillful means from your past lives.
Just as I have cultivated and purified my practice, So too have you awakened to these wondrous deeds.
Throughout immeasurable individual lands, I have made various offerings to oceans of Buddhas;
the fruits obtained through such practice, and these adornments, you all now behold.
Within this vast ocean of kalpas that knows no end, I have cultivated pure conduct in every land.
Your firm vow is inconceivable; you shall attain this supernatural power of a Tathāgata.
You shall make offerings to all Buddhas without exception, and all your buddha-fields shall be utterly pure.
Having cultivated sublime conduct throughout all kalpas, you shall become a Buddha of great merit.

Following the passage on the parinirvāṇa of that [first] Buddha, this section reveals the appearance of the second Buddha. The text consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that the previous Buddha has already passed away and the subsequent Buddha appears;
second, it clarifies the benefits obtained by beholding his marks; third, it praises his virtues and exhorts one to request his teaching.

This initial section clarifies the Buddha’s emergence: he appears at the very site of the previous Buddha’s *bodhimaṇḍa*. Following the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Mahāteja," it clarifies...
The section beginning with "The majestic light beheld the marks and obtained benefit" correctly clarifies the attainment of benefit.
Next, it sets forth ten kinds of Dharma-gates, concluding with the words, "Such ten thousand Dharma-gates as these.

Following this, the section beginning with "At that time, Great Majestic Light spoke in verse" praises his virtues and exhorts him to approach; the intent is to say that he has fortunately succeeded in seeing the second Buddha.
The verses consist of ten stanzas praising the virtues of the Buddha’s three karmas and exhorting the multitude to follow him together.
When Mahātejas uttered these verses, they were heard throughout all worlds, and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
When this Mahātejas spoke these verses, those who heard them first attained benefit.
Subsequently, Prince Mahātejas, together with his parents and retinue, went to the presence of the Tathāgata Paramitāsunetra-vyūharāja.

That Buddha preached for them the *Sūtra on the Adornment of the Purity of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm* (*Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-viśuddhi-vyūha-sūtra*). Regarding this, "the essential nature of the dharma-realm" refers to—
The "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensiveness). The "Pure Buddha" is the *Buddha*. "Adornment" is the *Avataṃsaka*.

The fact that there are many retinues reveals the nature of this Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*). Next, it clarifies that after the great assembly has heard this sutra, they immediately attain pure wisdom and ten kinds of great benefits.
The commentary (*śāstra*) correlates these ten benefits with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in their respective order, thereby manifesting the vastness of the Dharma.
Because it is great, the benefit obtained is extraordinary; that is to say, this present sutra contains the meaning of the sudden and perfect realization of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Once the assembly had already received this benefit through the majesty of the light, that Buddha spoke verses in praise and description. There are ten verses in total:

the first six praise his possession of supreme virtues and his future attainment of the ultimate fruit; the latter four state that because his practice is equal to the Buddha’s, he shall be like the Buddha.
[End of] testimony. The above concludes the account of the causes and conditions for Mahātejas encountering his second Buddha.
O Sons of the Buddha! After the Tathāgata Suvimalanetra-vyūharāja had entered parinirvāṇa, King Priyadarśana-buddhijña also passed away shortly thereafter.
The youth Mahātejas then ascended to the position of a universal monarch (cakravartin). That Maṇipuṣpa...
In the Great Forest of Branch-Wheels, the third Tathāgata appeared in the world, named Most Victorious Ocean of Merit (*Guṇasāgaravara*).

At that time, the Universal Monarch Mahātejas, perceiving the signs of that Tathāgata’s appearance, went together with his retinue, the fourfold army, all the people of the cities and villages, and carrying the seven treasures, to the place where the Buddha was. With...
He offered a great multi-storied pavilion adorned with all kinds of fragrant mani-jewels to the Buddha.
At that time, within that grove, the Tathāgata preached the *Sūtra on the Practice of the Universal Eye Radiance*, with as many sūtras as there are atoms in a world-system serving as its retinue.
When the Bodhisattva Mahātejaśrī heard this Dharma, he attained a samādhi named...

"Great Merit and Universal Radiance, because you have attained this samādhi, you are able to fully comprehend the ocean of merit and demerit of all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings across the past,
present, and future. Then, that Buddha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Light:

Excellent! You of great merit and majestic radiance, you who have now come to my presence out of compassion for the ocean of all sentient beings, have given rise to the supreme mind of the great vow for bodhi.
For the sake of all suffering beings, arouse the heart of great compassion and bring them to liberation.
One should become the refuge for all who are lost; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means.

If there is a bodhisattva who can remain steadfast and cultivate various supreme practices without weariness or indolence, they shall attain such wondrous wisdom—the most excellent, most sublime, and unimpeded understanding.
O Light of Merit, O Banner of Merit, O Abode of Merit, O Ocean of Merit!
All the vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—into these you, Great Light, are able to enter;
by means of these vast vows, you are able to enter the inconceivable ocean of all Buddhas.
The oceans of merit of all Buddhas are boundless; you, through your wondrous understanding, are able to see them all.
Within the lands of the ten directions, you behold all the infinite and limitless Buddhas.
The oceans of all the past practices of those Buddhas—all such things as these, you perceive them entirely.
If one dwells in this ocean of skillful means, One will surely enter the stage of wisdom.
This is the study that accords with all Buddhas; One will certainly attain omniscience.
Throughout oceans of all lands, You shall cultivate various practices for oceans of atom-like eons.
Having studied all the oceans of practices of all Tathāgatas, you shall attain Buddhahood;
just as you have seen all the oceans of lands in the ten directions, most exquisitely adorned and pure,
your own land shall be adorned and purified in that same way— this is what those with boundless vows shall obtain.
Now, this ocean-like assembly at the site of enlightenment, having heard your vow, has given rise to joy;
they all enter the vast vehicle of Samantabhadra, resolve their minds upon awakening, and dedicate themselves toward Bodhi.
Within each and every one of the boundless lands, they enter and practice throughout oceans of eons.
"By the power of all vows, one is able to fulfill all the practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Below this, it is revealed that the Buddha of Great Radiance encountered the appearance of the third Buddha. The name of that Buddha was Guṇasāgara (Ocean of Merit).
This means that his merit was already complete and could not be further increased. At that time, Prince Mahātejas had succeeded to the position of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
Therefore, together with his retinue and the fourfold army, he went to see the Buddha and offered a fragrant pavilion as an offering.
Then, that Tathāgata preached for him the *Sūtra on the Practice of Universal Eye Radiance* (*Samantacakṣur-ābhāsa-caryā-sūtra*). Because he saw [the universal eye]...
Because it is the Dharma, it is called the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*). Because its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called Radiance (*prabhā*).
Next, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahātejaḥprabha, having heard this Dharma, attained the Samādhi of Great Merit and Universal Radiance (*mahāpuṇya-samantaprabhā-samādhi*).

"Great merit" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because concentration constitutes the greatest merit, it is so named. "Universal radiance" refers to wisdom; it is quiescent and without...
"Not illuminating" is called "Universal Radiance. To speak of "merit and non-merit," merit refers to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while non-merit refers to essence (*svabhāva*).
This means that by simultaneously comprehending both essence and characteristics, one manifests the benefit of the perfect clarity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

However, although Wei-guang obtained ten benefits upon meeting the first Buddha, this was because his own power had not yet prevailed; when he met the second Buddha and obtained ten thousand benefits, it was because the Path had become even deeper.
Therefore, at present, he has attained only one [result], for his Path is already fulfilled.
Following the passage where that Tathāgata spoke these verses for Mahātejas, there are eleven stanzas concerning the Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that Tejas shall attain the sublime fruit.
Of these, the first four stanzas reveal the possession of the bodhicitta; the next four clarify his superior entry into the realm of the Buddhas; and the third...
There is one verse that shows the characteristics of its fruition, which is to attain equality with all Buddhas.
There are two verses that praise its present ability to benefit others by abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra. This concludes the explanation of the third Buddha encountered by Majestic Light.
O Sons of the Buddha, within that Great Forest of Mani Flower Branches, there appeared another Buddha named Universal Renown Lotus-Eye Banner.

At that time, Mahāteja passed away there and was reborn in the celestial city of the Śānta-ratna Palace atop Mount Sumeru as the Great Heavenly King named Vimalapuṇyaketu, together with a multitude of devas.
They all went together to the place where the Buddha was and made offerings by raining down clouds of precious flowers.

At that time, the Tathāgata preached for them the *Sūtra of the Universal Gate’s Radiant Illumination through Vast Expedient Means*, with as many sūtras as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds serving as its retinue.
When the assembly of celestial kings had heard this sūtra, they attained a samādhi named "The Treasury of Universal Gate Joy. By means of this—

By the power of samādhi, one is able to enter the ocean of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Having obtained this benefit, one emerges from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and returns to one's original place.
From here below, it clarifies how the majestic light encounters the appearance of the fourth Buddha. This Buddha is named Padmanetra-ketu (Lotus-Eye Banner).

In terms of its characteristics, it resembles a blue lotus; in terms of its virtues, the mind is unstained. Because its characteristics and virtues are lofty and manifest, its fame is proclaimed abroad;
because it crushes the heterodox and all beings take refuge in it, it is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*).

When that Buddha appeared in the world, Great Radiance passed away here and was reborn atop Mount Sumeru as the Great Heavenly King named Stainless Merit Banner (*Vimalapuṇyadhvaja*). This clarifies...
The place where the Bodhisattva receives the retribution for his practice is a celestial palace. This city is one of those listed at the beginning of this chapter.
At that time, having heard of the Buddha, the Heavenly King, together with the assembly of devas, went to make offerings.

Then, that Tathāgata preached for them the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Gate of Vast Expedient Means*. As for "vast expedient means," it refers to the provisional that accords with the real.

The absence of obstruction regarding the provisional and the ultimate is called "Great Expedient Means. The simultaneous illumination of phenomena and principle is the "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha).
It further states: "At that time, the Heavenly King, having heard this sutra, attained a samādhi named 'The Treasury of Universal-Gate Joy' (*Samantamukha-prīti-kośa*).

Because he heard the aforementioned universal-gate meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and dwelt securely in inexhaustible Dharma-joy, it is called a "Treasury. Through this, he realized and penetrated all realities.

Regarding the "Ocean of Marks" (Lakṣaṇasāgara): although the initial heading states that within this kalpa there will appear as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten Mount Sumerus, the current text mentions only meeting four Buddhas.

Furthermore, the sūtra text lacks any passage connecting the past with the present, nor does it mention matters such as manifesting proof or attaining benefits. Thus, we know that the transmission of the sūtra is incomplete. If...
As for the statement that [the Buddha] served many Buddhas over successive lifetimes, its textual details are largely self-evident.

This is all the more so when it concerns the fruit realized through the causes cultivated by Vairocana over vast eons; were one to recount those causes in full, they would be too numerous to surpass. To summarize them:
It should be said: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda was Vairocana. [Supplementary Note:

This section is titled "Manifesting the Fruit" (*phaloddeśa*). To speak of the cause (*hetu*) here is specifically to highlight the causes cultivated by our Teacher over vast eons (*kalpa*) as the means by which he realized this fruit.
This cause clarifies solely the cause of our Teacher; it is not [the answer to the question].
The ten questions concern the causes; the subsequent answers to these ten questions concerning the causes teach the causes cultivated by all bodhisattvas so that they may accord with this fruit.
Thus, it pervades the entire sutra. The preceding "Vairocana Chapter" is concluded.
The first section, from the beginning up to the encouragement to aspire for birth [in the Pure Land], generally constitutes the "Section on the Causality of What Is to Be Believed.

The subsequent twelve fascicles, from the start of the thirteenth fascicle through the fifty-second fascicle, generally constitute the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding."

Second Assembly: The Dharma Gate of the Ten Faiths Spoken by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in the Hall of Universal Radiance. This...
There will be six chapters of the sutra:
(The Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata; The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths; The Chapter on Radiant Awakening; The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity;
The Chapter on Pure Conduct; and The Chapter on the Worthy Leader—this is the first).
Chapter Seven: The Names and Titles of the Tathāgata.
Below this begins the third section, "Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding.

This comprises the twelfth through the thirteenth sūtras from the beginning of the second assembly, namely the "Bodhisattva-praśna-vyākaraṇa-parivarta" (The Chapter on the Questions and Explanations of the Bodhisattvas). To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to five gates.

Regarding the intent of the initial arrival: first, it clarifies the sequential arrival. Since the preceding section presented the fruit to inspire faith and joy, this section now clarifies the causal and fruitional understanding that gives rise to such faith;
thus, it follows next. Regarding the intent of the second assembly: among the factors for generating understanding, faith is primary.
Furthermore, while the preceding section presented the objects of faith, this section clarifies the practice of faith itself; thus, it follows next.
Regarding the three sections that follow: the preceding section cited the cause to manifest the fruit, thereby establishing the object of faith.
This present section cites the fruit to discern the cause, thereby clarifying the practice of faith. Within the fruit, the three karmas, the body being the aggregate of them, is presented first.

Furthermore, it answers from afar the question regarding the "Ocean of Names. The second part, the explanation of the names, is also threefold; the first division concerns the name "Practicing the Cause to Accord with the Fruit."

The Section on Generating Understanding (*utpāda-adhimukti-bhāga*). This refers to cultivating the perfect causes of the five stages to achieve the full fruition of the ten bodies, so that all bodhisattvas may understand these characteristics;

thus, they generate the understanding that accords with the fruition through the cultivation of causes. This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Second, the name of the assembly:
regarding the location, it is called the "Assembly in the Universal Radiance Hall. However, there are three interpretations. First, because the hall is composed of jewels...

First, because their light shines universally. Second, because the Buddhas emit universal light therein. Third, because the Buddhas expound the Dharma-gate of the Universal Dharma therein, and the light of wisdom illuminates the world;
for these reasons, they are given these names. Regarding the names of the three chapters: the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs" has already been explained.
To summon the essence is called a "name" (nāman); to manifest virtue is called a "title" (adhivacana). A name is specific, while a title is general. All Buddhas are thus... [omitted].
Because he possesses the ten titles, such as Śākyamuni and others, they are distinct; the Tathāgata is one of these ten titles.
In this chapter, the primary teaching establishes specific names according to the capacities of sentient beings and based on their respective virtues.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest retreat (araṇya-dharma-bodhimaṇḍa), having newly attained perfect awakening.
He sat upon the lotus-treasury lion throne in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
The following is the commentary on the text. For now, we shall follow this single assembly by dividing it into three parts: first, the Introduction; second, the Request; and third, the Exposition.
We begin now with the Introduction, which is identical to that at the beginning of the sutra, with the sole difference being the addition of the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Since this sutra was first expounded in its entirety all at once, even the introductions to the subsequent nine assemblies follow this initial exposition; how much more so for this one?
He ascends without moving; therefore, the location is now described. It is in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍapa*). The Commentary states:
"This hall is located approximately three *li* southeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa, at a bend in the River Kṣīranadī. The nāga of that river was created by the Buddha.
As for the name "Universal Radiance," it has already been explained in the preceding text. In reality, the Buddha speaks based upon the wisdom of universal radiance (*samantālokajñāna*).
This is the Universal Dharma. The causes and effects of the six stages are all perfectly accomplished based upon this wisdom;

therefore, the subsequent explanation that the two awakenings—Equal and Wondrous—still converge at the Hall of Universal Radiance is intended to reveal generally that they do not depart from this wisdom. This is the general principle of the entire work.
Thus, the present convergence at the Hall of Universal Radiance is none other than remaining at the Bodhi Tree; hence, it is established at the beginning of the introduction.

Sublime awakening is fully perfected; the two types of conduct are forever severed. One penetrates the dharma of signlessness, abides in the Buddha-abode, attains the equality of the Buddhas, and reaches the realm of non-obstruction.
Possessing a dharma that cannot be overturned, one’s practice is unimpeded; established in the inconceivable, one universally perceives the three periods of time.
These ten lines following "this wondrous realization" specifically manifest the virtues of the Lord; they also demonstrate the characteristics of attaining perfect enlightenment.
According to the text of the latter eight assemblies, the Buddha possesses twenty-one kinds of merit; the present text is incomplete. This shall be clarified later.
The commentary on these ten lines is very clear; fearing prolixity, I have not recorded it here.
He was accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of whom were in their final birth before attaining enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
They had all gathered together from other directions, having universally and skillfully observed the realms of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the realm of nirvāṇa;
as well as all karmic retributions, the sequences of mental activities, and all words and meanings pertaining to the conditioned phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

Without distinction of past, present, or future, at that time the bodhisattvas reflected thus: "If the World-Honored One would look upon us with compassion, we pray that he may act according to his pleasure.
This section below clarifies the perfection of the supporting retinue. If these multitudes, as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, were the light emitted previously...

As for those who were summoned, since they have already been questioned regarding the dharmas of the fruit, it would be inappropriate to designate them again; yet the text states that they "have gathered from other directions.

Therefore, we know these are newly assembled members of the assembly. Regarding the ten phrases beginning with "Next, he universally observes," the commentary states that these praise the virtues of the Buddha.
Next, from the passage "At that time, the bodhisattvas had this thought" onwards, they requested a portion [of the teaching]. First, the initial statement marks the intent of the request;
"If the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, would grant our wish," clearly indicates the opening of the inquiry.

Supplementary Commentary: Although there are fifty interrogative sentences in the section below, only forty constitute the primary questions, as the twentieth sentence is intended to explain the underlying meaning. These forty sentences differ from those in the first assembly;
the latter twenty sentences are identical, while the former twenty are largely the same with minor variations. Furthermore, regarding the preceding...
The latter is not the same as the former. The first ten phrases are identical to the thirtieth "Ocean" [chapter] mentioned previously.

In the previous assembly, the profound and vast nature of that which is observed was explained in general; here, however, the reliance (the Buddha’s body) and the supported (the environment) of the Tathāgata are explained specifically. Because the previous assembly served as a general overview, this assembly provides a specific manifestation.
Furthermore, since it is the basis for faith, the previous assemblies all employed the term "ocean," whereas here it simply mentions "lands" and so forth.
The first twenty phrases are called the "Ten Oceans of the Bodhisattva"; these enumerate the stages of practice such as the "Abodes" (*vihāra*) and so forth.

The former [set] applies universally across all assemblies, collectively manifesting the causes of both sequential progression (*pūrṇa*) and perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). This [latter set], however, pertains to the specific divisions, intending to manifest the characteristics of the distinct causes.
Although the subsequent twenty phrases are entirely identical [to the first], the former is general while this one is particular. Furthermore, the former refers to that which is believed.
Now, the established conclusion is being distinguished. This is intended to show that the essence of what is believed and what is established is not different.

The preceding section distinguished between the questions asked and those previously posed; its meaning was extremely detailed. Now, for the sake of both textual concision and semantic convenience, the text is divided into two parts:
the first ten phrases pose direct questions, while the latter thirty phrases cite examples to inquire further. Their meaning does not differ from the previous section. Furthermore...

There is one further point. Although the causes and effects of the Buddha previously cited merely revealed in general that the cause is profound and the fruit is vast, they did not yet specify the particular causes nor the fruits realized in accordance with those causes. Now, it is necessary to initiate practice and engage in cultivation.

Therefore, it is necessary to ask each question individually. Thus, when the initial question concerns the primary and secondary supports of the fruit, it mentions only the "land" (*kṣetra*) and not the "ocean," because the intent lies in sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), whereas the ocean implies perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
He reveals the buddha-fields, the abiding of the Buddha, the adornment of the buddha-fields, the nature of the Buddha-dharma, the purity of the buddha-fields,
the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the essential nature of the buddha-fields, the majestic power of the Buddha, the accomplishment of the buddha-fields, and the great enlightenment of the Buddha.

This precisely clarifies what was asked. In the initial inquiry regarding the results, there are five phrases each concerning the primary and secondary [realms], identical to those previously mentioned in the *Kṣetrasāgara* (Ocean of Lands).

Just as all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all worlds throughout the ten directions, act for the sake of bringing all bodhisattvas to fulfillment, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed, and for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, so as to cause all sentient beings to be forever free from...
Because it [is the means] for [overcoming] all afflictions; because it brings about the thorough understanding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
because it expounds all dharmas; because it purifies and eliminates all defilements; because it forever severs the web of all doubts; and because it uproots all worldly expectations.
Because it destroys all bases of attachment.
Below this, the second section introduces examples through a series of inquiries. The text is divided into three parts.

First, these ten phrases indicate what those Buddhas have taught, intending to clarify that they possess compassion (*karuṇā*). Second, the subsequent thirty phrases cite what they have taught, manifesting that they possess wisdom (*jñāna*).

The final phrase concludes with a formal request. The intention is that although the preceding sections have explained the Buddha’s vast cause and fruit, they have only revealed the perfectly interfused ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) without clarifying the distinct causal practices (*hetu-caryā*).

Therefore, these ten fruits are first presented, which correspond to the aforementioned perfectly interfused fruits; yet, because the specific causes for attaining these distinct fruits still remain unclarified, [the text] proceeds by citing...
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, out of great compassion, also speak of the causes for these distinctions, namely the practices such as the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) listed below.
Therefore, I now specifically request the reason for this. What follows is the answer to the questions posed;
it comprises six stages of cause and effect, each answering the inquiries therein in successive order.
The Supplemental Commentary states: What follows is the request for the causes, which is the formal response to the question concerning the "ocean of sentient beings" within the ten oceans.
Therefore, the six stages of causes are subsequently enumerated to encompass the subsequent text; thus, the Sub-commentary says that all [the following] answer this question.
It explains the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten treasuries, ten stages, ten vows, ten concentrations, ten supernormal powers, and ten summits of all bodhisattvas.
In the second section, beginning with "It explains the various bodhisattvas," he cites what was taught by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to make his request: "May [the Buddha] now..."
This is also explained according to the established pattern. These first ten phrases inquire about the cause, yet there are only nine; one phrase, "the ten patiences" (daśakṣānti), is missing.
The subsequent twenty phrases inquire about the fruit. In the commentary (*śū*), it is clarified that although the question lacks the "ten patiences," the subsequent answer-text does contain them.
Furthermore, while the question contains the "ten summits" (daśamūrdhan) but the answer lacks them, how much more so when the question contains only nine?
Now, in order to distinguish [the stages], the four grades from the ten *kṣāntis* downward shall collectively answer the question regarding the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

This is because this is the ultimate summit of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). In this way, one position would be lacking; therefore, the intention is to establish the ten *śraddhās* as a single position, whereby they become ten.
And he spoke of the stage of the Tathāgata, the realm of the Tathāgata, the spiritual power of the Tathāgata, the conduct of the Tathāgata, the powers of the Tathāgata,
the fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata, the samādhis of the Tathāgata, the supernormal knowledges of the Tathāgata, the masteries of the Tathāgata, and the unimpededness of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s eye, the Tathāgata’s ear, the Tathāgata’s nose, the Tathāgata’s tongue, the Tathāgata’s body, the Tathāgata’s mind, the Tathāgata’s eloquence, and the Tathāgata’s wisdom—these are the Tathāgata’s supreme qualities.
I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will likewise explain them to me.
The second section contains twenty questions concerning the fruits achieved, which are entirely identical to those in the first assembly.

Among them, the first ten phrases clarify the fulfillment of internal virtues; the subsequent ten phrases, beginning with "the Tathāgata’s eyes," clarify the manifestation of the essence and its characteristics.

Eloquence refers to the activity of speech; wisdom refers to the activity of mind; and supremacy refers to the activity of body. Following the pattern of the previous assembly, this section lacks only [the following].
The Buddha’s radiance. Next, the invitation is performed with the words: "May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise expound this for me.

The word "likewise" (*api*) is used because one desires to be equal to those other Buddhas. The section on the invitation is concluded. Below follows the response. First, the Tathāgata responds by manifesting signs.
Thereafter, Mañjuśrī spoke in reply.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, manifested supernatural powers for each according to their respective kind.

The following is the third section, the "Explanatory Section. Within this, the six subsequent assemblies answer the questions posed herein. Following the structure of the questions, this is also divided into three parts:

first, the initial three chapters answer the question regarding the fruit that serves as the basis; second, from the chapter "Clarifying the Questions" (*Mingyi pin*) onwards, answers the question regarding the causes to be cultivated;
and third, from the chapter "Inconceivable" (*Bùsīyì pin*) onwards, answers the question regarding the fruits to be accomplished. As for its equality...
Regarding cause and effect: the cause is the cause within the effect; it is the function of this effect, and therefore it is subsumed under the category of the effect.

Second, the separate enumeration. Within the first [section], there are two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s response by manifesting signs, because he was requested through mindfulness and because his realization is ultimate.
Second, Mañjuśrī’s response by means of speech, because he acts as an assistant to the Master and because he reveals [the meaning] through conventional language. Now, for the first [part]:
This section is divided into two parts: first, the Buddha manifests supernatural powers; second, the ocean-like assembly gathers like clouds. Regarding the first:

"knowing their mental intentions" refers to receiving the invitation through the recollection of those thoughts; "manifesting supernatural powers" refers to answering by displaying signs. As for the phrase "according to their kind," there are three meanings.

First, because it accords with the differences in what the doubters suspect: that is to say, manifesting forms so they may see, using sounds so they may hear, and providing silent assistance so they may understand—all these are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), for the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) appears suddenly and perfectly luminous. Second, because it accords with the doubters.

Because the categories of the [nine] assemblies differ, and because the objects of doubt in the third assembly differ, we know that the manifestations of signs in the first assembly pervade all nine assemblies.

Since the manifestation of supernatural powers in this assembly is common to one portion of them, the three subsequent assemblies all contain the statement that [the Buddha] did not leave the Bodhi tree.
Having manifested these supernatural powers, there was a world named Golden in the eastern direction, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.

The Buddha there was named Immovable Wisdom. In that world, there was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated and stood before the Buddha in the east.
He then transformed it into a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury and sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
To the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, there was a world named Wondrous Color. Its Buddha was named Unobstructed Wisdom.
There was a bodhisattva there named Chief of Enlightenment who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived—
Having paid homage, he immediately manifested a lion throne within a lotus treasury in the southern direction and sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
To the west, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Lotus Color;
the Buddha there is named Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness. There was a bodhisattva there named Chief of Wealth, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.

Sajū approached the place where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he paid his respects and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the western direction, whereupon he sat cross-legged.
To the north, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Campaka Flower Color;
its Buddha is named Wisdom of Dignified Conduct. There, a bodhisattva named Jewel Head, together with ten...
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field came together to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the northern direction, upon which they sat cross-legged.
To the northeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, there is a world named Utpala Flower Color; the Buddha there is named Wisdom of the Radiant Sign.
There was a bodhisattva there named Guṇarāja (Virtue Chief), who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he paid homage and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the northeast, whereupon he sat down cross-legged.
To the southeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world...
The land was named Golden Color, and the Buddha’s name was Ultimate Wisdom.
There was a bodhisattva there named Eyes on the Head, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived, he paid homage and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the southeast, whereupon he sat cross-legged. To the southwest, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten...
In worlds as numerous as atoms, there is a world named Ratnavarṇa. The Buddha there is named Jñānottama.
A bodhisattva named Vīryottama, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the southwest, upon which they sat cross-legged.
To the northwest, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Vajra-Color.
The Buddha there is named Sovereign Wisdom. A bodhisattva named Dharma-Crown, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they paid homage and immediately manifested a Lotus Treasury in the northwest.
Upon the lion throne, he sat cross-legged. Ten world-systems below, past as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world named Lapis Lazuli Color.

Its Buddha was named Brahma-Wisdom. There was a bodhisattva there named Wisdom Chief, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they paid homage and remained there in the region below.
He manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury and sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
Above, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world named Equal Color; the Buddha there was named Observing Wisdom.
From that place, a bodhisattva named Worthy Head, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they...
He paid homage. Immediately, he manifested in the space above a lion throne within a lotus treasury and sat cross-legged.
Second, having manifested his supernatural powers, the ocean-like assembly gathered like clouds; he then manifested signs to answer the questions posed in the first ten lines.
The manifestation of light answers the questions concerning Buddha-fields. That the fields possess golden colors and so forth refers to the adornments of those fields;

since they are formed of gold, it also answers the question regarding the substance of the fields. That the bodhisattvas in those fields are also the adornment of the fields is because they are adorned by the great jewels that are the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, they are pure and utterly pristine because the Buddha-field consists solely of bodhisattvas who have purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Because this land has accomplished the practice of purifying the buddha-field, the field itself is pure; because that which is cultivated is pure.

This above answers the five phrases regarding the environment as asked, while also answering the five phrases concerning the primary reward (*pratyātmika-vipāka*). Each of these lands has its own Buddha, and one sees the Tathāgata seated within the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*);

this answers the question regarding the Buddha’s dwelling. The manifestation of supernatural powers and the emission of light answer the question regarding his majestic power (*anubhāva*). It is named "Immovable" (*Acalā*).
Wisdom and so forth are the answer regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Seeing the Buddha turn the wheel of Dharma is the answer regarding the teaching of the Dharma.

The Buddha’s attainment of perfect enlightenment is the answer regarding *bodhi*. Although these phrases appear later in the text, their meanings are all fully contained herein, for the manifestation of light and awakening is precisely the manifestation of this.
The "Ten-Headed Bodhisattva" represents faith as the foremost; for in Sanskrit, the single name *Śrī* has four actual meanings.

First, "Head" (śiras); second, "Victorious"; third, "Auspicious"; fourth, "Virtuous. Because the translators used different terms for these at various times, the current text also refers to Mañjuśrī as "Head" (śiras).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, universally surveyed all bodhisattvas...
The assembly of bodhisattvas spoke these words: "O Sons of the Buddha, how truly rare are these bodhisattvas!

The Buddha-fields, the dwelling of the Buddhas, the adornments of the Buddha-fields, the nature of the Buddha-dharma, the purity of the Buddha-fields, the teaching of the Buddhas, the appearance of the Buddhas, the accomplishment of the Buddha-fields, and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas—all of these are inconceivable."
This is inconceivable. Why is this? O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas of all worlds in the ten directions know that the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ;
accordingly, they teach the Dharma to subdue them. This continues in such a manner throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
Below this, the second section, beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī," provides the response through discourse. This is divided into four parts: first, praising the rarity of the assembly;
second, from "O sons of the Buddha" onwards, restating the question and offering a general praise; third, from "Why is this? onwards, investigating the praise and providing a general explanation;
fourth, from "O sons of the Buddha, as for the Tathāgata... onwards, extensively revealing the inconceivable. Now, the first part is the heading. Previously, the assembly had harbored doubts.
Question: Why did the Buddha instruct Mañjuśrī to answer? It is because Mañjuśrī manifests his residence in this land; his birth is marked by ten signs of excellence;

he comes from other directions; his essence contains myriad virtues; he subdues Māras and restrains outsiders; his eloquence in debate is inconceivable; and his transformation of beings fills the realms as numerous as motes of dust.
Throughout the three periods of time, when the Way was first perfected in a previous kalpa, he was already titled the Honored King of the Dragon Lineage (Nāga-vaṃśa-rāja).

When he manifested the realization of Bodhi, he was again called Maṇi-ratna-akṣaya (Jewel Accumulation). He is truly the Mother of the Buddhas of the Three Times; how could he be the teacher of Śākyamuni alone?

He appears through his influence so that all may see him, and thus it is appropriate for him to speak. That he does not wait to be requested is because the Buddha’s own intention grants permission. Furthermore:
By means of Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom, which represents the reliance upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to establish all practices, he is made the foremost of those with faith.
First, there is the praise of rarity: the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s signs and the gathering of clouds from the ten directions are praised as rare.
Next, the ten phrases beginning with "O sons of the Buddha, the Buddha-lands are inconceivable" praise the ten fruits of merit that were inquired about.
...inconceivable. Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" interrogates and explains the grounds for this inconceivability.

"O Sons of the Buddha! Within this Sahā world, across all four continents, the Tathāgata manifests various bodies, various names, various physical forms, various heights and statures, various lifespans, various locations, and various [attainments]..."
Through various bases, various places of birth, various vocal actions, and various observations, he causes all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.

O Sons of the Buddha, within these four continents, the Tathāgata is sometimes named Sarvārthasiddha, sometimes Pūrṇacandra, sometimes Siṃhanāda, sometimes Śākyamuni, or sometimes the Seventh Sage. Or...
He is named Vairocana; or he is named Gautama; or he is named the Great Śramaṇa; or he is named the Most Victorious; or he is named the Guide.
Such names as these number ten thousand. He causes all sentient beings to know and see him individually.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the east of this world-system of four continents, there is another world named Sugupta. There, the Tathāgata is known by various names...
Vajra; or named Sovereign; or named Possessing Wisdom; or named Difficult to Conquer;
or named King of Clouds; or named Without Dispute; or named Able to be Master; or named Joyful Mind; or named Peerless;
or named Cessation of Discourse—such names as these number ten thousand. Thus do the Buddhas cause all sentient beings to perceive and know them individually.
Son, south of these four continents, there is a world named Dussaha (Difficult to Endure). There, the Tathāgata is known by various names:

sometimes as Śakra, sometimes as Ratnayaśas (Jewel Renown), sometimes as Vimala (Stainless), sometimes as Satyavādin (Speaker of Truth), sometimes as Vinetā (The Subduer), sometimes as Prāmodyasampanna (Endowed with Joy), sometimes as Mahāyaśas (Great Renown), sometimes as Hitakara (Benefactor), sometimes as Ananta (Boundless), or sometimes as...
Most Victorious. There are ten thousand such names as these, causing all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the west of this four-continent world system, there is another world named Priyamatī.
There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes he is called Varuṇadeva, sometimes Priyadarśana, sometimes Jayendra, sometimes Vinayāmara, and sometimes Bhūtamati.
Some are named "Reached the Ultimate," some "Joyful," some "Dharma-Wisdom," some "Task Accomplished," and some "Well-Abiding.
Such names as these number ten thousand. They cause all sentient beings to have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the north of this four-continent world-system, there is a world named "Possessing Lions. There, the Tathāgata is known by various names...

The Great Muni is named variously: sometimes as the Ascetic, sometimes as the Honored One of the World, sometimes as the Supreme Field of Merit, sometimes as the Omniscient One, sometimes as the Benevolent Mind, sometimes as the Pure One, sometimes as Elāpattra, sometimes as the Supreme Giver, or sometimes as the Attainer through Austerity.
Such names as these number ten thousand, causing all sentient beings to know him individually.
Behold, O sons of the Buddha! To the northeast of these four continents, there is another world named *Vipaśyanā* (Excellent Observation).

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes as *Māradamaka* (Subduer of Māra), sometimes as *Siddha* (Accomplished), sometimes as *Upaśama* (Quiescence), and sometimes as *Bhadradeva* (Worthy Deva).
Some are named Free from Greed; some are named Supreme Wisdom; some are named Equality of Mind; some are named Invincible; some are named Sound of Wisdom;
some are named Difficult to Appear. There are ten thousand such names as these, causing all sentient beings to perceive and know them individually.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the southeast of this four-continent world system, there is another world named Joy.

Joy. To those beings, the Tathāgata is known by such names as Supreme Majesty, Mass of Radiance, Omniscient One, Secret One, Liberated One, Abiding in Nature, Practitioner of Dharma, King of Pure Eyes, Great Heroic Strength, or Power of Diligence;
such names as these number ten thousand. He causes them—
Sentient beings each have their own distinct knowledge and vision. O Sons of the Buddha, to the southwest of these four continents, there is another world named *Sudṛḍha* (Extremely Firm).

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes he is called *Pratiṣṭhita* (Abiding), sometimes *Jñānarāja* (King of Wisdom), sometimes *Paripūrṇa* (Complete), sometimes *Acala* (Immovable), sometimes *Sudarśana* (Excellent Eye), sometimes *Mūrdharāja* (Crown King), sometimes *Vaśavartiruta* (Sound of Sovereignty), or sometimes...

Universal Giver; or named Sustainer of the Many Sages; or named Surpassing Mount Sumeru—there are ten thousand such names as these, causing all sentient beings to perceive and know each one differently.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the northwest of this four-continent world system, there is another world named Wondrous Ground (*Sudhara*).
There, the Tathāgata is known by various names, such as Universal Pervader, or Blazing Radiance, or...

Maṇi-keśa (Jewel Topknot), or named Smṛti-mān (Worthy of Recollection), or named Anuttarārtha (Supreme Meaning), or named Nitya-pramoda (Ever-Joyful), or named Svabhāva-viśuddha (Pure by Nature), or named Paripūrṇa-prabha (Perfect Light), or named Dīrghabhuja (Long Arms), or named Mūlasthita (Abiding in the Root).
Such names as these number ten thousand, causing all sentient beings to know and see them individually. O Sons of the Buddha, next below this four-continent world...
In that direction there is a world named Jvālāprabhā.

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes as Kuśalamūlasamudita, sometimes as Siṃhalakṣaṇa, sometimes as Tīkṣṇaprajña, sometimes as Suvarṇajvālā, sometimes as Sarvajñānin, sometimes as Niṣṭhānirghoṣa, sometimes as Hitakara, sometimes as Niṣṭhāgata, sometimes as Bhūtadeva, or sometimes as...
Universally Victorious (Samantavijaya). There are ten thousand such names as these, causing all sentient beings to have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
O Sons of the Buddha, above this four-continent world system, there is a world named Earth-Sustainer (Dharanidhara).
There, the Tathāgata is called Endowed with Wisdom (Jñānavat), or Pure Face (Vimalamukha), or Awakened Intelligence (Buddhimat), or Foremost (Agraja), or Practice (Caryā).

The Monk Deqing of Hanshan at Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty, extracts and elucidates the ninth chapter, "The Chapter on Enlightened Awareness.
There are ten reasons for the inclusion of this chapter: first, to answer the previous question regarding the fruit upon which one relies; second, to provide an extensive explanation of its name.
Regarding the "Chapter on Titles": First, because the general and specific aspects are manifold, it extensively and variously investigates them;

this constitutes mental karma. Second, it explains the essential nature of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). This is of the same category as the verses of praise found at the beginning of each of the three assemblies prior to the exposition of the true stage (*bhūmi*).
Third, it reveals the reality of pervasiveness; whereas previously only the Buddha’s names were shown to be pervasive, here the Buddha’s body is revealed to be pervasive.
The Four Truths are the pervasive aspect of the provisional within the real; this is the pervasive aspect of the real within the provisional. Fifth, because it reveals the verification [of this].
Although the two preceding chapters spoke of pervasiveness, the multitude had not yet witnessed it; now, the light reveals the pervasive aspect. Sixth, because it reveals universal pervasiveness.

Previously, it was merely called "pervasiveness" in terms of the distinct truths; now, in this single assembly, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, such that every single thing is simultaneously [present].
1. Because they share the same location, the same assembly, the same teaching, and the same pervasiveness; 2. because this seventh [point] manifests complete pervasiveness.
The former manifested differentiation, wherein all are individually able to pervade all; now it manifests non-differentiation, wherein all are immediately interfused and pervade all.
3. Because it serves as a model for the subsequent sutra; that is to say, the subsequent sutra concludes by stating that it "pervades all."

All are distinguished in this manner. This is because the Tathāgata’s Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) manifests its transformative power within all categories of worlds, such as those equal in size to Mount Sumeru, in a manner consistent with these examples.
Ninth, it demonstrates the characteristics of the aforementioned supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Regarding the statement above that he "manifests supernatural powers," how does he manifest them?
It is by remaining unmoved from a single assembly while pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Tenth, it is for the purpose of revealing that both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are coextensive.
There is no obstruction, because it causes one to relinquish attachment and follow the Dharma. Although this meaning is pervasive throughout, it is specifically revealed here in the text.

Because there are these various aforementioned meanings, this chapter follows. Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: "Radiance" (*āloka*) is the essence, while "Awakening" (*bodha*) is the function.

First, there are the two radiances of body and wisdom; as for awakening, there is the act of knowing and the state of being awakened. Furthermore, radiance possesses both the capacity to illuminate and that which is illuminated.

Illumination. To perceive means there is that which perceives and that which is perceived. When the Tathāgata emits the light of his body to illuminate the phenomenal realm (*dharmadhātu*), he causes Bodhisattvas to perceive and see the phenomenal realm.
Mañjuśrī manifests the light of wisdom to simultaneously illuminate both principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*), causing sentient beings to awaken to the nature and characteristics of phenomena.
This is because phenomenon and principle are mutually fused, constituting a single unobstructed realm. Thus, one attains a single phenomenon...
It thus pervades the boundless without destroying its original characteristics. Body and wisdom are non-dual, being a single, unobstructed radiance.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Radiance is called wisdom. Furthermore, these two radiances of body and wisdom do not obstruct the realm of awakening.
These three are perfectly interfused as the sole, unobstructed Dharma-realm; though it is equal and devoid of marks, it does not destroy radiance.
The title "Awakening of Faith" is so named because this work distinguishes that awakening within its chapters.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from beneath the wheels on his two feet.
This section below is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s emission of light; second, the extent of the illumination.
First, regarding the light emitted from beneath the feet: this symbolizes the four meanings of faith. First, it proceeds from below upward, signifying that faith is the very beginning.
Second, it originates from the most humble point. Third, it serves as the foundation for practice. Fourth, it reveals that faith encompasses the fruit, having already reached fulfillment.
The same applies to the meaning of the wheels. As for the phrase "ten billion rays of light," this refers to the number of lands illuminated throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Because there are ten billion of each,
it illuminates this trichiliocosm: ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Pūrvavidehas,

everything within them appeared clearly. Just as here one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne.

That is not the realization of the eye of the Path; yet if one knows the Tathāgata— That his essential nature and marks are non-existent—and through cultivation attains clear understanding, This person will swiftly become a Buddha.

Because Vairocana is currently seated in Jambudvīpa preaching the Dharma and emitting light, the primary assembly that is illuminated is first mentioned.
