Even if one were to contemplate for billions of nayutas of eons, the physical marks and majestic power of the Tathāgata would become ever more boundless.
The Tathāgata does not take these marks as his essence; he is rather the signless, quiescent Dharma-body.
Yet, he is fully endowed with all physical marks and dignified deportment, so that all in the world may behold him according to their own inclinations.
The Buddha-dharma is subtle and difficult to measure; no verbal expression can reach it.
It is neither a composite nor non-composite; its essential nature is quiescent and devoid of all marks.
The Buddha-body is unborn and transcends conceptual proliferation; it is not a phenomenon consisting of an aggregation of aggregates.
Having attained the power of mastery and possessing decisive vision, their conduct is fearless and transcends the path of speech;
body and mind are entirely equal, liberated both internally and externally. Abiding in right mindfulness for eternal kalpas, they are without attachment and unbound.
Those whose minds are pure and luminous act without defilement or clinging.
The eye of wisdom reaches everywhere, Broadly benefiting all sentient beings.
A single body becomes infinite, And the infinite returns to one. Thoroughly understanding all worlds, He manifests forms throughout everything.
This body has no origin, Nor does it accumulate from anywhere; It is due to the conceptual discrimination of sentient beings.
Seeing the various bodies of the Buddha, one discriminates the world with the mind; yet this mind has no inherent existence.
The Tathāgata knows this dharma, and thus one sees the body of the Buddha.
At that time, the light passed beyond hundreds of thousands of worlds, illuminating a million worlds to the east, as well as those to the south, west, and north.
It was likewise so for the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens; everything therein appeared clearly.
Within each of those Jambudvīpas, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lotus-treasury lion throne throughout ten buddha-fields.
He was surrounded by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a mote of dust.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands they had come from were the Golden World and so forth.
The Buddhas whom they had previously served were, namely, the Tathāgata Acalamati and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in each of all those places simultaneously uttered these verses before the respective Buddhas:
The Tathāgata is most sovereign, transcending the world and without dependence; Possessing all virtues, he delivers beings from the realms of existence.
Untainted and unattached, without conceptualization and without a basis for reliance, his essential nature is immeasurable.
All who behold him offer praise; his radiance is universally pure.
All worldly burdens are completely cleansed; Unmoving, one is free from the two extremes. This is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If one perceives the Tathāgata With body and mind free from discrimination, Then one will forever transcend all stagnation regarding all phenomena.
Throughout all worlds, In every place, one turns the wheel of Dharma.
Without intrinsic nature and nothing to be transformed, the Teacher spoke through skillful means.
Regarding all phenomena, there is no doubt; all conceptual proliferation is forever severed. One does not give rise to a discriminating mind; this is the recollection of the Buddha’s awakening.
Fully knowing the distinct characteristics of phenomena, one does not cling to verbal expressions; there is neither oneness nor multiplicity.
This is called following the Buddha’s teaching: Among the many, there is no single nature; In the one, there is likewise no multiplicity.
Thus abandoning both, one universally enters the Buddha’s merit. Sentient beings and their lands are all utterly quiescent;
Without support and without discrimination, One is able to enter the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Sentient beings and their lands—neither identity nor difference can be found. To observe them thus with skillful discernment is called knowing the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the light passed beyond a million worlds and illuminated a billion worlds in the eastern direction, as well as those in the south, west, and north.
In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, it was likewise so.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens; everything therein appeared clearly.
Within each of those Jambudvīpas, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lotus-treasury lion throne, extending across ten buddha-fields.

He was surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were the Golden World and so forth.
The Buddhas whom they had previously served were the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna) and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in each of all those places simultaneously uttered these verses at the feet of the respective Buddhas:
Your wisdom is peerless and your Dharma is boundless; you have transcended the ocean of all existences to reach the other shore.
Your lifespan and radiance are both incomparable; such merit arises from the power of skillful means.
You clearly understand all Buddha-dharmas and constantly contemplate the three periods of time without weariness.

Though perceiving objects, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination; this inconceivable one, through the power of skillful means, delights in contemplating sentient beings with the notion of non-arising.
Universally seeing all realms of existence, they have no notion of such realms;
they dwell constantly in meditative tranquility with an unattached mind. This is the power of skillful means of their unimpeded wisdom.
Skillfully penetrating all phenomena, they diligently cultivate the path to nirvāṇa with right mindfulness;

delighting in liberation and free from unease, these people of tranquil extinction possess the power of skillful means to exhort others toward the Buddha’s bodhi and lead them to the omniscience that accords with the dharma-realm.
Skillfully transforming sentient beings so they enter the Truths—this is the power of skillful means of abiding in the Buddha-mind.
All the teachings spoken by the Buddha are entered accordingly;
with vast wisdom that is unimpeded, one has reached the perfection of conduct in all places—this is the power of cultivating sovereign skillful means.
Constantly abiding in nirvāṇa like space, manifesting transformations according to the mind without exception;
this takes that which is signless as its sign, through the power of skillful means for those who have reached what is difficult to reach.
Day and night, months and years, kalpas, and the signs of the world’s beginning, end, formation, and destruction.
Thus recollecting and fully understanding, at this time, through the power of the skillful means of numerical knowledge,
one fully understands all sentient beings who undergo birth and death, as well as all names— whether material or immaterial,
with perception or without perception. This dwelling is the inconceivable power of skillful means.
All speech throughout the past, present, and future worlds can be fully understood;
knowing that the three periods of time are entirely equal—such is the power of this peerless skillful means.
At that time, the light passed beyond one hundred million worlds and universally illuminated ten billion worlds in the east, as well as those in the south, west, and north.
It was likewise so throughout the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Within each and every one of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens; everything contained therein appeared clearly.
Within each and every Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lotus-treasury lion throne, pervading ten buddha-fields.

He was surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, there was a great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, who came together to the place where the Buddha was.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands they had come from were, for instance, the Golden World.
The Buddhas whom they had previously served were the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna) and others.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in each location simultaneously uttered these verses at the presence of those Buddhas:

Having practiced all vast ascetic disciplines, diligent day and night without weariness or indolence, he has crossed over that which is difficult to cross and lets out a lion’s roar; his conduct is to universally transform sentient beings.
Sentient beings wander in the ocean of craving and desire, shrouded by the net of ignorance and oppressed by great sorrow.
Supreme benevolence and valor completely sever [delusions]; this is their vow and their practice.
The world is heedless, attached to the five desires, and undergoes manifold sufferings through unreal conceptualization;
To constantly restrain the mind by following the Buddha’s teachings and vow to deliver such beings—this is their practice.
Sentient beings, attached to a self, enter the cycle of birth and death; though one seeks its limit, it cannot be found.
By serving the Tathāgatas universally, they obtain the wondrous Dharma and proclaim it for their sake—this is their practice.
Sentient beings have no protector and are entangled by illness; they constantly sink into the evil realms, giving rise to the three poisons.
The fierce flames of a great fire constantly burn with heat; to deliver sentient beings from that state through a pure mind is their practice.
Sentient beings are deluded and lose the right path, constantly traveling on deviant roads into the dark house;
to light the lamp of the Great True Dharma for them, forever acting as a source of illumination, is their practice.
Sentient beings drift and drown in the ocean of existence, In boundless sorrow and hardship, unable to find rest;
For their sake, he constructs the great Dharma-ship To enable them all to cross over—this is his practice.
Sentient beings lack knowledge and do not see the source; Deluded and crazed within perilous difficulties.
The Buddha, out of compassion for them, builds the bridge of Dharma; To cause them to ascend by means of right mindfulness is his practice.

Seeing all sentient beings in perilous paths, Constantly oppressed by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, He cultivates immeasurable and boundless skillful means; Vowing to deliver them all is his practice.
Hearing the Dharma, they believe and understand it without doubt; realizing that nature is empty and quiescent, they are not startled or terrified.
Adapting their forms to the six realms throughout the ten directions, they universally instruct the deluded masses—this is their practice.
At that time, the light passed beyond ten billion worlds and shone everywhere across a hundred billion worlds in the eastern direction, as well as a thousand billion worlds.
World-systems; hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems; nayutas of billions of world-systems; hundreds of nayutas of billions of world-systems;

thousands of nayutas of billions of world-systems; hundreds of thousands of nayutas of billions of world-systems—in this way, they are innumerable, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable.
In all worlds within the dharma-realm and the space-realm—likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—all things are clearly manifested.
Within each of those individual worlds, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens;
everything therein is clearly visible. Within each of those Jambudvīpas, one sees as follows:
He came and sat upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, a great bodhisattva appeared in each of the ten directions, each accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all coming to the place where the Buddha was. These great bodhisattvas were, namely, Mañjuśrī...
The lands from which Mañjuśrī and the others had come were called the Golden World and so forth;

the Buddhas they had originally served were the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and so forth. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in each location simultaneously raised his voice and spoke these verses before his respective Buddha:
In a single thought, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons— Neither going nor coming, and likewise no abiding.
Thus understanding the affairs of the three periods of time, One transcends all expedient means and achieves the ten powers.
With a virtuous reputation peerless throughout the ten directions, Forever free from all hardships, one is always joyful.
They go everywhere throughout all lands, widely proclaiming and expounding such teachings;
for the benefit of sentient beings, they make offerings to the Buddhas, and according to their intentions, they obtain corresponding fruits.
They fully understand all phenomena in accordance with reality, manifesting spiritual powers throughout the ten directions.
From the beginning, with a mind of gentle patience in making offerings to the Buddhas, Entering deep meditative concentration to contemplate the nature of phenomena,
Universally exhorting sentient beings to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind, And thereby swiftly attaining the unsurpassed fruit—
Seeking the Dharma throughout the ten directions with no difference in intent, He causes his cultivation of merit to reach fulfillment.
Having completely eliminated both the marks of existence and non-existence, this person has true vision regarding the Buddha.
Traveling everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, they extensively proclaim the sublime Dharma to bring about benefit and welfare.
Abiding immovably in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), this person’s merit is equal to that of the Buddha.
The sublime Wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata— All of it consists of the factors of enlightenment.
If one can hear it and awaken to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), Such a person constantly sees the Buddha;
Yet they do not see the Ten Powers, for they are empty and like an illusion. Though they see, it is as if they do not see, like a blind man beholding forms.
Those who grasp at signs through discrimination do not see the Buddha; Only by being ultimately free from attachment can one see him.
Sentient beings differ according to their various karmas, Yet the Buddha’s body is unimpeded, pervading the ten directions.
Just as it is impossible to see them all, The same is true for seeing the Buddha.

Just as there are immeasurable lands in space, Neither coming nor going, pervading the ten directions, Arising, abiding, and decaying without any support— The Buddha’s pervasion of empty space is likewise so.
[This concludes] the worlds illuminated and pervaded by the light below; in all of them, Mañjuśrī recited these verses to describe the light.
Regarding the principle and phenomena of the central Dharma-realm: first, within the primary assembly, the verses collectively manifest that Bodhi transcends the realm of emotions.
From this point onward, in each successive section, the Buddha uses the light of his body to illuminate these matters, causing the multitude to behold them with their own eyes.

Mañjuśrī speaks the verses and the Wisdom Light praises and describes the phenomena and principles, causing the multitude to awaken and enter [the truth]. Now, the light shines beyond the Sahā world-system, arranged in successive layers.
In the ten buddha-fields, Mañjuśrī spoke verses that universally revealed the causes and fruits of bodhi.
Next, he illuminated a hundred worlds to reveal the eightfold marks of bodhi. Next, he illuminated a thousand worlds to reveal the essential nature of bodhi.
Next, he illuminated ten thousand worlds to reveal the characteristics of bodhi. Next, he illuminated a hundred thousand worlds to reveal his majestic power. Next, there was...
The fourth section answers regarding the virtue of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Next, it illuminates one million worlds to collectively manifest the virtue of internal and external inclusion.

Next, it illuminates one hundred million worlds to manifest the virtue of the functional capacity of skillful means (*upāya*). Next, it illuminates ten billion worlds to manifest the virtue of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that rescues and gathers beings.
Next, it illuminates one hundred billion worlds to manifest the virtue of the perfect pervasiveness of cause and effect. The intent is to manifest...
It is inexhaustible; therefore, there is no conclusion.
This is the beginning of the first section, "The Arising of Understanding through Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit," from the second assembly.

At the start of the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata," newly assembled bodhisattvas with mindfulness pose forty questions. The first ten questions are general inquiries regarding the fruit upon which they rely.
Next, there are thirty questions cited as examples: the first ten questions concern the cause, and the subsequent twenty questions concern the result.
Now, the preceding three chapters—the Buddha’s emission of light and manifestation of signs, along with Mañjuśrī’s discourse—collectively answer the first ten questions regarding the result.
Having thus completed the section on establishing the basis for the arising of understanding.

Next, the following provides the direct answer regarding the causes and conditions for generating understanding. First, it answers the question concerning the ten causal practices cultivated by the bodhisattva, beginning from the "Chapter on Clarifying the Questions" (*Wenming pin*) and extending through the forty subsequent chapters down to the "Chapter on Abiding Places" (*Zhuchu pin*) in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis.

Within this section, it teaches the "Ten Faiths" (*Shixin*)—namely, the three immediately following chapters—in order to cause those who have not yet attained faith to do so. Second, it teaches the "Ten [Abodes]" (*Shizhu*) in order to cause those who already possess faith to attain understanding.

1. Abiding. This occurs in the sixteenth sūtra, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru," where those who have already understood the three [practices] are made to practice; herein the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are taught. 2. Practice. This occurs in the nineteenth sūtra, "Ascending the Palace of the Yāma Heaven," where those who have already practiced the ten [practices] are made to arouse vows; herein the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught. 3. Vows. This occurs in the twenty-second sūtra, "Ascending the Palace of the Tuṣita Heaven," where those who have already... [the vows]... are made to... [arouse the resolve]. 4. Resolve. This occurs in the twenty-fifth sūtra, "Ascending the Palace of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven," where those who have already aroused the resolve are made to enter the stages (*bhūmi*); herein the ten stages are taught. 5. Stages. This occurs in the twenty-ninth sūtra, "Ascending the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven," where those who have already entered the stages are made to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; herein the ten powers (*daśa-bala*), four fearlessnesses (*catasraḥ vaiśāradyāni*), and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are taught. 6. Fruit. This occurs in the thirty-first sūtra, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra," where the practices of all bodhisattvas are fully explained. This is the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. For those who have aroused the aspiration, he causes them to enter [the path]; thus he teaches the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). This is found in the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the thirty-fourth sutra.

This is found from the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśasamādhi-parivarta*) to the "Chapter on the Abodes" (*Vihāra-parivarta*) of the fortieth sutra. Below this are twenty-three chapters of sutra that collectively answer the previous request for instruction.
The Tenth Chapter: Questions on the Ten Causes;
The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas’ Inquiry into Clarity, Number Ten.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed Bodhisattva Awakening Chief (Bodhyamati), saying: "O Son of the Buddha, the nature of the mind is one."
How is it that one perceives various distinctions? Namely: rebirth in the happy realms or the miserable realms; the completeness or deficiency of the sense faculties;
the similarities and differences in birth; being handsome or ugly; and the disparity between suffering and pleasure. Karma does not know the mind, and the mind does not know karma.

The recipient does not know the retribution, and the retribution does not know the recipient. The mind does not know the recipient, and the recipient does not know the mind. The cause does not know the condition, and the condition [does not know the cause].
The cause does not know [the effect], wisdom does not know its object, and the object does not know wisdom. At that time, the Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment answered in verse:
"You now ask about this meaning To awaken the ignorant masses. I shall answer according to their nature;
May you, O Benevolent One, listen attentively. All phenomena are devoid of activity, And likewise lack any intrinsic nature."
Therefore, all those things / Are each unaware of the other. / Just as the waters in a river / Rush onward in a turbulent current, / Each unaware of the others, / So it is with all phenomena;
/ And like a great mass of fire, / With its fierce flames breaking out at once, / Each is unaware of the others.
All phenomena are likewise: just as when a great wind arises, it encounters objects and fans them all, yet each is unaware of the others;
so too are all phenomena. Furthermore, just as the various elements of earth dwell in mutual dependence upon one another, yet each is unaware of the others; so too are all phenomena.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties—by these one constantly transmigrates, yet there is no agent who transmigrates.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally without birth;
it manifests as having birth, yet herein there is no agent of manifestation, nor is there any object manifested. [This applies to] the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body.
The mind, the intellect, and all the sensory faculties— All are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.

When one observes with a deluded mind through conceptual discrimination, it appears as if there were such a thing; Yet when observed with the inconceivable Dharma-eye, all are seen to be without intrinsic nature.
This vision is not inverted, whether regarding what is real or unreal, Or what is false or not false.
"Regarding the mundane and the supramundane, there is nothing but provisional verbal expression.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Vasumitra Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, all sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings.
How is it that the Tathāgata, according to the time, according to their lifespan, according to their bodies, according to their conduct, and according to..."
According to their understanding, according to their discourse, according to their mental inclinations, according to their skillful means, according to their reflections,
and according to their investigations— among such sentient beings, he manifests his body to teach,
transform, and subdue them. Then, the Bodhisattva Wealth Chief replied in verse:
This is the realm of those who delight in tranquility and possess great learning;
I have proclaimed it for you, so you should now receive it with careful attention. By analytically observing the internal body, one asks: "Who here is 'I'?
If one can understand in this way, they will realize the existence or non-existence of a self. This body is merely a conventional designation.
The dwelling place has no fixed location; one who thoroughly understands this body has no attachment therein.
By skillfully observing the body, one clearly perceives all things. Knowing that all phenomena are empty and false, one does not give rise to mental discrimination.
From what cause does life arise? And by what cause does it decline and perish?
Just like a whirling firebrand, its beginning and end cannot be known.
The wise are able to observe that all things are impermanent, that all phenomena are empty and selfless, and that they are forever free from all marks.
All retributions arise according to karma; they are unreal, like a dream, constantly perishing and decaying from moment to moment.
As it was before, so it is after; of all phenomena perceived in the world, the mind alone is the master.

Following its interpretations, one grasps at manifold signs; thus, through inversion, things are not seen as they truly are. All the discourses spoken in the world are merely conceptual constructions;
there has never been a single phenomenon that can enter into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Through the power of the perceiving subject and the perceived object, various phenomena arise; they perish swiftly without pausing for even a moment, and every thought-moment is exactly thus.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, all sentient beings..."
"All things possess the four great elements; they are without self and without what belongs to a self.

How, then, can there be the experience of suffering or pleasure, beauty or ugliness, excellence within or without, little or much experience, or retribution experienced in the present life or in future lives?
Yet, within the Dharma-realm, there is neither good nor evil. Then, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī replied in verse:
According to the actions one performs, Such is the retribution that arises.
The Buddhas have taught that there is no agent; It is like a pure, bright mirror: According to the objects reflected, The images that appear are each different.
The nature of karma is likewise; It is also like seeds in a field.
Each is unaware of the others, yet they naturally give rise [to effects]. The nature of karma is likewise.
Furthermore, it is like a skillful illusionist standing at a crossroads who manifests various forms and appearances;
the nature of karma is likewise. It is also like a wooden puppet operated by machinery, capable of producing all manner of sounds.
That is neither self nor non-self; the nature of karma is likewise so.
Just as various kinds of birds emerge from their eggs, their voices each being different, the nature of karma is likewise so.
For example, within the womb, all the sense faculties are fully developed, yet the physical form has no place of origin.
The nature of karma is likewise. Just as in the hells, various kinds of suffering have no place from which they originate, so too is the nature of karma.
For example, when a wheel-turning monarch achieves the seven supreme jewels, their point of origin cannot be found; so too is the nature of karma.
Furthermore, just as all worlds Are consumed by a great fire, Yet this fire has no place from which it comes— The nature of karma is likewise so.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa: "O Son of the Buddha, regarding what the Tathāgata has realized..."
It is but a single Dharma. Why, then, do you speak of immeasurable dharmas?
You manifest immeasurable lands, transform immeasurable multitudes, proclaim immeasurable sounds, display immeasurable bodies, know immeasurable minds, and manifest immeasurable supernormal powers.
You are able to universally shake immeasurable worlds, manifest immeasurable and sublime adornments, and reveal boundless varieties of realms.
"Regarding the realms: within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), these various differentiated characteristics are all unattainable. Then, the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇaketu replied in verse:
"The meaning of what the Son of the Buddha has asked is profound and difficult to comprehend; only the wise can know this."
Constantly delighting in the Buddha’s virtues, Just as the nature of the earth is one, And sentient beings dwell separately upon it without a thought of oneness or difference—
The Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise. Furthermore, just as the nature of fire is one and can burn all things,
Yet the flames themselves have no discrimination— The Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise.
Just as the great ocean is one, yet its waves and surges are ten thousandfold and diverse, while the water itself has no such variety—so too are the Buddhas' dharmas.
Just as the nature of wind is one, capable of blowing upon all things, yet the wind has not a single thought of diversity—so too are the Buddhas' dharmas. Just as the great clouds and thunder...
A rain falls everywhere upon all lands, yet there is no distinction among the drops;
so too are the qualities of the Buddhas, for they are one with the element of earth. They can produce various kinds of sprouts, though the earth itself possesses no differentiation;
so too are the qualities of the Buddhas. Like the sun when it is free from the veil of clouds, they shine universally throughout the ten directions.
The radiance has no difference in nature; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as the moon in the sky is seen by the entire world, yet the moon does not travel to those places—such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
For example, like the Great Brahmā King, who manifests his presence throughout the three thousandfold world-system, yet his body remains without distinction.
Such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Kṣemaṅkara Bodhisattva: "Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s field of merit is equal and without distinction;
why then do we see that the fruits of sentient beings’ giving are not the same, being as they are of various kinds?"
Regarding their various physical forms, various lineages, various faculties, various wealth, various masters, various retinues, various official ranks,
various merits, and various wisdoms, the Buddha’s mind remains equanimous toward them all.
There is no discrimination in thought. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mūrdhaja replied in verse:
"Just as the great earth is one, Yet sprouts grow according to each seed, So too is the Buddha-field of merit: Therein, there is neither enemy nor kin.
Furthermore, like water which is of a single taste, It appears different according to the vessel."
The Buddha-field of merit is likewise; it differs according to the minds of sentient beings.
Just as a skilled illusionist can cause the multitude to rejoice, so too is the Buddha-field of merit: it causes sentient beings to feel reverence and joy.
Like a wise and talented king who can bring delight to the great assembly, so too is the Buddha-field of merit.
Causing all beings to dwell in peace and happiness, Just as a pure, bright mirror Manifests reflections according to the forms before it, So too is the Buddha-field of merit:
One receives various rewards according to one's mind.
Just as the agada medicine Can cure all poisons, So too is the Buddha-field of merit: It extinguishes the afflictions of all suffering.
Just as when the sun rises, it illuminates the world, so too does the Buddha-field eliminate all darkness.
Like the pure full moon, which shines universally upon the great earth, so too does the Buddha-field;
it is equal in all places. It is like the Vairambha wind.
It causes the great earth to tremble everywhere; such is the Buddha-field of merit.
It moves the beings of the three realms of existence, like a great fire that can burn all things; such is the Buddha-field of merit that burns all conditioned phenomena.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Vīradatta Bodhisattva: "Son of the Buddha, the Buddha's teaching is one and the same for all sentient beings to perceive;
why is it that they do not immediately sever all the bonds of their afflictions and attain liberation?"

"However, there is no distinction between the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor between the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, nor between ignorance, craving, and attachment.
Thus, the Buddha’s teaching may be beneficial for some sentient beings and not beneficial for others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta replied in verse:
O Son of the Buddha, listen well; I shall now answer you according to reality.
Some attain swift liberation, while others find it difficult to escape.
If you wish to eliminate immeasurable faults and evils, you should always exert yourself with courageous diligence within the Buddha-dharma, just as even a tiny spark of fire can grow.
Just as damp firewood is quickly extinguished, so it is with those who are indolent within the Buddha’s teaching.
Like one drilling for fire who stops repeatedly before the flame appears—the intensity of the fire ceases accordingly—so it is with the indolent.
It is like a person holding a sun-crystal who does not use a substance to catch its reflection.
Fire can never be obtained [by seeking it in the wrong way], and so it is with the indolent.
It is like the glaring sun shining upon a child who closes his eyes; the child marvels, "Why do I not see it? So it is with the indolent.
Like a man without hands or feet, who wishes to pierce the entire earth with arrows made of mere blades of grass.

The same applies to those who are indolent: Just as if one were to take a single hair-tip And attempt to drain the waters of the great ocean until it is completely parched— The same applies to those who are indolent.
Or again, like the fire at the end of an eon arising, And attempting to extinguish it with a mere drop of water— Within the teachings of the Buddha, The same applies to those who are indolent.
"Just as one might see space sitting upright and unmoving, yet saying it 'pervasively leaps over' the indolent—so it is likewise.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Dharmottara Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, as the Buddha has said..."
If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold the True Dharma, they are all able to sever and eliminate all afflictions.
For what reason, then, are there those who receive and uphold the True Dharma yet do not sever them? It is because they are driven by the power of greed, hatred, and delusion;
by pride, concealment, anger, resentment, envy, stinginess, deceit, and flattery. There is no receiving and upholding of the Dharma that occurs apart from the mind.
"Why, furthermore, do various afflictions arise within mental formations? At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmottara replied in verse:
"O Son of the Buddha, listen well and attentively to the true meaning of what you have asked; it is not attained by mere extensive learning alone."
One who can enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata is like a person drifting on water; though fearing drowning, they die of thirst.
One who does not practice the Dharma, despite being well-versed in it, is just like this.
It is like a person who prepares a fine meal but starves and does not eat; one who does not practice the Dharma, despite being well-versed in it, is just like this.
Just as a person skilled in prescriptions and medicines Cannot save themselves from their own illness, So too is it with much learning If one does not practice the Dharma.

Just as a person counts another’s treasures Without having even half a coin for themselves, So too is it with much learning If one does not practice the Dharma. It is like being born into a royal palace...
Yet they suffer from hunger and cold, for they do not practice the Dharma. Much learning is likewise like this: it is like a deaf person playing music;
he pleases others but does not hear it himself. One who does not practice the Dharma despite much learning is likewise like this:
it is like a blind person painting various images; he shows them to others but does not see them himself.
One who does not practice the Dharma, though they have heard much, is just like this:
Like a sea captain who dies out at sea; One who does not practice the Dharma, though they have heard much, is just like this:
Like one standing at a crossroads, Speaking at length of many fine things, Yet lacking true virtue within themselves.
Not practicing is also like this.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Jñānaśrī Bodhisattva: "Son of the Buddha, within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is the foremost.
For what reason does the Tathāgata sometimes praise giving for the sake of sentient beings, and sometimes praise the upholding of precepts?"
Some praised patience; some praised diligence; some praised meditative concentration; some praised wisdom;

and others praised loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Yet, in the end, there was never anyone who attained liberation and achieved unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment through a single dharma alone.
Then, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī replied in verse:
O Son of the Buddha, you are most rare, Able to know the minds of sentient beings.

Listen attentively as I now explain the meaning of what you have asked: In the past, future, and present, Among all the Guides, there is not one who has attained the Way By teaching even a single dharma. The Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings.
The dispositions of beings differ from one another; according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, he teaches the Dharma in this way:
to the stingy, he praises giving; to those who violate the precepts, he praises morality;
to the wrathful, he praises patience; to the indolent, he praises diligence; to the distracted, he praises meditative concentration; and to the ignorant, he praises wisdom.
One who lacks benevolence is praised with loving-kindness; one who delights in harm is praised with great compassion;
one who is sorrowful is praised with sympathetic joy; and one with a crooked mind is praised with equanimity.

By practicing in this sequence, one gradually fulfills all the Buddha-qualities, just as one first establishes a foundation and subsequently builds a palace; the same applies to generosity and ethical discipline.
The fundamental basis for the various practices of Bodhisattvas is like the construction of city walls and moats;
In order to protect the multitude of people, patience and diligence are likewise used to guard all Bodhisattvas.
Just as a powerful king is looked up to and revered by the entire realm, so too are meditative concentration and wisdom that which the Bodhisattvas rely upon.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch is able to bestow all happiness, so too do the four immeasurables bestow happiness upon all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha: "O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones..."
If liberation is attained through only a single path, why do we now see that all Buddha-fields possess various and diverse phenomena?

That is to say, there are differences in the world-systems, the realms of sentient beings, the preaching of the Dharma, the means of training, the lifespan, the radiance, the supernatural powers, the assemblies, the pedagogical methods, and the duration of the Dharma’s abiding.
How is it that there is none among them that does not possess all the Buddha-dharmas?
When he was about to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse:
The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is always thus: The Dharma-King has but one single Dharma.
All those who are unimpeded Transcend birth and death by means of this One Path. The bodies of all Buddhas Are but this single Dharmakāya.
With a single mind and a single wisdom, Their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise so.
Just as they originally aspired toward Bodhi with a heart of dedication, They attain such lands, assemblies, and the preaching of the Dharma;
In all Buddha-fields, their adornments are entirely perfected, Yet they appear differently according to the various conducts of sentient beings.
Thus, these various manifestations— The Buddha-fields and the Buddha-bodies, The assemblies and the spoken teachings—
Such qualities of the Buddhas, Sentient beings are unable to see. Only those whose minds are already purified,
Whose vows are all fully perfected, And who have attained such clear realization, Are able to behold them here.
In accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings’ minds, And by the power of the fruits of their karma, Such differences in perception arise;
this is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. The Buddha-fields are without distinction, Free from both hatred and attachment;
Yet, according to the minds of sentient beings, They perceive them as diverse. It is for this reason that, within the world, [Such perceptions arise.]
The differences in what is seen do not stem from any fault of the Great Sages, the Tathāgatas; rather,
it is according to those in all worlds who are ready to be transformed that the Heroes among Men, the Buddhas, are always perceived—
such is the nature of the Buddhadharma.
At that time, the bodhisattvas said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, "O Son of the Buddha, we have each spoken according to our own understanding.
We pray that you, O Benevolent One, will expound with your sublime eloquence the entire realm of the Tathāgata.
What is the realm of the Buddha? What is the cause of the Buddha’s realm? What is the transcendence of the Buddha’s realm?"
These are the entries into the Buddha’s realm. What is the wisdom of the Buddha’s realm? What is the dharma of the Buddha’s realm?
What is the teaching of the Buddha’s realm? What is the knowledge of the Buddha’s realm? What is the realization of the Buddha’s realm?
What is the manifestation of the Buddha’s realm? What is the expansion of the Buddha’s realm? At that time, Mañjuśrī—
The Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"The profound realm of the Tathāgata Is equal in measure to empty space;
All sentient beings enter it, yet in truth there is nothing entered. The profound realm of the Tathāgata Consists of all supreme and wondrous causes."
Even if one were to proclaim it for billions of eons, one could never exhaust it.
According to their minds and wisdom, they guide and advance them all, causing them all to benefit. Thus do they deliver sentient beings.
They enter into all the realms of the Buddhas and all the lands of the world; their body of wisdom has no form.
This cannot be seen by others; it is the sovereign wisdom of the Buddhas. Unimpeded throughout the three times, such is the sphere of their wisdom.
Equal as space, the realm of phenomena and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately without distinction;
all is fully known. This is the domain of the Tathāgatas.
In all worlds, whatever sounds there may be, The Buddha’s wisdom comprehends them all accordingly, yet without discrimination.
They cannot be known by consciousness, nor are they the domain of the mind;
Their nature is fundamentally pure. He reveals this to all living beings: It is neither karma nor affliction.
Without substance and without abode, without illumination and without a path traversed, they practice equanimity throughout the minds of all sentient beings in the world;
universally present within the three periods of time, the Tathāgata fully and clearly realizes everything in a single thought-moment.

The purpose for the introduction of this chapter is both general and specific. The general purpose is that while the preceding three chapters have already answered the ten points regarding the basis for generating understanding, from here on we shall properly answer the causes and conditions for generating that understanding;
therefore, it follows immediately after. Regarding the causes for generating understanding:
First, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are answered. A stage is established by means of faith; since one is about to explain that which is established, one first explains that which establishes it.

Furthermore, this is a direct response to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and thus the following two chapters are brought forward in connection with it. This is because the question concerning the ten levels of faith was omitted from the previous inquiry.

As for Master Xianshou’s separate opening of the stage of faith: both the *Liang* commentary and the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) include a stage of faith; such is the case in this scripture as well.

Because there was no question [posed], it was said that [the teaching] was not established. Now, we do not debate whether a stage has been attained or not; rather, all three grades respond individually to the inquiry regarding faith.
Each of these separate assemblies has a question, and thus they are answered individually. Regarding those of the third grade who possess clear faith:

they have the virtues of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), with understanding serving as the foundation for the other two. This grade comes first. To explain the title: "Bodhisattva" refers to the person, and "Inquiry into Clarity" (*prajñā-pṛcchā*) refers to the question.
This dharma excludes the fruit and manifests the cause; therefore, it is called "bodhisattva. "Question" refers to an objection, while "clarification" refers to the response.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of questions: first, a general inquiry; second, an objection, which means to interrogate by means of reasoning—this is the intent of the present chapter.
There are likewise two kinds of responses: first, a direct reply based solely on the question, which is called a "response"; second, [a response] if both [question and answer] are for the sake of...

Explanation: To interpret by incorporating related meanings from other sources, using elegant language to praise and describe so that the principles are made clear and radiant is called "illumination" (*prabhā*);
this is the intended meaning of the present chapter. Furthermore, illumination dispels darkness; it refers here to being able to dispel the darkness of doubt in the questioner.

Thus, "illumination" here is "Dharma-illumination," for ten kinds of Dharma-illumination emerge from the questions of the ten bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called "Question-Illumination. This is the current chapter.

The "Chapter on Illumination" elucidates the contemplation of the principle of correct understanding; the subsequent chapter elucidates practice in accordance with conditions and vows; and the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" elucidates how the power of virtue encompasses all.
In this present chapter, ten bodhisattvas each preside over a gate to manifest ten kinds of profundity, which constitutes ten sections.

1. The first question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment (*Bodhimukha*), elucidates the profundity of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 2. The second question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Wealth (*Dhanamukha*), elucidates the profundity of teaching and transformation (*vinaya*).

3. The third question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Jewels (*Ratnamukha*), elucidates the profundity of karmic fruition (*karmavipāka*). 4. The fourth question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Virtue (*Guṇamukha*), elucidates the profundity of preaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).

5. The fifth question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Eyes (*Netramukha*), elucidates the profundity of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). 6. The sixth question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Diligence (*Vīryamukha*), elucidates the profundity of the true teaching (*saddharma*). 7. The seventh question, by Bodhisattva Chief of Dharma... [text ends]
The first question, by Samantabhadra, clarifies the profundity of the primary practice; the eighth question, by Jñānottara, clarifies the profundity of the primary and auxiliary practices;
the ninth question, by Bhadrapāla, clarifies the profundity of the single path; and the tenth question, by Mañjuśrī, clarifies the profundity of the Buddha’s realm.

These ten aforementioned profundities may also be correlated with the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), though the textual order does not correspond. The realm of Mañjuśrī and the Buddha corresponds to the stage of faith;
for Mañjuśrī presides over faith, and the Buddha’s realm is that which is to be believed. From the perspective of the sequence of initial aspiration, faith occupies the first place;
from the perspective of the ultimate limit of what is to be believed, it occupies the very last. This also clarifies the ten mental states (*citta*).

Because they follow a necessary sequence: the Chief of Diligence (*Vīryapramukha*) is the mind of progress; the Chief of Wealth (*Dhanapramukha*) is the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*), because he clarifies the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*);

the Chief of Virtue (*Guṇapramukha*) is the mind of concentration (*samādhi*), because the non-conceptual nature of the mind (*cittāsaṃkalpa*) constitutes the supreme concentration; and the Chief of Wisdom (*Jñānapramukha*) is the mind of insight (*prajñā*), which further serves as its own adornment.
Therefore, there are ten perfections (*pāramitā*). "Dharma-Head" refers to the mind of non-retrogression, for one does not fall back when practicing as taught.

"Jewel-Head" refers to the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla*), for the three clusters [of precepts] are without defect, like a precious gem. "Karma-Fruit" is profoundly deep, for it is that which is summoned by ethical discipline.
"Awakening-Head" refers to the mind of protecting the Dharma, for the profound nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is what is to be protected. "Eye-Head" refers to the vow...

The mind. [The distinction between] the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and so forth arises from the difference in their vows. Because the eyes can lead the body to proceed according to one's wishes, "Worthy Leader" (*bhadramukha*) refers to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
By returning to the One Path, one dedicates oneself to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

A single body and a single wisdom constitute the fruit of Buddhahood. As the text says: "Just as the mind of dedication and so forth directed toward awakening in the past... This is because it is perfect.
Each of these ten dharmas encompasses multiple meanings, which are explained in detail in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*); fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here.
The ten profundities listed above correspond to the sequence of the sūtra text.
At that time, within this Sahā world-system, all the various distinctions of sentient beings— namely, the distinctions of dharmas,
the distinctions of karma, the distinctions of worlds, the distinctions of bodies, the distinctions of faculties, the distinctions of birth, the distinctions of the fruits of observing precepts,
the distinctions of the fruits of violating precepts, and the distinctions of the fruits of lands— all appeared clearly through the Buddha’s spiritual power. Thus, in the east...
Throughout a hundred thousand billion nayutas of worlds— numberless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable,
inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable— that exhaustively encompass the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space,
all sentient beings and their diverse natures, even down to the differences in the fruits of their lands, are [manifested] entirely through the spiritual power of the Buddha.
Therefore, it appears with distinct clarity. It is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

This concludes the section on the manifested phenomena. Within this, first are the manifested phenomena, followed by the conclusion and generalization. Now, for the first part: by what cause do they appear?
The ten preceding verses were taught so that the light of the Dharma might enlighten the bodies and minds of sentient beings;
thus, the Buddha’s power was briefly manifested, providing a response through the display of signs, so that they might witness it with their own eyes and thereby experience joy and revulsion.
The Supplementary Commentary states: Carefully observing the concluding passage of the sutra text, it says:
"All the various phenomena of all sentient beings within this Sahā world, and so forth, are all clearly manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power. It further states:
"The various distinctions existing within all worlds throughout the unspeakable Dharma-realm and space-realm cannot be fully described. All [of these]...
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, these appear with distinct clarity. This is a world within the ocean of worlds illuminated by the supreme Buddha-light.

All the various distinctions among sentient beings in those worlds, as well as their diverse manifestations and phenomena, are all clearly perceived one by one due to the illumination of the Buddha-light. Therefore, now the nine-headed Bodhisattva...
"Sā" refers to the specific phenomena of cause and effect perceived within that light;
therefore, each [of the Buddhas] raises what they have seen to question Mañjuśrī, which is precisely to inquire about the causes of these distinctions.

Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the "nine-headed Buddha-realm" clarifies the fruits within those distinctions. The underlying meaning is that within the Dharma-realm, sentient beings are the internal cause.
Since there are various distinctions, practitioners must possess various distinct practices to clarify their respective remedies.
When these remedial practices are completed, each realizes the Buddha-realm within its own particular distinction as the distinct fruit.

Therefore, at the outset of generating understanding, one must first clarify these distinct characteristics and comprehend each one individually to establish the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).
For this reason, this chapter serves as the beginning of faith; it possesses profound significance.
If one were to conclude with this single question alone, how would it relate to the general purport of the entire scripture? The text is extensive, and the student...
I pray that you will clearly bear this in mind; I pray that you will not lose sight of the fundamental tenets.
The "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarification" concludes. *The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning commented upon by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá Yán Temple;
and the essentials extracted by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: On Pure Conduct (*Śīla-viśuddhi*).
Regarding the intent behind the introduction of this chapter: To ascend to the sublime stages, one must necessarily rely upon superior practice.

Since mere understanding devoid of practice renders extensive learning a vain expenditure, the preceding chapter elucidated understanding, while this chapter distinguishes practice. Furthermore, the preceding section clarified the contemplation that enters into principle; [this section now clarifies the conduct that accords with that principle].
[This is] practice. Now, the practices performed according to specific matters are being distinguished. Furthermore, the preceding [section on] making this vow follows the sequence of the meanings;
therefore, it follows here next. Regarding the explanation of the names: the three types of action (trikarma) following matters and traversing conditions are called "practices" (*pratipatti*).

Skillful vows that prevent wrongdoing, eliminate faults, and accomplish virtues are called "pure. Furthermore, the simultaneous practice of compassion and wisdom is called "practice. This practice transcends...
Because they are merely small, they are called "pure. Since the untainted (anāsrava) states of the two vehicles cannot benefit others universally, they are not true purity.
One who grasps this meaning finds that every step taken and every step set down is the mind of Mañjuśrī; every seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is the practice of Samantabhadra.
Because it is the mind of Mañjuśrī, the mind is free from turbidity and confusion; because it is the practice of Samantabhadra, these are the past cultivations of all Buddhas. All Buddhas...

This is the common practice of Bodhisattvas; "practice" here is analyzed according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) as "pure maintenance. Regarding the three essential principles (*piṇḍārtha*):
the principle is to prevent the mind from scattering by means of skillful vows in accordance with specific matters, thereby increasing the great practices of a Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom;
the goal is the accomplishment of the actual virtues of Samantabhadra. As for the scriptural text, concerning the matters traversed, it begins with leaving the household life and ends with...

Whether in sleep or waking, to always engage in practice is the conduct of phenomena (*dharma*). To encounter objects without confusion and skillfully master the principle of the identity of phenomena and noumenon (*dharmatā*) is the conduct of wisdom.

To simultaneously master both phenomena and noumenon such that they are unimpeded is the conduct of non-obstruction between phenomena and noumenon. To guide wisdom with vows so as not to stagnate in self-benefit is the conduct of great compassion.

The aforementioned two being non-dual is the conduct of the non-obstruction of compassion and wisdom. When encountering circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, the mind remains undisturbed...

"Chasing away and dispersing" refers to the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding). "Wisdom does not sink" refers to the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight). This is the simultaneous operation of both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, regarding objective phenomena, skillfully discerning the false from the correct is the appropriate vow for sentient beings; this is all the practice of *parikalpita-śūnyatā* (provisional observation).

Knowing that the body is empty and still, and that the mind is free from defilement, is the practice of *śūnyatā-śūnyatā* (emptiness observation). Seeing reality as it truly is is the practice of *madhyama-śūnyatā* (middle observation). Alternatively, one may first [practice] emptiness.
Subsequently, there is the provisional; or first the provisional and later the empty; or one, or two; or they are suddenly and fully present in a single thought-moment.

This constitutes the practice of the contemplation that wondrously penetrates the three truths. Furthermore, all practices accomplished are bestowed upon sentient beings; one does not give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles;
one remains patient and composed amidst both harsh and gentle circumstances; and while increasing wholesome qualities, the mind does not diverge from its object. This is wondrous penetration.
Skillfully turning toward the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they all vow to benefit sentient beings and together proceed toward Bodhi.

Unshakable by those of the Two Vehicles or by celestial Māras, they skillfully know the medicines and illnesses, making decisions without error; this is precisely the practice of cultivating the ten perfections in unison.
Furthermore, they all vow to benefit sentient beings and to achieve the virtues of Buddhahood. Seeing evil, they must cause it to be severed;
seeing good, they must cause it to be perfected. This is precisely the practice of the Four Great Vows.

Therefore, Zhishou summarizes all virtues to seek their causes, while Mañjuśrī instructs one to apply the mind skillfully to suddenly attain the manifold fruits. If one were to speak only of vows, would this not lead to confusion?
Ah! At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī questioned the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
[This section below first indicates Jñānaśrī’s inquiry. By citing his virtues, he seeks the cause; subsequently, Mañjuśrī answers, citing those virtues to reveal the cause.

First: Regarding these two bodhisattvas’ dialogue, they traverse various practices through skillful vows. Because wisdom must serve as their guide, the practices are proximate while the ultimate aim is remote; this is due solely to the excellence of their virtue.
Thus, Mañjuśrī represents the Prajñā that contemplates emptiness, while Śrīmati represents the Upāya that engages with existence.

Because engaging in phenomena does not lead to confusion regarding the principle, although he makes vows, he is without grasping; because contemplating emptiness does not neglect [existence]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Because of this matter, although he is quiescent, he does not realize [nirvana]. This constitutes the simultaneous movement through both the provisional and the ultimate, facilitated by this dialogue.
In the following section, which correctly presents what was asked, there are twenty "how-many" questions; these comprise a total of eleven segments, each containing ten phrases.

This constitutes one hundred and ten kinds of virtues. The first section clarifies the virtue of the three karmas being free from faults; second, attaining the capacity to be a vessel for transmission;
third, accomplishing manifold wisdom; fourth, possessing the causes and conditions for the Path; fifth, skillfulness regarding the Dharma; sixth, cultivating the causes of nirvāṇa;
seventh, fulfilling the bodhisattva practices; eighth, attaining the knowledge of the ten powers; ninth, [the virtue of] being honored and protected by kings.
Tenth, they are able to bring benefit; eleventh, they are transcendentally superior and noble. In all these cases, one asks: "By what cause is this obtained?
By practicing what conduct is it attained?
O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva obtain bodily, verbal, and mental actions that are free from fault? How does one obtain a body that is non-harming?
Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind: how does one attain indestructible actions of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain unbreakable actions of body, speech, and mind?
How does one attain non-regressive actions of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain immovable actions of body, speech, and mind?
How does one attain sublime actions of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain pure actions of body, speech, and mind?
Regarding karma: how does one attain bodily, verbal, and mental actions that are free from defilement? How does one attain bodily, verbal, and mental actions preceded by wisdom?
This correctly sets forth the questions, which are divided into two parts: first, a single section of ten phrases asking about the result in general; second, ten [phrases] asking specifically.
Explanation. First: By attaining these ten kinds of threefold action, one achieves the ten lower fruits. Because of being free from the three types of faulty action, one is preeminent and noble;
because of being without malice or harm, one constantly brings benefit; because of being without remaining afflictions and thus beyond reproach or defamation, the ten kings respect and protect one;
and because of being indestructible by adverse conditions, one attains the ten powers of a Buddha. By...
Because their practice is non-regressive, they fulfill the bodhisattva conduct.

Because they are far removed from all signs, they remain unmoving like suchness and thus establish the cause for nirvāṇa. Because their virtuous conduct is preeminent, they are skillful in the Dharma.

Because their essence is pure like space, they become endowed with the conditions for the Path. Because they engage with objects without defilement, they become worthy vessels capable of transmitting the Dharma.
Because they are preceded by wisdom, they accomplish manifold insights. Furthermore, because the latter ten can accomplish these [first] ten, they are called "fruits";
yet they also pertain to the "causes."
What is meant by being endowed with excellence of birthplace, excellence of lineage, excellence of family, excellence of physical form,
excellence of marks, excellence of mindfulness, excellence of wisdom, excellence of conduct, excellence of fearlessness, and excellence of awakening?
The following ten sections specifically clarify the five fruits: first, the single ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*); next, the four fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
next, the two fruits of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*); next, the single dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*); and finally, the two fruits of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Regarding the first ten phrases, these constitute the vessel for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), for when a Bodhisattva initiates practice, they must necessarily be endowed with these ten directions to achieve perfection.

Regarding the practice of the two benefits: as for what is called the "ripened fruit" (*vipākaphala*), it refers to a result that necessarily ripens at a different time than its preceding cause, ripens as a different category [from its cause], and ripens through transformation.
This is because it is the general characteristic of the causes and effects of good and evil as they are experienced.
Briefly stated, one who is born into the Buddha-family is fully endowed with the place of birth.
How does such a person attain superior wisdom, foremost wisdom, supreme wisdom, most excellent wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, and incalculable wisdom?
Inconceivable wisdom. Wisdom without equal. Immeasurable wisdom. Ineffable wisdom.

In the twentieth [section], there are four subsections below that clarify the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Regarding "human effort," it refers to any dharma produced by the power of another;
for example, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of a higher stage [arising] due to the power of the preparatory effort (*prayoga-citta*) of a lower stage.

They arise from the meditative concentrations free of outflows (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Among these four, the first is discernment through wisdom; the second is power, which refers to cultivation; the third is skillfulness, which refers to knowledge;
and the fourth is the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), which refer to the aids to cultivation. All of these are accomplished by means of the three types of action (*trividha-karman*).
What are the power of the cause, the power of aspiration, the power of skillful means, the power of conditions, the power of the object, the power of the faculties, the power of investigation,
the power of śamatha, the power of vipaśyanā, and the power of reflection?
The third power refers to the cultivation of the causes and conditions for the Path itself. All are called "powers" because each of these ten possesses the capacity to support the Path.
The first is the power of the cause, namely the *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth.
What is skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense bases, skillfulness regarding dependent origination,

skillfulness regarding the desire realm, skillfulness regarding the form realm, skillfulness regarding the formless realm, skillfulness regarding the past, skillfulness regarding the future, and skillfulness regarding the present?

The fourth skillfulness refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). All of these are explained in terms of the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*), because they are the wisdom that contemplates its cessation (*nivṛtti*).

How does one cultivate the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The factors of enlightenment: the factor of enlightenment of concentration and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The fifth category of the path-factors serves as an aid for cultivation. The aforementioned four are all results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
How does one attain the perfection of the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *śīla-pāramitā*, the *kṣānti-pāramitā*,
the *vīrya-pāramitā*, the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and the *prajñā-pāramitā*, as well as the perfection of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
The sixth is the fulfillment of the bodhisattva practice. The following two types clarify the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

"Dissociation" refers to exhaustion by means of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Wisdom" means discernment (*pravicaya*) and exhaustion (*kṣaya*), that is, extinction through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is manifested by dissociation.

Therefore, we shall now explain *visamyoga-phala* (the fruit of dissociation) by means of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation). This is because the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) serve as the remedies for all obscurations (*nīvaraṇa*).

How does one obtain the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma in the past, future, and present (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparāparatā-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*), and the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (*dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti-jñānabala*)?

The power of knowledge regarding liberation from the defilements of meditative absorption; the power of knowledge regarding recollection of past lives; the power of knowledge regarding the unobstructed divine eye; and the power of knowledge regarding the eradication of all habitual tendencies.

The seventh is the possession of the ten powers, which refers to the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). It is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and it is by means of this power that [the Buddha acts].
Only then will one attain liberation from bondage.
How does one constantly receive the protection of the kings of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, human kings, and Brahmā kings?
They are respectfully honored and provided with offerings.
That the eightieth king reveres and protects them is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

Regarding "sovereign," this means that, setting aside previously arisen conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), all other conditioned phenomena are termed "increasing" (*adhika*); now, the reverence and protection by the ten kings possess such power.
It is superior because it protects them by means of having already perfected its virtues.
How does it become a support, a rescue, a refuge, a resort, a torch, and a light for all sentient beings?
It acts as illumination, as guidance, as supreme guidance, and as universal guidance.

The ninth [point], "serving as a reliance for all sentient beings," and the following two sections clarify the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Regarding the term "uniform outflow" (*niṣyanda*):
it refers to that which flows forth in a manner equal to its own cause.
How is it that among all sentient beings one is the foremost, the great, the superior, the most excellent,
the sublime, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled?
The tenth is the foremost, the most excellent, and the most noble. To briefly explain its characteristics:

it is called "foremost" because the ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits is full and lacks nothing further. This is a general statement. It is "great" because its essence encompasses the entire *dharmadhātu*;
"excellent" because self-benefit is perfected; "supremely excellent" because benefit for others is ultimate; and "wondrous" because...
Because the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are exhausted; "supremely wonderful" because the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are exhausted;
"superior" because there is nothing below it that can equal it; "unsurpassed" because there is nothing above it; "unequaled" because there is no peer among those below;
and "equal to the unequaled" because all its peers are themselves unequaled. The reason for citing these extensively is to manifest the practice.
Because it is supreme. The preceding questions have now concluded.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed Jñānaśrī Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You have now asked these questions out of a desire to bring great benefit and great peace to many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of the welfare and happiness of devas and humans."
This meaning is divided into two parts within the second response. First, there is the praise of the benefits of the question:
"O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas skillfully employ their minds, they will obtain all supreme and wondrous merits. Regarding these...
In the Buddha-dharma, the mind is without obstruction. Abiding in the Way of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, one dwells among sentient beings without ever abandoning them.
One is able to thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena, severing all evils and perfecting all virtues.
One shall be like Samantabhadra, foremost in physical form, with all practices and vows fully accomplished, such that there is no phenomenon not mastered.
He is sovereign and serves as the second teacher for sentient beings.

Regarding the "second son of the Buddha" below, this directly answers his question: first, the virtues accomplished through causes are indicated; subsequently, specific matters are pointed out to reveal those causes.
First, "skillfully employing his mind" marks the cause; next, "attaining supreme and wondrous virtues" and below reveal the virtues accomplished.

The first is the general statement; the subsequent nine phrases, beginning with "in all Buddha-dharmas," specifically reveal [the virtues], which correspond respectively to the ten sections of virtue.
O Son of the Buddha, how should one apply the mind so as to be able to obtain all supreme and wondrous merits?
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva is at home, they should wish that all sentient beings realize the emptiness of the nature of the household and thus escape its oppressions;
and while serving their parents with filial piety, they should wish that all sentient beings...
Performing good deeds for the Buddha and protecting and nourishing all;
when gathered with wife and children, one should wish that sentient beings regard enemies and kin with equality and forever leave behind greedy attachment.
If one obtains the five desires, one should wish that sentient beings pull out the arrows of craving.
Ultimately peaceful and secure, amidst the assembly of musicians and performers,
may all beings find delight in the Dharma and realize that such performances are not real. If they are in a palace or chamber,
may all beings enter the ground of the sages and forever eliminate defiled desires.
When putting on a necklace, one should wish that all sentient beings abandon all false adornments and reach the place of ultimate reality.

When ascending a multi-storied pavilion, one should wish that all sentient beings ascend the tower of the True Dharma and see all things through and through. If there is anything to be given in charity...
At such times, may all beings be able to relinquish everything, their minds free from attachment even amidst gatherings and assemblies.
May all beings relinquish the phenomena of congregations and attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). If one should encounter hardship or peril, may all beings...
Moving with sovereign ease, their conduct is unimpeded.

Second, regarding the phrase "How, O Son of the Buddha," this explains the cause by pointing to specific instances to answer the preceding inquiry. First, the single sentence of the inquiry provides a general overview;
next, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the specific details are revealed; finally, the conclusion summarizes the benefits. Within the section on the specific details, there is one general point.
The one hundred and forty-one vows: the "one hundred" represents the perfect integration (*yuanrong*) of the ten stages of faith (*shixin*), wherein each stage fully possesses the ten [aspects].

The "forty-one" refers to the forty-one stages (*wei*). This clarifies that all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) belonging to these various stages can be purified by means of this, and all sublime practices (*viśeṣacaryā*) can be performed by means of this; therefore, there are one hundred and forty-one vows. [This is] the division.
This consists of ten sections. First, the eleven vows beginning with "When the Bodhisattva is at home" clarify the aspirations for the period of being a householder.
When renouncing the household life: "When entering a monastery, may all beings attain liberation through an unimpeded mind of renunciation. When entering a saṃghārāma, may all beings [attain this].
When preaching various non-contentious dharmas,
may all beings skillfully serve their teachers and elders, practice and cultivate wholesome dharmas,
and seek ordination; may they attain the dharma of non-retrogression.
With a mind free from hindrance, casting off worldly garments,
may all beings diligently cultivate roots of goodness and cast off the yoke of all sins. Shaving off hair and beard,
may all beings forever leave afflictions behind and attain ultimate quiescence.
When putting on the kāṣāya robe, one should wish that all beings have minds unstained by defilement and be endowed with the Great Path of the Sages. At the time of formally leaving the home life,
one should wish that all beings leave the home life together with the Buddha to rescue and protect all, taking refuge in the Buddha.
When taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
When taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean. When taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings...
Governing the great assembly, all things are without obstruction.
When receiving and studying the precepts, one should wish that all beings may skillfully learn the precepts and commit no evil.
