Receiving the instructions of the ācārya, one should wish that all beings be fully endowed with dignified deportment.
When practicing truth and receiving the instructions of the preceptor,
may all beings enter the wisdom of non-arising and reach the state of non-reliance. When receiving full ordination,
may all beings be endowed with all skillful means and attain the most supreme Dharma.
Second, there are fifteen vows regarding the time of leaving home and receiving the precepts:
When entering a hall or building, one should wish that all beings ascend the unsurpassed hall and dwell therein immovably.
When spreading out a bed or seat, one should wish that all beings...
When opening and blooming the wholesome dharmas and seeing the true mark, sitting upright with body straight,
one should wish that all beings sit upon the seat of Bodhi;
when sitting cross-legged with a mind free from attachment, one should wish that all beings have roots of goodness firmly established.
Attaining the Immovable Ground and practicing meditative concentration,
may all beings subdue their minds through concentration until it is ultimately complete without remainder. When practicing insight meditation,
may all beings see the reality of things as they truly are, forever free from conflict and dispute.
When releasing the cross-legged posture, one should wish that all sentient beings contemplate how all conditioned phenomena ultimately dissolve and perish.
(The third of the seven vows for sitting in meditation.)
When setting down the foot to stand, one should wish that all beings attain liberation of mind and abide immovably.
When lifting up the foot, one should wish that all beings emerge from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas. When putting on the lower robe, one should wish...
When putting on [undergarments], may all beings consume all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with shame and remorse;
when adjusting their robes and fastening their belts, may all beings restrain their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost. When wearing upper garments, may all beings...
Having attained the roots of goodness that lead to victory and reaching the further shore of the Dharma, when donning the saṃghāṭī, one should make this vow for all sentient beings:
"May they enter the foremost stage and attain the state of immovability.
These are the four vows and six aspirations to be recited when putting on the robe.
Holding a willow twig, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the ultimate purity of the sublime Dharma.
While chewing the willow twig, one should wish that the minds of all sentient beings be harmonized and purified, consuming all afflictions. When voiding excrement or urine...
At this time, may all beings abandon greed, anger, and delusion.
When the ritual for removing sinful dharmas is completed and one approaches the water, may all beings swiftly proceed toward the supramundane Dharma.
When washing away physical impurities, may all beings [attain purity].
Pure and supple, ultimately stainless— Washing one’s hands with water,
one should wish that all beings obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Washing one’s face with water, one should wish that all beings obtain the gates of the pure Dharma.
When bathing and rinsing oneself to be forever free from defilement and to fulfill the seven vows for the five realms of existence,
holding a mendicant’s staff in hand, one should wish that all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving.
Manifesting the path as it truly is, holding the alms bowl,
may all beings become vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans. Setting out toward the Way,
may all beings advance toward the conduct of the Buddhas and enter the state of non-reliance.
If one is on the road, one should wish that all beings be able to practice the Buddha-way toward the state of no-remainder; As one traverses the path,
one should wish that all beings tread upon the pure dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction, seeing the high road ascending.
When seeing a downward path, may all beings forever transcend the triple world, their minds free from cowardice or weakness.
When seeing a crooked path, may all beings humble their hearts and long cultivate the roots of Buddha-virtue. When seeing a downward path, may all beings...
Abandoning the wrong path and forever eliminating evil views, when seeing a direct road,
may all sentient beings have upright minds, free from flattery and deception.
Seeing a road covered in dust, may all sentient beings remain far removed from defilement.
Upon obtaining the pure Dharma and seeing a road free of dust,
one should wish that all sentient beings always practice great compassion, their minds moistened and supple. When seeing a perilous path,
one should wish that all sentient beings abide in the realm of the True Dharma and remain free from all calamities of transgression.
If one sees a great assembly, one should wish that all beings preach the profound Dharma so that all may be in harmony.
If one sees a great pillar, one should wish that all beings be free from the mind of self-contention, and have no anger or resentment. If one sees a grove of trees...
At such times, may all beings—gods and humans alike—be worthy of reverence and salutation.
If one sees a high mountain, may all beings have roots of goodness so transcendent that none can reach their summit. If one sees a thorny tree, may all beings...
May they swiftly cut away the thorns of the three poisons.
Seeing the lush growth of leaves, they should wish that all beings provide shade and shelter through meditative concentration and liberation.
Seeing flowers in bloom, they should wish that all beings attain the dharmas of the supernormal powers and so forth.
When flowers bloom, or when one sees tree blossoms, one should wish that all sentient beings possess marks like flowers,
complete with the thirty-two [major characteristics]. When one sees fruits,
one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the most supreme Dharma and realize the path to Bodhi.
If one sees a great river, one should wish that all beings enter the stream of the Dharma and flow into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
If one sees a marsh or a pond, one should wish that all beings swiftly awaken to the single-flavor Dharma of all Buddhas. If one sees a pool or a lake...
When seeing a well being drawn from, may all beings have their verbal karma fulfilled and be skillful in eloquent exposition.
When seeing a gushing spring, may all beings possess perfect eloquence and expound all dharmas.
Increasing skillful means, may the roots of goodness be inexhaustible.
When seeing a bridge or a path, one should wish that all sentient beings widely deliver all others, just like a bridge.
When seeing flowing water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain noble intentions.
Washing away the defilements of delusion and cultivating the garden of insight, may all beings,
within the garden of the five desires, weed out the grasses of craving; seeing the forest of sorrowlessness,
may all beings forever be free from greedy attachment and give rise to no further grief or fear.
If seeing a garden or grove, one should wish that all beings diligently cultivate all practices to proceed toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.
If seeing a person adorned with ornaments, one should wish that all beings take the thirty-two marks as their adornment. If seeing one without adornment...
When seeing those attached to pleasure and adornment, may all beings vow to abandon all finery and ornaments, and to fulfill the dhūta practices.
When seeing those who find no pleasure in attachment, may all beings vow to delight in the Dharma for themselves, loving it without ever forsaking it.
When seeing those who find no pleasure in attachment, may all beings vow to... [as above].
Amidst conditioned phenomena, may the mind find no delight;
Seeing those who rejoice, one should wish that all beings always attain peace and happiness;
Seeing those who suffer, one should wish that all beings obtain fundamental wisdom.
Seeing one who has eliminated all suffering and is free from illness,
one should wish that all beings enter into true wisdom and forever be free from the affliction of sickness. Seeing one who is diseased,
one should wish that all beings realize the body is empty and quiescent, and remain free from the dharma of discord and contention.
Upon seeing a person of handsome appearance, one should wish that all beings always give rise to pure faith in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Upon seeing a person of ugly appearance, one should wish that all beings do not give rise to attachment toward unwholesome things. Upon seeing a person who repays kindness...
When seeing those who repay kindness with ingratitude toward Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, may all beings be able to recognize their benevolence and virtue.
When encountering wicked people, may all beings refrain from retaliating against them.
If one sees a śramaṇa, may all beings [be inspired to cultivate such virtues].
Tranquil, pliant, and utterly supreme; Upon seeing a brahmin, one should wish that all beings forever maintain the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Upon seeing an ascetic who has abandoned all evil views, one should wish that all beings rely upon ascetic practice.
Upon seeing one who has reached the ultimate state and practices with integrity,
may all beings firmly maintain their resolve and conduct, never abandoning the path of the Buddha. Upon seeing one clad in armor,
may all beings constantly don the virtuous mail and advance toward the teacherless Dharma.
Seeing one without armor or weapons, one should wish that all sentient beings forever leave behind all unwholesome karma.
Seeing a person engaged in debate, one should wish that all sentient beings be able to completely subdue all opposing doctrines. Seeing a person of right livelihood...
At that time, one should wish that all beings attain a pure livelihood and do not feign dignified deportment.
If seeing a king, one should wish that all beings become Dharma-kings and constantly turn the wheel of the True Dharma. If seeing a prince, one should wish that all beings...
Born from the transformation of the Dharma, they become children of the Buddha.
Upon seeing an elder, one should wish that all beings may skillfully discern and judge, never practicing unwholesome dharmas.
Upon seeing a high minister, one should wish that all beings may constantly maintain right mindfulness.

In practicing the various wholesome deeds, there are fifty-five vows within the six [perfections]. When seeking the path and practicing the Way, they are divided into three parts: first, twelve vows concerning traveling upon the roads;
second, nineteen vows regarding the objects and environments perceived when seeing assemblies; and third, [vows] concerning seeing adornments.
Adorning those below, as described in the twenty-fourth vow regarding the people encountered along the way:
If one sees a city wall, one should wish that all sentient beings attain a firm and steadfast body and mind, never yielding to any pressure.
If one sees a royal capital, one should wish that all sentient beings...
When gathering together in merit, may the mind always be joyful;
when seeing those dwelling in the forest, one should wish that all beings be praised and looked up to by devas and humans.
When entering a village to beg for food, one should wish that all beings enter the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
With a mind free from obstruction, when entering the doors of others' homes,
one should wish that all beings enter the gates of all Buddha-dharmas. Having entered their houses,
one should wish that all beings attain entry into the Buddha-vehicle, which is equal throughout the three periods of time.
Seeing one who does not renounce [worldly things], one should wish that all beings never abandon the supreme dharmas of merit.
Seeing one who is able to renounce, one should wish that all beings forever attain liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms. If one sees an empty bowl, [one should wish...]
When seeing a full bowl, may all beings have minds that are pure and empty of afflictions.
When receiving honor and respect, may all beings be fully endowed with and perfected in all wholesome dharmas.
When reverently practicing all the Buddha-dharmas,
one should wish that sentient beings do not practice any unwholesome dharmas.
Upon seeing those who possess a sense of shame and remorse, one should wish that sentient beings be fully endowed with the practice of shame and remorse.
When guarding the sense faculties and seeing those who are shameless,
one should wish that all beings abandon shamelessness and abide in the path of great compassion. When obtaining fine food,
one should wish that all beings fulfill their aspirations and have no longing or desire in their hearts.
Upon obtaining unwholesome food, one should wish that all sentient beings may not fail to obtain the flavor of all samādhis.

Upon obtaining soft and tender food, one should wish that all sentient beings be permeated by great compassion, their minds and intentions becoming supple and gentle. Upon obtaining coarse and rough food, one should wish...
At that time, one should wish that all beings have minds free from defilement and attachment, severing worldly craving and love.
When eating food, one should wish that all beings take the joy of meditation as their sustenance and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
When experiencing flavors, one should wish that all beings...
Having attained the supreme flavor of the Buddha and being fully satiated with ambrosia, after the meal is finished,
may all sentient beings have their tasks accomplished and be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
When preaching the Dharma, may all sentient beings attain inexhaustible eloquence.
From the time of setting out from his home to enter the city for alms, when he extensively proclaims the essentials of the Dharma, may all beings at that moment vow:
"May they deeply penetrate the Buddha's wisdom. (The twenty-second vow of the Seven Vows.)
May they forever transcend the triple world. When entering the water, may they vow that all sentient beings enter into omniscience and know the equality of the three periods of time.
While bathing their bodies, may they vow that all sentient beings have no defilement in body or mind, and are radiant and pure both internally and externally.
In the intense heat of summer, may all sentient beings abandon all afflictions until they are entirely exhausted.
When the heat has subsided and the cool season begins,
may all sentient beings realize the unsurpassed Dharma and attain ultimate, refreshing purity.
When returning to bathe from the five rivers, or when reciting the sutras, one should make this vow for all sentient beings:
"May they accord with what the Buddha has taught, possessing dhāraṇī and never forgetting it. If they should behold the Buddha, may all sentient beings likewise do so."
Attaining the unobstructed eye, one sees all Buddhas.
When contemplating the Buddhas with clarity, one should wish that all sentient beings may become like Samantabhadra, upright, dignified, and beautiful.
When seeing a Buddha stupa, one should wish that all sentient beings be honored and revered as if they were stupas themselves.
Receiving the offerings of devas and humans, One contemplates the stūpa with a reverent mind;
one should wish that all sentient beings—devas and humans alike— be gazed upon by all.
Prostrating before the stūpa, one should wish that all sentient beings have a crown that no deva or human can behold.
Circumambulating the stupa, one should wish that all beings act without opposition and achieve all-encompassing wisdom. Circumambulating the stupa three times,
one should wish that all beings diligently seek the Buddha-way with minds that never grow weary, praising the virtues of the Buddha.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with all virtues;
Praising the Buddha’s marks and signs without end, may they cause all sentient beings to achieve the Buddha-body and realize the dharma of signlessness.
When reciting the Nine Existences and Ten Vows and performing circumambulations before the Buddha;
or when washing one's feet: May all beings be endowed with spiritual power, so that their actions are unimpeded;
and when resting at the proper time, may all beings... [be endowed with the power of timely rest].
May my body attain peace and security, and may my mind be free from agitation.
When first awakening from sleep, I vow that all sentient beings shall awaken to all-encompassing wisdom and look upon the ten directions.
These are the thirteen vows for the time of resting in peace both awake and asleep.
O Son of the Buddha, if Bodhisattvas apply their minds in this way, they will attain all supreme and wondrous merits,
such that none among the gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras, and others of the entire world,
nor any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, can shake them.
Next, a summary praising the benefits accomplished through the causes: if one can act as described above, one will skillfully employ the mind.

When the mind is employed in this manner, internal virtues become perfectly complete and external factors cannot disturb it. Because the mind roams within great wisdom, humans and devas cannot move it;
because the mind is crowned with great compassion, those of the Two Vehicles cannot move it. This concludes the "Chapter on Pure Conduct."
The Twelfth Chapter, "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (Bhadramukha), Part One.

Regarding the intent of this chapter’s inclusion: for practice to be not in vain, it must necessarily possess its corresponding virtues. Since the understanding and practice have already been perfected and wondrous, the resulting supreme virtues must be inconceivable.
This chapter follows because it gathers the preceding practices and vows to establish the functional application of the virtue of faith. Furthermore, the preceding...
Jñānaśīra raises the fruit to inquire about its cause; Mañjuśrī extensively reveals that cause.

Briefly indicating the fruit, he says one "attains all supreme and wondrous merits. Therefore, he asks Bhadrapāla to now elaborate upon these words. Thus, the opening verse of the gāthā follows the preceding section to initiate the subsequent one;

this is the underlying intent. Regarding the explanation of the name: the essential nature (svabhāva) that is supremely compliant, harmonious, and virtuous is called "Bhadra" (Worthy/Excellent); it signifies auspiciousness.
"Xiangsheng" (Wondrously Victorious) means that his virtue is transcendent and his name is foremost; it is by this name that he is called a Bodhisattva, and he expounds this Dharma.
"Xian" (Virtuous) is the "foremost," because as the head of the Three Virtuous Stages (*sanxian*), he encompasses all virtues; thus, the name "Xian" is specifically cited.

The Tiantai school establishes the Perfect and Sudden *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) for this chapter, stating: "This Bodhisattva hears the perfect Dharma, gives rise to perfect faith, and establishes the perfect [practice]."
Practice. Abiding in the stage of perfection (*yuan-wei*), one adorns oneself with perfect merit and establishes sentient beings through perfect power and function.
The present school is precisely the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-fa*). Its underlying intent has five aspects: first, faith, which is the arousal of perfect faith;

second, practice; third, the stages; fourth, merit; and fifth, function—all of which are permeated by perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). By means of this, the stages of faith encompass the stages of abiding, practice, penetration, and direction.
The merits of the five stages of the Grounds and Equal Enlightenment are such that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit;
for, in reality, all these stages are established based upon this faith.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had spoken of the great merit of the pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion, he desired—
In order to manifest the merits of the bodhicitta, he addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha in verse:
"I have now already explained to the bodhisattvas The pure conduct practiced by the Buddhas in the past;
You, too, should now within this assembly Expound upon the supreme merits of such practice."
This marks the intent of Mañjuśrī’s inquiry; it is a narrative device placed by the compiler of the sutra to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.

Regarding the merit of the bodhicitta, the text contains both its beginning and its end. From the perspective of the end, it reveals the extraordinary merit of the bodhicitta perfected through faith, which fully encompasses the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) because the causal practices have been exhausted.
From the perspective of the beginning, it refers merely to the vow to realize [enlightenment] within birth and death.
Since the myriad practices of enlightenment all depend upon this, it is now revealed. I have now composed one verse to correctly manifest its initial arousal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla replied in verse:
"Excellent! O virtuous one, you should listen attentively. Those various merits are immeasurable;
I shall now describe a small portion according to my ability, like a single drop of water from the great ocean.
Second, at that time, Bhadrapāla [and others] spoke extensively. First, the summary statement; next, "Excellent! O virtuous one," and so forth, is the main exposition.
This reveals the verses. There are four verses at the beginning, which offer humble praise and grant permission to speak. The first verse sets forth the chapter:
If there is a bodhisattva who, having first resolved their mind, Vows to seek the realization of Buddhahood’s bodhi, Their merit is boundless; It cannot be measured and has no equal.
How much more so for immeasurable and boundless eons— The merits of fully cultivating the stages and perfections;
Even all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, Together praising them, could not exhaust them.
Such are these boundless great merits; I shall now speak but a small portion of them.

For example, like the space traversed by a bird’s feet, or like a single atom of dust upon the great earth—this section below, within the actual prose of the text, first presents three verses as an outline.
By means of the virtues of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), it metaphorically brings forth the skillful practice that clearly manifests its profundity and vastness.
Within these, the first verse introduces the chapter on generating the mind; the second verse metaphorically brings forth [the subsequent stages].
Chapter on Practice. The subsequent verse permits an explanation of the boundaries [of the stages]. Question:

What is the distinction between this initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the initial arousal of the mind in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), as well as the "Chapter on the Merits of Arousing the Mind"? Answer:

The arousal of the mind herein encompasses both the beginning and the end, taking its majestic power (*vibhūti*) as its basis; it is the culmination of faith (*śraddhā*). Because it takes that [faith] as its root, it resides in the initial arousal. Therefore, [it is distinct from] the Ten Abodes.

The initial arousal [of the mind] is precisely that which constitutes this [stage], wherein that initial arousal is accomplished. This "arousal" (*praṇidhāna*) primarily signifies the act of initiating; its meaning also encompasses "opening.

That [latter] signifies "opening and developing," while its meaning also encompasses "initiating. Thus, the *Cittotpāda-parivarta* (Chapter on the Arousing of the Mind) specifically reveals the merits of the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Question: Since this faith is the first faith, how can it already possess the qualities of the subsequent [stages]?
[Question: Regarding the stages of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the virtues of Samantabhadra? [Answer: Ancient masters have explained this briefly through two approaches:
first, the approach of sequential arrangement (*paṭala-krama*); second, the approach of perfect interpenetration and inclusive synthesis.

"Sequential arrangement" refers to proceeding from the subtle to the manifest, from the shallow to the deep, ascending step by step to reach the further shore, as described in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, the *Bhadrakalpikāsūtra*, the *Śūraṅgamasamādhisūtra*, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and so forth.
The masters such as Gaṅgā and others have explained this. Regarding the "mutual fusion" (yuanrong) of the two, it means that a single stage is fully endowed with all stages, and so forth.
This is as taught in this sutra, and also as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other texts, where a single practice is endowed with all practices. Within this, there are two gates.
First, the gate of mutual dependence through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-lakṣaṇa-apekṣā-mukha*); second, the gate of the harmonious inclusion within the *dharmadhātu*.

Within this sutra, based on the meaning of the gate of dependent origination, there are four general explanations regarding the mutual inclusion of the stages and practices (*caryā-bhūmi*). First, some begin with the end;
this refers to those who possess the ocean of Samantabhadra’s virtues, including all stages and practices within this very gate. Second, some end with the beginning; and...

After the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), as explained in the sections on the ten concentrations (*daśasamādhi*) and the ten supernormal powers (*daśābhijñā*), either all stages are subsumed together—each individual stage within the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and so forth encompassing everything—because all reach the ultimate and achieve Buddhahood;
as explained below in the sections on the ten abodes and ten practices (*daśacaryā*). Alternatively, all stages are merged, and the virtues of practice become manifest.

As explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World," the preceding section was taught by way of the mutual interdependence of dependent origination. Regarding the second, the gate of the harmonious integration of the Dharma-realm:
it means that these various stages and the practices cultivated therein are all inseparable from the inexhaustible Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra.
However, this Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused and limitless; wherever one position is occupied, it immediately encompasses all others.
Now, within the gate of faith, there is nothing that is not included. The principle that all subsequent positions likewise encompass everything should be explained according to this.
Even though this sutra contains a sequential arrangement (*paṅ-pu*), it is nonetheless perfectly interfused (*yuan-rong*).
When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek enlightenment, it is not without cause or without condition;
they give rise to pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thereby generate the vast and great mind.
They do not seek the five desires, nor royal rank, nor wealth and abundance, nor personal pleasure, nor great fame.
Solely for the sake of eternally extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings, And to benefit the world, they resolve their minds;
Constantly desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all beings, They adorn the buddha-fields, make offerings to the Buddhas, Uphold the True Dharma, and cultivate all forms of wisdom;
It is for the sake of realizing Bodhi that they resolve their minds.
With a profound mind of faith and understanding ever pure, they revere and honor all Buddhas;
toward the Dharma and the Sangha, they act likewise. With utmost sincerity they make offerings and resolve their minds upon them;
they have deep faith in the Buddha and the Buddha’s Dharma, and they also believe in the path traversed by the sons of the Buddha.
And having faith in the unsurpassed Great Bodhi—by this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment.
Hereafter follows the explicit clarification of the excellence of generating the mind and practicing; the text consists of three hundred and forty-six and a half verses.
This is divided into five sections: first, the characteristics of the initial resolve; second, a brief demonstration of superior capacities;
third, the stages and practices possessed; fourth, the boundless great function; and fifth, the explanation of the profound principle through metaphors. Now, for the first:
from "The Bodhisattva resolves to seek Bodhi" onwards, five verses clarify the characteristics of the initial resolve.
Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of all merit; it nurtures all wholesome dharmas.
It severs the net of doubt and delivers one from the multitude of cravings, revealing the unsurpassed path to Nirvāṇa.
Faith is free from defilement and the mind is pure; it eradicates arrogance and is the root of reverence.
Faith is also the foremost wealth of the Dharma-treasury; it is the pure hand that receives all practices.
Through faith, one is able to practice giving with a heart free from stinginess; through faith, one can joyfully enter the Buddha-dharma;
through faith, one can increase wisdom and merit; and through faith, one will certainly reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Faith causes the faculties to be pure, bright, and sharp; The power of faith is firm and indestructible.
Faith can forever extinguish the root of afflictions; Faith can single-mindedly direct one toward the Buddha’s virtues.
Faith is unattached to sense objects; It brings one far from all hardships and attains the state free from hardship.
Faith can transcend the paths of all Māras, Revealing the unsurpassed path of liberation.
Faith is the indestructible seed of merit; Faith can cause the Bodhi tree to grow.
Faith can increase the most supreme wisdom; Faith can manifest all Buddhas.
Therefore, the sequence is explained according to the practice: faith and aspiration are most excellent and extremely difficult to find;
they are like a wondrous wish-fulfilling jewel existing within all the world.
Faith is the source of the path; below, a brief indication of its superior capacity is shown in seven verses.
If one constantly places faith in all Buddhas, Then one can uphold the precepts and cultivate the points of training.
If one constantly upholds the precepts and cultivates the points of training, Then one can be fully endowed with all meritorious qualities.
The precepts can bring forth the root of bodhi; Training is the ground for the diligent cultivation of merit.
Always acting in accordance with the precepts and the training, one is praised by all Tathāgatas.
If one always places faith in the Buddhas, one will be able to assemble great offerings.
If one is able to assemble great offerings, that person’s faith in the Buddha is inconceivable.
If one always faithfully reveres the Honored Dharma, then hearing the Buddha’s teachings will never bring satiety;
if hearing the Buddha’s teachings never brings satiety, that person’s faith in the Dharma is inconceivable.
If one always faithfully reveres the pure Saṅgha, then one will attain a faith that is non-retrogressive.
If one attains faith that does not regress, the power of that person’s faith cannot be shaken;
if the power of one’s faith cannot be shaken, then one’s faculties will become pure, clear, and sharp;
if one’s faculties are pure, clear, and sharp, then one can remain far removed from evil associates.
If one can distance oneself from evil associates, Then one will draw near to virtuous friends.
If one draws near to virtuous friends, Then one can cultivate vast and great goodness.
If one can cultivate vast and great goodness, That person will accomplish the power of great causes.
If a person accomplishes the power of great causes, Then they will attain a sublime and certain understanding.
If they attain a sublime and certain understanding, Then they will be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
From here below, there are fifty and a half verses concerning the stages and practices contained within the "Extensive Explanation of Faith," extending up to the section on the Bodhisattva Assembly.
It is likewise so for *śamatha*. This comprehensively encompasses the practices and virtues of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Now, first we shall clarify the practices possessed; next, we shall clarify the stages possessed. Within the section on the practices possessed, there are eight and a half verses. First, five verses clarify the Three Jewels (*triratna*) to establish the practice.
Next, from "If the power of faith is unshakable" onwards, the remaining three and a half verses clarify the establishment of successive practices.
Successively relying on prior merit, one abides in faith;
if one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas, then one can give rise to the bodhicitta;
if one can give rise to the bodhicitta, then one can diligently cultivate the merits of a Buddha.
If one can diligently cultivate the virtues of the Buddha, Then one will be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
If one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, Then one will skillfully practice expedient means.
If one skillfully practices expedient means, Then one will attain a mind of pure faith and joy.
If one attains a mind of faith and joy that is pure, then one attains the superior and most excellent state of mind.
Following this, the section beginning with "Next, for the sake of all Buddhas" clarifies the stages of practice possessed [by the bodhisattva].
There are thirty-nine verses in total, which are divided into four sections across four stages. Among these, the first three verses clarify the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
If one attains the superior and most excellent mind, Then one constantly cultivates the pāramitās;
If one constantly cultivates the pāramitās, Then one can fulfill the Mahāyāna;
If one can fulfill the Mahāyāna, Then one can make offerings to the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma.
If one can make offerings to the Buddha according to the Dharma, then one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha with an unmoving mind;
if one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha with an unmoving mind, then one will constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas.
If the two verses and a half beginning with "If one attains increase" are added, they clarify the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
If one constantly beholds immeasurable Buddhas, Then one sees that the body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding.
If one sees that the body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, Then one can know that the Dharma is forever indestructible.
If one can know that the Dharma is forever indestructible, Then one attains unimpeded eloquence.
If one attains unimpeded eloquence, one can then expound the boundless Dharma;
If one can expound the boundless Dharma, one can then compassionately deliver sentient beings;
If one can compassionately deliver sentient beings, one will attain a firm and steadfast heart of great compassion.
Next, the following three verses clarify the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
"If one can make the mind of great compassion firm, then one will be able to delight in the profoundly deep Dharma.
The thirty and a half verses that follow clarify the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The first two lines clarify the stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
If one can delight in the profound Dharma, then one can abandon the faults of the conditioned;
these two lines clarify the stage of freedom from defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
If one can abandon the faults of the conditioned, then one is free from pride and negligence.
If one is free from arrogance and heedlessness, Then one can benefit all beings simultaneously;
These four lines clarify the stages of the third and fourth bhūmis.
If one can benefit all beings simultaneously, Then one dwells within birth and death without weariness.
If one dwells in birth and death without weariness, Then one can be courageous and invincible;
these four lines clarify the five stages.
If one can be courageous and invincible, Then one can give rise to great supernormal powers.
If one can give rise to great supernormal powers, then one knows the conduct of all sentient beings;
these four lines clarify the six stages of the path.
If one knows the conduct of all sentient beings, then one can bring all living beings to fulfillment.
If one can bring all sentient beings to fulfillment, Then one can skillfully master the wisdom for gathering sentient beings.
If one attains the wisdom for gathering sentient beings, Then one can accomplish the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
If one accomplishes the four methods of attraction, Then one brings infinite benefit to sentient beings.
If one brings infinite benefit to sentient beings, Then one possesses supreme wisdom and skillful means;
These two and a half verses clarify the seven stages.
If one possesses supreme wisdom and skillful means, Then one abides in the courageous, unsurpassed path.
If one abides in the courageous, unsurpassed path, Then one can utterly destroy all demonic powers;
If one can utterly destroy all demonic powers, Then one can transcend the realms of the four Māras;
If one can transcend the realms of the four Māras, Then one attains the stage of non-retrogression.
If one attains the stage of non-retrogression, Then one attains the profound *dharmakṣānti* of non-arising;
If one attains the profound *dharmakṣānti* of non-arising, Then one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from all Buddhas.
These three verses clarify the stages of the eight grounds.
If one receives the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas, then all Buddhas will appear before one;
if all Buddhas appear before one, then one will realize the profound and secret application of spiritual powers;
if one realizes the profound and secret application of spiritual powers, then one will be remembered by all Buddhas.
If one is remembered by all Buddhas, Then one adorns oneself with the virtues of a Buddha.
These two verses clarify the nine stages (*navabhūmi*).
If one adorns oneself with the virtues of a Buddha, Then one attains a sublime, auspicious, and majestic body.
If one obtains a sublime and majestic body of wondrous merit, then that body will blaze like a mountain of gold;
if the body blazes like a mountain of gold, then it will be adorned with the thirty-two marks;
if it is adorned with the thirty-two marks, then it will be further embellished by the secondary signs.
If one is adorned with the secondary marks (anuvyañjana), Then the radiance of the body is immeasurable;
If the radiance of the body is immeasurable, Then there is the adornment of inconceivable light;
If there is the adornment of inconceivable light, Then from that light, various lotus flowers emerge.
When light issues forth from those lotus flowers, immeasurable Buddhas sit upon them, manifesting throughout the ten directions without exception; they are all able to discipline all sentient beings.
If one can thus discipline sentient beings, one will manifest immeasurable supernormal powers.
If one manifests immeasurable supernormal powers, One dwells in inconceivable lands and expounds inconceivable teachings,
Causing inconceivable multitudes to rejoice. If one expounds inconceivable teachings, One causes inconceivable multitudes to rejoice.
Then, by the power of wisdom and eloquence, One transforms and guides according to the minds of sentient beings.
If, by the power of wisdom and eloquence, One transforms and guides according to the minds of sentient beings,
Then taking wisdom as the precursor, The actions of body, speech, and mind are always without fault.
Below this, nineteen verses clarify the ten stages (*bhūmi*). This is divided into five sections. The first eight verses clarify the excellence of the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Among these, five verses clarify bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the next one verse clarifies verbal action (*vākkarman*); and the final two verses clarify mental action (*manaskarman*).
If one takes wisdom as the precursor, so that the actions of body, speech, and mind are always without fault,
then one’s power of aspiration will attain mastery, manifesting bodies everywhere in accordance with the various realms of existence.
If one’s power of aspiration attains mastery, one manifests bodies everywhere in accordance with the various realms of existence.
When they preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, their voices adapt to each type in ways that are inconceivable;
when they preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, their voices adapt to each type in ways that are inconceivable.
Then, regarding the minds of all sentient beings, they know them all in a single thought-moment without exception.
If, regarding the minds of all sentient beings, One knows them all in a single thought without exception,
Then one knows that afflictions do not arise, And will never again be submerged in birth and death.
The following four verses clarify the virtue of gathering in sentient beings through the three types of action.
If one knows that afflictions do not arise, One will never sink into the cycle of birth and death.
Then one attains the body of the dharma-nature of merit, Manifesting in the world through the power of the Dharma.
If one attains the body of the dharma-nature of merit, Manifesting in the world through the power of the Dharma.
Then one attains the ten stages and the ten masteries; Through the practice of the perfections, one achieves supreme liberation.
These two verses distinguish the attainment of the dharmas and the virtues of the culminating stage.
If one attains the ten stages and the ten masteries, One practices the perfections and achieves supreme liberation.
Then one attains the great supernormal power of consecration And abides in the most supreme samādhis;
If one attains the great supernormal power of consecration And abides in the most supreme samādhis,
Then in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions, One shall receive consecration and ascend to the rank [of Buddhahood].
If, in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions, one is to receive empowerment and ascend to the rank [of Buddhahood],
then all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall bestow ambrosia upon one’s crown with their own hands.
These three verses clarify the section on receiving empowerment through samādhi.
If one is graced by all the Buddhas of the ten directions Pouring the nectar of immortality upon the crown of one's head,
Then the body will become pervasive like space, Abiding unmoving and filling the ten directions.
If the body becomes pervasive like space, Abiding unmoving and filling the ten directions...
Then his conduct is without equal; neither gods nor worldlings can know it.
These two verses clarify that the Great Function is unfathomable and that this is also entering the stage of Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattvas diligently cultivate the practice of great compassion; their vow to deliver all beings shall never fail to bear fruit.
Whether they are seen, heard, or encountered, or even if one merely makes offerings to them, there is none who does not attain peace and happiness.
Through the majestic spiritual power of those Great Beings, the Dharma-eye remains forever whole, without deficiency or diminution.
The ten virtuous paths of action and all other supreme, excellent jewels are made to appear;
just as a mass of vajras in the great ocean produces various jewels through its power—
neither decreasing, nor increasing, nor ever exhausted— so too is the mass of a bodhisattva’s merit.

These three verses conclude by praising the functional efficacy [of the practice]. The first two verses provide the explanation in terms of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*); the following one verse provides the explanation through analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The third section above, concerning the stages and practices possessed [by the Bodhisattva], is now complete. The fourth section below concerns the boundless, great activity (*mahopayakauśalya*).
Below this are two hundred and three verses. The fourth section clarifies the boundlessly pervasive great function.

That which constitutes the boundlessly pervasive great function arises because the virtues of Samantabhadra pervade all times and places; since the *dharmadhātu* is limitless, ten gateways of samādhi activity are briefly distinguished:
first, the gateway of the perfectly luminous Sea-Seal Samādhi; second, the wondrous practice of the *Avataṃsaka*.

1. The samādhi-door of the three [realms]. 2. The samādhi-door of the triple Indra-net. 3. The samādhi-door of the hands extending vast offerings. 4. The samādhi-door of manifesting all dharma-gates. 5.
The samādhi-door of gathering sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). 6. The samādhi-door of conforming downward to the world. 7.
The samādhi-door of the light from the pores illuminating and benefiting [beings]. 8. The samādhi-door of the majesty and beauty of the principal and its attendants.
The Gates of Samādhi: The tenth is the Gate of the Boundless Functioning of Quiescence. Because there is no mind that is not in samādhi, all are termed "samādhi.

Their functions differ, so ten types are briefly distinguished. Furthermore, the first gate shows the arising of function from essence; the final one clarifies that function does not differ from essence;
and those in between all manifest the sovereign mastery of wondrous function.
In some lands where there is no Buddha, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
in some realms where the Dharma is unknown, he expounds the treasury of the sublime Dharma.
Without discrimination and without effort, in a single thought-moment, he pervades the ten directions.
Like the moonlight, whose shadow reaches everywhere, Through immeasurable skillful means, they transform all living beings.
Within those worlds of the ten directions, In every thought-moment, they manifest the attainment of Buddhahood,
Turn the wheel of the True Dharma, and enter into nirvana, Even to the point that their relics are widely distributed.
Sometimes they manifest the paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; sometimes they manifest the universal adornment of attaining buddhahood.
They manifest the forms of boys and girls, as well as devas, nāgas, asuras, and even mahoragas;
according to their inclinations, they cause all to see them.
The forms and appearances of sentient beings are each different, And their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable;
All such things can be manifested Through the majestic spiritual power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
Now, the first six verses clarify the Ocean-Seal Samādhi. Within these, the first five specifically clarify the pervasive scope of its functional activity.

The final [verse] summarizes the basis for the great function. Within the preceding [section], there are three parts. First, the initial verse generally clarifies the manifestation of Buddhas preaching the Dharma.
Next, one verse concerns the mastery of essence and function; that is, mindfulness is non-conceptual and movement is effortless.

Therefore, the mindfulness that is without mindfulness has a single thought pervading the ten directions, and the effort that is without effort gathers all classes of beings through many gates. Next...
First, the three vehicles; finally, the remaining classes. These collectively manifest the transformation of the ten dharma-realms. This concludes the first section:
the Gate of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi.
Adorning and purifying inconceivable lands, making offerings to all Tathāgatas.
He radiates great light that is boundless, And delivers sentient beings without limit.
His wisdom is sovereign and inconceivable; In his preaching of the Dharma, his speech is unimpeded.
Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, As well as wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers—
All these are sovereign through the power of the Buddha’s Flower Adornment Samādhi.
These ten lines below clarify the samādhi of the wondrous practice of the *Avataṃsaka*. By adorning the dharma-realm with myriad practices, one accomplishes the dharma-body;
this is "Flower Adornment. This concludes the second section: the Gate of the Flower Adornment Samādhi.
Entering samādhi within a single atom, they accomplish all meditative concentrations of atoms,
yet that atom does not increase in size; within that one atom,
inconceivable lands appear universally— some containing Buddhas, some without Buddhas.
Some are defiled, some are pure; some are vast, some are narrow;
some undergo formation, some undergo destruction; some abide uprightly, some abide horizontally;
some are like a mirage in the wilderness, and some are like Indra’s net in the heavens.
Just as that which is manifested within a single atom, so it is in all atoms;
this is the power of samādhi, liberation, and supernormal knowledges of these sages of great renown.
These four following verses clarify the gate of the Indra’s Net Samādhi. One enters it because the one and the many are mutually identical.

One will certainly achieve multiple meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). By achieving multiple concentrations, one causes all atoms to exist within a single atom, and within each and every atom, all buddha-fields (*kṣetra*) appear.
Since this occurs for every single atom such that all fields appear within them, it is said that one achieves the concentration of all subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The statement that "the atoms do not increase" means that their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not destroyed. [The following] two verses:
The manifestations of lands appearing within a single atom are clear and unimpeded like a flame; they appear in layers like Indra’s net.
This concludes the third, the Indrālaṃkāra Samādhi.
If one wishes to make offerings to all Buddhas, one enters this samādhi and manifests spiritual transformations.
With a single hand, one can pervade the three thousandfold world system, universally making offerings to all Tathāgatas.
All the supreme and wondrous flowers, ointments, powdered incenses, and priceless jewels existing throughout the ten directions—
all these emerge from the hand to make offerings to the Most Victorious Ones at the tree of enlightenment.
Priceless precious robes mixed with exquisite fragrances, Precious banners and streamers, all most beautifully adorned;
Flowers of pure gold and canopies of jewels— All these rain down from the palms of their hands.
Whatever wondrous things exist throughout the ten directions That may be offered to the Unsurpassed Honored One, [they all rain down].
From within his palms, everything without exception rains down in abundance; before the Bodhi tree, he offers these to the Buddha.
All manner of musical arts from the ten directions—bells, drums, lutes, and harps of many kinds—all produce harmonious, elegant, and wondrous sounds, none of which fail to emerge from his palms.
All the hymns of praise existing throughout the ten directions, extolling the Tathāgata’s true merits—
such various and wondrous words and phrases— are all manifested and proclaimed from within his palms.
The Bodhisattva’s right hand emits pure light, and from within that light, fragrant water rains down from the sky.
Universally sprinkling all Buddha-lands in the ten directions, Making offerings to all Lamps Illumining the World;
Again emitting light of wondrous adornment, Producing immeasurable precious lotus flowers.
The colors and forms of these flowers are all exquisite and sublime; With these, one makes offerings to all Buddhas.
Again, he emits a light called "Adorned with Flowers," In which various wondrous flowers gather to form canopies,
Scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, he emits a light called "Adorned with Fragrance," In which various wondrous incenses gather to form canopies.
They scatter universally throughout the lands of the ten directions, making offerings to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones;
they also emit light of powdered incense, with various heaps of powdered incense forming canopies,
scattering universally throughout the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, they emit a light called "Adorned with Garments," Which gathers various famous robes to form canopies,
Scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, they emit a light called "Adorned with Jewels," Which gathers various wondrous jewels to form canopies.
They scatter universally throughout the lands of the ten directions, making offerings to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones;
they further emit light adorned with lotuses, with various lotus flowers gathered to form canopies,
scattering them universally throughout the lands of the ten directions as offerings to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.

Again, he emits a light adorned with necklaces; various exquisite necklaces gather to form a canopy, which is scattered throughout all lands in the ten directions as an offering to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, he emits a light adorned with banners; those banners are radiant and resplendent, complete with every color.
Diverse and immeasurable, all exquisitely beautiful, With these they adorn the buddha-fields:
Canopies adorned with various miscellaneous jewels, And exquisite silk banners hanging together as ornaments;
Maṇi-jewel bells proclaim the voice of the Buddha, Which they hold aloft as offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
From his hands emerge inconceivable offering implements; thus he makes offerings to a single Teacher, and does so likewise before all Buddhas.
This is the power of the Great Being’s samādhi and supernormal faculties.
Verse four begins the section clarifying the gate of samādhi wherein vast offerings emerge from the hands. The first verse provides a general summary.
The heading: A single seal is subsequently tied; the intermediate section reveals it individually. To manifest its supreme excellence, one hand is briefly cited as the basis for offering.
Because in former times he offered with his hands to the Buddhas and gave to others, [this merit] pervaded the entire dharma-realm;
thus, the offerings flowing from the Truth (tathatā-pravṛtta) and so forth become inconceivable to all Buddhas. From the four hands, the Samādhi of Extensive Offerings emerges.
The Bodhisattva dwells within samādhi, employing various forms of mastery to gather in sentient beings;
through all the dharmas of merit practiced and immeasurable skillful means, they lead and inspire them.
Either by the gate of making offerings to the Tathāgata, Or by the gate of inconceivable generosity,
Or by the gate of asceticism and upholding the precepts, Or by the gate of unwavering patience,
Or by the gate of arduous effort and diligence, Or by the gate of tranquil meditative concentration.
Some through the gateway of decisive wisdom, some through the gateway of practiced skillful means,
some through the gateway of Brahma-abodes and supernormal powers, some through the gateway of benefiting others via the four means of attraction,
some through the gateway of the adornments of merit and wisdom, and some through the gateway of liberation via causes and conditions.
Either through the gateway of the powers of the faculties and the noble path, or through the gateway of the liberation of the śrāvakas,
or through the gateway of the purity of the pratyekabuddhas, or through the gateway of mastery in the Mahāyāna,
or through the gateway of impermanence and manifold suffering, or through the gateway of non-self and the absence of a life-principle.
Whether by means of the gate of detachment through impurity, or by means of the gate of the samādhi of cessation,
according to the various differences in the illnesses of sentient beings, they treat them all with the medicine of the Dharma;
and according to what the minds of sentient beings delight in, they satisfy them all through skillful means.
In accordance with the diverse conducts of all sentient beings, He brings them all to fulfillment through skillful means;
Such are the characteristics of this samādhi and its supernormal powers, Which no devas or humans can fathom.
The following eight verses clarify the samādhi-door that manifests all dharmas. This section is divided into four parts, the first of which is a single verse in summary.

This indicates the many gates. Next, there are five verses that specifically manifest twenty kinds of gates, such as offerings and so forth; these gates lead universally to entry into the fruit of Buddhahood.
The final one and a half verses conclude the many causes, which exist by virtue of the four *siddhāntas*. The first half-verse is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).
The subsequent half-verse is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint), which corresponds to the distinctions in practice. This is what should be [taught] accordingly.

The *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the person as a tenet) is thus established; what is called the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth as a tenet) is achieved. The latter half of the verse concludes that its function is difficult to fathom.
This completes the fivefold manifestation of the *dharmamukha-samādhi* (samādhi of the gateways of phenomena).

There is a wondrous samādhi named "Following Joy. Bodhisattvas dwelling herein observe universally and manifest themselves according to what is appropriate to deliver sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice and follow the transformation of the Dharma.
During times of famine and calamity within the kalpa, they provide the world with all manner of articles of pleasure.
They fulfill every wish as desired, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings;
whether it be food and drink of the finest flavors, precious garments, ornaments, and various wonderful objects, or even their royal thrones,
they are able to relinquish them all, causing those inclined toward generosity to be completely transformed by their example.
Some adorn their bodies with the marks and signs of excellence, decorated with exquisite garments, precious necklaces, and flower garlands;
they anoint their bodies with fragrant unguents and possess perfect deportment to deliver sentient beings.
They manifest whatever is esteemed by all the world—whether it be physical form, facial features, or clothing.
Manifesting universally according to need to satisfy their hearts, you cause those who delight in form to all follow the Way.
With the exquisite voice of the kalaviṅka and the wondrous sounds of the kokila and other birds, you are fully endowed with all kinds of Brahma-sounds;
according to what their hearts delight in, you preach the Dharma for them.
The eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates— by these all Buddhas deliver sentient beings. They likewise,
according to those various differentiated dharmas, transform and deliver sentient beings as is appropriate for the world,
[teaching] suffering and pleasure, gain and loss, and all such phenomena performed within the mundane world.
They are able to manifest in accordance with all circumstances to perform the same tasks as them;
by this means, they universally deliver all sentient beings from the myriad sufferings and afflictions of the entire world, which are deep, vast, and boundless like the great ocean.
They are able to endure performing these same tasks as others, causing them to obtain benefit and peace and happiness.

If there are those who do not recognize the Dharma of renunciation, Who do not seek liberation from the clamor and agitation [of the world], The Bodhisattva manifests for them the relinquishing of kingdom and wealth, Always delighting in the tranquility of mind that comes with leaving the home life.
For the home is a place bound by the fetters of craving; He desires to cause all sentient beings to be completely freed from it.
Therefore, this renunciant attains liberation; regarding all sensual pleasures, he remains without attachment.

The Bodhisattva demonstrates the practice of ten kinds of conduct and likewise practices all the dharmas of great beings, including the practices of the sages, without exception, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings whose lifespan is immeasurable, Whose afflictions are subtle and who possess every pleasure,
The Bodhisattva therein attains mastery; He manifests the suffering of old age,
sickness, and death, Or displays the presence of greed, hatred, and delusion, With the fierce fires of affliction constantly blazing.
The Bodhisattva manifests old age, sickness, and death in order to bring all those sentient beings to complete subdual;
he fully displays the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities,
as well as all his immeasurable merits, to deliver sentient beings.
The knowledge of others' minds, the instructions, and the supernormal powers—these are all the sovereign applications of the Tathāgata.
Those great beings all manifest them, being able to bring all sentient beings to complete subduing.
Through various gates of skillful means, the Bodhisattvas accord with worldly dharmas to deliver sentient beings.
Just as a lotus flower is not defiled by water, so too does one inspire deep faith while remaining in the world.
Below this, seventeen verses clarify the samādhi-door of gathering sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). The first verse provides a general summary.

The following section provides a detailed explanation. Regarding the "four means of integration" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*): first, giving (*dāna*); second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*); third, common purpose (*arthacaryā*); and fourth, beneficial conduct (*samānārthatā*).

Among these, the four verses beginning with "In an age of famine" illustrate the integration through giving. The two verses beginning with "Like the kalaviṅka bird" illustrate the integration through kind speech.

The two verses beginning with "The suffering and happiness of sentient beings" illustrate the integration through common purpose. The eight [verses] beginning with "If there are those who do not know" [illustrate the integration through beneficial conduct].
The verse clarifies the inclusion of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). "Beneficial conduct" refers to teaching the practice that leads toward meaningful goals in order to benefit sentient beings.
These eight verses clarify four sections. The first two verses clarify all-encompassing beneficial conduct.

The subsequent two verses, beginning with "The Bodhisattva demonstrates conduct," clarify beneficial conduct that fulfills requests; this refers to liberating sentient beings who are entangled by the eight fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Because it causes one to leave [unwholesome states], it is called "fulfilling requests. Alternatively, the two verses on desire represent beneficial conduct in all its forms:
the first verse concerns gathering those who should be gathered; the second verse concerns disciplining those who should be disciplined.
The two subsequent verses on mental recording and instruction represent beneficial conduct through all gateways; that is to say, for those who lack faith...

This is for the purpose of inspiring faith; it also serves as a summary of all beneficial conduct (*hitakriyā*). The section on the six means of integration (*ṣaḍsaṃgrahavastu*) for gathering sentient beings through the gate of samādhi is concluded.
With profound thought and deep talent, a king among those skilled in composition, his songs, dances, and discourses are cherished by all.
All the various arts and crafts in the world, there is none that this illusory master does not manifest;
he may become a householder or a leader of a town, a merchant or a guide for traders,
a king or a high minister, or he may act as a skilled physician well-versed in all treatises.
In some wildernesses he becomes a great tree; In others, he becomes excellent medicine or a treasury of many jewels.
He may become a wish-fulfilling gem that grants whatever is sought, Or he shows the right path to sentient beings.
If he sees a world first being formed, And sentient beings have not yet acquired the means for sustaining their lives,
At that time, the Bodhisattva acts as a craftsman, manifesting various types of work for them without causing affliction to living beings;
he merely expounds upon matters beneficial to the world,
such as incantations, medicinal herbs, and various treatises— indeed, he is able to explain all such things.
The supreme practices of all the ṛṣis, which beings such as gods and humans alike revere—
such difficult and ascetic dharmas, the Bodhisattva is able to perform them all as appropriate.
Sometimes he acts as an outsider or a renunciant, or he dwells in mountain forests, exerting himself with diligent austerity.
Sometimes they appear naked and without clothing, acting as teachers and elders among those multitudes;
or they manifest various modes of wrong livelihood, practicing what is unrighteous as if it were supreme;
or they manifest the various dignified demeanors of brahmins, serving as leaders within those assemblies.
Some undergo the five heats while turning with the sun; some observe the precepts of cattle, dogs, or deer;
some wear tattered rags and serve the sacrificial fire. To transform such as these, he acts as their guide;
sometimes he shows them visiting the temples of various devas, and at other times he shows them entering the waters of the Ganges.
He manifests the practice of eating roots, fruits, and the like; he constantly contemplates the supreme Dharma therein.
Sometimes he appears squatting or standing on tiptoe; sometimes he lies upon grass, thorns, or ashes;
or again, he lies upon a pestle seeking liberation, acting as the leader among that assembly.
Regarding such various types of non-Buddhists, observing their inclinations and engaging with them through shared activities, he demonstrated ascetic practices that the world could not endure.
Having caused them to witness these, he tamed those sentient beings who were deluded by false teachings;
they had dwelt in evil views and endured manifold sufferings.
For their sake, he preaches the sublime Dharma through skillful means, causing all to realize the truth of reality.
Whether through borderland incantations he speaks the Four Truths, or through excellent secret words he speaks the Four Truths,
or through human direct speech he speaks the Four Truths, or through celestial secret words he speaks the Four Truths.
The Four Truths are taught through the discrimination of syllables; The Four Truths are taught as the definitive meaning;
The Four Truths are taught to effectively refute the claims of others; The Four Truths are taught as being unmoved by external factors;
The Four Truths are taught in the languages of the eight classes of beings; Or the Four Truths are taught in all languages.
According to the languages and sounds they understand, he preaches the Four Truths to bring about their liberation;
all the teachings of the Buddhas are thus expounded without anything remaining unknown.
His sphere of speech is inconceivable—this is called the power of the Samādhi of Preaching the Dharma.
The seventh [chapter], "Profound Wisdom and Deep Talent," contains seventeen verses that correspond to the worldly samādhi gate.
This section has three parts: first, six stanzas on how the body conforms to the world to benefit sentient beings, manifesting as both the environment and its inhabitants;
second, six stanzas on manifesting as a non-Buddhist to save those of heterodox factions; third, five stanzas beginning with "Sentient beings are deluded" [on further manifestations].
The verse clarifies the great function of vocal karma. Next, the verse beginning with "All that exists" serves as a summary. It is not only the teaching of the Four Truths;

the same applies to the Six Perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth. By preaching the Dharma with a single mind, one attains the true nature of speech and is able to give rise to functions that accord with the various types of beings;
this is called the power of samādhi. This concludes the seventh section, the Samādhi of Conforming Downward to the World.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
the Great Vaipulya Scroll Ten-Four Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
the Great Vaipulya Scroll Fifteen Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
Extracted and Annotated by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Huángméishān Fǎyún Temple:
Chapter Twelve, Part Two, on the "Chapter on the Virtuous Leader" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta).
There is a supreme samādhi named Peaceful Bliss, Which can universally rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
It emits great light of inconceivable power, Causing all who see it to be fully tamed.
The eight verses and a half following this "Supreme Samādhi" clarify the samādhi of the light from the pores benefiting [beings].

Gate: Wisdom accords with the gate of liberation. Because compassion perfumes the actions of body, speech, and mind, one attains a body identical to the *dharmadhātu*, whose great functioning is boundless.
The light from a single pore touches all things, benefiting the myriad species throughout time and space; those who encounter it perceive it accordingly.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfect establishment of sentient beings. The main text is divided into five parts; the first verse provides the heading.
First is the general explanation of the name. Second, from "the light rays thus gathered" onwards, there is the specific explanation of the functional activity of the light from a single pore.

Third, from "as with one pore" onwards, there is the analogical revelation of the functional activity of the light from all pores. Fourth, from "according to their original practices" onwards, there is the explanation of the scope of the division.

Fifth, from "if there are those who hear" onwards, there is the benefit of hearing and believing the light. Now, for the first [point]: it is so named because it is spoken in terms of the recipients of the benefit.
Peace and bliss. The following text provides the formal analysis:
The light emitted is named "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa).
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly obtain benefit so that it is not in vain; by means of this, they shall achieve unsurpassed wisdom.
In the past, he manifested before all Buddhas, demonstrating the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the True Path, as well as Buddha-stūpas and images; therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Illumination," which eclipses the splendor of all the devas.
All obscurations of darkness are eliminated without exception; universally, he brings benefit to all sentient beings.
This light awakens all multitudes, causing them to hold lamps as an offering to the Buddha.
Because they offer lamps to all Buddhas, they attain the state of the unsurpassed lamp within the world.
He lit various oil lamps and butter lamps, as well as diverse kinds of bright torches, incense, exquisite medicinal herbs, and supreme jewel-candles;
by making these offerings to the Buddha, he attained this radiance.
Regarding the second section, the first part clarifies the functional activity of the light from a single pore, briefly explaining forty-four categories.
The function of the light is divided into ten sections: first, two lights manifest the Three Jewels; second, four lights cause [beings] to resolve upon the Great Mind;
third, two lights bring together and perfect merit and wisdom; fourth, two lights enter into principle and uphold the Dharma.
In the fifth [stage], there are six lights as the practice of the six perfections reaches completion. In the sixth, there are seven lights as the four immeasurables rescue and gather [beings].

In the seventh, there is one light that collectively manifests the three trainings. In the eighth, there are eight lights that variously manifest the myriad practices, with making offerings as the foremost.

In the ninth, there are six lights that cause the six sense faculties to be pure within, so that movement accords with principle. In the tenth, there are six lights that illuminate the six external sense objects.
Pure. All objects of touch are permeated. Now, at the beginning, there are two lights that manifest the Three Jewels.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Deliverance":
this light can awaken all sentient beings, causing them universally to give rise to the great vow-mind to deliver and liberate all living beings from the ocean of desire.
If one can universally give rise to the great vow-mind to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of desire,
then one will be able to cross over the four torrents and show the way to the city of liberation free from sorrow;
upon the great waters along all paths of conditioned existence, one shall construct bridges and rafts.
He disparages the conditioned and praises tranquility; therefore, he achieves this radiance.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Extinction of Craving.
This light awakens all beings, causing them to abandon the five desires and focus their thoughts exclusively on the exquisite flavor of the Dharma of liberation.
If one can renounce the five desires and single-mindedly contemplate the wondrous flavor of the Dharma of liberation,
then one may, with the Buddha’s rain of ambrosia, universally extinguish all the thirst and craving of the world.
By providing ponds, wells, and flowing springs as gifts, one shall single-mindedly seek the path to unsurpassed bodhi.
By disparaging the five desires and praising meditative concentration, one thus attains this radiance.
Furthermore, a light is emitted named "Joy";
this light can awaken all sentient beings, causing them to yearn for the Buddha’s Bodhi and resolve to realize the path of the Teacherless One.

Having fashioned an image of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, adorned with all the marks and seated upon a lotus throne, he constantly extols its most supreme merits; therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Beloved," which is able to awaken all sentient beings.
Causing their minds to delight in all Buddhas, And to delight in the Dharma and the Sangha;
If they always delight their minds in all Buddhas, And delight in the Dharma and the Sangha,
Then they shall dwell within the assemblies of the Tathāgatas And attain the unsurpassed profound *dharmakṣānti*.
Awakening immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to mindfully recite the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
and demonstrating the meritorious practices of generating the bodhicitta— thereby accomplishing this second light,
which consists of four lights and forty-four phrases, they cause [beings] to generate the Great Mind, namely the Four Great Vows. Regarding this:
In the first part, "Deliverance" refers to the vow to save sentient beings; next, "Extinction of Craving" refers to the vow to sever afflictions;
next, "Rejoicing" refers to the seeking of Bodhi; and next, "Delightful Love" refers to the study of the Dharma-gates.
Again, he emits a light named "Accumulation of Merit";
this light awakens all beings, causing them to practice various kinds of immeasurable giving.
Through this aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way, they establish great assemblies of giving without restriction; those who come seeking are all fully satisfied.
They do not allow their minds to suffer any lack; therefore, they achieve this radiance.
Furthermore, they emit a light named "Possessing Wisdom.
This light awakens all beings, so that within a single dharma, a single teaching, and a single thought-moment, they fully comprehend immeasurable gateways to the Dharma.
For the sake of all sentient beings, you distinguish the dharmas and definitively realize their true meaning;
you skillfully expound the dharma and its meaning without deficiency or diminution.
Therefore, this third light is attained, which consists of two lights that collectively perfect both merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Lamp of Wisdom.
This light awakens all beings, causing them to know that the nature of sentient beings is empty and tranquil.
It proclaims that all phenomena are non-existent, that all dharmas are empty and without a master, being like illusions, like mirages, and like the moon reflected in water.
Even as it is like a dream or a reflection, therefore this radiance is accomplished.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Sovereignty of Dharma";
this light awakens all beings, causing them to attain inexhaustible *dhāraṇīs* and to uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas.

Reverently making offerings to those who uphold the Dharma, serving and protecting all the worthy sages, and bestowing various forms of the Dharma upon sentient beings—for these reasons, one attains this fourth light.

This fourth light has two aspects: entering into principle and upholding the Dharma. The former involves wisdom entering the two emptinesses; the latter is endowed with the four [applications of mindfulness].
Dhāraṇī. Furthermore, he emits a light named "Able to Renounce.
This light awakens stingy sentient beings, causing them to know that wealth and treasures are all impermanent, so that they may constantly delight in wise giving with a mind free from attachment.

Avarice is difficult to subdue, yet he has subdued it; He understands wealth to be like a dream or a floating cloud, Increasing his pure mind of generous giving. Therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Dispelling Heat," This light can awaken those who violate the precepts.
Causing all to universally receive and uphold the pure precepts, Arousing the aspiration to realize the teacherless path,
Exhorting and guiding sentient beings to receive and uphold the precepts, And purifying all ten paths of wholesome action,
Furthermore, causing them to resolve toward Bodhicitta— For these reasons, this radiance is accomplished.
Again, he emits a light named "Adorned with Patience.
This light awakens those who harbor anger, causing them to eliminate hatred and abandon pride.
Sentient beings constantly delight in patience and gentle methods, yet they are violent and evil, difficult to endure; for the sake of Bodhi, their minds remain unshakable.
Always delighting in praising the merit of patience, one therefore attains this radiance.
Furthermore, a light is emitted named "Valiant," which awakens those who are indolent,
causing them to always revere and make offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness.
If one always reveres and makes offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness,
one will be able to transcend the realms of the four Māras and swiftly attain the unsurpassed Bodhi of a Buddha.
One should exhort and inspire sentient beings to advance, constantly and diligently making offerings to the Triple Gem.
