When the Dharma is about to perish, he single-mindedly protects it; for this reason, he attains this radiance.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Tranquility";
this light can awaken those with distracted minds, causing them to distance themselves from greed, hatred, and delusion, so that their minds no longer waver and they enter right concentration.
Having abandoned all evil associates and meaningless talk, and having praised the practice of meditative concentration in forest hermitages, one thus attains this radiance.
Furthermore, a radiance named "Wisdom Adornment" is emitted; this light awakens those who are deluded and confused.
Causing them to realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, With all faculties and wisdom fully penetrating;
If one can realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, With all faculties and wisdom fully penetrating,
Then one attains the Dharma of the Sun-Lamp Samādhi, And through the radiance of wisdom, achieves the fruit of Buddhahood.
One is able to relinquish both national wealth and one’s own person for the sake of Bodhi;
having sought and heard the True Dharma, one diligently expounds it for the sake of the multitude.
Therefore, this fifth light is accomplished, which consists of six lights and fifty-six phrases, clarifying the perfection of the practice of the Six Pāramitās.
Again, he emits a light named "Buddha-Wisdom"; this light awakens all sentient beings,
causing them to see immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, each seated upon a precious lotus flower,
praising the Buddha’s majestic virtue and liberation, and proclaiming the Buddha’s infinite sovereignty.
To manifest the Buddha’s power and supernormal faculties, he thus brings this radiance to fulfillment.
Furthermore, he emits a light named Fearlessness;
when this light touches those who are terrified, all poisons and harms inflicted by non-human beings are swiftly extinguished.
Able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings, Whenever encountering harm or affliction, they urge others to cease it;
Rescuing those in distress and aiding the solitary and destitute— By this, they attain this radiance.
Furthermore, they emit a light named "Peaceful Security," Which can illuminate those who are ill.
Causing all sufferings and pains to be eliminated, And enabling all to attain the bliss of right concentration and samādhi;
Bestowing excellent medicines to rescue the multitude from afflictions, With wondrous jewel-extended-life incense smeared upon their bodies,
And ghee, oil, milk, and honey provided as food and drink— By these means, this radiance is accomplished.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Beholding the Buddha. This light awakens those who are about to die, causing them to recollect and behold the Tathāgata.
Upon the end of their lives, they attain rebirth in that Pure Land. Seeing those facing death, he exhorts them to mindfully recite the Buddha’s name;
he further manifests sacred images for them to gaze upon with reverence.
So that they may deeply take refuge in and revere the Buddha, this light is thus produced;
furthermore, it emits a light named "Delight in the Dharma.
This light can awaken all beings, causing them to always rejoice in the True Dharma by hearing its exposition, transcribing it, and reciting it.
When the Dharma is about to perish, one is able to expound it, filling the minds of those who seek the Dharma;
through their love for the Dharma and diligent practice, they attain this radiance.
Furthermore, a light named "Wondrous Sound" is emitted, which awakens all bodhisattvas.
It can cause all sounds within the three realms to be heard as the voice of the Tathāgata by those who hear them;
with a great voice they praise the Buddha and offer bells and various musical instruments,
universally enabling the world to hear the Buddha’s voice— thereby this radiance is accomplished.
Again, he emits a light that bestows ambrosia; this light awakens all beings, causing them to abandon all heedless conduct.
It causes them to fully cultivate all meritorious virtues and to speak of how conditioned phenomena are not secure, being entirely filled with immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Constantly delighting in praising the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, one therefore attains this sixth light, which consists of seven rays and fifty-six phrases.
These clarify the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) through their saving and gathering [of beings]: first, one ray bestows happiness through loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
second and third, three rays extract suffering through compassion (*karuṇā*); third, two rays cause the arising of Dharma-joy (*muditā*); fourth, one [ray]...
The light causes them to achieve great relinquishment.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Most Supreme.
This light awakens all beings, causing them to universally hear from the Buddha the sublime Dharma of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Always delighting in praising all Buddhas— Their supreme precepts, supreme concentration, and sublime wisdom— Thus seeking the unsurpassed path, Therefore one attains this radiance.
The seventh [radiance] generally manifests the three trainings. Since the myriad practices are fully subsumed within the three trainings, it is called "Universal Renown."
Again, he emits a light named Jewel Adornment;
this light awakens all beings, enabling them to obtain inexhaustible treasuries of jewels.
With these various kinds of supreme and wondrous jewels, they make offerings to all Tathāgatas, presenting them as gifts to the Buddhas and their stūpas.
Furthermore, by bestowing gifts upon those who were poor and destitute, He attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Fragrant Adornment";
This light awakens all beings, causing those who hear it to find joy in their hearts, And they shall certainly attain the merits of Buddhahood.
With exquisite celestial incense, they anointed the ground, Making offerings to all the Most Victorious Lords;
They also constructed stupas and Buddha images, And for this reason, they have attained this radiance.
Furthermore, they emit a light named "Diverse Adornments," With countless jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies.
Incense is burned, flowers are scattered, and various music is played, filling both the interior and exterior of the city.

With the sounds of subtle and exquisite music, along with various offerings such as fragrant flowers, wonderful banners, and canopies, they adorn and make offerings to the Buddha; therefore, this radiance is attained.
Again, he emits a light named "Pure Adornment," Which makes the earth level like the palm of a hand, adorning the Buddha-stūpas and their sites;
For this reason, he is able to achieve this light.
Again, he emits a light named "Great Cloud," Which can raise fragrant clouds and rain down scented water.
By sprinkling water upon the stūpa and its courtyard, one thus achieves this radiance.
Furthermore, emitting a light named "Ornament," one bestows excellent garments and exquisite ornaments upon those who are naked;
by such giving, one achieves this radiance.

Again, he emits a light named "Supreme Flavor," Which enables those who are hungry to obtain fine food, Bestowing upon them various kinds of rare delicacies; Therefore, this light is brought to fulfillment.
Again, he emits a light named "Great Wealth," Which causes those who are destitute to obtain treasuries of jewels.
By bestowing inexhaustible objects upon the Triple Gem, one thus achieves this eighth light;
it consists of eight rays and forty-four phrases. It manifests various practices, with making offerings as the primary focus.
Of these, the first five pertain to the field of respect, while the latter three pertain to the field of compassion.
Again, he emits a light called "Pure Eyes," Which enables the blind to see all forms;
By offering lamps to the Buddha and the Buddha-stūpas, He thus achieves this radiant light.
Again, he emits a light called "Pure Ears," Which enables the deaf to hear clearly.
By providing music to entertain the Buddha and his stūpas, one thus attains this radiance;
furthermore, by emitting light, one’s nose becomes purified, so that all fragrances never before heard may be smelled.
By offering incense to the Buddha and his stūpas, one thus attains this radiance.

Again, he emits a light called "Pure Tongue," which is able to praise the Buddha with beautiful sounds and forever eliminate coarse, evil, and unwholesome speech; for this reason, he attains this radiance.
Again, he emits a light called "Pure Body," which causes those with deficient sense organs to become complete.
By prostrating with the body before the Buddha and his stūpas, one therefore attains this radiance. Furthermore,
by emitting light with a pure intention, causing those who have lost their minds to regain right mindfulness,
and attaining mastery in the practice of samādhi, one therefore attains this radiance.
The ninth [stage] has six lights; internally pure, it aligns the six celestial bodies with principle.
Furthermore, it emits a light of pure color, enabling one to behold the inconceivable forms of all Buddhas.
Adorned with a multitude of wondrous colors, it forms a stupa; therefore, this radiance is accomplished.
Again, he emits a light called "Pure Sound," Causing one to know that the nature of sound is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
Contemplating the dependent origination of sound as being like an echo, Therefore, this light is accomplished.
Again, he emits a light called "Pure Fragrance," Causing all foul odors to become fragrant and pure.
By washing the stūpas and the Bodhi tree with fragrant water, one therefore attains this radiance;
furthermore, by emitting a light of pure flavor, one is able to eliminate all poisons within flavors.
By constantly making offerings to the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and one’s parents, one therefore attains this radiance.
Furthermore, they emit a light that touches with purity, Causing all harsh sensations to become soft and supple.
Spears, javelins, swords, and halberds rain down from the sky, All of which are transformed into exquisite flower garlands.
With fragrant pastes upon the roads, Scented unguents, scattered flowers, and spread garments.
Welcoming and escorting the Tathāgata, causing him to tread upon it, for this reason one now attains such radiance.
Furthermore, emitting the light of the Dharma-purification, it enables all pores to expound the inconceivable, wondrous Dharma;
all sentient beings who hear it rejoice and attain awakening.

That which arises from causes and conditions has no arising; the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is not a physical body. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding like space; such is the light of the meaning of this teaching. Thus, in the tenth [section], there are sixteen lights and thirty-two phrases. Externally, they purify the six sense objects; when touching these objects, all become the Path. As for "go" (the character for "spear"): [The following is the phonetic/semantic gloss: *Go* (戈) — This is the sound of the letter *ga*. It signifies the cutting away of the three poisons and the five aggregates. It is the weapon that severs the bonds of affliction. It is the sword that destroys the darkness of ignorance. It is the wind that sweeps away the dust of delusion. It is the sun that dispels the gloom of the night. It is the moon that cools the heat of the passions. It is the fire that burns the fuel of karma. It is the water that washes clean the stains of defilement. It is the earth that supports the mountain of the Noble Path. It is the sky that encompasses the realm of the Dharma. It is the thunder that awakens the slumbering faculties. It is the lightning that reveals the brilliance of the Buddha-nature. It is the cloud that gathers the rain of the Dharma. It is the jewel that fulfills all wishes. It is the wish-fulfilling tree that provides the fruits of liberation. The *pingtou* is a halberd; the *ting* is a small spear.

Such as these are the gateways of light—limitless in number like the sands of the Ganges—all emerging from the pores of the Great Sage, each performing its respective function with distinct differentiation.
Second, in this manner, the following concludes the brief summary by revealing the extensive details. The light from the function of a single hair is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Just as the light emitted from a single pore is immeasurable and incalculable like the sands of the Ganges, so it is with every single pore.
This is the power of the Great Sage’s samādhi.
The third section, beginning with "As with one hair," illustrates by analogy the causal karma of all pores as well as the basis for their functioning, namely the power of samādhi.
This concludes the eighth section on the "Samādhi Door of Hair-Ray Illumination and Benefit.
Having thus finished explaining these forty-four doors, this final sentence at the end illustrates all hair-rays by analogy: as it is with one hair, so it is with all.
How much more so for one with abundant hair? The following explains the extent of his light:
"Just as he obtained this light through his past conduct, he now emits radiance in accordance with those who shared his past conditions;
such is the sovereign mastery of the Great Sage’s wisdom."
Those who in the past practiced together in meritorious deeds, And those who, with joyful devotion,
were able to rejoice in what was done— They all likewise behold this light.
If one personally cultivates various meritorious deeds, Making offerings to countless Buddhas, [they too shall see it].
Constantly aspiring to seek the Buddha’s virtues—this is what this light awakens one to.
Just as those born blind do not see the eyes [of others], it is not that the sun does not rise in the world;
rather, all who possess eyes see clearly, each according to their own pursuits, cultivating their respective tasks.
The radiance of the Great Being is likewise:
those possessed of wisdom all behold it, yet ordinary people of false faith and inferior understanding cannot perceive this light.
The palace of mani-jewels and the celestial chariot are polished and adorned with exquisite gems and sacred incense.
Those with merit naturally possess it; it is not something those without virtue can abide in.

The radiance of the Great Being is likewise: it shines upon and touches all those with profound wisdom, yet no one who possesses false faith, inferior understanding, or is a foolish ordinary person can see this light.
The following is the fourth section, which explains the scope of the light. That is to say: since such lights as these exist, why are they not seen now?

Those who possess the necessary conditions see them, just as one perceives light through its use; those without the conditions do not perceive them, remaining like the blind and the sightless in perpetual darkness.
Within this, twenty-eight phrases are divided into two parts. The first four lines of the initial verse provide a general explanation:
"according to their original conduct" refers back to the preceding causes, while "the light obtained" refers back to the preceding functional effects.

Thus, those who have past affinities or have previously practiced together will perceive these distinctions according to their respective visions. Next, six verses provide a detailed exposition; the first two verses concern the Dharma.
The latter four verses are explained through parables. There are two parables that clarify both seeing and not seeing, each with a doctrinal application (*dharmasaṃgati*).
For example, the metaphor of the sun illustrates light as the cause of benefit; in the application, it is said that the Dharma-sun is ever-bright.
Just as one who possesses eyes is able to see, there are three types of people who are unable to do so.

There are three types of those who do not see [it]: first, the ignorant and foolish; second, those with false faith among the non-Buddhists; and third, those of inferior understanding among the two vehicles.

These all lack the causes and conditions [to see it], like a person without eyes. The subsequent analogy of the jewel-adornment illustrates the benefit of the light of the correct [teaching] and clarifies that the Dharma-jewel exists eternally.
Depending on whether one possesses merit or lacks merit, one either encounters it or does not encounter it.

If there are those who hear this distinction of light, They can give rise to pure, profound faith and understanding, Forever severing all nets of doubt, And swiftly accomplishing the banner of unsurpassed merit.
(Verse 5) This single verse clarifies the benefits of hearing and believing in the light. That is to say, through faithful acceptance, understanding, and realization, one does not give rise to doubt.
They attain the fruit of Buddhahood. They do not harbor doubts regarding the Bodhisattva’s lack of radiance because they do not see it;
nor do they conclude that the light is useless because extreme suffering cannot be saved; nor do they dismiss its efficacy by claiming it is beyond the Bodhisattva’s power.
Therefore, it is said that "all doubts are forever severed. Thus concludes the eighth section: the Samādhi Door of the Beneficial Radiance of the Body Hairs.
There is a supreme samādhi capable of manifesting a retinue of adornments, all of which are sovereign;
throughout all the lands of the ten directions, the assemblies of the Buddha-sons are peerless.
There is a wondrous lotus light-adornment, its magnitude equal to a trichiliocosm.
His body sits upright, completely filling [the space]; this is the power of the supernormal knowledges of this samādhi.

Furthermore, surrounded by exquisite lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, the assembly of sons of the Buddha sits within them, abiding by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi.
Having accomplished great causes and conditions in past lives, these beings, who are fully endowed with the practice of the Buddha’s virtues, surround the Bodhisattva;
all together they join their palms, gazing upon him without weariness.
Just as the bright moon stands amidst the stars, so too does the Bodhisattva dwell among the assembly.
Such is the practice of the Great Being; through the majestic power of this samādhi,
just as he manifests in one direction, surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons,
so it is in all directions, abiding by the majestic power of this samādhi.

The ninth section, "The Samādhi of Supreme Excellence," contains six verses below it. These clarify the samādhi-gate of the majesty of the primary and attendant [deities], which is also the manifestation of samādhi.
The text is divided into three parts: first, one verse designates the gate and reveals its intent;

next, the four verses beginning with "There is a wondrous lotus" clarify the karmic functions of a single direction; therein, the first three are explained through the Dharma (dharma-deśanā), and the last is an analogy.

This is consistent. Since it is stated that the size [of the flowers] is equal to three thousand [great thousandfold worlds], this does not contradict the sequential order; they are inferior to those of the Ten Stages and Equal Enlightenment.

This is because the flowers received at the investiture of the Ten Stages measure a million times three thousand [great thousandfold worlds], while the quantity of the flowers of Equal Enlightenment pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Because this is revealed to be within the stage of faith, it is called the "unwavering sequence. Next, as with one verse in one direction, so it is illustrated for all ten directions.
There is a supreme samādhi named "Dharma-Directional Net" (Dharmadhātuprativedha), in which the Bodhisattva dwells and extensively reveals [the teachings].
Manifesting bodies everywhere in all directions, sometimes entering meditative absorption and sometimes emerging from it;
or entering right concentration in the east and emerging from concentration in the west,
or entering right concentration in the west and emerging from concentration in the east.
In some cases they enter right concentration in one direction and emerge from concentration in another;
thus their entry and emergence pervade the ten directions. This is called the power of the bodhisattva’s samādhi.
Throughout all the lands in the eastern quarter, there are immeasurable Tathāgatas.
Manifesting before them all, they approach them universally; abiding in samādhi, tranquil and unmoving,
yet in all the worlds of the western direction, they appear before all the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, and arising from that samādhi, they extensively perform immeasurable offerings.
Exhausting all the lands of the western direction, All the countless Tathāgatas appear before him;
He approaches them all universally while abiding in a samādhi, Tranquil and unmoving,
yet within all the worlds of the eastern direction, In the presence of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
All manifest arising from samādhi, extensively performing immeasurable offerings;
thus, in all worlds of the ten directions, bodhisattvas enter them without exception.
Some manifest in the stillness and immobility of samādhi, while others manifest in reverent worship of the Buddhas.

Entering right concentration within the faculty of the eye, he emerges from that concentration within the sphere of forms to manifest the inconceivable nature of form; no gods or humans are able to know this.
Entering right concentration within the sphere of forms, he emerges from concentration within the eye with an undisturbed mind.
He teaches that the eye is unborn and has no arising; its nature is empty, quiescent, and without action.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of the ear, he emerges from that concentration amidst the objects of sound.
He discerns all vocal sounds and languages, such that neither gods nor worldlings can comprehend them.
Entering right concentration within the object of sound, he emerges from that concentration amidst the objects of smell with a mind undisturbed;
he teaches that the ear is unborn and has no arising, its nature being empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of the nose, he emerges from that concentration amidst the objects of smell.
Universally obtaining all supreme and wondrous fragrances, Which neither gods nor people of the world can discern;
Entering right concentration within the sensory field of fragrance, Emerging from concentration through the nose with an undisturbed mind,
He teaches that the nose is unborn and without arising, Its nature being empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Entering right concentration within the tongue-faculty, he emerges from concentration amidst the objects of taste;
he universally attains all supreme flavors, yet neither gods nor worldlings can perceive this.
Entering right concentration amidst the objects of taste, he arises from concentration in the tongue with a mind undisturbed.
He teaches that the tongue is unborn and has no arising; its nature is empty, extinguished, quiescent, and without action.

Entering right concentration within the faculty of the body, he emerges from concentration amidst the object of touch, skillfully discerning all tactile sensations—something that neither gods nor worldly people can comprehend.
Entering right concentration within the object of touch, Emerging from concentration in the body with an undisturbed mind,
He speaks of the body as being without birth or arising, Its nature empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of mind, He emerges from concentration within the object of mental phenomena.
He discerns the characteristics of all phenomena, yet neither gods nor men can know them.
Entering right concentration within the objects of the mind, he emerges from that mental concentration with an undisturbed mind.
He speaks of the non-arising and non-origination of the mind; its nature is empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Entering right concentration within the body of a youth, he emerges from concentration within the body of a man in his prime;
entering right concentration within the body of a man in his prime, he emerges from concentration within the body of an elder;
entering right concentration within the body of an elder, he emerges from concentration within the body of a virtuous woman.
Entering right concentration within the body of a virtuous woman, emerging from concentration within the body of a virtuous man;
entering right concentration within the body of a virtuous man, emerging from concentration within the body of a bhikṣuṇī;
entering right concentration within the body of a bhikṣuṇī, emerging from concentration within the body of a bhikṣu.
The body of a bhikṣu enters right concentration; from that concentration, the bodies of those in training and those beyond training emerge.
The bodies of those in training and those beyond training enter right concentration; from that concentration, the body of a pratyekabuddha emerges.
The body of a pratyekabuddha enters right concentration; from that concentration, the body of a Tathāgata manifests and emerges.
Entering right concentration within the body of a Tathāgata, they emerge from concentration within the bodies of devas;
entering right concentration within the bodies of devas, they emerge from concentration within the bodies of great nāgas;
entering right concentration within the bodies of great nāgas, they emerge from concentration within the bodies of yakṣas.
Entering right concentration within the body of a yakṣa, emerging from concentration within the body of a ghost-spirit;
entering right concentration within the body of a ghost-spirit, emerging from concentration within a single pore;
entering right concentration within a single pore, emerging from concentration from all pores.
Entering right concentration from all pores, Emerging from concentration at the tip of one hair and entering right concentration at the tip of another hair;
Emerging from concentration within a single atom and entering right concentration within another atom, Emerging from concentration within all atoms.
Entering right concentration within all atoms, Emerging from concentration within the vajra-ground;
Entering right concentration within the vajra-ground, Emerging from concentration upon mani-trees;
Entering right concentration upon mani-trees, Emerging from concentration within the Buddha’s radiance.
Entering right concentration within the Buddha’s radiance, he emerges from concentration in rivers and oceans;
entering right concentration in rivers and oceans, he emerges from concentration in the element of fire;
entering right concentration in the element of fire, he emerges from concentration in the element of wind, his mind undisturbed.
Entering right concentration within the great element of wind, he emerges from concentration within the great element of earth;
entering right concentration within the great element of earth, he emerges from concentration within the celestial palaces;
entering right concentration within the celestial palaces, he arises from concentration in space with an undisturbed mind.
This is called the one of immeasurable merit; The samādhis of his mastery are inconceivable.
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions Could not exhaustively describe them even in immeasurable kalpas.
The tenth [chapter], "The Supreme Samādhi," consists of thirty-four and a half verses below this point, which clarify the boundless samādhi of quiescent activity.
The Gate. In terms of location, it is called the "Lattice of Directions" (*dig-jāla*); in terms of its characteristics, it constitutes quiescence and function.
It also generally reveals that, as discussed above, movement and stillness are non-dual. The text is divided into three parts. The first verse provides the title and offers a general explanation:

because the ten directions interlace, entering and exiting, vertically and horizontally, it is called a "lattice. Next, from "Alternatively, in the eastern direction... onwards, there are thirty-two and a half verses.

Third, the manifestation of functional activity (*karmakriyā*). The final verse summarizes the inconceivable nature. Within the section on functional activity, there are three parts: first, the two verses beginning with "Whether in the east" describe the mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) by means of entering and exiting through the interconnected directions of the ten quarters. Second, the twenty phrases following "Throughout the east" clarify the mastery over the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) through wisdom and perfect enlightenment. Third, [the remaining verses] clarify the mastery over the world of the Dharma (*dharmaloka*). Regarding the three [sections], under the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), there are one hundred and two phrases that collectively manifest mastery over the three worlds.
This is divided into four parts: first, under the faculty of the eye, forty-eight phrases concerning mastery over faculties and objects;
next, twenty-six phrases concerning mastery over the bodies of others, beginning with "within the body of a youth"; and next, ten phrases concerning the body of a spirit (*bhūta*).
"Subtle mastery. Next, the eighteen phrases beginning with "within all atoms" refer to mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The four phrases beginning with "this is called one of immeasurable merit" summarize the inconceivable nature [of these powers].
Supplementary Commentary: The principle of this Fangguang (Luminous Net) Samādhi is most profound and subtle.

Although there are many explanations in the commentaries, they all ultimately do not transcend the non-obstruction between *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, or between concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and between principle and phenomena.

To distinguish this non-obstruction, one must first clearly understand concentration and wisdom. Herein, "the arising of samādhi" refers to *vipaśyanā*, while "entering right reception" refers to *samādhi*. Although concentration and wisdom...

For the most part, these do not go beyond the two gates of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). To restrain [the mind] in a single place so that nothing remains undone is the gate of concentration on phenomena (*shiding men*).

To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind, accords with principle, and remains unmoving is the gate of concentration on principle (*liding men*). Clearly penetrating the characteristics of dharmas is the contemplation of phenomena (*shiguan*).

This is the contemplation that thoroughly understands the principle of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*). Nevertheless, when phenomena arise based on this principle, the phenomenal dharmas of the ten realms—both defiled and pure, including both the environment and its inhabitants—are entirely formed from this single principle.
Thus, although there are many phenomena, they are in fact only this one principle; therefore, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomenon is attained.

Consequently, when a Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in accord with the principle, because the principle is all-pervasive, the concentration is likewise all-pervasive. Therefore, upon entering even once...

This is precisely the entry into the manifold. If one contemplates through the phenomena (*dharma*), then the phenomenon and the principle (*li*) are entirely identical; thus, a single phenomenon is all phenomena.

Therefore, what arises in one place arises in all places. Because the principle and phenomena are perfectly pervasive, the place of entry is the place of arising, and the place of arising is the place of entry.
Since entering and emerging are free and unimpeded, self and other are equal, and the characteristics of the large and small [interpenetrate].

[The commentary] contains [this]: "Subtle and wondrous, it is difficult to conceive. Although the sub-commentary provides numerous detailed explanations, its meaning does not go beyond this. Therefore, it refers to it collectively, saying:
"If one can simply know that phenomena and principle are unimpeded and that faculties and objects are of one suchness, so that discursive thoughts do not arise, one will naturally enter [the path].
This is the wondrous gateway for entering the Dharma-realm; students should certainly contemplate it deeply. After a long time, they will surely attain awakening."
All Tathāgatas together proclaim: The karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable;
The transformations of the nāgas and the mastery of Buddhas, And the spiritual powers of Bodhisattvas are likewise beyond thought.
Though one wishes to demonstrate it through metaphors, there is ultimately no metaphor capable of illustrating this;
yet those of wisdom and discernment understand its meaning by means of similes.
The śrāvakas, whose minds abide in the eight liberations, possess mastery over all their miraculous manifestations.
Able to manifest many bodies from a single body, And again to make many bodies into one;
Entering the fire-samādhi within the void, Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, all while remaining in space;
Emitting water from the upper body and fire from the lower body, Or emitting fire from the upper body and water from the lower body.
Thus, within a single thought-moment, they manifest all manner of infinite and sovereign powers.
Since those who lack great compassion yet still seek the path of Buddhahood for the sake of sentient beings can manifest such inconceivable deeds,
how much more so those possessed of the sovereign power of great benefit?

Just as the sun and moon travel through space, Their reflections appear everywhere throughout the ten directions— In springs, ponds, marshes, and the water within vessels, And in all rivers, seas, and precious streams;
The physical forms of Bodhisattvas are likewise so: They manifest universally throughout the ten directions in an inconceivable manner.
These are all the dharmas of mastery over samādhi; only a Tathāgata can realize and comprehend them.

They are like the images of four kinds of troops in clear water—each distinct and without confusion—including many varieties of swords, halberds, bows, and arrows, as well as armor, helmets, chariots, and carriages of more than one kind.

According to all their various distinct characteristics, there is nothing that does not appear within the water, yet the water itself is fundamentally without discrimination; the samādhi of the Bodhisattva is also like this.
Within the ocean there is a deity named Good Sound, whose voice universally accords with the sentient beings of the sea.
All languages are analyzed and understood, Causing them all to be filled with joy.
Even that deity who possesses greed, anger, and delusion Is still able to skillfully comprehend all sounds;
How much more so, then, could one with the sovereign power of dhāraṇī Not cause the multitude to rejoice?
There was a woman named Prajñā (Eloquence), whom her parents obtained through prayers to the gods.
If one abandons evil and delights in the truth, she enters their body and produces wondrous eloquence;
even those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, she can follow and bestow eloquence upon them.
How much more so for a Bodhisattva endowed with wisdom—how could they not bring benefit to sentient beings?
Like a master illusionist who understands the nature of illusions, they can manifest all manner of infinite things;
in a mere moment, they display days, months, and years, as well as cities, abundant harvests, and great peace and happiness.
Even a magician who possesses greed, hatred, and delusion can delight the world through the power of illusion;
how much more so one who possesses the power of meditative concentration and liberation—could such a person not cause the multitude to rejoice?
When the devas and asuras were at war, the asuras were defeated and fled in retreat.
The weapons, chariots, and the host of followers— All fled at once and could not be seen.
If those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion Are still able to manifest such inconceivable transformations,
How much more so for one who dwells in the dharmas of supernatural powers and fearlessness— Why would they be unable to manifest sovereign mastery?
Śakra Devānām-indra has an elephant king; when that Lord of Devas desires to travel, it spontaneously manifests thirty-two heads.
Each head is fully endowed with six tusks, and upon each tusk are seven pools of water, pure, fragrant, and filled to the brim.
Within each of the pure ponds, there are seven lotus flowers exquisitely adorned;
upon each of these adorned lotuses dwell seven celestial jade maidens,
all skilled in the arts, who play various musical instruments and provide entertainment for Śakra.
That elephant may further cast off its original form and transform itself into a shape identical to the majestic appearance of the devas,
with every movement and posture exactly equal [to theirs]. Possessing such power of manifested supernatural transformation,
even one who has greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest these various supernormal powers.
How much more so for one who possesses the wisdom of skillful means, yet lacks mastery over the various meditative concentrations?
How could the transformation body of an asura stand upon the adamantine foundation at the bottom of the ocean,
with the seawater reaching only halfway up his body, while his head stands level with Mount Sumeru?
If those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest such great supernormal powers, how much more so for the Lamp that Illumines the World, who subdues the enemies of Māra?
When the gods and asuras wage war together, the supernormal power of Śakra is inconceivable; yet the sovereign majestic power of the Buddha is even more so.
In accordance with the number of the Asura hosts, he manifested supernatural powers equal to theirs to confront them.
When the Asuras conceived this thought—"Śakra Devānām Indra has come toward us;
he will surely bind my body with the fivefold bonds"—thereupon that entire host became despondent and distressed.
Śakra manifests his body with a thousand eyes, holding a vajra that emits flames;
clad in armor and bearing weapons, he is most majestic and awe-inspiring. When the asuras behold him, they all retreat and submit.
By the power of even such slight merit, he is yet able to crush and destroy his great enemies.
How much more so for one who delivers all beings! In the Trayastriṃśa Heaven, where the sovereign power of merit is complete, there is a celestial drum.
Born from the karmic retribution of the gods, it naturally produces this sound from the sky when it perceives that the hosts of devas are becoming heedless.
All five desires are entirely impermanent; Like a mass of foam on the water, their nature is false and deceptive.
All things are like dreams, like mirages, And also like floating clouds or the moon reflected in water.
Heedlessness is an enemy and a source of suffering; It is not the path to the Deathless, but the track of birth and death.
If one engages in various acts of negligence, one enters the mouth of the great fish of death.
It is the root of all suffering in the world; all noble ones loathe it.
Since the nature of the five desires is to decay and perish, you should take delight in the true Dharma.
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three heard this sound, they all ascended together to the Hall of Good Dharma.
Śakra preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, causing them all to accord with tranquility and eliminate craving and attachment.
Though that sound has no form and cannot be seen, it is still able to benefit the assembly of devas.
How much more so when he manifests a physical body according to the inclinations of beings' minds, yet fails to deliver all the multitudes of sentient beings?

When the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, the celestial drum, through the power of the devas' superior merit, emitted a sound to inform their hosts: "You should not give way to grief or fear."
When the devas heard this proclaimed voice, their grief and fear were entirely dispelled and their strength increased;
at that time, the asuras’ hearts trembled with dread, and the armies they led all retreated in flight.
The sublime samādhi of ambrosia is like a celestial drum, constantly producing the peaceful sound that subdues Māra.
The Greatly Compassionate One, the Benevolent Savior of All, universally causes all sentient beings to extinguish their afflictions.
Śakra, responding to all the celestial maidens—ninety-two nayutas in number—causes each of them to think in her own mind:
"The Heavenly King is sporting with me alone."
Just as the body of a celestial maiden universally responds, so it is within the Hall of Good Dharma;
in a single thought-moment she manifests spiritual powers, appearing before them all to preach the Dharma.
Although Śakra possesses greed, anger, and delusion, he is able to cause his retinue to be entirely joyful.
How much more so for one with great skillful means and supernormal powers—who could not cause all others to rejoice?
The six celestial kings of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations attain sovereignty within the desire realm;
yet, using karma, delusion, and suffering as a snare, they bind all ordinary beings.
If those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion can still exercise mastery over sentient beings,
how much more so one endowed with the ten kinds of sovereign power? How could such a one not cause all beings to practice together,
even as the Great Brahmā King of the Trichiliocosm in all the abodes of the Brahmā heavens?
They are all able to manifest their bodies seated there, Expounding the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice;

While they abide in the worldly path of Brahmā, Their meditative concentrations and supernormal powers are already as they wish— How much more so for those who have transcended the world and attained the unsurpassed state!
Yet, regarding meditative absorption and liberation, they are not yet fully sovereign.
Maheśvara, sovereign in wisdom, when the great ocean dragon king sends down rain,
can distinguish and count every single drop; within a single thought-moment,
he thoroughly discerns and understands the diligent cultivation and study throughout immeasurable billions of eons, having attained this supreme bodhi-wisdom.
How is it that in a single thought-moment, you universally know the minds of all sentient beings?

The karmic retributions of sentient beings are inconceivable; By the power of a great wind, you stir the vast oceans of the world, its mountains, and the celestial palaces, As well as the myriad species of things and the radiance of various jewels.
It can raise clouds and bring down great rain; it can also disperse and extinguish all vapors.
It can ripen all grains and bring peace and happiness to all living beings.
Yet the wind cannot learn the *pāramitās*, nor can it learn the various merits of the Buddhas.
They can already accomplish such inconceivable feats; how much more so those who have fulfilled all their vows!

Whether it be the various voices of men and women, the sounds of all birds and beasts, the roar of great oceans, rivers, and streams, or the thundering of clouds—they are able to please the minds of all sentient beings according to their inclinations.
How much more so for one who knows the nature of sound to be like an echo,
who has attained unimpeded and wondrous eloquence to preach the Dharma universally to all sentient beings—
how could such a one fail to cause the ocean of joy in the world to possess a rare and extraordinary quality, serving as the seal of equality for all?
The treasures of sentient beings and the flowing rivers, all are universally embraced without refusal;
those who possess inexhaustible meditative concentration and liberation likewise employ the seal of equality.
Regarding all sublime practices of merit and wisdom, they cultivate them all universally without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
When the Dragon King of the Great Ocean sports, he attains mastery over all places;

he raises clouds that pervade the four continents. Those clouds are adorned with various colors, and in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the color of those clouds is like pure gold.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it is the color of red pearls; In the Tuṣita Heaven, the color of frost and snow;
In the Yāma Heaven, the color of lapis lazuli; In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the color of agate;
In the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the color of crystal; Upon the great ocean, the color of diamond.
Among the kiṃnaras, it is the color of exquisite fragrance; in the abodes of the nāgas, the color of a lotus;
in the abodes of the yakṣas, the color of a white goose;
in Uttarakuru, the color of golden flames; and in Jambudvīpa, the color of green gems.
The other two continents are adorned with various ornaments, appearing according to the inclinations of the beings therein.
Furthermore, in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, it shines like lightning in the clouds or like the light of the sun;
in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it is like the light of the moon; and in the Tuṣita Heaven, it is like Jambu-river gold.
On the Yāma Heaven, it is the color of snow-white camphor; In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is the color of golden flames;
In the Heaven of the Four Kings, it is the color of various jewels; Within the great ocean, it is the color of red pearls;
In the realm of the Kiṃnaras, it is the color of lapis lazuli; In the abode of the Nāga Kings, it is the color of a precious treasure-store.
The abode of the yakṣas is the color of crystal; among the asuras, it is the color of agate.
In the realm of Uttarakuru, it is the color of fire-pearls; in Jambudvīpa, it is the color of indranīla.
In the other two continents, it is variously adorned, like the appearance of clouds and likewise like lightning.
The thunderous roar of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven is like the voice of Brahmā;
The sound of the celestial drum in the Nirmāṇarati heaven is like the sound of singing in the Tuṣita heaven;
The voices of the goddesses in the Yāma heaven, and in that Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Are like the various sounds of the kinnaras.
The sounds produced by the Four World-Protecting Kings and the various devas,
like the sound of two mountains colliding in the midst of the ocean, the sound of flutes and pipes among the kiṃnaras,
the sound of the kalaviṅka birds in the cities of the nāgas, and the voices of nāga maidens in the abodes of the yakṣas.
Among the asuras, the sound of celestial drums resounds; in the human realm, there is the sound of ocean tides.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, exquisite fragrances rain down, adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous flowers.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations, tāla flowers, māndārava flowers, and liquid perfumes fall.
In Tuṣita Heaven, maṇi jewels rain down, fully adorned with various precious ornaments;
the jewel in their topknots is like the light of the moon, and their exquisite garments are the color of pure gold.
In the Yāma Heaven, banners, streamers, and canopies rain down, along with flower garlands, unguents, and wonderful ornaments.
Exquisite garments of the color of red pearls, Various kinds of musical performances,
The wish-fulfilling jewels of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, And fragrances such as solid black aloeswood,
sandalwood, Uśīra, and kesarā— A rain of these falls, intermingled with wonderful flowers and scented water.
In the cities of the World-Protectors, delicious food rains down— complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, increasing strength—
and there also rains inconceivable multitudes of wondrous jewels, all created by the dragon kings.
Furthermore, within that great ocean, rain falls incessantly like the axle of a chariot.
Furthermore, there falls an inexhaustible rain of great treasuries of jewels, and also a rain of various kinds of ornamental gems.
In the realm of the kiṃnaras, there falls a rain of necklaces, lotus garments of many colors, and bālasirīṣa and mālatī perfumes; all manner of musical sounds are fully present.
In the cities of the nāgas, red jewels rain down; within the cities of the yakṣas, radiant maṇi-gems fall.
Among the asuras, weapons rain down to crush and subdue all enemies.
In Uttarakuru, exquisite necklaces rain down, as well as immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous flowers.
In the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī, there falls a rain of various kinds of ornaments;
in Jambudvīpa, there falls pure water— subtle, refreshing, and always timely—
which nurtures all flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs, bringing all crops to full maturity.
Thus, these immeasurable and wondrous adornments— various clouds, lightning, thunder, and rain—
the Dragon Kings can all produce with sovereign power;
yet their bodies remain unmoving and free from conceptualization as they dwell within the ocean of worlds, still manifesting this inconceivable power.
How much less could one who has entered the ocean of Dharma and is endowed with merit fail to perform great spiritual transformations?
The doors of liberation of those bodhisattvas cannot be revealed by any analogy;
yet, I shall now briefly describe their power of mastery through these various metaphors.
The fifth section concerns the profound purport of the metaphors of all Tathāgatas; it is also titled "The Section on Elevating the Inferior to Reveal the Superior.

Since the conduct and virtues of Samantabhadra described above reach the ultimate limit of the Buddha-realm, they pertain to a stage where faith is perfected. As this state transcends conventional norms, it deviates from what can be seen or heard.
Because those whose emotions are stagnant and who cling to the literal teachings have no means by which to find conviction, these proximate matters are cited here [to serve as an analogy].

This reflects the profound mystery and brings about awakening. It consists of seventy-nine verses, divided into three sections: the first two verses provide a general indication of the intended meaning of the metaphors;
the second section, comprising seventy-six verses, specifically elucidates the characteristics of the metaphors; and the final verse concludes by manifesting the excellence of the teaching.
Beginning from the metaphor of the Śrāvaka manifesting supernatural powers up to the metaphor of the Dragon King’s sport, there are twenty metaphors in total, each [illustrating a specific point].
This illustrates a single virtue of the Bodhisattva, as fully clarified in the commentary.
First, wisdom: vast wisdom, true wisdom, boundless wisdom, supreme wisdom, and preeminent wisdom—such a Dharma gate has now been explained.

This Dharma is rare and most extraordinary; if anyone, having heard it, can endure it, believe it, accept it, and praise and explain it—such an act is exceedingly difficult for all ordinary people in the world.
Those who have faith in this Dharma are extremely hard to find.
If there are those who diligently cultivate pure merit, they are able, by the power of past causes, to have faith in all sentient beings throughout all worlds.
Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas are few; those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha are even fewer still;
and those who proceed toward the Mahāyāna are extremely rare to encounter.
Those who aspire to the Mahāyāna are still considered easy to find; those who can have faith in this Dharma are twice as difficult to encounter.
How much more so those who uphold and recite it, explain it to others, practice according to the Dharma, and possess true understanding!
Even if one were to carry the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system upon their head for an entire kalpa without moving their body—
What they have done is not difficult; it is rather rare to find one who has faith in this Dharma.
To lift ten buddha-fields with one’s hand and remain suspended in mid-air for an entire kalpa—what they have done is not difficult;
it is rather rare to be able to believe in this Dharma.
If one were to bestow all articles of happiness upon as many sentient beings as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, their merit would not be supreme;
however, one who has faith in this Dharma is most supreme.
If one were to serve as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire eon, [their merit would not equal that of one who hears this Dharma].
If one is able to recite and uphold this chapter, its merit is most supreme, surpassing that [of the previous sections].
This is the third major section, the first of the "Comparison and Exhortation to Uphold" (the nine verses following the "Wisdom" section).
Such vast efficacy is within the reach of all people; yet to see it and not practice it is truly to deceive oneself. Therefore, even those of middling capacity can be exhorted [to do so].
This is the progression. It is divided into two parts. The first verse concludes what has been previously explained.

The subsequent eight verses, beginning with "This Dharma," clarify that it is difficult to find those who can receive and uphold it. Within these, the first verse provides a general indication, while the following eight provide specific clarifications.

Regarding the term "rare": the appearance of a Buddha is so remote that he is already difficult to encounter; yet, because he teaches this [Dharma] all at once immediately upon his initial enlightenment, it is rare. As for "extraordinary": it refers to—
The first [verse] is able to encompass the subsequent ones, specifically because it stands far beyond all other vehicles (*yāna*). The next half-verse cites a small example to illustrate the great.

Following that, the section beginning with "With three thousand... cites concrete matters for comparative measurement. Finally, one verse compares the difficulty of other practices, clarifying that only the recitation and upholding [of this teaching] is paramount.
Thus, the analogies illustrating the profound principle (*gambhīra-artha*) are concluded.
When the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha had spoken these verses, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways; the palaces of Māra were obscured;
the evil realms were stilled; and the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared before him, each stroking his head with their right hand and praising him in unison:
"Excellent, excellent! You have well expounded this Dharma. We all follow it."
Joy. The third major section, "Revealing the Actualization of Realization," contains four parts: first, because the great capacity of the world is stirred;
second, because the obscuration of Māra’s palace is a realm exclusive to the Buddha; third, because the cessation of evil destinies brings profound benefit and happiness; and fourth...

Because one realizes the Buddha-realm and accords with the Buddha-mind, the Buddha therein touches one’s crown, praises one as excellent, and rejoices in one’s merit; thus, all three karmas are realized.
One then exhorts others to have faith and practice. The intent of this chapter is to demonstrate that when faith is fulfilled, it encompasses and penetrates all the merits of the Buddha-fruit.
This is to manifest the perfect fusion and fullness of all virtues, serving as the stages of entry, abiding, and superior progress; therefore, this stage is named simply "Expedient Means.
The "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" concludes.
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifteen.
Essential Outline of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery at Mount Qingliang.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Kuang at Fayun Temple in Ming China, this third assembly is presided over by Dharma-Wisdom Bodhisattva in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace. It expounds dharma-gates such as the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
Its purpose is to bring understanding to those who have already developed faith. This section begins with the sixteenth fascicle and ends with the eighteenth, comprising a total of six chapters.
Sūtra.
(Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter on the Ten Abodes; Chapter on Brahma-Conduct;
Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment; Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma.)
Chapter Thirteen: Ascending to the Summit of Mount Sumeru.

Regarding the initial intent of this chapter, it first distinguishes the arrival of the assembly. Because they previously believed in the sequential order of these meanings, this serves as the formal response to the ten questions concerning the *vihāras* (stages).
In total, there are two sections: the former constitutes the expedient means for entering the *vihāras*, while this section clarifies the state of the true position (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Next follows this chapter. Regarding its sequence: the preceding chapter explained the perfection of faith; this chapter follows because it explains the stage of abiding (*vihāra*). Regarding the title:
in terms of the assembly, it is called the "Assembly at the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven"; in terms of the person, it is called the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati";
and in terms of the Dharma, it is called the "Assembly of the Ten Abidings. As for the name of the chapter, *Sumeru* is its formal name. This...
It is named "Wondrous High" (Sumeru). By the power of his sovereign mastery, the Tathāgata does not rise from the Bodhi tree but manifests there in response to the capacities of sentient beings;
therefore, it is said that he "ascends. This signifies that his status gradually increases and that he does not remain among humans, manifesting a state of pure station;
thus, he "dwells in heaven. If explained according to the contemplation of the mind: "Wondrous High" refers to samādhi; Sumeru is tranquil and motionless, without thought and without...
When the mind is neither restrained nor controlled, but rests naturally as it is, this is called the original ground of the mind. Entering the ocean of Buddha-wisdom, it is serene and immutable;
this is the bliss of the wondrous Dharma. Encountering objects with sovereign ease, it accords with the purity of the fundamental nature;
thus, adorned by these four virtues as jewels, one is the Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment, ascending to the summit of the Sumeru of the Dharma.

At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, throughout every world in the ten directions—in each and every Jambudvīpa of the four continents—the Tathāgata was seen sitting beneath a tree.
In each instance, there were bodhisattvas who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength, expounded the Dharma;
none of them failed to feel as though they were constantly in the presence of the Buddha.

Within this text, these six chapters are divided into two parts. The first two chapters constitute the preliminary preparation (*upāya*), while the latter four chapters constitute the actual exposition of the assembly.
Within the former [two], the first two consist solely of the causal process; the chapter on "Verses of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra*) possesses a dual significance:

first, it is the preliminary preparation, referring to the transformational master responding to the capacities of the audience in the preceding chapter; second, it is the assistance to the transformation, consisting of the praise of the Buddha.
Because the Dharma is expounded only when the primary [teacher] and the retinue are perfectly complete, the teachings of the three heavens all include verses of praise.
This is to reveal that the three stages of worthiness (trīṇi śaikṣāṇi) all possess distinctions based upon the Buddha’s wisdom, for apart from the Tathāgata’s wisdom, they have no self-nature.
Now, the first chapter is divided into ten sections: first, the simultaneous appearance of the wooden assembly; second, ascending without departing; third, each seeing [the assembly].

1. The Buddha arrives. 2. Each of the four [assemblies] decorates their respective palace thrones. 3. All five [groups] come together to invite the Buddha. 4. They all enter the palace simultaneously.

5. Musical instruments are silenced at once. 6. Each reflects upon their past causes. 7. They collectively praise the Tathāgata. 8. The palaces all become vast, magnificent, and pure. Regarding the phrase "at that time":
it refers to the time of the previous two assemblies, when the primary teachers and their retinues were gathered together to fully expound the teachings of those two assemblies.
This is the method [of the teaching]. Now, this "Clarifying Pervasiveness" (ming bian) is the first of the ten layers of exposition.
Regarding the ascent without separation, the commentary (*shu*) provides several interpretations.
At that time, the World-Honored One, without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree, ascended to the palace of Śakra on Mount Sumeru;
he ascended a second time while remaining immovable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw the Buddha approaching from afar before the Palace of Supreme Excellence.
A third time each [of the gods] saw the Buddha approaching;
he immediately used his supernatural powers to adorn this palace and prepared the Lion Throne of the Universal Radiance Treasury. That throne was entirely...
It was composed of exquisite jewels; ten thousand tiers rose up in supreme adornment. Ten thousand golden nets covered it from above.
Ten thousand kinds of curtains and ten thousand kinds of canopies were arranged in rows all around. Ten thousand silken fabrics formed hanging streamers.
Ten thousand pearl necklaces were interlaced everywhere. Ten thousand garments were spread upon the seats. Ten thousand devas...
Ten thousand Brahmā kings surrounded him from before and behind, and ten thousand rays of light shone resplendently.
Each of the fourth [assembly] adorned their palace seats.
At that time, Śakra, having respectfully prepared a seat for the Tathāgata, bowed with his body curved and palms joined, paying homage toward the Buddha.
And he spoke these words: "Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
We pray only that you will take pity on us and dwell in this palace."
Fifth, he invited the Buddha to reside in the palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted his invitation and entered the Palace of Sublime Victory. It was likewise so in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Sixth, they entered the hall simultaneously.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the musical sounds within the various palaces naturally ceased.
Seventh, the music ceased.
He immediately recollected the various roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke in verse.

This eighth [section] concerns each one recollecting their past causes and attaining the benefit of wisdom. Once distracted perceptions have ceased and supreme virtue manifests before him, he remains tranquil and free from discursive thought, giving rise to the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
As for "roots of goodness," this refers to the ten Buddhas mentioned below who once entered this hall and heard [the teachings].
Because it is an offering of the Dharma, and because it also manifests that one’s own mind-nature is identical to that of the Buddhas of the past:
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata, endowed with great compassion, The most supreme among all auspicious things— That Buddha once entered this hall; Therefore, this place is the most auspicious.”
Kanakamuni, whose vision is unimpeded, is the most supreme among all auspicious ones;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
Kāśyapa, who is like a mountain of gold, is the most supreme among all auspicious ones.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was free from the three stains; among all that is auspicious, he is supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Śikhin was free from conceptual discrimination; among all auspicious things, he was supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was like the full moon; among all auspicious things, he was supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Puṣya, who has realized the supreme truth, is the most unsurpassed among all that is auspicious;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Tiṣya possesses unimpeded eloquence; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Buddha Padmottara is pure and stainless; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Great Radiance of Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, the unsurpassed among all that is auspicious— That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In this world-system, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by means of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, praised the merits of the ten Buddhas in verse.
Likewise, the Śakra Kings of all the world-systems in the ten directions also praised the merits of the Buddhas in this same manner.
The ninth section is the "Joint Praise of the Tathāgatas. This means that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught the Dharma of the Ten Abodes at this very place.
The reason for praising these ten Buddhas specifically is to signify the teaching of the Ten Abodes and their inexhaustibility.

Each of the ten praised Buddhas is cited for one specific virtue; finally, it is concluded universally by stating: "In this world, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven praises the merits of the ten Buddhas."
The same was true for the worlds of the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Hall of Sublime Victory and sat cross-legged; suddenly, this hall became vast, spacious, and capacious.
Just as it is with the various abodes of the celestial hosts, so it is throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
each of the tenth halls is vast and expansive. As soon as the Tathāgata enters a hall, his awakened wisdom manifests before him, and suddenly it becomes vast and expansive.
Thus, body and mind are boundless. From "the ten directions below" onwards, the connection is established as inexhaustible.
Regarding the fourteenth chapter, the "Verse Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru":

as for the initial intent [of this section], having already clarified how the Lord of Transformation responds to sentient beings' needs, it now distinguishes the auxiliary manifestations that offer praise and glorification, and is about to expound upon the abiding [of the Dharma].
Section One: First, the presentation of the essential nature. Nature is precisely Buddha-wisdom; this chapter follows because it first extols the Tathāgata.
Second, regarding the explanation of the title: "Sumeru" refers to a location. It is called "Praise of the Buddha’s Virtues. Since there is praise based upon a location, this name is established.

Furthermore, "Summit" (mūrdhan) is used as praise to distinguish it from other locations. Third, regarding the central theme: it consists of the assembly of the multitude, the emission of light, and the verses of praise.

The thesis (*siddhānta*) is to establish the correct teaching as the goal (*prayojana*). Furthermore, the Buddha’s virtues are revealed as the thesis, while causing [beings] to know the abiding essence is the goal.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields, there came one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
They gathered there, their names being: Bodhisattva Dharmamati, Sarvamati, Vijayamati, Guṇamati, Vīryamati, Sumati, Jñānamati, Bhūtamati, Anuttaramati, Dṛḍhamati.
The lands from which they had come were as follows: [The land of] Cause...
In the world of Tāra-flower, the world of Padma-flower, the world of Jewel-flower, the world of Utpala-flower, the world of Vajra-flower,
the world of Exquisite Fragrance-flower, the world of Pleasing-flower, the world of Aruṇa-flower, the world of Nārada-flower,
and the world of Ākāśa-flower, [beings] each cultivated the pure life of brahmacarya in the presence of their respective Buddhas.

They proceeded. These were the Buddhas known as Viśiṣṭacandra, Akṣayacandra, Acalacandra, Vāyucandra, Jala-candra, Vimukticandra, Anuttaracandra, Nakṣatracandra, Viśuddhacandra, and Prabhāsvaracandra.
When these bodhisattvas had arrived at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and, according to the directions from which they had come, each manifested transformations.
Upon the lion throne of the Vairocana-garbha, he sat cross-legged.
Just as the bodhisattvas had gathered upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in this world-system, so it was in all world-systems;
the names of those bodhisattvas, their worlds, and the names of their Buddhas were all identical and without distinction.

Fourth, the explanation of the text. This chapter is divided into three sections: first, the section on the assembly; second, the section on the emission of light; and third, the section on the verses of praise.
Now, regarding the initial section on the assembly, there are ten points of correspondence: first, the correspondence of the gathering, as it occurs entirely through the Buddha’s power;
second, the correspondence of the leaders, as they are all great bodhisattvas; third, the correspondence of the retinues, as each is accompanied by the Buddha...

1. The number of buddha-fields [from which they come] is the same, being as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field. 2. The magnitude of the lands from which they come is the same, being from beyond as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields.
3. The names of the dharmas they represent are the same, for "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*).

4. The names of the worlds from which they come are the same, all being named "Flower" (*puṣpa*). 5. The Buddhas they serve are the same, all being named "Moon" (*candra*); the moon symbolizes the Buddha-fruit within these stages.
1. Wisdom illuminates and darkness ceases; its grace is refreshing and cool, for it pervades all suitable vessels. 2. Eight directions extend reverence;
their majestic deportment abides in the same essence, each dwelling in its own quarter. 3. Ten directions are bound together as one;
whether lands or persons, they all universally encompass the Dharma-realm, which is infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrously colored light from his two toes, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions;
from the summit of Mount Sumeru down to the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, the Buddha and the great assembly were all clearly manifested therein.
Second, from the section "At that time" onwards is the division on the Tathāgata emitting light. "From the two toes of his feet" means that the toes of the feet leave the ground;

having attained the power of mastery, he establishes a position from which there is no regression, and his movement is constant. The number [of rays] exceeds the previous count by a factor of one thousand.
Because the marks manifest and reveal [the truth], they are called "wondrous colors. They shine universally throughout the ten directions, revealing the single assembly of the Buddha.

When light illuminates all things, all things are likewise so; they overlap without obstruction, such that there is nothing that does not see one another, forming a great assembly of perfect clarity within the single Dharma-realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Buddha emits pure light, Universally revealing the Teacher of the World, Dwelling within the Palace of Supreme Excellence Upon the summit of Sumeru, King of Mountains.
All the Śakra-devānām-indras Invite the Buddha to enter their palaces.
With all ten wondrous verses, they praised all the Tathāgatas.
Within those great assemblies, all the hosts of bodhisattvas had come from the ten directions; having manifested seats, they sat down peacefully.
All the bodhisattvas in those assemblies were named exactly as we are, and the worlds from which they came—
The names are likewise so; the World-Honored Ones of their original lands all share these same titles.
Each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas, has purely cultivated the supreme practice.
O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery: throughout every Jambudvīpa, it is said that the Buddha is therein.
We now behold the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; so it is in all ten directions as well.

By the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, in every single world-system, beings who have resolved their minds to seek the path of the Buddha cultivate the practices of enlightenment based on such vows. The Buddha, by means of various bodies...
Wandering throughout all worlds, unimpeded within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is no one able to measure you.
Your light of wisdom shines eternally and universally, extinguishing the darkness of the world entirely. Since you are peerless in every respect, how could you ever be fathomed?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvajñāna, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to behold the Tathāgata constantly for hundreds of thousands of eons, If one does not rely upon the meaning of ultimate reality when contemplating the Savior of the World,
That person grasps at various signs, thereby increasing the web of delusion and confusion."
Bound within the prison of birth and death, blind and obscured, they do not see the Buddha. One should contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent;

Just as their characteristics of arising and ceasing are merely spoken of by way of provisional names, All phenomena are without arising, and all phenomena are without cessation. If one can understand in this way, [one attains liberation].
The Buddhas are ever manifest before one; the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Without grasping and without seeing—this emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha, which cannot be conceived or measured.
If one knows that the essential nature of all phenomena is thus, such a person will not be defiled or attached by afflictions.
Ordinary beings perceive all phenomena And merely revolve according to their marks.

Not understanding that phenomena are markless, they do not see the Buddha; The Muni is beyond the three times, Fully endowed with all marks, Abiding in non-abiding, Universal and immovable. Thus I contemplate all phenomena.
All have attained clear understanding; now they behold the Tathāgata.
There is no doubt whatsoever regarding the Dharma-wisdom previously taught by the Tathāgata concerning the true nature of reality.
From that, I have understood that Bodhi is inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānavara, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s great wisdom is rare and without peer;
All the worlds cannot reach it through thought. Ordinary beings observe falsely, Grasping at signs in an irrational manner.”

The Buddha is free from all signs; he cannot be seen by them. Those who are deluded and ignorant falsely grasp at the characteristics of the five aggregates and fail to understand their true nature. Such people do not see the Buddha.
One who thoroughly understands that all phenomena have no inherent existence—thus comprehending the nature of dharmas—sees the Buddha.
Thus one beholds Vairocana; Because of the preceding five aggregates, The subsequent aggregates arise in succession.
By understanding this nature, One sees the Buddha, inconceivable.
Just as a jewel in the dark cannot be seen without a lamp, If the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, Though one possesses wisdom, it cannot be understood.
Just as when the eyes are clouded by cataracts, one does not see pure and wondrous forms, so too a mind that is impure does not perceive the Buddhas’ teachings.
Furthermore, just as the bright, clear sun cannot be seen by the blind, those whose minds lack wisdom will never behold the Buddhas;
yet if one can remove the cataracts from the eyes, [one shall see].
Having abandoned the perception of form and not seeing any phenomena, one then attains the vision of the Tathāgata.
All the wisdom previously taught by the Buddhas— the Dharma of their Bodhi— I heard from him and thereby attained the vision of Vairocana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All phenomena lack true reality, yet people falsely grasp at the appearance of reality. For this reason, all ordinary beings wander through the prison of birth and death.
Regarding the teachings expressed through words and speech, those of small wisdom engage in false discrimination."
Therefore, obstacles arise; they do not understand their own minds. If one cannot understand one's own mind, how can one know the right path?
Due to their inverted wisdom, they increase all evils;
not seeing the emptiness of all phenomena, they constantly undergo the suffering of birth and death. Such people have not yet attained [liberation].
Because of the pure Dharma-eye, I formerly underwent manifold sufferings; this was due to my failure to see the Buddha.
Therefore, one should purify the Dharma-eye and observe that which ought to be seen.
If one attains the vision of the Buddha with a mind free from grasping, such a person is able to see the Dharma as the Buddha knows it.
If one sees the true Dharma of the Buddha, one is called a person of great wisdom.
Such a person possesses the pure eye capable of observing the world: non-seeing is itself seeing; it is able to see all phenomena.
If there is a view regarding phenomena, this is actually no seeing at all—the nature of all dharmas is thus.
Neither arising nor ceasing—how marvelous is the Great Teacher!
The Sublime Wisdom has already declared: "That which the Tathāgata realized, I have heard from him;
thus may we know the true nature of the Buddha."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"If one dwells in conceptual discrimination, Then the pure eye is destroyed.
Ignorance and false views increase, And one never sees the Buddhas. If one can understand false dharmas As they truly are, without inversion,"
Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true, one sees the Buddha and is thus purified. Where there is seeing, there is defilement;
this is not yet true seeing. To be far removed from all views—in this way one sees the Buddha.
