The worldly methods of speech are the false discriminations of sentient beings; know that all in the world is unborn.
This is indeed seeing the world; if one sees by seeing the world, then that seeing is the mark of the world as it truly is, equal and without difference. This is called the true seer.
If one sees with such equality and without discriminating among things, this seeing is free from all delusions; being untainted, one attains mastery.
All the various conceptual phenomena revealed by the Buddhas are entirely ungraspable, for their nature is pure.
The nature of phenomena is primordially pure; like space, it is without marks and cannot be described by anyone.
The wise contemplate in this way, remaining far removed from all conceptualizations.
Not delighting in any phenomena, there is likewise nothing to be cultivated here.
One who can see the Great Muni as described by Guṇamati is called a seer of the Buddha; for the essential nature of all conditioned formations is utterly quiescent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprajñā, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"How marvelous! The great heroes, the immeasurable Tathāgatas, Whose stainless minds are liberated—having crossed over themselves, they can deliver others.
I behold the Lamp of the World, who perceives reality without inversion."
As seen by those who have accumulated wisdom over immeasurable eons, all the activities of ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly reach exhaustion; their nature is like space.
Therefore, it is said that there is no exhaustion, yet even this "no exhaustion" is something that cannot be expressed, for its intrinsic nature is inexhaustible.
One may attain inconceivable exhaustion within the inexhaustible that has been taught; yet there are no sentient beings to be found, for such is the nature of sentient beings.
Thus one sees the Great Renowned One. To speak of "seeing" is called "non-seeing," and to speak of "sentient beings" is likewise so.
Whether it be seeing or sentient beings, one thoroughly understands them to be without intrinsic nature.
The capacity to see, that which is seen, and the seer—all are completely eliminated.

One who does not destroy the true Dharma understands the Buddha; if a person understands the Buddha and the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they can illuminate the world, just as the Buddha Vairocana, the Perfectly Awakened One, has skillfully revealed.
The Great Being of diligence and wisdom expounds the path of purity of the single dharma;
whether phenomena exist or do not exist, all such conceptualizations are extinguished. Thus one is able to see the Buddha abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Receiving the teaching of the Most Victorious One, The light of wisdom was immediately born. It shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, And one sees all Buddhas therein.
Within this, there is not the slightest thing; There is only the existence of provisional names."
If one calculates that there is a self or a person, one enters upon a perilous path.
Ordinary worldlings who cling to grasping reckon the body to be truly existent; yet the Tathāgata is not an object of grasping.
Those who lack the eye of wisdom will never be able to see this person, for they cannot perceive the Buddha throughout immeasurable kalpas.
One wanders through the ocean of birth and death; where there is contention, one speaks of birth and death.
Where there is no contention, that is nirvāṇa. Yet both birth and death and nirvāṇa are ultimately unattainable.
If one pursues these provisional names and becomes attached to these two dharmas, such a person does not accord with reality and fails to know the sublime path of the sages.
If one gives rise to such conceptions as "this is a Buddha" or "this is the most supreme," these are inverted views and not the true meaning;
thus one cannot see the Perfectly Awakened One. One who can know this true essence—the characteristic of quiescent *tathatā*—sees the Honored One of Perfect Awakening.
He transcends the path of language; all dharmas are spoken through words.
The true nature cannot be manifested; only through equanimity can it be seen. As with the Dharma, so too is the Buddha:
perfectly awakened regarding the past, the future, and the present, having forever severed the root of conceptual discrimination, he is therefore called a Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Real Wisdom, having heard the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to hear the names of the Buddhas;
Better not to experience immeasurable bliss than to fail to hear the names of the Buddhas. Therefore, in the past, throughout countless kalpas, I underwent suffering."
Wandering through the cycle of birth and death, they have not heard the name of the Buddha;
They do not perceive phenomena erroneously, but realize them as they truly are. Free from all signs of combination, this is called unsurpassed awakening.
The present is not a combination, and the past and future are likewise so; All phenomena are without marks.
This is the true body of the Buddha; if one can contemplate in this way, then one sees the profound meaning of all phenomena, the true mark of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
Seeing reality as it truly is, and not seeing the unreal as real— one who has such ultimate understanding is therefore called a Buddha.
The Buddha-dharma cannot be awakened to; realizing this is called awakening to the Dharma. All Buddhas cultivate in this way:
not a single dharma can be apprehended. Knowing that by virtue of the one there is the many, and knowing that by virtue of the many there is the one, all dharmas have no basis;
they arise merely from combination, with neither an agent nor an object of action.
Arising solely from the perception of karma—how can it be known to be thus?
Because nothing else exists apart from this, all phenomena are without abiding; no fixed location can be found.
The Buddhas dwell herein, ultimately unshakable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-mati, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Mahāsattva, Who has distanced himself from the notion of sentient beings;
Because none can surpass him, he is called 'Unsurpassed. The state attained by all Buddhas Is without fabrication and without discrimination."
The coarse does not exist, nor does the subtle; within the sphere of activity of all Buddhas, there is no calculation.
The Perfectly Awakened One is far removed from calculation; this is the true Dharma of the Buddha.
The light of the Tathāgata shines everywhere, extinguishing all darkness; yet this light has no illumination.
Nor is it without illumination; it is unattached to phenomena.
Without thought and without defilement, without dwelling and without location, it does not destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Within this, there is neither duality nor even unity. One who possesses great wisdom and sees clearly abides skillfully in accordance with reality.
In non-existence there is no duality, And even duality does not exist. That all in the three realms is empty—this is the vision of the Buddhas.
Ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding. The Buddha causes them to abide in the True Dharma;
All phenomena have no place of abiding. Awakening to this, one sees one’s own body: It is no-body, yet it is called "body."
Neither arising nor appearing, without body and without vision—this is the supreme body of the Buddha, as taught by the one of true wisdom.
Such is the nature of the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas; whoever hears this Dharma shall obtain the pure eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"How magnificent is the Great Radiance, The valiant and supreme being! For the sake of benefiting the deluded multitudes, he has arisen in the world.
With a heart of great compassion, the Buddha surveys all sentient beings."
Seeing those currently within the three realms of existence, Circulating and undergoing manifold sufferings— Except for the Fully Awakened One,
the Honored and Virtuous Guide, Among all devas and humans, there is none who can provide protection. If Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and the like Did not appear in this world, There would not be a single sentient being...

And they are able to attain peace and happiness; The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Along with the assembly of worthy sages, appears in the world To bestow happiness upon sentient beings. If one sees the Tathāgata, one gains great and wholesome benefit;
To hear the Buddha’s name and give rise to faith Is to be a stūpa for the world.
We have seen the World-Honored One, And having gained great benefit, Upon hearing such a wondrous Dharma, we shall all attain the Buddha-way.
All the bodhisattvas of the past, Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, attained the pure eye of wisdom;
They comprehended the realm of all Buddhas, And now they behold Vairocana.
My pure faith increases all the more; the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless.
Even if the Bodhisattvas such as Vyākarana-jñāna-ākṣaya and I, Dṛḍhamati, were to speak for countless billions of kalpas, we could not exhaustively describe it.
Third, at that time, the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions led by Dharmamati offer verses of praise. This consists of ten sections:

the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. Since Dharmamati is the master of the teaching, this section provides a general account of the events and meanings from beginning to end of this assembly and generally manifests the Buddha’s virtues;
the other nine sections extol the Buddha’s distinct, particular virtues. Thus, both the general and the specific together reveal [the Buddha’s majesty].
The Tathāgata’s unimpeded assembly: the names of these ten bodhisattvas also symbolize the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The teachings they expound symbolize the progressive advancement through those stages.
Now, first is Dharmamati of the East, because he has a comprehensive understanding of the Buddha-dharma.
Next is Sarvajñā of the South, because he understands the true nature of all phenomena due to the stage of the Pure Ground (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*). Then there is Vijayamati of the West.

Because they have purified their minds through the realization that the Buddha’s supreme wisdom accords with emptiness; because the one in the north, Guṇamati (Virtue-Wisdom), was born into the family of the Buddhas and skillfully understands the virtues of the Buddha;
because the one in the northeast, Vīramati (Diligence-Wisdom), diligently contemplates the ultimate truth and accumulates immeasurable goodness while remaining non-abiding;
and because the one in the southeast, Sumati (Good Wisdom), has accomplished *prajñā*.
That a mirror remains unmoved may be called "skillful. Regarding the wisdom of the southwest: it is named "wisdom" because its decisive judgment is unmoving.
Regarding the true wisdom of the northwest: it is called "true wisdom" because the mind is not inverted. Regarding the unsurpassed wisdom of the nadir:
it is called "unsurpassed" because it arises from the teaching of the Dharma King and is destined to succeed to the rank of a Buddha.

As for "Firm Wisdom" (Dṛḍhamati) in the zenith, because his power of wisdom has achieved invincibility, each of these bodhisattvas from the ten directions recites ten verses to praise the general and specific virtues of the Buddha.
The meaning of these verses is subtle and profound; there is an extensive commentary (*ṭīkā*) that explains them in detail.
Here, I have taken only the main outlines and have not recorded them in full.
Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes (*Daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the intent of this chapter’s introduction: since the preceding causes and conditions have already been clarified, it is now appropriate to manifest the main body of the teaching; thus, this chapter follows.

Furthermore, whereas the previous section distinguished the virtues of the Buddha as the basis (*āśraya*), this section distinguishes the ten abodes as that which depends upon it (*āśrita*); thus, this chapter follows. As for the explanation of the name: wisdom (*prajñā*)...
Abiding in principle, one attains the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, it is called "abiding. This Dharma of the ten abidings consists of four sections:
namely, the ten abidings, the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the merit of the initial resolve for enlightenment, and the illumination of the Dharma. These four sections are divided into two parts:

the first three sections pertain to the practice and virtues of the stage of abiding, while the final section pertains to superior progress toward the subsequent stages. In the preceding assembly, there was no superior progress; however—

This is because it is the stage of the means for proceeding, not yet having achieved the stage [of the actual ground]. Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) constitutes this stage; there is no further "proceeding" [beyond it].

Since the completion of the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) serves as the overall means for proceeding to the grounds, it also reveals the absence of conceptual differentiation and the departure from the characteristics of proceeding.
Now, the first chapter distinguishes the stages; the next chapter distinguishes the practices; and the final chapter distinguishes the virtues. The first is also termed "Understanding.
The text of this initial chapter is divided into seven sections: first, the section on samādhi; second, the section on empowerment; third, the section on arising; and fourth, the fundamental section.
The fifth is the section of exposition; the sixth is the section of realization; and the seventh is the section of verses in reiteration. Regarding the first:
at that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, entered the bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means.
This is the first section on Samādhi. Question: For what reason does one enter meditative concentration? Answer: Briefly stated, there are six reasons.

First, because this samādhi is the very essence (dharmatā) of the Dharma. Second, because it is not taught unless it has been realized. Third, to demonstrate that this Dharma is not an object of discursive thought or intellectual calculation.
Fourth, to observe the capacities of sentient beings and examine the Dharma accordingly. Fifth, to receive the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Buddha. Sixth, to perfect the ritual procedures (vidhi).

By the power of samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Dharmamati. They appeared before him and addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to enter this bodhisattva’s immeasurable..."
He then entered samādhi. "Good son, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-fields, have together empowered you through their spiritual powers.

Furthermore, by virtue of the power of the vows made by the Tathāgata Vairocana in the past, the power of his majestic majesty, and the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, you have entered this samādhi and are enabled to preach the Dharma for the sake of increase."
Because of the Buddha’s wisdom; because of penetrating deeply into the dharma-realm; because of thoroughly understanding the realm of sentient beings;
because of unimpeded entry; because of unobstructed conduct; because of attaining peerless skillful means; because of entering the nature of all-knowledge;
because of awakening to all phenomena; because of knowing all faculties; and because of being able to uphold and expound all dharmas—namely, the arousal of all bodhisattvas.
"Ten Abodes. Good son, you should expound this Dharma by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.

At that time, all the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dharmamati unimpeded wisdom, non-attached wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, non-deluded wisdom, non-differentiated wisdom, non-failing wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, untiring wisdom, and invincible wisdom. Why was this?
Therefore, because the nature of this samādhi-power is such, at that time each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.

This was the second stage of empowerment (*anugraha*). First, they empowered him by commanding him to preach the Dharma; this was the causal condition for the empowerment. Subsequently, it served to increase [his merit].

The eleven phrases beginning with "The Buddha’s wisdom" constitute the purpose of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Next, the passage beginning with "You should now, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound this Dharma" constitutes the characteristics of the empowerment.
First, the oral empowerment encourages the preaching in order to increase eloquence; next, the mental empowerment beginning with "arousing the ten kinds of wisdom" increases wisdom;
finally, the physical empowerment of touching the crown of the head increases majestic authority.
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati then arose from meditative absorption.
This third section on arising is summarized by four points: first, because the affairs of samādhi have been completed; second, because he has already attained supreme power;
third, because the time for teaching has arrived; and fourth, because meditative concentration is devoid of verbal expression.
He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of the Buddha, the dwelling place of a bodhisattva is vast, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space.
Sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva dwells in the household of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. I shall now explain that dwelling of the bodhisattvas, O sons of the Buddha."
There are ten stages in which a bodhisattva abides, which have been taught, will be taught, and are now being taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten? They are: the stage of initial resolve; the stage of purifying the ground; the stage of cultivation; the stage of noble birth; the stage of possessing great skillful means;
the stage of the correct mind; the stage of non-retrogression; the stage of the youthful prince; the stage of the Dharma prince; and the stage of consecration.
This is called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva, as taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
In the fourth primary section, there are three parts: first, the statement that "the dwelling place is vast," etc., which generally reveals the essential nature and characteristics;
second, the statement "there are ten kinds of dwellings," etc., which introduces the subject to be explained; and third, the inquiry "What are these ten? followed by the enumeration of their names.

Regarding this stage of abiding being called a "dwelling place": if considered in terms of its preeminence, one abides in *tathatā* (suchness) by means of profound *prajñā* (wisdom), and it is precisely through this that it becomes the dwelling place for practice and vows.
If considered from a general perspective, both abide within the house of the aforementioned three types of bodhicitta;
in the Sanskrit original, this is "house" (*kula*), which the older translations render as "lineage" (*gotra*). That is to say, the fourfold [lineage].

Among the [ten] lineages (*gotra*), this refers to the lineage of the cultivated seed (*abhyāsa-gotra*). It is because this family is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas that it is translated as "place of abiding" (*vihāra*).
There are many meanings in the commentary.

O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s stage of "Abiding in the Resolve" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*)? This Bodhisattva perceives the physical appearance of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to be upright and...
His physical marks and features are majestic and perfect; he is a joy for all to behold and is difficult to encounter. He possesses great power and majesty.
Whether they witness his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), hear his prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*), or listen to his instructions (*avavāda*);

or whether they see sentient beings undergoing various intense sufferings, or hear of the vast Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata—they give rise to the bodhicitta and seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This Bodhisattva takes these ten kinds of difficulties as his object of focus.

Having attained the Dharma, one brings it forth from the mind. What are the ten? They are: the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the retribution of good and evil karma; the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings;
the knowledge of the differences in various inclinations; the knowledge of the differences in various elements; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations;
the knowledge of the meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; the unimpeded knowledge of past lives; and the unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye.

The wisdom that is unimpeded; the wisdom that universally exhausts the outflows (*āsrava*) of the three periods of time—these are the ten. Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.

What are these ten? They are: diligently making offerings to the Buddhas; delighting in dwelling within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); acting as a leader for the world to cause them to eliminate evil karma;
constantly practicing instruction through the supreme and wondrous Dharma; praising the unsurpassed Dharma; studying the merits of the Buddhas; and generating...
They are constantly sustained by the presence of all Buddhas. Through skillful means, they expound the samādhi of tranquility and praise the transcendence of the cycle of birth and death.
They act as a place of refuge for suffering sentient beings. Why is this?

It is because they desire to cause the bodhisattvas' minds to expand ever further within the Buddha-dharma, so that whatever Dharma they hear, they may immediately understand it through their own insight without depending on the instruction of others.

The following section is the fifth part, the actual exposition. Within the text, the "sections for exposition" constitute the aspects of practice (*ākāra*). This explanation of the ten dwellings (*daśavihāra*) is divided into ten segments.

In each segment, there is first a formal inquiry followed by an explanation. Within the explanations, one first clarifies the "abiding in one's own stage" (*svabhūmi*) and subsequently clarifies the "progressive advancement" (*viśeṣagamana*).
Furthermore, the former refers to the state of dwelling, while the latter refers to the initiation of practice. Now begins the first: the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).
From "seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One" down to "seeking all-knowledge," this clarifies the conditions for generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). There are ten kinds of conditions.
Following this, from "this bodhisattva takes the ten kinds of difficult-to-attain dharmas as objects," the text correctly clarifies the generation of the mind by taking these objects as its sphere.

While it was previously stated that one "seeks all-knowledge," here it clarifies that the ten kinds of knowledge are precisely what constitutes all-knowledge; this is exactly the object of focus (*ālambana*).

This is the stage [of the bodhisattva]. Next is the second superior practice, which encourages the study of the ten dharmas. This means that one who seeks a superior station should exhort themselves and also exhort others to study;
these are listed as ten types, which do not go beyond compassion and wisdom. Making offerings to the Buddha serves as the general [foundation].
Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" provides an inquiry and explanation: why must one study this? It is because it causes one to attain both the general and specific benefits.
It is distinct, superior, and vast. These distinct benefits all aspire toward future stages, because this understanding arises from within and does not depend on the instruction of others.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground? In this dwelling, the Bodhisattva generates ten kinds [of aspirations] toward all sentient beings.

Mind. What are the ten? They are: the mind of benefit, the mind of great compassion, the mind of happiness, the mind of peaceful abiding, the mind of pity, the mind of gathering, the mind of protection, the mind of regarding others as oneself, the mind of a teacher, and the mind of a guide. These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are the ten? They are: reciting and practicing, extensive learning, emptiness... [text continues]

Dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, drawing near to spiritual friends, speaking with harmony and joy, always knowing the proper time for speech, having no fear or timidity in mind, thoroughly understanding the meaning [of the teachings], practicing in accordance with the Dharma, remaining far removed from delusion and confusion, and abiding immovably. Why is this?

It is because one desires to cause the Bodhisattva to increase great compassion toward all sentient beings; such that upon hearing the Dharma, they immediately attain self-awakening and understanding without depending on others.

Because he teaches them, the second stage, the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-parikarma-vihāra*), first causes sentient beings to give rise to ten kinds of mind; this is their own portion (*svabhāga*). Next, he exhorts them to study ten dharmas;
this is the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*). Next, he raises the question: why must one study these dharmas? It is said that they are guided by wisdom.
Compassion. Because it causes [the practice] to become increasingly superior.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva’s stage of cultivation? This bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena through ten kinds of practices.
What are these ten? Namely: contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent; that all phenomena are suffering; that all phenomena...
All phenomena are empty. All phenomena are without self. All phenomena are without agency. All phenomena are without flavor.
All phenomena do not correspond to their names. All phenomena have no location. All phenomena are free from conceptual discrimination. All phenomena lack solidity.
These are the ten. Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are:
observing the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm; observing the earth-element, water-element, fire-element, and wind-element;
and observing the desire-realm, form-realm, and formless-realm. Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause the bodhisattva’s wisdom to be clear and lucid, so that there may be...
Because one attains self-understanding upon hearing the Dharma without relying on the instruction of others, the third [stage] is practice.
First, regarding the stage of self-benefit: the ten kinds of contemplation of all phenomena constitute the practice for guarding against afflictions (*kleśa*).

Next, the encouragement to study the ten kinds of dharmas—namely, the contemplation of sentient beings and so forth—constitutes the practice for guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), because of the Lesser Vehicle...

One does not seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), because there is no desire for extensive knowledge. The subsequent interrogation implies: "It would suffice merely to contemplate impermanence;

what need is there for extensive knowledge? The explanation implies: "Contemplating emptiness does not obstruct extensive existence; for when both nature and characteristics are understood, the wisdom that comprehends phenomena becomes increasingly clear."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of Noble Birth? This Bodhisattva is born from the holy teaching and accomplishes ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: never regressing from the presence of all Buddhas and generating profound pure faith.
Skillfully observing phenomena, they thoroughly understand sentient beings, lands, worlds, karmic actions, retributions, birth and death, and nirvana;
these are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are the ten? They are:
to thoroughly understand all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; and to cultivate and accumulate [the wisdom of] the past, future, and present...
All Buddha-dharmas. He fulfills all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present. He thoroughly understands the equality of all Buddhas.
Why? Because he desires to advance toward equality of mind throughout the three periods of time;
whatever Dharma he hears, he immediately attains self-enlightenment without relying on the instruction of others.
The fourth stage is the Dwelling of Noble Birth (*janmakula-vihāra*). First, the explanation of its name: it is called "noble birth" because one is born from the holy teaching;
through the permeation of extensive learning, the outflowing (*niṣyanda*) untainted (*anāsrava*) teachings give rise to wisdom. Because one is born into the family of Bodhi, it is named "Noble Birth.
Regarding the ten factors of the initial stage, as for the term "non-retrogression," since one has been born from the holy teaching, one accomplishes the four [factors].
Wisdom: because one does not regress from one’s own abiding place while teaching and transforming sentient beings. Next, one is exhorted to study the ten dharmas as a further advancement.
Subsequently, the underlying intent of the inquiry is: "Why must one contemplate the three periods of time? The explanation of this intent is:

desiring to advance to the subsequent stage, where the ultimate and the conventional are equal, one contemplates the three periods of time universally without distinction; only then does one come to know their equality.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the perfection of skillful means?

It is when all the roots of goodness cultivated by this bodhisattva are for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings,
showing compassion to all sentient beings, liberating all sentient beings, and causing all sentient beings to be free from all calamities and misfortunes.
To cause all sentient beings to emerge from the suffering of birth and death; to cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith;
to cause all sentient beings to attain complete subduing; and to cause all sentient beings to fully realize nirvana.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are: knowing that sentient beings are infinite; knowing sentient beings...
Immeasurable. He knows that sentient beings are innumerable; he knows that sentient beings are inconceivable; he knows that sentient beings have immeasurable forms;
he knows that sentient beings are unfathomable; he knows that sentient beings are empty; he knows that sentient beings are without activity; he knows that sentient beings possess nothing;

he knows that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature. Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause their minds to become further increased and more excellent, so that they may be without [attachment].
Being free from attachment, one immediately attains self-understanding upon hearing the Dharma without depending on the instruction of others;

thus, there is the fifth dwelling, which is fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*). What are called the ten minds of one's own level (*svabhāga*) are also skillful means, followed by the stage of further advancement (*viśeṣa-gamana*).
The ten dharmas for encouraging study are likewise fully present. Next, the meaning of the inquiry and explanation is stated:

it is to simultaneously clarify that the profound nature and the vast characteristics mutually penetrate, becoming increasingly superior; such that form and substance are both forgotten, and all is free from defiled attachment, thereby accomplishing *prajñā*.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Abiding in the Rectified Mind? This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings and remains steadfast and unmoving in mind.
What are these ten? They are as follows: hearing praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, his mind remains steadfast and unmoving regarding the Buddha-dharma.

Hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, his mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma. Hearing praise or disparagement of a bodhisattva, his mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the practices performed by a bodhisattva, his mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing it said that sentient beings are finite or infinite, his mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Unshakable. Hearing it said that sentient beings have defilements or are free from defilements, his mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing it said that sentient beings are easy to deliver or difficult to deliver, his mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma.

Hearing it said that the dharma-realm is finite or infinite, his mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma. Hearing it said that the dharma-realm undergoes formation and destruction, regarding the Buddha-... [his mind remains fixed and unshakable].
The mind is settled and immovable within the Dharma. Upon hearing that the Dharma-realm may either exist or not exist, the mind remains settled and immovable within the Buddha-Dharma.
These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: all dharmas are signless; all dharmas are without essence; all dharmas are not to be cultivated; all dharmas...
There is nothing that exists. All phenomena lack reality; all phenomena are empty; all phenomena are without intrinsic nature;
all phenomena are like illusions; all phenomena are like dreams; all phenomena are without discrimination. Why is this?

It is because he wishes to cause his mind to further advance toward the attainment of the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Upon hearing any teaching, he immediately attains realization for himself.

Because understanding does not depend on the instruction of others, there is the sixth stage, the Abiding in Right Mind (*samyaktva-cittotpāda-vihāra*). Initially, regarding the ten minds of self-perfection (*svabhāva*), because one internally achieves *prajñā*, which is the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), they are all immovable;
thus it is called "Right Mind. Next, regarding the superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*), one is exhorted to study the ten dharmas, which encompass both hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).

[The text] explains: "Next, the inquiry and explanation state: 'This is like the Patience in Accordance (anulomikī-kṣānti). Because one desires non-retrogression in the subsequent stage and possesses patience, one does not regress;
this is precisely the Patience of Non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Non-retrogression? This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of dharmas and remains firm and unshakable.'"
[They] do not regress. What are these ten? They are: hearing that there is a Buddha or that there is no Buddha, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma;

hearing that there is the Dharma or that there is no Dharma, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma; hearing that there is a bodhisattva or that there is no bodhisattva, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there is the practice of a bodhisattva or that there is no practice of a bodhisattva, [their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma].

They do not regress from their central resolve. Upon hearing that there are bodhisattvas who practice for transcendence or those who do not practice for transcendence, they do not regress from their resolve regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Upon hearing that there were Buddhas in the past or that there were no Buddhas in the past, they do not regress from their resolve regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Upon hearing that there will be Buddhas in the future or that there will be no Buddhas in the future, they do not regress from their resolve regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that there is a Buddha in the present or that there is no Buddha in the present, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that the wisdom of the Buddha is finite or that the wisdom of the Buddha is infinite, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma.

Hearing that the three periods of time have a single characteristic or that the three periods of time do not have a single characteristic, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma. These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, this is the bodhisattva...
One should encourage the study of ten kinds of vast dharmas. What are these ten? They are: teaching that the one is the many; teaching that the many are the one;
the letter following the meaning; the meaning following the letter; non-existence being existence; existence being non-existence;

the signless being the sign; the sign being the signless; the absence of intrinsic nature being intrinsic nature; and intrinsic nature being the absence of intrinsic nature. Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause [wisdom] to increase.

One advances toward all phenomena with the excellent ability to transcend them; because one immediately attains self-understanding regarding whatever Dharma is heard, without depending on the instruction of others, this is the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*).
Regarding the fact that the ten qualities of this stage are all described as "non-retrogressive," it is because one has already entered this level.
It is "non-arising," because one knows that the Dharma heard is ultimately empty. Furthermore, in the preceding stage, one encounters phenomena to enter into principle, causing the mind not to waver;

now, one contemplates both phenomena and principle simultaneously, yet the mind does not regress. In the subsequent stage, one proceeds from principle toward phenomena, as the practice follows phenomena alone until it becomes fully matured.
For this reason, in the preceding stage, one merely endures praise or disparagement of the Triple Gem and so forth upon hearing them.
It was previously easy; now, hearing that there are both benefits and harms, one’s resolve deepens, and thus it becomes difficult to achieve patience. Therefore, it surpasses the preceding stage.

Furthermore, while the previous mention of "immovability" (akopya) referred merely to being able to rectify the mind, the present term "non-retrogression" (avaivartika) carries the sense of progressive advancement.

Next, the encouragement to study the ten kinds of vast dharmas constitutes "superior progress" (viśeṣagamana). Following this, in the section providing the analysis and explanation, the phrase "one who is well able to transcend" refers to this.
Because they do not sink into worldly affairs or principles, having attained mastery in the subsequent stage.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta)? This Bodhisattva dwells in ten kinds of activities.
What are these ten? They are: faultless conduct of body, faultless conduct of speech, faultless conduct of mind, taking birth according to one's will, and knowing...
They know the various desires of sentient beings; they know the various understandings of sentient beings; they know the various dispositions of sentient beings;
they know the various karmas of sentient beings; they know the formation and destruction of worlds; they possess mastery over the supernormal powers, their conduct being unimpeded—these are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten? They are: knowing all Buddhas...
They shake all buddha-fields, sustain all buddha-fields, contemplate all buddha-fields, and travel to all buddha-fields.
They wander through countless worlds, take possession of countless worlds, manifest bodies of sovereign transformation, and emit vast, all-pervading sounds.
In a single kṣaṇa, they serve and make offerings to countless Buddhas. Why is this?

Desiring to further advance toward skillfulness in all phenomena, so that whatever Dharma is heard may be understood by oneself without depending on the instruction of others—this is the eighth stage, the Youthful (Kumārabhūta).
Within this stage, the first three types of action (karma) are free from fault, and habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are forever abandoned; [only a Buddha]...
Attaining this occurs spontaneously and without effort; it is largely identical to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), as one is able to practice the untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore, there is no loss.

Next, the instruction to study the ten dharmas constitutes further progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) and is the practice of immovability (*acalā-caryā*). The first six [dharmas] concern mastery over the buddha-fields (*kṣetra-vaśitā*).

The latter four [perfections] consist of mastery over the three types of action (trikarma). These are identical to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), because one attains mastery over both form and the buddha-field.
Next, the text poses a question and provides an explanation: "It is for the sake of attaining skillfulness in entering the subsequent stage and for the sake of mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna*)."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Dharma Prince? This Bodhisattva skillfully knows ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten? They are:
skillful knowledge of the births of all sentient beings; skillful knowledge of the manifestation of all afflictions;

skillful knowledge of the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); skillful knowledge of the skillful means employed; skillful knowledge of immeasurable dharmas; and skillful understanding of all majestic demeanors... [and so forth].

...rituals. They are well-versed in the distinctions between worlds; they are well-versed in matters concerning the past and the future; they are well-versed in expounding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
and they are well-versed in expounding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten? Namely: skillfulness in the station of the Dharma King; the regulations and procedures of the station of the Dharma King; the station of the Dharma King...
Dwelling in the palace; entering the station of the Dharma King; observing the station of the Dharma King; the consecration of the Dharma King;
being sustained by the power of the Dharma King; the fearlessness of the Dharma King; the repose of the Dharma King; and the praise of the Dharma King. Why is this?

It is because one desires to further increase the mind so that it is without obstruction, such that whatever Dharma is heard is immediately understood through self-awakening, without depending on the instruction of others.

The ninth stage, the Abode of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputrabhūmi*). It begins with ten internal qualities: first, knowing the distinctions in the retributions received within the six destinies and four modes of birth;
continuing up to the tenth, knowing how to expound the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This is just as in the ninth stage, where one thoroughly understands the differences among the various conducts of sentient beings, and through teaching and taming them, proclaims the Dharma of the ultimate truth so that they may be disciplined.
This concludes the preceding section. Next, the ten dharmas are recommended for study as a means of superior progress.

The reason all are called "Dharma Kings" is that, having been referred to as "princes," they emulate the仪 (rites) of the Buddha and accord with the standards of his sons; furthermore, the term "position" (*sthāna*) refers precisely to their rank. The subsequent inquiry and explanation state:
it is because one wishes to cause them to advance further and attain the unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) of the subsequent rank.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Consecration? This Bodhisattva attains the accomplishment of ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten? They are: shaking countless worlds; illuminating countless worlds; sustaining countless worlds;
traveling to countless worlds; purifying countless worlds; and revealing [the Dharma] to countless assemblies.

Birth. Observing countless sentient beings, knowing the faculties of countless sentient beings, causing countless sentient beings to enter [the path], and causing countless sentient beings to be tamed—these are the ten.

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva’s body and bodily actions, their supernatural manifestations, their knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, and knowledge of the present, their accomplishment of buddha-fields, their mental sphere, and their wisdom.
Their spheres of activity are entirely unknowable; even Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Princes cannot know them.
Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study the ten kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas. What are these ten? They are: the wisdom of the three periods of time;

the wisdom of the Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom of unimpededness in the dharma-realm; the wisdom of the boundlessness of the dharma-realm; the wisdom that fills all worlds; and the universal... [text continues]
The wisdom that illumines all worlds; the wisdom that sustains all worlds; the wisdom that knows all sentient beings;
the wisdom that knows all phenomena; and the wisdom that knows the infinite Buddhas. Why is this?

It is because they desire to increase the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), so that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
The tenth stage, the Abode of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*). Within its preceding section, there are twenty phrases. The first ten phrases describe the qualities and functions accomplished therein;

the latter ten phrases praise its excellence as being difficult to fathom. Because this marks the conclusion of the stage, this additional section is added. The praises of its excellence all pertain to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Following this, there is an exhortation to study ten dharmas, all of which refer to the "wise one" (*jñānin*), meaning that one should study the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the Buddha.

The Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). One attains Buddhahood through the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) that fulfills this stage, because all other stages are subsumed within it and fully contained therein.

Next, the text raises a question and provides an explanation, stating: "As for the further study after accomplishing the ten superior knowledges, it is for the sake of desiring to attain the stage of the Buddha’s Knowledge of All Modes.
The section on the ten stages of abiding (*daśavihāra*) is concluded. Next, the proof is established.
At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways:
namely, they moved, moved everywhere, and moved all-pervasively; they rose, rose everywhere, and rose all-pervasively; they leaped, leaped everywhere, and leaped all-pervasively;
they quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked all-pervasively; they roared, roared everywhere, and roared all-pervasively; they crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed all-pervasively.

It rained celestial wonderful flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial flower garlands, celestial blended incenses, celestial precious robes, celestial clouds of jewels, and celestial ornaments.
Celestial music played spontaneously without being struck, emitting celestial radiance and sublime sounds.
Thus, atop Mount Sumeru within this world-system of four continents, above the palace of Śakra, the Dharma of the Ten Abodes was preached, manifesting various miraculous transformations.

All worlds throughout the ten directions are likewise so. Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, there came from each of the ten directions, passing through as many worlds as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.
They filled the ten directions and spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent! O Son of the Buddha, you have well explained."
This Dharma; we all share the same name, Dharmamati; the lands from which we come all share the same name, Dharmamegha;
the Tathāgatas in those lands are all named Subhadharma; and in the presence of our respective Buddhas, we also expound the Ten Abodes.
The assemblies, retinues, phrasing, and principles are in every respect identical, without increase or decrease. O Son of the Buddha, we have come here by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
This assembly shall bear witness for you. As it is in this assembly, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Sixth, the manifestation of reality through signs: first, auspicious omens appear to manifest reality—the earth quakes and offerings rain down; it is said that ten thousand Buddhas [appear].

"Buddha-field" (*kṣetra*) refers to those whose practice is still inferior. Thus, the passage "In this way, below, it is concluded that [this applies] throughout the ten directions" summarizes the universal application.

Next, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" introduces the Bodhisattvas who provide corroboration. "Speaking these words" means uttering words of praise and narration.

Next, the passage beginning with "We... cites others of the same kind to manifest the proof. Regarding the phrase "having the same names," it refers to the speakers, the locations, and the presiding masters of the assemblies. And...
The Dharma taught is identical in all cases, because this single assembly pervades all places. Because it is identical everywhere, it serves as a manifestation of realization;
thus it is said that just as it is in this assembly, so it is in all worlds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, surveyed the ten directions throughout the entire Dharma-realm and spoke in verse:
"I behold the most excellent wisdom-body, subtle and wondrous, Whose marks and embellishments are all perfectly complete."
Thus, with such reverence, it is extremely difficult to encounter; When a Bodhisattva courageously first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, they behold peerless great supernormal powers.

Hearing the teachings on the reading of minds and the instructions for sentient beings in all realms of existence regarding their immeasurable sufferings, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
I have heard that the Tathāgatas, the Universally Victorious Honored Ones, have fully accomplished all merits;
like space, they are without discrimination. By this, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind:
that the causes and effects of the three periods of time are called "possible," while our own inherent nature is called "impossible."
Desiring to fully comprehend the true meaning, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment;
desiring to fully comprehend, without exception, all virtuous and non-virtuous karmas throughout the past, future, and present worlds, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment.
Regarding all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis— whether defiled or pure, in their infinite varieties—
the Bodhisattva fully understands their entry, abiding, and emergence; by means of this, they first resolve their mind,
following the sharp or dull faculties of all sentient beings through such various powers of diligence.
Desiring to fully comprehend and discern them all, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
The various understandings of all sentient beings, and the differences in what their hearts delight in—
desiring to know such infinite things, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
The various realms of sentient beings are each distinct; Throughout all worlds, they are immeasurable.
Desiring to fully understand their essential nature, The Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Regarding all conditioned paths of practice, Each and every one has its destination.
Desiring to fully comprehend their true nature, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind;
All sentient beings in every world, drifting with their karma without a moment’s rest,
Desiring to obtain the divine eye to see them all clearly, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Whatever existed in past lives— such their essence and such their characteristics—
if one wishes to fully know those former abodes, the Bodhisattva generates this initial resolve; likewise,
regarding the various fetters and delusions of all sentient beings, their continuous manifestation and their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Desiring to fully comprehend them to their ultimate limit, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind;
following the various ways in which sentient beings are established,
he desires to know all their diverse discourses and paths of language according to worldly convention— this is why the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
All phenomena are beyond verbal expression; their nature is empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Desiring to fully comprehend this true meaning, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Desiring to cause all lands in the ten directions to tremble and to overturn all the great oceans, he thus first resolves his mind.
Possessing the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattva, by means of this, first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
wishing to emit light from a single pore, it universally illumines immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions,
awakening all beings within each ray of light— the Bodhisattva, by means of this, first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
Wishing to place all inconceivable Buddha-fields within the palm of one's hand without them being moved,
and understanding that all things are like illusions and transformations— by this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment;
wishing to place the sentient beings of immeasurable fields upon the tip of a single hair without any crowding.
Fully knowing that there is no person and no self, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
wishing to take a drop of seawater with a single hair and exhaust all the great oceans,
he fully discerns and knows their number— the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
All inconceivable world-systems, If ground down until not even a single particle remains,
And one wished to discern and know their total number— It is for this that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind.
Throughout the immeasurable eons of the past and future, Regarding all the signs of the formation and destruction of worlds.
Desiring to fully comprehend and exhaustively master them, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind;
desiring to know, without exception, all the dharmas of all the Tathāgatas of the three times,
as well as all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
All immeasurable and boundless worlds, wishing to lift them all up with a single hair,
and knowing their forms and characteristics exactly as they are— by means of this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment; likewise,
wishing to cause all the infinite and innumerable Cakravāḍa mountains to enter into a single pore.
Knowing all things, whether great or small, the Bodhisattva, by means of this initial resolve,
desires to use a single, wondrous, tranquil voice to universally respond to the various types of beings throughout the ten directions,
causing them all to be pure, clear, and fully understood; it is for this that the Bodhisattva generates this initial resolve.
The linguistic conventions of all sentient beings— To expound upon them with a single word, leaving nothing unexhausted;
Desiring to fully understand their intrinsic nature, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves to attain enlightenment.
There is no worldly sound or speech they do not produce, Causing all to understand and realize nirvana.
Desiring to obtain such a wondrous faculty of the tongue, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind;
desiring to cause all worlds throughout the ten directions— those undergoing formation and destruction—
to be seen and fully known as arising from conceptual discrimination, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, immeasurable Tathāgatas completely fill them;
desiring to fully understand the Buddha-dharma of those [Tathāgatas], the Bodhisattva thus first resolves the mind,
manifesting various transformations of infinite bodies, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds.
Desiring to fully comprehend all that arises from the mind, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the awakening mind.
Desiring to know, in a single thought-moment, the infinite and countless Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present worlds,
the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the awakening mind.
If one were to fully expound upon a single phrase of the Dharma, it would not be exhausted even in incalculable eons;
yet its words and meanings would each remain distinct. It is for this reason that Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds:
to follow all sentient beings throughout the ten directions according to their various modes of transmigration, birth, and cessation.
Desiring to clearly comprehend all in a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment;
Desiring to universally reach the ten directions with body, speech, and mental karma without obstruction,
and to understand that the three periods of time are all empty and quiescent, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment.

Once a bodhisattva has thus resolved their mind, they should be sent to the lands of the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas; by this means, they shall not regress from the bodhisattva path,
for with courageous vigor they seek the Buddha-way and dwell within birth and death without weariness.
I praise them for their sake so that they may practice accordingly; thus I cause them to have no regression.
Throughout the immeasurable lands of the worlds of the ten directions, I act as the honored lord within them all;
I speak thus to the bodhisattvas, thereby causing them to have no regression.
The most excellent, supreme, and foremost, the profound, subtle, and pure Dharma—
You urge the bodhisattvas to preach it to others; Thus teaching them to leave behind all afflictions,
you are peerless throughout the entire world, A state that cannot be shaken or overcome.
For the sake of those bodhisattvas, he constantly extols them; such is the teaching that causes them not to regress.
The Buddha is the Lord of Great Power in the world, endowed with all virtues;
he establishes all bodhisattvas therein, and by this teaching, he acts as the Supreme Man.
He has been able to go before and draw near to all the infinite and boundless Buddhas,
and is always sustained by the protection of those Buddhas; thus instructed, he shall never fall back,
and he fully expounds all tranquil samādhis without exception.
For those bodhisattvas, he speaks thus: by this, he causes them not to regress;
he crushes the wheel of birth and death within all states of existence.
He turns the pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma, remaining unattached to any world. For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he speaks thus.
For all sentient beings fallen into evil realms, Bound and oppressed by immeasurable, heavy sufferings,
He acts as their protector and refuge; Thus he speaks for the sake of all bodhisattvas—
This is the bodhisattva’s dwelling of the initial resolve, Single-mindedly seeking the unsurpassed path.
Just as I have taught this Dharma of instruction, so too do all Buddhas;
The Bodhisattva in the second stage, the Dwelling of Refinement, Should give rise to such a mind:
"May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions Be made to follow the teachings of the Tathāgata."
With a mind of great compassion for their benefit and happiness, Abiding in a heart of pity that gathers them in,
A heart that protects sentient beings as oneself, A heart that regards them as teachers and guides—
Having established such sublime and wondrous minds, One should next cause them to recite and study, seeking extensive learning.
Always delighting in tranquility and right reflection, Associating with all spiritual friends,
speaking with harmony and joy, free from coarseness; Speaking always with awareness of the proper time and without fear,
Thoroughly understanding the meaning and acting in accordance with the Dharma, One remains far removed from delusion, the mind unmoving.
This is the initial training in the conduct of enlightenment; those who can practice this conduct are true children of the Buddha.
I shall now explain what they ought to do; thus, children of the Buddha, you should train with diligence.
This is the third bodhisattva stage, the Abiding in Practice: one should diligently investigate according to the Buddha’s teaching.
All phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty; They lack a self or a person, and are devoid of activity.
All phenomena are not to be delighted in; They have no such thing as a name, no location, No conceptual differentiation, and no reality.
One who contemplates in this way is called a Bodhisattva.
Next, one should cause them to observe the realm of sentient beings, And likewise encourage the observation of the dharma-realm;
Exhaustively and without exception, one should everywhere encourage the observation Of the various worlds throughout the ten directions,
as well as space, And all that exists of earth, water, fire, and wind.

The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm— Exhort them all to observe these realms, examining each of their distinctions And their essential natures until they have fully mastered them;
Thus taught, they diligently practice. These are called the true children of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva in the fourth stage, the Dwelling of Noble Birth, is born from the various holy teachings;
having realized that all existents are non-existent, they transcend those phenomena and give rise to faith in the Dharma-realm.
Their faith in the Buddha is firm and indestructible, and as they contemplate the quiescence of all phenomena, their minds abide in peace.
He fully understands all sentient beings, That their essential nature is illusory and lacks reality;
The worlds, lands, karma, and its retributions, As well as birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—all are thus.
O Son of the Buddha, one who contemplates phenomena in this way Is born directly from the Buddha and is named a Son of the Buddha.
Having thoroughly understood and perfected the accumulation of all Buddha-dharmas throughout the past, future, and present ages,
one trains in this way to bring them to ultimate completion; thus,
one is able to observe all Tathāgatas of the three times as entirely equal.
Various distinctions cannot be found; one who contemplates thus penetrates the three periods of time.
As for those whom I praise and extol, these are the merits of the four stages of dwelling.
If one can practice diligently according to the Dharma, one will swiftly attain the unsurpassed Bodhi of a Buddha.
From this fifth stage, the bodhisattvas are said to dwell in the "Perfection of Skillful Means," having deeply entered immeasurable and subtle expedients.
The various merits and virtues cultivated by these bodhisattvas, which give rise to ultimate qualities and deeds, are all for the purpose of protecting and delivering all sentient beings.
Dedicated solely to their benefit and happiness, Always compassionate, you lead them to liberation;
To remove all hardships for every world, You draw beings from the realms of existence to joy.
Each and every one you tame without exception, Causing all to possess virtue and turn toward Nirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are boundless, immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable,
and beyond all calculation; those who hear and receive such a Dharma from the Tathāgata are the true sons of the Buddha in this fifth stage,
who have perfected skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
The Honored One of Great Wisdom and All Virtues has thus revealed this teaching:
The sixth stage, the Perfect Abiding of the Right Mind, Is free from delusion regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
Through right mindfulness and reflection, one is detached from conceptual construction, And cannot be shaken by any gods or humans.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, Of bodhisattvas and their various practices,
Of sentient beings— whether finite or infinite, With defilement or without defilement, those easy or difficult to deliver,
The dharma-realm— whether large or small, and its formation and destruction, Whether things exist or do not exist— their mind remains unmoved.
Past, future, and present— contemplating and reflecting with constant certainty—
that all phenomena are signless, without substance, without intrinsic nature,
empty, and unreal; like illusions and dreams, free from conceptual construction— one should always delight in hearing such meanings.

The seventh is the non-retrogressive Bodhisattva. Regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bodhisattva practice—whether they exist or do not exist, whether they emerge or do not emerge—even upon hearing such teachings, they do not waver or retreat.
Concerning all Buddhas of the past, future, and present worlds, whether they exist or do not exist, [they remain steadfast].
The Buddha’s wisdom is either finite or infinite; the three periods of time share a single characteristic, and various characteristics are one, while that which is one is many.
As the words follow the meaning, so does the meaning follow the words;
in this way, all things are established through mutual interdependence. This should be taught to those who have not yet retreated from the path.
Whether phenomena possess marks or are markless, whether phenomena possess intrinsic nature or lack intrinsic nature—
having heard these various distinctions and their mutual relations, this person attains the ultimate eighth Bodhisattva stage,
the Stage of Youthful Innocence (Kumārabhūmi), with the conduct of body, speech, and mind fully perfected.
All-pure and free from all faults, Taking birth at will with sovereign mastery,
Knowing the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, And their various differing dispositions,
As well as all phenomena that exist, And the signs of formation and destruction of the lands in the ten directions.
Having attained swift and wondrous supernormal powers,
they go at will to the abodes of all Buddhas in every place to hear the Dharma; they praise and practice it without weariness,
thoroughly understand all Buddha-fields, and shake, empower, and observe them.
Transcending immeasurable Buddha-lands, they travel through worlds beyond count;
They inquire about all the *asaṃkhyeya* dharmas, And possess complete mastery over whatever bodies they wish to assume.
Their skillful speech and tones reach everywhere, As they serve countless Buddhas.
The Ninth Bodhisattva Stage, the Prince’s Abode: He is able to perceive the differences in the births of sentient beings;

he knows all afflictions and habitual tendencies without exception. He thoroughly understands the skillful means employed in practice, as well as the distinct characteristics of various dharmas and their differing modes of conduct.
He discerns the differences between worlds and the distinctions between the past and future limits of time.
Just as they thoroughly understand all conventional and ultimate truths without exception,
so too do they skillfully establish the abodes of the Dharma King; wherever those abodes may be,
they enter the palace of the Dharma King and behold all that is seen therein.
The empowerment rites possessed by the Dharma King, The spiritual power of his sustaining grace,
and his fearlessness; His private chambers and his praises— By these instructions for the Dharma Prince,
He taught everything without exception, Causing his mind to be free from all attachment.
Having realized this and cultivated right mindfulness, all Buddhas appear before one;
as a true son of the Buddha who has received the tenth empowerment, one fulfills the supreme,
foremost Dharma and is able to shake countless worlds in the ten directions, with light radiating everywhere.
The Abbot goes forth without exception; Pure and adorned, he is fully endowed with all qualities.
He reveals the teachings to countless sentient beings, Observing and knowing their faculties to the very end.
His resolve to discipline them is likewise boundless, Causing them all to incline toward Great Bodhi.
They observe the entire dharma-realm and travel to all lands throughout the ten directions;
their bodies and the deeds performed by those bodies, as well as their supernatural manifestations, are difficult to fathom.
Regarding the various realms of the Buddha-lands of the three periods of time, even a prince cannot fully comprehend them.
The wisdom that perceives all as the three times; The wisdom that clearly understands all Buddha-dharmas;
The wisdom of the unimpeded and boundless realm of phenomena; The wisdom that fills all worlds;
The wisdom that illuminates and sustains the worlds; The wisdom that thoroughly knows all phenomena of sentient beings.
And knowing the boundless wisdom of perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata expounds it for them all so that they may fully realize it.
Thus, these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are all born through transformation from the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
according to their respective meritorious practices, no devas or humans can fathom them.
In the past, future, and present ages, those who have resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood are boundless;
they fill all the lands of the ten directions, and there are none who shall not attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
All lands are infinite, and the same is true for the worlds, sentient beings, and phenomena.
The afflictions, karma, minds, and inclinations each differ;
based upon these, one first gives rise to the thought of enlightenment and seeks the Buddha-way with a single moment of mind.
Even the worldlings, sentient beings, and those of the two vehicles cannot know this—how much less can they know the remaining meritorious practices?
All the worlds throughout the ten directions, One who can lift them all with a single hair—
Such a person, a child of the Buddha, Knows how to proceed toward the wisdom-practice of the Tathāgata.
All the great oceans throughout the ten directions, One who can exhaust them all by dripping them away with the tip of a hair—
That person can know this son of the Buddha, who in a single thought-moment cultivates meritorious deeds;
even if all worlds were ground into dust, they could distinguish and know their number.
Only such a person as this can see the path traversed by these bodhisattvas.
The Buddhas of the ten directions— past, future, and present— Along with all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas,
By means of various wondrous eloquences, Reveal and elucidate the initial arousal of the bodhicitta;
The merit of this arousal of the mind is immeasurable, Pervading and filling the realms of all sentient beings.
The collective wisdom of all cannot exhaustively describe it, let alone the remaining sublime practices.

Within the seventh section, the Section of Verses in Summary, there are one hundred verses in total. It is divided into two parts: first, ninety-one verses that correctly reveal the aforementioned dharmas;

Having spent hundreds of kalpas, even up to hundreds of thousands of nayuta-billions of kalpas, they give rise to the bodhicitta.
This is not merely for the sake of teaching so many sentient beings to practice the five precepts and the path of ten wholesome actions, nor to teach them to abide in the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments, nor to teach them to obtain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin.
[They generate the bodhicitta] for the sake of the fruit—the fruit of arhatship and the path of the pratyekabuddha;
for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is not interrupted; for the sake of pervading all worlds; for the sake of liberating all sentient beings in all worlds;
for the sake of fully knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds; and for the sake of fully knowing the multitudes within all worlds.
Because of the arising of defilement and purity; in order to fully know the intrinsically pure nature of all worlds;
in order to fully know the mental inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings; in order to fully know the death and rebirth of all sentient beings;
in order to fully know the faculties and skillful means of all sentient beings; in order to fully know all sentient beings...
Because they give rise to mental activity; because they seek the wisdom that fully knows the three periods of time of all sentient beings;
and because they seek the wisdom that fully knows the equality of the realms of all Buddhas, they resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

Below this, the text correctly reveals the comparison of the merit of generating the bodhicitta through eleven great metaphors: 1. the metaphor of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings;
2. the metaphor of swift steps across buddha-fields; 3. the metaphor of knowing the formation and destruction of kalpas;

4. the metaphor of skillfully knowing superior resolve; 5. the metaphor of skillfully knowing the faculties; 6. the metaphor of skillfully knowing inclinations and desires; 7. the metaphor of skillfully knowing expedient means.
8. The simile of skillfully knowing the minds of others; 9. The simile of skillfully knowing the characteristics of karma; 10. The simile of skillfully knowing the afflictions; 11.
The simile of making offerings to the Buddhas and giving birth [to the Bodhisattva]. Now, regarding these eleven similes, each subsequent one surpasses the preceding ones;

therefore, all the preceding ones are set aside as they are successively superseded by those that follow. Furthermore, within each individual simile, there are ten successive layers of minor sub-similes.

“Metaphor” (*dṛṣṭānta*). “The text is lacking” means it is abbreviated. Now, first is the metaphor for benefiting and gladdening sentient beings. First, from “Suppose there were a person” onwards, the extensive [explanation] is presented.
Next, “What do you think? is the interrogative inquiry. Next, the Devendra’s reply provides the extensive [explanation].
Next, from “Set this metaphor aside for a moment” onwards, nine minor metaphors are presented together. Next is the question, followed by the answer. Next is the Bodhisattva Dharmamati...

The word "sa" (he/that) refers to the subsequent comparison of its surpassing excellence; the following metaphors are used for illustration. This [present] lack of a minor metaphor is an abbreviation.

O Son of the Buddha, setting aside this metaphor for a moment: suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could pass through incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds in the eastern direction, and continued to do so in every thought-moment for as many incalculable eons (*kalpa*) as there are—no one would ever be able to reach the end of all those worlds.
One knows its limits. Furthermore, in a single moment of thought, a second person can traverse more worlds than the former person traversed in *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
in this manner, they continue through successive stages for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until reaching the tenth person.
The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were one hundred people in these ten directions, each of whom were to pass through all these worlds in this manner;
the limit of those worlds might be known, but no one can ever reach the limit of the roots of goodness possessed by a Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

As for knowing their limits: why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is not because a bodhisattva sets a fixed limit, thinking, "I shall only go to so many worlds" and then resolve upon the mind of enlightenment;
rather, they resolve upon the mind of enlightenment in order to fully know the worlds of the ten directions.
That is to say, they wish to fully know that a sublime world is itself a coarse world, and that a coarse world is itself a sublime world.
The world that is upright is the world that is inverted; the world that is inverted is the world that is upright.
The small world is the great world; the great world is the small world. The broad world is the narrow world;
the narrow world is the broad world. A single world is an unspeakable number of worlds.
Inexpressible worlds are themselves a single world; inexpressible worlds enter into a single world, and a single world enters into inexpressible worlds.
A defiled world is itself a pure world, and a pure world is itself a defiled world.
If one wishes to know the distinct natures of all worlds within a single hair-tip, [one must understand] all worlds...
Within a single pore of the realm, there is the singular essence of all bodies. Desiring to know how all worlds arise within a single world;
desiring to know that all worlds are without intrinsic nature;
and desiring to know all vast worlds in a single moment of mind without obstruction—for these reasons, one resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In the second section, concerning the analogy of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) traversed with rapid strides, first the extensive analogy is presented.

Next, it is demonstrated that the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve surpasses [the former] by transcending its faults. Why is this? The inquiry and explanation serve to show that the former cannot compare. Subsequently, for the sake of thoroughly understanding the ten directions, it is shown that this [resolve] surpasses the previous one.
