O Son of the Buddha, let us set aside this analogy. Suppose there were a person who, in a single moment of thought, could know the number of eons of formation and destruction of incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) in the eastern direction;
and suppose they continued to do so, moment after moment, for as many incalculable eons as there are.
No one would be able to know the limit of the number of those eons. Now, suppose there were a second person who, in a single moment of thought, could know the thoughts of that first person...
The number of eons known throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas is explained in detail in this manner, up to the tenth.

It is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. O Son of the Buddha, the limits of the number of eons of formation and destruction of these ten directions of incalculable worlds may be known;
yet, when a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [the number of such eons is beyond reckoning].
No one is able to know the limit of his roots of merit and virtue. Why is this?
It is because a bodhisattva does not resolve his mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* merely to know the number of kalpas of formation and destruction of such-and-such a world;
rather, he resolves his mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to fully know, without exception, the kalpas of formation and destruction of all worlds.
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is as follows: it knows that long eons and short eons are equal;
short eons and long eons are equal; a single eon and countless eons are equal; countless eons and a single eon are equal;
eons with Buddhas and eons without Buddhas are equal; and eons without Buddhas and eons with Buddhas are equal. One...
Within an unspeakable number of Buddha-aeons, there is one Buddha; within an unspeakable number of Buddhas, there is one aeon.
Finite aeons are equal to infinite aeons; infinite aeons are equal to finite aeons. Exhaustible aeons are equal to inexhaustible aeons;
inexhaustible aeons are equal to exhaustible aeons. An unspeakable aeon is equal to a single thought-moment.
Equanimity: a single thought-moment is equal to unspeakable eons; all eons enter into non-eons, and non-eons enter into all eons.

Because one desires to fully know, within a single thought-moment, all worlds of the past, future, and present—including their cycles of formation and destruction—one resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the first resolve.
The mind is adorned with great vows, possessing the supernormal knowledge that fully understands all kalpas.

Third, the analogy for knowing the formation and destruction of kalpas is presented: first, its vastness is established; next, from "In these ten directions... onwards, it is contrasted to demonstrate its transcendent superiority.

O Son of the Buddha, let this analogy be set aside for a moment. Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could know the various different understandings of all sentient beings in incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) in the eastern direction;
and suppose they continued to do so, in every thought-moment, for as many incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) as there are.
Then, suppose there were a second person who, in a single instant, could know all that the former person had known during those incalculable eons.

They give rise to various distinctions of understanding. In this manner, they continue for as many incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) as there are, proceeding sequentially through each stage up to the tenth.

It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. O Son of the Buddha, the limits of the various distinctions in the understandings of sentient beings throughout these ten directions can be known;
yet, when a Bodhisattva first resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the available portion.*
No one is able to know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness of the bodhicitta. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, it is not because a bodhisattva limits themselves to knowing the understandings of only so many sentient beings that they resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
rather, it is in order to fully know all the various distinctions among the sentient beings existing in all worlds.
Because they understand, they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. That is to say:

because they wish to know all distinct understandings as being boundless; because they see that the understanding of a single sentient being and the understanding of countless sentient beings are equal;

because they wish to attain the light of wisdom regarding the skillful means of inexpressible distinctions in understanding; and because they wish to fully know the various differences within the ocean of sentient beings.

Because they wish to exhaustively understand all [knowledges] without remainder; because they wish to fully know the various and immeasurable knowledges of the past, present, and future, whether wholesome or unwholesome;
because they wish to fully know similar knowledges and dissimilar knowledges;

because they wish to fully know that all knowledges are but a single knowledge and a single knowledge is all knowledges; and because they wish to attain the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge. They wish to fully...

Because he knows the distinctions between superior understanding and unsurpassed understanding, understanding with remainder and understanding without remainder, equal understanding and unequal understanding;

and because he desires to fully know the distinctions between understanding based on support and unsupported understanding, common understanding and uncommon understanding, limited understanding and limitless understanding,
differentiated understanding and non-differentiated understanding, wholesome understanding and unwholesome understanding, mundane understanding and supramundane understanding.

Because of these distinctions, they desire to attain the Tathāgata’s unobstructed wisdom of liberation within all subtle understandings, great understandings, immeasurable understandings, and understandings of the correct state;
and they desire to fully know, through immeasurable skillful means, the pure understanding, defiled understanding,
extensive understanding, concise understanding, subtle understanding, and coarse understanding of every single sentient being within the realms of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Because there is nothing remaining; because they wish to fully know, without exception, the web of all understandings— understanding through profundity, understanding through skillful means,
understanding through discrimination, spontaneous understanding, understanding arising in accordance with causes, understanding arising in accordance with conditions—
they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The fourth [section] provides an analogy for understanding "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*). As for "resolute conviction," its nature is to maintain a firm determination regarding a determined object, and its function is to be unshakable by others.
Here, it is briefly termed "conviction" (*mokṣa*), which refers simply to the discernment of an object.

First, a broad analogy is presented. Next, from "These multitudes of beings in the ten directions... onwards, the transcendence is explained. Next, from "Why is this? onwards, there is an interrogation followed by an explanation.

Within that, first there is an explanation by way of contrapositive negation (*paryudāsa*), and next, from "In order to know them exhaustively... onwards, there is a positive explanation (*anvaya*). This section, beginning with "In order to know them exhaustively," serves as the general summary.
Next, regarding "desiring to know what is below," there are eight phrases that collectively distinguish [the stages] by way of their characteristics.
Next, regarding "desiring to fully know," there are five phrases that individually clarify the characteristics of transcendence.

O Son of the Buddha, let this analogy be set aside for a moment. Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could know the differences in the faculties of all sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction;
and suppose they continued to do so, moment by moment, for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are.
Then suppose there were a second person who, in a single instant, could know all that the former person had known, moment by moment, throughout those asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
The differentiation of faculties. Thus it is explained in detail up to the tenth [direction]. It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
O Son of the Buddha, one might be able to know the limits of all the differentiations of the faculties of sentient beings in all these worlds of the ten directions;
yet, the merit and roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [are beyond such measure].

No one is able to know its limit. Why is this? It is because a bodhisattva does not set a fixed boundary, but rather resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of knowing the faculties of sentient beings in such-and-such worlds.
This is for the purpose of fully knowing all the various distinctions among the faculties of all sentient beings in all worlds, as explained at length, even unto...
One generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because of fully knowing the entire network of all faculties (*indriya*).

Fifth is the analogy of skillfully knowing the faculties. First, the extensive analogy is presented; next, from "In these ten directions... onwards, the transcendence [of that analogy] is distinguished.

O Son of the Buddha, let us set aside this analogy. Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could know the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction;

and suppose they continued to do so, moment by moment, for as many as incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, proceeding in sequence through the ten directions—east, south, west, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below—in the same manner. This...
One might be able to know the limits of all the desires and pleasures of sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
however, no one can know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, it is because a bodhisattva does not resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* merely for the sake of knowing the desires and pleasures of such-and-such sentient beings.
They resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to fully know the various desires and pleasures of all sentient beings in all worlds;
they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of extensively explaining, and even ultimately knowing, the entire web of all desires and pleasures.

Sixth, the illustration of the excellence of knowing aspiration (*chanda*). Aspiration refers to that which has the nature of longing for an object of desire, and its function is to serve as the basis for diligence;

it is subsumed under resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). First, the extensive [explanation] is presented; next, following the passage "this assembly of beings from the ten directions," the transcendence [of aspiration] is analyzed.

O Son of the Buddha, let us set aside this analogy. Suppose there were a person who, in a single moment of thought, could know all the various skillful means of the sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction;

and so it is described at length up to the tenth [direction]. Likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—it is the same for these ten directions. These various skillful means of the sentient beings in the ten directions may be...
Knowing the limit: no one is able to know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness of a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is because a bodhisattva does not set a fixed boundary, but rather aspires for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* solely for the sake of knowing the various skillful means for the sentient beings of that many worlds.
Third is the bodhicitta: for the sake of thoroughly knowing all sentient beings in all worlds through various skillful means,
and so forth, up to the desire to thoroughly know the entire web of all skillful means, one generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Seventh is the illustration of skillfully knowing expedient means. First, the extensive illustration is presented; next, from "In these ten directions... onwards, the surpassing [of that] is explained.

O Son of the Buddha, let us set aside this illustration for a moment. Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could know the various distinct minds of all sentient beings within countless worlds in the eastern direction, and so on, as extensively described, up to the worlds of these ten directions.
One may reach the limit of the various differentiated minds of all sentient beings;
however, no one can know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is not for the sake of knowing the minds of only so many sentient beings that a bodhisattva resolves upon [enlightenment].
They resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to fully know the various minds of infinite sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space;
indeed, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because they desire to exhaustively know the entire web of all minds.
Eighth is the analogy for skillfully knowing the minds of others. The meaning of "knowing the mind" encompasses both the king and his subjects. First, the extensive analogy is presented;
next, it is demonstrated how the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve surpasses [the former].
O Son of the Buddha, let this analogy be set aside for a moment. Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant,

could know the various distinct karmas of all sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction— and so on, as extensively described, until reaching the limit of what can be known regarding the various distinct karmas of all sentient beings throughout these ten directions—
yet a bodhisattva, from the very first moment they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
The limit of the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta cannot be known. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, it is not because a bodhisattva limits their resolve to the bodhi-mind merely for the sake of knowing the karma of such-and-such sentient beings;

rather, they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* desiring to know fully the karma of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, even unto the desire to know entirely the entire web of all karma.
Therefore, one resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Ninth, the analogy for skillfully knowing the characteristics of karma is presented; "karma" here refers to the wisdom regarding karmic retribution, as explained below in the context of the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).
First, a broad analogy is presented; next, the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve is shown to surpass it.

"O Son of the Buddha, setting aside this analogy for a moment: suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could know the various afflictions of all sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction, and continued to do so moment by moment for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are. This...
The various distinctions among all afflictions (*kleśa*) are such that no one can know their limit.

Suppose there is a second person who, in a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*), could know the distinctions among the afflictions of sentient beings known by the former person over *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Continuing in this manner for further *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and explaining it sequentially and extensively, one would eventually come to know the tenth [person]. [This applies likewise to] the four directions—south, west, north, and east.
The same applies to those above and below. O Son of the Buddha, it is possible to know the limits of the distinctions among the afflictions of sentient beings throughout these ten directions;
however, the limit of the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be known.

It cannot be known. Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is not for the sake of knowing the afflictions of sentient beings in only so many worlds that a bodhisattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Rather, it is for the sake of fully knowing the distinctions among the afflictions of all sentient beings in all worlds that they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Third is the bodhicitta, which is the desire to fully know each and every sentient being’s immeasurable afflictions— their light, heavy, dormant, and active afflictions—
as well as their various distinctions and types of vitarka and vicāra, in order to thoroughly purify all manner of defilements;
and the desire to fully know how to sever the affliction associated with ignorance and the affliction associated with craving.

Because he wishes to sever all fetters of affliction within all realms of existence; because he wishes to fully know and abandon the afflictions categorized as greed, the afflictions categorized as hatred, the afflictions categorized as delusion, and the afflictions categorized as equal parts, thereby cutting off the root of all afflictions;
because he wishes to thoroughly know the affliction of "I," the affliction of "mine," and the affliction of "I-conceit," awakening to the exhaustion of all afflictions without remainder. He wishes—

Because they fully know that the root afflictions and secondary afflictions arise from inverted discrimination, and because they give rise to the view of a self-identity which gives birth to the sixty-two views, they seek to subdue all afflictions.

Desiring to fully know the hindrances and the obstacles of affliction, they give rise to a mind of great compassion for the purpose of rescuing and protecting others, severing the net of all afflictions, and purifying the nature of omniscience. Thus they resolve.
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Tenth, the analogy for skillfully knowing the afflictions (*kleśa*) is presented. The afflictions possess roots, secondary factors (*anuśaya*), and so forth, as detailed in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only).

First, a broad analogy is presented; next, from "In these ten directions... onwards, the transcendence is distinguished. Within the section of inquiry and explanation: first, from "For what reason... onwards, it is initially demonstrated through negative implication (*paryudāsa*);

next, from "In order to know exhaustively... onwards, it is explained in general. Next, there are six sections for the specific explanation. The first section explains in general. The second, from "Desiring to know exhaustively...
onwards, is the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti*). The third, from "Desiring to know exhaustively... onwards, is the gate of afflicted conduct (*kleśa-carita*). The fourth...
1. The desire to fully know the lower gates of consciousness; 2. The desire to fully know the lower gates of the arising of signs;
3. The desire to fully know the lower gates of renunciation. There are many explanations for these meanings.

O Son of the Buddha, let us set aside this analogy. Suppose there were someone who, in a single moment of thought, were to offer to the east countless [Buddhas] all kinds of superior-flavored foods and drinks, fragrant flowers, garments, banners, flags, parasols, and canopies;
as well as most excellent monasteries, precious curtains and lattices, variously adorned lion-thrones, and many wonderful jewels.

They shall reverently honor, respect, prostrate to, and praise all Buddhas and all sentient beings in countless worlds, bowing their bodies and gazing up at them in an uninterrupted succession for countless kalpas.

Furthermore, they shall exhort those sentient beings to likewise make such offerings to the Buddhas, and after the Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa, each shall erect a stūpa for them; those stūpas shall be immeasurably high and vast, spanning countless worlds.
It is composed of various jewels and adorned in manifold ways.

Within each and every stupa, there are countless images of Tathāgatas, whose radiance shines universally throughout countless worlds for countless eons. It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
O Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is the merit of this person not great? Deva.
The Emperor said: "The merit of this person can only be known by a Buddha; no one else is able to fathom it.

Son of the Buddha, compared to the merit of a bodhisattva’s first aspiration for enlightenment, this person’s merit does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part. Son of the Buddha, let us set this aside."

This is the analogy. Suppose there were a second person who, in a single thought-moment, could perform all the acts of making offerings for a single person and for all sentient beings in countless worlds throughout countless eons;
and who, continuing in this manner moment after moment, used immeasurable kinds of offering materials to make offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas and to those in immeasurable worlds.

There are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable kalpas—whether they be the third person or even the tenth person—all likewise perform, within a single thought-moment, all the offerings previously made. They do so moment after moment in this manner;
[these offerings are] boundless, unequaled, incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, immeasurable, ineffable, and beyond description.

One may speak of the articles of offering used to make offerings to infinite—even to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas—and to all sentient beings within as many worlds, for infinite—even to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas.

Furthermore, after the parinirvāṇa of each Buddha, one may erect stupas for them; these stupas are so high and vast that they remain even throughout an entire kalpa, and it is likewise for all such cases.
O Son of the Buddha, these aforementioned merits do not equal even one hundredth part of the merit of a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve;
they do not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not limit himself to merely making offerings.
It is for the sake of the Buddhas that one resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is for the sake of making offerings to all the Buddhas of the past,
future, and present throughout the unspeakably unspeakable ten directions, as many as exist within the entirety of the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space,
that one resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Eleventh, the section on making offerings to the Buddha and [the resulting] rebirth. First, a broad analogy is presented: by making an offering to the Buddha as a single individual, there are merits both for the present life and for after death;
these are compared to reveal their excellence. Next, the merits of nine individuals making offerings to the Buddha are briefly explained and compared to reveal their excellence.

Finally, within the section of inquiry and explanation, the passage beginning with "Why is this? uses reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) to demonstrate the point. Then, the passage beginning with "For the sake of making offerings... [proceeds].
This concludes the sequential explanation. The third section, the analysis by way of analogy, is finished.
Having generated this mind, one is able to know all Buddhas of the past from their initial attainment of perfect enlightenment until their parinirvāṇa.
They are able to believe in all the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the future;

they are able to know all the wisdom of all Buddhas of the present; and regarding all the merits of those Buddhas, this bodhisattva is able to believe in them, accept them, cultivate them, attain them, know them, realize them, and accomplish them, becoming equal in nature to all Buddhas. Why is this?
This Bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment in order to ensure that the lineage of all Tathāgatas is never interrupted;
in order to pervade all worlds; in order to deliver all sentient beings of all worlds;
in order to fully know the formation and destruction of all worlds; and in order to fully know the defilement and purity of all sentient beings.
They resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the purity of the three realms of existence in all worlds;

they resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the mental inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings; they resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the faculties and skillful means of all sentient beings. For...

He resolves his mind because he wishes to fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings; he resolves his mind because he wishes to possess the wisdom that fully knows the three periods of time for all sentient beings.

The following section briefly demonstrates the divisions of the Dharma. The preceding metaphors revealed the vastness of the causes of the Great Mind; this section clarifies the profound excellence of its encompassed virtues.
This is also a praise of excellence and an exhortation to study. One is able to know that from the prior limit down to the final moment of mind, there is no attachment.
The text consists of five sections: first, the perfection of practice; second, because of the arousal of the mind, the wondrous fruit shall be accomplished;
third, it should be known that this person is equal to the Buddha; fourth, at the very moment the mind is aroused, one is able to perform the Buddha-work; fifth...
When the initial resolve first arises, great wisdom manifests before one; this is the perfection of the initial stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*).
Regarding "faith in words and so forth," it means that this bodhisattva is able to have faith in the Buddha’s wisdom because they have accomplished the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Consequently, they are able to receive the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), able to cultivate the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), able to understand the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), and able to realize the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
The ability to reach ultimate consummation is the cause; reaching ultimate consummation equal to that of a Buddha is the fulfillment of the fruit.
This means that because one’s capacity to realize and the object realized are equal and non-dual with those of a Buddha, the initial mind encompasses all stages.
Why is this? The following questions and explanations clarify the reason. Why does the initial mind fulfill the causal stage? The explanation states: because it is equal to true nature (*tathatā*).
Because it is without limit and because of the arousal of the mind,
one is constantly remembered by all Buddhas of the three periods of time; one immediately attains the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
and all Buddhas of the three periods of time immediately bestow upon one the sublime Dharma.
They are thus equal in essence to all Buddhas of the three periods of time. They have already cultivated the methods for the auxiliary path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;

they have accomplished the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they have adorned themselves with the unique Buddha-dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and they have fully attained the wisdom of the Dharma-exposition of all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because by generating this mind, one immediately attains Buddhahood.
Second, the sublime fruit shall be realized; that is, taking this generation of the mind as the cause, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Aspiring toward the fruit of perfect fulfillment, one will certainly achieve it. Regarding the realization of the nature [of reality] as the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*), the *Upadeśa* states that it is "attained immediately.
This refers to the meaning found in the Jin translation and the Sanskrit original, which state that "all herein are Buddhas."
It should be known that this person is equal to all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they are equal to the realm of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; they are equal to the merit of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
and they have attained the ultimate equality of the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies, as well as true wisdom.
The third point states that [the bodhisattva] is equal to the Buddha. This is because their resolve is uniform; for there is no distinction between the initial resolve and its ultimate fulfillment.
As soon as they give rise to this resolve, they are praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and are immediately able to preach the Dharma.
They teach and discipline all sentient beings in all worlds; they are able to shake all worlds;
they are able to illuminate all worlds; and they are able to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms in all worlds.
They are able to adorn and purify all lands; they are able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood within all worlds;
they are able to cause all sentient beings to attain joy; they are able to enter the nature of all dharma-realms;
they are able to uphold the lineage of all Buddhas; and they are able to obtain the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.
The fourth statement says that one is able to perform the Buddha-work. It consists of eleven phrases, all of which are attained as soon as they are initiated.
Regarding the phrase "attained as soon as," there are two meanings: first, in terms of the perfect interfusion of dharmas, because the initial resolve encompasses all stages;
second, by means of one stage encompassing another, such as attaining Buddhahood immediately upon the completion of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*).
This bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment does not have even the slightest attainment regarding the three times—
namely, whether it be the Buddhas or the Buddha-dharmas, the bodhisattvas or the bodhisattva-dharmas, the pratyekabuddhas or the pratyekabuddha-dharmas,
the śrāvakas or the śrāvaka-dharmas, the mundane or the mundane dharmas, or the supramundane or the supramundane dharmas.
Whether regarding sentient beings or the phenomena of sentient beings, one seeks only omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
With a mind that has no attachment toward any realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the fifth great wisdom manifests; this is because one seeks enlightenment through unattached great wisdom.

Furthermore, this universally explains the preceding four sections: because there is no attachment, the nature [of reality] is perfectly interfused, thereby able to accomplish and encompass all as one.
All merits. At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways:
namely, they moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; they rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; they surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere.

It leaped up everywhere; it shook, it shook everywhere, it shook equally everywhere; it roared, it roared everywhere, it roared equally everywhere; it struck, it struck everywhere, it struck equally everywhere.
They rained down celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial flower garlands, celestial robes, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments;
they performed celestial music, emitted celestial radiance, and produced celestial sounds.
This is the fifth major section of the text, "The Section on Making Offerings and Shaking the Earth," which describes auspicious omens.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, all named Dharmamati.
Each manifested his body before the Bodhisattva Dharmamati and spoke thus:

He said: "Excellent, excellent, Dharmamati! That you are now able to expound this Dharma is because we Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, also teach this Dharma. All Buddhas speak thus.
When you taught this Dharma, Bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields resolved their minds upon Bodhi. We [now...]"

All of them were granted their predictions: that in a future world, after passing through more than a thousand unspeakably many boundless kalpas, they would all attain Buddhahood within a single kalpa and appear in the world, all bearing the name Tathāgata Pure Mind (Vimalacitta), and all dwelling in worlds [of the same name].
Each is distinct. We shall all protect and uphold this Dharma, so that all bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may hear it in its entirety.
Just as in this Sahā world, upon the summit of Mount Sumeru within the four continents, this Dharma was taught so that all sentient beings might hear it and be transformed;
so too shall it be throughout the hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds in the ten directions.
In worlds as numerous as ten billion, countless, immeasurable, boundless, and peerless— beyond number, beyond measure, beyond thought, beyond calculation, and beyond description,
pervading the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space— the Dharma is likewise taught to edify sentient beings.
Those who preach this Dharma all bear the same name, Dharmamati, and it is entirely through the spiritual power of the Buddha, World-Honored One.
By the power of his original vow; desiring to manifest the Buddha-dharma; desiring to illuminate everywhere with the light of wisdom;
desiring to expound the true meaning; desiring to cause the realization of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); and desiring to bring joy to the entire assembly.
It is for the purpose of revealing the causes of the Buddha-dharma, for the purpose of attaining the equality of all Buddhas, and for the purpose of realizing that the dharma-realm is non-dual;
thus does he teach this Dharma.

This is the sixth major section, the "Section on Testimony from Other Realms. Because the virtues encompassed by the initial resolve are so profound and vast, there may be fear that they will be difficult to believe and accept;

therefore, the Buddha personally provides testimony. The text is divided into three parts: first, the Buddha’s direct realization; second, the testimony of the accomplishment of benefits, beginning with "You have said...";
and third, the summary of the inexhaustible, beginning with "Thus, in this Sahā world... This is the testimony of the Buddha that summarizes and extends [the teaching], not the sūtra itself.
It is the home.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati universally surveyed all the assemblies in the lands of the ten directions throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, desiring to bring all sentient beings to complete fulfillment;
desiring to completely purify the karmic fruits and retributions of all; and desiring to fully open [the way for them].
In order to manifest the pure dharma-realm; in order to completely uproot the roots of all defilements; in order to cause all vast faith and understanding to increase;
in order to cause all to know the faculties of immeasurable sentient beings; in order to cause all to know the equality of phenomena throughout the three periods of time;
in order to cause all to observe the realm of nirvāṇa; and in order to increase one's own pure virtues.
Because it is the root, [the Bodhisattva], receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke these verses.
This concludes the seventh section, the Section on Repeating the Verses. First, the meaning of the verses is analyzed. There are eleven lines;

the first and the last are the formal protocol for reciting the verses. They are separated [from the middle] because one wishes to show that the nine intermediate lines all rely upon the Buddha’s power. This encompasses...

Because of the ten directions, the middle nine [verses] clearly elucidate that for which [the teaching] is intended. The first is general; the remainder is specific. Within the specific section, there are four pairs: first, purifying karma to manifest principle;
second, removing delusions to open up faith—wherein false conceptualization serves as the root of defilement; third, knowing the illness to recognize the medicine;
and fourth, contemplating the pure cause of the fruit, whereby through benefiting others, one’s own karma becomes purified.
For the benefit of the world, they have resolved upon the Great Mind;
their minds pervade all sentient beings, lands, and the phenomena of the three times throughout the ten directions.
Reaching the ultimate limit of the ocean of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, equal to empty space and the Dharma-realm, they encompass every single world.
Just as all Buddhas go forth, so too does he resolve his mind without regression;
with compassionate thoughts, he never abandons sentient beings for even a moment.
Free from all affliction and harm, he universally benefits others, his radiance illuminating the world as a refuge. Protected by the Ten Powers, he is inconceivable.
They enter all lands throughout the ten directions, manifesting every form and appearance;
Like the Buddha’s merit and wisdom, vast and boundless, they cultivate the causes accordingly without attachment.
Some worlds face upward, some dwell sideways, and some are inverted; They are coarse, subtle, vast, or of immeasurable kinds.
As soon as a Bodhisattva gives rise to the supreme mind, they are able to travel everywhere without obstruction.
The sublime practices of Bodhisattvas are ineffable; they diligently cultivate them all while dwelling nowhere.
Seeing all Buddhas, they always rejoice, universally entering the profound ocean of their Dharma.
Out of compassion for all beings in the five realms, you cause them to remove defilements and become universally pure;
you perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas so that it is never severed, and you utterly destroy the palaces of Māra without remainder.
Having already abided in the equanimity of the Tathāgata, you have skillfully cultivated the subtle path of expedient means.
Giving rise to faith in the realm of the Buddha, Receiving the Buddha’s empowerment with a mind free from attachment;
Mindful of the debt of gratitude owed to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, With a mind like a vajra, indestructible,
One can clearly illuminate the conduct of the Buddha And spontaneously cultivate the practices of enlightenment.
The various distinctions among the realms of existence are immeasurable; Karmic fruits and minds are likewise not one.
Even down to the diverse differences in faculties and natures, Upon the single arousal of the Great Mind, all are clearly seen.
That mind is vast, equal to the Dharma-realm, Without support and unchanging, like space.
They proceed toward the Buddha’s wisdom without grasping; They clearly realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are free from conceptualization;
Knowing the minds of sentient beings, they have no notion of birth; Thoroughly understanding all phenomena, they have no notion of non-existence;
Though they universally discern, they are without discrimination; They travel to billions of nayutas of lands.
The immeasurable dharmas are a treasury of wondrous teachings; Observing them in accordance with reality, you can enter them all.
You know the faculties and conduct of sentient beings without exception;
Having reached such a state, O Honored One, your pure great vows are ever-conjoined. You delight in making offerings to the Tathāgata and never regress.
Those seen by humans and devas never tire of beholding them; they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Their minds are pure and without dependence; though they contemplate the profound Dharma, they do not grasp it.
Thus they reflect for immeasurable eons, remaining unattached throughout the three periods of time.
Their minds are firm and difficult to restrain or discourage; they proceed toward the Bodhi of the Buddha without hindrance.
Resolutely seeking the wondrous Way, they eliminate delusion and confusion; they traverse the entire Dharma-realm without complaint, knowing that the nature of all speech and phenomena is quiescent.
Entering only into True Suchness (Tathatā), they transcend all divergent interpretations.
"Observing all the realms of the Buddhas in accordance with reality, one attains mastery over the three periods of time with an unobstructed mind.
This second section, which explicitly reveals the verses, consists of one hundred and twenty-one stanzas. The text is divided into three parts:
first, eighty-two stanzas that skip ahead to praise the Dharma briefly; second, thirty-four stanzas that look back to praise by means of metaphors.
The comparison [of merits] consists of three verses; the conclusion consists of five verses that form an exhortation and praise, intended to inspire admiration and the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The profound nature and the difficulty of explaining [the subject] are praised throughout the three sections. Furthermore, because it serves as the basis for both the prose and the verse, it is not versified here and is thus omitted.

The initial section also divides into five parts. First, there are seventeen verses praising the first stage: the perfection of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*). Second, the Bodhi...

1. From "The Bodhisattva first sets out" (*sa prathamaṃ cittam utpādayati*) to the seventeenth verse: this anticipates the fourth [chapter], "Performing the Buddha-works. 2. From "The three abodes of the bodhisattvas" (*trīṇi bodhisattvavihārāṇi*) to the eighteenth verse:
this corresponds to the third [chapter], "Attaining equality with the Buddhas. 3. From "Proceeding toward enlightenment" (*bodhim abhimukhaḥ*) to the sixth and a half verses:

this corresponds to the fifth [chapter], "The manifestation of great wisdom. 4. From "Constantly exhorting the assembly" (*sadā saṃghaṃ samādāpayan*) to the twenty-third [verse]: [this corresponds to the sixth chapter].

One and a half verses. This verse praises the second stage, the attainment of the sublime fruit. The sequence of the text is not chronological because it demonstrates that these virtues have no before or after.
Now, for the first [verse]:
As soon as a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the vast mind, He is able to travel everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The Dharma gates are immeasurable and beyond expression; The light of wisdom shines everywhere, illuminating all with clarity.
Great compassion saves extensively, peerless and supreme;
A heart of loving-kindness pervades universally, equal to space, Yet makes no distinctions among sentient beings— Thus pure, you wander through the world.
All sentient beings of the ten directions are fully comforted; All that they do is truly real.
Always with a pure mind and no divergent speech, They are constantly protected by all the Buddhas together.
All that has occurred in the past is remembered, And all that is yet to come in the future is fully discerned.
Universally entering into the worlds of the ten directions, To deliver sentient beings and cause them to transcend,
The Bodhisattva is endowed with the light of wondrous wisdom; Thoroughly understanding causes and conditions,
they are free from doubt, Having severed all delusions, They thus traverse the Dharma-realm.
The palaces of the Māra kings have all been utterly destroyed; The cataracts of sentient beings have all been eliminated.
Free from all conceptual discrimination, their minds are unmoving; They thoroughly understand the realm of the Tathāgata.
The nets of doubt regarding the three periods of time have all been removed; They have given rise to pure faith toward the Tathāgata.
Through faith, one attains immovable wisdom; because that wisdom is pure, one realizes the truth.
To cause sentient beings to attain liberation, one benefits them universally until the end of time;
with long-term diligent effort, the mind never tires, even enduring the sufferings of hell.
Fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom, you thoroughly understand the faculties and desires of all sentient beings;
there is no karmic action or conduct that you do not perceive, and you preach the Dharma according to their inclinations.
Realizing that all things are empty and selfless, you cherish all beings with compassion, never forsaking them.
With a single, subtle voice of great compassion, they enter the world at large to proclaim the Dharma;
emitting great light of various colors, it universally illuminates sentient beings and dispels all darkness.
Within this light, Bodhisattvas sit upon lotus flowers, expounding the pure Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Upon a single hair-tip, they manifest myriad lands, Filled with great Bodhisattvas whose assemblies are vast;
Their wisdoms are each different, yet all clearly understand the minds of sentient beings.
The worlds of the ten directions are unspeakable in number, Yet in a single thought-moment, they traverse them all without exception.
Benefiting sentient beings and making offerings to the Buddhas, Inquiring about profound meanings in the presence of all Buddhas;
Regarding all Tathāgatas as one’s father, Cultivating the practices of awakening for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
Possessing skillful wisdom that penetrates the treasury of the Dharma, Entering the realm of deep wisdom without attachment.
Contemplating in accordance with reality, they expound the dharma-realm;
though they enter the wisdom that is inexhaustible throughout immeasurable eons, it has no fixed location.
Without weariness and without attachment, they are born into the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, realizing the wondrous Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Universally manifesting myriad forms for the sake of all living beings— just as a master illusionist can create anything—
he may manifest the initial cultivation of sublime practices, or manifest his first birth and renunciation of the world;
he may manifest the attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree, or manifest nirvana for the sake of sentient beings.
These seventeen verses perform the work of a Buddha.
The marvelous qualities in which the Bodhisattvas dwell Are the domain of the Buddhas alone;
they are beyond the body, speech, mind, and thought of the two vehicles, having been entirely eliminated, Yet they can manifest them all in various ways according to what is appropriate.
The various Buddha-dharmas attained by Bodhisattvas— Sentient beings who contemplate them fall into madness;
Their wisdom enters the limit of reality with an unimpeded mind, Universally manifesting the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
This is without equal in the world; How much more so when further increased by superior practices!
Although he has not yet fully perfected all-knowledge, he has already attained the sovereign power of the Tathāgata;
having established himself in the ultimate path of the One Vehicle, he has deeply entered the subtle and supreme Dharma.
Knowing well the proper and improper times for sentient beings, he manifests supernatural powers for their benefit.
Emanating bodies that fill all lands, They radiate pure light to dispel the darkness of the world.
Like a dragon king raising great clouds, They rain down wondrous showers everywhere to bring total fulfillment.
Observing sentient beings as like illusions and dreams, They constantly transmigrate due to the power of karma.
With great compassion, he pities and delivers all; for their sake, he expounds the unconditioned, pure nature of phenomena.
The Buddha’s power is likewise immeasurable, like space which has no bounds.
To enable sentient beings to attain liberation, he diligently practices for billions of eons without weariness.
Contemplating various sublime virtues, Skillfully cultivating the unsurpassed, supreme deeds,
Never forsaking any of the excellent practices, Single-mindedly mindful of generating all-encompassing wisdom;
Manifesting infinite bodies within a single body, Pervading every world throughout the universe.
His mind is pure and free from discrimination; The power of a single thought is thus inconceivable.
He does not discriminate among the various worlds, And regarding all phenomena, he is without conceptual construction.
Though he contemplates all phenomena, he does not grasp them; He constantly rescues sentient beings, yet there is nothing that is delivered.
All worlds are merely conceptualization; within them, various distinctions are known.

The realm of conceptualization is perilous and deep; to manifest supernormal powers and effect liberation is like the sovereign mastery of a magician—such too is the miraculous transformation of a Bodhisattva.
Your body pervades the Dharma-realm and all of space; according to the minds of sentient beings, there is nowhere you are not seen.

Free from both subject and object of discrimination, neither grasping at defilement nor purity, and having forgotten all notions of bondage or liberation— I only pray that you may universally bestow happiness upon all sentient beings.
The entire world is merely the power of conceptualization; Entering through wisdom, the mind is free from fear.
Contemplating all phenomena in this same way, One seeks them throughout the three times and finds them unobtainable.
One can enter the past to its ultimate limit, And enter the future to its ultimate limit.
Able to enter all present locations, Constantly and diligently observing that nothing exists, They accord with the dharma of nirvāṇa and cessation;
Abiding in non-contention and non-reliance, their minds are like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and peerless. Single-mindedly directed toward bodhi, they never regress.
Cultivating all supreme practices without retreat or fear, dwelling securely in bodhi without wavering;
clearly understanding the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the world throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm—
desiring to attain the most supreme and foremost path, the sovereign liberation of omniscience.
One should swiftly resolve upon the Bodhicitta, To forever exhaust all outflows and benefit all living beings.
[This concludes] the thirty-eighth verse, the third section: Attaining the Equality of the Buddhas.
With a mind pure and directed toward enlightenment, Its vast merit is beyond description;
yet for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I shall now proclaim it. All of you noble ones, listen well!
If all immeasurable worlds were reduced to dust, Within each and every mote of dust, there are immeasurable lands.
The Buddhas therein are all immeasurable; They can clearly perceive everything without grasping.
They well know that sentient beings have no notion of birth, And they well know that speech has no notion of speaking.
Their minds are unimpeded regarding all worlds; They thoroughly understand all things without attachment.
His mind is as vast as space; He fully understands all matters of the three periods of time, And all doubts and delusions are utterly extinguished.
Rightly contemplating the Buddha-dharma, he grasps at nothing;
In a single thought-moment, he visits infinite lands throughout the ten directions, Yet his mind remains free from attachment.
Thoroughly comprehending all the phenomena of suffering in the world, they abide entirely within the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where nothing arises.
To the presence of immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, they go to all those assemblies to pay their respects.
There, acting as the foremost, they shall question the Tathāgata regarding the various vows and practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas.
The mind constantly recollects the Buddhas of the ten directions, Without dependence and without grasping.
These four verses and a half of gāthās on the manifestation of great wisdom Constantly exhort sentient beings to plant roots of goodness, Adorning the buddha-fields to make them pure.
With unimpeded eyes, you observe all beings throughout every realm of existence within the three worlds;
you clearly perceive their infinite and boundless habitual tendencies, faculties, and inclinations, and you fully understand the mental dispositions of all sentient beings.
Thus, you preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.
They thoroughly penetrate all that is defiled and pure, Causing them to cultivate and enter the Path.
Into immeasurable and innumerable samādhis, The Bodhisattva can enter in a single thought-moment;
Regarding their mental images, wisdom, and objects of focus, They fully understand them all and attain mastery.
When Bodhisattvas attain this vast wisdom, they swiftly advance toward enlightenment without obstruction.
Desiring to benefit all living beings, they proclaim the Dharma of the Great Beings everywhere;
they well understand the long and short kalpas of the world, as well as months, fortnights, and days and nights.
The distinct natures of all lands are equal; Always diligently observing with heedfulness, they travel everywhere to the worlds of the ten directions.
Without grasping at any location, they purify all lands without exception, Yet they never give rise to the conceptualization of "purity."
Sentient beings, whether in what is possible or impossible, and the distinctions in the retributions of their various karmas—
by reflecting in accordance with these, one enters the Buddha-powers and understands them all completely.
One thoroughly knows the diverse natures of all worlds and the various ways they act and abide within the three realms of existence.
Those of sharp faculties, as well as those of medium and inferior faculties—
observing all such various inclinations regarding the pure and the impure, they clearly perceive the superior, the inferior, and the middling,
and explain the continuous succession of the three realms of existence for all sentient beings wherever they go.
The dhyānas, liberations, and various samādhis— Their causes for defilement or purity arise differently, As do the distinctions between past suffering and joy;
Through the power of purified cultivation, the Buddha perceives them all.
Sentient beings’ karma and delusions continue through the various realms of existence; By severing these realms, one attains nirvāṇa.
Various outflows never arise again; he fully understands them along with their habitual seeds.
The Tathāgata has exhausted all afflictions, and the light of his great wisdom illuminates the world.
Although the Bodhisattva has not yet realized the Buddha’s ten powers, he harbors no doubt regarding them.
Within a single pore, the Bodhisattva universally manifests immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions—
some defiled, some pure— and is able to fully comprehend all the various karmic actions therein.
Within a single atom, there are immeasurable lands, with immeasurable Buddhas and their sons.
The various lands are distinct and without confusion; as one, they are all clearly seen.

Within a single pore, one sees the ten directions; throughout the entire realm of empty space and all worlds, there is not a single place devoid of Buddhas. Thus, these Buddha-lands are entirely pure.
Within a single pore they see Buddha-fields, and further behold all sentient beings throughout the three times and six realms,
each distinct; day and night, month and season, there are those bound and those liberated—
such are these Bodhisattvas of great wisdom, who with single-minded devotion advance toward the station of the Dharma King.
Contemplating in accordance with the abode of the Buddha, they obtain boundless and great joy.
The Bodhisattvas manifest immeasurable billions of emanations to make offerings to all Tathāgatas;
their supernatural transformations are peerlessly supreme, and they are able to abide in every place where Buddhas travel.
In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, they were all praised and revered; they relished and savored the entire treasury of the Dharma.
Having seen the Buddhas and heard the Dharma, they diligently practiced it; like drinking nectar, their hearts were filled with joy.
Having already attained the supreme samādhi of the Tathāgata, they skillfully entered into all dharmas and their wisdom increased.
Faith is unshakable like Mount Sumeru; May you universally become a treasury of merit for all living beings.
With a vast and great heart of compassion extending to all, May you swiftly attain all-encompassing wisdom.
Always remaining without attachment or dependence, Be free from all afflictions and attain sovereign mastery.
With vast wisdom that compassionates sentient beings, Universally gathering all as one's own kin,
Knowing emptiness, signlessness, and the absence of reality, Yet acting with a mind that never slackens or retreats—
The measure of the merit of a bodhisattva’s resolve Could not be fully extolled even in ten million eons.
In order to bring forth peace and happiness for all Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, there are twenty-three and a half verses.
This constitutes the second chapter, "Attaining the Sublime Fruit. The text herein is divided into nine sections:
the first three and a half verses concern the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas; the next one and a half verses concern the attainment of Bodhi; the following one and a half verses...
1. Bestowing the Great Sublime Dharma; 2. One verse on the equality of the Buddha’s essence; 3. One verse on the cultivation of the auxiliary dharmas of the path;
4. Six verses on the powers and fearlessnesses of the Buddha; 5. Five verses on the adornments of the Buddha-dharmas; 6. Five verses on the wisdom of preaching the Dharma; 7.
One verse concluding with the inexhaustibility of these virtues.
To all sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions, I bestow peace for immeasurable eons,
Exhorting them to uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths, As well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and various samādhis. Furthermore,
through many more eons, I grant them peace and happiness, Causing them to sever all delusions and become arhats.
Though those masses of merit are immeasurable, they cannot compare to the virtue of generating the resolve for enlightenment.
Even if one were to lead billions of beings to become pratyekabuddhas, attaining the subtle path of the practice of non-contention,
when compared to the bodhicitta, neither calculation nor metaphor can reach it.
In a single thought-moment, one can pass through lands as numerous as atoms;
Even if such a journey continued for immeasurable eons, the number of these lands might still be measured.
Yet the merit of generating the Bodhicitta cannot be known, For the total number of eons in the past, future, and present is boundless.
These various kalpas may still be known, But the merit of generating the resolve is unfathomable.
With the bodhicitta pervading the ten directions, There is no discrimination that is not known;
In a single thought-moment, one clearly penetrates the three periods of time, For the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The sentient beings of the worlds in the ten directions, their desires, understandings, skillful means, and mental activities—even the limits of space—might be measured;
yet the merit of generating the bodhicitta is difficult to fathom.
The vows of the Bodhisattvas are equal to the ten directions, and their hearts of loving-kindness universally moisten all living beings.
Causing all to cultivate and perfect the merits of a Buddha, their power is thus boundless.

Regarding the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, and the distinct faculties, skillful means, and practices of each, they fully comprehend them all within a single thought-moment; the mind of omniscient wisdom is equal to all.
The various afflictions and karmas of all sentient beings, And the continuity of the three realms of existence, never cease for even a moment;
Though the limits of these may still be known, The merit of generating the bodhicitta is inconceivable.
Generating the mind can bring one away from karma and afflictions, And enable one to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Karma and afflictions being severed, the continuity of existence is broken; Universally attaining liberation throughout the three periods of time.

In a single thought-moment, they make offerings to boundless Buddhas, And likewise to countless sentient beings, Causing them all to receive fragrant flowers, exquisite garlands, Precious banners, pennants, canopies, and superior robes.
With exquisite foods, precious seats, and places for walking meditation, And various palaces all magnificently adorned,
With the wondrous jewels of Vairocana and radiant cintāmaṇi gems,
I thus maintain these offerings in every thought-moment, For unspeakable eons throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Though that person’s mass of merit may be vast, it does not equal the greatness of the virtue of generating the resolve for enlightenment.
Among the various analogies that have been taught, none can match the bodhicitta;
for all those who are honored as the World-Honored Ones throughout the three periods of time were born from the generation of this resolve.
The arousal of the mind is unimpeded and without limit; one cannot find its measure even if one seeks it.
Vowing that the wisdom of all-knowledge shall certainly be attained, all sentient beings shall be forever delivered.
This arousal of the mind is vast, equal to space, and gives birth to all merits, identical to the Dharma-realm.
His conduct is universally pervasive and without distinction; forever free from all attachments, he is equal to all Buddhas.
There is no Dharma gate into which he does not enter;
he can travel to all lands and thoroughly penetrate the realm of omniscience. All virtues and merits are fully accomplished.
Capable of relinquishing all things with constant continuity, Purifying the categories of ethical discipline without attachment,
Possessing the supreme and great merit, Always diligent and energetic, never regressing,
Entering deep meditative concentration and constantly reflecting, In perfect accord with vast wisdom.
This is the most supreme stage of the Bodhisattva, From which arises the path of Samantabhadra.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time Without exception protect and mindfully sustain those who first resolve their minds [on enlightenment].
With samādhis, dhāraṇīs, And supernatural transformations, they adorn it all together.
Sentient beings in the ten directions are immeasurable, And the worlds and empty space are likewise so;
Yet the resolve for enlightenment is more immeasurable than they, For this is that which gives birth to the Bodhicitta of all Buddhas—
The root of the ten powers, And also the root of the four analytical knowledges and fearlessnesses.
The eighteen unique qualities are likewise so; there are none that do not arise from the initial resolve of mind.

One thereby attains the bodies of all Buddhas adorned with physical marks, as well as the equal and wondrous Dharma-body, wisdom free from attachment, and the state of one worthy of offerings—all of these are obtained through the initial resolve of mind.
The bliss of all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, the meditative concentrations and samādhis of the form realm,
and all the samādhis of the formless realm— all these take the arousal of the bodhicitta as their root;
so too do the sovereign bliss of all humans and devas, and the various kinds of bliss found in the different realms of existence.
The various joys of the faculties of concentration, the powers, and so forth, all arise from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment.
By giving rise to this vast and expansive mind as their cause,
one is able to practice the six perfections and exhort all sentient beings to engage in right conduct, thereby attaining peace and happiness within the three realms.
Abiding in the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom of ultimate reality, you fully expound all sublime deeds;
you cause immeasurable sentient beings to sever their afflictions and karma and proceed toward nirvana.
Your light of wisdom is like the pure sun, and your perfection of all practices is like the full moon.
Virtue is ever full like the vast ocean; Stainless and unimpeded, it is equal to space.
Universally issuing forth infinite vows of merit, May all sentient beings be granted happiness.
Relying on these vows and practices until the end of the future, I shall always diligently cultivate them to deliver all beings.
Immeasurable great vows, inconceivable, May cause all sentient beings to be entirely pure;
Empty, signless, vowless, and without dependence, By the power of these vows,
may they all clearly realize that the self-nature of phenomena is like space, All quiescent and entirely equal.
The Dharma gates are innumerable and unspeakable; for the sake of sentient beings, they are taught without attachment.
The Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions all join in praising the first arousal of the mind;
this mind is adorned with immeasurable virtues and is able to reach the other shore, equal to the Buddhas.
Even if one were to speak for as many eons as there are sentient beings, one could never exhaustively describe his merits.
By abiding in the vast and great household of the Tathāgata, the phenomena of the three realms can provide no analogy.
[There are] thirty-four verses; these serve as analogies for comparison. Among them, the first fourteen verses directly correspond to what preceded.
[The] Simile. Next, there are twenty verses that provide a general explanation of the reasons [for this].
If you wish to know all the qualities of the Buddhas, You should swiftly resolve upon Bodhicitta.
This mind is the most supreme among all merits; It will surely result in the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom.
The mental activities of sentient beings may be counted, And the atoms within all lands are likewise so;
One might even reach the limits of empty space, But the merit of generating the Bodhi-mind cannot be measured.
It gives birth to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, And accomplishes all happiness in the world.
Increasing all supreme merits, Permanently severing all doubts and delusions,
Revealing all wondrous realms, Exhaustively removing all obstacles,
Accomplishing all pure lands, And giving birth to the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Those who wish to see all Buddhas of the ten directions, Who wish to bestow the inexhaustible treasury of merit,
And who wish to extinguish the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings— They should swiftly resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
These five verses conclude the section on virtues and exhort practice.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Volume Seventeen;
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Volume Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
Excerpts on the Meaning of the "Chapter on the Clarification of the Dharma" (Chapter 18) by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Kuāngshān.

Regarding the purpose for the introduction of this chapter: previously, the virtues accomplished within the current stage were clarified; now, the practice of further advancement toward the subsequent stage is clarified.

Furthermore, previously the supreme virtues of generating the bodhicitta were clarified; now, the specific characteristics of the practices possessed therein are distinguished. Thus, it follows in sequence. As for the explanation of its title:
according to the Sanskrit original, it should be translated in full as "The Chapter on the Radiance of Dharma" (*Dharmāloka-parivarta*). Taken as a whole, there are four meanings.

First is the wisdom of the Dharma-wisdom (*dharmajñāna*). Because it clearly illuminates and understands the phenomena of practice that proceed toward both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), it clarifies the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-dharma*).
Second, it clarifies the signifier, because it can manifest the practice; "Dharma" (*dharma*) refers to the signified, as it is that which may be followed as a rule.

This is the complete designation for the essence of the signifier, because it clarifies that there is a phenomenon (*dharma*) and because it is the illumination of the phenomenon. Thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

There are two interpretations: the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and the *dvandva* (dual). The third [interpretation] takes "wisdom" (*jñāna*) as the function of insight; "Dharma" refers to principle, practice, and fruition.

When object and wisdom are spoken of together, both are the objects of explanation. "The Dharma that is illumination" is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Fourth, the essence of the Dharma practiced is free from ignorance;
it is also exclusively the "Dharma that possesses illumination," which is the object of explanation. "Dharma is itself illumination" is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.

This is an analysis based on the two methods of *karmadhāraya* (attributive) and *tatpuruṣa* (appositional) compounds. As for the fundamental intent (*abhiprāya*), it clarifies that the dharmas are not uniform; briefly, there are four types: namely, teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*nyāya*), practice (*pratipatti*), and fruit (*phala*).

One seeks the teaching to awaken to the principle; contemplating the principle gives rise to practice; and when practice is perfected, one attains the fruit. In each case, the former is the "thesis" (*mūla*) and the latter is the "intent" (*abhiprāya*).
Furthermore, these four are all the thesis; they serve as the means for establishing the subsequent stages and for attaining superior qualities.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryamati addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
The commentary on the text is divided into three major sections: first, the section on the request for the teaching; second, the section on the actual teaching;

and third, the section on the conclusion of the teaching. Now, regarding the first: it consists first of prose (*gadya*) and subsequently of verses (*geya*). Within the former, there are also two parts. First is the description of the persons involved in the question and answer.
Since progress toward the higher stages cannot be achieved without diligence, it is through vigor and wisdom that the inquiry is posed.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they accomplish such immeasurable merit and are endowed with great adornment.

They ascend the vehicle of all-knowledge, enter the stage of the Bodhisattva’s correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), abandon all worldly dharmas, and attain the supramundane dharmas of the Buddhas.
They are sustained by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and are certain to reach the unsurpassed state.
The ultimate state of bodhi.
This section below is the second part, which formally presents the questions asked; it is also divided into two sections. First, acknowledging one's own prior superior virtues;

second, requesting the teaching on the practice of further advancement (*viśeṣa-gāminī-caryā*). Within the first section, there is first a general summary, followed by seven phrases beginning with "possessing greatness. The first [phrase]:

1. Mastery over virtues: this refers to the aforementioned adornments of the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). 2. Mastery over the vehicle: this refers to having already abided in the ultimate One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
3. Mastery over stages: because there is no regression from the stage. 4. Mastery over the path: because one abides in the cause for transcending birth. 5. Mastery over the Dharma.
Sixth, obtaining superior conditions, namely the protection and praise of the Buddhas and others. Seventh, receiving the future fruit, until reaching Bodhi.
Although these virtues are immeasurable, they do not exceed these seven.
How do those bodhisattvas practice within the Buddha’s teaching so that all Tathāgatas are filled with joy,
they enter the abodes where bodhisattvas dwell, all their great practices become purified, all their great vows are fully realized,
they obtain the vast treasury of the bodhisattvas, and they constantly preach the Dharma according to the needs of those to be transformed?
Yet they never abandon the practice of the *pāramitās*. They cause all sentient beings whom they keep in mind to attain liberation.
They succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it remains unbroken. Their roots of goodness and skillful means are entirely unfailing. O Son of the Buddha!
By what skillful means can those bodhisattvas cause these dharmas to reach fulfillment? I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me. These...
The great assembly was all delighted to hear this.
This request for an exposition of the superior progress consists of two parts: first, an inquiry into the essential nature of the practice to be accomplished;

second, an inquiry into the virtuous functions resulting from the accomplishment of that practice—since the destruction of ignorance and so forth constitutes those virtuous functions. This [section] first asks about the essential nature of the practice. There are ten questions.

The first five [verses] concern benefiting oneself while simultaneously benefiting others; the next four concern benefiting others while simultaneously benefiting oneself; the final conclusion shows that this is not in vain.
Afterwards, the following lines conclude the request.
Furthermore, as for all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they constantly and diligently practice to eliminate all the darkness of ignorance.
He subdues the dark forces and the enmity of Māra, restrains all non-Buddhists, and eternally washes away all defilements of the mind’s afflictions.
He is fully able to accomplish all roots of goodness, eternally emerge from all evil destinies and difficulties,
purify the sphere of all great wisdom, and achieve all the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas, the *pāramitās*, the *dhāraṇīs*, the *samādhis*, and the six supernormal powers.
He clearly understands the pure merits of the four fearlessnesses, which adorn all buddha-fields;
he fully accomplishes and perfects the marks and signs, as well as the activities of body, speech, and mind;

he thoroughly knows the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities of all tathāgatas, and the sphere of activity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, desiring to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
Upon birth, they take up Buddha-fields according to their mental inclinations and teach the Dharma appropriately according to the faculties and timing of beings.
They bring to full completion all manner of vast and immeasurable Buddha-activities, as well as other immeasurable qualities of merit, all practices, paths, and spheres of experience;
they swiftly attain equality with the merits of a Tathāgata.

The second question concerns the accomplishment of practice and the functioning of merit. It has two parts: first, questioning the causal practice; second, questioning the resultant meritorious qualities.
This [first] part concerns the cause. There are twelve matters: first, questioning how ignorance is extinguished; second, questioning the subduing of Māra;
third, questioning the restraint of externalists; fourth, questioning the severance of afflictions; fifth, questioning by what means the roots of goodness are accomplished; sixth, questioning...
1. How can one emerge from the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions? 2. What is the object purified by the seven inquiries? 3.
How are the merits of the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth accomplished? 4. How are the merits of the three types of action adorned and brought to fulfillment?
5. By what power of contemplation does one know the merits of the Buddha? 6. Furthermore, how are all objects and cognitions known? 7. What... [The text ends here.]

The Dharma is able to bring sentient beings to fulfillment, even performing the great work of a Buddha. The subsequent passage, "and furthermore, for immeasurable [aeons]," etc., concludes by showing the attainment of the merit of the fruit based on its causes.
Regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, during the hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas they practiced the bodhisattva path...
They collect the Dharma-treasury and are fully able to protect, reveal, and expound it. No demons or non-Buddhists can obstruct or destroy them.
They uphold the True Dharma without end. When they preach the Dharma in all worlds, the celestial kings, dragon kings, and...

The yakṣa kings, gandharva kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, human kings, and Brahmā kings—all these, as well as the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, shall provide protection.
All the worlds shall pay them homage and offer worship, collectively consecrating their crowns. They shall be constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas and all bodhisattvas.

They shall all likewise be filled with love and respect. Attaining the power of roots of goodness, they shall increase pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) and expound the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma.
Upholding the True Dharma as their own adornment, they shall fully expound the successive stages of practice for all Bodhisattvas.
The second section, following "regarding all Tathāgatas," reveals that his activity is equal to that of a Buddha; for by upholding the True Dharma (*saddharma*), he becomes equal to a Buddha.
This passage consists of ten phrases, the first of which serves as the general heading: namely, that "revealing, showing, and expounding" all refer to the True Dharma.
The remaining nine phrases clarify this: first, Māra cannot invade him; second, he maintains and practices [the Dharma]; third, he is protected externally by the kings.

First, being universally revered by the world; second, receiving the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of all Buddhas; third, being cherished and respected by Bodhisattvas; fourth, attaining all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*);
fifth, being able to expound the profound Dharma; sixth, gathering virtues to adorn oneself. Only when these nine qualities are attained is one called a "Protector of the Dharma" (*dharmapāla*).
Afterward, all those below requested [the teaching].
