The Fourth Assembly: In the Palace of the Yāma Heaven, the Bodhisattva of the Forest of Merit serves as the presiding host, expounding the Ten Practices and other teachings.

Dharma-gate. For those who have already understood it, this section causes them to practice. Beginning from the nineteenth fascicle and ending with the twenty-first fascicle, there are four chapters of sutra:
(The Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven Palace; The Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Yāma Heaven Palace; The Chapter on the Ten Practices; The Chapter on the Ten [Transferences]).
Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven (from the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*).

Regarding the initial intent [of this chapter]: it is to respond to the ten questions posed previously. It is not difficult to know; it is only the practice that is difficult. As stated previously: *...* (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*. The translation reflects the structure and content of the extant fragments.)
[Commentary: This practice is like the analogy of oil and light; as they correspond to the eyes and feet respectively, each further assists the other.

Therefore, it follows next. As for the sequence of the chapters: this assembly consists of four chapters divided into three parts. The first two chapters concern the causal conditions (*nidāna*) of this assembly; the next one chapter concerns the main teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*) of this assembly;

and the final one chapter concerns superior progress toward the subsequent stage. Within the section on the causal conditions, this present chapter first clarifies the response to resonance (*pratyāvedana*).

The Interconnection of the Path. The subsequent chapter clarifies the praise of virtues and the manifestation of the essence. As the previous assembly has concluded and the subsequent discourse is about to be presented, this chapter follows accordingly.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: there are three names for this assembly. First, according to its location, it is called the "Assembly in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven."

Yama is translated here as "Time" (Śakrābhilagna). He is the foremost of the celestial dwellers. This signifies that when engaging with existence to transform sentient beings through the ten practices, one must be appropriately attuned to the proper time.
Only by speaking at the right time will those who hear it be pleased and submit; only by acting at the right time will those who see it revere and follow.
Traversing existence by relying on emptiness, one enters the profound through phenomena; it is based on this that the teaching is expounded. With respect to persons, it is named the Forest of Merit;

with respect to the Dharma, it is named the Assembly of the Ten Practices. All three [names] are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds. As for the name of the subsequent chapter, it is largely the same as the assembly, meaning that one ascends to this stage without departing from the preceding three.

At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority, throughout every world in the ten directions—in each of the four continents, specifically in Jambudvīpa to the south and upon the summit of Mount Sumeru—the Tathāgata was seen dwelling amidst the assemblies.
All those bodhisattvas, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, expounded the Dharma; none of them failed to consider themselves as being constantly in the presence of the Buddha. At that time...
The World-Honored One did not depart from beneath any of the bodhi trees or from the summit of Mount Sumeru, yet proceeded toward the Jewel-Adorned Hall in the palace of the Suyāma Heaven.
At that time, the King of the Suyāma Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar and immediately employed his supernormal powers.
Within that palace, he manifested a lion throne of precious lotus-womb, adorned with a million tiers.
It was draped with a million golden nets and covered above by a million flower canopies, a million garland canopies, a million incense canopies, and a million jewel canopies.
There were likewise [a million] flower parasols, garland parasols, incense parasols, and jewel parasols.
A million [deities] were arrayed in circumambulation; a million rays of light shone forth in illumination;
a million kings of the Yāma Heaven paid homage with reverent prostrations; a million Brahmā kings leaped for joy; and a million bodhisattvas extolled and praised [him].
A million celestial musical instruments each played a million kinds of Dharma sounds in uninterrupted succession.
A million kinds of flower clouds, a million kinds of garland clouds, a million kinds of clouds of ornaments, and a million kinds of robe clouds completely covered [the space] on all sides.
A million kinds of mani-jewel clouds shone with brilliant light. These were produced from a hundred thousand kinds of roots of goodness. Hundred...
It is that which is protected and sustained by ten thousand Buddhas; that in which a million kinds of merit and virtue increase;
that which is purified and adorned by a million kinds of profound resolve and a million kinds of vows; that which is brought forth by a million kinds of practices;
that which is established by a million kinds of dharmas; and that which manifests through a million kinds of supernormal powers, constantly producing a million kinds [of phenomena].

The sounds of his voice revealed all dharmas. Then, having prepared a seat, that Heavenly King bowed his body with palms joined toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and with reverence and respect addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
We pray only that you will take pity on us and dwell in this palace. At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation and immediately ascended.
The jeweled palaces throughout all the ten directions were likewise so.
At that time, the Heavenly King, recollecting the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas, and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke these verses:
The Tathāgata Yaśas, renowned throughout the ten directions, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things;
he once entered this maṇi palace, And for this reason, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Ratnarāja, the Lamp of the World, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things.
He once entered this pure hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Priyadarśana sees without obstruction; among all that is auspicious, he is supreme.
He once entered this adorned hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, who illuminates the world, is the most supreme among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this sublime palace, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata benefits the world and is the most supreme among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Palace of Stainless Radiance; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Suprabuddha, who has no teacher and is supreme among all that is auspicious, Once entered this Palace of Precious Incense; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Jitendra, the lamp of the world, supreme among all that is auspicious—he once entered this Hall of Exquisite Fragrance; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Agati, the hero of discourse, supreme among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Hall of the Universal Eye; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata, endowed with all virtues, is supreme among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this Hall of Excellent Adornment; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Duṣkaracaryā benefits the world; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
He once entered this Hall of Universal Adornment; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In this world, the King of the Yāma Heaven, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, recollects the merits of the Buddhas of the past.
His virtues were proclaimed and extolled. In all the worlds of the ten directions, the kings of the Yāma heavens likewise praised the Buddha’s merits in this same way.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Maṇi-adorned Palace and sat cross-legged upon a lion throne within a precious lotus treasury.
Suddenly, this palace became vast and spacious, just like the dwellings of the celestial hosts.
The same applies to all worlds in the ten directions.

Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the text: this chapter is divided into ten parts. First is the "Original Assembly’s Perfect Pervasiveness," meaning that the subsequent assembly is taught while the preceding assembly remains undispersed.
Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, is "Ascending Without Departing. Third...
1. At that time, the heavenly kings descended; the heavenly kings beheld the Buddha. 2. Thereupon, by means of their supernormal powers, they each descended and adorned their palace seats.

(The remaining one million verses in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* separately manifest these marks of adornment. 3. At that time, those heavenly kings [descended]; they invited the Buddha to reside in their palaces.
4. At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation; the Tathāgata accepted the invitation. 5. At that time, the heavenly kings [descended]; each thought to himself...
1. The past cause: the eight verses beginning with "The Tathāgata of Eightfold Fame" praise ten Buddhas;

these Buddhas precede the ten Buddhas of the previous assembly, following their respective order. 2. At that time, the World-Honored One... [the Buddhas] ascended the hall together. 3. This hall suddenly...
[the place suddenly became vast enough to accommodate them].
The twentieth chapter, "Verses of Praise," from within the Yāma Palace.
The purpose of this [chapter] is to assist in transformation through praise and glorification, to explain the essential nature of practice, and to serve as the basis for that practice.
The fundamental intent and general purport of the verses of praise from the three heavens are largely the same; they differ only in their interpretation of practice, realization, and vows.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from worlds outside a number of lands equal to the atoms within a hundred thousand buddha-fields, there came to this assembly one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, and Bodhisattva Forest of Victory.

Sā. The Bodhisattva Forest of Fearlessness, the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse, the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, the Bodhisattva Forest of Power, the Bodhisattva Forest of Practice, the Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening, and the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom—the lands from which these bodhisattvas have come.
Namely, the world called Endowed with Affectionate Wisdom; the world called Banner of Wisdom; the world called Jewel Wisdom; the world called Supreme Wisdom;
the world called Lamp of Wisdom; the world called Vajra Wisdom; the world called Blissful Wisdom; the world called Sun Wisdom; and the world called Pure Wisdom.
In the world-system Brahmamati, these bodhisattvas each cultivated the pure conduct of brahmacarya under various Buddhas, namely:

the Buddha Constantly Abiding Eye, the Buddha Unsurpassed Eye, the Buddha Non-abiding Eye, the Buddha Immovable Eye, the Buddha Celestial Eye, the Buddha Liberation Eye, the Buddha Discerning Eye, the Buddha Radiant Mark Eye, the Buddha Supreme Eye, and the Buddha Deep Blue Eye. These bodhisattvas...
Once the Bodhisattvas had arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated themselves at his feet.
Then, in the direction from which each had come, they each miraculously manifested a lion-throne made of a treasury of *maṇi* jewels. Upon these thrones, they sat cross-legged.
Just as the Bodhisattvas had assembled in the Yāma Heaven within this world-system, so it was in all world-systems; such were the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas of those worlds.
All names and titles are entirely equal and without distinction.

Below this, the long passage consists of three sections: first, the gathering of the assembly; second, the emission of light; and third, the praise in verse. Now, regarding the first section, the gathering of the assembly, there are ten subsections.
This is the first: the cause for the gathering. Next, from "In the ten directions... onwards, the presiding deities are identified. Third, from "One by one... onwards...
1. Clarifying the retinue. 2. Descending from a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas]. 3. Belonging to [the assembly]. 4. Their names: listing the names below. 5.
The places from which these bodhisattvas descend. 6. The Buddhas whom each originally served at their respective locations.
7. The teachings established by these bodhisattvas upon their descent. 8. According to the direction from which they came, they participate without intermingling. 9. Just as in this world...
Within the realms, the lower fetters are universally exhausted.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrous-colored light from the tops of his two feet, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions;
within the Yāma Palace, the Buddha and the great assembly were all clearly manifested.

Second, at that time, light radiates downward from the feet; "feet" refers to the soles and the backs. This is because walking necessarily involves movement, and because the backs of the feet depend upon the wheels and toes to function.
This symbolizes that conduct depends upon faith and understanding to achieve its utility.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Buddha emits a great radiance, Universally illuminating the ten directions; All see the Honored One of Gods and Humans, Whose penetration is without obstruction.
The Buddha sits within the Yāma Palace, Pervading throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
This matter is most extraordinary, Rarely encountered in the world.
The King of the Suyāma Heaven offered verses in praise of the ten Tathāgatas; Within this assembly, we behold that In all places it is exactly so.
Those multitudes of bodhisattvas All share the same names as ourselves, Throughout all places in the ten directions.
They proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma; the worlds from which they come have no difference in their names.
Each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas, purely cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Those Tathāgatas all share the same name; their lands are all abundant and joyful, and their spiritual powers are entirely sovereign.
In all places throughout the ten directions, All say that the Buddha is here;
Some see him dwelling among humans, Others see him residing in celestial palaces. The Tathāgata dwells universally In all lands and realms;
We now behold the Buddha Abiding within this celestial palace, Just as he made his original vow for bodhicitta.
Pervading the worlds of the ten directions, the Buddha’s majestic power is thus all-encompassing and inconceivable.
Free from worldly cravings and endowed with boundless virtues, he has attained the power of supernormal faculties;
there are no sentient beings who do not see him as he travels through the worlds of the ten directions, unimpeded like space.
A single body is immeasurable bodies; its characteristics cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha’s merits are boundless—how could they be measured or known? Neither abiding nor departing, he universally enters the Dharma-realm.
Third, the explanation of the ritual for reciting verses. The discourse by the ten bodhisattvas is divided into ten sections. This is the first. The name of the bodhisattva is...
"Gunakusuma" (Forest of Merit) refers to one who has accumulated practice within themselves until their merit is perfected; thus it is called "merit.

Alternatively, when referring to the praise of the Buddha’s supreme virtues, it is called the "Forest of Virtue" (*guṇakusuma*). There are twelve verses which, as the presiding master of this assembly, provide a general summary of the universal events of this gathering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Great Teacher of the World, Stainless and Unsurpassed Honored One,
Whom it is difficult to encounter even in inconceivable eons— The Buddha emits a great radiance, Which none in the world fail to see."
For the sake of the multitude, you have extensively expounded the Dharma to benefit all living beings.
The Tathāgata has appeared in the world to dispel the darkness of ignorance for the sake of the world; such a Lamp of the World is rare and difficult to behold.
You have already cultivated the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
By this he illuminates the world; the Tathāgata has no equal.
One cannot find anyone to compare with him, for he does not perceive the reality of phenomena. The Buddha’s body and his sovereign supernormal powers are inconceivable;
he neither goes nor comes, yet he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If there are those who obtain sight or hearing of the Pure Teacher of Gods and Humans, they shall forever emerge from all evil realms and abandon all suffering.
Even if one were to practice the bodhisattva conduct for immeasurable and incalculable eons, one could not know this meaning; one could not attain Buddhahood even in inconceivable eons.
If one can understand this meaning, then making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas—
surpassing the merit of filling immeasurable lands with precious jewels and bestowing them all upon the Buddhas— one will not fail to attain enlightenment if one cannot know this meaning.

The second section clarifies the supreme merit. This distinguishes the wisdom that awakens one to this [truth] and removes darkness; because it is a wisdom difficult to encounter, it is called the Forest of Wisdom (*prajñā-vana*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Victorious Forest (*Jaya-vana*), empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
Just as in the first month of summer, The sky is clear and free from the veil of clouds, The blazing sun radiates its brilliant light, Pervading the ten directions without exception;
That light is immeasurable and boundless, Such that none can fathom or know it.
If even those with eyes find it thus, How much more so for those who are blind and in darkness? So too it is with all Buddhas.
Its merit is boundless, beyond the reach of inconceivable eons; No one can discern or know it.
All phenomena have no place from which they come, Nor is there any creator.
There is nothing from which they arise that can be distinguished; All phenomena have no coming, And therefore, they have no birth.
Because arising does not exist, cessation is also unattainable. All phenomena are without arising and likewise without cessation.
If one can understand in this way, such a person sees the Tathāgata.
Because all phenomena are without arising, their intrinsic nature is non-existent; thus should one discern and know them.
This person has realized the profound meaning because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
there is no one who can fully comprehend them. Thus understanding phenomena, they ultimately have nothing to understand.
Regarding that which is said to arise, they manifest in all lands; yet knowing the nature of those lands, their minds are never deluded.
Having observed the nature of the world and its lands exactly as they are, and being able to know this well-explained meaning of all things—
this is the third supreme forest. Because he has realized the profound Dharma of ultimate truth, he praises the Buddha’s unfathomable depth and vastness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Fearlessness, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The vast body of the Tathāgata Reaches the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm, Yet does not depart from this seat.”
Pervading all places, if one hears such a Dharma and reverently believes and delights in it,
one will forever leave behind the three evil realms and all sufferings and hardships. Even if one were to travel to worlds as immeasurable and incalculable as they may be,
with a single-minded desire to hear [it], one would encounter the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
Such are the teachings of all Buddhas; this is unsurpassed enlightenment. Even if one wished to hear them for a moment, no one would be able to obtain them.
Yet, those who in the past believed in such Buddha-teachings have already become the Honored Ones among Two-Legged Beings and act as lamps for the world. And those who shall hear them in the future—
Having heard of the Tathāgata’s power of mastery, those who are able to give rise to faith shall also attain Buddhahood.

If there are those in the present who can believe in this Buddha-dharma, they too shall achieve perfect enlightenment and preach the Dharma without fear for immeasurable and incalculable eons. This Dharma is extremely difficult to encounter.
If there are those who hear this, know that it is through the power of their original vows.

If there are those who can receive and uphold these teachings of the Buddhas, and having upheld them, proclaim them widely—if such a person were to attain Buddhahood, how much more so for one who exerts diligent effort, with a firm mind never abandoning [the practice]? Know that such a person is indeed like this.

The fourth stage of the certain accomplishment of Bodhi is called the Forest of Fearlessness, because through the power of faith and aspiration, one hears the profound teachings without fear; it is so named to praise the merit of one whose faith and inclination have become even deeper.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"If a person hears this rare and sovereign Dharma, They can give rise to a heart of joy and swiftly eliminate the web of doubt.
The One Possessing All-Knowledge and Vision Spoke these words himself:"
The Tathāgata knows all things; therefore, he is inconceivable.
There is no arising of wisdom from ignorance; the world remains perpetually in darkness.
Therefore, nothing can arise [from it], whether it be form or the formless. These two are not one; so too are wisdom and ignorance.
Their essences are each distinct and different, Like the characterized and the uncharacterized;
Birth-and-death and nirvana are differentiated as not the same, And so it is with wisdom and the absence of wisdom. When the world first comes into being, it has no mark of decay;
Wisdom and the absence of wisdom are likewise: These two aspects do not exist at the same time.
Just as the initial mind of a bodhisattva does not coexist with the subsequent mind, so too is it with wisdom and non-wisdom:
these two minds do not exist simultaneously. Just as the various groups of consciousnesses are each without mutual conjunction, so it is with wisdom and non-wisdom;
ultimately, they are without conjunction, like the agada medicine.
Just as one can extinguish all poisons, so too is the wise person; they can extinguish ignorance.
The Tathāgata is unsurpassed, and there is none equal to him; nothing can compare to him, and therefore he is difficult to encounter.

The fifth is to reject delusion and honor the true, and to reject ignorance and honor wisdom; this is called having a sense of shame and remorse. It praises the supreme benefits of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
All phenomena are without distinction, and there is no one capable of knowing them; only Buddhas know them, for their wisdom is ultimate.
Just as gold and the color of gold have no difference in their nature, so it is with what is dharma and what is non-dharma:
their essential nature is without variation, whether they be sentient beings or non-sentient beings.
Both are devoid of reality; such is the nature of all phenomena. In terms of ultimate meaning, neither exists.
Just as in the future age there is no characteristic of the past, so too are all phenomena:
they possess none of the various characteristics, for all such aspects are unreal, like the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
All phenomena are likewise thus; their intrinsic nature does not exist.
When Nirvāṇa is taught, two aspects are presented; all phenomena are likewise thus. Through conceptualization, distinctions arise;
just as there is that which is counted based upon the objects being counted, so too is the counter. That intrinsic nature does not exist.
Thus one understands phenomena, Like the method of calculation, Increasing from one to immeasurable numbers;
Though phenomena lack intrinsic nature, They are differentiated by wisdom.
Just as the world’s eons end in conflagration, Yet space remains unimpaired, So too is the Buddha’s wisdom.
Just as sentient beings throughout the ten directions each grasp at the characteristics of empty space, so too do the Buddhas perceive the world;

yet through false discrimination, they observe the sixth consciousness with diligent application, seeing that principle and phenomena are identical and without distinction, free from the marks of body and mind. Therefore, this is called diligence. Ten.
This verse offers a general praise of the Buddha’s virtues. The former [verse] refers to non-differentiation within differentiation; this [verse] refers to differentiation within non-differentiation.
These two chapters connect to reveal that they are neither identical nor separate, and they mutually establish one another.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Power Forest (Balavana), receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The realms of all sentient beings Are entirely within the three periods of time.
All sentient beings of the three periods Dwell entirely within the five aggregates (*skandhas*). The aggregates have karma as their root; Karma has the mind as its root.
Mental phenomena are like illusions, and the world is likewise so.
The world is not made by itself, nor is it made by another, yet it comes into being; it likewise undergoes destruction.
Although the world comes into being, and although the world undergoes destruction, one who thoroughly understands the world [is liberated].
These two should not be spoken of: what is the world (*loka*) and what is not the world?
"World" and "not-world" are merely distinctions of names. The phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) throughout the three times are called the "world";
their cessation is "not the world. Thus, they are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
How are the aggregates (skandhas) explained? What is the nature of the aggregates? Since the nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished, they are said to be unarisen.
When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished. This is the meaning of "unarisen. Since sentient beings are likewise so.
The Buddhas are likewise so; the Buddha and all Buddha-dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature.

I shall understand this thoroughly and explain it widely for others, so as to cause sentient beings to eliminate and eradicate these views. Therefore, although I now encounter suffering..."

Poison. One should endure it for the sake of compassionate mindfulness toward sentient beings, for the benefit of sentient beings, for the peace and happiness of sentient beings, out of pity for sentient beings, to gather in sentient beings, not to abandon sentient beings, to attain awakening oneself, to cause others to attain awakening, so that the mind does not regress, and to advance toward the Buddha-way. This is called a bodhisattva.
The third practice of the Mahāsattva is the practice of non-opposition.

This third practice of non-opposition is grounded in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). There are three kinds of patience: patience toward living beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and patience toward cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).

Because one accords with the nature of things through patience, it is called "non-opposition. One attains the patience regarding the true dharma (*bhūta-dharma-kṣānti*) and [realizes] non-self (*anātman*).
"Mine" (mamāyita) refers to the absence of resentment. To accord with things and to accord with the Dharma is what is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To accord with things means to have no conflict with phenomena; to accord with principle means to have no conflict with the Dharma. When phenomena and principle are without conflict, this is the meaning of non-arising and quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).

In the text, the initial section distinguishes the characteristics of patience. The two lines of scripture beginning with "constantly cultivating the dharma of patience" clarify the practice of patience.

Next, the two lines beginning with "not seeking fame or profit" reveal the freedom from faults. Next, the two lines of scripture beginning with "but one should simply form this thought" clarify the intention behind patience.
Below that is the actual cultivation of the practice of patience; first, it clarifies the patience of enduring enmity and harm, which is directed toward objects that are difficult to endure.
First, the five lines and a half of the sūtra beginning with "Thus accomplishing such patience" clarify verbal abuse and humiliation.

Next, the two lines of the sūtra beginning with "Furthermore, this assembly of sentient beings" clarify physical harm. Next, the passage "Thus, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), there was never a rest" clarifies long-term endurance.
Finally, the three lines beginning with "Encountering this extreme agony and torment" [clarify the intensity of suffering].
The first half of the sutra clarifies the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). Next, the three lines of sutra beginning with "At that time, he further thought...

clarify the patience of enduring suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanakṣānti*). Next, the three lines of sutra beginning with "Furthermore, he reflected... clarify the patience of discerning phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*).

Finally, the two and a half lines of sutra beginning with "For the sake of compassionately regarding sentient beings... clarify the cultivation of the intent for patience. This is called the conclusion of the names.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the unyielding conduct of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? This bodhisattva cultivates all forms of diligence, namely:

foremost diligence, great diligence, superior diligence, extraordinary diligence, most excellent diligence, most wondrous diligence, supreme diligence, unsurpassed diligence, unequaled diligence, and universal diligence.

Their nature is free from the three poisons. Their nature is free from arrogance. Their nature does not conceal [faults]. Their nature is free from stinginess and envy. Their nature is free from flattery and deception.
Their nature is inherently possessed of shame and remorse. They never practice diligence for the sake of harming even a single sentient being;
rather, they practice diligence solely for the sake of severing all afflictions, and they practice diligence solely for the sake of uprooting the source of all delusions.
They practice diligence solely for the sake of eliminating all habitual tendencies; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the realms of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the death and rebirth of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the afflictions of all sentient beings; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing all...
They practice diligence because sentient beings delight in it; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the spheres of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings; and they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the entire dharma-realm.
Therefore, they practice diligence. They practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the fundamental nature of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the equality of all Buddha-dharmas; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the equality of the three periods of time;
and they practice diligence solely for the sake of attaining the light of wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas.
They practice diligence solely for the sake of realizing the wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the single true mark of all Buddha-dharmas; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing that all Buddha-dharmas are boundless;
and they practice diligence solely for the sake of attaining the vast, definitive, and skillful wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, they practice diligence. They practice diligence solely for the sake of attaining the wisdom that discerns and explains the meaning of all phrases of the Buddha-dharma.
Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has accomplished such diligent practice, suppose someone were to say:
"Can you, for the sake of all sentient beings in countless worlds, for each and every sentient being..."
Therefore, they shall undergo all manner of sufferings in the Avīci Hell for incalculable kalpas.

May each and every one of those sentient beings encounter the appearance of innumerable Buddhas in the world; by virtue of seeing these Buddhas, may they fully experience all forms of happiness until they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
You, moreover, shall then attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You will be able to...
"Do you not? He replied, 'I am able. Furthermore, suppose someone were to say: 'There are immeasurable, incalculable great oceans;
you should exhaust them by dripping from them with the tip of a single hair. There are immeasurable, incalculable worlds, all ground into dust;
you must count each drop and each grain of dust, knowing their number entirely for the sake of sentient beings.'"
Thus, for that many eons, he experienced uninterrupted suffering in every moment of thought. Yet, upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva did not give rise to even a single thought of regret;
rather, his joy increased all the more, and he felt profound self-congratulation at having attained such great and wholesome benefit.
"By my power," he thought, "I shall cause those sentient beings to be forever liberated from all sufferings. With this, the Bodhisattva...
This practice of skillful means causes all sentient beings throughout all worlds to reach ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
this is called the fourth unyielding practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The fourth is the practice of being unyielding (*anavalīna*). Its essence relies upon the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). To be diligent without indolence or retreat is called "unyielding. "Yielding" (*nava*) means to bend or to be weak;
because one is firm and strong within oneself, there is no yielding or weakness. It is also said to be "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*);
because one constantly manifests transformations for the sake of sentient beings through merit, it is called inexhaustible. This means that if one were indolent, there would be exhaustion.
Among the three types of diligence in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, these are termed "non-retrogressive," "non-weak," and "non-contented.

In the text, the first section—beginning with "initially cultivating all forms of diligence" and consisting of two lines of fragmentary scripture—reveals the characteristics of diligence. Next, the passage "by nature free from the three poisons" reveals its freedom from faults;
this refers to difficult-to-practice diligence (*duṣkaravīrya*). Following that, the fourteen lines of scripture beginning with "merely for the sake of... clarify diligence.
Regarding the purpose [of this practice], there are four sections therein. First, it is solely for the sake of severing all afflictions; that is, for the severance of delusions.
Second, it is solely for the sake of knowing the realms of all sentient beings; that is, for the deliverance of beings. Third, it is solely for the sake of knowing the entire dharma-realm.

It is for the sake of knowing the Dharma; it is for the sake of attaining all Buddha-dharmas; it is for the sake of seeking the Dharma. The above section generally reveals the characteristics of diligence.
Following this, from "Having accomplished such diligent practice" onwards, there is a detailed explanation according to specific difficulties, which consists of two parts.

First, within the diligence of donning the armor: (1) for the sake of the sentient beings of the world enduring the sufferings of hell; (2) for the sake of delivering sentient beings, [one practices] for a long time...
For kalpas he endured suffering without a single thought of regret. Next, this is the diligence of benefiting and bringing joy through skillful means.
Finally, this is called the name of the concluding summary.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of being free from delusion and confusion? This bodhisattva achieves correctness...
Mindfulness: the mind is undistracted, firm and immovable, supremely pure, vast and immeasurable, and free from delusion.

By means of this right mindfulness, one skillfully understands all worldly languages and is able to maintain the verbal expressions of supramundane dharmas—namely, being able to maintain the verbal expressions of material and non-material dharmas, and being able to maintain the establishment of the intrinsic nature of material form.

Regarding verbal expressions, up to and including the verbal expressions that establish and maintain the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, his mind is free from delusion and confusion.
Within the world, as he dies here and is born there, his mind is free from delusion and confusion. Entering the womb and emerging from the womb, his mind is free from delusion and confusion.

Generating the aspiration for enlightenment with a mind free from delusion and confusion; serving spiritual friends with a mind free from delusion and confusion; diligently practicing the Buddha-dharma with a mind free from delusion and confusion;
recognizing the works of Māra with a mind free from delusion and confusion; and remaining detached from all demonic activities with a mind free from delusion and confusion.
Throughout unspeakable eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices with a mind free from delusion or confusion.
This bodhisattva achieves such immeasurable right mindfulness that, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya eons, they hear the true Dharma from all Buddhas,
bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends— namely, the profound Dharma, the vast Dharma, the adorned Dharma, and various forms of adornment.

The Dharma; the Dharma of expounding various bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; the Dharma of the adornments of Bodhisattvas; the unsurpassed Dharma of the light of the Buddha’s spiritual power;
the Dharma of pure definitive understanding through correct aspiration; the Dharma of non-attachment to all worldly phenomena;
the Dharma of discerning all worldly phenomena; the exceedingly vast Dharma; and the Dharma that, free from the cataracts of delusion, illuminates the realization of all sentient beings.

Regarding all worldly dharmas, both common and uncommon, the unsurpassed dharma of bodhisattva wisdom, and the dharma of mastery over all-knowledge—once a bodhisattva has heard such dharmas, they do not forget or lose them for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
their minds constantly recollect them without interruption. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated these throughout immeasurable kalpas.

While traveling, they never disturb or vex a single sentient being so as to cause them to lose right mindfulness, nor do they destroy the True Dharma or sever their roots of goodness, because their minds constantly increase and expand in vast wisdom.

Furthermore, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cannot be deluded or disturbed by various sounds, namely: loud and high-pitched sounds, coarse and turbid sounds, or sounds that cause extreme terror, or those that are pleasing...
Pleasant sounds, unpleasant sounds, sounds that disturb the auditory consciousness, and sounds that impair the six sense faculties—
when this bodhisattva hears such immeasurable and innumerable pleasant and unpleasant sounds, even if they were to fill incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds.
Never for a single thought-moment has his mind been distracted. That is to say: his right mindfulness is undisturbed; his objective sphere is undisturbed; his samādhi is undisturbed;
his entry into the profound Dharma is undisturbed; his practice of the bodhisattva conduct is undisturbed; and his arousal of the bodhicitta is undisturbed.

He is undisturbed in his recollection of the Buddhas; undisturbed in his contemplation of the true Dharma; undisturbed in his wisdom that transforms sentient beings; undisturbed in his wisdom that purifies sentient beings;
and undisturbed in his definitive realization of the profound meaning. Because he does not commit evil deeds, he has no obstruction of evil karma.

Because they do not give rise to afflictions, they have no obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Because they do not treat the Dharma with contempt, they have no obstruction regarding the Dharma through pride.

Because they do not slander the True Dharma, they have no obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). O Son of the Buddha, such sounds as those described above fill each and every *asaṃkhyeya* world;
throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, they have never been interrupted, and they are able to—
While they may destroy and disorder all the faculties of the body and mind of sentient beings, they cannot destroy the mind of this bodhisattva.

Having entered into samādhi and abiding in the noble Dharma, the bodhisattva contemplates and examines all sounds. He thoroughly understands the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sounds;
he thoroughly understands the nature of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sounds. Having heard them in this way, he gives rise to no attachment.
They do not give rise to anger; they do not lose mindfulness. They skillfully grasp signs without becoming stained by attachment.
They know that all sounds are non-existent and truly unattainable; they have no creator and no original limit. They are equal to the dharma-realm and without distinction.
In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes a tranquil body and mental activity, reaching all-knowledge.
They never regress. They skillfully enter all gates of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). They know that all samādhis share a single essential nature.
They comprehend that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without limit. They attain the true wisdom of all phenomena. They attain the profound samādhi that is free from sound.
They attain incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) gates of samādhi. They increase their immeasurable and vast heart of compassion (*karuṇā*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva attained countless hundreds of thousands of samādhis within a single thought-moment.
Hearing such sounds, his mind was not confused or disturbed, and he caused those samādhis to gradually increase and expand further. He formed this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in unsurpassed, pure mindfulness, so that they may attain non-retrogression regarding all-knowledge and reach the ultimate."
They achieve *nirvāṇa* without remainder; this is called the fifth practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the practice free from delusion and confusion.

This fifth practice of freedom from delusion and confusion relies upon the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*). Because wisdom (*prajñā*) supports meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and thereby eliminates both dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), it is termed "freedom from delusion and confusion.
The initial statement regarding "achieving right mindfulness" (*samyaksmṛti*) refers to right mindfulness as categorized under the side of calm abiding (*śamathapakṣa*). Right...
Mindfulness is itself concentration. Because that mind is free from the confusion of false thoughts, it is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Second, with respect to *vipaśyanā*, it is also called right mindfulness; this means not viewing objects one-sidedly, but clearly understanding their conditions.

As the Sūtra says: "Right mindfulness regarding all phenomena is never forgotten. Third, with respect to *dhyāna*, the simultaneous operation of calm abiding and insight is called right mindfulness. Below...
The Sūtra says: "By means of right mindfulness, one skillfully understands the world and so forth.

This means that clarity regarding objects is the sense of non-delusion (*amoha*), and not differing from the object of focus is the sense of non-distraction (*avikṣepa*). The subsequent sūtra states: "Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the mind is maintained constantly on a single object."
Wisdom that fully comprehends objects is identical to samādhi. Because it illuminates through wisdom, one is free from delusion; because it is right concentration, one is free from distraction.

The statement "the mind is without distraction" introduces the nine subsequent lines, which specifically clarify right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). The first line is the general summary of being undistracted.
This means: first, because it does not follow after objects, there is no distraction; second, because the two obstacles cannot destroy it, it is called "firm";
third, because various conditions cannot pull it away, it is called "immovable"; fourth, because it transcends the inferior to manifest the superior, it is called "supreme";
fifth, because it is untainted by other worlds, it is called "pure. These five points above explain the absence of distraction. The four meanings below explain the absence of delusion.

Sixth, it is called "vast" because it accords with the *dharmadhātu*. Seventh, it is called "great" because it leads toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Eighth, it is called "immeasurable" because its manifestation is difficult to measure.
Ninth, it is called "non-delusive" because it does not abandon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). These nine phrases are categorized individually into three types of dhyāna:
the first six are the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); the next two are the dhyāna that brings forth meritorious qualities; and the last...

First is the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings. The preceding section generally reveals the absence of delusion and distraction; the subsequent section, beginning with "Because of right mindfulness," specifically clarifies the absence of delusion and distraction.
First, it concludes the previous topic and introduces the following one. Second, from "Skillfully understanding the world" onwards, it reveals the capacity of right mindfulness.

The first two phrases present both [aspects] together; the subsequent section, beginning with "That which is for the sake of," explains them both. The former refers to the ability to maintain material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

The first five lines and a half of the sūtra generally distinguish the absence of delusion and confusion with respect to all objects. Following this, the passage beginning with "This bodhisattva accomplishes such...

specifically clarifies the absence of delusion and confusion in relation to that which is upheld. Within this, the first one line and a half of the sūtra concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
Next, the four lines and a half of the sūtra beginning with "That is to say" correctly reveal that which is upheld; the text contains fifteen [items].
[The first] sentence. Next, from "The Bodhisattva hears" downwards, one line of the fragmentary sutra concludes the absence of delusion and confusion.

Next, from "For what reason" downwards, two lines of the remaining sutra interrogate and explain the underlying cause. The following text specifically clarifies how the nine aforementioned meanings encompass the three types of dhyāna.
First, from the second instance, "Various sounds cannot delude or confuse him," there are sixteen lines of sutra that provide the explanation.

The preceding section on "the meditative absorption for dwelling in happiness in the present life" explains that from the so-called "lofty and great sound" down to the "profound meaning," there is no distraction;
this universally explains the absence of mental scattering. The phrase "not performing unwholesome deeds" explains steadfastness.
The phrase "as described above" explains immovability. The phrase "entering into samādhi" explains supremacy. The phrase "having heard thus" explains purity.

“Purity. This is the detailed explanation following “knowing all sounds. The above six sections conclude the explanation of the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Next, the five lines and a half of sūtra beginning with “In this way, the bodhisattva achieves... explain the dhyāna that draws forth merit (*guṇa-ākarṣaka-dhyāna*).

Within this, the two meanings of "great immeasurability" are explained. Next, the two lines of sūtra beginning with "then he forms such a thought" explain the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that benefits sentient beings.

This explains the absence of delusion among the nine types [of concentration], which refers to not becoming attached to the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyānāsvāda*) and failing to give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This constitutes delusion. Now, by guiding meditation through compassion, there is no delusion. This is called "naming the lower bonds.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful practice of manifestation? In this regard, the physical karma of this bodhisattva is pure.
Their vocal karma is pure; their mental karma is pure. Abiding in non-apprehension, they manifest the non-apprehensible karma of body, speech, and mind.
They are able to know that the three karmas are all non-existent; because they are without falsehood, there is no bondage.

Whatever they manifest is without intrinsic nature and without dependence. Abiding in the heart of non-substantiality, they know the self-nature of immeasurable minds and they know the self-nature of all phenomena.

Without attainment and without marks, it is profoundly deep and difficult to enter. Abiding in the true state of suchness and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one gives rise [to activity] through skillful means (*upāya*) yet remains free from karmic retribution.
Unborn and undying, one abides in the realm of *nirvāṇa*, abides in the nature of quiescence, and abides in the nature of reality that is without intrinsic nature.
Cut off from the path of language and transcending all worlds, there is no basis for reliance; one enters into the state beyond conceptual discrimination.
It is the dharma free from bondage and attachment. It enters the dharma of the reality of supreme wisdom; it enters the supramundane dharma that cannot be understood by any in the world.
This is the manifestation of the signs of birth through the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva.
Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva forms this thought: "All sentient beings have non-existence as their nature; all dharmas are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
It is their nature. All lands have non-characteristic as their characteristic. All three periods of time are merely verbal designations.
All verbal designations have no basis within all phenomena. All phenomena likewise have no basis within verbal designations.
When a Bodhisattva understands all phenomena in this way, they are all profoundly deep. All worlds are entirely...
Quiescent. All Buddha-dharmas are without increase. Buddha-dharmas are not different from worldly dharmas;
worldly dharmas are not different from Buddha-dharmas. Buddha-dharmas and worldly dharmas are neither confused nor distinct.
Having realized that the essential nature of the dharma-realm is equal, they universally enter the three periods of time and never abandon the great bodhicitta, remaining forever non-retrogressive.
They transform the minds of sentient beings and further increase their great compassion, serving as a place of reliance for all beings.
At that time, the bodhisattva further reflects: "If I do not bring sentient beings to maturity, who else shall?"
If I do not tame sentient beings, who shall tame them? If I do not transform sentient beings, who shall transform them?
If I do not awaken sentient beings, who shall awaken them? If I do not purify sentient beings, who shall purify them?
"This is what is appropriate for me; this is what I ought to do. Furthermore, he reflects:
"If I were to understand this profound Dharma by myself alone, I would attain liberation in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) as a solitary individual.
Yet all sentient beings are blind and sightless, entering upon a great perilous path, bound and entangled by various afflictions (kleśa), like those weighed down by..."
The sick person constantly suffers pain; dwelling in the prison of craving and attachment, they cannot escape on their own.

Not free from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama, they cannot extinguish suffering nor abandon evil karma. Always abiding in the darkness of ignorance, they do not perceive reality.
Transmigrating through birth and death, they find no way out, remaining amidst the eight difficulties and clinging to manifold defilements. Various...
Their minds are shrouded by afflictions and, deluded by false views, they do not practice the right path. Observing sentient beings in this way, the Bodhisattva reflects:

"If I were to abandon these sentient beings who are neither yet matured nor tamed, and instead realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), that would be improper. I shall first transform these sentient beings."
For unspeakably unspeakable eons, they practice the bodhisattva conduct. Those who are not yet matured, they first cause to reach maturity;

those who are not yet tamed, they first cause to be tamed. While this bodhisattva dwells in this practice, if any among the devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or all the world—including gandharvas and asuras—should even briefly behold them...

Those who dwell together with them, who honor, respect, serve, and make offerings to them, or even those who merely hear their name for a moment and it enters their hearts—all such actions shall not be in vain;
they will certainly and surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Excellent Manifestation (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
This sixth stage of excellent manifestation relies upon the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); its essence is *prajñā*.

Because wisdom can manifest and reveal the principle of the three truths, and because *prajñā* is present before one, it is named the Stage of Excellent Manifestation. It is so called because, by means of emptiness, it illuminates existence and is thus able to manifest.

He is born; therefore, he is called "Sudhana" (Excellent Appearance). Regarding the explanation of his characteristics: first, from the passage "This Bodhisattva’s bodily karma is pure" for two and a half lines of scripture, the aspects of his practice are briefly clarified.
Next, the aspects of his practice are explained in detail through three kinds of wisdom. First is "the wisdom that awakens accordingly.
Within this, starting with "first abiding in the mind of reality," the mental karma is indicated; next, starting with "abiding in the stage of correctness," [the verbal karma is indicated].

This demonstrates physical action (*kāyakarman*). Following "Abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa," the subsequent section demonstrates verbal action (*vākkarman*). Finally, "Entering into the state free from conceptual discrimination" serves as the summary.
Second, the five [points] clarify skillful wisdom (*kauśalyajñāna*), which has three parts: first, "This bodhisattva forms such a thought...

and so forth, which correlates principle with phenomena; second, "Thus understanding all... and so forth, which is the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; third, "Never abandoning or departing from... and so forth.
The great bodhicitta; compassion arising in accordance with reason; and the wisdom regarding the welfare of sentient beings. Regarding the latter, there are two parts. First, one further reflects:
"I shall not leave the immature masses behind, but shall establish the resolve to gather and deliver them.

Second, one places others before oneself. Within this, there are four sections. First: "If I myself were liberated... and so forth, which concerns gathering others while relying on one's own deliverance. Next: "But as for all those masses... and so forth.
1. Contemplating the cycle of rebirth for sentient beings. 2. The three bodhisattvas thus contemplate; this concludes the section on what is not appropriate. 3.

"I shall first transform them"—this is the resolution to first rescue them. 4. While subsequently abiding in this practice, the summary concludes by manifesting the benefits. This is the name of the concluding section.
