Chapter Twenty-one (Part Two): The Ten Practices.
"O Son of the Buddha, what is the unattached practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha, with an unattached mind, this bodhisattva is able, in every thought-moment, to enter incalculable worlds and to adorn and purify incalculable worlds."
With a mind free from attachment toward all worlds, they approach the presence of incalculable Tathāgatas,
where they pay respectful homage, serve, and make offerings with incalculable flowers, incalculable perfumes, incalculable garlands,
incalculable ointments, powdered incense, robes, rare jewels, banners, pennants, exquisite parasols, and various ornaments, each of which is incalculable.
They employ it solely for the purpose of making offerings. Such offerings are made for the sake of the ultimate unconditioned dharma and for the sake of abiding in the inconceivable dharma.

In every thought-moment, they behold countless Buddhas; yet toward these Buddhas their minds are without attachment, they have no attachment to the Buddha-fields, and they have no attachment even to the marks and signs of the Buddhas. They behold the radiance of the Buddhas and listen...
The Buddha preaches the Dharma, yet remains unattached. He is likewise unattached to the worlds of the ten directions, as well as to all the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Having heard the Buddha’s Dharma, his heart gives rise to joy; his resolve and power are vast, enabling him to embrace and practice all the bodhisattva deeds.
Yet, even regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, he remains unattached. This Bodhisattva, throughout unspeakable eons...
They see unspeakably many Buddhas appearing in the world, serving and making offerings to each and every one of them throughout unspeakably many eons, their minds never wearying or satisfied.
They see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and behold the majestic assemblies of bodhisattvas, yet they remain entirely without attachment.
They see impure worlds as well, yet they feel no aversion. Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas...
Because one observes in accordance with the dharmas of all Buddhas, within the dharmas of all Buddhas there is neither defilement nor purity;
neither darkness nor light; neither difference nor unity; neither reality nor falsehood; neither security nor peril; neither the right path nor the wrong path.
In this way, the bodhisattva deeply penetrates the dharma-realm to transform sentient beings, yet does not give rise to attachment toward those beings.
They uphold all dharmas, yet do not give rise to attachment toward those dharmas. They resolve upon the mind of enlightenment and abide in the dwelling of the Buddhas.
Yet they do not give rise to attachment toward the abodes of the Buddhas. Although there is verbal expression, their minds have no attachment to such expressions.
They enter the realms of sentient beings, yet their minds have no attachment to those realms. They thoroughly understand samādhi, being able to enter it and abide within it.
Yet, within the state of samādhi, their minds have no attachment. They travel to immeasurable Buddha-lands;
whether entering them, seeing them, or dwelling therein, their minds have no attachment to those lands. When they depart, they feel no lingering attachment.
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to remain without attachment, their minds are free from obstacles regarding the Buddha-dharma.
They fully comprehend the Bodhi of the Buddhas, realize the Dharma-vinaya, abide in the true teaching of the Buddhas, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, and dwell in the bodhisattva-mind.
They contemplate the methods of liberation for bodhisattvas; their minds are unstained by the dwelling places of bodhisattvas, and regarding the [Bodhi]...
The conduct of the Bodhisattva is likewise without attachment; he purifies the bodhisattva path and receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Having received this prediction, he reflects thus: "Ordinary people are foolish and deluded; they lack knowledge and vision, lack faith and understanding, and lack wise conduct.

They are stubborn, dull-witted, and greedily attached, wandering through the cycle of birth and death. They do not seek to see the Buddha, do not follow the enlightened guide, and do not trust the Tamer (*vināyaka*); they are lost."
They have mistakenly entered perilous paths; they do not revere the King of Ten Powers; they are ignorant of the Bodhisattva’s kindness; they are attached to their dwelling places;
upon hearing that all phenomena are empty, their hearts are greatly terrified; they distance themselves from the True Dharma and abide in false dharmas;

they abandon the level and easy path to enter difficult and treacherous ones; they turn their backs on the Buddha’s intent and follow the intent of Māra; and they stubbornly cling to existence within the various realms of being.
[He] relinquishes [them]. Thus observing all sentient beings, the bodhisattva increases great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and gives rise to various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) without attachment.

At that time, the bodhisattva further reflects: "For the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall, throughout every single land in the worlds of the ten directions, teach and mature them for unspeakably unspeakable eons (*kalpa*), just as I would for one being."
Birth. For all sentient beings, it is likewise; one never becomes weary or exhausted by this, nor does one abandon them and depart.

Furthermore, using the tip of a hair to measure the entirety of the Dharma-realm, one teaches and tames all sentient beings at the location of a single hair-tip for unspeakably unspeakable eons. Just as at one hair-tip, so it is at every single hair-tip.
It is likewise in all places. Even for as little as the snap of a finger, they do not give rise to the notion of "I" or "mine" through attachment to a self.

Throughout every single pore, until the end of future kalpas, they practice the bodhisattva conduct without attachment to the body, without attachment to phenomena, without attachment to mindfulness, without attachment to vows, without attachment to samādhi, without attachment to observation, and without attachment to tranquil concentration.
They do not cling to sense objects; they do not cling to teaching and disciplining sentient beings;
nor do they cling to entering the dharma-realm. Why is this? The bodhisattva forms this thought: "I should contemplate all dharma-realms as like an illusion;

the Buddhas as like shadows; the bodhisattva’s practice as like a dream; the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma as like an echo; and all worlds as like transformations produced by the retribution of karma."

Because they are sustained [by the dharmadhātu], differentiated bodies are like illusions, for they arise through the power of practice. All sentient beings are like the mind, for they are variously defiled.
All phenomena are like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for they cannot be altered. Furthermore, he reflects:
"I shall, throughout the entirety of space and pervading the dharma-realm, practice the bodhisattva path in the lands of the ten directions, attaining clear realization in every thought-moment."

Regarding all Buddha-dharmas, right mindfulness is present before them without any grasping or attachment. Thus observing the body as selfless, the bodhisattva perceives the Buddhas without obstruction.
To transform sentient beings, they expound all dharmas, causing them to give rise to immeasurable joy and pure faith in the Buddha-dharma.
They rescue and protect all beings with minds free from weariness; because they are free from weariness, throughout all worlds...

Regarding the realms: there are sentient beings who have not yet attained accomplishment and have not yet been tamed. [The Bodhisattva] goes to all such places and transforms and delivers them through skillful means.

Among those sentient beings, there are various sounds, various karmas, various attachments, various designations, various combinations, various cycles of transmigration, various actions, various spheres of experience, various births, and various...

Having passed away, he dwells securely therein by means of his great vows to teach and transform them, ensuring that their minds do not waver or regress, nor does he give rise to a single thought of defiled attachment.
Why is this? Because he has attained non-attachment and has no basis for dependence.
The complete purification and fulfillment of one's own benefit and the benefit of others is called the seventh practice of non-attachment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The essence of this seventh practice of non-attachment is skillful means (*upāya*). It is termed "non-attachment" because it does not abide in either phenomena (*dharma*) or principle (*tattva*).
Due to the act of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it does not abide in saṃsāra; due to the act of deliverance, it does not abide in nirvāṇa. Thus, it abides in neither.

Therefore, it is called "Non-attachment. This means that while contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one does not abandon existence (*bhava*); while traversing existence, one is not deluded regarding the void.

Practicing both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously, one dwells in neither of the two extremes; hence, it is named the "Practice of Non-attachment. Within the text, there are two explanations of its characteristics:

first, manifesting non-attachment within one's own stage (*svabhūmi*); second, manifesting non-attachment through superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*). Regarding the non-attachment within one's own stage, the first part clarifies—

One does not cling to pure objects. Next, one does not loathe defiled objects. The initial passage of the sutra, beginning with "This bodhisattva, with a mind free from attachment," clarifies non-attachment to pure objects;
that is, although he adorns the buddha-fields, his mind does not cling to the pure lands.

The subsequent passage, beginning with "Next, he goes to the presence of incalculable Tathāgatas," clarifies that although he makes offerings to the Triple Gem, he does not cling to the merit thereof.
Regarding "virtue," the reason for non-attachment is stated next as "for the sake of ultimate [enlightenment]," etc.

Next, from "in every thought-moment" onwards, four lines of the remaining sutra-text separately demonstrate the characteristics of non-attachment; this meaning encompasses both the Three Jewels and one's own spiritual cultivation, wherein there is no attachment whatsoever.
Next, from "this bodhisattva" onwards, it clarifies non-attachment over a long period of time. Next, it says, "seeing impure worlds."

Nor is there any aversion; one does not loathe defiled objects. Next, the two lines of further scripture beginning with "For what reason" interrogate and explain the cause for not loathing defiled objects:
it is because one contemplates them in accordance with the Dharma as being stainless and pure characteristics.
Next, the six lines of scripture beginning with "In this way, the Bodhisattva deeply enters" analogously manifest the myriad practices, whether pertaining to oneself or others. All...

"Without attachment. The first part clarifies the practice of one's own level (*svabhāga-caryā*); the second clarifies the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati-caryā*), which consists of three sections.

First, it clarifies the practice of self-benefit; next, it clarifies the practice of benefiting others; finally, it concludes by establishing the fulfillment of these practices. Now, for the first [section], it reiterates the preceding practice of one's own level.
Then, from "In the Buddha-dharma, the mind is without obstruction" onwards, there are eleven phrases that correctly manifest superior progress. Next, it clarifies...
Regarding altruism: first, one increases great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and subsequently, one must resolve to rescue [beings].

First, the two and a half lines of sūtra beginning with "Having received the prophecy" clarify the contemplation of those objects of compassion; those who are to be pitied fall into perilous paths because they are deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Next, the two and a half lines of sūtra beginning with "Not revering the Ten Powers" clarify the contemplation of those deluded regarding ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, they fall into perilous paths. Next, the Bodhisattva contemplates in this manner; the following one line of scripture clarifies the increase of compassion and non-attachment.
The preceding section clarified contemplating those who are objects of compassion; because they are pitiable, the mind subsequently seeks to rescue them.

Within this, the initial arousal of compassionate action is shown. The Bodhisattva at that time—[the following] three lines of scripture clarify that the mind is free from weariness. Furthermore, next...
The two lines of sutra text following "at the tip of a hair" clarify that his mind is vast; this is the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Next, from "not for even the duration of a finger-snap" down to the four lines of sutra text, he uses the few to illustrate the many, extensively manifesting his non-attachment (*asaṅga*).
Following this, the five and a half lines of sutra text beginning with "Why is this? explain the reason for his non-attachment: because his mindfulness is profound, his benefit is extensive.

It is simply because right mindfulness is present that there is no grasping or attachment. The preceding section clarifies superior progress; the following section concludes with the fulfillment of practice.
Within this, the two phrases regarding contemplating the body as selfless constitute the accomplishment of the practice for one’s own benefit.

Next, the one and a half lines of scripture beginning with "for the sake of transforming sentient beings" clarify tireless teaching and transformation. Following that, the four lines beginning with "because of being free from weariness and aversion" [elaborate on this point].

The Sūtra clarifies the characteristic of insatiability. Next, the two phrases beginning with "not allowing his mind" establish non-attachment. Following that, the two phrases beginning with "Why is this?
provide an inquiry and explanation, simultaneously concluding that the practices for the benefit of both self and others have been perfected.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice that is difficult to attain?

This bodhisattva accomplishes roots of goodness that are difficult to attain, roots of goodness that are difficult to subdue, most excellent roots of goodness, indestructible roots of goodness, and unsurpassable roots of goodness.
Inconceivable roots of goodness; inexhaustible roots of goodness; roots of goodness of sovereign power; roots of goodness of great majesty and virtue;

roots of goodness that share the same nature as all Buddhas. When this bodhisattva cultivates various practices, they attain the most supreme understanding within the Buddha-dharma, they attain vast understanding regarding the Bodhi of the Buddhas, and they never cease from the vows of a bodhisattva until the very end.
Throughout all eons, their minds never grow weary; they do not give rise to revulsion toward any suffering;
they cannot be moved by any demons; they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; they fully practice all the ascetic austerities of a bodhisattva;
they cultivate the bodhisattva path with diligence and without slackening; and they never retreat from their vows for the Great Vehicle. This is the bodhisattva’s secure abiding.

Having attained this difficult-to-attain practice, he is able, in every moment of thought, to transform birth and death throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) without relinquishing the great vows of a bodhisattva.
If any sentient beings serve, make offerings to, or even see or hear him, they all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although this bodhisattva realizes that sentient beings do not exist as substantial entities, [he continues his work].

Yet they do not abandon the realm of all sentient beings. They are like a boatman who does not dwell on this shore, does not dwell on the far shore, and does not dwell in the middle of the stream, yet is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the far shore because he travels back and forth without rest.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: they do not dwell in saṃsāra, nor do they dwell in nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, they do not abide within the middle stream of birth and death, yet they are able to ferry sentient beings from this shore and place them on the other shore—a place of peace, security, fearlessness, and freedom from sorrow and affliction. Moreover, they have no attachment to the numerical categories of sentient beings;
they do not abandon one sentient being while becoming attached to many, nor do they abandon many sentient beings while becoming attached to one. They do not increase the number of sentient beings.
The realm. It does not diminish the realm of sentient beings; it does not give rise to the realm of sentient beings; it does not extinguish the realm of sentient beings;

it does not exhaust the realm of sentient beings; it does not increase the realm of sentient beings; it does not differentiate the realm of sentient beings; it is non-dual as the realm of sentient beings. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva enters deeply into the realm of sentient beings as he does into the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). There is no duality between the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.

Within this non-dual dharma, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither arising nor ceasing; there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither grasping nor reliance, and neither attachment nor duality.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are non-dual within the dharma-realm. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
Through skillful means, they enter the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and abide in the signless (*animitta*).

Adorning their bodies with pure marks, they realize that phenomena lack intrinsic nature while being able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena. Without grasping at sentient beings, they are able to know the number of sentient beings;
without clinging to worlds, they manifest within Buddha-fields; and without discriminating between phenomena, they skillfully enter them.
The Buddha-dharma: profoundly penetrating its principles while extensively expounding its teachings;

fully understanding that all phenomena are the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) free from desire, yet never severing the bodhisattva path nor retreating from bodhisattva conduct; constantly and diligently practicing inexhaustible deeds, freely entering the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It is like drilling wood to produce fire; though the functions of fire are infinite, the fire—
It is not extinguished. In this way, the Bodhisattva’s work of transforming sentient beings is inexhaustible;
yet he dwells eternally in the world without being extinguished. He is neither ultimate nor non-ultimate; neither grasping nor non-grasping; neither dependent nor independent;
neither worldly phenomena nor Buddha-dharma; neither an ordinary person nor one who has attained the fruit. The Bodhisattva accomplishes such a mind that is difficult to attain.

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one does not speak of the Dharma of the two vehicles, nor does one speak of the Buddha-dharma; one does not speak of the world, nor does one speak of worldly dharmas;
one does not speak of sentient beings, nor does one speak of the absence of sentient beings; one does not speak of defilement, nor does one speak of purity. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are without stain and without grasping, neither turning nor regressing. Regarding suchness, the bodhisattva...
When practicing within this dharma that is quiescent, subtle, profound, and supreme, one does not give rise to the thought:

"I am currently practicing this," "I have practiced this," or "I shall practice this. One does not cling to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*), nor to the internal world, the external world, or the internal-external world.
All great vows, the *pāramitās*, and all phenomena are likewise non-existent.

It is so designated. Why is this? Within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is no dharma named "proceeding toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas" or "proceeding toward the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
There is no dharma named "proceeding toward the vehicle of the bodhisattvas" or "proceeding toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

There is no dharma named "proceeding toward the realm of ordinary beings. There is no dharma named "proceeding toward defilement," "proceeding toward purity," "proceeding toward saṃsāra," or "proceeding toward nirvāṇa."

Why is this? Because all phenomena are neither dual nor non-dual, just like space. Just as space cannot be found—whether in the past, future, or present—within the ten directions, yet it is not that space does not exist;
so too the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as unfindable, yet it is not that all phenomena do not exist.
Thus, in accordance with reality, there is no difference, and one does not lose what has been accomplished, universally demonstrating [this truth].
They practice all the bodhisattva deeds; they do not abandon their great vows as they subdue sentient beings and turn the wheel of the true Dharma.

They do not destroy cause and effect, nor do they contravene the sublime Dharma of equality. They are universally equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, never severing the lineage of the Buddhas.

They do not damage the true mark (*dharmatā*) and penetrate deeply into the Dharma. Their eloquence is inexhaustible; hearing the Dharma, they do not become attached, yet they arrive at the ultimate Dharma.
Reaching the very depths, he is well able to expound the Dharma with a mind free from fear. He does not abandon the dwelling of the Buddhas, yet he does not contravene worldly laws.
He manifests universally throughout the world without being attached to the world.

Thus, the Bodhisattva accomplishes this rare wisdom-mind, cultivates all practices, and rescues sentient beings from the three evil realms, teaching and taming them, and establishing them in the presence of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
On the path, he causes them not to waver. He further reflects: "The sentient beings of the world do not know how to repay kindness;
they instead harbor mutual enmity. They are attached to false views, deluded and inverted, foolish and lacking wisdom.

They have no faith, following after evil friends to give rise to various forms of unwholesome intelligence. Greed, craving, ignorance, and all manner of afflictions completely fill them. These are my..."

Regarding the sphere of practice for a bodhisattva: even if there were those who recognize kindness, possess intelligence and wisdom, and if good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) were to fill the world, I would not cultivate the bodhisattva path therein. Why is this?
Because toward sentient beings I have neither favoritism nor aversion, and I harbor no expectations; I do not seek even a single thread, a single hair’s breadth, or even a single word of praise.
He said: "Throughout all kalpas of the future, I shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices;
never for even a single thought-moment will I act for my own sake, but only desiring to deliver all sentient beings, causing them to be pure and to attain eternal liberation. Why is this?

As one who serves as a clear guide among sentient beings, the Dharma dictates that I should not grasp or seek anything for myself, but practice the bodhisattva path solely for the sake of sentient beings."
Causing them to reach the secure further shore and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—
this is called the eighth difficult-to-attain practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The eighth is the practice that is difficult to attain. Its essence relies upon the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*). In the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāva-bhūmi*);

second, the clarification of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*). Within the first part, one first clarifies self-benefit. This bodhisattva accomplishes the three lower practices described in the sutra as being "difficult to attain."

This clarifies the cultivation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Next, during the cultivation of the various practices, the remaining four lines of the sutra reveal the characteristics of these roots of goodness;
the text contains ten phrases. Because they have attained the most supreme state, they receive the name "difficult to obtain.

Next, the three lines of sutra following "abiding in this difficult-to-obtain practice" reveal the benefits accomplished by these practices. The first is the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*); next, [the text] distinguishes the benefit for others (*parārtha*).

He. Although this Bodhisattva has understood the eight sections and a half of sutra passages concerning sentient beings, there is a correspondence between the teaching (dharma) and the analogy (upamā).
Within this correspondence, it says: "not dwelling in the middle current of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Previously, birth-and-death was taken as this shore and nirvāṇa as the other shore;

now, speaking of the "middle current of birth-and-death" refers to the period from after the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) until before the attainment of Buddhahood—the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The three types of worthies still abide within the two deaths; therefore, the middle stream is itself birth-and-death. Thus it is said, "the middle stream of birth-and-death.
This does not mean that the interval between birth-and-death and nirvāṇa is called the "middle of birth-and-death.

Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" interrogates and explains the reason for non-abiding. There are two rounds of interrogation; the first begins from "Deeply entering the multitudes" and extends for two lines and a few characters.
The Sūtra first directly addresses the point of non-attachment. Next, the two lines beginning with "fully understanding all dharmas" re-examine the preceding meaning.
Following this, the seven lines of the remaining sūtra beginning with "The Bodhisattva thus... provide a dual conclusion for the two preceding lines, consisting of both the Dharma and its parable.

There is no attachment. However, fearing that one might still fall into the traces of compassion and wisdom, this [text] brushes them away.
Above, the practices of the two benefits were clarified; next, from "The Bodhisattva accomplishes such... onwards, the superior progress is clarified. First, the practice of wisdom is clarified;

next, the practice of compassion is clarified. First, the preceding stage of self-benefit is cited; next, from "Not teaching the Dharma of the Two Vehicles," the characteristics of the superior progress are correctly distinguished.
Entering the profound through phenomena, he therefore does not speak; this clarifies that being free from marks, there is no speaking.

Next, the four lines of scripture beginning with "For what reason" provide an inquiry and explanation to manifest the dual negation (*ubhayābhāva*). The intent is as follows: the reason for not speaking is, first, because there is no dharma to be spoken;
second, it clarifies that there is no mind that speaks, meaning that no conceptual thought is aroused. Next, the three lines of scripture beginning with "For what reason... [continue].

The Sūtra then explains the reason for "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*). Non-thought is so called because it accords with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Next, the four and a half lines of sūtra beginning with "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) investigate and reveal the dual negation (*ubhayābhāva*).
This consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). The intent of the investigation is as follows: "Since there is nothing to which one is attached..."

"Why is it that one cultivates the practice of the two benefits? This explains the underlying intent: because of the "double negation" (neither-nor), one is able to "dual-transport" (the union of wisdom and compassion);

because there is no duality, there is non-attachment; and because there is no non-duality, it does not hinder the arising of practice. Therefore, within this synthesis, first the non-obstruction between essence and characteristics is clarified;

next, from "universally bestowing" [onward], the establishment of meritorious virtues is accomplished. The above distinguishes the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*), while the below distinguishes compassion (*karuṇā*).

[The text] proceeds. First, the initial passage thus establishes the latter two lines, citing wisdom to manifest compassion. Next, the passage beginning with "In the three evil destinies" (from another sutra) correctly manifests the characteristics of compassion.

Next, the three lines of scripture beginning with "Then he further thinks" specifically address the transformation of the wicked, clarifying that the wicked are precisely those who are the objects of compassion.
Finally, the section beginning with "Even if there were" clarifies that if one is virtuous, they are not [the primary object of] transformation.

This is the context. Next, regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason," the subsequent three lines of the sutra provide an inquiry and explanation for the basis of universal transformation. The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Since it is the natural principle for a Bodhisattva’s transformative activity to be impartial, why is it that they focus exclusively on the wicked and abandon the virtuous?

The intent of the explanation is that a Bodhisattva has no fixed sense of intimacy or estrangement toward sentient beings; rather, they feel compassion specifically for those whose delusions are heavy and whose obstructions are deep.

Therefore, it is only those who commit evil that are transformed. If one seeks fame and profit, then transformation would be understood as gratitude; however, because there is fundamentally no seeking, the transformation is directed specifically toward the evil. Next, regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason," this further interrogates and explains why it is necessary to practice compassion without seeking. The interrogation asks: "The Bodhisattva and sentient beings are originally not mutually involved; for what reason does he compassionately rescue them throughout long kalpas? Without seeking, there is no attachment to self or others. Because there is no attachment, there is no obstruction. Because there is no obstruction, there is no separation. Because there is no separation, there is no distance. Because there is no distance, there is no distinction between self and other. Because there is no distinction between self and other, one naturally practices great compassion. Therefore, it is said: "Because there is no seeking, there is no obstruction; because there is no obstruction, there is no separation; because there is no separation, there is no distance; because there is no distance, there is no distinction between self and other; because there is no distinction between self and other, one naturally practices great compassion. "Seeking. The explanation of the meaning states that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas naturally guide [beings] in the same way; were it otherwise, they would not be called "enlightened guides.
This concludes the section on the superior progress. This is termed the "concluding summary of names."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of wholesome dharmas?

This bodhisattva acts as a cooling pool of Dharma for all the world—including devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and gandharvas—upholding the true Dharma and ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
Because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of pure radiance, they preach the Dharma and bestow predictions of enlightenment.
Their eloquence is inexhaustible. Because they have attained the dhāraṇī of the fulfillment of meaning, their analytical knowledge of meaning is inexhaustible.

Because they have attained the dhāraṇī of awakening to the true Dharma, their analytical knowledge of phenomena is inexhaustible. Because they have attained the dhāraṇī of explaining terminology, their analytical knowledge of language is inexhaustible.
Because they have attained the dhāraṇī of the unobstructed gateway to boundless phrases and inexhaustible meanings, their analytical knowledge of non-obstruction is inexhaustible.
It is inexhaustible: because they have received the empowerment of the Buddha’s *dhāraṇī* upon their crowns, their eloquence of joy is inexhaustible;

because they have attained the *dhāraṇī-gate* of awakening not through others, their eloquence of light is inexhaustible; because they have attained the *dhāraṇī-gate* of concordant eloquence, their concordant eloquence is inexhaustible;
and because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of etymological interpretation within the various bodies of meaning, the bodies of phrases, and the bodies of syllables.

Because he has attained the gate of the *anantamukha* (inexhaustible) analytical exposition, his inexhaustible eloquence is boundless; because he has attained the *anantāvarta-dhāraṇī* (the dharani of infinite revolutions), his inexhaustible eloquence is boundless.
This Bodhisattva, with firm great compassion, universally gathers in all sentient beings. Throughout the trichiliocosm, he transforms his body into golden color and performs the work of a Buddha.
According to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of various sentient beings, by means of his broad and long tongue, within a single...
Within a single sound, he manifests immeasurable sounds; preaching the Dharma according to the occasion, he causes all to rejoice.

Even if there were unspeakably many sentient beings with various karmic retributions gathered together in one place—an assembly so vast that it filled unspeakable worlds—and the Bodhisattva sat within that gathering, every single sentient being therein possessed [a distinct voice].

One may speak of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) assemblies. From each and every mouth, one can simultaneously emit hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of sounds, each with distinct words and distinct questions.
Within a single moment of thought, a bodhisattva is able to receive them all and respond to each, causing all doubts to be dispelled, just as in one assembly, so too in unspeakably many assemblies.

All are likewise. Furthermore, suppose that from every single tip of a hair, in every moment of thought, there emerge unspeakably unspeakable numbers of assemblies at sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
and let it be so for all tips of hair. Even if the kalpas of the future were to come to an end, these assemblies would never be exhausted.
Within each moment of thought, these assemblies, by means of their respective distinct languages...
In response to another inquiry: A bodhisattva is able to receive and comprehend all [questions] within a single thought-moment, without fear, without timidity, without doubt, and without error.

They form this thought: "Even if all sentient beings were to come together and question me with such verbal actions, I shall preach the Dharma for them without interruption or exhaustion, causing them all to rejoice and abide in the wholesome paths; furthermore, I shall cause them to well understand the One [Vehicle]."
He is able to expound all manner of teachings for sentient beings through every form of speech, yet he makes no conceptual distinctions regarding language.

Even if unspeakably many diverse words and phrases are brought forward as challenges, he comprehends them all in a single thought-moment and answers them all with a single voice, causing everyone to attain universal awakening without exception, because he has received the empowerment of omniscience. By means of this...
Because they have attained the treasury of non-obstruction; because they have attained the perfect radiance of all dharmas; and because they are fully endowed with the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Son of the Buddha, once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are established in the practice of wholesome dharmas, they are able to purify themselves.
Furthermore, by means of the skillful method of non-attachment, they universally benefit all sentient beings, yet they do not perceive any sentient being who attains liberation.
Just as in this trichiliocosm, so it is even throughout unspeakably many trichiliocosms;
they manifest bodies of golden hue and are endowed with sublime voices regarding all phenomena.
They perform the work of a Buddha without any obstruction. O Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accomplish ten kinds of bodies.
They are: the body that enters the boundless Dharma-realm yet is not a realm of rebirth (*gati*), because it extinguishes all worlds;
the body that enters the various realms within the boundless Dharma-realm, because it gives birth to all worlds; the non-arising body, because it abides in the equality of the non-arising Dharma.

Therefore, it is the non-extinguishing body, because all extinguished verbal expressions are unattainable. It is the non-substantial body, because it attains reality as it is (*yathābhūta*). It is the non-delusive body, because it manifests in accordance with conditions.
It is the non-transmigrating body, because it is free from dying here and being born there. It is the indestructible body, because the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is indestructible.
It is the single-characteristic body, because the paths of speech throughout the three periods of time are severed. It is the signless body, because it is skillfully able to...
By observing the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of bodies.

For the sake of nurturing all roots of goodness, he serves as a shelter for all sentient beings; for the sake of enabling them to attain great peace and security, he serves as a savior for all sentient beings.
He is a refuge for all sentient beings, because he acts as their great locus of reliance.
He is a guide for all sentient beings, because he causes them to attain unsurpassed liberation. He is a teacher for all sentient beings, because he causes them to enter into the true Dharma.
He is a lamp for all sentient beings, because he causes them to clearly perceive the retribution of karma. He is a light for all sentient beings, because he causes them to illuminate...
Because it is the profound and wondrous Dharma; because it serves as a torch for all three periods of time to cause the realization of the true Dharma;

because it serves as an illumination for all worlds to cause entry into the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); and because it serves as light for all realms of existence to manifest the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the ninth practice of wholesome dharmas of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. The Bodhisattva...
Abiding in this practice, one acts as a pool of the Dharma for all sentient beings to provide them with refreshing clarity, because it is able to exhaustively reach the source of all Buddha-dharmas.

The ninth is the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*); its essence is the power of strength (*bala-bala*). "Wholesome dharmas" refers to skillful preaching of the Dharma. Therefore...

These are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). Regarding "power" (*bala*): consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) is twofold—first, the power of analytical discernment (*cintā-bala*), and second, the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).

Based on these former powers as the catalyst, one preaches the Dharma. Fundamental activities are threefold: first, the power of retribution and supernormal faculties; second, the power of cultivated meditative concentration; and third, the power of transformation.
This stage is largely equivalent to the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*), which is the rank of a Dharma Master (*dharma-bhāṇaka*) who skillfully expounds the Dharma.

Therefore, first, the title is raised as a heading; second, the explanation of its characteristics has two parts: first, the internal development (*svabhāva*), and second, the superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
Within the section on internal development: this Bodhisattva is generally explained in the first seven lines of the sutra as being for the sake of all worlds;
next, from "obtaining pure radiance" onwards, in seven and a half lines of the sutra, it is specifically explained that he extensively upholds the True Dharma. Next, this Bodhisattva...
Below "The Firmness of Great Compassion" there are eighteen lines of scripture that extensively explain the non-interruption of the Buddha-seed. Within this, it is divided into three sections.
The first two and a half lines of scripture clarify the benefit of sentient beings through the three karmas; this is the river of great compassion. Next, from "Even if there were a person...

onwards, it employs hypothetical suppositions to demonstrate its profound superiority. Within this section, the initial passage beginning with "Even if there were unspeakable... clarifies the Great [Vehicle].
This section resolves doubts. It first clarifies that a single assembly is itself the river of *pāramitās*. Next, from the passage beginning "Suppose even a single hair-tip...

onwards, it clarifies the subtle resolution of doubts; that is, within the space of a single hair-tip, there are unspeakably many great assemblies as previously described—this is the river of *samādhi*.
Third, from the passage "And he forms this thought" onwards, it extensively resolves doubts throughout the entire text. The preceding mention of the multitude at the hair-tip refers to this.
There is still a measure [to be explained]. Now it is clarified that all assemblies, each possessing manifold speech, are fully capable of answering;

this is the River of the Knowledge of Vows (*praṇidhijñāna*). Next, by means of the phrase "having received the consecration of omniscience" (*sarvajñatābhiṣeka*), the underlying cause is explained in summary.

That is to say, the reason one is able to expound extensively is: first, because of the external assistance of other Buddhas; second, because of the freedom from obstruction within one's own treasury; third, because of the... [text fragment ends].

Because it illuminates the Dharma perfectly; because it possesses the wisdom capable of such illumination; for these reasons, it is called a "wholesome dharma" (kuśala-dharma). Thus, it does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.

The above has clarified the practice of one's own level (svabhūmi-pratipatti). Next, once this bodhisattva is established in the practice of wholesome dharmas, the superior progress (viśeṣa-gati) is clarified.
First, the own-level is restated; next, the superior progress is formally revealed. There are sixteen lines of sūtra, which are divided into four sections.
First, the one and a half lines of sutra beginning with "capable of purifying oneself" distinguish the meaning of the purification of the four rivers.

Next, the two lines of sutra beginning with "just as in this trichiliocosm... clarify that the four rivers enter the ocean without anything able to obstruct them, because there is no obstruction to transformation within the many world-systems.
Following the section beginning with "accomplishing the ten kinds of bodies," it distinguishes how these four rivers swirl and revolve.
Regarding the meaning of the "pond": the section beginning with "The Bodhisattva accomplishes... distinguishes the sense of tirelessly entering the ocean over successive kalpas via the four rivers.
Within the description of the "three circumambulations," it refers to the accomplishment of body, speech, and mental actions that accord with wisdom;
because these actions of body, speech, and mind flow into the ocean of wisdom from the four directions, "accordance" carries the meaning of "circumambulation. Next, "Bodhi... [and so forth].

The accomplishment of this [perfection] below specifically demonstrates freedom from weariness and fatigue. This refers to the four rivers entering the ocean without fatigue throughout successive eons;

likewise, the Bodhisattva, through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, cultivates the conduct of a Bodhisattva until the end of all future eons and enters the ocean of the Tathāgata without giving rise to weariness or fatigue.
For this reason, it extensively reveals how he acts as a savior and a refuge for sentient beings, and so forth. Above.
This clarifies the superior progress. Furthermore, this is called "concluding the name" and "abiding in this practice";
below this, there is praise for its excellence. "O Son of the Buddha! What is the true practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?

This Bodhisattva accomplishes the foremost speech of truth: as they speak, so they act; as they act, so they speak. This Bodhisattva trains in the [teachings] of all Buddhas of the three periods of time."
He speaks words of truth. He enters the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and becomes equal to the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
He attains the non-dual speech of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and follows the training of the Tathāgatas.

His wisdom is perfected. This Bodhisattva achieves the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible regarding sentient beings; the knowledge of the karmic retribution of the past, future, and present; and the knowledge of the sharpness or dullness of the various faculties.
The knowledge of various elements; the knowledge of various dispositions; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations;

the knowledge of the times and non-times for the arising of the defilement and purification of the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; the knowledge of recollecting past lives in all worlds; the knowledge of the divine eye;
and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows—yet they do not abandon any of the bodhisattva practices. Why is this? Because they desire to transform and guide all sentient beings.
In order to bring all beings to complete purity, this bodhisattva further gives rise to such a superior resolve:
"If I were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before establishing all sentient beings upon the path of unsurpassed liberation, I would be violating my original vow;
this is not what ought to be. Therefore, one must first cause all [beings]...
Only after all sentient beings have attained unsurpassed bodhi and nirvana without remainder shall I then become a Buddha.

Why is this? It is not because sentient beings requested me to resolve my mind on enlightenment; rather, I myself act as an uninvited friend for sentient beings, desiring first to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their roots of goodness and achieve all-knowledge. For this reason, I am the most supreme, remaining unattached to anything.
Because I am the foremost in the world; because I abide in the stage of the unsurpassed tamer; because I am free from cataracts, having realized the boundlessness of sentient beings;
because I have accomplished what was to be done, through the fulfillment of my original vows; because I am skilled in transformations, through the adornment of the bodhisattva’s merits;
and because I am a good refuge, being sustained by all the Buddhas of the three times—this Bodhisattva...
Because the Mahāsattva does not abandon his original vow, he attains entry into the adornment of unsurpassed wisdom;
he benefits sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied, and according to his original vows, he achieves ultimate fulfillment.

He possesses sovereign mastery of wisdom regarding all phenomena and causes all sentient beings to universally attain purity. In every thought-moment, he travels throughout the worlds of the ten directions. In every thought-moment...
They travel everywhere to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands;
in every thought-moment, they see unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas and their pure lands adorned by the Buddhas, manifesting the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas.
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, this bodhisattva manifests immeasurable bodies, universally entering all worlds without any dependence.
Within his own body, he manifests all lands, all sentient beings, all phenomena, and all Buddhas.
This bodhisattva knows the various conceptions, various desires, various understandings, and various karmas of sentient beings.
In response, he manifests his body according to what is appropriate for each being to bring them to discipline through various roots of goodness.
He contemplates all bodhisattvas as like illusions, all phenomena as like transformations, the appearance of a Buddha in the world as like a shadow, and all worlds as like a dream.

Having attained the inexhaustible treasury of the body of meaning and the body of letters, he possesses mastery over right mindfulness and definitively and thoroughly understands all dharmas with wisdom.

Wisdom is supreme. Entering the true mark of all samādhis and abiding in the stage of non-duality within a single nature, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—seeing that all sentient beings are attached to duality—abides in great compassion and practices this Dharma of quiescence.
Thus, they attain the ten powers of a Buddha, enter the Indra-net Dharma-realm, and achieve the Tathāgata’s unimpeded analytical knowledge.
Liberated, a hero among men, he utters the great lion’s roar; having attained fearlessness, he is able to turn the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma.
Having attained wisdom and liberation, he thoroughly understands all worldly realms, cuts off the revolving stream of birth and death, and enters the great ocean of wisdom.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he protects and upholds the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, reaching all...
The ocean of the Buddha-dharma is the source and depth of true reality (*dharmatā*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this practice of true reality, all those in the world—whether devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, or asuras—who draw near to them, are all caused to attain awakening, joy, and purity.
This is called the tenth practice of truth of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

The tenth is the practice of reality (*tattvayoga*). Its essence is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This means that, by means of two types of knowledge, one enjoys the dharma-bliss and brings sentient beings to maturity;
furthermore, it is "reality" because one can speak according to how one practices, and one can practice according to what one speaks.

First, the name is questioned; next, its characteristics are explained. First, this bodhisattva accomplishes the first [of the ten stages], etc.—this single line of sutra text generally reveals the name and essence. Next...

The specific characteristics of the practice are revealed in two parts. First, from the passage "this bodhisattva trains in the [teachings] of the Buddhas of the three times" onwards, the second section of the sutra provides a general outline of the chapters.
Second, there are five sections based on the detailed explanation: first, the accomplishment of wisdom; second, the non-dual speech of the Buddhas of the three times;
third, the commonality of roots of goodness with the Buddhas; fourth, entering the lineage of the Buddhas; and fifth, training in the reality of the Buddhas.

True words. The first three [sections] are as follows: First, this bodhisattva accomplishes the knowledge of the inclinations of sentient beings; this initially reveals the ten powers (*daśabala*) that are accomplished.
Second, "and does not abandon any bodhisattva practice" clarifies that one attains the fruit without abandoning the cause.

Third, from "Why is that? onwards, the reason is investigated and explained. Because the ten powers are the wisdom for transforming and giving birth [to others], they must be attained so as to purify sentient beings.
Because it is pure, one must not abandon the practice of the cause. Within the non-dual speech of the Buddhas of the three periods, there are three [points].

First, this Bodhisattva again gives rise to the following two lines and the remainder of the sutra; this first section takes up the violation of the vow by way of contrast and serves as a self-admonition that such [violation] should not occur.
Second, the single line and the remainder of the sutra beginning with "This is essential" (*yao dang*) provides a positive explanation. It is essential that one place others before oneself.
Third, the reason why the following two lines of the sūtra provide both an inquiry and an explanation of the underlying cause. There are two intentions in the inquiry:
first, why it is improper [to give] because it violates one's vow; second, why one must prioritize others before oneself. The explanation also has two distinct parts:
first, it was not at the request of sentient beings that I resolved to attain enlightenment; since I granted my consent despite being unasked, how could I now refuse to give?
This is what is appropriate. Next, it says, "I am the most excellent. For a Bodhisattva who guides others must put others first and themselves last;
otherwise, how could they be called the most excellent? Third, there are two aspects to sharing the same roots of goodness as the Buddha.

First, from "not abandoning the original vow" onwards, the virtues that have been perfected are indicated. Second, the specific characteristics of this shared nature are explained. First, regarding all dharmas:
Two phrases concern mental karma; their wisdom is identical. Next, the three lines of scripture beginning with "moment by moment, he travels everywhere" concern physical karma;
their supernormal powers are identical. Regarding the fourfold entry into the Buddha-lineage, there are two parts.

First, the two lines of scripture beginning with "This bodhisattva manifests immeasurable bodies" clarify that the body enters the world without dependence. Second, regarding the entry of wisdom into the lineage, there are two parts. First, knowing sentient beings...

Various perceptions clarify entry into the lineage of compassion (*karuṇā-gotra*). Next, contemplating all bodhisattvas as being like illusions clarifies entry into the lineage of wisdom (*jñāna-gotra*).
Within the fifth [section], "Learning the Buddha’s True Speech," there are two parts. First, by means of the various assemblies, the preceding is marked and the subsequent is initiated.

Second, from "Attaining the Ten Powers of a Buddha" onwards, the remaining four lines of the sutra result in the arising of function from fruition, manifesting the true reality (*dharmatā*) of speech and serving as the teacher.
The Lion’s Roar. Because he turns the wheel of the Dharma, the conclusion states: "Only by knowing the source of the true mark (*dharmatā*) can one speak words of truth.
This passage is largely identical to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. It signifies that within the perfectly integrated teachings attained by the Buddha, the fruits of each stage are perfected;

thus, one exhaustively investigates the true mark of phenomena—meaning that suchness, characteristics, power, and function all reach their ultimate source. Following this, it says: "Thereafter, the Bodhisattva dwells herein... and so forth.
The formation of the practice brings about benefit; this is called "the name of the concluding summary.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within the buddha-fields of the ten directions shook in six ways:
namely, they shook, shook everywhere, shook equally everywhere; they rose, rose everywhere, rose equally everywhere; they surged, surged everywhere, surged equally everywhere.

It quaked, it trembled, it shook everywhere, it shook equally everywhere; it roared, it thundered everywhere, it thundered equally everywhere; it crashed, it crashed everywhere, it crashed equally everywhere.
It rained down exquisite celestial flowers, celestial perfumes, celestial powdered incense, celestial garlands, celestial robes, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments.
Celestial music was played, celestial light was emitted, and the subtle, wondrous voices of the devas were proclaimed. It was just as in this world’s Yāma Heaven.
The celestial palaces proclaimed the supernatural transformations manifested by the teaching of the Ten Practices; it was likewise so throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, arriving together and filling the ten directions. They addressed Guṇākara:
The Bodhisattva Forest said: "O Son of the Buddha, excellent, excellent! You have skillfully expounded the practices of all bodhisattvas.
We are all named Forest of Merit; the worlds in which we dwell are all named Banner of Merit; the Tathāgatas in those lands are all named Universal Merit.
In the presence of our Buddhas as well, this Dharma is taught, along with its assemblies, retinues, terminology, and meanings."
The principle is likewise entirely thus, without increase or decrease. O Son of the Buddha, we have all come to this assembly by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness for you;
it is exactly so throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

The following is the sixth section, the Section on Scriptural Authority (*āgama*). First is the scriptural authority for the auspicious sign of the earth’s trembling; next is the scriptural authority for the arrival of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions;
and finally, from "O Sons of the Buddha, we... onwards, is the concluding summary that establishes universal applicability.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakanda, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed universally all the assemblies in the ten directions, extending throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
This was because he wished to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas would not be interrupted, and because he wished to purify the lineage of the Bodhisattvas.
It is because they wish to ensure that the lineage of their vows does not regress; because they wish to ensure that the continuity of the lineage of their practice remains constant;
because they wish to ensure that the lineages of the three periods of time are entirely equal; because they wish to encompass all the Buddha-lineages of the three periods of time;

because they wish to bring forth and expound all the roots of goodness they have planted; because they wish to examine all faculties; and because they wish to resolve the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Because of the activities of the mind of vital energy (*vāyu*), and because he desires to illuminate all the *bodhi* of the Buddhas, he spoke these verses:
With a single mind, I pay homage to the Honored One of Ten Powers, Who possesses stainless, pure, and unobstructed vision;
Whose sphere of activity is profound and far-reaching, beyond compare; And who dwells within the path that is like space.
Those most supreme among humans in the past, Of immeasurable merit,
unattached, Brave, foremost, and peerless— Those who have left the dust behind travel this path.
In all the lands of the ten directions in the present, They are well able to expound the ultimate truth.
Free from all faults and most pure, those who have no reliance travel this path;
All future lions among men, who wander everywhere throughout the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
Having given rise to the great compassion of all Buddhas, those benefactors travel this path.
The peerless Honored Ones of the three times naturally dispel the darkness of ignorance;
they are equal toward all phenomena. Those of great power who practice this path see everywhere throughout immeasurable and boundless realms, including all states of existence and all destinies.
Having seen this, their minds do not engage in discrimination; those who are unmoving practice this path.
They clearly understand all that exists within the dharma-realm;
in the ultimate truth, they are most pure, having forever destroyed hatred, pride, and delusion. Those possessed of such merit practice this path.
They skillfully discern all sentient beings and enter entirely into the true nature of the Dharma-realm;
they awaken spontaneously without depending on others.
Those empty ones travel this path, exhausting all empty lands throughout every realm, going everywhere to preach the Dharma and extensively employ parables.
The purity described cannot be destroyed; that supreme Muni practices this path with full endowment, firm and non-retrogressive.
Having accomplished the venerable and most excellent Dharma, through the power of his vows he reaches the inexhaustible further shore—this is the path traveled by those who have practiced well.
He is able to know and see, without exception, all the infinite and boundless stages, their vast and profound, wondrous realms;
he clearly understands every word and meaning of the path traversed by that Lion of Debaters, and he utterly subdues all opposing doctrines.
Having attained certainty in the Dharma and being free from all doubt, that Great Muni follows this path;
having distanced himself from all worldly afflictions, he universally bestows peace and happiness upon all sentient beings and acts as an incomparable, peerless guide.
That one of supreme virtue traverses this very path.
Constantly bestowing the gift of fearlessness upon sentient beings, you cause all to rejoice;

your mind is pure and free from defilement. That peerless one practices this path, with mental karma that is utterly refined and well-disciplined, free from all conceptual proliferation and verbal faults.
His majestic radiance is perfect and he is revered by all; that most excellent one practices this path.
Having entered the true meaning and reached the further shore, he dwells in the state of merit with a mind forever tranquil.
Protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, he never forgets; those who have extinguished existence practice this path.
Far removed from self, free from affliction and harm, He constantly proclaims the True Dharma with a great voice,
Pervading all lands in the ten directions; That peerless one practices this path,
Having already perfected the pāramitā of dāna, Adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits.
All sentient beings who see him rejoice; he of supreme wisdom traverses this path.
This ground of knowledge is profoundly deep and difficult to enter;
yet, through sublime wisdom, he skillfully abides with a mind that is ultimately unshakable. Firm in his conduct, he traverses this path.
They are able to enter all that exists within the dharma-realm; wherever they enter, they reach ultimate perfection.
Their supernormal powers are sovereign and leave nothing uncomprehended.
Those peerless Great Munis who practice this path of the light of Dharma diligently cultivate samādhi, which is free from dualistic characteristics.
Their minds are always in meditative absorption, delighting in tranquility; those who see all universally traverse this path.
Subtle and vast are the various lands, mutually interpenetrating yet each distinct;
they fully comprehend them all according to their respective realms—this is the path traversed by that King of Wisdom Mountains.
The mind is ever luminous and pure, free from all defilements;
Without attachment within the three realms, one upholds the various precepts and reaches the other shore. This one of pure mind practices this path;
their wisdom is boundless and ineffable, Pervading the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Skillfully training and dwelling therein, those of adamantine wisdom traverse this path—
the realm of all Buddhas of the three times— entering it with wisdom in its entirety and pervasively,
never for a moment giving rise to weariness or fatigue; such supreme beings traverse this path.
Skillfully discerning the dharmas of the ten powers, Thoroughly knowing all paths leading to every destination,
With unimpeded mastery over the body of karmic action,
That one of meritorious body practices this path throughout The infinite and boundless realms of the ten directions, Among all sentient beings who exist therein.
I shall protect and never abandon them; those fearless ones practice this path.
Diligently cultivating all the Buddha-dharmas, their minds are always vigorous and tireless as they purify all worlds.
These great dragon kings travel this path.

Knowing that the faculties of sentient beings are not the same, And that their inclinations and understandings are immeasurably diverse, They clearly penetrate all various realms; These universal enterers travel this path:
To the infinite lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions, They go everywhere to take birth, beyond all numbering.
Never for a single thought-moment do they give rise to weariness; those who rejoice practice this path.
They universally radiate immeasurable nets of light, illuminating all worlds.
Wherever that light shines, it enters into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); these ones of noble wisdom practice this path.
They cause the lands of the ten directions, numbering immeasurable billions of nayutas, to tremble, yet they do not allow sentient beings to feel any fear.
This is the path traversed by those who benefit the world;
they are well-versed in all methods of language and discourse, reaching ultimate mastery in answering difficult questions and responding to challenges.
Wise and discerning, there is nothing they do not know; this is the path traveled by those who possess fearlessness.
Skillfully understanding all lands—whether inverted or upright—they contemplate and analyze them until reaching the ultimate, causing all beings to dwell upon the ground of inexhaustibility;
this is the path traveled by those of supreme wisdom.
With immeasurable merits numbering in the nayutas, he has practiced all the perfections (pāramitās) in his quest for the Buddha-way.
This teacher of the world, who has transcended it through these inexhaustible practices,
possesses supreme eloquence and roars the lion’s roar.
Universally causing all sentient beings to reach the other shore—this is the path traversed by those of pure mind.
It is the foremost dharma for the Buddhas’ consecration;
having received this dharma-consecration upon their crowns, their minds dwell perpetually in the gateway of the True Dharma. Those of vast mind traverse this path.
All sentient beings are immeasurably diverse; Thoroughly comprehending their minds, they pervade them all.
Resolutely upholding the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, They practice this path like Mount Sumeru.
Within each and every word and phrase, They universally manifest infinite sounds.
Causing those sentient beings to understand according to their kind—this unimpeded vision traverses this path.
All dharmas of written words and spoken language—the wisdom enters them all well without discrimination, abiding within the realm of reality.
This is the path traveled by those who have realized the nature of vision.

Abiding securely in the profound ocean of the Great Dharma, they are well able to seal and determine all phenomena, having realized the true gateway of the signlessness of dharmas. This is the path traveled by those who see reality;
they go to every single buddha-field throughout immeasurable and boundless eons.
Observing and contemplating without a moment’s pause—this is the path traveled by those who are untiring.
The various names of immeasurable and countless Tathāgatas, each distinct from the others, they clearly perceive all upon a single hair-tip; this is the path traveled by those of pure merit.
Upon the tip of a single hair, one sees all Buddhas, Their number being immeasurable and beyond description;
All realms of phenomena are likewise so. Those sons of the Buddha who practice this path For immeasurable, boundless, and countless eons, Perceive them all clearly within a single thought-moment.
Knowing that their duration is neither fixed nor determinate—this is the path traversed by those whose conduct is liberation;
it enables those who behold it not to pass in vain, as all therein plant the seeds of causes and conditions for the Buddha-dharma, while remaining unattached in mind to what they do.
This is the path traversed by those Most Excellent Ones.
For *nayuta* eons he constantly encounters Buddhas, Never for a single thought-moment giving rise to weariness or aversion;

His heart’s joy increases ever further. This is the path traversed by Akṣayamati (Aśūnyadarśin), Which, throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, He has observed within the realms of all sentient beings.
I have never seen a single sentient being who has practiced this path traveled by this steadfast man;
he cultivates an infinite treasury of merit and wisdom,
acting as a universal pool of cooling virtues to benefit all living beings— this foremost person walks this path.
All the various categories within the Dharma-realm, Pervading space, beyond measure—
To know that they all abide in reliance upon verbal expression Is the path traversed by this lion’s roar;
Within each and every samādhi, One universally enters countless samādhis.
They have all reached the profound and subtle depths of the Dharma-gate; this treatise is called "The Moon," for its practitioners follow this path.
Through the power of patience and diligent cultivation, they reach the further shore;
able to endure the most supreme dharma of quiescent extinction, their minds are equanimous and unshakable—this is the path traversed by those of boundless wisdom.
In a single world, at a single seat, their bodies remain unmoving and eternally tranquil,
yet they manifest their forms everywhere; those of infinite body practice this path,
causing all immeasurable and boundless lands to enter together into a single atom.
Universally encompassing all without obstruction, they thoroughly understand this path through their boundless thoughts and actions, discerning what is possible and what is impossible.
They are able to enter universally into all bases of power and achieve the supreme powers of the Tathāgata;
this is the path traversed by those of foremost power.
Throughout the past, future, and present, he constantly and fully understands with wisdom all the infinite and boundless roots of karma;
this is the path traveled by those who possess thorough realization.
He discerns the proper and improper times in the world, and accordingly tames all sentient beings.
Complying with all that is appropriate without fail—this is the path traveled by those who have thoroughly mastered [the teachings].
Skillfully guarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, they constantly practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Free from all grasping and attachment, they subdue the hosts of Māra; this is the path traveled by those whose minds possess wisdom.
Having attained skillfulness regarding all phenomena, they are able to enter the state of equality that is suchness;
their eloquence in proclaiming the Dharma is inexhaustible. These practitioners of the Buddha-way have already perfected the gate of dhāraṇī;
they are well-established in the treasury of non-obstruction.
They have fully penetrated all dharma-realms; this is the path traversed by those who enter deeply.
All Buddhas of the three times are equal to them in mind and identical in wisdom;
they are of one nature and one characteristic, without distinction. This is the path traversed by those of unimpeded lineage.
Having already torn away the film of all ignorance, You have entered deeply into the vast ocean of wisdom;
Universally bestowing the pure eye upon all sentient beings, This is the path traveled by those with eyes.
Having perfected all the qualities of the Teachers, Your miraculous powers are equal and your conduct non-dual.
Attaining the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, this is the path traversed by those who have practiced well;
they wander throughout all worlds, universally raining down the boundless rain of the sublime Dharma,
causing all to attain definitive understanding of its meaning— this is the path traversed by those in the Cloud of Dharma stage.
One who is able to give rise to deep, pure faith in the Buddha’s wisdom and liberation, never regressing;
and through that faith, gives rise to the root of wisdom—this is the path traveled by those who practice well.
Such a one is able, in a single thought-moment, to fully comprehend all sentient beings without exception.
Having realized the self-nature of the minds of those sentient beings, they reach the path of practice of those who have attained the absence of nature;
throughout all lands of the dharma-realm, they are able to manifest emanations there in countless numbers.
Their bodies are most wondrous and peerless, beyond compare; this is the path of practice of those with incomparable conduct.
The Buddha-fields are boundless and beyond numbering; within them dwell immeasurable Buddhas.
Therein, Bodhisattvas appear before them all, attending upon and making offerings to them with deep reverence.
A Bodhisattva is able, by means of a single body alone, to enter into samādhi and abide in tranquil concentration.
They cause one to see their bodies as being beyond number, each and every one arising from samādhi.
The dwelling place of these Bodhisattvas is most profound and wondrous; their conduct and deeds transcend all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Their minds are pure and always joyful, able to cause all sentient beings to be filled with delight.
The various faculties and their skillful means are each distinct;
With wisdom, they clearly perceive them all and understand that these faculties have no basis.
They are able to skillfully distinguish the path for those who are difficult to tame through skillful means, And have attained mastery over all phenomena.
The worlds of the ten directions are each different, yet within them all they perform the work of Buddhas;
their subtle faculties and their conduct are likewise so, as they can extensively preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—who among those who hear it would not rejoice?
This is the path traveled through space by these [Bodhisattvas].
The eye of wisdom is pure and peerless, clearly perceiving all phenomena;
such skillful discernment of wisdom is the path traveled by those who are unequaled.
May all the inexhaustible and vast merit [accrued thereby] bring all spiritual practices to ultimate completion.
Causing all sentient beings to be entirely purified; this peerless one practices the path and universally exhorts others to cultivate the factors that assist the Way.
Causing them all to dwell securely on the stage of skillful means, he delivers countless sentient beings, yet never for a moment gives rise to the notion of "sentient beings."
Observing all capacities and conditions, he first protects their minds so that no conflict arises;
he universally shows sentient beings the place of peace and security.
This is the path traveled by those of skillful means, who have accomplished the supreme, foremost wisdom and are endowed with immeasurable, boundless knowledge.
Regarding all the immeasurable fearlessnesses, this is the path traversed by the wisdom of skillful means.
Within all worlds and all phenomena, one is able to enter them everywhere and attain mastery.
Furthermore, amidst all assemblies of people, one delivers countless sentient beings to liberation.
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, you beat the great Dharma drum to awaken all living beings;
as the supreme and unsurpassed master of Dharma-giving, this Immortal One practices this path,
sitting upright in the full lotus posture, filling infinite realms throughout the ten directions.
Yet his body remains unconfined; this is the path traversed by the Dharma-body.
Able to expound immeasurable and boundless teachings within a single meaning or a single phrase, its limits cannot be found—this is the path traversed by infinite wisdom.
Having well practiced the liberation of the Buddhas, Attaining the Buddha’s wisdom without obstruction,
They achieve fearlessness as heroes of the world; This is the path traveled by those of skillful means,
Who thoroughly know the oceans of worlds in the ten directions, And likewise know the oceans of all Buddha-fields.
They fully comprehend the ocean of wisdom and the ocean of Dharma; all sentient beings who behold them rejoice.
Sometimes they manifest entering the womb and being born; sometimes they manifest attaining perfect enlightenment at the site of awakening.
Thus they cause the world to see these infinite deeds performed by those on the path.
Within immeasurable billions of lands, he manifests his body entering nirvana;
yet in truth, he does not abandon his vows to return to quiescence. This Heroic Debater’s path is firm and subtle;
his single wondrous body is equal to the Buddha, without distinction.
According to the various different perceptions of all sentient beings,
The path traversed by those of the single true body is the dharma-realm of equality without distinction; Fully endowed with immeasurable and boundless meanings,
one contemplates the single characteristic with a mind that does not waver— This is the path traversed by the wise ones of the three periods of time.
Regarding all sentient beings and the Buddha-dharma, they establish and sustain them to ultimate perfection;

their power of upholding is equal to that of a Buddha. These supreme upholders practice this path, possessing unimpeded spiritual powers just like a Buddha, and their divine eye is unobstructed and most pure.
The faculty of hearing is unimpeded, excellently perceiving all sounds;
this one possesses the full array of supernatural powers that constitute the path of the unimpeded mind.
According to their wisdom, they achieve complete accomplishment, thoroughly knowing all things without peer; such is the path traversed by these wise and noble ones.
His mind is in right concentration, unwavering; his wisdom is vast and boundless.
He has clearly mastered all realms of experience and reached the further shore of all virtues—the path traversed by all seers.
He is able to deliver sentient beings according to their respective stages.
Their minds are ultimately never satiated; this is the path traveled by those who are ever-diligent.
All the Buddha-dharmas existing throughout the three times—they know and see them all.
Born from the lineage of the Tathāgatas, these sons of the Buddhas practice this path.
Having perfected speech that is harmonious and compliant, they skillfully subdue discordant discourse;
