always able to advance toward the Buddha’s bodhi, this is the path traveled by those of boundless wisdom.
A single light shines forth and touches all without limit, pervading every land throughout the ten directions.
Universally causing the world to attain great illumination—this is the path traversed by the Destroyer of Darkness.
According to what each should see, they all make offerings;
manifesting the pure body of a Tathāgata, he teaches and transforms hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings, and his adornment of Buddha-fields is likewise.
To cause sentient beings to transcend the world, they cultivate all sublime practices;
this practice is vast and boundless—how could anyone be able to know it?
Even if one were to manifest an unspeakable number of emanated bodies, they would be equal to the dharma-realm and empty space.
All together they praise those virtues, which could not be exhausted in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
The virtues of the Bodhisattva are boundless; all practices are fully perfected.
Even if immeasurable and boundless Buddhas were to speak for immeasurable kalpas, they could not exhaust them.

How much less could the world, including gods and humans, or all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, ever reach the ultimate end of praising and extolling [this] throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas?
The Seventh Section: Verses in Praise. First, the protocol for the discourse is revealed; next, the actual verses are presented. In total, there are one hundred [verses].
This single verse is divided into three major sections. First, one stanza generally expresses the taking of refuge in the teaching. Second, ninety-six stanzas correctly versify the preceding prose.
Third, four stanzas conclude with a praise of its profundity and vastness. Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the verses present the sequence [of the stages];
here, however, that sequence is omitted and it simply says, "one who practices this path. There are briefly four reasons for this: first, the preceding...

Thus, [the previous section] explained by means of the sequential arrangement (*paṭipāṭi*) of the stages from beginning to end. Now, I shall synthesize the preceding explanation so that there is no longer a distinction between beginning and end;
this is because I wish to reveal that within a single stage all practices are complete, and within a single practice all things are present.

Second, the former was based on distinct practices, whereas the present is based on universal practice; thus, the universal and the distinct are non-obstructive, and the two texts mutually clarify one another. Third, the former was based on... [text fragment ends].

The same teaching. Now, regarding the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), the identity and distinction are non-obstructive, for the sake of establishing the one Perfect Teaching (*ekakalpa-vyavasthāna*).

Fourth, whereas previously it was explained by way of unconfused eloquence (*asaṃkīrṇa-pratibhāna*), here it is explained by way of unrestrained eloquence (*anābhoga-pratibhāna*); thus, it is taught without depending on sequential order, as the verbal expression is uninterrupted.

Furthermore, while the former mostly concerns the cause (*hetu*), this mostly concerns the fruit (*phala*; or, alternatively, essence and function are more extensive or concise, and the general and specific alternate with one another).
This clarifies that they mutually arise from their reflections, manifesting the profound, vast, and inconceivable practices of the Bodhisattvas.

Although the subsequent text follows a sequential order, since its original names have been omitted, it is identical to the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) in its perfectly integrated practice.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya,
Scroll Twenty Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya,
Scroll Twenty-one Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, a Śramaṇa.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá-yán Monastery;
Excerpts by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Monastery on Mount Kuāng, clarifying the meaning.
Chapter Twenty-two: The Ten Inexhaustible Stores.

Regarding the purpose of this initial section, there are five general meanings: first, it is to answer the ten questions concerning the *daśanidhāna* (ten treasuries) at the beginning of the second assembly;

second, whereas the previous section elucidated the correct positions (*samyag-viṣaya*), the present section explains how to initiate practice based on those positions, and thus it corresponds to the "Chapter on Brahma" (*Brahma-parivarta*);

third, whereas the previous section treated specific practices according to the positions, the present section distinguishes the universal practices from beginning to end; fourth, whereas the previous section elucidated the practices for establishing the positions, the present section distinguishes the purification of those [practices].

[The practice of] conduct. Therefore, it is identical to the ten practices, such as faith and so forth, of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Five [of these] were previously explained as the culmination of one's own level;

now, the superior progress toward the subsequent stage is being distinguished. This is clarified in the same manner as the preceding explanation of the Dharma. According to the inquiry, this should have appeared after the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*); that it is distinguished here [is because...]
Briefly, there are two meanings. First, it is said that "treasury" (*kośa*) has two senses: in terms of the sense of inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), it occurs after the ten practices;
in terms of the sense of giving birth, it occurs before the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Its meaning thus applies to both locations, with question and answer mutually clarifying this.

Second, it is said that dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) has no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, its intrinsic nature consists simply in the preceding practice that is capable of being dedicated. Now, since these ten treasuries...

The ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) constitute the progressive advancement; because they are also the progressive advancement of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there is no separate stage of advancement following dedication.

This is a case of mutual illustration between the preceding and the succeeding, whereby the full meaning is revealed. Second, regarding the explanation of the name: "Treasury" (*garbha*) carries the sense of giving birth and accumulation.

This means that within the single treasury, its essence contains the *dharmadhātu*; it gathers all virtues and brings forth their functions, which are inexhaustible. It is metaphorically designated as such.

"Roundedly manifesting ten" is an explanatory gloss based on numerical association (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the three points of the essential purport (*abhiprāya*): the ten *piṭakas* constitute the essence (*mūla*), while the subsuming of what precedes and the attainment of what follows constitutes the goal (*prayojana*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma further addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."

There are ten kinds of treasuries. Regarding the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—those who have already spoken, those who shall speak, and those who now speak—the initial enumeration in the commentary on the text reveals their commonality.
By stating that they are spoken of equally throughout the three periods of time, it manifests their excellence and inspires compliance.

What are the ten? They are: the treasury of faith, the treasury of ethical discipline, the treasury of self-respect, the treasury of consideration for others, the treasury of learning, the treasury of generosity, the treasury of wisdom, the treasury of mindfulness, the treasury of retention, and the treasury of eloquence. These are the ten.
Second, the inquiry into their sequence and the enumeration of their distinct names: purity of mind is called faith (*śraddhā*); restraint is called morality (*śīla*);

honoring the virtuous and good is called self-respect (*hrī*); despising and rejecting the violent and evil is called shame (*apatrāpya*); consuming the vast teachings is called learning (*śruta*); relinquishing oneself to benefit others is called generosity (*dāna*);
discerning all phenomena is called wisdom (*prajñā*); causing the mind to remember clearly is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); and maintaining what has been remembered is called... [concentration].

They are maintained. Skillfully proclaiming what has been taught constitutes eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Each possesses its own specific function. However, mindfulness, wisdom, ethical discipline, shame, and dread of blame—these five—all take their essential nature as their substance.
The remaining five establish their names based on their functional activities. The first nine are for one’s own benefit; the last one is for the benefit of others.
Since faith is the foundation of all practice, it is explained first. Based on faith, one leaves behind faults; with shame and dread of blame as adornments, one practices ethical discipline.

Radiant and pure. The first three are practices for distancing oneself from faults; the remainder are all practices for advancing toward goodness. The foremost requirement for advancing toward goodness is extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

To practice according to what one has heard results only in merit and wisdom. Mindfulness causes these to increase and clarify, while wisdom ensures they endure for a long time. Eloquence is for the benefit of others;
therefore, the preceding seven are the seven noble riches (*saptāryadhanāni*), with wisdom as the primary guide. Thus, it is finally analyzed here. Next, the [following] two...
Guarding. The last [of these] is that which can accumulate and then disperse.
O Son of the Buddha! What is the treasury of faith (*śraddhā-kośa*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
This third reliance is explained in detail. The ten treasuries constitute ten sections; each section contains four parts, namely: the inquiry into the name.

This explains the characteristics, establishes the name, and distinguishes the benefits. Regarding the distinction of benefits, this type exists only in the first seventy [verses], while the remainder have none.
Now, first, the inquiry into the name:
this bodhisattva believes that all dharmas are empty, believes that all dharmas are signless, and believes that all dharmas are wishless.
He believes that all phenomena are without activity; he believes that all phenomena are without discrimination;
he believes that all phenomena have no basis; he believes that all phenomena are immeasurable; he believes that all phenomena are unsurpassed;
he believes that all phenomena are difficult to transcend; he believes that all phenomena are unarisen. If a bodhisattva can thus accord with all phenomena, pure faith arises.
Having gained faith, upon hearing that the teachings of all Buddhas are inconceivable, their minds are not cowed;
upon hearing that all Buddhas are inconceivable, their minds are not cowed; upon hearing that the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable, their minds are not cowed;
upon hearing that the dharma-realm is inconceivable, their minds are not cowed; upon hearing that the realm of empty space is inconceivable, their minds are not cowed.
Weakness. Hearing that the realm of nirvāṇa is inconceivable, the mind does not become timid or weak.
Hearing that the past world is inconceivable, the mind does not become timid or weak. Hearing that the future world is inconceivable, the mind does not become timid or weak.
Hearing that the present world is inconceivable, the mind does not become timid or weak. Hearing that entering all kalpas is inconceivable, the mind does not [become timid or weak].
He is not timid. Why is this? This bodhisattva possesses single-minded, firm faith in all Buddhas;
he knows that the wisdom of the Buddhas is boundless and inexhaustible, and that in each and every one of the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas.
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they have attained it, they are attaining it, and they will attain it;
they have transcended the world, they are transcending the world, and they will transcend the world; they have entered *nirvāṇa*, they are entering *nirvāṇa*, and they will enter *nirvāṇa*.
The wisdom of those Buddhas neither increases nor decreases; it is neither born nor extinguished; it neither advances nor recedes; it is neither near nor far; it is non-cognitive.
There is no relinquishing. This bodhisattva enters the wisdom of the Buddha and accomplishes boundless, inexhaustible faith.
Having attained this faith, their mind does not regress; the mind is not distracted, cannot be destroyed, is free from attachment, and is always rooted in the fundamental.
They accord with the noble ones; they dwell in the family of the Tathāgatas; they protect and uphold the lineage of all Buddhas;
they increase the faith and understanding of all bodhisattvas; they accord with the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas; and they give birth to the skillful means of all Buddhas.

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s treasury of faith. When a bodhisattva abides in this treasury of faith, they are able to hear, retain, and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, and explain them to sentient beings so that all may attain awakening.

The commentary is divided into three parts. First, the clarification of the characteristics of faith; second, from "If a bodhisattva... onwards, the clarification of the power of faith; third, from "This bodhisattva enters the Buddha...

onwards, the summary. Regarding the first part, there are ten phrases. The first three phrases clarify faith in the three emptinesses, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

The next three phrases clarify faith in the non-arising of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that there is no [intrinsic] activity.
Because they are unreal, there is no distinction between subject and object; because they lack substantiality, there is nothing upon which to rely.

These three sets of three phrases express faith in the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as being without intrinsic nature: first, it is immeasurable because it is vast and boundless; second, it is unsurpassed because it is most excellent; third, it is unfathomable because it is profound.
The final [set] expresses faith in the three natures collectively as being without intrinsic nature, entering the single contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Next...

Contemplating the power of faith: if a bodhisattva can thus [act], this correctly reveals the functional activity [of that power]. There are ten phrases [in the text], which universally derive from the preceding ten;
the preceding ten likewise all derive from these ten. If one correlates them with the preceding ten in reverse order, it means:

because one believes in the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda*), one is not timid regarding the Buddha-dharma, and so forth. Next, the section beginning with "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) interrogates and explains the basis for this lack of timidity.
This is because one possesses firm faith in both its profundity and vastness; for that which is believed in is exclusively the wisdom of the Buddha.
Next, the two and a half lines of scripture beginning with "In the ten directions" provide a specific explanation of the aforementioned faith in the Buddha’s wisdom.
This means that in the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable Buddhas have each realized *bodhi* and even entered *nirvāṇa*; therefore, [the object of faith is] wisdom.
It is boundless and immeasurable; even a single Buddha could not exhaust it, let alone one that extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time.

When a Bodhisattva possesses firm faith in this that does not waver, how could they have any timidity? Next, the passage beginning with "The wisdom of those Buddhas" explains why hearing of such profundity does not cause timidity.
This means that [notions of] increase, decrease, and so forth are all merely dharmas of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); for the essence of quiescent illumination is like—
Because it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), once a bodhisattva has established firm faith in this, how could they hear of its profundity and yet be cowed?
These two sections explain the ten preceding phrases regarding the inconceivable Dharma; these should be examined in detail according to the text.

Next, from "Having attained this faith" onwards, the benefits of having achieved such faith are revealed. There are eleven phrases [in this section], beginning with "The initial resolve does not regress."

The seven phrases beginning with "born into the family of the Tathāgata" clarify that the essence of practice is firm and stable. The subsequent four phrases beginning with "protecting and upholding" encompass inexhaustible virtues.
This is called the "concluding title. The section beginning with "the Bodhisattva dwelling herein" distinguishes the benefits.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of precepts of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

This bodhisattva accomplishes the precept of universal benefit, the precept of non-acceptance, the precept of non-abiding, the precept of freedom from regret, the precept of freedom from contention, the precept of non-affliction, the precept of freedom from impurity, the precept of freedom from craving, the precept of freedom from fault, and the precept of non-transgression. What is meant by "universal benefit"?
Increasing the precepts: This Bodhisattva upholds the pure precepts fundamentally for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
How is it that they do not receive the precepts? This Bodhisattva does not receive or practice any of the various precepts held by non-Buddhists;

rather, by their very nature, they are naturally diligent in reverently maintaining the impartial pure precepts of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the three periods of time. How is it that they do not abide in the precepts? This Bodhisattva...
When the Bodhisattva upholds the precepts, his mind does not dwell in the desire realm, nor does it dwell in the form realm, nor does it dwell in the formless realm.
Why is this? Because he upholds the precepts without seeking rebirth in those realms. What is the precept of being without regret?
This Bodhisattva constantly dwells in a state of mind free from regret. Why is this? Because he does not commit grave offenses, nor does he practice deceit or guile.
Because they have broken the pure precepts. What is the precept of non-contention? This bodhisattva does not disparage what was previously established, nor do they innovate new rules.
Their mind always accords with and inclines toward the precepts that lead to nirvāṇa; they fully receive and uphold them without any transgression.

They do not trouble other sentient beings by their observance of the precepts so as to cause them suffering; rather, they maintain the precepts with a heart that constantly wishes for all to be joyful.

Regarding ethical discipline: what is the discipline of non-harming? This bodhisattva does not, for the sake of training in spells or preparing medicinal prescriptions, use ethical discipline to harm sentient beings;
rather, they maintain ethical discipline solely for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings.
What is the precept of being unmixed? This bodhisattva does not cling to extreme views and does not maintain mixed precepts;

rather, they contemplate dependent origination and maintain the precepts of renunciation. What is the precept of being free from greed for gain? This bodhisattva does not manifest extraordinary signs to display their own virtue;
rather, they maintain the precepts solely for the sake of fulfilling the dharma of renunciation. What is the precept of being without fault?
He loses his precepts. This bodhisattva does not speak with self-conceit, saying, "I maintain the precepts.

Even upon seeing one who has broken the precepts, he does not disparage or revile them to cause them shame; rather, he maintains the precepts with a single-minded heart. What is meant by being without violation of the precepts?
This bodhisattva forever abandons killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter, as well as greed, malice, and wrong views.
Fully upholding these ten types of wholesome karma, when this bodhisattva maintains these unviolated precepts, they reflect:
"The fact that all sentient beings violate the pure precepts is entirely due to their inverted views; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can [remedy this]."
"Knowing that sentient beings give rise to perversion and violate pure precepts due to certain causes and conditions,
I shall accomplish unsurpassed bodhi and extensively expound the true Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to abandon perversion.
This is called the second treasury of precepts of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

The second is the treasury of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). In the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts: first, the listing of the ten names; second, the detailed explanation following that list.

Regarding the initial listing of the ten precepts, they all pertain to the three aggregates (*tripuṇya-skandha*). To highlight their specific characteristics: the first consists solely of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha*);

the last consists solely of restraint (*saṃvara*); and the middle eight pertain to both, as they serve to prevent transgressions and are thus entirely restraint, yet they also function to rescue and protect, which constitutes benefiting others.
The benefit [of this] can be understood as encompassing all that is wholesome. Next, the characteristics of the ten precepts are cited and explained in ten sections. Regarding the first, it asks:
"What is the precept of universal benefit? Since bringing benefit to sentient beings is the fundamental intention of a bodhisattva, this is clarified at the outset.

Second, what is meant by not receiving precepts? It refers to not receiving false precepts, such as those of the chicken or dog, because they have been established since one's youth and thus one’s movements do not exceed their boundaries.
Third, what is meant by non-abiding precepts? It refers to not delighting in dwelling within the three realms.
It is solely for the sake of seeking awakening and delivering sentient beings; it is not like that of those such as Nanda. Fourth, what is the precept of being without regret?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: For what reason does one maintain the precepts? It is for the sake of having no regret. For what reason is there no regret?
It is for the sake of joy, until the attainment of Great Nirvāṇa. Fifth, what is the precept of being without transgression?
Regarding the precepts for resolving disputes, there are four meanings herein. "Non-" (a-) signifies contrariety. First, not contravening established regulations, unlike Devadatta.
Second, not contravening *nirvāṇa*, because one does not grasp at signs. Third, not contravening the code of discipline (*vinaya*), because one maintains it in its entirety.
Fourth, not contradicting the benefit of sentient beings, because it does not afflict others. Sixth, what is the precept of non-affliction and non-harming?

Within this there are two meanings: first, not holding the precepts merely with the desire to afflict sentient beings—for example, hearing that an Arhat who held the precepts was able to subdue a dragon, and then immediately adopting them for that purpose;
second, not holding the precepts with the desire to achieve pure discipline by means of afflicting or harming sentient beings. As...
7. What is the precept of non-mixture? Holding precepts while harboring wrong views is called "mixed.
To sever the mixture of permanence and annihilation, one contemplates that the nature of conditions is detached; this is the absence of the mixture of afflictions, which is true renunciation.
8. What is the precept of being free from greedy seeking? It means not manifesting the possession of virtues for the sake of appearance.
One who possesses virtue [avoids] one of the five perversions. Having already seen pure conduct, [the text asks]: Ninth, what is the precept of being without fault?
It means not to disparage or revile others; as the *Caryāvatāra-sūtra* says: "When seeing one who has broken the precepts, do not speak of their faults or evils;
one should reflect that this person will also surely attain the Way after a long time. Tenth, what is the precept of being without transgression? This Bodhisattva...

The Bodhisattva forever abandons killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth. This explanation has two meanings. First, it clarifies the *saṃvara* (restraint), which is the foundation of the various precepts of the ten wholesome paths;

therefore, it is explained specifically here. "The Bodhisattva maintains these" and below, both accumulations are clarified together, because he gathers the virtues of enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called the concluding summary of the names.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of shame (*hrī-kośa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva recollects the various evils committed in the past and gives rise to shame. That is to say, the bodhisattva reflects within his own mind:
"Since beginningless time, I and all sentient beings have been each other's fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, sons, and daughters; we have all been possessed by greed, hatred, and delusion."
Due to pride, flattery, deception, and all other afflictions (*kleśa*), they cause one another harm and injury;

they mutually usurp and plunder, committing every kind of evil such as lewdness, violence, and killing. All sentient beings are likewise thus, fully creating manifold evils through their various afflictions;
for this reason, they do not respect one another, do not honor one another, and do not submit to one another.

They do not humble themselves before one another; they do not instruct or guide one another; they do not protect or cherish one another; instead, they kill and harm one another, acting as mutual enemies.
Reflecting upon myself and all sentient beings, I see that we have practiced shameless conduct in the past, future, and present.
There is not a single one of the Buddhas of the three periods who does not know and see this. If I do not now sever this shameless conduct, the Buddhas of the three periods will likewise behold me.
"How could I continue to act in this way without ceasing? This is utterly improper.
Therefore, I should single-mindedly eliminate [these faults] and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so as to extensively preach the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is called the third treasury of shame (*hrī-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The third section investigates and explains the treasury of *hrī* (self-respect). However, regarding the distinct characteristics of *hrī* and *apatrāpya* (shame before others), various explanations differ. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Self-respect (*hrī*) is inward shame;

shame before others (*apatrāpya*) is the disclosure [of one's faults] to others. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also says: "Inwardly giving rise to shame is self-respect; outwardly giving rise to shame is shame before others.
This is largely the same as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on the power of oneself and the Dharma..."
To revere and honor the virtuous and good is *hrī* (shame); this relies upon the power of the world. To despise and reject the violent and evil is *apatrāpya* (modesty).
Regarding the explanation [of the sūtra], first is the explanation of past misconduct as the practice of lack of shame (*ahrīkya*). The sūtra says: "That bodhisattva thinks to himself...
and so forth for four lines of verse. First is the self-reflection on lack of shame; next, from "all sentient beings... for two and a half lines of verse.
The explanation for compassion toward others is likewise. Next, the text explains how prior faults give rise to subsequent shame (*hrī*). The scripture states, "Reflecting upon my own self...

(the following two and a half lines of the sutra), which precisely reveals the characteristics of shame. First, one reflects on one's past transgressions and feels ashamed that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision perceive them;

this is the manifestation of shame through present practice. "Reflecting upon oneself" (*svam eva*) refers to internal self-reproach. Second, "Therefore, I ought... and so forth expresses the firm resolve.
Regarding the realization of abandonment (*prahāṇa-sākṣātkriyā*): the phrase "one who acts without shame in the past, future, and present" uses general wording with a specific intended meaning.

The Bodhisattva reflects upon his own past transgressions and, out of compassion for sentient beings, constantly practices throughout the three periods of time; thus, he single-mindedly abandons [shamelessness] to prevent it within himself and to subdue it.
When he arises again to preach this to sentient beings, both self and others are simultaneously eliminated. This is called the concluding summary of the name.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of shame of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva feels personal shame, thinking:
"In the past, I have greedily sought after various things among the five desires without ever being satisfied. Because of this, all afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion have increased.
I should not engage in such deeds again. Furthermore, he reflects: "Sentient beings lack wisdom; they give rise to..."
Possessing all manner of afflictions, they practice unwholesome dharmas; they do not show mutual respect or honor, even going so far as to become mutual enemies.
They commit every such evil without exception. Having committed them, they rejoice, pursue them, and praise them.
With the blind eye of evil wisdom, possessing no knowledge or vision, they enter the mother’s womb, take birth, and receive a defiled body.

Ultimately, this leads to white hair and wrinkled faces. A person of wisdom observes that these are merely impure phenomena born of lustful desire, as all Buddhas of the three periods of time have known and seen.
If I were still to engage in such matters now, [I would be acting contrary to their example].

This would constitute deceiving the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Therefore, I shall practice a sense of shame (*hrī*), swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and extensively expound the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called the fourth treasury of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the treasury of shame.
The fourth section provides an investigation and explanation of the "treasury of shame" (*hrī-kośa*). Within the explanation of its characteristics, there are three parts.
First, from the passage beginning "This bodhisattva, feeling shame for himself regarding the past," he reflects upon his own lack of shame and cultivates the practice of shame;

thus it says, "I should not now again engage in such deeds," which refers to the practice of shame itself. Second, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, he thinks: 'Sentient beings lack wisdom,'" he expresses compassion for those who lack [wisdom].
Because one feels shame for not awakening to suffering and its origin, it is said that there is "no knowledge or vision.

Next, regarding the passage "descending into the mother’s womb" and below, one practices the conduct of shame by looking back upon the world, vowing to benefit oneself and others. Within this, the section beginning with "first, descending into the mother’s womb" refers to the objects of shame.
Next, the section beginning with "possessing wisdom" refers to feeling shame toward others; this is external shame (*bāhya-lajjā*). Therefore, and so forth...
Resolutely determining the realization of cessation, that which is called the "impure dharma" is as follows: it is impure at its seed, being born from lustful desire;
it is impure in its dwelling place, while abiding within the mother’s womb; it is impure in its own characteristics and essential nature, becoming a defiled body;
and it is ultimately impure, with white hair appearing and the mind harboring [defilements]. This is termed the "name of the lower fetter."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s treasury of hearing? It is when this Bodhisattva knows that because this exists, that exists;
because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this arises, that arises; and because this ceases, that ceases.
These are worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas; these are conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas.
Dharma. There are dharmas that are determinate (*vyākṛta*) and dharmas that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). What is the principle that "because this exists, that exists"?
It means that because ignorance (*avidyā*) exists, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) exist. What is the principle that "because this does not exist, that does not exist"?

It means that because consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not exist, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) does not exist. What is the principle that "because this arises, that arises"? It means that because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises, suffering (*duḥkha*) arises. What...
Because this [condition] ceases, that [result] ceases. That is to say: because existence (*bhava*) ceases, birth (*jāti*) ceases. What are the mundane phenomena (*loka-dharma*)?

They are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). What are the supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*)? They are ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
What are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The realms and the realm of sentient beings. What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are space, nirvāṇa, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the abiding nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). What are determinate phenomena (*vyākṛta-dharma*)?

They are the four noble truths, the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya-phala*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), and the five... [powers].
The powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. What are the indeterminate phenomena? They are as follows: the world is finite;
the world is infinite; the world is both finite and infinite; the world is neither finite nor infinite;
the world is eternal; the world is non-eternal; the world is both eternal and non-eternal; the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal.

It is not that they are impermanent. It is that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa he exists; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa he does not exist; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa he both exists and does not exist;
after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa he neither exists nor does not exist. That the self and sentient beings exist; that the self and sentient beings do not exist;
that the self and sentient beings both exist and do not exist; that the self and sentient beings neither exist nor do not exist. How many Tathāgatas were there in the past?
[How many] will enter parinirvāṇa? How many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas will enter parinirvāṇa?
In the future, how many Tathāgatas, how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and how many sentient beings will there be?

In the present, how many Buddhas abide, how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas abide, and how many sentient beings abide? Which Tathāgata appeared first? Which śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha [appeared first]?
Who appears first? Which sentient beings appear first? Which Tathāgata appears last? Which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas appear last?
Which sentient beings appear last? What phenomenon is foremost at the beginning? What phenomenon is foremost at the end?
From where does the world come? To what place does it go? How many worlds are formed? How many...
When the world is destroyed, from where does the world come? Where does it go? What is the initial limit of birth and death?
What is the final limit of birth and death? These are called indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta-dharma*). The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought:
"All sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death lack extensive learning and are unable to understand this."
"Regarding all dharmas, I shall resolve my mind to uphold the treasury of much learning, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and preach the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. This is called the fifth treasury of much learning of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

The fifth section investigates and explains the *śrutaskandha* (the aggregate of hearing). Within this explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts: first, clarifying the dharmas that are known;

second, from the passage "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms such a thought" onwards, revealing the purpose of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). First, regarding the explanation of the dharmas that are known:
it is designated as the *śrutaskandha*. The commentary states: "Knowledge has hearing as its basis. In reality, however, it refers simply to extensive knowledge. As for what is known...

Regarding the Dharma of Knowledge, the initial heading lists ten dharmas, which are explained in seven sections. First, the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are cited and explained. "What is worldly existence?
and so forth refers to the dharma of dependent origination consisting of the twelve links. This sutra specifically clarifies that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Second, "What is the worldly dharma? and so forth clarifies that the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*) constitute the world.
3. What are mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*)? They are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). 4. What are supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*)?

They are the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*), namely, the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*). 5. What are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are the three realms (*tridhātu*). 6.

What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are the six unconditioned [phenomena], etc. Regarding these, there are differences in number between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; there are extensive explanations in the treatises. How so?
"Definable phenomena" (*vyākṛta-dharma*) refers to the Four Noble Truths and so forth. They are called "definable" because they are capable of producing desirable or undesirable fruits;
thus, they are termed "definable. This is a general explanation. In other contexts, "defining" refers specifically to the wholesome and the unwholesome;

here, however, it refers only to the wholesome. (7) What are "indeterminate phenomena" (*avyākṛta-dharma*)? Regarding the term "indeterminate," there are two senses: first, that which is not wholesome...
It is not evil. That which cannot produce either a desirable or undesirable fruit is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). This [definition] can only explain other passages;

however, in the present text, it refers specifically to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). It means that their false conjectures and irrational interrogations are not worth recording, and for this reason they are termed "indeterminate.
This does not refer to the contrast between good and evil. Furthermore, this indeterminate is also called "set-aside" (*sthāpanīya*).
"Indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) refers to that which should not be answered. Within these indeterminate dharmas, five types are briefly distinguished.
The first refers to the five lines of sutra concerning whether the world has limits; this clarifies the indeterminacy regarding the self (*ātman*).

Herein, non-Buddhists falsely calculate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), yet their errors do not exceed the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Next, the second [category] concerns how many [factors] exist in the past...
Regarding the descent [of the Buddhas]: as for clarifying the number of those in the holy ranks of the Three Vehicles, it cannot be recorded because they are boundlessly transverse.
Next, as for which Tathāgata descends first: it cannot be recorded because they are limitless vertically.
Next, as for where the world comes from when it descends: this interrogates the origin of the three worlds; the text contains six phrases.
The first two lines inquire about the world of sentient beings and the world of aggregates (*skandha*). The subsequent four lines concern the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
This is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that sentient beings have an initial birth;

they claim, for instance, that sentient beings come from darkness and return to darkness, or that the world is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*), which aggregate to form bodies and receptacles and disperse [when they dissolve].
This would then be reduced to atoms; all such views are sources of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and therefore should not be answered.

Next, regarding the fifth [question], "What is the initial limit of birth and death?"—the two subsequent lines concern the prior and posterior limits of birth and death. These non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that birth and death have a beginning and an end;
because they hold this with dogmatic certainty, it is a false view. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Great Sage..."
The fundamental limit (pūrvakoṭi) that has been spoken of cannot be apprehended; birth and death have no beginning, nor do they have an end.
If there is neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle? Therefore, within this, there is neither prior, nor subsequent, nor both together.
Because [the questioner] falsely conceptualizes a beginning and an end, it should not be answered. Thus, it is concluded: "This is called an indeterminate (avyākṛta) matter. Next, [it] proceeds:

This reflection below clarifies the intent of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). It means that because sentient beings lack learning and remain long submerged in birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one vows to uphold the treasury of learning (*śrutaskandha*) to realize enlightenment for oneself and benefit others. This is called the "concluding title."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of giving of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva practices ten kinds of giving, namely:
giving by apportioning; giving until exhaustion; internal giving; external giving; internal-and-external giving; all-encompassing giving; and giving of the past.
Future giving, present giving, and ultimate giving. Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva’s practice of partial giving?
This bodhisattva is by nature compassionate and fond of practicing generosity. If he obtains delicious food, he does not consume it for himself alone;
he must first give it to sentient beings before he eats. All things he receives are treated in this same way. When he eats for himself, he forms this [thought]:...
He reflects: "Within my body dwell eighty thousand families of worms who depend upon me. When my body is satiated with pleasure, they too are satiated;
when my body suffers from hunger, they too suffer from hunger. Now, as I partake of this food and drink, may all sentient beings everywhere obtain full satisfaction.
For the sake of giving to them, I eat this myself without craving its flavor. Furthermore, he reflects:
This is the reflection: "For a long night, I have been attached to this body, partaking of food and drink only to satisfy its hunger and thirst.
Now, by giving this food as a gift to sentient beings, may I forever sever my craving for this body. This is called the gift of partial reduction (*vibhāga-dāna*).
What is the bodhisattva’s gift of total exhaustion (*parikṣaya-dāna*)? Son of the Buddha, it is when this bodhisattva obtains various kinds of superior flavors, food, drink, and fragrances...
Regarding garments, flowers, and the necessities of life: if one uses them for one's own enjoyment, one will live in peace and longevity;
yet if one sets them aside to give to others, one will suffer poverty and meet an early death. At such times, there may be someone who comes and says, "You must give everything you possess to me.
The Bodhisattva reflects to himself: "Since beginningless time, I have lost countless bodies due to hunger."
"Never before have I obtained even so much as a hair’s breadth of benefit for sentient beings that would result in such wholesome gain.

Now, I too shall likewise sacrifice my life as I did in the past. Therefore, I must act for the benefit of sentient beings, relinquishing everything I possess according to their needs, and even at the cost of my very life, I shall have no regret. This is called 'exhaustive giving. What is..."
Bodhisattva’s Inner Giving. O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva is in the prime of youth, handsome and beautiful, his body adorned with fragrant flowers and fine garments.
Having just received the consecration to the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), he possesses the seven treasures and rules over the four quarters of the world.
At that time, someone might come and say to the king: "Great King, you should know that I am now aged and my body is afflicted by a grave illness."
"I am gravely ill, solitary, emaciated, and exhausted; my death will not be long in coming.
If I could obtain the flesh, blood, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and bones from the King’s body, my life would surely be saved.

I only pray that Your Majesty will not hesitate or hold anything back, but look upon me with compassion and grant this gift to me. At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself: "Now, as for this..."
After death, one must surely die; there is not even a single benefit [to be gained]. It is fitting that you abandon [this body] quickly in order to save sentient beings.
Having formed this thought, he gives with a mind free from regret; this is called internal giving (*adhyātma-dāna*). What is the external giving (*bāhya-dāna*) of a Bodhisattva?

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva is in the prime of his youth, possesses a beautiful complexion, and is endowed with all the marks [of excellence]. Adorned with famous flowers and superior garments, he has just received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
He had ascended to the rank of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin), possessed the seven treasures, and ruled over the four continents. At that time, someone might come and say to the king:
"I am now impoverished and oppressed by manifold sufferings; I pray only that Your Benevolence will take pity upon me in particular.
Grant me this royal throne so that I may provide for myself; I shall govern it and enjoy the blessings of kingship. At that moment, the Bodhisattva would think thus:
He said: "All prosperity must inevitably decline; at the time of decline, one can no longer further benefit sentient beings.
I should now fulfill their requests according to what they seek. Having formed this thought, he immediately gave it to them without any regret.
This is called external giving. What is the internal and external giving of a Bodhisattva? O Son of the Buddha, this—
When the Bodhisattva has attained the station of a Wheel-Turning King as described above, possessing the seven treasures and ruling over the four continents, someone may come and say to him:
"Your Majesty has long occupied this position of a Wheel-Turning King, yet I have never obtained it.
I pray only that Your Majesty relinquish it to me, and that you yourself become my servant. At that time, the Bodhisattva acts as follows:
He reflects: "My body, my wealth and treasures, and even my royal throne—all these are impermanent and subject to decay.
Now that I am in the prime of my strength and possess the whole world, and a beggar stands before me, I must seek the enduring Dharma by means of what is non-enduring.
Having formed this thought, he immediately bestows it upon them; even when using his own body to perform labor with diligence, his mind feels no regret. This is called...
The giving of both internal and external things. What is the universal giving of a bodhisattva?

Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, as previously described, occupies the position of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), possessing the seven treasures and ruling over the four continents. At that time, there are immeasurable people who are poor and destitute.
They approached him and spoke these words: "Great King, your fame is heard throughout the ten directions. Out of admiration for your reputation, we have come here.
We each now have a specific request; we pray that you will universally bestow your compassion so that our wishes may be fulfilled."

At that time, some of those poor people begged from the great king for his kingdom, others for his wife and children, and others for his hands, feet, blood, flesh, heart, lungs, head, marrow, or brain. Then the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"All unions of affection must inevitably end in separation; yet [giving these things] would bring no benefit to sentient beings. Now, I desire to forever abandon craving and attachment."

Thinking, "I shall fulfill the wishes of sentient beings with all these things that are destined to disperse," he gives them all away with a heart free from regret, and does not give rise to feelings of aversion or contempt toward sentient beings; this is called "universal giving" (*sarvadāna*).
What is the "past giving" of a bodhisattva? It is when this bodhisattva hears of all the merits possessed by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the past.

Having heard this, they do not become attached, but realize that it is non-existent; they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination, nor do they crave or relish it. They do not seek to grasp it, nor do they rely upon grasping.
Seeing all phenomena as like dreams, they find them to be without solidity. Regarding all roots of goodness, they do not give rise to the notion of existence, nor do they rely upon anything.
They merely expound the teaching for the sake of transforming and maturing sentient beings who cling to grasping, so as to bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity.
Furthermore, he observes all past phenomena; seeking throughout the ten directions, they are entirely unfindable.
Having formed this thought, he completely relinquishes all past phenomena. This is called the giving of the past. What is the future giving of a bodhisattva?
This bodhisattva hears of the practices cultivated by the Buddhas of the future and realizes they do not exist; he does not grasp at them.
He does not differentiate between signs. He desires to be reborn in the various Buddha-fields, yet he neither relishes nor clings to them, nor does he give rise to aversion toward them.

He does not dedicate his roots of goodness toward those realms, nor does he allow his roots of goodness to regress because of them. He constantly and diligently practices without ever abandoning them;
he merely wishes to gather in sentient beings by means of those realms, preaching the truth to them so that they may be brought to maturity for Buddhahood.
Dharma. Yet this Dharma has no location, nor does it lack a location; it is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far.
Furthermore, one reflects: "If a phenomenon is non-existent, it must not fail to be relinquished. This is called future giving. What is the present giving of a bodhisattva?
It is when this bodhisattva hears of the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma [Heaven]...
The Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven,
the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmapārṣadya Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābhā Heaven, the Apramāṇābhā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubha Heaven,
the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.

The gods of the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*), the Untroubled (*Avṛha*), the Heatless (*Atapa*), the Good to See (*Sudṛśa*), the Good Appearance (*Sudarśana*), and the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) heavens—
even upon hearing of the complete merits of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— his mind is neither deluded nor submerged, neither gathered nor dispersed.
He merely contemplates all conditioned phenomena as dreams and unreal, free from attachment, in order to cause sentient beings to renounce them.
They leave behind the evil realms; their minds are free from conceptual discrimination; they cultivate the bodhisattva path and, having accomplished the Buddha-dharma, expound it for others.
This is called "present giving. What is the "ultimate giving" of a bodhisattva?
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were immeasurable sentient beings, some of whom were without eyes, some without ears, and some without noses, tongues, hands, or feet.
He came to where the Bodhisattva was and addressed him, saying, "I am of meager fortune; my faculties are impaired and incomplete.

I pray that you, out of your benevolence and compassion, will employ skillful means to relinquish what you possess so that I may become complete. Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately gave it to him.
Even if, because of this sutra, one were to remain with impaired faculties for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one would not give rise to even a single thought of regret or regretful attachment.

Rather, one should contemplate that from the very moment of entering the womb, the body is an impure and minute form; it is a mass of fetal tissues, with faculties subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that this body has no reality, possesses no sense of shame or remorse, is not the property of the noble ones (*ārya*), and is foul, filthy, and impure.
It is clean. The bones and joints support one another, smeared with flesh and blood; from its nine apertures there is constant flow, detested and despised by others.
Having performed this contemplation, do not give rise to even a single thought of attachment. Furthermore, reflect thus: "This body is precarious and fragile, possessing no solidity.
Why should I now give rise to craving and attachment? I ought to bestow it upon others to fulfill their wishes, just as I [have done]..."
He acts in this way to guide all sentient beings, causing them to give rise to no craving for body or mind, so that they may all achieve the pure body of wisdom.
This is called ultimate giving; it constitutes the sixth treasury of giving of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
This explains the sixth treasury, that of giving (*dāna*). First, regarding the bodhisattva’s practice of the ten kinds of giving, the ten names are initially set forth and listed below.

In the subsequent explanation of their characteristics, they are explained according to their respective sections, forming ten segments. Each segment consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Now, among these ten types of giving, the first six constitute the relinquishment of things (*vastu-parityāga*), namely body, life, and wealth. The next three constitute the relinquishment of the mind (*citta-parityāga*). Namely: [The text continues with the specific list of the ten types of giving.]
Without grasping or attachment, the final simultaneous relinquishment is called "ultimate. Now, regarding the single phrase "How does the Son of the Buddha...

[the text] first indicates the practice of dividing and reducing one's portion for giving. Next, in the explanation, the passage beginning with "This bodhisattva, by nature compassionate and kind... first clarifies the characteristics of dividing and reducing the portion.
Next, the passage beginning with "When eating for oneself... clarifies skillful means in giving. Finally, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he thinks thus... addresses [the recipient].
This treats the obstacles to giving. This is called the "lower heading.

Second, as for "how the lower [giving] is exhaustively marked," the term "exhaustive" (*kṣaya*) refers to disregarding one's own life and emptying all that one possesses. Next, in the explanation of the characteristics: "this bodhisattva obtains various...
and so forth clarifies objects that are difficult to relinquish. Next, "or at times there comes a person... and so forth indicates the manifestation of the object of the request. Third.
The Bodhisattva reflects for himself and then correctly practices the act of giving; this is called the "concluding title.
Third, what is the Bodhisattva’s internal giving? Internal giving refers to the body. Next, from "this Bodhisattva" onwards, the objects of begging appear before him.

"Orphan" (*qiong*) means solitary; one who has no elder brother is called an orphan. Next, from "at that time, the Bodhisattva" onwards, he correctly practices the act of giving; this is called the [concluding] title.
The names of the categories: 4. What is the bodhisattva’s external giving? It is the royal throne.
When someone comes and begs for the realm, at that time one gives it away. 5. What is the bodhisattva’s internal and external giving?
The royal throne is the external; together with the body, it constitutes the internal. 6. What is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing giving? This refers to everything whatsoever...

There is. This clarifies that which is difficult to relinquish; because one ultimately relinquishes it through such means, this serves as a comprehensive summary. By citing what is difficult, the easy is encompassed.

A few instances are briefly cited, for if expanded, they would be boundless. Next, regarding the passage beginning with "At that time, there were immeasurable impoverished people," this clarifies the objects of begging appearing before one.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The mind forms this thought," this concerns the actual practice of giving. (7) What is it?
The Bodhisattva’s past giving—indeed, the giving of the three periods of time—is clearly characterized by non-attachment in its general nature.
Specifically, regarding the past, he does not give rise to longing; regarding the future, he preempts greedy seeking; and regarding the present, his mind is free from defiled attachment.
Now, the passage beginning with "This Bodhisattva, hearing of the past... clarifies that he has no attachment to the Buddha-dharma. Next, it says: "Furthermore, he contemplates..."
Examining the lower [time]: to have no attachment toward any phenomena is called past giving. Eighth, what is the bodhisattva’s future giving?
It is because of not being attached to future retributions. This refers to the passage beginning with "first hearing about the various Buddhas of the future" below.
This clearly reveals the cause of non-attachment in practice: not aspiring for the fruit of a pure land, not savoring its excellence, and not being weary of the task.
"Not dedicating" explains the former point, "not savoring"; "not regressing," and so forth, explain the latter point, "not being weary."
Because one cultivates those practices, next, regarding only the cause of desire for those objects, the following explains away a doubt. The doubt is:

"If one does not relish even the pure [objects], what is the purpose of cultivation? There are two points in the explanation. First, with respect to compassion: it is solely for the sake of gathering sentient beings.

Next, regarding the illumination of this Dharma, it is explained from the perspective of wisdom (*jñāna*). Because wisdom realizes that things do not exist, arising is itself non-arising; thus, one does not cling.
Because there is no obstruction to phenomena, this is the "arising of non-arising," and thus one practices. It is not a place of existence because it is in profound accord with principle (*li*);

it is not a place of non-existence because the characteristics of phenomena manifest. It is not internal because it is the objective sphere of the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*); it is not external.
Because the mind is purified, this is called future giving. Ninth, what is the present giving of a bodhisattva?

There are three aspects to its explanation: first, clarifying the objects to be relinquished; second, concluding with the mind of relinquishment; and third, resolving external objections. First, regarding the objects to be relinquished:
starting from the Four Heavenly Kings, the various heavens of the desire realm are listed; next, starting from Brahmā, the form realm is listed.
"The various devas," and so on down to "the śrāvakas," refers to the two vehicles (dvayayāna) as the objects to be relinquished.
Next, "having heard this, their minds are not deluded" and the following five phrases clarify the mind that is capable of relinquishing. Next, "in order to cause sentient beings...

provides an explanation to resolve doubts. The doubt is as follows: "If it is said that one does not accumulate wholesome causes, why then do you speak of the causes and effects of the five vehicles? The explanation says: "To rescue..."
The intense sufferings of the three miserable realms provide rest for humans and devas; they cease the deluded attachments of inferior views and employ the Two Vehicles to attract and guide beings.
This is done for the sake of others; it is not that [the Bodhisattva] does not abandon [their own welfare]. This is called present giving (*pratyutpanna-dāna*).
Tenth, what is the ultimate giving (*niṣṭhā-dāna*) of a Bodhisattva? Regarding the term "ultimate," there are briefly five meanings. First, the preceding...
Sixth, relinquishing wealth and life. Next, three [points] concern relinquishing the mind of attachment: (1) because it now encompasses the two preceding categories;
(2) because it generates great vows to cause beings to be free from attachment; (3) because it causes beings to attain the ultimate fruit;
(4) because by not giving rise to even a single thought of craving or attachment, one is free from subtle attachment; and (5) because it ultimately enables beings to receive real benefit. Next...
In the section explaining the characteristics, first it says, "Suppose there were immeasurable sentient beings," which clarifies that the objects of giving have appeared before one.
Next, "When the Bodhisattva hears this, he immediately gives," which refers to the actual practice of giving without hesitation.

Next, "He simply contemplates his own body," which reveals the reason for accomplishing renunciation; because he perceives that this body has many faults and afflictions, he must certainly relinquish it. Next, "As... [the text continues].
That which I have performed, I dedicate downward to all sentient beings; this is called ultimate giving.
Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva knows form as it truly is.
He knows the arising of form as it really is; he knows the cessation of form as it really is; he knows the path leading to the cessation of form as it really is.

He knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they really are; he knows the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they really is; he knows the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as it really is.
He knows as it really is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he knows as it really is ignorance; he knows as it really is the origin of ignorance;

he knows as it really is the cessation of ignorance; he knows as it really is the path leading to the cessation of ignorance. He knows as it really is craving; he knows as it really is the origin of craving;
he knows as it really is the cessation of craving; he knows as it really is the path leading to the cessation of craving. He knows as it really is the śrāvaka...

He knows. He knows the Dharma of the śrāvakas as it truly is; he knows the origination of the śrāvakas as it truly is; he knows the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas as it truly is. He knows the pratyekabuddhas as they truly are;
he knows the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas as it truly is; he knows the origination of the pratyekabuddhas as it truly is; he knows the nirvāṇa of the pratyekabuddhas as it truly is.
He knows the bodhisattvas as they truly are; he knows the Dharma of the bodhisattvas as it truly is; he knows the origination of the bodhisattvas...

He knows it as it truly is. He knows the *nirvāṇa* of the Bodhisattva as it truly is. How does he know it? He knows that it is constructed from the causes and conditions of various formations (*saṃskāra*) arising from karmic retribution;
that all things are false, empty, and without reality; that they are neither self nor solid;

and that not even the slightest dharma can be established as existing. Desiring to cause sentient beings to know their true nature, he extensively proclaims and teaches it for them. For him, he speaks.
What is it? It is said that all phenomena (*dharma*) are indestructible. What phenomena are indestructible? Form (*rūpa*) is indestructible;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are indestructible. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is indestructible;

the teachings of the Śrāvakas, the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the teachings of the Bodhisattvas are indestructible. Why is this? Because all phenomena are without action, without an agent, without verbal expression, and without location.
It is unarisen, not given, not taken, immovable, and without activity.

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such an immeasurable treasury of wisdom, they comprehend all phenomena through slight means; they naturally attain clear realization without depending on the awakening of others.
This wisdom is an inexhaustible treasury. It is called inexhaustible because it possesses ten kinds of inexhaustibility.

What are these ten? They are: the inexhaustibility of skillfulness in extensive learning; the inexhaustibility of attending upon spiritual friends; the inexhaustibility of skillfully discerning words and meanings;
the inexhaustibility of entering the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and by means of the wisdom of a single flavor...
Because their adornments are inexhaustible; because their accumulation of all merit and virtue with a tireless mind is inexhaustible;
because their entry into all *dhāraṇī* gates is inexhaustible; because their ability to discern the languages and sounds of all sentient beings is inexhaustible;
because their ability to sever the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings is inexhaustible; for the sake of all...
It manifests all the spiritual powers of the Buddhas for sentient beings, teaching, transforming, and subduing them so that their practice is uninterrupted and inexhaustible.

These are the ten. This is the seventh treasury of wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. One who dwells in this treasury attains inexhaustible wisdom and is able to universally awaken all sentient beings.

The seventh [section] explains the treasury of wisdom (*jñānagarbha*). Within the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts: first, clarifying the treasury of wisdom; second, explaining its inexhaustibility. Within the former, there are three sections.
First, the eight lines and a half of scripture beginning with "This bodhisattva knows form as it truly is" clarify the knowledge of objects as they truly are.
Next, the subsequent section explains the meaning of "knowing as it truly is" to reveal the characteristics of that which is known. It poses the question: "How does one know?"
The phrase "below, knowing from karmic retribution" provides the explanation. The intent of the explanation is as follows:

knowing the characteristics and knowing the nature without any obstruction constitutes what a Bodhisattva knows; knowing through non-knowing is what a Bodhisattva knows. Therefore, it is called "knowing in accordance with reality.
First, "knowing from karmic retribution" refers to clearly understanding suffering and its origin in terms of self-benefit. Next, it refers to benefiting others. This clarifies...

Having known cessation and the path, he next desires to cause sentient beings to know their true nature (*dharmatā*). He extensively proclaims this, marking the intent of his teaching as being precisely for the benefit of others.
Being able to know the true nature is the characteristic of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

That the Dharma is indestructible and its nature is that which is to be known is the characteristic of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). He extensively proclaims these as the unique characteristics of a Bodhisattva. Next, what does he teach?
The subsequent sequential interrogation and explanation consists of three layers in total. First, the interrogation asks: "By explaining what do you cause one to know the true nature?

The explanation states: "By explaining that which is indestructible. Next, the interrogation asks: "What kind of phenomena are indestructible? Are they the nature (*svabhāva*) or the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?"

This is the passage where the location of the inquiry is stated. The commentary explains that it is because characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are identical to nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is said that the five categories of phenomena and so forth are all indestructible.

Next, regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," the interrogation states: "We currently perceive all phenomena to be like a mass of foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, an illusion, or a dream—unsubstantial.
Why then do you say they are indestructible? The subsequent explanation provides three points in brief: first, the nature of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; [the remaining two points follow].

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because there is nothing that can be destroyed. If emptiness were to exist only upon destruction, it would not be primordially empty. Second, because emptiness is identical to reality (*tathatā*) and thus coextensive with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
If reality were to exist only upon destruction, then phenomena would exist outside of principle (*li*). Third, because that which is emptiness does not depend on destruction;
for destruction implies annihilation. There are ten phrases in the text. Following "The Bodhisattva accomplishes... and below, the final three [phrases] summarize the many [preceding points].
"Gateways to manifest skillfulness": there are further gateways, all of which take "non-apprehension" and so forth as minor expedients;
thus, the views of form and emptiness are exhausted, both "destruction" and "non-destruction" vanish, and one does not follow after objects. This is called "awakening not through others.
Following this, under the phrase "this treasury of inexhaustible wisdom," there are two explanations of inexhaustibility. The text contains ten phrases; these constitute [the section].
The title of the section is "The Lower Summary. Regarding those who dwell in this treasury, the following praises its benefits:
"O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s treasury of mindfulness? This bodhisattva abandons delusion and attains perfect mindfulness.
He recollects his past lives—one life, two lives, and so on, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, and a hundred thousand lives."
For a thousand births, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, through kalpas of formation, kalpas of destruction, and kalpas of both formation and destruction—

not a single kalpa of formation, not a single kalpa of destruction, nor a single kalpa of both formation and destruction— for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas,
and even up to immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, ineffable, inconceivable, and unfathomable [kalpas].
One may contemplate the name of a single Buddha for unspeakably unspeakable eons, up to the names of unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas;

one may contemplate a single Buddha appearing in the world to preach and bestow predictions of enlightenment, up to unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas appearing in the world to preach and bestow predictions of enlightenment;
one may contemplate a single Buddha appearing in the world to preach a *sūtra*, up to [unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas].
He speaks the *sūtras* taught by Buddhas appearing in the world who are themselves ineffable;
and as it is with the *sūtras*, so it is with the *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *nidāna*, *udāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*.
He recollects a single assembly, up to an assembly that is ineffably ineffable, and he recollects the preaching of a single [teaching].
He contemplates the Dharma, even to the point of expounding the ineffably ineffable Dharma.
He contemplates one faculty and its various natures, up to the ineffably ineffable faculties and their various natures.

He contemplates one faculty and its immeasurable various natures, up to the ineffably ineffable faculties and their immeasurable various natures. He contemplates one affliction and its various natures, up to...

The various natures of unspeakably unspeakable afflictions; the various natures of the single-samādhi mindfulness, up to the various natures of unspeakably unspeakable samādhis. This mindfulness has ten aspects, namely:
peaceful mindfulness, pure mindfulness, unclouded mindfulness, lucid mindfulness, dust-free mindfulness, mindfulness free from various kinds of dust, and stainless mindfulness.
Mindfulness. Radiant mindfulness. Delightful mindfulness. Unobstructed mindfulness. When a bodhisattva abides in these states of mindfulness, no one in any world can disturb them;
no heterodox arguments can move them; all their roots of goodness from past lives become completely purified;
they remain unstained by worldly dharmas; and they cannot be defeated by any māras or non-Buddhists. Upon transforming their bodies...
He does not forget anything regarding his successive births. His preaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible throughout the past, present, and future.
He dwells among sentient beings in all worlds without ever committing a fault. He enters the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas without obstruction.
He draws near to the presence of all Buddhas. This is called the eighth mindfulness of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Treasury.

Eighth, the explanation of the treasury of mindfulness (*smṛti-garbha*). Within the explanation of its characteristics, there are four parts. First, "abandoning delusion and confusion" identifies the essence of mindfulness.
Second, from "recalling the past" downward, thirteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the distinctions of what is recollected. Third, "this mindfulness has ten... [and so forth].
Planting the seeds of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*) constitutes the superior aspect of mindfulness; herein, there are ten phrases.
Next, the five lines of scripture beginning with "When the Bodhisattva dwells in this mindfulness" clarify the beneficial aspects of mindfulness. This is termed the "conclusion by name."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury-retention of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva retains the sūtras spoken by all Buddhas, with their phrases and meanings, without any loss or forgetfulness.
They retain them for one lifetime, up to unspeakably unspeakable lifetimes. They retain the name of one Buddha, up to the names of unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas.
They maintain for the duration of one eon, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of eons;
they maintain the prediction of enlightenment from one Buddha, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of predictions of enlightenment from Buddhas;
they maintain one sutra, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of sutras; and they maintain one assembly, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of assemblies.
They maintain the exposition of a single dharma, up to the exposition of unspeakably unspeakable dharmas.
They maintain a single faculty of infinite and manifold natures, up to faculties of unspeakably unspeakable natures.
They maintain a single affliction of manifold natures, up to afflictions of unspeakably unspeakable natures. They maintain a single samādhi.

"O Son of the Buddha, from the various natures up to the various natures of unspeakably unspeakable samādhis, this treasury of retention is boundless, difficult to fill, difficult to reach its bottom, difficult to approach, incapable of being suppressed, immeasurable and inexhaustible, endowed with great majestic power;
it is the realm of the Buddhas, which only a Buddha can fully comprehend. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
The ninth is the *Dhāraṇī-kośa*.
Regarding the ninefold explanation of the *Dhāraṇī-kośa*, there are three parts within the explanation of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). First, "This bodhisattva upholds all Buddhas...

and so forth, which specifically cites the meaning of the text. Second, "Upholding the name of a single Buddha... and so forth, which universally cites all dharmas. Third, "O Son of the Buddha, this *Dhāraṇī-kośa*... and so forth.
This clarifies the measure of his virtuous qualities. The text contains ten phrases. Next is the conclusion of the name.

O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of eloquence (*pratibhāna-kośa*) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva possesses profound wisdom and thoroughly understands the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
He extensively expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, never contradicting the sūtras of any of the Buddhas. Thus he speaks.
From a single category of dharmas up to unspeakably unspeakable categories of dharmas; from proclaiming the name of a single Buddha up to proclaiming the names of unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas;
likewise, proclaiming a single world, or proclaiming the prediction of enlightenment for a single Buddha.
He speaks of a single sūtra; he speaks of a single assembly; he speaks of the exposition of a single dharma; he speaks of the immeasurable and manifold natures of a single faculty;
he speaks of the immeasurable and manifold natures of a single affliction; he speaks of the immeasurable and manifold natures of a single samādhi;
