and even speaks of the immeasurable and manifold natures of unspeakably unspeakable samādhis. He may speak for a single day, or...
It may be spoken for half a month or one month; or it may be spoken for a hundred years, a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years;

or it may be spoken for one eon, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons; or it may be spoken for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons; or it may be spoken for incalculable, immeasurable, even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons.
While the number of eons might be exhausted, the meaning and principle of a single word or a single phrase are difficult to fathom.
Exhausted. Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has accomplished ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries.
Having accomplished these treasuries, he attains the presence of the *dhāraṇī* gate that encompasses all dharmas, with one million *asaṃkhyeya* *dhāraṇīs* as its retinue.
Having attained this *dhāraṇī*, he extensively expounds [the Dharma] for the sake of sentient beings through the light of the Dharma.
The Dharma. When he preaches the Dharma, he emits wondrous sounds from his broad and long tongue that fill all worlds throughout the ten directions.
According to their faculties and natures, he causes them all to be fully satisfied; their minds attain joy, and he eliminates all the entanglements and defilements of affliction.
He skillfully enters into all sounds, languages, characters, and eloquence, causing the Buddha-seed to flourish within all sentient beings.
He maintains an uninterrupted continuity of pure mind, and through the light of the Dharma, he expounds the teaching without exhaustion or weariness.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has accomplished an infinite body that exhausts empty space and pervades the entire dharma-realm.
This is the tenth treasury of eloquence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; this treasury is inexhaustible and without division.

It is without interruption, without cessation, without change, and without obstruction; it is without regression, profoundly deep and bottomless, difficult to enter, and universally enters the gateway of all Buddha-dharmas.

The tenth [section], the explanation of the *Vairocanagarbha*. Within the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are four parts. First, from "This bodhisattva possesses profound wisdom" (*ayaṃ bodhisattvo gambhīraprajñā*) onwards, the essence and function are summarized together.
Possessing both the illumination of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), the two kinds of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), is called "profound wisdom.

Second, from "He preaches a single category of dharma" (*eka-dharma-paryāyaṃ deśayati*) onwards, for four and a half lines of scripture, it reveals his ability to expound extensively. Third, from "Or, in a single day he preaches... (*atha vā ekadivasena deśayati*) onwards, for three lines...
In other sutras, it is explained that [the teaching] is performed over a long duration. Next, from "For what reason" onwards, there is an interrogation and explanation. The intent is to say:

the reason one is able to teach for a long duration is because of the accomplishment of the ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries (*akṣaya-kośa*). Since this marks the conclusion of these ten treasuries, it is said that one possesses the preceding ten treasuries.
Next, the five lines of scripture beginning with "When he preaches the Dharma" manifest the virtue of his eloquence (*pratibhāna*). This is...

The names of the sections are concluded below. Next, the passage beginning with "this treasury is inexhaustible" praises its benefits. Within this text there are ten phrases, whose meaning encompasses the seven types of eloquence.
First, "inexhaustibility" refers to the eloquence of abundant flavor, because many facts and principles emerge from each and every phrase.
Second is swift eloquence (*pratibhāna*), because one speaks immediately upon the desire to speak, without interruption.
Third is unerring eloquence, because it does not intersperse false errors within the profound principle. Fourth is uninterrupted eloquence, because it flows in a continuous, linked succession.

Fifth is appropriate eloquence, because it accords with the time and the capacity of the audience without deviation. Sixth is rapid eloquence, because it flows swiftly like a cascading river without obstruction. Thus [it is said].
The final four lines constitute the most supreme and wondrous eloquence among all worlds. This eloquence possesses five virtues:
first, it is as profound as thunder, which corresponds to the eighth line; second, because it is clear and heard afar, one does not regress, which corresponds to the seventh line;
third, its sound is mournful and elegant like that of the kalaviṅka bird, whereby it can universally enter into all Buddha-dharmas.
This refers to the tenth phrase. Fourth, it causes sentient beings to enter [the teaching] with love and reverence; fifth, those who hear it rejoice without weariness.
Therefore, it is difficult to gain entry. The first two [of these five] refer to the ninth phrase. The preceding section, based on the topical headings, has been explained individually.
O Son of the Buddha, these ten inexhaustible treasuries possess ten kinds of inexhaustible qualities that cause all bodhisattvas to ultimately achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
What are these ten? They are: because they benefit all sentient beings; because they are skillfully dedicated through original vows;
because they are uninterrupted throughout all kalpas; and because they awaken the mind throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space.
Because it is limited; because dedication is performed without attachment to the conditioned; because the realm of a single thought-moment is the inexhaustibility of all phenomena;
because the mind of great vows is unchanging; because it skillfully grasps all dhāraṇīs; because it is protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
and because it realizes that all phenomena are like illusions—these are the ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas that are able to...
All that is done for all worlds attains the ultimate, inexhaustible great treasury.
The fourth section, "The Disciples of the Buddha," provides a general praise of the superior capacities of the ten treasuries. This is divided into three parts: first, the heading and praise;

second, the inquiry and explanation beginning with "What are the ten..."; and third, the explanation itself, which consists of ten phrases organized into five pairs: (1) transforming those below and seeking those above; (2)... [text continues].
1. Vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive; 2. The three types of relinquishment accord with reality; 3. Unchanging and virtuous inclusion; 4.
External protection and internal illumination—therefore, these are considered supreme. Next follows the conclusion and praise in ten aspects.
After this, there should be verses and so forth, which may have been omitted, or perhaps the transmission of the sutra is incomplete. The fourth assembly concludes.
Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle Twenty-one and Fascicle Twenty-two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.

Fifth Assembly: The Dharma Gate of the Ten Dedications as Expounded by Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

To cause those who have already practiced to arouse their vows, there are three sections of sutra from the twenty-second fascicle through the thirty-third fascicle. Of these, the first two sections clarify the causes and conditions for the present assembly.
As for the three sections: [the third section... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. Based on the structure provided, this is the translation of the available portion.)
(Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace; Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace;
Chapter on the Ten Dedications) Chapter Twenty-Three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

From here below begins the fifth assembly, which expounds the Dharma of the Ten Dedications. First, regarding the purpose of its introduction: as for those who have previously gathered, it is primarily for their sake...

This answers the previous question regarding dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It refers to dedicating the preceding stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) toward true realization (*bhūta-prativedha*), extensively benefiting both oneself and others, so that one's conduct becomes all-pervasive and leaves nothing undone.
As the *Bodhisattva Mahāyāna-kośa Sūtra* states: "That which draws forth immeasurable fruits from a small root of virtue is the mind of dedication;
for the mind of dedication constitutes a great benefit. Therefore, [dedication] follows the practice.
This is clarified. Furthermore, as the previous practice of understanding and conduct has already been established, it causes compassionate vows to become ever more expansive.

Regarding the subsequent chapter that follows: since the preceding assembly has concluded, this serves to clarify what is to be taught hereafter. First, the place of teaching is clarified to manifest the Dharma; thus it is introduced. Second, regarding the explanation of the names:
first, the name of the assembly also has three meanings, identical to those of the two preceding assemblies. Second, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: Tuṣita is...
As for the location: the Buddha, by means of the body of the *dharmadhātu*, responds without arising; therefore, it is called "ascending.
That this is taught here indicates that its status is transcendent and superior, as it follows the proper sequence. Furthermore, while those above and below are heedless, this heaven is content;

thus, it represents the fulfillment of worldly practice and is therefore situated in the Heaven of Joyful Contentment (*tuṣita*). Moreover, because there is one who is in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) there, it represents Bodhi...

He uplifts his mind; because his meritorious practice is fulfilled, yet having accumulated merit over kalpas, he knows that his rank is still insufficient. He redirects his merit to his son and thus realizes there is still a surplus.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: though he has diligently and painfully accumulated practices, he sees no sign of surplus until he dedicates them to sentient beings, whereupon he knows he is self-sufficient.
Furthermore, among the six heavens of the desire realm, this one is situated in their midst, symbolizing the equilibrium of compassion and wisdom.

It is "even" (*ping*) because it abides in the center. Furthermore, those born in this heaven cultivate the three blessings—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration—whereas others do not possess them all, being partial or uneven in their practice;
therefore, it is described as such. Regarding the three essential tenets (*zongqu*), they are unified through the Ten Dedications (*shixiang*).

The Great Vow is the primary principle; the attainment of the stages is the goal. This chapter takes ascending to heaven and responding to spiritual resonance as its primary principle, and explains the direction toward it as the goal.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, throughout every world in the ten directions, in each of the four continents of Jambudvīpa—
In all of them, they saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree. Each had a bodhisattva who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, was expounding the Dharma;
none of them failed to feel as though they were always in the presence of the Buddha.

Fourth, the explanation of the text. This assembly consists of three chapters: the first two chapters concern the causes and conditions leading to this assembly, while the final chapter is the actual exposition.
As for why there is no further progression [beyond this], it is due to two reasons.

First, because this assembly marks the conclusion of the stage of the three types of worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*), subsuming the preceding stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) as a collective skillful means for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). From this point onward, it constitutes the dedication toward the actual essence [of the stages].
Regarding "superior progress," it is for this reason that [the stage] does not exist [as a separate entity]. Throughout this sutra, there are four such patterns:

first, concerning the transition from the fulfillment of practice to entering a stage, as in the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*, where the fulfillment of faith serves as the general means for both entering and abiding;

second, concerning the transition from the fulfillment of vows to the realization of realization, as in this dedication, where the completion of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* serves as the general means for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Third...

In terms of the fulfillment of effortful application (*sābhoga*), it refers to the stage of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), such as the eighth bhūmi, wherein the preceding seven bhūmis are subsumed as the means (*upāya*).

This constitutes the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. Fourth, in terms of the completion of the causal stage (*hetvavasthā*), it refers to the beginning of the tenth bhūmi, wherein the preceding nine bhūmis are subsumed as the means for entry. This refers to the point of fulfillment of the three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
This is a summary. As for the subsequent stages being interconnected, there are distinct skillful means; therefore, they are not of one type.

Second, when one is about to enter the [Bodhisattva] grounds, one must necessarily leave behind the characteristics of progressive advancement, as this serves as the skillful means for non-conceptualization.

Above, the superior progress was discussed; now, regarding the first two categories: the former involves the primary transformer responding to the capacities of sentient beings, while the latter category assists in the transformation by praising the Buddha. Now, within the first category:
This consists of ten major sections: 1. The entire assembly appears together; 2. Ascending without departing; 3.
Beholding the Buddha’s majestic abode; 4. Welcoming the Buddha and presenting offerings; 5. Observing the Buddha’s supreme virtues; 6. Inviting the Buddha to occupy the palace;

7. The Tathāgata accepts the invitation; 8. The Heavenly Kings obtain benefit; 9. Reciting verses of invitation by the power [of the Buddha]; 10. The Tathāgata takes his seat. This is the first section.

The initial mention of "spiritual power" (ṛddhi) refers to the universal cause; it does not necessarily imply the arising of the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), but rather denotes the mastery of mental force achieved through cultivation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his spiritual power, remained neither apart from beneath this Bodhi tree nor from the summit of Mount Sumeru.
From the Yāma Heaven palace, he proceeded to the Palace Adorned with All Wondrous Jewels in Tuṣita Heaven.

Second, at that time, it is said that he ascended without departing from the lower [world], meaning that the ten directions and all four assemblies previously mentioned ascended while remaining solemnly and without dispersing;
therefore, it is said "without leaving the Bodhi tree," and so forth. The intent of this explanation clarifies the horizontal [dimension].
Pervading the ten directions and encompassing the nine assemblies vertically, for the Buddha’s Dharma-realm pervades time and space.
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar and immediately prepared a lion throne of the maṇi-treasury within his palace.
That lion throne was composed of all manner of celestial, exquisite jewels, produced by the roots of goodness cultivated in the past.
It is attained. It is manifested through the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas; it is born from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya roots of goodness;
it arises from the pure dharmas of all Tathāgatas; and it is adorned and refined by the power of boundless merit.
The retribution of pure karma cannot be destroyed or impaired. Those who behold it rejoice with never-ending delight;
it is a supramundane dharma, untainted by the world. All sentient beings come to observe it, yet none are able to fathom its wondrous excellence.

The third section concerns the Manifestation of the Buddha’s Array. This is now explicitly revealed below. It consists of two parts: first, the array of a single direction; second, the conclusion extending this to all ten directions.

Within the first part, there are two divisions: first, a general revelation of the essence and virtues; second, beginning with "There are one million... and so forth, a specific elucidation of the essence and its functions.
Regarding the first [division], there are eleven phrases: the first phrase is general, while the remaining ten phrases are specific.
This section is divided into three parts. The first line describes its essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), as it is formed of jewels.
The next six lines describe its causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), namely past roots of goodness. The final three lines collectively manifest its extraordinary excellence.
It was surrounded on all sides by hundreds of billions of tiers.

Above it were spread hundreds of billions of golden nets, hundreds of billions of flower canopies, hundreds of billions of jewel canopies, hundreds of billions of garland canopies, and hundreds of billions of incense canopies.

Flower garlands hung down, and their fragrance perfumed everywhere. There were also hundreds of billions of flower parasols, hundreds of billions of garland parasols, and hundreds of billions [of other parasols].
The gods holding jeweled canopies stand in rows on all four sides, and a hundred trillion jeweled robes are spread upon them.

Within the second section, which clarifies essence and function, there are generally two hundred and ninety-nine kinds of hundred-trillion [manifestations], expanding upon the three preceding sections;
these constitute three distinct parts. First, from this point downward, there are two hundred and fourteen phrases that expand [upon the first].

The essential nature (*svabhāva*). Next, there are one hundred trillion verses on the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), with seventy-five lines below them that elaborate upon its extraordinary excellence.
Below the three million billion roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are ten lines that elaborate upon the characteristics of the cause.

The first of these primarily clarifies the adornment of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), while the latter two manifest the adornment of the sentient-being world (*sattvaloka*; *sattvadhātu*); both are the power of the world of wise and perfect enlightenment.
All say "one hundred million" because the rank increases by one hundred million for each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). These are divided into ten long sections from beginning to end:
the first nine are adornments of form, and the last one is the adornment of sound.
A hundred trillion pavilions were exquisitely radiant and adorned; a hundred trillion nets of *maṇi* jewels and a hundred trillion nets of jewels covered them from above.

Nets of precious necklaces hung down on all four sides, while a hundred trillion nets of ornaments, a hundred trillion nets of parasols, a hundred trillion nets of garments, and a hundred trillion nets of jeweled canopies were spread out.
Above it, a hundred trillion jeweled lotus nets bloom with glorious radiance; a hundred trillion jeweled incense nets emit a fragrance so exquisite that it delights the hearts of all beings.
The second pavilion consists of ten phrases. Furthermore, within the hall, pavilions were established, adorning the area surrounding the throne.
The pavilions were embellished with lattices;
a billion trillion jeweled bells hung from curtains, emitting harmonious and elegant sounds as they moved slightly. There were also a billion trillion precious sandalwood [incenses].
The fragrance of the canopies perfumed everywhere. There were a hundred trillion canopies of precious flowers, their blossoms in full and glorious bloom;
a hundred trillion canopies of robes of myriad exquisite colors, rare in the world;

a hundred trillion canopies of bodhisattvas, a hundred trillion canopies of various hues, a hundred trillion canopies of pure gold, a hundred trillion canopies of lapis lazuli, and a hundred trillion canopies of diverse jewels—all were spread out.
Above it, there were one hundred trillion canopies made of all kinds of jewels, adorned with great maṇi gems.

Thirdly, regarding the adornment of the ten-fold discerning canopies beneath the bell-canopies: these were arranged because they had already been established as coverings surrounding the front of the seat.
A hundred trillion exquisite jewel flowers adorned the surroundings on all sides. A hundred trillion *bimba* canopies were interspersed in marvelous patterns.
A hundred trillion jewel garlands and a hundred trillion incense garlands hung down from the four directions.
A hundred trillion celestial, solid fragrances pervaded everywhere with their scent. There were a hundred trillion celestial ornaments and necklaces, and a hundred trillion jewel-flower necklaces.
The body of the seat was adorned with a hundred trillion exquisite treasury jewel necklaces, a hundred trillion mani-jewel necklaces,
and a hundred trillion ocean-mani-jewel necklaces; it had a hundred trillion fine jeweled silks serving as hanging ribbons.
The fourth section, following the "Precious Flowers," consists of twelve phrases that distinguish the body of the adorned seat. *Bimbara* is translated here as "shadow-substance" (*yingzhi*);
this refers to the fact that within the adornments of the canopy, the shadows of external forms are manifested.
It was adorned with intervals of a hundred billion Indra-vajra jewels, a hundred billion sovereign maṇi jewels,
and a hundred billion treasuries of exquisite-colored pure gold.
It was illuminated by the radiance of a hundred billion Vairocana maṇi jewels and a hundred billion Indra maṇi jewels, and featured a hundred billion celestial firm maṇi jewels.
The windows and casements were made of jewels. A hundred trillion maṇi-jewels of pure merit displayed exquisite colors;
a hundred trillion maṇi-jewels of pure and wondrous treasuries formed the gates and portals;

and they were interspersed with a hundred trillion crescent-moon jewels, the most supreme in the world, a hundred trillion stainless-treasury maṇi-jewels, and a hundred trillion lion-faced maṇi-jewels.
It was adorned with magnificent ornaments. A hundred trillion *cittarāja* maṇi jewels fulfilled all desires;
a hundred trillion Jāmbūnada maṇi jewels, a hundred trillion *viśuddhagarbha* maṇi jewels, and a hundred trillion *indradhvaja* maṇi jewels all emitted radiance that completely covered it from above.
There were also a hundred trillion *rūpyagarbha* maṇi jewels... a hundred trillion [white silver] maṇi jewels.
A billion Sumeru-banner maṇi jewels adorn its interior.
Below the fifth, the Indra-vajra jewel, there are seventeen phrases;

these also adorn the four sides of the seat, all consisting of exquisite, wondrous jewels serving as windows, doors, and canopies, and they likewise adorn the body of the seat and its interior. This is the lotus.
The Flower Treasury (Kusumagarbha) does not refer to a lotus flower; rather, it is likely the name for the niche of the seat’s body.

There were one hundred trillion pearl necklaces, one hundred trillion lapis lazuli necklaces, one hundred trillion red-jewel necklaces, one hundred trillion maṇi necklaces, and one hundred trillion jewel-light necklaces. One hundred trillion...
Various kinds of maṇi-garland ornaments; one hundred trillion most delightful red pearl garland ornaments;
one hundred trillion maṇi-jewel garland ornaments with boundless colors and forms;
and one hundred trillion incomparably pure jewel garland ornaments—all these were draped all around as supreme radiant maṇi-jewel garland ornaments.
Adorned with a hundred trillion exquisite ornaments of mani bodies and a hundred trillion Indra-blue precious gems.
The following twelve phrases describe the sixth [ornament], the pearl necklaces (*muktā-hāra*), which hang down all around in magnificent array; such are those mani bodies.
The final two phrases appear to be somewhat abbreviated, as the "exquisite colored jewels" below have no concluding attribution.
There were ten million billion black sandalwood incenses, ten million billion incenses of inconceivable realms,
ten million billion exquisite incenses of the ten directions, ten million billion most supreme incenses, and ten million billion most delightful incenses, all of which emitted fragrance.
The fragrance pervades the ten directions. A hundred trillion *bimbara* fragrances are scattered throughout the ten directions.

A hundred trillion fragrances of pure light universally permeate sentient beings. A hundred trillion fragrances of various infinite colors universally permeate all Buddha-lands, never ceasing for an instant.
There are a hundred trillion unguents and a hundred trillion incenses. A hundred trillion...
A hundred million *utpala* incenses emit fragrances that spread forth, universally perfuming all things.
A hundred trillion *padmagarbha* aloeswood incenses produce great sounds. A hundred trillion *vihāra* incenses are able to transform the minds of the multitude.
A hundred trillion *aruna* incenses have fragrances that universally perfume, their flavors being sweet and delicious. A hundred trillion *avabodhana* incenses pervade all places, bringing awakening.
It causes the sense faculties of those who hear it to become tranquil. Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of incomparable kings of fragrances, adorned with various scents.
Beneath the seventh black sandalwood, there are sixteen phrases that use fragrance as an adornment. *Aruṇa* is translated here as...
A crimson-red hue prevailed.
There rained down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial flowers; clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial incenses; clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial powdered incenses;
clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *kūsuma* flowers; and clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *padma* lotuses.
Flower clouds: raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *utpala* flowers; raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *kubjaka* flowers;
raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *puṇḍarīka* flowers; raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial *māndārava* flowers;
raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of all kinds of celestial flowers; raining down clouds of hundreds of billions of celestial garments; raining down [clouds of] a hundred...
Ten trillion clouds of mani jewels rained down; ten trillion clouds of celestial canopies rained down;
ten trillion clouds of celestial banners rained down; ten trillion clouds of celestial crowns rained down; ten trillion clouds of celestial ornaments rained down;
ten trillion clouds of celestial jewel garlands rained down; ten trillion clouds of celestial jewel necklaces rained down; ten trillion clouds of celestial sandalwood rained down.
Fragrant clouds: they rained down hundreds of billions of clouds of aloeswood incense.
The eighth [cloud] rained down [the following] twenty phrases. Clouds were formed as adornments:
they erected hundreds of billions of jeweled banners, suspended hundreds of billions of jeweled pennants, and draped hundreds of billions of jeweled silk streamers; they lit...
There were a hundred trillion incense burners; a hundred trillion jeweled garlands were spread out; a hundred trillion jeweled fans were held; a hundred trillion jeweled whisks were grasped;
a hundred trillion jeweled nets of bells hung suspended, emitting wondrous sounds when stirred by a gentle breeze;
a hundred trillion jeweled railings surrounded it on all sides; and a hundred trillion jeweled *tāla* trees stood in successive rows. A hundred...
Ten trillion windows and casements were exquisitely adorned with wondrous jewels; ten million billion jewel trees surrounded it, casting down their shade;
ten million billion jewel pavilions extended far and wide, elegantly decorated; ten million billion jewel gates hung with necklaces of pearls;
ten million billion golden bells emitted sublime sounds; and ten million billion necklaces of auspicious signs hung down, pure and magnificent. Hundred...
Ten trillion *siddhikas* were capable of eliminating all evils. There were ten trillion golden treasuries woven with threads of gold.
Ten trillion precious canopies had poles made of various jewels, held aloft in orderly rows.
Ten trillion ornaments of every kind of jewel were interlaced as nets for decorative adornment.
The ninth section, "Establishing One Hundred Thousand," consists of forty-eight lines. The exterior of the seat is adorned on its four sides; herein there are four parts.

First, the twenty lines concerning miscellaneous adornments are arranged at the sides of the seat. Regarding the phrase "the pavilions extend far and wide," the *Jingfayun* (Cloud of Pure Dharma) states:
the Sanskrit term is *pamokha*, which here means a "canopy-carriage" (*zhangyu*). Since the term "pavilion" (*louge*) has already appeared in the preceding text, [this refers to] the jewels... all.
*Śvastikan* (底迦): the full term is *śvastyayan*, which means "possessing happiness. If one sees this sign, one will certainly obtain peace and joy.
Its shape is like the svastika.
A hundred trillion jewels of radiant light emit various kinds of radiance; a hundred trillion wheels of radiant light shine everywhere;
and a hundred trillion sun-treasury wheels and a hundred trillion moon-treasury wheels are all composed of jewels of immeasurable colors.
A hundred trillion fragrant flames and lights shine through with penetrating brilliance; a hundred trillion lotus treasuries bloom in fresh splendor;
and a hundred trillion jewel nets, a hundred trillion flower nets, and a hundred trillion incense nets completely cover the area above.
Next, regarding the nine phrases concerning the adornment of light beneath the Jewel of Radiance (*prabhā-ratna*):
as for the phrase "covered by a net," it is like a worldly lamp that protects nocturnal insects by creating a shimmering, translucent effect.

One hundred trillion celestial robes of precious jewels; one hundred trillion celestial garments of blue color; one hundred trillion celestial garments of yellow color; one hundred trillion celestial garments of red color;
one hundred trillion celestial garments of wondrous and marvelous colors; one hundred trillion celestial garments of various kinds of precious marvels;
one hundred trillion garments perfumed with various fragrances; and one hundred trillion [garments] made from all manner of jewels.
A hundred trillion ready-made garments of fresh white cloth are all beautifully spread out, bringing joy to those who see them.
These nine phrases describe the descent of the three types of celestial jewel-garments; the jewel-garments are spread out in solemn array.
A hundred trillion celestial bell-banners and a hundred trillion golden net-banners emitted subtle and wondrous sounds.
A hundred trillion celestial silk banners were fully endowed with all colors. A hundred trillion incense banners draped down nets of fragrance.

A hundred trillion flower banners rained down all kinds of flowers. There were a hundred trillion celestial robe-banners, hanging and spreading exquisite garments. There were a hundred trillion celestial maṇi-jewels.
Adorned with various banners and myriad jewels, it was embellished by hundreds of billions of celestial ornaments and banners.
Hundreds of billions of celestial garlands and various flower wreaths were arrayed on all four sides. Hundreds of billions of celestial parasols and banners had precious bells that chimed in harmony;
hearing them, all were filled with joy.
Under the bells and banners of the four heavens, there are ten lines: the first nine lines are adorned with the array of precious banners and the adornment of their colors and forms;
the tenth line below them is adorned with sounds.
A hundred trillion celestial conch shells produced wondrous sounds; a hundred trillion celestial drums produced great sounds;
a hundred trillion celestial *vīṇās* produced subtle and exquisite sounds; a hundred trillion celestial *mudrā* lutes produced great and wondrous sounds;
a hundred trillion varieties of celestial musical instruments played in unison; and a hundred trillion celestial instruments of sovereign joy produced sublime sounds.
As for the sounds: their voices pervade all buddha-fields. A hundred trillion celestial musical instruments produced music that was as delightful as an echo, responding universally to all.
A hundred trillion celestial drums emitted wondrous tones upon being struck.
A hundred trillion celestial *cintāmaṇi* lutes spontaneously produced sounds whose rhythms and melodies were in perfect harmony. A hundred trillion celestial various musical instruments emitted—
The wondrous sound extinguishes all afflictions.
The tenth heaven’s conch emits this wondrous sound; below, the adornment of the voice is explained. This section has two parts; first, ten phrases concerning the adornment of musical sounds.
A hundred trillion sounds of pleasing resonance offered praise and worship; a hundred trillion vast sounds offered praise and service;
a hundred trillion profound sounds praised the cultivation of practice; and a hundred trillion myriad exquisite sounds extolled the karmic fruits of the Buddha’s deeds.
One hundred trillion subtle sounds extolled the principle of reality as it is;
one hundred trillion unobstructed true sounds extolled the Buddha’s past conduct; one hundred trillion pure sounds praised his offerings to the Buddhas of the past;
one hundred trillion sounds of Dharma-gates praised the Buddhas’ supreme fearlessness; and one hundred trillion immeasurable sounds extolled all Bodhisattvas.
The merit of the Bodhisattva is inexhaustible. With a hundred trillion voices of the bodhisattva stages, he praises and reveals all practices corresponding to the bodhisattva stages.
With a hundred trillion uninterrupted voices, he extols the Buddha’s merit, which is likewise without interruption.
Regarding the twenty phrases of the "Dignified Sound of Dharma" following the "Joyful Mind": as for the *mudra* (or *mudrā*) among the preceding musical sounds, this is translated as "bee-drum.
This means that when the celestial music first begins to play, this drum is sounded first.
Regarding the first eleven phrases of the subsequent "Dignified Sound of Dharma," they praise the Triple Gem.
There were a hundred trillion voices of conformity that praised and extolled the conduct of seeing the Buddha;
a hundred trillion profound sounds of Dharma that praised the principle corresponding to unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena;

a hundred trillion vast sounds whose resonance filled all buddha-fields; and a hundred trillion unimpeded, pure sounds that caused all beings, according to their mental inclinations, to [attain realization].
The hundred trillion sounds of "Rejoicing" cause those who hear them to penetrate deeply into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The hundred trillion sounds of "Joyful Delight" cause those who hear them to have no obstacles in their minds, but to possess deep faith and reverence.
The hundred trillion sounds of the "Buddha-realm" are able to reveal the meaning of all phenomena according to the sounds they emit. The hundred trillion *dhāraṇīs*...
Her voice skillfully proclaims all the distinctions of the phrases of the Dharma, thoroughly resolving the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
her hundred trillion sounds of the Dharma are harmonious and flowing, perfectly blending with all music.

Thereafter, with the following nine phrases beginning with "In accordance with the sound," he expounded the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. The extensive explanation of the self-nature is complete.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds upon awakening, upon merely seeing this seat, further increased their resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*).

One hundred trillion bodhisattvas of the stage of "Cultivating the Ground" (*bhūmi-karman*) attained purity of mind and rejoiced. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas of the stage of "Practice" (*caryā*) attained realization.
They attained liberation and purity. One hundred trillion Bodhisattvas of Noble Birth dwelt in superior resolve and delight;

one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas Endowed with Skillful Means initiated the practices of the Mahāyāna; one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas Abiding in a Right Mind diligently cultivated all Bodhisattva paths;
one hundred trillion Non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas purely cultivated all Bodhisattva stages; and one hundred trillion [Bodhisattvas] like Youthful...
True Bodhisattvas attain the light of all Bodhisattva samādhis. Hundreds of billions of Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas enter the inconceivable realms of all Buddhas.
Hundreds of billions of consecrated Bodhisattvas are able to manifest the ten powers of immeasurable Tathāgatas.

The second major section extensively elucidates its extraordinary excellence. Previously, it was briefly stated that "those who see it never tire," and the characteristics of its benefits were also briefly clarified;
now they are extensively revealed. This includes the virtues and functions of the very seat itself, as well as the acts of reverence and offering, which further manifest its adornment.

The text consists of two parts: first, the elucidation of the benefits obtained; second, the presentation of the ritual offerings. The former comprises thirty-nine phrases, which are further divided into four sections.
The first ten phrases distinguish the benefits according to the stages [of practice].
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained mastery of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). One hundred trillion bodhisattvas gave rise to pure understanding.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas felt love and joy in their hearts. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas possessed indestructible, profound faith.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas possessed vast power and influence. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas saw their renown increase. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas...
He expounded the meaning of the Dharma so that wisdom might become certain: one hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained unconfused right mindfulness;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas gave rise to decisive wisdom; and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the power of hearing and retaining, thereby upholding all Buddha-dharmas.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas give birth to immeasurable and vast awakening and understanding. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas abide in the faculty of faith.
Regarding the twelve phrases following "attaining the ten thousand masteries," they variously explain the benefits obtained.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the dāna-pāramitā and were able to practice universal giving.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the śīla-pāramitā and fully maintained all the precepts.

One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the kṣānti-pāramitā, their minds remained unshakable, and they were able to endure and accept all the Buddha-dharmas. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the vīrya-pāramitā...
Honey. [They] are able to practice immeasurable diligence for transcendence.

One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the dhyāna-pāramitā, becoming fully endowed with the immeasurable radiance of meditative concentration. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the prajñā-pāramitā;
the radiance of their wisdom was able to shine universally. One hundred trillion bodhisattvas accomplished their great vows, all of which were completely pure. One hundred...

Ten trillion bodhisattvas attained the Dharma-gate of the Wisdom Lamp Illuminating All Dharmas; one hundred trillion bodhisattvas were illuminated by the Dharma-light of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas universally expounded the Dharma of transcending delusion throughout the ten directions.
Third, regarding the benefits derived from the practice of *dāna* (generosity):
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas universally enter all Buddha-fields; one hundred trillion bodhisattvas’ dharma-bodies reach all Buddha-lands;
and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas attain the voice of the Buddha, enabling them to extensively awaken others. One hundred...

Ten trillion bodhisattvas attained the skillful means for giving birth to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). One hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained the accomplishment of all dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*).
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas accomplished the wisdom of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*) like precious banners, able to universally manifest all Buddha-dharmas.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas were able to fully manifest the realm of the Tathāgata.
The four lines beginning with "Universally entering all Buddha-fields" and the following seven lines distinguish the benefits based on his great function.
The preceding four sections collectively clarify the attainment of benefits:
one hundred trillion celestial kings paid him respectful homage; one hundred trillion dragon kings gazed upon him without weariness; and one hundred...
Ten trillion yakṣa kings joined their palms above their heads; one hundred trillion gandharva kings gave rise to pure faith;
one hundred trillion asura kings severed their prideful minds; one hundred trillion garuḍa kings held silk ribbons in their mouths;
one hundred trillion kiṃnara kings leaped for joy; and one hundred trillion mahoragas...
The King gazed upon him with joy. A hundred trillion lords of the world bowed their heads in prostration.
A hundred trillion kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gazed upon him without blinking. A hundred trillion kings of the Yāma Heaven rejoiced and offered praise.

A hundred trillion kings of the Tuṣita Heaven prostrated themselves with their bodies. A hundred trillion kings of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven paid homage by touching their heads to his feet. A hundred trillion...
A hundred million kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven joined their palms in reverent salutation; a billion Brahmā kings observed with single-minded attention;
a billion Maheśvara kings made offerings with reverence; and a billion bodhisattvas raised their voices in praise.
Second, the respectful offerings of the devas. The text is divided into five sections.

The first seventeen lines explain in detail how the eight classes of beings, humans, devas, and bodhisattvas perform acts of reverence through the three modes of action (trikarma); the specific actions performed therein each accord with what is appropriate for them.
A hundred trillion celestial maidens made offerings with single-minded devotion; a hundred trillion devas of shared aspiration leaped for joy;
a hundred trillion devas who had dwelt together in the past praised him with exquisite voices; a hundred trillion Brahmakāyika devas prostrated themselves;
a hundred trillion Brahmapurohita devas joined their palms at their crowns; and a hundred trillion Brahmakāyika devas surrounded and attended upon him.
The Mahābrahmā deities, numbering in the hundreds of billions, praised and extolled his immeasurable merits.

The Ābhāsvara deities, numbering in the hundreds of billions, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. The Parīttābha deities, numbering in the hundreds of billions, proclaimed and praised how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha in the world.
The Apramāṇābha deities, numbering in the hundreds of billions, bowed from afar toward the Buddha. The Ābhāsvara deities, numbering in the hundreds of billions, praised the Tathāgata most highly.
It is rare to behold [them]. One hundred trillion Śuddhāvāsa devas arrived here together with their palaces;
one hundred trillion Parīttaśuddha devas prostrated themselves with pure hearts; one hundred trillion Apramāṇaśuddha devas cast themselves down from above, desiring to see the Buddha;
and one hundred trillion Śubhakṛtsna devas approached with reverence, respect, and offerings. One hundred...
Ten trillion Brahmakāyika devas recalled their past roots of goodness; one hundred trillion Parīttābha devas conceived a sense of wonder toward the Tathāgata;
one hundred trillion Apramāṇābha devas became resolutely respectful and gave rise to various wholesome karmas;
one hundred trillion Abhāsvara devas bowed their bodies in reverence; and one hundred trillion Avṛha devas, with firm roots of faith, paid homage with respect.
They prostrated. One hundred trillion gods of the Without-Heat Heaven joined their palms and recited the Buddha’s name with insatiable devotion.

One hundred trillion gods of the Good-to-See Heaven bowed their heads in salutation. One hundred trillion gods of the Good-Appearance Heaven contemplated making offerings to the Buddha with minds free from weariness.
One hundred trillion gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven paid respectful homage. One hundred trillion various kinds of gods were all filled with great joy.
With joy, they raised their voices in praise. A hundred trillion devas each performed adornments through skillful contemplation.
The twenty-six phrases from "The two goddesses focused their minds" onwards clarify exclusively the devas' reverent offerings through the three karmas.
A hundred trillion bodhisattvas and devas continuously guarded and adorned the Buddha’s seat.
A hundred trillion Flower-Handed Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of flowers; a hundred trillion Incense-Handed Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of incense;
a hundred trillion Garland-Handed Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of garlands; and a hundred trillion Powdered-Incense-Handed Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of powdered incense.
One hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Incense-Ointment Hands rained down all kinds of incense ointments;
one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Clothing Hands rained down all kinds of clothing; one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Parasol Hands rained down all kinds of parasols;
one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Banner Hands rained down all kinds of banners; one hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Pennant Hands rained down all kinds of pennants; one hundred trillion...
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi rains down all kinds of jewels; the Bodhisattva Śatasahasrakoṭyalaṃkārahasta rains down all kinds of ornaments.
These three bodhisattvas constitute the twelve sections concerning the world, clarifying the activities of the bodhisattvas and their offerings.
One hundred trillion sons of gods emerged from their celestial palaces and arrived at the place of the seat. One hundred trillion sons of gods, with pure faith, came together with their palaces.
One hundred trillion "born-noble" (*jāti-prabhava*) sons of gods supported the seat with their bodies.
One hundred trillion "anointed" (*abhiṣikta*) sons of gods supported the seat with their entire bodies.
Fourth, four verses on the descent from the celestial palaces by the sons of the gods: the bodies of the devas made offerings;
one hundred trillion *cintā* bodhisattvas contemplated with reverence; one hundred trillion *jāti-prabhava* bodhisattvas gave rise to pure minds;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas experienced joy in their faculties; and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas attained purity of their profound resolve.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas have purified their faith and understanding; one hundred trillion bodhisattvas have purified all their karmic actions;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas possess mastery over rebirth; one hundred trillion bodhisattvas radiate the light of the Dharma;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas have accomplished the stages (*bhūmi*); and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas are skillfully able to teach and transform all sentient beings.
The five reflections of the bodhisattva consist of the following ten phrases. The bodhisattva practices the offering of Dharma and also clarifies the benefits obtained;
the bodhisattva primarily clarifies the benefits obtained. As for why the devas speak only of offerings, it is because the offerings of the devas are the causes for such benefit.
Born from hundreds of billions of roots of goodness; protected and sustained by hundreds of billions of Buddhas;
perfected by hundreds of billions of merits; purified by hundreds of billions of sublime minds; adorned and cleansed by hundreds of billions of great vows;
brought forth by hundreds of billions of virtuous deeds; made firm by hundreds of billions of wholesome dharmas; and endowed with hundreds of billions of spiritual powers.
As manifested: accomplished through hundreds of billions of merits and praised by means of hundreds of billions of dharmas of praise.
The three hundred million roots of goodness [are] broad as the preceding causes and deep; the ten phrases may be understood. Therefore, this...

The reason why the adornments here are particularly abundant is twofold: first, because this heaven serves as the place of the Buddha’s final rebirth; and second, because his stage of excellence has reached its ultimate limit and his great compassion is universally pervasive.
These supreme manifestations are all the actual virtues of the Tathāgata’s sovereign mastery over the distinctions of the Dharma-realm as revealed by the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
They constitute the adornment of the non-obstruction between person and phenomena, and the seamless integration of the primary body and the environment.
It also indicates that the sublime practices accumulated prior to the aggregates are gathered in this stage.

[Supplementary Note: Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the sublime practices accumulated prior to the aggregates are gathered in this stage," the ten preceding *Akṣayagaṇanākośa* chapters correctly clarify the dharmas of practice that are to be gathered;
now, one is about to dedicate those practices to accomplish virtue. Therefore, with respect to...
This is illustrated by the facts. It clearly demonstrates the practice in which phenomena and principle are non-dual.

Just as the King of Tuṣita in this world offered a high throne for the Tathāgata to be seated upon, so too did the Kings of Tuṣita in all worlds likewise prepare seats for the Buddha, with such adornments and such protocols.
Their faith and aspiration were thus; their purity of mind was thus; their joyful appreciation was thus; their delight was thus; their reverence was thus;
their sense of wonder was thus; their exultation was thus; and their yearning admiration was thus—all of these being exactly equal.
Second, following this description of our world, the text concludes by extending [the account] to the ten directions.
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, having prepared a seat for the Tathāgata, gave rise to a heart of deep respect and,
together with hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeya Tuṣita devaputras, went forth to welcome the Tathāgata.
Fourth, regarding the section "At that time, [they] went down to welcome the Buddha and presented offerings," there are two parts within it: first, going forth to welcome and present offerings;
second, from "At that time, by the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power" onwards, seeing the Buddha and presenting offerings. Within the former, there is first the act of respectfully welcoming.
With a pure mind, they rained down clouds of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) colored flowers; they rained down clouds of inconceivable colored fragrances;
they rained down clouds of various colored garlands; they rained down clouds of vast and pure sandalwood; they rained down clouds of immeasurable and diverse parasols;

they rained down clouds of exquisite celestial garments; they rained down clouds of boundless and wondrous jewels; they rained down clouds of celestial ornaments; they rained down [clouds of... no limit.
They produced clouds of various kinds of incense and rained down clouds of all types of solid powdered incense, such as sandalwood and aloeswood.
Each of the hosts of devaputras emitted these clouds from their own bodies.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeya devaputras from Tuṣita, as well as the other hosts of devaputras present in the assembly, were filled with great joy and paid homage with reverent prostrations. Aśvaghoṣa.
The goddesses leaped for joy and, with longing admiration, gazed intently upon the Tathāgata.
Second, they offered worship from below with purity; therein, first, the various devas offered worship, all of which issued forth from their own bodies.
This not only manifests the power of the merit of the devas, but also signifies that the implements for bodily offering arise from within one's own mind.

Within the Tuṣita Palace, unspeakably many bodhisattvas dwell in mid-air, with diligent and single-minded devotion, using offering implements that surpass those of all the devas to make offerings to the Buddha and pay him reverent homage. [There were] incalculable sounds.
The music was played in unison at once.
Thereafter, Bodhisattvas descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to present offerings.
At that time, it was due to the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power and the outflow of his past roots of goodness—truly inconceivable.
By the power of his sovereign mastery, all the devas and devīs within the Tuṣita Palace see the Buddha from afar as if he were right before their eyes.
Second, regarding the arising of offerings to the Buddha: therein, first are the devas, followed by hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas, as clarified below.
They all gave rise to this thought: "The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter.

Now that we have seen one who possesses all-knowledge, is unimpeded regarding all phenomena, and is a perfectly awakened Buddha," they reflected and contemplated in this way, and together with the entire assembly, they simultaneously went out to welcome the Tathāgata.
Together they arose with joy at this auspicious encounter and went forth to welcome [the Buddha].
Each took celestial robes and filled them with all kinds of flowers, all kinds of incense, all kinds of jewels,
all kinds of ornaments, all kinds of celestial sandalwood powder, all kinds of celestial aloeswood powder, and one...
With powdered incense of all the celestial wondrous jewels, containing all celestial fragrant flowers and all celestial *mandārava* flowers,
they scattered them all as an offering to the Buddha.

The three sections below clarify the presentation of offerings; therein are three parts. First, ten lines describe scattering clothing as an offering to the Buddha, symbolizing the cultivation of quiescence (*śamatha*) to attain the fruit of enlightenment.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of Tuṣita devaputras dwelt in the midst of the sky;
all of them gave rise to minds directed toward the realm of wisdom regarding the Buddha, burning every kind of incense, whose fragrance formed clouds that adorned the sky.
Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha, they rained down clouds of all celestial flowers to adorn the void.
Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, they rained down clouds of all celestial canopies to adorn the void.
Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of offering toward the Buddha, they scattered clouds of all celestial garlands to adorn the void. Furthermore, they gave birth to faith toward the Buddha.
With a mind of understanding, they spread incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) nets of gold that completely cover space; all the jeweled bells constantly produce wondrous sounds.

Furthermore, conceiving a mind toward the Buddha as the most supreme field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), they adorn space with incalculable canopies and rain down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption.
Moreover, conceiving deep faith in the Buddha, they, with incalculable...
The palaces of the various devas adorned the void, and all celestial music produced subtle and wondrous sounds.
Furthermore, they conceived the thought that the Buddha was most supreme and difficult to encounter;

with clouds of celestial garments of countless varieties of colors, they adorned the void and rained down incomparable, diverse, and exquisite robes. Moreover, they gave rise to immeasurable joy and exultation toward the Buddha.
Citta, with incalculable celestial jewel crowns adorned the void. He rained down immeasurable celestial crowns that formed vast clouds.
Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha, he adorned the void with incalculable jewels of various colors and rained down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption.

The ten phrases following "two hundred thousand koṭis" clarify the arousal of the mind to rain down offerings. Adorning space reveals that the myriad practices cultivated accord with the emptiness of the dharma-nature;
the non-obstruction between emptiness and existence is the meaning of "adorning space."
One hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* devaputras all conceived pure faith toward the Buddha.
They scattered countless celestial flowers of various colors and burned countless celestial incenses of various colors as offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they gave rise to a mind of great adornment and transformation before the Buddha, holding countless celestial powders of sandalwood of various colors.

Incense: They scattered it before the Tathāgata. Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of joy and exultation toward the Buddha, they followed the Tathāgata, holding countless canopies of various colors.

Furthermore, giving rise to a superior mind toward the Buddha, they spread countless celestial robes of various precious colors along the road as an offering to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, giving rise to a pure mind toward the Buddha, they held...
Countless celestial jewel banners of various colors welcomed the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, conceiving a mind of superior joy toward the Buddha, they offered countless celestial ornaments of various colors as an offering to the Tathāgata.

Moreover, giving rise to indestructible faith toward the Buddha, they offered countless celestial jewel garlands as an offering to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, giving rise [to faith] toward the Buddha...
With incomparable hearts of joy, they held countless celestial banners of various colors made of divine jewels to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of devaputras, with minds that were disciplined, tranquil, and free from negligence,
held countless celestial musical instruments of various colors and produced exquisite sounds to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
The nine phrases beginning with "three hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* devaputras" describe various offerings being presented.
This signifies the mixed cultivation of the myriad practices; thus, the higher devas raise their offerings to the lower bodhisattvas.
There were hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas who had previously resided in the Tuṣita palace.
They were born from the dharma that transcends the three realms; born from conduct free from all afflictions; born from an all-pervading, unobstructed mind;
born from the dharma of profound skillful means; born from immeasurable and vast wisdom; and born from firm and pure faith.
It is that which has been increased; it is produced from inconceivable roots of goodness; it is accomplished through incalculable skillful transformations;
it is manifested by the mind intent on making offerings to the Buddhas; it is sealed by the dharma-gate of non-action;
and it surpasses all the celestial offering implements used to worship the Buddhas.

In the second section, regarding the bodhisattvas’ arousal of offerings, there are two parts. First, it clarifies the offerings of the *adhiṣṭhāna* (environmental) retribution resulting from perfected practice;

second, it describes how those bodhisattvas manifest the offerings of the *nirmāṇa* (primary) retribution by lowering their bodies. Within the first part, there are twenty-seven phrases, which are divided into three sections.
The first ten phrases concern offerings where many causes produce a single result; the next eight phrases concern offerings where a single cause produces a single result; and the final...
The ninth phrase is the offering of a single cause producing manifold fruits:
all jeweled canopies born from the *pāramitās*; all flower curtains born from the pure understanding of the realm of all Buddhas;
and all garments born from the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which enter into the adamantine Dharma.
All nets of bells produced by the mind that transcends all obstructions; all solid fragrances produced by the mind that realizes all phenomena are like illusions;
all exquisite thrones of various jewels for the assembly of Buddhas produced by the mind that pervades the entire realm of the Tathāgatas’ seats;
all jeweled banners produced by the tireless mind that makes offerings to the Buddhas; and the joy of realizing that all phenomena are like dreams.
The palace of all jewels where the Buddha dwells is born from the mental factor of joy (*muditā*).
Within this second [category] of one cause and one fruit, the cause and fruit are mutually similar; each has its own specific meaning according to the commentaries.
Clouds of all jewel lotuses produced from the roots of goodness of non-attachment and the roots of goodness of non-arising;
clouds of all solid fragrances; clouds of all flowers of infinite colors; clouds of all kinds of wonderful garments of various colors;
clouds of all infinite, pure sandalwood fragrances; clouds of all wonderful, adorned jewel canopies; and clouds of all burning incense.
Clouds of all manner of exquisite garlands and clouds of all pure ornaments, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and surpassing the offerings of all the devas,
made offerings to the Buddha.
Third, "Non-attachment" (asaṅga) and "Non-arising" (anutpāda): one cause, many fruits, and offerings. Non-attachment and non-arising are but one meaning.
Non-arising refers to principle (*tattva*); non-attachment refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). Only when these two are in accord do they constitute a single cause. The text contains nine phrases.

From each and every body of those bodhisattvas, there emerged unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, who completely filled the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.

Their minds were equal to those of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, arising from the non-perverted Dharma and empowered by the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgatas; they revealed to sentient beings the path of peace and security. They were endowed with...
These unspeakable names, phrases, and syllables universally enter into all the seeds of *dhāraṇīs* of immeasurable dharmas.
They give rise to an inexhaustible treasury of eloquence; the mind is free from fear, and great joy is born.
With unspeakably immeasurable and inexhaustible praises of reality as it is, one praises the Tathāgata without ever becoming weary or satisfied.
The second body issues forth offerings of the primary retribution. The text contains ten phrases. The first four conclude the welcoming of the Buddha and the presentation of offerings.
At that time, all the devas and the assembly of bodhisattvas beheld the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the inconceivable hero among men.
The fifth major section. At that time, all [the assembly]—this and below—clarifies beholding the Buddha’s supreme virtues.

This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the supreme virtues of the clouds of the Buddha’s body; second, from "At that time, the Tathāgata’s great compassion... onwards, clarifying the purpose of manifesting these supreme virtues.
Within the former, there are two parts: first, beholding the supreme virtues; second, from "Then that great assembly all saw... onwards, beholding [the manifestation].
The Application of the Buddha’s Light. First, one contemplates the Tathāgata in general; subsequently, one contemplates his specific virtues and marks.

Now, this scriptural text sequentially and fully reveals twenty-one kinds of the Tathāgata’s preeminent merits. The text is divided into three parts: first, the general contemplation of the Tathāgata;
second, the specific contemplation of his virtues and marks; and third, the conclusion that establishes the contemplative understanding. Herein begins the first part: the general contemplation.
His body is immeasurable and beyond calculation; he manifests inconceivable and manifold supernatural transformations, causing the hearts of countless sentient beings to rejoice greatly.

Pervading all realms of empty space and all dharma-realms, he adorns them with the adornments of a Buddha, establishing all sentient beings in roots of goodness and manifesting the spiritual powers of infinite Buddhas.
Possessing power that transcends all paths of language, he is revered by all the great bodhisattvas.
According to those who are to be transformed, he causes them all to rejoice. Abiding in the vast body of all Buddhas, his roots of merit and virtue are entirely purified;
his physical form is supreme, such that none can outshine it.
Second, regarding the section on the specific observation of the qualities of his body: the twenty-one qualities are divided into twenty sections, as the final two are combined.
However, within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, these twenty-one qualities consist of three general parts: first, the listing of the twenty-one phrases from the sūtra;
second, the establishment of the names of the merits by Asaṅga Bodhisattva as an explanation; and third, [the commentary] by Vasubandhu.
[The preceding] etc. However, the names in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) are employed to accord with the intent of the Sūtra. Now, each sentence shall be correlated accordingly. First:
this clarifies the *Sūtra on the Manifestation of Non-duality*, which is to say, it observes the Tathāgata’s merit of exclusively unimpeded transformation.
This is the naming established by Asaṅga; others follow this pattern.
The realm of wisdom is inexhaustible, born from the peerless samādhi; its body is boundless,
dwelling pervasively within the bodies of all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to rejoice greatly and ensuring that the lineage of omniscience is never severed.
The second section, from "wisdom" onwards, clarifies the approach to the signless dharma;
that is, the observation of the Tathāgata regarding the two signs of existence and non-existence, and the merit of entering true suchness, which is supreme and pure.
Abiding in the ultimate dwelling of all Buddhas, born into the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they cause incalculable sentient beings to attain pure faith and understanding.
They bring to fulfillment the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas and gladden their faculties.
With clouds of Dharma universally covering the void and the Dharma-realm, they teach and transform them without exception, according to the minds of sentient beings.
He brings them to fulfillment and causes them to abide in non-conceptual wisdom, surpassing all sentient beings.

The third [point] concerns abiding in the ultimate state of all Buddhas; this clarifies abiding in the Buddha-abode, specifically the merit of the Tathāgata’s effortless buddha-activities that never cease.
They attain all-knowledge and radiate great light; they cause all roots of goodness from past lives to manifest;
they cause all beings everywhere to give rise to the vast and great mind; they cause all sentient beings to abide in the indestructible wisdom of Samantabhadra;
they dwell pervasively in the lands of all sentient beings; they are born from the non-retrogressive True Dharma; and they abide in all equal dharmas.
Regarding the realms: they clearly understand the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and manifest unspeakably unspeakable varieties of the Tathāgata’s body;
these cannot be fully extolled by worldly speech, yet they enable all beings to constantly keep the Buddha in mind.

Pervading the entire dharma-realm to extensively deliver all sentient beings, they bestow the gift of Dharma according to the benefits desired by those who have first resolved their minds, thereby subduing them and causing their faith and understanding to become pure; they manifest inconceivable physical bodies.
Below the phrase "Fourth, obtaining all-knowledge," it clarifies the attainment of the equality of all Buddhas. As stated below,
"attaining the equality of the Buddhas" refers to observing that within the *dharmakāya*, the Tathāgata’s qualities— consisting of the basis, intention, and activity— are without distinction.

Observing all sentient beings with a mind free from attachment, they abide in unimpeded dwelling. Having attained the ten powers of a Buddha without obstruction, their minds are always tranquil and concentrated, never distracted. They abide in omniscience.
Fifth, observing the audience below clarifies reaching the state of non-obstruction; that is, one observes the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the merit that serves as the antidote to all obstacles,
his skillful exposition of the true meaning of various phrases and sentences, and his ability to penetrate deeply into the boundless ocean of wisdom.
It gives birth to an immeasurable treasury of merit and wisdom.
The sixth skillfully expounds the lower illumination of the irreversible Dharma;
that is, it contemplates the Tathāgata’s merit in subduing all non-Buddhist teachers.
Constantly, with the sun of the Buddha, they universally illumine the dharma-realm; according to the power of their original vows, they always appear and never vanish.
They dwell eternally in the dharma-realm, abiding where the Buddhas abide, without any change or alteration. They have no attachment whatsoever to "self" or "what belongs to self.
Abiding in supramundane dharmas, they are undefiled by mundane dharmas.
Seventh, they constantly employ the light descending from the sun of the Buddha so that their conduct is unimpeded;
that is, they observe the merit of the Tathāgata’s birth in the world, which is not obstructed by worldly dharmas.
He establishes the banner of wisdom throughout all worlds; that wisdom is vast, transcending the world, and remains unstained by attachment.
He uproots all sentient beings, causing them to emerge from the mire and place them upon the ground of supreme wisdom.
All his merit benefits sentient beings without ever being exhausted. He thoroughly understands the wisdom of all bodhisattvas and possesses resolute faith and inclination toward it.

He shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment. Through great compassion, he manifests unspeakably infinite Buddha-bodies with various adornments, and with wondrous voices, he expounds immeasurable teachings, fully satisfying the intentions of all sentient beings according to their needs.
Eighth, following all that has preceded, it clarifies that which is established as inconceivable; namely, the observation of the Tathāgata’s merit in establishing the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
This section is divided into two parts: first, distinguishing its profundity and vastness by way of the signified meaning (*vācya*).
Next, through great compassion, he manifests his body below to preach the Dharma. This establishes the teaching by means of the expressive doctrine (*vyañjana*).
His mind is ever-pure throughout the past, future, and present, causing all sentient beings not to cling to objective realms.

He constantly bestows predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas, enabling them all to enter the lineage of the Buddha, to be born into the family of the Buddha, and to receive the Buddha’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
The ninth section, following "Regarding the past, future, and present," clarifies wandering within the equal dharma-nature of the three periods of time;
that is, observing the merit of the Tathāgata’s bestowal of prophecy.
He constantly wanders through the ten directions without ever resting, yet remains without attachment or craving toward anything within the dharma-realm or the buddha-fields.
They are able to go everywhere, comprehending the minds of all sentient beings without exception. Their merit is world-transcending and pure;
they do not abide in birth-and-death, yet they appear universally throughout the world like reflections.
The tenth section, "Constantly Roaming the Ten Directions" and below, clarifies that his body is disseminated throughout all worlds;
it specifically elucidates the merit of the Tathāgata manifesting the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) and Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) in all worlds.
With the moon of wisdom, they universally illuminate the dharma-realm; they thoroughly comprehend that all things are ultimately unattainable.
Constantly, through wisdom, they know that all worlds are like illusions, like shadows, like dreams, and like magical transformations—all of which have the mind as their intrinsic nature.
Abiding thus, he manifests the body of a Buddha in accordance with the differing karmic retributions of sentient beings, their diverse inclinations, and their various faculties.
The Tathāgata constantly takes countless sentient beings as his object of focus and teaches them that all worldly phenomena arise from conditions.
He knows that the characteristics of all dharmas are entirely without marks, being only a single mark—the very foundation of wisdom.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to be free from attachment to all marks, he manifests within the world by displaying the nature and characteristics of all worldly phenomena,
and for their sake, he reveals unsurpassed bodhi.
The eleventh section, "Descending with the Moon of Wisdom," clarifies that there is no doubt or obstruction regarding the knowledge of all phenomena;
it specifically examines the Tathāgata’s merit of severing doubts. This passage consists of two parts: first, his own severing of doubts;
second, following the various assemblies, his ability to sever the doubts of others.
Desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings, he appears in the world to reveal the Buddha-way, enabling them to behold the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body;
by focusing their minds upon and recollecting these marks, they diligently practice until the characteristics of worldly afflictions are eradicated.
Cultivating the practices of enlightenment with an undistracted mind, one attains perfection in all gates of the Mahāyāna and accomplishes the benefit and purpose of all Buddhas.
The twelfth [section], beginning with "desiring to rescue and protect those below," clarifies the attainment of great awakening through the accomplishment of all practices; that is, contemplation.
Examining the Tathāgata’s merit of causing [beings] to enter various practices, there are two parts in the text.

First, causing them to enter by means of the teaching of the Dharma, so that those who have been shown the Buddha-way may awaken and enter it. Second, "causing them to obtain a vision" and below, causing them to enter by means of manifesting his physical body.
He is able to observe the roots of goodness in all sentient beings, yet he does not destroy their pure karmic retributions.
His wisdom is clear and penetrating, universally entering the three periods of time.
"Thirteenth, he is able to observe... and so forth, clarifying that his knowledge of all phenomena is free from doubt; that is, he observes...
Contemplating the merit of the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom that gives rise to future dharmas, he is forever free from all worldly discrimination.
He emits a network of light rays that universally illumines the ten directions, filling every world without exception.
His form-body is exquisitely beautiful, such that those who behold it never tire of it. By means of his great merit, wisdom, and supernormal powers...
He gives rise to the various practices of bodhisattvas; his mastery over the faculties and their objects is perfected; he performs all the works of a Buddha and, having performed them, vanishes.
The fourteenth [section], "Permanently Free from All Inferiority," clarifies that whatever body he manifests cannot be conceptually differentiated. Below, the sutra...
He merely said that his body was unfathomable; he then observed how the Tathāgata, in accordance with their respective inclinations,

manifested such meritorious qualities as being well-able to reveal the path of omniscience throughout the past, present, and future, universally raining down immeasurable *dhāraṇīs* upon all bodhisattvas,
causing them to give rise to vast aspiration and joy in upholding and practicing them.
Fifteenth, "skillfully able to reveal and teach" and below clarifies the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others;
that is, the observation of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable bases of reliance, his application of skillful means (*prayoga*) in taming sentient beings, and his meritorious qualities.
He has accomplished all the merits of the Buddhas, which are perfectly complete and blazingly radiant.
His body is adorned with boundless, wondrous colors, such that there is no one in any world who does not behold him. He is forever free from all obstructing dharmas;
he has attained purity regarding the true meaning of all phenomena and has gained mastery over the qualities of merit.
The sixteenth, "Accomplishing All," below, clarifies the attainment of the Buddha’s supreme other shore of non-dual dwelling;
it is the perfection of the merit of observing the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*.
He acts as a Great Dharma King, shining universally like the sun; he serves as a field of merit for the world, endowed with great majestic power.
He manifests transformation bodies throughout all worlds, emitting the light of wisdom to bring all beings to enlightenment.

Desiring to let sentient beings know that the Buddha is fully possessed of boundless merit, he binds his crown with the unimpeded silken cloth to receive his consecration, employing skillful means in accordance with the world to open their understanding.
He guides them. With his hand of wisdom, he comforts sentient beings; as a great king of physicians, he skillfully cures all ailments.
He is able to travel everywhere throughout the infinite lands of all worlds without ever resting. With the pure eye of wisdom, free from all obscurations, he perceives everything clearly.
Toward those sentient beings who commit unwholesome and evil deeds, he employs various means of discipline to lead them into [the path].

The Way consists in skillfully seizing the opportune moment without ceasing. If sentient beings give rise to a mind of equanimity, one immediately manifests for them the karmic retribution of equanimity.
