According to their mental inclinations and according to their karmic fruits, one manifests the body of a Buddha and performs various supernatural transformations to preach the Dharma, causing them to awaken to and understand the wisdom of the Dharma, so that their hearts are filled with great joy and their faculties leap with exultation.
Leaping forth, he beholds immeasurable Buddhas and gives rise to profound and heavy faith; he produces all roots of goodness and never again regresses.
The seventeenth [chapter], "The Great Dharma King," and below, clarifies the ultimate, wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata’s liberation, which is free from any intermixture;
that is, it elucidates the merit of the Tathāgata observing and manifesting various distinct Buddha-fields according to the superior inclinations [of beings].

All sentient beings, bound by their karma, sleep long in birth and death; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to awaken them, comforting their minds so that they are free from sorrow and fear.
Should any behold him, he causes them all to realize and enter the wisdom of the meaning of non-reliance.
With wisdom and skillful means, they thoroughly understand all realms; their majestic adornments are so sublime that none can outshine them.

The mountain of their wisdom and the fangs of their Dharma are entirely purified. They manifest either as bodhisattvas or as the bodies of Buddhas, leading all sentient beings to the stage free from affliction.
Adorned with immeasurable merits, it is brought forth into the world through the accomplishment of karmic actions.
All the adornments and purities of all Buddhas are none other than those achieved through the karma of omniscience.
Following the eighteenth [verse], "All Beings," which clarifies the realization of the Buddha’s level of equality that is without middle or extremes,
there follows the observation of the merit of the Buddha-body being without spatial limitations.
Constantly upholding his original vow, he does not abandon the world, acting as a steadfast and virtuous friend to all sentient beings.
Possessing the foremost purity and stainless radiance, he causes all sentient beings to behold him directly.

Toward the infinite and boundless beings of the six realms of existence, the Buddha follows them constantly with his supernormal powers and never forsakes them; should there be any who have planted roots of goodness together in the past, he causes them all to become pure.
Pure, yet toward all sentient beings in the six realms of existence, they do not abandon their original vows nor deceive them;
they gather them in entirely through skillful means of wholesome dharmas, causing them to cultivate pure karma and to destroy all the conflicts of Māras.
Nineteenth, "Constantly Guarding the Original Vow" and below clarifies that [the Tathāgata’s] excellence reaches the limit of the *dharmadhātu*.
That is to say, it observes the Tathāgata’s merit of constantly manifesting benefit and peace for all sentient beings until the very end of *saṃsāra*.
From the limit of non-obstruction, a vast power emerges. The most supreme Sun-Treasury is without hindrance;
it manifests its reflection within the realm of the pure mind, such that there is no one in all the worlds who does not behold it. It extensively bestows various dharmas upon sentient beings.
The Buddha is a treasury of boundless radiance. All his powers and wisdom are perfectly complete.

He constantly illuminates all sentient beings with a great light, fulfilling their aspirations according to their wishes. Free from all enemies, he is a supreme field of merit and the common refuge for all living beings.
Whatever offerings are made to him, he causes them all to become pure. Even by cultivating a small amount of wholesome conduct...
They shall receive immeasurable merit and cause all beings to enter the stage of inexhaustible wisdom.
They shall be masters who plant roots of goodness and purify the minds of all sentient beings; they shall be the most excellent and fertile fields for generating the merit of all sentient beings.
With profound wisdom and skillful means, they are able to rescue all from the sufferings of the three evil realms.
The twentieth section, from "the limit of non-obstruction" (*anāvaraṇakoṭi*) downward, reveals two phrases: namely, "exhausting the nature of space" and "reaching the limit of the future.
These refer to observing the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible and other such qualities. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* both possess these two phrases.
When expanded, there are twenty-one distinct phrases within them; here, the text combines them. The aforementioned cited qualities...
The name "Guṇaprabha" relies entirely upon Asaṅga. As for his explanations, the commentary (ṭīkā) mostly follows Sthiramati;
while there are slight differences from the *Lokottaraparivarta*, the general intent does not conflict. This shall be further demonstrated in the subsequent chapters.
Thus one has faith and understanding; thus one observes.
Thirdly, in this way, the conclusion is formed through contemplative understanding:
thus one enters the abyss of wisdom; thus one roams the ocean of merit; thus one reaches everywhere.
With the wisdom of space, one thus knows the field of merit of sentient beings; with such right mindfulness manifesting before them,

one observes in this way the marks and signs of all the Buddha’s deeds, observes in this way the Buddha’s universal manifestation throughout the world, and observes in this way the Buddha’s sovereign mastery of supernormal powers.

The final eight lines distinguish the subject that contemplates based on the qualities being contemplated. Within the first four lines, the former two concern internal qualities and the latter two concern external characteristics.
Regarding the former, it means that the Buddha’s immeasurable internal qualities do not transcend merit and wisdom;

the first two lines refer to the essence of merit and wisdom, while the next two lines refer to the function of merit and wisdom. Regarding the latter, the first line reiterates [the preceding point].
"Capable of observing" refers to right mindfulness, clarifying that this is not a distracted mind. The latter three phrases also distinguish the observer by way of the object observed.
The first phrase is general; the latter two are specific. "The cloud-body appearing everywhere" refers to the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
"Mastery of supernormal powers" refers to the aforementioned functional activities. This concludes the superior virtues of the Buddha’s cloud-body as observed above.
At that time, the great assembly saw that from every single pore of the Tathāgata’s body there issued forth hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays.
Each light ray possessed asaṃkhyeya colors, asaṃkhyeya purities, and asaṃkhyeya illuminations,
causing asaṃkhyeya multitudes to observe them, asaṃkhyeya multitudes to rejoice, and asaṃkhyeya multitudes...
Joyful! The deep faith of incalculable multitudes increases; the aspirations of incalculable multitudes become pure;
the faculties of incalculable multitudes become cool and serene; incalculable multitudes offer reverence and respect.

The second section clarifies how that great assembly perceives the Buddha’s light. Although there was a prior instance of such perception, it involved contemplating the virtues constantly possessed by the Tathāgata;
now, they behold them directly with their own eyes, and thus it is not the same. This section contains three parts: first, beholding the constant light;
second, beholding the emission of light; third, revealing the intent of the light. Regarding the first part, there are eleven phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
Among these, the first three are the marks of light, while the latter seven are the benefits of light.
At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s body emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable great radiances.
Each and every radiance possessed inconceivable colors and inconceivable lights, illuminating the inconceivable...
The Dharma-realm of the limits.
Second, in the passage "At that time, looking downward at the emission of light," first the physical characteristics are presented:
by the Buddha’s spiritual power, a great and wondrous sound is produced; that sound proclaims and expounds hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable [teachings].
The Discourse on Praise and Eulogy transcends all worldly speech and is accomplished through supramundane roots of goodness.

Furthermore, it manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable and subtle adornments, which could not be fully extolled even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable kalpas;
all of these arise from the inexhaustible mastery of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they manifest unspeakably many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, appearing in the world, causing all sentient beings to enter the gate of wisdom and understand the profound meaning.

They also manifest the transformations of unspeakably many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, causing all worlds to be equally pure. All such manifestations proceed from the Tathāgata.
The dwelling wherein all-knowledge arises is free from obstruction; it is also born from the inconceivable, supreme virtues cultivated by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable, wondrous jewel-flames appear, arising from the roots of goodness of his former great vows.
This is because he has once made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas and cultivated pure conduct without negligence.
Because of non-negligence; because the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) gives rise to unobstructed roots of goodness; to manifest the vast pervasiveness of the Tathāgata’s powers;
to sever the doubts of all sentient beings; to cause all to behold the Tathāgata;
to establish immeasurable sentient beings in roots of goodness; and to demonstrate that the supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) of the Tathāgata cannot be eclipsed or surpassed. Desiring—
It is so that sentient beings may universally enter the ultimate ocean; so that the bodhisattva assemblies from all buddha-lands may all gather here;
and out of a desire to reveal and demonstrate the inconceivable gates of the Buddha-dharma.

Subsequently, following the passage "The Buddha descended," there are five manifestations within the explanation of the functional activity of the light: first, the manifestation of preaching the Dharma;

second, the manifestation of adornments; third, the manifestation of the Buddha; fourth, the manifestation of supernatural transformations; and fifth, the manifestation of jewel-flame light. Following this, the four lines of scripture beginning with "In order to reveal the Tathāgata" clarify the intent behind manifesting the light.
At that time, the Tathāgata’s great compassion universally covers all, manifesting the adornments of all-knowledge.
Second, the following section clarifies the intention for manifesting supreme virtues. This text is divided into two parts:
first, it reiterates the previously manifested virtues.
The first desire is to cause sentient beings in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of worlds [to attain benefit].
The second desire is to clarify the manifestation of the underlying intention; this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the benefit for sentient beings below;

second, revealing the Tathāgata’s [wisdom] below to clarify the upward propagation of the Buddha-way. Regarding the first part, there are two sections: first, manifesting the causes; second, the World-Honored One...
The following section distinguishes the causes for manifest benefit. Herein is the first part: first, the enumeration of those who are benefited.

Those who have not yet developed faith shall develop it; those who have already developed faith shall cause it to increase; those whose faith has increased shall cause it to become purified; those who have been purified shall cause it to reach maturity;
and those who have reached maturity shall cause their minds to be disciplined. They contemplate the profound Dharma and are fully endowed with...
The light of their wisdom is immeasurable. They give rise to an immeasurably vast mind; their resolve for *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) never regresses.

They do not contravene the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and are not terrified by the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). They realize the principle of ultimate truth, fulfill all practices of the *pāramitās*, and purify all supramundane roots of goodness.
Like Samantabhadra, they attain the sovereign mastery of a Buddha and remain free from the realm of Māra.
The realms and sense-bases are the domain of all Buddhas. Having thoroughly understood the profound Dharma, one attains inconceivable wisdom.
One’s vows for the Mahāyāna never regress; one constantly beholds all Buddhas without ever being separated from them. One accomplishes realized knowledge and realizes immeasurable dharmas.
Endowed with the power of the treasury of boundless merit, one gives rise to a heart of joy and enters the stage of non-doubt. Free from evil and purified, one relies upon all...

With wisdom and vision, one remains unshakable in the Dharma and gains entry into the assemblies of all Bodhisattvas, constantly being born into the family of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.

Hereafter, for those who have not yet attained faith, the following section distinguishes the differing benefits. Regarding the textual meaning herein, if one follows the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), then from—
From the initial stage of faith up to the fulfillment of the stages (*bhūmi*), each section of the commentary provides specific indications.

If one considers the five initial phrases regarding the perfection of faith (*śraddhā*) as encompassing the various stages, each phrase corresponds to a single stage. From the phrase "contemplating the profound" (*gambhīra-darśana*) downward, the meaning applies to all stages, because in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), each stage encompasses all virtues.
This manifestation of such adornments by the World-Honored One is entirely accomplished by the roots of goodness accumulated in the past;
it is for the purpose of taming all sentient beings.
Second, the explanation of the manifest cause: since it is accomplished through the accumulation of merit, its benefit is profound and vast.

This also concludes the preceding causes and introduces what follows, for it reveals the great majestic power of the Tathāgata, illuminates the treasury of unimpeded wisdom, and manifests the Tathāgata.
Because his boundless supreme virtues are most intensely blazing; because he manifests the inconceivable great supernormal transformations of the Tathāgata;

because by means of his power of supernatural faculties he manifests the body of a Buddha in all realms of existence; because he demonstrates the infinite limits of the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations;
because his original vows have all been fully accomplished; and because he displays the courageous wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Because they are able to go everywhere; because they have attained mastery over all phenomena and thus become Dharma Kings; because they give birth to all gateways of wisdom; because they manifest the purity of the Tathāgata’s body;
because they further manifest their own bodies as most sublime and wondrous;

because they demonstrate the realization of the equal Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they reveal the treasury of the purity of roots of goodness; and because they manifest the world.

Because there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor for its supremely sublime form; because it manifests the marks of one endowed with the ten powers, causing those who behold it to never tire of doing so;
and because it acts as the sun of the world, illuminating the three periods of time.
The second section, "Revealing the Lower to Clarify the Propagation of the Buddha-Way Above," is divided into two parts: first, specifically manifesting the purpose;

second, from "Having attained mastery" onwards, citing the causes and concluding with praise. Within the former, there are twenty-seven phrases intended to reveal the twenty-one kinds of sublime qualities mentioned previously.
All the virtues of the Sovereign Dharma King manifest from his past roots of goodness;
even if all bodhisattvas were to praise and extol them throughout all kalpas, they could never be exhausted.
The second section cites the causes and concludes with a praise. The former cites the accumulation of causes; the latter praises their inexhaustibility.

At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, having prepared such various offerings for the Tathāgata, together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya Tuṣita devaputras, joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! We pray that you will look upon us with compassion and dwell in this palace.
This was the sixth occasion when the King of the Tuṣita Heaven invited the Buddha to reside in his palace as he descended from Tuṣita.
At that time, the World-Honored One, adorned with the adornments of a Buddha and endowed with great majestic virtue,
acted for the sake of causing all sentient beings to give rise to great joy, for the sake of causing all Bodhisattvas to develop profound awakening and understanding,
and for the sake of increasing the desire and delight of all the devaputras of Tuṣita, such that the King of the Tuṣita Heaven never grew weary of making offerings and serving him.
Therefore, because immeasurable sentient beings conceive the aspiration for enlightenment by recollecting the Buddha;
because the roots of goodness and merit planted by immeasurable sentient beings through seeing the Buddha are inexhaustible; because they are able to constantly give rise to pure faith;

because they see the Buddha and make offerings without seeking anything for themselves; because all their vows and aspirations are pure; and because they diligently accumulate roots of goodness without weariness or rest. They resolve...
Because he sought all-knowledge through his great vow, he accepted the invitation of the celestial king and entered the Hall Adorned with All Jewels.
As it was in this world, so it was in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Seventh: At that time, the World-Honored One descended; this section, "The Tathāgata Accepts the Invitation," is divided into two parts. First, accepting the invitation and entering the palace;
second, from "At that time, all... onwards, appearing in majesty after having entered. Within the first part, it first clarifies this world-system, and next, from "Just as in this world...
onwards, it establishes the universal application to the ten directions.
At that time, the Palace Adorned with All Jewels was spontaneously and exquisitely adorned, surpassing all the adornments of the devas;
it was completely covered on all sides by nets of every kind of jewel, and everywhere rained down clouds of the most sublime and wondrous jewels.

They universally rained down clouds of all kinds of ornaments; they universally rained down clouds of all kinds of precious robes; they universally rained down clouds of all kinds of sandalwood incense;
they universally rained down clouds of all kinds of solid fragrances; and they universally rained down clouds of all kinds of precious ornamental canopies.
They universally rained down inconceivable clouds of flower clusters and universally produced the sounds of inconceivable music, extolling the Tathāgata’s omniscience in every respect;
all these were perfectly consonant with the sublime Dharma.
All such articles of offering far surpassed those of the devas.
Upon his second entry, the splendor was manifested, revealing it to be the power of the Buddha; thus, he transcended all the devas.
At that time, within the Tuṣita Palace, the music and songs of praise resounded incessantly.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the mind of the King of Tuṣita was kept free from agitation, his past roots of goodness were brought to full maturity, and his immeasurable wholesome qualities were further strengthened.
They firmly increase their pure faith, arouse great diligence, give rise to great joy, purify their profound aspirations, and resolve upon bodhicitta;
they maintain unceasing mindfulness of the Dharma and possess dhāraṇī such that they never forget it.

In the eighth period, the Heavenly King descending from the Tuṣita Palace attains benefit. In the text, his mind is free from agitation and confusion; he attains the benefit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
From the passage "In the past... onwards, there is the benefit of advancing in goodness. Within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), he gathers the distracted and returns to stillness;

therefore, the sounds of music cease. This stage is transcendent and supreme; he attains the true nature of movement, and thus movement and stillness are non-dual. Therefore, the sounds of music flourish.
Yet his mind remained unmoved.
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty,
recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke these verses:
Ninth: At that time, the following verses of praise are offered based on [the Buddha's] power. However, recollecting past causes is also a sign of benefit;
therefore, these verses are established as the basis for the discourse. First, the verses of praise for this specific location are explained, followed by a general application to all ten directions.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Unobstructed Moon, The most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Adorned Palace, And therefore this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Vast Wisdom, The most excellent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Golden Hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past was a Tathāgata named Samantacakṣus, The most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Lotus Hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Coral, The most preeminent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Treasure Treasury Hall, Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Lion of Discourse, The most preeminent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this palace of the King of Mountains; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Sūryaprabha, the most excellent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Palace of Many Flowers; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Buddha named Anantaprabha, The most preeminent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Hall Adorned with Trees, Therefore this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Dharmadhvaja, The most preeminent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this precious palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past was a Tathāgata named Jñānapradīpa, the most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Gandhamādana palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Guṇaprabha, the most excellent among all auspicious ones;
he once entered this maṇi palace, and for this reason, this place is most auspicious.
Following this, the verses of praise were presented, consisting of ten stanzas, each stanza dedicated to one Buddha; each Buddha is distinct, though their specific virtues are not detailed here.

This Buddha is none other than one of the ten Buddhas mentioned previously in the sequence of assemblies; it is merely that his position is progressively deeper and the recollection of him becomes increasingly remote.
Just as in this world, the King of Tuṣita Heaven, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, praised the Buddhas of the past in verse.
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, the Tushita Heavenly Kings likewise extol the Buddha’s merits in this same manner.
This second section concludes by generalizing [the description] to all such worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon the lion throne of the mani-jewel treasury within the Palace Adorned with All Jewels.
Tenth: At that time, the World-Honored One descended and took his seat as a Tathāgata. This section is divided into four parts; the first clarifies the act of taking his seat.
The Dharmakāya is pure, its wondrous functions are sovereign, and it shares the same realm as the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Abiding in all-knowledge, it enters into the same single nature as all Buddhas. With the clarity of the Buddha-eye, it perceives all phenomena without any obstruction.
Possessing great majestic power, he travels throughout the entire Dharma-realm without ever resting.
Endowed with great supernormal powers, he is able to go everywhere to wherever there are sentient beings who can be transformed.
Adorning his body with the unimpeded adornments of all Buddhas, he skillfully knows the proper time to preach the Dharma for the multitude.
Second, the qualities manifested below the Dharma-body are also largely the same as the twenty-one virtues mentioned previously.
Inconceivable multitudes of bodhisattvas have each gathered together from various lands in other directions. This assembly is pure;
the Dharma-body is non-dual and has no basis of dependence, yet it is able to spontaneously manifest the activities of the Buddha-body with sovereign ease.
The third [inconceivable excellence] is the gathering of the lower assembly.

That is, his retinue is complete; having sat upon this seat, within that palace there spontaneously appear immeasurable and innumerable extraordinary, wondrous, and exquisite articles of offering surpassing those of the devas—namely, flower garlands, garments, ointments, powdered incense, and precious parasols.
Banners and streamers, music, songs, and praises—each of these things was beyond measure.
With a vast mind of reverence, respect, and worship, they made offerings to the Buddha; and it was likewise so for all the Tuṣita heavens throughout the ten directions.
Having sat upon these seats, the following section manifests the adornments: first, this world-system; subsequently, the ten directions conclude by universalizing [the application].
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-two;
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan;
with a commentary on the meaning by the śramaṇa Chengguan of Da Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang;
and edited and summarized by the śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace.

Regarding the intent for its initial appearance: previously, it was clarified how the Lord of Transformation responds to the call of sentient beings; now, it is clarified how those who assist in the transformation offer praise and exaltation, as well as the basis upon which the essence of the [Bodhisattva] stages rests.
Therefore, this chapter follows in sequence. As for the explanation of the text: it refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions within this palace.

Because it praises the Buddha’s actual virtues, it receives this name. Third, regarding the essential purpose: its essence (*piṭaka*) is the collection of verses praising him with the emission of light;
its aim (*prayojana*) is to teach the dedication of merit.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came one great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields.
They arrived at the place where the Buddha was from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields.
Their names were: Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, Dṛḍhadhvaja Bodhisattva, and Śūra... [and so forth].
Vīradhvaja Bodhisattva, Prabhādhvaja Bodhisattva, Jñānadhvaja Bodhisattva, Ratnadhvaja Bodhisattva,
Vīryadhvaja Bodhisattva, Vimaladhvaja Bodhisattva, Jyotirdhvaja Bodhisattva, and Dharmadhvaja Bodhisattva.

The main text is divided into three parts: first, the gathering of the assembly; second, the emission of light; third, the verses of praise. First, the single phrase concerning supernatural power indicates the cause for the gathering.
Second, the single phrase "from the ten directions" introduces the leaders. Third, the three phrases beginning with "one after another" specify their retinues.

Fourth, the phrase "descending from ten thousand Buddha-fields" indicates the place of arrival. Fifth, the list of names beginning with "their names were" enumerates the ten bodhisattvas, thereby identifying the principal figures.

Regarding the term "Dharmadhvaja" (Dharma-banner), there are briefly five meanings: 1. The meaning of "lofty emergence": it signifies the culmination of the stage of the three types of noble persons (*tri-śaikṣa*).
2. The meaning of "establishment": because great compassion and great wisdom establish sentient beings and *bodhi*. 3. The meaning of "orientation":

that is, through great compassion one gathers sentient beings, and through wisdom and vows one gathers wholesome qualities, thereby orienting oneself toward *bodhi*. 4. The meaning of "crushing the precious": like a fierce... [text fragment]
The banner represents the subduing of all demonic armies. Fifth is the meaning of extinguishing all fears, like the banner of Śakra, because one is not terrified by delusions or karma.
These various names, such as "Vajra" and so forth, signify the essence of the ten dedications and practices.
The lands from which they came were called the World of Wondrous Jewels, the World of Wondrous Bliss, the World of Wondrous Silver,
the World of Wondrous Gold, the World of Wondrous Maṇi, the World of Wondrous Vajra, the World of Wondrous Padma,
the World of Wondrous Utpala, the World of Wondrous Sandalwood, and the World of Wondrous Fragrance.
The fact that the five lands from which [the bodhisattvas] come are all called "Exquisite" (Miao) is due to the power of dedication; even minute virtues thereby pervade the entire dharma-realm.
Their specific names thus represent the dharma-gates practiced during the ten stages of dedication.
Each of them practiced the pure conduct of the brahmacarya under those buddhas, namely:
the Buddha Akṣayadhvaja, Vāyudhvaja, Vimuktidhvaja, Īryāpathadhvaja, Udayadhvaja, Nityadhvaja, Varadhvaja, and Vaśitādhvaja.
Brahmadhvaja Buddha and Avalokanadhvaja Buddha. When those bodhisattvas had arrived at the presence of the Buddhas, they prostrated at the Buddhas' feet.
The six Buddhas whom they originally served all shared the name "Dhvaja" (Banner) without difference in meaning;

the distinct names represent the cultivation of the wisdom of the ten transferences (*daśa-praṇidhāna*) and also represent the fruits of their respective stages. Seventh, when all those below had finished performing their respects...
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, there was immediately manifested a lion throne of exquisite jewel-treasury, completely covered and surrounded by a network of jewels.
As the assembly of bodhisattvas arrived from their respective directions, each sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
Eighth, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they descend and dwell with excellent deportment. Regarding the nature of the seats as "wondrous jewels":

the Ten Abodes take the Vairocana-treasury as their essence because they universally illumine all with the light of wisdom; the Ten Practices take the Lotus-treasury as their essence because their conduct is pure and free from defilement;
now, the Ten Dedications, being the locus of great compassion, universally encompass the realm of birth and death.
The myriad dharmas do not confine themselves to a single form; thus, the substance of the seat is simply called "wondrous jewel," unrestricted by category or kind.
Because its teaching and practice are all-pervasive, it encompasses and gathers in all sentient beings. Furthermore, a jeweled net is spread over its surface.
From his entire body, he emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of pure radiances.
These immeasurable lights all arose from the jewel of the Bodhisattva’s pure mind, which is free from all faults and evils and produced by great vows.
They manifested the sovereign and pure dharmas of all Buddhas. By the power of the Bodhisattvas’ impartial vows, they are able to universally save [all beings].
He protects all sentient beings and is a joy for all the world to behold; those who see him do not do so in vain, for he brings them all to subdual.
Ninth, his entire body emits light that benefits all things; this stage involves frequent engagement with compassion and wisdom to benefit all beings.
The assembly of bodhisattvas has all already accomplished immeasurable merit. That is to say:
they travel everywhere through all buddha-lands without obstruction; they behold the pure dharma-body which is without dependence;

and with their bodies of wisdom, they manifest infinite bodies that go everywhere throughout the ten directions to serve the Buddhas, entering into the immeasurable, boundless, and [inexpressible] states of the Buddhas.
The Dharma of sovereign mastery over thought abides in the gateways of immeasurable omniscience.

Through the radiance of wisdom, one thoroughly understands all phenomena and attains fearlessness regarding them. Whatever is expounded shall endure until the end of the future, with inexhaustible eloquence.
By means of great wisdom, one opens the gates of dhāraṇī; the eye of wisdom is purified as one enters the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). Wisdom...
The realms are without limit; they are ultimately pure, like empty space.

In this world, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the Tuṣita Heaven palace has gathered in such a manner. In all the Tuṣita Heaven palaces throughout the ten directions, bodhisattvas bearing these same names have likewise assembled.
The names of the Buddhas in the lands from which they came are also all [the same].
They are equal; there is no distinction.

Tenth, the brief praise of the supreme virtues of the Bodhisattvas below consists of eleven phrases: the first is general, while the remainder are specific. Within the specific section, there are ten gates.
Next, from "In this world" onwards, it concludes by extending [the description] to the ten directions.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of light rays from his two kneecaps, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions, as far as the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.

All those bodhisattvas beheld these signs of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations here; likewise, these bodhisattvas also beheld the signs of the spiritual transformations of all those Tathāgatas there. Just so...
These bodhisattvas all planted roots of goodness and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva together with the Tathāgata Vairocana in the past.
They have all awakened to and entered the profound liberation of the sovereign power of all Buddhas;
they have attained a body that is the undifferentiated dharmadhātu; they enter all lands while abiding nowhere; and they see immeasurable Buddhas, going to serve them all. In...
In a single thought-moment, one traverses the entire dharma-realm with sovereign non-obstruction. One’s mind and intentions are pure like priceless jewels.
Immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, constantly bestow their protective mindfulness and grant them their power.
Reaching the ultimate, foremost shore, one always dwells in supreme awakening through pure mindfulness. Moment by moment, one constantly enters the state of omniscience. By means of this...
Entering the small into the large, and entering the large into the small, they attain mastery and unhindered penetration.
Having attained the Buddha-body, they dwell together with the Buddhas and acquire all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
Their bodies arise from all-knowledge, and they are able to enter into every sphere traversed by all Tathāgatas. They expound immeasurable gateways of wisdom and reach the Great Vajradhvaja.
Having reached the other shore of wisdom and attained the vajra-samādhi, they sever all doubts and delusions.

Having already obtained the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas, they universally teach and transform countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings throughout all lands in the ten directions.
Although they remain unattached in all places, they are skillfully able to practice and study until achieving ultimate perfection, establishing [beings] in the One through expedient means.
All these bodhisattvas— such as those who have realized all phenomena, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas, unspeakably many, inexhaustible, and pure,
and who are treasuries of all the immeasurable merits of the three periods of time— all came together and assembled at the place where the Buddha was.
All that was seen by means of the light at the abodes of all Buddhas was likewise so.
Second, at that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from below; this section of the text is divided into four parts. First, regarding the knees from which the light is emitted:

they are called "knee-wheels" (*jānumaṇḍala*) because their position is relatively high, and furthermore, they symbolize the turning back of causes toward the fruit and so forth, involving both contraction and extension.
Because it is the characteristic of advancing toward [enlightenment]; furthermore, because compassion and wisdom guide one another, there is no fixed abiding in either contraction or extension.
Second, the number of downward rays emitted, numbering hundreds of thousands; third, the extent of the downward rays that universally illuminate;

fourth, the activity performed by those downward rays of the bodhisattvas, namely, causing those on this side and that side to see one another. Within this, there are three sections; the first correctly clarifies that.
"This mutual seeing"—the two lines beginning with "In this way" below explain the reasons for this seeing. They see one another due to two kinds of causes:
first, because of practicing together due to past causes; second, because of the perfection of present virtues.

The passage beginning with "All have already fully entered" below contains twenty phrases that describe the characteristics of the perfection of virtues. The section beginning with "In this manner" below concludes [the discussion].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, Nor is there any nirvāṇa; It is through the power of his original great vow.”
The manifestation of the sovereign Dharma—this Dharma is inconceivable. It is not within the sphere of the mind;
it is by reaching the other shore of wisdom that one beholds the realm of all Buddhas.
The form-body is not the Buddha, and the voice is likewise so; yet it is also not apart from form and sound that one perceives the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
Those of little wisdom cannot know the true realm of the Buddhas; Only those who have long cultivated pure deeds can understand it here.
The Perfectly Awakened One has no place from which he comes, Nor does he go anywhere;
yet his pure and wondrous form-body Is manifested through spiritual power throughout immeasurable worlds.
Manifesting the body of a Tathāgata, he extensively expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
his mind is free from attachment and his wisdom is boundless. He thoroughly understands all phenomena and universally enters the Dharma-realm, manifesting sovereign powers.
Regarding sentient beings and all dharmas, he understands them all without obstruction.
Universally manifesting all forms and appearances throughout all lands, if one desires to seek omniscience and swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment,
one should, with a pure and wondrous mind, cultivate the practices of bodhi.
If one beholds the Tathāgata and such majestic spiritual power, one should [take refuge] in the Most Victorious Honored One.
"Do not give rise to doubt regarding the offerings.
In the second verse of praise, there are ten bodhisattvas, which constitute ten sections. These also correspond sequentially to the ten directions.
In each case, the speaker and the ritual procedure are first indicated. Now, regarding the first, the Vajradhvaja of the East: this is the presiding master of the assembly.
The name contains both the general and the specific. Generally, it reveals that dedication does not transcend compassion and wisdom. "Vajra" means firm and sharp; this is the wisdom of compassion.
It is "firm" because even the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the two vehicles cannot destroy it; it is "sharp" because it cuts through afflictions that are difficult to sever.
Thus, it is said that "wisdom reaches the other shore," which is the compassion of wisdom. It is "firm" because it cannot be moved by attachment or views. It is... [nothing more].
It is not for the sake of profit. Therefore, throughout the text, it refers universally to *kṣatriya* beings. The Seventy-eighth Sūtra states:
"For example, a vajra is produced only from a vajra-source or a gold-source, and not from the source of other jewels.
The vajra of the bodhicitta is likewise; it arises only from the vajra-source of great compassion that protects sentient beings, namely, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
It arises from the locus of the gold of the sublime realm; it does not arise from the locus of the roots of goodness of other sentient beings.

Thus, one knows that "vajra" does not exclusively metaphorize wisdom. Those who attack [the term] *prajñā* fail to grasp this meaning, for they take only the designation and apply the vajra as a metaphor for *prajñā* alone.
[In the text], compassion rescues the nine classes of beings, yet there is nothing that is actually delivered. Compassion...
Wisdom that guides through its characteristics is what constitutes true *prajñā*. Its specific name is the compassion that protects and delivers sentient beings;
it is the wisdom that is free from the notion of sentient beings. There are ten verses in this hymn, extolling the Buddha’s merit of unimpeded quiescence and activity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata is supreme and peerless; Profoundly deep, he is ineffable.
Transcending the path of language, He is as pure as space. Behold the Lion among Men, And his power of sovereign spiritual transformations."
Having already transcended conceptual discrimination, yet causing it to appear as if discriminating, the Guide has expounded the profound and subtle Dharma.
For this reason, he manifests this peerless body;
this is great wisdom, the sphere of action of all Buddhas. If one wishes to understand it, [one must look here].
One should always draw near to the Buddhas, keeping the mental faculty constantly pure;
Making offerings to all Tathāgatas without ever feeling weary or fatigued, one is able to enter the Buddha-way.
Possessing inexhaustible merit and firmly abiding in the bodhicitta, thereby the net of doubt is removed, and one contemplates the Buddha without satiety.
One who penetrates all phenomena is truly a son of the Buddha. Such a person is able to understand the sovereign power of all Buddhas as taught by those of vast wisdom.
Desiring to take all phenomena as one's foundation, one should give rise to supreme aspiration;
with the resolve to seek unsurpassed enlightenment, if there is one who reveres the Buddha, [they shall attain it].
One who intends to repay the Buddha’s kindness will never be parted from him;
for what wise person, having encountered and heard the teachings of all Buddhas, would fail to cultivate pure vows and tread the path walked by the Buddhas?
The second, the "Firm One" of the South, symbolizes the indestructible dedication because the bodhicitta is firm and because one contemplates the Buddha without weariness.
The ten verses primarily clarify the Tathāgata’s qualities as the refuge for sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Valāgraketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as with clear and pure eyes, One perceives all forms because of the sun, So too is it with the pure mind:
Through the Buddha's power, one beholds the Tathāgata. Just as by the power of diligence, One can reach the very bottom of the ocean."
The power of wisdom is likewise so: one attains the vision of immeasurable Buddhas.
Just as what is sown in fertile, rich soil necessarily grows, so too in this ground of pure mind are all Buddha-dharmas produced.
Like a person who has discovered a treasure trove and is forever freed from the suffering of poverty, the Bodhisattva attains the Buddha-dharmas.
With a stainless and pure mind, like the *gadhā* medicine that can eliminate all poisons, so too is the Buddha-dharma;
it extinguishes the affliction of all defilements. This true and virtuous spiritual friend is praised by the Tathāgata;
through his majestic spiritual power, one is able to hear all the Buddha-dharmas.
Even if one were to bestow wealth and treasures upon the Buddha for countless eons, if one does not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha,
this is not called giving. The immeasurable varieties of physical marks adorn the Buddha’s body,
yet it is not by means of these physical marks that one can see the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Tranquil and eternally unmoving, yet able to manifest bodies everywhere,
filling the realms of the ten directions like the realm of empty space; the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus—
ultimately without arising or ceasing.
The third is the Bodhisattva of the West, Pure Mind Power Wisdom (Viśuddhamati-jñānabala). He perceives the Buddha as reaching the ultimate source and being equal to all Buddhas;
therefore, he is named "Valiant" (Vikrama). These ten verses collectively manifest the Tathāgata’s virtues of vast benefit through seeing and hearing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Light Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“In the human realm and the heavens, throughout all worlds, one everywhere beholds the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous form-body.
Just as the power of a single mind is able to give rise to various kinds of minds,”
In this way, the body of one Buddha universally manifests as all Buddhas;
awakening is a non-dual dharma and likewise devoid of all marks. Yet, within the midst of dualistic dharmas, he manifests a body adorned with marks.
Having realized that the nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, he arises like an illusion, his conduct being inexhaustible.
The Teacher thus manifests all Buddhas of the three times;
the Dharmakāya is entirely pure, yet according to those who are to be transformed, he universally manifests sublime form-bodies.
The Tathāgata does not think, "I create such a body," for it is manifested spontaneously, never giving rise to discrimination.
The Dharma-realm is without differentiation and has no basis of support;
yet, within the world, it manifests immeasurable bodies. The Buddha-body is not a transformation, nor is it non-transformed;
within the state of non-transformation, it displays transformed forms. Perfect Enlightenment is inexhaustible.
The Dharma-realm is equal to empty space, Profound and vast, without limit or bottom; All paths of speech are utterly cut off, yet the Tathāgata skillfully penetrates them.
He practices the Way in all places; In all lands throughout the Dharma-realm, his going is everywhere unimpeded.
The fourth Bodhisattva of the north, by the power of great compassion, employs the light of wisdom to illuminate that profound darkness, reaching everywhere without exception;
his name is Prabhāketu. The ten verses primarily manifest the Tathāgata’s virtue of pervasive transformation and function, which is identical in essence to his own being.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“If there is a person who can believe and accept The unimpeded knowledge of all-knowledge,
And cultivate the practices of enlightenment with a mind beyond measure, Throughout all lands, They universally manifest infinite bodies.”
Yet the body does not abide in any place, nor does it dwell within phenomena.
The supernatural power of each and every Tathāgata manifests bodies throughout inconceivable eons;
though one might exhaust all calculation, the number of sentient beings in the three periods of time could be known, yet that which the Tathāgata manifests remains beyond measure.
Their number cannot be grasped; at times they manifest as one or two, even appearing in immeasurable bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Yet in reality, there are not two kinds. It is like the pure full moon, which appears universally in all waters;
though the reflections are infinite, the original moon has never been two.
Thus, with unimpeded wisdom, he has attained perfect enlightenment;
he manifests universally in all lands, yet the Buddha-body is non-dual—it is neither one nor two, nor is it infinite.
According to those who are to be transformed, he manifests infinite bodies; the Buddha-body is not of the past.
Nor does it exist in the future; in a single thought-moment, it manifests birth, the attainment of enlightenment, and parinirvāṇa.
Like forms created by illusion, they are without arising and without origination; the Buddha-body is likewise manifested without any birth.

The fifth is in the northeast. Because it decisively resolves all matters regarding the realm of the Buddha’s quiescent activity without doubt, and because wisdom guides the myriad practices to give rise to them inexhaustibly, it is named "Wisdom Banner" (Jñānaketu).
These ten verses primarily praise the Tathāgata’s unimpeded virtue of manifesting and arising in response to beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Buddha-body is immeasurable, yet it can manifest a measurable form; In accordance with what is appropriate for beings to behold, the Guide appears in such ways.
The Buddha-body has no fixed location, yet it fills all places.
Just as space is without limit, so too is it inconceivable;
it is not a sphere of activity for the mind, and the mind does not arise within it. Within the realm of the Buddhas, there is ultimately no arising or ceasing.
Like what is seen by a person with cataracts, it is neither internal nor external; thus do the worlds perceive the Buddhas.
It should be known that it is likewise for the sake of benefiting sentient beings:
when the Tathāgata appears in the world, sentient beings perceive his appearance, yet in reality there is no arising in the world.
One cannot see the Buddha through lands, days, or nights; whether through years, months, or a single kṣaṇa—it should be known that all are thus.
Sentient beings speak thus: "On such-and-such a day, the Buddha attained enlightenment.
Yet the Tathāgata’s attainment of Bodhi is not actually bound to a specific day. The Tathāgata is free from conceptual discrimination; he is not of this world and transcends all numerical reckoning.
All the Guides of the three times appear in this very same way, just like the pure orb of the sun.
Not conjoined with the dark night, yet one speaks of a certain day and night; The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus:
throughout all kalpas of the three periods of time, it is not conjoined with the Tathāgata, yet one speaks of the Buddhas of the three periods, the Guides.
The Dharma is thus.
The sixth Bodhisattva of the southeast uses perfectly pure wisdom to illuminate the principle of equality.
Because he manifests unimpededly in accordance with all things like a *maṇi* jewel, he is named Ratnaketu (Jewel Banner). The ten verses primarily manifest his world-transcending virtue of equality.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The bodies of all the Teachers are identical, and their meanings are likewise so;
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, they appear in various ways according to what is appropriate. Behold the Honored Muni: His deeds are most extraordinary."
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena without exception, the Buddha-body is neither within nor without;
it manifests through the power of the Buddha. Such is the nature of the Dharma of the Guide:
according to the various classes of sentient beings and their accumulated karma from previous lives, there appear these manifold bodies.
The manifestations are each different; such are the bodies of all Buddhas.
Immeasurable and incalculable, they can only be excluded by the Great Awakened Honored One; none are able to conceive of them.
Just as my inconceivable mental karma cannot be grasped, so too is the Buddha inconceivable; he is not manifested by mental karma.
Just as inconceivable lands are seen in pure adornment, so too is the Buddha inconceivable, with no sublime marks not manifesting.
Just as all phenomena arise through a multitude of conditions, seeing the Buddha is likewise;
it necessarily relies upon manifold virtuous deeds, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Able to fulfill the hearts of sentient beings, such is the Dharma of all Buddhas;
They completely fulfill all vows throughout immeasurable lands. When the Guides arise in the world, they universally respond to the ten directions according to the power of their vows.

The seventh Bodhisattva in the southwest is named Vīryaketu (Virtue Banner). Because he diligently contemplates that the true and the responsive bodies of the Tathāgata are identical, he is able to be impartial and accord with all sentient beings. Ten verses clarify this meaning of sameness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The light of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom Universally purifies all worlds. Once the worlds have been purified, He reveals all Buddha-dharmas.
Should there be anyone who wishes to see Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings,"
There is nothing that does not accord with their mind, yet in reality there is no place from which [the Buddha] comes.
By taking the Buddha as their object of focus and maintaining undistracted mindfulness, such persons shall behold the Buddha.
Their number being equal to the scope of their minds, they accomplish pure and white dharmas and become fully endowed with all merits; they [attain] omniscience.
With single-minded devotion, never forsaking the mind, the Teacher acts for the sake of sentient beings;
he expounds the Dharma as is appropriate, manifesting the most supreme body wherever there are those to be converted.

He realizes that both the Buddha-body and all things in the world are devoid of self; having awakened to this, he attains perfect enlightenment and further preaches it for the sake of sentient beings.
All these lions among men, with immeasurable powers of mastery, manifest bodies such as mindfulness and the like, each body being distinct.
Such are the bodies in the world; the bodies of all Buddhas are likewise so.
To thoroughly understand their intrinsic nature is what is called "Buddha"; the Tathāgata knows and sees them universally.
Clearly understanding all phenomena—the Buddha-dharma and awakening—both are unattainable.
The Guide neither comes nor goes, nor does he abide anywhere. Being far removed from all perversions, this is called Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
The eighth [verse] concerns the Bodhisattva of the northwest: his essence is pure suchness (*tathatā*), capable of accomplishing the white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and further purifying the world;

thus he is named "Stainless" (*vimala*). Of the ten verses, most praise the Tathāgata’s pure virtues: the first six concern the purification of others, while the latter four concern self-purification.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constellation Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata has no abode, yet he dwells universally in all lands; He goes to every realm and is seen in all places.
According to the minds of sentient beings, He universally manifests all bodies.
The attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, And likewise the parinirvāṇa—these are inconceivable to all Buddhas.
Who can conceive of a Buddha? Who can see the Perfectly Awakened One? Who can manifest the most supreme?
All phenomena are suchness; The realm of all Buddhas is likewise so, Such that not even a single dharma exists.
Just as the intermediate state arises and ceases, sentient beings engage in false conceptualization.
To those who have thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena—that there is neither Buddha nor world—the Tathāgata appears everywhere to inspire faith and joy in sentient beings;
yet the essence of the Buddha cannot be apprehended, for even that is nothing seen.

If one can, within this world, remain far removed from all attachment, With an unimpeded mind, rejoice, and attain awakening to the Dharma— This manifestation of spiritual power is what is called a Buddha.
Throughout all times of the three periods, when sought, nothing whatsoever exists; If one can know it in this way, [one is a Buddha].
The mind, mental factors, and all phenomena— He knows and perceives them all. Swiftly attaining the state of a Tathāgata, he reveals this within his speech;
The sovereign power of all Buddhas, Perfect awakening transcends language, yet it is expressed through words as a provisional means.

The ninth [verse] concerns the bodhisattva Adhaḥsāgara. He understands that the Buddha’s body, which universally responds throughout the dharma-realm, does not depart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), just as the stars are brilliantly arrayed across the sky and cannot be bound or attached. Therefore, this is his name.
The tenth verse reveals this quality of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Dhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"It would be better to constantly endure all the sufferings of the world, Than ever to be far removed from the Tathāgata and fail to behold his sovereign power.
If there are sentient beings who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta..."
If one hears the Buddha’s name, one will certainly attain enlightenment.
If there is a person of wisdom who gives rise to the aspiration for the Way even for a single thought-moment, they will surely become a Supreme Honored One. Be careful not to give rise to doubt;
the Tathāgata’s power of mastery is difficult to encounter in immeasurable kalpas. If you give rise to even a single thought of faith—
One who swiftly ascends the unsurpassed path, Even if in every moment of thought They were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas—
If they do not know the true Dharma, it is not called making an offering. But if one hears such a Dharma as this— that all Buddhas are born from it—
Then even if they must undergo immeasurable suffering, They will not abandon the practice of Bodhi.
Upon hearing once of the Great Wisdom—the Dharma entered by all Buddhas—one becomes a guide of the three periods of time throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Even if one were to travel through all Buddha-fields until the end of the future, without seeking this wondrous Dharma, one would ultimately not attain Bodhi. For sentient beings since beginningless time...
For a long time wandering through birth and death, They did not understand the true Dharma. Therefore, the Buddhas have appeared in the world;
All phenomena are indestructible, And there is no one capable of destroying them.
With sovereign great radiance, they reveal them universally to the world.
The tenth bodhisattva from above, who knows the reality of dharmas and universally enters the dharma-realm, is named Dharmadhvaja because his practices and cultivation are all without limit.
Knowing the Dharma is called "Buddha"; therefore, he first praises the benefits of seeing the Buddha.
The first ten verses collectively manifest that the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear.
Regarding the first part of the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Ten Dedications" (*Daśa-pariṇāmanā-parivarta*):

as for the intent of its introduction, since the introductory section (*nidāna*) of this assembly has already been revealed, it is now appropriate to manifest the main teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*). Furthermore, it has already been presented in general.
The Buddha-wisdom is that which is relied upon; next, the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) that rely upon it are specifically revealed, and thus they follow hereafter.

Second, regarding the explanation of the name: "dedication" (*pariṇāmana*) means "to turn," and "orientation" (*abhimukha*) means "to proceed toward. Because one turns the myriad practices and proceeds toward the three destinations, there are ten distinct types of dedication.
The specific names of these ten will be explained in the "Fundamental Section" (*Mūla-bhāga*); the general term for dedication is now [to be discussed].
This shall be further clarified. Although the meanings of "following the direction of the object" are manifold, when these meanings are comprehensively subsumed, they do not exceed three points:
namely, sentient beings, bodhi, and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). The former two follow signs; the reality-limit is the departure from signs.
Expanding these three into ten, they are: (1) turning oneself toward others; (2) turning the few toward the many; (3) turning one's own causal practices toward [the goal].
1. Turning from practice toward realization; 2. Turning from cause toward fruit; 3. Turning from the inferior toward the superior; 4.

Turning from inference toward direct realization; 5. Turning from phenomena toward principle; 6. Turning from differentiated practice toward perfectly integrated practice; 7. Turning from the mundane toward the supramundane.

The ten types of dedication turn the practice that accords with principle toward the results accomplished through that principle. Among these ten meanings, the first three all dedicate toward sentient beings;
the next three all dedicate toward bodhi; the next two dedicate toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and the final two meanings apply to both the fruit and the limit of reality.
Regarding the third point, the essential aim: it is by means of an ocean of boundless practices that one accords with boundless great vows.
This is the primary tenet. To accomplish the virtues and functions of Samantabhadra is the ultimate goal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.

The commentary on the text consists of ten major sections: first, the Section on Samādhi; second, the Section on Bestowal of Power; third, the Section on Arising; fourth, the Section on the Fundamental;

fifth, the Section on Exposition; sixth, the Section on Auspicious Responses; seventh, the Section on Universal Connection; eighth, the Section on Testimony; ninth, the Section on Verses of Praise and Exhortation to Practice;
and tenth, the Section on the Measurement of Merit. Of these, the first two constitute the Section on Samādhi.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Vajradhvaja.
They all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you are indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Light of Wisdom."
Samādhi. Good son, this is because you are empowered by the combined spiritual power of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten hundred thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions;

it is also due to the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of Vairocana Tathāgata from the past, and because your own wisdom is pure and the roots of goodness of all Bodhisattvas have increased and become preeminent, enabling you to enter [this samādhi].
He expounds the Dharma while in this samādhi.

Second, regarding the entry into this samādhi, there is the section on the "bestowal of empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which has three parts. First, the general manifestation of the characteristics of the empowerment;
therein, first the appearance of the Buddha is clarified, followed by the praise of his excellence.
In order to cause all bodhisattvas to attain pure fearlessness; to be endowed with unimpeded eloquence; to enter the stage of unimpeded wisdom;
to abide in the great mind of omniscience; to accomplish inexhaustible roots of goodness;
to fulfill the unimpeded white dharmas; to enter the universal-gate dharma-realm; and to manifest the spiritual powers of all Buddhas—from the beginningless past...
Because mindfulness and wisdom are uninterrupted; because they attain the protection and sustenance of all Buddhas regarding their faculties;
because they extensively expound the manifold dharmas through immeasurable gateways; because they hear, fully comprehend, receive, and uphold them without forgetting;

because they gather all the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas; because they accomplish the supramundane aids to the path; because they do not sever the wisdom of omniscience; and because they bring forth great vows.
It is for the purpose of explaining the ultimate meaning; for the purpose of realizing the dharma-realm; for the purpose of causing all bodhisattvas to rejoice;
for the purpose of cultivating the roots of goodness that are equal to those of all buddhas; and for the purpose of protecting and sustaining the lineage of all Tathāgatas.
That is to say, it is the exposition of the ten dedications of the bodhisattvas.
The second section aims to clarify the purpose of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*). It consists of twenty-two phrases.

The first twenty phrases establish the goal to be accomplished through ten introductory phrases; the subsequent eleven phrases, beginning with "by means of immeasurable doors," clarify the activities performed;
and the final phrase provides a summary of their respective categories.

O Son of the Buddha, you should expound this Dharma by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. For you shall receive the Buddha’s protective mindfulness; for you shall dwell securely in the Buddha’s household;
for you shall increase supramundane merit; for you shall attain the radiance of *dhāraṇī*; for you shall enter the unobstructed Buddha-Dharmas;
for you shall cause the great light to universally illumine the *dharmadhātu*; for you shall gather the pure Dharmas free from fault; and for you shall abide...
Because it is the sphere of vast wisdom, and because he has attained the light of the unobstructed Dharma, at that time all Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immeasurable wisdom;
they bestowed unhindered eloquence; they bestowed skillful means for discerning the meaning of phrases;
they bestowed the light of the unobstructed Dharma; they bestowed a body equal to that of the Tathāgatas; and they bestowed infinite, distinct, and pure voices.
[They were endowed with] the voice; the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable samādhi of skillful observation; the wisdom of dedication of all indestructible roots of goodness;
the skillful means for accomplishing the observation of all phenomena; and uninterrupted eloquence in teaching all phenomena in all places. Why is this?
It is because of the power of the roots of goodness from entering this samādhi. At that time, all...

Each of the Buddhas stroked the crown of Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva’s head with their right hand. Having received this stroking of the head, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva immediately arose from meditative concentration.

Third, the passage beginning with "The third son of the Buddha" below explicitly reveals the characteristics of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Within this, there are initially ten phrases concerning the verbal empowerment (*vāg-adhiṣṭhāna*), which pertains to the activity of speech.

This is explained by way of increase. Next, the ten phrases beginning with "the Buddhas immediately bestow immeasurable wisdom" refer to the addition of wisdom through the secret empowerment of mental action (*manas-karman*).

Following this, the section beginning with "For what reason? refers to the addition of majesty through the empowerment of the body by touching the crown of the head. This concludes the section on arising from meditative absorption.

He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess inconceivable great vows that fill the dharma-realm, universally able to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
That is to say, they cultivate and study the dedication of merit of all buddhas of the past, future, and present."
The fourth section, "Addressing the Bodhisattvas," is divided into two parts within the main text. The first three lines provide a general definition of the nature of the vow as being inconceivable;
"aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) means seeking, which here refers to possessing the inexhaustible ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows—profound, vast, and inconceivable.

The subsequent lines reveal the characteristics of this inconceivability: because its essence permeates the *dharmadhātu*, its function universally protects and saves; therefore, it is called [the "Inconceivable"].
Great! Third, this explains how [the dedication] is difficult to conceive, because its practice is identical to that of the Buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha, how many kinds of dedication are there for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dedication for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which all the Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively expounded."
The second section provides a detailed exposition of the names and characteristics. The text is divided into four parts: first, the enumeration of the items and the inquiry regarding their names;
second, the statement "O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dedication," which indicates the number and reveals their excellence because they are taught by all Buddhas together.
What are these eleven? First is the dedication for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being.
Second is the indestructible dedication. Third is the dedication equal to all Buddhas. Fourth is the dedication that reaches all places.
Fifth is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit. Sixth is the dedication entering into all impartial roots of goodness.
Seventh, the dedication that accords with all sentient beings. Eighth, the dedication of the mark of true thusness (*tathatā*).
Ninth, the dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment. Tenth, the dedication of entering the infinite dharma-realm. O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of dedication of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which have been taught, will be taught, and are currently being taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
This enumerates the names of the ten dedications; their collective name has already appeared at the beginning of this chapter. Herein, their characteristics are briefly explained.
The two characters "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) both refer to the vow that performs the dedication. Terms such as "rescue and protection" (*trāṇa-rakṣā*) all refer to the practice of dedication.
All these are designated by names based upon their respective supports; terms such as "rescue and protection" are the specific characteristics of dedication.

That which extensively relieves through great compassion is called "rescuing and protecting all sentient beings. Because of great wisdom and non-attachment, it is said to be "detached from the multitude."
1. The characteristic of arising is the vast and non-erroneous mind. 2. Regarding the two types of non-destruction:
one attains indestructible faith in the Three Jewels and other such objects, and dedicates these roots of goodness through that [faith]. 3.

By dedicating in accordance with what the Buddhas of the three periods of time have done, one is called equal to all Buddhas. 4. Bodhisattvas cause those roots of goodness to reach all places. 5. Through dedication...

Because of this, one is able to accomplish the treasury of inexhaustible merit. Sixth, practicing goodness in accordance with principle; without conflict between phenomenon and noumenon, one enters into equality.
Seventh, benefiting sentient beings with a mind of impartiality through the roots of goodness. Eighth, the roots of goodness accord with suchness.

This constitutes the fulfillment of the dedication. Ninth, it is called "liberation" because it is not bound by signs and does not cling to views, as its activity is sovereign, such as the inconceivable liberation and others.
Tenth, it is the arising of function in accordance with the nature; that is, because one dedicates the roots of goodness of the dharma-realm toward the dharma-realm.
There is an extensive explanation in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), which is difficult to record in full. The above is a brief explanation of the specific names.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the enumeration of the lower stage.

O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s dedication of merit for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being"?
The fifth section for the Son of the Buddha, titled "The Section on the Lower Exposition," consists of ten parts concerning the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

Each part first presents a prose exposition followed by a verse summary. Within each prose exposition, there are two sections: first, the practice of the stage (*bhūmi*), and second, the fruit of the stage.
Where any element is incomplete, it should be understood from the text itself. Now, first, the title is cited: "Always, with a mind of non-characteristic (*animitta*), one constantly practices..."

Entering the six realms of existence as karmic retribution, they undergo various sensations without being subject to them; because they transform and redirect these states, they are called "Protectors" and so forth.
This is the citation of the name.

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), purifies the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), and cultivates the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
They give rise to the perfection of vigor, enter the perfection of meditation, and abide in the perfection of wisdom.
They cultivate immeasurable roots of goodness such as great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.

In the second part, the detailed explanation, there are two sections. First, the roots of virtue to be dedicated are clarified; second, starting from "when cultivating roots of virtue," the dedication itself is properly explained.
Now, for the first: ancient masters have designated this as the essence of the practice (*caryā-svabhāva*).
When cultivating roots of goodness, one should form this thought:

"May these roots of goodness universally benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to attain ultimate purity and forever leave behind the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama."
Immeasurable suffering and affliction.

Following this, the main section clarifying the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is divided into two parts. First, the dedication according to characteristics (*sanimitta-pariṇāmanā*) is clarified; second, the dedication free from characteristics (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*) is clarified starting from the passage "I should be like the sun.
Within the preceding text on the dedication according to characteristics, the first two lines of the sūtra provide a general explanation. Next, from here...

From the beginning until the end, for the sake of severing the doubts of sentient beings, there are one hundred and six lines of scripture that specifically clarify protection and rescue, divided into four sections:
first, protection through benefit and happiness; second, protection from suffering and affliction; third, protection by taking on suffering;
and fourth, protection through total liberation. These are indicated and manifested in sequence below.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva plants roots of goodness, they dedicate those roots of goodness in this way:
"May I act as a shelter for all sentient beings, so that they may be freed from all causes of suffering;

may I act as a protector for all sentient beings, so that they may be completely liberated from all afflictions; may I act as a refuge for all sentient beings, so that they may all attain freedom from [suffering]."
Because of all fears, he acts as a refuge for all sentient beings, so that they may reach omniscience.
He acts as a sanctuary for all sentient beings, so that they may attain the state of ultimate peace and security.

He acts as illumination for all sentient beings, so that they may obtain the light of wisdom and extinguish the darkness of delusion. He acts as a torch for all sentient beings, to shatter all of those [obscurations].
Because they dispel the darkness of ignorance, they act as lamps for all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the state of ultimate purity.
Because they lead them into the true Dharma, they act as guides for all sentient beings.
Because they grant them unimpeded great wisdom, they act as great guides for all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, by means of this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
These roots of goodness are dedicated in this way to equally benefit all sentient beings, ultimately causing them all to attain omniscience.

Following this, the text specifically elucidates the middle section, first clarifying the protection through benefit and happiness; this consists of ten lines of scripture, the first of which is general.
The heading. Next, there are ten phrases below which specifically reveal the departure from suffering and the attainment of happiness.
Finally, one and a half lines of scripture, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," summarize the benefit and joy.
