O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices dedication while guarding against those who are not their friends, they do so without any distinction from how they treat their own friends.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has entered into the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*).
Thus, they do not give rise to even a single thought of regarding any sentient being as not being a friend. Even if there should be a sentient being who, toward the Bodhisattva...
Even toward those with hearts of malice and harm, the Bodhisattva gazes with eyes of loving-kindness and never gives way to anger.

He acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to all sentient beings, expounding the True Dharma so that they may practice it. Just as the great ocean cannot be corrupted by any poison, so too is the Bodhisattva;
even when confronted by all who are ignorant, lacking wisdom, and ungrateful for his kindness, he remains free from resentment.
They are exceedingly cruel, arrogant, and conceited; their minds are blind and ignorant, failing to recognize wholesome dharmas.
Toward such evil beings as these, who inflict all manner of afflictions and harassments, he remains unmoved and undisturbed.

It is, for example, like the sun deity appearing in the world, which does not remain hidden or fail to manifest simply because those born blind cannot see it; nor does it fail to appear because of a city of Gandharvas.
Because it is obscured by such things as the hands of asuras, the Jambū tree, lofty crags, deep valleys, dust, mist, smoke, and clouds, it remains hidden and does not appear.
Nor does it remain hidden and fail to appear due to changes in the seasons.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise possesses great merit; his mind is profound and vast, and he maintains right mindfulness.
He observes [all things] without ever becoming discouraged. Desiring to bring his merit and wisdom to ultimate fulfillment, he gives rise to a resolute aspiration for the supreme Dharma.
With the light of the Dharma universally illuminating all meanings, he attains mastery of wisdom regarding all gateways to the teachings.
He constantly cultivates wholesome dharmas for the benefit of all sentient beings; he never mistakenly gives rise to a mind that abandons them, nor does he—
Sentient beings are by nature corrupt, evil, and clouded by wrong views and anger, making them difficult to tame;

yet, rather than abandoning them or failing to cultivate the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), they simply adorn themselves with the armor of the Bodhisattva’s great vows. They rescue and protect sentient beings, never regressing.
They do not withdraw from the Bodhisattva practice or abandon the path to enlightenment because sentient beings fail to recognize their kindness or repay their debt of gratitude. Nor do they...

When foolish and ignorant people gather together in one place and abandon all roots of goodness that accord with reality, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not give rise to weariness or aversion toward them, even though they commit transgressions and evils so numerous as to be unbearable. Why is this?
It is because, for example, the Sun Deity does not appear in the world for the sake of a single matter alone; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise.
It is so. One does not merely cultivate various roots of goodness for the sake of a single sentient being and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
rather, one cultivates roots of goodness and dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of universally rescuing and protecting all sentient beings.
Likewise, it is not merely for the sake of purifying a single Buddha-field, nor is it merely for...

Because they have faith in one Buddha; not merely for the sake of seeing one Buddha, nor merely for the sake of understanding one Dharma, do they give rise to the vow of great wisdom and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It is for the sake of universally purifying all Buddha-fields, for the sake of universally placing faith in all Buddhas, for the sake of universally serving and making offerings to all Buddhas, and for the sake of universal comprehension.
Because of all the Buddha-dharmas, they give rise to great vows, cultivate all roots of goodness, and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes all the Buddha-dharmas as their object of focus;
they give rise to a vast mind and a non-retrogressive mind, and throughout immeasurable eons, they cultivate and accumulate this rare and difficult-to-attain jewel of the mind. Together with...

All Buddhas are entirely equal. When a bodhisattva contemplates all roots of goodness in this way, their faith becomes pure, their great compassion firm, and they possess a profound mind, a joyful mind, a pure mind, a most excellent mind, a supple mind, a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of gathering and protecting, a mind of benefit, and a mind of peace and happiness, universally for the sake of all sentient beings. Truly...
This is the true dedication. It is not merely a matter of words. Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates their roots of goodness, they form this thought:
"By means of my roots of goodness, may all sentient beings in all realms of existence attain pure and perfect merit;
may it be indestructible, inexhaustible, and may they always receive the respect of the Right [Dharma]."
They maintain mindfulness without forgetfulness, attain decisive wisdom, and possess immeasurable knowledge. Their physical, verbal, and mental actions are adorned with the perfection of all merits.
Furthermore, they form this thought: "By these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings serve and make offerings to all Buddhas so that no such act goes in vain;
may they possess indestructible pure faith in the presence of all Buddhas and hear the True Dharma."

They sever all doubts and delusions; they retain [the teachings] in memory without forgetting and practice according to what has been taught. They give rise to a mind of reverence toward the Tathāgata; their physical actions are pure;
they dwell securely in immeasurable and vast roots of goodness; they are forever free from poverty, and the seven riches are fulfilled.

They constantly follow and study under all Buddhas, accomplishing immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous roots of goodness. They awaken to and understand with equanimity, abiding in omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
With unobstructed eyes, they regard all sentient beings equally; their bodies are adorned with all the marks of excellence, free from any blemish or deficiency.
His speech and voice are pure and sublime, his merits are perfected, his faculties are subdued, and he has accomplished the ten powers.

With a mind of goodness fully satisfied, he dwells nowhere upon dependence; he causes all sentient beings everywhere to obtain the bliss of the Buddha, attaining immeasurable abodes and dwelling where the Buddhas dwell.
Second, the explanation of receiving affliction and seeking protection consists of forty-five lines of scripture.

Within this, the characteristics of receiving affliction are first explained in twenty-seven lines of remaining scripture, extending up to the attainment of Bodhi. This section contains two layers of combined dharma and analogy.
Next, from "O Son of the Buddha... (etc. down to "by means of all Buddha-dharmas," there are seventeen lines of remaining scripture that explain the turning over [of merit].

Regarding the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*): herein, first the mind that rescues sentient beings is clarified; next, from "by means of all roots of goodness" onwards, the vows of dedication are distinguished;
subsequently, with the four lines of sutra beginning from "and again he forms this thought," the perfection of attaining the Dharma is clarified;

then, with the three lines of sutra beginning from "toward all Buddhas," the perfection of superior virtues is clarified; and finally, with the one line of sutra beginning from "causing all," the fulfillment of the fruit of virtue is clarified.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees sentient beings who, having committed evil deeds, undergo various heavy sufferings;
and because of these obstructions, they neither see the Buddha, nor hear the Dharma, nor recognize the Saṅgha—the Bodhisattva then forms this thought:
"I shall, within those various evil realms, undergo all manner of sufferings on behalf of these sentient beings, so as to bring them liberation. Thus does the Bodhisattva act.
When undergoing bitter suffering, they become even more diligent, neither abandoning nor avoiding it; they are without alarm or fear, without retreat or cowardice, and free from weariness.
Why is this? Because, according to their vows, they are determined to shoulder the burden of all sentient beings and bring them to liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects: "All sentient beings are subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death."

In all places of suffering and hardship, beings wander according to their karma; possessed by wrong views and lacking wisdom, they lose all wholesome dharmas. I should rescue them and cause them to attain liberation.

Furthermore, all sentient beings are entangled in the net of craving and shrouded by the veil of ignorance; stained by and attached to the various realms of existence, they pursue them without relinquishing them.
They enter the cage of suffering and perform the deeds of Māra; their merit and wisdom are utterly exhausted, and they constantly harbor doubts.
Failing to see the place of peace and unaware of the path to liberation, they revolve incessantly within the wheel of birth and death, perpetually submerged in the mire of all sufferings.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of great compassion and a heart of great benefit, desiring to bring all sentient beings to complete liberation.
He dedicates all roots of goodness and dedicates with a vast mind, as follows:
The dedication practiced by the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time is the dedication as described in the *Mahāpariṇāmanā-sūtra*.
May all sentient beings universally attain purity and ultimately accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, he reflects:
"My practice is intended to cause all sentient beings to fully achieve the sovereignty of unsurpassed wisdom; I do not seek liberation for my own sake."

[They] are liberated. Yet, for the sake of rescuing and aiding all sentient beings so that they may all attain the mind of omniscience, cross the stream of birth and death, and be released from all sufferings, [the Bodhisattva] further reflects:

"I shall universally undergo all manner of suffering on behalf of all sentient beings, so that they may emerge from the great abyss of immeasurable birth-and-death sufferings. I shall universally act on behalf of all sentient beings..."
May I be born in all worlds and within all evil destinies, and undergo every kind of suffering throughout all future kalpas;
yet may I always diligently cultivate roots of goodness for the sake of sentient beings. Why is this?
It would be better for me alone to undergo such manifold sufferings than to allow sentient beings to fall into hell. I shall [endure] those hells, the animal realm, and the perilous domains of Yama.
At this difficult juncture, I offer my own body as collateral to ransom all sentient beings in the evil realms and bring them to liberation. Furthermore, I form this thought:
"I vow to protect all sentient beings and never abandon them; what I have spoken is truthful and free from falsehood.
Why is this? It is because I have resolved to attain Bodhicitta for the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, and not for [myself].

One seeks the unsurpassed path for oneself, and does not cultivate the bodhisattva practice for the sake of seeking the realms of the five desires or the various pleasures within the three realms of existence. Why is this? Because worldly pleasure is nothing other than suffering;
it is the domain of the māras, that which the foolish crave, and that which the Buddhas rebuke. All sufferings and afflictions arise because of it. [It leads to] the hells, the hungry ghosts...
In the realms of ghosts, animals, and King Yama, there is anger, strife, and litigation; they revile and insult one another.
All such evils are caused by attachment to the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). Being addicted to the five desires, they distance themselves from the Buddhas and create obstacles to rebirth in heaven;
how much more so regarding the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus does the Bodhisattva contemplate these matters.
Worldly beings, craving the flavor of few desires, undergo immeasurable suffering; yet they never seek unsurpassed bodhi or practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of those five sensual pleasures.

Rather, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they resolve their minds to cultivate and fulfill the great vows, severing the snares of suffering for all beings and causing them to attain liberation. O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

The Bodhisattva further reflects: "I shall dedicate my roots of goodness in this way, so that all sentient beings may attain ultimate happiness, beneficial happiness, happiness that is not [merely] received, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of non-reliance, the happiness of immovability, immeasurable happiness, happiness that is neither abandoned nor regressed, the happiness of non-extinction, and the happiness of omniscience. He further reflects: "I shall..."

They act as guides for all sentient beings; they serve as generals; they hold aloft the great torch of wisdom, showing the path of peace and security so that beings may leave behind peril and hardship;
and through skillful means, they cause them to know the true meaning.

Furthermore, within the ocean of birth and death, they act as expert shipmasters of omniscience, ferrying all sentient beings across to the other shore. O Son of the Buddha, these are the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Sā thus dedicates all roots of goodness as follows: namely, to rescue and protect all sentient beings according to their needs so that they may emerge from birth and death;
to serve and make offerings to all Buddhas; to attain the unobstructed wisdom of omniscience;
to abandon all Māras and distance oneself from evil associates; to draw near to all Bodhisattvas and virtuous friends; and to extinguish all transgressions and offenses.
Regarding the purification of karma: it consists of the bodhisattva’s vast practices, vows, and immeasurable roots of goodness.
The third section, "Relieving Suffering on Behalf of Others," extends through the subsequent passage on immeasurable roots of goodness; it comprises forty-one lines of scripture and more.
Within this, there is first the general title "Relieving Suffering on Behalf of Others. The dedication text contains many sections, which are self-evident from the main text itself.
Thereafter, he summarizes the benefits of dedication by dedicating all roots of goodness in this manner:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has correctly dedicated all roots of goodness, he reflects thus:
'It is not because there are many sentient beings in the four continents that many suns appear; rather, a single sun rises and is able to illuminate them all universally.'"
All sentient beings, moreover, do not know day and night, nor do they travel, observe, or perform various deeds by means of their own bodily radiance;
rather, all these matters are accomplished through the emergence of the Sun Deva-son (Sūryadevaputra).
Yet that solar orb is but one and not two. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise practices roots of goodness and dedicates them.
At that time, one should form this thought: "Those sentient beings are unable to save themselves; how could they possibly save others?
I alone am resolute and without peer. I shall cultivate and accumulate roots of goodness and dedicate them in this way:

namely, for the sake of extensively delivering all sentient beings, for the sake of universally illuminating all sentient beings, for the sake of guiding all sentient beings, and for the sake of opening [the path] for them."
Because he awakens all sentient beings; because he looks back upon and nurtures all sentient beings; because he gathers and sustains all sentient beings;
because he brings all sentient beings to fulfillment; because he causes all sentient beings to rejoice; because he causes all sentient beings to find delight;
and because he causes all sentient beings to sever their doubts.
The fourth is the supreme dedication. This passage consists of ten lines of scripture: first, four lines clarify it through analogies; next, two lines apply the analogy to the Dharma;
and finally, four lines show how these combine to produce benefit.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects: "I should illuminate all beings universally like the sun, seeking no reward for my kindness.
Even when sentient beings commit evil, I am able to accept it all; I shall never abandon my vow because of this.
I will not abandon all sentient beings because of the evil of a single sentient being. Rather, I shall diligently cultivate roots of goodness and dedicate them universally."
May all sentient beings attain peace and happiness. Although one's roots of goodness may be few, one universally gathers in all sentient beings and performs a vast dedication with a joyful mind.
If there are roots of goodness that one does not wish to benefit all sentient beings, they are not called "dedication.
When each root of goodness universally takes all sentient beings as its object, it is then called "dedication. One establishes sentient beings therein...
Dedication through the nature of phenomena that is free from attachment; dedication by seeing that the self-nature of sentient beings is unmoving and unchanging;
dedication without dependence or grasping toward the act of dedication itself; dedication without grasping at the marks of roots of goodness;

dedication without discriminating the essential nature of karmic retribution; dedication without clinging to the marks of the five aggregates; dedication without destroying the marks of the five aggregates; not...

Dedicating by taking up karma; dedicating without seeking retribution; dedicating without being stained by causes and conditions; dedicating without discriminating that which arises from causes and conditions;
dedicating without attachment to names; dedicating without attachment to locations; dedicating without attachment to false dharmas;
dedicating without attachment to the marks of sentient beings, the marks of worlds, or the marks of mind and mental objects; and not giving rise to such thoughts.
Dedicating with inverted perceptions, inverted views, and inverted dedications; dedicating without clinging to the path of language; dedicating by contemplating the true nature of all phenomena;
dedicating by contemplating the mark of equality of all sentient beings; dedicating by sealing all roots of goodness with the seal of the *dharmadhātu*;
dedicating by contemplating that all phenomena are free from desire; and dedicating by understanding that all phenomena are without seed.
Planting roots of goodness is also like this. Contemplating that all phenomena are non-dual, without arising, and without ceasing—dedication is also like this.
By dedicating roots of goodness in such a manner, one practices the pure dharmas of counteraction; all roots of goodness thus accord with supramundane dharmas.
Without forming dualistic marks, one does not treat them as identical to karma, yet cultivates all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
It is not that one turns away from karma to attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor is omniscience identical to karma. Nevertheless, one does not attain omniscience apart from karma.
Because karma is pure like a reflection or a shadow, its maturation (*vipāka*) is also pure like a reflection or a shadow.
Because the maturation is pure like a reflection or a shadow, the wisdom of omniscience is also pure like a reflection or a shadow. It is free from "I" and "mine."
All agitated thoughts and conceptual discriminations are thus understood, and one dedicates [the merit] through skillful means by means of all roots of goodness.
This is the second major section, clarifying dedication free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāma*). It generally comprises eighteen lines of scripture.

First, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he thinks" consists of five and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies how the wisdom of deluded faculties guides the aforementioned great compassion.

It forms a non-conditioned [attainment]. Next, there are ten lines and a half of sutra text under the section "placing sentient beings," which correctly clarifies the characteristics of the mixed [practices].
First, it brings together the previous dedication to sentient beings to cause them to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Next, from the passage beginning with "by means of such roots of goodness" for five lines and a half, it brings together the previous dedication toward bodhi to enter the limit of reality.
When a bodhisattva dedicates [merit] in this manner, they liberate sentient beings without ever ceasing. They do not dwell upon the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Although they know that all phenomena are without karma and without retribution, they are skillfully able to produce all karmic results without contradiction or contention.
Thus, through skillfully cultivating dedication by means of such expedient means, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates in this way,
they are free from all faults and are praised by all Buddhas.
The second part summarizes the benefits. Because one conforms to and is free from duality, there is the benefit of being unimpeded and free from faults.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s first dedication, "Rescuing and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings."
The section on the names of the three fetters concludes above in the long prose.
At that time, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva surveyed all the assemblies in the ten directions, extending throughout the entire dharma-realm.
He entered into the profound meanings of the words and phrases, cultivated supreme practices with immeasurable minds, and universally covered all sentient beings with great compassion. Not...
He severs the lineage of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; he enters the treasury of the dharma of the merits of all Buddhas; he gives birth to the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
he is skillfully able to discern the minds of all sentient beings and knows when their planted roots of goodness have matured.
Abiding in the Dharma-body, he manifests a pure form-body. Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he then spoke these verses:
Having practiced the Way for inconceivable eons, with firm diligence and an unimpeded mind,
he sought to benefit all classes of living beings. Constantly seeking the meritorious dharmas of all Buddhas,
this peerless Tamer of the World cultivated his intent until it was exceedingly clear and pure.
They resolve their minds to universally rescue all sentient beings;
They are able to skillfully enter the treasury of dedication, Endowed with the power of courageous diligence, Possessing wisdom and penetration, their minds are pure.
Universally rescuing all living creatures, Their hearts are patient and unshakable.
The mind dwells well-established and peerless; the intellect is ever pure and filled with great joy.
Thus, one diligently practices for the sake of beings, just as the great earth universally receives all, seeking no happiness for itself, but desiring only to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
Thus arousing the mind of great compassion, one swiftly enters the stage of non-obstruction.
For the sake of rescuing all sentient beings throughout every world in the ten directions,
one should maintain a well-stabilized mind and practice such dedications of merit.
Practicing generosity with great joy, Upholding pure precepts without transgression,
With courageous diligence and an unshakable mind, They dedicate [merit] toward the Tathāgata’s omniscience;
Their minds are vast and boundless, Abiding steadfastly in the power of patience, unmoved.
Profound meditative concentration constantly illuminates and understands; Subtle wisdom is wondrous and inconceivable.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, One fully cultivates and purifies these practices.
All such merits are dedicated For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Great Being diligently cultivates all virtuous deeds;
Immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, he dedicates them all for the benefit of sentient beings, Causing them to abide in inconceivable, unsurpassed wisdom.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he remains in the hells throughout inconceivable eons.
Thus, never having a mind of weariness or retreat, with courageous resolve they always dedicate [their merit];
seeking neither form, sound, fragrance, nor taste, nor even desiring various exquisite tactile sensations,
they constantly seek the unsurpassed, most supreme wisdom solely for the sake of rescuing and liberating all living beings.
With wisdom as pure as space, they cultivate the boundless practices of a Great Being,
just as the Buddha practiced all dharmas. Those who thus constantly train and study travel through the various worlds as Great Beings,
able to bring peace and security to all living beings.
Causing all beings everywhere to rejoice, Practicing the bodhisattva path without weariness,
Eliminating all poisons of the mind, Contemplating and cultivating supreme wisdom,
Seeking no personal peace or happiness, But wishing only that sentient beings may be freed from suffering.
This person attains ultimate fulfillment through dedication; their mind is ever pure and free from all poisons.
Entrusted by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, they dwell in the city of the unsurpassed Great Dharma.
They are never stained by any form, and the same applies to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Their minds have forever transcended the three realms of existence; all their merits they dedicate entirely.
Regarding all sentient beings known and seen by the Buddha, they embrace them all without exception, vowing to bring them all to liberation, and practice with great joy for their sake.
Their minds dwell constantly in every thought-moment; Their wisdom is vast and beyond compare.
Free from delusion, with right mindfulness ever tranquil, All their karmas are completely purified.
Those bodhisattvas dwelling in the world Are unattached to all internal and external phenomena.
Just as the wind moves unimpeded through space, so too is the Bodhisattva’s application of mind;
all his physical actions are pure, and all his speech is free from fault.
His mind constantly turns toward the Tathāgata, and he is able to bring all Buddhas to complete joy.
To all the infinite lands throughout the ten directions, He travels to every place where Buddhas reside;
Therein he beholds the Honored One of Great Compassion, Whom he reveres and serves with total devotion.
His mind is ever pure and free from all faults, Entering all worlds without fear.
Having already established themselves in the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata, they further act as great reservoirs for the Dharma within the three realms;
with diligent effort, they observe all phenomena, contemplating them according to their existence and non-existence,
thus proceeding toward the principle of ultimate reality and attaining entry into the profound state free from contention.
By this, one cultivates and perfects the firm path, which no sentient being can destroy;
One skillfully and thoroughly realizes the nature of all phenomena, remaining universally unattached throughout the three periods of time.
Thus dedicating [merit] to reach the other shore, may all living beings be freed from every defilement.
Forever free from all bases of reliance, they have entered the ultimate state of non-reliance;
regarding the paths of speech of all sentient beings, according to their various types and distinctions,
the Bodhisattvas are able to explain them all individually, yet their minds are without attachment and without obstruction.
When a bodhisattva practices dedication in this way, the skillful means of their merit are ineffable;
they cause all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions to offer praise.

Second, at that time, the following section of verses in six lines is divided into two parts. First, the introduction of the ritual and its purpose: regarding the phrase "entering the profound words and meanings."

This is the explanation of the basis (*āśraya*). The section beginning with "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) also explains the basis, because it is spoken in reliance upon this. Furthermore, it explains the purpose (*prayojana*), as it is spoken for that sake.
Next, the section beginning with "inconceivable eons" (*acintyāḥ kalpāḥ*) formally presents the verses; there are twenty-eight verses, divided into two parts:
the first eight and a half verses praise the roots of goodness to be dedicated, and the latter nineteen and a half verses praise the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-caryā*).

The first seven and a half verses praise the aspect of following [phenomena]. The subsequent twelve verses, beginning with "Unprecedented," praise the practice of being free from aspects (*lakṣaṇa-vinirmukta*).
Within this, the first five verses correctly clarify being free from aspects; the latter seven verses, beginning with "In the ten directions," praise the benefits accomplished by the former.
The Dedication for the First Rescue of Sentient Beings is completed.
