This is the heading that introduces the inquiry. Regarding the term "indestructible" (*abhedyā*): it refers to attaining the name "indestructible" through firm and deep faith in the ten kinds of sublime objects, such as the earth-treasures and so forth.
However, these ten signify inexhaustibility, because faith penetrates both phenomena and principle. The *Mūla-karma-saṃgraha* states:
"To contemplate all dharmas as having only function and only names, which do not abide for even a single thought-moment—therefore they are called 'indestructible. This is it.
Knowing that the dedication of roots of goodness permeates all things in the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena, one is truly indestructible.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains indestructible faith toward all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.

Because they are able to serve all Buddhas; and because, regarding all bodhisattvas—even those who have first conceived a single thought seeking omniscience—they attain indestructible faith and vow to cultivate all bodhisattva roots of goodness without weariness.
One attains indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas because of the arousal of profound aspiration and joy.
One attains indestructible faith in all Buddha-teachings because of their protection, maintenance, and upholding.

One attains indestructible faith in all sentient beings because of viewing them with eyes of universal compassion and dedicating roots of goodness for the sake of universal benefit. One attains indestructible faith in all pure and white dharmas because of their universal...
Because they have accumulated boundless roots of goodness, they attain indestructible faith in the path of dedication of all bodhisattvas.
Because they fulfill their superior aspirations and inclinations, they attain indestructible faith in all bodhisattva Dharma-teachers.
Because they conceive the thought of the Buddha toward all bodhisattvas, they attain indestructible faith in the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas. They possess profound faith.
Because the Buddhas are inconceivable, [the bodhisattva] attains indestructible faith in the skillful means and practices of all bodhisattvas,
as they encompass various immeasurable and innumerable spheres of activity. Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus abides in indestructible faith,
regarding all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the teachings of the Buddhas...
If all sentient beings, within such various realms as these, plant roots of goodness that are immeasurable and boundless, causing the bodhicitta to increase further and further;
if they observe with vast, impartial compassion and accord with the practices performed by all Buddhas;
and if they gather all pure roots of goodness and enter the accumulation of merit for the sake of the true meaning—[this is the path].
He practices great giving and cultivates all merits, viewing the three periods of time with equanimity.
Within the second section, the extensive prose explanation, there are three major parts: first, presenting the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, clarifying the practice of dedication;
and third, clarifying the purpose for which the dedication is made. Now, for the first part: regarding the phrase "in the past, future, and present," there are ten [subsections].
The *Pañcaskandhaka-sūtra* first presents the roots of goodness to be dedicated. Within this, the initial ten lines of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* clarify the arousal of indestructible faith.
Following that, from "O Son of the Buddha, thus abiding... and below, the remaining lines of the sūtra clarify the planting of roots of goodness within the seeds of faith;
these consist of the first planting of roots of goodness, followed by the ten phrases beginning with "causing the bodhicitta... which clarify the cultivation of the bodhisattva path.
By means of such roots of goodness and merit, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dedicates them toward the vow for all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
They constantly behold all Buddhas, draw near to spiritual friends, and dwell together with all bodhisattvas.

They never for a moment abandon the mind that recollects all-knowledge, upholding the Buddha’s teachings and diligently guarding them. They transform and bring to maturity all sentient beings. Their mind...
They constantly dedicate [their merit] toward the supramundane path; they make offerings to and attend upon all Dharma masters;
they understand all phenomena and maintain them in memory without forgetting; they practice great vows until they are entirely fulfilled.

In this way, the Bodhisattva accumulates roots of goodness, accomplishes roots of goodness, increases roots of goodness, contemplates roots of goodness, fixes the mind upon roots of goodness, discerns roots of goodness, and cherishes them.

Delighting in the roots of goodness, cultivating the roots of goodness, and dwelling securely in the roots of goodness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having thus accumulated all these roots of goodness,
practices the bodhisattva conduct through the resultant fruits obtained from those roots of goodness.
In every thought-moment, they behold immeasurable Buddhas and serve and make offerings to them as is appropriate, with incalculable jewels and incalculable...
Flowers; incalculable garlands; incalculable robes; incalculable parasols; incalculable banners; incalculable pennants;
incalculable ornaments; incalculable attendants; incalculable floor decorations;
incalculable ointments; incalculable powdered incense; incalculable blended perfumes; incalculable burning incense; incalculable...
With profound faith, incalculable joy, incalculable pure minds, incalculable reverence, incalculable praise,
incalculable prostrations, incalculable jewel thrones, incalculable flower thrones, incalculable incense thrones,
incalculable garland thrones, incalculable sandalwood thrones, and incalculable cloth thrones.
Countless diamond seats; countless mani-jewel seats; countless precious silk seats; countless precious-colored seats;
countless precious walking paths; countless flower walking paths; countless incense walking paths;
countless garland walking paths; countless robe walking paths; countless...
Walkways interspersed with various jewels; walkways with canopies of all kinds of asaṃkhyeya precious silks;
walkways with all kinds of asaṃkhyeya precious tala trees; walkways with all kinds of asaṃkhyeya precious railings;
walkways covered by all kinds of asaṃkhyeya precious nets of bells; [walkways] with all kinds of asaṃkhyeya jewels...
Palaces: incalculable palaces of all kinds of flowers; incalculable palaces of all kinds of fragrances;
incalculable palaces of all kinds of garlands; incalculable palaces of all kinds of sandalwood;
incalculable palaces of all kinds of solid, wondrous fragrance-treasuries; incalculable palaces of all kinds of vajra. Incalculable...
All the *cintāmaṇi* palaces were exquisite and surpassed those of all the devas. There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) trees of various jewels,
incalculable trees of diverse fragrances, incalculable trees of precious garments, incalculable trees of musical instruments,
incalculable trees of precious ornaments, incalculable trees of wondrous sounds, and incalculable [trees of] the...
There were trees of precious gems; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) trees of precious silk brocades; incalculable trees of precious earrings;

and incalculable trees adorned with all manner of flowers, perfumes, banners, streamers, garlands, and parasols. Such trees as these spread their branches in lush profusion, casting dappled shade and adorning the palaces.
Furthermore, those palaces were adorned with incalculable railings and balustrades, and incalculable windows.
Adorned with windows; adorned with incalculable gateways; adorned with incalculable multi-storied pavilions;
adorned with incalculable crescent moons; adorned with incalculable canopies; covered above by incalculable golden nets; perfumed on all sides by incalculable fragrances;
and with incalculable garments spread upon the ground. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
With such various articles of offering as these, the Bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable, innumerable, unspeakable, and unspeakably many kalpas,
with a pure mind, honors, respects, and makes offerings to all Buddhas, never regressing and without ceasing.
After each and every Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, he likewise honors all their relics in the same manner.
They made offerings for the sake of causing all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith; for the sake of gathering the roots of goodness of all sentient beings;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to be free from all suffering; for the sake of the vast understanding of all sentient beings;
and for the sake of adorning all sentient beings with great adornments and immeasurable adornments. Whatever they did...
Because they have attained the ultimate; because they know that the appearance of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter; because they fulfill the immeasurable power of the Tathāgatas;
because they adorn and make offerings to the stupas and shrines of the Buddhas;

and because they uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas—such offerings made to the present Buddhas and to all their relics after their parinirvāṇa are, among all forms of worship, [superior] for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* eons.
It could not be fully expounded even in an eon.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of such [virtues] as these" onwards, the initial six lines of the remaining sutra clarify the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
First, it clarifies the dedication of roots of goodness; next, from "Thus accumulating roots of goodness" onwards, it clarifies the subsequent [dedication].

The dedication of roots of goodness for supreme retribution consists of twenty-five lines of scripture. Within this, the first section extensively lists the articles of offering, using asaṃkhyeya jewels to detail six categories.
Next, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, by means of these [offerings]... and the following two lines of scripture, it clarifies the offerings made to the present Buddhas.
Following that, one by one, it clarifies the offerings made to the śarīras (relics). Next, from the passage "In order to cause... and the following five lines...
The *Caryā-sūtra* clarifies the intention of making offerings in eleven phrases. Following this, from "In this way" onwards, it concludes the scope of the offerings.
Thus, one accumulates immeasurable merit for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, never regressing.
Without rest, without weariness, and without attachment; free from all conceptual thoughts, without dependence, and having forever severed all bases of reliance;
far removed from the notions of "I" and "mine"; it seals all gateways of karma with the seal of the Dharma as it truly is.
Attaining the non-arising of dharmas, they abide where the Buddhas abide; contemplating the nature of non-arising, they seal all objective realms.

With the Buddhas’ protective mindfulness, they dedicate their resolve; dedicating in accordance with the nature of all dharmas; dedicating through the skillful means of accomplishing what is to be done by entering the unconditioned;
dedicating through the skillful means of relinquishing all conceptual attachments to phenomena; and abiding in the immeasurable.
Skillful dedication; dedication that forever transcends all states of existence; skillful dedication that practices all deeds without dwelling on signs;
dedication that universally gathers all roots of goodness; vast dedication that universally purifies all bodhisattva practices;
dedication that resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; dedication that dwells together with all roots of goodness.

Dedication. Dedication with a mind of supreme faith and resolve. Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, although they follow the cycle of birth and death, they do not change; they seek all-knowledge and never retreat.
Amidst all states of existence, their minds are free from agitation, and they are able to deliver all sentient beings without being defiled.

Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they do not lose their unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*). The causes and conditions for the stages of a bodhisattva’s practice are inexhaustible;
no worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) can cause them to fluctuate. They are fully endowed with the pure perfections (*pāramitā*) and are able to accomplish all powers of a Buddha (*sarvajña-bala*).
In this way, the bodhisattva leaves behind all darkness of delusion, accomplishes the bodhicitta, reveals the light, increases pure dharmas, and dedicates them toward the supreme path.
Endowed with all practices, they are well able to discern with a purified mind that all phenomena appear entirely in accordance with the mind.
They know that karma is like an illusion, karmic retribution is like a reflection, all conditioned formations are like transformations, and dependently arisen phenomena are likewise.
All are like echoes. All the practices of a bodhisattva are like shadows.
They give rise to the unattached, pure Dharma-eye, whereby they perceive the vast realm of non-action, realize the nature of quiescence, and understand that all phenomena are non-dual.

Attaining the true mark of dharmas, they fulfill the bodhisattva practices and remain entirely unattached to any signs. They are skillfully able to practice the various activities of "sameness-in-purpose" (sāmānyārtha).
He never abandons pure and wholesome dharmas; he is free from all attachments and dwells in non-attached conduct.
Thus, through skillful reflection, the bodhisattva remains without delusion, does not contradict any phenomena, and does not destroy the causes of karma.

Clearly perceiving reality, he is skillful in dedication, knows the intrinsic nature of dharmas, and through the power of skillful means, brings karmic retribution to fulfillment and reaches the other shore.

With wisdom, one observes all phenomena and attains the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). All karmic roots of goodness are performed without effort, acting with mastery according to the mind.
Second, such cultivation below reveals the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This section contains three parts; first is the dedication itself.

The mind; second, the characteristics of dedication; third, the accomplishment of the practice of dedication. Regarding the first, there are four lines of verse in the remainder of the sutra that clarify the mind of dedication.
Within this, "not being separated from great compassion" implies the intention of dedicating [merit] to sentient beings.
"Being without attachment" implies the intention of being free from signs (*nimitta*). Next, the five lines of verse beginning with "in accord with the nature of all phenomena" clarify...
The characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) also manifest the dedication toward awakening (*bodhi*). There are eleven phrases.

Next, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, by means of all roots of goodness," the practice of dedication is established. Within this, the first phrase restates what preceded.

Then, from the phrase "Although [he] follows birth and death," there are ten phrases that correctly manifest the establishment of the practice of following [the world]. Because it accords with the previously mentioned *dharmatā*, he follows [it].
"Birth and death do not change. Next, the Bodhisattva [speaks] these one and a half lines of scripture to conclude the preceding and introduce what follows.
Next, with a pure mind, he speaks the remaining six lines and more of scripture to clarify the accomplishment of practice free from marks (*animitta*).

Because the preceding matters do not obstruct principle, one encounters all objects and realizes them as they truly are. All eleven phrases clarify the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) free from marks. Next, the Bodhisattva...
Thus, through these skillful means, the remaining three lines of the verse and the two lines of the subsequent sutra are joined together without obstruction to accomplish dedication.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner:

desiring to deliver and liberate all sentient beings, to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted, to remain forever free from the deeds of Māra, and to perceive the boundless nature of omniscience with faith and joy.

They renounce and depart from worldly realms, severing all defilements. They also vow that sentient beings may attain pure wisdom, enter profound skillful means, transcend the laws of birth and death, and obtain the roots of goodness of the Buddhas.
May they forever sever all demonic activities and universally seal all karmas with the seal of equanimity.
May they resolve their minds to pursue the all-encompassing wisdom of all modes and accomplish all supramundane dharmas.
The Dharma.
This is the purpose for which the third dedication is performed: to exclusively liberate all sentient beings and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed;
this is the objective of this dedication. Within it, demonic activities encompass all evil deeds of Māras and all such matters.
[These] signs merely violate the seal of the Dharma and are all the works of Māra.
Son of the Buddha, this is the second indestructible dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Third, the explanation of the title and its connection [to the preceding].
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they behold all the countless Buddhas;
they accomplish immeasurable, pure, and wondrous dharmas; they attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; they harbor no doubts regarding any dharma;
they are empowered by the spiritual authority of all Buddhas; they subdue all Māras and forever leave behind their karmic activities; and they achieve [perfection].
Born into noble status, they fulfill the bodhicitta; they attain unimpeded wisdom without depending on the explanations of others, and are skillfully able to elucidate the meaning of all dharmas.
By the power of their mental conceptions, they are able to enter all buddha-fields, universally illuminating sentient beings and causing them all to become pure.
Through this power of indestructible dedication, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gathers all roots of goodness and dedicates them in this manner.
The second fruit is also like the fruits of the ten stages, such as flexibility (*mṛdu*). First, it cites the time of attainment;
next, "attaining the vision" and below correctly distinguish the characteristics of the fruit; finally, "the bodhisattva" and below summarize its affiliation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveyed the ten directions and, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva has already attained an indestructible mind And practices all manner of wholesome deeds;
Therefore, he is able to bring joy to the Buddhas— The wise one dedicates [merit] by means of this."
Making offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, practicing generosity and upholding the precepts to subdue the sense faculties,
they act for the benefit of all sentient beings, universally causing all to be pure.
With all manner of supreme and exquisite incense and flowers, and with infinite varieties of excellent garments, they offer them all.
With jeweled canopies and various ornaments, they made offerings to all the Tathāgatas.
Thus making offerings to all the Buddhas for immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable eons,
they remained ever respectful, reverent, and joyful, never for a single moment giving rise to weariness or distaste.
With single-minded devotion, they contemplate all Buddhas, the great luminous lamps of all worlds.
All Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions appear before them as if seen with their own eyes;
for inconceivable and immeasurable eons, they practice various forms of giving without ever feeling weary.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, they have practiced all manner of wholesome dharmas in this very way;
even after those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, they never tire of making offerings to their relics,
adorning them with every kind of exquisite ornament and establishing inconceivable numbers of stupas and temples.
Having fashioned peerless and most supreme forms, adorned with pure gold from the treasure-store,
towering and lofty like the king of mountains;
having made offerings with a pure mind and deep respect, they further gave rise to thoughts of joy and benefit.
Abiding in the world for inconceivable eons, you rescue and protect sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation.
Fully knowing that all sentient beings are but conceptual constructions, you remain free from discrimination toward any of them;
yet you are able to skillfully discern the faculties of all beings, universally bringing benefit to the multitudes.
The Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates all merits—vast, supreme, and beyond compare;
yet he realizes that their essential nature is entirely non-existent.
With such certainty, he dedicates them all, observing all phenomena with his most excellent wisdom; therein, not a single phenomenon arises.
Thus, through skillful means, one cultivates dedication; The resulting merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible.
By these skillful means, one purifies the mind, Becoming entirely equal to all Tathāgatas.
The power of these skillful means is inexhaustible; Therefore, the reward of merit is boundless and infinite.
Having generated the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
They reach all worlds throughout the ten directions, Unimpeded by anything whatsoever.
When all Tathāgatas appear in the world, It is for the purpose of guiding the minds of sentient beings.
Observing according to the nature of the mind, Ultimately seeking it, nothing can be found;
All phenomena without exception Are entirely entered into suchness, devoid of intrinsic nature.
By means of this pure eye, one dedicates [merit], Opening the prison of birth and death for that world.
Though they cause all realms of existence to be completely purified, they do not discriminate among those realms;
knowing the nature of existence to be non-existent, they cause joy and purify the mind.
Without relying on even a single Buddha-field, they treat all Buddha-fields in this same way.
Nor does one become stained by conditioned phenomena;
Knowing that the nature of those phenomena has no basis, One cultivates and accomplishes all-encompassing wisdom through this, Adorning oneself with this unsurpassed wisdom;
Thus, all Buddhas rejoice— This is the bodhisattva’s work of dedication.
The Bodhisattva focuses his mind on all Buddhas, With unsurpassed wisdom and skillful means;
Just as the Buddha relies on nothing at all, May I cultivate and perfect these merits,
Focusing my mind on the rescue and protection of all beings, Causing them to remain far removed from all evil karma.
Thus benefiting all living beings, they maintain mindfulness and contemplation without ever abandoning it;
abiding on the ground of wisdom, they protect the Dharma. They do not seek nirvana through other vehicles, but aspire only to attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
Thus do Bodhisattvas skillfully dedicate their merit.
They do not grasp at the speech of sentient beings, nor at any of the false phenomena of conditioned existence;
though they do not rely on the path of language, they likewise do not cling to the absence of language.
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have fully realized all dharmas without exception.
Though knowing all things are empty and quiescent, they do not give rise to mental conceptions regarding emptiness;
with a single adornment they adorn all, nor do they produce discrimination regarding phenomena.
Thus they awaken all sentient beings, for all things lack intrinsic nature and there is nothing to be observed.
The second verse consists of twenty-five stanzas divided into three parts. The first two stanzas praise the roots of goodness to be dedicated and the dedication of the first section.
The next eighteen stanzas praise the practices of offering that are accomplished. The final five stanzas praise the purpose for which the dedication is made.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dedication equal to that of all Buddhas?
This is the third dedication, "Equal to All Buddhas. The prose section also has two parts: first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the stage.

Regarding the explanation of the name: according to the subsequent text, it refers simply to being equal to the path practiced by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and also equal to their roots of goodness.
The text says: "Just as all roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past, I likewise do so. Therefore, the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on Original Karma) states:
"The roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are practiced at all times," which also reveals their continuity. Thus, the following passage says:
"Together with his wife and children, he never for a moment abandoned the bodhicitta. This name is established based on what is "equal" [to that], namely, equality.
The dedication of all Buddhas consists in deeply penetrating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Its essence is the practice of universal-gate virtues.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva follows and trains in the path of dedication of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
When training in such a path of dedication, they perceive all forms, and even tactile objects and mental phenomena.
Whether encountering the beautiful or the ugly, they give rise to neither attachment nor aversion; their minds attain mastery, free from all faults and vast in purity.
They are joyful and delighted, detached from all sorrow and affliction; their mental faculties are supple and their senses are cool and serene.
Next, within the section that sets forth the title and provides a detailed explanation, first the dedication is revealed, followed by the clarification of the benefits achieved.

Within the dedication, first is the dedication according to characteristics, followed by the dedication free from characteristics. Within the dedication according to characteristics, there are again two parts:

first, clarifying the dedication of roots of goodness toward their respective objects; second, the dedication that universally encompasses all virtues. This is the first [part]. Thus, the following two lines...

The first half of the sūtra clarifies the roots of goodness to be dedicated. That is to say, when training in the Buddha-way, one achieves four types of pure mind regarding the six sense objects, whether they are adverse or favorable.
First, regarding the adverse and favorable, one achieves equanimity (*upekṣā*) in practice and is not dragged away by sense objects; this is called "mastery of the mind.

Second, because one purifies all afflictions through the vastness of compassion and wisdom toward ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle. Third, because one is free from the fault of sorrow, there is joy (*prīti*).
One delights in relinquishment and is free from sorrow, suffering, and affliction, because of the pliancy of the four dhyāna-concentrations.

Since the mind is supple and does not falsely grasp at objects, the sense faculties are cool and serene. These four purities of mind are the practice of one who studies the Buddha; they constitute the roots of goodness to be dedicated.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained such peace and happiness, they further resolve their mind toward dedication to all Buddhas, forming this thought:
"May the roots of goodness I have now planted cause the bliss of all Buddhas to increase even more excellently—
that is to say, the inconceivable bliss in which the Buddhas abide, and the peerless samādhi of the Buddhas."
The joy that is immeasurable; the joy of great compassion; the joy of liberation of all Buddhas; the joy of boundless great supernormal powers;
the joy of supreme, most honored, and great sovereignty; the joy of vast, ultimate, and immeasurable power;
the joy of tranquility free from all conceptual cognition; the joy of abiding in non-obstruction and perpetual right concentration; practicing non-duality.

The joy of unchanging practice. O Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has dedicated all roots of goodness to the Buddhas, they further dedicate these roots of goodness to other Bodhisattvas.
That is to say: they vow that those whose aspirations are not yet fulfilled shall attain fulfillment;
those whose minds are not yet purified shall attain purification; and those whose perfections (*pāramitā*) are not yet complete shall attain completion. To bring peace...
Abiding in the vajra-bodhicitta, they attain non-retrogression regarding omniscience. Without relinquishing great diligence, they protect all roots of goodness that constitute the gateway to bodhi.
They enable sentient beings to abandon ego-clinging (*asmimāna*), give rise to the bodhicitta, and fulfill their aspirations.
They dwell securely in all that Bodhisattvas abide in and attain the sharp and penetrating wisdom of Bodhisattvas.
Roots. By cultivating these roots of goodness, one realizes *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has thus dedicated all roots of goodness to the Bodhisattva path, he further dedicates them to all sentient beings, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings, even for as brief a moment as a single snap of the fingers, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and pay respectful homage to the Noble Sangha."
All those roots of goodness are free from obstacles. He recollects the Buddha’s perfection, recollects the skillful means of the Dharma, and recollects the venerability of the Sangha.
Never being separated from seeing the Buddha, his mind attains purity and he acquires all Buddha-dharmas. He accumulates immeasurable virtues and purifies all supernormal powers.

Abandoning all phenomena and free from conceptual thought, one dwells in reliance upon the teachings. Just as one dedicates for the sake of sentient beings, so too does one dedicate for the sake of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, one vows that all sentient beings shall forever leave behind all evil realms, such as the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the realm of King Yama, and that they may increase their aspiration for unsurpassed bodhicitta with single-minded devotion.

Diligently seeking all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they shall never slander the true Dharma of the Buddhas; attaining the peace and bliss of the Buddhas, their bodies and minds purified, they shall realize all-knowledge.
In the second section, "Correct Dedication," the objects of dedication for the five vehicles are presented. The text is divided into five parts: first, the Buddhas; second, the Bodhisattvas;

third, sentient beings with virtue; fourth, those of the two vehicles; and fifth, sentient beings with evil. The first line of scripture concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one.
Next, the passage beginning with "I now" and consisting of five lines of scripture correctly reveals the specific vows. The object of these vows is...
"May the Buddha increase. Now, although the Buddha’s virtues are already perfected, the reason for this prayer for increase is to express reverence and gratitude, and to manifest sincere respect.
It is like offering wild celery to a superior; when incense and flowers are offered to the Buddha, it is not that He requires them.

Following the section on the "Buddha's Son" (the Bodhisattva), this is the dedication [of merit] to the Bodhisattvas. First, it connects the preceding with what follows, which is the formal manifestation of the ten vows. Of these, the first six are as follows:

First is self-benefit. Next, "Afterward, he is able to bring about the four benefits for others" [refers to] benefiting others. Next, the five lines of sutra beginning with "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha...

explain the dedication for sentient beings who possess goodness. Next, the one line of sutra beginning with "Just as for sentient beings... clarifies the dedication for those of the Two Vehicles. Next, the three lines of sutra beginning with "Furthermore, may all...
clarify [the dedication] for sentient beings who possess evil; that is to say, not abandoning even the icchantikas. Above.
This consists of five sections. The first is dedicated toward bodhi; the remainder are dedicated toward sentient beings.
The preceding section has concluded the explanation of dedicating roots of goodness by means of their respective objects.
O Son of the Buddha, all the roots of goodness possessed by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are initiated and correctly initiated through great vows.
Accumulating and correctly accumulating, increasing and correctly increasing, they cause [these roots of goodness] to become vast, complete, and fully perfected.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells within a household together with wife and children, he never for a moment abandons the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
With right mindfulness, he contemplates the realm of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), delivering himself and others to ultimate attainment through skillful means.
He then transforms his own retinue, causing them to enter the wisdom of a bodhisattva and bringing them to maturity and liberation. Although he dwells together with them, his mind remains unattached;

yet, out of his fundamental great compassion, he remains in the household life. Out of a heart of loving-kindness, he accords with his wife and children, remaining free from any hindrance to the pure path of a bodhisattva.
Thus, although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva remains in the household, he performs all [deeds]...
In his activities, he never for a moment abandons the mind of omniscience; that is to say, whether putting on clothes, eating food, taking medicine, washing, rinsing, or anointing the body;
whether turning around, looking about, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—in all actions of body, speech, and mind.
Whether sleeping or awake, in all such activities, they constantly dedicate their minds to the path of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
They maintain focused mindfulness and contemplation, never abandoning it for a moment.

Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, they abide in the immeasurable great vows of bodhi, gather countless vast roots of goodness, diligently cultivate all virtues, and universally rescue all beings.
Forever free from all pride and negligence, they will resolutely proceed toward the stage of omniscience;
they will never again give rise to the intention to follow other paths, but will constantly contemplate the bodhi of all Buddhas and forever abandon all defiled phenomena.
Practicing all that is to be learned by bodhisattvas, they encounter no obstacles on the path to omniscience.
Abiding on the stage of wisdom, they delight in recitation and study; through immeasurable wisdom, they accumulate all roots of goodness.

Their minds do not crave or delight in any worldly realm, nor are they stained by or attached to the practices they perform. With single-minded devotion, they uphold the Buddha’s teachings. Thus is the bodhisattva.
While dwelling in the household life, they universally gather roots of goodness and cause them to increase, dedicating them toward the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, at that time, even when giving a single morsel or a single grain of food to an animal, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"May these beings abandon the animal realm, may they obtain benefit and peace, and may they ultimately attain liberation forever."
Crossing over the ocean of suffering, may they forever extinguish painful sensations, forever eliminate the aggregates of suffering, and forever sever the perceptions of suffering.
Regarding the mass of suffering, the practice of suffering, the causes of suffering, the root of suffering, and all locations of suffering—may those sentient beings all attain liberation from them.
Thus the Bodhisattva focuses his mind with single-minded devotion upon all sentient beings; taking those roots of goodness as the foremost, he dedicates them for their sake.
All-knowledge. When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they universally gather in all sentient beings and cultivate all roots of goodness, dedicating them all [to others].

They desire to cause them to forever leave behind the wilderness of birth and death, to attain the unimpeded bliss of all Tathāgatas, to emerge from the ocean of afflictions, and to cultivate the path of the Buddha-dharma.
With a heart of universal loving-kindness and vast power of compassion, they cause all beings everywhere to obtain [these benefits].
Pure joy consists in guarding the roots of goodness, drawing near to the Buddha-dharma, departing from the realm of Māra and entering the realm of the Buddha,
severing worldly planting and cultivating the seed of the Tathāgata, and abiding in the dharma of the equality of the three periods of time.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates all such roots of goodness— those already accumulated, those yet to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated— in this manner.
The second section, the dedication that universally encompasses all virtues, consists of twenty-nine lines of scripture and is largely divided into two parts.

First, it clarifies the detailed presentation of individual practices; second, it reveals the accumulation and dedication thereof. Within the first part, the initial two lines of scripture generally manifest its characteristics;
therein, "all roots of goodness" refers to those that have been initiated and so forth. All of these are [accompanied] by great vows...
This refers to being able to initiate [the practice] and so forth.

As for "correctly initiating" and so on, it means that according to what is initiated, accumulated, and advanced, one necessarily moves toward two destinations and seeks nothing else; being free from all faults is termed "correct.

Next, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the various matters are presented individually. First, four and a half lines of scripture clarify being unstained by defilement while following along with it. Next, although dwelling in...

The first four lines of the passage clarify that movement is in accord with the Way. Next, the following two lines are intended to benefit others and collectively manifest the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Subsequently, the four and a half lines beginning with "forever detached" specifically manifest ten phrases.
Next, the passage beginning with "Thus, the Bodhisattva... concludes the sequential account of the practices. Next, the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, at that time...
and continuing downward, secondly clarifies the accumulation and dedication [of merit]. First, it clarifies subtle accumulation: even a single morsel or a single grain is a most minute merit;
giving it to sentient beings constitutes a most inferior field. Yet, by accumulating these minute virtues, one also uses the Great [Vehicle]...
The vow is made so that [the merit] may be brought forth and transformed into the practice of dedication; hence it is called "subtle accumulation.
Next, the ten phrases beginning with "All make this vow" correctly clarify the practice of dedication, which is collectively termed "leaving suffering and attaining happiness.

Next, from "When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment" onwards, it clarifies long-term accumulation, because one begins to accumulate from the very moment the mind of enlightenment is first produced.
Because they have been accumulated, it is called "for a long time. The phrase "desiring to cause" refers to a mental vow. There are thirteen phrases in the text;
next, from "all such as these" onwards, is the summary. A single morsel or grain is what has manifested and accumulated;
that which has been accumulated since first generating the bodhicitta is already gathered. Since future merit must also necessarily be aroused, all are dedicated. Above.
Having completed the practice of the primary and secondary characteristics,
he further reflects: "Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past practiced by showing reverence and making offerings to all Buddhas,
delivering all sentient beings so that they might forever attain liberation, and diligently cultivated all roots of goodness, dedicating them all [toward enlightenment],"

They turn away without attachment. That is to say: they do not rely on form; they do not cling to sensation; they have no inverted perception; they do not engage in mental formations; they do not grasp at consciousness.
They abandon the six sense bases, do not dwell in worldly dharmas, and transcend the mundane. They know that all phenomena are like space:
they come from nowhere, neither arising nor ceasing, lacking any true reality, and free from defilement and attachment. Thus they remain far removed.
All conceptual views are unmoving, unchanging, indestructible, and indeclinable; they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Being signless and free from signs, they are but a single sign.
Thus, one deeply penetrates the nature of all phenomena and constantly delights in practicing the roots of goodness of the universal gate (*samantamukha*).
One beholds the assemblies of all Buddhas, just as were the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas of the past.
Dedication. I likewise dedicate in this manner. I understand these dharmas, realize these dharmas, and rely upon these dharmas.

I resolve my mind to practice without violating the characteristics of dharmas. I know that what is practiced is like an illusion, like a shadow, like the moon in water, and like a reflection in a mirror—manifested through the conjunction of causes and conditions, even unto the ultimate state of the Tathāgata.
...the ground. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"Just as the Buddhas of the past, when practicing the bodhisattva path, dedicated their various roots of goodness in this manner, so too do those of the future and the present.
I, now, should likewise resolve my mind as those Buddhas did, dedicating my various roots of goodness. Chapter [Number].
1. Dedication; supreme dedication; most supreme dedication; superior dedication; unsurpassed dedication;
unequaled dedication; dedication equal to the unequaled; incomparable dedication; peerless dedication; venerable dedication; exquisite dedication.
Equal dedication. Upright dedication. Dedication of great merit. Vast dedication. Skillful dedication.
Pure dedication. Dedication free from evil. Dedication that does not follow after evil.
Having thus correctly dedicated all roots of goodness, the bodhisattva accomplishes pure actions of body, speech, and mind, and dwells in the bodhisattva-abode, free from all faults.
They eliminate [faults], cultivate wholesome karma, and remain free from evil of body and speech. Their minds are without blemish; they cultivate omniscience and abide in a vast mind.
Knowing that all phenomena are without activity, they dwell in supramundane dharmas, untainted by worldly dharmas.
They analytically understand immeasurable karmas and achieve skillful means for the dedication of merit, forever uprooting all roots of grasping.
The Main Text.

Second, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he forms this thought," which concerns the Buddha’s dedication that is free from marks (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*): this refers to dedicating toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Within the preceding two [sections], it is taught that there is a sequence of priority and posteriority, yet their practice resides within a single mind (*ekacitta*). This section consists of two parts: first, equating with the past; second, [equating with] the future.
From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, [the text] deals with the present and the future. Regarding the first of these, it first presents that which is being compared.

The first two lines of the sutra state "without attachment," which indicates that while following appearances, one is simultaneously free from them. Next, it specifically reveals this freedom, saying:

"That is to say, not relying on form, etc.," which reveals the departure from delusion and the realization of the True. Next, "knowing all dharmas... and so forth explains the aforementioned non-attachment. Next...

Thus, entering deeply, he concludes the section on non-obstruction. This means that because he has already accorded with the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and now cultivates according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one encompasses all;
this is called the "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*) excellence. He sees all Buddhas. Having briefly explained the benefits achieved, next, from "Just as in the past...

onwards, he restates the preceding [section] to generally manifest the capacity for equality. Next, regarding the two and a half lines of sutra beginning with "Explaining these dharmas...", he provides a specific [exegesis].

This reveals the characteristics of equality. Next, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, he again thinks... down to "...the present and future," the first two lines of the sutra cite the precedent.
Next, from "I too should now... onwards, the text generally reveals the capacity for equality.

Next, the nineteen phrases specifically clarify the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The preceding section concludes the revelation of dedication; the following section clarifies the accomplishment of benefits.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the third dedication of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which is equal to that of all Buddhas.
Regarding the third [section], which explains the basis and concludes the name:
when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this dedication, they enter deeply into all the karmic paths of those who come, tending toward the state of a Tathāgata.
Possessing supreme and wondrous merit, they enter the realm of profound and pure wisdom without ever departing from the activities of all bodhisattvas.

Skilled in discerning subtle and skillful means (*upāya*), they enter the profound *dharmadhātu*. Thoroughly knowing the sequential stages of a bodhisattva’s practice, they enter the lineage of the Buddhas.
By means of skillful means, they analytically understand all phenomena (*dharma*) that are immeasurable and boundless.
Although they manifest their bodies within the world, their minds remain unattached to worldly phenomena.
This second stage of fruition distinguishes ten kinds of supreme virtues.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the method of dedication practiced by the Buddhas of the past,
and likewise study the conduct of all the Teachers of the future and present worlds;
they attain peace and happiness within all realms and are praised by all the Buddha-Tathāgatas.
With vast, radiant, and pure eyes, may all be dedicated toward the various pleasures of the body-faculty of the Greatly Wise Bodhisattva; likewise for the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—
may such immeasurable and supreme delights be entirely dedicated to all the Most Victorious Ones.
All the various wholesome dharmas of all worlds, And those accomplished by all the Tathāgatas—
I encompass them all without exception, And through rejoicing in them, I benefit sentient beings.
With immeasurable kinds of worldly rejoicing, I dedicate this for the sake of sentient beings.
May all the happiness possessed by the lions among men Cause all living beings to be fully perfected.
Whatever various joys are known and seen By all the Tathāgatas in every land,
May all sentient beings obtain them entirely, And become great, brilliant lamps illuminating the world.
Whatever supreme and wondrous bliss the Bodhisattva attains, he dedicates it entirely to all living beings;
though he dedicates for the sake of all beings, he remains unattached to that dedication.
As the Bodhisattva practices this dedication, he gives rise to a mind of immeasurable great compassion.
Just as the Buddha cultivated the virtue of dedication, may my own practice be fully perfected;
just as all the Victors have accomplished it, may there be the subtle bliss of the vehicle of omniscience,
as well as the immeasurable joy of the bodhisattva practices performed by me while in the world.
Manifesting entry into all realms for the sake of peaceful happiness, And constantly guarding the sense faculties for the sake of tranquility—
All of this is dedicated to all living beings, Universally causing them to cultivate and perfect supreme wisdom.
It is not that body, speech, and mind are themselves karma, Nor is there anything else apart from these.
By means of skillful expedients, they extinguish the darkness of ignorance;
thus cultivating and perfecting supreme wisdom, these Bodhisattvas perform all manner of practices.
Accumulating immeasurable and sublime merits, they accord with the Tathāgata and are born into the Buddha-family; remaining tranquil and undisturbed, they correctly dedicate their merit.
All sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions—
may I embrace them all and dedicate my roots of goodness to them, wishing that they may be fully endowed with peace and happiness;
I do not seek benefit for myself, desiring only that all beings may be secure and blissful.
Never for a moment giving rise to a mind of conceptual proliferation, But contemplating only that all phenomena are empty and selfless;
To all the infinite and most victorious Ones of the ten directions, And to every true son of the Buddha whom I behold—
I dedicate all my roots of goodness to them, Vowing that they may swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
May I gather all sentient beings of every world with an impartial mind, leaving none behind;
by means of all the virtuous deeds I have performed, may those beings swiftly attain Buddhahood.
These are the immeasurable and boundless great vows proclaimed by the Unsurpassed Guide.
May all the sons of the Buddhas be pure, And may their every heart’s desire be completely fulfilled.
Universally observing all worlds in the ten directions, I dedicate all merit to them, Vowing that they shall all possess sublime adornments; Thus do Bodhisattvas train in dedication.
The mind does not weigh out dualistic phenomena, but always realizes that all dharmas are non-dual.
Whether phenomena are dual or non-dual, there is ultimately no attachment therein.
All the various worlds throughout the ten directions are entirely the conceptual discriminations of sentient beings.
Regarding perception and non-perception, there is nothing to be apprehended; thus they thoroughly understand all perceptions.
When those bodhisattvas have purified their bodies, their minds are pure and free from blemish;
when their verbal karma is purified and free from faults, you should know that their minds are pure and without attachment.
With single-minded right mindfulness, I call to mind the Buddhas of the past, And likewise remember all the Teachers of the future,
as well as the Honored Ones among gods and humans in the present; I learn thoroughly from the Dharma they have taught,
for all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess wisdom that is clear, penetrating, and unimpeded in mind.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he dedicates his accumulated manifold deeds toward Bodhi.
He is the one of foremost wisdom, vast wisdom, non-false wisdom, non-erroneous wisdom,
impartial and true wisdom, pure wisdom— the One of Supreme Wisdom speaks thus.
The second verse section consists of twenty-four verses, divided into three parts: the first twenty-one verses praise the practices of the preceding stages;
the next two verses describe the fruits of those stages; and the final one provides a concluding eulogy.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dedication that reaches all places?
This fourth dedication, "Reaching All Places," also has two parts in its prose explanation: first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the stage.

Now, for the first, the name is cited and the inquiry is raised. As for the term "reaching all places": "reaching" refers to that which is able to reach, namely the roots of goodness and their offerings.
"Possessing all places" refers to the objects of offering reached by these roots of goodness.

This means that through great vows, one causes these roots of goodness and their offerings to pervade all times and places, making offerings to the fields of merit according to what is appropriate for each. As the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states:
"By the power of great vows, one enters all Buddha-fields to make offerings to all Buddhas. Thus, it is said they "reach all places."
The commentary has many meanings.
O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates all roots of goodness, he forms this thought:
"May the power of the merit of these roots of goodness reach every place, just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) reaches everywhere."
Reaching all things; reaching all worlds; reaching all sentient beings; reaching all lands; reaching all phenomena;
reaching all of space; reaching all of the three periods of time; reaching all that is conditioned and unconditioned.
Reaching all languages and sounds, may this root of goodness likewise reach everywhere to the presence of all Tathāgatas, making offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time:
may the vows of the past Buddhas be entirely fulfilled; may the future Buddhas be fully adorned;
and may it pervade the present Buddhas, their lands, their sites of enlightenment, and their assemblies.
Filling all of space and the Dharma-realm, may they, through the great power of faith and understanding, through vast and unobstructed wisdom,
and through the dedication of all roots of goodness, perform offerings with all manner of celestial articles of worship,
filling immeasurable and boundless worlds.

The second section, the detailed explanation based on the inquiry, has three parts: first, dedication toward the enlightenment of sentient beings; second, dedication toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
and third, the concluding praise of the benefits achieved. Within the first part, dedication toward sentient beings, there are first briefly nine lines of scripture that clarify this point.

There is the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). Regarding the principle: it refers to the power of aspiration and the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Because these two support one another, they are able to reach everywhere. Next, "just as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)" and following provides the analogy;

"the limit of reality" means that it is the ultimate boundary of the true nature of all phenomena. Next, "aspiration" and following applies the principle; first it is stated generally, and then "in the past" and following explains it specifically. First...

This refers to the entirety of the three periods of time and all places reached. Next, one should vow with faith and understanding, following the two lines below, as the remainder of the sutra clarifies the ability to reach and make offerings.
O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, pervade all of space..."
The empty dharma-realm arises from various karmas.

It comprises unspeakably many world-systems in the ten directions, unspeakable Buddha-lands, Buddha-spheres, and various worlds—immeasurable worlds, boundless worlds, inverted worlds, tilted worlds, upright worlds, and overturned worlds; all such worlds as these.
Abiding within the realms for the duration of their lifespan, they manifest various supernatural powers and transformations.
Therein, bodhisattvas through the power of their resolute conviction appear as Tathāgatas arising in the world for the sake of all sentient beings who are capable of being transformed.
By means of the wisdom that pervades all places, they universally reveal the immeasurable qualities of the Tathāgata.
Through sovereign spiritual power, the Dharma-body pervades everywhere without distinction, entering all dharma-realms with universal equality.
The Tathāgata-treasury body is neither born nor extinguished; through skillful means, it manifests universally throughout the world.
Because it realizes the true nature of phenomena and transcends all things, and because it has attained non-regressive, unimpeded power, it gives rise to the Tathāgata’s unobstructed vision.
Because they are within the lineage of vast majesty and power, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
with all the roots of goodness they have planted, makes a vow to offer to such Tathāgatas various exquisite flowers,
various exquisite fragrances, garlands, canopies, banners, pennants, robes, lamps, and all other kinds of ornaments as offerings. If...
The same applies to the images of the Buddha or the stupas and shrines of the Buddha. One dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner:

that is to say, with undisturbed dedication, single-minded dedication, dedicated according to one’s own intention, respectful dedication, immovable dedication, non-abiding dedication, non-reliant dedication, dedication free from the mind of a sentient being, and dedication free from a restless or competitive mind.
Dedication. Dedication with a tranquil mind.

Second, the section "The Two Sons of the Buddha" below extensively clarifies universal pervasion. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying universal pervasion by reference to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
second, clarifying universal pervasion by reference to the eternally abiding Buddhas. Regarding the former, it speaks of "unspeakable worlds."
This section generally clarifies the objects of offering. Next, from the passage "In all such worlds" onwards, it specifically clarifies the offerings.

First, the offering to those currently residing and living refers to the Buddhas of the present age. Among them, there are Buddhas of true recompense (*vipāka-buddha*) and Buddhas of provisional response (*upāya-pratibimba-buddha*).

Regarding the activities of the provisional response Buddhas who manifest their bodies to preach the Dharma, there are six lines and a half of scripture. Next, "O Son of the Buddha, by means of what they have planted... [and so forth].

The final two lines of the sutra clarify the practice of making offerings. Next, "if there are images of the Buddha," and so forth, clarifies making offerings to the Buddha as maintained in representations.
Next, "by dedicating these roots of goodness in this manner" generally reveals the mind of dedication;

that is to say, when previously dedicating roots of goodness to accomplish offerings and making offerings to the various fields of merit, one employs the mind in such a way. There are ten phrases in the text to manifest these ten [aspects].
Because of this mind, one is able to accord with principle through phenomena. Having finished explaining the offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions above, one further reflects:

throughout all kalpas—past, future, and present—within the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained all-knowledge and realized the path of Bodhi, each having distinct and various names according to their respective [lineages]. In these various...
At the time of their planting [of roots], they manifestly attain perfect enlightenment; all of them abide for a lifespan that extends to the end of the future.
Each one adorns their body with the adornments of the Dharma-realm. Their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
In all lands, they arise according to the occasion to perform the work of Buddhas. All such Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, I universally [venerate] through my roots of goodness.

Dedication: May these innumerable incense canopies, innumerable incense banners, innumerable incense flags, innumerable incense curtains, innumerable incense nets, innumerable incense images, innumerable incense lights, innumerable incense flames, and innumerable incense clouds [be dedicated].
Countless fragrant seats; countless fragrant walking paths; countless fragrant dwellings; countless fragrant worlds;
countless fragrant mountains; countless fragrant oceans; countless fragrant rivers; countless fragrant trees; countless fragrant garments;
countless fragrant lotuses; countless fragrant palaces; and immeasurable flower canopies—and so on, as extensively described.
Immeasurable flower palaces; boundless garland canopies, and so forth, up to boundless garland palaces;
incomparable ointment canopies, and so forth, up to incomparable ointment palaces; incalculable powdered incense canopies, and so forth, up to incalculable powdered incense palaces;
and inexpressible clothing canopies, and so forth, up to [inexpressible clothing palaces].
One may speak of palaces of raiment; of inconceivable canopies of jewels, and so forth, up to inconceivable palaces of jewels;
of immeasurable canopies of lamp-light, and so forth, up to immeasurable palaces of lamp-light;
of unspeakable canopies of ornaments, and so forth, up to unspeakable palaces of ornaments. One cannot...
There were unspeakably many mani-jewel canopies, unspeakably many unspeakable numbers of mani-jewel banners,
as well as mani-jewel streamers, mani-jewel curtains, mani-jewel nets, mani-jewel images, and mani-jewel lights.
Maṇi-jewel flames; maṇi-jewel clouds; maṇi-jewel thrones; maṇi-jewel walking paths; maṇi-jewel abodes;
maṇi-jewel buddha-fields; maṇi-jewel mountains; maṇi-jewel oceans; maṇi-jewel rivers.
There were mani-jewel trees, mani-jewel garments, mani-jewel lotuses, and mani-jewel palaces, all beyond description, beyond description.
Within each and every one of these realms, there were likewise countless railings.
With countless palaces, countless towers, countless gates and portals, countless crescent-shaped arches, countless defensive parapets,
countless windows, countless pure jewels, and countless ornaments— using such various articles of offering as these,
they reverently made offerings to the aforementioned Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The second section clarifies universal presence by way of the eternally abiding Buddha.

This means that his lifespan throughout the three periods of time extends to the very limits of the future, and he is likewise eternal because the three bodies and ten bodies are fused in unimpeded harmony. This differs from the preceding passage concerning stūpas and temples.
Within this section, there are three parts: first, dedicating roots of goodness as an offering to the Buddha; second, the vow to cause all [beings] below... [text continues].

Dedicate the roots of goodness from making offerings to the Buddhas to all sentient beings. Third, as in the following section, there is a general vow to universally encompass and dedicate the roots of goodness.
First, the four lines beginning with "As far as the Dharma-realm" [from] the remainder of the sutra clarify the objects of offering; next, they reveal the practice of the offerer.
The text says, "In this manner," and so forth—these three phrases conclude the preceding and introduce what follows. Next, the offering implements that are accomplished are enumerated.
The twenty-eight matters, such as the canopies of incense, are then presented one by one in succession, with each subsequent item increasing in number from the preceding one.

By means of these, the lower section establishes the practice of making offerings. The upper section generally reveals the Buddha’s own practice; the lower section takes this practice of offering to the Buddha and dedicates it to sentient beings.
May all worlds be rendered pure and may all sentient beings attain liberation,
dwelling on the stage of the Ten Powers and attaining unimpeded illumination of the Dharma within all phenomena. May all sentient beings be endowed with roots of goodness and be fully tamed,
their minds immeasurable and equal to the realm of empty space, traveling to all lands without obstruction.
They arrive and enter all lands to bestow all wholesome dharmas; they always obtain visions of the Buddhas and plant all roots of goodness.
They accomplish the Mahāyāna without clinging to any phenomena, fulfilling all virtues and establishing immeasurable practices.
They universally enter the boundless entire dharma-realm, accomplishing the supernatural powers of all Buddhas, and attaining the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes of knowing.
The second [verse] dedicates the roots of goodness from making offerings to the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings. This explicitly reveals the vow of dedication.

First, it generally reveals the purpose; next, the four lines of scripture beginning with "May all sentient beings" specifically reveal the vow to attain the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits.
Just as selflessness universally encompasses all phenomena, so too are my roots of goodness:
because they universally encompass all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, making offerings to them all without exception, and because they universally encompass all immeasurable dharmas.
Because they are able to penetrate all things without obstruction; because they universally encompass all the assemblies of bodhisattvas, ultimately sharing the same roots of goodness with them all;
and because they universally encompass all bodhisattva practices, fulfilling them all through the power of their original vows.
It universally encompasses all the dharmas of illumination of the bodhisattvas, because it thoroughly understands that all phenomena are without obstruction.

It universally encompasses the great supernormal powers of all buddhas, because it accomplishes immeasurable roots of goodness. It universally encompasses the powers and fearlessnesses of all buddhas.
It universally encompasses the gates of samādhi, eloquence, and dhāraṇī of all bodhisattvas, because it gives rise to immeasurable minds that fulfill all things;
it universally encompasses the skillful means of all Buddhas, because it clearly illuminates the non-dual Dharma and manifests the great supernormal powers of the Tathāgatas;
it universally encompasses the descent from heaven, birth, attainment of enlightenment, and turning of the wheel of the true Dharma by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
They tame sentient beings and enter parinirvāṇa because they have fully and universally honored and made offerings to all.
They universally encompass all worlds throughout the ten directions because they have completely perfected the purification of all Buddha-fields. They universally encompass all vast kalpas.
Because within it, the cultivation of bodhisattva practices appears without interruption; because it universally gathers all realms of existence, manifesting birth therein;
because it universally gathers all realms of sentient beings, fulfilling the practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
and because it universally gathers all afflictions and habitual tendencies, purifying them entirely through skillful means.
Because they universally comprehend all the faculties of sentient beings, fully understanding their infinite distinctions;

because they universally comprehend the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings, causing them to leave behind defilement and attain purity; and because they universally encompass all practices for transforming sentient beings.

Because they manifest bodies according to what is appropriate for beings; because they universally encompass all paths for those who should be guided; because they enter entirely into the realms of all sentient beings;
because they universally encompass the nature of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas; and because they protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.

Third, regarding the general vow of dedicating roots of goodness through universal inclusion: the preceding three sections have specifically elucidated roots of goodness, but they only spoke of accomplishing offerings to the Buddhas.
Now, wishing to demonstrate that these roots of goodness accomplish everything without exception, this section is further explained.
Herein, the first metaphor refers to the principle of the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*); it universally encompasses both principle and phenomena, leaving nothing unpermeated.
Next, regarding my various roots of goodness, there are twenty phrases in total according to the Dharma. The first twelve phrases comprise the virtues of self-benefit;
the subsequent eight phrases, beginning with "universally encompassing all," comprise the virtues of benefiting others.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they employ the method of non-apprehension as their skillful means.
They do not differentiate between karma and its retribution, nor do they differentiate between retribution and karma.
Although they are without differentiation, they universally enter the Dharma-realm; although they perform no action, they constantly abide in roots of goodness; although nothing arises...
Yet they diligently cultivate the supreme Dharma. Without believing in phenomena, they are able to penetrate deeply; without existing within phenomena, they fully know and see them.
Whether performed or not performed, [actions] are ultimately unattainable. They know that the nature of all phenomena is eternally without autonomy.
Although they perceive all phenomena, there is nothing seen; although they universally know all things, there is nothing known. In this way, the Bodhisattva attains thorough realization.
Regarding the sphere of experience: they know that all phenomena have causes and conditions as their basis; they perceive the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
they reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) where all phenomena are free from defilement; they understand that the world is entirely like a magical transformation;

they clearly realize that sentient beings are but a single dharma and possess no dual nature; yet they do not abandon the realm of karma, employing skillful means to demonstrate the unconditioned within the conditioned realm.

They act for the sake of the Dharma, yet do not destroy the characteristics of the conditioned; they demonstrate conditioned phenomena within the unconditioned realm, yet do not conceptualize the characteristics of the unconditioned.

Thus observing that all phenomena are ultimately quiescent, the bodhisattva accomplishes all pure roots of goodness and gives rise to a mind to rescue and protect sentient beings, their wisdom clearly penetrating all things.
Dharmasāgara constantly delights in practicing the dharma that transcends folly and ignorance. Having already fully accomplished supramundane merit, he no longer studies mundane dharmas.
He has attained the eye of pure wisdom, free from the cataracts of all delusions, and cultivates the path of dedication through skillful means.
The second section, from "the sons of the Buddha" down to "with all roots of goodness," concerns the dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The initial general heading states, "using non-apprehension as the skillful means. This briefly has two meanings:

first, by using non-apprehension to guide the preceding engagement with phenomenal characteristics, one enters into existence without becoming deluded regarding emptiness; this serves as the skillful means for entering into existence. Second, by relying on non-apprehension...
Entering into existence, one does not dwell upon non-attainment; this very non-attainment is itself a skillful means (*upāya*). This constitutes the skillful means for entering emptiness.
The present text encompasses both meanings, as it seeks to demonstrate that following characteristics and departing from characteristics are without temporal sequence.

Below, there are three distinct sections that separately clarify this. First is the primary clarification of the contemplative mind, which consists of ten phrases. The first [phrase] is: "Not [abiding] in karma..."
The middle section, consisting of the three phrases beginning with "discriminating retribution," clarifies the contemplation of phenomena as returning to principle.
This means that since phenomenal dharmas are empty, their characteristics are entirely exhausted and principle is fully manifested; therefore, karma and its fruits are both void.

Because karma is void, it lacks a substantial entity capable of summoning retribution—how much less could there be a fruit within the cause? Because retribution is void, it lacks a substantial entity by which to repay the cause—how much less...
This means: "Is there a cause within the fruit? If one speaks in terms of observing the mind, it is called "the function returning to stillness.

Next, the five phrases beginning with "Although there is nothing created, one constantly abides in the roots of goodness" clarify that principle does not obstruct phenomena; in terms of the mind, stillness does not obstruct function.
Within this, the first phrase indicates that while principle is devoid of the discrimination of subject and object, it does not obstruct the existence of that which enters [into it].
The dharma-realm entered by this wisdom: the second phrase refers to performing actions without fabrication; the third phrase refers to cultivating arising without origination;
the fourth phrase refers to being able to enter the profound through phenomena without the duality of subject and object of faith;

It is unimpeded. In terms of the mind, stillness and illumination flow as one. This is because phenomena are empty; they embrace principle such that there is no phenomenon that is not principle. Principle is real;

O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they accord with the hearts of all Buddhas;
they adorn and purify all Buddha-lands; they teach and bring to maturity all sentient beings;
they fully receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas; they become the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings; and they act as merchants for all...
The wise guide of humanity, acting as the sun’s orb that purifies all worlds, fills the entire Dharma-realm with each and every root of goodness;
he is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings, causing them all to be pure and fully endowed with merit. O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate in this manner, they are able to protect and maintain the lineage of all Buddhas;
they are able to bring all sentient beings to maturity; they are able to adorn and purify all buddha-fields; they are able to ensure that all karmic actions remain indestructible;

they are able to thoroughly understand all phenomena; they are able to contemplate all phenomena as non-dual; they are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions; and they are able to...
They thoroughly realize the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) free from desire; they are able to accomplish pure faith and understanding; and they are able to be fully endowed with sharp and keen faculties.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s fourth dedication, "Reaching All Places.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dedication, they attain bodily action that reaches all places, and are universally able to manifest in response to all [beings].
Because of the world, one attains speech-action that reaches all places, for one expounds the Dharma throughout all worlds.
One attains mental action that reaches all places, for one receives and upholds all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas.

One attains the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power that reaches all places, for one goes everywhere in accordance with the minds of sentient beings to respond to them. One attains the realization-knowledge that reaches all places.
Because they are able to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena, they attain the dhāraṇī and eloquence that reach all places;

because they cause sentient beings to rejoice according to their minds, they attain entry into the dharma-realm in all places; because they universally enter all worlds within a single pore, they attain the body that enters everywhere;
and because they universally enter the bodies of all sentient beings within a single sentient being’s body...
Because it is the body of all sentient beings, one attains the universal vision of all kalpas in every place, for within each and every kalpa one constantly beholds all Tathāgatas.
Because it is the mindfulness of all places, one attains the universal vision of mindfulness in every place, for within each and every moment of thought all Buddhas appear before one.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus attains the dedication that reaches all places.
One is able to dedicate roots of goodness in this manner.

All the lands throughout the ten directions, Are entirely without support and have no place of abiding;
