Chapter Twenty-Five, Part Three, on the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
O Sons of the Buddha, what is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The fifth is the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. In the prose section, the practice of the stage is first clarified.

Now, to first raise the inquiry and explain the name: because one dedicates through practices that take inexhaustible objects as their conditions, one accomplishes practices of inexhaustible merit and attains the fruit of the ten inexhaustible treasuries;
thus, it is named after both the dedicating practice and its fruit. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]...
It is a treasury of inexhaustible merit. Alternatively, "merit" itself is the "treasury"; thus it admits of both interpretations.

In relation to the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), dedication is the container and the inexhaustible merit is that which is contained. The same applies when considering the cause in relation to the fruit;
in both cases, this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive compound). The *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states: "Because one constantly bestows the Three Jewels upon others, it is called 'inexhaustible merit.'"
The "Treasury of Virtue" (Guṇagañja) takes the roots of goodness of the five gates as its essential nature. Within the second section, the detailed explanation, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, clarifying the practice of dedication; and third, concluding with the formation of virtue. Now, for the first part, there are eight phrases.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of the roots of goodness arising from the confession and removal of all heavy karmic obstructions;
the roots of goodness arising from prostrating and paying homage to all Buddhas of the three times; the roots of goodness arising from exhorting all Buddhas to preach the Dharma;
and through diligently practicing what he has heard of the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma, awakens to the inconceivable and vast realm.

The roots of goodness arising from the realms—namely, the roots of goodness produced by rejoicing in all the roots of goodness belonging to all Buddhas and all sentient beings of the past, future, and present; the inexhaustible roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;

and the roots of goodness obtained by the assembly of Bodhisattvas through diligent cultivation—all these roots of goodness of the Buddhas who have attained equal and perfect enlightenment throughout the three periods of time...
Having awakened, they turn the wheel of the true Dharma to subdue sentient beings. Bodhisattvas fully know the roots of goodness produced by those who give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.

They know the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time—from their first generation of the mind, their cultivation of bodhisattva practices, and their attainment of supreme awakening, up until their manifestation of entry into parinirvāṇa, and after their parinirvāṇa, the duration that the True Dharma remains in the world until its final extinction. Regarding such [roots of goodness]...
[They] all give rise to sympathetic joy regarding all roots of goodness.

Second, the explanation of the text: first, one takes four gates as the foundation of practice: (1) repentance (*pāpadeśanā*), (2) prostration (*vandana*), (3) entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), and (4) sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Now, regarding the first, "repentance": *chan* (懺) means to confess and reveal prior transgressions; *hui* (悔) means...
To reform the past and cultivate the future. Second, regarding "reverence": this refers to removing the obstacle of pride (*māna*) by giving rise to faith and respect for the wholesome.
Third, "entreaty" (*adhyeṣaṇā*) is called "supplication"; it removes the obstacle of slandering the Dharma by giving rise to the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion.

Regarding the four [practices] following "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*) for the sake of the past and future, these are for the purpose of celebrating and gladdening others; thus they remove the obstacle of envy (*īrṣyā*) by giving rise to impartial goodness. [End of] Text.

Whatever one has faith in and understood, whatever one has rejoiced in, whatever one has perfected, whatever one has accomplished, whatever one has practiced, whatever one has attained,
whatever one has realized, whatever one has upheld, and whatever one has increased— all of these are dedicated toward the adornment of all Buddha-fields,
just as throughout the boundless eons of the past in all worlds.

The sphere of activity of all Tathāgatas, namely: the immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-world systems known by the wisdom of Buddhas, recognized by Bodhisattvas, and experienced by those of great resolve;

adorned Buddha-fields arising from the flow and guidance of pure karmic actions, appearing in accordance with the needs of sentient beings, manifested through the spiritual power of the Tathāgatas, and the pure deeds resulting from the appearance of Buddhas in the world.
It is accomplished through the sublime conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Within it, all Buddhas attain the Way and manifest various sovereign spiritual powers.

Throughout the limits of the future, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who abide throughout the entire Dharma-realm—those who shall attain the Buddha-way and those who shall obtain all pure and adorned meritorious Buddha-lands—will do so within this entire Dharma-realm.
The realm is the realm of empty space; it is boundless and limitless, uninterrupted and inexhaustible.
It is born entirely from the wisdom of the Tathāgata and is adorned with immeasurable, wondrous jewels—namely, the adornment of all fragrances and the adornment of all flowers.
Adorned with all manner of garments, adorned with the treasury of all merits, adorned with the powers of all Buddhas,
and adorned with all Buddha-lands; there dwell pure assemblies who have shared karmic conditions and practiced together with the Tathāgata in inconceivable ways,
and who shall attain perfect enlightenment in future ages as all Buddhas.
This accomplishment is not seen by the world; only the pure eyes of Bodhisattvas can perceive it. These Bodhisattvas possess great majestic virtue and have planted roots of goodness in past lives.
They know that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations. They universally practice the various pure deeds of Bodhisattvas and enter the inconceivable, sovereign samādhi.
Through skillful means, they are able to perform the work of Buddhas, emitting the light of the Buddha...
The light shines universally upon the world without limit or end. All the present Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise adorn their worlds in this manner:
with immeasurable forms and appearances, immeasurable radiance and colors—all of which are accomplished through merit;
with immeasurable fragrances, immeasurable jewels, immeasurable trees, innumerable adornments, and innumerable palaces.
They enumerate sounds and voices, following along with past conditions and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). They manifest all adornments of merit without end, namely:
all adornments of incense, all adornments of garlands, all adornments of powdered incense, all adornments of jewels, all adornments of banners, and all adornments of precious silken fabrics. All...
Adorned with precious railings; adorned with incalculable nets of gold; adorned with incalculable rivers;

adorned with incalculable clouds and rains; with incalculable musical instruments playing subtle and wondrous sounds—by such infinite and innumerable articles of adornment, all things throughout the entire Dharma-realm and space-realm in the ten directions were adorned in incalculable ways.
The arising of various karmas is that which the Buddha fully understands and that which the Buddha proclaims.
Throughout all worlds, within all those buddha-fields— namely, adorned buddha-fields, pure buddha-fields, equal buddha-fields, exquisite buddha-fields,
majestic buddha-fields, vast buddha-fields, blissful buddha-fields, indestructible buddha-fields, and inexhaustible [buddha-fields]— [the Buddha knows them all].
Buddha-fields; immeasurable Buddha-fields; immovable Buddha-fields; fearless Buddha-fields; luminous Buddha-fields;
unopposed Buddha-fields; delightful Buddha-fields; universally illuminating Buddha-fields; adorned Buddha-fields; exquisite Buddha-fields;
skillful Buddha-fields; foremost Buddha-fields; superior Buddha-fields; distinguished Buddha-fields; most excellent Buddha-fields.
The most excellent buddha-field; the supreme buddha-field; the unsurpassed buddha-field; the peerless buddha-field; the incomparable buddha-field;
the ineffable buddha-field—all such adornments as exist in all buddha-fields of the past, future, and present.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through his own roots of goodness, directs his resolve in dedication, making this vow:
"May all the pure and adorned lands of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present adorn a single world-system;
may all the adornments found within those lands of all Buddhas be fully accomplished and entirely purified therein."
They are all purified; they are all gathered together; they are all fully manifested; they are all exquisitely adorned; they are all sustained.
As it is with one world, so it is with all worlds throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
In all Buddha-lands of the three periods of time, every kind of adornment is perfectly complete.
In the second section, which correctly elucidates the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), first, four lines of scripture conclude the preceding roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), stating:
"Whatever has been accumulated," and so forth. This briefly summarizes ten kinds of roots of goodness in their entirety, indicating that each and every one is dedicated.
Subsequently, from the words "all" (*sarvam*) onwards, the dedication itself is explained: first, the dedication to *bodhi*, and next, the dedication to sentient beings; both are present.
The practice of conforming to characteristics while remaining detached from characteristics involves correctly generating vows and practices within that conformity.
First, one dedicates them toward the Pure Land. As the sutra’s general heading states: "All are dedicated to adorning all Buddha-lands.
Now, there are two kinds of adornment: first, adornment by various jewels; second, adornment by the jewel of human beings. To specifically reveal the characteristics of these adornments:

Regarding the three periods of time: at the beginning of the sutra, it is first indicated that, as in the past, there were "boundless kalpas" and "immeasurable lands" in terms of time and space, just as the Buddha knows them.
The "lands received by Bodhisattvas," all of which are adorned, clarify the adornments of the past.
Next, from "pure karmic conduct" downward, it clarifies the perfection of the cause. From "all Buddhas" downward, it clarifies the perfection of the activity.

"Full. Next, from "extending to the limits of the future" onwards, the adornments of the future are presented. Next, from "extending to the limits of the Dharma-realm," nine distinct types of perfection are revealed;
these are condensed into five. First is the perfection of magnitude. Second, from the two lines beginning with "all [proceed] from the Tathāgata... [the remaining perfections follow].
1. The phrase "the fruit of clarity" (*vidyā-phala*) clarifies the perfection of the dharma. 2. The three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) clarify the perfection of the support (*adhiṣṭhāna*). 3.

The single phrase "wherein the Tathāgatas reside" clarifies the perfection of the sovereign (*prabhu*). 4. From "inconceivable" (*acintya*) down to "concordant practice" (*samācāra*), it clarifies the perfection of the retinue (*parivāra*).

Next, from "all present" (*pratyutpanna*) downward, it cites the adornment of the land in the present; from "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) downward, it specifically reveals this, wherein there are three perfections.
First, "form" refers to the perfection of shape and color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*). Next, "immeasurable light and color" refers to the perfection of hue (*varṇa*).
Third, "immeasurable fragrance" and so forth refer to the perfection of the dwelling place (*vihāra*). Next, "in this way" and so forth summarizes the adornments and lands of the three times.
Next, "that which is called" and so forth specifically reveals the objects of adornment, which consist of twenty-nine types; these collectively comprise ten categories.
Seventh is "Perfection. Next, through the following passage on the past, future, and present, the vows are fulfilled to adorn those [realms].
Within this, first one world is adorned; then, by the example of "as for one world," the entire universe is universally adorned, thereby manifesting the extent of the adornment.
It causes all lands throughout the dharma-realm to be endowed with all the adornments of the three periods of time.
Since a single buddha-land thus possesses inexhaustible adornments, one adornment is all adornments; likewise, the perfection of one manifests the perfection of all.
Layer upon layer, inexhaustible—only thus is the land of the *Avataṃsaka* truly perfected. This concludes the section on the adornment of the various jewels.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates his roots of goodness in this way:
"May all the great Bodhisattvas fill every Buddha-field that I cultivate; may those Bodhisattvas possess a nature of true reality and wisdom."
His wisdom is penetrating; he is well able to discern all world-realms and the realms of sentient beings. He enters deeply into the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Having abandoned delusion, he achieves mindfulness of the Buddha. He contemplates the Dharma as truly inconceivable;
he contemplates the Sangha as immeasurable and universally pervasive. He also contemplates relinquishment. The sun of the Dharma is full, and the light of wisdom shines everywhere. Thus he sees.

Unimpeded, they arise from non-attainment and give birth to all Buddha-dharmas. They act as the sovereign of the most excellent roots of goodness for the multitudes, giving rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhi.

Abiding in the powers of the Tathāgata, they proceed toward sarvajñā (omniscience), destroy all demonic activities, purify the realms of sentient beings, and penetrate deeply into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to forever leave behind inversion.
Their roots of goodness and great vows are entirely unfailing, just like...
These bodhisattvas fill that land. Born in such a place and possessing such virtues, they constantly perform the work of Buddhas.
Having attained the Bodhi of a Buddha, they possess pure radiance and the wisdom of the Dharma-realm. Manifesting supernatural powers, a single body fills the entire Dharma-realm.
Having attained great wisdom, they enter the sphere of activity of all-knowledge, skillfully discerning the non-...
They measure the infinite dharmadhātu and its meanings, remaining entirely unattached to any world-system while being able to manifest universally in all Buddha-lands.
Their minds are like space, having no point of reliance, yet they are able to discern the entire dharmadhātu.
They are skillfully able to enter and emerge from inconceivable and profound samādhis, proceeding toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience) and dwelling in the lands of all Buddhas. They have attained...
Possessing the powers of all Buddhas, they fearlessly reveal, demonstrate, and expound upon incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) dharmas.
They accord with the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and universally illumine the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas.
They are fully able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, know incalculable methods of language, and skillfully produce inconceivable varieties of vocal sounds. They enter...
In the unsurpassed state of the Buddha’s sovereign mastery, they travel unhindered throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
They practice the dharma of non-contention and non-reliance, free from conceptual discrimination.

They cultivate and expand the bodhicitta, attain skillful wisdom, and are well-versed in the meaning of words and phrases, able to reveal and explain them according to their proper sequence. May such beings as these...
Great Bodhisattvas adorn that land, filling it and distributing themselves throughout it in accordance with its nature, dwelling therein.
It is thoroughly cultivated and intensely cultivated; it is utterly pure and supremely pure; it is tranquil and profoundly serene.
Within a single Buddha-field, in every direction and location, there are likewise such infinite, immeasurable, boundless, and incomparable beings—incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, and...
[It is] immeasurable. Inexpressible, inexpressible numbers of great Bodhisattvas pervade and fill it.
As it is in one direction, so it is in all directions. As it is in one Buddha-field, so it is in all Buddha-fields throughout space and the entire Dharma-realm.
O Son of the Buddha, by means of these roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
He then dedicates [the merit] toward all buddha-fields; he skillfully dedicates it toward all bodhisattvas; he skillfully dedicates it toward all Tathāgatas;
he skillfully dedicates it toward the awakening of all Buddhas; he skillfully dedicates it toward all vast vows;
he skillfully dedicates it toward all paths of transcendence; and he skillfully dedicates it toward purifying the realms of all sentient beings.
They skillfully dedicate [these roots of goodness] toward all worlds, so that they may constantly see the Buddhas appearing in the world.
They skillfully dedicate [them] so that they may constantly see the Tathāgatas with immeasurable lifespans.

They skillfully dedicate [them] so that they may constantly see the Buddhas pervading the entire Dharma-realm, turning the unobstructed and non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma. O Son of the Buddha, by means of these roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
When dedicating in this manner, because one universally enters all buddha-lands, all buddha-fields are entirely purified.
Because one universally reaches all realms of sentient beings, all bodhisattvas are entirely purified.
Because one universally aspires for the appearance of Buddhas in all buddha-lands, throughout the entire dharma-realm and all buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas...
The body appears transcendent.
The second son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, is adorned by the Jewel of Men. This is also the aforementioned perfection of the supporting retinue.

The text consists of three parts: first, the general vow of what is accomplished; second, from "those various bodhisattvas" onwards, the specific manifestation of the preceding characteristics. First:
This section generally reveals the virtues. Next, from "skillfully able" (*śakto hi*) onwards, there are eighteen phrases that specifically reveal these virtues.

First, it clarifies the perfection of wisdom. Second, the four phrases beginning with "deeply entering" clarify the reality of the essence. Third, from "in this way" (*evam*) onwards, it concludes by describing the majesty of the virtues.
The phrase "born in such a place" refers to the aforementioned Pure Land; "possessing such virtues" refers to the preceding text; and "constantly performing Buddha-works" follows.
The following section reveals the vastness of his activity, which is divided into four parts, namely the four perfections (*pāripūri*). First, the perfection of activity is clarified;

above, the Buddha’s activity was distinguished, whereas here it is the Bodhisattva’s activity. Next, from “attaining great wisdom” onwards is the perfection of the vehicle, for he takes great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) as his vehicle.
This passage consists of eight phrases. Next, from “tending toward omniscience” (*sarvajñatā*) onwards is the perfection of fearlessness.

Full. Because there are no internal calamities and no external fears. Fourth, "conforming to the three times" refers below to the perfection of sustaining. Within this, first the capacity to receive is clarified;
next, from "knowing incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) languages" below, the capacity to teach is clarified;

next, from "vowing to cause... below, it is concluded by adorning the buddha-field. First, the pervasiveness of persons is generally manifested; next, the five phrases beginning with "perfuming and cultivating" conclude [the section].

The practice of virtue is profound. This means that through both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), and by means of wisdom and compassion alone, one perfumes and cultivates body and mind without interruption;
this is called "thorough cultivation. Because manifest delusions do not arise, it is called "pure"; because latent seeds and habitual tendencies do not emerge, it is called "extremely pure.
It is tranquil and harmonious; it is serene and at ease. This tranquility, harmony, serenity, and stillness are the very characteristics of quiescent illumination. Next—

Within a single buddha-field, the following section specifically demonstrates the pervasive nature [of the manifestations] while also revealing their great number. This consists of three parts: first, the presence of immeasurable quantities within a single field;
second, using the spatial dimensions as an analogy for the fields; and third, using the fields as an analogy for the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As stated in the *Gaṇanā-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Countless): "Upon the tip of a single minute hair, there are unspeakably many Samantabhadras."
The phrase "thus" (*evam*) refers to the aforementioned possession of all virtues. The above section generally reveals the practices and vows;
the following text summarizes the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of all roots of goodness...

(the six lines of sūtra text that follow). This indicates that it is not merely directed toward the Buddha’s Pure Land alone. There are ten phrases in the text; the first three conclude the preceding [section].
This has already been explained. The subsequent seven phrases clarify what was not yet elucidated. Next, the Buddha’s son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner;
this concludes the practice and its benefits, summarily encompassing the three types of worlds.
O Son of the Buddha, by means of such incomparable dedications, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva proceeds toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
His mind is as vast as space, without limit or measure;
he enters the inconceivable and knows that all karma and its retributions are entirely quiescent. His mind is ever-equal and boundless, universally able to penetrate the One.
Throughout the entire dharma-realm, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they do not discriminate between self and what belongs to the self;
they do not discriminate between the Buddha and the Buddha-dharmas; they do not discriminate between buddha-fields and their adornments and purifications;
they do not discriminate between sentient beings and their transformation; they do not discriminate between karma and the retribution of karma; and they do not cling to volition.
Furthermore, that which arises from reflection is the non-destruction of cause, the non-destruction of fruit, the non-apprehension of things, and the non-apprehension of dharmas.
It does not maintain that there is discrimination within saṃsāra, nor does it maintain that nirvāṇa is eternally quiescent; nor does it maintain that the Tathāgata realizes a Buddha-realm.
There is not even the slightest dharma that coexists with another dharma.
The second section, beginning with "The Buddha’s son reaches such states as these," clarifies the dedication that is free from marks, which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Within this passage, there are two parts: first, it clarifies how the wisdom that perceives reality merges with the limit of reality; second, it reveals how the virtue of being free from delusion accords with the limit of reality.
These two sections mutually reinforce one another through repetition. Now, regarding the first [section]: the initial phrase reiterates the previous dedication toward Bodhi;

the passage beginning with "his mind" correctly reveals the departure from signs (*animitta*). Being tranquil yet illuminating without limit, it constitutes entry into the inconceivable; thus, by means of phenomena, one accords with the Truth.
Therefore, it is always equal. By virtue of this, one is able to enter universally into the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), whether in terms of phenomena or principle, without obstruction;
this is called "all. Following the passage beginning with "Next, O Son of the Buddha," the text demonstrates its freedom from delusion through ten pairs of contrasts.

The first six negate the false attachment to existence, because [phenomena] are devoid of intrinsic nature due to being dependently originated. The next one negates the false attachment to emptiness, because [emptiness] is itself the reality (tattva). It does not...
Because they exist as obstacles; because one does not destroy conventional designations when explaining the true nature (*dharmatā*), one does not destroy cause and effect.

The latter three [points] concern the simultaneous negation of both emptiness and existence: that is, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa exist in mutual dependence, yet both are empty and unattainable.

The second [point] concerns the fusion of essence: the Buddha is the *dharmadhātu*; one should not use the *dharmadhātu* to further realize the *dharmadhātu*. The final phrase means "non-... [i.e., non-existence].
There is not even the slightest dharma that is entered by wisdom, nor is there even the slightest wisdom that enters into suchness.
The above has generally demonstrated the completion of the dedication toward Bodhi.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they universally bestow all roots of goodness upon sentient beings.
It is definitively matured; it teaches with impartiality; it is signless and objectless; it is beyond measure; it is without falsehood;
and it is far removed from all conceptual discrimination and attachment.
The second section, beginning with "The Buddha’s son," clarifies the dedication to sentient beings. The first sentence provides a general explanation:

it means that at the very time one previously dedicated [merit] toward enlightenment, one simultaneously dedicates those roots of goodness to sentient beings; hence the phrase, "at the time of dedicating in this manner."
Next, the specific characteristics of the lower stage of determination are revealed through seven phrases. The first two phrases concern the corresponding characteristics:

first, having no mind of abandonment; second, having no perception of enemies or kin. The subsequent five phrases concern the absence of characteristics: first, not perceiving the characteristic of sentient beings;

second, not grasping at the conditions for transformation; third, not weighing their faculties and natures; fourth, having no sense of self or others as those to be saved. The final phrase is a summary.
These seven phrases already encompass the entirety of the upward-directed conduct toward enlightenment. They universally clarify the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has dedicated in this manner, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness, namely, mindfulness of the three periods of time.
One attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of all Buddhas; one attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of mindfulness of all Bodhisattvas;
one attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of purifying all Buddha-fields; one attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of purifying the realms of all sentient beings;

one attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of deeply penetrating the Dharma-realm; and one attains inexhaustible roots of goodness by virtue of cultivating immeasurable minds equal to space.
Because of the realm, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness. Because they deeply understand the sphere of all Buddhas, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness.

Because they diligently cultivate and practice the deeds of a bodhisattva, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness. Because they thoroughly comprehend the three periods of time, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner, they attain inexhaustible roots of goodness.
He comprehends that within the realm of all sentient beings there are no sentient beings; he understands that all phenomena have no life-span; he knows that all phenomena have no agent;
he awakens to the fact that all phenomena have no *pudgala*; he realizes that all phenomena are free from anger and contention;
he contemplates that all phenomena arise from conditions and have no place of abiding; and he knows that all things are devoid of self-nature.
As for the basis: they realize that all lands are entirely without abiding; they observe that all bodhisattva practices likewise have no location;

and they see that all realms are entirely non-existent. Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus dedicates [merit], their eyes never see impure buddha-lands, nor do they see sentient beings with differing characteristics; there is not even the slightest [such thing].
The Dharma is that which is entered by wisdom, yet there is not even the slightest wisdom that enters into the Dharma.
One should understand that the body of the Tathāgata is not like empty space, for it is perfected by all merits and immeasurable, wondrous Dharmas;
and because, in all places, it causes all sentient beings to accumulate roots of goodness until they are fully satisfied. O Son of the Buddha, in every thought-moment, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
In the middle [of this stage], they attain the unspeakably unspeakable ground of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
They are fully endowed with all merit and virtue, have perfected pure roots of goodness, and serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings.

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has accomplished a treasury of merit like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), because they obtain every requisite for happiness according to their needs. Wherever they travel...
They are able to completely purify all buddha-lands. Wherever they go, they cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to become entirely pure.

Because they gather merit and cultivate all practices, O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate [their roots of goodness] in this way, they cultivate all bodhisattva practices; their merit is supreme, and their physical marks are beyond compare.
His majestic power and radiance surpass those of all worlds; neither Māra nor his followers can gaze upon him.

Fully endowed with roots of goodness, he has accomplished his great vows. His mind is vast and equal to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); in a single thought-moment, he is able to pervade immeasurable Buddha-fields.
His power of wisdom is infinite, and he thoroughly understands the realms of all Buddhas. In all...
The Buddha has attained profound faith and understanding. He abides in boundless wisdom. The power of his bodhicitta is as vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate as space.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the fifth inexhaustible treasury of merit dedication of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The third major section concludes the formation of merit through practice. There are four "sons of the Buddha," which, together with this [section], make five;

thus it consists of five parts. First is the formation of the merit of inexhaustible roots of goodness. Next, from "Sons of the Buddha" down to "with all roots of goodness," is the formation of the merit of the wisdom of the two emptinesses.
This passage contains ten phrases: the first four concern the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and the latter six concern the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Next, the Buddha...
From "The son [of the Buddha] reaches such a stage of dedication" onwards, it establishes the virtue of the purity of the objective sphere.

Next, from "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, in every thought-moment" onwards, it clarifies the virtue of the inexhaustibility of merit and wisdom. Next, from "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, at the time of such dedication" onwards, it clarifies the virtue of the transcendence and superiority of merit and wisdom.
Next, from "This is called... onwards, it explains the name based on its etymological interpretation and concludes the section by restating the title.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in this dedication, they attain ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries. What are these ten? They are:
attaining the inexhaustible treasury of seeing Buddhas, because within a single pore they see incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas appearing in the world;
attaining the inexhaustible treasury of entering the Dharma, because by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom they perceive that all dharmas entirely enter into a single dharma.
They attain the inexhaustible treasury of retention, because they uphold all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas without forgetfulness.
They attain the inexhaustible treasury of definitive wisdom, because they skillfully know the secret expedient means of all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas.

They attain the inexhaustible treasury of understanding the meaning and intent, because they skillfully know the principles, patterns, and boundaries of all phenomena. They attain boundless realization and comprehension...
The Treasury of Exhaustion: because one penetrates all phenomena of the three periods of time through wisdom that is like space;
one attains the inexhaustible treasury of merit and virtue, for it fills the intentions of all sentient beings and cannot be exhausted;

one attains the inexhaustible treasury of courageous wisdom-awakening, for it is able to completely eliminate the cataracts of ignorance and folly of all sentient beings; one attains the inexhaustible [treasury] of definitive eloquence...
Treasury. By expounding the Dharma of the equality of all Buddhas so that all sentient beings may fully understand it, they attain the inexhaustible treasury of the ten powers and fearlessnesses.
By fulfilling all the practices of Bodhisattvas and binding their crowns with the silk ribbon of detachment from defilement, they reach the state of unobstructed omniscience.
These are the ten. O Son of the Buddha, by means of these, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
When dedicating all roots of goodness, one attains these ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries.

Regarding the second [section], the Bodhisattva’s "Analysis of the Fruits of the Stages": "What are they? introduces the inquiry; "They are as follows" provides the explanation, consisting of ten phrases.

In each case, the name is first indicated, followed by the explanation of its meaning, and finally concluded with the phrase "this is for... [etc.]. Regarding the ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries:
the first six pertain to self-benefit; the next three to benefiting others; and the last one to the accomplishment of the fruition through the integration of practice.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva accomplishes the power of the profound mind, Attaining mastery over all phenomena.
Through the merit of exhorting and rejoicing, They skillfully dedicate it with unimpeded means."
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, Who have purified Buddha-fields throughout all worlds,
Possessing every merit without exception— I dedicate my merits toward pure lands in the same way.
All the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time, The Bodhisattvas contemplate them all with perfect clarity.
With a mind that encompasses them all without exception, one thus adorns all Buddha-fields throughout all kalpas of the three periods of time.
One might exhaust the kalpas of the three periods praising the virtues of a single Buddha-field,
yet the virtues of the Buddha-fields can never be exhausted.
All these Buddha-fields, without exception, the Bodhisattvas see entirely adorning a single Buddha-land; all Buddha-lands are thus,
for those sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, all born through transformation from the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Their minds are adorned with all virtues, filling every Buddha-field;
those Bodhisattvas are likewise fully endowed with bodies adorned by immeasurable marks and signs.
Their eloquence proclaims throughout the world, like the great ocean, inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattvas dwell securely in all samādhis; All their practices are fully perfected.
Their minds are pure and peerless, Their radiance universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Thus, throughout all Buddha-fields without exception, These Bodhisattvas completely fill them all.
Never having conceived thoughts of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor seeking the path of the Pratyekabuddha,
the Bodhisattva’s mind is thus pure; dedicating roots of goodness to all living beings,
he universally desires to cause them to achieve the Perfect Path and fully realize the knowledge of all Buddha-dharmas.
All the hosts of Māras and enemies throughout the ten directions Are utterly crushed by the Bodhisattva’s majestic power;
His valor and wisdom are invincible, And he resolutely practices the ultimate Dharma.
By the power of these great vows, All his dedications of merit are free from obstruction.
Entering the inexhaustible treasury of merit, they are forever without end throughout the past, future, and present.
Bodhisattvas skillfully contemplate all conditioned phenomena and thoroughly understand that their nature is not independent.
Having realized that the nature of all phenomena is thus, they do not falsely grasp at karma or its retribution.
There are no dharmas with form, nor any without form; there are no dharmas of perception, nor any of non-perception.
All dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, are entirely non-existent.
One thoroughly understands that all things are unapprehendable, for all dharmas arise through causes and conditions; their essential nature is neither existent nor non-existent.
Regarding causes, conditions, and that which arises, there is ultimately no grasping within them.
Amidst the sphere of the speech of all sentient beings, nothing at all can be apprehended;
one clearly understands that all signs are merely conceptual constructions, and realizes that all phenomena are entirely without self.
Just as the nature of sentient beings is fundamentally quiescent, so too does one understand all phenomena—completely encompassed within the three times—to be without exception.
Since lands and all karmic actions are equal, one dedicates through such wisdom; according to that awakening and understanding, meritorious deeds arise.
These various marks of merit are also understood as such; how could there be anything further to be attained therein?
With such a stainless mind of dedication, one never attempts to weigh the nature of all phenomena, for one realizes that their nature is non-nature.
One neither abides in the world nor departs from it.
All the manifold virtuous deeds performed, I dedicate them entirely to all living beings.
May they all thoroughly realize their true nature, And may all conceptual discriminations be dispelled.
May every single false view Be completely abandoned without exception.
Free from all feverish afflictions, they are ever cool;
dwelling in the unimpeded stage of liberation, these Bodhisattvas do not destroy any phenomena, nor do they annihilate the nature of phenomena.
Understanding all phenomena to be like echoes, they remain entirely unattached to anything whatsoever.
They thoroughly know all sentient beings of the three periods of time, arising entirely from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
they also know their mental inclinations and habitual tendencies, yet they never destroy or annihilate any phenomena.
They penetrate the nature of karma as being non-karma, and yet they do not contradict the characteristics of all dharmas.
Furthermore, one does not destroy the karmic fruits and retributions; One explains that the nature of all phenomena arises from conditions.
Knowing that sentient beings have no birth, And that there are no sentient beings who transmigrate, There are no real sentient beings to be spoken of;
It is only based on worldly convention that they are provisionally designated.
The second verse section consists of twenty-five verses. The first verse provides a general summary of the roots of goodness to be dedicated.
The remaining twenty-four verses double as summaries of the aforementioned dedication of roots of goodness and conclude the formation of benefits through practice.

Within this, there are first eleven verses summarizing the aspect of following signs (*sanimitta*), followed by thirteen verses summarizing the aspect of being free from signs (*animitta*). This concludes the fifth dedication.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s dedication that accords with all firm roots of goodness?
This is the sixth dedication: the dedication that accords with all firm roots of goodness. The prose section also has two parts:

namely, the stage of practice and the fruit of the stage. Regarding the explanation of the name within the practice: it means that all the virtuous deeds being cultivated accord with and enter into the firm Dharma.
Because it is the nature [of reality], the subsequent text states: "This is then to be in accordance with the true abiding.

The section on the fundamental divisions is named "Entering All Equal Roots of Virtue. "Entering" means being in accordance; "equality" means being firm, for the principle of equality cannot be destroyed.
If one accords with this principle of equality, one then accords with all roots of virtue. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "This is then to be in accordance with the Buddha."

Regarding "abiding" and so forth: this does not merely mean that the phenomenon conforms to the principle; rather, when the phenomenon and the principle conform to one another, they receive the name "equality.
Only such equality is called "firm. This designation is established based on the roots of goodness being dedicated and the actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) toward which they are directed.
It may also be called "firm roots of goodness," wherein firmness is itself the root of goodness. If, by...
The roots of goodness that accord with and strengthen [the bodhisattva’s resolve] likewise encompass three meanings; they take unimpeded roots of goodness as their very nature.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva may become a sovereign ruler presiding over a great kingdom, his majestic virtue pervading far and wide.
His fame shook the world; none among his enemies failed to submit and obey. All his proclamations and edicts were strictly in accordance with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Holding a single parasol, he provided universal shade over the myriad regions. As he traveled throughout the land, there was no place he could not reach.

He bound a stainless silken cloth upon his crown; sovereign in the Dharma, all who beheld him were humbled. Without execution or punishment, they were moved by his virtue and followed his transformation.
He gathers all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and provides for them all as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells securely in such sovereign merit; he possesses a great retinue that cannot be broken, is free from all faults so that those who behold him never tire, and is adorned with merit such that his primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are perfected, and his physical form and limbs are perfectly proportioned and complete.
They attain a body as firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa; they achieve great power that cannot be overcome or subdued;
they obtain pure karma and become free from all karmic obstructions;
and they fully practice all forms of giving—whether by bestowing food and drink of the finest flavors, or vehicles, or clothing, or flower garlands, various incenses, ointments, seats, and dwellings.
He joyfully bestowed as alms his palaces and residences, exquisite lamps and candles, medicinal decoctions and medicines, precious vessels, and magnificent jeweled chariots;
he gave away well-trained elephants and horses, all of which were richly adorned.

Furthermore, there were those who came to beg for the throne upon which the king sat, or canopies, or parasols, or banners, flags, and various precious ornaments, including the jeweled crown upon his head and the bright pearl within his topknot—even unto the king himself.

In all positions, they are without any stinginess. If they see sentient beings within prisons and dungeons, they relinquish all wealth, treasures, wives, children, and kinsmen, even their own bodies, to rescue them and bring about their liberation.
If they see prisoners who are about to be executed, they immediately sacrifice their own bodies to take the place of those lives.
Or, if they see someone come to beg for their skin, head, or hair, they joyfully bestow these upon them without any regret.
Without stinginess, they give away their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, head, hands, and feet; their flesh, blood, marrow, and bones; their heart, kidneys, liver, and lungs;
their large and small intestines; their thick and thin skin; and even the flesh and fingernails of their fingers and toes—with a joyful heart, they bestow all of these entirely.
Or, for the sake of requesting the unprecedented Dharma, they cast themselves down into a deep, great fire.
Or they fall into pits. Or, for the sake of upholding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, they endure all manner of suffering and poison with their own bodies.
Or, for the sake of seeking even a single word of the Dharma, they are able to relinquish everything within the four seas.
They constantly transform and guide sentient beings through the True Dharma, causing them to cultivate wholesome deeds and abandon all evils. If they see sentient beings harming others...

He rescues those with compassionate hearts, causing them to abandon their sinful karma. If he sees the Tathāgata achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, he extols and praises him so that all may hear and know.
Or he gives land, constructing monasteries, dwellings, and halls as places of residence;
or he gives servants to perform service and labor; or he gives his own body to those who come to beg; or he gives...
The Buddha, for the sake of rescuing the Dharma, rejoices with exultation; for the sake of sentient beings, he serves and makes offerings to them.
He may relinquish his royal throne, cities, towns, villages, palaces, gardens, wives, children, and retinue, fully satisfying all their requests as they arise.
Or he may relinquish all goods necessary for life, universally establishing great, unrestricted assemblies of giving (*amogha-mahā-dāna*), wherein the multitude...

He gives rise to various fields of merit. Whether they come from afar or from near, whether they are wise or foolish, handsome or ugly, male or female, human or non-human—though their mental dispositions differ and their requests vary—he bestows gifts upon them all equally, causing each to be fully satisfied.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices such giving, he generates a mind that is skillfully restrained.
He dedicates them all, as follows: by skillfully gathering form, he accords with and strengthens all roots of goodness;

by skillfully gathering feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he accords with and strengthens all roots of goodness; by skillfully gathering royal sovereignty, he accords with and strengthens all roots of goodness;
by skillfully gathering retinues, he accords with and strengthens all roots of goodness; by skillfully gathering requisites...
It accords with and consolidates all roots of goodness; it skillfully gathers and bestows charity; it accords with and consolidates all roots of goodness.
Within the second broad explanation, there are two parts: first, clarifying the body that serves as the basis for practice; second, clarifying the practice that arises based on that body.
Regarding the body as the basis, one first attains the stage, for the body is the root of the myriad practices and the stage is the ground upon which the path is traversed.
Now, the Emperors and Kings have clearly attained their positions; yet, having a position necessarily entails possessing virtue, and thus they are next called "Endowed with Virtue.
The Sūtra states: "His majestic virtue is widely diffused. The following four lines of the Sūtra clarify the virtue of sovereign leadership.

Next, the remaining three lines of the Sūtra beginning with "The Bodhisattva dwells securely in this manner" clarify the virtue of the excellence of the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Following this, based on the body, [the text] arises...
In the section "Practicing: Fully Cultivating All Forms of Giving," first the dedication according to characteristics is clarified, followed by the dedication free from characteristics.

The former consists of dedicating toward enlightenment and dedicating toward sentient beings; the latter, the dedication free from characteristics, consists of dedicating toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Now, within the section on the secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are three parts. First, a general presentation and enumeration of the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāma*).

Second, an extensive exposition of the dedication of roots of goodness based on that presentation. Third, a summary of the various gateways of the dedication of roots of goodness. Regarding the first part, the presentation and enumeration, it says:
"fully practicing all forms of giving. This refers to the objects given; the nineteen lines of the sūtra summarize this.
These are listed here. Subsequently, sixty distinct categories are opened up. Next, it says, "The sentient beings therein," which identifies the field of giving;
it indicates that for all who give, no distinction is made between the worthy and the foolish, and all are fully satisfied according to their respective requests.

Following this, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, when giving in this manner," onwards, the mind of dedication of the giver is revealed; in relation to what precedes it, this constitutes the act of giving itself.

This is the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). Therefore, it is said that "at the time of such giving, one arouses a well-restrained mind," because this anticipates the subsequent mind capable of dedicating [merit].
Thus, it is said "one arouses a well-restrained mind. Because one dedicates in this manner, all the various sections of dedication listed below are permeated by this very mind.
Specifically, the six types of "well-restrained goodness" (*kuśala-saṃgraha*) listed below collectively encompass [this principle].
Thus far, regarding the donor, the recipient, and the gift itself:
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates their roots of goodness in this manner according to the infinite and boundless nature of the gifts bestowed.
That is to say, when giving sublime and excellent food to sentient beings, their mind is pure; regarding that which is given...
Regarding all things, they are without greed or attachment, and without any sense of regret or stinginess; they practice giving fully.
May all sentient beings obtain the food of wisdom, their minds free from hindrance, understanding that the nature of food is devoid of anything to be craved or clung to.

May they take pleasure only in the food of Dharma-joy and renunciation, becoming filled with wisdom, abiding firmly in the Dharma, gathering roots of goodness, and purifying both the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body.
They wander about out of compassion for sentient beings, manifesting as fields of merit by receiving morsel-food.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives food.

In the second section, "The Disciples of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*), within the detailed explanation of the text according to its passages, there is first a general presentation of the practice of giving (*dāna*).

Next, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, each is explained individually; there are sixty sections, and within each of these, there are four parts: first, the act of giving; second, the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); [and so forth].
The three pairs conclude with two lines. Fourth is the dedication for the sake of [others]. If the object of dedication is omitted, there are only three.
Alternatively, the latter two sections may be combined as a pair concluding the dedication for the sake of [others]; this classification should be noted. Now, first is the offering of food.
Food is the life-force of the world; both the noble and the lowly depend upon it equally. Therefore, it is explained first. The text consists of only three parts.

First, the practice of giving is clarified, stating that the mind is pure because it is free from the faults of giving. This means that one practices giving without seeking fame, profit, karmic rewards, or out of fear.
"Not being greedily attached" refers to the volition of non-attachment (*alobha-cetanā*). "Having no regard for stinginess" [refers to the absence of parsimony].
This is the thought free from stinginess. Furthermore, at the time of giving, there is no attachment; after giving, there is no regret or parsimony.

Whatever one practices in giving, one shares it with all sentient beings; being complete in both principle and practice, this mind is present at the beginning and also runs through all subsequent sections.
Next is the vow for all sentient beings, which constitutes the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). However, that vow is specifically for the sake of sentient beings.

May they be born [in the presence of Buddhas] and attain Buddhahood; thus he dedicates [the merit] toward Bodhi. The following cases are all to be understood accordingly. This constitutes the second pair of concluding verses for the lower [grade].
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives a drink, he dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner. What follows...

That is to say, they vow that all sentient beings shall drink the water of the flavor of the Dharma; they shall diligently practice and cultivate until they are fully endowed with the Bodhisattva path;

they shall sever worldly thirst and craving, constantly seeking the Buddha-wisdom and remaining detached from the realm of desire; they shall attain the joy and bliss of the Dharma, and their bodies shall be born from the pure Dharma;
they shall always use samādhi to regulate and collect their minds, enter the ocean of wisdom, raise great clouds of the Dharma, and pour down [the rain of the Dharma].
The Dharma-rain. This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives drink.
Within the second [section on] giving drink, there are also three parts: first, the actual practice of giving; next, the two following phrases which introduce the subject;

and next, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of the vow, beginning with "That is to say. All subsequent sections follow this pattern. However, the vows themselves are issued in accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
The previous vows were fulfilled one by one in this very way.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva bestows various kinds of pure, superior flavors— namely, sour, bitter, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—
and all these diverse tastes are perfectly moist and complete, able to bring the four great elements into a state of peace and harmony.

Harmonious. Their physical bodies are full and robust; their strength is vigorous. Their minds are pure and they constantly experience joy. When swallowing or chewing, they do not cough or feel any obstruction.
Their faculties are sharp and clear; their inner store is replete. Poisons cannot invade them, and diseases cannot harm them.
From beginning to end, they are free from affliction and forever attain peace and happiness. With these roots of goodness, they dedicate them in this way, namely, making this vow:
May all sentient beings obtain the supreme flavor; may they be filled with ambrosia.
May all sentient beings obtain the flavor of the wisdom of the Dharma and fully comprehend the functions of all flavors.

May all sentient beings obtain the immeasurable flavor of the Dharma and thoroughly penetrate the Dharma-realm, dwelling securely within the great city of the ultimate reality. May all sentient beings become great clouds of the Dharma.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, may they universally rain down the rain of Dharma to teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings obtain the flavor of supreme wisdom, their bodies and minds filled with unsurpassed Dharma-joy.
May all sentient beings attain non-attachment toward all superior flavors and remain unstained by any worldly tastes, constantly and diligently practicing all [virtues].
The Buddha-dharma. May all sentient beings attain the flavor of the One Dharma, realizing that all Buddha-dharmas are entirely without distinction.
May all sentient beings attain the most supreme flavor, riding upon omniscience until the end without ever regressing.
May all sentient beings attain entry into the non-differentiated flavor of the dharmas of all Buddhas, being fully able to discern all faculties. May all...
Sentient beings increase in the flavor of the Dharma and constantly attain fulfillment in the unimpeded Buddha-dharmas.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give the flavor [of food], in order to cause all sentient beings to diligently cultivate merit and virtue,
so that they may all be fully endowed with the body of unimpeded wisdom.
Third is the gift of flavors. For those who wish to obtain the supreme flavor, the Buddha takes whatever enters his mouth and transforms it all into nectar.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives a vehicle, he dedicates the roots of goodness in this way:
that is to say, he vows that all sentient beings shall fully attain the vehicle of omniscience and ride upon the Great Vehicle, which is... [inexpressible].
The vehicle that destroys [samsara], the most excellent vehicle, the supreme vehicle, the swift vehicle, the vehicle of great power, the vehicle endowed with merit, the supramundane vehicle,
and the vehicle that gives birth to immeasurable bodhisattvas— this is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives vehicles.

Fourth is the gift of vehicles. The meaning encompasses both carriages and horses; in the vows, these are all intended as substitutes for one's own feet, because later, at the sixteenth [vow], the gift of vehicles is treated separately. Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives clothing, they dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner: ...the garments that cover the body, which ward off cold and heat, and provide protection against wind, sun, and rain; the garments that adorn the body, which beautify the physical form and bring joy to the eyes of others; the garments that satisfy the body, which provide comfort and eliminate weariness; and the garments that protect the body, which guard against the harms of thorns, brambles, and weapons. May all sentient beings obtain such clothing, and may they never again suffer from the afflictions of cold, heat, wind, sun, or rain. May they always be adorned with the robes of the Dharma, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled garment of the Tathāgata’s great compassion. May they always be clothed in the pure, stainless, and unsullied robes of the precepts, and may they never again be separated from the robes of the three trainings. May they always be clothed in the robes of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the eighty minor marks, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom. May they always be clothed in the robes of the thirty-two major marks, and may they never again be separated from the robes of the sublime marks of a Great Man. May they always be clothed in the robes of the five supernormal powers, the six supernatural knowledges, the four bases of power, and the eight liberations, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great spiritual penetrations. May they always be clothed in the robes of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great liberation. May they always be clothed in the robes of the ten stages, the ten powers, the ten dedications, and the ten dharma-spheres, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great bodhisattva conduct. May they always be clothed in the robes of the ten paramitas, the ten dharanis, the ten vows, and the ten practices, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great skillful means. May they always be clothed in the robes of the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten grounds, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great bodhi. May they always be clothed in the robes of the four immeasurables, the four unhindered knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and the four fearlessnesses, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great turning of the wheel of Dharma. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three gates of liberation, the three non-outflows, the three jewels, and the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great nirvana. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of samadhi, the three kinds of wisdom, the three kinds of liberation, and the three bodies of the Buddha, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great dharmakaya. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of purity, the three kinds of emptiness, the three kinds of non-arising, and the three kinds of non-extinction, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great ultimate reality. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-self, the three kinds of non-attachment, the three kinds of non-obstruction, and the three kinds of non-discrimination, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great true thusness. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-birth, the three kinds of non-death, the three kinds of non-coming, and the three kinds of non-going, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great eternal stillness. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-form, the three kinds of non-sound, the three kinds of non-smell, and the three kinds of non-taste, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great signlessness. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-touch, the three kinds of non-object, the three kinds of non-mind, and the three kinds of non-consciousness, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great wishlessness. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-existence, the three kinds of non-non-existence, the three kinds of non-being, and the three kinds of non-non-being, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-action. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-grasping, the three kinds of non-rejection, the three kinds of non-acceptance, and the three kinds of non-refusal, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-attachment. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-clinging, the three kinds of non-abandoning, the three kinds of non-holding, and the three kinds of non-releasing, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-duality. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-coming, the three kinds of non-going, the three kinds of non-staying, and the three kinds of non-resting, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-dwelling. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-birth, the three kinds of non-destruction, the three kinds of non-increase, and the three kinds of non-decrease, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-arising. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-ceasing, the three kinds of non-perishing, the three kinds of non-change, and the three kinds of non-transformation, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-extinction. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-defilement, the three kinds of non-purity, the three kinds of non-increase, and the three kinds of non-decrease, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-differentiation. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-emptiness, the three kinds of non-non-emptiness, the three kinds of non-mark, and the three kinds of non-non-mark, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-conceptualization. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-wish, the three kinds of non-non-wish, the three kinds of non-desire, and the three kinds of non-non-desire, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-attachment. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-arising, the three kinds of non-ceasing, the three kinds of non-coming, and the three kinds of non-going, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-duality. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-birth, the three kinds of non-death, the three kinds of non-sickness, and the three kinds of non-old-age, and may they attain the supreme, peerless, and unexcelled robe of the Tathāgata’s great non-conditioning. May they always be clothed in the robes of the three kinds of non-grief, the three kinds of non-lamentation, the three kinds of non
That is to say, he vows that all sentient beings shall obtain the garment of shame and modesty to cover their bodies; that they shall abandon the evil practice of nakedness and heterodox paths;
that their complexions shall be lustrous and their skin fine and soft; that they shall achieve the supreme bliss of all Buddhas and attain the most pure knowledge of all modes.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva when giving clothing.
Fifth is the gift of clothing. The gift of clothing can bring about a wondrous complexion, for clothing wards off the cold and causes the facial features to appear lustrous and moist.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly practice the giving of various kinds of flowers:
namely, exquisite fragrant flowers; flowers of various colors; immeasurable and wondrous flowers; *sudarśana* (well-seen) flowers; delightful flowers;
flowers that bloom in all seasons; celestial flowers; human flowers; flowers prized and loved by the world; and most fragrant, pleasing flowers. By means of such as these...
With immeasurable exquisite flowers, they make offerings to all Buddhas currently residing in the world, as well as to all stūpas and shrines after the Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa;
or they may offer them to those who preach the Dharma, or to the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, all bodhisattvas, spiritual friends,
śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, parents, kinsmen, and even down to their own selves and all other beings.
When giving to those who are poor, destitute, and without shelter, one dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings attain the flowers of the samādhis of all Buddhas and be able to cause all dharmas to fully blossom;
may all sentient beings attain a heart of joy like that of one who beholds a Buddha, never feeling weary or satiated; may all sentient beings...
May what they see accord with their wishes, and may their minds remain free from agitation. May all sentient beings fully practice vast and pure deeds.
May all sentient beings constantly mind their virtuous friends with unchanging hearts.
May all sentient beings be like *agada* medicine, able to eliminate the manifold poisons of all afflictions. May all sentient beings attain fulfillment.
Great Vows: May all beings become kings of unsurpassed wisdom. May the sun of wisdom of all sentient beings shatter the darkness of ignorance.
May the pure moon of bodhi of all sentient beings increase and reach fulfillment.
May all sentient beings enter the great jewel-island, meet spiritual friends, and fully accomplish all roots of goodness. This is called bodhi...
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives flowers, he dedicates the roots of goodness for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain pure and unobstructed wisdom.
Regarding the sixth offering of flowers: first, the objects offered are enumerated; subsequently, the recipients of the offering are clarified, as well as one's own self.

This is because one’s own body is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and a vessel for the Dharma; by relying upon it, one advances on the Path. Therefore, giving one’s own body is infinitely superior to giving external things.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives a garland, they dedicate all their roots of goodness in this manner. What... [is attained]...?

That is to say, he vows that all sentient beings shall be pleasing for others to behold; that those who see them shall admire and praise them; that those who see them shall regard them with intimacy and kindness;

that those who see them shall love and delight in them; that those who see them shall thirst for and yearn after them; that those who see them shall have their sorrows dispelled; that those who see them shall give rise to joy; that those who see them shall leave behind evil;
and that those who see them shall always attain proximity to the Buddha and, through purity, obtain omniscience. This is the [vow] of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When the Bodhisattva offered the garland, he dedicated the roots of goodness.
This was the seventh offering of a garland. A "garland" (*mālā*) refers to flowers strung together like a ring to serve as head-ornament, or used as a necklace for the body.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives incense as a gift, they dedicate the roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the fragrance of ethical discipline (*śīla-gandha*).

May they attain ethical discipline that is unimpaired, unmixed, unstained, free from remorse, free from entanglements, free from feverish affliction, free from transgression, boundless, supramundane, and the perfection of a Bodhisattva."
Honey-like precepts. May all sentient beings, by virtue of these precepts, fully accomplish the precept-body of all Buddhas.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives incense, for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain the complete and unobstructed aggregate of precepts.

Eighth is the offering of incense. According to the ten perfections below, the myriad practices are all fragrant; this term applies universally to the precepts because they overturn the filth of breaking them. There are twelve vows:
first, "without deficiency," meaning to fully maintain the three clusters of pure conduct (*triskandha*);

second, "without admixture," meaning not to mix with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); third, "without defilement," meaning to have no stained mind. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Even [not wearing] a stained ring..."
The sound of bracelets. It is also called "defiling the bodhisattva precepts. Fourth, freedom from regret: this means not committing a grave offense (*āpatti*).
Those who commit grave offenses generally give rise to remorse. Fifth, freedom from entanglement: this means that even if an offense is committed through negligence, one feels deep shame and remorse.

To knowingly commit an offense, to commit it repeatedly without feeling shame or remorse, to be deeply attached to transgression, and to view transgression as merit—this is what is meant [by the opposite].

1. Freedom from entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). 2. Freedom from fever (*paridāha*). 3. Freedom from transgression (*avyatikrama*). This means that because it is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no heat of delusion;

and because it is constantly maintained as it was at the beginning, there is no transgression. 4. Boundlessness (*ananta*). 5. Supramundane (*lokottara*). This means that because it is associated with the Path (*mārga*), one is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Because it accomplishes supramundane practice. Regarding the ten *pāramitās*: it means that by remaining far removed from the two vehicles (*yāna*) and perfectly cultivating the ten perfections, one is then called "unviolated" in the bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
This is the morality praised by the wise. The final phrase concludes the cause by showing its fruition.
That is to say, one-fifth part.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives powdered incense, they dedicate their roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings give fragrance that perfumes everywhere, and may they all be able to generously relinquish everything they possess. May [one...]
May the fragrance of the precepts of all sentient beings universally permeate them, so that they may attain the ultimate pure precepts of the Tathāgata.
May the fragrance of patience of all sentient beings universally permeate them, so that they may be free from all treacherous and harmful intentions.

May the fragrance of diligence of all sentient beings universally permeate them, so that they may constantly don the armor of Mahāyāna diligence. May the fragrance of meditative concentration of all sentient beings universally permeate them, so that they may abide in peace...

Abiding in the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas, may all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of wisdom, attaining the Sovereign of Unsurpassed Knowledge in a single thought-moment.
May all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of the Dharma, attaining fearlessness regarding the unsurpassed Dharma.
May all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of virtue, accomplishing all great merit and wisdom. May all...
May the fragrance of the bodhi of all sentient beings universally permeate them, so that they may attain the ten powers of a Buddha and reach the other shore.
May the sublime fragrance of the pure white dharmas of all sentient beings universally permeate them, forever extinguishing all unwholesome dharmas.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give fragrant ointments.

Ninth is the gift of scented ointments. In all ten perfections, there is the inciting and nurturing of the bodhicitta; they expel obscurations and evils, and thus all are termed "fragrance.
