Twenty-sixth: Giving the crown of the head with its skin intact; this refers to the *uṣṇīṣa* (the fleshy protuberance on the head). There are six [points] regarding the practice:

first, he feels joy upon seeing the beggar because he abides in the *gotra* (spiritual lineage); second, his speech is pure in both words and intent because he is free from the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*);
third, he takes up a sharp blade and performs the physical act of renunciation because his activity is supreme; fourth, he maintains right mindfulness as he yearns for [this deed].

The upward stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is superior because its mental karma (*manaskarman*) is preeminent. Fifth, it is because it skillfully establishes the principles of the truths (*satya-nyāya*) among all phenomena through the inclusion of signlessness (*animitta*).

Sixth, it is because it is superior by virtue of relying on a resolute will to emulate [the Buddhas]. This, along with dedication (*pariṇāmana*), constitutes the seven types of supremacy that constitute the *pāramitās*.
Regarding the various acts of giving mentioned before and after this, the text is mostly abbreviated and omitted; however, because the internal giving is so urgent, it is treated specifically.
Marked as most supreme; the mark of the invisible crown of the head, for even in the higher realms there are others [who possess it].
According to the Sanskrit original, the Buddha’s hair-mark is clockwise (right-turning).
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his eyes in charity to all who come to beg, just as in the Joyful Practice of Bodhi.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the same acts of giving as King Candraprabha and other immeasurable bodhisattvas.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives his eyes, he generates a mind of pure giving of eyes; he generates a mind of pure wisdom-eye;
he generates a mind that relies upon the light of the Dharma; he generates a mind that realizes the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; and he directs [the merit] toward vast wisdom.
With a wise mind, they give rise to a mind of impartial generosity equal to that of the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
They give rise to unimpeded vision and the arising of indestructible, pure faith. Toward those who beg, they give rise to a mind of joyful acceptance.

This is for the sake of ultimately attaining all supernormal powers; for the sake of generating the Buddha-eye; for the sake of increasing the vast bodhicitta; and for the sake of cultivating great compassion.
Out of compassion and in order to subdue the six sense faculties, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva directs his mind toward such a Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives away his eyes, he conceives a heart of loving joy toward the beggar.

He does so to establish a sacrificial assembly that increases the power of the Dharma, to abandon worldly attachment, views, and negligence, to sever the bonds of desire, and to cultivate Bodhi. Following...
The mind of those who seek [his help] remains unshakable; he does not oppose their intentions but fulfills them all, while constantly practicing non-dual equanimity in accordance with them.
He dedicates these roots of goodness as follows: "May all sentient beings obtain the most supreme eye to guide and instruct all;
may all sentient beings obtain the unobstructed eye to open wide the treasury of wisdom. May...
May all sentient beings obtain the pure fleshly eye, its radiance penetrating and clear so that nothing can obscure it.
May all sentient beings obtain the pure celestial eye, seeing clearly the karmic fruits of birth and death for all beings.
May all sentient beings obtain the pure Dharma-eye, able to enter the realm of the Tathāgata in accordance with it. May all sentient beings obtain the wisdom-eye, and abandon...
May they be free from all conceptualization and attachment. May all sentient beings be endowed with the Buddha-eye, fully awakening to all phenomena.
May all sentient beings achieve the Universal Eye, reaching all realms without obstruction.
May all sentient beings achieve the pure eye that is free from the cataracts of ignorance, realizing that the realm of sentient beings is empty and non-existent.
May all sentient beings be endowed with pure, unobstructed eyes and attain the ultimate ten powers of a Tathāgata.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives his eyes,
for the sake of enabling sentient beings to obtain the pure eye of omniscience.
Twenty-seventh: Giving the Eyes. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of giving: giving food and drink is inferior; giving precious jewels is middling;

and giving one’s head, eyes, and five viscera is superior. Within this passage, there are four sections: first, the identification and citation of examples, such as the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana and others;
second, the bodhisattva’s subsequent arousal of the superior mind; third, [the section on] "for the sake of ultimate... and so forth.

The "Clarifying Conduct" (*Caryā-vibhāga*) explains the mental factors (*caitta*). The four sections for the Buddha-sons below manifest the ritual procedures. The dedication of practice and vows (*pariṇāmana-praṇidhāna*) completes the ten eyes;
this is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the *Lokātīta* chapter.

O Son of the Buddha! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to give their ears and noses to those who beg for them, just as King Śreṇika, the Bodhisattva Aśoka, the Bodhisattva Vijitāvaśin, and countless other bodhisattvas did.
At the time of giving, they draw close to the supplicants and single-mindedly cultivate the practices of all bodhisattvas.
Possessing the lineage of the Buddhas, they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas and remain mindful of all...

The practice of giving cultivated by a bodhisattva constantly and diligently gives rise to the enlightenment of all Buddhas, purifies the faculties, merits, and wisdom, and observes that within the three realms of existence there is not a single thing that is solid or permanent.

They vow to always behold all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, to accord with and recollect all Buddha-dharmas, and to know that the body is illusory, empty, and non-existent, having nothing for which they might feel greed or attachment. Thus does the bodhisattva...
When giving their ears and noses in this manner, their minds remain constantly tranquil as they subdue the sense faculties.

They strive to rescue sentient beings from perilous and evil calamities, cultivating all wisdom and merit. Entering the great ocean of giving, they thoroughly comprehend the meaning of the Dharma and fully practice all paths.
Relying on the conduct of wisdom, they attain mastery over the Dharma, exchanging their non-solid bodies for solid ones. O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away their ears, they dedicate these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings attain unimpeded ears and universally hear the sounds of all teachings being expounded;
may all sentient beings attain unobstructed ears and be able to fully understand and comprehend all voices; may all sentient beings attain [ears] like those of...
...it comes to the ear. All things are clearly understood without any obstruction.

May all sentient beings attain pure ears, such that they do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts based on the auditory faculty. May all sentient beings attain ears free from deafness, causing deluded consciousness never to arise again.
May all sentient beings attain ears that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, so as to fully know all things.
The Sound of the Buddha-Dharma: May all sentient beings attain unimpeded ears and awaken to all unhindered dharmas.
May all sentient beings attain indestructible ears, skillfully knowing all treatises such that none can refute them.
May all sentient beings attain universally hearing ears, vast and pure, serving as kings among all ears. May all sentient beings be endowed with...

They attain the divine ear as well as the Buddha-ear. This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away their ears, for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to obtain completely pure ears.
Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away their nose, they dedicate it in this way: that is to say, they vow that all sentient beings shall obtain a prominent and straight nose.
May they obtain a nose of secondary marks; a nose of auspicious characteristics; a nose that is lovely and delightful; a pure and wondrous nose; a compliant nose; a prominent and distinguished nose;
a nose that subdues enemies; a well-seeing nose; and the nose of a Tathāgata. May all sentient beings obtain a face free from anger and resentment;
may they obtain a face of all dharmas; may they obtain an unobstructed face; and may they obtain a well-seeing face.
He attains a face that is compliant, a pure face, a face free from faults, a face as perfect as that of a Tathāgata, a face that pervades all places, and a face of immeasurable beauty.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives his nose, for the sake of causing sentient beings to ultimately enter into the teachings of all Buddhas. For...
To cause sentient beings to ultimately embrace all Buddha-dharmas; to cause sentient beings to ultimately and fully understand all Buddha-dharmas;
to cause sentient beings to ultimately uphold and maintain all Buddha-dharmas;
to cause sentient beings to ultimately and constantly behold all Tathāgatas; to cause all sentient beings to fully realize and attain the gateways of the Buddha-dharmas; for...
It is to cause sentient beings to ultimately achieve an indestructible mind; to cause sentient beings to be able to clearly illuminate and understand the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
to cause sentient beings to universally adorn and purify all Buddha-lands;
and to cause sentient beings to all obtain the body of great majestic power of the Tathāgata. This is the giving of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
At the time [of giving] the nose, one dedicates the roots of goodness.
Second and eighth, the giving of ears and nose: at the time of practicing this giving, one abides in a superior mind characterized by six kinds of excellence.
First, possessing the Buddha-lineage is the excellence of abiding; second, mindfulness of all inferior activities is the excellence... Third... [text fragment].

1. The supreme excellence of constant diligence in relying [on the teachings]; 2. The supreme excellence of conforming to purity; 3. The supreme excellence of the resolute intention to rescue those who are inferior; 4.
The supreme excellence of skillful means for the growth and development [of those who are inferior]. Regarding the ten aspects obtained within the final aspiration:
The nose resides in the center of the face, and from it beauty or ugliness arises; therefore, one should establish vows in accordance with its characteristics.

Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell securely in the stage of the firm and sovereign ground, they are able to give their own teeth to all sentient beings, just as in the past did the Bodhisattva King Flower-tooth and the Bodhisattva Six-tusked Elephant King, and others.
There were immeasurable bodhisattvas and so forth. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives his teeth, his mind is pure—rare and difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower.
That is to say: he gives with an inexhaustible mind; he gives with a mind of great faith; he gives with a mind that accomplishes immeasurable renunciation at every step;
he gives with a mind that subdues all the sense faculties; he gives with a mind that relinquishes everything—all of it.

The gift of the mind of wisdom and aspiration; the gift of the mind that seeks to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; the great gift; the ultimate gift; the superior gift; the most excellent gift;
the gift of the body’s essential parts without any feeling of resentment. At that time, the bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings obtain sharp and white teeth, become supreme reliquaries (stūpas), and receive offerings from devas and humans.
I make this offering. May all sentient beings obtain even and level teeth, like the marks and signs of a Buddha, without gaps or deficiencies.
May all sentient beings attain a disciplined mind and skillfully enter the bodhisattva practices of the pāramitās.
May all sentient beings have mouths that are perfectly pure, with teeth that are bright white and clearly manifest. May all sentient beings obtain...
I call to mind the adornment of the teeth: may my mouth be pure and free from any loathsome appearance.
May all sentient beings achieve and possess forty teeth that constantly emit various rare and wondrous fragrances.

May the minds of all sentient beings be well-tamed and disciplined; may their teeth be fresh and clean like white lotuses, and may they be adorned with the auspicious *svastika* symbol swirling within the patterns of their enamel.
May all sentient beings have lips that are fresh and pure and teeth that are white and clean. May they emit immeasurable light that shines everywhere.
May all sentient beings have teeth that are firm and sharp, such that no grain remains whole when they eat; may they be free from attachment to flavors and become supreme fields of merit.
May all sentient beings constantly emit radiance from between their teeth, bestowing upon them the [stages] of the Bodhisattvas.

This is the first prediction. This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives his teeth, in order to cause sentient beings to possess all-knowledge and to have pure wisdom regarding all phenomena.
The twenty-ninth is the gift of the teeth. Regarding the phrase "abiding securely in the state of firm mastery" at the beginning of the practice of this gift:
this refers to those who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*) and above. Among the ten vows, only the third is spoken of solely in terms of the mind;
it teaches that wisdom can subdue afflictions and lead one to the further shore, just as teeth subdue food so as to nourish the Dharma-body. The remaining [vows] are spoken of in terms of the teeth.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is approached by someone who comes to beg for their tongue,
they address that beggar with a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), using gentle and affectionate speech. Just as in the past the Bodhisattva King of Upright Face,
the Bodhisattva of Non-retrogression, and countless other Bodhisattvas did, so too, O Son of the Buddha, does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva act toward those in all realms of existence.
When he was in the midst of taking birth, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings came to beg for his tongue.

At that time, the Bodhisattva seated those people upon lion thrones; with a mind free from anger, a mind free from malice, a mind free from resentment, a mind of great majestic power, a mind born of the lineage of the Buddhas, and abiding in the mind of a Bodhisattva’s dwelling.
With a mind that is never turbid or distracted, dwelling in a mind of great power, with a mind unattached to the body and a mind unattached to speech,
he placed both knees upon the ground, extended his tongue from his open mouth to show it to the beggar, and addressed him with compassionate and gentle words:
"This body of mine now belongs entirely to you; you may take my tongue and use it as you please, so that all your aspirations may be fulfilled.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicated his roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings obtain a universal tongue, capable of proclaiming and teaching all methods of speech. May all sentient beings..."
May they obtain tongues that can cover their faces; may all their words be non-dual and entirely true.
May all sentient beings obtain tongues that universally cover all Buddha-lands, manifesting the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings obtain soft and supple tongues, constantly experiencing exquisite, pure, and superior flavors. May all sentient beings obtain tongues of eloquence.
May they be able to sever all nets of doubt in the world. May all sentient beings obtain tongues of radiance, capable of emitting countless billions of rays of light.
May all sentient beings obtain tongues of certainty, whose eloquent exposition of all dharmas is inexhaustible.
May all sentient beings obtain tongues of universal subduing, skillfully able to reveal all secret essentials.
May all speech be received with faith and acceptance. May all sentient beings attain tongues of universal eloquence, skillfully entering the great ocean of all languages.
May all sentient beings attain tongues that skillfully expound all dharma-gates.

They have reached the further shore of all knowledge regarding speech. This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives their tongue, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain perfect and unimpeded knowledge.
The thirtieth is the gift of the tongue. One should establish ten superior resolves for the future.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives his head to those who come to beg, he acts as did the Bodhisattva Most Supreme Wisdom, the Great Man King of Kāśi, and other great Bodhisattvas in their practice of giving, desiring—
To achieve the head of supreme wisdom that enters into all phenomena; to achieve the head that realizes great enlightenment to rescue sentient beings;
to be fully endowed with the head that perceives all phenomena as the most foremost; to obtain the head of pure wisdom through right view;
to achieve the head of non-obstruction; to realize the head of the first stage; and to seek—

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells securely in these dharmas and practices them with diligent effort, desiring to become the foremost of those with supreme wisdom in the world; desiring to achieve the pure crown of wisdom that none in the three realms can behold;
desiring to attain the manifestation of the sovereign crown of wisdom that reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions;

and desiring to fulfill the sovereign crown of mastery over all dharmas that cannot be destroyed. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells securely in these dharmas and practices them with diligent effort.

Through such practice, one enters the lineage of all Buddhas. Training in the Buddha’s conduct of giving, one generates pure faith toward all Buddhas, increases roots of goodness, and causes all supplicants to attain satisfaction. One’s mind becomes pure and immeasurably joyful;

with a pure heart and resolute understanding, one illuminates the Buddha-dharma, gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), dwells in equanimity, and all the sense-faculties are gladdened.
May merit increase in advance; may a wholesome aspiration arise; and may one always delight in practicing vast and extensive deeds.
At that time, the bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:

namely, may all sentient beings obtain the head of a Tathāgata and attain the invisible crown, such that they cannot be eclipsed by anyone anywhere and become the most preeminent leaders within all Buddha-fields.
His hair curls to the right, radiant, pure, and lustrous. Adorned with the svastika mark, it is rare in the world.
He possesses the head of a Buddha; he has achieved the head of wisdom; he is the foremost head among all worlds; he is the complete head; he is the purified head.
To become one who sits at the site of enlightenment with the perfection of the head of wisdom— this is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away their head,
for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the most supreme dharma and accomplish unsurpassed great wisdom.
The thirty-first [chapter], "Giving the Head," is intended to clarify the purpose for which giving is performed.

There are ten types, all of which relate to the Buddha’s wisdom: first, entering into principle; second, guiding through compassion; third, perceiving phenomena; fourth, abandoning hindrances; fifth, harmonizing phenomena and principle;

sixth, serving as a refuge; seventh, transcending the inferior; eighth, seeing the mark of beginninglessness; ninth, the sovereign function of principle; and tenth, [realizing] suchness within phenomena.
It is true; therefore, it cannot be destroyed. Furthermore, the practice of giving is also supreme.

Son of the Buddha, there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who give their hands and feet to all sentient beings, such as the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent, the Bodhisattva King Without Sorrow, and countless other Bodhisattvas, throughout various realms of existence. In these various [realms]...
In every place of birth, he gives away his hands and feet; taking faith as his hand, he undertakes deeds of benefit.

Moving back and forth in constant circulation, he diligently cultivates the True Dharma. May he obtain the "Precious Hand" and practice giving with that hand, so that his actions are never in vain and he fulfills the Bodhisattva path.
Constantly extending his hand, he intends to provide vast kindness; he walks with steady steps, courageous and fearless, possessing vigor through the power of pure faith.
It proceeds to eliminate the evil realms and bring about the realization of Bodhi. O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives in this manner, with an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind, they open the gateways of the pure Dharma and enter the ocean of all Buddhas.
They perfect the hand of giving to provide for all throughout the ten directions, sustain the path to omniscience through the power of their vows, and abide in ultimate freedom from defilement.
The mind of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body is uninterrupted and indestructible; no demonic activities can cause it to waver.
Relying upon spiritual friends, one strengthens that mind and practices the perfection of generosity alongside all bodhisattvas.

Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks the wisdom of omniscience for the sake of all sentient beings and gives away his hands and feet, he dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner:
That is to say: may all sentient beings be endowed with supernormal powers and all obtain the "precious hand.
Having obtained the precious hand, may they each respect one another and conceive of one another as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), making mutual offerings of various jewels.

Furthermore, may they offer various treasures to all Buddhas, raising clouds of exquisite jewels that pervade all Buddha-lands, causing all sentient beings to give rise to hearts of mutual compassion.
They do not harm one another. They travel through all Buddha-fields, dwelling securely in fearlessness. They naturally possess ultimate supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Furthermore, they cause all to obtain the jewel-hand, flower-hand, incense-hand, robe-hand, parasol-hand, garland-hand, powdered-incense-hand, ornament-hand, boundless-hand, immeasurable-hand, and universal-hand. Having obtained these hands, by means of their supernatural power...
He constantly and diligently visits all buddha-fields. He is able to touch all buddha-worlds with a single hand;
he holds all sentient beings with his sovereign hands. He attains the mark of exquisite hands that emit immeasurable light;
he is able to universally cover sentient beings with a single hand. He achieves the Tathāgata’s marks of webbed fingers and copper-colored nails. At that time, the Bodhisattva...
With the hand of great vows, he universally covers all sentient beings. He vows that all sentient beings shall always joyfully seek unsurpassed bodhi and give birth to the great ocean of all merits.
Upon seeing those who come to beg, he rejoices without weariness, entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma and sharing in the Buddha’s roots of goodness.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his hands and feet.
Thirty-second: Giving Hands and Feet. These two matters are combined as a single vow. Faith is the cause for the hands; its fruit is the ability to rain down jewels.

Conduct is the cause for the feet; its fruit is the ability to walk. Following the passage "Next, O Son of the Buddha," the actual giving begins. The term "pure mind" refers to the vow for the hands within the context of the actual giving;
the subsequent section clarifies the mind for giving the feet. Thus, by abiding on the stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to sustain the body; therefore, the vow is to abide [on these stages].

The stage of wisdom can accomplish the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*); because it is free from the defilements of the mind, it can manifest the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because the dharma-body is profound and still, it is indestructible;
because the realization of wisdom continues perpetually, there is no interruption.

O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give their own blood from their bodies as a gift to sentient beings—such as the Bodhisattva Dharmakarma, the Bodhisattva Rājā Sukhacitta, and other immeasurable Bodhisattvas—they do so while dwelling within the various realms of existence.

At such times, they give rise to the mind that accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they give rise to the mind that yearns for and reveres Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), and they give rise to the joy of cultivating the Bodhisattva path.

He cultivates the mind of practice; he gives rise to a mind that does not grasp at painful sensations; he gives rise to a mind that delights in seeing beggars; he gives rise to a mind that does not disdain those who come to beg;

he gives rise to a mind directed toward all bodhisattva paths; he gives rise to a mind that guards all bodhisattva renunciation; he gives rise to a mind that increases and expands the bodhisattva’s virtuous giving;
he gives rise to a non-retrogressive mind, an unceasing mind, and a mind free from attachment to self. By means of these...
One dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner: namely, may all sentient beings attain the fulfillment of the dharma-body and the wisdom-body;
may all sentient beings attain a body free from weariness and fatigue, like a diamond;
may all sentient beings attain an indestructible body that cannot be harmed; and may all sentient beings attain a body like a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
They manifest universally throughout the world without end or limit. May all sentient beings attain a body that is lovely, pure, subtle, and firm.
May all sentient beings attain a body born of the Dharma-realm, identical to that of the Tathāgata, being without any dependence.
May all sentient beings attain a body of wondrous jewel radiance, such that no one among all people in the world can obscure it.
May all sentient beings attain a body that is a treasury of wisdom, attaining mastery within the realm of the deathless.
May all sentient beings attain a body like an ocean of jewels, such that all who see it receive benefit and none do so in vain. May all sentient beings...
One attains a body like space, which cannot be defiled by the afflictions and sufferings of the world. This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives his own blood,
performed with a Mahāyāna mind, a pure mind, a vast mind, a joyful mind, a celebratory mind, a glad mind, a superior mind, a peaceful mind, and an unturbid mind.
The thirty-third [practice] is the gift of blood from one's own body after it has been wounded. Regarding this, twelve superior thoughts arise toward all those who are inferior.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees someone begging for the marrow and flesh of his body, he speaks with joy and gentle words to the beggar, saying:
"Take the marrow and flesh of my body as you please. He is like the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, the King of All-Givers.

When Bodhisattvas and other immeasurable bodhisattvas, throughout various realms of existence and diverse places of birth, give their marrow and flesh to supplicants, their joy is vast and their resolve to give increases.

They cultivate roots of goodness together with all bodhisattvas, free themselves from worldly dust and defilement, and attain profound aspiration and delight. Giving their bodies universally, their minds never exhaust; they are thus fully endowed.
With immeasurable and vast roots of goodness, they embrace all jewels of sublime merit.
They practice according to the Dharma of Bodhisattvas without weariness, their minds always delighting in the merit of giving. Providing for all without exception, their hearts feel no regret.

They discern that all phenomena arise from conditions and lack intrinsic substance; thus, they do not crave the act of giving nor its karmic rewards. Whatever they encounter, they treat with equanimity.
Bestowal. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives in this manner, all Buddhas appear before them, for they perceive them as fathers and receive their protective mindfulness.
All sentient beings appear before them, so that they may universally cause them to dwell securely in the pure Dharma.
All worlds appear before them, so that they may adorn and purify all Buddha-lands.
Therefore, all sentient beings appear before them, because they universally rescue and protect them with a heart of great compassion.
All Buddha-ways appear before them, because they joyfully contemplate the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
All Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present appear before them, because they together fulfill all roots of goodness. All fearlessnesses appear before them...
First, because one is able to utter the supreme lion’s roar, all three periods of time appear before one.
Because one attains the wisdom of equality and observes universally, all worlds appear before one.
Because one makes vast vows to cultivate bodhi throughout all future kalpas, all the tireless practices of all bodhisattvas appear before one. One makes innumerable...
Because of the vastness of their immeasurable mind, O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give their marrow and flesh, they dedicate these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings attain a vajra-body that cannot be destroyed;
may all sentient beings attain a firm and dense body that is forever without deficiency or decay; may all sentient beings attain the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Their bodies shall be as adorned and pure as the body of a Buddha.
May all sentient beings attain a body endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, adorned by the thirty-two primary characteristics.

May all sentient beings attain a body beautifully adorned with the eighty secondary signs, fully possessing the ten powers that are indestructible. May all sentient beings attain the body of a Tathāgata, reaching ultimate perfection.
Pure and immeasurable. May all sentient beings attain a firm and solid body, indestructible by any maras or adversaries.
May all sentient beings attain a body of one mark, identical in physical characteristics to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
May all sentient beings attain an unimpeded body, pervading the realm of empty space with their pure Dharma-body.
May all sentient beings attain the body of the treasury of Bodhi, universally capable of containing all worlds.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks all-knowledge by giving his marrow and flesh, so that all sentient beings may attain [it].
Because the Tathāgata possesses an ultimately pure and immeasurable body, he gives his marrow and flesh as the thirty-fourth gift.
These two matters are combined with his vow; the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*) is as described in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give their own hearts to those who come to beg,
like the Bodhisattva Aregyā (Unrepenting) and the Bodhisattva Asaṅgarāja (King of Non-obstruction), as well as other immeasurable great Bodhisattvas,

they learn the mind of sovereign giving, cultivate the mind of universal giving, and practice the mind of the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of generosity) when bestowing their hearts upon beggars. Thus they achieve perfection.
With a mind directed toward the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), he trains in the mind of giving of all bodhisattvas;
a mind that relinquishes everything without exhaustion; a mind habituated to bestowing everything; a mind that bears the burden of the practice of giving of all bodhisattvas;
a mind of right mindfulness in which all Buddhas appear before him; and a mind that makes offerings to all who come as supplicants without interruption. Thus does the bodhisattva...
When a Mahāsattva gives such gifts, his mind is pure: for the sake of delivering all sentient beings;

for the sake of attaining the state of enlightenment endowed with the ten powers; for the sake of practicing in reliance upon his great vows; for the sake of desiring to abide securely on the bodhisattva path;
for the sake of desiring to accomplish omniscience; and so as not to abandon his original vow. By means of these...

One dedicates all roots of goodness in this way: that is to say, may all sentient beings attain the Vajra-treasury mind, which cannot be destroyed by any surrounding mountains of vajras; may all sentient beings attain the Vajradhātu-mind adorned with the svastika sign;
may they attain a mind that is immovable, a mind that is fearless, and a mind that benefits the world.
They constantly possess an inexhaustible mind. They attain the mind that is a treasury of wisdom, the great banner of valor. They attain a mind as firm and solid as the banner of Nārāyaṇa.
They attain a mind as inexhaustible as the ocean of sentient beings. They attain an indestructible mind, a treasury of Nārāyaṇa.
They attain a mind that extinguishes all demonic activities and the hosts of the māra armies. They attain a mind free from fear. They attain a mind of great majestic power.
They attain a mind of constant diligence; they attain a mind of great valor; they attain a mind free from alarm and fear; they attain a mind donned in the adamantine armor;
they attain the supreme mind of all bodhisattvas; they attain the fulfillment of the light of the Buddha-dharma and bodhi;
and they attain the sitting beneath the bodhi tree, abiding securely in the true Dharma of all Buddhas, free from all delusions, and accomplishing everything.

The mind of wisdom. Attaining the accomplishment of the mind of the ten powers—this is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the mind of giving, in order to cause sentient beings to be unstained by the world and to fully possess the mind of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
The thirty-fifth is the mind of giving. By means of it, ten superior minds arise from below; subsequently, twenty minds of aspiration are revealed.
Regarding "Vajragarbha": "garbha" (matrix/store) signifies firmness, and "vajra" is also firm. This refers to the wisdom of the Buddha-stage, which cannot be destroyed by worldly dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva encounters those who beg for their intestines, kidneys, liver, or lungs, they give them all away.

Just as the Bodhisattva Sudatta, the Bodhisattva Mārajit-viśeṣarāja, and countless other great Bodhisattvas did when practicing this giving—upon seeing a beggar approach, their hearts were filled with joy and they gazed upon them with eyes of love—for the sake of seeking Bodhi, in accordance with...
Whatever is required, he gives it all away without any regret in his heart. He contemplates that this body is devoid of solidity;

"I should give this to others so that they may obtain a solid body. Furthermore, he reflects that this body will soon perish and cause revulsion in those who see it, being devoured by foxes, wolves, and hungry dogs.
This body is impermanent and must eventually be abandoned to be eaten by others. It is without...
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, they realize that the body is impermanent and the ultimate in defilement.

Attaining awakening regarding the Dharma, they give rise to great joy. With a heart of reverence, they gaze intently upon the beggar who approaches, perceiving them as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) come to protect them.
Whatever is requested, there is nothing they do not bestow, exchanging this non-substantial body for that which is substantial.
Stabilizing the Body. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices giving in this manner, they dedicate all their roots of goodness, making these vows:
"May all sentient beings attain a body that is a treasury of wisdom, pure both internally and externally.
May all sentient beings attain a body that is a treasury of merit, capable of universally sustaining all aspirations for omniscience. May all sentient beings attain a most sublime body."

With sublime fragrance within and radiance emanating without, may all sentient beings attain a body that is not manifest in its abdomen, being upright from top to bottom with well-proportioned limbs and joints.
May all sentient beings attain a body of wisdom, nourished, gladdened, and made to grow by the flavor of the Buddha-dharma.
May all sentient beings attain an inexhaustible body, practicing and dwelling securely in the profound nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
May all sentient beings attain the body of the pure treasury of dhāraṇīs, manifesting all dharmas through wondrous eloquence.
May all sentient beings attain a pure body, such that both body and mind are purified within and without.
May all sentient beings attain the body of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of profound contemplation and practice, filled with wisdom and raining down the great rain of Dharma. May...

May all sentient beings attain a body of inner tranquility, and externally act as kings of the banner of wisdom for the sake of sentient beings, emitting great radiance that universally illumines all.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas when giving their intestines, kidneys, liver, and lungs.

In order to cause sentient beings to attain pure dwelling both internally and externally through unimpeded wisdom, [the Bodhisattva] performs the thirty-sixth giving of the intestines, kidneys, liver, and lungs.
These four matters are unified and dedicated, giving rise to ten superior states of mind.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give their limbs, members, and bones to beggars— just as Dharmagarbha Bodhisattva, Prabhāsarāja Bodhisattva,
and countless other great Bodhisattvas did when giving their bodily parts, limbs, and bones—
they perceive the coming of the beggar and give rise to a mind of affection and delight, a mind of joy, a mind of pure faith, a mind of peace and happiness, and a mind of valor.
A mind of loving-kindness, a mind of non-obstruction, a pure mind, and a mind that grants whatever is requested.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives their own bones, they dedicate these roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings attain bodies like those of emanations, never again receiving bodies of bone, flesh, and blood; may all sentient beings attain golden [bodies]..."

A body of adamantine nature, indestructible and invincible. May all sentient beings attain the perfectly complete Dharma-body of omniscience, born within the realm that is unbound, unattached, and unfettered.
May all sentient beings attain the body of the power of wisdom, with all faculties perfected, uninterrupted, and indestructible.
May all sentient beings attain the body of the power of the Dharma, through the power of wisdom.
May they attain mastery and reach the other shore. May all sentient beings obtain a firm and solid body, whose substance is real and never subject to decay or destruction.
May all sentient beings obtain a body that accords with conditions, teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings attain bodies permeated by wisdom, possessing the great strength of Nārāyaṇa’s limbs and joints.
May all sentient beings attain bodies of firm continuity that are never severed, forever free from all exhaustion and fatigue.
May all sentient beings attain bodies of great power that abide in stability, fully endowed with the great strength of diligence. May one...
May all sentient beings attain the universal Dharma-body that pervades the world and abide in the station of immeasurable, supreme wisdom.
May all sentient beings attain bodies endowed with the power of merit and virtue, benefiting all who behold them and remaining far removed from all evils.
May all sentient beings attain a body that has no dependence and may they all be fully possessed of non-reliant, non-attached wisdom. May all sentient beings...
May they attain a body sustained by the Buddhas, constantly protected by the empowerment of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings attain a body that universally benefits all living beings, capable of entering all realms of existence.
May all sentient beings attain a body that manifests everywhere, universally able to illuminate and manifest all Buddha-dharmas. May all sentient beings attain the perfection of vigor.
Advancing in their person, they single-mindedly and diligently cultivate the wisdom-practices of the Mahāyāna.
May all sentient beings attain a pure body free from pride, arrogance, and haughtiness; may their wisdom always abide peacefully, unmoved by distraction.

May all sentient beings attain a body of firm practice, accomplishing the karmic deeds of universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) of the Mahāyāna. May all sentient beings attain the body of the Buddha-family, forever...
To transcend all birth and death in the world— this is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives his own body and bones,
for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain all-knowledge and eternal purity.

The thirty-seventh [section] concerns the distribution of the bones of the limbs and joints. Previously, it was mentioned that "marrow" refers to what lies within the bones; that has already been clarified.
Now, the opening of the limbs and joints is treated as a distinct matter, for when the joints and members are disarticulated, they were not previously listed among the columns.

As for the phrase "without the realm of attachment," this refers to the realm of *nirvāṇa*. Within the context of that which is performed, it is said that one who attains omniscience possesses wisdom as the foremost of the ten thousand virtues.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees someone come with a sharp blade in hand begging for his skin, he gives rise to joy and his faculties are filled with delight, as if someone had bestowed upon him a profound kindness.
He goes out to meet them, welcomes them, and provides them with a seat."
He bid him sit. Bowing low with reverence, he formed this thought: "This beggar who has come is most difficult to encounter;
he has come to seek from me in order to fulfill my vow for omniscience and to bring me benefit. With a joyful and serene countenance, he spoke to him, saying:
"I now renounce this body of mine entirely. Whatever skin you require, take and use it as you please. Just as...
Just as in the past, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapārśvamṛgarāja, and other immeasurable great bodhisattvas were no different,
at that time the bodhisattva dedicates his roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings obtain skin so subtle that it is like the pure physical marks of a Tathāgata, such that those who see it have no [weariness]."
May [all beings] be weary of [suffering]. May all sentient beings obtain indestructible skin, like a vajra that nothing can destroy.
May all sentient beings obtain golden skin, as pure, bright, and clean as the finest Jāmbūnada gold.
May all sentient beings obtain skin of immeasurable colors, manifesting pure hues according to their mental inclinations. May all...
May sentient beings obtain pure and exquisite skin, fully endowed with the auspicious marks of a Tathāgata—serene, supple, and pure.
May all sentient beings obtain the foremost complexion, a naturally pure appearance beyond compare.
May all sentient beings achieve the pure complexion of a Tathāgata, adorning themselves with the various marks and signs of excellence. May one...
May all sentient beings obtain exquisite skin that emits great radiance, universally illuminating all things.
May all sentient beings obtain skin like a net of light, emitting ineffably perfect radiance like a lofty banner in the world.
May all sentient beings obtain moist and lustrous skin, such that all physical forms are entirely pure. This is the [vow] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

When giving his own body’s skin, he dedicates the roots of goodness so that all sentient beings may attain all the adorned and purified Buddha-fields and be fully endowed with the great merits of a Tathāgata.
The thirty-eighth [practice] is the giving of the skin of one’s body. Regarding the phrase "purifying the Buddha-fields" found therein: this is because the skin constitutes the external appearance.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his fingers of the hands and feet to those who beg, just as the Bodhisattva Firm Diligence did.
The Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Jambudvīpa and countless other great bodhisattvas were at that time of serene and joyful countenance;
their minds were peaceful and virtuous, free from delusion, and they rode upon the Great Vehicle.
They sought no sensual desires and prized no fame or reputation, but gave rise solely to the vast intention of a bodhisattva, remaining far removed from all stinginess and envy.
Free from defilement, they single-mindedly turn toward the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata.

Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives in this manner, they gather all roots of goodness and dedicate them entirely, making this vow: "May all sentient beings obtain long, slender fingers, no different from those of the Buddha.
May all sentient beings obtain well-proportioned fingers, symmetrical from top to bottom. May all sentient beings obtain..."
His copper-colored nails are raised and pure, translucent and clear.
May all sentient beings obtain the fingers of the supreme great man of omniscience, capable of grasping and upholding all dharmas.

May all sentient beings obtain the fingers of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*). May all sentient beings obtain the fingers of a great being, slender, long, and perfectly even. May...
May all sentient beings obtain fingers with the mark of wheels; may their finger joints be perfectly round with lines that curl to the right.
May all sentient beings obtain fingers that swirl like the *svastika* on a lotus flower, adorned with the marks and signs resulting from the karma of the Ten Powers.
May all sentient beings obtain fingers that are treasuries of light, emitting great radiance that illuminates unspeakably many Buddha-worlds. May all...
May all sentient beings attain well-arranged fingers, skillfully distributed with webbed membranes complete.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives his fingers, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain purity of mind.
Thirty-ninth: Giving the Fingers of the Hands and Feet. Regarding the purpose for which this is done: it is said that one who attains a pure mind obtains the fingers by means of that mind;
thus there are ten vows. O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks the Dharma, if someone should say to him: "If you can give me [your fingers]..."
"I shall give you my flesh-and-nail fingernails. The Bodhisattva replied, "Give me only the Dharma; as for the flesh-and-nail fingernails, take them as you please.

Just as the Bodhisattva Sovereign King Seeking the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible, and countless other great Bodhisattvas, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, desired to reveal, expound, and benefit sentient beings through the True Dharma.
In order that all may attain complete fulfillment, the Bodhisattva gives away his fingernails and the flesh attached to them to those who beg.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way: namely, "May all sentient beings obtain the copper-colored nails of the Buddhas;
may all sentient beings obtain moist and lustrous nails, adorned with the secondary marks of excellence; may all sentient beings..."
May all sentient beings obtain the nails of omniscience, endowed with the mark of a great man, which are naturally luminous, pure, and possess the supreme power of penetration.
May all sentient beings obtain incomparable nails, remaining unstained by and unattached to any worldly realm.
May all sentient beings attain the light of exquisite, adorned fingernails that universally illumines all worlds.
May all sentient beings attain indestructible fingernails that are pure and without flaw.

May all sentient beings attain fingernails with the characteristics of skillful means for entering all Buddha-dharmas, and may their vast wisdom be entirely purified. May all sentient beings attain...
Well-formed nails. There is no karmic fruit of the Bodhisattva that is not pure and sublime.
May all sentient beings obtain the nails of the Great Guide of All-Knowledge, which emit a treasury of wondrous light in immeasurable colors.

This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his fingernails, including the flesh, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, in order to cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with all [virtues].
Because of the Buddha’s power of unimpeded wisdom-nails,

he performs the fortieth act of giving by offering his nails along with the flesh. Just as a physical nail is not defiled by dust and grime, so too the wisdom-nail is not defiled by the appearances of objects.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, they treat it with reverence and respect, perceiving it as something difficult to encounter.

If someone capable of explaining it should come and say to them, "If you can cast yourself into a fire-pit seven fathoms deep, I shall bestow the Dharma upon you," the Bodhisattva, having heard this, leaps for joy and reflects: "For the sake of the Dharma, I should even remain for a long time in [the fire-pit]..."
In the hells and all other evil realms, one undergoes immeasurable suffering; how much more so when, upon merely entering a fire-pit among humans, one is able to hear the Dharma!
How marvelous that the True Dharma is so easily obtained! One need not endure the immeasurable torments of hell;
simply by entering a fire-pit, one may immediately hear it. Therefore, for my sake, speak [the Dharma] as I enter this fire-pit, just as King Suprabha sought the sublime Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vajracintin, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, entered a pit of fire.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicated these roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings abide in the omniscient Dharma in which the Buddhas abide, never regressing from unsurpassed bodhi. May all sentient beings be freed from all perils and hardships."
May they receive the peace and happiness of the Buddha. May all sentient beings attain a mind free from fear and be liberated from all terrors.
May all sentient beings always joyfully seek the Dharma, being fully endowed with the adornments of the various dharmas of delight.
May all sentient beings leave behind all evil realms and extinguish the blazing fires of the three poisons. May all sentient beings always obtain peace and happiness.
May they be endowed with the supreme and wondrous bliss of the Tathāgata. May all sentient beings attain the bodhicitta and forever leave behind the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion.
May all sentient beings fully attain the bliss of all bodhisattva samādhis and behold all Buddhas with great joy in their hearts.
May all sentient beings skillfully expound the True Dharma and reach ultimate, eternal [realization] regarding that Dharma.
Without forgetfulness, may all sentient beings be fully endowed with the wondrous bliss of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and ultimately abide in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva mahāsattva throws himself into a pit of fire for the sake of seeking the true Dharma,
in order to cause sentient beings to leave behind obstructive karma and all attain the fire of wisdom.
Forty-first: Seeking the Dharma by Entering the Practice of Fire. Seven feet are called a *ren*.

O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, for the sake of seeking the True Dharma, analyzes and expounds it, opens the path of the Bodhisattva, reveals the way to Bodhi, and proceeds toward supreme wisdom.
Diligently cultivating the ten powers, he extensively demonstrates the mind of omniscience and attains unimpededness.
The Dharma of Wisdom: To cause sentient beings to dwell in purity within the bodhisattva realm, when diligently cultivating great wisdom and protecting the Buddha’s bodhi,
one undergoes immeasurable suffering and affliction with the body, just as the Bodhisattva Seeking the Good Dharma, the Bodhisattva Valiant King,
and countless other great bodhisattvas underwent immeasurable suffering for the sake of seeking the Dharma, even unto its full acquisition.

For the sake of seeking the Dharma, he shall undergo all the sufferings that ought to be endured by those extremely wicked persons who are shrouded by the evil karma of slandering the true Dharma and possessed by the deeds of Māra; he dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner.
That is to say: may all sentient beings forever be free from the oppression of all suffering and affliction, and achieve peaceful bliss and sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
May all sentient beings forever be free from all sufferings and attain all forms of happiness.

May all sentient beings forever extinguish the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkhaskandha*) and, illuminating their present bodies, constantly experience peace and joy. May all sentient beings transcend...
May they accomplish the wisdom and conduct that transcend the prison of suffering. May all sentient beings behold the path of peace and security and leave behind all evil realms.
May all sentient beings attain the joy of the Dharma and forever sever all forms of suffering.

May all sentient beings eternally uproot all suffering, loving one another with compassion and free from any intent to harm. May all sentient beings attain the bliss of the Buddhas and depart from the cycle of birth.
The suffering of death. May all sentient beings achieve pure and peerless peace and happiness;
may no afflictions or distresses be able to harm them. May all sentient beings obtain all supreme joys, ultimately becoming fully endowed with the unimpeded bliss of a Buddha.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva when undergoing various sufferings for the sake of seeking the Dharma.

It is for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, causing them to leave behind perilous difficulties and dwell in the state of omniscience— a realm of liberation free from all obstructions.
The forty-second [example] is like that of the one who sought the Dharma and protected it by enduring manifold sufferings, such as grinding his bones to powder in the City of Fragrance (Gandhavatī).
"O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva occupies a royal throne in search of the True Dharma, they conceive of even a single word,
a single letter, a single phrase, or a single meaning as something difficult to obtain. They are thus able to completely relinquish everything within the sea-like realm."
Whether near or far, they are able to relinquish their lands, cities, and towns; their people, treasuries, gardens, ponds, houses, dwellings, groves, flowers, and fruits;
even all manner of rare and wonderful objects, palaces, towers, wives, children, kinsmen, and royal thrones.
Amidst that which is unstable, they seek the stable Dharma, exerting themselves for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
They seek the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas and the path of omniscience that is ultimately pure.
Just as the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇarāja, and countless other great Bodhisattvas diligently sought the True Dharma—

even for as little as a single syllable— they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, maintaining right mindfulness of all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time with deep affection and joy.

In their practice, they never crave fame or gain; they renounce all worldly sovereignty and royal positions to seek the state of a Buddha, the Sovereign Dharma-King. Their minds have no attachment to worldly pleasures;

they nourish their hearts with supramundane dharmas and remain forever free from all worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), dwelling in the non-proliferated dharma of all Buddhas. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
At that time, one dedicates all roots of goodness in this way: namely, may all sentient beings always delight in giving and relinquish everything;
may all sentient beings be able to renounce all they possess without any regret in their hearts;
may all sentient beings constantly seek the true Dharma, not begrudging their bodies, lives, or the necessities of life; may all sentient beings...
May they all obtain the benefits of the Dharma and be able to sever the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings attain a wholesome desire for the Dharma and their minds always rejoice in the True Dharma of the Buddhas.

May all sentient beings, in seeking the Buddha-Dharma, be able to relinquish their bodies, lives, and royal thrones, and with a great mind cultivate unsurpassed Bodhi. May all sentient beings revere...
I revere the True Dharma; may I always deeply love and delight in it, not sparing even my own body or life.
May all sentient beings protect and uphold the Dharma of the Buddhas, which is so difficult to encounter, and may they constantly and diligently practice it.

May all sentient beings attain the light of the Buddhas' Bodhi and accomplish the practices of enlightenment without depending on others for realization. May all sentient beings be able to constantly observe all things.
The Buddha-dharma extracts the arrows of doubt so that the mind attains peace and stability.

This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva relinquishes their kingdom and city in search of the True Dharma; it is for the sake of enabling sentient beings to perfect their knowledge and vision, and to always abide upon the path of peace and stability.
Forty-third: Seeking the Dharma, one renounces everything within the sea. That is, one renounces the royal throne and all that it governs. O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva acts as a great king, he attains mastery over the Dharma. He universally carries out his commands and edicts to eliminate the karma of killing.
Within Jambudvīpa, in all cities, towns, and villages, he causes all slaughter and butchery to be strictly prohibited and brought to an end. There shall be none.
To all classes of living beings—whether two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—he universally grants fearlessness with a heart free from deceit or plunder.
He extensively cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva, treating all things with benevolence and compassion, never inflicting harm or affliction.

He gives rise to a mind of wondrous jewels to bring peace and security to sentient beings, establishing deep resolve and joy in the presence of all Buddhas. He constantly abides himself in the three kinds of pure precepts, and furthermore...
He causes sentient beings to abide thus. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva establishes all sentient beings in the five precepts so that they forever sever the karma of killing.
He dedicates these roots of goodness in this way: namely, he vows that all sentient beings shall give rise to the bodhicitta and be endowed with wisdom;
that they may forever preserve their life-span without end; and that all sentient beings...
Dwelling for immeasurable eons, they make offerings to all Buddhas; through reverent and diligent cultivation, their lifespan further increases.
May all sentient beings fully practice and depart from the laws of old age and death; may no calamities or poisons harm their lives.
May all sentient beings fully achieve a body free from illness and affliction, possessing mastery over their lifespan and able to abide therein according to their will. May one...
May all sentient beings attain inexhaustible life, remaining for kalpas as vast as the future to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, teaching and taming all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings become gateways of longevity, within which the roots of goodness of the ten powers may increase.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with roots of goodness; may they attain inexhaustible life and fulfill their great vows.
May all sentient beings behold all Buddhas, making offerings and serving them, and dwell in inexhaustible longevity while cultivating roots of goodness.
May all sentient beings, under the Tathāgatas, skillfully train in what is to be learned, attaining the joy of the noble Dharma and inexhaustible life. May...
May all sentient beings attain the life-faculty that is eternally abiding, free from aging and illness, and enter the wisdom of the Buddha through courageous and diligent effort.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), who has forever severed the karma of killing,
for the purpose of enabling sentient beings to attain the perfect wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha.

The forty-fourth [case] concerns a king who, for instance, puts an end to killing and so forth. To abide oneself in the threefold pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) and to cause others to abide in the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) constitutes the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
Since killing is the first of the five precepts, this term is used universally. From the perspective of the victim, however, it is the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees sentient beings harboring cruelty in their hearts, who damage the male organs of humans and livestock, thereby causing their bodies to become mutilated and making them undergo various agonies, he perceives this situation and gives rise to great compassion to rescue them in pity.
He causes all the people of Jambudvīpa to abandon such karma. At that time, the Bodhisattva speaks...
That person said: "What have you done to commit such evil karma? I possess treasuries numbering hundreds of thousands of millions, and all manner of articles of pleasure are fully provided therein.
Whatever you may require, I shall give it to you entirely. The multitude of sins you have committed arose from this;
I now exhort you not to do such things. The work you have performed is contrary to reason. Even if...
"What is gained [from this] could be of what use? To harm others for one's own benefit—such a thing can never be.
Such evil conduct and all unwholesome dharmas are not praised by any Tathāgata. Having spoken these words, he immediately gave away all his articles of pleasure and enjoyment.
Furthermore, with kind speech, he expounded the sublime Dharma for him, causing him to rejoice. The...
That is to say, he demonstrates the teachings of tranquility so that they may be believed and accepted; he causes the elimination of unwholesome states and the cultivation of pure karma;
and he causes them to give rise to mutual compassion and refrain from harming one another. Upon hearing this, those people forever abandon evil deeds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way: namely, "May all sentient beings possess the physical form of a great man and achieve the state of a Tathāgata."
With the mark of the horse’s concealed organ, may all sentient beings possess the male form, give rise to a courageous mind, and cultivate all pure conducts (*brahmacarya*).
May all sentient beings be endowed with heroic strength, always act as leaders, abide in unimpeded wisdom, and never regress.
May all sentient beings fully attain the body of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), forever leave behind lustful thoughts, and be free from...
There is attachment. May all sentient beings fully accomplish the dharmas of a son of good family, their wisdom increasing and praised by all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings universally attain the power of a great man, always able to cultivate the roots of goodness of the ten powers.
May all sentient beings never lose or destroy the male form, always practicing...
This merit and wisdom are unprecedented dharmas. May all sentient beings be without attachment or bondage amidst the five desires, and may their minds attain liberation.
May they grow weary of and depart from the three realms of existence to abide in the bodhisattva practice.
May all sentient beings achieve the status of the foremost wise man, such that all honor, believe in, and submit to their transformation. May all sentient beings be fully endowed with bodhi.
This is the wisdom of a true man; before long, he shall become a supreme Great Hero.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva prohibits all that destroys the male form, in order to cause sentient beings to possess the form of a true man.
They are all able to protect all virtuous men (*satpuruṣa*). Born into the families of sages and saints, they are fully endowed with wisdom.
They constantly and diligently cultivate the supreme practices of a man, possessing the utility of a man. They are skillfully able to manifest the seven paths of a man.
They are fully endowed with the lineage of the virtuous men of all Buddhas, as well as the correct teaching of a man, the valor of a man, the diligence of a man, and the wisdom of a man.
The noble husband is pure; he causes all sentient beings everywhere to ultimately attain this.
Forty-five: Saving those with physical impairments. First, observing the situation, compassion arises. Next, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva...

onwards, he uses the analogy of a legal admonition. Third, from "Having spoken these words... onwards, he saves them through both material wealth and the Dharma. Regarding the salvation by material wealth:

The present suffering caused by harm; the future suffering that can be brought about by such harm—these are shown to be extinguished in tranquility. By cultivating the path of pure karma, one eliminates the causes of accumulation (*samudaya*).
Regarding the past account of a eunuch who saved five hundred oxen from having their bodies mutilated: through the power of his roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), he was endowed with male organs.
Within the practice of dedication, he cultivated various holy conducts (*brahmacarya*) to ensure the necessary restraint of the mind, and subsequently attained liberation.
One who possesses desire will certainly not have physical faults; though possessing the form of a man, he differs from women.

One who possesses the qualities of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*) must necessarily harbor virtue and morality in his heart. Among the four things to be practiced by those below, one should give rise to the conduct of a great man.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If all men and women possess four dharmas, they are called 'great men' (*puruṣa*). First, associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); second, listening to [the Dharma]..."
1. Hearing the True Dharma. 2. Contemplating its meaning. 3. Contemplating its meaning. 4. Practicing according to the teaching.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Essential Outline*, Fascicle Twenty-seven;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Essential Outline*, Fascicle Twenty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan;
with a commentary on the meaning by the śramaṇa Chengguan of Dafangguang Fo Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang;
and edited and summarized by the śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Five, Part Six: The Ten Dedications.

O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a Tathāgata appear in the world and proclaim the True Dharma, making it heard everywhere with a great voice, crying out, "A Tathāgata has appeared in the world!
A Tathāgata has appeared in the world! so that all sentient beings may obtain [this benefit]...
Upon hearing the Buddha’s name, they abandon all conceit and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Furthermore, they are exhorted to see the Buddha swiftly, to bring the Buddha to mind, to take refuge in the Buddha, to focus their attention upon the Buddha, to contemplate the Buddha, and to praise the Buddha.
Moreover, for them he extensively explains that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, appearing but once in tens of billions of *kalpas*. Through this, sentient beings attain...
Upon seeing the Buddha, they gave rise to pure faith; leaping for joy and filled with gladness, they honored and made offerings to him.

Furthermore, at the Buddha’s presence, they heard the names of various Buddhas and subsequently encountered countless other Buddhas. They planted roots of goodness and cultivated them until they increased.
At that time, due to having seen the Buddha, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings all attained purity.
Having attained ultimate subdual, those sentient beings all conceive of the Bodhisattva as a supreme spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Through the Bodhisattva, they achieve the Buddha-dharma; by means of the roots of goodness planted over countless eons, they universally perform the work of a Buddha throughout the world.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reveals [the truth] to sentient beings so that they may see the Buddha, with...

One dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner: namely, by vowing that all sentient beings shall go to see the Buddhas of their own accord without waiting for exhortation or inducement, and that they may serve and make offerings to them so as to bring them all joy.
One vows that all sentient beings shall always delight in seeing the Buddhas, never abandoning this aspiration from their hearts.
One vows that all sentient beings shall always diligently cultivate vast wisdom and uphold all [teachings].
The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas: may all sentient beings, upon hearing any sound, awaken to the Buddha-dharma;

may they cultivate the bodhisattva practices for immeasurable kalpas. May all sentient beings abide securely in right mindfulness, constantly beholding the appearance of the Buddhas with the eye of wisdom.
May all sentient beings not dwell on other activities, but always remember seeing the Buddhas and diligently cultivate the ten powers. May...
May all sentient beings, in all places, constantly behold all Buddhas, fully realizing that the Tathāgatas pervade the entire dharma-realm of space.
May all sentient beings attain the sovereign body of a Buddha, universally achieving enlightenment and preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
May all sentient beings encounter spiritual friends and constantly hear the Buddha-Dharma, attaining [insight] regarding all Tathāgatas.
To destroy [wrong] faith. May all sentient beings be able to praise the appearance of all Buddhas, so that all who see them may attain universal purity.

This is the dedication of roots of goodness by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas when praising the appearance of Buddhas in the world, in order to cause sentient beings to see all Buddhas, to make offerings and serve them, and to achieve ultimate purity in the unsurpassed Dharma.
Forty-sixth: Praising the Appearance of the Buddha. As in the verses of the youth Mahātejas, he proclaims universally, etc.

First, regarding the practice of giving, this refers to the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Within this, there are benefits obtained from the gift of the Dharma: first, the benefit of being freed from delusions upon first hearing the name;
second, the benefit of initiating practice upon seeing the physical body; third, the benefit of increasing reverence through praise; and fourth, the benefit of progressive increase.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva may relinquish the great earth, either to offer it for the construction of monasteries for the Buddhas,
or to offer it for the use of Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends as they please, or to offer it to the Saṅgha as a dwelling place. Or...

They give to their parents, or to other individuals, to the various fields of merit such as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and even to all who are poor, destitute, and homeless, as well as the other four assemblies; they give according to their wishes so that none lack anything.
Or they give to the construction of Tathāgata stūpas and temples; in all such places, they provide and prepare all necessary provisions and utensils.
One may use them as one pleases without any fear. Whenever a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away land in any direction, they dedicate their roots of goodness in this way:
"May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the ground of pure omniscience and reach the further shore of all the practices of Samantabhadra. May all sentient beings attain the ground of dhāraṇī."

May they correctly maintain all Buddha-dharmas through right mindfulness. May all sentient beings attain the power of upholding [the Dharma] and be able to constantly protect all the Buddha-teachings.
May all sentient beings attain a mind like the earth, such that their intentions toward all beings are always pure and free from evil thoughts.
May all sentient beings uphold the seeds of all Buddhas and accomplish the various [qualities of] Bodhisattvas.
The stages of the grounds are continuous and without interruption. May all sentient beings universally serve as a place of peace and security for all;
may they all be tamed and established upon the path of purity. May all sentient beings, like all Tathāgatas, benefit the world;
may they universally and diligently cultivate and abide in the power of the Buddhas. May all sentient beings universally become those who are... for the world.
May they all find delight and be established in the unsurpassed bliss of the Buddhas.

May all sentient beings attain skillful means and abide within the dharmas of the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses. May all sentient beings obtain earth-like wisdom and practice all Buddha-dharmas with mastery.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives the great earth. For...
It is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain the ultimate, pure ground of all Tathāgatas.

The forty-seventh is the "gift of the great earth. The term "great earth" is used here merely as a general designation; though it is listed briefly among the various fields of merit (*kṣetra*), it actually encompasses all of them.
As for the mention of "specific individuals," this refers to those who possess wealth and resources, because [the gift] is not motivated by respect or compassion toward them.
It is said that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) must essentially be one who benefits me.
However, there are four different types of fields for giving—respect, compassion, gratitude, and virtue—as explained in various commentaries.

In this context, the bodhisattva’s mind of giving is such that compassion and wisdom are equal to space, the objects given exhaust the entire Dharma-realm, and the fields of giving encompass all ordinary and holy beings throughout the ten directions; thus, these three factors [are perfected].
The emptiness of nature is profound and bottomless; these three matters are extraordinary and peerlessly supreme. These three matters are vast and pervasive without limit;

these three matters are mutually fused and entirely unimpeded. Within the ten vows of the practice of dedication, the first pertains to the stage of fruition, while the remaining nine pertain to the causal stages.
O Son of the Buddha! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives servants as gifts to offer to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
or he gives them to the Jewel of the Sangha; or he presents them to his parents, who are supreme fields of merit;
or again, he serves those suffering from illness and pain, ensuring they lack for nothing so that their lives may be sustained; or he bestows them upon the poor, the destitute, and the orphaned.
All others have no attendants; some guard the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgatas, while others transcribe and uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
They provide hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of servants and laborers at all times, and these servants are all wise, skillful, and naturally disciplined and compliant.
They are constantly diligent and energetic, free from indolence, and endowed with integrity.
A mind that is peaceful, a mind of happiness, a mind of benefit, a mind of benevolence, a mind of reverence, a mind free from resentment, and a mind free from enmity;
one who is able to act for the benefit of others in various ways according to what is appropriate to the customs and regions of those recipients.
Furthermore, all these arise from the maturation of the Bodhisattva’s pure karma; in skills, arts, crafts, and mathematics, there is nothing they do not master, and they are highly proficient.
They serve and attend to them so as to gladden their hearts. At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:

namely, they vow that all sentient beings may attain a mind of harmony and docility; that all roots of goodness cultivated in the presence of all Buddhas may cause all sentient beings to accord with and make offerings to all Buddhas, and to be able to hear and receive everything spoken by the Buddhas; and that one—
May all sentient beings be taken into the care of the Buddhas, constantly contemplating the Tathāgata with no other thoughts.
May all sentient beings never allow the lineage of the Buddhas to be broken, and diligently cultivate all roots of goodness that accord with the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings always and diligently make offerings to all Buddhas, never letting a single moment pass in vain. May all sentient beings uphold and preserve all the Buddhas.

Sublime meaning! With pure speech, one wanders fearlessly. May all sentient beings always delight in seeing the Buddha, never feeling satiated in their hearts, and may they not spare even their own bodies or lives in the presence of the Buddhas. May all sentient beings attain the vision of all Buddhas.
With a mind free from attachment and detached from worldly dependencies, they vow that all sentient beings shall take refuge only in the Buddha, forever leaving behind all false objects of refuge.
