They vow that all sentient beings shall follow the path of the Buddha, their minds always joyfully contemplating the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives servants and attendants, in order to cause all beings—

Because it gives rise to the state of being far removed from dust and defilement, purifies the Buddha-ground, and enables the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body of sovereign mastery, [the Bodhisattva] performs the forty-eighth gift:
that of servants. A "tóng" (僮) refers to a young and beautiful attendant for the purpose of personal service; a "pú" (僕) refers to one who maintains and guards [the household].
This is to prepare them for labor and service. Yet, one does not release them from their status as slaves to give them away to others, thereby causing them to remain servants.
This is because in the ocean of a bodhisattva’s practice, there is no virtue that is not cultivated. If one were to release them to become free, three deficiencies would arise:

first, the ocean of practice would be incomplete; second, the original vow of those servants would remain unfulfilled; and third, the fruit of Buddhahood would lack this merit of responding to the needs of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his own body to those who come to beg, at the time of giving he generates a mind of humility;
he generates a mind like the earth; he generates a mind that endures all sufferings without wavering; he generates a mind that serves sentient beings without weariness;
and he generates a mind that dedicates all roots of goodness toward all sentient beings, just as a compassionate mother does.

He possesses a mind of universal compassion. Toward all foolish, treacherous, and extremely wicked beings who commit various forms of aggression and oppression, he maintains a heart of complete forgiveness.
Abiding securely in the roots of goodness, he diligently serves others. At that time, the bodhisattva dedicates all these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings never lack anything according to their needs; may they constantly practice the conduct of a bodhisattva without interruption.

Without interruption, they do not abandon any of the aims and benefits of a bodhisattva; they dwell securely on the path practiced by bodhisattvas; they thoroughly comprehend the equal dharma-nature of bodhisattvas;
they attain inclusion within the lineage of the Tathāgatas; they abide in truthful speech and maintain the conduct of a bodhisattva, causing all worlds to attain the pure Buddha-dharma;
with profound resolve and faith-understanding, they realize the ultimate of the Dharma, and cause all...
Sentient beings give birth to pure and superior roots of goodness; they abide in great merit and possess all-knowledge.

Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, they cause all sentient beings to constantly make offerings to all Buddhas, to understand all dharmas, and to receive, uphold, read, and recite them—neither forgetting nor losing them, neither destroying nor dispersing them—and their minds are well-tamed, bringing those who are untamed to taming.
They train them through the dharma of tranquility, causing those sentient beings to abide in such matters before all Buddhas.
Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, they cause all sentient beings to become the foremost stūpas, worthy of receiving various offerings from the world,
and cause all sentient beings to become the supreme field of merit, attaining the wisdom of a Buddha and awakening all.
May all sentient beings become supreme recipients; may they universally benefit all sentient beings;
may all sentient beings achieve the highest welfare and benefit; may they be endowed with all roots of goodness;
may all sentient beings become the foremost field of merit for giving; may they obtain immeasurable rewards of merit; and may all sentient beings...
May they attain liberation from within the three realms; may they act as the supreme guides for all sentient beings;
may they be able to show the world the path of reality; may they cause all sentient beings to obtain sublime *dhāraṇī* and fully uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
and may they cause all sentient beings to realize the immeasurable, foremost realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), which is coextensive with space.
The unimpeded right path— this is the dedication of roots of goodness by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when giving his own body,
for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain the body of immeasurable wisdom worthy of offerings.
Forty-ninth: Sacrificing one’s own body as a servant. Regarding the dedication for the practice, there are twenty vows:
the first ten advance goodness, and the latter ten maintain it.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva hears the Dharma with joy and gives rise to pure faith, they are able to offer their very body.
They nurture all Buddhas; they joyfully delight in faith and understanding of the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma; they conceive the thought of their parents toward all Buddhas;
they read, recite, receive, and uphold the Dharma of the unobstructed path; they universally enter the gates of all roots of goodness—the great jewels of wisdom of countless nayutas of dharmas;
their minds constantly keep in mind immeasurable Buddhas; they enter the profound and far-reaching principles of the Buddha-realm; and they are able to...
With the subtle and secret Brahma-voice of the Tathāgata, he raises the clouds of the Buddha-dharma and rains down the rain of the Buddha-dharma.
With courageous mastery, he is able to analytically explain the foremost ground of the Omniscient One.

He fully accomplishes the vehicle of Sarvajñā (all-knowledge), and through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great dharmas, he brings all the faculties to fulfillment. O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
Having heard such a Dharma from the various Buddhas, he rejoiced immeasurably and dwelt securely in the True Dharma.
He severed his own doubts and caused others to sever theirs as well. His mind was ever serene and expansive; his merits were fully perfected and his roots of goodness complete.

His intention was constantly continuous in benefiting sentient beings, and his mind was never depleted. He attained the most supreme wisdom and became the Vajragarbha, drawing near to all the Buddhas.
The Buddha purifies all buddha-fields and constantly and diligently makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way: namely, may all sentient beings attain the most supreme body in its entirety.

May they be sustained by the protection of all Buddhas. May all sentient beings always draw near to the Buddhas and dwell in reliance upon them, constantly beholding and revering them without ever being separated.
May all sentient beings attain a pure and indestructible body, fully endowed with all merit and wisdom. May all sentient beings always diligently make offerings to the One...
I take refuge in all Buddhas. May they practice the ultimate Brahma-conduct of non-attainment. May all sentient beings attain a selfless body and be free from the notions of "self" and "mine.
May all sentient beings be able to manifest bodies everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, appearing like reflections without coming or going.
May all sentient beings attain a body of mastery, traveling universally throughout the ten directions without a self.
May there be no grasping. May all sentient beings be born from the body of the Buddha and dwell in the supreme abode of the Tathāgata’s family.
May all sentient beings attain the Dharma-power body, possessing the great strength of forbearance that cannot be destroyed by any.
May all sentient beings attain the incomparable body and accomplish the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. May all sentient beings achieve...
The body of supramundane merit is born within the pure *dharmadhātu* of non-apprehension;

this is the dedication of roots of goodness by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva offers their body to the Buddhas, so that all sentient beings may dwell forever in the household of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Fifty: Hearing the Dharma with Joyful Delight and Sacrificing the Body as an Offering to the Buddha. "Practicing giving" refers to the two types of offerings—material wealth and the Dharma—which constitute the essence of the initial practice.
"Rejoicing" refers to the practice of self-benefit; "being able to" refers to the practice of benefiting others.

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives his own body as an offering to all sentient beings, desiring to cause them universally to accomplish roots of goodness and to remain mindful of those roots of goodness. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva vows that his own body shall become a great bright lamp.
It is able to universally illuminate all sentient beings; it serves as a source of manifold delights for them.

It is able to universally embrace all sentient beings; it serves as a treasury of the sublime Dharma. It is able to universally sustain all sentient beings; it serves as pure radiance. It is able to universally awaken and enlighten all sentient beings;
it serves as the light and shadow of the world. It causes all sentient beings to constantly behold it; it serves as the cause of their roots of goodness.
As a condition, may they cause all sentient beings to always encounter them;
as true spiritual friends, may they cause all sentient beings to receive their instruction and guidance; as a level path, may they cause all sentient beings to tread upon it;
as unsurpassed, complete peace and happiness, may they cause all sentient beings to be free from suffering and purified; as a bright and pure sun, may they universally act for the world.
...equally benefiting all. At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings always draw near to the Buddhas and enter the ground of Buddha-wisdom; may all sentient beings attain conforming wisdom and abide in unsurpassed enlightenment;
may all sentient beings always dwell within the assemblies of the Buddhas with their minds well-subdued; may all...
May all sentient beings have a standard for their conduct and be endowed with the majestic deportment of a Buddha.

May all sentient beings fully attain nirvāṇa and deeply understand the meaning of the Dharma. May all sentient beings be endowed with the practice of contentment and be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

May all sentient beings abandon ignorance and desire, and abide in the aspiration and joy of the Buddha. May all sentient beings give birth to supreme roots of goodness and sit [in the seat of enlightenment].
Bodhi Tree. May all sentient beings slay the thieves of affliction and be free from the mind of enmity and harm.

May all sentient beings fully possess and uphold all Buddha-dharmas. This is the dedication of roots of goodness by which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives his own body as a gift to all sentient beings, desiring to benefit all sentient beings and cause them to attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
Because it is a place of peace and security.
Within the fifty-first practice of giving one’s own body to all sentient beings, there are also two types of practice: the practice of phenomena (*dharma*) and the practice of things (*vastu*).
In the subsequent section where the Bodhisattva explains them individually, if categorized by things, the body is like the light of the sun and moon, or a river and a pond.
One provides springs and wells for the benefit of sentient beings because one has attained mastery over the bodies of the threefold world.
If considered in terms of the Dharma, this refers to the illumination of the lamp of Dharma and the benefits of the sun of Dharma, and so forth.
Within the practice of dedication, since the practice of giving involves approaching birth through the body, one vows to transform sentient beings by bringing their bodies close to the Buddha.

O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva personally serves all Buddhas with his own body. In the presence of all Buddhas, he reflects upon repaying their profound kindness as if they were his parents.
He gives rise to deep faith and joy toward all Tathāgatas and, with a pure mind, protects the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
Abiding in the teachings of the Buddhas, he leaves behind worldly perceptions, is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and accords with all Buddhas. Free from...
The realm of Māra. Thoroughly penetrating all that the Buddhas practice and becoming a vessel for all the Buddha-dharmas, the bodhisattva at that time dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings attain a pure mind and adorn themselves with the jewel of omniscience; may all sentient beings abide in excellent self-mastery and remain far removed from...
May they be free from all unwholesome karma. May all sentient beings obtain indestructible and steadfast retinues, and be universally able to embrace the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings become disciples of the Buddhas and reach the stage of Bodhisattva consecration. May all sentient beings always be sustained by the Buddhas and forever remain free from...
May all unwholesome dharmas be eliminated. May all sentient beings follow the Buddhas and practice the most supreme dharmas of a Bodhisattva.
May all sentient beings enter the realm of the Buddha and all receive the prediction of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vyākaraṇa*).
May all sentient beings be entirely equal to all Tathāgatas; may there be no Buddha-dharma in which they do not possess mastery.
May all sentient beings be fully embraced by all Buddhas, always able to cultivate karmic actions free from grasping and attachment.
May all sentient beings always serve as the foremost attendants of all Buddhas, practicing under all Buddhas...
The practice of wisdom. This is the dedication of roots of goodness by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who serves all Buddhas:
desiring to realize the bodhi of all Buddhas; desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings; desiring to transcend all three realms;
desiring to achieve a mind free from affliction and harm; and desiring to attain immeasurable and vast bodhi. Desiring...

They achieve the wisdom that illuminates the Buddha-dharma. This is for the sake of constantly receiving the gathering-in of all Buddhas; for the sake of attaining the protection and sustenance of all Buddhas;
for the sake of aspiring with faith and understanding toward all Buddha-dharmas; for the sake of accomplishing roots of goodness equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and for the sake of perfecting a mind free from regret and realizing all the qualities of a Buddha.
Fifty-second: Giving the Body to Serve All Buddhas. Within this practice, there is also the maintenance of the mind and the maintenance of the body.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away all things within the realm, even the royal throne;
he is able to relinquish them all. Regarding worldly affairs, his mind attains mastery; he is without attachment, without bondage, and without any lingering craving. He remains far removed from them.
They abandon evil karma and benefit sentient beings. They do not cling to the fruits of karma, nor do they delight in worldly dharmas.

They no longer crave or become defiled by any place of birth. Although they dwell in the world, they are not born from this realm; their minds do not cling to the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
Their minds have no dependence or dwelling upon internal or external phenomena. They never forget any of the bodhisattva practices and are never separated from them.
O virtuous friends, upholding the vast practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, they always delight in serving all spiritual friends.
At that time, the bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:

namely, may all sentient beings become great Dharma Kings, attaining mastery over the Dharma and reaching the further shore; may all sentient beings become Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma, who crush [all obstacles].
May all afflictions and hostile thieves be extinguished. May all sentient beings abide in the sovereign throne of the Buddha, attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and expound the Buddha-dharma.
May all sentient beings abide in the realm of the Buddha and be able to turn the unsurpassed, sovereign wheel of Dharma.
May all sentient beings be born into the family of the Tathāgata and, within the sovereignty of the Buddha, protect and uphold the lineage of the Buddhas forever.
May it never cease. May all sentient beings reveal and teach the True Dharma of the immeasurable Dharma Kings, and may they bring to fulfillment the state of boundless great Bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings dwell in the pure Dharma-realm as Great Dharma Kings, manifesting the appearance of Buddhas appearing in succession without interruption.
May all sentient beings become kings of wisdom within all worlds, transforming and guiding the multitudes.

May they never abandon this for even a moment throughout their lives. May all sentient beings universally become donors of the Dharma for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, the space-realm, and all other worlds, enabling them all to abide in the Mahāyāna.
May all sentient beings attain the status of sovereigns who are fully endowed with all virtues, equaling the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. This is...
He dedicates the roots of goodness from his gift of the royal throne for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
desiring to cause all sentient beings to ultimately abide in a state of peace and security.
In the fifty-third [chapter], "The Giving of the Kingdom," from the possession of all things up to the royal throne, the first part clarifies the practice of material deeds (*vastukriyā*).
The subsequent sections clarify the relinquishment of the mind (*cittatyāga*). He cast aside his imperial chariots like discarded sandals; what bondage could there be?

O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees someone come to beg for the king’s capital, its magnificent great city, and all the customs duties collected at the frontier passes, he gives them all away without any stinginess in his heart.

He directs himself solely toward Bodhi, making great vows, abiding in great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), practicing great compassion (*karuṇā*), and with a joyful mind, benefiting all sentient beings. By means of this...
With vast wisdom, they understand the profound Dharma; they abide in the equal nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
They resolve their minds for the sake of seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); because they give rise to deep delight in sovereign dharmas;
because they seek to realize sovereign wisdom; because they purely cultivate all meritorious virtues; because they dwell in firm and vast wisdom; and because they extensively gather all [virtues].

By virtue of these roots of goodness, through the aspiration to practice all Buddha-dharmas, through the spontaneous awakening to the dharma of great wisdom, through abiding securely in the bodhicitta without regression, and through cultivating all bodhisattva practices and vows to reach the ultimate limit of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), one practices giving.
One dedicates these roots of goodness in this way: that is to say, may all...
May all sentient beings be able to adorn and purify immeasurable buddha-fields, offering them to the Buddhas as dwelling places.
May all sentient beings always delight in residing in *āraṇya* hermitages, remaining tranquil and unmoving.
May all sentient beings never rely upon royal capitals or villages, but find joy in stillness and forever attain ultimate liberation. May all sentient beings...
May they be born with a mind that never takes pleasure in or clings to anything in the world; may they always delight in remaining far removed from worldly speech.
May all sentient beings attain a mind free from greed and give away all they possess without any regret in their hearts.
May all sentient beings attain a mind of renunciation and abandon all domestic affairs. May all sentient beings attain a mind free from stinginess and constantly practice generous giving.
May all sentient beings attain a mind free from attachment and leave behind the ways of household life.
May all sentient beings be freed from all suffering and eliminate all calamities, misfortunes, and fears.
May all sentient beings adorn and purify all worlds throughout the ten directions and offer them to the Buddhas. This is the root of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s giving of a royal capital.
Dedication: It is for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to completely adorn and purify the buddha-fields.
Fifth and forty-fourth: The Gift of the King’s Capital City.
O Son of the Buddha! All the women of the inner palace, the retinue of attendants, and the female musicians belonging to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva—these are all...
Their countenances were upright and handsome, and they were endowed with every talent. Their speech, laughter, singing, and dancing were all exquisite and skillful.
They adorned their bodies with various garments and diverse flowers and perfumes; those who beheld them rejoiced, never wearying of the sight.
Such jewel-women numbered in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, all born from the virtuous karma of the Bodhisattva, existing with sovereign mastery according to his will.
Reverently complying without fail, he gives everything in alms to all who come to beg;
yet therein he has no heart of fondness, no heart of longing attachment, no heart of indulgent clinging, no heart of bondage, no heart of grasping, and no heart of greedy defilement.

With a mind free of conceptual discrimination, a mind free of pursuit, a mind free of grasping at signs, and a mind free of longing, the bodhisattva at that time contemplates all roots of goodness and dedicates them for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain liberation;
he dedicates them for the sake of attaining the joy of the Buddha-dharma; and he dedicates them so as to attain firmness within what is not firm, thereby attaining the vajra-like state.
One dedicates with a mind that wisdom cannot destroy; one dedicates for the purpose of entering the Buddha’s place of enlightenment;

one dedicates for the purpose of reaching the other shore; one dedicates for the purpose of attaining the unsurpassed bodhicitta; one dedicates for the purpose of being able to comprehend all phenomena through wisdom;
one dedicates for the purpose of giving birth to all roots of goodness; and one dedicates for the purpose of entering the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in such dharmas, they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas;
they increase the pure and supreme causes of all Buddhas; they give birth to the most excellent path of omniscience; they enter deeply into the vast intellectual activities of Bodhisattvas;
they eliminate all worldly defilements and afflictions; they are constantly able to provide offerings and gifts to the field of merit; and for the sake of all sentient beings, they proclaim...
He preaches the sublime Dharma, skillfully establishing beings so that they may practice all pure conducts and constantly and diligently gather all roots of goodness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:

namely, he vows that all sentient beings shall always obtain the retinue of immeasurable samādhis, and that the Bodhisattva’s supreme meditative concentrations shall continue in uninterrupted succession. He vows that—
May all sentient beings always delight in seeing the Buddhas and enter the Samādhi of the Adornments of All Buddhas.
May all sentient beings achieve the inconceivable meditative concentration of Bodhisattvas and play with mastery in immeasurable supernormal powers.
May all sentient beings enter the samādhi of reality as it is and attain an indestructible mind. May all sentient beings fully obtain the profound [wisdom] of Bodhisattvas.
Samādhi: May all sentient beings attain mastery over all meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) and achieve liberation of mind, perfecting the retinue of all samādhis.
May all sentient beings become skillful in all varieties of samādhi.
May they be able to fully grasp the characteristics of all samādhis. May all sentient beings attain the Samādhi of Supreme Wisdom and be universally able to study the gates of all samādhis.
May all sentient beings attain the Unobstructed Samādhi, entering deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without ever falling back or losing it.
May all sentient beings attain the Non-Attached Samādhi, their minds constantly in right reception (*samāpatti*), never grasping.
These two dharmas constitute the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives away all members of his inner palace and retinue.
It is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain an indestructible and pure retinue;
it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain the retinue of a bodhisattva; it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to [attain... entirely.
In order to bring the Buddha-dharma to fulfillment; in order to cause all sentient beings to fulfill the power of all-knowledge;
in order to cause all sentient beings to realize unsurpassed wisdom;
in order to cause all sentient beings to obtain compliant retinues; and in order to cause all sentient beings to obtain fellow practitioners of the same resolve.
Because they dwell together; because they desire to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with all merit and wisdom;
because they desire to cause all sentient beings to accomplish pure roots of goodness; because they desire to cause all sentient beings to obtain a harmonious and virtuous retinue;
and because they desire to cause all sentient beings to accomplish the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
It is because they desire to cause all sentient beings to achieve sequential and rational eloquence for skillfully expounding the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
because they desire to cause all sentient beings to forever abandon all mundane roots of goodness and collectively cultivate supramundane pure roots of goodness;
and because they desire to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their pure karma and achieve [enlightenment].
It is for the sake of all pure dharmas; it is because he desires to cause all Buddha-dharmas to manifest before all sentient beings, universally adorning them with the light of the Dharma.
Fifty-fifth: Giving the Inner Palace Retinue. There are two [points]: first, the maiden is beautiful and endowed with virtue; second, the purity of mind in giving to those below.
Regarding the dedication within the practice, there are two parts: first, the intention for dedication; second, the actual manifestation of dedication. Now, for the first:
as the sequence of events is nearing its conclusion, the literary flow expands slightly. This section of text runs through both the preceding and following passages. (Jin Dynasty)
In the original text, the two characters "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) both appear at the beginning of the phrases; this signifies dedication toward *bodhi*.

In the present scripture, they appear at the end of the phrases, which signifies the intent of dedication. In the first section, there are ten phrases. Below the words "O Son of the Buddha," the preceding meaning is restated.
From the words "born into the family of the Tathāgata" onward, the subsequent points are restated by way of example. There are likewise ten phrases. [End of] Western Region [text].

The literary style frequently reverses the preceding phrasing in this manner. To clarify the ten vows within the section on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), each individual vow incorporates the ten preceding meanings.
The term "samādhi" used throughout refers to the ease and tranquility of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); because the body and mind are supple, they are likened to a woman.
Thus, Sudhana says: "The woman of concentration constantly serves and attends [him]."

O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to give away even his beloved wife and children, just as in the past the Crown Prince Sudāna, the Bodhisattva King Śrīkūṭa, and countless other Bodhisattvas did.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, mounting the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), practices all-encompassing giving and purely cultivates the Bodhisattva path of generosity. His...
With a pure mind free from regret, they relinquish all that is cherished to seek omniscience.

They cause all sentient beings to purify their profound aspirations and resolve, so that they may accomplish the practices for awakening and contemplate the bodhisattva path, recollecting the Buddha’s awakening and abiding in the lineage of the Buddhas.
Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has fulfilled such a mind of giving, they resolutely seek the body of a Tathāgata.
He observes his own body as being bound to all beings and lacking autonomy;
furthermore, he universally embraces all sentient beings with his body, like a treasure island, bestowing upon them everything they need to satisfy those who are not yet fulfilled.
In this way, the Bodhisattva protects and mindfully attends to sentient beings, desiring to make his own body the foremost stūpa so that all may everywhere give rise to joy.
Desiring to give rise to a mind of equanimity toward the world; desiring to act as a cooling pool for sentient beings;
desiring to bestow all peace and happiness upon sentient beings; desiring to act as a great benefactor for sentient beings;

possessing sovereign wisdom and thoroughly understanding the practices performed by Bodhisattvas—may I thus adorn myself with such great vows, proceed toward omniscience, and fulfill the unsurpassed aspiration.
The field of merit of wisdom universally contemplates all sentient beings, constantly following and protecting them, while being able to accomplish one's own benefit.
The light of wisdom shines universally throughout the world. One always diligently recollects the bodhisattva’s mind of giving and constantly delights in observing the realm of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with a mind of liberation that is neither bound nor attached, spreads...
Giving to one's wife and children, one dedicates the roots of goodness thus gathered in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings abide in the bodhi of the Buddhas, manifest transformation bodies that pervade the entire dharma-realm, and turn the wheel of non-retrogression;
may all sentient beings attain a body free from attachment, traveling throughout all buddha-fields by the power of their vows; and may all sentient beings abandon hearts of love and hatred.
May they sever the fetters of greed and anger. May all sentient beings become children of the Buddhas and follow the conduct of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings give rise to a sense of self toward the Buddhas that is indestructible.
May all sentient beings always be children of the Buddha, born through transformation from the Dharma. May all sentient beings attain the ultimate state and achieve the realization of the Tathāgata.
Sovereign wisdom. May all sentient beings realize the Bodhi of the Buddha and be forever free from afflictions.
May all sentient beings be able to fully expound the path to the Bodhi of the Buddha and always delight in practicing the unsurpassed gift of Dharma.
May all sentient beings attain a mind of right concentration, unshakable by any conditions. May all sentient beings...
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he attains supreme perfect enlightenment and reveals the Dharma to immeasurable sons and daughters of good family who are born from the transformation of the Dharma.
This is the dedication of the roots of goodness from the giving of one’s wife and children by a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fully realize unimpeded liberation and non-attached wisdom.
The fifty-sixth [practice] is the giving away of wife and children. These two matters fulfill his vows. To introduce the topic and cite examples:
Sudāna (which means "Good Love" or "Lovely Love")—his story is recounted very extensively in a certain sutra. Next, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva...

and below, the mind capable of giving is clarified. First is the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*); next, from "accomplishing" (*sādhanā*) and below, is the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), which constitutes the purpose of the practice. Self-...
Contemplating one's own body, one observes that the body is not solid; how much more so, then, is this true for wife and children?

Next, with the passage beginning "Furthermore, below," one cultivates the two benefits of self and others through firm practice. Next, within the section on the practice of dedication beginning with "Next, O Son of the Buddha," there are eleven vows.
The first is based on the mind of giving, intended to make it universal. The next two are vows established regarding the wife. The following three and the final one [are as follows].
He establishes vows based on his children, regarding those who have been born from his own heart as if they were his own flesh and bone.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorns his dwelling and all its necessities, giving away everything requested by supplicants.
He practices the dharma of generosity without attachment to his home, remaining far removed from all discursive thoughts and mental observations concerning domestic life, and feeling weary of them.
Regarding the household, its activities, and the means of livelihood, they do not crave them, do not savor them, and their minds have no attachment.

Knowing that the household is easily ruined, their minds are constantly weary of it and inclined toward renunciation; they find no pleasure or delight therein at all. Desiring only to leave the home-life to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, they adorn themselves with the teachings of all Buddhas.
They relinquish everything entirely without any regret in their hearts, always acting as [disciples] of the Buddhas.
He is praised. He bestows his dwellings, wealth, and possessions—whatever he has at hand—as gifts, his mind free from attachment.
Upon seeing those who beg, his heart gives rise to joy and celebration. At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings renounce their wives and children, and achieve the supreme bliss of leaving the household life. May all...
May all sentient beings be liberated from the bonds of the household and enter the homeless state, practicing the holy life within the teachings of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings cast off stubborn defilements and take delight in all forms of giving with a mind that never regresses.

May all sentient beings forever leave behind the ways of the household, possessing few desires and knowing contentment, without hoarding or accumulating anything. May all sentient beings transcend the world.
Dwelling in the homes of worldly people, they enter the family of the Tathāgata. May all sentient beings attain the unobstructed Dharma and eliminate all paths of hindrance.
May all sentient beings be free from attachment to their families; though appearing to dwell at home, may their minds be without clinging.
May all sentient beings be skillful in transforming and guiding others; while not departing from the ways of householders, may they expound the wisdom of the Buddha.
May all sentient beings, though their bodies remain within the home, dwell with minds that always accord with the Buddha's wisdom.

May all sentient beings, while on the ground of the household life, abide upon the ground of the Buddha, universally causing immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy. This is...
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives away their home as an act of generosity, they dedicate the roots of goodness for the sake of causing sentient beings to accomplish the various practices,
vows, supernormal powers, and wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Fifty-seventh: The Gift of Houses and Estates.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives various gardens, groves, terraces, pavilions, and places of play, pleasure, and adornment.
He forms this thought: "I shall create excellent gardens for all sentient beings; I shall..."
I shall manifest the joy of the Dharma for all sentient beings. I shall bestow upon all sentient beings a mind of gladness.
I shall demonstrate boundless joy and bliss to all sentient beings. I shall open the gate of the pure Dharma for all sentient beings.
I shall cause all sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy. I shall cause all sentient beings...
Having attained the Bodhi of a Buddha, I shall cause all sentient beings to fulfill their great vows;
I shall act toward all sentient beings as a compassionate father; I shall cause all sentient beings to observe with wisdom;
I shall bestow upon all sentient beings the necessities of life; and I shall give birth to all sentient beings as a compassionate mother.

The Great Vow to Increase All Roots of Virtue. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices these roots of virtue in this manner, they do not give rise to weariness or aversion toward sentient beings who are evil, nor do they mistakenly conceive a mind of abandonment.
Even if all sentient beings throughout the world were to remain entirely ungrateful, the Bodhisattva would never harbor resentment toward them from the very beginning. They do not give rise to...
With a single thought, they seek to repay [the kindness of others], desiring only to extinguish their immeasurable suffering and affliction.

Toward all worlds, their minds are like space, free from any defilement or attachment. They universally contemplate the true nature of all phenomena and give rise to great vows to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings.
They never grow weary of or abandon the Mahāyāna aspiration, extinguishing all views and cultivating the equanimity of all bodhisattvas.
Practice and Vow. O Son of the Buddha! Having observed in this manner, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gathers all roots of goodness and dedicates them all.
That is to say: he vows that all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, may give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas and achieve the mind of the unsurpassed garden.
He vows that all sentient beings may attain the immovable dharma and cause them all to see all Buddhas.
With joy, may all sentient beings delight in the garden of the Dharma and attain the sublime bliss of the gardens within the buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings attain a pure and wondrous mind, and constantly behold the groves of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers.
May all sentient beings attain the playful delights of the Buddha and always skillfully sport within the realm of wisdom. May all sentient beings attain the power to roam...
May they sport in joy, traveling everywhere to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment in all Buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings achieve the playful liberation of Bodhisattvas, performing the practices of a Bodhisattva throughout all future eons with minds free from weariness.
May all sentient beings behold all Buddhas filling the Dharma-realm, giving rise to the vast mind and dwelling in the groves of the Buddhas. May all sentient beings...
Being born, they are able to go everywhere to all Buddha-fields, making offerings to the Buddhas in each and every field.
They vow that all sentient beings may attain a mind of wholesome desire and purify and adorn all Buddha-fields.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness from giving all gardens, groves, terraces, and pavilions by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in order to cause sentient beings to see all [Buddha-fields].
Because the Buddha sports in all the gardens and groves of the Buddhas,

the fifty-eighth [section] on "Bestowing Gardens and Groves" and so forth first sets forth the initial thought; next, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it describes the transcendence of faults and the perfection of virtues.
O Son of the Buddha! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva convenes hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of immeasurable and innumerable vast assemblies for giving.
All these are pure and approved by all Buddhas; they never cause harm or affliction to even a single sentient being.
They cause all beings everywhere to distance themselves from all evils, purify the three paths of action, and achieve wisdom, establishing countless hundreds of thousands [of such assemblies].
Throughout *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* kalpas of pure realms, they have accumulated immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* excellent articles of life,
and having resolved upon the most difficult-to-attain bodhicitta, they practice boundless giving.
He causes all sentient beings to abide in the path of purity, giving rise to pure faith and understanding that is good in the beginning, middle, and end.
According to the inclinations of hundreds of thousands of billions of immeasurable sentient beings, he causes them all to rejoice. With great compassion, he rescues and protects all.
They serve and make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, desiring to bring all Buddha-seeds to fulfillment.

They practice generosity with a mind free from regret, increasing the faculty of faith and perfecting sublime conduct. Moment by moment, they advance further in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings resolve upon the Great Vehicle and fully accomplish the giving of the Mahāyāna.
May all sentient beings be able to practice the great assembly giving, exhaustive giving, excellent giving, most supreme giving, unsurpassed giving, and the most unsurpassed, unequaled giving.
This is giving. It is giving that transcends all worldly giving; it is giving praised by all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings become supreme donors, striving to rescue beings from the evil realms and causing them all to enter the path of unimpeded wisdom.
Cultivating roots of goodness through the vow of equality as it truly is, one attains the non-discriminative wisdom that realizes one's own objective realm.

One vows that all sentient beings may dwell securely in the wisdom of tranquil meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), enter the path of immortality, and perfect all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom.
With courageous diligence, they shall be fully endowed with the adornments of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the Buddha-dharmas, reaching the further shore never to regress.
May all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving without ever becoming weary;
may they provide for and succor sentient beings without ceasing until they reach the ultimate, unsurpassed knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
May all sentient beings constantly and diligently plant all roots of goodness, reaching the further shore of immeasurable merit. May all sentient beings always receive the protection of the Buddhas.
They are praised by all; they act as great benefactors for the entire world. Their merit is complete and fills the Dharma-realm;
they illuminate the ten directions, bestowing unsurpassed bliss. May all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving and extensively gather roots of goodness.
May they impartially gather in all beings and lead them to the other shore. May all sentient beings achieve the most supreme giving, universally causing—
May sentient beings abide in the foremost vehicle. May all sentient beings practice timely giving and forever leave behind untimely great giving, reaching its ultimate consummation.
May all sentient beings accomplish virtuous giving and reach the further shore of the great giving of the Buddha, the Great Man.
May all sentient beings ultimately and constantly practice the great adornment of giving.
May they take all Buddhas as their teachers, drawing near to them all and offering great worship.
May all sentient beings abide in pure giving, accumulating immeasurable merit equal to the Dharma-realm and reaching the other shore. May all sentient beings, for the sake of all worlds, act as...
Great donor! Vowing to deliver all beings and abide in the stage of the Tathāgata—this is the dedication of roots of goodness from the great assembly of giving by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to practice the unsurpassed gift, the ultimate gift of a Buddha, the accomplished gift, the indestructible gift, the gift that makes offerings to all Buddhas, the gift free from resentment, the gift that rescues sentient beings, and to bring them to fulfillment.
The gift of all-knowledge; the gift of constantly beholding all Buddhas; the gift of excellent diligence;
and the vast gift of accomplishing all bodhisattva merits and the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Fifty-ninth: Establishing a Great Assembly for Almsgiving. Next, regarding "All those below [the noble ones] leave faults behind and accomplish virtues":

one selects firewood for cooking and filters water for use; not begging forcefully is called "not troubling sentient beings. Now, many act contrary to this—how could such things constitute great benefit?

"Opening and establishing [the assembly]" briefly indicates the ritual procedures. "Arising that which is extremely difficult to obtain" and below clarifies the basis upon which the giving is performed.
The mind accomplishes the pāramitās. Within the practice of dedication, there are fifteen vows.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives away all necessities of life, his mind is free from greed or attachment and he does not seek karmic retribution.
Having no expectations for worldly wealth or pleasure, he is free from the mind of false conceptualization and skillfully contemplates the Dharma. For...
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he thoroughly contemplates the true nature of all phenomena.
According to the various differences among sentient beings and their respective needs and aspirations, he provides immeasurable means of livelihood;
all his adornments are exquisitely beautiful. He practices boundless giving, practices universal giving, and practices the giving of both internal and external things. He practices...
At the time of this giving, one increases the power of aspiration and joy; one attains great merit and accomplishes the jewel of the mind.
One is always able to protect all sentient beings, causing them all to give rise to supreme vows. From the very beginning, there has never been a thought of seeking recompense.

All roots of goodness are equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and through them, one brings the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) to full perfection. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
The Bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness from this giving to sentient beings, wishing that all sentient beings may be pure and disciplined;
wishing that all sentient beings may eliminate their afflictions; and wishing to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings, with a pure mind, pervade the entire Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment.
May the wisdom of all sentient beings fill the void of space and the Dharma-realm.

May all sentient beings attain all-knowledge, universally entering the three periods of time to tame sentient beings, and at all times constantly turning the pure, non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma. May...
May all sentient beings possess all-encompassing wisdom and be skillfully able to manifest supernatural powers and expedient means to benefit living beings.

May all sentient beings be able to awaken to and enter the Bodhi of all Buddhas, and throughout all future kalpas, constantly proclaim the True Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions without ever resting, so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it. May one...
May all sentient beings, having cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva throughout immeasurable eons,
attain complete perfection. May all sentient beings, in all worlds— whether defiled or pure, small or large, coarse or subtle, inverted or upright,
adorned with a single ornament or various ornaments— be able to expound upon all the worlds as they are described in their respective numbers.

In all realms, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without exception. May all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, constantly perform all the buddha-activities of the three periods of time, teaching and transforming sentient beings toward omniscience.
Sixtieth: The Giving of Requisites. Because it is impossible to exhaustively explain each category through individual doors, at the end all requisites are explained collectively.
The text consists of only two parts: first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication. Since this concludes the preceding section, the final two [of the four] are omitted.
Now, for the first part, there are four sections. The first concerns the freedom from faults at the time of giving, by means of abandoning the mind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
1. Because they are equal. 2. "Well-considered" and below distinguishes the basis of giving. 3. "According to the various assemblies" and below correctly clarifies the practice of giving.
4. "Practicing this" and below reveals the virtues accomplished. Within the subsequent practice of dedication, there are ten vows that provide for many kinds of livelihood;
these vows are also categorized as follows: 1. The vow to give cleansing implements; 2. The vow to give brooms for sweeping.
The Vow for Requisites (*pariṣkāra-praṇidhāna*). Furthermore, since the requisites are explained collectively, the vow is also generated collectively and need not be assigned individually.

O Son of the Buddha! A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva provides all that sentient beings require according to their needs, using such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) things as these, in order to ensure that the Buddha-dharma continues without interruption, universally rescuing all through great compassion.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they abide in great compassion and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva. They never violate the teachings of the Buddha.
Through skillful means, they practice all manner of virtues and do not sever the lineage of all Buddhas.

Granting whatever is requested without weariness or fatigue, they relinquish everything without ever having a moment of regret. Constantly and diligently, they dedicate their merit toward the path of omniscience. At that time...

Beings of various forms and types from the lands of the ten directions, those born in various realms of existence, and all manner of fields of merit, all gather together and come to the Bodhisattva’s abode seeking various things.
Upon seeing them, the Bodhisattva universally perceives and accepts them; his heart gives rise to joy as if seeing a virtuous friend.
With great compassion and pity, he intends to fulfill their wishes; his mind of renunciation increases without ceasing.
He was neither weary nor disheartened; according to whatever they sought, he caused them all to be fully satisfied, thereby freeing them from the suffering of poverty.

At that time, the beggars were filled with great joy and celebration, spreading his virtues far and wide through their praises. His excellent reputation spread to distant lands, and all came to seek refuge in him.
Upon seeing this, the bodhisattva experienced immeasurable joy. Even if one were to experience the pleasures of Śakra for hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta kalpas;
the pleasures of the Yāma heaven for incalculable kalpas; the pleasures of the Tuṣita heaven for immeasurable kalpas;
the pleasures of the Sunirmita-vaśavartin heaven for boundless kalpas; and the pleasures of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven for incomparable kalpas—none of these could be counted.
For incalculable eons he enjoys the bliss of a Brahmā king; for incalculable eons he enjoys the bliss of a wheel-turning monarch ruling over the three thousandfold world system;
for inconceivable eons he enjoys the bliss of the Śubhakṛtsna devas; and for ineffable eons he enjoys the bliss of the Śuddhāvāsa devas—yet none of these can compare [to what follows].
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees a beggar approaching, he feels joy, love, and delight; he exults and leaps for joy as his faith increases.
Their aspiration is for purity; their faculties are harmonious and compliant; their faith and understanding are fully perfected, even progressing toward the bodhi of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates these roots of goodness for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
he dedicates them for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings; he dedicates them so that all sentient beings may attain...
They dedicate for the sake of great benefit; they dedicate so that all sentient beings may attain complete purity;
they dedicate so that all sentient beings may all seek awakening; they dedicate so that all sentient beings may all attain equanimity;
they dedicate so that all sentient beings may all attain a virtuous and wholesome mind.
They dedicate [their merit] so that all sentient beings may enter the Mahāyāna;

they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may attain virtuous and excellent wisdom; and they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may be fully endowed with the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, fulfill the vehicle of the ten powers, and manifest perfect enlightenment.
Third, following the various classes of sentient beings, there is a general summary of the dedication of the roots of goodness across many categories.

Since these specific instances cannot be exhausted individually, they are explained here collectively. This section has two parts: first, the summary of the roots of goodness, which refers to the preceding practice of giving;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the summary of the dedication. Regarding the first part, there are two sections. The first summarizes the objects given, meaning that the objects given by the Bodhisattva are—

It stops at sixty; therefore, it is equalized by means of the *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable). Next, in order to conclude the purpose of the giving, the "Dharma of the Buddha" is used to tie the section together.
Taking the beginning and connecting it to the end constitutes the "purpose" (*prayojana*). If one relies on "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth, these constitute the "basis" (*āśraya*).

However, the "purpose" applies universally to both self and others, whereas the "basis" is that in which one's own mind abides. At the end of the three periods and ten directions, the "ability to give" (*dāna-śakti*) is concluded.
Regarding the mind, there are four points herein: first, generating joy toward many fields of merit and thereby departing from faults;
second, explaining that as the fields of merit become more numerous, the joy becomes increasingly vast, as seen in the passage beginning "At that time, the beggars...";

third, comparing and demonstrating its vastness through the passage beginning "Even if...", which shows that the pleasures enjoyed by ten kings do not equal the joyful mind of a bodhisattva; fourth, the bodhisattva seeing the beggars...
The following section concludes the joy that is vast and deep. What kind of joy does a bodhisattva experience upon seeing a beggar?

It is because their practice of giving has matured and their obstacles to giving have been exhausted. Second, the Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, uses these roots of goodness to conclude the previous dedications;
here, however, he merely concludes the purpose for which they were dedicated, thereby revealing that the preceding individual dedications were not exhaustive.
It emerges from this. The above has completed the general exposition of the practice that accords with signs. Hereafter follows the departure from signs.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner, his actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely liberated;
they are without attachment, without bondage, without the notion of a sentient being, without the notion of a life-principle, and without the notion of a person (*pudgala*).
The perception of a person; the perception of a youth; the perception of a being; the perception of an agent; the perception of an experiencer;
the perception of existence; the perception of non-existence; the perception of this world or the next world; the perception of dying here and being born there;

the perception of permanence; the perception of impermanence; the perception of the three realms of existence; the perception of the absence of the three realms of existence; neither-perception-nor-non-perception—just so.
This is a dedication that is neither bound nor liberated; a dedication that is neither karma nor the retribution of karma;
a dedication that is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; a dedication that is neither thought nor having thought;
a dedication that is neither mind nor being without mind. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, it is called the dedication of the unattached.

Not clinging to the internal; not clinging to the external; not clinging to the subject that perceives; not clinging to the object perceived; not clinging to causes; not clinging to effects; not clinging to phenomena (*dharma*); not clinging to non-phenomena (*adharma*);
not clinging to volition; not clinging to non-volition; not clinging to form (*rūpa*); not clinging to the arising of form; not clinging to the cessation of form;

not clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*); not clinging to the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; not clinging...

The cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can remain unattached to these phenomena, they will not be bound by form, nor bound by the arising of form, nor bound by the cessation of form;

they will not be bound by feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor bound by the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor bound by the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If they can remain unbound to these phenomena in this way—
Thus, one does not understand all phenomena. Why is this? There is not the slightest phenomenon that is currently arising, has already arisen, or will arise;
there is no phenomenon that can be grasped and no phenomenon that can be clung to. The self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is such:
they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are neither one nor two, neither many nor immeasurable, and neither small nor large.
It is neither narrow nor broad; neither deep nor shallow; neither quiescent nor discursive; neither a locus nor a non-locus; neither dharma nor non-dharma;
neither essence nor non-essence; neither existent nor non-existent. When a bodhisattva observes all phenomena in this way, they are seen as non-dharmas.
Within the realm of language, one follows worldly convention to establish what is non-dharma as dharma, without interruption.
Regarding all paths of action, they do not abandon the bodhisattva practice and never regress in their quest for omniscience.
They understand that all karmic conditions are like dreams, sounds are like echoes, sentient beings are like shadows, and all phenomena are like illusions;
yet they do not destroy the power of causes, conditions, and karma. They understand that the function of all karma is vast and comprehend that all phenomena are ultimately without agency.
He practices the path of non-action without ever ceasing for even a moment.

This is the second major section of the text: when the Buddha’s son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner, he performs a dedication that is free from signs (*animitta*), which directly faces the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and accords with *nirvāṇa*. This demonstrates the profundity of his practice. [End of] the preceding section.

The obstruction of practice and the vastness of depth occur simultaneously; it is merely said that they do not coexist. First, the correct elucidation of the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viveka*);
second, the passage beginning "observing in this way" explains how one is not hindered by following characteristics. The initial general statement regarding liberation is the summary:

"Not clinging to liberation, not bound by bondage—this is true liberation. Next, the two [sections] within the detailed exposition: first, because internal conceptualizations of characteristics are severed, there is none...
Bondage and liberation. From the passage "Thereafter, O Son of the Buddha... downwards, because one touches objects while remaining free from defilement, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

First, by the phrase "having no notion of a sentient being," etc., one first severs the notion of a self (*ātman*). Next, by the phrase "having no notion of existence," etc., one severs the notion of phenomena (*dharma*).

Next, by the phrase "In this way, it is not bound," etc., the perfection of practice is revealed. Next, from the passage "When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner," etc., is the second [section].

Because contact with objects is without defilement, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Within this, the statement "not clinging to the internal or external" first clarifies non-clinging, which is to say that the *dhātus* and *āyatanas* are empty.
Next, the statement "not clinging to form (*rūpa*) and so forth" reveals non-clinging to the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Following this, the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, if one can thus... clarifies non-bondage to the aggregates. In this way, the three categories [of *skandha*, *dhātu*, and *āyatana*] have been dispensed with. Next...
If one can [understand this], it clarifies below that they do not understand. If there were originally no bondage, who would seek its resolution?

To abandon bondage while grasping for liberation is still not to be free from bondage; therefore, he again dismisses it. By dismissing it until there is nothing more to dismiss, one becomes suddenly free of reliance, and the principle naturally accords with the profound mystery.
Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" interrogates and explains the reason why [the mind] is devoid of characteristics. First, the intent of the interrogation:
It is asked: "Suppose we provisionally establish that the substance of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not non-existent; yet now there is no attachment to it. What is the reason for this?

The explanation below states that it is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus. That is to say, the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally unarisen; their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is such that they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Next, the passage "neither one nor two" specifically clarifies what is to be relinquished. This means that while the preceding [text] merely stated...
"Detachment. From what phenomena is there detachment? It refers to "one," "two," and so forth. There are ten pairs of phrases in the text.

Next, from the passage "The Bodhisattva observes in this way" onwards, it clarifies that one is not obstructed by following these characteristics. This is because ordinary people, due to their habitual attachments and rigid grasping, encounter words and produce stagnation;

upon hearing of the characteristic of detachment, they believe it contradicts the previous discourse on following characteristics, thereby losing sight of the practice of karmic results and bodhi. Therefore—
To summarize and synthesize this briefly:
O Son of the Buddha, when these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they universally dedicate all that is possible and impossible toward the nature of omniscience.
In every respect, they dedicate everything without ever regressing. For what reason?
It is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It is called dedication because it eternally carries one across the world to the further shore;

it is called dedication because it eternally brings one out of the aggregates (*skandha*) to the further shore; it is called dedication because it carries one across the path of language to the further shore.

It is called dedication because one leaves behind various perceptions and reaches the further shore; it is called dedication because one forever severs the view of a self-identity and reaches the further shore;
it is called dedication because one forever abandons the basis of dependence and reaches the further shore;

it is called dedication because one forever cuts off all conditioned activity and reaches the further shore; it is called dedication because one forever emerges from all states of existence and reaches the further shore.

Because they have forever abandoned all grasping and reached the other shore, it is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Because they have forever transcended worldly phenomena and reached the other shore, it is called dedication.

Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they are then in accord with the abiding of the Buddhas, in accord with the abiding of the Dharma, in accord with the abiding of wisdom, in accord with the abiding of enlightenment, and in accord with the abiding of the ultimate meaning.
The dwelling of conformable dedication; the dwelling of conforming to objects; the dwelling of conforming to practice; the dwelling of conforming to reality; the dwelling of conforming to purity.
Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate in this manner, they thereby fully comprehend all dharmas and serve all Buddhas;
there is not a single Buddha whom they do not serve. There is no... [text ends]
There is not a single dharma that is not to be honored with offerings; there is not a single dharma that can be destroyed; there is not a single dharma that can be contravened;
there is not a single thing to which one may become attached; and there is not a single dharma from which one may feel weary or seek liberation.

One does not perceive even the slightest destruction or decay within any internal or external phenomena, nor do they ever violate the path of dependent origination; for the power of the Dharma is fully perfected and lacks nothing.
Rest. O Son of the Buddha! This is the sixth dedication of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which accords with and strengthens all roots of goodness.
[End of] the third major section. From "This Bodhisattva" onwards, the names of the dedications are explained. First, the general explanation. First, abiding in all...
Wisdom is its own root of virtue, for by means of it one can accomplish the various meanings explained below.

Having already explained the meaning of "equality" and "conformity," the text next provides a specific explanation. For what reason is it called "dedication"? Below, this is raised as a provisional inquiry to explain the meaning of dedication.
Next, from the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dedicates in this way," the text explains "conformity."

This is "conformity to the meaning" (*anuloma-artha*). The intent is that if one can thus dedicate [merit] while remaining free from signs (*animitta*), it naturally conforms to the Buddha-dharma, wisdom, and so forth, because the Buddha-dharma and such are in fact the very essence (*tattva*).
Third, regarding this dedication by the three types of sons of the Buddha, the text next explains the meaning of "making all roots of goodness firm.
One might also raise the following objection: "The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is signless; how then can it be called 'firm'? Truly...

If there is no distinction at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), how can it be called "all"? The intent of this explanation is as follows: only such a dedication that is free from characteristics (*animitta*) is termed "firm.
This is because anything possessing characteristics can be destroyed; therefore, by merely being able to remain free from characteristics, one spontaneously accomplishes all virtues.
This is because all virtues take the limit of reality as their essence. Below, the Buddha says: "This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."

This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s sixth dedication, which accords with and fortifies all roots of goodness. Having explained the name of the dedication, the practice of the higher stage is concluded;
now follows the fruit of the lower stage.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dedication, they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and [their resolve] becomes firm and unshakable.

They do not regress from entering the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). They cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), accord with the meaning of the Dharma, accord with the nature of phenomena, and accord with all firm roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
They accord with all perfectly fulfilled great vows and are fully endowed with the quality of acceding to that which is firm;
they cannot be destroyed by any *vajra*, and they attain mastery over all phenomena.
The second major section clarifies the fruit of the stage when abiding in this dedication; in accordance with the departure from duality, these ten fruits are summoned.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveyed the ten directions, surveyed the assembly, and surveyed the dharma-realm.
One enters into the profound meaning of words and phrases; cultivates an immeasurable and vast mind; universally covers the world with a heart of great compassion;
perpetuates the seed-nature of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; and enters into the merits of all Buddhas.
Having accomplished the body of the sovereign power of all Buddhas, he observes the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings.
According to the degree to which their roots of goodness have matured, he manifests a form-body based on his dharma-nature body. Sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he spoke these verses:
The Bodhisattva manifests his body as a king; among all worldly positions, he is peerless.
His merit and majestic radiance surpass all others, universally bringing benefit to all living beings.
His mind is pure and free from attachment; sovereign in the world, he is honored and revered by all.
He widely proclaims the True Dharma to instruct all people, universally causing sentient beings to attain peace and security.
In his present life, he is born into a noble clan and ascends the royal throne; constantly relying on the Right Teaching, he turns the Wheel of Dharma.
By nature he is compassionate and kind, free from cruelty or tyranny; the ten directions look up to him with reverence, and all follow his transformation.
With wisdom and discernment ever lucid, Endowed with all physical marks and talents,
He governs the entire realm, and none do not obey; Having crushed and subdued the demonic armies until none remain,
He upholds the pure precepts without transgression, Resolute and patient, remaining unshakable.
May I forever vow to eliminate all thoughts of anger and resentment, and always delight in practicing the various teachings of the Buddhas.
With food, drink, incense, garlands, clothing, chariots, horses, couches, mats, seats, and lamps—
may the Bodhisattvas provide these entirely for the relief of others, as well as all other immeasurable varieties.
They practice giving for the sake of benefiting others, causing them to develop a vast and expansive mind;
toward those in exalted positions as well as others, their intentions are entirely pure and they give rise to joy.
These Bodhisattvas provide for all without exception, able to relinquish everything both internal and external.
One must ensure that the mind remains forever pure, never allowing even a moment of narrow-mindedness or inferiority to arise;
whether giving away one's head or eyes, or giving away one's hands or feet,
skin, flesh, bones, marrow, or any other thing— one relinquishes everything with a heart free from stinginess.
The Bodhisattva, dwelling in the rank of a great king, of noble lineage and honored among men, extends his tongue from his mouth as a gift to all living beings;
his heart is joyful and free from grief or attachment.
By virtue of those merits from the giving of his tongue, he dedicates them to all sentient beings.
May all universally rely upon these excellent causes and conditions To fully attain the broad and long tongue of the Tathāgata;
Whether giving away their wives and children or their royal throne, Or offering their own bodies as servants,
Their minds are pure and always joyful, Such that in all these things there is no sorrow or regret.
Whatever they seek, he bestows it all; He provides relief at the proper time without weariness.
He can relinquish everything he possesses, Satisfying all who come to him in search of aid.
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, he gives away his own body, Practicing various austerities in pursuit of Bodhi.
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he relinquishes everything;
seeking supreme wisdom without regressing, he hears the True Dharma from the Buddha.
To universally save all living beings, he personally sacrifices his own body to serve as an attendant, giving rise to a heart of immeasurable joy.
Seeing the World-Honored One, the Great Guide, who is able to bring vast benefit through a heart of compassion,
he then leaped for joy and gave rise to gladness; hearing and receiving the profound flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma,
he dedicated all the roots of goodness possessed by that Bodhisattva toward all sentient beings.
Universally rescuing and protecting all without exception, forever enabling them to attain liberation and eternal peace and joy;
the Bodhisattva’s entire retinue possesses dignified and majestic physical forms and eloquent wisdom.
They are fully endowed with various adornments: flower garlands, garments, and ointments.
These retinues are most rare; the Bodhisattva is able to give them all away.
Solely seeking perfect enlightenment to deliver all beings, he never abandons such a mind for even a moment.
The Bodhisattva reflects with such earnestness and fully practices all manner of vast and great deeds.
Dedicating it all to all sentient beings, they give rise to no mind of grasping or attachment.
The Bodhisattva relinquishes that great royal throne, as well as the kingdom, cities, palaces, towers, pavilions, and gardens;
regarding servants and attendants, he is entirely without stinginess.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he traveled everywhere, bestowing gifts and thereby instructing all living beings;
they were all led to transcend to the shore beyond.
Beings of infinite varieties and distinctions gathered from the worlds of the ten directions and came to rest there.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva’s heart rejoices; he fulfills whatever they lack.
Just as the Buddhas of the three times have dedicated [their merit], the Bodhisattva likewise cultivates such deeds.
Following the conduct of the Honored One who tames men, he studies it all and reaches the other shore.
The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena: who is it that can enter these phenomena? How does one enter?
What is it that is entered? Thus, the Bodhisattva’s mind of giving abides nowhere;
the Bodhisattva dedicates [merit] through skillful wisdom and the methods of dedication.
The Bodhisattva dedicates toward the true meaning; within those dharmas, there is no attachment and the mind does not discriminate among any karmas.
Nor is there defiled attachment to the fruits of karma;
knowing that the nature of bodhi arises from conditions, they enter the profound dharma-realm without opposition.
There is no karma within the body, nor does it abide dependent upon the mind;
through wisdom one understands the nature of karmalessness.
Because of causes and conditions, karma is not lost, yet the mind does not falsely grasp at past phenomena, nor does it crave or cling to future events.
Not dwelling in the present, they thoroughly realize that the three periods of time are entirely empty and quiescent.
These Bodhisattvas have reached the further shore of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Having transcended the worldly stream of birth and death, their minds are humble and ever-pure.
Contemplate thoroughly the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, The twelve bases, and your own body;
Seeking awakening within each of these, Their essential nature is ultimately unattainable.
Do not grasp at the characteristic of the permanence of phenomena, Nor do you cling to the characteristic of annihilation.
The nature of phenomena is neither existent nor non-existent; The sequence of the principles of karma is ultimately inexhaustible.
One does not dwell upon any phenomena, Nor among sentient beings, nor in awakening, Nor within the ten directions, the lands, or the three times; Ultimately, when sought, nothing can be found.
If one can contemplate all phenomena in this way, then it will be as the Buddhas have understood them:
though one seeks their intrinsic nature, it cannot be found; yet the conduct of the Bodhisattva is not in vain.
The Bodhisattva realizes that phenomena arise from conditions and does not contradict any of the paths they practice.
He reveals and explains the tracks of all karmas, desiring to bring all sentient beings to complete purity;
this is the path traveled by the wise, as taught by all Tathāgatas.
By reflecting in accordance with it, one enters the true meaning and spontaneously awakens to attain Bodhi.
All phenomena are without arising and without ceasing; They likewise neither come nor go.

One does not die here to be born there; Such a person awakens to and understands all Buddha-dharmas, Thoroughly penetrating the true nature of all phenomena, Yet remaining free from discrimination regarding that dharmatā.
Knowing that phenomena have no intrinsic nature and are without discrimination, this person skillfully enters the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The dharma-nature pervades all places; all sentient beings, lands, and the three periods of time exist therein without exception, yet no form or characteristic can be apprehended.
All that is realized by all Buddhas is entirely encompassed without exception;
though they teach all phenomena of the three times, such phenomena as these are all non-existent.
As the characteristics of all phenomena pervade everywhere, so too does the Bodhisattva’s dedication.
Thus dedicating [merit] to all sentient beings, may they never regress within the world.
