This is the second section, the *Geya* (Verses). First, the introductory context is stated; then follows the actual verses. There are forty-one verses in total.
The first five verses praise the supporting body (*āśraya*). The subsequent thirty-five verses, beginning with food and drink, praise the practice undertaken based upon that body.
Following this, there are five and a half verses that accord with the subsequent sections, versifying the meanings of "conformity" (*anuloma*) and so forth within the explanation of the names,
while also versifying the fruits of the stages. *The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-Eight.
Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Fascicle Twenty-Nine Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan Commentary on the Meaning by the Monk Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery
The Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Kuang at Fayun Monastery,
clearly elucidating the twenty-fifth chapter on the Ten Dedications, Part Seven:
O Sons of the Buddha, what is the dedication of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that accords with all sentient beings?
The seventh is the dedication that accords with all sentient beings. The prose section also has two parts: first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the stage.

Regarding the first, in citing the text and explaining the name: it is because one benefits [beings] with roots of goodness and an equal mind. "Equal" (等) means impartiality, encompassing both the subject and the object.
The objects to be accorded with are sentient beings who are equal in their lack of marks (*animitta*); the subject that accords with them is the wisdom-mind.
"Shining equally. This derives its name from dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). "Equal" means to accord with. Thus, the *Mūla-karma-sūtra* states:

"By observing that parents, whether good or evil, possess no dual characteristics because they are of a single unified nature, it is called the dedication of observing all sentient beings in accordance with [reality].
Some say that "good and evil" refers to enemies and kin; these two are equal, for both arise within the *dharmakāya*.
All are called "parents. The good parents are skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); the evil parents are ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Since delusion and craving are not extinguished, yet illumination and liberation arise, there is no duality of characteristics. When wisdom accords with this non-duality, it is called the "single integrated mark" (*ekasaṃyuktalakṣaṇa*).
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, according to all the roots of goodness he has accumulated—

namely, small roots of goodness, great roots of goodness, extensive roots of goodness, numerous roots of goodness, immeasurable roots of goodness, various kinds of roots of goodness, roots of goodness as numerous as atoms,
incalculable roots of goodness, boundless roots of goodness, inconceivable roots of goodness, and... [inexpressible roots of goodness]...
The roots of goodness of measure; the roots of goodness of the Buddha-realm; the roots of goodness of the Dharma-realm; the roots of goodness of the Saṃgha-realm;
the roots of goodness of the realm of spiritual friends; the roots of goodness of the realm of all sentient beings; the roots of goodness of the realm of skillful means;

the roots of goodness of the realm of cultivating various virtuous minds; the roots of goodness of the internal realm; the roots of goodness of the external realm; [the roots of goodness of] the non-...
The roots of goodness that take as their object the peripheral factors for aiding the path; the roots of goodness of diligently practicing all forms of relinquishment;

the roots of goodness of establishing supreme resolve and ultimately upholding pure precepts; the roots of goodness of enduring everything without failing to accept it; the roots of goodness of constant vigor with a mind that never regresses;
the roots of goodness of entering immeasurable samādhis through great skillful means; and the roots of goodness of thoroughly examining with wisdom.
Roots of goodness; roots of goodness that know the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings; roots of goodness that accumulate boundless merit;
roots of goodness that diligently cultivate the practices and conduct of bodhisattvas; and roots of goodness that universally cover and nourish all worlds. O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice and abide in these roots of goodness, enter into them, embrace them, accumulate and prepare them, and attain purity of mind through realization;
when they manifest and give rise to them, they attain a mind of forbearance that closes the gates to the evil realms.

They skillfully restrain their sense faculties, are fully endowed with dignified deportment, remain far removed from perversions, and perfect their right conduct, thereby becoming worthy vessels for all Buddhas.

They are vessels of the Dharma, capable of acting as the fertile field for the merit of sentient beings. They are held in the mindfulness of the Buddhas, lengthening the roots of goodness of the Buddhas.

Abiding in the vows of all Buddhas, they perform the deeds of all Buddhas. Their minds attain mastery equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time. They proceed to the Buddha’s place of enlightenment and enter the power of the Tathāgatas.
Possessing the physical marks and signs of a Buddha, they transcend all worlds. They take no pleasure in being born in the heavens; they do not crave wealth or pleasure; they do not cling.
All conditioned phenomena and all roots of goodness are entirely dedicated as a treasury of merit for all sentient beings.
Abiding in the ultimate path, they universally cover all things; they pull sentient beings out from within the path of falsehood and cause them to dwell securely in all wholesome dharmas.
Throughout all realms, they are uninterrupted and inexhaustible, opening the gate of omniscient bodhi and establishing it.
They establish the majestic banner of wisdom upon the pure Great Way, universally manifesting themselves to all worlds to eliminate defilements.

With minds well-tamed, they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas; they purify the Buddha-lineage and are fully endowed with merit. Acting as great fields of merit, they serve as a refuge for the world.
They establish all sentient beings, causing them all to become pure, and constantly and diligently cultivate all roots of goodness.
The second part, the extensive explanation, consists of two major sections. First, the clarification of dedication;

second, the discernment of the benefits accomplished, beginning with the passage: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices such dedication... The first of these also has two parts.

First, the roots of goodness to be dedicated are distinguished; subsequently, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, with pure resolve, gather [these roots] below and are about to dedicate them.
Within the preceding dedication, there are again two parts: first, the actual cultivation of the roots of goodness;

second, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, regarding these roots of goodness below, cultivate and thereby accomplish virtues. It may also be understood that the former is the essence and the latter clarifies the practice.

Regarding the application: the preceding section contains thirty-one phrases, divided into three parts. First, the eleven phrases beginning with "according to what has been accumulated" clarify the extent of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Second, the ten phrases beginning with "the roots of goodness that are the Buddha’s realm" clarify the objective conditions upon which the goodness relies.
Third, the ten phrases beginning with "diligently cultivating all relinquishment of the roots of goodness" clarify the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the roots of goodness. The former...
Eleven: each of these subsumes the subsequent twenty; reflect upon this and it will become clear. Next, the virtues accomplished through cultivation are explained.

First, regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the "Son of the Buddha," the text first restates what has already been cultivated in the section on these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). This passage consists of ten phrases.

Next, the passage beginning with "attaining the capacity for patience" (kṣānti) and spanning five lines of the sutra explicitly reveals the perfection of virtues. Within this, the first section clarifies the virtues of self-benefit;

the text contains ten pairs [of opposites]. Next, the passage beginning with "becoming a treasury of merit for all sentient beings" and spanning five lines of the remaining sutra clarifies the virtues of benefiting others.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a pure mind and the power of the resolve for bodhicitta, cultivates various roots of goodness, they form this thought: "These roots of goodness are accumulated by bodhicitta;
they are contemplated by bodhicitta; they are initiated by bodhicitta; and they are the object of the aspiration of bodhicitta."
This is augmented by the bodhicitta. It is entirely for the sake of compassion for all sentient beings; it is entirely for the sake of seeking all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
it is entirely for the sake of accomplishing the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Tathāgata. When one forms such a thought, roots of goodness increase and one never regresses.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further forms this thought: "May I, by means of these roots of goodness..."
Throughout all future kalpas until the roots of karmic retribution are exhausted, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva,
dedicating them all exclusively to all sentient beings, universally and without exception, vowing that incalculable worlds be filled with precious jewels,
incalculable worlds be filled with clothing, and incalculable worlds be filled with exquisite fragrances.
Incalculable worlds are filled with ornaments; incalculable worlds are filled with immeasurable mani-jewels;
incalculable worlds are filled with exquisite flowers; incalculable worlds are filled with the finest flavors.
Incalculable worlds are filled with wealth and goods; incalculable worlds are filled with couches and seats, canopied with jeweled curtains and spread with exquisite garments;
incalculable worlds are filled with various kinds of adorned jeweled crowns.
Suppose a single person were to constantly come and request these items throughout all future kalpas, and one were to bestow them as gifts upon him. Even so—
Having grown weary, they take rest; as it is with one person, so it is with all sentient beings.

Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives in this manner, they have no mind of hypocrisy, no mind of expectation, no mind for reputation, no mind of regret, and no mind of feverish distress;
they simply give rise to a mind that single-mindedly seeks the path to all-knowledge.
A mind that relinquishes everything; a mind of compassion for sentient beings; a mind that teaches and brings them to maturity;
and a mind that causes all to dwell securely in the wisdom of omniscience. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates their roots of goodness in this way:
throughout all future eons, they constantly practice giving while dwelling in the mind of the wisdom of omniscience. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...

Again, he forms this thought: "For the sake of even a single sentient being, I wish to cause the world-systems of incalculable numbers (*asaṃkhyeya*) to be filled with precious elephants, complete with their seven limbs, of an exceedingly gentle and well-trained nature, upon which golden banners are erected and covered with golden nets, adorned with various exquisite jewels, and which I shall give as a gift.
I vow to cause the world-systems of incalculable numbers to be filled with precious horses."
Like a king of dragon-horses, adorned with various ornaments made of many jewels, he offers them as a gift.
He makes the vow: "May incalculable worlds be filled with female musicians, all capable of performing and playing various sublime melodies, and may I offer them as a gift.
He makes the vow: "May incalculable worlds be filled with men and women, and may I offer them as a gift. May he...
They fill incalculable worlds with their own bodies, resolve upon bodhicitta, and practice giving.
They vow to fill incalculable worlds with their own heads, give rise to a mind of non-negligence, and practice giving.
They vow to fill incalculable worlds with their own eyes and practice giving. They vow to fill incalculable worlds with their own...
With his own body’s flesh, blood, and marrow filling its center, he holds it without any sense of attachment and offers it as a gift.
He vows to fill incalculable worlds with sovereign kingships and offers them as a gift;
he vows to fill incalculable worlds with servants and laborers and offers them as a gift. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with such various things as these, dwells for all future kalpas in a vast mind of universal giving and bestows them upon a single sentient being.
Just as with one sentient being, he bestows them in this same manner upon every sentient being throughout the entire realm of beings.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path in a single world-system for all future kalpas.
He practices by giving such things as these to a single sentient being, and likewise provides for all sentient beings until they are all fully satisfied.
As it is in one world, so it is in all worlds throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm;
his great compassion covers all universally without ever ceasing, and he universally bestows pity, providing whatever each requires.
He makes offerings, ensuring that his practice does not cease even when encountering adverse conditions, nor does he give rise to a mind of weariness for even the duration of a finger-snap.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices giving in this way, he gives rise to these states of mind:
namely, the unattached mind, the unbound mind, the liberated mind, the mind of great power, the profound mind, the well-restrained mind, and the non-grasping mind.
A mind free from the notion of a self; a well-tamed mind; an undistracted mind; a mind free from false conceptualization; a mind endowed with the nature of various jewels;
a mind that does not seek karmic retribution; a mind that thoroughly understands all phenomena; a mind abiding in the great dedication of merit; a mind that skillfully resolves all meanings;
a mind that causes all sentient beings to abide in unsurpassed wisdom; a mind that gives rise to the light of the Great Dharma; entering...
The mind of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Second, regarding the section on gathering [merit] for dedication, the first five lines of the sūtra clarify that one should dedicate by recollecting the causal dharmas that are the roots of cultivating virtue.
Next, within the major section on dedication, there are three parts: first, dedicating toward sentient beings and toward bodhi...
[The Buddha] said: "Furthermore, when a son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dedicates [merit] in this way, he does not cling to karma;

this clarifies dedication toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Thirdly, 'Sons of the Buddha, by means of these roots of goodness, they universally bestow them upon the world'—this concludes the three types of dedication.
Regarding the first: dedicating one's own virtues and vows to become requisites in order to bestow them upon the multitude."
[The section on] "Generating [the Resolve]. The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects thus:

'May I, by means of these roots of goodness, [dedicate them as follows]'... Below this, two lines and more of the sūtra first provide a general manifestation of the essential aspiration; next, they clarify the actual practice. First is the vow to accomplish external giving (*bāhyadāna*).
This passage consists of four sections. The first begins: "May it cause the jewels of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds... below which follow five lines.

Other sutras reveal the vastness of giving because it extends through each *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa. Next, the two lines of scripture beginning with "Suppose there were one person who, until the end of future kalpas...
distinguish the boundlessness of giving, as it involves long durations, many fields of merit, and being insatiable in accordance with requests.
Third, the three lines of scripture beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when giving in this manner... clarify the excellence of giving, as it is free from faults and accords with principle.
Fourth, it is said: "O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas take all roots of goodness from the preceding section and consolidate them into two practices.

That is to say, through the practice of dedication, they accomplish the practice of giving. The former accomplishes external giving; the latter, through the power of vows, accomplishes internal giving.
This passage consists of four sections. First: 'O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas further act as follows...'"
Below the "Recollection" (念) section, there are twelve lines of scripture that clarify the vastness of giving by addressing a single field (*kṣetra*).

This means that giving to all sentient beings constitutes many acts of giving, because each [sentient being] is as numerous as the *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas]. Second, from "The Bodhisattva, by such means as these...

onwards, one case is used as an example for the rest to demonstrate that the giving is limitless. Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva, in a single world-system... onwards, the location is cited as an example.
The section on "Bases" summarizes the meaning of these practices; there are six infinities: first, the object; second, time; third, the mind; fourth, the field; fifth, the gift; and sixth, the basis.
Following the passage on "Great Compassion," the conclusion establishes the activities performed, which encompass these six infinities.

From the line "When the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, give in this way" onwards, five lines of scripture reveal the excellence of giving, its freedom from faults, and the virtues it accomplishes, consisting of twenty mental states.

The first [verse] cites what precedes to introduce what follows; the subsequent section below correctly elucidates the point. Through nineteen moments of mind, one accomplishes the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) endowed with seven excellences:
namely, the first six moments of mind constitute the excellence of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); the next five moments of mind constitute the excellence of purity (*viśuddhi*);
the next three moments of mind constitute the excellence of abiding (*sthiti*); and the final two moments of mind constitute the excellence of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).
The first is the excellence of aspiration, which is the excellence of intention, meaning that one feels compassion for all beings.
The latter two mental states constitute the excellence of the basis, as they rely upon the bodhicitta.

Having concluded the first part—dedicating one’s own virtues to become the requisites for enlightenment—the second part of the text below concerns dedicating these [virtues] so that the masses may be fully endowed with both material wealth and the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates the roots of goodness he has accumulated in this manner with every thought-moment.
That is to say: may all sentient beings have abundant wealth and treasures, lacking nothing;
may all sentient beings achieve an inexhaustible treasury of great merit; and may all sentient beings be fully endowed with all forms of peace and happiness.
May it be joyful! May all sentient beings increase the karma of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
May all sentient beings fulfill immeasurable, supreme, and foremost dharmas. May all sentient beings attain non-retrogression in the vehicle of omniscience.
May all sentient beings universally behold all Buddhas of the ten directions.
May all sentient beings forever be free from the defilements and dust of worldly delusions. May all sentient beings attain a pure and equanimous mind.
May all sentient beings leave behind all places of hardship and attain all-knowledge. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, like...
At the time of this dedication, one generates a mind of joy for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and peace;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain a mind of equanimity; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in a mind capable of relinquishment;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in a mind of universal giving; for the sake of causing all sentient beings...
Because they abide in a mind of joyful giving; because they cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving that is forever free from poverty;
because they cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving all material wealth;
because they cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving immeasurable material wealth; and because they cause all sentient beings to abide in universal and boundless giving.
Because of the mind of universal giving; in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of uninterrupted giving throughout all future kalpas;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving that relinquishes everything without regret or affliction;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving that relinquishes all requisites for life; in order to cause one...
Because all sentient beings abide in a mind of conforming generosity; because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of inclusive generosity;
because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of vast generosity;

because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving offerings of immeasurable ornaments through renunciation; and because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to abide in non-attachment.
Because of the mind of giving: in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the mind of impartial giving;

in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving with the supreme power of a vajra; in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving with the radiance of the sun;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving that gathers the wisdom of the Tathāgata; and so forth.
In order to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the retinue of roots of goodness;

in order to cause the roots of goodness and wisdom of all sentient beings to be constantly present before them; in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the perfection of an indestructible pure mind;
in order to cause all sentient beings to accomplish the most supreme and pure roots of goodness; in order to cause one—
In order that all sentient beings may attain awakening from the sleep of afflictions;
in order to cause all sentient beings to eliminate all doubts and delusions; in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the pure merit of equal wisdom;
in order to cause the merit of all sentient beings to be perfected so that it cannot be destroyed; in order to cause one...
Because all sentient beings are endowed with the pure and immovable samādhi; in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the indestructible knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to fully accomplish the immeasurable, pure, and supernatural powers of a bodhisattva;
in order to cause all sentient beings to cultivate and accumulate roots of goodness free from attachment; in order to...
Because all sentient beings contemplate all Buddhas of the past, future, and present with a pure mind;
in order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure and supreme roots of goodness;

in order to cause all sentient beings to eliminate all obstructive dharmas that hinder the Path created by actions in various places; and in order to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with unimpeded purity.
Because it is the dharma of impartial merit; so that all sentient beings may, with a vast mind, constantly mindfulness of all Buddhas without weariness or negligence;
so that all sentient beings may always draw near to all Buddhas and diligently make offerings to them;
and so that all sentient beings may extensively open all gates of wholesome roots and universally perfect all pure dharmas.
In order to cause the immeasurable mind, the vast mind, and the supreme mind of all sentient beings to be entirely pure;
in order to cause all sentient beings to achieve a mind of pure and equal giving;
in order to cause all sentient beings to uphold the śīla-pāramitā and other perfections of all Buddhas so that they are pure; and in order to cause all sentient beings to attain great endurance.
Because of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and remain forever without indolence;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in immeasurable meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and be able to give rise to various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom (*jñāna*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to know the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) which realizes that all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For...
In order to cause all sentient beings to perfect the boundless pure dharma-realm;
in order to cause all sentient beings to fully accomplish all pure roots of goodness of the supernormal powers;

in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in impartial conduct and accumulate wholesome dharmas until they are entirely perfected; and in order to cause all sentient beings to skillfully enter into all Buddhas.
Because its sphere of influence is entirely pervasive; in order to cause the physical, verbal, and mental karma of all sentient beings to be universally purified;
in order to cause the karmic fruits and retributions of the wholesome deeds of all sentient beings to be universally purified;

in order to cause all sentient beings to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena and thereby attain universal purification; and in order to cause all sentient beings to thoroughly comprehend the true meaning and thereby attain universal purification.
Because of purity: in order to cause all sentient beings to cultivate all supreme practices for universal purity;
in order to cause all sentient beings to fulfill all great vows of bodhisattvas for universal purity;
in order to cause all sentient beings to realize all merit and wisdom for universal purity; in order to cause all sentient beings to achieve...
Because they dedicate all roots of goodness of the same essence so that the vehicle of omniscience may be universally perfected;
because they desire to cause all sentient beings to adorn and purify all Buddha-lands so that they may be universally perfected;
because they desire to cause all sentient beings to see all Buddhas without attachment so that they may be universally perfected; and because they desire to cause all sentient beings...
Because he is fully adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence, which are universally perfected;

because he causes all sentient beings to obtain the sixty kinds of vocal tones, so that their speech is truthful and worthy of trust and acceptance, and because he causes them to be adorned by hundreds of thousands of kinds of dharmas, thereby perfecting the Tathāgata’s unimpeded merit of wondrous voice; and because he causes all sentient beings to achieve...
Because of the unimpeded and impartial mind adorned with the ten powers;
in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the inexhaustible light of the Dharma and all eloquence of all Buddhas, universally and perfectly fulfilled;
in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the supreme, fearless lion’s roar of the heroes among men; in order to cause all sentient beings to attain all...
Because he turns the irreversible and inexhaustible wheel of Dharma through wisdom;

because he causes all sentient beings to understand all phenomena and to reveal and expound them in universal perfection; because he causes all sentient beings to cultivate pure and wholesome dharmas at the proper time in universal perfection;
and because he causes all sentient beings to achieve the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma of the Teacher.
Because they are equally pure; in order to cause all sentient beings to universally fulfill the single adornment, the immeasurable adornments, the great adornments, and the adornments of all Buddhas;
in order to cause all sentient beings to equally enter and pervade all realms throughout the three periods of time;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to be able to travel to and visit all Buddhas.
Because there is nowhere throughout all lands where they do not hear and receive the True Dharma;

because they cause all sentient beings to attain the benefit of wisdom and become honored by the world as equals to the Buddhas; because they cause all sentient beings to know all phenomena through omniscience, achieving universal perfection;
and because they cause all sentient beings to perform unshakable karma and attain the fruit of non-obstruction. Everywhere...
Because it is perfected; so that all sentient beings may cause all their faculties to attain supernormal powers and thereby know the faculties of all sentient beings;
so that all sentient beings may attain undifferentiated, equal wisdom and be universally purified within the dharma of the single characteristic;
and so that all sentient beings may never contradict the principle in any virtuous [deed].
Because they are fully endowed with all faculties; in order to cause all sentient beings to clearly penetrate all the sovereign supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas;
in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the inexhaustible merit and wisdom of all Buddhas, such that their merit and wisdom are entirely equal;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta and understand all dharmas.
Because it is equal, of one mark, and without deficiency; because it causes all sentient beings to thoroughly understand the True Dharma as the supreme virtue and field of merit in the world;
because it causes all sentient beings to achieve impartial and pure great compassion as a field of great power for all donors;
and because it causes all sentient beings to become firm and foremost, such that none can [overcome them].
Because it prevents destruction; because it ensures that all sentient beings who behold it will certainly receive benefit and be unable to overcome it;
because it causes all sentient beings to fulfill the most supreme mind of equanimity;
because it enables all sentient beings to skillfully comprehend all phenomena and attain great fearlessness; and because it causes all sentient beings to emit a single ray of light.
Because it clearly illuminates all worlds throughout the ten directions;
because it causes all sentient beings to universally cultivate the diligent practice of all bodhisattvas without weariness or regression;

because it causes all sentient beings to universally fulfill all vows of practice through a single vow of practice; and because it causes all sentient beings to universally hear [the Dharma] with a single sublime voice.
Because all may attain liberation; because it is to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the pure mind of all bodhisattvas;
because it is to cause all sentient beings to universally encounter all spiritual friends and receive their guidance;
and because it is to cause all sentient beings to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and subdue sentient beings without ceasing.
To cause all sentient beings to possess wondrous eloquence and fully manifest all sounds, extensively expounding the Dharma according to their capacities without interruption;
to cause all sentient beings to be able to know all minds with a single mind through the equal dedication of all roots of goodness;
and to cause all sentient beings to always delight in accumulating all roots of goodness and to establish them therein.
For the sake of pure wisdom in sentient beings; in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the body of pure merit and wisdom of omniscience;
in order to cause all sentient beings to skillfully know the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, observe them, and dedicate them so that they may be universally accomplished;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to attain omniscience and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.

Because it is universally perfected: to cause all sentient beings to attain the wisdom of fully endowed supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), such that by manifesting in one place, they manifest in all places;

to cause all sentient beings to attain the wisdom of universal adornment, such that by adorning and purifying one assembly, they adorn and purify all assemblies; to cause all sentient beings, regarding...
Because in one buddha-field, all buddha-fields are universally perceived;

because it causes all sentient beings to adorn all buddha-fields with every kind of ornament—unspeakable ornaments, immeasurable ornaments, and inexhaustible ornaments—pervading them everywhere; and because it causes all sentient beings, in a single...

Because it is able to definitively resolve the profound meaning of all phenomena; because it causes all sentient beings to attain the supreme and foremost sovereign supernormal powers of all Tathāgatas;
because it causes all sentient beings to attain the sovereign supernormal powers of all merits that are neither identical nor different;
and because it causes all sentient beings to be fully endowed with all equanimities.
Because they universally use these roots of goodness to consecrate the crowns of all Buddhas;
and because they cause all sentient beings to fully attain the pure body of wisdom, becoming the most honored and supreme among all states of existence. O Son of the Buddha!
In this way, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas compassionately benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them all to be purified and to remain far removed from stinginess and envy.

They experience supreme and wondrous bliss; they possess great majestic power and virtue; they give rise to profound faith and understanding; they are forever free from anger and all obscurations and turbidity;
their minds are pure, upright, gentle, and supple; they are devoid of flattery, crookedness, delusion, and folly;
they practice the path of renunciation with firmness that cannot be destroyed; their mind of equanimity never regresses; and they fully achieve and perfect the power of pure, white dharmas.
Skillfully dedicating merit without affliction or loss, they constantly cultivate correct practice to subdue sentient beings, extinguishing all unwholesome karma.
They practice asceticism with all roots of goodness and further exhort sentient beings to engage in cultivation, causing them to fully undergo all sufferings for the sake of all conscious beings.
With the eye of great wisdom, they observe these roots of goodness and know them all to be...
Its nature is wisdom. It employs skillful means to dedicate [merit] to all sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may fully abide in the state of all pure merits;
so that all sentient beings may be able to embrace all roots of goodness and know the nature and meaning of all merits; and so that all sentient beings may universally purify...
For the sake of all roots of goodness; so that all sentient beings may plant various wholesome dharmas within the sphere of the field of merit with a mind free from regret;

so that all sentient beings may universally be able to embrace all other sentient beings, leading each and every one toward omniscience; and so that all sentient beings may universally gather in all that is to be gathered.
Because each and every root of goodness is associated with an impartial dedication. Furthermore, one dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:
namely, vowing that all sentient beings may attain ultimate peace; vowing that all sentient beings may attain ultimate purity;
vowing that all sentient beings may attain ultimate bliss; and vowing that all sentient beings may attain ultimate...
Liberation! May all sentient beings ultimately attain equality. May all sentient beings ultimately achieve thorough understanding.
May all sentient beings ultimately abide securely in all pure and wholesome dharmas. May all sentient beings obtain the unobstructed eye.
May all sentient beings skillfully harmonize their minds. May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the ten powers.
To subdue sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they do not cling to karma;

they do not cling to its retribution; they do not cling to the body; they do not cling to material things; they do not cling to buddha-fields; they do not cling to directions; they do not cling to sentient beings;
they do not cling to the absence of sentient beings; they do not cling to all phenomena; and they do not cling to the absence of all phenomena. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
When the Bodhisattva thus dedicates [merit], he bestows these roots of goodness universally upon the world, making this vow: "May all sentient beings fulfill the Buddha-wisdom;
may they attain a pure mind and clear, lucid wisdom; may their inner minds be tranquil and remain unmoved by external conditions;
and may they increase and perfect the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices dedication in this manner.
At that time, he transcends all and none can surpass him; though all the words and expressions of every world were used together to praise him, they could never exhaust his virtues.

He universally cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva, is able to travel to all buddha-fields, perceives all Buddhas everywhere without obstruction, and is likewise able to see all the bodhisattvas in all worlds.
Their conduct consists of using skillful means to analyze the profound words and meanings of all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having attained *dhāraṇī*, they expound the sublime Dharma without interruption throughout all future kalpas.
For the sake of sentient beings, in every thought-moment, throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds, they universally manifest their bodies like reflections to make offerings to all [Buddhas].
The Buddha, in every thought-moment, adorns and purifies unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands,
causing them all to be universally pervaded by the wisdom of practicing the purification of Buddha-fields without ever feeling weary or satisfied. In every thought-moment,
he causes unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings to attain purity, accomplishment, equanimity, and fulfillment regarding all of those [Buddha-lands].
In all lands, they diligently cultivate all the *pāramitās*, gather in sentient beings, and accomplish pure karma.

They attain unimpeded ears and, in each and every Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-worlds, they hear, receive, uphold, and practice with diligent application, never giving rise to a single thought of abandonment. They abide therein...
The bodhisattva’s supernormal power is without attainment, without reliance, without activity, and without attachment.

In a single moment, or even in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, they manifest bodies that travel everywhere to unspeakably many Buddha-worlds, seeing them all as equal to those of the other bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva conduct in this way, they are still able to bring it to full completion.
Immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable pure merits cannot be fully exhausted even by recollection and praise, let alone the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi. All buddha-fields are equally pure;
all sentient beings are equally pure; all bodies are equally pure; all faculties are equally pure; all...
The equality and purity of karmic results; the equality and purity of all assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
the equality and purity of all perfected practices; the equality and purity of the wisdom of skillful means regarding all phenomena;
the equality and purity of the dedication of all vows of the Tathāgatas; the equality and purity of the spheres of supernormal power of all Buddhas. The Buddha...

Son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates [merit] in this way, they attain the dharma-gate of pure joy in all virtues, adorned by the perfection of immeasurable merit. When dedicating in this way, sentient beings do not conflict with all buddha-fields;
buddha-fields do not conflict with all sentient beings; buddha-fields and sentient beings do not conflict with karma; and karma does not conflict with buddha-fields or sentient beings.
Birth does not contradict volition; volition does not contradict the mind; volition and the mind do not contradict the objective realm; the objective realm does not contradict volition and the mind.
Karma does not contradict retribution; retribution does not contradict karma. Karma does not contradict the path of karma; the path of karma does not contradict karma.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not contradict characteristics; characteristics do not contradict nature. The arising of phenomena does not contradict nature; the nature of phenomena does not contradict arising. The lands...
The equality of equanimity does not contradict the equality of sentient beings. The equality of sentient beings does not contradict the equality of buddha-fields.
The equality of all sentient beings does not contradict the equality of all phenomena. The equality of all phenomena does not contradict the equality of all sentient beings.
The equality of the limit of detachment does not contradict the equality of all sentient beings abiding in peace. All...
Sentient beings abide in equanimity that does not deviate from the limit of detachment. The past does not deviate from the future; the future does not deviate from the past;
the past and future do not deviate from the present; and the present does not deviate from the past and future.
The equality of the world does not deviate from the equality of the Buddha; the equality of the Buddha does not deviate from the equality of the world. This is the practice of the Bodhisattva.
It does not contradict all-knowledge; all-knowledge does not contradict the bodhisattva practice.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates in this way, they attain equality of karma, equality of retribution, equality of body, equality of skillful means, equality of vows, equality of all sentient beings, and equality of all buddha-fields. They attain...
They attain equality in all conditioned phenomena. They attain equality in omniscience. They attain equality with the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
They attain the service of all Buddhas. They attain the making of offerings to all Bodhisattvas. They attain the planting of all roots of goodness. They attain the fulfillment of all great vows.
They attain the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings. They attain the thorough knowledge of all karma. They attain the service of...
One makes offerings to all spiritual friends; one gains entry into all pure assemblies and maṇḍalas; one attains thorough penetration of all correct teachings;
and one achieves the fulfillment of all wholesome dharmas.
The second cycle is the dedication of practice, which aims to cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with wealth and the Dharma. This major section is divided into three parts:
first, the dedication through compassion; second, "Furthermore, he exhorts the assembly" and below, the dedication of things;
third, "Furthermore, with all roots of goodness, dedicating them in this way," and below, the ultimate dedication. Now, for the first: it says, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva..."
Having accumulated roots of goodness, the following section clearly elucidates the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). First, there is a general statement; then, the ten vows are specifically revealed.

The first vow concerns the abundance of wealth, because it consists of the giving of material things (*āmiṣadāna*); the remaining vows all possess the Dharma, because they accumulate the foundation of virtue.

Next, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dedicates in this way," the purpose of the dedication is clarified. This begins with a formal citation, followed by an explanation according to the meaning.
This is explained separately. Within this section, there are one hundred and ten sentences in total. The text is divided into two parts:

the first seventy-two sentences establish the sequential progression (*pan-pu*) from the cultivation of causes to the attainment of the fruit; the latter thirty-eight sentences establish the perfect fusion (*yuan-yong*) whereby the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.

These two being mutually unimpeded constitutes the intent of dedication. Furthermore, the former represents the stage of self-maintenance (*zi-fen*), while the latter represents the stage of superior advancement (*sheng-jin*).

The preceding section on the distribution [of the teachings] is divided into six parts. The first, intended to cause all sentient beings to descend [into the path], consists of fourteen lines of scripture and twenty-one phrases.
It is for the purpose of causing them to practice the conduct of those at the head of the noble ranks within the happy realms; however, it exclusively clarifies the practice of giving (*dāna*).

At the end, the phrase "the practice of giving that encompasses the wisdom of the Tathāgata" refers to illuminating the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*) and being free from all conceptual discrimination.
Because they are identical to bodhi. Second, the ten phrases beginning with "in order to cause all roots of goodness" refer to the practice within the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*);
the spiritual lineage is precisely the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*). Third, the ten phrases beginning with "in order to cause all sentient beings... [refer to the subsequent stages].

This causes the completion of the practice during the stage of "Practice through Understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). The tenth [verse] mentions "immeasurable," which refers to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

The arousal of the mind of understanding occurs within the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), because it involves the arousal of the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). The fourth [section] consists of ten phrases beginning with "for the sake of causing all sentient beings to achieve purity.
This causes the completion of the practice of the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) during the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*). The fifth is for the sake of...
The ten phrases beginning with "the bodily, verbal, and mental karma of all sentient beings" refer to the practice within the stage of attaining equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

therefore, each contains the word "universal" (*sarva*). The eleven phrases beginning with "to cause all sentient beings to be endowed with the primary and secondary marks" refer to the conduct within the stage of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the sixty kinds of voice, the *Śāstra* (Commentary) explains them as sixty-four sounds.
Because sound possesses eight case-roles (*vibhakti*): namely, the nominative, accusative, instrumental, ablative, dative, genitive, locative, and vocative;
these are the eight case-roles, each possessing specific qualities, namely: being harmonious, supple, clear, easy to understand, free from error, and free from the defects of being weak or feeble.
Vast and profound, the eight eights comprise sixty-four kinds.

The second section, consisting of thirty-eight phrases beginning with "to cause all sentient beings to be able to proceed," clarifies the practice of perfect integration (*yuanrong xing*), wherein the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
This passage is divided into four parts. First, ten phrases cause sentient beings to fulfill their causal practices within the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Second...

The ten phrases following "in order to cause all sentient beings to thoroughly comprehend the True Dharma" are intended to bring about the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Second, regarding the phrase "the great field of the Dharma": it means that by planting even a small root of goodness therein, one is able to destroy great delusions.
Third, from the eight phrases beginning with "fully possessing all the pure minds of Bodhisattvas."
This causes the causal practices within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to reach fulfillment.

The ten phrases following "causing the attainment of all-knowledge and the realization of equal and perfect enlightenment" cause the fruit of Buddhahood to reach fulfillment. The third section below concludes these benefits.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus feels compassion... onwards, it connects the preceding with what follows. Next, it says "all... [and so forth].

The section beginning with "causing purification" specifically reveals the characteristics of the benefits; it consists of thirteen phrases that manifest two kinds of births and encompass all virtues.
The first three phrases manifest a superior and sublime birth: two phrases represent the cause and one phrase represents the result.

"Purification" refers to observing the precepts and thereby receiving a human or celestial body. "Being free from stinginess" refers to practicing generosity and thereby attaining great wealth and status among humans and celestials. These constitute human and celestial wealth and status.
This is the "Excellently Sublime Birth," which possesses great majesty and virtue. The subsequent ten phrases reveal the "Birth of Merit.

As for the "Birth of Merit," it refers to the definitive path to victory. To possess great wealth and status among gods and humans while lacking faith, understanding, and so forth, does not constitute the "Birth of Merit.
The above concludes the dedication of compassion; the following text further exhorts sentient beings to practice it.
In the second section on "Exhorting Beings to Dedicate," the middle part first causes compassion and wisdom to proceed together so as to accomplish dedication;

next, it clarifies the intent of dedication for those below. This passage contains six phrases. Third, through the phrase "dedicating all roots of goodness in this manner," it concludes with ultimate dedication.
Thus ends the first major section: dedicating [merit] to the bodhi of sentient beings.
The second major section of the text: "When the Son of the Buddha thus dedicates [merit], he dedicates it to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

First, he restates the preceding [section] regarding following after signs; next, with the words "not clinging," he correctly reveals the departure from signs. The text contains ten phrases in five pairs.
"Not clinging to all phenomena" means that one realizes the emptiness of phenomena. "Not clinging to the non-existence of all phenomena" means that even emptiness is empty.

Therefore, in the third major section, "The Son of the Buddha: When a Bodhisattva Dedicates in This Way," the following summarizes the three kinds of dedication. This follows closely from what precedes it;
that is, while the former is free from signs (*animitta*) yet not obstructed by following signs (*nimitta*), this concludes the preceding text at a distance.

"Universally bestowing upon the world" is dedication to sentient beings; "vowing to bring about the attainment of Buddhahood" is dedication to enlightenment (*bodhi*); [and] "attaining purity... [is dedication to the Dharma].
"Purifying the lower" refers to dedicating [merit] toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), thereby accomplishing the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This concludes the summary of the capacity for the three types of dedication. This marks the end of the first section—explaining dedication—in the preceding general overview and detailed exposition.
The second major section of the text below explains the accomplishment of benefits; that is, the vast merit accomplished through this practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

This section is divided into four parts. First, from the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva practices such dedication," and extending for fourteen lines of scripture, it clarifies the vast merit of the causal stage.
Second, "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus practices... [and so forth].

1. Cultivating the merit of purity in the lower stages of fruition. 2. Third, O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus dedicates [merit], this clarifies the virtue of mastery that accords with conditions.
3. Fourth, O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus dedicates [merit], they attain the equality of karma;

this clarifies the virtue of the equality of the exhaustion of marks. The first two sections concern benefiting according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter two sections concern being free from characteristics.
Furthermore. First, within the text, it first restates the time when the benefit is accomplished, showing that this benefit is realized precisely at the time of correct practice.
Next, from "surpassing" onwards, the actual manifestation is shown; there are twelve phrases, the first two of which are general, while the subsequent ten are specific manifestations.
Following this, from "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva practices in this way," onwards, the pure virtues of the resultant stage are clarified. First...

The current state is now set forth as appropriate: if the virtues of the preceding causes are already thus inexhaustible, how much more so must the virtues of the resulting fruit be; how could they ever be measured?
Next, the ten phrases beginning with "All Buddha-fields are equal" provide a pre-emptive explanation of the characteristics of that which is to come.

This refers to the manifestation of the fruit; briefly stated, there are these ten. The first six present the complete and perfect characteristics of the fruit, while the latter four cite the causes to manifest the fruit. That is to say:

This fulfillment of the fruit results from the perfection of the cause. When the third son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, thus dedicates [merit], he eliminates contradictions regarding the quality of mastery (*vaśitā*).

This initial summary has two intentions: first, it summarizes the preceding section; second, it introduces what follows. The first [intention] concerns the accomplishment of the qualities of the fruit.
The virtues of the fruition are boundless; what has been stated above cannot exhaust them. Therefore, it is said that "all merits are pure.

Second, this concludes the general summary of cause and effect, having finished [explaining] how they benefit according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, wishing to clarify that attaining benefits according to characteristics entails the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vinirmukta*), it is summarized as:
"attaining all merits" up to "perfectly adorned. Because of this, there is no contradiction.

...is equal. Next, there are four sections for correctly clarifying the reconciliation of contradictions. First, within the section on the non-contradiction of phenomena with phenomena (*dharmadharmāvirodha*), there are three sub-sections.
First, at the time of such dedication, sentient beings do not contradict all lands and so forth; herein there are eleven pairs.

The first six pairs clarify the non-contradiction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāvirodha*). The subsequent two pairs, beginning with "the nature of phenomena does not contradict," clarify the non-contradiction of phenomena and principle (*dharmatattvāvirodha*).

Contradiction. The equality of the three lands does not contradict the [preceding] three pairs below. There is no contradiction between principle and principle; there is no contradiction when the three dharmas above are compared with one another.
Next, the passage beginning with "The past does not contradict the future" (one and a half lines of scripture) clarifies that there is no contradiction across the ages.
"The equality of the three times" below refers to the absence of contradiction regarding the dharmas of time. Fourth, "Bodhisattva practice does not contradict... below.
In terms of cause and effect, there is no contradiction. The four characteristics are exhausted in the virtue of equality. The text consists of two sections.
First, when a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva, thus dedicates [merit], he attains the equality of karma. Initially, he attains the benefit of the equality of detachment from signs;
subsequently, from the passage "serving all Buddhas" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the benefit of not destroying various signs. The extensive explanation is now complete.
Below, based on the commentary, the title is explained.
"O Son of the Buddha! This is the seventh dedication of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which accords with and conforms to all sentient beings.
The preceding section, which comprehensively clarifies the practices of the stages, is now complete. Below, the fruits of the stages are elucidated.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish this dedication, they are able to crush all Māras and enemies;
they extract the thorns of desire and attain the bliss of renunciation. Abiding in non-dual nature, they possess great majesty and virtue to rescue and protect sentient beings.
As kings of merit with unimpeded spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), they travel to all lands and enter the state of cessation. Possessing all bodies, they bring about enlightenment.
In the practice of *sādhana*, they attain mastery of mind over all practices and vows; they discern and fully understand all phenomena (*dharma*);
they are able to manifest universally in all Buddha-fields; they attain unimpeded ears to hear all sounds within all fields;
they attain the eye of pure wisdom to behold all Buddhas without ever for a moment turning away from them; and their minds achieve roots of goodness in all spheres of experience.
There is no high or low. Regarding all phenomena, they attain non-apprehension.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness accordingly to all sentient beings in this manner.
The second major section distinguishes the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the distinction between "accomplishing benefit" (*siddhi-hita*) and "attaining fruit" (*phala-prāpti*):

accomplishing benefit refers to the process within the stages, while attaining fruit refers to the completion of those stages. There are twenty-one phrases; the first restates what preceded, and the last summarizes the whole.

The nineteen intermediate phrases are subsumed under nine fruits. The first is the fruit of severing defilement (*saṃkleśa-prahāṇa-phala*), which consists of vanquishing Māra and his adversaries—meaning the cessation of adverse conditions—and uprooting [afflictions].

1. The fruit of severing the causes of evil through the desire [to do so]. 2. The fruit of realization and entry, which is the direct realization of the bliss of liberation and abiding in the realization of non-duality as the cause.
3. The fruit of benefiting others, which possesses great majestic power and is thus the cause for protecting sentient beings.

4. The fruit of internal and external transcendence, referring to internal virtues and external applications. 5. The fruit of unimpeded application toward all lower realms and tranquility. 6. [The sixth...]
1. The vast fruit of all lower vows and aspirations; 2. The fruit of the distinction between lower wisdom and supernormal powers; 3.
The fruit of attaining unhindered mastery over lower vision and hearing; 4. The fruit of fulfilling lower cultivation regarding all objects.
Of these, the former is accomplished while the latter is not attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Whatever meritorious deeds the Bodhisattvas perform— Subtle, vast, profound, and far-reaching—
even those practiced for but a single thought-moment, They are all able to dedicate toward the boundless."

Whatever means of sustenance the Bodhisattvas possess are of every variety, abundant and beyond measure—hundreds of millions of fragrant elephants and precious horses yoked to chariots; their clothing and treasures are all exquisite and wonderful.
Or they offer their heads, eyes, hands, and feet; or they give their own flesh, marrow, and bones.
Pervading all throughout the immeasurable lands of the ten directions, they universally bestow [merit] so that it fills them all;
all the virtues cultivated throughout immeasurable eons are entirely dedicated for the sake of rescuing and liberating all living beings, their minds never regressing until the very end.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the supreme practice of dedication,
universally bringing peace and happiness to the three realms and causing all to attain the unsurpassed fruit.
The Bodhisattva universally gives rise to impartial vows, in accordance with the pure karma they have accumulated.
I dedicate it all as a gift to all living beings; such a great vow I shall never abandon.
The Bodhisattva’s power of aspiration is limitless and unimpeded, embracing all worlds.
Thus dedicating to all living beings, I have never for a moment abandoned the mind of discernment.
May all sentient beings possess clear and lucid wisdom; May their generosity and observance of precepts be entirely pure;
May they practice with diligence, never wearying or ceasing;
With such great vows, may Bodhisattvas dedicate their merit to reach the other shore And universally open the sublime gates of the pure Dharma.
Their wisdom is equal to that of the Two-legged Honored One;
having attained the ultimate realization of the true meaning through discernment, they have mastered the speech of Bodhisattvas. Their various forms of wisdom are likewise so;
they preach the Dharma according to principle without obstruction, yet their minds remain unattached therein.
Always regarding all phenomena as neither dual nor non-dual,
and being free from both duality and non-duality; knowing that these are all merely the path of speech,
and that all worlds are entirely equal— there is nothing that is not the mind, speech, or all karma.
Sentient beings are like illusions and have no reality; All karmic retributions arise from this.
Whatever exists within all the worlds, The various retributions are each different;
None are not accomplished by the power of karma. If karma is extinguished, they all come to an end.
The Bodhisattva observes all worlds, In which the actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely equal;
He causes sentient beings likewise to abide in equality, Just like the peerless, Great Holy One.
The Bodhisattva dedicates all his virtuous deeds To cause the physical forms of all sentient beings to be pure.
Fully endowed with merit and skillful means, equal to the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men,
may the Bodhisattva benefit all living beings; dedicating the entirety of this ocean of merit,
may his majestic radiance transcend the world and he attain a body of courageous and great power.
May all the merits I have cultivated cause the world to be universally pure;
As the Buddhas are pure and peerless, so too are sentient beings pure.
The Bodhisattva attains skillfulness in meaning And is able to know the most supreme Dharma of all Buddhas.
By dedicating these through various skillful means, may all beings come to understand that all phenomena are empty like the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva;
may they realize that all worlds are non-existent,
devoid of creation or a creator, yet that the karmic retribution of sentient beings is never lost.
All phenomena are quiescent, yet not [inherently] quiescent; Free from these two, one knows with a discerning mind that such discrimination is a worldly view.
Entering the stage of right determination, all discrimination is exhausted;
Such true children of the Buddhas arise from the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and Transformation-body.
He is able to thus skillfully dedicate [merit], whereby all doubts and delusions in the world are completely extinguished.
The second section, consisting of twenty-one verses in *śloka* meter, is divided into three parts: first, eleven verses praising the dedication;

second, nine verses praising the accomplishment of benefit; and third, one verse concluding with praise. Within the first part, there are two sub-divisions; the first half-verse praises the object [of dedication].
The dedication of roots of virtue. The remaining verses summarize this dedication; therein, it is divided into three parts.
First, the first three and a half verses summarize the dedication of one’s own cultivated virtues, wishing them to become requisites for giving to sentient beings.

Second, the next five verses summarize the further dedication of this giving, wishing that sentient beings may be fully endowed with the wealth of the Dharma. Third, [the section beginning with] "The Bodhisattva’s words... [and so forth].
The two verses [from] the *Gāthā* praise the dedication to the *bhūtakoṭi*. The section beginning with "Knowing all worlds" praises the accomplishment of benefit. This consists of three parts:
first, the two initial verses praise the vastness of the causal virtues; next, the five verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva contemplates" praise the purity of the resultant virtues.
Subsequently, the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that the characteristics of the two following verses are entirely equal. Following this, the three subsequent verses provide a concluding eulogy.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang.
The Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Kuang at Fayun Monastery, during the Ming Dynasty,
extracted [this section] from the twenty-fifth chapter on the Ten Dedications, Part Six:
"O Sons of the Buddha, what is the dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva characterized by True Suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā)?"
The eighth is the dedication of the mark of true thusness (*tathatā*). In the prose section, the practice of the stage is explained first, followed by the fruit of the stage.

Within the former, the name is designated; as for the explanation of the name: roots of goodness combine to form the dedication. The name is established based on its support (*āśraya*), and its meaning extends to both the agent and the object.
Therefore, the *Mūla-karma* states: "It constantly illuminates the two truths of existence and non-existence; all phenomena are a single unified mark."
Therefore, if the Sanskrit original were complete, it would read: "The dedication of the characteristics and the intrinsic nature of True Suchness.

Here, "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the qualities (guṇa-lakṣaṇa), and "nature" (svabhāva) refers to the essence (tattva-svabhāva). Because these two are neither identical nor separate, they are mentioned together;

yet, for the most part, the qualities are emphasized, as their very nature is constituted by the seal of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-mudrā). What distinguishes this from what precedes and follows is that, in the seventh assembly, phenomena are directed toward principle.
Therefore, it is called "equality. This clarifies that when phenomena are exhausted, principle manifests; thus, practice is identical to suchness.
The ninth [section] clarifies arising from essence to function, and the tenth clarifies that function is identical to essence, and essence is identical to function.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses clear and lucid right mindfulness, and his mind dwells firmly therein.
Free from delusion, he practices with single-minded devotion; his profound resolve is unshakable as he accomplishes indestructible karma. He advances toward omniscience, never turning back.

Aspiring to seek the Mahāyāna with courage and fearlessness, they plant the roots of all virtues to bring universal peace to the world. Giving birth to superior roots of goodness, they cultivate pure and wholesome dharmas.
Their great compassion increases and their jewel-like mind achieves fulfillment; they constantly keep the Buddhas in mind and uphold the True Dharma.
With firm faith and joy in the bodhisattva path, they accomplish immeasurable, pure, and wondrous roots of goodness;
they diligently cultivate all merits and wisdom to become masters who give rise to the many wholesome dharmas for sentient beings, dedicating them through the skillful means of wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva surveys with the eye of wisdom all roots of goodness, which are immeasurable and boundless. Regarding these roots of goodness, at the time they are being cultivated—
whether in seeking their conditions, in preparing them, in purifying them, in entering into them, in applying diligent effort,
in initiating practice, in attaining clear realization, in exercising precision, or in revealing them— all such things possess various gateways and varieties.
Various objects, various characteristics, various matters, various divisions, various practices, various names,
various discriminations, various origins, and various cultivations— all the roots of goodness contained therein are established by a mind directed toward the vehicle of the Ten Powers;
they are all dedicated toward omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), being solely [for that purpose].
There is no duality. One dedicates all roots of goodness in this way: namely, the vow to attain the cultivation of bodhisattva practices through a perfectly complete and unimpeded physical karma;
the vow to attain the cultivation of bodhisattva practices through a pure and unimpeded verbal karma;
the vow to achieve the establishment of great perfection through unimpeded mental karma; and the vow to attain a perfectly complete and unobstructed mind that purely cultivates all things.
Regarding the practices of all Bodhisattvas: may they give rise to a mind of immeasurable and vast generosity to provide for all infinite sentient beings;
may they attain mastery over the mind regarding all dharmas and manifest the great light of the Dharma that nothing can obstruct;

may they attain clear penetration into the sphere of all-knowledge and resolve upon the bodhicitta to universally illumine the world; and may they maintain constant right mindfulness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Contemplate the Tathāgata as ever present before you. May you dwell in the perfection of superior aspiration and resolve.
May you remain far removed from all māras, enemies, and adversaries. May you attain stable abiding in the wisdom of the Buddha’s ten powers.
May you universally gather in sentient beings without ceasing, and may you attain samādhi to travel through all worlds, remaining unstained by the world. May you abide in all worlds...
May there be no weariness throughout the realms; may the teaching and transformation of sentient beings never cease.

May I give rise to immeasurable wisdom born of reflection and skillful means to accomplish the inconceivable path of a bodhisattva. May I attain the wisdom that is not deluded regarding all directions and be able to fully distinguish all worlds.
May I attain the power of wisdom regarding sovereign spiritual paths, such that within a single thought-moment, I may adorn them all.
I vow to purify all buddha-fields. I vow to universally enter into the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and perceive that all worlds are entirely pure.
I vow to give rise to non-discriminative wisdom and, within a single field, enter into all fields.
I vow to manifest all manner of adornments of every field and to teach and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. I vow...
Within a single buddha-field, they manifest the boundless dharma-realm; it is likewise for all buddha-fields.
May they attain the wisdom of great supernormal powers of mastery, so as to be able to travel everywhere to all buddha-lands.
O Son of the Buddha, by means of their various roots of goodness, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas vow to adorn all buddha-lands and vow to pervade all worlds.
Realm. May I attain the accomplishment of wisdom-observation. Just as I dedicate for my own person, so do I dedicate for all sentient beings.
That is to say: may all sentient beings forever leave behind all realms of hell-beings, animals, and the Lord of Death (Yama);
may all sentient beings eliminate all karma that constitutes obstacles; may all...

May sentient beings attain a universal mind and impartial wisdom. May all sentient beings, toward both enemies and kin, embrace them with equanimity, bringing them all to peace and happiness and purifying their wisdom.
May the wisdom of all sentient beings be perfected, and may their pure light shine everywhere.
May the wisdom born of reflection of all sentient beings be fully accomplished, realizing the ultimate truth. May all...
Sentient beings, through their pure resolve, seek enlightenment and attain immeasurable wisdom. May all sentient beings be able to universally manifest the abode of peace and security.

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly dedicates with a virtuous mind in this way, in order to cause all sentient beings to encounter the cool clouds and rain down the rain of Dharma; in order to cause all...

Because sentient beings constantly encounter the supreme field of merit; in order to cause all sentient beings to be able to skillfully enter the treasury of the bodhicitta and maintain it for themselves;
in order to cause all sentient beings to be well-established by leaving behind all hindrances and entanglements;
in order to cause all sentient beings to obtain unimpeded supernormal powers and wisdom; in order to cause all...
Because sentient beings attain bodies of mastery that manifest universally;
because they cause all sentient beings to accomplish the most supreme knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), so that universal benefit may arise without being in vain;

because they cause all sentient beings to universally gather all categories of beings and bring them to purity; and because they cause all sentient beings to be able to ultimately realize all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).

In order to cause the minds of all sentient beings to be unshakable and free from obstruction, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva may see delightful lands, gardens, groves, trees, grasses, flowers, fruits, famous incenses, exquisite garments, rare jewels, wealth, and various articles of adornment;
or they may see pleasant villages, towns, and settlements; or they may see the majesty and virtue of kings themselves.

Abiding there, he may see a dwelling place free from all clamor and distraction. Having seen this, through the wisdom of skillful means, he diligently practices and cultivates, giving rise to immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous merits.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he earnestly seeks wholesome dharmas with a mind free from negligence.
He extensively gathers all manner of goodness, like a great ocean, universally covering all things with inexhaustible virtue for the sake of the multitude of good deeds.
Regarding the locus upon which the Dharma relies: through the skillful means of dedicating all roots of goodness, one remains free from discrimination.
One reveals immeasurable varieties of roots of goodness; with wisdom, one constantly observes all sentient beings, and the mind perpetually recollects the realm of roots of goodness.
By means of roots of goodness that are equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*), one dedicates them to sentient beings without ceasing. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
At that time, one dedicates all roots of goodness in this way: namely, may all sentient beings attain the delightful vision of all Tathāgatas;
may they see the true nature of phenomena as perfectly equal and impartial, free from grasping and attachment, and completely pure.
May all sentient beings behold all Tathāgatas and perform most delightful and perfect offerings.
May all sentient beings be reborn in all pure Buddha-fields that are free from afflictions and most delightful.
May all sentient beings attain the vision of the most delightful Dharma of all Buddhas. May all sentient beings always joyfully protect and uphold it.
May all bodhisattvas practice what is delightful. May all sentient beings obtain the eye that delights in spiritual friends and see them without obstruction.
May all sentient beings always behold all delightful things without opposition.
May all sentient beings realize all delightful dharmas and diligently protect and uphold them. May...
May all sentient beings attain pure light within the delightful dharmas of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings cultivate the various bodhisattva practices of renouncing all that is dear and cherished.
May all sentient beings attain fearlessness and be able to expound all delightful dharmas. May all sentient beings attain the supreme... of all bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings attain the most delightful and profound samādhi. May all sentient beings attain the most delightful dhāraṇī-gates of the bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings attain the most delightful wisdom of thorough investigation of the bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings be able to manifest the most delightful sovereign supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas. May one...
May all sentient beings be able to proclaim the delightful, profound, and wondrous Dharma within the great assemblies of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings be able to skillfully reveal and expound upon the most delightful and diverse phrases.
May all sentient beings always be able to give rise to the most cherished and joyful impartial great compassion.

May all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, give rise to the most cherished and joyful mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and may their faculties always be filled with joy and gladness.
May all sentient beings be able to enter the most cherished and joyful families of all Tathāgatas. May...
May all sentient beings attain the practice of delightful subjugation, subduing sentient beings without ceasing.
May all sentient beings attain the most delightful and inexhaustible eloquence of all bodhisattvas to expound upon all dharmas.
