May all sentient beings, throughout unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, abide in all that is delightful.
Throughout the worlds, they teach and transform sentient beings with minds free from weariness or fatigue.
May all sentient beings, through immeasurable skillful means, universally be able to awaken to and enter the most delightful Dharma-gates of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings attain delightful and unimpeded skillful means, knowing that all phenomena have no fundamental basis. May all sentient beings attain...
They delight in the limit of freedom from desire; they know that all phenomena are ultimately non-dual and sever all obscurations.
They vow that all sentient beings may attain the delightful limit of freedom from desire and realize the equal and true nature of all phenomena.
They vow that all sentient beings may fully perfect all the most delightful, non-conceptual dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings attain the vajra-treasury mind of diligence and accomplish the delightful path of omniscience.
May all sentient beings possess delightful and unimpeded roots of goodness, subduing all enemies that are the afflictions.
May all sentient beings attain the delightful gateways of omniscience and manifest throughout the world.
Attaining perfect enlightenment, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates such roots of goodness, they obtain the light of wisdom and are sustained by spiritual friends.
The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shines brightly upon their mind, forever extinguishing the darkness of ignorance as they diligently practice the True Dharma.
They enter into all intellectual activities, skillfully train in the stages of wisdom, and spread forth their roots of goodness until they are fully perfected.
The Dharma-realm: through wisdom, one dedicates [merit] to exhaustively reaching the very source and bottom of all bodhisattvas' roots of goodness;
through wisdom, one enters deeply into the ocean of great skillful means, thereby accomplishing immeasurable and vast roots of goodness.
In the second major section, the detailed explanation, there are three parts. First, the dedication according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvartinī pariṇāmanā*).
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of these roots of goodness... onwards, the dedication free from characteristics (*alakṣaṇā pariṇāmanā*).
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner... onwards, the benefits achieved through the dedication. Regarding the first:
This section is divided into two parts: first, the accumulation of merit and its dedication; second, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dedication when seeing inferior objects of contact.
Within the first part, there are also two sections: first, clarifying the essential nature of the practice to be dedicated;

second, at that time, the Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom gathers [the merit] below and is about to dedicate it. Now, for the first: "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva possesses clear and lucid right mindfulness."
This explains the accumulation of the provisions (*sambhāra*). The text contains ten phrases. The first is general, referring to "right mindfulness being firm and clear.

The remaining nine are specific. The first three phrases concern right mindfulness directed toward *bodhi*. "Distant from delusion" means the sense of clarity; "practicing with focused intent" constitutes right mindfulness.
Right mindfulness is concentration (*samādhi*), while clarity is wisdom (*prajñā*); thus, concentration and wisdom are practiced in union.
It is the source of the Way. Second, because it accords with principle and is immovable, it is called the "profound mind. Since conditions cannot obstruct it, it accomplishes indestructible karma;
this is steadfast abiding in one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Seeking Buddhahood without regressing is steadfast abiding in superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).

Next, the four lines concern right mindfulness for the transformation of beings. The first line is the general summary: courageously seeking universal salvation for the sake of the Great Dharma. The following three lines...
There are distinctions. First, the simultaneous application of compassion and wisdom serves to clarify *prajñā* (wisdom) and acts as the foundation for all virtues.

Second, advancing in goodness and eliminating outflows constitutes right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Third, the increase of compassion and the perfection of wisdom constitute firm abiding. Regarding the latter two [categories], there is right mindfulness toward the Three Jewels:

first, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, protection of the Dharma; and third, faith in the Saṅgha. "Right mindfulness" occurs in the preceding line, while "firmly established" corresponds to the subsequent phrase. This is the reflection.
This is a brief summary. This constitutes the essence of the dedicatory practice for the accumulation of provisions. Next is the accomplishment of the qualities of the immeasurable lower dedication.
The text contains four phrases; the first three conclude the preceding section. It is called "immeasurable" because it does not merely consist of ten [qualities].
Two or three [points] unify and encompass these [virtues], which do not transcend merit, wisdom, and great compassion. The final phrase concerns the dedication performed after rebirth;
the subsequent text summarizes what is to be dedicated. It says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva, with the eye of wisdom, universally observes...
This first provides a general heading for the observation of roots of goodness. Next, "Those various roots of goodness... specifically reveals them. Finally, "In this way, all... provides a summary.
Because there are many categories and gateways, it is called "various. There are ten phrases in the text, which refer to the many distinctions among the conditions sought previously.
Next, the section beginning with "Among these... concludes the original intent of the practice; since the original intent is thus established, how could one not dedicate [the merit]?
The preceding section generally clarifies the essence of the acts to be dedicated, while the following section correctly clarifies the dedication itself. First, the dedication:
Bodhi. Second, dedication for the sake of sentient beings. The Sūtra says: "Dedicate all roots of goodness in this manner. This first refers to the dedication toward Bodhi.
The text contains twenty vows, which are divided into three parts. The first ten vows are the aspiration to accomplish the practice of wisdom; these constitute the cause and fruit of Bodhi.
The subsequent vows, beginning with "attaining samādhi," and the following four vows, concern the universal benefit of sentient beings; these constitute the transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karma*).

Regarding cause and effect: the three vows beginning with "attaining mastery over supernatural powers" and the six subsequent vows constitute the cause and effect of universally adorning the Buddha-field, which is the Pure Land.
The preceding section generally dedicates [merit] toward Bodhi; the following section states that "the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, by means of all roots of goodness...
and so forth, dedicating it toward sentient beings. First, the previous [vows] are cited to introduce what follows; next, the object of the vow is all sentient beings.
This gives rise to the explicit teaching on dedication. The text contains eight phrases. The first two phrases express the vow to be free from the three obstacles;

the term "obstacle" here carries the dual sense of hindrance and affliction (*kleśa*). The next four [phrases] establish the four wisdoms (*jñāna*). The final two [phrases] conclude with the two fruits;

since these are not limited to the four wisdoms alone, they are described as "immeasurable. Following this, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva always, with this mind... and so forth.
The *Eightfold Practice Sūtra* summarizes the purpose [of the preceding]. Above, the section on the accumulation of merit and its dedication has been concluded.
Below, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a delightful land... onwards, the second part clarifies the dedication upon encountering objects.

This is largely equivalent to the *Pure Conduct Sūtra*’s practice of making vows in response to encountered objects. Within this, there are five parts; first, "seeing what is delightful," etc., enumerates the objects.
1. Seeing the object. 2. Having seen these matters and below, observing the object to accomplish virtue; that is, increasing compassion and wisdom. 3.
"With all roots of goodness" and below, a general explanation of dedication, which is also the merit of dedication. 4. "At that time, the Bodhisattva" and below, a specific explanation of dedication.
5. "O Son of the Buddha" and below, the benefits accomplished through dedication. The first three are understandable. Now, the fourth is explained specifically.

In the section on the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), the first sentence provides a general heading. It refers back to what was stated in the preceding section on the cultivation of practice, namely:
"Dedicating all roots of goodness through skillful means. Since it was not yet known what the characteristics of such dedication are, it says: "At that time, dedicating in this manner.

The subsequent section, beginning with "That which is called," provides a specific explanation. This explains the phrase "in this manner" by showing that there are thirty-one vows, each of which states "to cause... [the following].

It is attained. Regarding the phrase "lovely and desirable": it refers to the arising of lovely and desirable wholesome states through seeing lovely objects, and the aspiration to accomplish lovely and desirable virtues.
The commentary (*śāstra*) explains this with multiple meanings.

Next, from the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas cultivate such roots of goodness," the fifth section concerns the benefits accomplished by dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This text contains ten phrases, which are subsumed into five pairs to manifest the four [aspects].
The benefits are as follows: First, through the influence of causes upon conditions, internal wisdom becomes clear and one is externally sustained by spiritual friends;

this is the benefit of removing obstacles. Second, through the influence of conditions upon causes, one is externally graced by the illumination of insight while internally extinguishing the darkness of delusion; this is the benefit of learning. Third, through diligent cultivation, one enters the activities of the three types of wisdom;
this is the benefit of clarity in learning. Fourth, through the realization of superior learning, one’s own excellence universally suffuses all; this is the benefit of realization and entry. Fifth...

Exhausting the source of all excellent merit, one enters the ocean of true wisdom. This constitutes the benefit of the two adornments and serves as the foundation for advancing toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because one penetrates it through ultimate wisdom, the preceding section on following appearances is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner: namely, by not clinging to the world, not grasping at sentient beings,
with a mind that is pure and without dependence, maintaining right mindfulness of all phenomena while remaining free from discriminatory views,
never abandoning the sovereign wisdom of all Buddhas, and not contravening the correct dedication of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Gate. They accord with all equal and true dharmas, not destroying the true mark of the Tathāgata.

They contemplate the three periods of time as equal, being free from the mark of a sentient being, and skillfully follow the Buddha-way. They skillfully expound the Dharma and deeply understand its meaning. They enter the most supreme stage and awaken to the true Dharma.
Their wisdom is perfected and their faith and joy are firm. Although they skillfully cultivate right action, they know...
The nature of karma is empty. One realizes that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; one knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
One contemplates all meanings and various activities, conforming to worldly conventions of speech without attachment.

One eliminates all causes and conditions for clinging and knows the reality as it is. One contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is entirely quiescent and realizes that all phenomena are identical.
First, the mark of reality: knowing that the marks of all phenomena do not contradict one another; dwelling together with all bodhisattvas;
practicing their path and skillfully gathering in sentient beings; entering the gate of dedication of all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present;
having no fear or alarm in one's mind regarding the teachings of all Buddhas; and causing all sentient beings to attain universal purity through an immeasurable mind. Regarding...
In the worlds of the ten directions, they do not give rise to the mind that grasps at "self" or "what belongs to self.

They make no conceptual distinctions regarding the various worlds and do not produce defiled attachment toward any objective realm. They diligently cultivate all supramundane dharmas and have neither grasping nor reliance toward any worldly things.
Their right view regarding the profound and wondrous path is firm and stable; they are free from all false views and realize the truth.
Dharma.
The second major section: Dedication Free from Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-parāvṛtti*). This differs slightly from the preceding dedications.

Previously, there was a greater emphasis on subsuming characteristics back into their nature (*dharmatā*), with little focus on arising characteristics based upon that nature. Now, this primarily manifests the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa-avyāghāta*) as the basis for [dedication].

Because it is the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), the preceding heading all refers back to the time of following after the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, it is not necessary to correlate this with what preceded to establish its non-obstruction;
therefore, the word "time" is absent. The text is divided into two parts: first, a direct explanation of the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

second, from the analogy below, a detailed analysis in contrast to suchness. Regarding the first part, there are again two sections: first, practice in accordance with suchness; second, from "As the dharmas of all Buddhas... onwards.
Following the benefit of suchness: at the beginning, one practices the simultaneous application of śamatha and vipaśyanā, without clinging to existence or non-existence.

The text states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way, namely, without clinging... This first section clarifies that śamatha pacifies false grasping without contradicting essence and function.
Next, it says: "Equally contemplating the three periods of time... This clarifies the contemplation of emptiness and existence; faith and wisdom are both perfected.
The first phrase contemplates true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in order to skillfully accord with the subsequent contemplation of wondrous existence (*prajñapti-sat*).

The following statement, "Although one skillfully cultivates right action, one knows that the nature of action is empty," clarifies the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real. The first phrase establishes the thesis; it takes non-obstruction as its thesis.
Next, one realizes that all phenomena are like illusions, sharing the same analogy; for the nature of an illusion is that while it has a form, its substance is empty.

Next, one knows "all [phenomena]" and below, which applies the analogy and sets forth the underlying cause. The cause is stated as: because they are produced by conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Next, the passage beginning with "toward the Buddha-dharmas, the mind is without alarm or fear" describes the benefits of conforming to suchness (*tathatā*). This text contains ten phrases arranged in five pairs, which...
The four minds become increasingly firm: 1. Above, one dwells in the profound Dharma; below, one purifies sentient beings.

This is the vast mind (*vaipulya-citta*). 2. The notions of self and other do not arise, and worldly views are utterly severed. This is the non-perverted mind (*aviparyāsa-citta*). 3. One is unstained by sense objects and diligently practices for the supramundane.
4. One does not rely on the mundane world, and the right path alone remains firm. The first two [of these four] constitute the first mind, which is non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*).
Because *nirvāṇa* is supreme, these five false views are stilled. Realizing that the true substance is identical, it is the eternal mind;

because of this compassion of identical substance, one never abandons it. The above has directly addressed dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); the second [section] provides a detailed analysis in contrast to the *Tathāgata*.

This section of text concerns the dedication according to suchness (*yathābhūta-pariṇāmanā*). First, the outline of the meaning is presented. This section is briefly analyzed by means of five gates. First, the explanation of the names:
"True" (*zhen*) means reality, indicating that it is not false or illusory; "Suchness" (*ru*) means as-it-is, signifying the absence of change.

This is the interpretation of the Dharma-character school (*dharmalakṣaṇa-vāda*). If one follows the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-vāda*), they say: "Unchanging is True," and "Conforming to conditions is Suchness."
The first is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Because it is unchanging, it is not identical with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
because it conforms to conditions, it is not different from conditioned phenomena. The second is called "category" (*jāti*). It may be one, two, three, seven, or even ten;
these various types of categories are explained individually in the commentaries. The third is the discernment of virtuous functions, which refers to the first...

First, as the basis and support; second, as the object for the cultivation of contemplation; and so forth, up to the three greatnesses (*mahattva*) and so on, as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*, all of which manifest the functions of its virtues.
Fourth, regarding the differences in doctrinal interpretation, one may infer them through reflection. Fifth, concerning the commentary on the text:

although there have been numerous ancient commentaries on these "One Hundred Gates," the present sub-commentary does not adopt them; rather, it shall proceed by means of the ten categories (*kośa*), correlating them with the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
1. "As it is" (*tathatā*), being initially full, pervading all, and characterized by signlessness (*animitta*) and so forth, refers to the meaning of the pervasive *tathatā*.
2. Among the two [meanings], that which cannot be measured and has no counterpart refers to the meaning of the supreme (*parama*). 3.

Among the three [meanings], being unimpeded regarding phenomena and serving as the eye for all phenomena refers to the meaning of the excellent outflow (*srotas*). 4. Among the four [meanings], non-attachment, non-abiding, and so forth refer to the absence of grasping (*anupādāna*).
Regarding the meaning of "receiving": among the five [aspects], being ultimately inexhaustible and without change is the meaning of "no distinction in category.

Among the six, having no parts and a nature that is unarisen is the meaning of "no distinction between defilement and purity. Among the seven, being omnipresent and abiding in both existence and non-existence is the meaning of "the dharma has no parts.
Among the eight, the nature is pure and the nature is equal is—
The meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing: that which pervades all phenomena within the nine [categories] is the Buddha’s realm, which is the meaning of mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
That which abides in all stages (*bhūmi*) and accomplishes all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth within the tenth [category] is the meaning of mastery over action (*karma-vaśitā*).

The remaining meanings therein may be inferred by analogy. They are revealed individually according to each stage (*bhūmi*), yet only ten aspects (*tathatā*) are taught, as each stage possesses them all.

These ten times ten make one hundred, intended to reveal that the virtues of *tathatā* are immeasurable and boundless. Before the stages, they are cultivated universally; at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they are fully equalized;

and the Tathāgata realizes them to their ultimate limit. The meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) here refers to initiating practice in accordance with *tathatā*, the essence of which is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

However, although people believe in the virtue of suchness (*tathatā*), they still remain deluded regarding the virtue of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, the virtue of suchness is used as a metaphor for the virtue of dedication.
If one takes the literal meaning of the text: "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) means that the essence and characteristics of true suchness pervade all places;
because the roots of goodness dedicated [to it] are like suchness, they likewise pervade all things without limit. Within each of the hundred gates, there are two phrases; the former is...
The "virtue of that which is common" refers to the virtue of the lower roots of goodness being able to equally dedicate [merit]. The first part outlines the structural meaning;
the second part provides an exegesis following the text.
For example, just as True Suchness (tathatā) pervades all places without limit or boundary, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It pervades all places without limit or boundary. Just as true suchness (tathatā) has reality as its nature, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā).
It understands that all phenomena have reality as their nature.
Just as true suchness constantly maintains its original nature without change, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness maintain its original nature from beginning to end without alteration.
For example, just as true thusness (tathatā) has the naturelessness of all phenomena as its nature, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it realizes that all phenomena have naturelessness as their nature. For example, just as true thusness has signlessness as its characteristic, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it realizes that all phenomena have signlessness as their characteristic. For example, if there were anyone who could attain true thusness...
There is ultimately no regression. The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: whoever attains it will never regress from the teachings of all Buddhas.
Just as True Suchness (tathatā) is the sphere of activity for all Buddhas, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness the sphere of activity for all Tathāgatas.
Just as True Suchness is free from the marks of objective spheres (viṣaya-lakṣaṇa), so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.

Yet it functions as an objective sphere (*viṣaya*). The dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*) is likewise: free from the characteristics of an objective sphere, it functions as the perfected sphere of all Buddhas of the three times.
Just as True Suchness (*tathatā*) is able to establish [all things], the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise:
it is fully able to establish all sentient beings. Just as the nature of True Suchness is eternally compliant, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: it continues unceasingly in accordance with [conditions] throughout all future kalpas.

Regarding the first ten phrases of the commentary: the first section reveals that [the nature] is present within conditions; therefore, there is nothing that is not pervasive. Second, it clarifies that because it is unchanging, it is called "real.
Third, it clarifies that because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it is said to "constantly maintain its original nature. Fourth...

5. Showing its nature (*lakṣaṇa*). These five [points] are explained exclusively in terms of the "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*). The next two are explained in relation to wisdom (*jñāna*), and thus they constitute the object of wisdom.
8. It reveals that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not an object, yet it is taken as an object;

this is because one must forget all objects in order to accord with the object that is Suchness, for the fundamental nature of Suchness is non-conceptually-constructed (*aprajñapti*). 9. This refers to the conceptually-constructed Suchness. 10. This refers to...
Regarding the meaning of "as usual": in the following ninety sections, ten items shall constitute one gate in succession.
For example, just as True Suchness (tathatā) cannot be measured, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā);

it is equal to the realm of empty space and the minds of all sentient beings, such that none can measure it. For example, just as True Suchness pervades all things, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is likewise thus: within a single kṣaṇa, it universally pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) is eternally abiding and inexhaustible, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it is ultimately inexhaustible.

12. Regarding "pervading all": this means that whether it be form or mind, large or small, and so forth—even down to the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) and the momentary (*kṣaṇika*)—all are fully perfected, for they are not merely partially filled.
Just as true thusness has no counterpart, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:
it is universally able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas without counterpart.
Fourteenth, regarding the peerless counterpart: because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not coexist with falsehood.
For example, just as the essential nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is firm and solid, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

its essential nature is firm and solid, incapable of being thwarted by any afflictions or delusions. For example, just as true suchness cannot be destroyed, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is likewise so. No sentient beings can destroy it;
the fifteen afflictions cannot destroy it; and the sixteen types of persons cannot destroy it.
Just as true thusness has illumination as its essence, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, for it universally illuminates.
And this constitutes its nature.
Seventeenth: quiescent yet ever-illuminating; wisdom is the functioning of suchness.
For example, just as true thusness (tathatā) is omnipresent, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā) in all places.

There is nothing that is not pervaded by it. Just as true thusness (tathatā) is omnipresent throughout all times, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā) omnipresent throughout all times.
Just as the nature of true thusness is eternally pure, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness eternally pure.
Abiding in the world yet with a fundamentally pure body—just as true thusness (tathatā) is unimpeded regarding all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it circulates everywhere without obstruction. Just as true thusness serves as the eye for all phenomena, so too does this dedication.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so; it can serve as the eye for all sentient beings.
Since, as the twenty-second [point], its essence is illumination, why would it lack the eye that gazes?
For example, just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from weariness, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

one constantly practices all the various bodhisattva deeds without ever becoming weary. For example, just as the essence of *tathatā* is profoundly deep, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
its nature is profoundly deep. For example, just as *tathatā* does not possess a single thing, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is also thus. One thoroughly knows that its nature is such that not a single thing exists.
Just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) does not manifest, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; its essence is subtle and difficult to perceive.
Just as *tathatā* is free from all defilements and obscurations, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness. The eye of wisdom is pure and free from the obscurations of ignorance.
For example, just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) has no equal, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it accomplishes all bodhisattva practices in a manner that is supreme and peerless. For example, just as the essence of *tathatā* is quiescent, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is well able to accord with the dharma of quiescence. For example, just as *tathatā* has no root, [so too is the dedication of roots of goodness].
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so: it is able to enter into all dharmas that are without root.
As for what is meant by "without root," it is because there is nothing prior upon which to rely; it is precisely because there is no fundamental basis for abiding.
For example, just as the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is boundless, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*).
It purifies sentient beings in numbers that are boundless. For example, just as the essence of true suchness is unattached, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is ultimately free from all attachments. Just as true thusness (tathatā) is without obstruction, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it eliminates all worldly obstructions. Just as true thusness is not within the sphere of worldly activity, so too is this dedication.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus; it is not something that can be practiced by those in the world.
Just as the essential nature of true suchness (tathatā) is non-abiding, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; all of birth and death are not places where it dwells.
For example, just as the nature of true thusness (tathatā) is without activity, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā).
One completely relinquishes all that is done. For example, just as the essence of true thusness abides in tranquility, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It abides in reality. Regarding the thirty-seventh point, "abiding":
because it abides in reality by way of non-abiding—just as true thusness is in common conjunction with all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
They are in accord with all bodhisattvas through hearing, practicing, and cultivation.
Just as true suchness is eternally equal in nature within all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness. They cultivate the practice of equanimity toward all worlds.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) is not separate from all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it does not abandon the world until the end of the future limit. Just as true thusness is ultimately inexhaustible among all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is inexhaustible in its dedication toward all sentient beings.
Forty-first, regarding ultimate inexhaustibility: although it exists within all phenomena, its essence remains constant even when those phenomena are exhausted.
Furthermore, while situated precisely within phenomena, it cannot be exhausted, for it is like the space within a mustard seed.
For example, just as true thusness (tathatā) is not in conflict with any phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

it does not conflict with any of the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time. For example, just as true thusness universally encompasses all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it fully encompasses the roots of goodness of all sentient beings. For example, just as true thusness [is not in conflict] with all phenomena...
It shares the same essential nature. The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so: it shares the same essential nature as the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Just as True Suchness is never separate from all phenomena, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so.
It encompasses and sustains all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Just as true thusness cannot be eclipsed, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
no world can eclipse it. Just as true thusness is unshakable, so too is this dedication.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus: no demonic activities whatsoever can shake it.

Just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from defilement and turbidity, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; in practicing the bodhisattva path, there is no defilement or turbidity.
Just as true suchness (tathatā) is without change, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā).
Just as the mind that takes pity on sentient beings is without change, so it is. Just as true suchness is inexhaustible, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It cannot be exhausted by any worldly phenomena. Just as the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is eternally awakened, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is universally able to awaken to all dharmas.
Regarding the fifty-first nature, "the constant awakening of speech":

because it can internally permeate and give rise to weariness with cyclic existence and the aspiration for liberation, it is like true thusness (tathatā), which cannot be lost or destroyed. The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this;
it gives rise to supreme vows toward all sentient beings that are never lost or destroyed.
The fifty-second [quality] is being indestructible. While abiding in birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is not defiled by defilement;
thus, just as true suchness (*tathatā*) is able to provide great illumination, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*).
By means of the light of great wisdom, it illuminates all worlds.
Fifty-three is the Great Radiance of Wisdom, because it universally illumines the dharma-realm.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) is ineffable, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it cannot be expressed by any words whatsoever.
Fifty-fourth: The ineffable *tathatā*.
Just as *tathatā* sustains all worlds, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it can sustain all the practices of bodhisattvas. Just as *tathatā* conforms to worldly discourse, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It accords with all speech of wisdom. Just as true suchness pervades all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:
it manifests great supernormal powers and achieves perfect enlightenment throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions.
Just as true thusness is without discrimination, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it makes no distinctions among any worldly things. Just as true thusness pervades all bodies, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.

Within the immeasurable bodies that pervade the lands of the ten directions, it is like the nature of true thusness (tathatā), which is without arising; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so.
Through skillful means, it manifests birth yet has no birth; it is like true thusness, which is not absent from anywhere.

The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time, one manifests spiritual powers universally, being present everywhere.
Regarding the sixty-first point, "being nowhere not present": above, it pervades all things, thus being without limit; now, it follows each [particular].
Every single dharma is entirely contained within it.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) pervades the night, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā);
throughout every night, it emits great radiance and performs the buddha-work.
The sixty-two [kalpas] within a day and night, up to the exhaustion of the future, are each a single thought-moment and a long kalpa.
Because each is gathered according to suchness and each relies upon suchness, one is able to mutually gather and mutually enter thought-moments and kalpas.
Just as true suchness pervades the day, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:

it causes all sentient beings during the day to behold the Buddha’s miraculous transformations, hear him turn the wheel of non-retrogression, and, being free from defilement and pure, none shall pass their time in vain.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) pervades both the half-month and the full month, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā).
Through skillful means, one attains mastery over the successive seasons of all worlds, knowing all times within a single thought-instant.
Just as *tathatā* (suchness) pervades all years, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
abiding for immeasurable eons, it brings all faculties to clear maturity and causes them to be perfected.

Just as *tathatā* pervades the kalpas of formation and destruction, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; abiding through all kalpas, it remains pure and unstained while teaching and transforming sentient beings.

They cause all to be purified. Just as True Suchness extends to the end of the future, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness extend to the end of the future, cultivating all the pure and wondrous practices of Bodhisattvas, fulfilling great vows without ever regressing.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) pervades the three periods of time, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it causes all sentient beings to see the Buddhas of the three periods of time in a single instant, never for even a single thought-moment being abandoned or separated from them.
Just as true thusness pervades all places, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it transcends the triple world and extends everywhere.
They attain complete mastery. Just as true thusness abides within both existence and non-existence, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
They thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena of existence and non-existence are ultimately pure.
Regarding the seventy abodes, there is no deluded conceptualization of existence or non-existence, because existence and non-existence are not ultimately real.
For example, just as the essential nature of true thusness (*tathatā*) is pure, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.

By means of skillful means, one gathers the factors conducive to enlightenment to purify all bodhisattva practices. For example, just as the essential nature of true thusness is luminous and stainless.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so: it causes all bodhisattvas to attain a samādhi of clear and pure mind.
The seventy-two modes of awakening constitute clarity; freedom from discursive thought constitutes purity.
Just as the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is stainless, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it remains far removed from all defilements and fulfills all pure intentions. Just as true suchness is devoid of self and what belongs to self, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
with a mind purified of self and what belongs to self, one fills the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
Earth. Just as the essential nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is equal, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
one thereby attains the equality of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), which illuminates all phenomena and removes the cataracts of ignorance.

Just as *tathatā* transcends all numbers and measures, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it is endowed with the great power of the vehicle of omniscience that transcends all numbers and measures.
They are stored together and abide therein. They give rise to vast clouds of Dharma throughout all worlds in the ten directions;
just as True Suchness (tathatā) abides in equality, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It brings forth all bodhisattva practices and dwells equally upon the path of omniscience; just as True Suchness pervades all sentient beings.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise. It fulfills unimpeded omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and manifests before all realms of sentient beings.
Just as True Suchness (*tathatā*) is without discrimination and universally abides within the wisdom of all sounds, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is fully endowed with the wisdom of all speech and sounds, and is able to manifest them everywhere.

They manifest various sounds and voices to instruct and enlighten sentient beings. Just as True Suchness (tathatā) is eternally free from the mundane world, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it causes all sentient beings to forever transcend the mundane world.
Just as the essential nature of True Suchness is vast and great, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it is fully capable of upholding the vast Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The Dharma is never forgotten or lost. One diligently cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva, without interruption, just as true suchness (tathatā) is without cessation.

The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Desiring to establish all sentient beings upon the ground of great wisdom, one cultivates the bodhisattva practices throughout all eons without interruption, just as the essential nature of true suchness is vast.
Pervading all phenomena extensively, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Purifying mindfulness without obstruction, it universally encompasses all vast dharma-gates;
just as true thusness (tathatā) universally encompasses all classes of beings, the universal dedication of roots is likewise so.
It realizes wisdom of immeasurable categories and cultivates the true, wondrous practices of all bodhisattvas; just as true...
Just as there is nothing to be grasped or clung to, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it grasps at nothing whatsoever regarding all phenomena, extinguishing all worldly attachments and causing them to be universally purified.

Just as the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is immovable, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it abides securely in the perfect conduct and vows of Samantabhadra, ultimately never wavering.
It is unshakable. Just as true thusness is the realm of the Buddhas, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it causes all sentient beings to fulfill the realm of all-encompassing great wisdom and extinguishes the realms of afflictions, rendering them entirely pure.
Just as true thusness cannot be overcome, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it is not thwarted by any of the works of Māra.
It cannot be subdued by the heterodox arguments of the karma-mārga heretics.

Just as true thusness (tathatā) is neither something to be cultivated nor something not to be cultivated, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā). One relinquishes all false conceptualizations and attachments, making no distinction between cultivation and non-cultivation.
The eighty-nine [factors] are not to be cultivated because there is nothing to be attained; yet they are not not to be cultivated because they constitute the sphere of the noble ones.
For example, just as true suchness has no retrogression or abandonment, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness. One constantly beholds all Buddhas.
They give rise to the bodhicitta, adorned with great vows that they never again abandon or retreat.
Just as true thusness universally encompasses all worldly speech and sounds, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

it enables one to attain the supernatural powers and wisdom of all diverse speech and sounds, and to universally produce all manner of verbal expressions. Just as true thusness [pervades] all phenomena...

There is no seeking for anything; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, causing all sentient beings to mount the vehicle of Samantabhadra and attain liberation, such that they have no craving or seeking regarding any phenomena. It is, for example, like true thusness abiding in all stages.

The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: it causes all sentient beings to abandon the worldly ground and dwell upon the ground of wisdom, adorning themselves with the practices of Samantabhadra, just as true thusness (tathatā) is without interruption; the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this.
Attaining fearlessness regarding all phenomena, they proclaim the Dharma everywhere according to the various sounds of their kind.
It is said that there is no interruption. Just as true suchness is free from all outflows (*āsrava*), so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*):
it causes all sentient beings to achieve the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and thoroughly comprehend all dharmas, thereby perfecting the untainted merits of *bodhi*.
Regarding the "ninety-five who have abandoned all outflows" (*āsrava*): according to the Sanskrit original, this is *anāsrava*, which means "without outflows.
Here, it is said they have "abandoned" them because their nature is fundamentally abandoned, just as the essence of the mind is free from discursive thought.
For example, just as true thusness (tathatā) cannot be corrupted or disturbed by even the slightest phenomenon such that it would cause even a fraction of it to fail to be awakening,
so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā). It universally causes all phenomena to be awakened to,
its mind being immeasurable and pervading the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
96. It is said: There is not even the slightest phenomenon capable of causing disruption or confusion such that it would prevent even a small portion from being awakened.
Just as there is nothing among insentient things that is not awakening, so too there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not awakening.
For example, just as true thusness (tathatā) has no beginning in the past, no end in the future, and no difference in the present, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:
for the sake of all sentient beings, one constantly gives rise to the bodhicitta anew at every moment,
universally vowing to purify them and cause them to forever leave behind birth and death.
Regarding the ninety-seventh point, concerning "the past is not a beginning," etc.: the initial limit of the past is called the "beginning" (*ādi*);

the future is the "end," and is thus termed the "conclusion" (*anta*). The present appears to exist, yet because it is divided into the already-past and the not-yet-come, there is no momentary duration.

Therefore, it is called "different. Now it is clarified that although True Suchness pervades the three periods of time, its essence transcends the three periods and the characteristics of beginning, middle, and end;
thus, the universal statement is negated. Dedication is also like this: although one generates vows anew for sentient beings at every moment, [its essence remains beyond temporal distinctions].
Just as that suchness pervades the three periods of time and is now eternally free from the characteristics of birth and death,
it is only then termed "pure.
For example, just as suchness makes no distinctions within the three periods of time, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
In the present, every thought-moment is constantly awakened; in the past and future, all are entirely pure.
Just as True Suchness (tathatā) accomplishes all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It gives rise to all great vows and skillful means, and accomplishes the vast wisdom of all Buddhas. Just as True Suchness is ultimately pure, so too is this dedication.
It does not coexist with any afflictions; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise, for it can extinguish the afflictions of all sentient beings and bring to fulfillment all pure wisdom.

Regarding the statement "non-differentiation across the three periods of time": previously, this was explained through the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), showing how it differs from the three periods; now, it is explained through the method of affirmation (*vidhi*), showing that it is eternally without differentiation.
In the following text, there are still two further analogies, totaling one hundred gates, which are applied to the ten aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The dedication that transcends signs is hereby concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they attain equality with all Buddha-fields, because they universally adorn and purify all worlds;
they attain equality with all sentient beings, because they universally turn the wheel of the unobstructed Dharma for them.
Because of the wheel, one attains the equality of all bodhisattvas, for they universally give rise to the vows for omniscience.
One attains the equality of all buddhas, for one observes that the essence of all buddhas is non-dual.

One attains the equality of all phenomena, for one universally knows that the nature of all phenomena is immutable. One attains the equality of all worlds, through the wisdom of skillful means that skillfully understands the one.

Because all paths of speech are transcended, one attains equality in all bodhisattva practices. Because all various roots of goodness are dedicated without exception, one attains equality at all times.
Because one diligently cultivates the Buddha-work without interruption at all times, one attains equality at all times.
They attain equality in the fruits of all karma, because they are entirely free from attachment to any mundane or supramundane roots of goodness and have brought them all to ultimate fulfillment.
They attain equality in the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas, because they manifest the deeds of a Buddha in accordance with the world.
Son of the Buddha, this is the eighth dedication, the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The third major section, concerning the benefits realized through dedication and the conclusion of the title, may be understood as follows:
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they realize immeasurable gates of pure Dharma.
They are able to perform the Great Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata with mastery and fearlessness, and through skillful means, they teach and bring to maturity immeasurable bodhisattvas.
Sā. At all times, without ever resting, he attains the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect body, a single body that pervades all worlds;
he attains the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect voice, a single sound that awakens all sentient beings;
he attains the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect power, capable of universally containing all lands within a single pore.
They attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), placing all sentient beings within a single atom.

They attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect liberation (*vimokṣa*), manifesting the realms of all Buddhas and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) within the body of a single sentient being.
They attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect samādhis, universally able to manifest everything within a single samādhi.
Through samādhi, they attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect eloquence, such that even a single phrase of the Dharma remains inexhaustible until the end of the future,
completely eliminating the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings. They attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect endowment with the ten powers of a Buddha,
manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.

The second major section, "The Bodhisattva Abiding Herein and Below," clarifies the fruits of the stages. First, it restates the causes for attainment; subsequently, from "Correctly Attaining" onwards, it correctly reveals what is attained.

There are ten phrases in the text: the first is general, while the remaining ones are specific. All are described as "immeasurable" because they are identical to the vastness and inexhaustibility of Suchness (*tathatā*).
All are described as "attaining Buddhahood" because they are identical to that which the Buddha has realized. Thus, they perform the work of a Buddha.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, this is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in accordance with the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
[The passage] beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" below serves as a general conclusion and demonstration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva’s aspiration and joy always abide securely; With firm right mindfulness, they are free from delusion and confusion.
Their mind is supple and ever-cool, Accumulating boundless meritorious deeds.”
The Bodhisattva is humble and compliant, never acting in opposition; all his aspirations are entirely pure.
Having attained the great radiance of wisdom, he is well able to illuminate all karmic actions.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the vastness of karma, its various distinctions being most rare and marvelous.
Resolutely practicing without regression, they thereby benefit all living beings;
The various and immeasurable types of karmic actions, the Bodhisattvas diligently cultivate them all;
Accordant with the inclinations of sentient beings and never opposing their wishes, They cause the minds of all to be pure and filled with joy.
Having ascended the stage of the Honored One, the Tamer of Men, free from all feverish afflictions and with an unimpeded mind,
he thoroughly understands both phenomena and their meanings. For the benefit of all living beings,
he diligently practices the various virtuous deeds cultivated by Bodhisattvas— immeasurable, innumerable, and of diverse kinds.
Knowing all those conceptual constructions, one dedicates for the benefit of all sentient beings;
with sublime wisdom, one constantly contemplates the ultimate, vast, and true principle,
severing all states of existence without exception, dedicating well according to that suchness.
Just as true suchness pervades all, so too do Bodhisattvas universally encompass all worlds.
By dedicating with this mind, they cause all sentient beings to have nothing to do;
the Bodhisattva’s power of aspiration pervades all, just as true suchness is nowhere not present.
Whether seeing or not seeing, mindfulness pervades all; All is dedicated through merit.
Abiding thus at night and abiding likewise by day, Abiding for half a month or a full month, Abiding for a year or even for an eon— Such is the practice of True Suchness (tathatā).
All that exists in the three times and all buddha-fields, All sentient beings and all phenomena—
They all abide therein, yet abide nowhere; Dedicating through such practice,
Just as the true nature of reality is its original essence, So does the bodhisattva give rise to the great mind.
Tathatā is present everywhere; through such practice, one dedicates [the merit].
Just as the fundamental nature of Tathatā is such that not a single dharma within it fails to obtain its own nature—that is true nature—through such karma, one dedicates [the merit].
As is the characteristic of *tathatā*, so too is karma; as is the nature of *tathatā*, so too is karma.
As the nature of *tathatā* is fundamentally real, karma is likewise identical to *tathatā*.
Just as *tathatā* has no limit, karma likewise has no boundary.
Yet within this, they are without bondage or attachment; therefore, these karmas attain purity.
Such wise and true children of the Buddha have firm and unshakable aspirations;
through the power of their wisdom, they skillfully penetrate and enter the treasury of the Buddhas' expedient means.
The Dharma King has awakened to the true Dharma; therein is neither attachment nor bondage.
Thus, his sovereign mind is unimpeded, and never has he seen a single dharma arise.
The activities performed by the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya appear to all worlds as mere reflections.
It is taught that the characteristics of all phenomena are all without characteristic; to know such characteristics is to know the Dharma.
A Bodhisattva who abides in this is inconceivable; within it, thought cannot reach its end.
Entering this state of the inconceivable, both thought and non-thought are utterly stilled.
Reflecting thus upon the nature of all phenomena, they thoroughly comprehend all distinctions among karmic actions;
all grasping at a self is extinguished, and they abide in merit, immovable.
All the karmic fruits and retributions of Bodhisattvas are sealed by inexhaustible wisdom.
Thus, that which is of an inexhaustible nature is itself exhausted; therefore, through the means of inexhaustibility, it is extinguished.
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the mind does not exist externally, nor can it be found within;
knowing that the nature of the mind is non-existent, both self and phenomena are transcended in eternal quiescence.
Those sons of the Buddha know thus: the nature of all phenomena is eternally empty and quiescent;

there is not a single dharma that can be created. Like the Buddhas, they have awakened to non-self and understand that all worlds are entirely equal in their essential nature to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Seeing this inconceivable mark, one is thus able to know the dharma of signlessness.
If one can abide in this profound dharma, one will always delight in practicing the bodhisattva conduct.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, one is adorned with great vows and never regresses.
Thus they transcend the world, Not giving rise to the deluded discrimination of birth and death;
Realizing that their own minds are like illusions and transformations, They diligently cultivate all practices to deliver all beings.
With right mindfulness, the Bodhisattva contemplates the world, Seeing that everything arises from the conditions of karma.
Desiring to rescue and deliver others, he cultivates all practices, universally gathering those within the three realms without exception.
He thoroughly understands the various differences among sentient beings— all of which are discriminated by perception and mental formations—
and observes them with complete clarity, yet without destroying the true nature of all phenomena.
The wise one understands all Buddha-dharmas And dedicates through such practice out of compassion for all sentient beings, Causing them to correctly contemplate the true Dharma.

[This is] the second section, the Verses in Praise (Geya), consisting of twenty-nine stanzas. It is divided into two parts: first, the formal presentation of the verses; second, the six initial stanzas that praise the practice.
Regarding the essence (*tattva*): therein, first, the two verses concern the essence of the practice dedicated; next, four [verses] concern the practice of dedication itself.
Third, there are sixteen verses praising dedication free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*). Within these, first, nine verses provide a detailed analysis in contrast to the Tathāgata;
next, seven verses summarize by directly clarifying it according to the dharmas. The final six verses praise the benefits accomplished through dedication; the last verse concludes the dedication.
Preface. *The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirty;
*The Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirty-One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
commentary on the meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá Yán Temple;
and edited and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Five, Part Nine: The Dedication of Non-Attachment, Non-Bondage, and Liberation.
O Sons of the Buddha, what is the dedication of non-attachment, non-bondage, and liberation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The ninth is the dedication of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation. In the prose commentary, there are likewise first the practices of the stage and subsequently the fruits of the stage.
Within the former, first the name is cited and its significance raised. To explain the name:

it means that the wisdom of principle (*prajñā*) has no dependence and is not bound by the delusions of attachment to the characteristics of subject and object. Because of this, it is termed "liberation. This explanation is given in terms of the essential nature of the practice.
Therefore, the *Mūlakarma* states: "Because all phenomena are non-dual, prajñā is unborn, the two truths are equal, and the three periods of time are a single unified mark.
Furthermore, liberation also possesses sovereign function, such as the inconceivable and so forth;
this refers to its activity and application. By gathering roots of goodness, all are dedicated through the three karmas of Samantabhadra, which are infinitely sovereign.
Because of the function of virtue. Question: From what is there no bondage or attachment? It refers to the ten [factors], beginning with the mind.

This is because one possesses within oneself the fruits of mental, physical, and vocal karma, as well as the Buddha-activities performed, the worlds, the Buddha-fields, sentient beings, dharmas, wisdom, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is asked: By what is one not bound or attached? Briefly, it is as explained above; specifically, there are ten matters.

Five pairs: First, because one has departed from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one is not bound by saṃsāra; because one has emerged from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), one does not cling to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Second, by departing from the grasping of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*), one is not bound by external objects; by departing from the attachment of the seventh [consciousness], one does not cling to the internal.

Third, by departing from the bondage of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), one has no clinging to seeds (*bīja*). Fourth, by not grasping at existence (*bhava*), one is not bound; by not adhering to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one does not cling. Fifth, there is no...

The fetters of the afflictive hindrances and the fetters of the cognitive hindrances—whether coarse or subtle—are all bound by attachment. If considered with respect to a single phenomenon, one is bound due to attachment;

the meaning is as explained in the general [section]. Alternatively, "bondage" and "attachment" have a single meaning here, which receives its name from the unimpeded great function that pervades both the subject and object of dedication.
With respect to liberation from the afflictive hindrances, being without bondage and without attachment is itself liberation. This is explained in terms of function.
Liberation is precisely liberation from bondage and attachment. If one looks toward the mind and so forth, it is likewise a mind free from bondage and attachment;
thus, both the aforementioned essence and function together constitute its nature.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva conceives a sense of reverence toward all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

That is to say, he conceives a sense of reverence toward the mind that seeks to transcend birth and death; he conceives a sense of reverence toward the mind that gathers in all roots of goodness; he conceives a sense of reverence toward the mind that aspires for all roots of goodness;
he conceives a sense of reverence toward the mind that regrets all past transgressions and karmic actions; and he conceives a sense of reverence toward [the mind that] follows...

They give rise to respect for the roots of goodness of joy; they give rise to respect for the mind that pays homage to all Buddhas; they give rise to respect for the mind that joins palms in reverence;
they give rise to respect for the mind that prostrates before stupas and shrines; they give rise to respect for the mind that exhorts the Buddhas to teach the Dharma;
and toward all such various roots of goodness, they give rise to respect, accord with them, and accept them with patience.

The second part, the extensive explanation, is divided into three major sections: first, the explanation of the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the practice of dedication;
and third, from "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this way" onwards, the benefits accomplished by the dedication.
Within the first section, there are six lines of scripture. The first phrase provides a general heading indicating respect; specifically, there is...
Ten phrases.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regards those roots of goodness with respect, accords with them, and finds them acceptable, they ultimately give rise to joyful delight and firm faith-understanding.
They themselves abide therein and cause others to abide therein, diligently cultivating non-attachment.
They freely accumulate [merit], attaining the superior resolve and delight that dwells within the realm of the Tathāgatas; their power increases until they fully attain all knowledge and vision.
They dedicate all roots of goodness in this manner: namely, with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they accomplish the physical karma of Samantabhadra;
with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they purify the verbal karma of Samantabhadra; with a mind that is unattached...
One dwells with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated. One fulfills the mental actions of Samantabhadra.
With this unattached, unbound, and liberated mind, one initiates the vast diligence of Samantabhadra.
In the second dedication practice, the first son of the Buddha [recites] three lines of scripture following those roots of goodness;
he continues to advance in his cultivation, intending to perform the dedication. Next, within the section that correctly elucidates the meaning of the practices of aspiration, there are ten gates.

The main text is divided into two parts: first, a detailed exposition of their characteristics; subsequently, "O Son of the Buddha, with those roots of goodness, one dedicates in this manner... and so forth.
This refers to the conclusion of many sections on the absence of mental bondage. Within the preceding section, there are two parts: first, the dedication of sentient beings and bodhi;
second, "O Son of the Buddha, with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one dedicates without discrimination," which is the dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The former clarifies vastness; the latter reveals profundity. Regarding the vast dedication mentioned previously:

There are sixty-one gates; within those that are most profound there are twenty gates, and when combined with the preceding twenty gates of honoring and advancing in practice, there are one hundred gates in total, manifesting the inexhaustible, perfect fusion of the profound and the vast without obstruction.
This constitutes the vast dedication. Based on the sixty-one gates of vastness, it extensively reveals the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra’s virtues.
The main text is divided into two parts. First, regarding the passage beginning with "By means of all roots of goodness," within the four gates, three accomplish the three karmas;
this is because none of the subsequent gates transcend the three types of wisdom. The final one, diligence, universally governs the myriad practices.
Therefore, within this state, the mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated is the mind capable of dedication;

the accomplishment of the physical karma of Samantabhadra is precisely what is dedicated. Others should all be understood in this manner. The aforementioned roots of goodness are themselves the objects of dedication;
thus, the term "roots of goodness" flows downward into the eighty gates [of practice] herein. This single dedication does not aspire to the attainment of Buddhahood.

The vow "to become Samantabhadra" means that because Samantabhadra pervades both the stages prior to and subsequent to [enlightenment], one does not abandon causal practice even after attaining the Way, but continues until the end of the realm of sentient beings to bring them benefit and happiness; thus, one vows to become Samantabhadra.
This simultaneously encompasses the two dedications of bodhi and sentient beings. In the specific explanations below, within each individual gate, there is the mastery over the entire dharma-realm.

Regarding the function of virtue—whether as principle or practice, wisdom or object, one's own cultivation or the generation of others, essence or function, cause or fruit, person or dharma—each of these individually encompasses all phenomena; therefore, they do not follow one another.
The preceding section of the sutra contains four general gateways that summarize the meaning of the classification; the following are the specific gateways.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they are fully endowed with the Samantabhadra Unobstructed Sound Dharani-gate;

their voice is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions. With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they are fully endowed with the Samantabhadra Vision of All Buddhas Dharani-gate;
they constantly behold all Buddhas of the ten directions. With a mind that is unattached...
With a mind liberated from bondage, they achieve the *dhāraṇī* gate of understanding all sounds;

they preach immeasurable teachings using all voices. With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they achieve the *dhāraṇī* gate of Samantabhadra’s abiding throughout all eons, universally cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva throughout the ten directions.

The separate section is briefly divided into two parts. The first twenty-three gates reveal the ultimate realization of Samantabhadra’s own nature (*svabhāva*), which is Samantabhadra within the state of abiding (*sthiti*).
The latter thirty-four gates reveal the ultimate realization of Samantabhadra’s superior progress (*viśeṣa-uttara*), which is Samantabhadra after the state of abiding.

These two divisions are non-obstructive, constituting the virtues of Samantabhadra. The former represents the perfection of cause and the fulfillment of fruit; the latter represents the attainment [of that fruit].

The Path does not abandon causal practice; therefore, both sections contain both cause and effect. Now, the first part is divided into three: first, four [sections] establish the merit of Samantabhadra’s dhāraṇī;
second, twelve gates establish the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra; third, seven gates establish the vows for Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Furthermore, the virtues of these various gates are all categorized according to the three karmas. Now, the first is the general [introduction].

It is maintained that these also possess three types of activity: first, the dhāraṇī of vocal activity; second, the vision of the Buddha through bodily activity; and third, comprehension through mental activity.
The latter refers to the time and place of the application of these three activities.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra.
Within the body of a single sentient being, they manifest the cultivation of all bodhisattva practices, continuing without interruption throughout all future eons.
As it is with the body of one sentient being, so it is with the bodies of all sentient beings. With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they accomplish...
By the sovereign power of Samantabhadra, he universally enters all sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and universally manifests before all Buddhas to cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
With a mind of liberation that is unattached and unbound, he accomplishes the sovereign power of the Buddha Samantabhadra;
within a single gateway, he manifests for unspeakably unspeakable eons without end, causing all—
All sentient beings attain entry through a mind of liberation that is unattached and unbound, thereby accomplishing the sovereign power of Samantabhadra Buddha.
Within various gateways, they manifest for unspeakably unspeakable eons without end, causing all sentient beings to attain entry.
Their bodies appear universally before all Buddhas; by means of this—
With a mind of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra.
In every thought-moment, they cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to abide in the mind of the wisdom of the ten directions without weariness.
By means of this mind of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra, manifesting all Buddhas within the bodies of all sentient beings.

Through supernormal powers, they cause all sentient beings to abide in the practices of Samantabhadra. With a mind of liberation that is unattached and unbound, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra.

Within the speech of all sentient beings, they produce the speech of all sentient beings, causing every single sentient being to abide upon the ground of omniscience. By means of this unattached and unbound [mind]...
With a mind of liberation, they achieve the sovereign power of Samantabhadra;
within the body of each and every sentient being, they universally accommodate the bodies of all sentient beings, causing them all to perceive themselves as having achieved the Buddha-body.
With a mind of liberation that is unattached and unbound, they achieve the sovereign power of Samantabhadra, such that they can adorn all worlds of the ten directions with a single flower.
With a mind of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra;
emitting great sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, these are heard throughout all Buddha-lands, gathering in and taming all sentient beings.
With a mind of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra, [extending] to the end of the future... [incapable of being exhausted].
They speak for unspeakable eons, and in every moment they are able to enter all worlds universally.
By the spiritual power of the Buddhas, they adorn them according to their thoughts. With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they accomplish the sovereign power of Samantabhadra.
Throughout all kalpas dwelling until the end of the future, they are constantly able to enter universally into all worlds, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood and appearing in the world.
With a mind of liberation, unattached and unbound, they accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra;
with a single light shining universally throughout all worlds as far as the limits of space, they accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra with a mind of liberation, unattached and unbound.
Attaining immeasurable wisdom and possessing all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they preach various dharmas.
With a mind of liberation—unattached and unbound—they accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra. They enter the Tathāgata’s inconceivable supernatural wisdom that endures through all kalpas.
With a mind of liberation—unattached and unbound—they accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra. They abide in all the Tathāgatas throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm.
They come to this place to cultivate all bodhisattva practices through the spiritual power of the Buddha. Their physical, verbal, and mental actions are never weary or indolent.
With a mind of liberation—unattached and unbound—they accomplish universal and true practice. They do not deviate from the meaning, nor do they undermine the Dharma.
Their speech is pure, their eloquence is inexhaustible, and they teach and discipline all sentient beings, causing them to...
One shall attain the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas. With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, one cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra.
Upon entering a single dharma-gate, one emits immeasurable light that illumines inconceivable dharma-gates;
as it is with this one dharma-gate, so it is with all dharma-gates. Attaining unimpeded penetration, one shall ultimately achieve [the goal].
The Ground of All-Knowledge: dwelling in the bodhisattva practice with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated;
attaining mastery over all phenomena and reaching the further shore of Samantabhadra’s adornments;
observing and penetrating every single realm through all-knowledge, yet such all-knowledge remains inexhaustible.
The second section consists of twelve gates that establish the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra. Within this, there are two parts:
first, nine vows concerning the sovereignty of subsuming the one within the many; second, three vows beginning with "emitting great sounds," which clarify vast sovereignty.
The third [section] consists of seven vows for accomplishing the conduct of Samantabhadra (*Samantabhadracaryā*). Within this, there are two parts:
first, the vow "to accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra," and the four subsequent vows beginning with "one light shines universally," which accomplish the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Next, the three vows beginning with "accomplishing the conduct of Samantabhadra without contradicting the meaning" accomplish the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), thereby manifesting the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit. The above twenty-three sections clarify the universal [conduct].
Having thus brought the perfection of one’s own excellence to completion,
with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one shall, from this life until the end of the future,
dwell in the conduct of Samantabhadra without ever ceasing. One shall attain all-knowledge and awaken to the ineffably ineffable true Dharma, and regarding that Dharma—
Ultimately, there is no delusion. With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one cultivates the deeds of Samantabhadra.
Possessing mastery in skillful means, one attains the light of the Dharma and clearly perceives, without obstruction, all the practices performed by Bodhisattvas.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one cultivates the conduct of Samantabhadra and attains the wisdom of all skillful means, knowing all directions.

It is as follows: namely, the skillful means of the immeasurable; the inconceivable skillful means; the skillful means of the bodhisattvas; the skillful means of omniscience; the skillful means for the discipline of all bodhisattvas;
the skillful means for turning the immeasurable wheel of Dharma; the skillful means regarding unspeakable times; the skillful means for expounding various teachings;
