the skillful means of the boundless treasury of fearlessness; and the skillful means for expounding all dharmas.
Without any other expedient means, one dwells in the conduct of Samantabhadra with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, thereby accomplishing the physical karma.
This causes all sentient beings who see it to rejoice and not give rise to slander;

they resolve to attain bodhicitta, never to regress, and ultimately become pure. By practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one attains realization.
Possessing the pure wisdom of the languages of all sentient beings, they are fully adorned with every form of speech;

universally responding to all beings, they cause them all to rejoice. With a mind of liberation—unattached and unbound—they abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra and establish a most excellent resolve.
Possessing a pure mind, they attain vast supernormal powers and vast wisdom.
They travel everywhere throughout all vast worlds and vast lands to hear all the unspeakably vast teachings of all Tathāgatas spoken for the sake of vast multitudes of sentient beings—
the vast treasury of perfect adornments— with a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, thereby fulfilling the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Through the dedication of practice and vows, they attain the pure body, pure mind, and pure understanding of all Buddhas.
They encompass the merits of the Buddhas and abide in the realm of the Buddhas. With the seal of wisdom shining universally, they manifest the pure karma of Bodhisattvas.
Skillfully entering into all differentiated phrases and meanings, they demonstrate the vast sovereignty of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, appearing for the sake of all sentient beings.
They attain perfect enlightenment. With a mind liberated through non-attachment and non-binding, they diligently cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra’s faculties.

They obtain the faculty of keen intelligence, the faculty of harmonious discipline, the faculty of mastery over all phenomena, the inexhaustible faculty, the faculty of diligently cultivating all roots of goodness, and the faculty of equality regarding the spheres of all Buddhas.
They receive the great prediction of non-retrogression for all Bodhisattvas.
The faculty of diligence; the faculty of the vajra-realm that realizes all Buddha-dharmas;
the faculty of the vajra-flame illuminated by the wisdom-light of all Tathāgatas; the faculty of mastery in discerning all faculties;
the faculty that establishes immeasurable sentient beings in omniscience; the boundlessly vast faculty; the perfectly complete faculty; and the pure, unobstructed faculty.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and attain the spiritual powers of all bodhisattvas.

These are: the spiritual power of immeasurable and vast strength; the spiritual power of immeasurable sovereign wisdom; the spiritual power of manifesting throughout all buddha-fields without moving their bodies;
the spiritual power of unimpeded, uninterrupted sovereignty; and the spiritual power of universally gathering all buddhas.
The spiritual power of placing all buddha-fields in a single location; the spiritual power of a single body pervading all buddha-fields;

the spiritual power of sporting in unimpeded liberations; the spiritual power of sovereign mastery in a single thought-moment without any deliberate effort; the spiritual power of abiding in the natureless and the non-reliant;
and the spiritual power of sequentially establishing unspeakable numbers of worlds within a single pore while traveling throughout the entire dharma-realm to visit all Buddhas.
The second major section, which clarifies the ultimate stage of supreme advancement, contains thirty-four gates and is divided into three parts.

First, there are nine gates that encompass the virtue of the vast and sovereign mastery of all phenomena. Second, there are fifteen gates concerning the mutual identity and mutual interpenetration of phenomena.

Third, there are ten gates concerning the power of the spiritual capacity to manifest the Dharma-body for all sentient beings, enabling them all to enter the gate of great wisdom. This concludes the second major section.
The Profound Virtues. Third, there are ten sections clarifying the profound virtue of subtle containment and support.
This section is divided into six parts: first, from "From this arising... downwards, three vows establish wisdom;
second, from "Accomplishing bodily action... downwards, two vows establish benefit; third, from "Establishing a sublime resolve... downwards, one vow establishes vastness.
Regarding karma: the fourth [vow] states, "To fulfill the conduct of Samantabhadra," which includes one vow for the purification of the three karmas;

the fifth states, "To diligently cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra," which includes one vow for planting all roots of goodness, among which the three karmas are further distinguished by fourteen roots.
All are designated by the name "faculty" (*indriya*) because they function as superior and preeminent causes for the manifestation of meaning.

First, regarding the three faculties such as the "acute" (*tīkṣṇa*), they pertain to the six [faculties] beginning with the eye, together with the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*). The others pertain to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, the inexhaustible faculty of faith also includes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Next is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) for ardent cultivation; next, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) of all Buddhas; and next, the faculty of non-retrogression.

This is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*). The remaining seven are all wisdom (*prajñā*). The sixth is the vow to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and attain the spiritual powers of all bodhisattvas;
this refers to the power of the vow and the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. This concludes the vast and sovereign virtue of the nine preceding sections that encompass all dharmas.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one enters the gateway of Samantabhadra and gives rise to the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Through sovereign wisdom, in a single thought-moment, one universally enters immeasurable buddha-fields; with a single body, one accommodates and contains immeasurable buddha-lands.

They attain the wisdom that is able to purify Buddha-lands. Constantly observing and beholding infinite Buddha-lands with wisdom, they never again give rise to the mind of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
With a mind of liberation—unattached and unbound—they cultivate the expedient practices of Samantabhadra.
They enter the realm of wisdom, are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, abide in the path of the bodhisattvas, and become fully endowed with the unspeakable.
He possesses an ineffable, immeasurable, and inconceivable, most excellent mind. He practices immeasurable vows without ever resting.
He thoroughly understands all dharma-realms of the three periods of time. With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, he accomplishes the pure Dharma-gate of Samantabhadra.
Within the space of a single hair-tip, he completely encompasses and pervades the entirety of empty space and the entire dharma-realm.
He speaks of all unspeakable lands, causing them all to be clearly seen as if they were the space of a single hair-tip;
throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, at every point the size of a hair-tip, it is likewise so.
With a mind of liberation, unattached and unbound, he accomplishes the profound mind and skillful means of Samantabhadra, manifesting within a single thought-moment the entirety of a sentient being.

One can contemplate the thoughts of kalpas that are expressible and those that are inexpressible; thus, one may even contemplate the thoughts of as many kalpas as there are sentient beings currently existing.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one enters the stage of skillful means for the practice of Samantabhadra’s dedication.
Within a single body, one is able to encompass all the bodies throughout the entire dharma-realm—bodies that are inexpressibly inexpressible—yet sentient beings...
The realms neither increase nor decrease. As it is with one body, so it is with all bodies throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they accomplish the skillful means of Samantabhadra’s great vows.
Having abandoned all inversions of thought, mind, and view, they universally enter the spheres of all Buddhas and constantly behold the Buddhas’ emptiness.
The pure Dharma-body of the realm of space and so forth is adorned with the marks and signs of perfection;

its spiritual powers are sovereign, and it constantly reveals and expounds the teaching through sublime sounds, unimpeded and uninterrupted, causing those who hear it to receive and uphold it as taught.

Within the body of the Tathāgata, one finds nothing at all to be apprehended. With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, one cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra and dwells in the stages of a bodhisattva. In...

In a single thought-moment, they enter all worlds—namely, the unspeakably unspeakable worlds of the ten directions arranged like Indra’s net, including worlds that are upright and worlds that are inverted, throughout all vast realms.

By means of the skillful methods of differentiation within Indra’s net, they universally discern the entire dharma-realm; they enter a single world by means of various worlds. By means of the... [incomplete source text]... not...
One may speak of immeasurable worlds, both expressible and inexpressible, entering into a single world.
One may cause all immeasurable worlds established within the entire dharma-realm to enter into a single world;

one may cause all immeasurable worlds established within the entire space-realm to enter into a single world, yet without destroying their established characteristics, causing them all to be clearly seen. By means of this...
Abiding in a mind that is unbound and liberated, they cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Having received the empowerment of the Buddhas, they enter the stage of skillful means within a single thought-moment.

They bring to full completion and dwell securely in the jewel-like wisdom of all practices, being able to fully comprehend all conceptualizations—namely, the conceptualization of sentient beings, the conceptualization of phenomena, the conceptualization of lands, the conceptualization of directions, the conceptualization of Buddhas, the conceptualization of time, the conceptualization of karma, and the conceptualization of conduct.

The perception of realms; the perception of liberation; the perception of faculties; the perception of time; the perception of upholding; the perception of afflictions; the perception of purity; the perception of maturation;

the perception of seeing the Buddha; the perception of turning the wheel of Dharma; the perception of understanding the Dharma upon hearing it; the perception of subduing; the perception of the immeasurable;

the perception of renunciation; the perception of various stages; the perception of immeasurable stages; the perception of the Bodhisattva’s full comprehension; the perception of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation; the perception of the Bodhisattva...

The perception of a *sattva*; the perception of a bodhisattva arising; the perception of a bodhisattva being formed; the perception of a bodhisattva disintegrating; the perception of a bodhisattva passing away; the perception of a bodhisattva being born;

the perception of a bodhisattva attaining liberation; the perception of a bodhisattva possessing mastery; the perception of a bodhisattva maintaining [the teachings]; the perception of a bodhisattva’s sphere of activity;
the perception of the formation and destruction of kalpas; the perception of light; the perception of darkness; the perception of day; the perception of night; the perception of the half-month.
They are able to fully comprehend within a single thought-moment all such perceptions as the perception of change over a month, a season, or a year;

the perception of going, the perception of coming, the perception of standing, the perception of sitting, the perception of sleeping, and the perception of waking. Yet, they remain free from all perceptions and without conceptual differentiation;
they sever all hindrances and are without attachment. The wisdom of all Buddhas fills their minds. All...
The Buddha-dharma causes their roots of goodness to grow. They become one body with all Tathāgatas and are embraced by all Buddhas.
Free from defilement and pure, they study and practice all the Buddha-dharmas until they reach the other shore.
With a mind of liberation, unattached and unbound, they cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra for the sake of all sentient beings, giving birth to the jewel of great wisdom. In...

Within each and every mind, one knows immeasurable minds. According to their bases, their discriminations, their lineages, their actions, their karmic functions, their characteristics, and their thoughts and perceptions—one clearly perceives all their various differences without exception.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one accomplishes the jewel-like wisdom of Samantabhadra’s great vows.
Within a single location, one knows infinite, ineffable locations; as it is with one location, so it is with all locations.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one cultivates the ground of wisdom for the practices of Samantabhadra.
Within a single karma, one is able to know immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable karmas;
each of these karmas is created by various conditions, and one clearly knows and sees them. As it is with one karma, so it is with all karmas.
With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one cultivates the wisdom of Samantabhadra that knows all phenomena, and within a single phenomenon, one knows...
The ineffable Dharma that cannot be spoken: within all phenomena, one knows a single phenomenon;
thus, while these various phenomena are each distinct, they are without obstruction, without contradiction, and without attachment. By means of a mind liberated from attachment and bondage—
Abiding in the conduct of a bodhisattva, they attain the unimpeded ear-faculty of Samantabhadra.
Within a single utterance, they know unspeakably unspeakable utterances, with their infinite and boundless varieties and distinctions, yet without attachment.
Just as with one utterance, so it is with all utterances; thus, with a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they proceed.

They cultivate the wisdom of Samantabhadra, initiate the practices of Samantabhadra, and abide on the stage of Samantabhadra. Within each and every dharma, they expound unspeakably unspeakable dharmas.
These dharmas are vast, with manifold distinctions, and are adapted to inconceivable skillful means for the purpose of teaching, transforming, and gathering in sentient beings.
Throughout immeasurable time and at all times, they act in accordance with the needs of all sentient beings.
To explain: according to their faculties and at appropriate times, he preaches the Dharma using the Buddha’s voice.
With a single sublime sound, he causes all the immeasurable sentient beings in the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment—whose number cannot be described—to rejoice.

All the Tathāgatas are filled with immeasurable Bodhisattvas who pervade the Dharma-realm; they establish supreme resolve and give rise to vast vision, ultimately and thoroughly understanding the One.
They sever all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Abiding in the stage of Samantabhadra, they are able to realize and enter into every teaching as it is proclaimed, moment by moment.
In a single instant, they increase immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable masses of great wisdom.
Thus they continue to expound for all kalpas of the future, cultivating vast practices equal to space in all lands until they achieve perfection.
Fulfilling [all roots], with a mind of liberation that is unattached and unbound, they cultivate the gates of practice of Samantabhadra’s faculties,
becoming great kings of conduct. Within each and every faculty, they are able to fully know immeasurable faculties, immeasurable mental inclinations,
and the wondrous practices arising from inconceivable realms.
The second section consists of fifteen gates, clarifying the mutual interpenetration of marks and the vast, layered virtues. It is divided into six parts.
First, there are three gates that enter the gate of Samantabhadra: (1) the gate of practice, (2) the gate of wisdom, and (3) the gate of phenomena.

Next, following the passage "Accomplishing the skillful means of the profound mind of Samantabhadra," there are three gates concerning the fulfillment of the skillful means of Samantabhadra through vows.
First, the skillful means of the profound mind; second, the skillful means of dedication; third, the skillful means of the great vows.

Regarding the entry into the stage of Samantabhadra through two gates: the first involves entering at the beginning while abiding on the bodhisattva grounds; the latter states that one attains the Buddha’s consecration, clarifying the final accomplishment.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the designation of the knower and the known; second, the enumeration of what is to be known; [and third, the explanation of how they are realized].

Knowledge of perceptions (*saṃjñā*) consists of fifty-two types. Their activities, conduct, realms, understandings, faculties, and so forth, are all known by the wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*).

"Holding" (*dhāraṇa*) means to maintain or grasp. The "stages of good and evil" (*kuśalākuśala-bhūmi*) refers to the boundaries of abandonment and realization. For a bodhisattva who has attained accomplishment, these consist of correct practice and right livelihood;
for a bodhisattva who has failed, they consist of precepts, views, and wrong livelihood. The remainder may be understood accordingly. The fourth [point] concerns all sentient beings.
The practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct gives rise to the jewel of great wisdom; herein follow four gates that accomplish the great wisdom of Samantabhadra:
first, the wisdom accomplished through conduct, which knows nothing because there is no sentient being not reached, for its practice consists in transforming all beings;

second, the wisdom of great vows, which knows no place not reached, for its vows encompass universal transformation; third, the wisdom that exhausts karma, which thoroughly understands causes and conditions; and fourth, the wisdom that accords with reality.

Because of knowing the nature of transformation. Fifth, it is said that one attains the unimpeded ear of Samantabhadra; below this are two gates: the accomplishment of Samantabhadra’s hearing and speaking.
First, there is nothing the ear does not hear; second, there is nothing the tongue does not express. Sixth, it is said that one cultivates the gate of practice of all the faculties of Samantabhadra;
below this is one gate: the accomplishment of the virtue of knowing faculties, because it encompasses all within one. Within this, it says:
The Great Practitioner King, because he possesses universal knowledge of the faculties and mastery over transformative conduct,
has twenty-four gates above him.
With a mind of liberation, unattached and unbound, he abides in the great heart of dedication to the practices of Samantabhadra, attaining a form that is exceedingly subtle.
Wisdom: wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of bodies; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of lands; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of eons;

wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of worlds; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of directions; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of time; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of numbers; wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of karmic retribution;
and wisdom regarding the extreme subtlety of purification—all such things, which are extremely subtle, [are known] within a single thought-moment.
They are able to understand all things completely, yet their minds are neither terrified nor deluded; they are undisturbed, unscattered, unturbid, and not inferior.
Their minds are focused on a single object; their minds are well-settled in tranquility, well-discriminating, and well-established.

With a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, they abide in the wisdom of a bodhisattva, cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra without weariness or fatigue, and are able to know the One.
The destinies of all sentient beings are extremely subtle. The death of sentient beings is extremely subtle. The birth of sentient beings is extremely subtle.
The abiding of sentient beings is extremely subtle. The dwelling places of sentient beings are extremely subtle. The categories of sentient beings are extremely subtle.
The realms of sentient beings are extremely subtle. The conduct of sentient beings is extremely subtle. The grasping of sentient beings is extremely subtle. The clinging of sentient beings...
The conditions are extremely subtle; all such things, being extremely subtle, can be fully known within a single thought-moment.
With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, one establishes a profound aspiration and joy to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.

One is able to know the extremely subtle ways in which all Bodhisattvas, from their initial resolve, cultivate the Bodhisattva path for the sake of all sentient beings. Thus does the Bodhisattva [know].
The dwelling place is extremely subtle. The supernormal powers of the bodhisattva are extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s wandering through immeasurable buddha-fields is extremely subtle.
The bodhisattva’s light of Dharma is extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s pure eye is extremely subtle.
The bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the supreme mind is extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s approach to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas is extremely subtle.
The assembly is exceedingly subtle. The wisdom of the bodhisattva’s gateways of dhāraṇī is exceedingly subtle.

The exposition from the treasury of all eloquence on the stages of the bodhisattva’s immeasurable fearlessness is exceedingly subtle. The characteristics of the bodhisattva’s immeasurable samādhis are exceedingly subtle.
The wisdom of the bodhisattva’s samādhi that beholds all Buddhas is exceedingly subtle. The wisdom of the bodhisattva’s profound samādhis—
It is extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s samādhi-wisdom of great adornment is extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s samādhi-wisdom of the dharma-realm is extremely subtle.
The bodhisattva’s samādhi-wisdom of sovereign supernormal powers is extremely subtle.
The bodhisattva’s samādhi-wisdom of maintaining vast practices until the end of the future is extremely subtle. The bodhisattva’s production of the immeasurable...

The samādhi-wisdom of the differentiation [of dharmas] is extremely subtle. The samādhi-wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s birth before all Buddhas, diligently practicing offerings and never abandoning them, is extremely subtle.

The samādhi-wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of all that is profound, vast, unobstructed, and unimpeded is extremely subtle. The Bodhisattva dwells in the ultimate stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

The stage of wisdom in conduct, the stage of great supernormal powers, the stage of the definitive meaning, and the extremely subtle wisdom of the *vimala* (stainless) samādhi—all such extremely subtle things he is able to fully know. With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, he cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra.
He fully knows the extremely subtle wisdom established by all bodhisattvas and the [extremely subtle] bodhisattva stages.
Subtlety: The immeasurable practices of bodhisattvas are exceedingly subtle; the generation and dedication of merit by bodhisattvas are exceedingly subtle;
the attainment of the treasury of all Buddhas by bodhisattvas is exceedingly subtle; the wisdom of observation of bodhisattvas is exceedingly subtle;

the power of the vows and spiritual faculties of bodhisattvas is exceedingly subtle; the exposition of samādhis by bodhisattvas is exceedingly subtle; the mastery of bodhisattvas in all directions is...
It is exceedingly subtle. The seal of the Bodhisattva is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva in his final birth before enlightenment is exceedingly subtle.
The Bodhisattva’s birth in Tuṣita Heaven is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the celestial palace is exceedingly subtle.
The Bodhisattva’s adornment and purification of the Buddha-land is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva’s observation of the human realm is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva emits a great light.
The clarity is extremely subtle. The excellence of the bodhisattva lineage is extremely subtle. The assembly at the bodhisattva’s site of enlightenment is extremely subtle.
The birth of the bodhisattva throughout all worlds is extremely subtle. The manifestation by the bodhisattva of the death of all bodies within a single body is extremely subtle.
The entry of the bodhisattva into the mother’s womb is extremely subtle. The dwelling of the bodhisattva...
The mother’s womb is exceedingly subtle. While dwelling within the mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva freely manifests the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment throughout the entire dharma-realm;
this is exceedingly subtle. While dwelling within the mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva manifests the spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
this is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva manifests the event of his birth; this is exceedingly subtle. The Bodhisattva performs the lion’s stride and takes seven steps.
The wisdom is exceedingly subtle. The bodhisattva’s skillful means in manifesting residence within a royal palace is exceedingly subtle.

The bodhisattva’s renunciation of the world and cultivation of the practice of self-discipline is exceedingly subtle. The bodhisattva’s sitting beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment is exceedingly subtle.
The Bodhisattva’s destruction of the hosts of Māra and his attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are exceedingly subtle.
The Tathāgata sitting upon the seat of enlightenment and emitting great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions is exceedingly subtle.
The Tathāgata’s manifestation of immeasurable supernatural transformations is exceedingly subtle. The Tathāgata’s lion’s roar of the Great Parinirvāṇa is exceedingly subtle. The Tathāgata...
Subtly and minutely is the taming of all sentient beings without obstruction; subtly and minutely is the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s sovereign mastery, like the adamantine bodhicitta;
subtly and minutely is the Tathāgata’s universal protection and mindfulness of the realms of all worlds;
and throughout all future kalpas, the Tathāgata universally performs buddha-activities in all worlds.
It is extremely subtle that there is no rest; it is extremely subtle that the Tathāgata’s unimpeded spiritual power pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
it is extremely subtle that the Tathāgata universally manifests the attainment of Buddhahood in all worlds throughout the entirety of space to discipline sentient beings;
it is extremely subtle that the Tathāgata manifests immeasurable Buddha-bodies from a single Buddha-body; it is extremely subtle that the Tathāgata, regarding the past...
Throughout the three periods of time—past, present, and future—they abide in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), their sovereign wisdom being exceedingly subtle.
They are able to fully comprehend all such subtleties and achieve complete purity. They are universally able to manifest throughout all worlds;

in every thought-moment, they increase their wisdom, attaining perfection without regression. Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva without [hindrance].
Resting in the stage of the Samantabhadra Dedication, they are endowed with all the virtues of the Tathāgatas.
They never weary of or abandon the conduct of Bodhisattvas, giving rise to the manifest realm of Bodhisattvas. All their immeasurable skillful means are utterly pure;
they universally desire to bring peace and security to all sentient beings while practicing the Bodhisattva path, thereby accomplishing the great majesty of Bodhisattvas.
The Ground of Virtue (*guṇabhūmi*). One attains the aspirations and inclinations of all bodhisattvas; acquires the gateway of the Vajradhvaja dedication;
gives birth to the treasuries of merit within the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); is constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas;

enters the profound and wondrous Dharma-gates of all bodhisattvas; expounds the meaning of all that is true and real; becomes skillful in the Dharma without error or loss; and gives rise to the Great...
They vow never to abandon sentient beings. Within a single thought-moment, they fully know that all minds are the treasury of the realm that is not the mind.
In that which is not the mind, they manifest birth within the mind. Remaining far removed from speech, they abide in wisdom.
They practice the same conduct as all bodhisattvas and, through the power of mastery, manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way. Until the end of the future, they are eternally without [ceasing].

Resting for as many eons as there are sentient beings in all worlds—constructions established by the discursive speech of deluded thoughts—they are able to manifest them all through the power of their spiritual penetrations and vows.
With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and attain the most subtle wisdom regarding the realm of all sentient beings;
that is to say, the most subtle wisdom that discerns the realm of sentient beings. The multitude...
The extremely subtle knowledge of the verbal designations for the realm of beings; the extremely subtle knowledge of attachment to the realm of beings;
the extremely subtle knowledge of the diverse categories within the realm of beings; the extremely subtle knowledge of the homogeneous categories within the realm of beings;

the extremely subtle knowledge of the immeasurable destinies within the realm of beings; and the extremely subtle knowledge of the inconceivable various conceptual constructions produced within the realm of beings.

Wisdom: the wisdom that perceives the immeasurable and extremely subtle defilements of the realm of sentient beings; the wisdom that perceives the immeasurable and extremely subtle purification of the realm of sentient beings.
Thus, regarding all such realms of sentient beings that are extremely subtle, they are able, within a single thought-moment, to know them all as they truly are through their wisdom.
They extensively gather in sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them, revealing various [teachings].
This gate of pure Dharma causes one to cultivate the vast wisdom of a bodhisattva; it manifests immeasurable transformation bodies that bring joy to all who behold them.
With the light of the sun of wisdom, it illuminates the bodhisattva’s mind, causing awakening and mastery of wisdom.
By means of a mind liberated through non-attachment and non-binding, one cultivates the conduct of Samantabhadra for the sake of all sentient beings in all worlds, until the ultimate end is reached.
The extremely subtle wisdom regarding the realm of space, the dharma-realm, and all worlds; that is to say: extremely subtle wisdom regarding small worlds;
extremely subtle wisdom regarding large worlds; extremely subtle wisdom regarding defiled worlds; extremely subtle wisdom regarding purified worlds;
extremely subtle wisdom regarding incomparable worlds; and extremely subtle wisdom regarding diverse worlds.
Wisdom: the extremely subtle wisdom regarding vast worlds; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding narrow worlds; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding worlds adorned without obstruction;
the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the appearance of Buddhas throughout all worlds; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the preaching of the True Dharma throughout all worlds;
and the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the universal manifestation of the body throughout all worlds.
Wisdom that emits great light throughout all worlds with extreme subtlety; wisdom that manifests the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas throughout all worlds with extreme subtlety;
wisdom that displays all sounds through a single voice throughout all worlds with extreme subtlety;
and wisdom that enters the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment in all Buddha-fields throughout all worlds.
They possess the extremely subtle wisdom that perceives all dharma-realms and buddha-fields as a single buddha-field;
the extremely subtle wisdom that perceives a single buddha-field as all dharma-realms and buddha-fields;
the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all worlds to be like dreams; and the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all worlds to be like reflections. They know all...
With the extremely subtle wisdom that perceives the world as like an illusion, one understands it thus;

thereby giving birth to all paths of the bodhisattvas, entering the conduct of Samantabhadra, and possessing the wisdom and supernormal powers of Samantabhadra’s contemplation, one cultivates the bodhisattva practices constantly without rest.
They attain the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas; endowed with unimpeded bodies, they abide in non-reliant wisdom.
They harbor no grasping or attachment toward any wholesome dharmas; in the movements of their minds, nothing at all is apprehended. In all places, they give rise to the perception of detachment.
One conceives the thought of pure cultivation regarding the bodhisattva practices; one conceives the thought of non-attachment toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Adorned with various samādhis, one’s wisdom accords with the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, one enters the gate of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s practice and attains the extremely subtle wisdom of the immeasurable dharma-realm, expounding all things.
The subtle wisdom of the dharma-realm; the subtle wisdom of entering the vast dharma-realm; the subtle wisdom of discerning the inconceivable dharma-realm;
the subtle wisdom of discerning all dharma-realms; the subtle wisdom of pervading all dharma-realms in a single thought-moment;
the subtle wisdom of universally entering all dharma-realms; knowing all...
The extremely subtle wisdom that perceives the non-apprehensibility of the dharma-realm; the extremely subtle wisdom that contemplates all dharma-realms as being without obstruction;
the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all dharma-realms to be without arising;
the extremely subtle wisdom that manifests spiritual transformations within all dharma-realms—all such extremely subtle aspects of the dharma-realm are [perceived] through vast wisdom.
Knowing things as they truly are, they manifest the conduct of Samantabhadra with mastery over all phenomena, causing all sentient beings to be fully satisfied.
Without abandoning the ultimate meaning and without clinging to phenomena, they give rise to impartial and unimpeded wisdom.
Knowing the source of non-obstruction, they do not dwell in any phenomena and do not destroy the nature of phenomena. Truly undefiled like space, they accord with the world.
Arising from conventional discourse, it opens the gate to the true meaning and reveals the nature of quiescent extinction.
Regarding all objects, it is without dependence or dwelling, free from conceptual discrimination, and clearly perceives the vast establishment of the *dharmadhātu*.

It realizes that all worlds and all phenomena are equal and non-dual, remaining detached from all attachments. With a mind liberated from both attachment and bondage, one cultivates the conduct of Samantabhadra.
They practice the extremely subtle wisdom that generates all kalpas;

that is to say, the extremely subtle wisdom that takes unspeakable kalpas as a single thought-moment, the extremely subtle wisdom that takes a single thought-moment as unspeakable kalpas, the extremely subtle wisdom that enters one kalpa through incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, and the extremely subtle wisdom that enters incalculable kalpas through one kalpa. With this length...
The extremely subtle wisdom that enters long eons through short eons; the extremely subtle wisdom that enters short eons through long eons;

the extremely subtle wisdom that enters eons with Buddhas and eons without Buddhas; the extremely subtle wisdom that knows the numerical count of all eons; the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all eons as non-eons;
and the extremely subtle wisdom that perceives all eons of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment.
Wisdom. Thus, all such eons, however extremely subtle they may be, are known by the Tathāgata’s wisdom as they truly are within a single thought-moment.
He attains the mind of the sovereign of the perfect conduct of all bodhisattvas; he enters the mind of Samantabhadra’s conduct;

he possesses a mind free from all conceptualization, divergent paths, and frivolous proliferation; he gives rise to a mind of great vows that never tires; and he universally beholds immeasurable worlds.
A mind filled with an infinite net of Buddhas; a mind capable of hearing and retaining the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and the practices of all Bodhisattvas;
a mind that, having heard of the vast conduct for comforting all sentient beings, never forgets it;
a mind capable of manifesting the appearance of Buddhas in the world throughout all kalpas; and a mind that performs unshakable practice in every single world until the end of the future.
Resting the mind, they fill the bodies and minds of bodhisattvas throughout all worlds with the physical actions (*kāyakarman*) of the Tathāgata.
With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra and become non-retrogressive.
They attain the most subtle wisdom regarding all phenomena—namely, the most subtle wisdom regarding profound phenomena and the most subtle wisdom regarding vast phenomena.
The extremely subtle wisdom regarding the various dharmas; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the adornment of dharmas; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the immeasurability of all dharmas;
the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the entry of all dharmas into a single dharma; the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the entry of a single dharma into all dharmas;
the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the entry of all dharmas into non-dharmas; and the establishment of a single [dharma] within the absence of dharmas.
The extremely subtle wisdom that does not contradict any phenomena; the extremely subtle wisdom that enters all Buddha-dharmas through skillful means without exception;

and likewise, the extremely subtle wisdom regarding all the dharmas established by all the various conventions and expressions in all worlds—all such wisdoms are equal to those [Buddhas], unimpeded, and known exactly as they truly are, whereby one attains entry into the boundless Dharma.
Regarding the realm of the mind: dwelling with firm resolve in the deep mind of each and every dharma-realm, one accomplishes unimpeded conduct.
Filling all the sense-faculties with omniscience, one enters the skillful means of right mindfulness within the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Accomplishing the vast merits of all Buddhas that pervade the dharma-realm, one universally enters the bodies of all Tathāgatas and manifests all the bodily actions of Bodhisattvas, in accordance with...
They expound the Dharma in accordance with the languages of all worlds. They attain the mental karma of wisdom empowered by the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
They give rise to immeasurable skillful means and the *sarvajñā* (omniscience) that discerns all phenomena.
With a mind liberated from attachment and bondage, they cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and give rise to all most subtle wisdom. Regarding these matters...
That is to say: the wisdom that knows all lands to be extremely subtle; the wisdom that knows all sentient beings to be extremely subtle;
the wisdom that knows the retributions of all phenomena to be extremely subtle; the wisdom that knows the minds of all sentient beings to be extremely subtle;
the wisdom that knows the timing of all Dharma-teachings to be extremely subtle; the wisdom that knows the entire dharma-realm to be extremely subtle; and the wisdom that knows all...
The extremely subtle wisdom that exhausts the three periods of time throughout the realm of empty space; the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all paths of speech;
the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all worldly activities; and the extremely subtle wisdom that knows all world-transcending activities.
...up to the knowledge of the extremely subtle wisdom regarding the path of all Tathāgatas, the path of all Bodhisattvas, and the path of all sentient beings.

They cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva and abide in the path of Samantabhadra. Whether in letter or in meaning, they know them all as they truly are. They give rise to the wisdom that [all things] are like reflections;

they give rise to the wisdom that they are like dreams; they give rise to the wisdom that they are like illusions; they give rise to the wisdom that they are like echoes; they give rise to the wisdom that they are like transformations; they give rise to the wisdom that they are like...
The wisdom of emptiness arises; the wisdom of tranquil extinction arises; the wisdom of the entire dharma-realm arises; the wisdom of non-reliance arises;
and the wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas arises.
Third, there are ten gates that clarify the profound virtue of subtle containment and support, namely: the vow to attain the [wisdom] of Samantabhadra...
The Dharma of Subtle Wisdom (*sūkṣmajñāna-dharma*). Because the objects known are subtle, the wisdom that is able to know them is also subtle.

There are two reasons for this subtlety: first, because it is difficult to know; second, according to the tenet of the sūtras, within a single dharma all dharmas are vividly and simultaneously manifested.
Thus, as the text says: "The karmic retributions of sentient beings are subtle," and so forth. These ten gates constitute the ten [chapters].
Section. In the initial presentation and enumeration: first is the knowledge of the subtle dharmas of the world.

The initial mention of the "great mind of dedication" (mahā-pariṇāmanā-citta) indicates the virtue that is cultivated. Next, the passage beginning with "attaining the extremely subtle form" lists the dharmas attained.

Finally, the passage beginning with "all such extremely subtle [dharmas]" concludes by describing the virtue of the capacity for such knowledge. This consists of not fearing the profound and not being deluded regarding phenomena.

"Principle" (*li*) refers to order; "confusion" (*luan*) means error. "Scattered" (*san*) means lack of concentration; "turbid" (*zhuo*) means defilement. "Inferior" (*lie*) means lacking capability. Now, all these are the reverse.

The first part clarifies the departure from faults; the second reveals the perfection of virtues. "Single-pointed object" (*yi-yuan*) means focusing exclusively on one sphere, and thus there is no scattering.

"Wholesome tranquility" (*shan-ji*) means the mutual forgetting of both mind and object, and thus there is no confusion. That which is precisely meditative concentration (*ding*) is known as "skillful discernment" (*shan-fenbie*).
Therefore, one is not deluded. To stop while illuminating is called "skillful stopping," and thus one is not afraid; this is the virtue of being able to know.

Because it resides in the first gate, its meaning extends through the following nine gates. Second, it is said that there is no weariness or fatigue; this is the subtle wisdom that knows the destinies of sentient beings.
Third, it is said that one establishes profound resolve and aspiration; this is the subtle wisdom that knows the virtues of the bodhisattva practices. [The following] lists what is known...
There are twenty phrases in the middle section. The first ten are distinct explanations, while the latter ten collectively clarify samādhi.

This fourth [section] concerns the knowledge of the bodhisattva’s stages, virtues, great functions, and wisdom; it consists of two parts. The first establishes the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct through a mind free from attachment.

Next, it says, "fully knowing all," which refers to the dharmas obtained below; there are forty-one kinds. The first eleven matters concern the perfection of practice once the stages (*bhūmi*) have been established.

Next, it says, "the Bodhisattva is born in Tuṣita Heaven," followed by thirty matters that clarify the fulfillment of the stages and the manifestation of great function, such as the appearance of the eight signs (*aṣṭābhinirhāra*).
Among these, there are distinctions between the names of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, as well as differences regarding cause and fruit.
All of these are merely matters within the midst of practice. Third, it is said that such [qualities] as these constitute the subtle, lower concluding virtue of being able to know;

that is to say, they constitute the virtue of the sovereign mastery of Samantabhadra. Virtue is also termed "benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*). This arises universally from the subsequent various wisdoms. There are twelve lines of scripture.
Fifth is the wisdom that knows the subtle aspects of the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*); this has three parts. First, by means of...

The final phrase of Asaṅga’s commentary indicates the basis for his qualities. The second [verse] previously mentioned, "knowing the destinies of sentient beings," refers to the objective domain of the knowledge of one's own karma among the ten powers (*daśabala*).
This present passage, "knowing the realm of sentient beings" (*sattvadhātu*), takes *dhātu* to mean "nature" (*prakṛti*); therefore, the two are not identical.
Therefore, the *Jin jing* (Jin Scripture) says: "Entering the subtle nature of sentient beings. Next, it says:
"Attaining all realms of sentient beings," followed by the wisdoms obtained therein, which consist of ten phrases. The first is general; "that which is called" below is specific.
Regarding the phrase "the realms of the distinctions of sentient beings," one may also say "the realms of the distinctions of sentient beings. The third says: "All such as these."

The following summarizes the qualities of knowledge (*jñeya-guṇa*). There are six types of knowledge regarding the subtle nature of the world (*loka-sūkṣmatā-jñāna*), which are threefold. First, the general heading is indicated by "without attachment" (*asaṅga*) and so forth.
Second, the specific details are revealed by "namely, the extremely subtle knowledge of small worlds" (*tadyathā kṣudra-loka-parama-sūkṣma-jñāna*) and so forth.

This comprises twenty-one types of knowledge: the first nine directly refer to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); the next nine clarify its enjoyment (*paribhoga*); and the final one concerns the manifestation of many forms (*aneka-ākāra-kriyā*).
This is also the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the latter three, there is correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) without attachment.

The third [verse] states, "Thus understanding," which concludes by manifesting the virtue of the knower. The seventh is the wisdom that knows the subtlety of the three realms; this manifests the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as phenomena that are themselves the principle.
Therefore, it says "all dharma-realms. This refers to the principle within phenomena. Furthermore, it says "non-arising" and so forth, which is also the first [point].
This indicates the basis. Next, the passage beginning with "attaining the immeasurable" lists the wisdom obtained; the first phrase is general, while the remainder is specific.

Following this, the passage beginning with "in this way" concludes by describing the virtues of the one who possesses such knowledge. Eighth is the knowledge that enters the subtleties of the kalpas, which also has three parts.
First, by means of "unattached" (*asaṅga*), the basis for the qualities is indicated. Second, by "namely" (*yad uta*), the wisdom obtained is listed.
Third, by "such as these," the quality of the knower is concluded. [Regarding] the ninth, the subtle wisdom of unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*):
first, the heading; second, by "namely," the specific wisdom obtained is detailed. The text contains ten phrases, which in meaning comprise four layers. First, the essence of phenomena is complete.

1. Virtue; 2. Entering the equality of all bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), which clarifies the mutual identity of phenomena and their function; 3. Entering that which is not the dharma and so forth, which clarifies the mutual identity of principle and phenomenon;

4. Entering skillful means without distinction, which is the mastery of essence and function. Following this, the passage beginning with "such as these" concludes by describing the virtue of being able to know.
The tenth is the subtle wisdom that comprehensively knows all things exhaustively without remainder. (These are the ten phrases in the Jin translation.)
All [of these] contain the phrase "without remainder. The text is divided into four parts: First, from "by means of non-attachment" (*anāsaṅga*) onwards, there is a general statement of the basis.
Second, from "that is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, there is a detailed enumeration of the dharmas attained; this restates the ten preceding gates, with some names being slightly modified.
Third, from "or not equal" onwards, the meanings are all identical. Fourth, from "furthermore, up to knowing all" onwards, there is a conclusion regarding what was not explicitly stated.
The four points beginning with "like an illusion" below reveal the virtues of the knower; these also have both general and specific aspects. The general aspect arises from what preceded.
The specific aspect corresponds, in order, to the ten preceding phrases: first, because external lands are reflections of the mind, one who now knows the lands knows them as reflections.
Second, because the perceptions of sentient beings appear [unreal], they are said to be like dreams. Third, karmic retribution is produced through illusion.

Therefore, it is like an illusion (1). Fourth, the nature of the mind is quiescent, yet through conditions and stimuli it manifests as diversity; therefore, it is said to be like an echo (2). Fifth, at the time of speaking, it is like a transformation (3).
Sixth, it is the very realm of emptiness (4). Seventh, language is fundamentally quiescent (5). Eighth, it is the very dharma-realm (6). Ninth, the mundane world has no basis (7).
Tenth, supramundane practice is itself the Buddha-dharma (8). The above collectively clarifies the dedication toward Bodhi in relation to the preceding [sections].
Having finished [dedicating] for the sake of all sentient beings, the following dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the practice of detachment from signs.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated.
He does not discriminate between the world and worldly phenomena; he does not discriminate between bodhi and the bodhisattva. He does not discriminate...
They do not differentiate between the bodhisattva’s practice and the path of deliverance; they do not differentiate between the Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas;
they do not differentiate between those who have been disciplined by sentient beings and those who have not been disciplined;

they do not differentiate between roots of goodness and their dedication; they do not differentiate between self and other; they do not differentiate between the object given and the recipient of the gift.
One discriminates neither the conduct of a bodhisattva nor perfect enlightenment, nor does one discriminate between phenomena or wisdom.

The second major section concerns the dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This section contains ten pairs of concepts: first, the pair of the provisional and the real; second, the pair of person and phenomenon;
third, the pair of essence and function, which includes five internal pairs all concerning the subjective and objective; and ninth, the pair of cause and effect, [leading to] perfect enlightenment.
Awakening (*bodhi*) refers to a person’s realization of the Dharma; it differs from the aforementioned *bodhi*. The tenth [category] consists of the teaching and the wisdom of the teaching;
because there is no conceptual discrimination, each and every one enters into reality. Above, its characteristics were extensively revealed.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates those roots of goodness in this way: namely, with a mind free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated;

with a body free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated; with speech free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated; with karma free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated;
with retribution free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated; and with the world free from attachment, free from bondage, and liberated.
The Buddha-field is liberation through non-attachment and non-binding; sentient beings are liberation through non-attachment and non-binding;
phenomena are liberation through non-attachment and non-binding; wisdom is liberation through non-attachment and non-binding.

The second major section, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, summarizes the various gateways. Because the mind is without bondage, it causes the body and all else to be entirely free from attachment and bondage.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates merit in this manner, it is as when the Buddhas of the three periods of time were themselves Bodhisattvas...

They cultivate dedication and practice dedication; they study the dedication of the Buddhas of the past, accomplish the dedication of the Buddhas of the future, and abide in the dedication of the Buddhas of the present.

They dwell securely in the path of dedication of the Buddhas of the past, do not abandon the path of dedication of the Buddhas of the future, and follow the path of dedication of the Buddhas of the present. They diligently cultivate the [dedication] of the Buddhas of the past...

The Buddha-dharma: accomplishing the equality of all future Buddhas, fully knowing the equality of all present Buddhas, and fulfilling the equality of all past Buddhas; abiding securely in the equality of all present Buddhas.
They traverse the realm of all past Buddhas, abide in the realm of all future Buddhas, and equalize the realm of all present Buddhas.
They attain the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, possess the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
dwell in the conduct of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and accord with the realm of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

The third major section clarifies the benefits achieved through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It first restates [the preceding] and then reveals [the subsequent]. This revelation consists of ten phrases:

the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. Among the specific ones: (1) "dedication" refers to the actual engagement in practice; (2) "path" refers to constantly traversing the tracks of the Dharma;
(3) "dedication to the teaching"; (4) "equalizing wisdom"; (5) "the objective sphere"; and (6) "the transcendence of meritorious practice."
1. Cultivating these roots of goodness of the Buddha; 2. Clearly perceiving the original source and accomplishing the nature of a Tathāgata;
3. Unimpeded compassion and wisdom as the sphere of practice; 4. The inexhaustible essence and function as the boundary of the objective realm.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s unattached, unbound, and liberated mind.
The third section concludes with the phrase "possessing a mind," which is stated because the explanation has been set forth extensively from the beginning.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they cannot be destroyed by any of the Vajra-circled mountain ranges.
Among all sentient beings, their physical form and marks are supreme, with none able to equal them.

They are fully capable of crushing all the evil deeds of Māras and manifesting throughout all worlds in the ten directions to cultivate the bodhisattva practices, desiring to awaken even a single being.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they employ skillful means to expound the teachings of the Buddhas and attain great wisdom.
Their minds remain free from confusion regarding the Buddha-dharma. In whatever place they are born, whether walking or standing still, they always encounter an indestructible retinue.
They are able to receive and uphold, with pure mindfulness, the true Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, practicing it throughout all future kalpas.
The bodhisattva practice is constant and without rest; it is free from all dependence and attachment. The practices and vows of Samantabhadra increase and become fully perfected.
One attains omniscience, performs the Buddha-work, and accomplishes the sovereign spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.
The second stage of fruition consists of three types of results: first, the result of present accomplishment; herein, one first achieves self-benefit and subsequently desires to benefit others below.

Second, the result of future attainment while remaining in the lower realms; herein, one first achieves self-benefit and subsequently, until the end of the future, simultaneously benefits both self and others.
Third, the result of ultimate perfection as indicated by Samantabhadra; herein, cause and effect are non-obstructive.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Throughout the ten directions, toward the peerless Honored Ones, I have never once given rise to a thought of contempt.
In accordance with the meritorious deeds they cultivate, I likewise pay them homage and give rise to reverence."
All the merits one cultivates, neither for oneself nor for others,
are always dedicated with the mind of supreme faith and understanding for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
never for a moment does one give rise to a mind of pride, nor does one ever harbor thoughts of inferiority.
All the physical and other actions of the Tathāgata, as well as the various roots of goodness he has cultivated through diligent practice— all these are for the benefit of all sentient beings;
abiding in a profound mind and vast understanding, they dedicate them toward the state of merit of the Honored One among Men.
All the immeasurable varieties in the world— The various skillful, marvelous, coarse, subtle, vast,
and profound matters— There is none that they do not practice or fully comprehend.
Regarding all the various bodies in the world, They enter into them all with the equality of their own body.
Having attained realization through practice herein, they achieve the gateway of wisdom and never regress.
Regarding the infinite varieties of world-systems— subtle, vast, inverted, or upright—
the Bodhisattva, by means of the gateway of wisdom, perceives them all within a single pore.
The mental activities of sentient beings are immeasurable; They can cause them all to enter equally into the single mind.
Through the gateway of wisdom, they awaken them all completely, So that they do not regress from their practices.
The faculties, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings— Each of the superior, middling, and inferior grades are different.
All things are profoundly deep and difficult to know; yet, according to their inherent nature, they can fully comprehend the various karmas of sentient beings.
Distinguishing each among the superior, middling, and inferior grades, the Bodhisattva enters deeply into the power of the Tathāgata, seeing all clearly and universally through the gateway of wisdom.
Inconceivable and immeasurable eons can be made to enter equally into a single thought-moment;
having seen this, they pervade the ten directions and cultivate all pure deeds.
Regarding the past, future, and present, they understand that their characteristics are each distinct.
Yet they do not contradict the principle of equality; this is the practice of great-minded clarity and penetration in the world.
The conduct of sentient beings is diverse—sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden—in immeasurable varieties.
The Bodhisattvas fully know these distinct characteristics, and they also know that all such characteristics are ultimately without characteristics.
The sovereign power of spiritual transformations manifested by all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions is vast and inconceivable;
yet Bodhisattvas are able to discern and know it all.
Within the Tuṣita heavens of every world, these lions among men naturally awaken to enlightenment.
His merit is vast, pure, and peerless; he can perceive all things according to their essential nature and characteristics.

Sometimes he manifests his descent into a mother’s womb; through immeasurable, sovereign, and great spiritual transformations, he becomes a Buddha, preaches the Dharma, and demonstrates parinirvāṇa, pervading the entire world without a moment’s rest.
When the Lion among Men was first born, all those of supreme wisdom— Śakra, Brahmā,
and the other lords of the devas— honored and attended him with reverence;
throughout the ten directions, without exception, within the immeasurable and boundless realms of reality, there was none who did not do so.
Without beginning or end, without distance near or far, the Tathāgata manifests his sovereign power;

having appeared as the Honored Guide among men, he walks seven paces in each direction, desiring to awaken all sentient beings through the sublime Dharma; for this reason, the Tathāgata gazes everywhere.
Seeing all sentient beings submerged in the ocean of desire, Enveloped by blindness, darkness, and ignorance, The Sovereign among Men manifests a smile;

Reflecting that he shall rescue them from the suffering of the three realms of existence, The Great Teacher utters this wondrous sound of the lion’s roar: “I am the foremost honored one in the world.”
One should kindle the bright lamp of pure wisdom To extinguish the darkness of ignorance within birth and death.
When the Lion-King of Men appears in the world, He universally radiates immeasurable great light,
Causing all evil realms to find rest, And forever extinguishing the manifold sufferings and hardships of the world.
At times he manifests dwelling in royal palaces, and at times he manifests leaving home to practice the path;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he displays such sovereign power that when the Tathāgata first sits at the site of enlightenment, the entire great earth trembles.
The worlds of the ten directions all receive its light, And sentient beings of the six realms are all freed from suffering.
It causes all the palaces of Māra to tremble, And awakens the minds of sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Those who have previously received transformation and those who practice the path— All are made to understand the true meaning.
All the lands throughout the ten directions enter entirely into a single pore without exception;
within the infinite lands of every pore, he universally manifests his supernormal powers.
All the skillful means expounded by all Buddhas, he awakens to them all accordingly.
They speak that which all Tathāgatas have not spoken; they are able to understand and diligently cultivate [this teaching] so that it pervades the trichiliocosm.
All the hosts of Māra who raise strife and commit immeasurable varieties of evil are entirely extinguished by the gateway of unimpeded wisdom.
Whether the Tathāgata is in various Buddha-fields, or manifests in the palaces of the devas,
or appears in the Brahma-heavens, the Bodhisattvas encounter no obstacles whatsoever;
the Buddha manifests infinite and diverse bodies, turning the pure and wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
Even throughout all kalpas of the three periods of time, one cannot find its limit;
The precious throne is high, vast, and peerless, Pervading the immeasurable realms of the ten directions, adorned with various wondrous marks; The Buddha sits upon it, inconceivable.
Surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, Pervading the entire extent of the Dharma-realm,
He reveals the immeasurable practices of Bodhi— The path by which all the Most Victorious Ones proceed,
The deeds performed by the Buddhas according to their suitability, Immeasurable and boundless, equal to the Dharma-realm.
The wise one, by means of a single skillful method, thoroughly understands all things without exception;
through the sovereign supernatural powers of the Buddhas, they manifest all manner of diverse bodies—
sometimes appearing as infinite births within the various realms of existence, and sometimes appearing surrounded by a multitude of celestial maidens.
In immeasurable worlds, he manifests leaving the home life, attaining the path of Buddhahood,
and even reaching final parinirvāṇa; he distributes his body to establish stupas and temples—
such are the various boundless practices that the Guide expounds as the dwelling place of the Buddha.
May all the great virtues of the World-Honored One, And all his vows and practices, be fully realized;
When dedicating those roots of goodness, One abides in such skillful means.
Thus cultivating the conduct of enlightenment, The mind never becomes weary or indolent.

All the great supernormal powers possessed by the Tathāgata, As well as his boundless and supreme merits, And even all the various modes of worldly knowledge— He knows them all completely, without exception.
Such is the Lord among Men; In accordance with all his various spheres of experience,
In a single thought-moment, they fully awaken to all things, yet never abandon the practices of enlightenment.
They are able to understand and accord with every subtle action of the Buddhas and the diverse phenomena of all lands;
having perfected their dedication of merit, they reach the further shore.
Throughout all kalpas, whether numbered or unnumbered, the Bodhisattva understands every thought;
thus they skillfully enter the practice of enlightenment, constantly and diligently cultivating it without ever regressing.
They behold all the infinite lands throughout the ten directions, whether they are defiled or pure.
And all those Tathāgatas, as well as the Bodhisattvas, they are able to discern and know them all;
in every thought-moment they clearly perceive inconceivable and immeasurable eons.
Thus, throughout the three periods of time without exception, they fully cultivate and purify the practices of a Bodhisattva.
Entering with equanimity into all minds, And entering with equal exhaustion into all phenomena and empty buddha-fields;
Fully knowing those supreme practices, The arising of sentient beings and all dharmas, And all the various kinds of wisdom— [Note:
This verse is a translation of a passage from the *Gandavyūha-sūtra* (Entry into the Dharma Realm), specifically from the section on the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.]
The supernormal powers of the Bodhisattva are likewise so; all such things are inexhaustible.

Each of the subtle wisdoms is distinct, yet the Bodhisattva encompasses them all without exception, thoroughly knowing both their common and specific characteristics. Thus they practice these vast deeds.
Throughout the immeasurable Buddha-fields of the ten directions, The sentient beings therein are each infinite;
their destinies, births, and species are manifold and distinct.
Having mastered the power of abiding and practice, they fully know all things Of the past, future, and present worlds—every single one of those who are the Guides.
If one knows this and dedicates [merit], then one is equal in practice to those Buddhas;
if one can cultivate this dedication, then one studies the path traveled by the Buddhas.
One shall attain all the virtues of the Buddhas, as well as all the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Nothing in all the worlds can destroy them; All that they have studied is fully accomplished.
They shall attain the recollection of all Buddhas, And constantly behold the lamps of all worlds.
The sublime conduct of these Bodhisattvas is immeasurable, And their qualities and dharmas are likewise so.
Having already abided in the supreme conduct of the Tathāgatas, they fully know the sovereign powers of all Buddhas.

(This is the second section, the Verses of Application, consisting of fifty-one stanzas. It is divided into two parts: first, the verses on the practices of the stages; second, the verses on the fruits of the stages.)
The preceding section consists of three parts. First, the first three verses praise the roots of goodness to be dedicated.
Second, the following forty-four verses praise the practice of dedication. Third, the final two verses praise the benefits achieved through that practice.

Within the section on the practice of dedication, the first verse praises the ultimate fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s own path (*svabhāva-niṣṭhā*), while the remaining verses praise the ultimate fulfillment of his superior progress (*viśeṣa-niṣṭhā*).

The preceding prose section contained three categories of qualities: first, the quality of vastness through the threefold inclusion; second, the quality of entering into the layered (re-repeated) profundity; and third, the quality of subtle containment.
Now, these are summarized in verse, but here only the subtle aspect is revealed. This is divided into ten parts: the first consists of three verses summarizing the subtle wisdom regarding the world;
the second consists of one verse summarizing the realms of sentient beings, as they are distinguished by their respective modes of conduct.
Three verses praise the fifth [topic], the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*). "Realm" (*dhātu*) refers here to the nature of the faculties (*indriya-gotra*).
Four verses praise the third [topic], the virtues of the bodhisattva’s practice; a bodhisattva is also designated by the term "sentient being.
Fifty verses and below praise the fourth [topic], the great function of the virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*); herein there are three parts. First, one verse provides a general summary. Next...
23. The eight characteristics of cause and effect are praised in separate verses. The final three verses praise the virtues of the one who possesses this knowledge.

The verse beginning with "six categories" praises the eighth, the knowledge of eons (*kalpa-jñāna*). The verse beginning with "the ten directions" praises the sixth, the knowledge of worlds (*loka-jñāna*).
The two verses beginning with "in every moment of thought" praise the seventh, the knowledge of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*). 9. Exit.

The first verse following "Upon birth" praises the ninth, the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*). The two verses beginning with "All subtle [aspects]" below praise the tenth, the knowledge of all dharmas (*sarvadharmajñāna*).
The four verses beginning with "Past and future" below praise the fruit of the stage of accomplishment and benefit, which may be understood accordingly.
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha,
Volume Thirty-One and Volume Thirty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá-yán Monastery;
Excerpts by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Monastery on Mount Kuāng, Explaining the Meaning.
Chapter Twenty-five, Part Ten: The Ten Dedications.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s “Infinite Dedication Equal to the Dharma Realm”?

Regarding the tenth dedication, the Infinite Dedication Equal to the Dharma Realm, the prose section first treats the practice of the preceding stage and subsequently the fruit of the succeeding stage.
The preceding citation from the "Extensive Explanation of Names" explains the etymology [of *dharmadhātu-praveśa*]: it means that by invoking the great function of the *dharmadhātu*, one enters it.
The term "etc. (*ādi*) signifies the meaning of "entering" (*praveśa*). Therefore, in the "Fundamental Section," it is named "Entering the *Dharmadhātu*.

The immeasurable *dharmadhātu* is that which is entered. What phenomena are able to enter it? Briefly, there are four: first, the phenomena of the conduct to be transformed, namely, the practice of the gift of Dharma which accords with the *dharmadhātu*.

First, because of giving. Second, because the essential nature of the practices performed is vast and boundless. Third, the wisdom capable of redirecting [merit]. Fourth, the virtues to be redirected;

that is to say, by means of great wisdom that accords with the dharma-realm, one redirects roots of goodness equal to the dharma-realm toward the great function identical to the dharma-realm, thereby perfecting the essential nature of practice within the dharma-realm. This constitutes the ultimate fulfillment of the stages. Therefore...

The designation "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm) is applied according to its actual nature. To what kind of dharmadhātu does this refer? It encompasses four meanings: first, the dharmadhātu of equal principle;
thus the Sūtra says, "in accordance with the nature of the dharmadhātu. Second, the dharmadhātu of equal phenomena;

as the Sūtra says, "wishing to see the immeasurable Buddhas who tame beings within the equal dharmadhātu, and the immeasurable sentient beings within the equal dharmadhātu. Third, the dharmadhātu of equal principle... [text continues].
Regarding the *dharmadhātu* of non-obstruction between phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*):

the Sūtra says, "May all sentient beings become Dharma-preachers who cultivate the path of signlessness, adorning themselves with all manner of sublime marks. Thus, the non-obstruction of marks is of this same category.
Fourth is the *dharmadhātu* of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*). The Sūtra says, "Within every Buddha-field, manifest all Buddha-fields. However...
These four matters are entirely identical to the four kinds of *dharmadhātu*. They are fused and non-dual; thus, that which is able to equalize is itself that which is equalized.
There are not two distinct entities upon which one can rely. Therefore, what is called "entering" above refers to entering where there is nothing to enter.
The *Mūlapravṛtti* merely states that the *dharmadhātu* is without equal; the term "entering" carries precisely this meaning. The commentary explains: "to awaken to all phenomena."
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the Middle Way without marks (*animitta*), because all phenomena are illuminated by a single characteristic.
This first Middle Way is that which is entered; that all are illuminated by a single characteristic is the means of entry. These two are non-dual, and this is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, it cannot be designated merely by the name "phenomenal Dharma-realm. As for the term "immeasurable," in terms of principle (*li*), it is...
It is without measure. In terms of phenomena, there is no numerical limit. The previous dedication clarified that function arises based on the essence;

this clarifies the non-obstruction between essence and function. Being perfectly consummate and sovereign, it takes the merit of the Dharma-gift, along with all its corresponding qualities and the great skillful means of Samantabhadra’s sovereignty, as the essential nature of this stage.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has a stainless silk ribbon bound upon his crown and abides in the rank of a Dharma Master.
In the second part, the extensive explanation, the main text is divided into three sections: first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, from "With these roots of goodness...
onwards, gathering and preparing for the dedication; third, "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner..."

Abiding in the lower stage, one dedicates [merit] to achieve benefit. Regarding the first part, the initial section clarifies the bodily status upon which the practice depends; the second section extensively explains how practice arises based on that status.
Now, for the first part, the phrase "free from defilement" (*vimalā*) and so forth refers to attaining the *vimalā-samādhi* and receiving the rank of wisdom as described in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Because one internally attains this samādhi, which consecrates the crown of the mind, one externally manifests the sign of a white silk turban.
The method of binding the crown is designated by way of analogy as the "Stainless Silk Ribbon. Possessing this sign of realization, one attains that samādhi;
manifesting the perfection of the stage, one is then able to rain down the Dharma to benefit all sentient beings—this is called the stage of the Dharma Master (*dharmabhāṇaka*).

Furthermore, the fulfillment of this stage consists of five levels in total. First is the fulfillment of faith, as described in the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*, whereby one receives the empowerment of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
1. Regarding the perfection of attainment, such as ascending to higher stages; 2. Regarding the perfection of understanding, such as the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*); 3.

Regarding the perfection of what is fulfilled, such as the tenth practice of entering the *indrajāla* (net of Indra) dharmadhātu; 4. The perfection of skillful vows, as distinguished in this stage; 5.

Regarding the perfection of realization, as explained in the context of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Within these five layers, wherever one is established, it necessarily contains both principle and practice.

Because they are mutually corresponding, all are said to have their stages fulfilled (*pūrṇa*). If one considers them from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), then the fulfillment of even a single stage is itself the ultimate;
nothing further remains to be awaited. Furthermore, if one attains one stage, one simultaneously attains the others.

Within the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the stage of receiving office, there are differences according to the various gates, such that the five stages are distinct. Yet, as the essence of the Dharma is interpenetrating, they are entirely encompassed without obstruction.
Extensively practicing the gift of Dharma, they give rise to great compassion to establish sentient beings in the state of peace.
