They constantly act for the benefit of others through the bodhicitta without ceasing, nurturing roots of goodness by means of that bodhicitta, and serving as guides and teachers for all sentient beings.
They show the path of omniscience to all sentient beings. For the sake of all sentient beings, they act as the sun of the Dharma-treasury;
the radiance of their roots of goodness shines universally upon all. Their minds are impartial toward all sentient beings, and they cultivate various virtuous practices without ceasing.
With a pure mind free from defilement and mastery over wisdom, they do not abandon any roots of goodness or the path of practice.
Acting as great wise leaders for all sentient beings, they cause them all to enter the secure and correct path, serving as guides and heads for all beings.

They cause all roots of goodness and dharmic practices to be cultivated. For the sake of all sentient beings, they act as indestructible and steadfast virtuous friends, causing their roots of goodness to increase and reach fulfillment.
Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas take the gift of Dharma as primary;
they give rise to all pure and white dharmas and embrace the mind that inclines toward omniscience through their sublime vows.
Their power is ultimate and firm; they have accomplished increase and possess great majestic virtue.
Relying on spiritual friends with a mind free from flattery or deception, they contemplate and investigate the infinite realms of all doors of wisdom.

Regarding the second [section], "Arising Practice Based on the Stages," there are two parts: first, the explanation of the arising of practice; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the manifestation of the perfection of that practice.

Furthermore, the former clarifies benefiting others, while the latter clarifies self-benefit. Moreover, the former clarifies the stage of one's own nature (*svabhāva*), while the latter manifests superior progress (*viśeṣa*).

Now, within the first of these, there are eleven phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific. These specific points clarify that compassion and the other [immeasurables] are all the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). As for this Dharma...
Generosity is the wondrous method for generating understanding, the root of initiating practice, the gradual steps for entering the noble path, and the bridge for crossing the sea of suffering.
As the ancient masters have said, within this sutra, the Way is propagated by relying upon persons;

it frequently extols the superior virtues of the Dharma Master and expresses the Dharma by entrusting it to practice, often citing Samantabhadra as the conclusion of each chapter. Thus we know the Dharma...
The merit of this giving is beyond comparison with that of material giving. Within this, there are ten phrases: first, bringing peace to beings through compassion;
second, benefiting beings without ceasing—these two constitute the vast mind. Third, nurturing the great mind; fourth, ultimate discipline and guidance—these two constitute the foremost mind.
Fifth, the universal illumination of the sun of Dharma; sixth, equally exhorting others to cultivate goodness—these two...
This is the constant mind. Because it constantly loves sentient beings as it does itself, it is called "equanimity. The seventh is the pure mind of non-obstruction, which is the non-perverted mind.
The eighth is called the "Merchant Leader" because he shows the jewel-island of the fruit;
this jewel-island is the fruit of nirvāṇa and bodhi. The ninth is that he guides them by means of the causes of the ten thousand practices; these two constitute the first mind.
The tenfold increase and non-destruction constitute protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*). It begins by causing the arousal of the mind of enlightenment and ends by bringing it to fulfillment;

for who, indeed, is a sage other than one who possesses both a beginning and an end? Next, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva takes the gift of Dharma as foremost," which below reveals the perfection of his practice.
First, it reiterates the aforementioned gift of Dharma; the following five phrases, beginning with "receiving and sustaining" (*parigraha*), correctly reveal its fulfillment.
[He] contemplates thus: "That which is directed toward is merely these roots of goodness.
By means of these roots of goodness, I dedicate them in this way: may I obtain the cultivation, accomplishment, increase, and vast expansion of all unobstructed spheres;
and may I obtain [the opportunity] to hear even a single phrase or a single verse within the Buddha’s true teaching."
I shall uphold and expound this. May I attain mindfulness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present in all infinite and boundless worlds, equal in extent to the Dharma-realm.
Having attained such mindfulness, I shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices.

Furthermore, may I, by means of these roots of goodness from the recollection of the Buddha, cultivate the bodhisattva practices for the sake of a single sentient being in a single world throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
Just as it is for one world, so it is for all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Just as it is for one sentient being, so it is likewise for all sentient beings.

Through skillful means, he adorns himself with great vows for every single one of them throughout all future kalpas, never ceasing to perceive Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and constantly beholding them.
The Buddhas appear before them; there is not a single Buddha appearing in the world whom they do not have the opportunity to approach.

Regarding the pure brahmacarya praised and taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they vow to practice it until it is entirely perfected—namely, a brahmacarya that is unbroken, unimpaired, unmixed, and stainless.

The loss of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). There is no obscuration of the holy life. The holy life praised by the Buddha. The holy life that is without dependence. The holy life that is without attainment.
It increases the pure holy life of a bodhisattva. The holy life practiced by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The unimpeded holy life. The unattached holy life. The non-contentious holy life. The non-extinguishing holy life. The holy life of stable abiding. Without...
This is the holy life (*brahmacarya*): the unshakable holy life, the undisturbed holy life, the non-hostile holy life.

Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice such pure holy life for their own sake, they are then able to do so universally for the sake of all sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to dwell securely and causing all sentient beings to attain full understanding.
May all sentient beings achieve fulfillment. May all sentient beings attain purity. May all sentient beings become stainless.
May all sentient beings attain illumination. May all sentient beings be free from the defilement of dust.
May all sentient beings be free from all obscurations. May all sentient beings be free from...
[They eliminate] all fevers and afflictions. They cause all sentient beings to be free from all fetters and bonds.
They cause all sentient beings to be forever free from all evils. They cause all sentient beings to be without harm or affliction, ultimately pure. Why is this?
Because if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cannot purify their own Brahma-conduct, they cannot cause others to attain purification. As for themselves...
One who has regressed from the holy life cannot cause others to be free from regression;
one who has ruined the holy life oneself cannot cause others to be free from ruin; one who has abandoned the holy life oneself cannot cause others to remain constantly un-abandoned;
and one who is indolent in the holy life oneself cannot cause others to not become so.
Being indolent, they do not themselves give rise to faith and understanding toward the holy life (*brahmacarya*), nor can they cause others' minds to give rise to faith and understanding.
They do not themselves abide securely in the holy life, nor can they cause others to attain such secure abiding.
They do not themselves realize entry into the holy life, nor can they cause others' minds to attain realization. They themselves abandon the holy life, and cannot...
They cause others never to abandon [the path], yet they themselves waver within the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and cannot cause the minds of others not to waver. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in unerring conduct and teach the unerring Dharma; their words are truthful, and they practice according to what they have taught.
With body, speech, and mind purified, they are free from all defilements and abide in unimpeded conduct, extinguishing the one...
All obstacles. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains a pure mind for himself and expounds the Dharma of the pure mind to others.

He personally cultivates harmony and patience, using all roots of goodness to subdue his own mind, and causes others to cultivate harmony and patience, using all roots of goodness to subdue their minds.
He himself leaves behind doubt and regret, and also causes others to forever leave behind delusion and regret. He himself attains pure faith, and also...
He causes others to attain indestructible pure faith; he himself abides in the True Dharma and also causes sentient beings to dwell securely in the True Dharma.
Regarding the second section on "Inclusion and Dedication," there are twenty-one gates in total for the subsequent text. This major section is divided into three parts:
first, nine gates that individually correspond to the eleven phrases of roots of goodness to clarify dedication—this constitutes the "self-part" (*svabhāga*); next, four gates...
This generally clarifies the intent of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Within the third section, there are eight gates that further clarify dedication through distinct approaches;

this is the "Superior Progression" (*viśeṣagamana*). First, it consists of nine segments. The first is the vow to hear the Dharma, see the Buddhas, and cultivate the practices of the two benefits (*dvividha-artha*).
Regarding the first two lines: among them, the first expresses the vow in general, while the remainder specifically elucidate it.
Now, for the very first line, the preceding [context] is cited; from "may I attain" onwards, the actual wording of the vow is revealed.

As for "all objects" (*sarvaviṣaya*), the literal phrasing is restricted to the initial section, but its meaning comprehensively encompasses all twenty-one sections of dedication, as all of these constitute "all objects. This refers to "all objects."
Vast as the Dharma-realm, with no obstruction between principle and phenomena, or phenomenon and phenomenon, may such a state be fully increased and accomplished.
Next, there are two specific clarifications within the middle section. First, it says: "May I, within the Buddha’s true teaching, hear, receive, and uphold even a single line of scripture.
This constitutes the aforementioned meaning of extensively practicing the giving of the Dharma. Second, it says:
I pray that I may remember the one and a half lines of scripture below. I pray that I may practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) so as to accomplish supreme benefit without ceasing.
Within this, first, the practice of recollecting the Buddha is correctly elucidated;

next, there is the prayer that by means of these roots of goodness (kuśalamūla), the four lines of scripture below shall dedicate the merit of recollecting the Buddha toward accomplishing the two benefits (svārtha and parārtha). Within this latter section, there are also two parts: first, [the dedication] generally for all beings.
One practices the bodhisattva path throughout all times and places. Hereafter, the text specifically clarifies the cultivation of the brahma-conduct;
as it is the foundation of the myriad practices, it is explained in detail. This section contains three parts; first, one verse from another sutra.

This first section summarizes the vows. Next, from the passage beginning with "That which is called not breaking the holy life" (*brahmacarya*) down to four and a half lines of scripture, the practices to be cultivated are enumerated.
Within this, there are twenty types of holy life (*brahmacarya*), which for the most part correspond to the ten realms listed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
These are: being unimpaired, unbroken, unpierced, unmixed, following the path, unattached, praised by the wise, sovereign, and conforming to meditative concentration.
Fully endowed [with these], one universally takes the general precepts as the foundation. Now, the ten [precepts] are expanded into twenty-one.

The Commentary follows the sequence of the Sūtra to reconcile the ten precepts. Regarding the fact that the Sūtra places the "non-breaking" [precepts] first, this refers to upholding the four grave and the ten heavy [offenses].
If one violates this, it is like a broken vessel that is no longer functional. Second, "without flaw" refers to maintaining the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension);
"flaw" is like a chipped vessel, yet it can still be repaired. Third, "without admixture" refers to maintaining the preparatory practices (*prayoga*);

if one recollects matters of broken precepts, speaks with a defiled mind, or hears the sound of bracelets and anklets, all such instances are termed "admixture. Fourth, "without stain" refers to maintaining...
A *pāyattika* offense is like a flaw in white jade; though it might be polished away, one should not allow it to occur.
Regarding the six points of non-failure, these correspond to a concentrated mind; one does not err even in a *duṣkṛta* (minor transgression), for the six conditions cannot destroy them.
The first three do not pierce the precepts; to pierce them is like a leaking vessel, incapable of receiving the Path. The first six are all matters of restraint (*saṃvara*). Seven.

1. It is praised by the wise. 2. The eight kinds of non-reliance refer to not relying on fame, profit, or karmic retribution. 3. Non-attainment refers to not attaining that which can uphold [the precepts] or that which is upheld.

4. Next, the increase of the lower three [categories] all follow the path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*). 5. The tenth excludes the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). 6. The eleventh reveals that this is the practice of a Buddha. 7.
The twelfth is able to penetrate even what is not the path; therefore, it is called "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*). 8. The thirteenth...

Non-attachment (*anāsaṅga*) means that upon seeing reality, one becomes a sage (*ārya*). The four qualities following "non-contention" (*araṇā*) constitute the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*):

first, because one contemplates the path as possessing both phenomena and principle; second, because phenomena and principle do not conflict; third, because by acting in accordance with principle, the mind is never extinguished;
fourth, because the mind can reach the principle, it is called "abiding securely"; and fifth, because it surpasses all others, it is called "incomparable."
Following the "Immovable" [Samādhi], all that follows pertains to the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*). This refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi:

while not arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests all modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*); though manifesting the forms of the ten dharma realms, there is no precept that is not practiced, yet one remains tranquil and unmoving.
Favorable conditions cannot disturb one, and adverse conditions provoke no anger. It further states: "O Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
The seven lines of scripture beginning with "Able to... constitute the third section, which resolves objections and establishes the argument. An anticipated objection (*vāda-pratibandha*) states:
"If a Bodhisattva’s resolve is to place others before oneself, does it not contradict this to first practice for one's own sake?

Therefore, the text below explains: "Merely practicing for oneself is itself a benefit to sentient beings. This also establishes the aforementioned point regarding establishing sentient beings in the bodhicitta.
And through the bodhicitta, one nurtures the roots of goodness. This section consists of two parts: first, the direct explanation;

second, a further inquiry and clarification. Now, for the first part: the single phrase "If one can... provides a general explanation, while the subsequent passage beginning with "causing all... provides a specific exposition consisting of twelve phrases.
This section generally clarifies the observance and violation [of precepts]. Next, regarding the interrogation and explanation beginning with "For what reason," there are two parts:

first, the direct interrogation and counter-explanation; second, the repeated interrogation and conformative explanation. Now, for the first part, the direct explanation, there are eight lines of scripture containing ten phrases.
The intent of the interrogation is: "Since the practices of self and others differ, how can one's own practice be considered that of another? The intent of the explanation is: "If one's own body..."

[The Buddha] replied: "It is so. Because his command was not followed, he himself acted, thereby benefiting sentient beings. Next, the passage beginning with "For what reason? provides a further inquiry and explanation in six lines of scripture. The intent of the inquiry is: although a whetstone is not sharp itself, it can sharpen a blade; even if one does not practice oneself, how could that hinder benefiting others? Why, then, do you now say that [the Buddha] cannot benefit them? The meaning of the explanation is as follows: [The Buddha said: "Good son, for example, there is a king who possesses great power and authority. He issues a decree to all his subjects, commanding them to go forth and cultivate fields. At that time, there is a person among the subjects who is lazy and indolent; he does not wish to cultivate the fields and instead remains at home. The king’s decree is thus not carried out by him. The king thinks to himself:

'If I myself do not cultivate the fields, how can I expect the people to cultivate them? Thinking thus, the king himself goes out to cultivate the fields. When the people see the king cultivating the fields, they all follow his example and cultivate their own fields. Because the king cultivated the fields, the people were benefited. Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise. He has great spiritual power and authority, and he issues a decree to all sentient beings, commanding them to cultivate the roots of goodness. Yet sentient beings do not wish to cultivate the roots of goodness and instead remain in the house of afflictions.

The Tathāgata thinks: 'If I myself do not cultivate the roots of goodness, how can I expect sentient beings to cultivate them? Thinking thus, the Tathāgata himself cultivates the roots of goodness. When sentient beings see the Tathāgata cultivating the roots of goodness, they all follow his example and cultivate the roots of goodness. Because the Tathāgata cultivated the roots of goodness, sentient beings were benefited. This is the meaning of the explanation. The analogy of the whetstone is used because, while the stone is not sharp, it enables the blade to become sharp; similarly, although the Tathāgata is already perfected, he acts to demonstrate the path so that sentient beings may follow and be benefited. However, if sentient beings do not follow, the Tathāgata’s own cultivation cannot produce the same effect of benefit as when they do follow. This is why it is said that [in such cases] he cannot benefit them. This concludes the explanation.
It is said that if one commits an offense oneself and then instructs others [to do so], it constitutes a perversion. A bodhisattva is free from perversion;

their words and deeds must necessarily accord with one another. Therefore, only by acting as one speaks can one speak as one acts. In the text, this is first explained in general terms, and subsequently, from the section beginning "The Bodhisattva," it is specifically revealed.
This concludes the first section.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates the roots of goodness produced by this Dharma-giving in the following way:
"May I obtain all the inexhaustible Dharma-doors of all Buddhas, and universally analyze and explain them for all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice and attain fulfillment of heart.
May I destroy all the heterodox arguments of external paths. May I be able..."
For the sake of all sentient beings, they expound the ocean of the Buddhas' teachings throughout the three periods of time.
For each and every dharma, they give rise to its respective meaning and principle; for each and every dharma, they provide its name and terminology; for each and every dharma, they establish it;

for each and every dharma, they explain it; for each and every dharma, they reveal it; for each and every dharma, they open its gateway; for each and every dharma, they lead to its realization; for each and every dharma, they investigate it.
Within the single state of a single dharma, they fully attain the boundless and inexhaustible treasury of dharmas;

they obtain fearlessness and are endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), extensively analyzing and explaining them for the sake of sentient beings without end until the limits of the future.
This is because they desire to cause all sentient beings to establish supreme vows and to give rise to unimpeded and unfailing eloquence. This is because they desire to cause all...

All sentient beings were filled with joy. Desiring to cause all sentient beings to accomplish the radiance of all pure dharmas and to expound them through their respective languages without interruption;

desiring to cause all sentient beings to have deep faith and joy, to abide in the wisdom of omniscience, and to discern all phenomena so as to be free from delusion—this thought arose: "I shall, throughout..."
Throughout all worlds, they diligently practice for the sake of all sentient beings, attaining infinite sovereign bodies that pervade the entire dharma-realm,
attaining infinite vast minds that pervade the entire dharma-realm, and possessing infinite pure voices equal to the dharma-realm.
They manifest immeasurable assemblies in *maṇḍalas* equal to the *dharmadhātu*. They cultivate immeasurable bodhisattva activities equal to the *dharmadhātu*.

They attain immeasurable bodhisattva abodes equal to the *dharmadhātu*. They realize immeasurable bodhisattva equanimity equal to the *dharmadhātu*. They study immeasurable bodhisattva teachings equal to the *dharmadhātu*.
They abide in immeasurable bodhisattva practices equal to the *dharmadhātu*. They enter [the state] equal to the *dharmadhātu*.
The dedication of immeasurable bodhisattvas is the dedication performed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with all their roots of goodness,
for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fully achieve omniscience.

The second section is the aspiration to expound [the teaching] extensively for the benefit of oneself and others. It also completes the preceding passage concerning the Teacher as a Guide who reveals the path of omniscience.
This section consists of three parts; first, a single phrase on the gift of Dharma introduces the preceding topic and initiates the subsequent one.

Next, regarding what is called "the lower [section]," there are two parts that correctly clarify the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The first part is a general aspiration for attaining the Dharma, which consists of four sections:
first, attaining the Dharma; second, liberation; third, benefiting sentient beings; and fourth, crushing and destroying [afflictions]. Next, the passage beginning with "May I be able to...

specifically clarifies the propagation of the Dharma, explaining the four meanings of the preceding text. This section consists of five divisions, the first two of which provide a general clarification.
Next, under each individual dharma, the attainment of the dharma is clarified. Third, from "obtaining fearlessness" onwards, the ability to expound [the Dharma] is clarified.

Fourth, the four lines of sutra beginning with "desiring to cause all... clarify the intended audience (the *kai*). Fifth, the five and a half lines of sutra beginning with "he had this thought" clarify the cultivation of virtues for oneself;
that is, diligently cultivating for the sake of others while simultaneously perfecting one's own virtues, thereby accomplishing the ten [powers].

Regarding the cultivation of merit: the first two [perfections] are said to be "pervasive," as they pervade both principle and phenomena; the remaining eight are said to be "equal," as they include equality and unimpededness.
Next, in the concluding summary beginning with "This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of all roots of goodness...

and so forth, the aforementioned cultivation of one's own virtues is also for the sake of gathering in sentient beings; therefore, it is further reiterated: "in order to cause sentient beings to achieve all-knowledge. Above.
The second section is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates their roots of goodness in this way: that is to say, desiring to behold infinite Buddhas equal in extent to the Dharma-realm;
to tame infinite sentient beings equal in extent to the Dharma-realm; and to maintain [the teachings] equal in extent to the Dharma-realm.
They pervade immeasurable buddha-fields; they realize the immeasurable wisdom of bodhisattvas equal to the dharma-realm;
they attain the immeasurable fearlessnesses of bodhisattvas equal to the dharma-realm; they accomplish the immeasurable dhāraṇīs of bodhisattvas equal to the dharma-realm;

they obtain the immeasurable inconceivable abodes of bodhisattvas equal to the dharma-realm; they are endowed with immeasurable merits equal to the dharma-realm; and they fulfill [virtues] equal to the dharma-realm.
The roots of goodness for the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings. Furthermore, by virtue of these roots of goodness, may I attain equality in merit,
equality in wisdom, equality in power, equality in fearlessness, equality in purity, equality in mastery,
equality in perfect enlightenment, equality in preaching the Dharma, equality in meaning, equality in certainty, and equality in all supernormal powers.
Equanimity. May all such dharmas be fully perfected for all sentient beings, just as they have been attained by me, so that they may obtain them exactly as I have, without any difference.

The third section concerns the aspiration to perfect the practice of the two benefits. This constitutes the aforementioned "Method for Becoming a Treasury of the Dharma," as it attains wisdom, beholds the Buddhas, and so forth, all of which universally illuminate.
This section contains two parts: first, five lines of scripture that generally clarify the two benefits;

second, four lines of scripture beginning with "Furthermore, I vow by this... which specifically elucidate the two benefits. This thus completes the preceding discussion on [the practice] among all...
The minds of sentient beings are equal. First, one attains equality with the principle through oneself; subsequently, one causes all things to be equal to oneself by means of what has been attained.
The third section is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates his roots of goodness in this way: that is to say, as the Dharma-realm.
It is immeasurable. The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so; the wisdom attained is ultimately without measure.
Just as the dharma-realm is boundless, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Seeing all Buddhas has no limit;
just as the dharma-realm is infinite, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Traveling to all Buddha-fields is without restriction.
Just as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is boundless, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

just as the cultivation of bodhisattva practices in all worlds has no limit, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness that are uninterrupted like the realm of phenomena, abiding in omniscience forever without cessation.
Just as the realm of phenomena is of a single nature, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
They share the same nature of wisdom as all sentient beings. Just as the dedication of roots of goodness that are inherently pure like the dharma-realm is likewise;
it causes all sentient beings to reach ultimate purity. Just as the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with the dharma-realm is likewise;
it causes all sentient beings to fully accord with the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. Just as...
The dedication of roots of goodness as the adornment of the dharma-realm is likewise so: it causes all sentient beings to be adorned with the practices of Samantabhadra.
The dedication of roots of goodness that, like the dharma-realm, cannot be lost or destroyed is likewise so.
It causes all bodhisattvas to never lose or destroy their various pure practices.
This fourth gate of aspiration and conduct accords with the dharma-realm, accomplishing supreme mental purity free from defilement, as well as mastery over wisdom.
Because movement accords with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is nothing that can defile it. Therefore, the conclusion states: "One never loses or destroys any pure practices.

This chapter for the most part accords with the principle of the Dharma-realm; just as wisdom arises from principle, it is thus identical to the Dharma-realm, which is precisely the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
The fourth section is completed.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
that is to say, may he serve all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with these roots of goodness and cause them all to rejoice;
may he, by means of these roots of goodness, swiftly enter into the nature of omniscience; and may he, by means of these roots of goodness, cultivate all [virtues] in all places.
Wisdom. May all sentient beings, by virtue of these roots of goodness, always be able to go and visit all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings, by virtue of these roots of goodness, always see the Buddhas and be able to perform the Buddha-work.
May all sentient beings, by virtue of these roots of goodness, constantly behold the Buddhas and never give rise to a mind of indolence or negligence regarding the Buddha-work. May...
By this root of goodness, may all sentient beings always behold the Buddha, their minds joyful and pure, never regressing.
By this root of goodness, may all sentient beings always behold the Buddha and skillfully understand his teachings.
By this root of goodness, may all sentient beings always behold the Buddha and give rise to no attachment. By this...
May these roots of goodness cause all sentient beings to always behold the Buddhas and attain unimpeded realization.
May these roots of goodness cause all sentient beings to always behold the Buddhas and accomplish the practices of Samantabhadra.
May these roots of goodness cause all sentient beings to always see all Buddhas appearing before them, never for a moment departing. May these roots of goodness...
May all sentient beings always behold the Buddhas and give birth to the immeasurable powers of Bodhisattvas.
By these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings always behold the Buddhas and never forget or lose any of the dharmas.

The fifth gate: "May I obtain the vision of the Buddha and the understanding of the Dharma. This section consists of fourteen and a half lines of scripture, listing fourteen vows that establish one as a Great Wise Caravan Leader (*mahāśreṣṭhī-sārthavāha*).
The first three [vows] constitute the self-perfection of the nature of wisdom; these are the virtues of the Caravan Leader. The remaining [vows] are for the sake of sentient beings;
these are the duties of the Caravan Leader. Thus ends the fifth gate.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner: that is to say, he dedicates them in accordance with the unarisen nature of the Dharma-realm;
he dedicates them in accordance with the fundamental nature of the Dharma-realm; he dedicates them in accordance with the intrinsic nature of the Dharma-realm;
he dedicates them in accordance with the non-dependent nature of the Dharma-realm; he dedicates them in accordance with the non-forgetful nature of the Dharma-realm; as such...
Dedication as the emptiness and lack of intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm; dedication as the quiescent nature of the dharma-realm;

dedication as the nature of the dharma-realm being without location; dedication as the nature of the dharma-realm being without transition or movement; dedication as the nature of the dharma-realm being without differentiation.
The sixth section concerns the vow to understand the *dharmadhātu*. This refers to the *dharmadhātu* as principle (*li*). How could this passage be named after its phenomenal characteristics?
Yet, herein it says "as" (*ru*); the Jin translation says "understand" (*jie*). Because understanding accords with principle, it is termed "as.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the aforementioned secure and correct path. The text contains ten phrases: first, not changing according to conditions; second, not clinging to its own...
1. Nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is the fundamental basis of all phenomena (*dharma*). 2. The three kinds of suchness (*tathatā*) are likewise thus; this is its own essence (*svabhāva*). 3.

It is not that which serves as the support for the subject or object. 4. It is never momentarily separated from suchness. 5. Following conditions while lacking intrinsic nature is itself the nature of suchness.

6. Even the absence of intrinsic nature is non-existent; it is primordially quiescent. 7. It is non-dual in nature because it is free from subject and object. 8. It does not follow the three periods of time. 9. Ten...
Of one flavor and equal. The sixth section is concluded.

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates all roots of goodness arising from the Dharma-giving—namely, all that is proclaimed, all that brings awakening, and everything else associated with it—in this way: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood."
May all sentient beings become unsurpassed Dharma masters, constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and through skillful means establish all sentient beings in omniscience.
May all sentient beings become invincible Dharma masters, such that no interrogations or challenges can ever exhaust them. May all sentient beings become unobstructed Dharma [masters].
Master, you have attained the unimpeded light of all dharmas; may all sentient beings become Dharma-teachers who are treasuries of wisdom, able to skillfully expound all Buddha-dharmas.
May all sentient beings become sovereign Dharma-teachers of all Tathāgatas.

May they be well able to discern the wisdom of the Tathāgata. May all sentient beings become Dharma-teachers with eyes like those of the Buddha, preaching the Dharma as it truly is without depending on the instruction of others.
May all sentient beings become Dharma-teachers who retain all the Buddhas' teachings in memory.
May they preach the Dharma according to the truth, without contradicting the words or their meanings.

May all sentient beings become Dharma teachers who practice the path of signlessness, adorning themselves with all sublime marks, radiating immeasurable light, and skillfully entering into all phenomena.
May all sentient beings become Dharma teachers of the Great Body, whose bodies pervade all lands and raise great clouds of Dharma to pour down rain.

The Dharmas of all Buddhas: May all sentient beings become Dharma-preachers who protect the treasury of the Dharma, erecting the banner of invincibility to guard the teachings of all Buddhas, and ensuring that the ocean of the True Dharma suffers no deficiency or diminution.

May all sentient beings become Dharma-preachers who are suns of all dharmas, attaining the eloquence of a Buddha to skillfully expound all teachings. May all sentient beings become those with the skillful means of sublime sound.
Dharma Master, you have skillfully expounded the treasury of the boundless Dharma-realm.
May all sentient beings become Dharma Masters who reach the further shore of the Dharma, opening the treasury of the True Dharma through wisdom and supernormal powers.

May all sentient beings become Dharma Masters who dwell securely in the True Dharma, proclaiming the ultimate wisdom of the Tathāgata. May all sentient beings become those who thoroughly comprehend all phenomena.
Dharma Master, you are able to expound immeasurable and inexhaustible merits.
May all sentient beings become Dharma Masters who do not deceive the world, and through skillful means, lead others to enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
May all sentient beings become Dharma Masters who destroy all hosts of Māras, being well-able to discern and understand all demonic activities. May all sentient beings be embraced by all Buddhas.
Receiving the Dharma Master, may they abandon the mind that grasps at "I" and "mine," and may all sentient beings become Dharma Masters who bring peace and security to the entire world,
accomplishing the bodhisattva’s power of aspiration for the preaching of the Dharma.
The seventh section: May all sentient beings become Dharma-teachers. This refers to becoming a leader as described above; a "leader" (導首) is precisely a Dharma-teacher.
Whereas previously one acted for others, now one causes others to act. There are twenty-two sūtras that enumerate twenty types of Dharma-teachers.

The seventh [type] is called "like the eye," because it is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) rather than through hearing or seeing. The ninth is the mark of the signless (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*).
Because of their wondrous marks. Twentieth: they possess only the power of preaching the Dharma to bring peace to the world. The seventh section is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner:
that is to say, he does not dedicate them out of attachment to karma; he does not dedicate them out of attachment to retribution; he does not dedicate them out of attachment to the mind.
Dedication. One does not dedicate by way of attachment to phenomena; one does not dedicate by way of attachment to things;
one does not dedicate by way of attachment to causes; one does not dedicate by way of attachment to words, sounds, or voices;
one does not dedicate by way of attachment to names, phrases, or syllables; one does not dedicate by way of attachment to dedication itself. One does not...
One dedicates for the sake of benefiting sentient beings without attachment.
The eighth gate is dedication without grasping, which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This and the ninth [gate] fulfill the aforementioned "indestructible and firm spiritual friend. There are ten phrases that clarify the conditions for firmness. The eighth gate is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates his roots of goodness in this manner: that is to say, he does not dedicate them for the sake of attachment to the realm of forms;
he does not dedicate them for the sake of attachment to the realms of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
he does not dedicate them for the sake of seeking birth in the heavens; he does not dedicate them for the sake of seeking sensual pleasures; nor does he dedicate them out of attachment...
They dedicate [their merit] for the sake of the realm of desire; they do not dedicate it for the sake of seeking followers; they do not dedicate it for the sake of seeking sovereignty;
they do not dedicate it for the sake of seeking the pleasures of birth and death; they do not dedicate it for the sake of attachment to birth and death;

they do not dedicate it for the sake of delighting in the various realms of existence (*bhava*); they do not dedicate it for the sake of seeking the pleasure of union; they do not dedicate it for the sake of seeking what is... [acceptable].
One dedicates because of being free from attachment to objects of pleasure; one dedicates not for the sake of harboring a mind of malice; one dedicates so as not to destroy roots of goodness;
one dedicates without relying on the triple world; and one dedicates without clinging to the various dhyānas, liberations, or samādhis.
They dedicate [their merit] because they do not abide in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they dedicate it solely for the sake of teaching and taming all sentient beings;
they dedicate it solely for the sake of fulfilling the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); they dedicate it solely for the sake of attaining unimpeded wisdom;
they dedicate it solely for the sake of attaining unobstructed, pure roots of goodness; they dedicate it solely for the sake of causing...
They dedicate [their merit] so that all sentient beings may transcend birth and death and realize great wisdom;
they dedicate it solely to ensure that the mind of great bodhi remains indestructible like a vajra; they dedicate it solely to accomplish the ultimate dharma of immortality;
and they dedicate it solely to adorn the lineage of the Buddhas with immeasurable ornaments and manifest omniscience.
They dedicate with mastery; they dedicate solely for the sake of seeking the great supernormal knowledge and wisdom that illuminates all dharmas of a bodhisattva;

they dedicate solely for the sake of practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra in all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm and space-realm, fulfilling it without regression and donning the armor of firm great vows, so that all sentient beings may abide on the stage of Samantabhadra.
I dedicate [these roots of goodness] so that, for the sake of liberating sentient beings throughout all future kalpas without ever resting,
I may manifest the unimpeded light of the stage of omniscience, which is eternally uninterrupted.

The ninth section concerns the abandonment of faults and the accomplishment of virtues. It is divided into two parts: first, the abandonment of faults through seventeen phrases, which constitutes the avoidance of conditions that lead to destruction;
second, the accomplishment of virtues for those below, which clarifies the purpose of the practice—namely, to become an indestructible and steadfast spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding the first part, the preceding fifteen matters protect against the activity of afflictions (*kleśa*), while the sixteenth, "If one is liberated from the three... [is as follows].
Ignorance is the cause of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) alone. The various dhyānas and samādhis are causes common to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Those who have not yet attained them do not seek them;
those who have already attained them do not cling to them. Who, then, would further seek death? As for what is called "seeking birth," it is because birth inevitably leads to death.

Those who seek union—except for the bliss of nirvāṇa—all involve conjunction with something. For the śrāmaṇera to seek a dragon is to direct his aspiration toward harboring poison; he vows to become a Māra.

The King immediately destroys wholesome dedication. Next, the passage of nine and a half lines beginning with "merely for the sake of teaching and taming" reveals the accomplishment of virtuous qualities;
it clarifies that what is undertaken is also what is sought. The ninth section concludes.
Thus ends the first nine sections, which individually correspond to the ten phrases on the dedication of roots of goodness.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate those roots of goodness, they do so with a mind such as this:
that is to say, they dedicate with a mind of equality regarding intrinsic nature; they dedicate with a mind of equality regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
they dedicate with a mind of immeasurable equality regarding all sentient beings; they dedicate with a mind of equality regarding non-contention; they dedicate with their own...
One dedicates with a mind of equanimity that has no arising of intrinsic nature; one dedicates with a mind free from confusion regarding all phenomena;
one dedicates with a mind that enters the equality of the three periods of time; one dedicates with a mind that gives birth to the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
one dedicates with a mind that attains non-retrogressive supernormal powers; and one dedicates with a mind that brings to completion the practices of omniscience. Furthermore,
They dedicate [their merit] so that all sentient beings may forever be free from all hells;
they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may not enter the realm of animals; they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may not go to the abode of King Yama;
they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may eliminate all factors that obstruct the Path.
I dedicate [these roots of goodness] so that all sentient beings may fulfill all roots of goodness;
I dedicate them so that all sentient beings may turn the wheel of Dharma at the appropriate time and cause all to rejoice;
I dedicate them so that all sentient beings may enter the wheel of the ten directions; I dedicate them so that all sentient beings may fulfill the boundless [qualities] of a bodhisattva.
They dedicate [the roots of goodness] for the sake of the vow for the pure Dharma.
They dedicate them so that all sentient beings may fulfill the vessel of the bodhicitta that accords with the instructions of all spiritual friends.

They dedicate them so that all sentient beings may receive, uphold, and practice the profound Buddha-dharma, thereby attaining the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas. They dedicate them so that all sentient beings...
One dedicates [merit] so that the unobstructed practices of all bodhisattvas may be constantly present;
one dedicates so that all sentient beings may always see the Buddhas appearing before them; one dedicates so that the light of the pure Dharma may be constantly present for all sentient beings;
and one dedicates so that all sentient beings shall never be parted from the fearless great bodhicitta.
They dedicate [their merit] so that it may constantly manifest before them; they dedicate so that the inconceivable wisdom of all sentient beings and bodhisattvas may constantly manifest before them;

they dedicate so that all sentient beings may universally rescue and protect other beings, causing the mind of pure great compassion to constantly manifest before them; they dedicate so that all sentient beings, by means of the unspeakably unspeakable...
They dedicate [their merit] so as to adorn all Buddha-fields with supreme and wondrous ornaments.
They dedicate it so that all sentient beings may destroy the nets of karma consisting of all demons and strife.
They dedicate it so that all sentient beings may practice the bodhisattva path without any dependence upon any Buddha-field. They dedicate it so that [all sentient beings...]
One dedicates [merit] because all sentient beings have generated the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*) and enter the vast gateway of all Buddha-dharmas.
The second major section consists of four gates that collectively reveal the intent of dedication.

Therefore, at the beginning, it does not say "furthermore, with these roots of goodness," but simply says "when dedicating those roots of goodness. This clearly distinguishes [the stages]. The first gate clarifies what should be done.

Toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and toward sentient beings. The second section clarifies that one should be directed toward bodhi; the third section clarifies that one should be free from faults;
the fourth section clarifies the attainment of benefit. The first section has two parts: first, it clarifies that one should be directed toward the limit of reality;

subsequently, for the sake of those below, it clarifies that one should be directed toward sentient beings. Within the first part, there are ten phrases and ten types of mind, which are stated as follows:
Intrinsic nature is immutability; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is conformity with conditions. Sentient beings are persons; non-contention is the Dharma.
When principle and phenomena do not deviate from their own nature, that which arises is nothing that arises; all phenomena thus horizontally encompass primordial quiescence.
The three periods of time enter vertically without distinction. By taking the knowledge of the dharma-nature as a condition, the seeds of Buddhahood are produced;
relying on the nature and relying on its function, there is no time of retrogression or loss. Illuminating this reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the practice of true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) is established.

Next, it says: "Furthermore, in order to cause all sentient beings... This clarifies that one should turn toward sentient beings. There are eighteen practices [mentioned here], while other sutras list twenty.
Regarding the purpose: seventh, it is called the wheel of the ten powers because it completely subdues [all adversaries].

Fourteenth, it is called the fearless bodhicitta because one does not fear that saṃsāra is long-lasting, that sentient beings are difficult to deliver, that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is difficult to realize, that the myriad practices are difficult to cultivate, or that enlightenment is vast and remote. This concludes the first of the four gates.
O Son of the Buddha, furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates these roots of goodness with pure right mindfulness;
dedicates them with certainty of wisdom; dedicates them with the complete knowledge of all skillful means of the Buddha-dharma;
dedicates them for the sake of accomplishing immeasurable and unimpeded wisdom; dedicates them out of a desire to fulfill the pure and sublime mind; for the sake of all...
They dedicate for the sake of sentient beings abiding in great loving-kindness; they dedicate for the sake of all sentient beings abiding in great compassion;
they dedicate for the sake of all sentient beings abiding in great sympathetic joy; they dedicate for the sake of all sentient beings abiding in great equanimity;
they dedicate for the sake of permanently leaving behind the two attachments and abiding in superior roots of goodness; and they dedicate for the sake of contemplation, observation, and discernment.
They dedicate [their merit] for the purpose of expounding all dharmas of dependent origination; they dedicate it for the purpose of establishing the mind of great heroic valor;
they dedicate it for the purpose of establishing the treasury of the banner of invincibility; they dedicate it for the purpose of destroying all hosts of Māras;
they dedicate it for the purpose of attaining a pure and unobstructed mind regarding all dharmas; and they dedicate it for the purpose of practicing all bodhisattva deeds without regression.
They dedicate [their merit] because they transform it; they dedicate it because they seek to attain a mind that joyfully pursues the foremost and supreme Dharma;
they dedicate it because they seek to attain a mind that joyfully pursues the sovereign purity of all qualities and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*);
they dedicate it to fulfill all vows, to eliminate all contention, and to attain the unimpeded, pure Dharma of the Buddha’s sovereignty, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings.
They dedicate [their merit] for the sake of the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.

They dedicate it so as to attain the adornment of the hundred-thousandfold radiance of the sun of wisdom—the most supreme and extraordinary Dharma of the Tathāgata—which universally illuminates all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharmadhātu.
They dedicate it out of a desire to tame all sentient beings, always satisfying them according to their inclinations, never abandoning their original vows until the end of time.
In the future, having heard the true Dharma and practiced the Great Deeds, they shall attain pure wisdom and stainless radiance;
severing all pride, extinguishing all afflictions, tearing asunder the net of craving, and shattering the darkness of ignorance,
they dedicate [their merit] because they are fully endowed with the stainless and unobstructed Dharma, so that for all sentient beings throughout incalculable eons they may always...
They dedicate their merit so as to diligently cultivate all practices for omniscience without ever regressing, to cause each and every being to attain unimpeded, wondrous wisdom,
and to manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas without rest.
In the second section, there are twenty-four dedications directed toward Bodhi. The first three phrases are abbreviated by one character each in order to complete the number twenty.
Among these, the first twenty dedications clarify the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit;
the final two clarify that having attained the fruit, one does not abandon the cause, continuing to transform sentient beings until the end of the future. The second section is concluded.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates roots of goodness in this manner, they should not be greedily attached to the realms of the five desires within the three realms of existence. Why is this? A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should dedicate with roots of goodness free from greed;
they should dedicate with roots of goodness free from hatred; they should dedicate with roots of goodness free from delusion; they should...
One should dedicate the roots of goodness of non-harming; one should dedicate the roots of goodness of being free from pride; one should dedicate the roots of goodness of being without guile;
one should dedicate the roots of goodness of being upright; one should dedicate the roots of goodness of diligent application;
and one should dedicate the roots of goodness of cultivation.
The third section clarifies that one should abandon faults.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they attain pure faith; they joyfully accept and endure the practices of a Bodhisattva;
they cultivate the pure path of the Great Bodhisattvas; they possess the lineage of the Buddhas and attain the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Abandoning all evils and distancing oneself from the deeds of Māra, one draws near to virtuous friends to fulfill one’s own great vows.
Inviting all sentient beings, one establishes a great assembly for giving.
The fourth gate clarifies the attainment of benefits. The above four gates complete the exposition on the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates the roots of goodness produced by this gift of Dharma in the following way:
namely, to cause all sentient beings to obtain pure and wondrous voices; to obtain soft and gentle voices; to obtain the voice of the celestial drum;
to obtain immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable voices; to obtain lovely and delightful voices; to obtain pure voices; and to obtain pervasive voices.
They attain voices that pervade all Buddha-fields; they attain voices adorned with hundreds of thousands of nayutas of unspeakable merits;
they attain lofty and distant voices; they attain vast and expansive voices; they attain voices that extinguish all distraction; and they attain voices that fill the entire Dharma-realm.
They attain the grasping of the linguistic sounds of all sentient beings. They attain the wisdom of the boundless vocal sounds of all sentient beings.
They attain the wisdom of all pure linguistic sounds. They attain the wisdom of immeasurable linguistic sounds.
They attain the wisdom of the most sovereign voice that enters into all sounds. They attain all pure and adorned voices. They attain all...
The sound of being insatiable with the world; the sound of attaining ultimate non-attachment to all worlds;

the sound of attaining joy; the sound of attaining the pure speech of a Buddha; the sound of attaining the renown of teaching all Buddha-dharmas while remaining free from the cataracts of ignorance, which is heard everywhere;
the sound of enabling all sentient beings to attain the adornment of *dhāraṇīs* for all dharmas. He attained these sounds.
They proclaim the sounds of all infinite varieties of Dharma teachings; they attain the sound of reaching everywhere to the infinite assemblies within the Dharma-realm;
they attain the sound of universally upholding the inconceivable vajra-words of the Dharma; and they attain the sound that reveals all dharmas.
They attain the treasury of sounds of wisdom that can explain the distinctions between expressible and inexpressible words and phrases;
they attain the sound of explaining all phenomena without attachment and without interruption; they attain the sound of the radiant illumination of all phenomena;
they attain the sound that enables all worlds to be purified and ultimately reach omniscience; and they attain the sound that universally encompasses the phrases and meanings of all phenomena.
They attain the voice of sovereign, unimpeded mastery sustained by supernormal powers, and the voice of wisdom that reaches the further shore of all worlds.
Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, they cause all sentient beings to attain a voice that is not inferior and a voice free from fear.

They attain the voice free from defiled attachment; they attain the voice that gladdens all assemblies at the site of enlightenment; they attain the voice that accords with what is exquisite and beautiful;
they attain the voice that skillfully expounds all Buddha-dharmas; they attain the voice that severs the doubts of all sentient beings and causes them all to awaken;
they attain the voice endowed with perfect eloquence; and they attain the voice that universally awakens all sentient beings from the long night of sleep.
Ghoṣa. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates all roots of goodness in this way:
that is to say, he vows that all sentient beings may attain a pure Dharma-body free from all faults and evils;

he vows that all sentient beings may attain pure and wondrous merit and virtue free from all faults and evils; he vows that all sentient beings may attain a pure and wondrous [nature] free from all faults and evils.
[May they attain] the marks. May all sentient beings attain the fruit of pure karma, free from all faults and evils.
May all sentient beings attain the mind of omniscience, pure and free from all faults and evils.
May all sentient beings attain the immeasurable, pure bodhicitta, free from all faults and evils. May all sentient beings attain thorough knowledge, free from all faults and evils.
The skillful means for purifying the faculties: May all sentient beings attain pure faith and understanding, free from all faults and evils;
may all sentient beings attain pure, diligent cultivation of unobstructed conduct and vows, free from all faults and evils;
may all sentient beings attain pure right mindfulness, wisdom, and eloquence, free from all faults and evils.
The third major section consists of eight gates that further clarify dedication through alternative perspectives; this constitutes "superior progress. The text is divided into four distinct parts:
first, two gates on dedicating to sentient beings; second, two gates on dedicating to bodhi;
third, two gates collectively revealing the purpose; and fourth, one gate on dedicating to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Now:

The first section is divided into two parts. The former part concerns the aspiration to attain the perfect voice; the latter part concerns the universal endowment with these virtues. Now, for the first part:

because it pertains to the rank of the Dharma Master, there are twenty lines of scripture intended to cause all beings to likewise attain the perfect voice for expounding the essentials of the Dharma.

Forty-five kinds of vocal sounds are enumerated. The commentary (*śāstra*) offers many explanations. Next, the passage beginning "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, by means of these roots of goodness...

clarifies that all sentient beings are collectively caused to possess merit. The text contains ten phrases: the first five phrases indicate the fulfillment of the fruit, while the latter five phrases indicate the perfection of the cause.
Among these eight [sections], the first two gates have concluded the dedication toward sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates all roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings in this way:
"May I attain various kinds of pure and wondrous bodies—namely, the body of radiance, the body free from turbidity, and the undefiled body."
The pure body; the utterly pure body; the body free from dust; the utterly dust-free body; the stainless body; the delightful body; the unobstructed body.
It manifests the images of all karmic actions in all worlds; it manifests the images of all speech in all realms;
it manifests the images of all established dwellings in all palaces, just as various forms and colors appear in a clear, bright mirror.
It manifests spontaneously, demonstrating to all sentient beings the practice of great bodhi; demonstrating to all sentient beings the profound and wondrous Dharma;
demonstrating to all sentient beings their various merits; demonstrating to all sentient beings the path of cultivation;

demonstrating to all sentient beings the practices for accomplishment; demonstrating to all sentient beings the vows and conduct of Bodhisattvas; and demonstrating to all sentient beings within a single world-system.
In all worlds, Buddhas arise in the world. They manifest to all sentient beings the supernatural powers and transformations of all Buddhas;
they manifest to all sentient beings the inconceivable power of liberation of all Bodhisattvas;
and they manifest to all sentient beings the nature of omniscience, which is the fulfillment of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. By means of these, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
The subtle, pure body [of the Buddha] skillfully gathers in all sentient beings, causing them all to achieve the pure merit of the body of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The second section, consisting of three gates, is the dedication toward Bodhi. It is divided into three parts: the first gate attains the correct fruit; the next gate...

Second, the perfection of the causes for the fruits. Regarding the latter section on the fulfillment of the fruit of the environment, first, there are ten phrases concerning the fruits obtained by sentient beings as mentioned above;
each of these should have many variations, but here we shall elaborate only upon the first instance of a single body, and the others may be understood by analogy.
The text consists of three parts: first, the explanation of attaining the body; second, the manifestation of the body’s functions; and third, the conclusion of what has been established.

Now, regarding the first part, the initial phrase presents the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while the section beginning with "That which is called" presents the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The "body" is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); the remaining elements are the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Their formation and dissolution can be understood accordingly. Furthermore, these ten bodies pertain both to phenomena (*dharma*) and to wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding the first, "light," this refers to the light of the body and the light of wisdom. There is nothing that is not...

1. Because it illuminates, its two aspects are free from the obscuration of darkness, for they are capable of penetrating and discerning. 2. Its essence is not subject to defilement; its pure virtues are fully internalized, like a jade stone free from flaws or obscurations.
3. It is not merely temporarily pure. The first three [points] distinguish this based on its essence (*tattva*);

the subsequent three clarify it in relation to its objects (*viṣaya*). 4. It is not defiled by dust; this corresponds to the aforementioned "purity" (*viśuddhi*). 5. Even the most subtle atoms do not adhere to it; this corresponds to...

1. Utmost purity. 2. Untainted by the eight defilements; facing the superior, one remains unstained. 3. Regarding internal virtue, the exhaustion of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is called "freedom from dust" (*vītaraja*);
the extinction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is called "utter freedom from dust. The non-abiding of the cognitive objects of knowledge is called "freedom from mental impurity" (*cittamala*).
4. Possessing the nine marks and all virtues. 5. The physical form fills the *dharmadhātu*; wisdom pervades the ten directions. 6. Mountain.
The principles of the river cannot obstruct it. Next, the passage beginning with "In all worlds" clarifies the arising of function based on the body.

The first four [verses] concern the function of the form-body (*rūpakāya*): the first three encompass the single body within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), while the last one gathers the myriad phenomena into a single body.
Next, the five lines beginning with "Manifesting to all sentient beings" demonstrate the function of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). Finally, it demonstrates the bodhisattva practice.
May [this] descend and penetrate the functions of the two bodies. The subsequent statement, "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of such [practices]," concludes what has been accomplished.
This marks the end of the first gate within the second section on the orientation toward Bodhi.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates the roots of goodness arising from this gift of Dharma in this way:
"May my body abide throughout all worlds to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva. May all sentient beings who see me not do so in vain;
may they resolve upon bodhicitta and never again fall back; may they accord with the meaning of reality and remain unshakable. In all worlds..."
Throughout all kalpas of the future, they abide in the bodhisattva path without weariness or fatigue. Their great compassion is impartial and universal, its measure equal to the dharma-realm.
Knowing the faculties of sentient beings, they preach the Dharma according to the appropriate time, never resting.

They maintain constant right mindfulness toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), not relinquishing it for even a single moment. All Buddhas are ever present before them, and their minds are constantly in right mindfulness.
Never for a moment did they grow lax; they cultivated all roots of goodness without any hypocrisy. They established all sentient beings in omniscience so that they would never regress.
They were fully endowed with the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas, sustained the great clouds of Dharma, and received the great rain of Dharma.
They cultivate the bodhisattva conduct; they enter into all sentient beings, enter into all buddha-fields, enter into all dharmas, and enter into all three periods of time.

They enter into the wisdom of the karmic retributions of all sentient beings, enter into the wisdom of the skillful means of all bodhisattvas, enter into the wisdom of the manifestations of all bodhisattvas, and enter into the wisdom of the pure realms of all bodhisattvas.
Entering the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas and entering the entire boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one dwells therein and cultivates the bodhisattva practices.
Within the second section, concerning the fulfillment of the two fruits through a single gateway of aspiration, there are two parts; first, the practice of arising function from within the principle.

Regarding the subsequent passage, "Entering all that is inferior," this refers to entering the profound practice through phenomena. First, there is the initial formation of the conditions for practice, because the body dwells in accordance [with reality].

Next, regarding "Sentient beings see... and below, this concerns the non-emptiness of benefiting others. Following that, regarding "In the presence of spiritual friends... and below, this simultaneously encompasses both self-benefit and benefit for others.

Next, in the phrase "Entering all assemblies of sentient beings... and below, this pertains to the entry into profound practice through phenomena, wherein wisdom accords with and enters the unmanifest.

The boundless Dharma-realm is entered by the wisdom-pervading body. The eight superior and two intermediate stages of dedication toward Bodhi constitute the completion of the cause for the fulfillment of the one gate and two fruits.
At the beginning of the final fascicle, within the section on Bodhi, three parts clarify the fulfillment of the fruit of the dependent environment through the one gate.

Chapter Twenty-five, Part Eleven: The Ten Dedications.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates the roots of goodness cultivated through the gift of Dharma in this way:
"May all Buddha-fields be entirely pure, adorned with unspeakably unspeakable arrays of ornaments.
May each and every Buddha-field be as vast in extent as the Dharma-realm, consisting solely of goodness, unimpeded, and pure."
Radiant light. Within it, all Buddhas manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment. Within the pure realm of a single buddha-field, one can manifest all buddha-fields;
as it is with one buddha-field, so it is with all buddha-fields.
The third section, the first gate, concerns the aspiration for the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*). The text is divided into two parts: first, a general exposition;

second, a detailed explanation of each individual point. Regarding the first part, there are ten phrases. First, one phrase cites the preceding section to introduce the following. Next, the passage beginning with "May all Buddha-fields...
correctly reveals the characteristics of the aspiration. These consist of: (1) the aspiration for purity, (2) the aspiration for adornment, and (3) the aspiration for universal extent.
1. Pervasive; 2. Pure in its four dimensions; 3. Wholly virtuous; 4. Free from obstructions; 5. Possessing pure radiance; 6. Where Buddhas appear; 7. All-encompassing integration; 8.

Using one instance as an illustration for the rest; 9. The expansion of a single buddha-field is equal to the entire Dharma-realm, while the contraction of a single buddha-field manifests everything without exception.
This expansion and contraction are unimpeded within this single buddha-field, and as it is with one buddha-field, so it is with every buddha-field. Thus it is established.
For later generations, this is solemn. If it is thus for every atom, how much more so for every world-system (*kṣetra*)?
Each and every world-system is adorned with ornaments of pure, wondrous jewels—equal in extent to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), immeasurable and boundless.
That is to say, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) pure jewel thrones spread with various precious cloths. Incalculable...
Precious canopies and jeweled nets were draped and spread; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious parasols reflected one another through all their exquisite jewels.
Incalculable clouds of jewels rained down various treasures everywhere; incalculable clusters of jewel flowers were pure and pervasive.
Incalculable railings and balustrades made of various jewels were pure and magnificently adorned. Incalculable jewel bells constantly played—
The subtle and wondrous voices of all Buddhas pervade the Dharma-realm. Countless jewel lotuses, in various precious colors, bloom with radiant splendor.
Countless jewel trees stand in rows on every side, their flowers and fruits composed of immeasurable exquisite jewels.
There are countless jewel palaces where immeasurable bodhisattvas dwell. There are countless jewel towers...
The pavilion was vast, expansive, lofty, and magnificent, extending far and wide. It featured incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jeweled battlements, exquisitely adorned with great jewels.
There were incalculable jeweled gates and portals, draped all around with wonderful jewel necklaces.
There were incalculable jeweled windows, purified and adorned with inconceivable jewels. There were incalculable jeweled *tāla* trees, shaped like half-moons.
It was composed of a multitude of jewels; all such things were adorned with various precious gems.
Stainless, pure, and inconceivable, there was nothing that did not arise from the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata, being fully endowed with the adornments of countless treasuries of jewels.

In the second section, which provides a detailed exposition, there are two parts: first, the specific manifestation of the jewel-adornments; second, the application of these to other adornments following the passage "As with the jewel-adornments.
Regarding the first part, it is divided into three sections: first, a general indication of each of the [ten] items; second, a detailed exposition;

and third, a summary beginning with "This is for the sake of the bodhisattvas. Within the detailed exposition, there are two further divisions: first, a general manifestation of the jewel-adornments; second, [the address] "O Son of the Buddha."
Regarding all those [qualities] below, the "Adornment of the Jewel of Humans" is explained in detail:

whereas previously [in the middle section] there were only ninety-four numerical categories using the term *asaṃkhyeya*, the Jin translation consistently uses the expression "immeasurable *asaṃkhyeyas*.
Since the initial enumerated items merely say "immeasurable," the word *asaṃkhyeya* is not one among the various numbers; rather, it is a term signifying "the incalculable."

If "fixed" were taken as a numerical count, it would result in limitation. Now, within the ninety-four precious trees, those that possess immeasurable wonderful jewels serving as flowers and fruits constitute the first.
Within the palaces, the immeasurable bodhisattvas constitute the second.
Following the initial section which reveals the causes, the countless jewel treasuries constitute the third. Within each and every necklace...
There are four types of sublime adornments of a thousand bodhisattvas; within the lower jeweled branches are inconceivable birds as the fifth;
and within the jeweled flowers are immeasurable bodhisattvas as the sixth, totaling one hundred items. The text is divided into two parts:
first, eighteen matters are briefly presented to clarify their excellence; first, the matters are listed to clarify them, and subsequently, "in this way, all... [is stated].
The following passage cites causes to manifest their excellence:
Furthermore, there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel rivers that flow forth all pure and wholesome dharmas; incalculable jewel oceans are filled with the water of the Dharma;

Jewel sashes hung suspended in the air, their adornment exquisite and sublime. There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel couches, capable of producing various subtle sensations of pleasure.
There were incalculable wonderful jewel swirls, manifesting the eye of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna-cakṣus*) of the Bodhisattvas.
There were incalculable jewel necklaces; each necklace was the supreme and wondrous adornment of hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattvas. There were incalculable jewels...

Mountains of jewels serve as its walls, surrounding it in a complete enclosure that is pure and unobstructed.

There are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel fragrances, whose scents universally permeate all worlds. There are incalculable jewel manifestations; each manifestation pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*.
There are incalculable jewel radiances; each radiance manifests every kind of light.
Next, there are eighty-two further items that extensively elucidate [the subject]. These are divided into five sections.

The first section consists of twenty-four items, which are adorned solely with external jewels; among these, two or three are also designated by their specific names and explained through Dharma-gates.
For the time being, they shall be categorized according to the majority.
Furthermore, there were incalculable jewel lights; the light of pure wisdom clearly illuminated all phenomena.
Furthermore, there were incalculable unimpeded jewel lights, each individual light pervading the entire Dharma-realm. There were incalculable jewel locations.
All manner of jewels were fully present. There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) treasuries of jewels that revealed the treasures of all the true Dharma (*saddharmakośa*).
There were incalculable jewel banners, with the banner-signs of the Tathāgata rising loftily aloft.

There were incalculable jewel sages, possessing the pure and perfect forms of great wisdom sages. There were incalculable jewel gardens, which gave birth to the bliss of the various *samādhis* of the bodhisattvas.
Incalculable jewel-sounds: the Tathāgata’s wondrous voice universally manifests throughout the world. Incalculable jewel-forms:
each and every form emits immeasurable rays of light from the sublime Dharma. Incalculable jewel-signs: each and every sign utterly transcends all other signs.
Incalculable jewel-dignities: those who behold them all give rise to the joy and delight of bodhisattvas. Incalculable...
The Jewel Heap: all who see it give birth to the Jewel Heap of wisdom. It is the abode of incalculable jewels;
all who see it give birth to the jewel-mind of excellent dwelling. There are incalculable jewel garments; those who wear them give birth to the peerless samādhi of all bodhisattvas.
