The Dharani-gate.
Second, there are further incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) jewel-lights, beneath which there are fifteen matters.
These are designated by their names as matters and explained by way of dharma-gates, because it is intended to reveal that these very matters constitute the dharma-gates.
There are incalculable treasures of cultivation; those who behold them see that all jewels are the fruits of karma, which are definitively pure.
There are incalculable treasures of unimpeded knowledge and vision; those who behold them attain the pure Dharma-eye that encompasses all things.
There are incalculable treasures of the treasury of light; those who behold them achieve the treasury of great wisdom.

The cultivation of the Three Jewels consists of the following three matters, which refer exclusively to the Dharma-gates; they manifest that the Dharma itself is noble, rather than requiring reliance upon external objects.
There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel thrones upon which the Buddha sat and uttered the Great Lion’s Roar. There were incalculable jewel lamps that constantly emitted light.
The light of pure wisdom shines forth. Countless *asaṃkhyeya* jewel *tāla* trees stand in successive rows, encircled by jeweled cords and adorned with purity.
These trees further possess countless jewel trunks that rise upward from their bases, straight, upright, and perfectly polished.
Countless jewel branches, adorned with various kinds of jewels, grow densely together, while inconceivable birds soar among them.
They gather therein. Constantly emitting sublime sounds, they proclaim the True Dharma. Countless (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel leaves radiate the light of great wisdom, pervading all places.
Upon each of countless jewel flowers, immeasurable bodhisattvas sit in the full lotus posture, traveling everywhere throughout the Dharma-realm.
From countless jewel fruits, those who behold them shall attain the non-retrogressive wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The transformation of the fruit: there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel villages, where those who see them abandon the worldly ways of the village;

there are incalculable jewel cities, filled with unimpeded sentient beings; there are incalculable jewel palaces, wherein the King dwells, endowed with the Nārāyaṇa body of a bodhisattva—valiant, firm, clad in the armor of the Dharma, and with a mind that never regresses.

The five treasures and the assembly of beings comprise eighteen matters below, which manifest within the internal body as the six sense organs and the three karmas;

all are termed "treasures" because they are perfectly luminous and worthy of esteem. These aforementioned matters—whether pure or mixed, whether pertaining to the environment or its inhabitants—are all unimpeded, for they are all evoked by the cause of the non-obstruction of phenomena in phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

For example, regarding the precious robes and other such things produced with tranquil patience as their cause, I fear that a detailed exposition would be too prolix to manifest clearly.

they dedicate for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide securely in all pure dharmas;

One dedicates [merit] for the sake of fulfilling and purifying the path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Within the third major section, regarding the purpose of dedication through two categories, the first category should be for the sake of sentient beings, and the latter category should be for the sake of *bodhi*.
Now, for the former, there are twenty-three phrases; although the wording of the first two phrases...
In the first [section], the meaning applies to both places. The third [section], "accomplishing sentient beings," serves as the general statement; all that follows is specific.
From the initial confidence in one's own mind to the ultimate attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), the texts are all explicit.
O Son of the Buddha, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has dedicated all roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings in this manner,
he further dedicates these roots of goodness with the desire to universally fulfill and expound the power of all pure practices,
and with the desire to achieve the majestic power of pure conduct and attain an unspeakably unspeakable ocean of Dharma.
Therefore, they dedicate [their merit]. They dedicate because they wish to be fully endowed with the light of pure wisdom equal to the Dharma-realm within each and every ocean of dharmas.
They dedicate because they wish to reveal and expound the distinct phrases and meanings of all dharmas.
They dedicate because they wish to accomplish the boundlessly vast Samādhi of the Light of All Dharmas. They dedicate because they wish to accord with the Three...
They dedicate [their merit] for the sake of the eloquence of all Buddhas of the world. They dedicate it desiring to accomplish the sovereign bodies of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
They dedicate it out of reverence for the delightful and unobstructed Dharma of all Buddhas.
They dedicate [their merit] so as to fulfill the heart of great compassion, never retreating in the rescue and protection of all sentient beings;
desiring to accomplish the unimpeded wisdom of inconceivable and diverse dharmas, their minds are free from defilement and their faculties are pure.
They dedicate [their merit] because they wish to universally enter all assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

They dedicate [their merit] because they wish to constantly turn the equal and non-regressive wheel of Dharma within all such Buddha-lands—whether inverted or upright, coarse or subtle, vast or narrow, small or large, defiled or pure.
They dedicate [their merit] because they wish to attain fearlessness in every moment of thought. They dedicate [their merit] because they wish to be without...
They dedicate [their merit] for the purpose of exhausting all varieties of eloquence by revealing and expounding the light of the sublime Dharma;

they dedicate it for the sake of seeking all that is wholesome with joy, generating the resolve to practice so that the faculties become increasingly superior, attaining the great supernormal knowledge of all dharmas, and being able to fully comprehend all phenomena;
they dedicate it with the desire to approach and make offerings at all assemblies and sites of enlightenment.
To nourish all sentient beings, one dedicates [merit] so that they may hear all dharmas and be made to rejoice.
Second, regarding the dedication toward Bodhi, it clarifies the fulfillment of cause and effect; its great function is inexhaustible, and this is likewise evident.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
that is to say, by dedicating through abiding in the immeasurable abidings of the Dharma-realm; by dedicating through abiding in the immeasurable bodily actions of the Dharma-realm;
by dedicating through abiding in the immeasurable verbal actions of the Dharma-realm; by dedicating through abiding in the immeasurable mental actions of the Dharma-realm; by abiding in...
One dedicates equally to the immeasurable forms of the *dhātu*. One dedicates equally by abiding in the immeasurable feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of the *dharmadhātu*.
One dedicates equally by abiding in the immeasurable aggregates (*skandha*) of the *dharmadhātu*. One dedicates equally by abiding in the immeasurable elements (*dhātu*) of the *dharmadhātu*.
One dedicates equally by abiding in the immeasurable sense bases (*āyatana*) of the *dharmadhātu*. By abiding in the *dharmadhātu*... [immeasurable... one dedicates equally.
They perform the dedication of equality within the measure; they perform the dedication of external equality through abiding in the immeasurability of the *dharmadhātu*;

they perform the dedication of equality through the immeasurable arousal [of bodhicitta] while abiding in the *dharmadhātu*; they perform the dedication of equality through the immeasurable profound mind while abiding in the *dharmadhātu*;

they perform the dedication of equality through immeasurable skillful means while abiding in the *dharmadhātu*; and they perform the dedication through immeasurable faith while abiding in the *dharmadhātu*.
They understand the dedication of equality: they dedicate with the equality of the infinite faculties dwelling within the *dharmadhātu*;

they dedicate with the equality of the infinite beginnings, middles, and ends dwelling within the *dharmadhātu*; they dedicate with the equality of infinite karmic retributions dwelling within the *dharmadhātu*;
they dedicate with the equality of infinite defilement and purity dwelling within the *dharmadhātu*; they dedicate with the equality of the infinite... dwelling within the *dharmadhātu*.
They dedicate equally for all sentient beings. They dedicate equally by abiding in the infinite Buddha-fields of the Dharma-realm.
They dedicate equally by abiding in the infinite dharmas of the Dharma-realm. They dedicate equally by abiding in the infinite lights of the world within the Dharma-realm.
They dedicate equally by abiding in the infinite Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm. By abiding...
They dedicate with the equality of the immeasurable bodhisattva practices and vows of the dharma-realm.

They dedicate with the equality of the immeasurable bodhisattvas’ emergence from the dharma-realm. They dedicate with the equality of the immeasurable bodhisattvas’ teaching and taming within the dharma-realm.
They dedicate with the equality of the non-duality of the immeasurable dharma-realm within the dharma-realm. They dedicate by abiding in the dharma-realm...
The fourth dedication is to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
It consists of twenty-nine phrases, all of which speak of the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*); this refers to the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
All of them state "abiding"; this means that wisdom accords with the principle within phenomena, for there is nothing upon which it abides. Thus, it is called "abiding."
This is because one enters into the meaning [of reality] by means of abiding. The non-duality of the *dharmadhātu* is precisely the meaning of "equality.

The initial mention of "immeasurable abiding" refers to the fact that all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are what is to be dwelled in; now, by means of the "abiding of non-abiding," these are identical to the immeasurability of the *dharmadhātu*.
All other cases should be understood in this manner. This concludes the eight preceding sections.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure body of the dharma-realm;
they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure speech of the dharma-realm; they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure mind of the dharma-realm;
and they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure conduct and vows of all bodhisattvas within the dharma-realm.
Abiding in the infinite equality and purity of the assembly within the dharma-realm;
abiding in the infinite equality of the dharma-realm, extensively expounding the pure wisdom of all dharmas for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
abiding in the infinite equality of the dharma-realm, able to enter bodies throughout all worlds in the entirety of the dharma-realm; abiding in the infinite equality of the dharma-realm.
All phenomena are luminous, pure, and fearless. With a single voice, he completely severs the web of doubts of all sentient beings;

according to their faculties and inclinations, he causes them all to rejoice. He abides in the supreme knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), within the dharma of liberation characterized by the powers, fearlessnesses, sovereign supernormal powers, and vast merit.
The third major section concerns the benefits accomplished through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This passage consists of ten phrases, all of which speak of "abiding securely.
One is able to attain such security because of the resonance with the aforementioned wisdom. The body and so forth are, in their differentiated aspects, phenomenal phenomena;
now, they are equal and pure. This equality and purity is the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu*. This purity of the *dharmadhātu* is that which is attained.
Wisdom abides in perfect identity with the *dharmadhātu*. Through eight modes of abiding, it accomplishes the latter two functions:

first, each single sound universally severs the doubts of sentient beings; second, it abides in the supreme qualities of a Buddha. Although the qualities of a Buddha are numerous, four are briefly enumerated:

namely, the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*), and the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). These are called "vast qualities. In contrast to the aforementioned seed-like wisdom, [this is]...
The two adornments of the Buddha are the dharma of transcendence.
Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s tenth dwelling: the immeasurable dedication equal to the Dharma-realm.
Third, the explanation of the conclusion of the title. The practices of the higher stages are now complete.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus dedicates all roots of goodness, such as the gift of Dharma, they fulfill the immeasurable and boundless bodhisattva practices and vows of Samantabhadra, and are able to completely adorn and purify the entire dharma-realm, which is coextensive with space.
In all Buddha-fields, may all sentient beings likewise attain such [realization], fully accomplishing boundless wisdom and comprehending all phenomena.
In every thought-moment, they see all Buddhas appearing in the world;
in every thought-moment, they see the immeasurable and boundless sovereign powers of all Buddhas—namely, the vast sovereign power, the... [unlimited sovereign power].
The power of mastery over attachment; the power of unimpeded mastery; the power of inconceivable mastery; the power of mastery in purifying all sentient beings;
the power of mastery in establishing all worlds; and the power of mastery in manifesting ineffable speech.
The power of sovereign mastery in manifesting according to the occasion; the power of sovereign mastery in the wisdom of supernatural penetrations that abides in non-retrogression;

the power of sovereign mastery in expounding the entire boundless realm of phenomena without exception; the power of sovereign mastery in giving birth to the boundless eye of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
and the power of sovereign mastery in hearing and upholding the true Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas through unobstructed auditory consciousness.
The power of sitting cross-legged in a single body throughout the infinite dharma-realms of the ten directions without encroaching upon or obstructing any sentient beings;
and the power of sovereign mastery over the infinite dharmas of the three periods of time through the entry of perfect wisdom.
Furthermore, one attains immeasurable purity, namely: the purity of all sentient beings; the purity of all Buddha-fields; the purity of all phenomena;
the purity of the wisdom that universally knows all places; and the purity of the boundless wisdom that pervades the realm of empty space.
One attains the wisdom of all differentiated speech and sounds, universally responding to sentient beings through various modes of expression.
Pure. It emits immeasurable, perfect light that universally illumines all boundless worlds and is pure.

It gives birth to the wisdom of the practices of all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time and is pure. In a single thought-moment, it universally enters the assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and its wisdom is pure.
It enters all boundless worlds, causing all sentient beings to...
They have performed what was to be done for purification. In this way, all these are fully possessed, all are accomplished, all have been cultivated,
all have attained equality, all are manifest before them, all are known and seen, all are entered into,
all have been observed, and all have attained purity, reaching the further shore.
The second major section concerns the fruits [of the practice]. It is divided into three parts. First, the indication of the causes for attaining them.

Second, beginning with "Thus, having perfected the conduct of Samantabhadra," the specific enumeration of the three types of fulfilled fruits attained. First, the fulfillment of causal benefit; second, the fulfillment of the mastery of seeing the Buddhas, beginning with "In every thought-moment...
This first part provides the heading, while the subsequent section, beginning with "That is to say, vast and... specifically elucidates it through seven lines of scripture, all of which...
Because both essence and function, as well as principle and cognition, are entirely without obstruction, this is the sovereign mastery of the Buddha.

Thirdly, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, one attains immeasurable purity," there are six lines of scripture below it. This refers to the fulfillment of the fruit of purity, which arises from purifying the obstacles of afflictions and perceiving the purity of the nature (*dharmatā*).

This was also previously indicated; specifically, the following lines are listed. Next, regarding the two lines of scripture beginning with "In this manner," etc., they conclude that which is capable of attaining [this state].
Regarding the characteristics: "equality" refers to being free from the subject that knows and the object known. The preceding section concludes the general exposition of the main teaching.
The following six proofs establish the five preceding topics at the beginning of the Ten Dedications.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways:
namely, they moved, moved universally, and moved everywhere; they rose, rose universally, and rose everywhere; they surged, surged universally, and surged everywhere;
they quaked, quaked universally, and quaked everywhere; they roared, roared universally, and roared everywhere; they crashed, crashed universally, and crashed everywhere.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, and because such is the nature of the Dharma, there rained down a multitude of celestial flowers, celestial garlands, celestial powdered incense,
various celestial fragrances, celestial garments, celestial jewels, celestial ornaments, celestial maṇi gems, celestial aloeswood incense, celestial sandalwood incense,
exquisite celestial parasols, various celestial banners, and multicolored celestial pennants, along with incalculable devas.
There were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of unspeakable celestial sounds of the sublime Dharma; inconceivable celestial sounds of praising the Buddha;
and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) celestial sounds of joy, all exclaiming, "Excellent!
Immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of nayutas of devas paid respectful homage and prostrated. Countless sons of gods constantly kept the Buddhas in mind and longed for the Tathāgata.
With hearts never abandoning immeasurable merit, countless sons of heaven performed various musical performances, singing hymns of praise and joy to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

Hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya devas emitted great light that universally illuminated all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of space and pervaded the Dharma-realm, manifesting the infinite asaṃkhyeya realms of all Buddhas. Thus did the Tathāgata transform.
The body surpasses all devas.
This is the sixth major section, "The Portents of Auspicious Response" from the passage beginning with "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the shaking of the earth to engender faith; second, the passage beginning with "By the Buddha’s spiritual power and because the Dharma is thus," which describes the offering of worship to manifest practice. Regarding the former...
The middle section has three parts. The first two phrases establish the causes for making offerings. Second, "a rain of various celestial flowers" refers to external material offerings.
Next, the six lines of scripture beginning with "the bodies of incalculable devas" refer to the three internal karmas.
Just as this Dharma was taught here in the Tuṣita Heaven palace of this world, so it was likewise in all the Tuṣita Heaven palaces throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The seventh major section, "As in this world," concludes by extending [the teaching] to the ten directions.

Because this is a discourse that universally pervades all directions, it follows the pattern of the various previous assemblies, which either conclude with auspicious responses or conclude with the summary of the teaching; therefore, this is established as a separate chapter.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came to the assembly bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten million buddha-fields.
Pervading the ten directions, they all spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound these great dedications."
"O Son of the Buddha! We are all of one name, called Vajradhvaja.
We have all come from the world-system Vajraprabhā to this land from the presence of the Buddha Vajradhvaja.

In those worlds, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, this Dharma was preached to an assembly of followers; its phrasing, words, and meanings were exactly like this, neither more nor less. We..."
All have come from those lands by the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness for you, just as I have come to this assembly to bear witness for you.
It is likewise with all the assemblies of bodhisattvas in the palaces of the Tuṣita heavens and the Jewel-Adorned Halls throughout all worlds in the ten directions who have come to bear witness.
The Eighth Major Section: At that time, furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the section on the "Supporting Realization" (adhigama) is presented.
As for the term "one million," it is because its stage surpasses the preceding one. This concludes the prose section above.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed all the assemblies in the ten directions as far as the reaches of the Dharma-realm.
Having thoroughly understood the words and their meanings, he expanded his vast mind and encompassed all sentient beings with great compassion.
He binds his mind in steadfast dwelling within the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

He skillfully enters into all the qualities of the Buddhas' merit and accomplishes the sovereign bodies of all Buddhas. Observing the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, he discerns and knows all the roots of goodness they have planted.
In accordance with the Dharma-body, he manifests for them a body of pure and wondrous form. At that very moment—
Then he spoke in verse.
This is the ninth major section: the section on praising with verses and exhorting practice following the passage on Vajra. It consists of two parts; first, the statement of the intent.
The Bodhisattva has perfected the wisdom of the Dharma; Awakening to and understanding the boundless gateways of the True Dharma, He is a Teacher and Guide who illuminates the Dharma with light;
Thoroughly knowing the unimpeded and true Dharma, The Bodhisattva is a great guide of the Dharma, Revealing the profound and rare-to-be-attained teachings.
Guiding immeasurable multitudes throughout the ten directions, they cause all to dwell securely within the True Dharma.
Having already drunk from the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, the clouds of Dharma rain universally upon the worlds of the ten directions.
The Sun of Dharma appears in the world, proclaiming the wondrous Dharma to benefit all living beings.
Always a rare donor of the Dharma, he thoroughly understands the skillful means for entering the Dharma;
the pure light of the Dharma illuminates his mind, and he is ever fearless in preaching the Dharma to the world.
Having well cultivated a mind of mastery over the Dharma, he is able to awaken to and enter all gateways of the Dharma.
Having accomplished the ocean of profound and wondrous Dharma, you universally beat the Dharma drum for all sentient beings;
You proclaim the profound and rare Dharma, nurturing all merits through the Dharma;
Possessing a mind of pure joy in the Dharma, you manifest the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings to the world.
Consecrated by all Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma, The body of the treasury of wisdom of the nature of phenomena is fully realized;
One thoroughly understands the true reality of all phenomena And abides securely in all wholesome dharmas.
This is the foremost gift practiced by Bodhisattvas, Which is praised and rejoiced in by all Tathāgatas.
All that he does is approved by the Buddhas; By this, he achieves the state of the Honored One among Men.

The Bodhisattva accomplishes the wondrous Dharma-body, Personally born through transformation from the teachings of all Buddhas, To act as a lamp of Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings, Proclaiming immeasurable and most supreme teachings.
In accordance with the sublime Dharma-gift practiced, one likewise contemplates those roots of goodness;
for the sake of sentient beings, all the various merits performed are dedicated through wisdom.
All the qualities that constitute the merit of attaining Buddhahood are entirely dedicated and bestowed upon all living beings.
May all beings be purified and reach the further shore of the Buddha’s adornments;
may the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions all possess immeasurable and vast adornments—
adornments such as these, inconceivable in number, may they all be used to adorn a single land.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata;
Like the true sons of the Buddha, Samantabhadra, may they adorn themselves with all merits and achieve great supernormal powers, Traveling to and pervading every world-system.
May all sentient beings without exception, All be led to practice the Bodhisattva path;
Awakened by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
May all infinite sentient beings throughout the ten directions Become exactly like Samantabhadra, Fully accomplishing the supreme conduct.
The various and diverse merits accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
may such boundless virtues as these cause all sentient beings to be fully perfected.
May Bodhisattvas, endowed with sovereign power, go forth to study all that ought to be learned.

Manifesting all great supernormal powers, Bodhisattvas are able, in a single moment of thought, to visit countless Buddhas as numerous as sentient beings throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions;
furthermore, within a single hair-tip, they can encompass all phenomena and perceive them all with perfect clarity.
The sentient beings of the world are immeasurable, yet the Bodhisattvas are able to discern and know them all;
the Buddhas are as immeasurable as these beings, and with a great mind, they make offerings to them all until none are left—
offering various kinds of named incenses and exquisite flowers, as well as robes of many jewels, banners, and canopies.
Pervading and filling the entire Dharma-realm, I resolve to universally make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within a single pore, I clearly behold Buddhas of inconceivable and infinite number;
It is thus within every single pore, As I universally prostrate to all the Lamps of the World.
Bowing with reverence, body upon body in succession, I likewise praise all these infinite,
most supreme ones with words. Throughout every kalpa until the end of the future,
The offerings made to each and every Tathāgata are as infinite in number as all sentient beings.
Thus making offerings to a single Tathāgata, one likewise does so for all Tathāgatas;
by offering and praising all the Tathāgatas throughout every kalpa of that world,
even if the number of kalpas in the world were to come to an end, the Bodhisattva’s offerings would never cease or grow weary.
Throughout all the various kalpas of every world, one practices all the deeds and reverently makes offerings to a single Tathāgata for as many kalpas as there are;
never becoming weary or satisfied throughout all these kalpas,
just as one would offer to a single Buddha for immeasurable kalpas, so too does one offer to all Buddhas.
Nor does he discriminate regarding the number of eons; He never grows weary or fatigued by the acts of making offerings.
The Dharma-realm is vast and boundless; The Bodhisattva observes it all with perfect clarity.
Within this space, he spreads great lotus flowers everywhere, And bestows them upon Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings.
The precious flowers, fragrances, and colors are all perfect;
Pure, adorned, and exceedingly subtle, beyond all worldly comparison. I hold these to offer to the Honored One among Men.
Throughout infinite lands as numerous as sentient beings, Exquisite jeweled canopies fill them all.
To make offerings to a single Tathāgata, one should likewise offer to all Buddhas in this same way.
This unexcelled and most supreme fragrant ointment, never before seen in any world,
is used to make offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Humans for as many eons as there are sentient beings.
With powdered incense, burning incense, and most excellent flowers, With robes of various jewels and all manner of ornaments—
Thus making offerings to the Most Victorious Ones, Serving them with joy and never wearying;
Equal in number to all sentient beings, these lamps illuminating the world, In every thought-moment, accomplish Great Bodhi.
Furthermore, with boundless verses, they praise and make offerings to the Tamer of Men,
the World-Honored Buddhas, as numerous as all sentient beings; they cultivate unsurpassed,
sublime offerings for as many eons as there are sentient beings, extolling them in this way without end.
While thus making offerings to all Buddhas, through the spiritual power of the Buddhas,
one sees everywhere throughout the ten directions the infinite Buddhas;
and all roots of goodness whatsoever belonging to the past, future, and present, as they abide in the practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
May I always cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra, And swiftly attain stable abiding on the stage of Samantabhadra.
May all immeasurable sentient beings in the world, Whom all Tathāgatas know and see,
Be fully endowed with qualities like those of Samantabhadra, And be praised by the wise.
This is the practice of dedication cultivated together by the great beings of the ten directions;

the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have taught it to me. This practice of dedication is most unsurpassed, and among all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is none who excels it.
May all beings without exception attain awakening, And may they always act as Samantabhadra does in his practice of dedication.
Just as he practices giving, So too shall they firmly uphold the prohibitions and precepts,
Exerting diligence for a long time without retreat or fear, With patience and gentleness, their minds unshakable.
Through meditative concentration, they hold the mind constantly on a single object; through wisdom, they comprehend all objects as being identical to samādhi.
They penetrate the past, future, and present, such that no one in the world can find their limit.
The physical, mental, and verbal activities of these Bodhisattvas—all such deeds are utterly pure.
All practices, without exception, are entirely equal to those of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
like the dharmadhātu, they are free from discrimination, and all conceptual proliferation and attachment are forever exhausted.
Like nirvāṇa, they are without obstruction; the mind is always thus, detached from all grasping.
The methods of dedication employed by the wise, As taught in their various ways by all the Tathāgatas, Dedicate every root of virtue; Thus they are able to accomplish the path of the Bodhisattvas.
Sons of the Buddha, learn well this dedication, And all immeasurable practices and vows will be fulfilled.
Comprehending the entire dharma-realm without exception, One is thus able to accomplish the powers of the Sugata.
If one wishes to fulfill the vast and sublime conduct Expounded by the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Should properly abide in this dedication; Such a son of the Buddhas is named Samantabhadra.
The actual exposition of the verses also consists of two parts: first, the clarification of the tenth dedication; second, the praise of its excellence and the exhortation to practice it.

Next, seven verses praise the practice of dedication, which is divided into three sections. First, the two verses beginning with "In accordance with the practices performed" provide a general summary of the preceding nine sections of dedication.
Second, the single verse beginning with "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions" praises the dedication for adorning the fields. Third, [the section on] the Tathāgata...

All four subsequent verses constitute the dedication for the sake of others. Regarding the "Perfection of the Three Qualities of Bodhisattvas," there are twenty verses below that describe the results of the stages (*bhūmi-phala*).
This is divided into three parts: first, one verse on seeing the mastery of the Buddha, which states that one sees the mastery of the Buddha only through one's own mastery;
second, seventeen verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva is able, in a single thought-moment," which praise the attainment of purity.
Within a single moment of thought, one universally enters the assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; this is the purity of wisdom.
Since the previous [verse] mentioned "entering," it must involve making offerings; therefore, this is explained extensively here.

This is a manifestation of power and cannot be subsumed under the preceding vows regarding what is accomplished. The final two verses, beginning with "The past and the future," summarize the tenth dedication.

However, the above has been categorized based on coarse characteristics for the time being. Since the Bodhisattva’s spontaneous eloquence encompasses all aspects in its essential nature and the general intent remains no different, it is not discussed in detail here.
The preceding section on the individual verses is concluded.

The following second part consists of a concluding eulogy and exhortation to practice, which applies generally to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-praṇidhāna*). Within this, there are nine stanzas divided into two sections; first, the six stanzas beginning with "This is [the path] of the ten directions."
The person who practices these deeds does so to praise their excellence; that is to say, they are the practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas as taught by the Tathāgata.

Because they consist of practices such as those corresponding to the characteristics of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and practices that transcend the characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are preeminent.
The final three verses concerning the wisdom of the subsequent stage summarize this praise and exhort one to practice.
All sentient beings may be counted, And the mental capacities of the three periods of time may also be known;
Yet the limits of the merit of such sons of the Buddhas, Samantabhadra, Can never be measured.

One could reach the end of space by measuring it with a single hair, And one could count the number of atoms in all the lands; But the boundless ocean of their virtues Cannot be fathomed even by the Buddhas themselves.
Thus, the conduct, dwellings, and vows of these great sages, the sons of the Buddhas, are immeasurable.
This is the end of the tenth chapter on the Great Text; the final two verses compare their merits. Since these virtues are limitless, they should be cultivated.

[This is] the practice. Now, as for the manifestation of these virtues as profound, supreme, lofty, and far-reaching: first, because it is the teaching of perfect interfusion; second, because it concerns the power of extraordinary vows;
and third, because from the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) upward, there are successive gradations of status. At each conclusion, it says:
"If one considers the power of extraordinary vows, it exceeds this even further and cannot be known by calculation. Do not say that because this [stage] is profound, the [lower] stages are inferior.
The fifth assembly above is concluded.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
commentary on the meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
and edited and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fāyún Temple on Mount Kuāng in Ming China.
The sixth assembly was preached by Vajragarbha Bodhisattva in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Regarding the first part of the twenty-sixth chapter, "The Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*):
the intent behind its introduction is to provide a remote response to the questions concerning the ten stages posed by Samantaprabha. Indeed, no merit is established in vain; in the end...
There must necessarily be a destination. Previously, the explanation of the causes for the stages of the noble ones—namely, understanding that guides conduct and vows—was concluded.

Now, the establishment of the fruits of the stages of the sages—namely, wisdom that realizes the profound *tathatā* (suchness)—is presented; therefore, this assembly has come forth. The former was the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), while this is the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*).

Teaching serves as the cause for realization, because realization is precisely the realization of the teachings concerning the three minds mentioned previously. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "This hearing..."
Although the perfuming (vāsanā) is of an outflowing nature (sāsrava), it possesses the nature of being the seed for supramundane mind; this is precisely the meaning [of the text].

Furthermore, "assembly" (hui) is equivalent to "chapter" (pin), because within a single assembly there is only one chapter. Therefore, the explanation of the fundamental tenet and its purpose is no different between the chapters and the assemblies.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names: there are three types of names for the assemblies. First, those based on the names of persons, such as the *Vajra* [Assembly].

The Assembly of the Tathāgata. Second, according to the location, it is called the Assembly of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. This means that others manifest the instruments of pleasure, which one then enjoys for oneself;
this represents the ground entered, wherein one realizes suchness without conceptual mind, yet gives rise to activity through post-meditative wisdom without obstruction.

Activity arises through the enjoyment of others, not from one's own affairs, because self and other act in mutual dependence to attain mastery, and because one attains the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) free from desire.
Thirdly, regarding the dharma, it is named the "Assembly of the Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-samāja*), which is synonymous with its title.
The reason it receives this name is that "stage" (*bhūmi*) means "to sustain"; it sustains millions of *asaṃkhyeya* merits.
It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it generates all causes and effects; it is so named because it generates and sustains the Buddha-wisdom.
There is another translated version titled the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and yet another titled the *Anupūrvasamudgata-sarvajñatā-guṇa-sūtra*.
It is called "gradually perfected" (*anupūrva-samudgata*) because each subsequent stage surpasses each preceding one. Regarding the three essential points: first, the general [summary], and then...

They are distinct. In general, there are two meanings. First, taking the stages of practice—where wisdom and the abandonment and realization of the grounds are correlated with specific positions—as the primary focus, it takes the manifestation of the characteristics of perfect, non-obstructive interpenetration as its ultimate goal.
Second, both of the preceding [meanings] serve as the primary focus, while taking the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood as the ultimate goal.
Regarding the subsequent distinctions: these distinguish [the present section] from the preceding general summary. Briefly, there are ten points. First, regarding the basis:

it is exclusively the ocean of fruition, an ineffable nature, because it is free from the duality of subject and object of realization; although this applies throughout the entire treatise, it is precisely elucidated in this chapter.
Second, that which is realized is stainless *tathatā* (suchness). Third, regarding wisdom: it refers to both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom, and also includes skillful means. Fourth...

Regarding what is to be abandoned: this refers to being free from the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles. Regarding what is to be cultivated: on the first stage, one cultivates the practice of aspiration;

on the second stage, the practice of ethical discipline; on the third, the practice of meditative concentration; on the fourth, the practice of the path; on the fifth, the practice of the four truths; and on the sixth, the practice of dependent origination.

1. The practice of the seven factors of enlightenment; 2. The practice of purifying the buddha-field; 3. The practice of preaching the Dharma; 4. The practice of receiving the position [of Buddhahood]. Regarding the six [stages] in terms of cultivation and accomplishment, there are four practices:

namely, first, the practice of faith and aspiration on the first stage (*bhūmi*); second, the practice of ethical discipline; third, the practice of meditative concentration; and fourth, from the fourth stage upward, all are the practice of wisdom.
Among these, the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are those that accord with the practices of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). From the seventh stage onward...
This is the wisdom of the bodhisattva. Seventh, in terms of the practice associated with the stages (*bhūmi*), each of the ten stages is associated with one of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Eighth, in terms of the dharmas, there are three virtues: the virtue of realization (*adhigama-guṇa*), the virtue of scripture (*āgama-guṇa*), and the path of non-abiding (*apratisthita-mārga*); these constitute the virtues of the ten stages.

Ninth, in terms of the vehicles to which they are associated, the first, second, and third stages are associated with the vehicles of humans and devas; the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are associated with the [Śrāvaka] vehicle...
The three vehicles of the world and those above the eighth stage, which are supramundane, constitute the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). These various vehicles are taken as the dharmas of this stage.
The ten essential points are condensed into six, for it is through these that the definitive tenets are distinguished; this shall be clarified in the "Section on the Fundamentals" (*Mūla-bhāga*).
Among these ten, the numbers two, three, four, eight, and ten pertain to both the perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*) and the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*). The first pair is a negation of both.
Because it is beyond words. All others are sequential (prabandha), for they mostly manifest the degrees of depth and shallowness by relying on provisional stages.

If one integrates that sequence with perfect interfusion (yuanrong), then there is nothing that is not interfused. Therefore, when the specific is subsumed under the general, all take the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) as their primary tenet.

If one considers the specifics within the specifics, then each stage is itself a primary tenet; yet, when discussing their ultimate aim individually, it does not differ from the general aim. Question: Why?

Is it that the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) reveals the virtue of perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), while the stages from the grounds upward manifest a sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) to indicate their relative shallowness and depth? Answer: This is to reveal the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). How is it revealed?
In the positions of the Three Vehicles, there is a sequential arrangement prior to the grounds and perfect fusion from the grounds upward.

Now, in the position of the One Vehicle, both sequential arrangement and perfect fusion exist throughout both the stages prior to the grounds and the grounds themselves. If both are presented together, then [the former... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.)*

The latter is not different from the former. If the sequential arrangement (*pratipatti*) prior to the stages were identical to the perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*) upon the stages, it would be entirely the same as the Three Vehicles, which are shallow before and deep after.

Furthermore, this would resemble a case where sequential arrangement and perfect interpenetration are treated as distinct teachings and practices; one would fail to realize that the teachings and practices of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) are neither identical nor separate.
Therefore, while the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) merely manifests perfect interpenetration—already surpassing the Three Vehicles—the stage of the grounds [manifests] much more.

The sequential arrangement (*pindapāta*) is clarified in order to manifest its transcendent superiority. What are these superior characteristics? They refer to the fact that from the beginning to the end of the stage of worthiness (*bhadra-avasthā*), one has already attained perfect fusion and mastery.
From the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) onward, it is profoundly deep, beyond the reach of words. If this were not expressed by way of stages, how could its depth be manifested?
If it did not encompass the three vehicles (*triyāna*), how could its vastness be manifested? Therefore, it is like the tracks of a bird in the sky—[the tracks exist, yet they leave no trace].
The traces [of the teaching] accord with emptiness. The ten virtues of the great ocean are such that each virtue is like the ocean itself.

Within each stage (*bhūmi*), all the merits of every stage are fully contained; within each phrase, it is said that by the power of supreme vows, they exceed even this and cannot be numbered or known.
Therefore, Vajragarbha waited for five requests before he finally spoke, and Vasubandhu [analyzed them] by means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of "perfect interfusion" (yuanrong) lies precisely herein. Furthermore, this single assembly constitutes a single chapter;
the absence of the "Expedient Means" (upāya) and the "Advancement" (viśeṣagamana) sections is exactly this point. There are two reasons for the omission of the Expedient Means:

first, to signify that the True Dharma is non-dual and transcends expedients; second, to comprehensively encompass the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) as the very method for entering the [Bodhisattva] grounds.

This is because it is expedient. There are also two meanings for the absence of further progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*): first, because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are like those of a Buddha, there is no further destination;
second, because the categories such as the ten concentrations (*daśasamādhi*) constitute this very progress. If that is so, why are they explained separately in other assemblies?

Because it contains two meanings: first, it opens up this superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) so as to achieve equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); second, the superior progress toward the Buddha’s practice is profound and far-reaching.

If one were to establish "expedient means" (*upāya*) and "superior progress" as separate categories, one would be unable to encompass the preceding and following stages or manifest their perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*).
That the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are profoundly deep lies precisely herein. The stage prior to the [first] ground is simply "before my ground. How could it be otherwise?
"The clouds are deep and different from those upon the earth. This interpretation is particularly subtle; students should reflect upon it. The supplementary commentary states:
Regarding the assembly in the celestial palace, it should have followed the ritual of the first three assemblies, where the Heavenly Kings prepared seats and praised the Buddha with verses.
That this is not present here is due to three reasons. First, this heaven is the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
It is fully provided for one's own enjoyment. Since it is thus with the devas, the Buddha likewise acts according to his transformations;

therefore, it is not necessary to arrange seats or offerings. Second, it reveals that the wisdom of the ground transcends the world and accomplishes tasks without deliberate thought, as it is free from contrived activity.
Third, the merit and practice accumulated through the three preceding stages of worthiness are consolidated here to constitute the virtues of this ground, as in other cases.
Because it is a transformation [sūtra], there is no specific mention of this in the scripture;

however, since this meaning exists, the subsequent scriptural text is explained according to its major sections, which comprise ten divisions in total: first, the Introduction (Nidāna); second, the Section on Samādhi (Samādhibhāga).
1. The Section on the Threefold Increase; 2. The Section on Arising; 3. The Section on the Main Body; 4. The Section on the Request; 5. The Section on the Correct Exposition;
6. The Section on Images; 7. The Section on Benefits; 8. The Section on Verses. Now, the first:

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Maṇi-jewel Treasury Hall of the palace of the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas.
All these bodhisattvas were non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and had all gathered from worlds in other directions.
They dwelt in the realm where the wisdom of all bodhisattvas abides and had entered into one...
They enter the sphere of all Tathāgatas' wisdom and practice with tireless diligence.
They are skillfully able to manifest various supernatural powers and perform all manner of deeds, teaching and taming all sentient beings without missing the proper time.
To fulfill all the great vows of a bodhisattva, they diligently cultivate all practices throughout all worlds, all eons, and all lands, never for a moment becoming weary.
They rest, fully endowed with the bodhisattva’s accumulations of merit and wisdom that aid the path; they universally benefit sentient beings without ever becoming exhausted;

they reach the ultimate further shore of all bodhisattvas’ wisdom and skillful means; they manifest entry into both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa without ever abandoning the cultivation of bodhisattva practices;
and they skillfully enter all bodhisattva meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis.
With the supernormal power of the *pātra* (alms bowl) and clear wisdom, they attain mastery in all their undertakings.

Having acquired the sovereign spiritual powers of all bodhisattvas, in a single moment and without any physical movement, they are able to go to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Tathāgatas.
As leaders among sentient beings, they request the Buddhas to preach the Dharma and protect and maintain the wheel of the true Dharma of all Buddhas. By means of...
With a vast mind, they make offerings to and serve all Buddhas; they constantly and diligently cultivate all the deeds and practices of Bodhisattvas.
Their bodies appear universally throughout all worlds, and their voices pervade the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Their mental wisdom is unimpeded, and they universally perceive all the merits of all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time, having fully practiced them all.
It is fully perfected; even if one were to speak for unspeakable eons, one could not exhaust it.
Now, this initial introduction also ascends without being separated from it. As for the phrase "at that time," it refers to the moment of first attaining perfect enlightenment.
At that point, the ten bodies are first fulfilled, and clouds of inexhaustible bodies pervade the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, he ascends without moving.
The treatise states: Because this Dharma is supreme, the time, the master, and the assembly are all supreme. This means that at the time of its initial formation, the time is supreme.
The World-Honored One is the master among masters, and Vajragarbha is the master of the exposition.

Since this supreme Dharma is expounded by a Buddha of the initial formation with a distinguished body (*vairocana-vigraha*) and a Great Bodhisattva, the master is supreme. The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven surpasses the five lower heavens.
Because it abides at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), its location is superior.

Because it is accompanied by great bodhisattvas, distinguishing it from those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and because they have all newly assembled having come from other directions, the assembly is superior. As it says below: "Abiding with all bodhisattvas... and so forth.

Praising the excellence of his virtues. This passage praising his virtues consists of twenty phrases. The first two phrases concern the objective realm in which the All-Knowing One abides during the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

These briefly clarify the fulfillment of the "self-benefiting practice" (*svārtha-caryā*) of the first phrase: namely, the wisdom that is unimpeded regarding both the provisional and the ultimate, abiding in a realm where the absolute and the conventional are fused as one.

Here, object and wisdom are identical; because it is an abiding without abiding, it is called "abiding. The subsequent phrase clarifies the fulfillment of the "practice for the benefit of others" (*parārtha-caryā*).

One who realizes what the Buddha has realized is a Tathāgata; one who practices with tireless diligence is a Bodhisattva. Next, the sixteen phrases beginning with "skillfully able to manifest" are explained:
the first thirteen phrases elaborate upon the stage of self-benefit (*svabhāga*), while the final three phrases elaborate upon the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

The preceding section consists of two parts. The first three phrases clarify the perfection of the cultivation of practice; the remaining ten phrases, beginning with "endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva," praise the complete and perfect excellence of his virtues and functions.
Next, the three phrases beginning with "His body manifests everywhere" extensively describe his sublime progress, which refers to the vastness of the three karmas.
Finally, the two phrases beginning with "All have already" serve as the concluding summary.
Their names were: Vajragarbha Bodhisattva; Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva;
Padmagarbha Bodhisattva; Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva; Padmaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva; Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva; Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva;
Vimalacandragarbha Bodhisattva; Sarvabuddhakṣetrasamantavyūhagarbha Bodhisattva; and Vairocanajñāna [Bodhisattva].
Gandhagarbha Bodhisattva, Mañjughoṣagarbha Bodhisattva, Candanaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Puṣpaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Kusumaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva,
Utpalaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Devaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Puṇyagarbha Bodhisattva,
Asaṅgapariśuddhajñānaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva, and Nārāyaṇa.
Bodhisattva Guṇagañja; Bodhisattva Vimalagañja; Bodhisattva Vimalanirbhāsagañja; Bodhisattva Nānāpratibhānavyūhagañja;
Bodhisattva Mahāprabhājālagarbha; Bodhisattva Śuddhatejaprabharājagañja; Bodhisattva Suvarṇavyūhamahāpuṇyaprabharājagañja; and Bodhisattva Sarvalakṣaṇavyūhaśuddhaguṇagañja.
Sā. The Bodhisattva Vajrajvālāguṇalakṣaṇavyūhagarbha; the Bodhisattva Prabhājvālāgarbha;
the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājaprabhāsa-ālokagarbha; the Bodhisattva Gaganāsaṅgajñānagarbha; and the Bodhisattva Manojñāghoṣāsaṅgagarbha.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī-guṇa-sarvasattva-praṇidhāna-garbha, the Bodhisattva Sāgara-vyūha-garbha, the Bodhisattva Meru-guṇa-garbha,
the Bodhisattva Viśuddha-sarvaguṇa-garbha, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-garbha, the Bodhisattva Buddha-guṇa-garbha,
and the Bodhisattva Vimukti-candra— these and others, numbering countless, immeasurable, boundless, and incomparable.
An incalculable, inexpressible, inconceivable, immeasurable, and ineffable assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
whose names were established in accordance with their virtues, consisting of forty groups; of these, Vajragarbha was the presiding speaker for the first [group], and subsequently...

Vimukticandra serves as the presiding petitioner. The thirty-eight members of the assembly who share the same name, "Treasury" (Gaṇḍa), signify that the dharmas of the stages (bhūmi) contain and encompass all virtues and give rise to the functional efficacy of the fruits. The one at the end, named Vimukticandra, is the leader who requests the Dharma;
he is so called because he dispels the darkness of doubt for the assembly like the moon at night. Among them, Sūrya means "moon" in this context.
Furthermore, *kusuma* means "delightful"; it is a name for flowers. Such enumerations as these are difficult to measure at their lower limit.
With the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha as their leader, [they were present].
The fifth [section] identifies the speaker. Question: Since there are many bodhisattvas, why does only Vajragarbha speak? Answer:
Because all afflictions are difficult to destroy, and this Dharma is able to shatter them; his roots of goodness are as firm and solid as a vajra, therefore he is spoken of by no other name.
Question: What is meant by "Vajragarbha"? This explains the meaning of "garbha" (matrix/storehouse). Answer: It refers to the matrix (garbha).

This is called "solidity" (*khara*). It is like the core of a tree; just as the heartwood of a tree is firm and dense, capable of producing branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, so too is the wisdom of the earth (*pṛthivī-jñāna*), which can produce cause and effect.
In this sense, it is called a "store" (*garbha*) because it stores [the potential]. Furthermore, it is like a fetus dwelling within a womb.
Therefore, its solidity is like that of a diamond (*vajra*); it is like a "diamond-store" (*vajragarbha*). This refers to the embryo (*bīja*) residing within the womb (*garbha*).
It is sustained by virtuous karma and is firm and indestructible; yet it is called "growth. This is termed an "ālaya" (storehouse) with reference to that which is stored therein.
Both metaphors possess the sense of growth.
The Supplementary Commentary states: As for Vajragarbha’s exposition of the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*), it is because the golden wheel supports the seeds of the world-system;

because the great earth has diamond as its essence; and because the very bottom of the earth is the "diamond-limit" (*vajrānta*), signifying that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) constitutes the essence of the dharmas of the stages.

Regarding the term "storehouse" (*garbha*), the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* speaks of the "consciousness-storehouse" (*vijñāna-garbha*) and the "Tathāgata-storehouse" (*tathāgatagarbha*). It is said that the consciousness-storehouse has three aspects.
The meaning of "store" (*ālaya*) refers to that which stores, that which is stored, and that which is clung to as a self.

This is because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) can store all seeds of both the defiled and the pure, and it is also the locus where those seeds are stored, remaining neither lost nor destroyed throughout long kalpas.
Because it is clung to as a self, this present storehouse consciousness is the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store). The *tathāgatagarbha*, in turn, is the Dharma...
The treasury of the body and wisdom is named "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This is because all pure and sublime merits of the Buddha-stage are sustained solely by this wisdom, and it is also that in which those various merits are accumulated as the four virtues of true permanence, purity, wondrousness, and bliss.

Because it remains undiminished and indestructible until the end of the future, it carries the meaning of a "repository" (*garbha*). Therefore, this Bodhisattva is established by name based on the Dharma;

for he expounds the Dharma realized through self-attestation (*pratyātma-adhigama*). Furthermore, this signifies the diamond-like wisdom-mind (*vajra-jñāna-citta*) that shatters all stubborn ignorance.
Thus, although there are many assemblies, this alone is specifically mentioned here. The commentary (*śāstra*) has not yet reached this point. [End of] the above.
The introductory section is concluded.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi of the Great Wisdom Radiance.

This is the second section on samādhi. "At that time" refers to when the assembly had already gathered. Vajragarbha entered meditative absorption because, as the leader of the assembly, he knew that he ought to speak;
thus, he first entered samādhi. Because he perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind, he relies upon the Buddha’s power.
"The light of great wisdom" is the name of the samādhi. Samādhi is a general term; [here it specifically denotes] wisdom.
This is the essence; radiance is its function. Realizing suchness is called wisdom (*prajñā*); illuminating phenomena is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because these two are unimpeded and can destroy the delusions of views as well as ignorance, they are termed "radiance.
Because they can sever great delusions, realize the Great Principle, and achieve the Great Fruit, they are called "Great. Because knowledge merges with the Principle, it is termed "entry."

Having entered this samādhi, there are six sections in the third part concerning the "Additional Merit" (*anugraha*) of entering this samādhi: first, identifying the cause of the additional merit; second, the manifestation of the Buddhas who bestow the additional merit immediately thereafter;
third, praising his attainment of concentration with the words "In this way," and so forth; fourth, "O son of good family, this... [and so on].
This section below distinguishes the causes and conditions for the bestowal of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The five desires serve as the objects for which the bestowal of empowerment is performed.
From "Good son" onwards, the specific characteristics of the empowerment are individually revealed. Now, regarding those who have already entered this samādhi:
if one has not yet entered meditative concentration, the Buddha does not bestow empowerment upon them. Therefore, Vajragarbha alone is specially empowered because he has attained this samādhi.
Immediately, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him ten billion buddhas—
each as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields— all sharing the same name, Vajragarbha.

Second, regarding the manifestation of the Buddhas who bestow empowerment, there are five points: first, the time when the Buddhas appear is identical to the time when [the Bodhisattva] enters meditative concentration;
second, the distance from which they descend from the ten directions; third, the number of Buddhas who bestow empowerment in each case;

fourth, their shared name as Vajragarbha, indicating that the names bestowed upon them are identical because the path revealed is the same; and fifth, their appearing before him, manifesting their bodies to inspire faith.
The mention of "ten billion" is intended to manifest their inexhaustibility by means of a round number.

As for the phrase "appearing simultaneously under the same name," it signifies that the dharmas of the stages are realized and taught identically by all Buddhas; this is because while the persons differ, the path is the same, and it is also due to the original vows of Vairocana.
He spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent! Vajragarbha is indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
This third instance of joint praise for attaining samādhi reveals the presence of an augmenting cause.
"Good son, these are the empowerments bestowed upon you by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms in ten billion Buddha-fields,
through the power of the original vows and the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
This is also due to your superior power of wisdom.
The fourth pair distinguishes the causes and conditions for the bestowal of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Within this, there are four statements and four causes and conditions:

first, because the accompanying Buddhas bestow empowerment together; second, because of the original vow of the presiding Buddha; third, because of the manifestation of the majesty of the presiding Buddha; and fourth, because of the wisdom of the one in meditative concentration.

Because of [his] power, there are two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): first, secret empowerment; second, manifest empowerment. Secret empowerment comes first, as manifest empowerment resides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It is because he wishes to have you explain to all bodhisattvas the light of the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas, namely:
Because it causes entry into the stage of wisdom; because it gathers all roots of goodness; because it skillfully discriminates all Buddha-dharmas; because it extensively knows all phenomena;
because it is well able to expound the Dharma; because non-conceptual wisdom is purified; because one is untainted by any worldly dharmas;
because supramundane roots of goodness are purified; because one attains the sphere of inconceivable wisdom; because one attains the first...
Because it is the sphere of wisdom of all-knowing ones; because it causes one to attain the beginning and end of the ten stages of a bodhisattva;

because it explains, according to reality, the distinct characteristics of the ten stages of a bodhisattva; because it takes all Buddha-dharmas as its object of mindfulness; because it cultivates the discernment of untainted dharmas;
because it skillfully adorns itself with the light of great wisdom through excellent selection and observation; and because it skillfully enters into certainty.
Because it is the gateway of wisdom; because it fearlessly elucidates the Dharma in successive order wherever one dwells;
because it attains the radiance of unimpeded eloquence; because it abides securely in the stage of great eloquence; because it recollects the bodhisattva mind without forgetfulness;
because it brings all realms of sentient beings to maturity; and because it is able to reach all places to definitively awaken them.

The fifth section clarifies the purpose of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The text contains twenty phrases: the first ten concern the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*), and the latter ten concern the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha*).
Now, regarding the first: it generally reveals that there are three intentions behind the empowerment. First, all bodhisattvas are the intended recipients (*vineya*).
Second, the light of the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas is the teaching to be proclaimed. Third, [it is to cause them...]
"Entering the stage of wisdom," and so forth, describes the benefits of this teaching. Furthermore, it enables one to attain the ten stages of a bodhisattva;

based on these ten phrases, there are ten items concerning altruistic practice. Although the sutra contains twelve phrases, the treatise combines the seventh and eighth phrases, resulting in only eleven.
The first phrase serves as the general heading, while the remaining ten constitute the specific details.
"Good son, you should skillfully explain the distinctions of this dharma-gate. This is because you have been empowered by the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom through the Buddha’s spiritual power;
because you have purified your own roots of goodness; because you have universally purified the dharma-realm; because you have universally gathered in all sentient beings;
because you have deeply entered the wisdom-body of the dharma-body; because you have received the empowerment of all Buddhas; and because you have attained all..."
Because it is the most sublime body in the world; because it transcends all worldly paths; because it is the pure supramundane roots of goodness;
and because it fulfills the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

The sixth section, which specifically reveals the characteristics of the empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), has three parts: first, the empowerment of speech; second, the empowerment of mind; and third, the empowerment of body.

Herein is the first [the empowerment of speech], which consists of eleven phrases. The first is general, while the others are specific. Within the general part, he is exhorted to expound the distinct characteristics of the Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) through eloquence born of joy, establishing them skillfully in accordance with both principle and phenomena; therefore, it says: "You should explain with eloquence. Regarding what is to be explained...
Regarding the various meanings found in the commentary on each of the ten points:
at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha a body that could not be eclipsed or surpassed; they bestowed unimpeded eloquence for joyful exposition;
they bestowed pure wisdom for skillful discernment; they bestowed the power of skillful recollection and non-forgetfulness; and they bestowed skillful decisiveness.
The wisdom of clear realization through meditative concentration; the wisdom of awakening that reaches all places; the sovereign power of accomplishing the Path;
the fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata; the eloquence and wisdom of the omniscient ones to observe and discern the various Dharma-gates;
and the supreme adornment of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

Regarding the second [section], the "Additions of Intention" (*manas-adhikāra*), there are two parts: first, the actual presentation; second, the inquiry into and explanation of the reason for the partial additions.

Within the former, there are ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining are specific. Regarding the initial [general] part: [the Buddha] bestows upon them bodily action (*kāya-karman*) that is unobscured and non-appropriated; he bestows upon them vocal action (*vāk-karman*) characterized by unhindered joy and eloquence;
and he bestows upon them mental action (*manas-karman*) consisting of wholesome, distinct, and pure wisdom, and so forth. Thus, the final phrase says: "He bestows all..."

The Tathāgata’s supremely sublime activities of body, speech, and mind are fully adorned. Although there are many meanings in the commentaries and exegeses, I shall now briefly set forth their characteristics. Why is this?
Because the nature of the dharma of attaining this samādhi is such; because it arises from original vows; and because of the thoroughly pure and profound mind.
Therefore, because of the wheel of well-purified wisdom; because of the well-accumulated aids to the path; because of the well-cultivated and refined activities;
because of being mindful of immeasurable vessels for the Dharma; because of knowing their pure faith and understanding; because of attaining the dhāraṇī free from error;
and because of being well-sealed by the seal of wisdom of the dharma-realm.
"Why is this so?"—the following passage explains the reason for the partial bestowal of grace in order to demonstrate that [the Buddha] is capable of bestowing it through his own power.

The reason for explaining it specifically in terms of mental action (*manas-karman*) is that the mind is the fundamental basis. The initial inquiry asks: "If the compassionate power of the Buddhas were to be deficient..."

It may be granted that there is partial emphasis. Since he possesses the power to bestow [this samādhi] and the compassion to do so universally, why is it that in the preceding ten instances of partial emphasis, Vajragarbha alone is singled out while others are not?
The subsequent explanation of the text contains ten phrases: the first is general, and the rest are specific. The general title is "attaining this samādhi.
By the nature of the Dharma, partial emphasis is appropriate; others do not receive it because they have not attained this [samādhi]. This is the reason for its attainment.
Samādhi possesses eight kinds of purity, namely the following eight phrases. The first four constitute purity for one’s own benefit, while the latter four constitute purity for the benefit of others.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands and stroked the crown of the head of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva.

Because the three bodies increase their majestic power and cause it to arise, it is said that "each extends [the hand]"; this means they extend it without leaving their original place, which is the unimpeded nature of prolonging and contracting.
Since all Buddhas touch [them], it is said that "each extends"; this is the unimpeded nature of the one and the many.
This is the supernormal power of mastery over the mind (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*) among the four unhindered powers.
Having touched his head with the crown of his hand, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva arose from samādhi.

This is the section on arising after the fourth touching of the head. The reason for arising is that the matters of the samādhi have been concluded, he has attained superior power, and the time for exposition has arrived;
furthermore, because meditative concentration is devoid of verbal expression, it is necessary to arise. [End of] the fifth section of the main text.

The section on the fundamental divisions below is universally proclaimed as a brief indication of the essential framework; for the sake of an extensive treatment, the text is divided into three parts.

First, it clarifies the six determinations (*ṣaḍ-niyama*) as the substance of the ground (*bhūmi*). Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, what are... onwards, it enumerates the ten names to manifest the characteristics of these determinations.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... onwards, it cites the concurrent teachings of the ten directions to demonstrate the supreme importance of this ground.
He addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha! The vows of all bodhisattvas are well-determined, pure, and beyond perception.
They are as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extend to the end of the future.
They pervade all buddha-fields to rescue and protect all sentient beings, are guarded by all Buddhas, and enter into the past and the future."
The stage of wisdom of all present Buddhas is the essence of the first ground.
In the text, the first sentence serves as the introductory announcement, while the section beginning with "O sons of the Buddha" correctly elucidates it.

Within this, the first sentence provides a general explanation, and the subsequent section beginning with "unmixed" provides a detailed exposition. Regarding the phrase in the general explanation, "the bodhisattva’s vow is well-determined":
It designates the person and manifests the Dharma; thus it is called "Bodhisattva. Because one makes a vow to seek toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it is termed a "vow" (*praṇidhāna*);
this refers to the generation of the bodhicitta within the first stage (*bhūmi*). The reason this vow is explained as being "well-determined" is that it is embraced by true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
That is to say, it guides and encompasses this vow so that all things accord with principle, providing definitive discernment and rectitude.

Because it is fixed. This refers to one who has already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*); this is the certainty of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-niścaya*). It is not the designation "certainty of vow and acceptance" (*praṇidhāna-parigraha-niścaya*) belonging to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) prior to the stages.
Within the subsequent section, this "good certainty" (*kuśala-niścaya*) is of six kinds, corresponding to the six phrases of the sutra.

First, "unmixed" (*asaṃbhinna*) refers to the good certainty of the aspect of contemplation (*lakṣaṇa-pratyavekṣaṇa-kuśala-niścaya*), because the contemplation of *tathatā* has the single flavor of its aspect. That is to say:
The true essence of the object-condition is the single flavor of object and wisdom; this constitutes the characteristic of contemplation, being free from the admixture of conceptual signs.
Second, "the two are invisible" means it is the truly good and definitive, not an object of any worldly realm, because it is supramundane.
That is to say, this true gnosis transcends the destructible phenomena of the world; therefore, it is called "true. True...
Because it is real, it is not seen by worldly knowledge. Third, "vast as the dharma-realm" refers to the determination of supreme goodness;
the treatise explains this generally as being because it is the great dharma-realm and the root of all Buddhas.

Fourth, "ultimate like space, reaching to the end of the future" refers to the determination of causal goodness; because this wisdom is quiescent yet constantly active, it serves as [the basis for activity].
It has impermanence as its cause; because it is eternally quiescent in its functioning, it serves as the cause for the fruit of permanence.
This means that while Nirvāṇa is eternal quiescence, the essence of wisdom is not non-existent; therefore, it extends to the very limits of the future.

That which pervades all Buddha-fields and protects all sentient beings is the "Great Good Determination" (*mahā-kuśala-niścaya*), meaning that one acts in accordance with the practice of benefiting others; this is precisely what is meant by "universally covering."

It is called "Great" (*mahat*). This means that because of the preceding causes, through goodness one does not abide in *saṃsāra*. Because of this great goodness, through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) one does not abide in *nirvāṇa*.
The sixth [point], "for the sake of all," refers to the determination of being free from cowardice; because one enters the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*), one is not cowardly.
The six aspects are perfectly integrated, as can be understood by analogy with what precedes. The above six determinations are presented for clarification.
The essence of the stages (*bhūmi*). Below, the characteristics of the stages are enumerated in response to an inquiry.
"O Son of the Buddha! What are the stages of wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas?
