Next, within the enumeration of the characteristics of the stages, there are four sections. First, the inquiry is posed to introduce the topic. Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, [the characteristics are] presented.
The enumeration and the explanation are identical. Third, from "What are these? onwards, the number is questioned and the names are listed. Fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva...
onwards, the name is concluded and its excellence is revealed. First, regarding the initial section:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten stages of wisdom for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. All Buddhas of the past, future, and present [abide therein]."
That which has been said, that which shall be said, and that which is being said now—I also speak in this same way.

The two [phrases] "has been" and "shall be" cite the number to manifest their commonality; because they bring about generation, maintenance, and sustenance, they are spoken of as identical across the three periods of time.

The word "identically spoken" (同說) refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the earth in its textual expression, while its meaning encompasses the substance (*dravya*) of the earth. That which is spoken of identically across the three periods of time is the sixfold determination of the substance of the earth.
...as well. What are the ten? First is the Ground of Joy; second, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement;
third, the Ground of Radiant Light; fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer; sixth, the Ground of Manifestation; seventh, the Ground of Far-Going; eighth...
These are: [the first is] the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); the ninth is the Good Wisdom Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*); and the tenth is the Dharma Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Among these three enumerations of the grounds, the ten grounds are taught to counteract the ten obstacles, to realize the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), and to accomplish the ten supreme practices.
The commentary (*ṭīkā*) cites the treatise (*śāstra*) to explain their meaning in detail; here, I shall briefly extract the ten obstacles. The first is the ordinary...

Namely: first, the obstruction of the notion of self; second, the obstruction of wrong conduct; third, the obstruction of dullness and ignorance; fourth, the obstruction of pride regarding the understanding of the Dharma;

fifth, the obstruction of pride regarding the purity of one’s own body; sixth, the obstruction of subtle afflictions; seventh, the obstruction of the habitual tendencies toward subtle signs; eighth, the obstruction of applied effort regarding the signless;
ninth, the obstruction of being unable to skillfully benefit sentient beings; and tenth, the inability to attain mastery over all phenomena.

Regarding the obstructions: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that within each obstruction there are two types of delusion (*moha*). These are the delusions that obstruct and the delusions that are severed;
upon severing them, one realizes the ten *tathatās*. This will be explained in detail below. For now, we shall briefly explain the names of the stages according to this treatise. The treatise says:

"First, having accomplished the unsurpassed practice of benefiting oneself and others, one realizes the initial stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) and gives rise to great joy; thus it is named 'Joy' (*pramuditā*)."

The Ground (Bhūmi). Because one has now attained initial accomplishment through the cultivation of the preceding three stages, and because this is a newly attained state of the noble ones (*ārya*), there is the arising of joy.

Second, because it is free from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to errors and transgressions of the precepts, and because it is endowed with pure morality, it is called the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Third, because phenomena appear clearly through the illumination of hearing, reflection, and meditation, it is the Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). That is to say:
It is called the "Luminous Ground" (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*) because one attains the characteristic marks of the light of wisdom of the fourth stage;

this sutra refers to it exclusively as "Emitting Light," meaning that by accomplishing superior meditative concentration and the great dharma-dhāraṇī, one is able to emit the boundless light of wondrous wisdom—this name is derived from its subsequent stage.
It is called the "Blazing Ground" (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) because the fire of knowledge can burn the fuel of the afflictions without forgetting—this is "blazing."

This is the "Flame of Wisdom. It is the fire of fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), which can burn away the fuel of afflictions—the pride of relying on one's ability to hear, retain, and not forget the teachings of the preceding stage.
Fifth, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjaya*) because its supramundane wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver;
that is to say, because the ultimate truth and conventional reality are non-contradictory, they are extremely difficult to conquer. Furthermore, as it is both supramundane and...

He is able to conform to worldly conventions; skillfully proficient in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), he is able to deliver those who are biased or stagnant, and is truly difficult to surpass.

Sixth, because the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) has reached its interval and great wisdom manifests before him, it is called the "Manifest" stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). This means that through skillful mastery of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he induces non-conceptualization, which is termed the "practice of wisdom.
Because this is as intimate as being witnessed with one's own eyes, it is called "manifest. Seventh, excellent cultivation...

The stage of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*) is so named because the application of effort in signless practice reaches its culmination, thereby transcending both the mundane path and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles.
This has three meanings: first, having skillfully cultivated the signless, one reaches the limit of the signless; second, the application of effort has reached its ultimate point;

and third, it surpasses the preceding stages. The eighth stage is called the Immovable (*acalā*) because the practice of retribution has become fully matured, such that signless practice is continuous and uninterrupted.

"Movement. This has three meanings. First, by abandoning the activities of the triple world and giving rise to the fruit of transformation (*pariṇāma*), it is called "retributive activity" (*vipākacaryā*).
Because one initiates activities based on this which are spontaneously accomplished, there is no movement through effortful application.

Second, having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and the wondrous wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*), there is no movement regarding signs. Third, because these two are uninterrupted, there is no movement of afflictions (*kleśa*). Nine.
Because one attains the power of non-obstruction and achieves the practice of benefiting others through the preaching of the Dharma, it is called the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
Although one attains unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), it is not yet fully "excellent"; only when one preaches universally and benefits all universally can it be termed "excellent.

On the tenth ground, because one attains the great Dharma-body and possesses complete mastery, it is called the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā*). This has two meanings: first, one attains the great Dharma-body which is like a cloud, capable of...
The teaching of the Dharma is like rain, for it is employed with mastery. Second, because they are able to receive the great clouds and rains of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, these ten stages of the Bodhisattva have been taught, will be taught, and are being taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The names of the four summaries reveal their excellence.
"O Son of the Buddha, I do not see any buddha-field wherein the Tathāgata does not teach these ten stages.

This third section of the commentary cites the universal teaching throughout the ten directions to manifest the essential excellence of these stages, intending to cause sentient beings to give rise to a thirst [for them].

Because of this reverence, there are two parts in the text. First, it says that he neither sees nor speaks; this is a reductio ad absurdum (paryudāsa) which reveals that throughout the ten directions, both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* Buddhas do indeed speak.

Why is this? Because this is the supreme path toward Bodhi for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, and it is also a gateway to the light of the pure Dharma—namely, the analytical exposition of the various stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattvas. O Son of the Buddha, this point cannot [be grasped by ordinary means].
This is inconceivable; that is to say, it is the wisdom realized by all bodhisattvas. This consists of two parts:

first, the inquiry into the reason for the teaching, and second, the explanation of that reason. The inquiry asks: "Since the Buddha-lands are not identical and the modes of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) also differ, why must the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) be taught in every case?
The intent of the explanation is that these are the most supreme. That is to say, all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); their essence is suchness.

One becomes a sage. Apart from this realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*), all [other teachings] are merely provisional; therefore, this is essential and superior. The preceding concludes the "Section on the Fundamental Nature" (the sixth).
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva spoke these words. Below is the "Section on the Request," which consists of three parts: first, having finished speaking, he remains silent;
second, from "At that time" onwards, the three families make five requests; third, from "At that time, Vajragarbha observes... onwards.
This permits an explanation of the limits [of the teaching]. The reason for remaining silent is that one who intends to speak must first maintain silence;

this is so as to cause the great assembly to yearn with longing and request the teaching. There are briefly two reasons for awaiting such a request: first, to increase the Bodhisattvas' reverence for the Dharma;
second, because the previous exposition of the stages (*bhūmi*) and their praise of excellence increased their aspiration, it is now intended that within this request...
Because the arising of understanding is superior. How does this understanding arise? It means that by virtue of being requested, the reasons for speaking or remaining silent are established;

the profound nature of the ground, which transcends words and thought, is revealed so that the assembly first gains understanding, and subsequently, when hearing the sections of the teaching, they do not grasp them merely according to the sounds.
Because it is free from erroneous interpretations, there is consequently a third section that provides a definitive exposition. First:
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had spoken these names of the ten bodhisattva stages, he remained silent and did not further elaborate upon them.
Having spoken these initial words, he remained silent. Within the second request, there are three distinct sections, which are divided into three parts:
first, the request by Vimukticandra; second, the request by the Great Assembly; and third, the request by the Tathāgata. As for the reason why these three groups were required:

The leaders of the assembly proclaimed it, those present yearned for it with thirsting devotion, and the Master of Transformation further exhorted him; only when these matters were complete was the task fulfilled.

Furthermore, "the Buddha’s request" is precisely what is meant by "addition" (*adhiṣṭhāna*); this means that although the assembly had already made their request, it required the majestic radiance of the Lord Buddha before he could be fit to speak.
It is also called "instruction" (*śāsana*), because the Tathāgata’s teaching and exposition clarify that Vajragarbha’s discourse transmits the Buddha’s teachings. Moreover, as for the preceding...
The first two requests seek to clarify that the dharmas of this stage are cultivated by practitioners; the latter request seeks to clarify that these dharmas are realized by the Buddha.
There are six sections in the text consisting of three requests and three refusals, which, as the refusals and requests alternate, may be further divided into five segments:

(1) the request arising from the suspicion of wondering at the silence; (2) the refusal based on the profundity of the Dharma being difficult to receive; (3) the praise of the assembly’s capacity to hear, followed by the request.
Fourth, the cessation due to the incapacity for harm: although there are those who are capable, there are also those who are incapable. Fifth, the request by praising both the person and the Dharma:
this means that because the Dharma is profound, even those incapable of hearing it should be taught, as they will receive the Buddha’s protection.
Thereupon, Vajragarbha’s reasoning was exhausted and he could no longer refuse the request.
At that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas heard the names of the ten bodhisattva stages but did not hear their explanation. They all felt a deep yearning and thought to themselves:
"For what cause and for what reason does the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha speak only of the names of the ten bodhisattva stages?"
The title is given but not explained. Within the first request, there are two parts:
first, the great assembly observes his silence and gives rise to doubt; second, Vimalakīrti rises into the air and voices his doubt as a request. Regarding the first:
the phrase "for what cause and for what reason" is an expression of wonder and suspicion. It serves as the cause for the discourse.
Is it that he is unable to speak? Or is it because the audience is incapable of hearing it?
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, questioned the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in verse:
2. Raising Doubts as a Request. First, the introduction of the request based on the assembly’s doubts:
Why does the one of pure awakening, who is endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and merit, proclaim the various supreme and wondrous stages but not explain them?
All are certain that he is courageous and free from cowardice.
For what reason do you speak of the names of the stages, yet do not expound their wondrous meanings?
This assembly all desires to hear them; their minds are free from timidity. We pray that you will explain them in detail for us;
this gathering is entirely pure, free from indolence, refined and clean, and capable of remaining firm and unshakable.
Endowed with merit and wisdom, they gaze at one another with mutual reverence;
all look up with single-minded devotion, like bees thinking of fine honey, or like those parched with thirst longing for nectar.
(2) Second, the formal request by means of verse consists of five stanzas. These clarify that there is no fault in preaching or listening; therefore, [the Buddha] should preach. First:

The first verse concerns the speaker and is free from fault; it dispels the assembly’s doubt as to the cause [of the teaching]. The latter four verses concern the listener and are likewise free from fault;

they also dispel the assembly’s doubt as to the conditions [for hearing the teaching]. Now, regarding the first: why is it that the praise of the speaker’s pure awakening as being free from fault does not provide an explanation?
Indeed, there are three kinds of faults in preaching the Dharma: first, not preaching due to stinginess or envy; second, [not preaching due to]... [text truncated]
Laziness is not mentioned. Third, those lacking the power of eloquence do not delight in speaking. Now, one is free from these three faults:

first, by being endowed with virtues such as non-aversion, one is free from the faults of stinginess and envy; second, because the name "Exalted and Sublime Stage" has already been explained previously.

Therefore, there is no fault of indolence in preaching the Dharma. Third, because he possesses the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) in joyful exposition, there is no fault of lack of joy in preaching.

Second, regarding the four verses on praising the listeners for their absence of faults: the first two verses praise the assembly of those born together [as disciples], the next one verse praises the assembly of those born separately [as ordinary beings], and the final one verse praises both together.
Now, of these first two verses, they praise the faculties and inclinations; the preceding verse praises the faculties.
Therefore, it is called "decisive. The subsequent verse praises the desire [to hear], stating "desiring to hear.

If one has desire but lacks the faculty (indriya), one will not understand even if one hears. If one has the faculty but lacks desire, one will not accept it even if one hears. Thus, both must be praised.

The meaning here clarifies that those who possess only the faculty but lack desire are incapable of hearing the Dharma. Now, the preceding verse is decisive regarding the teaching; [this verse is decisive] regarding the principle.

[The commentary] states: "To possess the two certainties [of faculties and aspiration] while having faculties that are not currently manifest, yet possessing the aspiration currently manifest as expressed in this verse, constitutes certainty through both teaching and realization;
therefore, one is fit to receive [the teaching]. Since he possesses both faculties and aspiration, I pray that you will explain the wondrous meaning of the various stages.
The second single verse praises the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Because it simply refers to them as the "assembly," it praises both their faculties and aspirations. First...

The first phrase serves as the general statement. Because the mind is free from turbidity, it is called "pure. The subsequent three phrases serve as the specific details, which distinguish and depart from the six turbidities (*ṣaḍ-kaṣāya*).
First is the turbidity of lack of desire, meaning the mind lacks any savoring [of worldly things]; this is remedied by departing from indolence.

Second is the turbidity of deportment, meaning one is not reverent and solemn; this is remedied by strict discipline. Third is the turbidity of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), such as craving for fame and so forth; this is remedied by purification.
1. One treats it by means of [the antidote of] non-conceptualization. 2. The turbidity of divergent thoughts refers to the defilement of arrogance, the defilement of contempt, and so forth;
all these are termed "divergent thoughts. Now, one treats this by means of firm practice and immovability. 3.

The turbidity of insufficient merit refers to having very few roots of goodness and thus taking no pleasure in dwelling in those teachings. One treats this by means of possessing merit. 4. The turbidity of ignorance refers to being deluded and dark.
Because [the meaning] is not yet understood, wisdom is used to treat it. The final verse praises both assemblies for their attendance and service throughout all four verses.
Furthermore, the bee’s longing for honey and the thirsty person’s desire for a drink serve as metaphors for the aspiration for the flavor of the joy of Dharma and liberation.
Again, by mentioning "fine honey" and "ambrosia," the excellence of the Dharma is revealed; such is the depth of the yearning and thirst of the great assembly, and thus they ought to [listen].
Thus it was said. At that time, having heard this teaching, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, possessed of great wisdom and fearlessness,
spoke these verses for the sake of the sons of the Buddha, desiring to bring joy to the hearts of the assembled multitude.
The second dharma is profound and difficult to receive; first, the intention is set forth for the joy of the assembly—this is the general manner of response.
The deeds of the bodhisattva stages are the fundamental source of all supreme Buddhas. They are revealed and explained through analysis as being foremost, rare, and difficult to encounter;
they are subtle and difficult to perceive, transcending thought and surpassing the realm of the mind.
The five verses from the response, which are divided into four parts, clarify that those who hear [of] the Buddha’s realm are all bewildered.
The first two verses concern the difficulty of explaining the Dharma, dispelling the doubt raised above regarding the cause.

Within this, "difficulty" refers to the general characteristic; as for what is difficult, it means it is difficult to attain and difficult to realize. There are four ways in which it is difficult to attain.
1. It is difficult to attain because it is subtle; this indicates that it is not an object of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). 2.

It is difficult to see and difficult to attain because it is also not seen by the "mind's eye" of the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). 3. It is difficult to attain because it is free from discursive thought (*niṣprapañca*);

furthermore, it is not an object of mundane wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Since the wisdom of the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*) is true cultivation, it is not an object of the preparatory cultivation involving the conceptual mental factors of those prior to the stages (*pūrvabhūmika*). 4. It transcends...
Because it is the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*), it is difficult to attain. It is not only beyond the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmipūrva*);

it is also not the domain of the wisdom attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-jñāna*) by those born of retribution (*vipākaja*) who have already ascended the grounds. That is to say, the matured (*vipāka*) consciousness arising from the transformation of the basis (*pariṇāmika*) is called "born of retribution.

Because one can immediately know wisdom such as impermanence upon birth, it is called "well-attained wisdom of the path of cultivation" (*sukhalabdha-bhāvanā-mārga-jñāna*). This is because it does not [function as] illumination...

Because it is the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), it also does not fathom the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*). Knowing impermanence and so forth while the mental state of the path of cultivation has not yet been forgotten is called the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*).

Since this applies to all stages prior to the seventh, as they are all capable of emerging from contemplation, and because one has well attained the wisdom of the path of cultivation—which is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and not fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)—and since this is not the object of the four minds, whose object is it? It is the Buddha’s.

It is because of wisdom. What is this wisdom? It is the vision of the true meaning. The reason it is difficult to explain is that one fears the listener might grasp at what they hear, thereby giving rise to delusion.
Holding the mind like a vajra, with deep faith in the Buddha’s supreme wisdom, and knowing that the ground of the mind is without self—one may hear this sublime Dharma.

(Verse 2.1) This verse reveals the difficulty of hearing [this teaching]. However, one who possesses such virtues is able to hear it; by contrast, this serves to highlight its rarity. Furthermore, it is intended to...

Because it enables one to learn through hearing, the first phrase serves as the general statement: that is, if one maintains a mind for listening to the Dharma as firm as a diamond (*vajra*), one will be able to hear.
The second phrase refers to the firmness of decisive faith.

Deep faith means that even if one’s own intellect cannot reach the Buddha’s wisdom, one reverently infers that the Buddha’s wisdom is not within one’s own domain; this is the characteristic of deep faith. The Buddha is supreme.
"Wisdom" refers to the two types of wisdom—expedient and real—as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. As the Sūtra states: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable;
its gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Therefore, it is called "supreme wisdom. Regarding "firmly realizing," there are two meanings.

First, "knowledge" is that which realizes; second, the "mind-ground" is that which is realized—namely, the phenomena upon which the two kinds of emptiness and true reality depend, referring to the characteristics of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
The term "selflessness" applies to both the subject that realizes and the object that is realized.

To understand these two categories as they truly are constitutes the wisdom of the non-existence and existence of the two emptinesses of self and phenomena. The final phrase concludes this: having known what is difficult to hear...
The meaning is as follows: Only when one possesses the two aforementioned firmnesses does one hear the subtle and supreme wisdom described above.
It is like a painting in the sky, like the appearance of wind in the sky; the discernment of the Muni’s wisdom is likewise extremely difficult to perceive.
The third section consists of one verse, which uses metaphors to illustrate the teaching of hearing (*śruta*).
The supplementary commentary states: "Regarding these two metaphors, the *Vyākhyā* (the *Śāstra*) contains many explanations; here, they are explained collectively according to their meaning.

The metaphor of space represents the Buddha’s non-reliant wisdom (*anāśraya-jñāna*), for the Sūtra says: 'The Buddha’s wisdom is like space, having nothing upon which it relies. The metaphor of painting represents the characteristics of the teaching (*lakṣaṇa-deśanā*). Wind..."

The analogy refers to the characteristics of the Śrāvakas; both are without any basis. Because the wisdom of the stages (bhūmi-jñāna) is difficult to hear, it is combined [with the preceding] and stated:
"The wisdom of the Muni is thus; its differentiation is extremely difficult to perceive."
I contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom, Supreme and inconceivable; None in the world can receive it, Thus he remains silent and does not speak.

This fourth verse, consisting of one stanza, raises the difficulty and concludes with silence. Its meaning is that speaking and hearing are fundamentally based upon realization and vision; since [this wisdom] is difficult to see, it cannot be spoken.
"What benefit would that bring? Moreover, it is difficult to believe; therefore, I remain silent.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in gold-colored speech:
The third section is the Moon of Liberation’s praise of the assembly’s fitness to hear the teaching and his request for it to be spoken.

Although he has already offered praise previously, he praises them again here because hearing the aforementioned words is difficult to attain through faith and realization; this demonstrates that this assembly possesses faith, realization, and the capacity [to understand].
The prose section first sets forth the request:

"O Son of the Buddha, this assembly has now gathered in its entirety; they possess deeply purified intentions, perfectly cleansed thoughts, have well cultivated all practices, have well accumulated the aids to the path, and have been able to draw near to hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, thereby accomplishing immeasurable merit."

Roots of goodness. Below this, the formal request is made. This section has three parts: first, the assembly is described; second, from "well-purified" (*suviśuddha*) onwards, their virtues are praised.
The text contains ten phrases: the first is general, and the remaining nine are specific. The first virtue is a well-purified profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*), which is free from...

It is called the "well-purified mind" because it is purified by both teaching and realization. First, because it is fully endowed with the practice of all virtuous deeds, it is the "purity of teaching" mentioned below.
Second, because it accords with the principle, it is the "purity of realization" mentioned below.

Regarding the nine phrases concerning the "thoroughly cleansed reflection," the first five phrases refer to the purity of teaching, while the latter four phrases—beginning with "abandoning"—refer to the purity of both teaching and realization. That is to say, practicing in accordance with the teaching is termed...

Regarding the purities (*śraddhā*): the realization of principle and the arising of practice are termed "purities of realization" (*avetyaprasāda*). Now, regarding the first five phrases: first, "skillfully purifying thought" refers to purity of aspiration;
second, "skillfully cultivating all practices" refers to purity of seeking the three types of action (*trikarma*); third, "skillfully gathering the aids to the path" refers to purity of birth;
fourth, "skillfully being equanimous" refers to purity of receiving and upholding [the teachings]; and fifth, "accomplishing the roots of goodness" refers to purity of practice.
Abandoning delusion and confusion, one is free from defilement; with a profound mind of faith and understanding, one does not follow the teachings of others within the Buddha-dharma.

These four phrases constitute the "purity of realization" (*avetyaprasāda*). Regarding "abandoning delusion and confusion": in the Path of True Vision (*darśanamārga*), one resolves the principles without doubt, as all ignorance has been destroyed.
Second, "being free from defilement" refers to the purity of non-practice (*apracāra-viśuddhi*) within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). One...
Because all afflictions do not function, the afflictions themselves are defilements; this non-functioning is their non-existence.

Third is the purity of deep-seated conviction and understanding through insatiability, which means not delighting in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) because of one's resolute faith in the supreme qualities of the Buddha.
Fourth is the purity of not following the teachings of others regarding the Buddha-dharma, which refers to [the stage of] proceeding toward the bodhisattva grounds.
Having exhausted the path and established right practice, the praise of his virtues is concluded:
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You should now expound this by virtue of the Buddha's spiritual power;
these bodhisattvas are all able to realize and know such profound matters."
Second, the request for instruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"May you explain the most secure state, The supreme conduct of the Bodhisattvas, And the differentiation of the stages."
"Purified wisdom attains perfect enlightenment; this assembly is free from all defilements. Their resolve and understanding are entirely clear and pure;
having served immeasurable Buddhas, they are able to know the meaning of this stage.
Regarding these two verses within the second set of double verses: the first verse directly cites the Dharma to make the request, while the second verse reiterates the preceding meaning.

At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said: "O Son of the Buddha, although this assembly has gathered with pure and virtuous reflections, having abandoned ignorance and doubt, and does not rely on the teachings of others regarding the profound Dharma."
Fourth, the inability to endure harm and cessation. In the prose section, the praise is first summarized.

Regarding the reason for the subsequent mention of "harm," although it is so, there are other sentient beings of inferior understanding who, upon hearing these profound and inconceivable matters, will for the most part give rise to doubt and confusion.
Throughout the long night, they have experienced various forms of decline and affliction. Out of compassion for them, I remained silent.

Later, when they earnestly raised objections and violated my request, I considered that those of inferior understanding—including ordinary people and followers of the Lesser Vehicle—are all vessels for delusion regarding the Dharma;
thus, they frequently give rise to doubt, which by its very nature contradicts right practice and signifies hesitation. As for the "deluded," their minds are confused regarding...
"Reasoning" refers to its ability to destroy wholesome dharmas; this clarifies present harm. "Throughout the long night" and below clarify future harm.
"I pity these" and below conclude with the refusal of their request through silence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Though this assembly is pure and possesses vast wisdom, Profound, sharp, and capable of discernment,
Their minds are as unshakable as the king of mountains, And cannot be overturned, like the great ocean."
There are those who have not long practiced and have not yet attained understanding;
they follow consciousness rather than wisdom, and hearing this, they give rise to doubt and fall into evil realms. Out of compassion for such as these, I do not speak [of them];
furthermore, there are two types within the verses. The first verse summarizes the preceding section, while the latter verse summarizes the subsequent section regarding those who are incapable.

There is a deficiency. In the fifth section of the following text, within the request that praises both the person and the Dharma, the reason for requesting again is to demonstrate that his doubts must be severed;
how could he possibly avoid this? To avoid it and fail to speak would entail many faults. What are these faults?
One will not be able to accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha once more, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will rely upon the Buddha’s spiritual power to analyze and explain this inconceivable Dharma. Such persons shall receive the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and give rise to faith and acceptance.
Why is this? When the Ten Stages are being taught, it is the natural law for all Bodhisattvas to thus obtain the protection of the Buddhas."
Mindfulness. Because they attain protective mindfulness, they are able to give rise to heroic vigor within this stage of wisdom.
Why is this? Because this is the initial practice of Bodhisattvas for accomplishing all the Buddha-dharmas.
For example, just as all writing and calculation are fundamentally based on the alphabet, and there is nothing whatsoever that is ultimately separate from the alphabet; so it is, O Son of the Buddha.
All Buddha-dharmas take the ten stages as their foundation. Through the ultimate accomplishment of cultivation in these ten stages, one attains all-knowledge.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will expound this for us; this person will surely be protected by the Tathāgata and will come to believe and accept it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! Please expound upon the practices for entering the stages of enlightenment.
There is not a single Sovereign of the Ten Directions who does not protect and mind this root of wisdom;
it is the abiding in wisdom that is ultimate, from which all the Buddha-dharmas arise.
Just as letters and numbers are subsumed within the alphabet, so too are the Buddha’s teachings dependent upon the stages (bhūmi).
In the fifth pair of verses, which praise both the person and the Dharma, there are likewise two parts: first, in the prose section, the request is initially indicated;
then, from "For what reason" (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) onwards, the request is explained; and finally, from "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, the request is concluded.
The Supplementary Commentary states: This section of the prose commentary has many interpretations.

The general meaning is that although there may be sentient beings who are incapable [of receiving it], when this Great Dharma is now preached, the Buddha will certainly protect and mind them (*anuparigṛhṇāti*). If they receive his protection and mindfulness, he will also cause them to believe and accept it.
As for why the Buddha must protect and mind them: because the Dharma of all Buddhas is necessarily based upon both teaching (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*). Therefore, he establishes...
This is an analogy of words. It is now stated that the wisdom of the earth is the root of the Buddha-dharma; it shall certainly be protected and remembered by the Tathāgata.
The meaning of the subsequent verse may also be understood accordingly.
At that time, the assembly of great bodhisattvas, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
speaking in verse: "O you of supreme, stainless wisdom, With boundless analytical eloquence, You proclaim words that are profound and beautiful."

Corresponding to the ultimate truth, maintaining pure conduct through mindfulness, possessing the ten powers, accumulated merit, eloquence, and discernment of meaning—this most excellent stage is now being taught.
With concentration, morality, and a rightly established mind, free from conceit and false views, this assembly is without doubt; we only pray to hear this sublime discourse.

Like one who thirsts for cool water, like one who hungers for delicious food, like one who is ill and remembers a potent medicine, or like a bee craving fine honey— we are just the same; may we hear the Dharma of the Deathless.
O you of excellent and vast wisdom, please explain the entry into the stages, and the attainment of the ten powers and unimpeded knowledge.

Regarding the second assembly of the ocean-like multitude who collectively requested [the teaching] from the Sugata concerning all practices: they personally declared that they possessed both faculties and desires.

Within this, there are four and a half verses at the beginning that praise the person; following the words "Excellent! (*sādhu*), there is one verse that praises the Dharma to bring about benefit. Regarding the praise of the person:
There are two verses. The first five lines praise the speaker, establishing his own realization as the authoritative teaching (*śāstra*).

The final three lines praise his ability to lead others to enter [the path]. The subsequent two and a half verses praise the listeners. The first verse, beginning with "stability and morality," praises the faculties (*indriya*) possessed by the assembly.

The following verse, beginning with "like one who thirsts," praises the aspiration (*chanda*) of the assembly, demonstrating that the great multitude’s seeking of the Dharma has become increasingly profound. The final [verse]... [is] excellent.
This single verse praises the benefits of the Dharma.
From here on, the Tathāgata’s empowerment is requested. Although the two families previously made four requests to manifest the excellence of the Dharma, they still required the Buddha’s empowerment.

Thus far, the roles of principal and attendant have been distinguished; the principal—the Buddha—manifested only the empowerment of mind. Now, however, he wishes to provide it fully through body and speech as well.

Therefore, the Buddha adds further [teaching]. Moreover, whereas previously he bestowed [the teaching] through silence and majestic power (*vibhūti*), now there is a formal request for addition; thus, he speaks with this added [instruction], which is not the same as before.
When superior power is exerted upon the inferior to provide instruction, it is called "addition" (*ādhāna*); because this addition encourages the speaking, it is termed a "request" (*adhyeṣaṇā*).
"Bestowal" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is equivalent to "request. In the preceding section on bestowal, the great assembly was not included. As for this present bestowal:

if it had been bestowed immediately in the previous section, there would have been no basis for the Speaker’s three instances of silence. If it were not bestowed here, the requestor’s earlier statement that he has obtained the Buddha’s protective mindfulness (*buddhānubhāva*) would be contradicted.
Thus, it would be without efficacy. The above summarizes the intent of the classification.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from between his eyebrows a pure radiance named "Flame-Light of Bodhisattva Power," with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays of light as its retinue, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions such that none were left untouched.
It pervaded everywhere, causing the sufferings of the three evil realms to all find rest. It further illuminated the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, manifesting the inconceivable power of all Buddhas.
It also illuminated all worlds in the ten directions and the bodies of the Bodhisattvas empowered by all Buddhas to preach the Dharma.
Having performed these deeds, it formed a great cloud-net of radiant light in the sky above.

Abiding upon the platform, the first [section] concerns the Buddha’s light-bestowing empowerment. Within the prose, there are generally eight activities and two bodies; specifically, the long prose contains seven activities and two bodies.
In the verse, however, only the activity of requesting is clarified. First, this Buddha’s light shines upon the ten directions; subsequently, the Buddhas of the ten directions...

The light is emitted to illuminate this direction. As the two lights mutually illuminate one another, they must necessarily see each other. Both sections contain two bodies and seven activities. Now, for the first:
first, the essence, nature, and function of the light are clarified; from "having performed these deeds" onwards, the actual deeds performed are clarified.
Now, first: to clarify the source of the light, it is mostly applied from above to below, using the light from between the eyebrows.

This also symbolizes that the Middle Way is about to be expounded. Emerging from the "Pure" section, this now clarifies the essence and function. There are six activities in the text. First is the activity of awakening, which is the essence of the light;
that is to say, after the light has illuminated the bodies of the Bodhisattvas, they themselves awaken to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power.

Because it is the light of awakened illumination, it is called "Flaming Radiance" (Jvalanaprabha). Regarding the two hundred thousand [rays] below, they are the karma of the cause, for they are able to produce retinues.

Regarding the three universal illuminations below, this is the karma of expansion and contraction: when expanded, they universally illuminate the ten directions; when contracted, they return into the constant radiance.

In the current text, the section on "karma of the scrolls" is omitted. Fourth, the "karma of cessation" below the three evil realms, because it brings all suffering to rest. Fifth, the "karma of subjugation":
in the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, it states that all the palaces of Māra are obscured and made invisible; this passage is missing from the current text.

Sixth, furthermore, the "karma of reverence" below "illuminating all," which manifests the Buddha’s assembly to inspire reverence in sentient beings. Seventh, furthermore, the "demonstration" below "illuminating the ten directions."

Regarding the "manifest karma": this is specifically for the purpose of enabling both the audience and the speaker to receive the Buddha’s empowerment so that they may be capable of listening and speaking.

The name "receiving a body" (longxing shoushen) is established primarily based on this [empowerment]. From the phrase "having done this" (*kṛtvā*) onwards, the second section correctly reveals what was accomplished.
This is one of the two bodies. Regarding the "two bodies": first is the meteoric body (*ulkā-kāya*), so called because it travels to and fro through other world-systems;
second is the solar-like body (*āditya-kalpa-kāya*), which means that just as the sun dwells in space, this very [body] acts as a terrace in the upper sky.
In terms of the body, there is substantiality (*svabhāva*); in terms of activity (*karman*), there is utility (*upayoga*).
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise did so. From between their eyebrows, they emitted pure rays of light;
the names, retinues, and functions of these lights were entirely identical to those here.
Furthermore, having illuminated this Sahā world—including the Buddha, the great assembly, and the body and lion throne of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva—they formed a great mass of light in the space above.
The Mingyunwang (Cloud-Net) Terrace is precisely what is illuminated by the light emitted from the Buddhas of the twenty directions; yet their activities also pervade the ten directions.
Since their seven karmas and two bodies are no different from those of this Buddha, it is said that they are "entirely identical."
At that time, from within the Hall of Radiance, by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, these verses were spoken.
The second verse clarifies the request for the activity; its basis, in relation to what precedes it, still pertains to the body.
The Buddha is unequaled and equal to space; his immeasurable, supreme merits throughout the ten directions make him the most excellent among humans and the highest in the world.

Regarding these five verses on the addition of the request within the *Śākyasiṃha-dharmadeśanā*, they are divided into two parts: the first four add the request for what is to be taught, and the last one instructs on the limits of the teaching.
In the preceding section, the first two verses constitute the request by citing the Dharma, while the latter two verses constitute the request by citing the benefits.

Within the former, the first verse correctly reveals the performance of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the subsequent verse reveals the purpose for which the empowerment is performed. Regarding the phrase "the highest in the world" in the first of these:
it is called "the highest in the world" because it possesses four kinds of supremacy. These four supremacies are: first, supremacy of mastery, meaning that one's activities are unimpeded.
Therefore, it is said that he is not subdued by others; "others" refers here to the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

Because he is free from these two obstacles, he is liberated, sovereign, and unstained like space—this is what the Sūtra calls "the peerless peer" (*asamasama*). Second, his power is superior; "power" refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*), for they can subdue the enemies of false knowledge.
Third, his retinue is superior, consisting of immeasurable supreme merits; thus, he is the most excellent among humans.

Fourth is the excellence of lineage, meaning excellence of family name; that is, the Lion of the Śākyas, because the Śākya clan constitutes the noble progeny of the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).

Due to these four aforementioned meanings, he is called the Dharma King and is named the Supreme among the Worldly. Now, to this person who possesses such supreme virtues, the title "Vajragarbha" is added.
"O Son of the Buddha, you should, by the power of all Buddhas, Open this most excellent treasury of the Dharma-King:
The vast wisdom and sublime practices of the various stages. By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, explain them in detail.

The second verse adds a purpose for doing so: it is because one wishes to cause the meaning of the Dharma-treasury to be opened and understood. Regarding "the most excellent treasury," there are... [text continues]

There are two kinds: first, the treasury of meaning (*arthapiṭaka*); second, the treasury of words (*vyañjanapiṭaka*). The treasury of meaning refers to the sublime and wondrous practice (*viśeṣacaryā*).

"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the various practices of the bodhisattvas, namely the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). "Sublime" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the realization of reality (*tattvapratisaṃvit*), which is the path of realization (*darśanamārga*).

"Wondrous" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the excellence of supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), which is the non-abiding path (*apratisthita-mārga*). Because it is unimpeded regarding both defilement and purity, it is called "supernatural power. Thus it is revealed.
It reveals the profound, subtle, supreme, and excellent meaning. The "Two-Syllable Treasury" refers to the vast wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*) and their detailed exposition.
Above, the request for the Dharma was made;
if one is empowered by the strength of the Sugata, one shall obtain the jewel of the Dharma and it will enter one's heart.
The second section, "Requesting by Way of Manifesting the Benefits," demonstrates that the Dharma being taught provides benefit for others at three distinct times.

This section is divided into two verses, which are further subdivided into three parts. The first half-verse concerns the benefit at the time of hearing: if one receives the supreme empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the Jewel of the Dharma enters the mind, resulting in the benefit of hearing and retaining it.
As the previously mentioned Vimukticandra requested: "This inconceivable Dharma shall receive the protection of the Tathāgata."
Reflecting thus, one gives rise to faith and acceptance.
"The stainless stages are fulfilled in succession" and "also possessing the ten powers of the Tathāgata"—this half-verse concerns the benefit during the time of cultivation.
The upper line refers to the perfection of the causes during cultivation; the lower line refers to the fulfillment of the fruit that is cultivated.
"Even if one dwells amidst the waters of the ocean or within the fires of the kalpa, if one is capable of receiving this Dharma, one will certainly hear it.
Those who harbor doubts and do not believe shall never again hear such a teaching.
The final verse reveals the benefit of generating [faith] in turn; that is, those who possess the seeds of firmness. The first half of the verse clearly explains those who have faith accordingly.

The latter half of the passage serves as a counter-illustration to highlight the loss incurred by those lacking faith. "Those of the adamantine lineage" refers to those who possess the adamantine seed;

because they are able to hear [the teaching] even while situated within the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). Regarding the "heavenly son of hell," the three levels are simultaneously perfected.

The intent here is to reveal that those who possess faith and acceptance can hear this sutra even while in the difficult places of the evil realms, for such difficulties do not constitute an obstruction.
It is said so because it has been heard [in scripture]. The ocean waters and the kalpa-ending fire are difficult places for rebirth.
This is because the dragon palaces within the great ocean belong to the evil destinies of the animal realm.

As for those within the kalpa-ending fire, this refers to the second dhyāna of the form realm as a "good destiny," for while the fire burns the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna is not destroyed; furthermore, the gods and humans above the second dhyāna are long-lived.
Even those in the realms of long life or the heavens who face hardships may hear this sutra.

The *Būyì* (Supplementary Commentary) states that this collectively reveals the excellence of the Dharma; because the seeds of hearing [the Dharma] become firm, the sutra employs the analogy of a person consuming a small amount of *vajra*.
However, the various meanings in the *Shù* (Commentary) are largely subsumed within this point.
One should explain the path of superior wisdom regarding the various stages (bhūmi), which is practiced through the successive sequence of entering, abiding, and progressing;
from this arises the knowledge of dharmas regarding the sphere of practice, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Regarding the second single verse, within the section on the limits of the teaching: "one should explain the various stages" is a general exhortation. [The following] explains the stages.
What is the meaning? It refers to the explanation of the three gradual phases of extensive wisdom across the various stages (*bhūmi*) contained within the preceding syllables.
What are these three? First, the gradual phase of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); second, the gradual phase of realization (*adhigama*); and third, the gradual phase of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

These constitute the three types of wisdom—preparatory (*prayoga*), fundamental (*maula*), and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)—within the ten stages, serving as the initial, middle, and final characteristics of each stage. This is the excellence.
The path of wisdom (*jñāna-mārga*) is like a cause, because the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) serves as the gradual sequence for the attainment of superior wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*).

Next, "entering and abiding in succession" refers to the sequence of realization. "Entering" (*praveśa*) is the mind that enters the stages (*bhūmi*), and "abiding" (*vihāra*) is the mind that dwells within the stages.

Because there has been no turning toward other stages (*bhūmi*), one emerges from the mind of the stage through successive progression; because one turns from stage to stage, the very place where one abides is established.

Thus, these three minds constitute the gradual sequence of realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*). Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can only comprehend the conventional through correct and authentic practice;
therefore, it is called the gradual sequence of practice. As for "dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*), it precisely designates the subsequently attained wisdom.

The essence of wisdom is designated as "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) because it distinguishes phenomena as its object. This wisdom arises from two conditions: first, because it realizes the ultimate truth, it is said to arise from practice;
second, because it externally comprehends the conventional, it is said to arise from the object.

That is to say, one practices within the conventional realm by means of the practice of direct realization; this is subsequently attained knowledge (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna). The phrase "benefiting sentient beings" concludes [the section].
The benefit of this exposition is also the meaning of the direct realization of the realm of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as explained extensively in the commentary.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva surveyed the ten directions and, wishing to increase the pure faith of the great assembly,
spoke these verses:

The following is the third section, the "Allowance for Exposition. This means that what is to be explained does not exceed the two great categories of meaning; this constitutes the scope of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Within this, first the manner of exposition is set forth, and subsequently the verses themselves are revealed. Now, first, the observation of the ten directions is the setting forth of the manner of exposition.
One observes the Buddhas of the ten directions because one is about to rely upon their power, and thus there is no conceit. One observes the ten directions...

Because the intent is that [the teaching] shall universally benefit all, there is no partiality; thus, both the preceding and following passages state that "by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, one universally observes the ten directions.
The phrase "desiring to cause the great assembly to increase their pure faith" explains the purpose of the discourse:

it means that the assembly already possessed faith and was deeply thirsting for what they were to hear; now, by further revealing and explaining the two great [realms] of the Bodhisattva Stages (*bhūmi*), the listeners' [faith] is further augmented.

It is capable of receiving the correct meaning; it does not grasp [the teaching] literally. This is called "increasing pure faith. As for the term "meaning" (*artha*), it is called "great" because it is profound and vast;
this is a name derived from its actual nature. It is called "explanation" (*nirukti*) because it expresses and manifests; since one attains that meaning by means of this explanation, it is so named.
Based on that meaning, it is called "Great. Because it is spoken of as "Great," it relies upon the designation conferred by others.

Within this, first there is the greatness of the meaning (*artha-mahattva*), followed by the greatness of the teaching (*deśanā-mahattva*), and finally the discernment of their mutual integration. Regarding the greatness of the meaning, there are three aspects.

First, from the perspective of the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), it may be generally indicated so that people may know it exists; thus it is called "that which can be spoken of" (*vaktavya*). However, it cannot be pointed out specifically to show it to a person.
It is unspeakable. Second, regarding the locus of realization: since the principle realized is free from characteristics and names, it is said that "this dharma is not spoken of nor heard.
Because this very speech that negates speech corresponds to that dharma, it is called "speakable.

When one says that this negation of names is "unspeakable," third, regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*): because it is easily understood through apophatic expression (*paryudāsa*), it is called "speakable."

It is said that because direct expression fails to reach it, it is "unspeakable. This is the first of the three great meanings. Next, within the context of what can be spoken, there are also three points.
First, regarding the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*): its modes of activity in accordance with phenomena can be distinguished by words and phrases, and thus it is "speakable";
yet, because it is supramundane (*lokottara*), it is "unspeakable. Second, regarding the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*): this refers to mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).
Because it is observed, it can be said [to exist]. However, because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) within that observation does not arrive [at the ultimate], it is called "inexpressible.

Third, regarding the dharma of provisional assignment to stages: because this can be used as a provisional representation to lead people to understand the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is called "expressible";
yet because this cannot be taken as the ten stages themselves, it is called "inexpressible. Finally, regarding the middle way of mutual fusion... this...
The six dharmas above each describe the ocean of fruition; this is precisely non-explanation. This explanation of non-explanation is non-dual and both are fused;
one may understand this by reflecting accordingly. The preceding exposition of the intended meaning is now complete.
The path of the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, is subtle and difficult to comprehend;
it is beyond thought and free from all conceptualization, and though one seeks to see it, it cannot be found. It is without arising and without cessation, pure by nature and eternally tranquil.
Only those of stainless wisdom and intelligence can traverse the sphere where that knowledge operates.
The second part clearly presents the verses, which consist of twelve verses divided into two sections. The first seven verses clarify the greatness of the meaning (*arthamāhātmya*);

the latter five verses elucidate the greatness of the teaching (*deśanāmāhātmya*). Within the first section, the first four verses generally clarify the subtle nature of the stages (*bhūmisūkṣmatā*). This is further divided into two parts:

the first two verses provide a general clarification, while the subsequent two verses provide a specific clarification. [The remaining verses are as follows: one verse clarifies by way of analogy; one verse demonstrates through contrast; and one verse...

This is illustrated by verses. At the beginning, the first two verses correctly reveal the subtle characteristics of the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*). This is because they are explained in reliance upon the stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*).

That is to say, the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) is the essence; it is "subtle" because it is difficult to know. "Great Sage" (*maharṣi*) refers to the Buddha. The "Path" is that which is realized. In other words, the subtle wisdom of the stages is the cause;
by relying on the cultivation and realization of this wisdom, one attains the fruition of accomplishment. Therefore, [the text] points to...
The wisdom of this stage is the Buddha-way. The subsequent six phrases clarify the reason for its subtlety.

"Non-thought" means that it is not the sphere of a mind characterized by discursive thought and conceptualization; because the essence of wisdom is without thought, it is said to be "free from thought."
The following five phrases clarify that the time of realization is extremely subtle. The first phrase is a general inquiry, because it is difficult to obtain a correct vision [of this].
The subsequent four phrases distinguish four types of subtlety. The first refers to the extreme subtlety of merit (*guṇa*):

it is neither arising nor ceasing, namely, non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, the merit of which consists in the unimpeded harmony between quiescence and function. The second phrase refers to the extreme subtlety of purity, meaning that its nature is free from...
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are never absent; therefore, it is eternally quiescent, which is *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity).

Regarding the third phrase, "free from defilement" (*vimala*), this refers to the subtlety of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-caryā*). That is to say, within the wisdom of contemplation, one is free from the defilement of ignorance (*avidyā-mala*).
Regarding the fourth phrase, "the wise person," this refers to the subtlety of the basis (*āśraya*). A "wise person" is one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*) and above, possessing such wisdom.
These four aforementioned subtle elements differ from those of ordinary beings and the Śrāvakas, as they collectively manifest the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent; they are non-dual and inexhaustible.
They are liberation from all realms of existence, the equality of *nirvāṇa*, neither beginning, middle, nor end, and cannot be expressed by words.
Transcending the three periods of time, its characteristic is like empty space.
The following two verses specifically manifest the subtle characteristics; that is, the essential characteristics of the subtle. This wisdom has two aspects.

The first two lines clarify the aspect of sameness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because the essence of wisdom is empty and quiescent. The subsequent six lines clarify the aspect of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), as the stages of wisdom differ.

Because they are distinct. Regarding the statement that "the first two phrases refer to the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth," it means that the essence of this wisdom is fundamentally empty and quiescent.

Why is it said to be "identical"? This is precisely the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*). It is identical to all Buddhas above, and identical to all sentient beings below, for all sentient beings possess this.
It is horizontally identical to all phenomena because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*). This suchness is...
Because their own-being (*svabhāva*) is empty, all things take emptiness as their intrinsic nature.

The nature of wisdom and the nature of form are fundamentally without distinction, for all things possess the nature of bliss. The subsequent phrase provides a specific explanation of the meaning of emptiness.

The Commentary, relying on the Sūtra, states: "There is non-duality and inexhaustibility. This explanation, based on this phrase, distinguishes it from the three kinds of emptiness and encompasses the characteristics of true emptiness. (3)
Regarding those who cultivate emptiness: Bodhisattvas on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) whose minds are distracted by emptiness have three kinds of doubt.
First, they doubt that emptiness annihilates form and thus grasp at a nihilistic emptiness; this loses sight of the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness and constitutes the slander of denial (*apavāda*).

Second, they doubt that emptiness is distinct from form and thus grasp at an emptiness external to form. Third, they doubt that emptiness is a substantial entity and thus grasp at emptiness as being existent. Now, when it is said that [emptiness] exists...

It is not a cessation; therefore it is said that "form is itself emptiness. To say they are "not two" means that there is no wisdom of emptiness distinct from this [emptiness], nor is there anything else separate from emptiness.
To say they are "not exhausted" means that emptiness is not a substantial entity that can be transformed or extinguished;
therefore it is said that "emptiness is itself form. There is no separate emptiness apart from this. Apart from these three aspects of emptiness, one sees that the self-nature is fundamentally empty.
It is the Tathāgatagarbha. This commentary explains it based on the sūtra and the śāstra. Following "liberation," there are six phrases which refer to the nirvāṇa of purified skillful means;

that is to say, because it differs from the cultivation and abandonment practiced by ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, it is the very nature of wisdom, and thus constitutes "nature-purity" (prakṛti-viśuddhi).
To transcend the obstacles of affliction through wisdom is the purification of skillful means.

To be liberated from the various realms of existence (*gati*) means that one attains freedom from the defilements of those realms for the sake of liberation. Regarding "equality," it is because the nature of the world is itself *nirvāṇa*;
since birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, it is not like the two vehicles which turn their backs on birth-and-death. That is to say:
Only when there is no interruption throughout the three periods can one speak of the severance of delusions; hence it is said that this does not pertain to the beginning, middle, or end.

The final three phrases clarify the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The first phrase is the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom), which is the characteristic of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), namely non-conceptual observation.

Its essence transcends all names and words; true wisdom arises within. The second phrase refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*, which is the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
This means that by transforming the basis of impermanence, it transcends the three periods of time. Third, its characteristic is like space; this is the characteristic of liberation.
This means that unlike the śrāvakas, who still possess two obstacles, these two obstacles have now both vanished; thus, it is unimpeded like space.
This characteristic of difference arises because one has attained the aforementioned identity, thereby establishing this difference and manifesting that prior identity.
Therein lies the purity of being free from obstacles, like a melted gold casting an image; the image is not external to the gold.
The conduct of the Buddhas is quiescent; no words can reach it. The practice of the stages is likewise difficult to describe and difficult to receive.
This second verse, consisting of one stanza, illustrates the subtlety of the conduct of others. Within it, the first half reiterates that the wisdom of the preceding stage is beyond words.
The first half [of the verse] serves as the analogy; the second half properly cites the practices of the stages (*bhūmi-caryā*) as the object of the analogy.

That is to say, by using the wisdom of the higher stages as the analogy, it reveals that the practices of the stages are exceedingly subtle and tranquil. This tranquility constitutes their common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity is tranquil by its very nature.

Cessation (*nirodha*) is precisely the characteristic of difference (*visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa*). The purification through skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*) and nirvāṇa require wisdom that takes cessation as its object; they do not pertain to cessation by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*).

These two types of nirvāṇa are the domain of the Buddhas, and thus it is said that words cannot reach them. "The practitioner realizes" refers to this. That "words cannot reach" them means that both speaking and listening are difficult.
As for the analogy in the second half [of the verse], it means that not only is the wisdom of realization (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) thus profound.
"Profound. Furthermore, it is difficult to describe the practice of the retinue of wisdom (*jñāna-parivāra*). The six perfections, such as generosity (*dāna*), constitute this retinue of wisdom.
Although "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the essence of the ground, the intent here is to cite the ground in order to include its practice; thus, it is called "ground-practice" (*bhūmi-caryā*).

Since one takes these grounds and their wisdom to cultivate generosity and the other perfections, it is termed "concordant practice" (*sādhāraṇa-caryā*). This is because one practices in accordance with those [perfections]. This, then, constitutes the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
It is the retinue of realized wisdom.
Wisdom arises as the Buddha-realm; it is beyond thought and transcends the path of the mind. It is not accessible through the gates of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases;
it is known by wisdom alone, for the intellect cannot reach it.

The third section, consisting of one verse, clarifies the subtle by means of contrast. It reveals the subtlety by contrasting it with hearing, reflection, and so forth. The first phrase presents the essence of the dharma:
"wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*) that is produced; this refers to the fundamental wisdom elucidated in the preceding five verses.

"Produced" (*utpanna*) refers to both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), both of which contemplate suchness (*tathatā*). Suchness is the realm of the Buddha. Next, the two lines beginning with "not recollecting" (*a-smṛti*)... [and so on].

The phrases clarify that it is difficult to describe. Among them, the first phrase is difficult to describe because it is not a mental factor (*caitasika*). It is "not recollection" because it is not the object of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

It is "beyond the path of the mind" because it is not the object of the wisdom of consciousness born of maturation (*vipākaja-vijñāna-jñāna*). Consciousness born of maturation is explained above in the section on the "Refutation of Invitations.

The next phrase clarifies that it is distinct from the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], as it does not consist of matter, mind, faculties, or objects; therefore, it cannot be described.
The word "expound" (*shuo*) does not appear in the scriptural text because the "gate" (*men*) itself is the expounding. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, expounding is taken as the gate of wisdom.
As for the phrase "that which cannot be heard," it is known only by realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*), for the meaning is beyond the reach of hearing.
Thus, one relies on wisdom and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Just as the tracks of birds in the sky are difficult to describe and difficult to point out, so too the meaning of the ten stages cannot be fully comprehended by the mind.
This fourth verse uses a metaphor to illustrate the subtlety of the stages. Here, the metaphor does not refer to empty space in any other location. Furthermore...
One does not take the traces of sand and soil; one takes rather the traces of birds in the sky.

Because the traces of birds in the sky cannot be pointed out or demonstrated, the preceding metaphor of the wind-drawn lines was intended to manifest the meaning of silence and non-discourse. Herein, the metaphor and the difficulty of explanation are presented.

The assembly was truly free from attachment, and [the Buddha] consented to preach for them; however, his intention was different. This is because there are many faults in grasping the meaning according to the sound with an attached mind.
His purpose was to lead the great assembly to realize for themselves how to abandon such faults; therefore, he explained that it is difficult to speak and difficult to hear.
Through compassion and the power of aspiration, He enters the stages of practice from birth;
The successive perfection of mental and physical conduct is not an object of discursive thought. This realm is difficult to perceive; it may be known, yet it cannot be described.
From here below, the second section further elucidates the Great [Vehicle] to inspire correct faith. These five verses are divided into three parts; the first consists of one verse.

The first half-verse correctly elucidates the meaning of the great accomplishment of speech (*vāda-siddhi*). The second section consists of three verses that demonstrate the author’s own faultlessness and admonish the assembly to eliminate errors.
The third section consists of half a verse indicating the limits of the exposition; this serves merely as the cause for the discourse. Now, regarding the first point:

as for the "three accomplishments," the first is the greatness of the cause (*hetu-siddhi-mahattva*), which refers to compassion and the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) serving as the basis for initiating practice; therefore, it is so named.

First is the greatness of the cause (*hetu-mahattva*). Second is the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause, which refers to the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) serving as the causes for supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*);

because its arising is not instantaneous, it is called "gradual. Third is the greatness of the accomplishment through the teaching of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which refers specifically to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

Because true cultivation accords with reality, it is like the state of direct realization; yet, because it can be expressed through verbal designations, it is termed "teaching" (*deśanā*). Thus, there are the two characters "teaching" (*jiao*) and "speaking" (*shuo*).

This correctly distinguishes the great meaning: it is not like the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), because [the former] cannot be so described. Regarding the "greatness of the accomplishment of the cause," this refers to the first two phrases.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is for the benefit of others; aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) encompasses both benefits; and power (*bala*) encompasses the aforementioned three.

It is called "power" because its cultivation through these two benefits differs from that of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). The subsequent phrase refers to the merit of the two benefits: the arising of the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Practice" (*caryā*) precisely signifies the meaning of "cause. Second, the gradual accomplishment of greatness refers to the second character.

Third, regarding the perfection of the teaching that explains the accomplishment of cultivation, there are two types: first, the cultivation of fulfillment, which consists of the first eight characters;

second, the cultivation of contemplation, which consists of the final two phrases. At the ultimate stage of true cultivation, all worldly concerns are utterly stilled, and one is able to fulfill [the path].

Earth-wisdom (*bhūmi-jñāna*) is called "fulfillment cultivation" (*pūrṇa-bhāvanā*). When true wisdom arises within, its tranquil illumination is distinct and clear; this is called "contemplation cultivation" (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*).

Just as a polished bright mirror has no impurity that is not cleansed, so it is with fulfillment cultivation; just as nothing is not penetrated when reflected in it, so it is with that contemplation cultivation.

The two types of cultivation are like those in the supramundane [path]; they merely constitute the conclusion of the causal stage (*hetu-bhāga*). Only when one attains direct realization and abandons cultivation does it truly qualify as the resultant stage (*phala-bhāga*).

In the text, "contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*); "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom of true cultivation; and "mind" (*citta*) refers to the essential substance of the mind in true cultivation.
This means that only when the mind of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) is absent can it be called the perfection of the mind of true cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, it is accessible only through the wisdom of true cultivation; thus it is said: "The practice of wisdom is not an object of discursive thought.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "this is the realm" within the section on the cultivation of contemplation, it refers to the realm of true cultivation. That it is "difficult to see" means it cannot be seen through hearing and reflection; this should be understood.
This can only be known through the true cultivation of the tranquil illumination of one’s own mind; to know it is to see it. Since it is difficult to see, it is also difficult to explain.
Nevertheless, it is manifested through gradual cultivation and is subsumed within the discourse on the Great [Vehicle], though it differs from the stage of fruition. It is simply a profound meaning.
Through the power of the Buddha, I shall expound this; you all should receive it with reverence.
Such an entry into the practice of wisdom could not be fully described even in billions of eons; I now speak only in brief.
Listen with single-minded respect to the true meaning without remainder, as I, relying on the Buddha’s power, proclaim this sublime Dharma in a subtle and wondrous voice.
"By way of metaphor, through the power of immeasurable Buddhas, All [words] enter my body.

This second section on the Buddha’s power clarifies that he himself is free from fault and exhorts the assembly to avoid error. It consists of three verses. The first half-verse provides a general explanation;
the latter two and a half verses provide a specific exposition. Regarding the former: because both speaker and listener each have two faults, [the teaching would not be effective].
Because it can be realized, both [the speaker and the listener] are shown to be free from faults. Regarding the two faults of the speaker: first, the Buddha does not rejoice in [ordinary] speech;
now, since it is said that "by the power of the Buddha, this is expounded," we know that the Buddha has already rejoiced in it.

Second, [ordinary speech] is unequal; now, since it is said "you all should receive it," there is no sense of self or other. Regarding the two faults of the listener: first, the fault of contention regarding views, which is to say, "my dharma is that..."
The Dharma is not [to be grasped] in such a way; thus one clings to various views. Second, one does not give rise to reverence for the teacher of the Dharma.
