Now, by causing them to receive it with respect, both faults are simultaneously abandoned: because of reverence for the Dharma, there is no fault of contention;

because of reverence for the person, there is no subsequent fault. Next, two and a half verses specifically clarify the middle section, extensively elaborating upon the power of receiving and respectfully accepting what has been taught.
It is divided into three sections. The first verse reveals the exposition; the next verse reveals the reception; and the latter half-verse reveals the reliance on power.
This matter is difficult to proclaim; I shall now speak of but a small portion.

The third section, the "Exposition of the Delimitation," consists of half a verse. The phrase "this locus" refers back to the preceding meaning, stating that the two great [elements] constitute this locus.
"A small portion" merely indicates the cause; as for the fruit-portion, it is inexpressible. There are two senses of cause and fruit:
first, with respect to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is taken as the fruit-portion, while the skillful means (*upāya*) is provisionally [assigned to the cause].
The "dharmas as causes" refers to the fact that while they can be described by relying on dharmas, realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*) is ineffable.

Furthermore, since the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) serve as the cause for reaching the ocean of the ultimate fruit, and because that ocean of the fruit to be reached is beyond words and thus ineffable, the dharmas of the stages mentioned here refer only to the causes.
If one considers the vastness of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows...
The void and the profound darkness share the same ocean of fruition; both are ineffable. The tracks of birds in the sky serve as a metaphor precisely to illustrate this.
From here below, the seventh major section clarifies the threefold analysis within the "Section on Exposition": first, the purpose; second, the explanation of the names;
third, the explanation of the text. Now, regarding the first, the purpose: since the ritual of invitation has concluded, the boundaries have already been shown, and its... [text continues]

The ground is the reality (*vastu*). Since the reality of the ground is difficult to clarify, it is manifested by means of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). These characteristics constitute the causal portion (*hetvaṃśa*).

From this point onward, the characteristics of the grounds are explained in detail so that, by investigating these characteristics, one may attain the reality. Therefore, this [section] has come into being. Furthermore, the section on "requesting" (*pṛcchā*) gives rise to correct understanding.
Following this, its practice and cultivation are revealed; therefore, it follows next. Second, the explanation of the title:

because it extensively expounds and sets forth the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is called the "Explanatory Section" (*nirdeśa-vibhāga*). Third, the explanation of the text: the ten stages constitute ten sections. Within the first stage, there is a sevenfold analysis:

first, the purpose (*āgama-artha*); second, the explanation of the name (*nāma-nirukti*); third, the abandonment of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-prahāṇa*); fourth, the realization of principle (*tattva-adhigama*); fifth, the accomplishment... [text fragment ends].

[The section on] Practice. Six, Attaining the Fruit. Seven, Explaining the Text. First, regarding the intent of its introduction: among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), this is the first stage because one eliminates obstacles, realizes the principle, and attains the nature of a noble one (*ārya*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the name: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that "one first acquires the nature of a noble one;
fully realizing both forms of emptiness, one is able to benefit oneself and others, thereby giving rise to great joy. This has three meanings. First, attaining the rank.
Second, the realization of principle; third, the accomplishment of practice. Because of these three, it is called "Supreme Joy" (pramuditā). Regarding the third point, the severing of hindrances:

the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that the hindrance of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is what is severed. An "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) refers to a worldling; this is termed the "hindrance of the self-conception of a worldling.
It obstructs the first stage (*bhūmi*) and is what is severed therein. For this reason, it is said that two [hindrances] are severed in the first stage.
There are two types of delusion and their corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*): first, the delusion of attachment to a self and phenomena, which is the obstacle of ordinary beings;

second, the delusion regarding the defilements of the miserable realms, which refers to the various karmas and fruits of the miserable realms. Although these latter are not themselves delusions, they are subsumed under the category of delusion.

Each of the nine lower stages likewise possesses two such delusions. Regarding the four principles to be realized: by severing the aforementioned obstacles, one realizes the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).
This means that this *tathatā* (suchness) is manifested by the two kinds of emptiness; there is not a single dharma that does not exist within it.

Regarding the five types of practice accomplished [by this], there are briefly four kinds: first, the practice of giving (*dāna*) accomplished through cultivation based on its preeminence; second, the sixteen great practices arising from what is accomplished;
third, the ten practices such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, which are accomplished through cultivation; and fourth, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), which are the actual practices.

There is nothing among these that is not cultivated. Regarding the fruits obtained, there are briefly four kinds: first, obtaining the four fruits such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) at the time of attaining perfection in one's respective stage;

second, obtaining the fruit of great wealth through the practice of giving (*dāna*); third, obtaining the fruit of the cessation of all obscurations by penetrating the emptiness of those obscurations;
and fourth, obtaining the fruit of the wisdom and principle of the three natures and the three non-natures. However, the above...

Most of the various sections primarily concern sequential progression (*paṭītyasamutpāda*). However, if one considers them from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), then by a single severance, all are severed;

by a single realization, all are realized; by a single practice, all are practiced; and by a single attainment, all are attained. The seventh section, the Explanation of the Text, is divided into two parts:

first, the prose (*gadya*); second, the verse (*śloka*). Within the former, if one were to divide it directly according to the scriptural text, there should be two parts: the first clarifies the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Later, regarding the Bodhisattvas, the Sons of the Buddha, who dwell in this stage, they mostly become kings of Jambudvīpa as a fruit of the lower stages.

The preceding section first provides a detailed explanation; the subsequent phrase, "The Sons of the Buddha," is the concluding summary of the name. Within the preceding section, there are three parts; the first clarifies the entry into the mind.
Next, "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva takes great compassion as the foremost," and so forth, clarifies the mind of abiding on the ground (*bhūmi*).
Following this, "O Son of the Buddha, having dwelt in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), by the power of his great vows he beholds many Buddhas," and so forth, clarifies his mind of emergence.

The textual structure of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is for the most part like this throughout. For now, we shall follow the treatise (*śāstra*) to analyze it; within the prose (*gadya*) portion, it is divided as follows.
Second: first, the section explaining the initial stage; second, the section on comparative evaluation beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells herein.
Within the former, according to the treatise, there are one hundred phrases in total, divided into three sections. The first forty phrases clarify the section on dwelling.
The second part consists of thirty phrases beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Joy," which is the section on the Explanation of Names;

and the latter part consists of thirty phrases beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva dwelling in Great Compassion," which is the section on Abiding. If one were to calculate their relative superiority comprehensively, these constitute the four divisions of the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Regarding the first [division], "dwelling" refers to the arising of the supramundane bodhicitta and firmly maintaining the First Stage. Furthermore...

Because there is no falling back or loss, it is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Since the three minds are realized simultaneously within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each stage encompasses the three preceding positions.

Among these, the section on "abiding" (*sthiti-bhāga*) subsumes the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*); the section on "explaining the name" (*nirukti-bhāga*) subsumes the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*);
and the final two sections subsume the protection of sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a sentient being.
Dedication. Now, within the first hundred phrases of this prose section, the initial forty phrases clarify the stage of abiding (*sthiti-bhāga*).

O Son of the Buddha: if there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, well-cultivated various practices, well-accumulated the aids to the path, well-made offerings to all Buddhas, well-collected pure dharmas, been well-guided by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and well-purified their profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*), they establish themselves...
Vast resolve; giving rise to vast understanding; compassion manifesting before one.
Now, regarding the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the text is divided into two parts: first, the specific manifestation of the dharmas of the stage; second, from "The Bodhisattva dwells thus...

onwards, the conclusion of the entry into the position of the stage. Within the former, there are forty phrases divided into four sections. The first ten phrases concern the basis of what kind of body.
What is the meaning of the next ten phrases? For what reason are there ten phrases regarding the three realms of existence (*tribhava*)?

What are the characteristics of the ten phrases regarding the four [realms]? First: the ten phrases concerning the planting of deep roots of merit constitute the basis for the body. Next, one seeks the wisdom of the Buddha.
It serves as the meaning of the objective referent (*ālambana*). Third, having great compassion as the foremost is the cause for generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*).

Fourth, the transition from being an ordinary person to attaining the state of an *ārya* is the characteristic of the benefit and merit of generating the resolve. Now, regarding the first [section], upon what body do the ten phrases depend?

First, "If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness"—this phrase is the general statement. "Sentient beings" refers here to those who possess understanding and practice. It says:
Regarding "deeply planted": in terms of the sequential progression (*saṃbhāra*), one has already accumulated the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) over the course of one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*;

hence it is called "deeply planted. In the treatise, this is termed "thickly gathered" (*gāḍha-saṃcita*). There are nine distinct phrases, corresponding to nine types of gathering. Of these, the first six pertain to the practice of guarding against afflictions (*kleśa*).

The latter three protect the practices of the two vehicles. Regarding the "nine collections," the first is the collection of practice (*caryā-saṃgraha*), which refers to skillfully cultivating all practices and skillfully establishing the retinue of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because the three aggregates (*skandha*) are not one, they are termed "all. Since impure *śīla* does not give rise to samādhi, this is clarified at the outset.
The second is the collection of concentration (*samādhi-saṃgraha*), which refers to skillfully gathering the factors that assist the path and skillfully establishing their retinue.

Because of samādhi, it is called a "retinue" (parivāra) since concentration serves as the support for wisdom. Third, the accumulation through close attendance (*upaniṣad-saṃbhāra*) refers to the excellent worship of the Buddhas;

this is because one desires to accumulate the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) by making offerings to the Buddhas. Fourth, the accumulation through gathering (*saṃgraha-saṃbhāra*) refers to the excellent gathering of pure and white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), namely, relying upon hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).

Depending on whether these consist of names, meanings, essential natures (*svabhāva*), or distinctions (*viśeṣa*), and whether they are superior or inferior, they constitute the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
It is called "pure white" (*śukla*) because it remedies all obscurations and outflows. The fifth attainment is that of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), who provides excellent guidance;
this occurs because one attains external instruction through internal cultivation and realization. This practice of realization is the wisdom of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

It is further divided into higher and lower stages, established as the level of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*). The higher levels are identical to the stage of application (*prayoga*); the lower four have already [been attained].
Entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Sixth, the accumulation of the purified mind refers to the thoroughly purified profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).

Because one has attained supramundane right knowledge, there is non-conceptual wisdom regarding the objects of perception; since no object whatsoever is apprehended and various signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are not grasped, it is called "thoroughly purified.
Because this wisdom accords with reality, it is termed the "profound mind. Seventh, the extensive accumulation refers to establishing the extensive [collection].

Because of the greatness of their great resolve, profound mind, and vast benefit; because the eighth, the accumulation of faith, gives rise to expansive understanding by seeking the wisdom of all-knowledge;

and because the ninth, the manifestation [of virtue], is the manifestation of compassion, as they practice compassion extensively and never abandon it for even a moment—therefore it is called "manifestation.
This is because those of the Lesser Vehicle lack the aspiration to seek Buddhahood and the mind to benefit sentient beings.
The latter three protect it. The ten preceding phrases clarify by what body [the Buddha] relies; the following clarify for what purpose:
for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom, for the sake of attaining the ten powers, for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses, and for the sake of attaining the Buddha’s equanimity.

Because these dharmas are equal; because of the desire to rescue all worlds; because of the desire to purify great compassion; because of the desire to attain the non-remaining wisdom of the ten directions;
because of the desire to purify all buddha-fields without obstruction; because of the desire to know all three periods of time in a single thought-moment;
and because of the desire to turn the great wheel of Dharma without fear.

Regarding the meaning of the ten phrases in the second [section]: they are for the purpose of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. First, the characteristics of seeking that fruit are specifically revealed;

subsequently, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the generation of the mind is summarized. Now, regarding the initial ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining ones are specific.
Generally, it is called "Buddha-wisdom," which refers to the unsurpassed wisdom that knows, abandons, realizes, and cultivates. This wisdom has nine distinct varieties.

All seek it. First is the Buddha-wisdom of Single Power (*eka-bala*), whose activity is to provide questions and predictions (*vyākaraṇa*); because it answers according to the capacities of beings by means of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Second is the Buddha-wisdom of Fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), whose activity is to destroy false views; it is called "Great" (*mahat*) to distinguish it from that of Bodhisattvas.

Third is the Buddha-wisdom of Equality (*samatā*), which realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*), and whose activity is to instruct sentient beings so they may realize and enter [this truth]. Fourth is the Wisdom of Rescue...
1. Buddha-wisdom: the activity of transforming sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). 2. Pure Buddha-wisdom:

the activity of being able to rescue and sustain [beings], because it purifies hatred through compassion and mercy. 3. Non-remainder Buddha-wisdom: the activity of constantly observing the world’s sentient beings with the Buddha-eye;
it is called "non-remainder" because it observes them pervasively throughout the ten directions. 4. Untainted Buddha-wisdom: by means of non-obstruction...

The Buddha-wisdom that is unimpeded adorns its *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment and its supports); its function is to spontaneously manifest transformations so as to inspire faith and joy in others. The eighth is the Buddha-wisdom of awakening;
its function is to know, in a single thought-moment, the minds and mental factors of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

The ninth is the Buddha-wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma; its function is the skillful means of liberation. Thus, in each of these nine phrases, the essence of wisdom is first indicated in general, followed by—

This reveals their activities: the first three are for one's own benefit, and the latter six are for the benefit of others. Within the benefit of others, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the practice of benefiting others;
compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are the mind that benefits others; and the final four are the wisdom that benefits others.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind—within this second summary of the arousal of the mind—the phrase "gives rise to such a mind" refers to the ten preceding minds. This constitutes the arousal of the bodhicitta.
As for the treatise stating that among the six preceding determinations, the vow is "well-determined," this means that the vow is...
The arousal of the bodhicitta within the first bhūmi refers precisely to these ten minds. What is the meaning of what was stated above?
It is because there is the sense of seeking the Buddha’s wisdom. What is the cause for what is stated below?
Having great compassion as its foremost quality, with wisdom as its preeminent feature, embraced by skillful means, and sustained by the most supreme profound resolve;
possessing the immeasurable powers of a Tathāgata, characterized by excellent observation and discernment, the power of valor, the power of knowledge, and the manifestation of unimpeded wisdom;
conforming to spontaneous wisdom and capable of receiving all Buddha-dharmas; it teaches and transforms through wisdom, as vast as...
The *dharmadhātu* is ultimately like space, extending to the end of the future.
Third, by means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the text clarifies the cause by which such a mind is generated; that is, it is for the sake of sentient beings through great compassion.
There are ten phrases in the text: the first is general, while the others are specific. There are nine specific types, the first of which is "superior greatness."

Because the wisdom regarding the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) increases as one’s conduct becomes subtle; whereas if one understands only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), such wisdom does not increase.
The two types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*) and so forth encompass the "great" because they include the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) through flexibility and adaptability.

The third is the greatness of supreme purity (*viśuddhi*). "Purity" here carries the sense of being "supreme," meaning that one has directed the mind toward the Great Vehicle (*mahācitta*) with the vow to exhaust the suffering of all sentient beings.
The realm is inexhaustible in its benefit; therefore, it is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).

Fourth, the "immeasurable power of the Tathāgata" refers to immeasurable greatness, because it encompasses the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Tathāgata to inspire faith in sentient beings. Fifth, "skillful observation and so forth" refers to the "greatness of certainty":
to have certain faith and understanding in the supreme, wondrous Dharma is called "skillful observation and discernment"; regarding all sentient beings, [to have] certainty...
Concentration is the power of valor, for it is capable of definitively counteracting the obstacles that are to be remedied.

Wisdom is the power of knowledge, as unimpeded wisdom manifests before one. This connects with the preceding phrase. Sixth is the greatness of conformity to spontaneous wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which is the greatness of conformity itself.
Seventh is the greatness of receiving and upholding, as it involves taking up the supreme Dharma and bestowing it upon sentient beings. Eighth is the greatness of breadth...
As vast as the dharma-realm, it is the most supreme greatness. As the nine ultimate stages below, it is the greatness of abiding in exhaustion.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the stage of ordinary beings and enter the rank of bodhisattvas.
They are born into the family of the Tathāgatas; no one can speak of any fault in their lineage. They leave behind the worldly realms and enter the supramundane path, attaining—

This is the dharma of a bodhisattva. Abiding in the station of a bodhisattva and entering into the equality of the three periods of time, one will certainly attain unsurpassed enlightenment within the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Regarding the fourth section, "The Signs of the Bodhisattva, the Son of the Buddha," it specifically reveals the signs of the benefits obtained upon entering this stage.
The text consists of nine phrases: the first is general, while the remaining eight are specific. The phrase "one who has first given rise to such a mind" refers back to the preceding two sections.
"One immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings" because one has attained the supramundane noble path.
Second, below "entering the bodhisattva stage," there are eight distinct types of faults; in the treatise, for each, the principle is stated first followed by a simile.
This entry into the noble stage means being born into the family of the Tathāgata, just as a prince is born into a royal household; thus, every sentence contains a corresponding analogy. First:
1. Transcending the stage of entry: the initial formation of the supramundane mind is like the process of first dwelling in the womb;
this is the analogy for the dharma. 2. Being born into the family of the Tathāgata: this is the analogy for the dharma of being born into the family. 3. Having no deficiency in lineage:

this is the analogy for a son, because one gives birth to the practice of the Mahāyāna. 4. Being free from the defects of mundane lower paths: because it is not tainted by outflows (āsrava), it is like...
The body of the King is similar to the Dharma; thus, the fifth point concerns the excellence of attaining the Bodhisattva-dharma, which is the essence of the Dharma itself.
Taking great compassion (mahākaruṇā) of the same essence as the Bodhisattva’s body is analogous to how a king takes the governance of the state as his essence.

The sixth point concerns the excellence of abiding in the Bodhisattva’s station; that is, abiding in the non-abiding path (apratisthita-mārga), which differs from that of ordinary beings and Śrāvakas, just like a worldly king.
The son does not dwell in base or vulgar ways. Seventh is the fault of entering the equality of the three periods of time:
this refers to realizing the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*) to sustain the life of wisdom. Just as a life is cut short if it lacks nourishment, one would be unable to succeed to the lineage.
Eighth is the fault of falling below the Tathāgata’s certainty: by ensuring the Buddha-lineage is not severed, one attains the unsurpassed path, just as in the world...

The prince’s resolve is firm and established, and he is certain to succeed to the throne; this is called "resemblance through accomplishment. This collectively demonstrates his dissimilarity with those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
When a bodhisattva abides in such a dharma, it is called "abiding in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because of its correspondence with immovability.
The second stage of the bodhisattva is the dwelling in the lower fetters and entering the position. "Dwelling in such dharmas" refers to the four preceding sections.
"Named dwelling in the Stage of Joy" (Pramuditā-bhūmi) signifies the meaning of the first stage. "Because it corresponds with immovability" explains the meaning of "dwelling":
first, because one has realized the true principle and will no longer lose it; second, because those of other vehicles cannot move [the bodhisattva] from it.
The first forty lines above conclude the section on the "Abiding" (vihāra). The thirty lines below explain the "Exposition of Names" (nāmanirdeśa).

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), they achieve abundant joy, abundant pure faith, abundant love and delight, abundant serenity, abundant exultation, abundant elation, abundant valor, abundant freedom from strife, and abundant freedom from affliction and harm.
There is no malice or resentment.
In the second major section, "The Explanation of Names," there are thirty phrases. The first phrase provides a general heading;

the next ten phrases clarify the characteristics of joy (*muditā*); and the final twenty phrases clarify the causes of joy. These are now explained individually. The passage beginning with "accomplishing" (*samanvāgata*) provides the detailed explanation.
Regarding the ten phrases within the characteristic of joy (*prīti-lakṣaṇa*), there are first three general types of joy: 1. **Joy of Abundance**:

This refers to the mind’s delight upon entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). 2. **Joy of Essence**: This is the joy associated with the feeling (*vedanā*) that arises upon emerging from meditation. 3. **Joy of the Faculties**:

Because the preceding mental joy fills the interior and extends outward, the five faculties (*indriya*) become pliant and harmonious. Therefore, this characteristic of joy is also termed [the joy of the faculties].

Regarding "Joy" (*prīti*), there are nine phrases within its specific classification. The first six constitute the essence of the practice of joy for one's own benefit; the latter three manifest the capacity of joy for the sake of transforming others.
Because this is a joy that arises from internal contemplation of the mind itself—a joy that is itself devoid of [ordinary] joy—it differs from the fluctuating joy of the second dhyāna;
therefore, it is called "Supreme Joy. It is the pinnacle of joy. The above explains the characteristics of joy.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy, they give rise to joy by recollecting all Buddhas;
they give rise to joy by recollecting all Buddha-dharmas; they give rise to joy by recollecting all bodhisattvas; they give rise to joy by recollecting all bodhisattva practices;
they give rise to joy by recollecting the pure perfections (pāramitās); and they give rise to joy by recollecting the excellence of the bodhisattva stages.
They give rise to joy. They give rise to joy by reflecting that the Bodhisattva is indestructible. They give rise to joy by reflecting that the Tathāgata teaches and transforms sentient beings.
They give rise to joy by reflecting that he is able to bring benefit to sentient beings.
They give rise to joy by reflecting that he has entered the skillful means of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Second, there are twenty phrases that manifest the causes of joy. First is joy because one recalls what is to be attained; second is joy because one recalls what is currently being attained.
Each has ten phrases. Now, for the first [section]: the first phrase is general, while the others are specific. Regarding the general statement, "recalling all Buddhas":
This means that one thinks, "Just as the Buddhas have attained [this], so shall I also attain it. Therefore, it is judged to be mindfulness of what is to be attained.

There are nine distinct types: first, mindfulness of the Buddha's Dharma; second, mindfulness of the Buddha's Bodhisattvas; third, mindfulness of the Buddha's practices; fourth, mindfulness of the Buddha's purity.
Fifth is the excellence of mindfulness of the Buddha; sixth is the indestructibility of mindfulness of the Buddha; seventh is mindfulness of the Buddha’s teaching and transformation;
eighth is mindfulness of the Buddha’s benefit; ninth is mindfulness of the Buddha’s entry. All these involve mindfulness of the Buddha for the sake of attaining Buddhahood.
Again, he forms this thought: "I feel joy because I am turning away from all worldly realms; I feel joy because I draw near to all Buddhas;
I feel joy because I distance myself from the stage of ordinary beings; I feel joy because I approach the stage of wisdom;
I feel joy because I have forever severed all evil destinies; and I act as a refuge for all sentient beings."
They give rise to joy because they abide in their proper place; they give rise to joy because they behold all Tathāgatas;
they give rise to joy because they are born into the realm of the Buddhas; they give rise to joy because they enter into the equality of all Bodhisattvas;
and they give rise to joy because they are far removed from all terrors, such as the bristling of body hair.

In the second reflection on what is presently attained, there are two parts: first, the explicit clarification of that which is reflected upon; second, the analysis and explanation following the raised questions (beginning with "For what reason?").
Within the former, there are ten phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.

The general statement, "I have turned away from all worldly spheres," means that I have turned away from all matters of grasping and attachment characteristic of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). However, these matters are both coarse and subtle.
The coarse refers to the objects of the six external sense-fields, as these are universally the objects of grasping for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The subtle refers to the establishment of a slight object before one, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*); this too is an object of grasping for ordinary beings prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
There are another nine types of transformation and departure. In contrast to the preceding [section], what are the characteristics of these nine phrases, both general and specific?

Although the textual order does not follow [the previous sequence], the essential nature (*dharmatā*) is entirely identical. This is because they reflect the characteristics of the previously mentioned benefits and virtues, and because they distinguish themselves from the preceding stages by being dissimilar to them.
Therefore, each is individually correlated and explained in the commentary.
Why is this? Once this bodhisattva has attained the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all fears are completely abandoned.
That is to say: the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of the miserable destinies, and the fear of the majesty of great assemblies.
Such fears as these are all permanently left behind.

Second, the detailed interrogation and explanation in response to the objection. Because the abandonment, transformation, and separation involve extensive textual meaning, they are interrogated and explained again.
There are four levels of meaning, namely that there are respective causes and effects for both fear and separation; yet the text is divided into five sections. First, the general interrogation.
1. A general answer by enumerating the names; 2. A threefold inquiry; 3. Citing the causes to reveal the characteristics; 4. From "In this way, the Bodhisattva...
onwards, concluding the response to the initial inquiry. Now, the intent of the initial inquiry is: Why is it said here that one is "free from fear"? The intent of the subsequent answer is:
Because the five fears are obstacles to the first stage (*bhūmi*); when the first stage is attained, one is naturally free from them. Furthermore:
Freedom from these [fears] is precisely the benefit of this stage. The reversal of fear is called joy (*prāmodya*), and this characteristic is most manifest.
Why is this? Because this Bodhisattva has abandoned the notion of self (*ātma-saṃjñā*); since he does not even cherish his own body, how much less so his material possessions?
Therefore, he has no fear regarding livelihood. He does not seek offerings from others, but devotes himself solely to giving and bestowing upon all.
Sentient beings. For this reason, there is no fear of ill repute. Being far removed from the view of self, there is no notion of a self;

for this reason, there is no fear of death. Knowing for oneself that after death one will certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for this reason, there is no fear of the evil realms.
As for my aspirations and joys, there is no one equal to me in all the world, much less anyone superior; for this reason—
There is no fear regarding the majesty and power of the great assembly.
The third inquiry explains the reason for being free from fear. This single inquiry contains four meanings:
first, why is it called the fear of not being able to make a living? Second, by what cause do these five fears arise?
These two [questions] concern the cause and effect of fear. Third: why is it called "perpetual separation"? Fourth: by what cause is this perpetual separation attained?
These two [questions] concern the cause and effect of the separation from fear. If one attains the cause of separation, the result naturally ceases to exist.
Next, the four [verses] provide the answer by citing the cause to manifest its characteristics; that is to say, they correctly cite the cause of separation to manifest the state of being separated.

Regarding the characteristic of the result (*phala-lakṣaṇa*): this is presented by way of contrast to reveal the fear of causes and the fear of the characteristic of results. Generally, there are four intentions that respond to the four preceding inquiries.
For example, "If one does not love one's own body, how much less so one's possessions"—this indicates being free from the cause of the fear of non-sustenance (*ājīva-śāthya*).

By contrast, it reveals that loving the body and possessions is the cause of the fear of non-sustenance. If one does not fear non-sustenance, this constitutes being free from the cause of fear; thus, by contrast—
The fear of being unable to subsist is the fruit of this [fear]. The remaining four cases are analogous.
Furthermore, the abandonment of the cause is itself the remedy, while the dread itself is that which is to be remedied.
In this way, the bodhisattva remains far removed from such things as alarm, fear, and the bristling of body hair.
Fifth, the bodhisattva thus concludes the preceding section by answering the initial inquiry. Previously, it was asked: "How is it possible to remain free [from these]?"; now, the answer is given:
"It is because of the three preceding sections that one is able to remain free. The thirty preceding lines have completed the explanation of the names; the following three...
The tenth section, on Abiding:

O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva takes great compassion as the foremost priority; his vast aspiration and resolve cannot be thwarted or destroyed, and he further diligently cultivates all roots of goodness until they reach fulfillment.
From here begins the third major section: "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, by means of great compassion...
This section on abiding in the stages has three parts: first, a general explanation of abiding; second, a specific elucidation of abiding, beginning with the words "That is to say...";

and third, a summary of abiding, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, because the Bodhisattva has accomplished... Now, for the first part, there are three sentences. The first is: "Great compassion as..."
First, this is the cause of abiding. All that a bodhisattva practices is for the sake of sentient beings, with compassion as the foundation of their conduct;
therefore, it is called "foremost. Second, the vastness of their aspiration and resolve cannot be thwarted or destroyed; this is the contemplation of abiding.

That is to say, the profound mind that accords with reality is "great," and thus afflictions cannot destroy it. Compassionate transformation that encompasses all things is "vast," and thus the Lesser Vehicle [cannot overcome it].
It can be destroyed. By diligently cultivating all roots of goodness for three watches of the night, one attains accomplishment; this is the stage of abiding securely.
Below, thirty distinct phrases specifically reveal this secure abiding, which is divided into three sections.
That is to say: because faith is predominant; because of abundant pure faith; because of the purity of understanding; because of certainty in faith; because of the arising of compassion;
because of the accomplishment of great loving-kindness; because the mind is free from weariness; because of the adornment of shame and remorse;
because of the accomplishment of gentleness; and because of reverently following and honoring the Buddha’s teachings and Dharma.
The second section, which specifically elucidates "abiding," clarifies the previously mentioned diligent cultivation of the roots of goodness. How does one diligently cultivate them?
The text contains thirty phrases that demonstrate three kinds of accomplishment: first, the accomplishment of faith; second, the accomplishment of practice;
and third, the accomplishment of dedication. Faith is the beginning of practice; next, one initiates practice based on faith; finally, one dedicates the practice to perfect virtue. Thus it is said:
Regarding the sequence of practice: first, there are ten phrases concerning faith. "Superior" (*adhimātra*) refers to the objects listed below, such as the truths and realities;

profound conviction and certainty regarding these is termed "superior. Within this category, there are nine points: the first six concern the initial arising of faith, while the latter three concern the growth of faith resulting in aspiration.
Among the former, the first two pertain to one's own benefit, and the latter four to the benefit of others.
Because they cultivate roots of goodness day and night without weariness; because they draw near to spiritual friends; because they always delight in the Dharma;
because they seek out extensive learning without weariness; because they correctly contemplate the Dharma as it has been heard;
because their minds are free from attachment and clinging; because they do not crave gain, fame, or honor; and because they do not seek any material necessities for life.
Because one gives birth to a mind like a treasure that knows no satiety.
Regarding the nine phrases on the accomplishment of practice during the second night: they generally speak of "no satiety," which refers to uninterrupted cultivation (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).

Specifically, there are eight collections. Of these, the first seven concern the practice of instruction, while the last one concerns the practice of realization. Within the former [seven], the first two are as follows:
The skillful means for gathering the Dharma consist of: first, the gathering through proximity, which is to associate with virtuous friends with the intent of not forgetting any dharmas;
second, the gathering through delighting in the Dharma, which is to take joy in the mind during questions, answers, debates, and explanations.

The subsequent five phrases describe the sequential cultivation of practice, among which the first three concern internal contemplation and conduct in accordance with principle. The first is the gathering through extensive learning, which refers to hearing.
1. Wisdom (*prajñā*). 2. The collection of correct contemplation is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). 3.

Non-attachment is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because within *samādhi* there is no dependence or clinging. The latter two are practices of detachment in accordance with conditions: namely, 6.

the collection of non-greed, which is the practice of few desires, because one does not seek what has not yet been attained; and 7. the collection of non-seeking. 8. The collection like a jewel is the perfection of the practice of realization.
Because it is constantly present before them; because they seek the stage of omniscience; because they seek the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities of a Tathāgata;

because they seek the perfections and the factors conducive to enlightenment; because they are free from all guile and deception; because they are able to act according to their words; and because they always protect truthful speech.

Therefore, because they do not defile the family of the Tathāgata; because they do not abandon the bodhisattva precepts; because they give rise to the mind of omniscience that is as immovable as the king of mountains;
because they do not abandon worldly affairs while accomplishing the supramundane path;
because they gather the factors conducive to enlightenment without weariness; and because they constantly seek the ever-higher, most excellent path.
The third section, "Seeking All-Knowledge," concerns the fulfillment of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Seeking all-knowledge is the dedication toward enlightenment (*bodhi*).

It consists of twelve phrases. The first phrase refers to the object sought, which is termed the "home" (*kula*), because the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*) is the locus of that seeking.
The subsequent eleven phrases constitute the causes for this seeking. The first [of these] seeks suchness (*tathatā*).

"Power of coming" (*āgati-bala*) and so forth clarify the contemplation that seeks [the goal]. The remaining ten phrases clarify the practices that seek it. The initial seeking of the various perfections (*pāramitā*) is called "unobstructed seeking" (*anāvaraṇa-paryeṣaṇā*);
this means that because one seeks the non-attached dharmas of the various perfections, one is able to eliminate obscurations.

The subsequent nine phrases are distinct, as they specifically counteract various obstacles. The first is "seeking detachment," which counters flattery and crookedness; when seeing a beggar, one might falsely manifest [virtue] in order to seek [gain].
Skillful means (upāya): first, because one is consistently without the intention to give;

second, being able to practice as one has spoken, which seeks to remedy false speech—namely, promising and then not giving, and so forth—and this remedies two stains within the perfection of generosity (dāna); third, guarding one's conduct, which remedies one stain within the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla).

Because one does not conceal transgressions. Fourth is the unblemished seeking, which remedies the single stain of impurity: namely, the activity of harassing others is a blemish because it defiles the Tathāgata’s house of benefit.
Fifth is the non-abandoning seeking, which remedies the single stain of [lack of] vigor. Sixth is the immovable seeking.
This treats two defilements of dhyāna: first, the distracted mind that clings outwardly, which is treated by means of a mountain;

second, the inability to subdue recollective thought and discrimination, which is treated by means of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*). The following three phrases treat the three defilements of prajñā.
This refers to the seven types of seeking that achieve non-abandonment, which remedy the stains of the path of non-abiding by counteracting their obstacles.

Eighth is the seeking of accumulation, which remedies the stains of the path of assistance by counteracting their obstacles. Ninth is the constant seeking, which remedies the stains of the realization of the path by counteracting its obstacles;

this is because, regarding the superior and sublime dharmas of realization, the aspiration and desire of the mind are slight. The above concludes the section on dedication and achievement; below is the summary.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva accomplishes such methods for purifying the stages, they are said to be "dwelling securely in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy.
Regarding the third summary: the thirty preceding phrases extensively describe the fulfillment and accomplishment of diligent practice; this refers to that diligent practice.
There are four: first, faith; second, aspiration; third, diligence; and fourth, skillful means. Faith refers to acceptance and certainty.
Aspiration refers to the longing for and pursuit of those practices. Among the first ten phrases, the first seven constitute faith, while the latter three constitute aspiration.

The next ten refer to diligence (*vīrya*), which involves the actual practice and cultivation. The final ten refer to the practice of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), because they constitute the mastery of seeking [the goal].
This is called "abiding within the section on the exposition of this stage. Therefore, it says: "having accomplished these dharmas that purify the stage."
This is called "Abiding. The preceding section on the stage of Abiding is concluded.
Below follows the fourth section, the "Analysis of Superiority," which has three parts: first, the superiority of the vow, which serves as a marker for its vast and far-reaching scope;

second, the superiority of practice, which consists of cultivation based upon the vow; and third, the superiority of the beneficial fruit, which refers to the accomplishment of the stages and practices. Now, the first is introduced.

[Answer: Indeed, its ultimate meanings (*paramārtha*) are numerous; however, when summarized, they do not exceed three types: namely, aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), practice (*caryā*), and wisdom (*jñāna*).

Because these three traverse the stages (*bhūmi*), they become manifold. To explain them briefly, there are ten stages: first, the excellence of the initial generation of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*); second, ... [and so forth].
1. Superiority of faith; 2. superiority of the three liberations; 3. superiority of practice; 4. superiority of vows (the above are the three minds); 5. superiority of realization and entry; 6.
superiority of the provisional and ultimate wisdom that transcends the seventh stage; 7. superiority of initiating practice without effort; 8. superiority of being equal to all Buddhas; 9.
superiority of the ultimate, which refers to the fulfillment of the fruit of the three minds of all Buddhas; therefore, this section now clearly elucidates practice.
The vows are supreme. They are called "perfectly interfused" because they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Within a single vow, all vows are fully contained;

this is precisely the entry into the layered, profound [realms] and the perfect interfusion of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*). This is the meaning of the commentary (*śāstra*), though the specific passage has not yet been recorded here.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy, they are able to accomplish such great vows,
such great valor, and such great activities.

The second part, the actual explanation of the text, is divided into two sections. First, the ten vows are revealed to manifest the practice of self-benefit. Second, the ten "exhaustive phrases" (*daśa-paryantapada*) are explained as being shared with all sentient beings.
Regarding the first section, there are four parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration beginning with "That is to say...";

third, the summary conclusion beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy..."; and fourth, [the statement] "By means of these ten gates of vows... and so forth.
The first section below clarifies the inclusion of the retinue. The initial ten vows manifest the practice for one’s own benefit. The first [vow] is a general heading.

The phrase "is able to accomplish" encompasses the following three sentences. The single phrase "in this way" marks the commencement of the formal commitment. Next, "great valor" refers to the arousal of skillful means.
Finally, "the three great functions" signify that the vow has been fulfilled and the practice accomplished.
This refers to generating a vast, pure, and resolute understanding, whereby one reverently makes offerings to all Buddhas with every possible article of worship,
leaving nothing remaining; as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space,
and continuing without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.

The first section, the "Vow of Making Offerings," generally clarifies the act of offering. The *Śāstra* states that offerings are made to the "superior field," which encompasses both the teacher and the Triple Gem;

however, because the Buddha is the most preeminent, it speaks here only of making offerings to the Buddha. Next, the passage beginning with "as vast as the Dharma-realm" reveals the excellence of the vow.
It is said that [this vow] is great in its inclusion of merit within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as vast as space, and as enduring as the future limit;
it clarifies the scope of the vow throughout all kalpas.
Furthermore, he made these great vows: "May I receive the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas; may I encompass the bodhi of all Buddhas;

may I protect the teachings of all Buddhas; may I uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas—vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future, without ceasing throughout all kalpas."
Second, the vow of upholding. The first phrase indicates the vow; this upholding is also called the vow to protect the Dharma. Next is the aspect of the vow’s practice:

all four phrases encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others. "Up" (śīla) means to receive and accept; "gathering" (saṃgraha) means to include within one's scope, meaning to gather and bestow the true Dharma.
"Protecting" (rakṣā) means to guard; "upholding" (dhāraṇa) means to sustain, meaning to guard and maintain the true Dharma. Next is the vow beginning with "vast" (udāra).
By virtue of their power, they encompass the scope of all vows throughout all kalpas.

Furthermore, they make a great vow: "May I go before every Buddha who appears in all worlds—from descending from the Tuṣita heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, birth, renunciation, attaining enlightenment, teaching the Dharma, to manifesting parinirvāṇa—and attend upon them all."
He provides close service and acts as the leader of the assembly, receiving and practicing the True Dharma. He turns it forth simultaneously in all places;
it is as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and continues without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
The vow for the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma: the first phrase indicates the locus of the turning throughout all worlds, namely when descending from Tuṣita and manifesting the eight signs;
the following two phrases encompass the skillful means of the Dharma.

Next, the two phrases beginning with "in all places" clarify that the turning of the Dharma is instantaneous and universal. Finally, the two phrases beginning with "vast and great" express the merit of the vow throughout all kalpas.
This concludes the section on the downward transition.
Furthermore, he makes a great vow: "May all bodhisattva practices be vast, immeasurable, indestructible, and unmixed;

may they encompass all the *pāramitās*, purify all the stages (*bhūmis*), and [comprehend] their general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, characteristics of formation, and characteristics of disintegration."
All the practices of Bodhisattvas are explained exactly as they are. They teach and transform all beings, causing them to receive and practice these teachings so that their minds may increase.
These practices are as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space; they continue without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
Fourth is the cultivation of the vow for the two benefits. The aspiration that all [beings] may clarify their practice is the aspect of the vow.

The inclusion of the various *pāramitās* constitutes the essence of practice; next, the purification of all karmas constitutes the activity of practice. The general characteristics below clarify the skillful means of practice.

The six aspects being perfectly interfused constitutes self-benefit; "explaining according to reality" constitutes benefit for others. Next, "teaching and transforming all beings" clarifies the increase of the mind;
"vast" and following clarify the virtue of aspiration; the final phrase clarifies the scope of the aspiration.
Furthermore, he made this great vow: "I vow that for all realms of sentient beings—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; bound within the three realms; entering all places of birth among the six destinies;
and comprised of name-and-form—I shall teach and transform every such being as these, causing them to enter the Buddha-dharma."

May they cause all worldly destinies to be forever severed; may they cause [beings] to dwell securely in the path of the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), as vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.

Fifth is the vow to mature sentient beings. Regarding the first aspect of this practice, the clarification of the sentient beings to be converted: there are generally ten categories that encompass all beings within the three realms.
They differ only in terms of coarseness and subtlety: those with form are coarse, while those without form are subtle;

those with perception are coarse, while those without perception are subtle; those who are neither with nor without perception are subtle, while those who are neither without perception nor non-perception are coarse. [These include] the four modes of birth.
Beings belong to the six realms of existence. Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth; hungry ghosts are born through both the womb and transformation;
those in the hells, the various heavens, and the intermediate state (antarābhava) are born solely by transformation. Among humans, there are those born from eggs:

for instance, the wife of the Vaiśya Viśākha gave birth to thirty-two eggs, each of which produced a son; likewise, the queen of the Pañcāla king gave birth to five hundred eggs, each containing a son.

Moisture-born beings are like King Mūrdhaja, who was born from a blister on his crown. Those born by transformation are like those at the beginning of a kalpa; at that time, all humans were born by transformation.
I have taught and transformed them all to cause them to enter [the path]. This refers specifically to what is to be done:

namely, causing those who have not yet developed faith to believe and enter the Buddha-dharma, and causing those who already have faith to realize and enter it. "Severing the worldly destinies" refers to karma, afflictions, and suffering.
The three paths encompass both cause and effect. Next, regarding the capacity for vast and great virtues, throughout all kalpas and their respective limits, one further makes a great vow:
that in all worlds—vast and immeasurable, coarse or subtle, abiding in disorder, inverted, or upright;
whether entering, moving, or departing; differentiated like a net of Indra’s jewels, and infinitely diverse in the ten directions—one may [attain] these various distinctions.

Their wisdom is clearly manifest as direct knowledge and vision; it is as vast as the Dharma-realm, as ultimate as space, and continues without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
Sixth is the vow of service (*paricaryā-praṇidhāna*). This is the vow to go to all buddha-fields to constantly see the Buddhas and always reverently serve and listen to them.
Regarding the characteristics of all forms of inferior service, first the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is clarified, and next the subject that knows (*jñātṛ*) is distinguished.

Within the former, there are three distinct types: first, all aspects (*sarva-ākāra*); second, the aspect of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-ākāra*); and third, the immeasurable aspect (*apramāṇa-ākāra*).
Now, because the characteristics of the initial realm differ, it is called "all. Because the small contains the large, it is called "immeasurable.

Regarding "coarse and subtle," this clarifies the substantial nature of being coarse or refined, meaning that karmic retributions and so forth are distinct. "Disordered abiding" refers to different modes of establishment:

"disordered" means not following a regular order; "inverted" means the world-systems are turned upside down; "upright" means the world-systems are facing upward. "Entering" or "traversing" refers to moving through them.
If one dwells, it refers to the coming and going upon the path of the world. First, entering in accordance with others means that what belongs to another is gathered into oneself;
departing means being gathered by others. As for "moving," it refers to coming and going without remaining still, like the distinctions within Indra’s net.

That is, the characteristics of the true meaning are such that the lands and their essences share a single substance; they do not maintain their own individual natures but interpenetrate one another, like the jewels in Indra’s net.

Because it is like a net, it is called "reality" (*tattva*). "Wisdom clearly understands all" distinguishes the capacity for knowing; that is to say, because the characteristics of the true meaning can be known only by wisdom.
"Vast" and below refer to the virtue of aspiration; "all" and below refer to the boundaries.
Furthermore, he made a great vow: "May all lands enter into one land, and one land enter into all lands.
May immeasurable Buddha-fields be universally pure, adorned with arrays of light and various requisites.
May they be free from all afflictions, and may the path of purity be accomplished therein. May immeasurable beings of wisdom fill them, universally entering into the vast [reality]."
The great realm of all Buddhas manifests in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
It is as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as empty space; it continues until the end of the future, without ceasing throughout all kalpas.
Seventh is the vow for the purification of the Buddha-land. This is the aspiration to purify one’s own land by establishing the True Dharma and enabling sentient beings to practice it.
Within the characteristics of this practice, there are seven types of purity in total:

first, purity of identity, because all share the same *dharmatā*, such that the one and the many mutually interpenetrate; second, universal adornment and purity, which is the purity of mastery, like a *maṇi* jewel.
The beauty or ugliness of the jewels is thus revealed; as purity and impurity are perfectly interpenetrated, it is said that "all are universally pure.

Third, from "the assembly of light-radiating implements" downward, it clarifies the purity of adornment, which is the purity of marks (*lakṣaṇaviśuddhi*). Fourth, from "free from all... downward, it clarifies the purity of enjoyment (*paribhogaviśuddhi*).

This refers to the purity of enjoyment, because by utilizing this land, one leaves behind faults and accomplishes virtues. Fifth is the purity of the dwelling place of sentient beings through immeasurable wisdom below;
this refers to the fact that it is inhabited by those endowed with virtue. Sixth is the purity of the cause for universal entry below;

this refers to taking the pure consciousness of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the penetrating wisdom of subsequent cognition (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as a basis. Therefore, it is said to be "the realm of all Buddhas. Seventh is [the purity] according to sentient beings below...
The fruit is purity. This refers to manifesting according to the occasion. The final two phrases concern the scope of one's virtues and powers.
Furthermore, one makes a great vow: may I share the same resolve and conduct as all bodhisattvas; may I be free from resentment and jealousy while accumulating all roots of goodness;
may I share the same single object of focus as all bodhisattvas, always gathering together in assembly without ever being separated, acting according to their will.
They are able to manifest various forms of the Buddha-body. According to their own minds, they are able to know the power, majesty, and wisdom of the realm of all Tathāgatas.
They attain non-retrogressive *ṛddhi* (supernormal powers) and travel through all worlds, manifesting their forms in all assemblies and universally entering all places of birth.
They accomplish the inconceivable Mahāyāna and cultivate the vast conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Just as the *dharmadhātu* is ultimately like space, it continues without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
This is the eighth [aspect], non-separation from the vow. It is the vow that one shall never be separated from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of attaining identical practice with them.
Within the characteristics of this practice there are twelve phrases: the first phrase is general, the final phrase is a conclusion, and the ten in between are specific.

This separately clarifies the bodhisattva practices. The first five stages of cultivation are identical; the latter stage, "Attaining Non-retrogression," shares the same functional qualities as the final five stages.
This concludes the section on cultivating bodhisattva practices. The phrase "Vast and Great" below refers to the scope and limits of these qualities.
Furthermore, he made this great vow: "May I ride upon the wheel of non-retrogression and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, such that my actions of body, speech, and mind shall never be in vain.
May those who see me even for a moment become certain of the Buddha-dharma; may those who hear my voice even briefly attain true wisdom;

and may those who give rise to pure faith even momentarily forever sever their afflictions. May I obtain a body like that of the Great King of Medicine Tree, and may I obtain [a nature] like that of a wish-fulfilling jewel."
Body: Practicing all bodhisattva practices, as vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, continuing until the end of the future, without rest throughout all kalpas.
Ninth is the aspiration for benefit: the vow to constantly perform deeds that benefit sentient beings at all times so that no moment is spent in vain.

Regarding the aspects of this practice, there are two parts. First, a general explanation: it means that by mounting the wheel of the Dharma through non-retrogressive mindfulness, one brings benefit to others through all three types of action (body, speech, and mind).
Second, a specific explanation of how even a brief encounter is not in vain, which has two points. First, the performance of the deed is certain and will not...
"Empty. Because the three karmas can bring peace and happiness: that is to say, seeing the conduct of the body and hearing the Dharma spoken by the mouth can give rise to wisdom;
mindfulness of the true virtues of the mind prevents the arising of various delusions. Obtaining [benefits] like those under a great medicinal king tree is "non-empty" regarding subsequent benefit.
Both metaphors illustrate the extraction of suffering: the tree extracts the suffering of illness, and the jewel extracts the suffering of poverty. "Vast," etc.

Regarding the scope of his virtuous power, he further made a great vow: "May I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in all worlds, without ever departing from even a single hair-tip;
and upon every hair-tip, may I manifest my initial birth and renunciation."
He proceeds to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), attains perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), turns the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), and enters *nirvāṇa*.

These are the ten vows for the attainment of perfect awakening. He vows that he and all sentient beings shall simultaneously attain unsurpassed bodhi, so as to constantly perform the deeds of a Buddha.
Within the aspects of practice, there are two parts: first, the realization of the essence of bodhi, which is the spontaneous perfection of one's own cultivation; next—
Without departing from a single hair-pore, one performs the activities of awakening; that is, the ceaseless movement for the sake of others. There are seven kinds of such activity.
First, from "not departing from a single hair-pore" to "entering nirvana," this is the activity of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

Every hair-tip is a place of attaining Buddhahood. While it was stated above that "all worlds" refers to the vast expanse of the ten directions, here it refers to the pervasiveness throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Within each and every infinitesimal point at the tip of a single hair, he attains enlightenment through the eight phases of manifestation,
because there are always sentient beings therein who can be transformed.
Having attained the power of great wisdom within the realm of Buddhahood, he manifests [enlightenment] in every thought-moment in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings.
He attains Buddhahood and causes others to attain nirvāṇa.
Second is the activity of teaching the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which means teaching the Four Noble Truths so that beings may realize reality.
By means of a single *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he knows that the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is itself the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
Third is the activity of teaching and transforming through realization. By means of the single, ultimate, non-dual bodhi, one accords with the nirvāṇa that is differentiated yet intrinsically pure;
thus, there is no further extinction. To preach this teaching of realization so as to inspire faith in sentient beings is called the activity of teaching and transforming.
He preaches the Dharma with a single voice, causing the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice.
This is the fourth type of activity of preaching the Dharma:
because he accords with the capacities [of beings] through a single voice, he manifests entry into Great Nirvana while never ceasing his bodhisattva practices.
Fifth, the karma that does not sever the lineage of the Buddha: Nirvāṇa is eternally abiding, where movement and stillness are non-dual.

Although the twin śāla trees signify the end of his manifestation, this serves to increase the compassionate longing of sentient beings; thus it is said he "manifests entry. Since this is not eternal extinction, he constantly performs the Buddha-work, and thus the lineage of the Buddha is never severed.
This is the principle of attaining the fruit without abandoning the cause.
It reveals the ground of great wisdom, wherein all phenomena are established.
The six wheels do not abide in karma; the ground of great wisdom is the single reality, which is precisely Buddha-wisdom.
It can give rise to all things and ultimately returns to this; therefore, it is called a "ground. Yet, the gates of wisdom differ in ten thousand ways according to the capacities of beings.
It is named "The Establishment of All.

By means of the supernormal power of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-abhijñā*), the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-abhijñā*), and the supernormal power of illusion (*māyā-abhijñā*), one exercises mastery over transformations that fill the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

These are the seven types of sovereign activity (*vaśitā-karman*). The three types of supernormal powers are the basis for this sovereignty. Regarding the supernormal power of Dharma-knowledge: it contemplates all...

Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics; because those with the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery can manifest their own bodies through birth, abiding, and cessation, and exercise sovereign control over their size according to their will;
and because those with the supernormal power of illusion can transform external objects so that nothing does not accord with their intentions.
Vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as empty space, it continues without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
This demonstrates the extent of its virtuous power.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells on the Stage of Joy, they give rise to such great vows, such great courage, and such great activities.
This summarizes the ten vows. The ten vows above are concluded.
Taking these ten gates of vows as the foremost, one fulfills one million *asaṃkhyeya* great vows.
Section Four of the main text clarifies the inclusion of retinues from this point onward;
that is to say, within each of these ten great vows, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* great vows serving as its retinue. Thus, these ten vows encompass them all.

There is nothing that is not exhausted. The preceding section clarifies the ten vows, concluding with the manifestation of one’s own diligent practice; the following ten "exhaustive" phrases are shared with all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, these great vows are accomplished through ten exhaustive phrases. What are these ten? They are as follows: [The first is] sentient beings...
The realm of sentient beings is exhausted; the realm of worlds is exhausted; the realm of empty space is exhausted; the realm of phenomena is exhausted; the realm of nirvāṇa is exhausted;

the realm of the appearance of Buddhas is exhausted; the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is exhausted; the realm of the objects perceived by the mind is exhausted; and the realm of the objective spheres entered by the Buddha’s wisdom is exhausted.
The turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom exhaust the realms.

These are shared with sentient beings through ten inexhaustible phrases; that is to say, the aforementioned ten vows are all for the sake of sentient beings, and by virtue of these ten inexhaustibilities, the previously established great vows are all rendered inexhaustible.
The first phrase serves as the general heading. The section beginning with "What are they? provides the detailed analysis and explanation.

There are ten phrases concerning sentient beings; the first serves as the general [heading], while the remaining nine serve as the particulars. This is because they all collectively establish the meaning of delivering sentient beings.
The term "exhaustively" (*jin*) is used because there is no exhaustion or cessation.

If the realm of sentient beings were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted. If the worlds, and even the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, the turning of wisdom, and the turning of the realms were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted.

However, because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, and because even the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, the turning of wisdom, and the turning of the realms are inexhaustible, these roots of goodness of my great vow are without end.
Regarding the fulfillment of the two great vows, first there is a reductio ad absurdum (paryudāsa), followed by the explanation of why they are inexhaustible for the sake of sentient beings.
Having concluded the superiority of the first vow within the initial comparative evaluation, the following section concerns the superiority of the second practice.
O Son of the Buddha, once a bodhisattva has made such great vows, they will attain a mind of benefit, a pliant mind, a compliant mind,
a tranquil mind, a disciplined mind, a mind of cessation, a humble mind, a moistened mind, an unshakable mind, and an unclouded mind.
The second section, "The Sons of the Buddha Excel in Practice Below," concerns the comparative analysis of practice, which consists of ten types of practice.

This is divided into three parts in the text: first, clarifying the mind upon which the practice relies; second, from "Accomplishing Pure Faith" onwards, revealing the characteristics of the practices accomplished;

and third, from "Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas thus... onwards, concluding with the names and essence of the ten [practices]. Now, for the first part: because the previous great vows have permeated the mind.
Thus, the ten mental states beginning with "attaining benefit" serve as the basis for initiating practice, because one attains mastery in performing the subsequent ten practices.
These ten practices are divided into nine, as compassion and pity are combined.

The second section specifically elucidates the modes of practice (*ākāra*) through ten categories: first, faith-practice; second, compassion; third, loving-kindness; fourth, generosity; fifth, tirelessness;
sixth, knowledge of the sūtras and śāstras; seventh, understanding worldly dharmas; eighth, the adornment of shame and dread of blame;
ninth, firm strength; and tenth, making offerings to the Buddha.
Those who have perfected pure faith possess the functional power of faith: they are able to believe in the entry into the original practices of the Tathāgata;

they believe in the accomplishment of all the pāramitās; they believe in entering the various supreme stages (bhūmis); they believe in the accomplishment of the powers (balas); they believe in the possession of the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradyas);

they believe in the growth of the indestructible, unique Buddha-dharmas; they believe in the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas; and they believe in the emergence of that which is without center or periphery.
The Buddha’s realm. One enters the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata through faith; one achieves the fruit through faith. To state it briefly:
it is because of the power of the teaching regarding all bodhisattva practices up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that one has faith.
In the second part, the actual explanation, there are first two lines establishing that the accumulation of virtues constitutes the person.

Next, from "capable of faith" (*śraddhā*) onwards, the characteristics of faith are explicitly revealed in eleven lines, which are divided into three sections. First, the single line "capable of faith in the Tathāgata" is a general faith in both cause and fruit.
Second, the nine lines beginning with "faith in the accomplishment" specifically clarify cause and fruit. Among these nine, the first two lines serve as...
The [first] is the cause; the remaining seven are the results. To state the essential point in a single phrase:
it is the ground of wisdom that universally believes in all causes and results. O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva further reflects:
"The true Dharma of the Buddhas is thus profound, thus tranquil, thus quiescent, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, and thus unstained."
Thus it is immeasurable; thus it is vast.

Second, the two practices of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are distinguished in pairs. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the three contemplations as the skillful means;
second, clarifying the practice that arises when the Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings. Regarding the former, the three contemplations constitute three sections.
Section. The nine phrases following "The True Dharma of all Buddhas" clarify the contemplation that is far removed from the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
First, it is stated generally that "the Buddha-dharma" is so because it can be manifested only through the realization of the Buddha's teachings.
It is profound because it possesses all the subsequent meanings. Specifically, there are nine kinds of profundity.
Yet the minds of ordinary beings fall into false views.
Second is the contemplation of the fullness of all suffering, which is explained by means of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Although the twelve links of dependent origination comprise karma, afflictions, and suffering, the present discussion refers only to the "contemplation of suffering" because karma and afflictions are the causes of suffering. As stated in the following passage:

This consists of two sections. First, the general explanation of the false views of ordinary beings; second, the specific explanation of the three links via four and a half lines of scripture beginning with "ignorance" (*avidyā*);
and finally, the specific explanation of the remaining nine links via the section beginning with "the field of the three realms."
Shrouded by ignorance, they raise the high banner of arrogance; they enter the net of craving and wander through the dense forest of flattery and deception, unable to emerge on their own.
Their minds remain associated with stinginess and envy without relinquishing them, constantly creating the causes and conditions for rebirth within the various realms of existence.

Subsequently, beneath the obscuration of ignorance, there are separately nine kinds of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The first five [factors] are ignorance, which thus comprise five kinds of wrong view.
The next three are formations (*saṃskāra*), and the last one is the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Why are karma and the seed of consciousness also called "wrong view"?
It is because they are associated with wrong view and are led by wrong view. The reason the category of ignorance is extensive is to manifest the single [nature of delusion].

All afflictions are capable of providing the moisture that brings about the arising of karma; however, at the stage of generating karma, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) increases, and thus it is explained in detail.
