Arrogance (*māna*), flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) are all as explained in the treatise.
Greed, hatred, and delusion accumulate all karmic actions, which increase day and night. Driven by the wind of resentment and anger, the fire of the mental consciousness blazes without ceasing;
whatever karma is performed is entirely associated with perversion.
The next three phrases clarify the *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) link. The first phrase, "greed and hatred," refers to the accumulation of karma through wrong views.

Next, the two subsequent phrases—"blown by the winds of anger and resentment"—specifically clarify the *saṃskāra* link. These winds blow upon the fire of consciousness, causing wrong views to blaze intensely;
that is, the mental karma of internal thought acts as the wind of affliction. Furthermore, whatever actions one performs constitute the karma of wrong views, which simultaneously involves movement.
Body and speech;

the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the flow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and the flow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). These give rise to the seeds of mind and consciousness in a continuous succession.

Among these, the three flows of desire—down to the ninth [moment] of the mind, mental faculty, and consciousness—are the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) as induced by false view. The subsequent [moments] clarify this.
The three branches of the past limit have been concluded.

Below, the nine branches of the middle and future limits are explained, whereby the sprouts of suffering arise again within the field of the three realms. That is to say, name-and-form arise together and are inseparable;

as this name-and-form grows, the village of the six sense bases is produced. Within these, contact arises through mutual encounter; from contact, feeling arises; and because of feeling, craving arises.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because craving increases, grasping (*upādāna*) arises. Because grasping increases, existence (*bhava*) arises.

Regarding the latter nine factors among the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the text is divided into three sections. First, from "in the three realms" down to "existence arises," it clarifies their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
By "specific characteristics" is meant the present factors such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); this is because their essential forms are distinct. Next, there is...
"From birth until the end of the mass of suffering" clarifies the characteristic of similarity (*sādharmya*). Regarding the characteristic of similarity:

it means that the two future links are also similar to the present ones, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. "The three" refers to the middle [links]. "Down to being like a reflection" clarifies the characteristic of inversion (*viparyāsa*).

First, regarding their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): the "three realms" are the places where one is born; they further give rise to the sprouts of suffering, which is what is called [the characteristic of inversion].
It is form (*rūpa*). To say that they arise together and are inseparable means that they arise together and are inseparable from the *ālayavijñāna*.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the fundamental consciousness has three aspects: first, the self-aspect (*svalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the essence of the fundamental consciousness itself; second, the causal aspect (*hetulakṣaṇa*), which refers to the seed-consciousness;
and third, the resultant aspect (*phalalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Because these three aspects exist, they share a common cause.

Regarding the result: what is now meant by "co-arising and not separate" is intended to mean that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), taking the held seeds of defilement as its cause, brings about name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its maturation fruit (vipākaphala).
Thus, one half of the causal characteristic of the consciousness link resides in the past, maintaining the remaining causes of defilement;
the other half serves as the basis for the subsequent name-and-form. Therefore, it is said to be "together with" them.

Regarding "birth" (*jāti*): it means that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises solely from the seeds based upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), without being mixed with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Therefore, of the three branches of the past, there are only two and a half branches; of the middle and future existences, there are nine and a half branches. It is only in this way that the meaning of continuity (*saṃtati*) is revealed.
As name-and-form grows, it becomes the remaining eight branches; they do not possess separate substantial entities.
Because there is birth, there arise aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress. In this way, sentient beings give rise to and grow within a mass of suffering.
The two [phases of] birth and aging-and-death equally manifest the characteristic of similarity (*sādharmya*).

To speak of the characteristic of similarity means that the two factors of the future [existence] are likewise identical to those of the present, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. Since birth and death are alike, their suffering is also alike. As it is said:
This concludes the preceding twelve links. Of these, the first two and a half links serve as the conditions for growth, while the subsequent nine and a half links are that which grows.
All of these are empty; they are devoid of self and what belongs to a self, lacking cognition, awareness, agency, or experience, being like grass, wood, or stone.
The wall is also like a reflected image.
Regarding the phrase "within these" in the context of the three inverted characteristics, it refers to the aforementioned twelve links of dependent origination.

The section beginning with "all are empty" clarifies the reason for their being inverted: because one perceives existence where there is emptiness, it is called an inversion; this is because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature.

"Empty. This explains the meaning of emptiness by way of being free from "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*). It is empty of a person (*pudgala*), and empty of the phenomena that are the objects [of perception].

The phrase "without cognition" (*ajñāna*) below explains the absence of self and what belongs to self. Cognition and awareness (*buddhi*) are common to both outsiders and the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

The Sāṃkhya outsiders assert that awareness is the characteristic of the spirit (*puruṣa*); the Vaiśeṣika assert that knowledge (*jñāna*) is the characteristic of the spirit. Both cling to the spirit as the self. Now, there is neither cognition nor awareness.

In its ultimate nature, the self is fundamentally non-existent. If one follows the perspective of the Hīnayāna, with respect to the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is called "feeling" (*jue*) and the other three aggregates are called "cognition" (*zhi*).
With respect to the six sense bases (*āyatana*), body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) is called "feeling," while the remaining five are called "cognition.

Because the five aggregates perform karma, they are termed the "agent" (*kartṛ*); because the aggregates receive retribution, they are termed the "experiencer" (*bhoktṛ*). Now, all such [conceptions] are refuted.
All say there is none. This is like the analogy of grass and trees below, which signifies the meaning of lacking sentience.
Yet all sentient beings do not awaken to this and do not know it.

Third, regarding that inverted contemplation of both [suffering and pleasure]: false suffering is fundamentally empty, yet one attains it without awakening; true bliss is fundamentally present, yet one fails to realize it.

To lose [the truth] and not know it—seeking pleasure while far from it and approaching suffering—is called "perversion" (*viparyāsa*). The three preceding contemplations constitute the conclusion of the preparatory means (*upāya*).
Seeing that sentient beings do not attain liberation from such a mass of suffering, the Bodhisattva consequently gives rise to Great [Compassion].
With compassion and wisdom, he further reflects: "I must rescue all these sentient beings and establish them in the state of ultimate peace and happiness.
Thereupon, the great light of the wisdom of loving-kindness arises.
Second, the correct arousal of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). First, it clarifies the arising of compassion, meaning that seeing suffering, one should pull [beings] out of it.

Next, it further establishes the arising of loving-kindness, meaning that since they lack happiness, one should grant it to them; for it is said that those who possess suffering necessarily do not know happiness.
Thus concludes the superior practice of the two types of compassion within the ten practices. Below follows the practice of giving (*dāna*).

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accords with such great compassion and great loving-kindness, and dwells in the first stage with a profound and respectful mind, they feel no stinginess regarding any object; seeking the great wisdom of a Buddha, they practice great relinquishment.
The fourth is the practice of giving (*dāna*). This section consists of three parts: first, a general explanation of the practice of giving; second, a specific elucidation of the objects given;

and third, a summary of the completion of the practice. Regarding the first part, there are five phrases. The first clarifies the basis upon which giving relies, namely, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Second, by means of "profound and heavy" and below, its stage of practice (*pratipatti*) is revealed, because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is attained at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

By "at all [beings]" and below, the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the gift are clarified. "Seeking the great wisdom of the Buddha" reveals the purpose (*prayojana*) of the giving. This concludes the name of the practice of giving.
Whatever there may be that can be given—namely, wealth, grain, treasuries, gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and other such items;
precious jewels, necklaces, and ornaments for adorning the body;

elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, male and female slaves, subjects, cities, towns, villages, gardens, groves, palaces, towers, wives, concubines, sons, daughters, and all those both internal and external.
One's retinue and all other precious objects of enjoyment, as well as one's head, eyes, hands, feet, flesh,
blood, marrow, and bones— all parts of the body— are not to be begrudged. Second,
regarding all inferior and specific items of giving, this specifically clarifies that, as stated above, there is no stinginess whatsoever in giving.
There are two kinds: first, external giving, which refers to wealth, grain, the four requisites, and so forth; second, internal giving, which refers to one's head, eyes, and so forth.
This is practiced for the sake of seeking the vast wisdom of all Buddhas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of great relinquishment while dwelling in the First Stage.

Third, the concluding summary of the accomplishment of practice for the sake of the lower [stages]. First, the summary of the purpose: this is called the "correct conclusion of the accomplishment of practice.
However, the practice of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) should fully comprise the three types of giving; here, it mentions only material giving (*āmiṣadāna*) because it is predominant.

Fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) is attained only from the second and third stages onward, while the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is practiced from the fourth stage upward. Thus concludes the four types of giving.
O Son of the Buddha, because the bodhisattva, with this mind of great compassionate giving,

seeks out further all mundane and supramundane matters of benefit for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings without weariness or fatigue, they immediately achieve the state of a mind free from weariness.

The fifth is the practice of tirelessness. Within this, there are three parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, "furthermore" and so forth, which correctly reveals the characteristics of the practice;
third, "thereby attaining" and so forth, which concludes by establishing the practice as a whole. The fifth, the practice of tirelessness, is complete.
Having attained a mind free from weariness and fatigue, one’s mind will have no timidity regarding any sūtras or śāstras.
Because there is no timidity, one immediately achieves mastery of the wisdom of all sūtras and śāstras.
The sixth stage is the knowledge of the practice of the sūtras and śāstras.
Having attained this knowledge, one is well able to deliberate upon what should and should not be done.

Toward all sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—one acts accordingly, according to their capacity, and according to their habitual inclinations. For this reason, the bodhisattva achieves the status of a World-Honored One.

Wisdom. The seventh is the accomplishment of worldly wisdom (*loka-jñāna*). "According to what is appropriate" means according to what is suitable for the individual's capacity; that is, by means of whatever dharma is fitting.

"According to one's own power" means according to what one's own intellectual power can accomplish, or according to what another's intellectual power is capable of. "According to what has been practiced" means...
Manifesting in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, as explained in the treatises according to what is appropriate,

once worldly wisdom has been perfected, one knows the proper time and the proper measure, adorning oneself with shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), and diligently cultivates the path of self-benefit and the benefit of others;
thus, one achieves the adornment of shame and remorse.

The eighth is the practice of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). "Knowing the time" specifically clarifies the mode of practice (*ākāra*). There are three kinds of time: first, the time of mindfulness;

this refers to the times when it is appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, because there is not a single moment of interruption. Second, the time of day and night;

one should maintain the mind during the day, and likewise not neglect it during the first, middle, and last watches of the night. Third, the time when what is undertaken must never be abandoned. This is...
Know the proper measure. This means acting according to one's own capacity, applying both affection and exertion so as not to exceed one's limits and thereby cause exhaustion or desistance.
At this time, one cultivates the practices for the dual benefit of self and others as set forth in the preceding eight sections.

With the "sleeping snake" of the afflictions no longer intermingling day or night, one adorns oneself with the raiment of shame and dread of blame. These are the eight practices of shame and dread of blame.
Within this practice, one diligently cultivates renunciation, remaining non-regressive and non-retrogressive, thereby achieving firm strength.

The ninth is the achievement of firm strength; that is to say, it is the aforementioned sense of shame and dread of blame. Within the two types of beneficial conduct, one desires to seek liberation early;
thus, one should be diligent and not regress from one's own portion, nor turn back from superior progress. This is the ninth: the practice of firm strength.
Having attained firm strength, one diligently makes offerings to the Buddhas and is able to practice the Buddha’s teachings exactly as they were taught.
This is the tenth practice, the practice of making offerings. This practice of offering material goods and services encompasses both types of offerings.
O Son of the Buddha, in this way the bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas that purify the stages (*bhūmi*). They are: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, equanimity, being free from weariness;
knowledge of the various sūtras and śāstras; skillful understanding of worldly dharmas; firm power of shame and dread of blame; making offerings to all Buddhas;
and practicing in accordance with the teachings.
The third major section, "O Son of the Buddha," concludes the ten names, their essence, and their function. First, the essence and function are concluded:

that which is referred to as the "essence and function" refers to these ten as the dharmas that purify the various stages (*bhūmi*), because they counteract the ten obstacles. Next, the names are concluded with the words "That which is called... and so forth. Regarding the essence and function: these ten are precisely the dharmas for purifying the various stages, because they treat the ten obstacles.

The hindrances are as previously explained. Question: In the previous section on the Stage of Abiding (*anusthāna-bhūmi*), there were thirty phrases, which were also termed faith, compassion, and so forth;
how does this differ from them? The treatise answers: The former refers to purification, whereas the dharmas of this stage are restricted to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Now, all these [practices] exhaustively purify the obstacles of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Because these ten kinds of dharmas are able to purify and cultivate all the stages, the second superior practice—based on aspiration and its cultivation—is hereby concluded.
The third major section: the superior evaluation of the benefits of the fruit, which constitutes the fruit of the stages (*bhūmi*). There are four kinds of fruits: first, the fruit of refinement;

second, the fruit of setting forth; third, the fruit of retribution-gathering; and fourth, the fruit of vow-knowledge. They are collectively termed "fruits" because they are fully perfected within the stages.
Specifically, "refinement" refers to tempering and maturing [the faculties] so that one may provide offerings and gather in [beings] for their transformation.
Faith and the other ten practices are that which is to be refined. Through the performance of offerings and so forth, faith is made supple and serviceable according to one's will;
therefore, it is called "refinement" (*karmanya*). The analogy of refining gold below [in the text] makes its meaning very clear.

Second, regarding "setting out" (*prasthāna*): "setting out" means to advance, and "setting toward" means to move forward; it refers to setting out from this stage and moving toward each subsequent stage.
It serves as that which is set forth. This is very similar in meaning to the parable of the inferior merchant. Third, regarding the fruit of the maturation of rewards (*vipākaphala*):

the body of a royal station is called "retribution" (*vipāka*) because it compensates for causes; it is called "appropriation" (*saṃgraha*) because it receives the fruit once the causes have been established. Fourth, the power of internal realization and aspiration.
Mastery over teaching and wisdom causes the application of activity to be boundless; therefore, it is called the fruit of the knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).

Regarding the text, the "setting forth" (*prasthāna*) is restricted to the first stage (*bhūmi*), but its meaning extends through all ten stages. For the remaining three, their meaning is restricted to the first stage, while their text extends through all ten stages.
O Son of the Buddha, once a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy, through the power of their great vows they are able to see many Buddhas—
namely, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas,
many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of quadrillions of Buddhas, many quintillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of quintillions of Buddhas.
Many thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

The fifth is the fruit of the four stages, which constitutes four distinct parts. Now, first is the fruit of refinement (*praśrabdhi*). This passage contains the dharma, the metaphor, and the application. Within the dharma, there are four points:
first, seeing the Buddha as the condition for refining one's practice; second, [the realization that] all [phenomena] below are the essence of the practice being refined; third...
The first two [stages] distinguish the modes of practice for descending to other levels. The latter four are the maturation of the Bodhisattva’s practice through refinement as they descend.

Regarding the first [of these], the power of the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) is the cause for seeing the Buddha; this power encompasses both spiritual power (*bala*) and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Thus, the treatise states:

"By means of superior supernatural powers and illusions, one sees the Buddha in his form-body (*rūpakāya*); by means of the power of correct vows, one sees the Buddha as the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This refers to the Buddha as the dharma-body of merit.

Regarding the phrase "many hundreds," this refers to many hundreds and many thousands. However, since the one already encompasses the many, in principle, one truly enters the Flower-Treasury Sea of Lands and beholds the cloud-like bodies of the Dharma-realm.

With a universal mind and a profound mind, they honor, revere, serve, and make offerings to them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life, offering these gifts to them all.

They likewise make offerings to the entire Saṅgha, dedicating all these roots of goodness toward unexcelled enlightenment. O Son of the Buddha, it is because this Bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas...
Therefore, one attains the dharma of maturing sentient beings.
Second, regarding the essence of the practice being refined, it is called "refining" because one enters practice through practice, just as gold is placed in fire.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of entry: first, entering merit, which refers to the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas; this removes the defilement of meager merit. Second, by means of this...
When the roots of goodness descend into the unsurpassed fruit, they are immediately turned upward; this removes the defilement of inferiority.
Third, O sons of the Buddha, when this bodhisattva descends into the mind of great compassion, it constitutes the practice of benefiting sentient beings; this removes the defilement of indolence.
The first two means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—namely, generosity (*dāna*) and pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*)—are used to gather sentient beings.

As for the latter two means of attraction, they are practiced solely through the power of faith and understanding; they have not yet been fully mastered. Among the Bodhisattva’s ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is predominant, though the other perfections are not unpracticed;
they are simply cultivated according to one's strength and capacity.
Regarding the third section, the characteristics of the distinct stages (*bhūmi-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): first, we shall consider them in terms of the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*).

Now, while these four means of attraction are still methods for benefiting sentient beings when viewed in relation to what precedes them, they constitute the characteristics of the distinct stages when viewed in relation to what follows. Because they provide the opportunity for benefiting sentient beings, they are explained here. Kind speech (*priyavāditā*) is the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
Since generosity (*dāna*) is perfected in the first stage, it is said that two [means] increase; this is taught as the mark of realization for each distinct stage. Each is thus explained.

There is one increase. Because the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are difficult to differentiate, they are manifested through their association with the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). In reality, however, each stage fully cultivates all of them;
they are perfectly interfused according to their true nature, such that each contains all.
As this bodhisattva diligently practices—making offerings to all Buddhas and teaching and transforming sentient beings—they do so entirely by practicing the dharmas of the pure stages (*bhūmi*).
All their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are dedicated toward the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), which becomes increasingly bright and pure.
It becomes supple, perfected, and serviceable according to one's will.

Regarding the maturation of the practices to be refined (*parikarma*), three entries are subsumed in total. First, it cites making offerings to the Buddhas and generating through transformation as the "refiner" (*parikarman*).
Faith and other pure dharmas are taken as the "refined" (*parikārya*). Later, the aforementioned dedication is raised as the "refiner" of faith and the other pure dharmas.
As for the term "successively" (*paryāya-paryāya*): this refers to how these [dharmas of] faith and so forth are purified across the three stages within the first bhūmi; that is, the first...
While dwelling on this stage, one realizes the previously cultivated conditions and causes them to become true cultivation; thus, it is already once purified.

Furthermore, within the second section on the comparative evaluation of practices, it is purified once more in contrast to the methods for removing hindrances. Now, after this stage, one again undergoes three further cultivations; therefore, it is said to be "progressively purified."
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a skilled goldsmith who repeatedly smelts gold in fire, making it increasingly bright and pure, until it becomes supple and perfected,
fit for use according to one's will.
In the second analogy, the goldsmith represents the bodhisattva; the gold represents faith and the other [perfections]; and the fire represents the three practices, such as making offerings.
Since these three practices are not singular, one enters them repeatedly. "Tempering and achieving perfection" refers to the accomplishment of the practice through refinement.

Before faith and the various practices have realized the Truth, they are merely practices of cultivation based on conditions (*pratyaya*) serving as antidotes; their essence is false cognition (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). Upon realization...

Only after realizing the Truth does one come to know that faith and the other [virtues] are not merely present now; they are, in fact, the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the Tathāgatagarbha, with the True Mind as their essence.
Now that the Truth has been realized, the Truth is manifested by means of signs (lakṣaṇa); therefore, the distinction between subject and object is established.
The Bodhisattva is also like this. Making offerings to all Buddhas and teaching and transforming sentient beings are all for the sake of practicing the dharmas of the pure stages.
All roots of goodness are dedicated toward the stage of omniscience, which becomes increasingly bright and pure;
it is harmonized, perfected, and rendered serviceable at will.
The third point, the correspondence with the Dharma, may be understood by analogy with the parable. O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the First Ground, they should seek out and inquire from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained within this ground, never feeling weary or satisfied, desiring to bring them to fulfillment.
Regarding these dharmas of this stage, one should likewise seek out and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and spiritual friends concerning the characteristics and the fruits attained within the second stage, never feeling satiated, in order to bring those dharmas of that stage to fulfillment.
In this same manner, one should also investigate and inquire regarding the characteristics and the attainment of the fruits within the third, fourth, fifth, sixth,
seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, never becoming weary or satisfied, for the purpose of accomplishing the dharmas of those stages.

Within the second section, the "Fruit of Setting Out," there are two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the fruit of setting out; second, the summary of the characteristics of the stage, beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha.
The former consists of four sections: 1) the Dharma (the teaching); 2) the metaphor; 3) the application; and 4) the conclusion. Within the section on the Dharma, there are also four parts:
1) the question; 2) knowledge; 3) practice; and 4) arrival. "Knowledge" refers to clear understanding, which is the actual capacity for setting out. However, due to...
Question: It is known through inquiry. The reason for questioning first is that knowledge lies in practice; through practice, one will surely reach the goal.

Although the first stage (*bhūmi*) is already fulfilled, the reason for questioning again is twofold: first, to inquire about further advancement; second, because within a single stage all the merits of every stage are fully contained.
Regarding the question on the characteristics and the attainment of the fruit: "characteristics" refers to those possessed within each respective stage.
This is because they consist of the characteristics of the obstacles and their remedies; that is to say, the characteristics of the subject and object of observation in the various stages (*bhūmi*).

"Attainment" refers to the correct realization of supramundane wisdom. "Fruit" refers to the acquisition of mundane and supramundane wisdom through the power of having realized that [supramundane] wisdom.

The marks are the wisdom of skillful means; attaining this is the fundamental wisdom. The fruit is the subsequently attained wisdom. Because the subsequently attained wisdom takes conventional reality as its object, it is called "worldly";
yet because it is non-conceptual, it is also called "transcendent."

This bodhisattva skillfully knows the obstacles to the stages and their remedies; skillfully knows the formation and destruction of the stages; skillfully knows the characteristics and fruits of the stages; skillfully knows the cultivation for attaining the stages;
skillfully knows the purification of the dharmas of the stages; skillfully knows the progression from stage to stage;

skillfully knows what is possible and impossible regarding each stage; skillfully knows the superior wisdom of each stage; skillfully knows the non-retrogression of each stage; and skillfully knows...
The second is the clear knowledge that purifies all the bodhisattva stages and leads one to enter the stage of a Tathāgata;
it is known through questioning, for it is understood to be no different from the question itself.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus well understands the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), they initiate practice in the first stage without interruption;
in this manner, it continues until they enter the tenth stage without any cessation. By means of the light of wisdom of these various stages, they achieve the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Third, regarding the Bodhisattva’s practice of descending: it should be understood that he subsequently descends from there.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a caravan leader who is skilled in expedient means and wishes to lead a multitude of merchants to a great city;
before setting out, he first inquires about the merits and defects along the way, as well as whether the places where they might rest are safe or perilous.
Thereafter, having fully equipped the provisions for the path, they perform what is to be done.

O Son of the Buddha, although that great caravan leader has not yet set out, he is able to know all matters of safety and danger within the journey; he skillfully weighs and examines them with wisdom.
Providing all that was required so that there was no lack, he led the multitude of merchants until they reached that great city in safety;
both he and the people were entirely freed from distress and calamity.
In the second analogy, the first analogy contains two preliminary methods: first, the method of non-delusion;

the "traveling on the road" metaphor represents the cultivation of causes, while "stopping and dwelling" represents the attainment of stages. Because each has its respective obstacles and remedies, they are termed "safety and danger.

Second, the method of requisites; because it involves the accumulation of provisions, non-delusion primarily concerns the benefit of others, whereas the requisites primarily clarify self-benefit. Next...

"O Son of the Buddha, that great merchant leader is understood through the following analogy: 'skillfully using wisdom' is the analogy for practice; 'the four [stages]' up to the end is the analogy for arrival.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva merchant leader is also like this: dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he skillfully knows the obstacles and their remedies for all stages."
He masters [the stages] up to thoroughly knowing all the bodhisattva grounds and their pure transition into the Tathāgata ground.

Thereafter, he becomes fully endowed with the provisions of merit and wisdom. He leads all sentient beings through the vast wilderness and perilous difficulties of birth and death, enabling them to reach the city of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) in safety, such that neither his own person nor the sentient beings undergo any suffering or hardship.

In the third correspondence, first the correspondence regarding knowledge is established; subsequently, the correspondence regarding practice is set forth. "Peaceful" corresponds to arrival. In the parable, practice is abbreviated;
in the correspondence, the question is abbreviated. This is intended merely to reveal the underlying meaning.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should always cultivate the sublime pure deeds of the various stages with tireless diligence, until entering the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The fourth section, which provides a concluding exhortation, may be understood accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called a brief explanation of the gate for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas entering the first stage of a Bodhisattva.
Were it explained extensively, there would be immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya varieties of matters.
The second section, "The Disciples of the Buddha," concludes the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*). Since the cultivation of practice has been completed, the conclusion is made here.

What was previously explained was a partial description because the scope was profound; what is stated here is exhaustive because it is detailed. Thus, that which was not fully exhausted before is now fully expressed.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this first stage (*bhūmi*), he frequently becomes a king of Jambudvīpa, possessing great nobility and sovereign power, and constantly protects the True Dharma.

[The third major section, "The Resultant Reward," which concerns the excellence of benefit, is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the results for those living as householders; second...]

If this bodhisattva wishes to descend to the fruit of leaving the household life, there are again two parts within the former: first, the superior body, which manifests the excellence of his retribution;
second, the ability to perform great giving, which clarifies the excellence of that superior fruit. Now, for the first [point], regarding the king of Jambudvīpa:
The Iron Wheel-Turning King constantly protects the True Dharma; this should be considered the excellence of his conduct.
He is able to gather in sentient beings through great giving, skillfully removing the defilement of their stinginess and greed.
He constantly practices great giving without end, employing the four means of attraction: generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
Second, regarding the superior fruits that transcend [the former]: based upon the aforementioned royal retribution, one initiates superior practices, which constitute the fruit of this body.

This consists of two parts: first, practice; second, aspiration. Within the first part, there are also two: first, great compassion for the benefit of others, which refers to both giving and gathering [disciples].
In this way, all actions performed are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Saṃgha,

never apart from mindfulness of fellow bodhisattvas, never apart from mindfulness of bodhisattva practices, never apart from mindfulness of the pāramitās, never apart from mindfulness of the stages (bhūmis),
never apart from mindfulness of the powers (bala), never apart from mindfulness of the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and never apart from mindfulness of the unique qualities (āveṇika).
The Buddha-dharma, up to and including not being separated from mindfulness and being fully endowed with the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes.
Second, not losing one's own benefit: because when one is actually performing the work of benefiting others, one is not separated from mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth.
That is to say, by dedicating the work of benefiting others toward enlightenment, one accomplishes deeds of great merit; because no conceptual discrimination arises.
Eliminating all deluded thoughts, because one accords with principle and merges with the essence, it is said that they are "not separate.
Furthermore, one forms this thought: "I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings;
the most excellent, the most preeminent, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the commander, and even [the leader] of all."
Regarding the basis of the knowledge of knowledge (*jñānajñāna*):
there are further eleven phrases that clarify the subsequent vow. The first seven concern one's own virtues, while the latter four concern the gathering and transformation [of others].

The first [phrase] is exclusively general, meaning that the state of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is supreme and exalted. "Sublime" (*praṇīta*) and so forth are exclusively specific; "victorious" (*viśiṣṭa*) and "great" (*mahat*) are both general and specific.
They are also distinct. "Guiding" (nāyaka) refers to discerning the meaning of the Dharma; "leading" (vināyaka) means causing others to attain realization by extinguishing all afflictions.
The latter two refer to wisdom, representing cause and effect respectively. "Directing" (praṇāyaka) means teaching and commanding entry into the right path;
the final phrase refers to teaching and transforming through great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
If this bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life and practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they are able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires,
and go forth to study the Way according to the Tathāgata’s teaching. Having gone forth, they practice with diligent vigor and,
in a single moment of thought, attain one hundred samādhis, behold one hundred buddhas, know the spiritual powers of one hundred buddhas, and can shake one hundred buddha-fields.
He can traverse a hundred Buddha-worlds, illuminate a hundred Buddha-worlds, and transform the sentient beings of a hundred worlds.
He can abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas, know the events of a hundred kalpas each in both the past and the future, enter a hundred Dharma-gates, and manifest a hundred bodies.
Within each body, he can manifest a hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue.
Regarding the second [section], the fruits of renunciation: first is the abandonment of the secular life to enter the monastic order;

subsequently, "having already left" and so forth refers to practicing as a member of the community and attaining the superior karma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). There are two types of such superior karma: first, the excellence of *samādhi*.

This refers to the essence of supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The excellence produced by the two types of *samādhi* means that through *samādhi*, one attains such things as the vision of the Buddhas;

the text contains eleven phrases that clarify these two benefits. The first two phrases concern self-benefit: (1) "seeing a hundred Buddhas" refers to the ten bodies of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the ten directions, each numbering ten;
(2) "knowing their spiritual power" means apprehending the empowerment they bestow. The next four phrases concern the benefit [of others].

First, for those with the capacity for faith, he moves world-systems and manifests supernatural powers. Next, for those with the capacity for awakening, he travels to other lands, illuminates them with light, and directly imparts the Dharma.

Next, there are two phrases concerning the vertical discussion of the two benefits: prolonging his life to remain throughout kalpas. Finally, the last three phrases concern the swiftness of the two benefits.

If, by means of the Bodhisattva’s extraordinary power of aspiration, they manifest with sovereign mastery beyond these numbers— for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas— it would be impossible to calculate or know them.
The fourth is the fruit of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*). Having long accumulated right vows, because wisdom illuminates within, its sovereign manifestations are difficult to fathom.
This demonstrates that the hundredfold distinctions of the stages mentioned above are not fixed. Now, practice accords with the *dharmadhātu*;
this is the virtue of perfect interfusion and reality. Therefore, it is said to "transcend this. The following verse provides the summary.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person accumulates manifold virtues, Is fully endowed with pure and white dharmas, Makes offerings to the Honored One of Gods and Humans, And follows the path of compassion;
If their faith and understanding are exceedingly vast, And their aspirations and inclinations are likewise pure."
To seek the wisdom of the Buddha, One generates this unsurpassed mind.
(II) The second section, the *udāna* (verses), consists of forty-six and a half verses. It is divided into two major parts: first, the actual verses corresponding to the preceding prose;

second, the concluding summary. Within the first part, there are four sections. The first, consisting of eleven verses, corresponds to the "Abiding" (*vihāra*) section. This is further divided into four subsections; the first two correspond to the "Basis" (*āśraya*).
By what body?
Through the power of omniscience purified in every way, as well as the fearlessnesses;
by accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas to gather and protect the multitudes of sentient beings; and for the sake of attaining great compassion and turning the supreme wheel of Dharma.
To purify the Buddha-lands, they give rise to this most supreme mind;
In a single thought-moment, they know the three periods of time without discrimination. Though various times differ, they manifest them to the world.
Briefly stated, they seek all the supreme merits of the Buddhas, And give rise to a vast and expansive mind.
Regarding the meaning of the next four verses on the equality [of the bodhisattva] with the realm of empty space:
Compassion as the precursor, wisdom as the primary, Conjoined with skillful means, And a mind purified by resolute faith.
The Tathāgata’s immeasurable power and unimpeded wisdom are manifest before him; having realized this for himself without depending on another, he is fully endowed with the qualities of a Tathāgata.
Next, the two verses explain by what causes one generates this most excellent mind.
When a Son of the Buddha first gives rise to such a wondrous jewel-mind, he transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters the sphere of the Buddhas’ activity.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, his lineage is without blemish and he is equal to the Buddhas.
He is certain to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment as soon as he has given rise to this mind.
One immediately attains entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*), Whose resolve and delight are unshakable.
For example, like the king of great mountains, The final three verses describe what characteristics he possesses:
Abounding in joy and abundant love and delight, And likewise possessing abundant pure faith, With a mind of supreme and great courage.
With a heart of jubilation, far removed from strife, affliction, and malice;
modest, respectful, and upright; well-guarding all the sense-faculties—[he possesses] all the wisdom of the peerless Saviors of the World.
The second section consists of five verses explaining the names. First, two and a half verses praise the characteristics of joy.
The lines "In this place I shall attain" and "Recalling [this], joy arises" praise the nature of joy;
the remaining verses praise the causes of joy. Within these, the first half-verse praises the recollection of what will be attained.
Upon first attaining entry into the First Stage, one immediately transcends the five fears:
fear of lack of livelihood, fear of death, fear of ill repute, fear of the miserable realms, and fear of assemblies.
Because they are free from attachment to "I" and "mine," these sons of the Buddhas remain far removed from all such fears.
The final two verses praise the present attainment of mindfulness:
Always practicing great loving-kindness and compassion, Constantly possessing faith and reverence, Equipped with the virtues of shame and dread of blame,
Increasing wholesome qualities day and night, Delighting in the true benefit of the Dharma, And having no craving for the various sensual desires.
The third section, consisting of six verses, concerns abiding in the stages (*bhūmi*). The first one and a half verses praise the accomplishment of faith:
Contemplating the Dharma as it has been heard, One practices free from grasping and attachment; Not coveting gain or honor, One delights solely in the Buddha’s bodhi.
Seeking the Buddha’s wisdom with a single mind, One applies oneself with diligence and no other thought.
Next, one and a half verses praise the accomplishment of practice:
In practicing the perfections, One remains far removed from flattery, vanity, and deception;
One practices exactly as taught and abides in truthful speech, Neither defiling the family of the Buddhas Nor abandoning the bodhisattva precepts.
Not delighting in worldly affairs, one constantly benefits the world; practicing virtue without weariness, one seeks ever more excellent paths.
Thus, delighting in the Dharma, one accords with the meaning of merit.
(The final three verses praise the accomplishment of dedication.)
Constantly giving rise to the mind of great aspiration, I vow to behold all Buddhas;
Upholding the teachings of all Buddhas, I shall embrace the path of the Great Sages.
Always generating such vows, I shall practice the most supreme conduct to bring all sentient beings to maturity, Adorning and purifying the Buddha-lands throughout all Buddha-fields.
The sons of the Buddha completely pervade all, Equal and sharing a single mind; All their deeds are not in vain.
At every tip of a hair, They simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment.
Such great vows as these are immeasurable and boundless, Reaching as far as space, sentient beings, The realm of phenomena, and nirvāṇa.
When a Buddha appears in the world, the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom-mind, that which is entered by the Tathāgata’s knowledge,
and the three turnings— should all these have an end, only then would my vow come to an end;
as long as they are without end, so too shall my vow remain.
The following twenty-two and a half verses constantly arise to compare and evaluate the excellence [of this practice]. Within this section, there are three parts;
first, six and a half verses compare the excellence of the vow:
Thus one makes the great vow, With a mind that is supple and well-disciplined, Able to have faith in the Buddha’s qualities.
Observing sentient beings, he knows they arise from causes and conditions; Thus he gives rise to a mind of compassion, thinking:
"Sentient beings are thus suffering; I should now rescue and liberate them.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he practices various kinds of giving: His royal throne and precious jewels, even his elephants, horses, and chariots.
Whether it be head, eyes, hands, or feet, Even unto the very flesh and blood of his body, He is able to relinquish all of it, Attaining a heart free from sorrow or regret.
Seeking various scriptures and treatises, His mind never grows weary;
He skillfully understands their meanings and purposes, And is able to act in accordance with worldly ways, Adorning himself with a sense of shame and remorse.
The practice becomes increasingly firm; One makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Honoring and respecting them.
(The following six verses praise the measurement of practice.
Thus constantly cultivating and practicing, Without weariness day or night, One's roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Just as fire refines true gold, so the Bodhisattva dwelling herein purifies the ten stages;
their activities are unimpeded, and they are fully endowed with continuity.
These ten subsequent verses praise the result through comparison. Of these, the first two verses praise the result of pliancy.
Just as a great caravan leader, for the benefit of the merchant folk, Inquires about the path— its dangers and ease—
to reach the great city in safety, So too should one know that the Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage Is likewise courageous and unobstructed, reaching the tenth stage.
The next two verses praise the fruit of setting forth.
Abiding in this first stage, one acts as a great king of merit;
transforming sentient beings through the Dharma with a compassionate mind free from harm, one rules over Jambudvīpa, such that there is nowhere his transformative conduct does not reach.
Causing all to abide in great equanimity and achieve the wisdom of a Buddha;
Desiring to seek the most supreme path, one relinquishes their own royal throne.
If one can, within the Buddha’s teaching, Vigorously and diligently practice, Then one will attain a hundred samādhis, Behold a hundred Buddhas, And cause a hundred worlds to tremble.
The illumination of their conduct is likewise; they transform sentient beings in a hundred lands, enter into a hundred Dharma-gates, and are able to know the events of a hundred eons.
They manifest a hundred bodies and appear with a hundred bodhisattvas as their retinue.
The next five verses summarize the fruit of retribution.
As for the line "If by the power of sovereign vows," it exceeds this number immeasurably;
the latter half-verse summarizes the fruit of the knowledge of vows.
I have briefly described a small portion of the meaning of this stage; were one to wish to analyze it in detail, even billions of eons would not suffice.
Such is the supreme path of the Bodhisattvas, which benefits all living beings.
Thus, I have now completed the explanation of the Dharma of the First Stage.
The two verses conclude the exposition. The first Joyous Ground (Pramuditā-bhūmi) is finished.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
commentary on the meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang;
and edited and summarized by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter, Part Two: The Second Ground, the Stainless (Vimalā).

Regarding the reason for its presentation, the *Śāstra* states: "Having thus realized the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), by means of the supramundane path and based upon pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), the second Bodhisattva ground, the Stainless, is explained. As for the term "state of certainty":

This refers to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*), which is supramundane (*lokottara*). Based upon this, one cultivates the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), of which ethical discipline (*śīla*) is foremost.

Although the preceding stages involve the realization of truth, there may still be lapses in discipline due to inadvertent transgressions. Furthermore, the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) are used to clarify the respective stages.

Since this precept was bestowed previously, it is explained next. The following eight [stages] follow this same principle. Regarding the term "free from defilement" (*vimalā*): Maitreya says that it is because one has utterly distanced oneself from the defilement of violating the precepts;
that is to say, it is achieved through one's innate nature, rather than being a precept guarded through deliberation as on the first stage (*bhūmi*).

It is also called "superior precept" (*adhiśīla*). Abiding in this stage, one abandons the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to that which is associated with the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
A portion of [inherent] birth and the three types of karma arising from erroneous transgressions can obstruct the second bhūmi.

For this reason, it is said that on the second bhūmi one abandons two delusions along with their coarse residues (*dausthulya*). First is the delusion of subtle erroneous transgression, which is the aforementioned portion of the innate [birth];
this is capable of giving rise to karma. Second is the delusion regarding various courses of action, which refers to the three types of karma arising from those erroneous transgressions.
Regarding the term "supreme *tathatā*": it means that this *tathatā* possesses boundless virtues and is the most supreme among all phenomena (*dharma*).
This is also because, by reversing the fault of violating the precepts, one achieves boundless virtues; thus, through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one attains supremacy.
Upon hearing of these most supreme and subtle stages, the minds of all the bodhisattvas were completely purified;
they were all filled with joy, rose from their seats, and leaping into the midst of the air,
scattered exquisite flowers above while simultaneously offering praise together.

Next is the formal explanation of the text, which is divided into three parts: first, the section on praise and request; second, the section on the formal exposition; and third, the section on the restatement in verse.
Now, for the first part: the five verses are divided into two sections. The first three celebrate having heard about the first bhūmi, while the latter two request the exposition of the second bhūmi.
Regarding the former, the first two verses describe the narrator’s celebration of joy through the three types of action (body, speech, and mind).
Excellent, Vajragarbha! You of great wisdom and fearlessness have well explained the dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas on this stage.
[The text] concludes the preceding request and introduces what follows with these words of praise.

The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure and that they delighted in hearing all the characteristics of the practices belonging to the second bhūmi, immediately requested Vajragarbha: "O Greatly Wise One, please expound upon this;
the sons of the Buddha all delight in hearing about the second bhūmi wherein they dwell."
The latter two [sections] consist of the initial introduction and the subsequent request.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already cultivated the first stage and wishes to enter the second stage, they should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve."
In the second section, the "Section on the Correct Exposition," the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) are first clarified, followed by the manifestation of the fruits of the stages.

Within the former, there are two parts: first, the "purity of arousal," which is the mind that enters the stage; second, the "mind that dwells in the stage," beginning with the passage: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells here in the Stainless [Stage]...
The correct practice within the stage itself is called "purity of essence. This arises from the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*).
This is called "Initiating Purity. The first part [of this section] has three divisions: the heading, the enumeration, and the conclusion. This is now the first, the heading.

"Deep mind" (*gambhīra-citta*) refers to profound accord with both principle and phenomena; therefore, "deep" is designated as the heading while "straight" (*ṛju*) is enumerated [in the body]. Though the meaning is one, the names differ.

As for "straight mind," it causes the innate purity of one's own essence and the accomplishment of natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*). There are two types of natural morality: first, that which is formed through long-term accumulation; second, that which is true...

Just as there is no stain of broken precepts within the nature of reality (*tathatā*), it is now called "maintaining suchness" (*tathatā-dhāraṇa*). Because it causes the nature to be perfected, it is termed "accomplishment.

What are these ten? They are: a straightforward mind, a supple mind, a capable mind, a disciplined mind, a tranquil mind, a purely wholesome mind, an unadulterated mind, a mind free from attachment, a vast mind, and a great mind.

In the enumeration of the two inquiries, there are ten phrases. The first phrase is the general [category], while the remaining nine are the specific [categories]. Within the specific categories, the first four are the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*);
the next three are the gathering of virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*); and the final two are the benefiting of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā*).
By means of these ten mental states, the bodhisattva attains entry into the second stage, the "Stainless" (*vimalā*).

This constitutes the third phase: the stage of entering through the completion of preparatory practices. Because these aforementioned ten mental states have been accomplished in their superior grade and are utterly perfected, one enters this abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla-vihāra*).
These ten mental states serve as the purity of initiation; regarding the first of the following sections, the "purity of the essential nature" (*svabhāva-śuddhi*):

The three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) are explained as follows, divided into three: first, the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*); second, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*);

and third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*). These three groups of precepts encompass the preceding three stages: the first encompasses the Stage of Preparing the Ground (*caryā-pratipatti-sthiti*);

the second encompasses the Stage of Beneficial Conduct (*anugraha-caryā*), because therein one contemplates how sentient beings fall into evil states and so forth; and the last encompasses the Stage of Unbreakable Dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*), namely:
The vow of wisdom and so forth does not impair the Jewel of the Dharma and the others. Restraint (saṃvara) pertains to both abstention and performance;
the gathering of virtue (kuśalasaṃgraha) concerns only virtuous conduct. These two [vows] pertain to one's own benefit, while the latter [vow] pertains solely to the benefit of others.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), this initial section on ethical discipline (*śīla*) is divided into three parts. First is the designation of its basis, which refers to the predominance of the ethical discipline of the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.
By nature, they are naturally far removed from all killing; they do not keep weapons or staves, nor do they harbor resentment.

Possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, they are fully endowed with benevolence and forbearance. Toward all sentient beings who possess life, they constantly give rise to thoughts of benefit and loving-kindness.
Such a bodhisattva does not even distress sentient beings with an evil mind, much less toward another whom they perceive as a living being.
Therefore, one carries out acts of killing with a heavy heart.
Second, the actual manifestation of the precepts: within this, there are the ten paths of wholesome karma, which constitute ten sections. Now, first is the abstention from killing.
This is divided into two parts. First, a general explanation; second, a specific exposition beginning with "not keeping" [livestock]. Now, for the first:

"naturally and inherently avoiding" belongs to the category of abstaining from killing, yet its meaning encompasses the following nine precepts. This refers to the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) as naturally perfected, which constitutes the natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*).

However, there are three kinds of detachment (*virati*): first, detachment through formal commitment, which refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); second, detachment through skillful means, which refers to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*);
and third, detachment by its very nature (*svabhāva*), which refers to the Bodhisattvas who have realized the ultimate true nature and whose own being is inherently undefiled.

Furthermore, there are four types of detachment: detachment from active manifestations (*samudācāra*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); detachment from seeds (*bīja*) upon entering the stages; and the removal of transgressions to reveal the [Buddha-]nature.

"Purity" corresponds precisely to the second stage (*bhūmi*). Next, the three types of renunciation (*virati*) within the intermediate state are specifically revealed: first, renunciation of causes, which means being free from the causal conditions for killing;

second, renunciation through the application of antidotes regarding all lower [states], which means being free from the methods of killing; third, renunciation through the conduct of the fruit, as in "the Bodhisattva...
and so forth, which refers to being free from the karmic act of killing itself. Since one is currently not killing, it is called "renunciation of the fruit."

By nature, he does not steal. A bodhisattva always knows contentment with his own resources and, out of compassion and forbearance toward others, has no desire to encroach upon or damage their property.
If an object belongs to another, he perceives it as such; he never gives rise to a thought of theft regarding it.
He would not take even a blade of grass if it were not given, much less any other means of livelihood.

The second [precept] is abstaining from stealing. The first phrase provides a general definition: taking what is not given by means of irrational methods that damage another's wealth is called "stealing.

Within the specific explanation, there are also three parts: first, abstention through the cause; second, abstention through the antidote, beginning with "in relation to others"; and third, abstention through the fruit of practice, beginning with "if the object.
Regarding the cause, "cessation" refers to having few desires, and "contentment" refers to being self-sufficient; one should even give rise to cessation regarding what one already possesses.
He is content; therefore, he commits no theft.
By nature he is free from sexual misconduct. A bodhisattva is satisfied with his own wife and does not seek the wives of others.

Even toward the wives or concubines of others, women protected by their kin, those betrothed through a matchmaker, or those protected by the Dharma, he does not give rise to even a single thought of lustful attachment.
How much more so for those who engage in such acts, or those that are contrary to the Way.

Third is the abstention from sexual misconduct. That which deviates from principle is called "perverse" (邪); deep attachment is called "lust" (婬). Within this category, there are also three parts. First is abstention by cause:
this refers to being content with one's own wife. This also has two meanings: first, internal contentment, which abandons the causal basis [of desire].

Second, regarding the wife’s form as being self-sufficient: because he has abandoned the causes for taking and keeping [a wife], this is due to the fact that his manifested retribution is similar to that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), who likewise appears to have wives and concubines in accordance with worldly custom. Second, regarding the abandonment through its antidote:
this means not seeking the wives of others, because his present conduct is pure; nor does he seek the form of a wife for the future, as the wives of others need not even be mentioned. Third.
Regarding the abandonment of misconduct with the wives of others, there are also coarse and subtle levels. The subtle refers to the arising of the intention; the coarse refers to the actual act.
As for the nature of not lying, a bodhisattva always speaks words that are truthful, real, and timely, even in dreams.
One may speak words that conceal [faults] out of patience, yet without the intention to do so; how much less would one intentionally commit an offense? Fourth is the abandonment of false speech.
To act contrary to one's perception and to turn away from the mind is what is called "false. This is divided into two parts: first, abandonment through antidotes;

second, abandonment through the practice of the fruit, starting from "even unto... Now, for the first, abandonment through antidotes: this refers to abandonment at the level of the cause, not as a separate category.

The clarification of the cause has two meanings. First, there are no external objects; that is, because there are no external objects such as weapons, staves, wives, or wealth, there is no cause for their acceptance or possession.
Second, there is no distinct cause; that is, the mere intention to deceive others is itself the cause of lying.

There is no separate factor such as greed that serves as a distinct cause, because a distinct cause is simply the arising of that [deceptive] mind. Apart from that deceptive mind, [there is no other cause].
This refers to truthful speech. Truthful speech is the antidote to a distracted mind; therefore, the separation [from distraction] through its antidote is itself the cause of separation.

This differs from the three bodily [actions], each of which possesses all three types of separation, whereas the four vocal [actions] possess only two, and the three mental [actions] possess only one.
By nature, he does not engage in double-tongued speech. Regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattva harbors no mind of alienation and no mind of malice or harm.
He does not repeat these words to others for the sake of breaking apart those people, nor does he repeat those words to this person for the sake of breaking apart this person.
He does not cause what is not yet divided to be divided, nor does he increase what has already been divided. He takes no pleasure in alienation and does not delight in it.
To abstain from divisive speech: not to engage in divisive talk, not to utter words that cause division—whether true or untrue.
The fifth [precept] is called "abstaining from double-tongued speech" because it prevents discord. Regarding the accomplishment of divisive speech, there are two types of separation:
first, separation through remedial action; second, separation through the subsequent conduct of those already divided. As for separation through remedial action, it is as follows:
Non-disruptive conduct pertains exclusively to the mind. Conduct that is detached from its results pertains to both the mind and physical action;
this is the distinction.

By nature, one does not engage in harsh speech—namely, speech that is poisonous and harmful, speech that is coarse and rugged, speech that causes suffering to others, or speech that incites anger and resentment in others.

One completely abandons all such speech as: speech in one's presence; speech in one's absence; vile and wicked speech; vulgar and base speech; speech unpleasant to hear; speech that does not please those who hear it;
speech of anger and resentment; speech that burns the heart like fire; speech of enmity and bondage; speech of feverish affliction; unlovely speech; speech that is not delightful;
and speech capable of destroying both one’s own body and the bodies of others. One renounces all such forms of speech.
He constantly utters words that are moistening, gentle, pleasing to the mind, delightful to hear, bringing joy to those who hear them,
penetrating the hearts of people, elegant and refined, beloved by many, and gladdening many.

The speech of one whose body and mind are leaping with joy is such that the sixth [type of speech], which is not coarse or vulgar, is called "abstaining from harsh speech. This is divided into two parts: first, abstaining through the practice of the fruit;

second, "constantly practicing" and so forth. Since this is in contrast to the subsequent karmas and is viewed in relation to the remedial practice of the fruit, it does not follow the complete sequential order; therefore, the remedy is revealed first.

The latter [section] concerns that which is able to abandon [the faults]. Now, within this initial clarification of the practice of abandoning, we first clarify that which is to be abandoned, and subsequently clarify that which is able to abandon it.
In the former [section], there are seventeen phrases, each with its own distinct meaning. The first four phrases collectively manifest the essence and function of evil speech;
the subsequent thirteen phrases further elaborate upon these four. The commentary contains many meanings.

By nature, he does not engage in frivolous speech. The bodhisattva always delights in speech that is well-considered, timely, truthful, meaningful, in accordance with the Dharma, consistent with reason, skillfully disciplining, and decisive after due deliberation according to the occasion.
This bodhisattva maintains such careful consideration even in jest; how much more so when intentionally uttering words of distraction?
The seventh is called frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) because its words are improper; it is like ornate embroidery. This can be understood as a general abandonment.

Within the specific [abandonments], there are also two parts: first, the antidote, and second, the resultant practice. Regarding the former, among the eight types of speech, the first serves as the general heading.
Therefore, the subsequent summary states: "Even in jest, one should always deliberate before speaking. Thus, a bodhisattva always delights in the three reflections before speaking.
Then there will be no distraction. The seven subsequent phrases are distinct. The single character "time" (*kāla*) is both general and specific.

As for its general sense, the preceding statement regarding "deliberate reflection" means that one’s thoughts accord with the proper time; thus, whether speaking or remaining silent, one acts with moderation. As for its specific sense, the seven types of speech below all clarify their respective times. Briefly, there are three meanings:

first, the time of teaching and transformation, which refers to being in accordance with the capacities of those to be taught. Second, [the time of... Third, [the time of... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated).
The three types of speech regarding the Dharma of actual meaning at the time of instruction consist of the three forms of admonitory speech that accord with reason and so forth;

these correspond to the five meanings found in the Vinaya: first, *prajñapti* (proclamation), which refers to the disciplinary treatment of those who have committed an offense; second, *anuśrāvaṇā* (authorization), which refers to the authorization of those who are without offense;
third, *codanā* (accusation), which refers to the accusation of those who possess faults; and fourth, *vinayana* (subduing), which refers to subduing through appropriate means of restraint.
Regarding "skillful subduing": the fifth point, "causing joy," refers to praising those who possess genuine virtues so as to inspire them;
hence it is called "definitive. Regarding "weighing according to the occasion": whether it be a prohibition or a permission, a formal censure or a reprimand, all must be appropriate to the time.
Therefore, he summarizes these two points. In the section on the Bodhisattva’s subsequent fruits and conduct, he likewise uses light matters to illustrate heavy ones.
By nature, he is not covetous. Regarding the wealth and resources of others, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to a greedy mind;
he neither desires nor seeks them.

This is the eighth [perfection], the abandonment of greed. Below this are the three mental [actions]. As for those that serve as antidotes, since greed and the like constitute karmic existence (*karmabhava*), they are to be countered.

This is the root; there is nothing else upon which it depends. Therefore, it is not a resultant action. Since it is not a result, one cannot further establish a distinct cause for it; thus, it exists as a single entity.

Now, the first [aspect], "separation from greed," refers to the mind that is free from the desire for seeking. Within this, there are three distinct points: first, regarding the objects of others' property;
second, regarding the things used by others as their sustenance; and third, the non-arising of greed and other such afflictions. This clarifies...
The distinctions are as follows: the initial desire is called "seeking"; next, the hope that [the object] shall belong to oneself is "vow.

By nature free from anger and hatred, the bodhisattva constantly gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of harmony and moisture, and a mind of embracing.
They forever abandon malice, resentment, enmity, harm, and the feverish affliction of distress, and always contemplate...
Acting in accordance with kindness and compassion to provide benefit and aid.
Ninth, because one is free from anger and its poisonous venom, it is called "freedom from hatred. Within this section, there are three parts: first, specifically revealing the remedy;

second, permanently abandoning [the cause] to generally reveal that which is to be remedied; third, constantly reflecting [on the antidote] to categorize the general benefit of the remedy. Specifically:
The six types of mind within the middle [section] are subsumed by the treatise into five: first, the cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness toward enemies;
second, the cultivation of a mind of benefit toward those who commit evil deeds; third, the cultivation of a mind of compassion and joy toward those in poverty and suffering;

fourth, the cultivation of a mind of harmony and moisture toward sentient beings—this is termed "moistening" (*li-run*) in the treatise because it remedies their attachment to what is unprofitable; fifth...
One should give rise to a mind of gathering-in toward those who have resolved upon bodhicitta, in order to lead them to fulfillment.
Furthermore, one should be free from wrong views; the bodhisattva abides in the right path, does not practice divination, and does not adopt improper precepts.
Their mental vision is upright, being without deception or flattery, and they possess resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The tenth [point] is to be free from irrational investigation. The statement that "nature is detached" (*svabhāva-vivikta*) is merely an abbreviation of the text.

Within the specific [treatments], seven types of false views are countered: First, for those abiding in the Right Path, the view of other vehicles is countered; for the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) in relation to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is not the Right Path.
Second, the practice of divination is countered, which is the view of false discrimination; this is indeed a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Now, as for...

Good fortune, misfortune, regret, and blame arise from love and hatred; therefore, they are called "wrong views. Third, not adopting evil precepts counteracts the attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Fourth, a mind and view that are upright counteract the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Fifth, being without deception counteracts the view of concealment (*mrakṣadṛṣṭi*).
Sixth, through non-deceit, one counteracts the false manifestation of unreal views. Seventh, by descending into the Buddha-dharma, one counteracts the view of impurity.
Son of the Buddha, in this way the bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the ten paths of wholesome action, constantly and without interruption.
The third section, "The Son of the Buddha," concludes the section on superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).

Having finished the summary of the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*), he further reflects: "All sentient beings who fall into the evil destinies do so without exception because of the ten unwholesome courses of action."

Second, he further reflects upon the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). This means that it is not merely that the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*) are unimpaired and uninterrupted;

rather, the constant gathering of virtuous dharmas must likewise be without interruption or deficiency. This section is divided into three parts: first, a brief contemplation on the arising of non-virtue and the initiation of practices for gathering virtue;
second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, an extensive contemplation on obstacles and their remedies, initiating practices for gathering virtue; third, "In this manner... [and so forth].
This concludes the summary and exhortation to practice. The first section is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of contemplative wisdom;
second, from "Therefore" onwards, the clarification of the arousal of vows and practices. Regarding the first:
"Therefore, I shall personally cultivate correct practice and also exhort others to cultivate correct practice. Why is this? If..."
It is impossible for one who cannot practice correct conduct oneself to cause others to do so.

As for those who subsequently give rise to the practice of aspiration, because they contemplate the evil causes and effects of sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion and cultivate the two harmonious practices.
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects: "The ten unwholesome paths of action are the causes for rebirth in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts."
The second [section], the extensive contemplation on the arising of the remedies for obstacles within the inclusion of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*),
