refers to contemplating the fivefold categories of wholesome dharmas— namely, those of humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. It means that with respect to the supremely pure wholesome qualities of a buddha,
one gives rise to the *adhimukti-citta* (resolute mind) in order to seek, study, and practice the pure conduct of the precepts that include wholesome dharmas.
The ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) are the cause for rebirth among humans and devas, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Subsequently, the contemplation of the ten wholesome paths encompasses all dharma-gates. However, when distinguished by their general characteristics, all wholesome states are capable of acting as antidotes, because they accord with principle and benefit sentient beings, whereas the opposite constitutes evil.
The text consists of five sections; this is the first: the ten wholesome actions of humans and devas.
Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated with wisdom— yet because the mind is narrow and inferior,
because of fear of the triple world, because of the absence of great compassion, and because of understanding through hearing the voice of another— they result in the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The second section distinguishes the virtues of the three vehicles, each consisting of three parts. Now, first is the virtue of the Śrāvaka vehicle: first, the virtues to be cultivated are indicated;
next, from "by means of wisdom" onwards, the difference in the exertion employed is revealed; finally, it is concluded as the Śrāvaka vehicle, thereby establishing it as one's own vehicle.

Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated and purified, one achieves the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha because of awakening through self-realization rather than the instruction of others,
due to the lack of the skillful means of great compassion, and by realizing the profound law of dependent origination.

Third is the excellence of the pratyekabuddhas. Regarding the differences in their practice, the first phrase provides a general clarification: because they are able to cultivate it, it is called "cultivated purity";

yet, as they have not cultivated it to perfection, it is not called "complete. "Expedient means" refers to the teachings, for when pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, the ninefold canon (navāṅga-dharma) does not exist.
Furthermore, these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated to purity because the mind is vast and immeasurable; because they are endowed with compassion;
because they are embraced by skillful means; because they give rise to great vows; because they do not abandon sentient beings; because they seek the great wisdom of all Buddhas;
because they purify the various bodhisattva stages; because they purely cultivate all the perfections; and because they bring about enlightenment.
The vast and great conduct of the Bodhisattva.

Fourth, among the differences in the application of the ten wholesome paths of the Bodhisattva, there is the cultivation and purification [of these virtues]. This is the mind of self-benefit; "vast" refers to the benefit of others;
"immeasurable" refers to the Mahāyāna mind. These constitute the essence of the practice for the dual benefit [of self and others], being fully endowed with compassion and pity. This is...
The bodhisattva’s application of skillful means is subsumed by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), which is the power of his compassion.

The generation of great vows is the purification of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), corresponding to the first stage (*bhūmi*). Second, not abandoning sentient beings corresponds to the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).

Although he has attained quiescence, he does not abandon sentient beings; this corresponds to the eighth stage. Third, the aspiration for the Buddha-wisdom and so forth corresponds to receiving the [great]...
Regarding the stages, this corresponds to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, because these progressively superior ten paths of wholesome action are pure in every respect, and because one thereby realizes the ten powers (*bala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), all Buddha-dharmas are fully accomplished. Therefore, I shall now practice the ten wholesome actions equally. One should...
This causes all things to be fully endowed with purity.
The fifth [quality] is the Buddha’s excellence; "higher and higher" (uttarottara) is the general category. All the subsequent items are specific instances, of which there are four types.

The meaning clarifies that the preceding matters pertain to the Buddha, while the final one concerns the Bodhisattva’s aspiration for equality. Within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he attains mastery and complete proficiency.
Only then can it be called "fully endowed. It also extinguishes habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and is therefore termed "pure.
A bodhisattva should train in such skillful means (*upāya*).
The concluding exhortation is as may be understood.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects: "The ten unwholesome paths of action—the superior ones are the cause for rebirth in hell;
the middling ones are the cause for rebirth as an animal; and the inferior ones are the cause for rebirth as a hungry ghost."
The thirtieth [topic], the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings regarding the ten unwholesome paths of action, consists of two long sections.
First, a detailed explanation of gathering in sentient beings; second, the conclusion on the ethical discipline of benefiting others, beginning with "In this way, one maintains the precepts.

Within the former, it is shown that this ethical discipline has five increasing meanings: first, wisdom; second, aspiration; third, practice; fourth, accumulation; and fifth, the fruit of accumulation.

First, regarding "the wise": this refers to those who skillfully understand the causes and effects of the suffering of sentient beings. The text is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation of knowing the causes;

second, a specific manifestation of knowing the effects within the intermediate and lower realms; third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the conclusion establishing the causes of suffering. Now, within the initial general section:

the effects consist of the three different miserable destinies (*durgati*), while the causes consist of the three temporal stages of progression. This is termed [the "Chapter on Causes"] in the treatise.
Regarding the distinction of time, the commentary contains many meanings.
Among these, the transgression of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness.
The ten unwholesome actions are divided into ten [results]. First, regarding killing: by taking life, one causes premature death so that the natural lifespan is not completed;

thus, one obtains a short life, which is the direct outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the primary evil. Second, because the victim suffers while still alive, the perpetrator incurs much illness, which is the outflow of the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, being terrified [by the act], one lacks vital radiance, which induces external predominant conditions (*adhipati*); thus, one's requisites and material goods lack luster.
The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
Second, because one steals and thus damages another's wealth, one incurs poverty; because one prevents others from enjoying their possessions as they intend, one lacks mastery over shared property;
and as a result, external crops and seedlings are destroyed by frost and hail.
The sin of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits:
first, their spouse will not be chaste or virtuous; second, they will not obtain a retinue according to their wishes.

Among the three types of sexual misconduct, because one uses various means to seduce one's own wife so that she is not chaste and virtuous, the defilement of such lust results in external odors, filth, and dust.
As for the transgression of lying, it likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they obtain two kinds of retributive fruits.
The retribution is twofold: first, one is frequently subjected to slander; second, one is deceived by others.

These are the outflows of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Furthermore, slander pertains to the contradiction of the object, while being deceived pertains to the contradiction of the mind, because [the latter] speaks what is not real.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive results:
first, their retinue will be estranged; second, their kinsmen will be wicked.

Fifth, among the types of divisive speech, because it causes others to alienate their kin and friends and turn them into enemies, the sin of harsh speech likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they constantly hear unpleasant sounds; second, their speech is frequently embroiled in contention and litigation.
Among the six types of evil speech, because the substance of the speech is evil and its function is evil, one’s words are constantly contentious and cause distress to others.

The transgression of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they will obtain two kinds of retributive fruits.
The retribution is twofold: first, one's words are not accepted by others; second, one's speech is not clear.

Regarding the seventh [unwholesome path], frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): because one's words are not accepted by others and the listener does not comprehend them, and because one's speech is itself confused and incoherent.
The transgression of greed also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their minds know no contentment; second, they have much desire and are never satiated.

Among the eight types of covetousness, because one is dissatisfied with what has already been obtained and craves what has not yet been obtained, the transgression of malice likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they will receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are constantly subjected by others to the seeking of their faults; second, they are perpetually troubled by others.
Regarding harm:
among the nine forms of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), two types are similar outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the former, being light at first and heavy later.
This is because, seeing what is disagreeable, one seeks out its faults; and secondly, because one intends to afflict and harm that object.
The sin of wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, being born into a family of wrong views; second, having a mind that is deceitful and crooked.
The ten wrong views lead one to be reborn into a family of wrong views; because their mental vision is not upright, they are full of flattery and crookedness.
Son of the Buddha, these ten unwholesome paths of action can produce such immeasurable and boundless masses of great suffering.
The three fetters constitute the cause of suffering, for from them arises this boundless mass of suffering.
Therefore, the bodhisattva forms this thought: "I shall distance myself from the ten unwholesome paths;
taking the ten wholesome paths as my garden of Dharma, I shall delight in and dwell securely therein."
The second is the Bodhisattva’s lower clarification of vows. Based on wisdom, one gives rise to vows; the vow is for the sake of sentient beings so that they may cultivate goodness themselves.

It is simply this: may they abandon evil causes and evil fruits, which will then vanish of their own accord; may they cultivate good causes and good fruits, which will then arrive of their own accord.
One dwells within it oneself and also exhorts others to dwell within it.
Third, "dwelling oneself in lower practice" refers to initiating practice based on one's vows, because one cultivates according to one's pledges.

Within this, first, one initiates one's own practice based on the aforementioned vows; subsequently, "also exhorting others in lower [practice]" refers to correctly gathering sentient beings based on that very self-practice.
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further gives rise toward all sentient beings a mind of benefit,

a mind of peace and happiness, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of embracing, a mind of protection, a mind regarding them as oneself, a mind regarding them as a teacher, and a mind regarding them as a great teacher.
The fourth section, "The Son of the Buddha Below Clarifies the Accumulation," explains that because one relies on superior compassion for sentient beings, ten kinds of minds arise.
That is to say, based on the previous "gathering of virtue," the arising of compassion to gather in sentient beings is called "superiority in ethical discipline" (*śīla-adhipati*).

Now, relying on this superior compassion with the desire to extract sentient beings from suffering, the compassionate mind is able to initiate activities that benefit sentient beings; therefore, it is called "accumulation. "Accumulation" means benefiting others.
...the mind. Within this, there are eight distinct aspects regarding sentient beings: first, causing those who engage in unwholesome conduct to abide in wholesome conduct;
thus it is called "benefiting. Second, causing those who suffer to attain peace and happiness. Third, extending loving-kindness toward those who are hostile or hateful without retaliating.
Fourth, feeling compassion for those in poverty and suffering with the desire to rescue them. Fifth, [extending compassion] toward those who are happy...
1. To give rise to compassion for those who are heedless; 2. To gather those among external paths and lead them to right faith;
3. To protect fellow practitioners so that they do not fall back; 4. To take into oneself all sentient beings who have made the vow for enlightenment; 5.
To regard those sentient beings who ride the path of the Mahāyāna and advance toward it with the same respect as one’s own teacher; 6. To observe the accumulation [of the requisites].
Those who possess sufficient merit revere [the teacher] as if he were the Great Master. Because the latter two are subsumed together as a single *bodhi*, there are only eight [perfections].
Regarding the fifth, one forms this thought: it is the gathering of the fruit below. Based on the aforementioned compassionate mind, one gives rise to a superior and sublime desire;

because of the desire to rescue and deliver [sentient beings], there are generally four types of sentient beings concerning that aforementioned rescue and deliverance: first, those who transform sentient beings who are subject to perversion; second, [those who transform sentient beings who are attached to the cycle of birth and death]; third, [those who transform sentient beings who are attached to the Lesser Vehicle]; and fourth, [those who transform sentient beings who are attached to the Great Vehicle].
1. Transforming sentient beings who seek sensual desires. 2. Transforming sentient beings who seek existence. 3. Transforming sentient beings who seek the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Within the text, these are divided into ten categories: the first has one category; the second has five categories; the third has two categories; and the fourth has two categories.
In each case, it says, "Furthermore, he thinks thus. Each passage contains two parts: first, observing those to be transformed; second, "I shall now... [descend].
One arouses the mind of deliverance. The former refers to that which is to be remedied, and the latter refers to the remedy itself.

Now, within each of the ten classes of beings, there are those who can be delivered by the aforementioned ten types of minds. Among these ten, the first resolves erroneous views, while the remaining nine counteract erroneous conduct.
First, he forms this thought:
"Sentient beings are to be pitied; they have fallen into the dense forest of wrong views, unwholesome wisdom, evil desires, and evil paths.
Among those to be converted first, he transforms those sentient beings who are inverted. Within those initially transformed, wrong view is the primary factor, namely the four inversions.
Seeking outside of reality is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The two inversions of permanence and pleasure are termed faulty wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
The two inversions of self and purity are termed faulty desire (*duriccha*). The "dense forest of evil realms" summarizes these wrong views as the cause of all faults;
they are what must be remedied.
I cause them to abide in right view and practice the path of reality so that they may later be able to cure [themselves].
Abiding in right view reverses the aforementioned false views; the path of reality reverses the aforementioned dense forest of evil paths.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings discriminate between self and other, mutually destroying one another;
their strife, contention, and malice burn fiercely without ceasing. I shall cause them to abide in unsurpassed great compassion."
The second [section], the transformation for sentient beings who seek sensory desires, has five categories. It is divided into two parts:

the first three transform [the perception of] the faults arising from obtaining and enjoying the five sensory desires; the latter two transform the faults occurring during the pursuit of the five sensory desires when they have not yet been obtained.
Within the former [three], there are further three sections: 1) the enjoyment of non-common wealth; 2) the enjoyment of insatiable wealth; and 3) the enjoyment of accumulated wealth.
Wealth. First: not sharing with others what one has already acquired; this gives rise to the fault of anger (*dveṣa*) at the time of expenditure.

First, the objects of treatment are clarified: mutual destruction is twofold. First, quarreling within speech; second, discriminating between self and other, which constitutes resentment within the mind.
From "hatred" (*pratigha*) downward, its intensification is summarized: by means of hatred...

Therefore, one should cultivate mindfulness as a remedy. When evil conduct of body and mind blazes forth without ceasing, one can treat the middle state by using loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to counteract hatred.
The loving-kindness of the Tathāgata is called unsurpassed.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings greedily grasp without satiety, seeking only wealth and profit, and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood.
I shall cause them to abide in the Dharma of right livelihood, which consists of pure actions of body, speech, and mind."
Second, regarding those who never tire of transforming sentient beings through material wealth: when they seek [wealth], they never tire, thereby giving rise to the fault of greed.
Within the first [category] of what is to be remedied, there are two parts: first, insatiable grasping, which clarifies that the inner mind is difficult to satisfy;

second, those who seek only material gain manifest this through body and speech, sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). This concludes the three types of action (*karmapatha*). Next, right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) serves as the remedy for these.
He treats them thus.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings are constantly pursued by the three poisons, and because of them, their various afflictions blaze forth.
They do not understand how to resolve to seek the skillful means for liberation. I shall cause them to extinguish the great fires of all afflictions."
They are established in the place of cool nirvana.

Third, there are sentient beings who receive and store accumulated wealth; they accumulate it without dispersing it, thereby following the production of the three poisons and increasing the faults of affliction.

Regarding the initial treatment of the middle [category]: attachment gives rise to greed, and its dissipation through use gives rise to anger; delusion pertains to the former two. These are called "various" [afflictions].
Regarding the blazing intensity of the afflictions (*kleśa*): this refers to how, through the repeated enjoyment and indulgence in precious objects, one is consumed by the fires of the afflictions.
Because of delusion and confusion regarding this, one lacks the intention to seek liberation; thus it is said that "one does not know the essential way out.
Among the remedies, *nirvāṇa* is cool, for therein the fire of the afflictions is extinguished.

Furthermore, he reflects: "Because all sentient beings are covered by the heavy darkness of ignorance and the thick film of false views, they enter the dense forest of the aggregates (*skandha*), lose the light of wisdom, and wander upon the perilous paths of the wilderness, giving rise to various evil views."
I shall cause them to attain the unobstructed, pure eye of wisdom, so that they may know all phenomena as they truly are and no longer follow the teachings of others.
Next, there are two pairs of vows: to transform those sentient beings who have not yet attained the five desires and are wasting their time in pursuit of them, thereby creating further karma.
This is divided into two parts. The first clarifies the pursuit of rewards in the present life, whereby one commits various unwholesome deeds.

The second clarifies the pursuit of rewards in future lives, whereby one creates causes for contaminated merit (*sāsrava-kuśala*). Herein is the first part. First, regarding that which is to be remedied, there are four kinds of faults:

(1) the fault of the mind being shrouded by ignorance; (2) the fault of entering into the shadows and depths, increasing evil and distancing oneself from the wholesome; and (3) wandering through vast wildernesses and dark paths.
This clarifies the fault of experiencing the retribution of suffering. Regarding the fourth point, the fault of giving rise to wrong views is that there is no correct antidote.
Later, within the capacity for treatment, one first attains the pure eye of wisdom; because what is seen is according to reality, one does not follow the teachings of others.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings dwell within the perilous path of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
They have entered the net of evil views and are bewildered by the dense forest of ignorance.
Following false paths, they engage in inverted practices. Like blind people without a guide, they mistake that which is not the path of deliverance for the path of deliverance."
They have entered the realm of Māra and are seized by evil marauders; they follow the mind of Māra and remain far removed from the Buddha’s intent.
I shall pull them out from such perilous difficulties and cause them to dwell in the fearless city of omniscience.
Second, seeking future retribution through transformation. This refers to the fault of practicing contaminated virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*) that accords with perilous paths;

namely, by being deluded regarding the supreme truth of transcendence (*lokottara-paramārtha*), one performs meritorious and immovable karma (*puṇya-aniñjya-karma*) in pursuit of future rewards, thereby remaining perpetually on perilous paths.

In the preceding section on the objects of treatment, there are ten phrases, divided into three parts. First, birth and death are the very essence [of the problem]; the retributions of humans and devas are precarious.
Therefore, it is called a perilous path. Second, the matter of being on the verge of falling into the perilous path below consists of eight phrases.

Being deluded regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path corresponds to two phrases for each in sequence. First, "on the verge of falling" clarifies the existence of suffering. Second, "entering the net of evil views" correctly clarifies delusion regarding suffering.
Third, "for the sake of the ignorant and base" clarifies delusion regarding the cause of origination (*samudaya*). "Following after" clarifies the act of creating that origination. As...

The phrase "blind" below reveals the absence of the essence of the Path (*mārga*). "Lacking a guide" indicates the deficiency of the conditions for the Path. This clearly explains delusion regarding the Path; it is not the Path of definitive deliverance.
The phrase "entering Māra" below indicates being truly deluded regarding Cessation (*nirodha*) and the presence of obstacles to cessation.

That is to say, entering the six sense-objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*) is like being plundered by evil bandits. The following two lines clarify what is lost. Next, within the section on the "remedy," [the text speaks of] "pulling out from the perilous."
The Way. It is the total departure from the aforementioned evils and the abiding in the City of Fearlessness; this is the place of detachment.

Having concluded the transformation of sentient beings who seek [desire], he further reflects: "All sentient beings are submerged by the waves of the great torrential flood and have entered the flow of desire and existence."
They swirl in the eddies of birth and death within the flood of ignorance and the flood of views;

they are tossed about in the river of craving, where turbulent currents rush and surge so violently that there is no leisure for contemplation, as they are pursued and never left by thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness.

The third [section] concerns the transformation of sentient beings who seek existence; it consists of two parts. The first part concerns the differentiation of paths, namely the transmigration through the five destinies (*pañcagati*);
the second concerns the differentiation of realms, namely the confinement within the bonds of the three realms (*tridhātu*). Now, for the first part: first the faults, then the remedies.

Within the faults, the initial phrase serves as the general summary, while "entering desire" and so forth provide the specific details. The general summary refers to the fault of being submerged in the great river—that is, being adrift and drowning in the six destinies.
Regarding that great river, the reason for its submerging [beings] within is explained as follows. Next, entering the stream of desire (*kāma-ogha*), it is further distinguished below:
the great torrent of waves has three characteristics. First, the drifting of its own substance, which is the cause and effect of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).

Second, the arising of difficulties caused by the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as a basis; that is, being situated amidst many harms. Third, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) below immediately become established.
A great loss! One loses the path to liberation. Now, the primary nature [of this river] has five characteristics:

first, depth; second, flow; third, name; fourth, drifting; and fifth, vastness. First, regarding "depth": because it is fully endowed with the immeasurable waters of the four floods (*ogha*), it constitutes the river of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, "the swirling of birth and death" refers to its flow. Generally, the four floods above represent the profound cause of affliction; therefore, this [river] is deep.
The bitter fruits flow constantly without exhaustion; this refers to those who are swept away and tossed about by the river of the three cravings (*tṛṣṇā*).

Although it was previously explained that the four floods (*ogha*) do not encompass all delusions, because craving moistens birth and death, those who are particularly subject to being swept away and drowned receive the name "river.

Regarding the phrase "the four rapids rush," etc., this refers to being swept away. This has two meanings: first, to reveal the urgency of the river, hence it is said that the rapids rush and surge violently.
This means that although one cherishes the body and desires it to endure for a long time, it does not remain still from moment to moment; this is the time of being swept away and drowned.
Second, because of its urgency, one cannot know things as they truly are, nor can one see the other shore of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that there is no leisure for contemplation.

Fifth, regarding "being pursued by the awakening of desire and so forth," this refers to the expansion [of the afflictions]; that is, following after the five objects of sensory desire. Thus it is said.
It is called "Vast. Sinking and drowning therein, the rākṣasa of the view of a self seizes them and carries them forever into the dense forest of craving and desire;
they develop deep attachment to what they covet and dwell upon the high ground of the conceit of "I am."
The second [section] raises four difficulties. First is "clinging": being attached to the cave-dwelling of the self and what belongs to the self, one cannot move forward;
thus it is said that the rākṣasa of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) seizes hold therein. Second is "bringing back from below":
having previously abandoned desire and been about to be born in a higher realm, due to the clinging of the view of a self, one returns once more to the midst of desire-thoughts in the lower realms.
Third, attachment to what is craved in its inferior or middling forms; that is, because one seeks and becomes attached to pleasures such as desire at the time of enjoyment.

Fourth, those who dwell on the high ground of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") increase their pride; that is, while engaged in the act of enjoyment, they harbor *māna*, *atimāna*, and *mānātimāna*, exalting themselves and disparaging others.
Because pride causes the mind to become haughty, it is likened to a high ground or plateau.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are established as a village. There is no one to provide good rescue, and there is no one capable of delivering [beings].
Regarding the three great losses of the Three Knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*): first, the loss of having no intention to emerge from the good realms;

this is because, by establishing the six sense bases as a village, there is no wholesome cause. Second, the loss of having no rescue from the evil realms; this is because there is no condition for rescue. Third, the absence of anyone capable of delivering [them].

"Departing for another place and losing [the opportunity]" means that by abandoning virtuous conduct, one is born in places of adversity where one does not encounter a Buddha. Since these two conditions are both lacking,
I shall arouse great compassion toward them and provide rescue through all roots of goodness, so that they may be free from calamity and affliction."
Free from defilement and tranquil, he dwells upon the jewel-island of all-encompassing wisdom.

Subsequently, he first gives rise to a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) within the state of meditative mastery; next, he accomplishes the activities of transformation through various lower states. There are six such activities of transformation.

First, providing good causes, meaning taking the six perfections and myriad practices as a boat and raft. Second, acting as a condition for rescue. Third, ensuring there is no suffering or affliction.
Fourth, causing one to leave behind the defilement of accumulation. Fifth, realizing the tranquility of nirvana. Sixth, enabling the attainment of the great wisdom of bodhi.
These are all the reversals of the aforementioned [unwholesome] thoughts.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings dwell in the prison of the world, beset by manifold sufferings and afflictions. They constantly harbor love and hatred, giving rise to anxiety and fear;
they are bound by the heavy shackles of craving and fettered by the dense forest of ignorance which serves as a covering and obstruction."
Within the three realms, they are unable to emerge on their own. I shall cause them to forever leave the three states of existence (*tribhava*) and abide in unobstructed great *nirvāṇa*.

Second is the clarification of the distinctions between the realms: first the faults, then the remedies. Within the faults, the first phrase serves as the general heading: "bound to the three realms."

Bondage is like a prison; one seeks a place within existence, which is why it constitutes a fault. Next, the various secondary [faults] specifically clarify that there are five faults that follow one in the worldly prison:
first, the matter of suffering, which refers to the various kinds of suffering;

second, the exhaustion of wealth, meaning that when one loves the means of livelihood but cannot obtain them through seeking, or when one hates poverty but cannot distance oneself from it; third, separation from what is loved, which refers to relatives...

Separation from what is loved constantly gives rise to sorrow and fear. Fourth is the bondage of existence (*bhava-bandhana*), which means that even if one is born in the higher realms, one is still bound by the shackles of craving.
Fifth is obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), which means that although one may attain the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis, one is still shrouded by ignorance and thus contradicts right view.
Next, regarding the remedies: if one understands as it truly is the characteristic of the three realms as being false and illusory.
Thus, one becomes free from obstacles and realizes the fruit of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, one reflects: "All sentient beings are attached to a self; they do not seek escape from the cave-dwelling of the aggregates.
Relying on the empty village of the six sense bases, they give rise to the four types of inverted conduct and are afflicted by the venomous snakes of the four great elements."
Slain by the hostile thieves of the five aggregates, they undergo immeasurable suffering.
I shall cause them to abide in the most supreme state of non-attachment—namely, the unsurpassed nirvāṇa in which all obstacles are extinguished.

The fourth [section] concerns the transformation of sentient beings who seek through false ascetic practices (*brahmacarya*). This has two parts: first, transforming those who seek through false ascetic practices, causing them to abandon the false and return to the correct;
second, transforming those of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) who share similar methods, causing them to abandon the provisional and return to the ultimate.

Regarding the first part, we first clarify the faults, where the initial phrase serves as a general summary: namely, the fault of clinging to a self (*ātman*). Although the attachments of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are manifold, because...
The self is the basis; views such as those of eternalism and annihilationism all arise from this. Next, regarding the aggregates (*skandhas*), six points are specifically clarified below.

The first three points involve losing the path, and thus one is far removed from the bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The latter three points involve losing cessation (*nirodha*), and thus one is fully possessed of all suffering. Regarding the beginning:
because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive of a self, it is said that they do not seek liberation from the aggregates. This applies universally.
Calculating the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one gives rise to the four inversions; hence it is called "inverted conduct.

Within the latter three [sufferings], the first is the suffering of the discordance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), namely the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. The second is the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) following one’s every step. The third is the immeasurable suffering of the six feelings (*ṣaḍvedanā*) from enemies and thieves.
Because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are attached to a self (*ātman*), they are unable to attain liberation. Regarding the subsequent treatment, the superior [remedy] arises from calculation.
Therefore, I give rise to attachments in various places; only the Great Nirvāṇa is the place free from attachment.
The Bodhisattva instructs them to contemplate its defects and know its true nature; because both persons and phenomena are empty, it is called the supreme, unattached place, the unsurpassed Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings possess narrow and inferior minds; they do not practice the path of supreme omniscience.
Although they wish to attain liberation, they take pleasure only in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. I shall cause them to abide in the vast Buddha-dharma and vast wisdom."
The second transformation is identical to the Dharma of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the initial arising of faults, there are three: first, the fault of not seeking the great cause;
being indolent in benefiting sentient beings is narrow-minded, and failing to realize the boundless Buddha-dharma through regression is inferior.

Second, the fault of not practicing the lower [path] while not aspiring for the great fruit. Third, although [they] desire the lower [path], it clarifies the fault of their practice; these are sentient beings of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi). In reality...
There exists the Dharma of liberation through the Mahāyāna, yet one may practice the Hīnayāna; subsequently, one treats the vast Buddha-dharma, namely the various pāramitās and the myriad practices.
That which is attained from the stages (bhūmis) upward is termed "vast. All these are the causal dharmas of the Buddha. Wisdom encompasses both cause and effect;
as opposed to the previous narrowness and inferiority, this is collectively termed "vast."
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus guards and upholds the precepts, they are well able to increase the mind of compassion and mercy.

This constitutes the second summary of the precepts for gathering sentient beings. Guarding and upholding the precepts refers to the aforementioned *saṃvara* (restraint), as well as the gathering of wholesome dharmas;
thus, being able to increase the mind of compassion and mercy is the precept of benefiting others. This concludes the stage of the Superior Mark (*adhimātra-nimitta-bhūmi*).
The fruit of the lower stages.
Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stainless Stage (vimalā-bhūmi), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas;

that is to say, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, and many trillions of Buddhas.
One sees many hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, and so on, up to seeing many hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of Buddhas.

This is the fruit of the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi-phala*). It is characterized solely by the absence of further [deliberate] exertion (*anābhoga*). The third fruit is the same as before; all are superior to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Regarding the first, the fruit of refinement (*praśrabdhi-phala*), there are three aspects: namely, the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their synthesis. Within the teaching, there are three parts. First, seeing the Buddha serves as the condition for refining one's practice.
Toward all Buddhas, with a vast mind and a profound mind, they pay homage, respect, and reverence, serving and making offerings of clothing,
food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all requisites for life. They likewise make offerings to the entire Saṃgha,
and dedicate these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Next, following the passage "Regarding all Buddhas," the text clarifies the ability to refine one's practice.

Within this, one first makes offerings to the Buddhas with a mind of deep respect, and furthermore, receives and practices the dharma of the ten paths of wholesome action according to what has been received.
Until reaching enlightenment, one shall never forget or lose it.

Later, when receiving the Dharma from the various Buddhas, one further receives the ten wholesome actions; that is, one studies the ten wholesome actions of the Buddhas. This is because it is the ground of the precepts.
Because this bodhisattva has, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, envy, and broken precepts,
their generosity and observance of the precepts are pure and fully perfected.

Third, regarding the purification through refinement within the "inferior" category of Bodhisattvas—compared to the "superior" category mentioned previously—it is because they have abandoned the two types of defilements, namely stinginess/envy and the breaking of precepts.
It is like pure gold placed in alum stone and refined according to the proper method; having been freed from all impurities, it becomes even more brilliant and pure.
It is the same for a bodhisattva dwelling in this Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*):

throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of eons, because they have distanced themselves from the stains of stinginess, envy, and broken precepts, their generosity and ethical discipline are pure and fully perfected.
Regarding the two metaphors: in the former case, because the precepts of a bodhisattva in the first stage (*bhūmi*) were not yet pure, their giving was likewise not pure.

Now, having abandoned the two defilements, it is called "purified. While the gold of the first stage was merely refined by fire to remove external impurities, here it is placed in alum, whereby both the internal purity of its essence and its brilliance are revealed;
thus it is said to be "all-pure. The application of this to the Dharma can be understood accordingly.

O Son of the Buddha, among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva predominantly practices kind speech (*priyavāditā*). Among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he predominantly practices ethical discipline (*śīla*).
As for the others, it is not that he does not practice them; rather, he practices them according to his strength and capacity.
Second, among the practices specific to this stage, because one is free from the four faults of speech, loving speech (*priyavāditā*) is particularly predominant.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called a brief explanation of the second stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Third, the summary of the stage:
A bodhisattva dwelling in this stage frequently becomes a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), serving as a great Dharma lord who possesses the seven jewels and sovereign power.

Second, regarding the bodhisattvas dwelling here, this section summarizes the fruits of retribution. First, the householder stage is clarified; subsequently, "if they so desire" and so forth clarifies the renunciant stage.
Within the householder stage, there are two parts. First, the superior body, namely the Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).

They are able to remove the stains of stinginess, greed, and broken precepts from all sentient beings. Through skillful means, they cause them to abide securely within the ten paths of wholesome action.
Acting as great donors, they provide for all inexhaustibly through the four bases of sympathy: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
All such deeds they perform are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
He does not depart from the mindfulness that is fully endowed with the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, he forms this thought: "Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, and the supreme."
It is unsurpassed, even serving as the basis for the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Subsequently, it can eliminate the lower and clarify the superior fruit.
If this bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life to practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they will then be able to renounce their home and wife.
Having renounced the five desires and left the household life, he practiced with diligent vigor;

in a single moment of thought, he attained a thousand samādhis, beheld a thousand Buddhas, and understood the spiritual powers of a thousand Buddhas. He was able to shake a thousand worlds and even manifest a thousand bodies.
In each individual body, one is able to manifest a thousand bodhisattvas as an entourage.
Second is the ripening fruit of the result of renunciation;
if manifested through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it exceeds these numbers, spanning hundreds of kalpas and thousands of kalpas.
Even over the course of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
Third, if one were to take the fruit of the bodhisattva’s lower vow-knowledge, it would be the same as that of the first bhūmi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Uprightness, flexibility, and adaptability; Subjugation, tranquility, and pure goodness;
The swift emergence from birth and death with a vast mind— By means of these ten mental states, one enters the second stage."

The third section, consisting of the stanzas in *śloka* meter, contains fifteen verses. It is divided into three parts. The first ten verses concern the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). Within this, there are four sub-sections;
the first of these consists of one verse that praises the ten types of mind.
Abiding here, one accomplishes the merit of ethical discipline: Far removed from taking life, one does not harm or injure;
Likewise, one abstains from stealing and sexual misconduct. Free from lying, slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter, One does not covet material wealth and is always compassionate.
With a straightforward mind on the right path, one is free from flattery and deceit.

Avoiding peril and abandoning pride, being supremely gentle and compliant, acting according to the teachings without negligence—these two verses in pairs summarize the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
In the hells and as animals, they undergo manifold sufferings; as hungry ghosts, they are scorched by blazing, fierce flames.
All things arise from the causes of transgression; I shall leave them behind and dwell among those who practice the Dharma of reality.

Therein, one may receive rebirth at will, even up to the bliss of meditative concentration in the Peak of Existence, as well as the paths of the Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Buddhas—all of which are accomplished through the ten wholesome actions.
Reflecting thus with heedfulness, one maintains pure precepts oneself and teaches others to protect them;
these two and a half verses summarize the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings undergoing manifold sufferings, one causes the mind of great compassion to increase even further.
Ordinary fools, with their deviant wisdom and incorrect understanding, are constantly indolent, resentful, and full of disputes;
they greedily seek after sensory objects without ever reaching satisfaction.

I should cause them to eliminate the three poisons and be freed from the great darkness of delusion that shrouds and covers them, so that they may enter the great perilous path and the net of false views.
Trapped within the cage of birth and death by the power of resentment, I shall cause them to destroy the thieves of Māra.
Adrift upon the four currents, their minds submerged and drowning, they burn within the three realms in immeasurable suffering.
Regarding the aggregates as my dwelling, I abide therein; for the sake of delivering them, I diligently practice the Way.
If those who seek liberation have inferior resolve and abandon the supreme wisdom of the Buddha,
I desire to establish them in the Mahāyāna and inspire in them diligent vigor without weariness.
These four and a half verses summarize the precept of gathering in sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here accumulates merit; Beholding immeasurable Buddhas, he makes offerings to them all.

Cultivating goodness for billions of eons, his virtue becomes even more radiant; Like refining true gold with excellent medicine, The Son of the Buddha dwelling here acts as a Wheel-Turning King, Universally transforming sentient beings through the practice of the ten wholesome paths.
He cultivated all wholesome dharmas to achieve the Ten Powers and save the world;
Renouncing his royal throne and treasures, he immediately abandoned the household life to rely on the Buddha’s teaching.
With courageous diligence, in a single thought-moment, he attained a thousand samādhis and beheld a thousand Buddhas.
All the various kinds of supernormal powers—on this stage, the bodhisattvas are able to manifest them all.
The deeds performed through the power of their vows exceed even this; with immeasurable mastery, they deliver sentient beings.
(These two verses and four lines praise the fruit of the stages.)
The supreme conduct of Bodhisattvas practiced by those who benefit all the worlds—thus has the merit of the second stage been expounded for the sake of the sons of the Buddha.
(One verse concludes the praise of what has been taught. The second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*), is hereby completed.

The third is the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*). The reason for coming [to this stage] is that the sequence of meaning follows from the previous [grounds of] ethical discipline (*śīla*) to this [ground of] meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, while the first three grounds were analogous to the mundane practices of generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline, and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the first two grounds have already completed the practices of generosity and ethical discipline; now, on this ground, cultivation is revealed.
Therefore, it is said in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*: "In the preceding stages, one is able to maintain the subtle categories of ethical discipline, yet has not yet attained their worldly perfection."
This stage is taught as the cause for attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and the dhāraṇī of perfect hearing of the Dharma;

it is intended to encourage their cultivation and study. As for the term "Radiant" (*prabhākari*), the *Jñānaprasthāna* calls it the "Light Stage," while the root treatise calls it the "Illuminating Stage" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

"Light" (*āloka*) and "clarity" (*prabhā*) are distinct designations for the eye itself; in both cases, the character "arising" (*utpāda*) is omitted. In the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, it is called the "Stage of Luminous Wisdom" (*prajñābhūmi*);

since wisdom is also clarity, the essential meaning is identical. Now, summarizing the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* and various other sūtras and śāstras, there are three general meanings for establishing the name "Emitting Light" (*prabhākari*).
First, the ten kinds of faith of the initial stage (*bhūmi*) are taken as that which emits [the light]. Superior...

One takes the retention of what has been heard as the light that is emitted; for it is only after one has fully established oneself in the stages (*bhūmi*) that one begins to hear the Dharma and cultivate the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By means of the light of practicing the sublime Dharma through hearing, the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is manifested."
Therefore, it is named the "Radiant Ground" (Prabhākarī-bhūmi). Second, taking the retention of what has been heard as the producer and superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the produced;
third, taking both superior meditative concentration and dhāraṇī as the producers, with the realization of the characteristics of light in that fourth ground as the produced.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Having accomplished superior meditative concentration and the great dhāraṇī of the Dharma, one is able to produce the light of boundless sublime wisdom. Therefore...
The ten pure minds are exclusively that which can produce; the realization of the signs of luminosity is exclusively that which is produced.

Regarding the obstacles to be abandoned, the term "obscuration" (*avaraṇa*) refers to the dullness and darkness of consciousness—specifically, a portion of the innate *jñeyāvaraṇa* (cognitive obscuration) that causes the loss of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.
This obscuration obstructs the superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage. Upon entering the third stage, one is able to eliminate it forever.
They are abandoned. For this reason, it is said that in the third stage, two types of delusion (*moha*) along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:

first, the delusion of desire and greed (*kāmarāga*), which obstructs the superior stage and its cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*); second, the delusion regarding the perfection of *dhāraṇī*, which obstructs the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-prajñā*) as well as those *dhāraṇīs* themselves.
If categorized according to what is realized, it is solely in terms of the *dhāraṇī* that one speaks of realizing the "superior flow" (*viśeṣa-srotas*).
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "This refers to the teaching that flows from this True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is far superior to other teachings.
The practice it accomplishes consists solely of dhyāna and the quest for the Dharma; the fruit it attains likewise consists of the Dharma and dhyāna."
The four immeasurables, the five supernormal powers, and so forth, are all subsumed within meditative concentration. The explanation of the names is now complete.
Upon hearing of the practices of this stage, the sons of the Buddha—whose bodhisattva realm is inconceivable—all pay homage with joyful hearts; they scatter flowers into the air as an offering.

Next, the actual explanation of the text is divided into three parts: first, the section on praise and request; second, the section on the formal exposition; and third, the section on the summary verses.
Regarding the first part, the six verses are divided into two sections: the first three celebrate what has preceded, and the latter three request what follows.
Within the former, the first verse is the narration by the compiler of the sutra.
Praise be to you, Great Mountain King! With a heart of compassion, you take pity upon all sentient beings.
You have excellently expounded the dharmas of the wise’s discipline;
these are the characteristics of practice within the second stage, the subtle conduct of all Bodhisattvas—true, without variation, and without distinction.
"Desiring to benefit all sentient beings," thus he spoke these two most pure verses of praise.
The former verse possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the latter verse possesses compassion (*karuṇā*). Therefore, it says "to benefit.

Furthermore, the former verse concerns the aspect of the teaching (*deśanā-lakṣaṇa*), hence it says "discipline" (*vinaya*). The latter verse concerns the aspect of realization (*adhigama-lakṣaṇa*), hence it says "sublime. "Reality" (*tattva*) refers to that which accords with [the truth].
Because it is the principle; because there is no difference, for the thousand sages share the same path; because there is no distinction, for the principle permeates all phenomena.
All humans and devas offer worship. I pray that you will expound upon the wisdom-activities corresponding to the dharmas of the Third Bhūmi, and reveal them fully according to their actual scope.

The Great Sage’s teachings on generosity and ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, as well as skillful means, compassion, and the path—all these pure practices and vows of the Buddha were explained;

the latter three verses were requested by [the author], while the first two verses of the middle section were requested by the great assembly. The preceding verse requests the dharmas of the three stages in their entirety.

This refers to the activity of the three knowledges (*jñāna*) corresponding to those teachings. The subsequent verse separately requests the practice of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), as they are present throughout each stage (*bhūmi*).
Compassion and loving-kindness are the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). The "path" refers to the power of the path. The Buddha’s pure conduct is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying: "O Fearless Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, may you please explain the entry into the third bhūmi and its various merits for those of gentle mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
The Bodhisattva, having already purified the second bhūmi and desiring to enter the third bhūmi, should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*).
Within the section on the correct exposition of the second [bhūmi], the practices of the bhūmi are first clarified, followed by the fruits of the bhūmi.

This former section consists of four parts: (1) the section on initiating the practice of renunciation, (2) the section on the practice of renunciation, (3) the section on renunciation, and (4) the section on the fruit of renunciation. In this bhūmi, one cultivates dhyāna.

Because one feels revulsion toward and subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*), and also feels revulsion toward meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it is called the "ground of revulsion" (*nirvedabhūmi*). The mind that correctly abides in this ground dwells within the eight dhyānas; therefore, it is simply called "revulsion.
The initial mind that enters the ground, which contemplates and cultivates those practices, is called the "stage of the practice of revulsion" (*nirvedāṅga*).

The skillful means for proceeding to the ground give rise to those practices of revulsion. Within the mind that fulfills the ground, the attainment of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth constitutes the fruit of this revulsion. Now...

The first section contains three parts. First, the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of the subsequent. Second, from "What are... onwards, the ten types of mind are interrogated and enumerated.

Third, from "The Bodhisattva, by means of these... onwards, the practice is concluded as entering the stage. Regarding the first part, the heading is established: "Ten kinds of profound mind" (*daśa-vidha-gambhīra-citta*).

The *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* refer to this as the "mind of profound mindfulness" (*gambhīra-smṛti-citta*), which differs from the second stage where it is simply called "profound mind. This means that one further contemplates by means of these ten minds.
This is because of the ten profound resolves (*adhyāśaya*).

What are these ten? They are: the pure resolve, the settled resolve, the resolve of weary detachment, the resolve free from greed, the non-retrogressive resolve, the firm resolve, the resplendent resolve, the courageous resolve, the expansive resolve, and the great resolve.
Second, the interrogation enumerates ten states of mind, which are divided into four pairs of meanings. The first pair of two lines refers to the fundamental establishment;
the next pair of three lines refers to the cultivation initiated through skillful means; the following pair of three lines refers to the accomplishment after cultivation;
and the final pair of two lines refers to mastery over virtuous functions. Within these four pairs, each preceding element is free from faults.
The latter clarifies the accomplishment of virtue. First, regarding "the pure mind," this refers to the departure from faults;

that is, by relying on the pure mind of the second bhūmi, one proceeds toward the pure mind of this [third] stage. Second is "the abiding mind," which relies on not abandoning one's own vehicle (yāna) and the aforementioned ten [factors].
Since these two rely on the former, they are called the "fundamental establishment. Next, regarding the second pair, the cultivation through skillful means (*upāya*), therein—
The first two phrases eliminate faults: the first eliminates future desires, and the second eliminates present greed. The final phrase constitutes the cultivation of wholesome progress.
Within the third pair, the first phrase eliminates faults, meaning that because the afflictions of one's own stage cannot destroy it, it is called a "firm mind.
The latter two phrases clarify the flourishing of the wholesome, meaning mastery over the entry and emergence from the eight dhyānas.
"Valiant" means not falling back or losing [one's resolve]. Regarding the fourth pair, it is called "vast" because one does not delight in what is narrow or limited;
it is called "great" because one relies on mastery over others and does not abandon sentient beings.
By means of these ten mental states, the bodhisattva attains entry into the third stage (*bhūmi*).

Entry into the stage occurs through three types of cultivation: namely, by bringing to mind and reflecting upon the aforementioned ten mental states, one enters the dwelling of superior mind (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*).
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the third stage, they contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as they truly are:
namely, as impermanent, suffering, impure, insecure, subject to decay, not long-lasting, arising and ceasing in every moment,
not born from a prior limit, not going toward a future limit, and not abiding in the present.

The second section, on the practice of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*), has three parts: first, the practice of guarding against afflictions by contemplating that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are to be reviled;
second, seeing thus, the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) while seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Because they deeply contemplate sentient beings and abandon narrow and inferior minds;

and because these three types of bodhisattvas thus weary of and depart from lower practices, yet embrace the skillful means of practice, desiring to gather sentient beings without departing from the ultimate skillful means of unobstructed wisdom.
Furthermore, these three sections subsume the first three stages: the first and half of the second subsume the stage of practicing cultivation (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*).
Next is the practice of guarding against the narrow and inferior mind of the Hīnayāna and subsuming it under non-hostility; this is because of compassion.
The latter section subsumes all Buddhas through dedication, as one contemplates Buddha-wisdom to deliver sentient beings.

Now, the initial passage contains twenty phrases, divided into two parts: the first ten phrases contemplate impermanence, thereby knowing the essential nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); the latter ten...

Regarding the phrase "observing that there is no refuge," this points out the fault in relation to persons. This initial section is divided into three parts. First, it reveals the observation of impermanence;

"time" refers to having already established oneself upon the ground. Second, "next, observing all... and below, this generally identifies the object of observation, namely conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

Third, "that which is called... and below, this specifically demonstrates its characteristics. There are ten phrases in the text: the first is general, and the others are specific. Generally, it is termed "impermanence."
The treatise states: "In this context, because the formations of life do not abide, the formations of life are impermanent phenomena. Non-abiding is the meaning of impermanence.
Within the specific [explanation], there are nine phrases that collectively manifest this meaning of impermanence, namely, that there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
Furthermore, one contemplates that these phenomena offer no refuge and no support; they coexist with sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; they are bound by love and hatred;
they give rise to ever-increasing grief and distress; they never remain stable; the fires of greed, anger, and delusion blaze without ceasing;
and entangled by manifold calamities, they increase day and night—illusory and unreal.
The second section further contemplates the following ten phrases to clarify that there is no rescue. The first phrase provides a general manifestation;
it refers to this "Dharma," which is the aforementioned impermanence. Now, contemplating it again, one sees that one cannot escape birth, aging, sickness, and death.

It is like mountains from the four directions closing in, leaving no place to flee and no one capable of providing rescue. There are nine distinct phrases that address birth, aging, sickness, and death, of which the first four are as follows:
By means of death, the lack of rescue is revealed; because this characteristic is manifest, it is explained first.
First, "having no refuge" means that while impermanence has not yet arrived, there is no one to rely upon for protection to prevent its arrival.

Second, "possessing sorrow" means that once impermanence has arrived, there is no one capable of rescuing one; the intention here is that one fears death, and thus harbors sorrow. Third, "possessing grief" refers to birth...
The aggregates undergo transformation and decay; the signs of death manifest before him. During this interval, his tears and snot increase even more.

As he who dwells with the four types of suffering and affliction is about to relinquish his life, the four great elements disperse, and his grief and pain intensify as his mind becomes tormented by feverish distress.
Next, regarding the second pair, one does not recognize that the affairs of livelihood are suffering, but falsely conceives them as pleasure; this refers to the five pursuits (*paryeṣaṇā*).
Because the objects of livelihood involve both the adverse and the favorable, one is bound by attachment and aversion. Sixth, at the time of enjoyment, suffering is abundant while pleasure is meager.
It is said that sorrow and distress increase ever more; for when one receives [them] and does not dispel them, all manner of calamities gather.
When they are employed, they cause ruin and damage, as if destroying one's own life. Therefore, it is said that suffering is manifold. These two types of sentient beings share this same condition:

at the time when the body is old, its prime years and robust complexion cannot be rescued or made to remain. The latter two concern illness; the first is the cause of illness, namely the eight [afflictions].
In youth and vigor, one possesses the three feelings, such as pleasure; therefore, greed and the like constantly burn within, leaving no room for the water of the Dharma.
This blazing fire is difficult to extinguish. Ninth, in the time of declining years, one is entangled by manifold ailments, like a tree about to rot;
these increase day and night, and none can provide escape. Old age is the very condition for sickness; it is illusory and unreal. This concludes the preceding nine points. Above.
Guarding against the conduct of afflictions, having seen this,
one becomes increasingly weary of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and advances toward the wisdom of the Buddha. Seeing that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable,
unequaled, immeasurable, difficult to attain, unmixed, free from affliction, free from sorrow, and culminating in fearlessness.
The city. No longer retreating, one is able to rescue immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and hardship.
The second [section] protects the practice of the Hīnayāna; the text contains thirty phrases. The first ten phrases protect the small mind, while the latter twenty phrases protect the narrow mind.
Now, the first phrase is general; it first concludes the preceding [section], meaning that having previously contemplated impermanence, one has become weary [of saṃsāra].
Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*): next, because one observes that there is no refuge, revulsion increases further. One hastens toward the Buddha’s wisdom;

having clarified the subsequent stages of birth, one correctly guards the small mind (*parītta-citta*) in order to seek the Buddha’s great wisdom (*mahājñāna*). Next, following the section on seeing the Buddha, there are ten distinct phrases divided into two parts.

The first five comprise the greatness of merit (*guṇa-mahattva*), which is the seeking of the Buddha’s *bodhi*; the latter five comprise the greatness of purity (*viśuddhi-mahattva*), which is the seeking of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the fruition: *bodhi* (enlightenment) is termed "attainment" because it is accomplished through cultivation; *nirvāṇa* is termed "purity" because it is primordially present and free from obstructions.
First, regarding the greatness of the encompassing qualities: (1) its cognitive function is inconceivable because it cannot be fathomed;

(2) its sublime activity is peerless because it has no equal; (3) it is pure because it consists solely of benefiting others; (4) it is difficult to obtain because it is beyond reproach; (5) it is unlike [other states]...
Because it is not of the heterodox paths, it is free from admixture. It encompasses five kinds of greatness of merit, followed by five kinds of greatness of purity.
In terms of meaning, there are three [aspects]: first, being without affliction, which means being free from the habits of delusion because ignorance is not intermingled;

second, being without sorrow, which means being free from the basis of the suffering of suffering because its root has perished; third, attaining nirvāṇa, which has two meanings: first, attaining the essence, which refers to reaching...

The City of Fearlessness. Second, regarding the attainment of function: it refers to the ability to establish great deeds. Because one does not abide in saṃsāra, it is said that there is no longer any regression;
because one does not abide in nirvāṇa, one is able to rescue immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and hardship.
When a bodhisattva thus perceives the immeasurable benefit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and perceives the immeasurable faults and afflictions of all conditioned phenomena,
they give rise to ten kinds of compassionate concern for all sentient beings.
The second is the protection against a narrow mind. The text contains twenty phrases: the first ten express compassion for those who are submerged in suffering;

the latter ten resolve upon their rescue. Within the former, it first restates [the previous point]: seeing the benefits of the Buddha’s wisdom, one is grieved that sentient beings do not attain them;

observing the faults of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), one takes pity on those dwelling therein. This restatement of the preceding [point] gives rise to compassion; this serves as the cause for the subsequent [section].
What are these ten? They are: seeing sentient beings solitary and without refuge, one gives rise to a heart of compassion;

seeing sentient beings impoverished and destitute, one gives rise to a heart of compassion; seeing sentient beings burning with the fires of the three poisons, one gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeing sentient beings imprisoned within the jails of the various realms of existence (*bhava*), one gives rise to a heart of compassion; seeing... [the rest of the passage].
He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings are constantly shrouded and obstructed by the dense forest of afflictions.

He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings fail to practice skillful observation. He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings lack the desire for wholesome dharmas.

He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings have lost all Buddha-dharmas. He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings follow the current of birth and death.
The mind of compassion (*anukampā-citta*): seeing that sentient beings have lost the means to liberation, one gives rise to a heart of pity.

These are the ten [points]. Second, the section beginning with "What are the two? correctly reveals the practice of compassion (*karuṇā-caryā*). There are ten phrases in the text; the first is general and the remainder are specific.

The general [point] is that pity arises because they are solitary and without reliance. Now, these sentient beings are distanced from the Compassionate Honored One above and do not benefit others below; therefore—
Regarding "solitude": there are nine distinct types of solitude and lack of reliance. The first two pertain to sentient beings who seek through desire (*kāma-īṣaṇā*):

first, because they have already attained [objects] yet their minds know no satiety, they are destitute and without reliance; second, because they do not cease seeking what they have not yet attained, they are consumed by the fires of the three poisons.
This is what is meant by having "much desire and much seeking. The next three pertain to sentient beings who seek through existence (*bhava-īṣaṇā*): first, [they are] obstructed by suffering...
First, the fruit of hell. Second, because they are obscured by the accumulation of causes, it is called the "dense forest of afflictions" (*kleśa-gahana*). Third, there is no path of discernment;

since they are born into the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) and do not hear the Dharma, how could they possibly realize cessation? The latter four refer to sentient beings who seek the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The first three pertain to the Hīnayāna: first, they practice minor causes and do not seek the superior, virtuous dharmas of the Great Cause;

second, they preserve minor fruits and fail to seek Bodhi, thereby losing the Buddha-dharma; third, they do not attain Great Nirvāṇa and remain long subject to the cycle of changeable birth and death.
The last one pertains to non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); although they seek liberation, because their practices are erroneous, they lose the skillful means.
Thus perceiving the immeasurable suffering and affliction of the realm of sentient beings, the bodhisattva arouses great diligence and forms this thought:
"I must rescue these sentient beings; I must liberate them; I must purify them; I must deliver them; I must establish them in the state of goodness."
One should cause them to dwell in stability; one should cause them to rejoice; one should cause them to know and see; one should cause them to be tamed; one should cause them to attain nirvāṇa.
Second, the bodhisattva thus makes a firm resolve to rescue and deliver others. In this section, the first part summarizes what preceded and introduces what follows.

From the phrase "making this reflection" onwards, the text correctly reveals the mind of rescue. There are ten phrases, which correspond to the ten preceding classes of beings to give rise to these ten minds. First:
1. To rescue those who are solitary and destitute; 2. To liberate them from poverty; 3. To purify the three poisons; 4. To cross over the prison of existence (*bhava*); 5.
To dwell in the open air, free from obstructions; 6. To abide in skillful observation; 7.
To give rise to joy through the desire for wholesome dharmas; 8. To know that the nature and characteristics [of the mind] are identical to the Buddha-dharma; 9. To subdue the sense faculties.
Because it does not follow the currents. Tenth, because it should cause one to attain nirvāṇa through the means of liberation.

Section Two: The Division on the Practice of Aversion has three parts. The preceding [sections] on guarding against afflictions and guarding against the practices of the Hīnayāna are concluded. Below is the third:
the practice of gathering through the cultivation of skillful means.
In this way, the bodhisattva becomes weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena; in this way, they compassionately regard all sentient beings;
and they know that the wisdom of omniscience possesses supreme benefit.
The third is the practice of the means of gathering [beings] (*saṃgrahavastu*). This refers to cultivating the practice of the means for gathering sentient beings.
Therefore, the sutra below asks: "By what means can one rescue and deliver them? It then states that this is known to be inseparable from the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*) and so forth;
this is precisely the means for gathering sentient beings. The text consists of four sections: first, the cause for initiating the practice of gathering; second, performing this...

1. Contemplating the lower [level], one seeks the skillful means to encompass practice. 2. Then one forms this thought: contemplating the lower [level], one seeks the skillful means to gather sentient beings.
3. "The Bodhisattva, in this way... and so forth: practicing based on contemplation. This first section is divided into two parts: first, citing the previous two practices as the three causes;
second, "desiring to rely on... and so forth: clarifying the arousal [of the mind] by relying on those three causes. Now...
First: "In this way, one feels weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena" restates the protection of conduct against afflictions;
it serves as the cause for abandoning the causes of false conceptualization. Second: "In this way, one compassionately regards all sentient beings" restates the protection of a narrow mind;
it serves as the cause for not abandoning any world. Third: "Knowing that the wisdom of omniscience possesses supreme benefit" restates the protection of [the aspiration for] the Lesser Vehicle.
The mind is the cause for the arousal of diligence; that is to say, having known the supreme benefits of the Buddha’s wisdom, one clearly practices that path in order to enter it.
Among these three causes, the first and the last are wisdom, while the middle one is compassion. Compassion and wisdom serve as the causes for the skillful means capable of saving [beings].
Desiring to rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom to rescue and deliver sentient beings,
the later aspirant reflects upon these three causes, wishing to employ beneficial wisdom to save those beings who are worthy of compassion.
He reflects thus: "These sentient beings have fallen into the midst of the great suffering of the afflictions.
By what skillful means can I rescue and deliver them, causing them to abide in the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa?"
