The second type, the practitioner who seeks through skillful means, likewise contemplates that the aforementioned sentient beings have fallen into the midst of conditioned afflictions, karma, and suffering, and desires to cause them to be eternally extinguished so they may attain Great Nirvana; because they do not yet know the skillful means, they seek them through contemplation.
He then formed this thought: "I wish to deliver sentient beings and cause them to abide in nirvāṇa. This does not depart from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation.
The wisdom of unobstructed liberation does not depart from the realization of all phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).

The realization of all phenomena as they truly are does not depart from the light of wisdom regarding non-action and the practice of non-arising. The light of wisdom regarding non-action and the practice of non-arising does not depart from meditative excellence."

The wisdom of skillful and definitive observation. The wisdom of skillful and definitive observation regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is not separate from skillfulness in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Third, within the means for gathering sentient beings through reflection, there are five types of skillful means: first, the unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Buddha; second, the realization of reality as it is on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*);
third, the wisdom of practice as it is on the fourth stage; fourth, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the third stage; and fifth, likewise [the concentration] of the third [stage].
The ground is extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). Among these five, from the subtle to the manifest, each subsequent stage arises based on each preceding one.
Now, when we examine them in reverse order to seek their root, we find that they are all mutually dependent and inseparable. Within these five, extensive learning is the agent of origination;
the Buddha’s wisdom is solely the object of origination; and the three intermediate factors serve as both the agent and the object of origination.
Having thus observed and understood, the Bodhisattva redoubles their diligent seeking and cultivation of the True Dharma.

This is the fourth reliance: the practice based on reflection (*cintāmayī bhāvanā*). Since it was previously traced back to its origin in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), one now proceeds in the forward order by first seeking the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) and initiating the practice of hearing.
In the text, the preceding section is first concluded and the subsequent section introduced; below, the actual practice of seeking is formally initiated.

Day and night, he only aspires to hear the Dharma, to delight in the Dharma, to rejoice in the Dharma, to rely on the Dharma, to follow the Dharma, to understand the Dharma, to accord with the Dharma, to arrive at the Dharma, to abide in the Dharma, and to practice the Dharma.
Subsequently, day and night, he correctly initiates the practice of seeking. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the practice of seeking the Dharma; second, the Bodhisattva...
Thus, the following clarifies the causes for seeking practice. Now, the initial passage contains ten phrases, which correspond to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) and consist of four sections.

The first three pertain exclusively to hearing (*śruta*); the fourth, fifth, and sixth pertain to both hearing and reflection (*cintā*); the seventh pertains exclusively to reflection; and the final three pertain exclusively to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Within this, the constant hearing throughout the day and night at the beginning demonstrates diligent practice; the nine qualities beginning with "joy in the Dharma" demonstrate...
This is right practice: seeking the Dharma above and seeking the causes below.
Thus, when a bodhisattva diligently seeks the Buddha-dharma, they have no stinginess regarding any precious wealth;
they see no object as difficult to obtain or particularly weighty. They regard only those who can expound the Buddha-dharma with the thought that such persons are difficult to encounter.

Regarding the second [section], the causes for seeking practice, there are two parts: first, the cause of constant and diligent seeking; second, the cause of correct practice, beginning with the passage "In this way, the bodhisattva...

and so forth. Now, concerning the first: what serves as the cause for that constant and diligent seeking? It is shown to be the ultimate exhaustion [of attachment] through revering and honoring the Dharma.
This section is divided into six parts; the first is a general clarification of valuing the Dharma more than material wealth.
Therefore, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, a bodhisattva is able to relinquish all internal and external wealth.
In these two pairs of internal and external things,
there is nothing that cannot be practiced with reverence, nothing that cannot be abandoned through the removal of pride, and nothing that cannot be served.
Yet there is nothing that one cannot do; there is no hardship that one cannot endure.
Third is the reverent service of internal wealth: that is, the mind is respectful and abandons pride, while the body serves and forgets its own suffering.
If one hears a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, the great joy that arises is superior to obtaining the precious treasures that fill a trichiliocosm;
how much more so when one gives away external wealth!
If one hears a single verse of the True Dharma not previously heard, the great joy that arises surpasses the attainment of the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

If one obtains a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, which can purify the bodhisattva practice, it surpasses the attainment of the rank of Śakra or Brahmā for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
The five positions of lightness are heavy dharmas. The positions of kings of men and gods are ultimately impermanent; the fruit is the Dharma King through the meaning of the verses and teachings.
If someone were to say, "I possess a single verse of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, which can purify the bodhisattva practice," and you now...
"Even if I must enter a great pit of fire and undergo extreme suffering, I shall give it to you. At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"For the sake of purifying the bodhisattva conduct through even a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, I would desire to cast myself down from as high as the Brahma Heaven, even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with raging fires, in order to witness it for myself."

I accept it; how much less could I fail to enter a small fire pit? Yet now, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, I should endure all the manifold sufferings of the hells, let alone the various minor pains and afflictions of human beings.
Sixth is the dharma of sweetness and bitterness and gravity. A single phrase of the Dharma can exhaust the source of suffering; thus, even many kalpas in hell may truly be considered sweet.
In this way, the bodhisattva exerts diligent effort to seek the Buddha-dharma, observing and practicing according to what has been heard.
Regarding the subsequent section on "Correct Practice," the initial part summarizes what preceded it, while the following portion explicitly reveals the characteristics of its causes.

That is to say, meditative reflection and correct contemplation in a secluded place constitute the cause for practice. If one follows the sequence of the sutra text, this [initial summary] is merely a heading for the subsequent passage.
Having heard the Dharma, this bodhisattva collects the mind and dwells in composure. In a secluded place, he reflects thus:
"One attains the Buddha-dharma by practicing according to what has been taught; it cannot be purified through mere words alone."
The third major section, the Section on Aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-bhāga*). To summarize its seven cultivated characteristics: the preceding [sections] clarified hearing and reflection;

here, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) is revealed. This is the fourth among the five types of skillful means: the analytical wisdom of definitive observation regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna-kauśalya-nirvedha-cintā-jñāna*).

The treatise asks: "What is the Section on Aversion? It is when this bodhisattva, having heard all phenomena, knows them as they have been taught and practices accordingly, thereby attaining Buddhahood.
Dharma. Entering the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the formless realms (*ārūpya*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):

these are not places of delight. One is not defiled by them because one must certainly act [in this way]. That is to say, "not delighting" and "not being defiled" is the meaning of "disgust" (*nirveda*).

These immeasurable supernormal powers are the fruit of that disgust. The scriptural passage describes cultivation through seven aspects: first, based on what one cultivates; second, how one cultivates; third, in what place...

1. Cultivation (*bhāvanā*). 2. For what reason is it cultivated? 3. When is it cultivated? 4. What is cultivated? 5. For what purpose is it cultivated? These seven aspects are condensed into three major sections:
the first four concern the practice of cultivation; the next two concern the actual entry [into the path]; and the last one concerns the intent of that entry. Now, regarding the first:
having heard the Dharma, upon what does this bodhisattva rely for cultivation? It is because he relies on the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Next, the summary:
Regarding how one practices once the mind is settled: it is because the method of gathering the distracted mind and abiding is the characteristic of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Next, as for "in a secluded place," this refers to the location where one practices. Next, as for the reflection that follows, "why does one practice?"—it is because one must engage in practice in order to realize the goal.
Among these seven characteristics, four have already been established. Furthermore, this is not merely verbal; it is comprehensive.
Regarding speaking and listening: it is not that one attains purity merely by hearing the sounds and characters of words;
rather, all things are simultaneously delusion and reality, perfectly interfused and sovereign, arising spontaneously and without the duality of preference or aversion.
O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage (Prabhākārī-bhūmi), regarding the first summary of the second entry: at what time is there cultivation and realization?

It is said that the time of samādhi is the time of practice, while the completion of that very practice is the time of entry into realization. The subsequent passage, beginning with "having become free from desire for evil," etc., [explains this].

What is it that is cultivated? What is it that is realized through cultivation? This refers to the realization of the eight meditative absorptions (*aṣṭa-samāpatti*). The meaning of these eight absorptions has been extensively explained in many commentaries;

here, this sub-commentary briefly analyzes them according to four sections: first, the intent of their inclusion; second, the etymological explanation of their names; third, their essential nature (*svabhāva*); and fourth, the explanation of the text.
Regarding the first, the intent of their inclusion, the subsequent scripture states: "Because one merely accords with the Dharma, one acts without being defiled."
[The commentary] states: For what purpose does one enter the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the immeasurables, and the supernormal powers? It is for the sake of five kinds of sentient beings.

First, for the sake of those sentient beings who are arrogant due to the bliss of dhyāna, one enters the various dhyānas; that is to say, they have attained worldly dhyāna and rely upon it to give rise to pride.

Second, for the sake of those sentient beings who are arrogant due to the liberation of the formless realm, one enters the formless concentrations; that is to say, [they have attained them and thus become conceited].

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) take this as their realization of nirvāṇa and rely upon it to give rise to pride. The Bodhisattva demonstrates entry into the eight dhyānas and, because he transcends each of them, subdues them.
Third, for the sake of sentient beings suffering from affliction, he enters the immeasurables of loving-kindness and compassion;

he enters the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) so that they may be established in a wholesome state and granted eternal happiness, and he acts so that their suffering may be resolved and they shall not undergo it again.

1. One enters the immeasurable state of compassion (*karuṇā*). 2. Fourth, for the sake of liberating sentient beings, one enters the immeasurable states of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*);

that is, one rejoices because they have attained what they themselves have freed from agitation and turmoil. 3. Fifth, for the sake of sentient beings who have taken refuge in the wrong way, one enters superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to cause them to develop right faith;
furthermore, one demonstrates the entry into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) so that others may emulate it. Thus, one skillfully disciplines and refines oneself.

The sequence of their placement is as it ought to be according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Since they are not even comparable to the self-benefit of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), how could they be equated with ordinary worldlings or non-Buddhists?
Next, regarding the explanation of the names: *dhyāna* is a term from the Western language (Sanskrit), which here [in Chinese] is translated as "calm contemplation" (*jinglü*).

"Calm" (*jing*) means tranquility; "contemplation" (*lü*) means discernment. Thus, through calm one can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and through contemplation one can achieve correct observation. Among the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), there is also calm.

The *avitarka* (without applied thought) states: although one can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one cannot achieve correct contemplation (*samyak-darśana*). In the *kāmadhātu*, there is applied thought but no tranquility (*avyupaśama*);

although one can achieve correct contemplation there, one cannot sever the fetters. Therefore, only the *rūpadhātu* alone receives this designation. Next, regarding the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*):
because within these four stages one transcends all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they oppose and subvert all that is material.

Because of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is impossible for material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) to arise therein. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The formless (*ārūpya*) refers to that which is without form;

because all [factors] therein are without form, they receive the name 'formless. Next, regarding their specific names: the first four dhyānas—first, the first dhyāna is a meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) with vitarka and vicāra, possessing five factors (*pañcāṅga*), namely:
vitarka, vicāra, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*). It is also called 'joy born of concentration.'"
The "ground of bliss" refers to the state of having abandoned the joy and pleasure obtained by birth in the desire realm.

The second dhyāna, which is free from vitarka and vicāra, possesses four factors: namely, internal purity, joy, bliss, and concentration. The third dhyāna, which is free from joy, possesses five factors.
This refers to equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and concentration; it is also called the stage of sublime bliss free from joy.

This is because, having abandoned the joy and bliss of the lower realms, one attains sublime bliss. The fourth dhyāna is a meditative absorption free from bliss and possesses four factors: equanimity, mindfulness, neutral feeling, and concentration.

It is also called the "ground of purity through equanimity and mindfulness. The specific names for the formless realms will be explained below. Third, regarding the explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*):

the *Vibhāṣā* states that there are two kinds of dhyāna. First, that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*), which is comprised within the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*) and consists of one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*), because it has wholesome meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its intrinsic nature.
Second, that obtained by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), which is bound to its respective level and consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The nature has no form as its essence; it is simply the exclusion of form, while the remaining meanings are the same as before. Within the Mahāyāna school, there is likewise no divergent path.

If one brings the characteristics back to the nature, then all eight branches of meditative concentration are entirely empty. If phenomena are exhausted and principle manifests, everything is the Tathāgatagarbha.
When all is obliterated and there is no place of reliance, both concentration and distraction vanish. If phenomena and principle are perfected...
Rong: One is all. Fourth, the explanation of the text: first, the clarification of the four dhyānas; second, the exposition of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Within the four dhyānas, each is further condensed into four parts: (1) the removal of hindrances; (2) the application of antidotes; (3) the benefits; and (4) the samādhi that serves as the basis for those two.

That is to say: being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one dwells in the first *dhyāna*.
Now, to explain the first *dhyāna*: "being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states" clarifies the removal of obstacles.

This phrase "being free from" applies throughout the following three [stages]. Because one is free from the five objects of desire, it is called "freedom from desire. Because one has severed the ten unwholesome paths of action, it is called...
In order to abandon evil, one removes the five hindrances; therefore, it is called "abandoning unwholesome states.

As for the phrase "abandoning evil and unwholesome," this refers to the various evil and unwholesome states produced by the causes of afflictions and desire, namely, the misconduct of body and speech. This provides a general analysis of all unwholesome states within the desire realm.
Having already clarified the abandonment of obstacles, there are two [factors]: with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). These constitute two branches. This is...
These are the antidotes for cultivation; in the new translations they are termed *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought). Both are coarse at first and subtle thereafter.
*Vitarka* refers to seeking; *vicāra* refers to examining. The coarse nature of the mind is called *vitarka*, while the subtle nature of the mind is called *vicāra*.
Third, "joy and bliss born of seclusion" refers to the benefit of cultivation: because one is separated from desire, evil, and so forth, joy arises;
because the body and mind are tranquil and one attains the bliss of liberation, it is called "bliss. For this reason, it is termed a "beneficial factor.
Fourth, "dwelling in the first dhyāna" refers to the samādhi that serves as the basis for those two; that is, being attentive toward the object of focus.

Right observation and one-pointedness of mind serve as the basis for their respective remedies and beneficial factors, because investigation (*vitarka*) and so forth proceed by relying on the power of concentration.
Since the obstacles to be abandoned lack the nature of active application (*anabhisamskāra*), they do not serve as a basis for those [factors].
As for the term "initial," it refers to this being the very first stage of advancing upward from the desire realm. Thus it is said.
"Abiding" means to dwell securely.

Having stilled directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*), with internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, one dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

In the second dhyāna, the cessation of vitarka and vicāra is that which is to be abandoned as an obstacle. Vitarka and vicāra are the initial movements that give rise to the three consciousnesses, thereby disturbing the second dhyāna;
just as when pure water is disturbed by waves, nothing can be seen, the first dhyāna is able to remedy this.
This constitutes that which is to be remedied; thus, when the illness is exhausted, the medicine perishes.
"Internal purity with a one-pointed mind, free from vitarka and vicāra" refers to the practice of the remedy. "Internal purity" means that faith is equanimous, causing the internal mind to be pure.
"One-pointedness of mind" explains the meaning of "internal": it takes only the *dharmadhātu* as its object, unlike the first dhyāna, which possesses the three consciousnesses. Therefore...
The *Abhidharma* states that in the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), mental activity (*citta-vṛtti*) occurs in six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

In the stage of the first dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna*), mental activity occurs in four bases, namely, excluding the nose and tongue. From the second dhyāna upward, mental activity occurs in only one base, because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-kāya*) alone takes the mental object (*dharmārambaṇa*) as its condition.

It is explained that there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*) to clarify the meaning of "purity" (*śubha*), as this differs from the first dhyāna, which possesses both applied and sustained thought. [End of previous section]

The cessation of vitarka and vicāra is manifested as the antidote to their opposites; this mention of "non-existence" does not imply the non-existence of the antidotes themselves, and thus it is not redundant.

Third, regarding the phrase "joy and bliss born of concentration": these two factors constitute the benefits of cultivation. In the first dhyāna, one rejoices in turning away from sensual desires and evils, and is thus called "born of seclusion.
Now, one rejoices in the subsiding of the mind’s vitarka and vicāra, and is thus called "born of concentration," like a clear mirror.
The waters are stilled; thus, body and mind are at ease and joyful. Abiding in the second dhyāna, which relies upon that very samādhi, one is detached from joy.

Abiding in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, one experiences bliss with the body—this is what the noble ones describe as abiding in the third dhyāna, experiencing bliss through the faculty of equanimity and mindfulness.
In the third dhyāna, "being detached from joy" refers to the obstacle to be abandoned; that is, the factor of benefit in the second dhyāna.
Because the agitation produced by the conceptualization of a joyful mind causes distraction, it must be eliminated as the third dhyāna becomes increasingly tranquil.

Second, "abiding in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension" refers to the three factors of the antidote for practice. First, "abiding in equanimity" is the mental state of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This excludes neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). The treatise calls it "equanimity of mental application" (*citta-saṃskāra-upekṣā*), because the mind, having been brought into balance through application, abandons the fault of that joy.
Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "One who dwells in equanimity does not tolerate the joy that has already arisen; they abide in a state of equality, rectitude, and immovability."
Second, "possessing mindfulness" means that within the practice of joy (*prīti*), one does not forget but maintains clear recollection.

Third, "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*) means that if at times mindfulness is lost during the practice of joy, one dwells in correct mindfulness by making a discernment regarding this, namely, dwelling in equanimity (*upekṣā*). These latter three are identical to the previously mentioned "internal purity";
however, as they are progressively cultivated to a superior degree, they are here distinguished separately as being profound, subtle, and tranquil; thus, they are able to act as antidotes.

The lower stages are characterized by agitation and restlessness. The experience of bliss in the three bodies constitutes the branch of benefit. The experience of bliss in the first body specifically clarifies the essential nature of this branch;
that is to say, being free from the agitated mind of joy belonging to the second dhyāna, one attains supreme tranquility and great pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
With both body and mind in a state of bliss, because the body exists within that bliss, the mental bliss is also termed "bodily bliss. Next...

Regarding the statement by the Noble Ones that one experiences the bliss of equanimity (*upekṣā-smṛti-sukha*) while abandoning existence (*bhava*), this establishes the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
That is to say, the lower stages lack such bliss as well as uninterrupted equanimity; while the higher stages possess equanimity, they lack bliss.

Therefore, the Buddhas and their disciples declare that the third dhyāna alone possesses both the capacity for equanimity and right mindfulness and awareness, while simultaneously experiencing bliss. Thus it is said.
Among all forms of bliss, the bliss of the third dhyāna is supreme. Abiding in the third dhyāna, he relies upon that very samādhi;

having abandoned pleasure and previously eliminated pain, with the cessation of joy and sorrow, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
In the fourth dhyāna, the abandonment of pleasure and the prior removal of pain, along with the cessation of joy and sorrow, constitute the "separation from hindrances.

The superior pleasure of the third dhyāna is a detriment here; it is like a gravely ill person listening to exquisite music—it acts as a hindrance to the fourth dhyāna and must therefore be eliminated.
Thus, it is said that "pleasure is abandoned. One who attains this meditative concentration transcends all suffering and pleasure. Therefore...

The general summary states: "First, one eliminates suffering," and so forth. The word "first" (先) pervades the following three [stages]. That is to say, in the second dhyāna, one first eliminates the sensation of suffering;

in the third dhyāna, one first extinguishes the sensation of joy; and in the first dhyāna, one first extinguishes the sensation of grief. Together with the present cessation of pleasure, these constitute the extinction of the four sensations.
The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*). In all other dhyānas, this is explained first.

[This section] treats [the subject]. Now, here first the beneficial [factors] are clarified. Following the previous general statement that there are no four types of sensation (*vedanā*), it immediately mentions "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*aduḥkhāsukha*) to clarify that among the five sensations, there is only one:
equanimity (*upekṣā*). Because this is immovable, [it is said]: "The third dhyāna is pure in equanimity and mindfulness.

These two are the factors of antidote (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*), and they are also called the "ground" (*bhūmi*). In the third dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness coexist with the craving for pleasure; this [verse] severs that pleasure.

Because of affection, it is called "pure. When the mind of joy is restless, one must always maintain clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). When the sensation of pleasure is deep and subtle, one need only maintain equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*).
If one wishes to manifest this purity from afar, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "All calamities and afflictions of the lower stages have been severed."
Because it is free from the eight calamities—namely, vitarka, vicāra, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and inhalation and exhalation—the equanimity and mindfulness therein are pure.
Consequently, the mind of this dhyāna abides without movement. Abiding in the fourth dhyāna, one relies upon those two [factors].
However, when entering a higher form-sphere concentration, the physical appearance of the body is as if remaining within a room; whereas when entering a lower [concentration], [it is otherwise].
The four formless [attainments] are like being situated in space. Having concluded the four dhyānas above, we shall first explain the intent of the four formless attainments below.
Regarding the second category, the four formless concentrations—namely, the sphere of infinite space and so forth—their names refer to a state of one-pointedness of mind;

what, then, is their distinction? The *Abhidharmakośa*, in its "Chapter on Concentration," clarifies this distinction: they are established as four names because they involve the abandonment of the defilements of the lower stages. That is to say, by abandoning the [defilements of] the first...

The fourth dhyāna establishes the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); departing from the sphere of infinite space, it establishes the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Since the distinctions are thus established, from what are they named? Furthermore, the verse says: "The three beginning with 'infinite space' are named according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*);
'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' is named because of its dullness and inferiority. This refers to the stage of preparatory application prior to cultivating the meditative concentration.

Because one has grown weary of and overcome form (*rūpa*), one forms a resolute perception (*adhimokṣa-saṃjñā*) and contemplates infinite space. When this preparatory application (*prayoga*) is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
By growing weary of the perception of space, one perceives that consciousness is non-existent; this should be understood by analogy.

As for the fourth [sphere], because its perception is dull and inferior—meaning it lacks the clear, superior perception of wisdom found in the lower stages—it receives the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*); it is so named because it possesses a perception that is faint and inferior.

Because it is not "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," it is said that the first three formless attainments receive their names from their preparatory stages (*prayoga*), whereas the fourth formless attainment receives its designation based on its essential nature (*bhāva*).
Furthermore, each of these four emptinesses (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc. also possesses four aspects, namely: being free from hindrances (*vighāta-vigama*), and so forth.

Although the scriptural text mentions only three phrases, the meaning implicitly contains all four; specifically, the first phrase, "being free from hindrances," includes the sense of "possessing the counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*). According to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng): [text continues].

In the *Mūlakarma*, each of the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) possesses five factors: perception (*saṃjñā*), protection (*rakṣā*), tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). As in the first formless absorption of infinite space:
one becomes weary of the signs of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and gives rise to the perception of space; this is the immediate antidote.

Protecting against those signs of form so that they do not manifest is what is meant by "tranquility" (*śamatha*); this is the present departure from hindrances. The practice of the boundlessness of space is the illumination [of insight].
To be clearly manifest is the meaning of contemplation; this is the first benefit. Single-mindedness is the basis for those two.

Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells in the base of infinite space.

Now, first is the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). This refers to contemplating space as having the aspect of being infinite, which can extinguish the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*) and settle the mind in the concentration of space;
thus it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. These four spheres are called "spheres" (*āyatana*) because they are the places where sentient beings grow and dwell.
The three phrases within the text constitute three distinct sections. First, the clarification of being free from hindrances; second, the discernment of benefits;
and third, the elucidation of the basis. This is the first section. By linking the three phrases of the sūtra into a single semantic unit, there are three sub-sections.

Regarding "being free from hindrances," this refers to being free from the three types of obstructive, curved matter (*rūpa*): first, visible and obstructive matter, which refers to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). This one—
That which is "visible" (sanidarśana) is so called because it is observed by the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

These ten elements—the five faculties and the five objects—possess form (*rūpin*) and possess resistance (*sapratigha*). Because their substance is form, they are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and mutually obstruct one another;
therefore, they are called "possessing resistance. Second, regarding "invisible and resistant form," this refers to the five faculties, such as the eye.

The same applies to sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. The three types of "form that is invisible and non-obstructive" refer to the unmanifest form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Here, the phrase "transcending all perceptions of form" means passing beyond the characteristics of visual consciousness; this clarifies the transcendence of visible and obstructive forms.

Second, "the cessation of perceptions of obstruction" refers to the cessation of the perceptions associated with the synthesis of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses; this is their cessation.

It is invisible and non-obstructive. Regarding the three [aspects], "not recollecting variety" means not recollecting the perceptions associated with the synthesis of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because mental consciousness discriminates all phenomena (*dharma*), it is termed "variety. When this ceases, it is invisible and non-obstructive.
Although the mental consciousness takes non-material objects as its domain, it is currently concerned only with the various [perceptions] that arise when taking material form as its object;

these are all called "conception" (*saṃjñā*). In the Hīnayāna, because one remains within the realm of form and has not yet abandoned the appearance of form when practicing this meditative concentration, it is not said that "form is extinguished," but rather that "conception is extinguished.
This is because conception grasps the characteristics of form, and thus it is specifically extinguished. In the Mahāyāna, however, it is definitively only...
The cessation of perception. If one speaks of the formless by transcending the perception of form, then when space and consciousness subsequently cease, there should be no consciousness or space.
If one were to suddenly cultivate the concentration on emptiness within the realm of form, then the objects of the six consciousnesses would all be extinguished.

Having already clarified the separation from hindrances, how is it counteracted? Within the first three phrases, the term "non-recollection" contains the counteractive measure; that is to say, non-...

Because one discriminates between objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, why does one not recollect them? It is because one perceives non-self (*anātman*). This is said to be "non-self" in reference to the actual antidote of a Bodhisattva;
however, if relying on the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) state, one merely cultivates the practice of revulsion toward coarseness as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Second, entering the infinite space is the benefit of this cultivation: that is to say, when the perceptions of the three forms cease, one enters the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is vast and open.
Because it is infinite. Those who dwell in the third [dhyāna], the Sphere of Infinite Space, rely upon that samādhi as their support.
The final three concentrations are identical to this.
Transcending the Sphere of Infinite Space entirely, they enter the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and dwell in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Second is the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Because the mind takes internal consciousness as its object and forms the aspect of "infinite," it is so named.

The first [attainment], the Transcending of the Sphere of Infinite Space, clarifies the departure from obstacles. What is it that constitutes an obstacle? External mental attention is coarse; therefore, it is an obstacle.

What is the antidote? It is because one perceives the faults of coarse conceptualization in those external mental objects. Second, entering the "infinite consciousness" is the benefit of this practice.
While the previous section clarified the relinquishing of the external, the present section distinguishes the taking of internal objects as its focal point. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Regarding the pure sixfold body of consciousness, having correctly apprehended the signs within that which can be cognized, one abides in resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) by means of mental construction (*parikalpa*)."
Through the power of contemplative observation of the sign of infinite consciousness, preceded by this preparatory application (*prayoga*), one attains entry into the fundamental state (*maula*).
Thereafter, it should be understood that, relying upon this,
one transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), abiding therein.

The third station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is the state where both the internal and external are non-existent. The initial transcendence of the station of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) clarifies the departure from hindrances.
Why must one transcend it? Because the objects of recollection are coarse. How does one apply the remedy? By perceiving the faults and afflictions of coarse recollections and objective entities.
Next, entering the state of having nothing whatsoever is the benefit of practice; previously, one has already abandoned the external.

Because it takes the internal as its object, it is considered coarse thought. Since there is nothing to be grasped, the grasper also does not exist; thus, the absence of both internal and external is what constitutes benefit.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that when one progresses beyond the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), one seeks further objects outside of that consciousness but finds nothing at all.
This meaning clarifies that since consciousness itself is coarse, and because there is nothing further outside of consciousness, [the sphere of nothingness] is non-existent.
All [beings] abide in the sphere of nothingness; these two are the bases.
Transcending the entire sphere of nothingness, they abide in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In the fourth [dhyāna], the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no clear perception belonging to the seven lower stages; rather, there is a dull and inferior perception, and it is for this reason that it is so named.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is the obstacle to be abandoned. How is this countered?

By seeing that "there is nothing" (*naivāsti kiṃcit*)—that is, by perceiving the faults of coarse conceptualization and discursive thought—as the antidote. Once nothingness is stilled, [one enters the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception].
What is meant by "coarse"? It is because there is still the perception of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyasaṃjñā*). A sentence is missing in the Sūtra, whereas it is complete in the Śāstra-Sūtra. It says:
"Knowing that the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is peaceful, one then practices for its benefit and enters into neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These two are the bases of support. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "First, one enters the meditative attainment of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatanasamāpatti*)."
Having transcended all perceptions of existence, one now further transcends the perception of non-existence; therefore, it is called "neither-perception.

Furthermore, it is called "not non-perception" because it is not like the state of non-perception or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), wherein all perceptions have been entirely extinguished and only a subtle perception remains, which functions by taking the object of non-perception as its condition. It is precisely in this state...
Transcending superior resolve, one then transcends the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) to enter the fundamental dhyāna (*maula*).

The reason why [the non-Buddhists] do not transcend the three realms is that they take the object of "non-conception" (*asaṃjñi*) as their focus; since this is itself a subtle form of conception, the non-Buddhists fail to realize it and mistake it for *nirvāṇa*.

As they have not yet attained the state of being without an object (*anālambana*), how could they be free from the mind and its objects? Moreover, they reckon this very state to be the self. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* uses the metaphor of a fire upon one's head.

However, if one recognizes these afflictions and seeks further advancement, yet finds nothing to be attained despite seeking the higher objects of focus, then—due to this non-attainment—one ceases and does not proceed, thereby attaining the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

If one has not yet attained this absorption, first becoming weary of mental signs and subsequently no longer engaging in perception, one enters the absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Now, to further discuss cultivation according to the primary truth (*paramārtha*):

Briefly, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are indicated as follows: contemplating that form is itself emptiness and resting the mind in emptiness is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Next, knowing that both emptiness and form do not transcend the mind is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Next, the mutual forgetting of both mind and objects constitutes the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Next, one also abandons the perception of nothingness. Taking the sphere of nothingness as its object is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one does not take this sphere of nothingness as an object, then all taints are forever stilled.
He acts solely in accordance with the Dharma, yet without any attachment or delight.
This is the third entry into the mind: he merely follows the method of transforming sentient beings, unlike ordinary people who possess craving for flavors and the like.
The third section on the factors of aversion is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva’s mind accords with loving-kindness; it is vast, immeasurable, non-dual, infinite, without counterpart, unobstructed, and free from affliction.
It reaches everywhere throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, pervading all worlds.
The fourth major section clarifies the fruit of his renunciation. It is called "fruit" because it is that which is induced by the aforementioned eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
This section is divided into three parts: first, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), which are the fruit of the skillful means of practice;

second, the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which are the fruit of the application of practice; and third, a summary of the bodhisattva’s mastery over the various dhyānas. Now, as for the first [part]:

Regarding those who are first enlightened: ordinary beings, relishing meditative absorption, transmigrate through the three realms; those of the Two Vehicles, ascending upward, mostly tend toward quiescence;
whereas Bodhisattvas, by means of meditative absorption, give rise to compassion for the four types of sentient beings according to the four immeasurables as set forth in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

One arouses loving-kindness (*maitrī*) by taking as an object sentient beings who seek happiness; one arouses compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those who suffer; one rejoices in those who possess virtue; and one remains untainted by those who are deluded.

These four are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because they take immeasurable objects as their domain. If explained according to their general characteristics, all of them have meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature.
If they are clarified individually: loving-kindness has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essence, consisting in the bestowing of happiness; compassion consists in the removal of suffering.
Harm is its essence. Joy (muditā) has rejoicing in others as its essence; non-envy is its essence. The abandonment of delusions regarding self and others is itself joy and equanimity (upekṣā).

The text is divided into two parts: first, the specific manifestation of the practice of loving-kindness (maitrī); second, starting from "abiding in compassion" (karuṇā), the remaining three are manifested by analogy.

Within the first part, there are twelve phrases. The phrase "the mind conforms to loving-kindness" serves as the general heading. Regarding "conforms," there are two meanings: first, the mind does not...
Moving toward tranquility, all movements are imbued with compassion. Second, one follows after all things with a compassionate mind, like a calf following its mother.

There are three types of compassion: first, compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*); second, compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*); and third, objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).

"Object" (*ālambana*) refers to the act of taking something as an object of mindfulness. The first takes the conventional person (*pudgala*) as its object, wishing to grant them happiness; this is common to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Next—

Taking the emptiness of persons as the condition, there are only the phenomena of wholesome and unwholesome actions, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), used for the purpose of teaching and transforming others; this applies to the Hīnayāna.
Third, taking the emptiness of the essence of sentient beings as the condition with the desire to cause them to awaken and enter [the truth]; this applies to the Mahāyāna. Now, regarding the first:
furthermore, these seven phrases contain eight meanings, which are subsumed into four groups. The first four phrases speak of bestowing happiness and correctly manifest the aspects of the practice.
"Vast" means bestowing the pleasure of the desire realm, because the objects of desire are extensive and manifold. "Great" means bestowing shared joy and happiness;

that is, because it is accompanied by the sensation of joy (*prīti*) in the first and second dhyānas. It is called "great" because it is preeminent. "Immeasurable" means that from the third dhyāna upward, one is free from suffering and free from joy, and because it is profound, it is called immeasurable.
"Non-dual" means that the three types of happiness are bestowed with equality. Next, the two...

Regarding the remedy for obstacles: even toward those who are enemies because they are not loved, one bestows happiness; therefore, there are no obstacles of enmity. Toward those who are kin because they are loved, one likewise bestows happiness;
this is not a matter of partiality, and thus there is no obstruction. Since the mind is free from both love and dislike, it constitutes no obstacle. Next is the first purity:
this refers to the absence of physical and mental disharmony and obstacles such as the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); this is the purity of practice.

"Purity" (*śubha*) and "compassion" (*maitrī*). The subsequent phrase, "absence of affliction," subsumes the result. Compassion arises as the primary fruit (*maulaphala*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

through the residual force (*anuśaya*) of that compassion, it arises as the secondary fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In both cases, there is no occurrence of suffering or affliction.

Therefore, when practicing loving-kindness, the sūtras state that there are fifteen benefits: namely, peaceful sleep, peaceful awakening, protection by devas, protection by humans, having no bad dreams while asleep, and [peaceful] awakening...
Always joyful, one cannot be swept away by water, burned by fire, wounded by a blade, or harmed by poison.

One is constantly reborn in auspicious realms and perpetually experiences happiness. As a direct retribution, one attains the Brahma world; as a residual retribution, one becomes a king of men; and as a distant fruit, one becomes a Buddha.

Furthermore, within this there are many kinds of fruits: first, the fruit of immediate retribution, which is to be constantly reborn in lower realms; and second, the fruit of subsequent retribution, which is the direct...

The retribution for the Brahma-world is the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) expected from a superior birth; the retribution for the lower realms is the primary ripening fruit. The residual retribution of a human king is the fruit of cultivation (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Furthermore, the initial "human effort" fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*)—such as being unable to be swept away by water—is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Constantly being born in the lower realms is the ripening fruit. Residual retributions and so forth are the fruits of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Becoming a Buddha is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). By cultivating a single thought of loving-kindness, these three types of retribution are not [experienced].

The five fruits are severed and all are perfected; not a single hair’s breadth of effort is wasted, yet the merit and retribution are infinite. I hope that future students will reflect upon and cultivate this.
The above explains the compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*). Next, "pervading all places" refers to the compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).
Transversely it pervades the ten directions; vertically it penetrates the three realms. All phenomena (*dharma*) therein can be taken as objects of mindfulness.
"Phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of both noble and ordinary beings, as well as all phenomena consisting of the differentiated activities of sentient beings;

these are called "conditioned by phenomena" (*dharmālambana*). Regarding the latter two lines concerning "objectless" (*anālambana*), there are two types of objectlessness: first, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); [the second is the absence of external objects].
"Objectless" (mūrdhābhisamaya) means vertically exhausting the emptiness of all phenomena; thus it is said, "throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Second, "pervading to the objectless" reveals that emptiness has no boundaries, horizontally exhausting the entirety of space. The final phrase, "pervading all worlds," summarizes the aforementioned compassion.
Thus, one accomplishes immeasurable meanings.
Abiding in compassion, joy, and equanimity is likewise so.
The three categories may be understood by analogy. The above clarifies the fruits of the four immeasurables.
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva attains immeasurable powers of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). He is able to shake the great earth;

he can manifest many bodies from a single body, or a single body from many bodies. Whether hidden or manifest, he passes through stone walls, mountain barriers, and obstructions without hindrance, as if through empty space.
He travels cross-legged through the air like a flying bird; he enters the earth as if it were water, and treads upon water as if it were solid ground.
On the earth, his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, and he rains down water like a massive cloud.
Although the sun and moon possess great power in the sky, he can reach out and touch them with his hand. His body is sovereign, extending even as far as the Brahma-world.
The second [section], "The Buddha-sons Attain the Five Supernormal Powers," clarifies the fruit of the application of practice.

Previously, they inwardly harbored a mind of compassionate salvation; now, outwardly, they manifest the function of saving living beings. Their wondrous application is unfathomable, hence it is called "supernormal" (*śiddhi*); their mastery is unimpeded, hence it is called "penetration" (*abhijñā*).

There are five items in this text: first, the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhivisaya*); second, the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*); third, knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); fourth, recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); fifth, [the knowledge of death and rebirth].

The divine eye (divyacakṣus), because it is categorized as belonging to the mundane world, possesses only five [faculties]. External forms and the internal body are both objects of the supernormal power (ṛddhi);

when these undergo various transformations, they receive the name "supernormal power" (ṛddhi). It is also called "basis of supernormal power" (ṛddhipāda) because it is accomplished by means of desire, effort, mind, and investigation.

It is also called "according to wish" (kāmacāra) because it is accomplished according to one's will. The remaining names are easy to understand. Now, this is discussed in terms of the three types of action for the benefit of sentient beings.

First, by means of the body, he arrives at the place of the recipient. Next, by means of two types of vocal action: with the divine ear, he hears the Buddha preaching the Dharma and hears the various dialects of the multitude;

then, through the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, having fully understood all the various sounds and voices, he takes the Dharma previously heard and, according to the intent of what was heard, further employs whatever different language is appropriate to bestow it upon them.
Next are the two types of mental action (*manas-karman*). Through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), one knows which realm or seed they belonged to in the past;

through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one sees their future benefits at a distance or nearby, and accordingly transforms them. Now, regarding the first, the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*):

first is the general explanation, followed by the specific manifestation of the ability to move downward. Within the general section, the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to attaining [the powers] through general cultivation. However, these supernormal powers rely upon the four dhyānas and are most frequently...
Based on the fourth [dhyāna], one attains three kinds of mastery within the specific [attainments]: first, mastery over the world, because one causes the great earth to tremble;
second, mastery over the body and its lower parts by means of a single body; and third, mastery over the performance of actions through solid walls and other obstacles.
This Bodhisattva’s divine ear is purified and surpasses that of humans;
they hear all sounds of humans and devas, whether near or far, even down to the sounds of mosquitoes, gadflies, horseflies, and flies—all these they are able to hear.
The second day concerns the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). First, its essential nature is generally indicated: it is the "pure divine ear. This purity has two meanings:
first, it is produced from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are pure because they are induced by meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), having departed from the dharmas of the desire realm;
second, it is because it hears with precise clarity, being free from all obstructions. By this, it surpasses the human ear. The following section explains its function in full detail.
The meaning of "surpassing humans" is that he knows everything, even the most subtle things, from afar.
By means of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), this bodhisattva knows the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are:
he knows a mind with attachment as a mind with attachment, and he knows a mind free from attachment as a mind free from attachment; likewise for a mind with aversion and a mind free from aversion.
The mind: a deluded mind; a mind free from delusion; a defiled mind; an undefiled mind; a narrow mind; a broad mind; a great mind;
an immeasurable mind; a contracted mind; a non-contracted mind; a distracted mind; a non-distracted mind; a concentrated mind; a non-concentrated mind;
a liberated mind; an unliberated mind; a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind; a defiled mind; an undefiled mind. Broad.

The mind, and that which is not a broad mind, he knows all as they truly are. In this way, the bodhisattva knows the minds of sentient beings through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Within the third supernormal power (*abhijñā*), there are three parts: first, the general [statement]; "knowing the minds of others" applies generally to both kings and commoners;

next, the specific [details] beginning with "namely"; and finally, the conclusion beginning with "the bodhisattva, in this way. Within the specific section, there are twenty-six types of mind, each with its own mode of activity (*ākāra*).

However, with the exception of the four minds such as the "small" [defilements], all others are clearly explained as being either obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) or remedies (*pratipakṣa*), and are distinguished by their association with the wholesome or the unwholesome;

these are subsumed into nine categories. First, the initial six minds clarify the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). They are called "secondary" because they arise in accordance with conditions in association with the primary afflictions (*kleśa*);

it is not on account of being minor defilements that they are termed "secondary. As for the mention of "possessing greed" (*sānu-rāga*) and so forth, these refer to the three types of... [text truncated]

The roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), as well as the three roots of goodness, serve as the antidotes. The two types of minds associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth clarify the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Third, the four minds—small and so forth—are termed "arising" (*jāti*); these are categorized according to the neutral mind of maturation (*vipāka-citta*). In the human realm, the mind is small.

The desire realm heavens are "broad" (*vistīrṇa*); the form realm heavens are "vast" (*mahat*); and the two liberations of the formless realm are "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), because they employ the mental modes of the "infinity of space" and "infinity of consciousness.
The two higher [liberations] are not so. Regarding the four *dhyānas*, there is the practice of the learner’s samādhi.

"Concentration" (*samkṣepa*) refers to binding the mind to an internal object by means of the practice of calm abiding (*śamatha*); "non-concentration" (*asamkṣepa*) is so called because it is either too dull or...
Because of a single object of focus: "distracted" refers to excessive elevation, as it flows and scatters toward the five objects of sensual pleasure;

"not distracted" refers to the clear manifestation of the sublime object of focus. The first two [terms] are defined in terms of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the latter two are defined in terms of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the fifth, there are two types of mind that clarify the attainment of samādhi: those who are concentrated, because they have correctly entered the fundamental dhyāna;

and those who are not concentrated, because they have not yet entered it or have emerged from it. Regarding the sixth, there are two types of mind that clarify the attainment of liberation: those with bondage and those without bondage.
Seventh, there are ordinary persons with a remainder; their overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is a remnant of the aforementioned types.

Because they attain the four dhyānas and claim them to be the four fruits, their coarse habitual practice is termed "surpassable" (*sottara*); the absence of this is their subtle habitual practice, termed "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*).

Eighth, there are two kinds of mind: deluded practice and correct practice. In the treatise and sutras, these are called "seeking" and "not seeking. Seeking fame and reputation is what is meant by "mixed."
Defiled; the opposite of this is non-defiled. Among these nine, there are two types of mind. In the Mahāyāna, the attainment of both compassion and wisdom constitutes "extensiveness";

if either is lacking, it is not extensive. These nine categories do not exceed three types: the first two are afflictions (*kleśa*), the next one is suffering (*duḥkha*), and the remainder are all karma.
Karma is merely of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome. To know them all as they truly are means to examine the facts of reality with precision.
Because one perceives the reality of principle, one does not perceive phenomena as being external to the mind, nor is it the case that there is no object to be known.

If the characteristics of self and other are mutually exhausted, then one’s mind is of the same substance as the minds of all sentient beings; thus, there is nothing external to the mind. Because the subject and object are not destroyed, there is knowing.
Furthermore, the minds of others are the general, while all others are the particular. This is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in which the six aspects are perfectly interfused.
This is the realization of true knowledge.
This bodhisattva recollects and knows the distinctions of immeasurable past lives. That is to say, they recollect and know one life;
they recollect and know two lives, three lives, four lives, and so on up to ten, twenty, thirty, and even up to a hundred lives and immeasurable hundreds of lives.
Through immeasurable thousands of births, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births;

through eons of formation, eons of destruction, and eons of both formation and destruction—through immeasurable eons of formation and destruction—I was once in such a place, with such a name, such a clan, such a lineage, such food and drink, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure. Having died there, I was born in such a place...
He can recollect his various past lives with their specific details: from such-and-such a place he died and was born in this place; having such a form, such a physical appearance, and such a voice;
thus he can remember all the infinite distinctions of the past.

The fourth is the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*). First, it provides a general heading identifying who is able to recollect, namely, the wisdom of past abodes.

Next, under the section beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*), it provides a detailed exposition. Finally, under the section beginning with "In this way, in the past," it provides a summary. Within the detailed exposition, the first part concerns what is recollected:
namely, events from one lifetime up to many eons; this indicates the duration of the recollection. Next, under the section beginning with "I once," it explains how one recollects.

This refers to the distinctions among the characteristics of mindfulness. "Mindfulness" refers to the fact that names differ within those causal conditions. "Surname" refers to the family name of one's parents;
for example, the clans such as Kāśyapa refer to the noble or lowly status of the Kṣatriya caste and so forth. The rest may be understood accordingly.
This bodhisattva’s divine eye is purified and surpasses that of human eyes.

He sees sentient beings at the time of their birth and death—whether of beautiful or ugly appearance—and as they go according to their karma toward happy or miserable destinies. If those sentient beings have accomplished evil conduct of body...

They have accomplished misconduct of speech and accomplished misconduct of mind; they revile the noble ones and are possessed of wrong views and the causes and conditions for the karma of wrong views.
At the breaking up of the body after death, they will inevitably fall into an evil destination and be born in hell.
If those sentient beings have accomplished good conduct of body, accomplished good conduct of speech, and accomplished good conduct of mind; if they do not revile the noble ones...
Possessing right view and the karmic causes and conditions of right view, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will certainly be reborn among the gods in the happy realms.
The Bodhisattva knows all this through his divine eye exactly as it is.

The fifth is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*). The treatise clarifies the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), as they differ in terms of their faculties and objects.
First, it generally reveals the capacity to see: who is able to see? It is the one with the divine eye; "pure" because of seeing with precision, and "transcending humans" because of seeing from afar.
Next, it specifically reveals what is seen by first observing the fruits that have existed since beginningless time within the cycle of birth and death. Following this...

Regarding the causes of karma: how do those sentient beings perceive them? They perceive cause and effect differently [from one another], as explained in the section on the "Good Gathering of Precepts" in the second bhūmi.
This concludes the section on the bodhisattvas below.
This bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis;

yet, he does not take birth according to their power, but rather takes birth within those places where the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) can be fulfilled, through the power of his aspirational vow.
The third section summarizes mastery (*vaśitā*). It concludes proximately with the fruit of revulsion (*nirveda*) and distantly with the preceding revulsion.

Regarding "mastery over what": it refers to the aforementioned dhyānas and so forth. "Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas. "Samādhi" refers to the samādhis such as the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), namely loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest.
"Samāpatti" is translated here as "equilibrium" (*tingdengzhi*); this is likely a scribal error by the translator. It should properly be rendered as *samāhita*.

By means of this, one is said to be "equanimously induced" (*samāhita*), because the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are precisely what is induced. What is meant by "mastery"? It refers to the wisdom that can enter and emerge [from concentration];
thus, discursive agitation (*vikṣepa*) cannot bind it, for when the mind arises, its functions manifest in accordance with that mind.

Great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) do not follow along with rebirth; thus, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) cannot bind them. If one were not to be born in accordance with dhyāna, what would [the purpose] be?
Regarding the place of birth: without discriminating between the pure and the impure, one is born wherever the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) can be fulfilled.

That is, one is born in the same place as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this is the place where [the factors] can be fulfilled. As for those who act through the power of vows (*praṇidhāna*), they are not born through the bondage of karma.
Having completed the practice of the higher stages, the fruit of the lower stages [is attained].
O Son of the Buddha, when this bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Ground (Prabhākārī-bhūmi), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas;
that is to say, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta Buddhas.

The second fruit. The three realms constitute three distinct categories. Within the first, the fruit of refinement (*mṛdu-karaṇa*), there are three parts: the dharma-explanation, the analogy, and their synthesis.

First is the condition for refining practice; next, from "all" (*sarva*) onwards, it clarifies the practice that performs the refining; finally, from "seeing the bonds" (*bandhana-darśana*) onwards, it clarifies the purity resulting from what has been refined.
With a vast and profound mind, they respectfully revere, serve, and make offerings to them,
presenting all necessities of life— robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites— and likewise making offerings to the entire community of monks.
They dedicate these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, maintaining reverence toward those Buddhas.

They listen to the Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity. This Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, but exist by way of causes and conditions.

Next, within the clarification of the refinement of practice, there is first the practice of merit, then the practice of dedication, and finally the cultivation of the practice of wisdom. It is said that one contemplates...
That all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing is the contemplation of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Within pure phenomena, because no increase is perceived, there is no arising;
within afflictions and delusive thoughts, because no decrease is perceived, there is no ceasing.

That which exists through causes and conditions means that pure phenomena arise from conditions and thus have nothing that can be increased, while delusive phenomena cease through conditions and thus have nothing that can be decreased.
Furthermore, because these three stages fulfill the mundane world, one practices this true contemplation within meditative concentration.
One gives rise to the wisdom of the non-arising practice of the subsequent stage, which is precisely the skillful, definitive wisdom of observation.
The fetters of views are first extinguished; all fetters of desire, form, existence, and ignorance become increasingly subtle and thin.
Because they have not been accumulated for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, wrong greed, wrong anger, and wrong delusion are all completely severed.
All roots of goodness become even more radiant and pure.

Regarding the two aspects of purification through refinement (*pariśodhana*), first the severance of delusions is clarified, followed by the refinement of the subtle as distinct from the coarse. Within the former, the five bonds (*bandhana*) are the afflictions of the five stages (*pañca-vāsa*).
If the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are combined, they constitute four bonds, which are also called the four floods (*catasra oghāḥ*).

As for the prior extinction of the bond of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*), this is because the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) have already been severed during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "all desires and so forth," the *Śāstra* states:
Within all paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the three bonds (*bandhana*) and their causes—the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*)—are all rendered subtle and thin.
This refers to the "causes," namely the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*) of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Because they are extinguished simultaneously with the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of that same stage, they are termed the "habitual tendencies of ignorance. Here, "habitual tendency" has the meaning of "seed. Next, regarding the immeasurable...
The following passage distinguishes the subtle from the coarse; that is to say, it refers to the severing of the subtle.
Because one has not accumulated the three unwholesome roots for many kalpas, the subtle seeds are gradually severed and the roots of goodness become increasingly pure.

Regarding the phrase "many kalpas," the *Renwang jing* states that while the first stage (*bhūmi*) passes through four asaṃkhyeya kalpas, each subsequent stage increases in duration. This is because the subtle obstacles are difficult to sever, and thus the kalpas required increase progressively. Much...

Because kalpas are not accumulated, false greed and the like are severed; however, only their subtle habitual tendencies remain, because the coarse [afflictions] have already been severed by the path of seeing in the first bhūmi and the path of cultivation in the second bhūmi.
As the roots of goodness become increasingly purified, the preceding [faculties] such as faith and so forth [are likewise transformed].
O Son of the Buddha, it is like pure gold that, when skillfully refined and smelted, does not decrease in weight but becomes increasingly bright and pure.
The metaphor of "not decreasing in weight" means that one’s revulsion toward the world surpasses that of the preceding stage;
because faith and the other faculties have entered the fire of revulsion, their mastery is neither lost nor diminished.

The Bodhisattva is also like this. Abiding in this Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), because they do not accumulate [unwholesome states], all wrong greed, wrong hatred, and wrong delusion are completely severed.
All their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) become increasingly bright and pure.

This Bodhisattva possesses a mind of patience, a gentle and mild mind, a harmonious and compliant mind, a joyful and beautiful mind, a non-angry mind, an unshakable mind, an unpolluted mind, and a mind free from...
The mind of superiority and inferiority, the mind that expects no recompense, the mind of gratitude, the mind free from flattery, the mind free from deception,
and the mind free from treachery and partiality all become purified.

Of the three combinations, two are presented here. First, the preceding section establishes the purity of practice; subsequently, from the words "this bodhisattva" onwards, the purity of patience (*kṣānti*) is specifically revealed.
Since patience increases on this stage, it is explained in detail. There are thirteen mental states. The first two lines constitute the general summary:

first, the ability to endure insults and harms inflicted by others; second, skillfully protecting the minds of others, meaning that even when others treat one with harshness and aggression, one guards their hearts.
I, however, urge it forward with gentleness; therefore, the subsequent lines separately explain these two. Within that separate explanation, there are initially two types of mind:
first, the mind of discerning and skillfully protecting the minds of others; second, the harmonious and compliant mind, which [arises] because others commit evil against the Bodhisattva.

Suspecting that the bodhisattva might harbor anger or resentment, the bodhisattva manifests as a companion to harmonize with him. For those whose minds are joyful and beautiful, he instructs and guides them with pleasant speech (*priyavāda*).
Next, he distinguishes [the practice] by means of the three types of mind: regarding the endurance of harm, this means that when harm is inflicted upon the body, one does not become angry;
when the mouth insults and degrades, one remains unmoved; and when the mind harbors jealousy or malice, one cannot be defiled by grief or affliction. Next...
There are three mental states that emerge from the two aforementioned causes and are characterized by an absence of pride and contempt.
Because one has long since abandoned arrogance in the past, one does not exalt oneself or disparage others; through this, one is able to endure with gentleness and protect others.

The latter two are the causes for not changing even when subjected to harm: first, because one does not expect gratitude in return, one endures being wronged while benefiting others; second, [the second cause is...]

One who has received kindness always keeps it in mind and repays even small favors with great gratitude. Therefore, since sentient beings have been kind to me, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that I should practice patience toward them.
The latter three mental states reveal how the former two are free from obstacles: although one is compliant and protects others, this is not flattery;

because one truly seeks their benefit, one does not deceive. This is because the mind is free from concealment, sycophancy, and crookedness—whereas "crooked" refers to being sycophantic and deceitful.

Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva excels particularly in beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). Among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he excels particularly in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
He does not fail to cultivate the others, however, practicing them according to his strength and capacity.
This concludes the second section on the specific characteristics of the stages for this bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the Bodhisattva’s third stage, the Luminous (Prabhākari).
This concludes the third summary exposition of the characteristics of the stages.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

This constitutes the second [of the two types of] ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). In all subsequent descriptions of ripened fruits in the stages below this one, the text is divided into two parts; first, the superior body.
They are able to use skillful means to cause all sentient beings to abandon and leave behind craving and desire. Whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action,
or cooperation— whatever actions they perform— they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never depart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha,
and even never depart from mindfulness of the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Next, regarding the supreme fruits mentioned above, first is the stage of one’s own practice (*svabhāga*).
One further reflects: "I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings;
I shall be the superior, the most excellent, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, and even the basis for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). If...
