Because they are able to be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they are called those who constantly and diligently practice.
Because they seek to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind, they are called those who hold the Dharma in great esteem and reverence.

Because they act according to the teachings in the presence of all Bodhisattva Dharma-teachers, they are called those whose minds are without obstruction. Because they always move within the world through great skillful means (*mahopāya*), they are called...
"Being one who day and night remains far removed from other thoughts" means that one constantly delights in teaching and transforming all sentient beings.

The subsequent seven phrases concern superior progress: (5) initiating the practice of the Buddha-dharma; (6) initiating the practice of purifying the buddha-field—this constitutes the pair of the environment and its inhabitants;

(7) initiating practice based on the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, because it consists of both the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the *dharmakāya*; (8) initiating [practice] based on what the Buddha performs.

[The ninth is] the practice of manifesting the three secrets (*triguhyavajra*). This pair constitutes the correspondence between external appearance and internal secret. The [first] four above all give rise to bodhicitta.

The ninth is the practice of revering the Dharma, which proceeds by relying on those superior to oneself. The first five above pertain to self-benefit; the latter two pertain to the benefit of others.

The tenth is the practice of vowing to take up existence (*saṃsāra*); the eleventh is the practice of distancing oneself from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). These immediately manifest the distinction between what is correct and what is not.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices with such diligence, they transform sentient beings through the gift of giving;
they transform sentient beings through kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

In the third section on the excellence of teaching and transforming sentient beings, there are two parts. First, the actual clarification of the transformation of sentient beings; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva...

onwards, the conclusion regarding the accomplishment of benefit through practice. Now, for the first part, there are two divisions. First, the general gathering of sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

They manifest physical bodies to teach and transform sentient beings; they expound all dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings; they reveal and explain the bodhisattva practices to teach and transform sentient beings;
they display the great majestic power of the Tathāgata to teach and transform sentient beings; they demonstrate the faults and sufferings of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings;
they praise the wisdom and benefits of the Tathāgata to teach and transform sentient beings; and they manifest great spiritual powers...
He transforms sentient beings through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). He transforms sentient beings by means of various skillful practices (*upāya*).

Subsequently, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are explained individually; the text contains eight phrases. First, manifesting the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is the means of attraction through "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*), because he accords with sentient beings by manifesting himself among their own assemblies.
Second, expounding the Dharma is the means of attraction through "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*), as it consists of truthful words and the Dharma.
Speech has the nature of loving speech (*priyavāditā*). Among all forms of loving speech, it is mostly explained in terms of its exposition.

The three types of "revealing" [the path] below are all subsumed under beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). This phrase demonstrates the bodhisattva practice for those sentient beings who lack skillful means regarding awakening.
This is the very nature of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). Fourth, for those sentient beings who are weary of the Mahāyāna, one demonstrates the Buddha’s majestic power;

this constitutes all forms of beneficial conduct, as it causes those who have not yet attained [realization] to attain it. Fifth, because worldly sentient beings delight in and are attached to wealth and status...
He reveals their faults and perils, clarifying that although their status is high, they possess great sorrow and much calamity despite their vast wealth.

Sixth, for those who lack faith in the Mahāyāna and have not previously practiced superior goodness, he praises the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Seventh, for the ignorant followers of external paths, he demonstrates his supernatural powers.
The first three constitute difficult-to-practice beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). The eighth generally reveals beneficial conduct in all its aspects and through all its gateways;

thus it is said to employ "various skillful means. However, agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*) may also be applied here, because that agreeable speech demonstrates what is to be learned, which constitutes beneficial conduct.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to thus diligently employ skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings;

his mind constantly continues in succession toward the wisdom of the Buddha, and the roots of goodness he cultivates never regress. He always diligently studies and practices the sublime dharmas of conduct.

Next, regarding the formation of benefits through practice, first is the summary of what precedes it. In the section beginning with "The mind constantly... and continuing with "attaining the wisdom of Buddhahood," it is shown that for the sake of transforming sentient beings, one further seeks superior power;
the remainder clarifies that what has already been accomplished is made irreversible, while what has not yet been accomplished is further cultivated.
The section on the excellence of those fruits is concluded. Below follows the excellence of conforming to worldly knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices all worldly arts and crafts without exception.
The fourth major section, "The Superiority of Accordance with Worldly Wisdom," clarifies the remedies for defiled obstacles.

"Defilement" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), and "obstacles" refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This text is divided into three parts: first, a general presentation of many categories; second, a detailed demonstration of their characteristics, beginning with the words "That is to say";
and third, a concluding summary of the benefits, beginning with the words "And furthermore. Herein is the first part, the general presentation.
These refer to writing and mathematics.

To distinguish and clarify these five fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that because Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage study the five fields of knowledge, they are divided into five.
First, writing and mathematics constitute the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), which generally remedies the cognitive obstacles regarding worldly wisdom.
"Words and letters" refers to the collections of names, phrases, and syllables; these are established as the provisional designations of phenomena within the science of phonology (*śabda-vidyā*).
"Calculation" refers to the establishment of numerical enumeration; therefore, it remedies the obstacles of grasping, rejecting, and the arising of doubt.
He thoroughly mastered the arts of calligraphy and seal-carving, as well as earth, water, fire, and wind, and all manner of treatises.

From "the two arts of calligraphy and seal-carving" up to "thoroughly mastered," this refers precisely to *hetuvidyā* (logic). "Thoroughly mastered" (*xiantongda*) is the very meaning of "illumination" (*ming*).

The discourses of various theorists—including speculative discourse (*saṃjñā-vāda*), contentious discourse (*vivāda-vāda*), disparaging discourse (*apa-vāda-vāda*), orthodox discourse (*anuvāda-vāda*), and instructional discourse (*upadeśa-vāda*)—are of many kinds.
The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind are subsumed within contentious discourse, because the various false views hold differing positions;
for instance, the Lokāyatas maintain that earth alone is the cause, while others assert that everything is composed of atoms.
Therefore, the non-Buddhist practitioners who follow Water and Wind take water and wind as their causes, because the world is formed from water and is supported by the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).

The fire-worshipping non-Buddhists take fire as their cause, because fire brings things to maturity. As for maps, charts, seals, and insignia, these are merely conventional arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), following what is heard in the world.
Furthermore, these maps and charts are also valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) within the context of correct teaching; they are the objects of governance.

The obstacle of forgetfulness regarding the performance of tasks. The treatise states: taking, giving, and entrusting constitute obstacles to the performance of tasks; hearing the Dharma and contemplating it constitute obstacles to understanding;
and whether one acts or does not act, has acted or has not yet acted, should act or should not act—all these constitute obstacles to karma.
Seals and insignia are also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, they remedy the obstacles of not guarding or protecting the objects to be grasped; "seal" refers here to a jade seal.
Moreover, they are like excellent prescriptions and medicines that treat all illnesses; madness, emaciation, demonic possession, and sorcery can all be eradicated by them.

The third is the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*). This refers to the remedies for the afflictions and obstacles of disease characterized by poison that arise when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of sentient beings are out of harmony.

It is called "skillful" because it effectively cures and eliminates [the illness] through skillful means; it is called "skillful" because once eliminated, the illness does not arise again. Regarding the categories of disease from insanity to the symptoms of *gū* (sorcery/venomous spirits):

therein, insanity and so forth pertain to the internal four great elements, while ghosts and so forth pertain to external sentient beings. As for *gū*: *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the Buddhist sciences (*vidyāsthāna*), specifically discussing the science of medicine within the context of the five fields of knowledge.*
Poisons are of two kinds, as there are both plant poisons and snake poisons.
He was skilled in all matters such as writing, calligraphy, praise, chanting, song, dance, instrumental music, performance, laughter, jesting, and conversation.

Regarding the layout of kingdoms, cities, villages, towns, palaces, residences, gardens, groves, springs, streams, ponds, pools, grasses, trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs, everything was arranged with perfect appropriateness.
He thoroughly knows the locations of all treasuries containing gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and so forth, and brings them forth to show them to others.
He skillfully observes the sun, moon, and stars; the cries of birds; earthquakes; auspicious and inauspicious signs in dreams at night;
and the bodily marks of fortune and misfortune, such that there is not a single error in his discernment.
Fourth is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*). "Literary composition and eulogistic verse" refers to writing, calculation, measurement, and seals;

since these are subsumed under the category of craftsmanship, they are included here. "Literature" (*wen*) refers to prosody and rhyme; "penmanship" (*bi*) refers to the composition of prose; "eulogy" (*zan*) refers to manifesting virtue; and "verse" (*yong*) refers to the expression of sentiment.

Next, from "singing" up to "discourse" refers to the craft of music; one is thoroughly skilled in these matters, which together with the two preceding texts all serve as remedies for the obstacle of distress and affliction (*daurmanasya*).
From "kingdoms and cities" up to "what is appropriate" refers to the craft of construction; "grass, trees, flowers, and fruits" also encompasses the craft of agriculture.
This serves as the remedy for the obstacle of lack of joy (*anabhirati*). From "gold" up to "showing it to others" refers to...
The craft of producing [artifacts] is the remedy for the obstacle of attachment.
The craft of divination regarding the sun and moon until they reach the point of no error is the remedy for the obstacle of the causes of faults and evil within the portion of karmic retribution.

The sun, moon, and five planets constitute the seven luminaries, along with the twenty-eight lunar mansions; thus one knows the celestial phenomena above, and by earthquakes, one knows the terrestrial phenomena below, even at night.
When dreams reach their fulfillment in good or ill fortune, one immediately understands human sentiments; when birds sing, one observes the nature of the birds—these too are moved by human sentiment.
All are auspicious and without error, for they collectively investigate the three superior powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity).
Observing the precepts leads to meditative absorption, the immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
The fifth category, the internal science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) of observing the precepts, remedies five kinds of defilement: first, observing the precepts remedies the defilement of violating them;

second, entering meditative absorption remedies the defilement of sensual desire; third, the supernormal powers remedy the defilement of false refuge; fourth, the immeasurables remedy the defilement of improper conduct.

The defilement of merit refers to the practice of seeking the "merit of Brahma" (*brahmavihāra*) through rituals such as animal sacrifice; it is countered by the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

Fifth, the defilement of falsely cultivating liberation is countered by the four formless attainments. The explanations provided above rely primarily on the *Mūlaśāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapters three, four, five, and six;
however, there are further distinct principles therein.
As well as all other worldly matters, he reveals them all for the sake of benefiting sentient beings without causing them harm or distress,
gradually leading them to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
Third, regarding the establishment of the benefit: this gives rise to mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) endowed with four characteristics.

First, because there is no obstruction within what would otherwise be obstructive, it is said that one does not cause harm or affliction to sentient beings. Not knowing the facts of a matter is termed an "obstruction."
Furthermore, matters that cause harm and distress are obstacles distinct from the matter at hand; now, there are no such distinct obstacles as hunting and the like.
Second, it provides faultless happiness, which constitutes benefit; that is to say, even though one does not cause harm, one does not act to cause them to become attached either.
Third, it initiates purity, which consists of universally practicing and revealing [the Dharma]; that is to say, it is able to give rise to the factors that assist the Path.
The fourth is the purity of application, which gradually causes one to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma; that is, because one attains purity by means of this.
Thus concludes the section on the superiority of mundane wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*durjayā*), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas—
namely, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
To all of them they pay homage, revere, serve, and make offerings with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
They offer all their means of livelihood as gifts and also make offerings to the entire Sangha.
They dedicate these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In the presence of the Buddhas, they listen to the Dharma with reverence;
having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity. Furthermore, within the teachings of those Buddhas, they go forth into homelessness. Having thus gone forth...
Having already established the household, he further hears the Dharma and attains *dhāraṇī*, becoming a Dharma-preacher who retains what he has heard.
Abiding in this stage for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, and even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* kalpas,
all his roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
The second section of the major text concerns the fruits. There are also three fruits. Within the first, the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), there are four parts:

first, the practice of pliancy; second, the purity of teaching and wisdom; third, the characteristics of the specific stages; and fourth, the concluding explanation of the characteristics of the stages.

Regarding the first [of these four], there is the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy, and the synthesis. Within the principle, regarding the internal arising of practice, it says: "Furthermore, one who hears the Dharma and attains *dhāraṇī*. This refers to the treatise.
It is said that those who do not attain the *dhāraṇī* of meaning manifest their inferiority in contrast to the superior; this is because the *prajñā* has not yet become manifest before them.

As for why they are able to attain the *dhāraṇī* of hearing, it is because they have attained two things that are difficult to obtain: first, at the beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are able to attain the ten kinds of impartial mind (*samacitta*), which are otherwise difficult to obtain.
In the second bhūmi, one delights in supramundane knowledge while manifesting mundane knowledge;

because this non-abiding path is difficult to attain yet can be attained, these two difficulties serve to distinguish its excellence from inferior states, thereby enabling the attainment of hearing and retention (*śrutadhara*). This differs from the third bhūmi, where hearing and retention pertain solely to the mundane.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like pure gold that becomes even more brilliant and pure when polished with mother-of-pearl.
In this analogy, the polishing of the pure gold with mother-of-pearl represents the realization-wisdom (*jñāna*) which accords with reality as it truly is, just as the gold itself;
the light of the teaching-wisdom (*śāsana-jñāna*) is able to manifest reality as it truly is, just like that mother-of-pearl.
The roots of goodness possessed by the bodhisattvas on this stage are likewise thus; through contemplation and observation with skillful means and wisdom, they become increasingly bright and pure.
This can be understood through the threefold synthesis.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Difficult-to-Conquer stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), they accomplish meritorious qualities through the wisdom of skillful means such that the roots of goodness of the lower stages cannot reach them.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the light of the palaces of the sun, moon, and stars, which is sustained by the power of the wind and cannot be destroyed;
nor can it be shaken by any other wind. So too are all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattva on this stage.
It is likewise so. Through the wisdom of skillful means, one observes it with constant persistence such that it cannot be destroyed;
nor can it be shaken by any of the worldly roots of goodness of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or mundane beings.
Regarding the "sun, moon, and so forth" within the second [section], the purity of teaching and wisdom: the treatise states that by relying on the *āgama*, the light of wisdom increases;
because it surpasses the wisdom of the preceding stage, it means it excels the radiance of the jewels of the preceding stage.
Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the dhyāna-pāramitā is predominant; yet it is not that the others are not cultivated, for they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity.
This concludes the third distinct stage of practice.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the brief explanation of the fifth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā).
To conclude, the characteristics of this stage are as follows:
when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, exercising sovereign mastery over all sentient beings.
They subdue all the heterodox views of external paths and enable sentient beings to abide within the true reality (*satya*).

Whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—indeed, in all such actions they perform—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor from mindfulness of the Dharma, nor from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the possession of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes. Furthermore...
He forms this thought: "I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished among sentient beings;
the sublime, the most subtle, the supreme, the unsurpassed, and even the one upon whom all-knowledge relies.
If this bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, in a single moment he attains ten billion samādhis, beholds ten billion buddhas, and knows ten billion [kalpas].
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he can shake a thousand billion buddha-worlds, and even manifest a thousand billion bodies;
each body manifests a thousand billion bodhisattvas as its retinue.
Second is the fruit of the maturation of rewards.
If one manifests through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it exceeds these numbers;
even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
Third is the fruit of the knowledge of vows.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva’s fourth stage is already purified; He contemplates the equality of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.”
With the mind of ethical discipline, one removes doubt regarding the path and what is not the path; observing in this way, one enters the fifth stage.

With the foundations of mindfulness as the bow and the faculties as sharp arrows, with the right efforts as the horse and the bases of supernatural power as the chariot, and with the five powers as sturdy armor, one shatters the enemy hosts; courageous and unretreating, one enters the fifth stage.
Shame and modesty are his garments, the factors of enlightenment his wreath; Pure precepts are his incense, dhyāna his unguent;
Wisdom and skillful means are his exquisite adornments. He enters the grove of dhāraṇīs and the garden of samādhi;
The power of wish-fulfillment is his feet, right mindfulness his neck; Compassion is his eyes, wisdom his tusks.
The Lion among Men roars the cry of non-self; having destroyed the enemy of afflictions, he enters the fifth stage.
This third section of verses in praise consists of twenty-two stanzas, divided into three parts: first, seventeen stanzas praising the practice of the stage;

second, four stanzas praising the fruit of the stage; and third, one stanza concluding the exposition. Within the first part, there are again three sections; the first five stanzas consist of three lines each.
The antidote to the pride of superiority. Among these, the first four verses praise the ten equalities.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this fifth stage, they further cultivate the supreme and pure path, aspiring for the Buddha-dharma with non-retrogression, and contemplating loving-kindness and compassion without weariness.
Having accumulated the supreme merit of merit and wisdom, through diligent application and skillful means, he contemplates the higher stages;
empowered by the Buddha’s power, he is endowed with mindfulness and wisdom.
The remaining two verses are as in the *Caryāgīti*.
Thoroughly knowing the Four Truths as they truly are— The characteristics of the conventional truth and the ultimate truth,
The distinctions between the truths, the establishment of the truths, The truth of phenomena, the truths of origination and cessation, the path-truth,
And even the unimpeded truth of the Tathāgata— Though such contemplation of the truths is subtle and profound,
Not yet having attained unimpeded supreme liberation, one generates great merit by means of this;
therefore, one transcends worldly wisdom.

The second [section], consisting of six verses and three lines of verse, concerns the knowledge of the lower [stages] and the path of non-abiding (*apratisthita-mārga*). Within this, the first two verses constitute the first [part].
Wisdom is purified regarding the dharmas known through verses and phrases.
Having contemplated the truths and realized that conditioned phenomena are deceptive in essence and lack solidity,
one attains a portion of the Buddha’s compassionate light and seeks the Buddha-wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings.
Contemplating the prior and posterior limits of all conditioned phenomena, one sees beings wandering in a cycle of suffering within the darkness of ignorance and the bonds of feeling;
devoid of self, person, or life-span, they take up grasping as their cause and undergo future suffering. One seeks their ultimate limit, yet it cannot be found.
Wandering in delusion with no time of return—these pitiable ones I must deliver.

Within the house of the aggregates, there are snakes and the arrows of various views; the fire of the mind blazes fiercely, the darkness of ignorance is heavy, and one is swept away by the river of craving, too distracted to look back.
Sunk in the ocean of suffering, they lack a guide to illuminate the way.
Having known this, one exerts diligent vigor; all that is done is for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Following this, the next four and a half verses observe the diligent skillful means for teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Among these, the first verse generally observes the falsity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and gives rise to a mind of compassion. The subsequent one and a half verses observe through the perspective of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The Madhyamaka contemplates suffering arising from conditions. Next, one and a half verses contemplate the heavy suffering of the body; the latter half-verse is the contemplation of great compassion.
It is said: "One who possesses mindfulness and wisdom... up to one who has realized the skillful means."
They practice merit and wisdom without weariness, honoring the learned without fatigue;
their lands and physical marks are all adorned.
All such things are for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to transform all worlds, and they are well-versed in the arts of writing, calculation, and seals.
Furthermore, they are well-versed in all medicinal prescriptions, curing all manner of illnesses until none remain.
Their literary compositions, songs, and dances are all exquisite; their palaces, residences, gardens, and ponds are entirely peaceful and secure.
They reveal many kinds of precious treasuries to others for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as earthquakes, and even the physical marks [of a Buddha], are observed;
the four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the supernormal powers are all manifested for the benefit of the world.
This third verse is called the "Superiority of the Result," consisting of four and a half verses. The first half-verse summarizes the merit.

Virtue is supreme. The following verse concerns the supremacy of practice; therein, the phrase "all this for the sake of sentient beings" also praises the supremacy of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
The wise one dwelling on this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (Duranjaya-bhūmi) Makes offerings to nayutas of Buddhas and also listens to the Dharma.
Just as fine jewels polish true gold, so all roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Like the stars in the empty sky, sustained by the power of the wind, they remain unharmed and unmoved;
like a lotus flower that is not defiled by water, such is the Great Being’s conduct in the world.
Dwelling here, he mostly acts as the King of Tuṣita; He can crush the various false views of heterodox paths, And all the virtues he cultivates become the wisdom of a Buddha.
Vowing to attain the Ten Powers to save sentient beings, He further practices great diligence, Immediately making offerings to billions of Buddhas.
"Attaining the shaking of buddha-fields is likewise so; what is accomplished through the power of vows exceeds this.
These four verses praise the excellence of the arising of worldly knowledge and describe the fruit of the stages.

Thus has the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), the true path for those supreme among men, been fully expounded by me through various skillful means for the sake of the sons of the Buddha;
the three fruits may now be known. The fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer, is concluded.
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Thirty-Six;
Essential Outline of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Thirty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan.
Commentary on the Meaning by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
Extracted by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Six on the Ten Stages, Part Four.
The sixth stage, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). The reason it follows is that the wisdom associated with the various truths has already been explained;

next, the wisdom associated with the flow and cessation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained. Because this is entrusted to the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas, it follows immediately after.

Furthermore, while the fourth stage transcends the world, it is not yet able to conform to worldly ways; the fifth stage is able to conform but cannot yet shatter the views of defilement and purity. This [sixth] stage...
One observes the undefiled and pure dharma-realm in order to destroy those views.

Although in the preceding stage one was able to abandon both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through a mental orientation that turned away from the former and toward the latter exclusively, one was still unable to observe the flow of saṃsāra as it truly is.
Furthermore, because of the great degree of revulsion felt toward it, one was unable to dwell extensively in the mental orientation of signlessness. For this reason...
Because this stage must be brought to fulfillment, one practices with diligence to achieve that perfection; therefore, it follows next.
It is called "Manifest" because the *Vyākhyāyukti* states that the wisdom of the contemplation of neither abiding in saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa is manifest.
This refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*). Because one practices the dual contemplation during the preceding five stages, [the realization] is brought to manifestation.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that after the two matters of subduing Māra, all the dharmas of the Bodhisattva path manifest before one; this also refers to the initial [stage].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, citing the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, speaks of "manifestly observing the flow and turning of all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) and further practicing extensively in signlessness (*animitta*).

The meaning is that one can only bring [the realization] into manifestation by extensively cultivating the signless (*animitta*). This refers to the initial stage of the grounds (*bhūmi*), as it involves observing the ten types of equality.

As for "observing the process of transmigration" (*pravṛtti*), this refers to having already entered the grounds; only then does one observe dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"By means of the wisdom of dependent origination, one can cause the Prajñāpāramitā to manifest. This interpretation is correct.

Following the present sutra, this is explained in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*). As An-hui’s commentary states: "It means that within this stage, one abides in the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*).
By the power of this wisdom, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is brought to manifestation, whereby one realizes that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure.

Second, from the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he thinks" down to the eleven lines of scripture concerning the observation of the characteristics of dependent origination, the arising of inverted delusions through conditions is clarified;
this is answered by the treatise, which explains and resolves the [objection regarding] non-existence.

Regarding my own interpretation: from the passage "The three sons of the Buddha" down to "all are equally unobtainable," there are nine lines and a half of scripture that clarify the sequence of conditions by which delusion arises from the truth and gives rise to the false.
This is precisely what the treatise clarifies regarding the characteristics of phenomena. First, in establishing this, one will contemplate dependent origination;
first, one explains the establishment of non-self to definitively determine the fundamental tenet. To unify all through this single principle reveals that all ten gates are established.
There is no self. This is the correct destruction of the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self.
One should reflect: "All births in the world arise from attachment to a self; if one is free from this attachment, there will be no place for birth."
In the main body of the commentary, the first section establishes the non-existence of a self, which constitutes the fulfillment of the treatise’s title.

The initial statement—that all worldly arising and ceasing result from attachment to a self—indirectly cites deluded sentiments to clarify that the notion of a self is irrational, as it is merely the nature of suffering and its origination (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).

If one is free from this attachment, there is no place for rebirth. This directly follows the scriptural text to clarify that the mind which understands [this] is not the self, as it pertains to the Path and Cessation.

Thus, the meaning of "no-self" is established. The treatise states that regarding those born in the places where a body is received, the habitual tendencies of self-grasping merely cause the distinction between self and other; therefore, the treatise says: "Among the five destinies..."

Regarding the distinctions between birth and death: if there are distinctions among the five destinies, they are summoned solely by karma. The preceding section has definitively established the absence of self;
the discussion is now concluded. The following section provides the explicit response.

The second [section], concerning the conditions for the arising of inverted delusions, is explained as the response in the treatise. This is done to resolve external challenges; thus, there are two challenges and two responses.
First is the challenge that interrogates the principle based on emotional attachment, to which the response shows that such emotion deviates from correct principle.

Second is the challenge that interrogates reality based on the characteristics of constant seeking after existence or non-existence, to which the response shows that these characteristics do not depend upon a self (*ātman*). Regarding the first, the challenge states: "If there is truly no self, why is there attachment?"
"I" is like seeing a person in empty space where no person exists; one who fixates on "I" does not adhere to non-self, for they clearly believe there is a self.
To this, the answer is: it is due to ignorance that one clings to a self where there is no self, not because a self actually exists—just as one with cataracts sees flowers in the sky.
The second objection asks: if there truly is no self, why do you have such craving and attachment?
Regarding the self: it is only when one clearly understands that there is a self that one speaks of its arising through the sequence of conditions for birth in the world.
The answer is: it is precisely because of the absence of a self that one conceives of a self; with delusion and craving as the root, one creates karma through inverted confusion.
"Up to old age and death. What is there to be grasped? The answer is that the intention is precisely this. The preceding section sets forth the intention.
Regarding the text, there are twelve lines of sūtra, divided into three parts: first, it clarifies how delusions arise in accordance with the conditions for defilement;

second, from "By these causes and conditions" onwards, it correctly observes through wisdom in reverse order, concluding by responding to the absence of self; third, from "The Bodhisattva, in this way" onwards, it proceeds according to the person.
The summary of the contemplation. First: Now, although the twelve links constitute twelve distinct factors without interruption, many treatises subsume them into four categories.

First, the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), which refer to the two causes of the past—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—because they project the seeds for the five effects beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Second, the projected factors (*ākṣipta-aṅga*), which refer to the five effects of the present.
That is, the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they are brought forth by the preceding two members. Third, the productive members (*janaka-aṅga*):

namely, the three present causal members, which are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*), because they directly produce future birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Fourth, the produced members (*janya-aṅga*).
This refers to birth, old age, and death, as these are produced in close proximity to craving and grasping. The above represents the general intent of various treatises.
Herein, however, birth and projection are distinguished by way of a single set of cause and effect across two lifetimes;
whereas if one relies on the two sets of cause and effect across three lifetimes, birth and projection mutually interpenetrate. This sutra contains both perspectives.
Furthermore, he reflects: "Ordinary worldlings lack wisdom; they cling to a self and constantly seek existence or non-existence.
Regarding the initial delusion that gives rise to conditions for defilement, these are first divided into five parts based on the twelve links [of dependent origination].

From the beginning up to 'constantly seeking existence or non-existence,' this explains the link of ignorance (*avidyā*). Lack of wisdom is delusion (*moha*); constantly seeking existence or non-existence is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*). However..."

The cessation of all afflictions throughout the three periods of time is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because it is taken as a summary [cause] that initiates and moistens the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

If restricted to two periods of time, although all afflictions are capable of initiating and moistening [existence], ignorance is designated as such because its power is predominant at the stage of initiating karma.
It is defined solely as that which initiates the wholesome or unwholesome karma that directly brings about future rebirth.

Its essence is the desire for permanence within existence, because one wishes for things that are pleasant to endure forever; it is the seeking of cessation regarding the unconditioned, because one vows to bring about the extinction of things that are painful within existence.
Improper reflection gives rise to deluded conduct and leads one onto a wrong path. One accumulates and increases the courses of action consisting of demerit, merit, and the imperturbable.
Second is the branch of clear comprehension; the text contains seven phrases: the first three concern the faults of conduct, while the next three concern the essence of conduct. The latter...
This is concluded in a single phrase. The first phrase, "improper reflection," refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) conjoined with mental formations;

the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* explains this as the cause of ignorance and includes it within the category of ignorance itself. Because the preceding and succeeding [phrases] are linked, cause and effect are presented interchangeably.

The next phrase reveals the fault in terms of the person: one who gives rise to deluded practice is necessarily an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), for they seek [liberation] with ignorance as their cause.
Because there is the creation of karma, the First Ground states that "all actions performed are associated with inversion.

The subsequent phrase reveals the fault in terms of the phenomena themselves; the Treatise says this is because it demonstrates incorrect practice regarding the state of liberation. If one proceeds along the path to nirvāṇa, only then is it the correct path.
The next three phrases distinguish the essence of practice through its correspondence with the three types of action (*trikarma*); [the first] is volition (*cetanā*) which creates the three...

Regarding the [three types of] formations (*saṃskāra*): those arising from delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*)—which, being contrary to correct faith and understanding, give rise to the afflictions and the evil karma of the three miserable realms, as well as the karma for the specific retributions of humans and gods—are all termed "unwholesome formations" (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*).

Those arising from delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*)—which, not knowing that the three realms are entirely suffering, falsely conceive them to be happiness, and give rise to wholesome karma of the desire realm—are termed "meritorious formations" (*puṇya-saṃskāra*), as are the pure karmas of the eight dhyānas.
This is called "immovable formations. The subsequent phrase concludes the branch of formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

This means that having acted without regret, there is accumulation and growth, and because there is flux (*saṃsāra*), one plants the seeds of the mind within all formations; these are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and with grasping (*sopādāna*).
Next, the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is explained. This means that once [volitional] formations (*saṃskāra*) have been set in motion, they permeate the mind;

because this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is thereby enabled to attract future birth, aging, and death, it is termed a "seed. If there were no permeation by formations, it would ultimately fail to become a seed.

Therefore, it is said that "the seeds of the mind are planted within the various formations. These refer to the five factors, beginning with consciousness, which are projected [by karma]; they exist within a single [moment].
The moment (*kṣaṇa*) is that which is accumulated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*); it has no prior or posterior [parts]. The *Śāstra* states:

"In this context, the 'arising of the seeds of mind' indicates birth, old age, and death; the 'essential nature' refers to the two future fruits. This explains that the seed serves as the direct cause.

The statement that "it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and with grasping (*sopādāna*)" establishes the meaning of being a seed for the aforementioned [fruits]; that is to say, the seeds of verbal designation (*nāma-vyavahāra*) such as formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
All [factors] are generally untainted (*anāsrava*); however, because they are currently associated with the three taints (*āsrava*), they are termed "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*).

This is just as, in the first stage (*bhūmi*), the seeds of the mind arise through the four floods (*ogha*) such as desire and so forth. Tainted existence is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); tainted grasping is clinging (*upādāna*).
Because craving and clinging provide moisture, they are able to summon future existence (*punar-bhava*).

Furthermore, there arises subsequent birth, aging, and death. That is to say: karma is the field; consciousness is the seed; it is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; moistened by the water of craving;
irrigated by the sprinkling of self-conceit; and as the net of views increases, the sprout of name-and-form is produced.
Next, the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is explained. The first two lines of the text contain two meanings: first, they establish the meaning of the "seed" mentioned above;
because the mind that initiates birth and death acquires the designation of a "seed. Second, they provide a general indication of the subsequent meaning;

since the active manifestations of name and so forth are all [the causes of] birth, old age, and death, this is equivalent to the first stage, where the sprouts of suffering subsequently arise within the field of the three realms. That is to say:

The detailed explanation below also has two meanings. First, it generally concerns the twelve [links], from consciousness up to the production of the sprout of name-and-form; this means that consciousness produces the sprout of name-and-form.
Second, it is to demonstrate that since the ten causes have already been fully established previously, the branch of existence (*bhava*) is now analyzed as producing old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*);
thus, name-and-form is placed at the beginning, being explained in its proper sequence. This is because of the five factors, such as the preceding single mind and so forth.

It is with outflows and with grasping; because it is moistened by craving and grasping, it gives rise again to future existence (*punarbhava*). This indicates that the member of existence (*bhavāṅga*) produces two fruits.
Now, the specific characteristics of the member of existence are further elucidated.
The supplementary commentary states: This branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) takes birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as its primary fruits.
This meaning is frequently cited from the treatises in this sub-commentary, making it most difficult to comprehend.

This is because it is commonly taught that the twelve links of dependent origination generally refer to ignorance conditioned by formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*) as the fundamental cause and condition for the cycle of birth and death across the three periods of time. Within these twelve...
Zhi [Dao-lun] then restricts [the scope of ignorance] to two lifetimes; that is, sentient beings who create karma in the present life take up birth and death in the future.
Therefore, this ignorance is not the same as the ignorance that first arises. This is because the *Chao* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*) quotes the intention of Master Yuan, saying:
There are four types of ignorance (*avidyā*): first, ignorance regarding principles, which applies throughout from beginning to end;

second, ignorance that initiates karma, which exists prior to the formations (*saṃskāra*); third, ignorance that conceals karma, which exists after the formations and before consciousness (*vijñāna*);
fourth, ignorance of rebirth, which is simultaneous with consciousness or occurs after it—occurring after consciousness when viewed in relation to the seeds of the past mind-consciousness.
It is expected that the [karmic] formations arise simultaneously with consciousness; this is now the fourth link, ignorance at the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhi-avidyā*).
Previously, in the analysis of the link of ignorance, it was stated that "ordinary beings, lacking wisdom, cling to a self. This clarifies that ignorance is the root of the creation of karma.
In meaning, this corresponds to the two types of ignorance: that which initiates karma (*pravartaka-avidyā*) and that which conceals karma (*āvāraka-avidyā*). Therefore, it says next:

Improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) constitutes the limb of formations (*saṃskāra*). By implication, it should precede formations. Next, it is said that planting the seed of the mind within various formations constitutes the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
By implication, this should follow formations, because this seed of consciousness is the direct cause that draws forth future birth and death.
Next is the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which is indicated by the statement: "Furthermore, there arises subsequent existence... and so forth.
"Old age and death" refers to the fact that birth and death are directly invited by the seeds of prior consciousness;

however, since the beginning of birth starts from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the Commentary points out that this is the fourth ignorance, namely "rebirth. Therefore, regarding the preceding link of consciousness, it is said to be "with outflows and with grasping.
The Commentary states: "Outflows" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and "grasping" refers to clinging (*upādāna*). Because they are moistened by craving and clinging, [the seeds ripen].
It is capable of summoning future existence (*punarbhava*). This future existence, in turn, belongs to the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Therefore, the preceding commentary states that within the limb of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*), ten causes are already complete; this is to distinguish how the limb of existence gives rise to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Thus, in the future [sequence], name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is placed at the beginning, and the factors are explained in their proper order. These ten causes are spoken of solely in reference to the present, wherein delusion regarding selflessness constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*).
Improper reflection constitutes the activity of performing good or evil deeds. Through this activity, seeds are received as consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because it acts as the cause for birth and death, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which subsumes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). In every present moment, these ten causes are fully present.
As the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) quotes from the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, the correct principle does not go beyond this. If one speaks of the causes and effects of two lifetimes:
In the section concerning the gate of arising delusion from truth that follows later, the commentary states:
"For now, we shall consider this in terms of the *bhavāṅgas* (factors of existence). There are six conditions in the text: first, karma as the field, which is the seed of *saṃskāra*;
it serves merely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to that which is produced. Second, consciousness as the seed, which refers to the five seeds beginning with consciousness."

"Later, birth and death act as the proximate causes and conditions. The treatise explains this collectively by stating that they "accord with and grasp the activities of demerit and merit," because karma serves as the ground.
This precisely clarifies the accordance with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), whereby it gathers the seeds of the preceding consciousness (*vijñāna*) to form the link of existence (*bhava*).
Third, "enveloped by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*). The treatise takes up the ignorance mentioned in the preceding sutra; therefore, it says, "as previously stated, [there is] ignorance..."
Because it is obscured by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), this [ignorance] takes up the "equal" [ignorance] and initiates it, acting as a remote auxiliary.

Furthermore, it serves as an illustration of the past life by analogy with the present life. According to the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this is not the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmārambhaka-avidyā*), but rather the ignorance that covers karma (*āvāraka-avidyā*);
it is also subsumed under craving (*tṛṣṇā*). It is the delusion regarding external dominant results (*bāhya-adhipati-phala-moha*).
Fourth, the water of craving provides moisture. The *Śāstra* points to the aforementioned craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and non-existence as an illustration;

this is also identical to what was previously designated as "contaminated" (*sāsrava*). This is because the former is subsumed under craving for existence and ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas within the former [category of] ignorance, craving refers specifically to the craving that initiates karma (*karmābhisamskāra-tṛṣṇā*).
Since the present [craving] is the craving that moistens karma, it is not the same. Fifth, the self...

The "irrigation by pride" (*māna*) is the limb of grasping (*upādāna*). It is only through repeated irrigation that the sprout of existence (*bhava*) arises, for the grasping of "self-identity" (*ātma-vāda*) and so forth constitutes the pride of self (*asmimāna*);

if one were to realize non-self (*anātman*), such [grasping] would not arise. Furthermore, the growth of the "six nets of views" is also the limb of grasping, as it is subsumed under the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*).
Since all views arise with the three [wrong] views as their root, they cause the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)... [to be obscured].
Because it cannot be destroyed, it is called a "net. The general explanation in the treatise states: "Thus abiding, thus arising.

This refers to the mind that gives rise to the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Because of ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is caused to abide in the stage of karma, whereby the mind of name-and-form arises.
Now, while the previous seed of consciousness is concealed within the other four [aggregates], we shall briefly analyze its manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
The basis for its collective retribution is intended to reveal the principle that consciousness and name-and-form arise sequentially;

furthermore, it is intended to reveal that these exist both as seeds and as manifest states. Thus, there is a distinction between what is hidden and what is manifest. Nevertheless, since name-and-form and so forth must necessarily have the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as their support, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Within the field of the three realms, the sprouts of suffering grow once again—namely, name-and-form together."
Regarding "birth" (*jāti*): the *Śāstra* states that it arises together with the *ālayavijñāna*.

This refers to what follows in the text: name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arise simultaneously with consciousness; as name-and-form increase, the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise; through the mutual encounter of the faculties, contact (*sparśa*) arises; from the encounter of contact, sensation (*vedanā*) arises; following sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises through the longing for existence;
as craving increases, grasping (*upādāna*) arises; as grasping increases, becoming (*bhava*) arises; and once becoming has arisen, one exists within the various realms of rebirth (*gati*).
The arising of the five aggregates is called birth. Once born, their decay and transformation is aging. Their final passing away is death.
At the time of aging and death, various fevers and afflictions arise. Because of these fevers and afflictions, sorrow, lamentation, and all manner of suffering converge.
Next, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the other eight links are to be explained as they arise, as clarified in the subsequent section.

However, the intent of this present section is to answer the reason for taking birth; therefore, it sets forth all the afflictions (*kleśa*) in their various modes of manifestation and concealment, rather than focusing on their explicit characteristics.
This is clarified in the subsequent text.
For this reason, although there is arising through causes and conditions, there is no one who arises; although there is spontaneous cessation, there is no one who ceases.
Through right wisdom, one contemplates in reverse order. This response regarding the absence of a self concerns the first two lines, which clarify non-self with respect to birth. It simply says:
The accumulation of ignorance and so forth does not arise through a self. Furthermore, the first phrase excludes the absence of a cause, while the second phrase excludes false causes.
The latter two phrases clarify non-self with respect to cessation; because things are of a momentary nature that perishes, they are such without the need for an external agent.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the characteristics of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in accordance with reality.
Third, regarding the person, he forms a contemplative observation. One who observes in this manner accords with the principle of dependent origination.
The preceding clarifies the response; the following clarifies the characteristics.

Regarding the sequence of conditions for the delusion of the great text, wherein the true is lost and the false arises, this refers to the distinctions among the characteristics elucidated in the treatise. The treatise states:

"If there were no self within causes and conditions, by what characteristic would they abide? Causes and conditions assemble and proceed; that which is termed their respective characteristics is called 'abiding'."
After birth, there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Deluded regarding the principles of the Truths, one gives rise to the accumulation of signs (*nimitta*).

Nevertheless, the mutual correspondence between the answer and the question indicates that these are the continuous succession of the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*). How, then, are the distinctions between these two layers of causal conditions? Briefly, there are five differences.

First, the former refers to the conditions arising from the deluded self, which is the attachment to a self; this [latter] refers to the conditions arising from delusion regarding the truths, which is delusion regarding the ultimate meaning.
Second, the former refers to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); this refers to the sequence of conditions.

Therefore, the former generally includes the ten causes and one basis arising together as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), whereas here it speaks exclusively of the single sequence. Third, the former encompasses all three time periods.
The World [honored one], because he allows the ten causes to span a single lifetime, takes them to mean they also span all five lifetimes.

This [text], however, refers only to the three lifetimes, because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are treated solely in terms of the present; thus, it takes them to mean they also span a single lifetime.

The preceding passage intended to clarify that the three lifetimes are fully complete; since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are mentioned within ignorance (*avidyā*), [craving] is not mentioned separately within the present.

Because they are clarified herein, the three time periods mutually possess concealment and manifestation; it is not admitted that they interpenetrate. The five [preceding] points answer objections, while these [present] points distinguish the characteristics.
Since this accords with the intent of the treatise, there are these five differences. Both sections distinguish conditions and together clarify continuity;
they collectively refute delusion and inversion, and thus are merely bound together as ten.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects: "Because one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

The three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) clarify the sequence of the conditions for delusion that arises from the true, giving rise to the false, and the appearance of characteristics. Within this passage there are also two parts: first, the conformity [to the truth], and afterwards...

[This refers to] the reverse order. Regarding the first member of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the forward order, "ignorance" (*avidyā*), it is said that one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

However, all twelve members arise based upon the Reality (*tathatā*) and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the following verse states: "When observing the true meaning of all causes and conditions, they are empty.

Yet, ignorance initially and directly deludes regarding the principle of the Truths (*satya*), thereby giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Since these arise horizontally from emptiness, [they are thus characterized].
It cannot be restored to its original state; therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) alone receives the designation of "delusion. As the *Śāstra* on the Sūtras states:
"The ultimate truth among all truths refers to the Four Noble Truths. Thus, the remedy for delusion regarding the true meaning is called the "Four Noble Truths."
That which is deluded is the actual reality; that which is capable of deluding is ignorance (*moha*). There exists a distinct obscuring phenomenon called "ignorance" (*avidyā*);
it is not merely a negative designation (apavāda) indicating the absence of knowledge.
The fruit of the karma performed is *saṃskāra*;

this is the second member of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Karma refers to the three types of karma, such as unwholesome action (*pāpa*) and so forth, because it is the fruit arising from that ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, the verse says: "The volitional karma performed is the fruit of delusion. The commentary states: "Among these, it is the fruit of the karma produced by ignorance."
That which is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) refers to the essence of the fruit produced. This "essence" refers to the essence of the formations (saṃskāra), for it is precisely name-and-form.

Master Yuan’s commentary on the *Śāstra* states that the formations have three meanings: mental karma is "name," while bodily and vocal karma are "form. Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says there are two kinds of name-and-form:
first, name-and-form as means (*upāya-nāmarūpa*), and second, name-and-form as designation (*abhidhāna-nāmarūpa*). If one speaks of "conditioned by name-and-form," [it refers to the latter].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself the skillful means (*upāya*) for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). If one says that consciousness conditions name-and-form, that is what is designated as name-and-form. Now, taking volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as the skillful means for name-and-form:
the initial mind upon which these formations depend is consciousness.
Second is the consciousness link (*vijñāna-aṅga*). The treatise states: "Among these, consciousness is so called because it is the basis for that [name-and-form].

Here, "that" refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This passage contains a syntactical inversion; it should read "based upon those. Therefore, the treatise and the sūtra state: "Based on the formative forces, there is the initial consciousness.
This means that through the perfuming of the mind by the formative forces, there exists the essence of the future fruit, continuing until its actual manifestation.
The four aggregates of grasping that arise simultaneously with consciousness constitute "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
This is the fourth member of dependent origination. The first term, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), refers to the active (*pravṛtti*) member of consciousness;

as a seed, it is exclusively the *ālayavijñāna*, whereas in its active state, it encompasses all six consciousnesses. Since the present context distinguishes the active from the seed state, the term "simultaneous" (*saha*) is used.
The four aggregates arise; since the aggregate of consciousness already belongs to the dependent consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increases to become the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).

Regarding the two branches of the five and six sense bases: this refers to the stage when the faculties are fully developed after four weeks [of gestation]. When the six sense bases are bright and flourishing, it is called "increase" (vṛddhi).

The sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is established by form; the remaining five are established through their increase. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "From the arising of the eye and other faculties, prior to the triad [of the next stage], there are the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The conjunction of the three factors—the faculty, the object, and consciousness—is contact (*sparśa*)."
The sixth limb is contact (*sparśa*). This means that although there is a conjunction of the three, one has not yet fully understood the causes of the three types of sensation;
it is merely the act of contacting.
Contact arises together with sensation.
The seventh is the branch of feeling (*vedanā*). It is analyzed into three types of feeling that experience contact; this is called "arising together with contact.
Among these, the first four arise only as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Attachment to feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The eight factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*): because one is entangled in and yearns for the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) among the three types of sensation, it is called "attachment" (*rakta*).

This refers to greed (*lobha*) of middling and inferior grades. Although this [craving] generally takes both internal and external fruits as its objects, most treatises take the external environment as its primary object.
The external dominant fruit arises.
The increase of craving is grasping (*upādāna*).
Although the nine factors of grasping belong to other afflictions, because the moistening by craving is predominant, they are said to be the increase of craving. However, regarding the [last] two...
The two branches [craving and grasping] encompass both the manifest and the seeds. That is to say, craving as a seed increases and becomes grasping;

since grasping is the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the seed of craving, they are essentially the same greed. Initial [craving] is termed "craving," while its intensification is termed "grasping.
Thus, this very seed of craving is itself the seed of grasping. Therefore, both of these two branches encompass both the manifest and the seeds.
The outflowing karma (*āsrava-karman*) arising from grasping (*upādāna*) constitutes "existence" (*bhava*).
There are ten members of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Because these karmas arise within the internal mind through internal grasping, they are termed "outflowing.

Since this karma directly brings about future results, it is called "existence. This refers to the three periods of time and differs from the previous [classification] which combined craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
The moistening karma and so forth are called "existence" (*bhava*). These three preceding types of karma have already been separated from the manifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth;
thus, the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) from karma constitutes birth (*jāti*).

Regarding the eleven branches of birth, they are said to arise from karma in terms of their predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). This begins from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until the point before decay and transformation.
All stages are termed "birth.
The maturation of the aggregates is "aging. The disintegration of the aggregates is "death.

Regarding the twelve links of aging-and-death, the state of various transformations is what is termed the maturation of the aggregates; therefore, the substance of these latter two links [is that state].
These pertain to all five aggregates and consist exclusively of active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

Having completed the upward contemplation, one who is deluded and confused at the time of death feels attachment and separation; the distress within the heart and chest constitutes sorrow (*śoka*), while the shedding of tears and lamentations constitute grief (*parideva*).

In the five sense faculties, it is suffering (*duḥkha*); in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is grief (*daurmanasya*). When grief and suffering increase further, they become affliction (*upāyāsa*).
In this way, there is only the growth of the tree of suffering.

Subsequently, when observing in reverse, there are four [aspects]: first, the formation of suffering; second, the formation of non-self (*anātman*); third, the formation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); fourth...
The summary of the ultimate truth. First: ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) lead to consciousness (*vijñāna*), up to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which constitutes the sprout of suffering.
Craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*), leading to becoming (*bhava*), which constitutes its nourishment. Birth, old age, and death constitute the tree of suffering.

From the sprout to the nourishment, this signifies growth. Furthermore, the first two [links] are the roots; the next two are the trunk; the next two are the branches; the next three are the flowers; and the last...
The second is the fruit:
the absence of self and the absence of what belongs to a self.
Through the absence of self and the absence of what belongs to a self, non-self is established.
There is no agent and no experiencer.
The non-existence of an agent and an experiencer constitutes emptiness.
Furthermore, one reflects thus: "If there were an agent, there would be an action; if there were no agent, there would likewise be no action."
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both are unattainable.

Fourth, by using the self as an analogy for phenomena, the excellence [of the teaching] is established. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is profound by virtue of ten aspects:
six meanings based on impermanence (*anitya*), one meaning based on suffering (*duḥkha*), one meaning based on emptiness (*śūnya*), and two meanings based on selflessness (*anātman*).
Now, regarding the six meanings: first, [a phenomenon] arises from its own seed and also depends on other conditions;
second, it arises from others and also depends on itself; third, both [of these] are devoid of functional activity; fourth, the nature of these two causes is not non-existent.

These four points constitute the previous section’s statement that they arise due to causes and conditions alone, and that there is no agent who assembles them. Fifth, although they are beginningless, their...
The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are established and yet perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*). Although these six perish moment by moment, they appear to remain stable.

These two [aspects] are both spontaneously extinguished as before, and there is no agent of extinction. Regarding the first meaning based on suffering (*duḥkha*): it is of a single flavor of the characteristic of suffering, yet appears as if it has three characteristics;
thus, it is concluded that it is a "tree of suffering. Regarding the second meaning based on emptiness (*śūnyatā*): it refers to being devoid of sentient beings and an agent (*kartṛ*).
The experiencer appears as if not separate from the experience; yet, right now, there is neither agent nor experiencer. Regarding the two meanings based on selflessness:
first, although in reality there is no self, the appearance of a self and what belongs to a self arises; yet, right now, there is neither "I" nor "mine.
Second, although in the ultimate sense it is inexpressible, it is said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena can be described; thus, one further reflects as follows:
The six lines of scripture below fully encompass the ten meanings.

Since the preceding conditions and marks are all merely semblances of objects, this inverse contemplation directly reveals the non-obstruction between the true nature and its characteristics; therefore, it constitutes the contemplation of the profound dependent origination.
It is precisely here. The above concludes the detailed contemplation of the distinctions among the marks of the truths.
Second, regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion: this first gate corresponds to the first of the four contemplations, namely, the contemplation of delusion and inversion.
The treatise provides a general explanation, stating: "In whatever place one is attached, there is both delusion and inversion."

Because it is a contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*). This refers to the nature and characteristics of delusion (*moha*) regarding the points of attachment within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein one erroneously clings to "mine" (*mamakāra*).
The subsequent detailed explanation states that it clarifies how delusion follows its objects of confusion to establish two types of inversion (*viparyāsa*).

First, [the section] up to "there is no place of birth" clarifies that one is confused regarding the selflessness (*anātman*) of the nature of conditions; by clinging to a self, one establishes an inversion. Because of this attachment to a self, then...
The arising of illumination within the world is an inversion (*viparyāsa*). If one is free from this attachment, there is no place for such arising.

By implication, this attachment must necessarily be an inversion. Second, following the first section [of the previous chapter], this initial gate clarifies how ignorance conditions the arising of doubt and inversion.
Because of a lack of wisdom, one constantly seeks after existence and non-existence, becoming mired in the two paths of annihilationism and eternalism; hence, it is called "doubt."

To clarify that the continuity of the characteristics of conditions is an inversion, the Bodhisattva now accords with the ignorant and inverted state of those sentient beings and gives rise to compassionate observation;
this is called the "contemplation of phenomena" (*vastu-vipaśyanā*). Third, regarding the contemplation through the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*):
among the nine types of contemplation, this section subsumes the entirety of the first contemplation and half of the second, namely, the initial establishment and the response to the two.
The text is titled "Discrimination of Defilement and Purity. This has two meanings: first, attachment to a self is defilement, while detachment from a self is purity;

second, because of attachment to a self, the arising of conditioned marks through objective conditions is defilement, while because of detachment from a self, the cessation of conditioned marks through objective conditions is purity.

The subsequent passage of the sutra belongs to the second [category], which relies on contemplation (vipaśyanā). That is to say, although one relies upon the ultimate truth (paramārtha), because of ignorance—

This immediately gives rise to various defilements; thus, it serves as the basis for defilement (*saṃkleśa-āśraya*). When one perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these conditions are extinguished, and it then becomes the basis for purity (*vyavadāna-āśraya*).

Because of ignorance within the contemplation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satyābhisamaya*), they constitute the appearance of conditions (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Because of ignorance within the contemplation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-bhāvanā*), this results in perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Nevertheless, the scriptural passage concerning the single gateway of the aforementioned continuity is non-dual; it is divided into three according to its meaning. First, the perversion is explained.

First, one contemplates the wisdom of all modes (sarvajñatā) by realizing that although delusions arise based on conditions, there is no self-existent entity. Next, one contemplates the wisdom of the aspects of the path (mārgajñatā) by following the process of the deluded inversions.
Finally, one contemplates the wisdom of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) by thoroughly investigating the nature and characteristics of delusion and awakening, as well as defilement and purity.

Furthermore, the first corresponds to the fundamental [wisdom], the second to the subsequently attained [wisdom], and the last to the unimpeded [wisdom]. Thus, although there is no "mine," the characteristics are not destroyed.

Arouse great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Since both subject and object are fundamentally empty, one practices compassion without attachment. By simultaneously exhausting both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one does not stagnate in either self or other.

When the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are unified within a single mind, unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) is perfected. How could profound *prajñā* not then manifest before one? This is true even for a single gate; how much more so when the remaining nine are added.
The first section, the Gate of the Succession of the Links of Existence (*bhavāṅga*), concludes above. Below begins the second [section], the One...
The Section on Being Subsumed by Mind.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects: "All that exists within the three realms is but the single mind.
Within this second section on being subsumed by the single mind, this one gate contains many meanings; for now, it shall be divided into two parts.

Separate. First is the section on "Pushing the Branches Back to the Root. Second is the "Section on the Mutual Support of the Root and the Branches," beginning with the passage "The Tathāgata, in this regard... Now, for the first:

according to the three contemplations of the *Śāstra*, the first—contemplating based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—corresponds to the second contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which comprises half of this present section.
The *Śāstra*’s introduction asks: "What is the differentiation of the ultimate? Thus it is realized... the ultimate.
Because one attains liberation through the contemplation of that single meaning, this clarifies the purpose of cultivating contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), seeing the nature of conditions brings liberation from the bondage of conditions.

Although the treatise and the sūtra state that "all are produced by the one mind," the intent is to take the "one mind" as the agent of production; therefore, it is called the contemplation of the ultimate truth. The treatise says: "It is merely..."

"Single-mindedness" (ekacitta) means that all of the triple world is merely the transformation of mind; this statement is general in scope. "Transformation" (pariṇāma) carries the meaning of arising and activity, as well as the meaning of transmutation.
Nevertheless, this single phrase is cited in various teachings alike to establish the proof of Mind-Only (cittamātra).
