How does a single mind produce the triple world? Briefly, there are three meanings: first, persons of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) believe that external objects exist.

They do not understand that it is "mind-only. Even if they hear of the "one mind," they interpret it in one of three ways: first, they claim that although the mind is the sole truth, its manifestations are transformations of the mind and are therefore not all the mind itself;
second, they identify the *ālayavijñāna* of maturation as the "one mind," asserting it is called "one mind" simply to exclude the existence of external objects;
third, they refer to the pure "one mind" of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is called "one mind" because, in principle, there is no duality of substance.
The first "single-mindedness" (ekacitta) is not intended for this contemplation. The latter two "single-mindednesses" clarify the meaning of the sūtra’s intent and apply to all three contemplations.
Taking the pure single-mindedness as the first contemplation, these two subsequent states of mind constitute the latter two contemplations.

The latter two single-mindednesses are summarized here as in the *Wenming* (Questions on Illumination); if fully expanded, they comprise ten types, but the text is too voluminous to record here. Next, the second...
The Gate of the Basis for the Fundamental and the Derivative. From here until the end of the ten gates, all are distinctions within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Since the characteristics of conditions are fundamentally quiescent, one should only contemplate the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Why, then, does one further contemplate the distinctions of conventional truth? The treatise states:

"By contemplating conventional truth in accordance with it, one enters the ultimate reality. The conventional serves as the expression of the ultimate; only by realizing that the conventional lacks intrinsic nature does one see the ultimate.
[The text continues: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If one does not know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one cannot attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This analytical observation of the distinctions within conventional truth consists of six [sections], which subsume the first eight sections and a half. First, as for what constitutes defilement (*kleśa*):

this is the observation based on defilement, which simultaneously explains both the dependent (the basis) and that which depends upon it (the defilement). This subsumes this half-section. Second, the "observation of causes," because it observes the causes of defilement; this subsumes the next...

2. Contemplation that subsumes [the truths] (saṃgraha-vipaśyanā): because it subsumes only suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya). 3. Contemplation that guards against faults (doṣa-rakṣā-vipaśyanā): because it guards against the false views of ordinary beings. 4.

Contemplation that neither loathes nor delights (an-udvega-an-anurāga-vipaśyanā): because it prevents minor pride (parītta-māna). The above three [contemplations] each subsume one gate in their respective order. 5. Profound contemplation (gambhīra-vipaśyanā):
because it reveals the subtle principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as transcending emotional grasping. This subsumes the final three gates. Now, this half...

The "gate" refers to the contemplation of the basis of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). Because the divisions of causes and conditions constitute defilement, and this basis of defilement relies upon the one mind, the Treatise states:
"This is the distinction between the two truths. For pure reality alone does not arise, and solitary delusion cannot be established.
The truth of the single mind and the conventionality of defilement—these two are in harmony, forming a collection of causes and conditions.
Regarding this, the Tathāgata has analytically expounded the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all of which are established based upon this single mind.

Next, within the section on the Basis and Support of the Fundamental and the Derivative, there are two parts. First is the general statement: that is to say, based upon the one mind, the twelve [links] are differentiated;
thus, the twelve are supported by the one mind. The specific mention of "the Tathāgata says" is because the one mind is instantaneously complete [in all things], and none but a Buddha knows this.
This means that having manifested the past awakening to the nature of conditions, [the Tathāgata] subsequently gives rise to the equal continuity [of teaching].
Because it is transmitted through successive oral tradition.
Why is this? Craving for objects arises together with the mind. The mind is consciousness (*vijñāna*); the object is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Delusion regarding these formations is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which arises together with ignorance and the mind is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form is the six [sense bases] (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—the three [internal bases] combined with the [three external objects]—constitute contact (*sparśa*). Feeling (*vedanā*) arises simultaneously with contact. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the lack of satiety regarding feeling.

Grasping (*upādāna*) is the failure to relinquish what craving has seized. That which gives rise to the various links of existence is becoming (*bhava*). What is called "arising" is birth (*jāti*). The maturation of birth is aging (*jarā*).
The disintegration of aging is death (*maraṇa*).
The subsequent inquiry states: "The twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are arranged across the three periods of time, with the preceding inducing the succeeding.

Why, then, is it now said that they all depend upon the single mind? This means that the Teacher skillfully demonstrates that not only are the three periods of time inseparable from the single mind, but that within a single momentary thought (*ekakṣaṇa-citta*), the twelve links are instantaneously complete.
This further clarifies that the sequence of before and after is likewise inseparable from the single mind. This is [the teaching of] the *Abhidharmakośa*.

The ninth section clarifies the twelve links of dependent origination in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Since this section contains many aspects of dependent origination, it is not necessary here to follow them in their sequential order;
rather, the intent is to demonstrate that they are all instantaneously present within a single mind.

Regarding the phrase "following after matters of desire, which arise simultaneously with the mind," this refers generally to the various objects of engagement. Since the objects of desire are manifold, one may take any single instance thereof. At [that time]...

Within a single thought-moment, all twelve links are present. This means that when one engages in this act of craving, it necessarily arises dependent upon the mind, which further discriminates the preceding object;
thus, the mind is the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). As for the "act" (*saṃskāra*), the act of craving is itself the performance of mental karma (*manas-karman*).

If it manifests through body or speech, these are likewise two types of action. Not knowing the faults of craving and its capacity to bring about suffering is termed "delusion regarding action" (*saṃskāreṣu sammohaḥ*).
"Delusion" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*). That which arises simultaneously with ignorance and the mind is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).

"Name-and-form" is a collective term that serves as the basis for these two; since "name" arises together [with form], the *Jin jing* (Dharmaguptaka version) states: "The locus upon which consciousness relies is name-and-form. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The three aggregates co-arising with consciousness are collectively termed 'name-and-form'. This intends to clarify that by means of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) itself...
Because it is the link of sensation (*vedanā*). As for "the growth of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)," the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"The faculties that abide in name-and-form are designated as the six destinies. This means that while the six faculties are distinct, they are established as six by distinguishing the specific [faculties] based upon the general [basis].

Thus, they are called "abiding in name-and-form. Greed necessarily takes an object as its contact (*sparśa*), and sensation necessarily experiences contact; therefore, greed is itself craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and thus there is no sensation apart from it.

Disenchantment (*nirveda*). That which is embraced by craving and not relinquished is the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*). Craving and grasping moisten the preceding six factors to constitute existence (*bhava*).

Therefore, the mere arising of the preceding members of existence is the meaning of "existence. That which arises from existence refers to the aforementioned dharmas; their arising is the meaning of "birth" (*jāti*).

Because the maturation of what has been born constitutes aging (*jarā*), the birth of a thing is itself its alteration. The decay and destruction of what has aged constitutes death (*maraṇa*); [this occurs] in an instant.

Because that [birth] ceases, and because its characteristics are subject to destruction, the Sūtra says: "That which is born is immediately subject to cessation. This is not taught for the sake of the ignorant;
if this were not severed, it would be called a continuous bond (*saṃdhi*). The twelve links of dependent origination, in their respective stages, are all termed "phases" (*avasthā*).

These very phases, following one another from beginningless time, are called "distant continuity" (*dūra-anubandha*). This principle applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, or alternatively, to the six [links].
The eight consciousnesses are merely different [in aspect]. Who would believe this principle if it were not based on the authority of the Holy Teachings (*āptāgama*)?

This text precisely analyzes the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as being simultaneous yet distinct in substance (*bhinnadravya*). If they were simultaneous and identical in substance, they would likewise possess all twelve links: delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*);
when there is outflow (*sāsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*), it is termed formative action (*saṃskāra*); its substance is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*), and it is also name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Form (*rūpa*) is also the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*). Contact (*sparśa*) is so named because it encounters its object; feeling (*vedanā*) because it experiences the object; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) because it is stained by the object;

grasping (*upādāna*) because it clings to the object; becoming (*bhava*) because it brings about retribution; birth (*jāti*) because the aggregates manifest; and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) because they are the transformation and cessation [of those aggregates].
These twelve links—whether analyzed according to three lifetimes, two lifetimes, or one lifetime—are all explained as in the first section. They exist simultaneously yet possess distinct natures.
They are of the same essence, as stated in this very text.

Regarding the contemplation of the distinctions among the truths of the marks [of phenomena] mentioned above, within the second [contemplation], which concerns the contemplation in accordance with great compassion, it corresponds to the second [point]: seeking liberation elsewhere.
This refers to ordinary beings who, due to ignorance and perversion, constantly [seek it] within the *ālayavijñāna* and the *ādānavijñāna*.
Seeking liberation, one instead seeks it elsewhere within the "mine" (*ātmiya*).
Therefore, the Sūtra clarifies that there is only this single mind, and that apart from the mind, there are no self or dharmas; one should seek [liberation] within this single mind.

Third, regarding the contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this corresponds to the second reliance on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which clarifies that this dependent origination relies upon two kinds. First, it relies on the... [text fragment ends]

The first meaning has already been explained as before. The second, "based on mind-consciousness," refers to the present text; whereas the former referred exclusively to the pure, this applies to both the defiled and the pure.

The meaning of "based on" is as previously stated. Furthermore, the former [section] concerned the arising of delusion based on the True [Nature], while this [section] clarifies that delusion is based upon the True [Nature].
The second section, the "Gate of Being Subsumed by the Single Mind," is concluded. Below begins the "Gate of Assisting Accomplishment through One's Own Karma."
O Son of the Buddha, herein ignorance has two functions: first, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding their objects of perception;

second, it acts as the cause for the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Volitional formations also have two functions: first, they can produce future retribution; second, they act as the cause for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness also has two functions: first, it causes the continuity of all states of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It acts as the cause for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form also has two functions: first, it mutually assists and completes one another;
second, it acts as the cause for the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases also have two functions: first, each individually perceives its own respective object;

second, they act as the cause for the arising of contact (*sparśa*). Contact also has two functions: first, it is able to touch upon the objective conditions; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*).

The origin of sensation (*vedanā*). Sensation also has two kinds of functions: first, it is able to experience objects such as the pleasant and the unpleasant; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving also has two kinds of functions: first, it becomes attached to desirable objects; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the continuity of all afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the origin: existence (*bhava*) also has two kinds of functions: first, it can cause rebirth in other realms of existence; second, it acts as the productive cause for birth (*jāti*).
Birth also has two kinds of functions: first, it can give rise to the aggregates (*skandha*); second, it acts as the productive cause for aging (*jarā*). Aging also has two kinds of functions:
first, it causes the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*); second, it acts as the productive cause for death (*maraṇa*).
Death also has two kinds of functions: first, it can destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); second, because there is no conscious awareness, the continuity [of existence] is not severed.

Below this, in the third section, the "Gate of Assisting the Accomplishment of One's Own Karma," there are also three parts. First, regarding those who practice contemplation according to the characteristics:

the following two gates correspond to the contemplation of causes. There are two types of contemplation of causes: first, the contemplation of external causes; second, the contemplation of internal causes.
Now, regarding what is called "other-cause" (*parahetu*): it refers entirely to the fact that a subsequent member arises dependent upon a preceding member.

This serves to exclude the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). Within the context of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), this excludes a primordial essence (*pradhāna*) and refutes such causes as intrinsic nature.

The observation of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is termed "skillful means" (*upāya*), because it reveals the characteristics of causes and conditions. Since volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise solely from ignorance (*avidyā*), it is termed the "self-cause" (*svahetu*).
This distinguishes it from other causes that can produce volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Now, this particular gateway is precisely the "other" cause.

The Sūtra clarifies that each has two functions: first, its own function; second, its auxiliary function. Yet, both are termed "other" because it is specifically through ignorance (*avidyā*) being deluded regarding the object of perception (*ālambana*) that it becomes the cause for volitional formations.
If one were to understand the object of perception, how could false formations arise? Furthermore, at the beginning...
The first clarifies that one’s own karma is the manifesting cause, while the second clarifies that others are the manifesting condition.

The remaining eleven links should be understood by analogy in this manner. Furthermore, the cause for arising is itself the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); it is termed a "cause" here because it is explained according to its general sense.
Since there are many conditions with differing meanings, the Sūtra selects the essential ones based on their definitive existence. That is to say, only...
There is predominance. Each of the twelve links has its own primary function, which does not differ from the two preceding categories.
The Master [Vasubandhu] explains only the two functions of old age and death (jarāmaraṇa) because of this objection; he cites one example to represent all.
However, since ignorance (avidyā) has no cause and old age and death have no fruit, each of the first twelve links serves as the productive cause for the subsequent link. As for old age and death...
If there were no fruit, for whom would it serve as a cause? The meaning of the sutra reveals that it serves as the cause for ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, ignorance is not without a cause, and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are not without a fruit. Therefore, it is said that because of non-awakening (*abodha*), the continuity is never severed;
this "non-awakening" is precisely ignorance. For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are like a revolving ring or a water-lifting wheel.
There is no interruption. This conversely reveals that if one is able to awaken and know [this], there will be no further birth and death.
The Master of the Treatise generally takes the two types of karma as the cause for future birth; thus he says that the destruction of the five-aggregate body can act as the cause for future birth.
Because it is not seen or known, it can act as the cause for future birth. The intent clarifies that when the preceding aggregates merely cease, the subsequent aggregates arise. Therefore...

The first serves as the cause. Subsequently, the mind’s lack of knowledge is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). With ignorance as the cause, the twelve links of dependent origination continue in an uninterrupted succession.

Second, regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): among the four types of contemplation, the following four sections clarify the third, which concerns seeking liberation through heterodox paths.
The Treatise states that there are three kinds of causes for perversion (*viparyāsa*): the causal factor of nature (*prakṛti-hetu*), the self-...
Regarding causes: there are four types of causes—causes of suffering, causes of asceticism, and causelessness. These are refuted respectively by the four gates. The first three are false causes;
therefore, they are collectively termed "perversions. The last one is causelessness. As for these four causes, the first is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is the nature of darkness (*tamas*).
This refers to the Sāṃkhya school’s reckoning that this is the cause of all objects of knowledge; that is, knowing this primordial nature...
Because they have attained liberation. What was previously stated—that seeking liberation in another realm reveals the irrationality of their principle—is not the case here;

although "the knowable" (*jñeya*) is mentioned, the intended meaning refers to the non-existence of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Second, this refers to the view of Kārakoḍa, who reckons that Maheśvara is the causal source.
First, it is the belief that Maheśvara causes sentient beings to suffer when he is angry with them and causes them to experience happiness when he rejoices in them; thus, one seeks his favor.
Second, it is the view of Saṃjaya, who holds that ascetic practices are the cause of cultivation; by merely practicing austerities to repay past karma, one attains liberation.
Third, it is the doctrine of no-cause, held by Ajita, which maintains that sentient beings do not obtain anything through causes, and that all phenomena [arise without cause].
It is natural. One who understands this attains liberation. Sentient beings seek [causality] within false causes and the absence of cause;
thus, the Sūtra employs the correct to refute the false by presenting four gateways, causing them to seek therein. This gateway immediately shatters the nature of darkness (*tamas*);

that is to say, the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) each possess two kinds of karma, which are able to produce those phenomena of dependent origination. It is not [spontaneous].
Due to the nature of darkness (*tamas*), if the conditions for the preceding link are severed, the subsequent link will not continue; thus, one attains liberation within a single lifetime.
As for you, despite your nature of darkness persisting for eighty thousand kalpas, there shall be no liberation.

Thirdly, regarding the contemplation through the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this corresponds to the second contemplation of skillful means (*upāya*). That is to say, each of the links of dependent origination possesses two types of karma. For...
One initiates the subsequent expedient means (*upāya*). If each preceding [factor] is extinguished, then each subsequent one will not arise; this is the expedient means for liberation.

In the fourth section below, the "Gate of Non-Separation," three gates are the same as before. First is the characteristic of truth (*satyalakṣaṇa*), which corresponds to the contemplation of its own cause (*svahetuvipaśyanā*).
The meaning of "one's own cause" can be seen in the preceding text. Furthermore, the Treatise states that "contemplation of one's own cause" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth.
Regarding the cause of self-arising: because one observes the nature of conditions, it means that without the preceding link, the subsequent link does not exist.

For example, since volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth do not exist apart from ignorance (*avidyā*), ignorance is solely the cause of their own arising. Because it is the "self," it causes the formations to continue without interruption;
because it is the "cause," it is merely said to "assist in their completion. If it were only the case that the formations exist without being separate from ignorance, then...

If they were identical, one could not say that "volitional formations (saṃskāra) have ignorance (avidyā) as their condition. If volitional formations existed entirely apart from ignorance, this would constitute an excessive separation;

ignorance would then not be the cause of volitional formations. Therefore, the treatise states: "If they were different, [the causal relationship] would not be established. They are neither identical nor separate."
Thus, the name "self-cause" is established through two meanings. Therefore, the verse from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is cited:

"Phenomena produced by various causes and conditions are neither identical to their causes, nor are they different from their causes; they are neither annihilated, nor are they eternal. The first line is a general statement.
The second line [explains] that what is produced is not the producer itself. Furthermore, "nor are they different from their causes" means that from...

Because it is able to produce that which is produced, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. It is not eternal because it is not identical [to what is produced], and it is not annihilated because it is not different [from what is produced].
O Son of the Buddha, herein, from "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions aging and death," by means of ignorance and so forth...
Birth is the condition that causes formations through to old age and death to remain uninterrupted, because it assists in their accomplishment.
Within the fourth section, the "Door of Non-Abandonment," there is first the forward order and then the reverse order. Regarding the discussion in the forward order, it says:
"Ignorance is of two kinds: first, the time of the seed; second, the time of the fruit. Among these, the time of the seed causes formations to remain uninterrupted. There is...
Regarding the two types of meaning, that which is manifested as a causal object: the "seed" (*bīja*) is the cause, and the "fruit" (*phala*) is the active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Although the fruit of active manifestation has already passed away, it is not grasped [as the primary object]; rather, because the seed continues, it ensures that the activity is not severed and can assist in the accomplishment of that activity.
Therefore, at the time of grasping the seed, one may also designate the initial arising of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the "seed," which then migrates to...
The time of proceeding is called the fruit. By the power of the preceding meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), it causes the proceeding to be uninterrupted;

because this uninterrupted proceeding assists in the accomplishment of the proceeding, the "time of the son" is specifically singled out. The other eleven links all possess two times; they are to be understood by this same principle.
Regarding the statement that "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease," and so on up to "with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease":
because ignorance through to birth do not act as conditions, they cause the cessation of all formations through to aging and death, since they no longer provide assistance for their formation.
Next is the reverse contemplation. The treatise states: "The prior limit and the posterior limit are extinguished; the middle limit likewise does not exist. Therefore, it is not spoken of.

The twelve links of dependent origination do not transcend these three limits. Since the past and future do not exist, how could there be a middle? Therefore, it is not said that there is the meaning of being uninterrupted or assisted in its formation.
Furthermore, because it is not spoken of, once [the links] are extinguished, all preceding meanings are extinguished as well; thus, they do not depend [on such assistance].
1. Explaining the distinctions between the "son" (cause) and the "fruit" (result), etc. 2. Regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

within the refutation of the causes of perversion, [it is shown that] while some take Īśvara as the cause of sentient beings, here ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are taken as the causes of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth;

since these do not even arise from other links [of dependent origination], how could they possibly arise from Īśvara? 3. Regarding the contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are without agency.
As for "the former": since the former causes the latter to continue without interruption, and by assisting in the formation of the latter, the latter lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
How then could the former act as a cause for the latter? Thus, the characteristic of taking non-action as a condition is the objective domain of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

O Son of the Buddha, herein, the non-cessation of ignorance, craving, and grasping constitutes the path of afflictions; the non-cessation of formative action and existence constitutes the path of karma;
and the non-cessation of the remaining factors constitutes the path of suffering.

The fifth is the section on the non-interruption of the three paths. First, within the *lunxiangdi* (依論相諦) among the six contemplations, this is termed the "contemplation that subsumes transgressions" (*sheguoguan*).

This name is situated within the "single-mind gate" (*yixinmen*). Second, regarding the "basis and support of the root and the branches" (*benmo yichi*), it means that by subsuming the twelve links under the three paths, it is revealed that the links of existence (*youzhi*) subsume only suffering (*duḥkha*), while karma and afflictions (*karmakleśa*) constitute the faults of cause and effect.
The cause is suffering itself, which is the fruit; there are also both reverse and direct [orders of observation]. In the first [section], the "direct observation," the text contains two meanings.
First, regarding the three periods of time: ignorance in the past and craving in the present are termed "afflictions. Although they are both afflictions, [the distinction is made as follows:]...

In the past, one was deluded regarding the ultimate limit (*pūrvānta*) and designated by the name "ignorance" (*avidyā*). In the present, the drawing forth of future existence is due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).

From their beginning to their end, these factors manifest and mutually clarify one another. Regarding *saṃskāra* (formations) and *bhava* (existence), these are both karma: past karma is called *saṃskāra*, while present karma is called *bhava*.

Although they are equally karma, that which has already been determined in the past receives its designation according to its actual characteristics, whereas that which has not yet occurred in the future does not.
Karma has the capacity to possess these; it receives its designation based on its functional efficacy. The five fruits in the present and the two fruits in the future are all equally suffering.

Those with manifest retribution have already been determined and receive their names according to their current characteristics. Those in the future have not yet arisen, so they are established based on their underlying afflictions (*doṣa*).

If categorized by the two time periods, the first ten share the same period; thus, the afflictions are of two types: those that can incite and those that can moisten. Although there are various afflictions...

All [these factors] are capable of producing moisture. At the stage of initiating karma, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) increases; at the stage of moistening karma to bring about rebirth, the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) increases.
Each receives its name according to its predominant function. Since there is no separate perfuming or initiation [of karma], it is solely ignorance that repeatedly irrigates [the seeds];

therefore, craving and grasping are distinguished [as a single factor]. Karma also has two types: that which is not yet moistened and that which is already moistened. That which is not yet moistened is called "formative action" (*saṃskāra*), because it is the initial performance [of an act]. That which is... [already moistened...]

"Moistening" refers to existence (*bhava*), because it is proximate to that which is about to arise. If one takes the seeds of consciousness and so forth collectively as the object of moistening, they are likewise subsumed under suffering (*duḥkha*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "A portion of the member of existence is subsumed under karma. Regarding the statement that all three paths are uninterrupted:
That is to say: from the three afflictions arise the two karmas; from those two karmas, in turn, arise the seven sufferings;
and from the seven, the three arise again. Thus it is like a revolving wheel.
By discerning the limits of the past and future, one cuts off the three paths. In this way, these three paths are devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self"; there is only arising.
Cessation is like a bundle of reeds.
Next, the inverse contemplation is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of abandonment through antidotes:

this means that by severing ignorance and formations of the past limit, as well as craving, grasping, and becoming of the future limit, the seven types of suffering do not arise. Second, following the phrase "these three paths," the explanation of abandonment of their intrinsic nature follows.
Therefore, Viśuddhamati said: "All worldly phenomena consist solely of cause and effect and lack a self; they merely arise from empty dharmas and, in turn, produce empty dharmas.
Thus, the causes and effects of arising and ceasing are like two bundles of reeds that stand supporting one another."
If one cannot achieve [liberation] alone, then one knows there is no inherent nature; thus, both types of self are empty.

Second, within the contemplation of great compassion, this corresponds to refuting the heterodox path’s pursuit of the middle way through ascetic practices based on causal calculations. That is to say, they take karma and delusion as the causes of suffering;
wishing to seek liberation, they believe one must sever delusions and karma and practice asceticism. This gives rise to false conceptualization, and the mind of asceticism is itself...
These are afflictions (*kleśa*). How could such afflictions possibly be the cause of the bliss of liberation?

This is the fifth entry into the contemplation of the truths (*satyāvatāra*) within the contemplation of the characteristics of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because it concerns the three paths of the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*).

That is to say, since delusion, karma, and suffering all constitute the "origin" (*samudaya*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Birth, old age, and death in the present life are suffering; consciousness and the other [four aggregates] in the future life are suffering."

The fifth point is explained according to their categories. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that all twelve [links] are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This implies that karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) pertain to both truths;
when viewed through reverse contemplation, they constitute the Truths of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the Path (*mārgasatya*), because the cessation of discriminative thought is itself the path.

Furthermore, the substance of the three paths is identical to the three virtues of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), because *nirvāṇa* and *buddha-dhātu* are the single truth of reality (*eka-tattva*).
Moreover, "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to observing the past; "consciousness through sensation" refers to observing the present;
and "craving through existence" refers to observing the future. Thereafter, these continue to evolve in succession.

The sixth is the section on the cycle of the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika-saṃsāra-mukha*). First, regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), it is called the "contemplation that guards against faults" (*doṣa-rakṣā-vipaśyanā*), because it explains how one guards against the three faults across the three periods.

The commentary on the text follows both a reverse and a direct order. Within the direct order, it first clarifies the three periods as they appear in succession; therein, it subsequently clarifies the flow of transmigration through the three periods.
Now, for the first point, it says: "Ignorance conditions formative forces (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*). This is the contemplation of the past. Regarding this contemplation:
There are two meanings. First, one contemplates the present as being produced by two past causes.
Second, one recognizes that consciousness and so forth are the effects of those past [causes] and future [conditions]. Cause and effect are mutually connected and reciprocally established;
it is only in this way that one is said to "see the meaning of past causes," which is able to prevent three faults. To say that "consciousness up to feeling" is the contemplation of the present...
Regarding "that which exists," there are also two meanings: first, observing that present consciousness and so forth are obtained through past karma;
second, further knowing that consciousness and so forth can obtain future retributions, because they do not encounter an antidote and thus give rise to craving and the like based upon them.
Since these are now being witnessed directly, they are divided into two directions to clarify their two meanings.
To say that "craving" up to "existence" refers to observing the future is because this cause of the future will certainly obtain its future fruit; it is thus fixed in one direction.

Furthermore, regarding the transmigration through the three periods of time, as long as one has not obtained the antidote, there is a subsequent life, and from that subsequent life one transmigrates again into another subsequent life.
This would lead to an infinite regress. Having already understood [the faults regarding] the three time periods, how does one guard against these errors?

They concern both the external and the internal. Three types of errors are established regarding the phenomena of causes and conditions: first, the error that all bodies arise simultaneously. Why is this? Because there is no distinct cause.
This error arises from the preceding [argument] regarding its own cause; that is to say, since there is no *īśvara* (Lord) or other such distinct cause, [all things would arise at once].

Regarding causes: ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) alone serve as the causes for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the subsequent links. Since there are many kinds of volitional formations, why do the six destinies not arise simultaneously?
Second, there would be the fault that one’s own karma would not be experienced as its retribution.

Why? Because there is no agent (*kartṛ*). This fault arises from the notion of non-arising through conditions; the "agent" is simply the self (*ātman*). Third, there would be the fault of the loss of karma. Why? Because [the action] has not yet...
Because the karma that has already yielded its retribution has ceased, this fault arises from the condition of impermanence.

Having thus identified the fault, how is it to be guarded against? It can be guarded against by perceiving the three time periods (*trikāla*). Furthermore, there are three meanings regarding the karma of faults.

Therefore, retribution cannot be obtained. First, because it has not yet been performed; second, because although performed, it has not yet been moistened; third, because an antidote has been attained. Now, "acting without conditions" indicates that [the action] has already been performed;
the five [factors], beginning with the manifest consciousness (*vijñapti*), indicate that it has already been moistened;

and the presence of the three—craving, grasping, and becoming—indicates that an antidote has not yet been attained. Since there is a distinction between actions that have already been moistened and those that have not, this constitutes the difference.
Regarding causes: if they have already been moistened, one receives the retribution of birth; if they have not yet been moistened, one receives subsequent retribution.

Since there is a distinction between what has been moistened and what has not, how could the six realms of existence be received simultaneously? This constitutes a distinct cause; what need is there for an "Isvara" (Creator)?

Since one creates diverse causes oneself and thus invites two types of retribution oneself, it is not received by another body. How can you say that one's own karma does not entail receiving retribution? As for the "provisional self"...
"What use is it for me to create [karma]? If karma has already been performed and lacks the conditions for counteraction or nourishment, it will then arise. One knows that karma is not lost;
although the cause may have previously ceased, its force continues. Since one is presently seen to receive the retribution, it cannot be said to be lost.
This is the third point regarding transcendence.
Regarding "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease": this is a cessation through dependence (*apekṣā-nirodha*).

This is the reverse contemplation (*pratiloma-anupaśyanā*), which carries the sense of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*). That this [subsequent] cessation occurs because of that [prior] cessation is cessation through dependence.

Furthermore, because one contemplates the capacity for cessation as distinct from cessation by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*), it is called "dependence. Thus, the twelve links of dependent origination across the three times...
All things are complete; yet, according to the traces of transformation—whether hidden or manifest—they are divided into three.
This is to make known that past causes have summoned the vessel of present suffering, and to cause the severing of craving so that future fruits do not arise.

Thus, ignorance is brought to an end by the blade of wisdom, the waters of craving are parched by the fire of knowledge, the high nets are opened across the six realms of existence, and one transcends beyond the eight directions of birthlessness.

Second, regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion: it remedies the views of non-Buddhists who seek a middle [existence] without cause by demonstrating the causality across the three time periods.
Since the two [factors] of the prior limit are the five causes for the middle limit, and the three [factors] of the middle limit are the two causes for the subsequent limit.
If such things as these did not exist, sentient beings would also not exist. Since this cause exists, how can one say they do not?

Third, regarding the contemplation of the characteristics of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-lakṣaṇa*), one should enter into reliance upon contemplation through the power and lack of power [of the three times]. The *Śāstra* states:

"Because the transformation is superior across the prior, middle, and subsequent limits. This means that from the perspective of being causes, these three limits are all termed "possessing power," whereas from the perspective of being effects...
The aspect of meaning is termed "powerlessness. If categorized according to the three times, the past is powerless with respect to the future two [times];

in the middle period, craving and so forth are powerful with respect to the future, but powerless with respect to the present. By means of these three periods, he transforms those ordinary beings, causing them to enter with faith, rely [on the teachings], and practice;
this is the most excellent among methods of transformation. Investigating in this manner constitutes the objective domain of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The seventh is the section on the accumulation of the three types of suffering. First, regarding the contemplation of characteristics according to the truths, this corresponds to the fifth of the six contemplations within the "Gate of Single-Mindedness," namely, the contemplation of non-disgust through disgust.
The *Śāstra* states: "One becomes weary of various subtle sufferings, because one discriminates that all sensations (*vedanā*) are suffering.
This refers to the subtle *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering inherent in conditioned formations). It further states: "And one becomes weary of various coarse sufferings."

Therefore, regarding these [forms of suffering]—namely, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*)—ordinary beings do not feel weary of them, whereas Bodhisattvas do. Furthermore, regarding the first [type], subtle suffering (*sūkṣma-duḥkha*), the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) do not feel weary of it, yet Bodhisattvas do.

Although the followers of the Two Vehicles know that the neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), they do not exhaustively understand its subtle aspects, its immeasurable characteristics, or the suffering of transformation (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*); therefore, it is said that they "do not know."

Furthermore, the twelve links of existence are termed the three types of suffering. Among these, ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth up to the six sense bases constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Contact and sensation constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). The remainder constitutes the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

7. The Section on the Accumulation of the Three Kinds of Suffering. Within this text, there are also both progressive and regressive orders. In the progressive order, the explanation proceeds from the perspective of increasing characteristics to correlate them with the three types of suffering.

The first five [links] have the characteristic of constant flux (saṃskāra) prominently displayed, and are thus called *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*. The two links of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) involve the encounter with the arising of suffering;
therefore, they are called *duḥkha-duḥkhatā*. The remaining [links] merely destroy happiness, and are thus called *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*. Old age and death destroy birth, and likewise...
This is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
The cessation of formations through the cessation of ignorance constitutes the abandonment of these three types of suffering;

this can be understood through reverse contemplation (*pratiloma-anupaśyanā*). Second, regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the following four sections correspond to the fourth [stage], "Seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*).
"False liberation" refers to not recognizing true liberation and seeking liberation through the suffering of the three realms and the like;

therefore, it is called a "false pursuit. True liberation possesses four characteristics: first, the characteristic of being free from all suffering; second, the characteristic of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
third, the characteristic of being far removed from defilement; and fourth, the characteristic of being supramundane (*lokottara*). These four are precisely the bliss and permanence of *nirvāṇa*.
"Purity and Self. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "To be sovereign and detached from worldly dharmas is called 'Self.

Thus, the following four sections of the sūtra clarify that there are only the four delusions and no four virtues. Now, this [section] clarifies that there is suffering and no bliss; hence the treatise says:
"That matter of the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) follows along, even unto the bonds of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). That...
If one reckons the formless realms (*ārūpya*) to be *nirvāṇa*, is this not a false perception of suffering? Third, regarding the contemplation of the characteristics of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*):
this corresponds to the seventh [stage], the contemplative entry of faith characterized by either overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or the absence of overweening pride.

Not knowing subtle suffering as it truly is constitutes overweening pride; if one knows subtle suffering, it is not overweening pride. This [contemplation] brings about knowledge where there was previously none.
This is called "Entrance through Faith.

The eighth is the gate of the arising and ceasing produced by conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), also called "Lack of Self-Nature Following Conditions. The first [gate] is based on the contemplation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).

The following three gates all clarify the profound contemplations of the six modes of observation within the gate of the one mind (*ekacitta*). These are known as the "seeking by means of the four propositions" (*catuṣkoṭi*).
All conditions are devoid of arising. To arise from non-arising is called "profound contemplation. This gate is named "not self-arising" and "not other-arising.
The ninth gate is named "not co-arising," and the tenth gate clarifies "not arising without cause.

There are briefly two meanings for explaining these four propositions: first, the refutation of error; second, the revelation of principle. That which is falsely conceptualized outside of principle is called "error."

When perversion perishes, principle becomes manifest; when principle becomes manifest, delusion perishes. Now, the four—self, other, and so forth—are the objects of calculation and the basis for attachment.
The single word "not" (*bù*) is both the medicine and the principle. The principle of the exhaustion of birth does not transcend these four categories of self and so forth.

If self and the others did not exist, where would birth find its locus? Therefore, by negating them with "not," delusion perishes and principle becomes manifest. Yet, as for that which they calculate...

Each of these has three categories. First, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) assert that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the self, Brahmā is the other, the aggregation of atoms is the common [cause], and spontaneity is the causeless.
These four views are also held by the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Ājīvika, and Lokāyata schools.
Second, the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) assert that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is the self, while the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is...
This "other" refers to the fact that this maturation (*vipāka*) is not consciousness itself; it is said in relation to unwholesome states and contaminated wholesome states.
As for the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it is "common. To calculate that ignorance arises by relying on emptiness is also called "causelessness.

This superior calculation also applies to those within the Mahāyāna who cling to signs (*nimitta*). Third, according to the Mahāyāna: the resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*) are taken as "self," and the various conditions (*pratyaya*) are taken as "other."

The combination of these constitutes the "common" (sādhāraṇa); their separation constitutes the "causeless" (ahetu). Furthermore, regarding the ālayavijñāna, its own seeds constitute the "self" (sva), while the various conditions constitute the "other" (para);

the combination of these constitutes the "common," and their separation constitutes the "causeless. Moreover, when a phenomenon arises from the True [Suchness] it is "self," and when it arises from the delusory it is "other";
the combination of these constitutes the "common," and their separation constitutes the "causeless. Although the calculations [of these positions] are numerous, they are merely being elucidated here.
All speculative theories based on [false] reasoning naturally perish. The revelation of the principle is twofold: first, profound contemplation by way of non-arising;
second, profound contemplation revealed by way of the non-obstruction between arising and non-arising. Within the former, there are briefly two explanations.

First, explaining through successive stages that phenomena arise from conditions and therefore do not arise of themselves (*svataḥ*); since there is no "self," toward what could one speak of an "other" (*parataḥ*)? Furthermore, all...

Because phenomena are collectively considered "self," and because from the perspective of another, that other is also "self," since there is no such thing as an "other," there is no arising from another.

Since neither self nor other can be established, with what could they be combined to constitute "both"? If even that which has a cause does not arise, how could that which lacks a cause possibly arise?
This second point is explained by way of the mutual negation of causes and conditions; thus, the Abhidharma states: "Because of the existence of one's own seeds, [phenomena] do not arise from..."
Because it depends on various conditions, it is not self-produced; because it lacks independent agency, it is not co-produced; because it possesses causal efficacy, it is not causeless.
If this were so, since its own seeds exist, would it not be self-arising? How could one say it is "unborn"?
This merely uses the concept of "self" to refute the "other," rather than establishing a "self. The next phrase uses the concept of "other" to refute the "self. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
Just as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena does not reside within conditions, so it is with the following two lines; examine this carefully.
Second, regarding the unimpeded [nature]: results arise solely from causes and conditions, each of which possesses two meanings, namely, being entirely efficacious.
It is entirely powerless. If the conditions were entirely powerful in relation to the fruit, then the cause would be entirely powerless;

therefore it is said that "the cause does not produce, but the conditions produce. Thus it is said that [the cause] does not arise from itself. The same applies to the case where the cause is entirely powerful in relation to the fruit.
Therefore, it is said that [things] do not arise from conditions, because they arise from their own causes; thus, they do not arise from another.

Third, they do not arise together, because the two powers do not coexist simultaneously. Fourth, they do not arise without cause, because the two lack power when not coexisting. This further has two meanings:
first, regarding function, the functions of the powers interpenetrate, which carries the sense of mutual inclusion; that is to say, the powerful encompasses the powerless. Thus, [the ten...]

The Chapter on Forbearance states: "The Bodhisattva skillfully understands the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Within a single dharma, he understands the manifold; within manifold dharmas, he understands them as one.
Second, based on the essence (*svabhāva*), there is both emptiness and non-emptiness. This is the meaning of the identity of existence and appearance (*sanimitta*):

it means that not only do causes return to conditions through their power, but also that the essence of the cause is manifested by means of conditions. It fully encompasses both cause and condition; the cause is like space."
Because they are empty, the preceding text states that "one is many and many are one," and so forth. Power and its absence must necessarily coexist;
therefore, they are constantly mutually identical and interfused. This is what is meant by inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, regarding "ignorance as the condition for volitional formations," the causal condition of ignorance is able to produce all volitional formations.

Within the gate of the arising and ceasing of the eight causal conditions, this is also called the profound contemplation of the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*), which likewise possesses both forward and reverse orders.
In the initial section on sequential contemplation, the Sūtra states, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," which is the citation (*nirddeśa*).

It further explains, "The causal condition of ignorance is able to produce all volitional formations," which is the exposition (*vyākhyāna*). The Treatise states, "The factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are not created by another; they arise from their own causes.

This uses the principle of non-production by another to explain the word "condition" (*hetu*) in the Sūtra. That is to say, because the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arises solely from ignorance, it is described as having its "own cause" (*svahetu*). This is precisely...
The first is the contemplation of the cause from above (*ūrdhva-hetu-vicāra*). Second, it is not self-made, because it arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).

This explains the word "condition" (*pratyaya*) in the Sūtra by means of the principle of non-self-arising; that is, the link of *saṃskāra* merely takes ignorance as its condition, and there is no substantial entity of *saṃskāra* existing within ignorance that arises from itself.
This is the contemplation of the cause from another (*para-hetu-vicāra*). It is designated as a "cause" simply by selecting [the primary factor] and excluding those that do not produce it directly.

It is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*) because it makes what precedes manifest and is not distant from what follows; it does not refer to the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the four conditions.
Regarding "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease": because ignorance is absent, the various formations are also absent. The same applies to the rest.
This can be understood through reverse contemplation. Second is the contemplation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

among those who seek erroneously, they reckon the realm of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth to be *nirvāṇa*, and further reckon sublime practices to be liberation; yet these are neither permanent nor eternal, but are merely subject to arising and ceasing, and are thus to be pitied.
Third is the contemplation based on the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). This and the subsequent section are termed the "contemplation of the beginningless. This includes:

There are two meanings. First, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), it is said that causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are the basis of arising and ceasing. Because birth and death have no limit, causes and conditions are beginningless.

Second, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is said that when one perceives the gathering of dharmas through conditions, there is no inherent nature (*prakṛti*) upon which to rely;

therefore, they are called "beginningless. This is what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* means when it says: "All dharmas are established based on the root of non-abiding. Thus, this refers to the true nature of both defilement and purity.
All are without beginning or end. Because it is revealed that defilement can be eliminated, it is said to be "without beginning. Thus, the Treatise states:
"Because the middle limit arises from causes and conditions, the subsequent limit arises"; this refers to the eighth section. "Because it conforms to bondage" refers to the ninth section.
This means that a single thought-moment arising from conditions is itself non-arising; therefore, it has no beginning.
The reason it does not speak of "arising at the initial limit" is intended to reveal that there is no beginning. Now, the non-arising of delusion is itself non-birth.
Furthermore, that "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" is the arising of bondage; that "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" is the cessation of bondage.
The same applies to the rest.
The ninth gate, the arising and cessation of bondage, is also called "appearing as if existent or non-existent. This is first observed by the Omniscient One.

In the middle [section], it clarifies that [ignorance and formations] do not arise together. First, regarding the sequential contemplation: in the Sūtra, it is stated only that ignorance serves as the condition for formations (*saṃskāra*), causing formations to be bound to ignorance;

this is dependent origination. Yet, as for why they are "not co-arising," the Śāstra says: "Because they are not produced by both; because they arise only in accordance [with conditions]; because there is no knower;
and because at the time of their production, they do not abide. The meaning is that formations merely accord with ignorance.
It is clear that conditions cannot produce [an effect] without [the presence of] what is not produced, for since there is no cognizer of them, they do not act as a duality.
If this is so, then it is simply the conformity with production that constitutes "co-arising"; why insist on a cognizer? Therefore, the conclusion states:

"Since things arise from conditions, they do not abide for even a single moment; who, then, could be said to 'co-arise'? This is because, according to the Abhidharma, there is no functional activity [in conditions]. Furthermore, the treatise says: "The conjunction..."
That is, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). How, then, could they arise through combination? Next, regarding the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nirodha*), one contemplates in reverse order:
cessation merely means the cessation of bondage. Since there is no co-arising, how could there be co-cessation? To speak of "arising" is merely a designation for bondage.

Second, regarding the contemplation of great compassion: when those non-Buddhists seek liberation through such means as the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the Bodhisattva contemplates that these are merely defiled fetters and not the true, pure virtue of *nirvāṇa*.

Third, regarding the contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): it clarifies that within beginningless contemplation, [these states] arise by conforming to bondage and have no fundamental basis.

Furthermore, "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" is the contemplation that accords with non-existence; "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" is the contemplation that accords with exhaustion and cessation.
The same applies to the remaining [links].
The first is the gate of contemplation on the exhaustion of non-existence (*asarva-bhāva-kṣaya-vipaśyanā-mukha*), also named "merging into equality.

In the initial contemplation of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vipaśyanā*), it is revealed within profound contemplation that [phenomena] are not without cause. Within the initial contemplation in forward order (*anuloma-vipaśyanā*), because formations arise dependently from ignorance, dependent origination is itself without intrinsic nature;
therefore, it is said to "accord with non-existence" (*asarvatā-anuloma*). Next, in the contemplation in reverse order (*pratiloma-vipaśyanā*), cessation is likewise dependently originated.
Cessation. Only when there is no cessation through the condition of cessation does one accord with the principle of exhaustion and cessation.

However, when the treatise explains the contemplation in accordance with the sūtra as "this accords with existence," it reveals that dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature; therefore, it cannot be non-existent. Although the two sūtras differ, they share the same name, "dependent origination";

thus, it is not without cause. What fault is there in being without cause? If things were produced without a cause, the cause of production would produce [them] eternally, and [the effect] would not...
It does not arise. Why? Because there is no fixed cause. This is a refutation by concession (*anujñā-viparyaya*).
Furthermore, it could never arise; why? Because it would arise without a cause. This is a refutation by denial (*apavāda*) of its arising.

Therefore, arising without a cause is not what the Buddha’s teaching delights in, because such causelessness can give rise to great false views. Second, this is an observation in accordance with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

This refers to seeking a distinct liberation wherein non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to be *nirvāṇa*.
Because this [sphere] exists, it is not supramundane; thus, it lacks the quality of selflessness (*anātman*). Yet, they falsely reckon this to be liberation, and therefore it is to be pitied.

Third, regarding the contemplation through the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it corresponds to the ninth of the various contemplations. This is the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Because they accord with existence (*bhava*), there are distinctions such as craving for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; hence it is called "various.
This means that while truly conforming to existence, one has not yet lost the conformity to non-existence (*vibhava*). The foregoing concludes the separate explanation of the ten gates.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus contemplates dependent origination in ten ways—both in direct and reverse order—namely:
by way of the continuity of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); by way of being subsumed within a single mind; by way of the differentiation of one's own karma; by way of mutual inseparability;

by way of the non-interruption of the three paths; by way of contemplating the past, present, and future; by way of the accumulation of the three types of suffering; and by way of arising through causes and conditions.
Because of cessation; because of the bondage of arising and ceasing; because of the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence.

This concludes the third section, summarizing the ten names. Since it is stated that one contemplates both in reverse and in direct order, the two gates of "one mind encompassing" and "assisting the accomplishment of one's own karma" mentioned previously must include the reverse contemplation;
their omission there was merely due to brevity in the text. Now, regarding this reverse and direct contemplation:
In the *Abhidharma*, the fourth [chapter] is titled "Defilement and Purification" (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*). Within defilement and purification, there are respectively the reverse and the direct orders.

As the treatise states: "Because of the reverse and direct orders of defilement; because of the reverse and direct orders of purification. Regarding defilement, the direct order refers to "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth.
Who is it that opposes? It is through the accumulation of old age and death, up to ignorance. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* asks: "Due to the existence of what does old age and death exist?
Thus, the former phrase investigates the cause, while the latter phrase examines the cause. Regarding the forward and reverse order of purification:
when ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease—this is the forward order (*anuloma*). Due to the cessation of what [does ignorance cease]?

Therefore, the cessation of old age and death is not contrary [to the sequence]. The current text omits this briefly; it merely distinguishes between the "contrary" and "concordant" based on defilement and purification.

Regarding the term "all dependent originations" (*sarva-pratītyasamutpāda*): "all" (*sarva*) refers to the twelve links rather than just one. Each preceding link acts as a condition (*pratyaya*) to cause each succeeding link to arise.
Furthermore, because one wanders through the various realms of existence bound by afflictions (*kleśa*) and arises there again and again, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

it is also called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). "Arising" (*samutpanna*) carries the meaning of "origination" (*utpāda*), and this is also explained in terms of the fruit. Nevertheless, each [section] encompasses three contemplations, their essential structures arranged like a constellation;
now, they are again subsumed under ten primary gates. The first gate clarifies the arising of the causes of defilement and purity; the second clarifies...
The source of dependent origination consists of ten gates: first, cause and effect are both empty; second, their mutual formation is without activity;
third, the principles of the truths are set forth; fourth, their functional powers intersect; fifth, suffering is exhausted and pride is eliminated; sixth, form is subsumed within the beginningless;

seventh, existence and non-existence have no fundamental basis; eighth, the ultimate and the conventional are not in conflict. Furthermore, these ten gates, when condensed, do not exceed five meanings: the first concerns how delusion regarding principle gives rise to phenomena.
Next is the gate of the mutual support of principle and phenomena; next are the six gates of the fulfillment of phenomena; the ninth is the simultaneous sublation of both principle and phenomena;

and the final one is the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena. Thus, these four gates do not exceed the scope of principle and phenomena. If one proceeds from the mutual penetration of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, there is a layering of interpenetration;
if one relies on the dual fusion of the forward and reverse movement of principle and phenomena, the true gate is profoundly still.
Therefore, the *dharmatā* of dependent origination is most profound and most profound. This very conditionality is called the causal Buddha-nature (*hetu-buddhadhātu*).

The wisdom that contemplates conditions is the causal nature of the cause (*hetu-hetudhātu*). When this causal cause reaches its fruition, it becomes the Bodhi-nature; when the causal nature reaches its fruition, it becomes the Nirvana-nature.
The non-obstruction between cause and effect is the nature of dependent origination. One must contemplate this solely by emptying oneself of self.

The Supplementary Commentary states: This sutra takes the dependent origination of the dharma-realm as its central tenet. What is called dependent origination does not transcend the principles and phenomena, causes and effects, of the ten dharma-realms.
Furthermore, these causes and effects are merely the inverse and direct transformations of the twelve links of dependent origination based upon the one mind.
Thus, it is known that the purport of the entire sutra consists entirely of the dharma of dependent origination. Regarding the preceding three stages of the worthy ones...

The practice of cultivation consists entirely of actions that follow conditions (*pratyaya*), whereas what is realized upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*) is the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, the objects of contemplation in the first, second, and third stages involve entering the *dharmadhātu* by means of a forward contemplation (*anuloma*) of defiled conditions;

the object of contemplation in the fourth stage involves entering the *dharmadhātu* by means of a reverse contemplation (*pratiloma*) of pure conditions. Consequently, the objects of contemplation in the fifth stage consist of the integration of the defiled and the pure.

[This] is consistent. However, this has been observed solely from the perspective of sequential and discrete progression; therefore, upon reaching this sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*), there is a detailed explanation of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

This brings together all preceding contemplations and subsumes them within the single mind, thereby manifesting entry into the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of phenomena-to-phenomena (*shishi wuai*) by means of the non-obstruction of principle-and-fact (*lishi wuai*).
Consequently, the conclusion of the sutra text is clear, and the commentary (*ṭīkā*) likewise concludes here.

There are five intentions, which form four gates. These four gates are precisely the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Herein is fully demonstrated the general gate of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai guanmen*).
Furthermore, according to the commentary based on the treatise, each gate contains three contemplations (*guan*), and each contemplation subsumes ten gates.

Through this layering of the hidden and the manifest, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wuai dharmadhātu*) is revealed. This constitutes the entirety of the sutra.
The principles of contemplative practice are fully revealed within the ten gates of the twelve links of dependent origination.

That is to say, the profundity of dependent origination is demonstrated to show the fundamental tenet of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because the scriptural text is vast and its purport is profound and subtle, I have provided only a brief indication here.
The above concludes the ten gates; below is the summary of the Great Text on the Path of Non-Abiding.
The section on the excellence of practice is concluded.

This is the third major heading. Because the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, act in accordance with this [teaching] down to the subsequent [stages] without contradiction, the excellence of that fruit is clarified.
Since this also subsumes the stage of the "Abiding in Right Mindfulness," one knows that [all things] arise through dependent origination. Hereafter—

Because one encompasses the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*), the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*) and so forth manifest before one. According to the treatise, there are five characteristics of the fruit (*phala*):

first, the excellence of attaining counteractive practices (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) and the excellence of being free from hindrances (*āvaraṇa-vigama*); second, the excellence of attaining cultivation (*bhāvanā-prakarṣa*); third, the excellence of attaining meditative absorption (*samādhi-prakarṣa*);

fourth, the excellence of attaining an indestructible mind (*abhedyacitta-prakarṣa*); and fifth, the excellence of attaining the power of mastery (*vaśitābala-prakarṣa*). Each of these has a son of the Buddha (*jinaputra*) as its witness.
Discrimination: Only in the second section are there two "sons of the Buddha.
Sons of the Buddha, it is by means of these ten kinds of aspects that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dependent origination.

The first section has two parts: first, clarifying the excellence of the antidotes; second, from "In this way, the bodhisattva... onwards, clarifying the excellence of being free from hindrances. Regarding the first:

these are the three gates of liberation, also called the three samādhis. *Samādhi* receives its name based on its own essential nature, whereas *vimokṣa* (liberation) receives its designation in dependence upon something else.
Because these three can lead to the liberation of nirvāṇa, they are called "gates. Within this section, there are two parts.

The first part restates what preceded; the latter part correctly elucidates the present topic. Regarding the first [point], its meaning is the same as that of the five fruits, because by means of the ten preceding contemplations, one attains these three fruits of emptiness and so forth.
That is to say, by taking these three contemplations of emptiness as their objects, one attains the first and third fruits;

by taking the three contemplations of compassion as their objects, one attains the second and fourth fruits. When comparing the three to the first, the first serves as the antidote, while the three are...
That which is accomplished consists of four aspects: with respect to the two pairs, two are the means of cultivation and four are the firm foundations.
The fifth arises from both types of contemplation; it may also arise through successive progression. Because there is an antidote, one is free from hindrances;

because one is free from hindrances, practice becomes superior; because there is an antidote, samādhi becomes superior; and because samādhi is superior, the mind is not destroyed. Thus, mastery is attained.

Knowing that there is no self, no person, and no life-span; that all things are empty by nature; and that there is neither an agent nor an experiencer—one then attains the gateway of liberation of emptiness, which manifests before one.
Below this, the three emptinesses are correctly revealed, each with its own specific exposition followed by a summary. Within the first gateway of emptiness, there are three specific expositions.

The first three phrases clarify the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Next, the emptiness of intrinsic nature clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This above clarifies that the substance of the two selves is empty.
Third, the absence of agent and recipient reveals that the activity of the two selves is empty. Because their substance is empty, they are both [non-existent].
The enabling cause receives its fruit. The commentary concludes:

"Because the present [state] is the merging of wisdom with its object, one contemplates that all links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are by nature extinguished, ultimately liberated, and without the arising of even the slightest dharma-characteristic.
At that moment, the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before one."

Within the gate of the signless (*animitta*), there are also three [aspects]. The first is the cessation of hindrances. This means observing that all factors (*aṅga*) are by their very nature extinguished.
That is to say, if one enters the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and neither attains emptiness nor grasps the mark of emptiness, then the task is accomplished.

If one views phenomena as having existed previously and now being non-existent, claiming this to be emptiness, or if one grasps the mark of emptiness, this is not true knowledge of emptiness; therefore, it is so named.
Obstruction. Therefore, by cultivating the signless (*animitta*) and realizing the cessation of self-nature, one does not grasp at the obstruction of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Second, the reason for not grasping is that the antidote has been attained; that is, knowing that emptiness is itself empty is called ultimate liberation (*atyanta-vimukti*).

Third, since there is now the ability to treat the object of treatment, conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) no longer functions; thus it is said that "not even a slight dharma arises as a sign" (*na kiṃcid-dharmasya nimittam utpadyate*).
When both subject and object are stilled, the signless manifests before one.
Having thus entered into emptiness and the signless, there is no further seeking or wishing, except for the foremost great compassion that transforms sentient beings;
at that moment, the liberation door of wishlessness manifests before one.

The three gates of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) also possess three aspects: first, the basis, which refers to the fact that one can attain wishlessness only by relying on the previously entered emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*);
second, the essence, which is the absence of any aspiration or seeking, as one does not seek after the triple world (*traidhātuka*) and so forth;

third, the excellence, which refers to the birth through transformation by means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), as it surpasses the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Furthermore, the aforementioned three types of emptiness universally take the reality of all phenomena as their object.
He contemplates that the characteristics of the world are themselves the characteristics of nirvāṇa; thus, he is also not the same as those of the two vehicles.

In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the three gates of liberation, abandoning the notion of self and other, abandoning the notion of an agent and a recipient, and abandoning the notions of existence and non-existence.
