In the second section, which clarifies the excellence of being free from hindrances, the preceding cultivation is first restated, because one attains freedom through such cultivation.

First, the abandonment of the notion of emptiness is that which is abandoned by the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*). Next, the abandonment of the notions of existence and non-existence is that which is abandoned by the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-mukha*), as there is nothing to be sought.
Having already understood how one is free from hindrances, one may ask: in what sense is this "excellence"? The Sūtra says:
The middle three phrases concern the successive superiority of the fifth, fourth, and fifth stages, as well as the preparatory means (*prayoga*) for this stage.

That is to say, within the fifth stage, by means of the ten kinds of profound and tranquil equanimity of mind, one distances oneself from the pride of bodily purity characteristic of the fourth stage.

This is superior because it employs profound emptiness to extinguish those two forms of selfhood. Second, within the fourth stage, one uses the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to counteract the third stage.

Regarding the pride of [perceiving] the emergence and disappearance of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth, this stage is superior because it employs the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) to abandon such conditioned experiences.
Third, the preparatory means (*prayoga*) of the previous stage merely employed the ten types of equality to break down and reveal existence and non-existence;

now, at the fulfillment of this stage, one employs the profound signlessness (*animitta*) to dismantle and eliminate existence and non-existence. Since everything is thus completely swept away, this stage is superior.

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s great compassion increases further; he practices with diligent effort in order to bring to fulfillment those factors of enlightenment that are not yet complete.
Regarding the second [section], the excellence of practice, there are two parts. First, a general explanation of cultivating the mind:
because one practices within a mind where compassion (*karuṇā*) has increased, even for those who have not yet perfected *bodhi*, this also serves as the objective for practicing self-benefit.

As for "compassion having increased," it refers to the three types of compassion that arose after previously contemplating the ten equalities; now, through the contemplation of the ten gates of objects, one’s compassion for sentient beings ensnared by delusion increases even further.
The Dharma.
He reflects thus: "All conditioned phenomena proceed when there is a combination [of causes], and do not proceed when there is no combination.
They proceed when conditions assemble, and do not proceed when conditions do not assemble. Thus I know that conditioned phenomena possess many faults and afflictions; I should..."
He severs these causes and conditions of conjunction; yet, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, he does not ultimately extinguish all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Next, the middle two [verses] are specifically revealed: first, the explanation of cultivation; second, the explanation of the excellence of cultivation. Now, regarding the first: again—

Two: First, the courageous undertaking of practice, meaning that one exerts effort when first beginning the cultivation. Second, from "The Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, it clarifies that the resolve of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*) ensures that the practice will ultimately reach fulfillment.
Furthermore, the former refers to courageous cultivation through compassion and wisdom; the latter refers to the ultimate realization of both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the former [the courageous undertaking], there is first wisdom and then compassion; within wisdom, there is first knowledge and then revulsion. Of these, the first consists of the two upper lines.

This clarifies that conditioned existence arises through the conjunction of conditions. That is to say, when karma and afflictions mutually support one another, conditioned phenomena are produced, as in the case of "ignorance conditions volitional formations" and so forth.
The latter two phrases clarify whether the conditions for existence are complete or deficient. "Accumulation" refers to completeness;

that is, if either karma or afflictions are lacking, rebirth will certainly not occur, just as there may be volitional formations but they lack the moistening power of craving and so on. The subsequent section, beginning with "I am thus," expresses weariness. Having understood this...

The conditioned is characterized by the fault of suffering; one must certainly sever the causes of its compounded aggregation. Yet, while cultivating compassion to benefit sentient beings, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva thus contemplates the conditioned as having many faults and evils, as being devoid of intrinsic nature, and as neither arising nor ceasing.

The two great masters first cultivate the stage of renunciation (*vidūṣaṇā*) within the initial [stage] of the middle path. Seeing that those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) abound in faults, they renounce them because these are obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*).
Next, from the passage "furthermore, they lack intrinsic nature" (*na svabhāvo 'sti*) onwards, they realize the nature [of reality].

By understanding that the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, they are able to extinguish all obstructions and merge with the principle (*tattva*).

While constantly giving rise to great compassion and not abandoning sentient beings, one immediately attains the manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is called the "Light of Unobstructed Wisdom.

Having accomplished such light of wisdom, although one cultivates the causes and conditions of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one does not dwell within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena is quiescent, one likewise does not dwell in quiescence.

Within the section on cessation: because the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have not yet been perfected, the second [section] concerns the excellence of practice, which refers to the manifestation of the excellence of non-abiding. Thus, there are three kinds of excellence:
first, the initial two phrases clarify the excellence of the cause of *prajñā*, for it is by means of this non-abiding that one builds upon the aforementioned great wisdom.

First, because of the arising of compassion. Second, one immediately attains the manifestation of the inferior *prajñā*. *Prajñā* is the general name; "unobstructed wisdom" (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) is its specific designation.
Although the unimpeded Buddha-wisdom has not yet been fully accomplished, this present *prajñā* is now able to illumine this wisdom.
The preceding sign of this wisdom is called "light" (*āloka*). Light is itself the gate. Third, one accomplishes in this manner.

The latter [verse] emphasizes the superior function of *prajñā*; it is also the characteristic of non-abiding. That is to say: the first two lines show that while engaging with phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one does not lose sight of the principle;
thus, one does not abide in the conditioned. The latter two lines show that while perceiving the principle (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not destroy phenomena;

thus, one does not abide in the unconditioned. This is because one realizes the equality of the conditioned and *nirvāṇa*. Consequently, through the wisdom of *bodhi*, one does not abide in what is to be accomplished.

Because the aids to the path of wisdom are not yet fulfilled, one does not abide in the conditioned; because the aids to the path of merit are not yet fulfilled, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, because both are not yet fulfilled, one abides in neither.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*): the samādhi of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*),

the samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of the foremost emptiness (*agrya-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of combined emptiness (*saṃyoga-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of arising emptiness (*utpāda-śūnyatā*),

the samādhi of emptiness that does not differentiate according to reality (*yathābhūta-avikalpa-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of emptiness that does not abandon or depart (*aparityāga-apagamana-śūnyatā*), and the samādhi of emptiness that is neither detached nor non-detached (*vigama-avigama-śūnyatā*).

Samādhi. Third, regarding the excellence of samādhi, there are two parts. First, the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is explained; subsequently, from "these ten signless [dharmas]" onwards, the remaining two are illustrated by analogy.
Within the former, there are again two sections. First, the ten foremost [bodhisattvas] are cited; from "from this bodhisattva" onwards, they are summarized.

There are many ways to organize these categories. Regarding the first ten among them, the commentary based on the *Śāstra* is somewhat difficult to reconcile. Next, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it explains them as follows: "The first eight are the emptiness that realizes true reality (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*);

the latter two are the emptiness that gives rise to function (*kārya-śūnyatā*). To speak of 'entering emptiness' refers to internal emptiness and external emptiness, because they consist of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) of the internal and external.
'Intrinsic nature' refers to the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), for it has not only been non-existent from the present moment."

It is called "emptiness. The emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is identical in substance to this. As for "the first emptiness," it is called the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

This means that while the preceding [type of] emptiness was merely empty of the ultimate meaning, here it is clarified that whether there is existence or non-existence, they are fundamentally empty from the beginning.

Therefore, that sutra says: "Whether it is 'it exists' or 'it does not exist,' these are called the emptiness of emptiness. Whether it is 'it is' or 'it is not,' these are called the emptiness of emptiness."

This means that even this [negation] must itself be empty in its essence. Such "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) is precisely where the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) become lost;

Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage penetrate only a small portion of it, and thus it is called the "first emptiness. Its name is the same as "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā), which is designated as Prajñāpāramitā.
When combined, these constitute "internal and external emptiness" (adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā), because they are both joined and not joined. When they arise, there is existence.

The first is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The eighth is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), because that which is as-it-is (*yathābhūta*) is itself unconditioned. Regarding the two [terms] "non-abandonment" and so forth, both their names and meanings differ.

If one wishes to reconcile them: the ninth is the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), because the beginningless does not depart from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and is itself empty.
The tenth is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), meaning that both departing and not departing are equally non-existent.
With these ten gates of emptiness samādhi as their primary focus, this bodhisattva brings forth hundreds of thousands of emptiness samādhis before them.
Likewise, with these ten gates of signlessness and ten gates of wishlessness samādhi as their primary focus,
they bring forth hundreds of thousands of signless and wishless samādhi gates before them.
The subsequent knots may be understood accordingly.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they further cultivate and bring to fulfillment the indestructible mind, the resolute mind, the purely virtuous mind, the profound mind, the non-retrogressive mind, the unceasing mind, the vast mind, and the... [inexhaustible mind].
The mind of the limit, the mind seeking wisdom, and the mind associated with skillful means and insight are all fully perfected.
This is the fourth fruit of the indestructible mind. The following two sections also subsume the dedication of all roots of goodness that accord with firmness;
this constitutes the advancement of virtue and the subsequent initiation of great practice. Now, for the first [point]: regarding the "indestructible mind," it is because—

Obstacles are extinguished and practice is perfected; whether it be wisdom or compassion, neither shall ever regress or perish. The text contains ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.
There are nine kinds of non-retrogression: (1) the determination of the principle through faith is called the "resolute mind";

(2) the adaptability and flexibility of practice is called the "wholesome mind"; (3) the absence of fear regarding the profound is called the "profound mind"; (4) not regressing from one's own vehicle...
1. It is called the non-retrogressive mind. 2. The fifth is the unceasing mind of superior progress. 3. The sixth is the expansive mind that dissolves the distinction between self and other.
4. The seventh is the boundless mind that benefits sentient beings without limit. 5. The eighth is the mind seeking wisdom, which seeks the knowledge of the stages (*bhūmi*). 6.
The ninth is the mind of skillful means and wisdom, which skillfully transforms sentient beings; this may also be correlated with the preceding ten [bodhisattva stages].
The mind of samādhi is indestructible by means of clarity. Nine are all firm and are said to be indestructible.
Ten are all complete and are called fully perfected.
O Son of the Buddha, by means of this mind, the bodhisattva accords with the Bodhi of the Buddha; he does not fear heterodox arguments and enters the stages of wisdom, free from...
The path of the two vehicles leads toward the wisdom of the Buddha; no demons of affliction can obstruct or destroy it.
Abiding in the luminosity of the bodhisattva’s wisdom, one skillfully cultivates all dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Skillful means and wisdom are always in mutual accord, and the factors of enlightenment are constantly practiced without abandonment.

The fifth [power], the power of mastery (*vaśitā-bala*), is superior. First, its characteristics are revealed; subsequently, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, its limits are defined. Within the former section, there are ten phrases:
the first is general, and from "without fear" onwards, they are specific. Generally speaking, "this mind" refers to the ten minds mentioned previously.
"Conforming to the Bodhi of the Buddha" means being able to deeply enter and incline toward it. As the *Śāstra* says: "One attains the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā."
It is superior in power because it is able to penetrate deeply; thus, one knows that the ten preceding minds are all minds in which *prajñā* is manifest.
Within the nine distinct phrases, one attains mastery and proceeds by relying on the aforementioned ten indestructible minds:
first, not fearing heterodox arguments, which is the power to subdue others; second, ascending into the ground of wisdom, which is the power to sever doubt and attain the Dharma.

1. Because it is empty (*śūnya*). 2. The power of the non-propelling of one’s own vehicle, because it is free from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). 3. The power of faith in the secret place, because it proceeds toward the wisdom of the objective realm.
4. The power of diligence that cannot be destroyed by any Māras. 5. The power of firmness in subduing afflictions, because it abides in the clarity of wisdom (*jñāna-vidyā*). 6.
The power of universal subduing, because it is endowed with the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*) and is unstained while dwelling in existence (*bhava*). 7. The power of transformation.

This corresponds to the ninth stage of skillful means mentioned previously. The power of purifying the nine obstacles to knowledge is the aforementioned higher pursuit of the ground of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*).
Since the former wisdom abides in the center, it guides the two types of compassion; whereas this wisdom abides at the end, thereby manifesting the distinct characteristics of compassion and wisdom.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain the preeminence of the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and attain the third kind of sharp and compliant patience (*kṣānti*).
This is because they accord with and do not contradict the true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
In the second bond, because of the manifestation of *prajñā*, compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) becomes clear and sharp.
As for the "third," it is because it is the most superior among the three grades of patience. Thus concludes the excellence of its fruit.
The preceding section of the Great Text has already been completed. Regarding the fruit of the lower stages:

O Son of the Buddha, once a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas—namely, many hundreds of Buddhas, up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of Buddhas.
In the second section of the major text, regarding the fruits, three points are the same as before. Within the section on "Pliability" (*praśrabdhi*), there are four parts:

first, the practice of pliability; second, the purity of teaching and wisdom; third, the specific characteristics of the stages; and fourth, the concluding explanation of the names of the stages. Within the first part, there are the dharma, the metaphor, and the application.
Within the dharma, there are three sections; the first concerns the conditions for refining the practice.
With a vast mind and a profound mind, they offer, revere, respect, and praise [the Buddhas].
They provide all necessities of life—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and so forth—and likewise make offerings to the entire Saṅgha.
They dedicate these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus, they show reverence toward all Buddhas.
They listen to the Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, attaining the light of wisdom of the samādhi of reality as it is.
They practice accordingly, maintaining it in memory without forsaking it, and further attain the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
Next is the ability to refine one's practice. Within this, "having heard and received and maintained" refers to the attainment of the *dhāraṇī* of meaning.

The light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*) of samādhi is the meaning that is maintained. "Practicing in accordance [with it]" indicates the cause for attaining the *dhāraṇī* of meaning. By what means does this occur?
It is because, by relying on the excellence of the aforementioned three samādhis, one attains such *śamatha* and so forth, thereby recollecting and maintaining [the teachings].
The preceding section primarily reveals the capacity to sustain; furthermore, from "having attained" onwards also refers to that which is sustained.
Throughout hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, all roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
It is purified by the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*), becoming even more luminous and pure because it has liberated itself from those obstacles.
Furthermore, this is due to having previously realized that treasury of the Buddha’s teachings (*buddhadharmakośa*).
It is like genuine gold, which becomes even more luminous and pure when repeatedly polished with lapis lazuli gems (*vaiḍūrya*).
In the analogy, pure gold represents the realization of truth and also represents faith and so forth. Lapis lazuli represents the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).

By being repeatedly polished by this wisdom of skillful means, it causes the light of the teaching-wisdom (*deśanā-jñāna*) to emerge from the supramundane realization-wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*), becoming even more excellent than before.
The roots of goodness possessed by the bodhisattvas on this stage are likewise thus. Through the wisdom of skillful means, they observe them accordingly;
they become increasingly bright and pure, increasingly tranquil and extinguished, and cannot be eclipsed by anything.
Within the synthesis, skillful means and wisdom correspond to the aforementioned non-abiding path. This corresponds to the preceding lapis lazuli;
"observing in accordance with it" corresponds to polishing and refining it repeatedly until it becomes even more brilliant and pure, because Prajñā manifests.
"Becoming further quiescent" refers to the realization-wisdom that is liberated from those obstacles.
For example, just as moonlight illuminates the bodies of sentient beings, bringing them cooling relief and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of wind-circles,

so too are all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas on this stage. They can extinguish the blazing fires of affliction of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings,
and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of māra-paths.

Second, the purity of the wisdom of the teaching is explained. Because the moonlight is more vast and superior than that of the preceding stage, the metaphor is taken solely from the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
Regarding the "four kinds of wind-wheels" (*vāyumaṇḍala*), these refer to the four types of wind-wheels—such as the "appearing" and the "supporting"—that emerge;

they are not the four [great] wheels [of the world-system], because those are not winds that cause disintegration. Furthermore, where there is a wind of disintegration, the four [great] wheels do not exist.

Having not yet examined the sūtras and śāstras, I do not dare to make a definitive judgment. For now, I shall explain it according to its meaning as the winds of the four seasons: The spring wind is called the "Harmonious Wind" (*hefeng*);

it is a metaphor for the *kleśamāra* (demon of afflictions), for it accords with the mind of attachment. The summer wind is called the "Scorching Wind" (*yanfeng*); it is a metaphor for the *skandhamāra* (demon of the aggregates), for there is much heat and distress.

The autumn wind is called the "Cool Wind" (*liangfeng*) or the "Golden Wind" (*jinfeng*); it is a metaphor for the *mṛtyumāra* (demon of death), for when the fruit ripens, it is gathered and harvested.

Therefore, the winter wind is called "cold wind," which is a metaphor for the celestial Māras. Because they destroy the storehouse of a person's goodness, practicing the conduct of the four Māras constitutes the path of Māra.
Among the ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva, the prajñāpāramitā is predominant; it is not that the others are not cultivated, but rather—
According to one's power and according to one's lot.
Second, the specific characteristics of the stages.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the brief exposition of the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Manifestation (Abhimukhī).
This is the fourth stage, the Ground of Radiance (*Arciṣmatī*).
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a celestial king of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, exercising mastery over their activities.

They cannot be defeated or discouraged by any questions or challenges posed by śrāvakas. They are able to cause sentient beings to eliminate the pride of self (*asmimāna*) and to penetrate deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). They spread...

Whether practicing generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation, all such activities are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, up to and including mindfulness of the possession of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes. Furthermore, he forms this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes relies."
If this bodhisattva practices with diligent vigor, in a single moment of thought they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of samādhis,
and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas as their retinue.

Within the category of the fruit of retribution, it is said that no one is able to defeat him when questioned by Śrāvakas; this is because he already knows the stages, conditions, and so forth of the two vehicles.
If, however, he manifests through the sovereign power of his vows, he exceeds these numbers, even reaching hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas.
Even eons cannot calculate its number.
This is the fruit of the wisdom of the three vows.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Having perfected the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena are signless and devoid of intrinsic nature;
they are unborn and unceasing, fundamentally pure, free from conceptual proliferation, without grasping or abandoning,
their essential character quiescent like an illusion, and non-dual as existence and non-existence, transcending all discrimination.
Contemplating in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in this way—this wisdom is accomplished as one enters the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*).

This third section of verses on the perfection of clear and sharp compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) consists of twenty-two verses, divided into three parts: the first seventeen verses praise the practice of the stages; the next four...

The verses concern the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*). The final [section] provides the concluding summary; the preceding middle section consists of three parts. First, the first two verses and one line praise the antidote to superior pride (*abhimāna*).
Second, ten verses and three lines praise the excellence of practicing the path of non-abiding (*apratisthita-mārga*).
Third, four verses praise the excellence of its fruition. Now, for the first part:
In observing the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the world, there are three parts.
The first line of verse reveals the nature of the mind and its objects:
"Through the power of the darkness of delusion, the world arises; if that darkness of delusion is extinguished, the world does not exist."

Contemplating all causes and conditions as empty in their true sense, yet not destroying the utility of conventional designations and their harmonious integration—therein is no agent, no recipient, and no volition. All conditioned phenomena arise like clouds;
ignorance is the failure to know the True Reality. The karma of intentional action is the fruit of delusion.
"Consciousness arises together with name-and-form;

thus, up to the mass of suffering"—these nine verses and one line constitute a separate exposition clarifying the contemplation of characteristics, which is divided into ten sections. The first section consists of two and a half verses that explain the arrangement of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
One thoroughly understands that the three realms depend upon the mind; The twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so.
Birth and death are all produced by the mind; If the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted.
These two verses summarize [the teaching] into the single mind. Since it is said that if the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted, one thereby knows that...
One may consider this as referring solely to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). It is said that "relying on the mind" refers to the union of the true and the deluded;

once the delusion within the true has ceased, the truth within the deluded is nonetheless not absent. Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "It is only the mental characteristics (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) that cease, not the essence of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*) that ceases."
The functions of ignorance are twofold: failing to understand conditions serves as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Thus it continues until old age and death; from this, suffering arises without end.
(One verse in three lines praises the distinctions of one's own karma.)
With ignorance as a condition, it cannot be severed; when those conditions are exhausted, all are extinguished.
(The first half-verse of the fourth stanza: these factors are inseparable.

Delusion, craving, and grasping are the branches of affliction (*kleśa*); volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are the branches of karma (*karman*); the rest are suffering (*duḥkha*).
The five and a half verses praise the non-interruption of the three paths:
From ignorance up to the six sense bases, these are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); Contact and feeling are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
The remaining links of existence are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). If one perceives non-self, these three sufferings are extinguished.
The Seventh Section: The Six-One Verses on the Accumulation of the Three Sufferings.
Ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past; Consciousness through feeling evolve in the present;
Craving, grasping, and becoming produce future suffering. If these conditions are severed, the limit is reached and all ends.
Verse 71 reiterates the cycle of rebirth across the three time periods:
"Ignorance is the condition for the bondage of birth; when one attains liberation from conditions, that bondage is exhausted.
Verses 8a through 14b skip ahead to restate the ninth [verse] concerning the bonds of arising and ceasing.
From causes arises the fruit; when separated from them, it ceases. Contemplating this, one knows that its nature is empty.
(The first half of verse nine reiterates the arising and ceasing of dependent origination.
Following along with ignorance, all existences arise; if one does not follow along, all existences cease.
"When this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that likewise does not exist"—this verse of thirteen lines observes the exhaustion of all that exists.
Through ten modes of reflection, the mind is freed from attachment; the continuity of the links of existence is subsumed within a single mind.
One's own karma, non-separation, and the three paths; the three time periods, the three sufferings, arising from causes and conditions,
bondage, origination and cessation, and conformity to inexhaustibility—
these five phrases in the third verse conclude the ten names.
Thus universally contemplating the process of dependent origination— Without agent, without recipient, and without reality;
like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection of light, And like a fool chasing a mirage— By observing in this way, one enters into emptiness;
Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached, one attains the signless.
Having realized their emptiness and falsity, there is nothing to be wished for; one acts solely out of compassion for sentient beings.
Among the three verses on the excellence of that fruit, the first two verses concern the excellence of the remedy (*pratipakṣa*).
The Great Being practices the gate of liberation, Increasing his great compassion as he seeks the Buddha-dharma;
Knowing that all conditioned phenomena arise through cooperation, His resolve is firm and he diligently practices the Path.
This verse praises the excellence of his practice.
The gate of the emptiness samādhi possesses hundreds of thousands [of aspects]; the signless and the wishless are likewise so.
The subsequent half-verse praises the excellence of the samādhis:
"In wisdom and compliant patience, all are supreme; liberation and wisdom are brought to full perfection."
The final two lines of the verse generally praise the latter two excellences, as their meaning applies to both.
Furthermore: With a profound mind, one makes many offerings to the Buddhas;
Within the Buddha’s teachings, one cultivates the Path and attains the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, increasing roots of goodness, Like gold and lapis lazuli that have been polished and refined.
Just as the moon’s coolness pervades all things, And the four winds cannot destroy it when they strike,
so too does this ground’s Bodhisattva transcend the path of Māra, and likewise extinguish the fever of afflictions for all living beings.
On this ground, one often becomes a benevolent wheel-turning king, transforming and guiding sentient beings to eliminate their conceit.
All that they do is sought for the sake of all-knowledge; They have already completely surpassed the path of the śrāvakas.

The bodhisattvas on this stage exert themselves with diligence, Attaining hundreds of billions of samādhis, And also beholding various immeasurable Buddhas, Like the sun in the sky during the height of summer.
The results of the stages and so forth can be understood from the four verses that follow.
Profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive or know—
such as this sixth stage of the Bodhisattva, which neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas can comprehend— I have now proclaimed for the sake of the Buddha’s sons.
The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), is concluded with this summary verse.

Regarding the seventh stage, the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*): the reason for proceeding [to it] is that the dwelling in wisdom associated with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-yukti-prajñā-vihāra*), which was entrusted to the level of the Pratyekabuddhas, has already been explained;

next, the dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra*) involving application and effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-sābhoga*) is explained, which is entrusted to the Bodhisattva stages. This is why [the seventh stage follows].

It comes. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Although on the preceding stage one was able to dwell frequently in signless mental attention (*animitta-manasikāra*), one was not yet able to cause that signless mental attention to be practiced with uninterrupted and flawless continuity. To fulfill this now, there follows this 'coming.

Furthermore, because the previous effort was not yet perfected, it is now brought to fulfillment; thus it is called 'far-reaching' (*dūraṅgama*). This is as stated in the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only).
Because one emerges from the contemplation of the mundane and the paths of the two vehicles at the final limit of the stage of effort within the signless dwelling (*animitta-vihāra*).

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Because one is able to enter far into the signless mental application (*manasikāra*) that is without deficiency and without interruption, and because it is contiguous with the pure stages (*śuddhabhūmi*), it is called 'Far-Going' (*dūraṅgama*).
There are two meanings for establishing the name 'Far-Going': first, it has come from afar..."

Regarding the limit of effort: second, because this final stage of effort can travel far into subsequent states, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it is "far from the three realms" and "near the station of the Dharma King," and is therefore called the "Distant Ground" (*dūra-bhūmi*). However, the practice of being able to travel far is precisely the signless (*animitta*);
thus, the obstacle to be abandoned is precisely the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle signs, namely, the attachment arising in the sixth ground.
Because the manifestation of subtle characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) has been extinguished, this characteristic of arising and ceasing consists of two types of ignorance:
first, the ignorance of the manifestation of subtle characteristics, which refers to the grasping at the existence of subtle characteristics of arising within the flow of dependent origination;

second, the ignorance of seeking the signless through exclusive mental attention, which refers to the grasping at the existence of subtle characteristics of cessation. This is because one has not yet attained [the state] by exclusively attending to the signless with diligent pursuit.

One is able to initiate superior practices within emptiness; it is only upon reaching this stage that one can sever them. Because one constantly abides in the signless (*animitta*), one does not cling to arising.
Furthermore, because one no longer exerts mental effort to seek the signless, one is able to realize the suchness (*tathatā*) of the non-differentiation of phenomena.
This is because one understands that the various teachings are identical to the signlessness of suchness. Because one is able to empty...

Because there arises superior practice within the midst [of non-conceptuality], it constitutes the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*). These two practices proceed in tandem, even until the fruit of signlessness (*animitta*) is attained.
Thus, one should know that through pure signlessness, the arousal of practice is not obstructed.
At that time, the hosts of devas rejoiced in their hearts; They scattered jewels that formed clouds abiding in the sky,
Universally emitting all kinds of wondrous sounds, Addressing the Most Victorious and Pure One,
Who has mastered the wisdom of ultimate truth And accomplished hundreds of billions of merits.
The Lotus among Men, Unattached, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, expounds the sequence of profound practices.
Next, the formal explanation of the text also consists of three parts. First, within the praise and request, there are twelve verses; the first ten are praises.
Regarding the latter two invitations, the preceding section is divided into four parts. The first two verses describe the praise offered by the celestial hosts:

The Sovereign Heavenly King, dwelling in the midst of space, Emanated great radiance that illuminated the Buddha’s body, And also scattered clouds of the most sublime and wondrous incense, Universally making offerings to the One who has removed all sorrow and affliction.
Next follows a verse. The Lord of Devas, Cloud of Light, makes offerings to the Buddha to signify that his wisdom accords with the Dharma-body.
At that time, the assembly of devas were all filled with joy; they all raised beautiful voices in unison to offer praise:
"Having heard these merits of this stage, we have already obtained a great and excellent benefit."
A single verse concerning the three realms of existence was heard with joy by the host of devas.
At that time, the celestial maidens’ hearts were filled with delight, and they vied with one another to play tens of millions of kinds of musical sounds.
By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, voices within those sounds collectively uttered these words:
The four verses on the existence [of the gods] consist of six stanzas in which celestial maidens praise the Buddha with music. Among them, the first reveals the causes and conditions of the sound:
"Your majestic deportment is tranquil and peerless; You are the World-Honored One who can subdue the unsubduable.
Having already transcended all worlds, You traverse the world to proclaim the wondrous Path."
Though manifesting various immeasurable bodies, they know that each body is ultimately non-existent;
skillfully using words and speech to explain all dharmas, they do not grasp at the marks of letters or sounds.
Traveling to hundreds of thousands of lands, they offer the most excellent gifts to the Buddhas.
With mastery of wisdom, they are free from attachment;
though they do not conceive the thought of their own Buddha-land, they diligently teach and transform all sentient beings, yet harbor no sense of "other" or "self.
Although they have already cultivated and perfected vast goodness, they do not give rise to attachment toward those wholesome dharmas.
The remaining five verses clearly express words of praise. Among them, the first four verses praise the unimpeded activity of tranquility:

Seeing that all worlds are constantly ablaze with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, He remains entirely detached from all conceptual thoughts, And exerts the power of great compassion and diligence.

The latter part clarifies the source from which the activity arises—namely, the non-obstruction of compassion and wisdom. Since he is about to explain their simultaneous practice, he praises this by relying on its power:
"All the devas and devīs, having offered various kinds of worship and praise,"
They all remained silent at the same time, gazing up at the Honored One among Men, wishing to hear the Dharma.
Then Vimukticandra again made this request: "The minds of this great assembly are pure;
[they wish to hear] the characteristics of the practices within the seventh stage. We pray that the Son of the Buddha will proclaim them for us."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying: "O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage and wishes to enter the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā,
he should cultivate ten kinds of paths of superior excellence arising from skillful means and wisdom."
Within the second part, the Section on the Correct Exposition, there are two: first, the practice; second, the result. Within the practice, there are five distinct types of characteristics:
(1) the distinction of the antidote to the practice of effortless ease; (2) the distinction of the antidote to its obstacles; (3) the distinction of the excellence of the dual practice;
(4) the distinction of the superiority of the preceding higher stages; and (5) the distinction of their results. Among these five, the first is as follows:
This is the expedient means for entering the stages (*bhūmi*); it corresponds to the mind of entry. The remaining four constitute the stage of abiding.

The mind of emergence resides in the fruit. Furthermore, within the stage of abiding, the first is the initial stage of abiding; the next one is the stage of correct abiding; the next one, although mentioned later, in meaning encompasses the beginning and the end;
and the final one is the completion of the stage. Regarding the initial statement of "delighting in non-action," this refers to delighting in the contemplation of emptiness through *prajñā*.
This refers to the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics (*sūkṣma-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*).
Although this stage possesses non-attachment as its antidote, the fact that it still involves limited scope (*sopamāna*) and effortful application (*sābhoga*) constitutes another obstacle.
Therefore, one cultivates immeasurable and effortless practice (*apramāṇa-anābhoga-caryā*) as the antidote. Third, because the obstacles of defilement have been exhausted, [this stage is attained].

The simultaneous practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. According to the Four Clarifications (*Sì míng*), the effort of this stage surpasses that of the preceding six stages and excels those of the subsequent three;
"subsequent" refers to the latter [three]. Fifth, because the stage is fulfilled, the fruit of simultaneous practice is explained.

Now, within the first section, there are four parts: first, the conclusion of the heading; second, from "What is it? onwards, the inquiry that reveals its characteristics; third, "The Bodhisattva, by means of such... [and so forth].

This concludes the section on the function of practice. From "The four enter" onwards, its limits are clarified. First: having fully completed the practices of the six stages, this summarizes the preceding meaning;
for it concerns the practice of signlessness (*animitta*) which is to be remedied. Since the practice of signlessness through *prajñā* is fulfilled, one might become attached to this [attainment];
therefore, it is not yet the practice of increase (*utkṛṣṭa*). Next, from "desiring to enter below," its designation is clarified following the ten [stages].

These various skillful means (*upāya*) constitute the remedy. That is to say, the previous delight in non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and lack of clarity regarding skillful means cannot give rise to superior practice;
it is not the sublime path. Now, by means of the ten kinds of wisdom regarding the non-abandonment of sentient beings and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), [one attains this].
One considers this to be capable of cultivation. Cultivating the preceding mind of joy is called "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-prajñā*);

it is thus able to grasp the superior practices (*adhimātra-caryā*). Therefore, it is called "arousing the distinguished path. This is precisely because one cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one does not abide in emptiness;

this is expedient wisdom within emptiness. Because one engages with existence (*bhava*) within emptiness, one does not abide in existence; this is the distinguished path within existence. The path is thus...
This is practice. It is called "supreme" (*adhipati*) because the practice performed is extraordinary. In what respect is it supreme?

That is to say, within the mundane and supramundane states previously entrusted [to the practitioner], it is superior to the mundane because it is emptiness, and it is able to surpass the supramundane because it is capable of engaging with existence (*bhava*).
Although one also cultivates compassion in the first six stages and does not abide in non-existence, one is unable to emerge from quiescence (*śānti*).

Because they practice emptiness as a deliberate effort, they do not attain the name of "excellent skillful means. Although they engage in the practice of emptiness, they are largely attached to emptiness;
thus, this is merely called the "remedy for delighting in non-action."
What are these ten? They are: although one skillfully cultivates the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one does not abandon sentient beings through compassion;
although one attains the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, one delights in constantly making offerings to the Buddhas;

although one enters the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, one diligently accumulates merit and virtue; although one is far removed from the triple world, one adorns the triple world; although one is ultimately...

Having extinguished the flames of all afflictions (*kleśa*), they are nevertheless able to give rise to the flames of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings.

Although they know that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, mirages, transformations, the moon reflected in water, and images in a mirror—being non-dual in their intrinsic nature—they nonetheless engage in the infinite distinctions of actions according to the mind. Although they know...
All lands are like empty space, yet one can adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous conduct.
Although one knows that the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma-body is inherently bodiless, one adorns the body with the marks and signs of excellence.
Although one knows that the nature of the Buddhas' voices is empty, quiescent, and ineffable, one is able to produce various sounds according to all sentient beings.
With pure voices of diverse distinctions, although they understand with all Buddhas that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment,

they nevertheless cultivate various practices through various characteristics, various times, and various kalpas, in accordance with the mental inclinations and conceptual discriminations of sentient beings.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies the inquiry: the reason why these superior practices attain a supremacy that is unsurpassed is due to the ten points below.
Each point consists of two phrases; in all cases, the upper phrase contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while the lower phrase engages with existence (*saṃsāra*).

When the upper phrase attains the lower, it constitutes the skillful means and wisdom within emptiness. When the lower phrase attains the upper, it constitutes the distinguished practice within existence. Thus, they are not [separate].
Because they stagnate in emptiness and existence, [the text] proceeds with these words. The Master of the Treatise subsumes the ten [perfections] into four kinds of merit;
that is to say, the first three each constitute one, while the latter seven constitute one. First, the initial phrase concerns the cause for guarding against unwholesome conduct (*duṣcarita*).

There are two types of unwholesome conduct in a Bodhisattva: first, taking no delight in the benefit and happiness [of others]; second, giving rise to craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*). Now, by virtue of the preceding phrase...
There is no attachment or [wrong] view. By virtue of the latter phrase, one is able to bring benefit and happiness.

If either of these two were lacking, there would be misconduct; now, one protects through both phrases. This serves as the basis for compassion free from attachment and view. The "two" refers to the superior bases of wealth and body.
Because of making offerings to the Buddha, one protects wealth and body; because of attaining equanimity, both matters are [equally protected].
Victorious. As for victorious wealth, it accords with whatever objects are required. As for the victorious body, one takes whichever type is desired at will.

The three types of protection are the causes for the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); these roots of goodness consist of diligently accumulating merit as provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).

Now, this is accumulated by means of the wisdom of emptiness itself, which constitutes the superior cause for attaining that victory. All the meritorious dharmas now being accumulated become increased.
The practice of the higher perfections (pāramitās) is termed "protection" (*rakṣā*). Although they possess compassion, these are all due to the superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*);

thus, the first three are all for one's own benefit. The latter seven are likewise for the benefit of others. Taken together, these constitute the fourth category: the causes and activities for gathering and sustaining sentient beings.
This constitutes seven types. The first involves taking birth in accordance with objects; the next two involve transforming others to cause them to leave behind hindrances;

and the final four involve gathering others to establish them in goodness. Regarding the first: taking birth through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is for the purpose of acting as a leader among sentient beings;

thus, one must adorn the three realms. Since this is birth by aspiration alone and not due to karma or afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said to be "far removed. The second [type] is explained as being for the sake of providing remedies.
This means that by demonstrating the arising of afflictions, one intends to treat and sever them while knowing their nature is quiescent; only then does this constitute the primary treatment.
Now, because one sees that they are eternally quiescent from the outset, [this is established]. Third, it is for the sake of extinguishing the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

There are four types of such obscurations, as explained in the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*) within the context of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). It enables one to perform immeasurable activities—such as composing books and treatises—in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
And it acts as the remedy. Fourth, because of the gathering of the great assembly of the Dharma, one undertakes the practice of adorning the land for the sake of sentient beings;

this clarifies the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment). The following three clarify the *mūla-vipāka* (the primary body). Through the three wheels, one benefits sentient beings. Fifth is the bodily action (*kāyakarman*):

by manifesting a body where there is no body, one causes [beings] to produce the five blessings—namely, through seeing, hearing, approaching, making offerings, and practicing. One’s own body is without...
The first is because his body is identical to the Dharma-body; the same applies to the following two. The sixth is because his verbal karma turns the wheel of the Dharma.

The seventh is because his mental karma provides excellent explanations in response to questions regarding that which has neither length nor brevity, records the events of the three periods of time, and initiates practices throughout the three periods of time.
By means of these ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom, the bodhisattva initiates sublime practices and enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage.
Regarding the third summary of superior capabilities, the commentary states: "These ten kinds of initiated sublime practices collectively correspond to..."
Regarding the treatment of "appropriation" (*parigraha*), the two lines—upper and lower—are paired as "mutual oppositions" (*sādharmya-pratipakṣa*).
By means of these upper and lower [lines], each is able to act as an antidote: the upper line treats the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*), while the lower line treats the Hinayana.
Because their respective treatments differ, these two forms of appropriation are called "excellent practices" (*viśiṣṭa-caryā*) that serve as antidotes to the aforementioned obstacles.
Having entered [this stage], this practice is constantly present before one; this is called dwelling in the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*).

Fourth, regarding the clarification of the boundaries: because the state of signlessness (*animitta*) is uninterrupted, the name "Signless Stage" (*animittabhūmi*) is established from this point onward.
This also subsumes the previously mentioned "Non-Retrogression Dwelling," which differs from the preceding six stages; in those six, once the dwelling is attained, it is subsequently relinquished.

Entering the mind of the stages (*bhūmi*) by means of entry through cultivation and understanding, rather than entry through practice; because one enters here by means of practice, one constantly practices without abandoning it, which is called the "non-retrogressive dwelling" (*avivartana-vihāra*).
The preceding section on the primary remedies is concluded.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this seventh stage, they enter the infinite realms of sentient beings and enter the infinite activities of the Buddhas for teaching and transforming sentient beings.

The following is the second section: the distinctions in the remedies for those obstacles. This subsumes the aforementioned practice of non-attachment, as it involves immeasurable applications that are all characterized by non-attachment.
Regarding these "remedies," there are two aspects: first, the cultivation of immeasurable types [of practices] to remedy the previously mentioned finite obstacles;
second, from the passage "this bodhisattva forms this thought" onwards, the cultivation of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) to remedy [the remaining obstacles].
The preceding section concerned the practice with effort (*sābhoga-prayoga*) and the obstacles thereto. Now begins the first [section], which consists of twenty phrases organized into ten pairs.
Within each pair, the first phrase clarifies that the objective realm is infinite, serving as both the object of knowledge and the field of conversion.
The second line clarifies that the Buddha’s meritorious deeds are immeasurable, as he is able to know and transform.

When Bodhisattvas enter into that Buddha’s transformation to transform sentient beings themselves, these essentials are subsumed into five, namely the five immeasurable realms (*apramāṇa-dhātu*). The first one corresponds to the immeasurability of sentient beings; the treatise states:

"In accordance with whichever sentient beings are to be transformed. This [first] correspondence serves as the general category, while the ten subsequent correspondences all serve as... [specific instances].
It is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. As for the phrase "what kind," it refers to the fact that their types are not one; this explains the term "immeasurable" in the sutra.
Because he transforms sentient beings through immeasurable activities according to the inclinations of their many diverse types, [the term is used].
They enter the infinite network of worlds; they enter the infinite pure lands of all Buddhas.
This constitutes a pair of two. Where do sentient beings dwell? It is said they dwell in the infinity of worlds, because they transform others through pure conduct.

They enter into the immeasurable varieties of differentiated phenomena; they enter into the immeasurable wisdom of the manifest enlightenment of all Buddhas; they enter into the enumeration of immeasurable eons;
and they enter into the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas’ realization of the three periods of time.
There are three pairs [of categories], and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is immeasurable. This refers to by what kind of wisdom one transforms [beings].

The first pair is the wisdom that horizontally exhausts all phenomena; the second pair is the wisdom that vertically exhausts the three periods of time. Both are the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Regarding these two pairs, in terms of their objects of knowledge, they are both the immeasurable dharma-realm.
They enter into the infinite differences in the faith and understanding of sentient beings; they enter into the infinite manifestations of the various names and forms of the bodies of all Buddhas;
they enter into the infinite differences in the desires, inclinations, and faculties of sentient beings;

they enter into the infinite languages and sounds of all Buddhas that bring joy to sentient beings; they enter into the infinite varieties of mental activities of sentient beings; and they enter into the infinite [manifestations] of all Buddhas.
He fully understands vast wisdom.
There are four sets of three pairs. These clarify the immeasurable realms of discipline (*vinaya*). Regarding the first two pairs, they clarify by means of what kind of mind [this is accomplished].

Within those, the first pair concerns the various celestial bodies according to the inclinations and faiths of sentient beings; herein, the Bodhisattva manifests through a body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Therefore, it is said that the mind follows its inclinations by practicing celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*) in common with others, thereby attaining a great body;

the speech follows its faith, for it explains those practices through the body of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-kāya*). The second pair knows that the faculties and desires of the past were not the same, because it teaches according to their faculties using sounds appropriate to each class.
The next pair concerns "by what kind of practice," which means knowing the mental activities of the present.

The same. Because the antidotes are explained by means of the practices that lead everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*), one enters into the immeasurable faith and understanding of the Śrāvaka vehicle; one enters into the immeasurable paths of knowledge taught by the Buddhas to inspire faith and understanding;
one enters into the immeasurable accomplishments of the Pratyekabuddhas; and one enters into the immeasurable gateways of profound wisdom taught by the Buddhas.

Entering. Entering the immeasurable skillful practices of all bodhisattvas; entering the immeasurable matters of the Great Vehicle compendia taught by all Buddhas, thereby enabling bodhisattvas to attain entry.
There are five sets of three pairs that clarify the realm of the skillful means of discipline (*vinaya-upāya-dhātu*). The treatise asks: "In which vehicle are they established?

It means they are established within the Three Vehicles (*tri-yāna*). The first pair is taught for *śrāvakas* as the path of wisdom (*jñāna-mārga*) in order to lead them to realize cessation (*nirodha*).

The second pair is taught for *pratyekabuddhas* as profound wisdom (*gambhīra-jñāna*) in order to enable them to know dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The final pair is taught for *bodhisattvas* as the matters of the accumulation of the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*).
Because they employ skillful means to engage with existence, the treatment of the obstacle of limited existence is hereby concluded.
This Bodhisattva reflects: "Such immeasurable realms of the Tathāgatas cannot be fully known even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas;
I must, therefore, accomplish them all with a mind that is effortless and non-conceptual."
[This] is fulfilled.
Second, within the cultivation of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), there are two parts: first, the preparatory application for seeking; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva...
onwards, the actual manifestation of the practice. Now, regarding the first: first, the preceding immeasurables are restated as the objects to be sought. I [have] all...

Regarding the lower stage, which sets a period of practice to apprehend that object through non-action and signlessness without discrimination: this means not grasping at essential natures or characteristics.

To forget conditions and illuminate equally is precisely the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*). When this is further augmented by non-action and signlessness, it becomes even more excellent.

However, this is a matter of following one's natural disposition (*prakṛti*), not resulting from diligent exertion (*vīrya*). It proceeds spontaneously, where the absence of effort accords with the Way;
thus it is called "effortless" (*anābhoga*). This is realized at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Now, because the mind must abide therein, it is said that "one should [apply] it.
Since the practice involving effort has already been fulfilled, this constitutes "effortless cultivation"; yet it is not like the effortless spontaneity of the eighth stage.

O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva observes in this manner with profound wisdom; constantly and diligently cultivating the wisdom of skillful means, they give rise to the sublime path and abide therein immovably.

In the second section, which clearly elucidates the middle [path], first the preceding contemplative wisdom is restated; next, from "constantly and diligently practicing" (*sadā-udyukta*) onwards, is the characteristic of cultivation;
and from "expedient means" (*upāya*) onwards, is the dharma to be cultivated—namely, the wisdom of expedient means within emptiness and the distinguished practice within existence (*bhava*).
Since one has already cultivated with the wisdom of non-exertion and signlessness, one is able to remedy the obstacles of exertion and signs.

Subsequently, by abiding immovably, the characteristics of perfected contemplation are manifested; this is the perfection of practice as immovability, which is not like the immovability of signs and functions at the eighth stage.
This concludes the treatment of the obstacles of functional effort.

There is not a single moment of rest, abandonment, or cessation. Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or even in sleep and dreams, one has never for a moment been associated with hindrances or obstructions.
Third, there is not a single moment of inferiority or dualistic practice; this section on the distinction of excellence is divided into four parts. First and second...

The practice of the two [aspects] is uninterrupted. Second, one never abandons inferior faith for the sake of the superior. Third, this Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, is able to accomplish great benefit.

Fourth, O Son of the Buddha, these ten are the distinctions among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). Among these four, the first three are specifically manifested, while the last one encompasses them all in general.
Among the three, the former one is self-perfection (*svabhāga*), and the latter two are progressive advancement (*viśeṣagamana*). Now, regarding the first: there is none.
The phrase "there being not even a single moment of rest or abandonment" precisely clarifies the meaning of the uninterruptedness of the simultaneous practice of both [calm abiding and insight].

This means that one does not relinquish the previously established unmoving calm abiding (*śamatha*) and the investigative insight (*vipaśyanā*). To practice these two modes simultaneously is the simultaneous practice;

"not resting for even a single moment" is the meaning of uninterruptedness. The subsequent passage beginning with "walking, standing, and so forth" clarifies the timing of this uninterruptedness, referring to the four postures as well as sleeping and waking. Raising [the mind]...
One who is in a dream uses the indistinct to illustrate the discerning;
one should never abandon such contemplation.
Regarding the second, the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* states: "Within that immeasurable wisdom, the meaning of distinction appears as a manifest adornment."

"Because of single-minded mindfulness" means single-mindedly accepting and assenting; this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Because one constantly maintains faith in the ten previously mentioned immeasurables, the two adornments, and the realm of the Buddhas, it is called "supreme."
This Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, is constantly able to fulfill the ten pāramitās. Why is this?
Because in every thought-moment they practice the Buddha-dharma with great compassion as their primary guide, directing themselves toward Buddha-wisdom.
All roots of goodness are bestowed upon sentient beings for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom; this is called the dāna-pāramitā. It is able to extinguish all afflictions.

Heat is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). To have compassion as one's primary motive and not to harm sentient beings is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
To seek the supreme wholesome dharmas without ever becoming weary or satisfied is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
For the path to omniscience to be constantly present before one and never to be distracted is called the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). To be able to endure...

That all phenomena are without arising and without cessation is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). That it can give birth to immeasurable knowledge is called the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*).
That it can seek the ever-higher, most excellent knowledge is called the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*).
That no heterodox arguments or hosts of Māras can obstruct or destroy it is called the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*). To understand [all things] as they truly are—
All dharmas are called the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).
Regarding the second point, "accomplishing great benefit": in a single thought-moment, one suddenly possesses the practice of the ten perfections.

Because the benefit and purpose are vast, it is termed "accomplishing" (*kṛta*) as these are cultivated and brought forth in every thought-moment. The text has two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a critical inquiry and explanation beginning with "What... (*kena*). [The inquiry:]

It is said that while the practices of the ten perfections differ, how can they be perfected within a single thought-moment? The commentary on this text is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the reason why they can be possessed:

because compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem. Second, from "All those... onwards, it reveals the characteristics of what is possessed; herein, *dāna* (generosity) encompasses both compassion and wisdom.

Patience (*kṣānti*) is defined solely in terms of compassion (*karuṇā*), while the remaining [perfections] are all defined in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*). However, regarding these ten aspects herein, the intention is to show that the ten aspects are distinct within a single moment of thought.
The first six are self-evident; I shall therefore explain only the latter four. Engaging with phenomena through skillful means (*upāya*) is called "immeasurable wisdom."
By means of this wisdom, one is further able to give rise to practices and vows such as generosity to gather in sentient beings; therefore, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Within these vows, by virtue of this vow-wisdom, although one seeks the ever-higher *pāramitās* of the eighth stage and above, [one does not fall into the extremes].
Because they encompass those superior practices, next, among the powers (*bala*), by means of this wisdom one remains far removed from the obstacles to giving and so forth;
thus, one is not moved by them. Among the knowledges (*jñāna*), by means of this wisdom one understands, as they truly are, all the various distinctions of giving and so forth.
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, these four characteristics are all established according to their function. [This is] a single thought-moment.
They are fully present in every thought-moment; it is only when the initial resolve to practice reaches this stage that they are attained.
O Son of the Buddha, these ten pāramitās are all fully realized by the bodhisattva in every thought-moment.

Thus, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and so forth, up to all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) are briefly explained.
The Dharma is perfectly fulfilled in every moment of thought.

Within the distinctions of the four factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), there are four aspects: the first two comprise the accumulation of merit, while the latter two involve the elimination of faults.
First, relying on Mahāyāna practice: this refers to the ten perfections for one's own benefit, which constitute the "Great Meaning.

Second, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) rely upon the teaching and transforming of sentient beings. Third, the four supports (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth rely upon the supreme purification of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
That is to say, one takes the four supports as the dwelling place and the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) as the basis for practice, cultivating the thirty [virtuous qualities].
Through these seven categories, one attains purification from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). It is called "sustenance" (*dhṛti*) because it maintains its own nature;

it is also called the "four families" (*catur-kula*) because they are the abodes wherein one dwells. These four are: first, the family of *prajñā* (wisdom), which is that which illuminates; second, the family of the truths (*satya-kula*).

This is that which is illuminated. Third is the family of abandoning afflictions; fourth is the family of the purification of suffering. By means of the first two superior activities, one is freed from these delusions and sufferings.
Fourth, briefly stated, is the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) based on the lower [stages], because there is nothing not fully possessed;
thus one is freed from the dust-like ignorance (*avidyā*). The three pairs of superior practices have now been concluded.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Buddha,
do Bodhisattvas fulfill all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) only within this seventh stage, or are they also able to fulfill them within all the stages?"

Regarding the fourth [section], the distinction of superiority over the preceding higher stages, there are two parts. First, it clarifies how [the seventh stage] is superior to the preceding six stages;

second, it explains why the Bodhisattva, from the beginning, is superior to the subsequent three stages. "Superiority" (viśeṣa) carries the sense of being preeminent (adhika). Within the first part, there are two sub-sections.
First, he asks. The intent of the question is: if they were already complete previously, why speak of them here alone? If they were not yet complete previously, how could this be accomplished?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied: "O Son of the Buddha, within the ten stages, bodhisattvas are able to fulfill enlightenment."
Regarding the classification of the stages: however, the seventh stage is the most preeminent. Why is this?
Because in this seventh stage, the practice of effortful application is fulfilled, and one enters into the eye of wisdom while remaining within the sphere of practice.

The subsequent response consists of three parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; and third, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections. First, the specific manifestation of the superior characteristics of this stage.

"The fulfillment of the practice of effort" means that one's own level (*svabhāga*) is perfected, whereby one attains entry into the lower [stages] through superior progress toward the subsequent [stages].

By virtue of these two meanings, it surpasses the wisdom of the preceding [stages], namely the realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) of the eighth stage. "Mastery" refers to the great function of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and the ten [powers].

"O Son of the Buddha, regarding the [Bodhisattvas] such as those with mastery: in the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the Bodhisattva seeks all Buddha-dharmas through aspiration, they fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
In the second stage, because they are free from the stains of the mind; and in the third stage, their aspirations increase further and they attain the light of the Dharma."
Therefore, because one enters the path in the fourth stage, because one accords with worldly activities in the fifth stage, because one enters the profound dharma-gates in the sixth stage,
and because one gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas in the seventh stage, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are in every case fully perfected.
The second [point] generally indicates the characteristics of fulfillment in all the stages (*bhūmi*), thereby providing a remote explanation for the statement that "all ten stages are fulfilled.

It also provides a proximate explanation for the expression regarding the fulfillment of effort in the seventh stage. Therefore, the treatise poses the question: "In what way are the practices of skillful means (*upāya-caryā*) fulfilled within this stage?"
"Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to functional effort. Because one is endowed with the ten expedient means, the treatise itself explains:
"Within those other mundane and supramundane [stages], one further initiates superior practices.

Thus, regarding the statement that "in these seven stages one initiates all Buddha-dharmas," this refers to the first three being mundane and the subsequent three being supramundane; these are each distinct from one another.
Regarding "excellent conduct": it is called "fulfilled" because it is now fully present within all [stages].

It is complete within the vows of the first stage (*bhūmi*), complete within the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the second stage, and complete within the learning (*śruta*) of the third stage. As for the statement that "vows increase," it is because one desires to benefit sentient beings by relying on the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
the rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the term "all" in the context of the seventh stage, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
It is said that the merits of the Buddha are attained in the seventh stage, accomplished in the eighth stage, perfected in the ninth stage, and fully realized in the tenth stage.
Because there remains a slight residual obstacle, it is not yet called "pure. Freedom from this [obstacle] is precisely pure bodhi.
Why is this? Because from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva accomplishes the portion of wisdom involving effortful application (*prāyogika-jñāna*).
By the power of this, from the eighth stage up to the tenth, all practices free from effortful application (*anābhoga-caryā*) are fully accomplished.
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were two worlds: one place is defiled and the other is purely pure; the space between these two is difficult to traverse.

It may be crossed; however, except for a bodhisattva who possesses great skillful means, supernormal powers, and the power of vows, O Son of the Buddha, it is likewise with the various stages of a bodhisattva.
There are practices of defilement and practices of purity;
it is difficult to cross between these two, except that a bodhisattva who possesses the power of great vows, skillful means, and wisdom is able to cross over.

Second, the explanation of the three stages subsequent to the [first] two superior ones. This section contains four parts: first, the teaching; second, the analogy; third, the application; and fourth, the extension of the discussion from the inquiry.

Now, for the first part: first, the interrogation; second, the explanation. The intent of the interrogation is: "Why is it that while each of the first six has only one, it is only upon reaching the seventh that all are complete?
The explanation states: "Because they were accumulated from the beginning and have now reached completion here. This answers the preceding interrogation. For this reason...

This is able to bring about the accomplishment of the superior practices of the three subsequent stages. This "surpassing what follows" and "surpassing what precedes" refers to the ability to enter the eighth stage;
"surpassing what follows" causes the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of the subsequent stages to be accomplished, up to the tenth stage.

This is because one must reach the state of effortlessness through the accumulation of effort. Thus, within the state of integration there are mixed defiled practices, and it integrates with the world of defilement.
The realm (*dhātu*). However, there are two meanings: first, it refers to the preceding six [stages]; second, it extends to the preceding seven.

When pure conduct (*viśuddha-caryā*) merges with the purely pure world, this refers to the final three stages. Regarding the "intermediate stage difficult to traverse" (*antara-duṣkara*), there are likewise two meanings:
first, if the sixth stage is considered mixed, then the seventh stage is the intermediate; if the seventh stage is entirely mixed, then from the seventh to the eighth is the intermediate.
It is said: "The intermediate stage. That which is difficult to traverse is like the distance from Sahā to Sukhāvatī, where the pure and the defiled realms are utterly separated.
The difficulty of traversing the first six and the last three stages is likewise. One must attain the great vows and skillful means of this stage to be able to transcend them;
