The text consists of three parts: first, the single body responds universally while remaining without [discursive] mind; second, the two [aspects of] speech expound according to capacity; third, the final analogy concludes that the mind is ever-present.

In the sūtra, since it specifically mentions the "mind of supreme wisdom" (*anuttara-jñāna-citta*) as demonstrating the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the provisional and the ultimate are clearly distinguished.
Having praised the Buddha with such millions of kinds of beautiful voices, they remained silent.
Vimukticandra then said: "Now that this assembly is pure, I pray that you will explain the practices to be cultivated on the ninth stage."
The third request for instruction.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is by means of such immeasurable wisdom that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects and investigates."

The second part, the Section on Correct Exposition, first clarifies the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*). This text consists of four sections: First, the accomplishment of the skillful means of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*).

This stage is called the "Stage of the Dharma-preacher" because it can give rise to eloquence for preaching the Dharma; the establishment of the practice that leads to this stage is termed "skillful means.
Second, the accomplishment of wisdom (*jñāna*), because one possesses the wisdom capable of knowing the Dharma. Third, the accomplishment of entering into practice.

This is because one has attained mastery over the mental activities of those to be converted. Fourth is "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*), because one bestows the teaching correctly according to their faculties.

Among these four, the first is the stage of "entering the mind," while the remaining three are all stages of "abiding in the mind. These also encompass the three positions; this shall be understood below.

However, within the eighth [stage], one merely purifies Buddha-fields and converts sentient beings; it is through the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) on this ground that one converts sentient beings.

Birth. This is because one is able to teach and transform others by accomplishing all marks (*sarva-lakṣaṇa*). "All marks" refers to possessing the four aforementioned divisions. Within the first division, there are three parts.
First, the preceding section is cited to introduce the subsequent one, as one has previously attained the wisdom that is equal regarding the two truths (*satya*).

That is to say, the Buddhas exhort one to give rise to immeasurable wisdom, which involves deliberation and observation; this constitutes reflection and cultivation (*cintā-bhāvanā*). Next, one further intends to descend into the correct [practice].
Manifesting skillful means: third, having attained entry and completed the preliminary practices for entering the stages (*bhūmi*),
desiring to further seek increasingly superior quiescence and liberation, one again cultivates the wisdom of the Tathāgata, enters the secret dharma of the Tathāgata,
contemplates the nature of inconceivable great wisdom, purifies all *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* gates, and becomes fully endowed with vast [qualities].
Possessing great supernormal powers, they enter diverse worlds, cultivate the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), follow all Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma,
and do not abandon the power of their original vows of great compassion.
Next, the main text clearly presents ten phrases, which do not depart from the two benefits [of self and others]. The *Śāstra* states that "each [set] of five and three phrases is a manifestation":
the first phrase is for the benefit of others, and the second phrase is for one's own benefit; hence it says "each.

The subsequent five phrases are for the benefit of others, and the final three are for one's own benefit; hence it says "five and three. The term "manifestation" applies throughout the preceding four sections. The first phrase is based on...
They attain the perception of liberation in the formless realm for the sake of transforming sentient beings and benefiting others, thereby leading them to attain Great Nirvāṇa;
thus it is said they are "superior. Second, because they have not yet attained ultimate self-benefit, they further cause [beings] to cultivate the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Third, relying on bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature, they transform them so that they enter the secrets of the Tathāgata—the three mysteries.

Fourth, for the sake of transforming and benefiting those sentient beings who can be transformed through wrong mindfulness, one causes them to observe inconceivable wisdom so that they may attain right mindfulness;

this refers to observing non-thought (*amanasikāra*) to perceive the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Fifth, for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet known the Dharma, one turns the wheel of Dharma so that they may come to know it;
this refers to the fact that the gates of pure *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* are all the bases upon which the teaching of the Dharma relies.
Sixth, for the sake of sentient beings who have taken refuge in what is false, he possesses great supernormal powers in order to cause them to enter the True Dharma.

Seventh, for the sake of sentient beings born in the heavens through faith, he causes them to enter the Buddha-pure lands of various worlds. The preceding five [perfections] are for the benefit of others.

Within the three types of self-benefit, the lower three [perfections] correspond to the eight qualities of the Buddha’s inner realization of wisdom (*pratyātma-vedya-jñāna-guṇa*). Thus, the [eighth perfection] corresponds to the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*) and so forth.

The ninth corresponds to the quality of grace in external transformation through the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana-parārtha-guṇa*). The tenth corresponds to the quality of abandonment in non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa-prahāṇa-guṇa*).
One attains entry into the Bodhisattva’s ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*).
Having entered this position through the practice of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), one achieves mastery in the skillful means of the Dharma teacher.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Stage of Excellent Intelligence, they know, as they truly are, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The practice of the Dharma; the practice of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas; the practice of mundane and supramundane dharmas; the practice of conceivable and inconceivable dharmas;
the practice of determinate and indeterminate dharmas; the practice of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the practice of the Bodhisattvas; the practice of the Tathāgata stage;
the practice of conditioned dharmas; and the practice of unconditioned dharmas.

The second is the accomplishment of wisdom. From here downward, two or three sections comprise the stage of the Prince (kumārabhūmi), as knowing the dharmas and knowing the faculties are both the protocols of a Dharma King.
For now, we rely on the accomplishment of wisdom. In the text, the first phrase generally knows the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):

namely, that the pure and the defiled are non-dual, which is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Subsequently, from "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) downward, they are progressively distinguished in detail. First, regarding pure dharmas, there is an opening...

Regarding the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*): when practices such as giving and ethical discipline are cultivated with a mind that grasps at signs (*nimitta*), they are associated with the taints and are thus called "tainted.

The untainted is the opposite of this. These two are further distinguished within the category of the untainted: that which precedes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called "mundane" (*laukika*), while that which follows the path of seeing is called "supramundane" (*lokottara*).
Thirdly, regarding these same two categories, the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane is termed "conceivable" (*cintya*); this refers specifically to the mundane.

That which transcends the world is called inconceivable (*acintya*). Fourth, within that which is conceivable (*cintya*) yet possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), that which is certainly able to bring about realization is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*);
that which is moved by conditions is termed "non-concentration.

Furthermore, the Buddha-nature is fixed (*niyata*), while all other dharmas are entirely unfixed, such as the three categories of beings (*triniṣyanda*) and so forth; these will be explained in the text below. Fifth, this summarizes and opens up all the aforementioned virtues.
The three vehicles emerge [from this]. That is to say, the truths (*satya*), bases (*āyatana*), perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth, all pertain to the aforementioned four [truths].

Only the single fruit of Buddhahood is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and so on, and thus belongs to the fruit of the Bodhisattva vehicle. Sixth, within the teachings of the three vehicles, they demonstrate the practice in accordance with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

That is to say, the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), the nature of the bases (*āyatana-svabhāva*), the further shore (*pāra*), and ultimate reality (*tattva*) are all termed unconditioned. The truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)...
The wisdom arising from conditions that realizes and cultivates is entirely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). All [qualities] of the Tathāgata are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is because the conditioned wisdom of a Buddha is not taught as ultimate, and because *nirvāṇa* causes the characteristics of the conditioned to be concealed. The noble ones of the three vehicles rely upon this to initiate their practice;
because they rely upon these distinctions, it is called "conforming practice" (*anuloma-caryā*). Thus, the supreme wisdom is accomplished.
By means of such wisdom, this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the thicket of the minds of sentient beings, the thicket of afflictions,
the thicket of karma, the thicket of faculties, the thicket of inclinations, the thicket of natures, the thicket of desires, and the thicket of latent tendencies.
The thicket of rebirth; the thicket of the gathering of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); and the thicket of the distinctions among the three aggregates.
Second, the explanation of the accomplishment of entering into practice, which has three parts: first, the general presentation of the headings;

second, the detailed explanation based on the headings, beginning with "This bodhisattva knows as it truly is..."; and third, the concluding summary of establishment, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva, in accordance with..."

[The section on] "Abiding. Now, regarding the first part, there are eleven forests (*vanas*). Because the meaning of the *Śāstra* (Commentary) is somewhat difficult to explain, I shall now extract the essential points of the *Śāstra* to serve as a supplementary commentary (*pūryārtha*).
The supplementary commentary states: According to the *Śāstra*, these eleven dense forests (*ghana-vanas*) take the "mind of sentient beings" as their general heading; therefore...
The treatise explains that the mind is the common basis (*āśraya*), because it serves as the shared support for the ten subsequent defiled and purified states.
Since the Bodhisattva relies upon this [mind] to know them, it is called the "basis. The other ten are specific. These ten do not transcend the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

What are called the three afflictions are namely: afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Thus, the treatise says: "They depend on afflictions, karma, and birth. However, regarding the afflictions...

The karma of affliction (*kleśa-karma*) refers to the karma of delusion; "birth" (*jāti*) refers to the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*). This collectively clarifies the meaning of the ten "dense forests" (*gahana*).
However, the ten forests mentioned below are further condensed into seven: first, the forest of afflictions is delusion; second, the forest of karma is indeed karma;

third, the four forests concerning the faculties, inclinations, dispositions, and desires are collectively categorized as karma; and fourth, the forest of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is the seed of defiled delusion.
The fifth is the forest of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which encompasses both defiled and pure tendencies. The sixth is the forest of rebirth, which is the fruit of suffering.

The seventh is the forest of the three groups (*triskandha*), which generally concerns the spiritual capacities of the noble ones and ordinary beings, including those who are fixed and those who are not fixed in time.

For these reasons, the latter ten forests are condensed into seven. Thus, the treatise explains these seven, saying: "Based on common defiled afflictions, based on the defiled and pure [factors], and so forth."

This concerns the determinate and indeterminate timing. The text consists of four sections: 1. Relying on the commonality refers to the fact that the faculties, inclinations, dispositions, and the four forests are all collectively karma.
2. Relying on defilement refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). These are called "defilement" because they are the seeds of afflictions;

they lie dormant within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), causing the mind to become stained. 3. Defilement and purity of the afflictions refer to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). 4. Relying on... [text continues]
The determinate and indeterminate times are themselves the three clusters (*trikaṇḍa*) and the two forests (*vana*).

However, because the three clusters of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the two forests pertain to all three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it is said that "the other two pertain to all three. Furthermore, it is said that they do not exceed these three:

namely, that the *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) are afflictions (*kleśa*), while the roots and so forth are karma (*karman*). Now, the three clusters of latent tendencies and the two forests likewise do not exceed these three categories of defilement. These ten—
They are all termed "dense forests" (*gahana*) because they are numerous; thus they are called a "forest. They are called "dense" (*ghana*) because they are difficult to know.

Furthermore, these ten names are as analyzed in the "Chapter on the Arousing of the Mind" (*Cittotpāda-paṭala*). As for "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), it encompasses two meanings: first, residual habits; second, the perfuming of seeds.
As will be explained below, this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings. That is to say: the characteristic of arising in a mixed manner;

the characteristic of rapid transformation; the characteristic of being subject to decay or not; the characteristic of lacking physical form; the characteristic of being without limit; the characteristic of purity; the characteristic of being defiled or stainless; and the characteristic of bondage.

The characteristic of non-binding; the characteristic of that which is produced by illusion; the characteristic of being born according to the various realms of existence—these hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and even immeasurable such characteristics are all known as they truly are.
The second chapter provides an extensive explanation. The text consists of nine sections;

however, because the categories of nature (*dhātu*), understanding (*buddhi*), and desire (*chanda*) are combined into one example, there are now ten gates briefly presented within the first section, which are subsumed into eight by merging the second and third, and the last two. First, the characteristic of differentiation:

this refers to the sixfold distinction between mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding their "arising in combination," it is asserted that these eight [consciousnesses] take objects as their conditions.

They arise simultaneously; therefore, they are called "arising together" (*miśra*). This is because they must necessarily coexist with their [respective] objects, as even the minimum number consists of the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

The second pair, "swift transition" (*āśu-vartana*), explains the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by combining the two lower [phases]. This means that because the four characteristics involve flux, "swift" refers to the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*);

the essence of duration is precarious and swiftly moves toward change. "Transition" (*vartana*) refers to the characteristic of alteration (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*). "Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) refers to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). Not...

Dissolution is the characteristic of arising. The three that lack form or substance are the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is because one contemplates that mind as being detached from mind.
How is it detached? It means that neither body nor mind can be apprehended. "Body" (*kāya*) carries the sense of a collection of physical bases;

it is thus identical to the essence of the arising of faith, which is detached from discursive thought (*manasikāra*). Fourth is the characteristic of boundlessness, which is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); it accords with the practice toward immeasurable objects.

Because of the grasping of the elements (*dhātu*), and because the objects grasped differ, they are called "self. Of the four characteristics mentioned above, the first is the characterized (*lakṣya*), and the second is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
These two are both characteristics of the mind. The third is the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the mind; since nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristic differ, they combine to form the essence of the mind.
The fourth is the function (*vṛtti*) of the mind. These four are common to both the defiled and the pure. The subsequent four clarify...
The pure mind follows conditions. The fifth purity is the characteristic of being unstained by its own nature;

it is the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*), the non-empty nature that serves as the basis for both the real and the false. Being stained yet unstained is called "purity by nature.
The following two phrases refer to being unstained yet stained. Regarding "the six defilements are without defilement": they are identical to afflictions (*kleśa*) yet not identical to afflictions.

The characteristic of being "with-outflows" (sāsrava) is that while it follows conditions, its nature is eternally free from outflows. Regarding the seventh [point], the characteristics of being "bound" and "not bound"—whether they share the same latent tendencies (anuśaya) or not—the meaning does not differ from what preceded;

there is only a distinction between their seeds and their manifestation. The eighth [point] combines two phrases into one, both termed the "characteristic of the cause," because birth is received in accordance with causes.
Bodhisattvas are born through the power of illusory wisdom and vows, whereas other sentient beings follow [their karma].
He knows how karma produces rebirth in the various realms of existence.
Furthermore, he knows the various characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), namely: the characteristic of long-term persistence; the characteristic of boundless origination;

the characteristic of arising simultaneously with and not abandoning [the mind]; the characteristic of being identical in meaning whether dormant or active; the characteristic of being associated or dissociated with the mind; and the characteristic of following along with the realms of existence.

He knows, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of taking birth and abiding; the characteristics of the distinctions within the three realms; the characteristics of the afflictions such as craving, views, delusion, and pride that penetrate like arrows;
and the characteristics of the uninterrupted continuity of the causes and conditions of the three karmas—briefly stated, he knows all eighty-four thousand [afflictions] as they truly are.

The second explanation of the dense forest of afflictions (*kleśa-gahana*) also has three parts. Within the specific section, nine phrases are subsumed into three types of matters because the latter seven are combined.
First is the characteristic of entering from afar, reaching as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

this refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*) within the four abodes, while extending downward to the diamond-like [samādhi], which is explained here in terms of the seeds (*bīja*). "For a long time" means it has followed one continuously since beginningless time. Second is the boundless arousal.
This refers to the characteristic of being difficult to know. "Boundless" means that because one has cultivated immeasurable roots of goodness, [the afflictions] are induced;

they are "induced" because they give rise to delusion (*kleśa*). Since delusion coexists with goodness, it is difficult to discern—namely, the "afflictions superior to the sands of the Ganges" mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The three [types of] co-arising constitute the following seven phrases, which together form the characteristic of defilement; that is, the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). This refers to...

Afflictions also arise together with karma; because both arise simultaneously, they are divided into three parts. The first three phrases clarify the defilement of afflictions in terms of their essential nature.

First, "simultaneously arising and inseparable" clarifies that which is bound according to its locus. This phrase generally clarifies both the agent and the object. The object bound is the deluded mind;
that is, the delusions and the deluded mind mutually engage in the same activity, hence it is called "simultaneously arising."
Birth is itself the phenomenon (*vastu*). However, although delusion (*moha*) is not termed the "deluded mind" (*vikalpa-citta*), apart from the mind, upon what could delusion abide?

Therefore, their mutual dependence is called "not abandoning one another. Regarding the two—dormancy (*prasupti*) and arising (*udaya*)—one meaning is this: by what is one bound? It is said that the proclivities (*anuśaya*) act as the binder;

the proclivities are themselves the latent tendencies (*anusaya*), while "arising" refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Through active manifestation driven by the proclivities, one fails to attain liberation.

This is because the manifest [defilement] and its seed share the same nature as the affliction (*kleśa*). However, while the following section clarifies that the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) do not necessarily coexist with their manifest forms, here it is held that the manifest must arise from the latent proclivities.
This is like how a seed may exist without a sprout, whereas if a sprout exists, a seed must necessarily be present;
thus, they are said to have the "same meaning" (*ekārtha*). Third, regarding whether they are associated (*samprayukta*) or dissociated (*viprayukta*) with the mind, this refers to...
The matter of bondage. This "matter" is the true mind itself. If it were associated with the names of those deluded defilements, it would be bondage rather than liberation.

Because the nature of the mind is pure, it is said to be "non-associated," demonstrating that liberation is possible. Second, regarding the following passage on "following the realms of existence" (*gati*), there are two phrases which clarify the defilement of afflictions in relation to birth.
As the *Śāstra* states: "Because the matter of the body is the cause for birth in the paths and realms"—this refers to the arising and accumulation of the retribution of suffering.
The "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) arises from phenomena. The first phrase refers to the cause of the Path; the second phrase refers to the cause of the realms (*dhātu*).

Regarding the three types of craving and views, the latter two phrases are designated as "defilement of afflictions" (*kleśasaṃkleśa*) in terms of karma. The first phrase clarifies the causal role of karma among the three divisions, as it obstructs liberation. As for the "three divisions":
craving refers to those who, within the pursuit of desire, seek present retribution and engage in the practice of sensual enjoyment. Views—
This is the pursuit of false brahmacarya. Delusion (*moha*) is the pursuit within the quest for sensual desire (*kāma-cchanda*) that practices evil deeds for the sake of seeking present retribution.
Thus, the treatise says: "Sentient beings who lack precepts, for the sake of slight pleasure in the present, practice various evil deeds;

their delusion is extreme. Arrogance (*māna*) pervades the three aforementioned [quests], yet it mostly belongs to views (*dṛṣṭi*). The quest for existence (*bhava-cchanda*) belongs to birth, as it is subsumed under defilement (*kleśa*); this is omitted here. Above.
All three [afflictions] equally obstruct liberation. Their faults are difficult to extract, like an arrow deeply embedded in wood;

thus, even when non-Buddhists attain the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), they still remain associated with views and pride. This is the intended meaning of the treatise. Furthermore, it may be understood that afflictions such as craving and attachment pervade the seven consciousnesses;
hence, they are said to be "deeply embedded. The following phrase clarifies that these delusions conform to worldly bodily and verbal actions.

Regarding mental karma (*manas-karman*): because it does not sever the causes of arising, the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are clarified in the section on the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).

In this present commentary, there are many meanings; roughly speaking, by dividing greed, hatred, and delusion (*rāga*, *dveṣa*, *moha*), each possesses twenty-one thousand [afflictions], thus totaling eighty-four thousand.
Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of all karmas: namely, the characteristics of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; the characteristics of being manifest or non-manifest;

the characteristic of arising simultaneously with the mind and not being separate from it; the characteristic of having a causal nature that perishes moment by moment yet accumulates results in succession without loss;

the characteristics of having maturation or no maturation; the characteristics of receiving various retributions such as black-for-black and so forth; and the characteristic of being like a field that is immeasurable.

The characteristics of the distinctions between ordinary beings and noble ones; the characteristics of receiving birth and receiving [results] in the present or in the future; the characteristics of those who ride the vehicles and those who do not, and of those who are fixed or unfixed—briefly stated, even up to the eighty-four thousand [afflictions], he knows them all as they truly are.
The third [section], the explanation of karma, also has three parts. Within the detailed section, there are ten phrases that constitute nine types of distinctions, as the last two are combined.
The first phrase concerns the distinction of the causes of the paths; that is, it generally explains the three natures as the causes for the six destinies.

Projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) consists of the wholesome and unwholesome, each having three grades, as already explained in the second stage. Completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) pertains to all three natures. The permeation of names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*) is also...

It encompasses all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), as it is accepted that these serve as causal seeds. Furthermore, in the seventeenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the three natures as causes are contrasted with the five kinds of fruits;
since even the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) can bring about fruit, the Master [Vasubandhu] generally treats all three as causes for the path.
Since afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot bring about maturation (*vipāka*), the Master’s statement that all three are causes for the path intends specifically to take only the wholesome (*kuśala*).
"Evil is the cause. Regarding the phrase "the two, the informative and so forth," this refers to their specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).

The Sūtra commentary states that these are characterized as "done" or "not yet done," and both take volition (*cetanā*) as their intrinsic nature. The Commentary says: "There are two kinds of this: first, at the time of deliberation (*tarka*)."
This exists in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), because it consists solely of the volition (*cetanā*) that deliberates.

This has not yet performed its function. Second, at the time of performing an action, there is determinative volition; if it pertains to body or speech, it is solely the volition that initiates movement.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The volition that moves the body is called bodily karma (*kāyakarman*); the volition that initiates speech is called vocal karma (*vākkarman*). Third, it arises simultaneously with the mind.
"Non-separation" refers to the differentiation of skillful means. It means that the mind arises together with [the seeds] and perfumes the mind, because they do not produce fruits separately.

That is to say, the seeds of karma are not separate from the mind, just as the attainment of fruit is not separate from the seed. This refers to the volition of karma arising together with the motivating mental consciousness;

once it has arisen according to its being wholesome or unwholesome, it immediately perfumes the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to form the seeds of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. These seeds resemble [their causes].
Because it can act as a perfuming agent, it is said that it does not produce a separate fruit; this is the meaning of "not being apart.

Regarding the phrase "the self-nature of the four causes perishes moment by moment" and so forth: this refers to the complete accumulation of the distinctions of the fruit. That is to say, because the causal karma from beginningless time is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), its self-nature perishes moment by moment;
hence it is called "exhausted. This demonstrates impermanence. Nevertheless, the efficacy that sustains and brings about the fruit does not perish or vanish.

Therefore, it is said that the fruits gather like clouds and are not lost; this demonstrates that there is no annihilation (*uccheda*). Although the preceding moment ceases, the succeeding moment continues to exist; hence, it is called "successive" (*anupūrva*).
Furthermore, while the cause may be instantaneously perfumed, the fruit arises successively, as in the case of the five [consciousnesses] such as cognition (*vijñāna*).

Regarding the characteristics of these five having retribution (*vipāka*) or being without retribution, the treatise states: "The distinction between those that have already received their fruit and those that have not yet received their fruit. This refers to past births.

Karma that has already been experienced in the present is called "having retribution" (*savipāka*). Karma whose subsequent retribution has not yet been experienced is called "without retribution" (*avipāka*);

this does not mean it is entirely non-existent. There is another principle: namely, karma that has already been repented is held to be without retribution, while that which has retribution can be known.

Regarding the "six types of black-black and so forth" karmas, these are established as distinctions based on their mutual comparison; that is, the four types of karma are contrasted with one another to form these distinctions.
Therefore, the first two pairs contrast the black with the white, while the latter two contrast the tainted (*sāsrava*) with the untainted (*anāsrava*).

As for what is called "black-black," it refers to the very first among the four, because both its cause and its fruit are evil, and furthermore, because both its cause and its fruit are associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
This refers to the karma of the three miserable realms (*durgati*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) equals the remaining three types: namely, second, white-white karma;

and third, black-white karma, which is the wholesome karma of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Because it is mixed with both good and evil within its causal stage, its retribution is likewise a mixture of the desirable and the undesirable.

Fourth is non-black, non-white karma; this refers to all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma, because it lacks maturation (*vipāka*). In contrast to the aforementioned black and white karmas, the name "neither" is established.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of manifold retribution," this is because the three aforementioned realms of existence (*bhava*) possess such characteristics. As the treatise states: "Because karma is accumulated and accomplished.
According to the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa*, black and white karma are explained in terms of the continuity (*saṃtati*) [of the individual], for there is not a single...
Karma that is both black and white has a single ripening; this is because the two are mutually contradictory. Regarding the term "continuum":
either the intention is black while the application is white, as in performing acts of respect and service for the sake of deceiving others;

or the intention is white while the application is black, such as when one speaks harsh words out of compassion for a disciple. If one examines it by way of the mind, it is precisely through a deceitful mind that these actions are carried out.

Regarding the respectful service, it may also be performed simultaneously. Although the remaining points are collected [in other texts], they are explained extensively in the eighth and sixteenth chapters of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
As for the "seven immeasurables," they refer to the distinctions among causes and conditions. That is to say, consciousness is the cause and karma is the field;

according to the differences in the elevation and depression of the field, the seeds likewise undergo many distinctions. Therefore, the treatise and the sūtra state that "the fields of karma are immeasurable."

8. The distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) refers to the distinction between that which has already been accumulated and that which has not yet been accumulated; for [the former] has already accumulated worldly [karma], whereas [the latter] has not yet accumulated supramundane [karma]. 9.
The distinction between the determined and the undetermined regarding the twelve phrases clarifies the determination or non-determination of the three types of time and retribution.

That is to say, performing an action in the present and receiving its fruit in the present is called "receiving in the present" (*pratyutpanna-vedanīya*). Next is obtaining the fruit in a future birth...

This is called "retribution upon birth" (*upapadyavedanīya*). It is named "subsequent retribution" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) because it is received only after one has passed through the third birth from the present life.

Within these three types, each has both determinate (*niyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*) aspects. That is to say, for the first two [types], the timing is determinate; for the retribution itself, it may be either determinate or indeterminate. For the last one, both the timing and the retribution are common to being either determinate or indeterminate.
The tenth phrase clarifies the determinacy or indeterminacy regarding the vehicles (*yāna*) and non-vehicles; "vehicle" here refers to the Three Vehicles.
Practicing only the activities of one's own vehicle is called "fixed" (*niyata*). Practicing this vehicle at one time and that vehicle at another is called "unfixed" (*aniyata*).
That which is not a vehicle refers to the mundane world, as it lacks the sense of being conveyed out [of saṃsāra]. The fixed is difficult to deliver, while the unfixed is easy to deliver.
Regarding the mention of "eighty-four thousand" within the summary verse: since the causes of delusion are thus, the karma arising from them is likewise.

Thus, the various gates such as the faculties (*indriya*) all constitute eighty thousand. By reversing these, one reveals the gates of the perfections (*pāramitā*), the gates of samādhi, and so forth.

Furthermore, one knows the characteristics of the inferior, middling, and superior faculties, as well as the characteristics of distinction and non-distinction between the prior limit and the posterior limit, [and] the superior and middling [stages].

The characteristics of the lower [realms]; the characteristic of being co-arisen and inseparable from afflictions; the characteristics of those who ride the vehicle and those who do not, and of those who are fixed and unfixed;

the characteristic of being thoroughly matured and pliant; the characteristic of shifting, changing, and disintegrating according to the net of faculties; the characteristic of being superior and incapable of being destroyed; the characteristic of the distinction between falling back and not falling back;
and the characteristic of being distant, following along, arising together, and being dissimilar—in brief, up to eighty-four thousand such characteristics, he knows them all as they truly are.

In the fourth [section], the explanation of the faculties (*indriya*) has two parts: first, the individual analysis, and second, the summary. Within the individual analysis, ten aspects are differentiated into nine categories because the fifth and sixth are combined.
First is the explanation of the differentiation of the vessel (*bhājana*), meaning the vessel to whom the Dharma is taught;

this refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), which possess lower, middling, and superior degrees, and are thus categorized as dull, middling, or sharp—meaning that there is slowness or speed in receiving the teachings and principles. Furthermore, and...

To what extent does the distinction between the transformation of the two faculties (indriya) occur? The past and future constitute the prior and posterior limits (pūrvānta and aparānta), while the present is already fixed.
The distinction is discussed in relation to these two limits; that is, the prior, superior, middle, and inferior faculties undergo mutual transformation across the three time periods.

If a subsequent faculty transforms into a middle or superior faculty, then the prior faculty becomes inferior; if a subsequent faculty transforms into an inferior faculty, then the prior faculty increases. This is the distinction.
Regarding the meaning: "non-reversal" implies equanimity, which is non-differentiation. Therefore, the treatise states that there are "subsequent and prior faculties.

Because the prior faculty increases from the inferior to the equanimous, there is a distinction among the three natures; that is, when the faculties of the three vehicles—such as the Bodhisattvas—are compared with one another, they are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
Thus, this is not the same as the first [category], which applies universally to all three vehicles. Fourth, there is the distinction of defilement by afflictions, namely:
The five faculties of feeling, such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, attain predominance in accordance with afflictions such as greed (*lobha*).

The two characteristics of the five and six [faculties] refer to the distinction between the determined (*niyata*) and the undetermined (*aniyata*). Regarding the first phrase, "vehicle" (*yāna*) and "non-vehicle" (*ayāna*), both are explained in terms of being matured (*pakva*) or not matured (*apakva*).
Within the Mahāyāna, those who are matured are determined, while those who are not matured are undetermined. Within the Hīnayāna, those who are matured are undetermined and can be redirected.
Because it is Mahāyāna. Those who are not yet mature are fixed, as they attain liberation according to their respective vehicles.

If they are worldly and not of a vehicle, they are not fixed, for they can still be transformed and led into the Path. As for those who are not yet mature, their retribution is already fixed; therefore, one temporarily sets them aside.
This refers to the "pure relinquishment" that awaits the proper time for transformation while remaining within the world. The subsequent phrase concerns those who are fully matured.
Being pliant and one-pointed is concentration. The six faculties, which are like a net that is light, shifting, and fragile, constitute the differentiation of conforming activity.
This is because one knows that the eyes and other faculties gain predominance by conforming to their respective objects. Within this, there are three types of conforming activity.

First, following in accordance with the body: this refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) which are mutually and successively bound to one another, like a net for fish or birds that allows no liberation;
therefore, they are called the "net of the faculties" (*indriyajāla*). This is the internal object of practice. Second, following in accordance with arising and ceasing:

this means that their substance is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), arising and abiding only briefly; therefore, they are called "light. Because they are easily subject to change and extinction, they are called "transient and decaying. Third, contemplative practice.

Grasping at signs and acting accordingly; this refers to external objects. Thus, the treatise and the sūtra speak of "grasping at signs," which is omitted in the present text, or it may be included within the "net of the faculties.
The seven types of purity of the śrāvakas are superior when compared to the practice of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Because the faculties of the two vehicles are capable of accomplishment through the extinction of hindrances, afflictions cannot destroy them.
This constitutes the eighth distinction of the purity of the bodhisattva; it encompasses all three types of retrogression and non-retrogression.

The ninth, "distantly following," and so forth, demonstrates the distinctions in the inclusion of all faculties, meaning that the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) collectively subsume all faculties.
Third, there are three stages: first, the initial commencement, which is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*);

second, the application, which is the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), so called because one is currently practicing the path; and third, the ripening of the fruit, which is the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

This means that the preceding faculties such as faith arise together with these three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), yet they differ according to their relative strength across these three stages from beginning to end.
It is called "remote following. These three faculties are so named because they exercise sovereignty over the cultivation of the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and *nirvāṇa*.
Among these nine [faculties] mentioned above: the first two pertain to faith and the others; the third, fifth, seventh, and eighth pertain to all faculties throughout the three vehicles;

the fourth pertains to the five feelings; the sixth pertains to the six faculties beginning with the eye; and the ninth pertains to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). This may be accepted as a rough explanation.
If explained in detail, they are inexhaustible; therefore, it concludes by stating "up to eighty-four thousand.

Furthermore, one should know that regarding the various levels of understanding—soft, medium, and superior—the various dispositions—soft, medium, and superior—and the various inclinations—soft, medium, and superior—all are briefly described as being "up to eighty-four thousand."

The fifth example concerns the three dense forests (*gahana*), namely: nature (*prakṛti*), understanding (*buddhi*), and desire (*icchā*). These three accord with the faculties (*indriya*) and their natures (*prakṛti*) as they enter [into realization].
Since citing one case allows the other three to be inferred, all are treated briefly by way of illustration.

Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), namely: the characteristic of arising together with the deep-seated mind (*adhyāśaya*); the characteristic of arising together with the mind;

the characteristic of the distinction between being associated with or dissociated from the mind; the characteristic of persisting for a long duration; and the characteristic of being unextracted since beginningless time.
It is characterized by being diametrically opposed to all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

it is characterized by the bondage of taking birth through the continuity of the three realms; it causes the manifestation of an infinite continuity of mental states; it opens the doors to the various sense bases (*āyatana*); it is solid and difficult to cure;
and it is characterized by the attainment or non-attainment of specific stages and locations. It can only be uprooted by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

[The] Characteristics. Sixth, the explanation of the *anuśaya* (latent tendencies). First, regarding the general [definition]: in the Zhongjing (Zhong-a-han jing), the Jin translation, and the *Śāstra*, these are all termed *paryavasthāna* (outbursts/afflictions).

The *Śāstra* states that their meaning is "to follow along" (*anugata*) and "to pursue" (*anusṛta*). This is like a public official’s messenger who pursues sentient beings, finds an opportunity, and binds them; this is precisely what "following along" means.

"Sleep. It is called "sleep" because it follows, pursues, and envelops the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This refers exclusively to the seeds (*bīja*) and is not the same as the minor schools (*hīnayāna*), which maintain that there are twelve distinct phrases.
The treatise subsumes these into two categories: the first six clarify *where* it pursues, and the latter six clarify *by what* it pursues.
Now, for the first [section], there are five parts. First, combining the initial two phrases, it clarifies the location in terms of the mind. Regarding the first phrase:

The phrase "the retributive mind follows along" clearly reveals that the latent *ālayavijñāna* has long been dwelling in peace; it is called "profound" because it has existed since beginningless time and is subtle and difficult to perceive.

The subsequent phrase, "it does not follow along with non-retributive minds," refers to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the discriminative object-consciousness (*vastuvijñaptivijñāna*), which arise inseparable from manifest phenomena;
thus, it simply says "mind," referring to the point where they momentarily revolve.

Regarding the two aspects of association and non-association: with respect to the three realms (*dhātu*), [the afflictions] are associated only with the mind of their own respective realm and not with the mind of another realm.
Therefore, the treatise states that there are distinctions of desire, form, and formlessness, or superior, intermediate, and inferior.

Because the delusions of the formless realm are subtle, they are designated as "inferior" and so forth. Although the nature of these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is fully present [in all], [they are categorized according to their specific manifestation].

The manifest afflictions also possess the sense of being non-associated [with the mind]. Regarding the third point, the "aspect of long-term persistence," this is explained in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*) and locations (*sthāna*).
The treatise states that they persist "up to the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*). However, the term "Peak of Existence" carries two distinct meanings.

First, reaching the summit of the vajra; second, reaching the summit of the three realms of existence (*bhavāgra*). Here, taking the meaning common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it is simply called "the summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*).
While the treatise and the sūtra merely say "entering from afar," here it is said "for a long duration," because from time immemorial one has ascended as far as the summit of the ninth stage.
Fourth, the characteristic of not being uprooted from the beginningless. This clarifies the location by way of time; since the location is boundless, [the cycle continues].
Time, too, has no beginning. Only wisdom can terrify the thieves that are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Since one has never yet possessed the wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one cannot pull [the mind] out [of saṃsāra]. Regarding the fifth point, "equal to all meditative concentrations" (*dhyāna*), this clarifies the locus in terms of practice.

Because the latent tendencies pursue [the practitioner], they prevent worldly meditative concentrations and the like from extinguishing the mind of craving, views, and so forth; they are unable [to do so].
Because it conforms to correct practice, it is termed "contrary. Thus, the following verse says: "The objects of meditative concentration are expelled, yet one still regresses.
Below this, regarding the three realms, it clarifies by what means [the afflictions] pursue; that is, it reveals the characteristics of their pursuit.
Because of these characteristics, they are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies). These are of six kinds: first, the uninterrupted pursuit within the three higher realms of existence (*bhava*).

Pursuit (*anubandha*). This is why the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) continue without interruption in a similar succession: it is because they are bound by these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is like a sleeper in the world who cannot rise from his bed. Second, distant-time pursuit:

this refers to the aforementioned beginningless time, wherein it causes the mental continuum to manifest as limitless. It is like the dream-mind of a sleeper in the world that continues in succession. Third, opening...

Regarding the "gateways of the various bases" (*āyatana-dvāra*), they follow and accompany the arising of a single body; that is to say, upon the aforementioned single body, both resultant and non-resultant minds clearly follow and accompany it.
This is like a sleeper who sees and hears within a dream. Within this, there are two meanings:

first, when the six kinds of consciousness are gathered and produced through the gateways of the eye and other sense organs, [the mind] causes them to arise simultaneously with itself; therefore, it is called "opening the gate."

This clarifies the external pursuit of the expedient mind (*upāyacitta*). The two treatises state, "and because of the perfuming of the *ālayavijñāna*. This clarifies the internal perfuming of the retributive mind.

In the text of the sūtra, beneath the character "gate" (*mén*), there is additionally the character "accumulate" (*jí*); this refers to the *ālaya* as the mind that accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena].

However, because these various locations serve as common bases, the meaning is implicitly contained within this sutra. Fourth, "solidity that is difficult to cure" refers to the persistence of what is unreal;
that is, when practicing dhyāna and so forth, one fails to attain the true antidote. This unreal solidity is like deep sleep in the world:
one cannot be awakened by loud sounds, as there is no means to arise from it. Fifth, regarding "the place of the ground" and so forth...
It is subtle and persistent; for it persists as a body of afflictions within the six sense bases throughout the nine stages, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Now, regarding these nine stages, there are two senses: first, in terms of the nine stages of the three realms, although [the afflictions] are accomplished in all of them, [they differ in their mode of persistence].
Because they are subtle, one does not know how many instances of their formation exist. For example, it is like a sleeper who, in a dream, believes he is awake.
Second, because these [defilements] still persist even in the tenth stage, where wholesome wisdom constitutes the nine stages, they are called "subtle non-attainments.

Since they are partially eliminated within this stage, the following verse says: "Only when extinguished by the vajra-path are they finally and utterly gone. Sixth, the separation from suffering follows.
"Expelling" means that only supramundane noble paths consisting of non-conceptual wisdom can extract [the seeds], just as one who is asleep must be touched to wake up.

Furthermore, it refers to knowing the various characteristics of taking birth, namely: the characteristic of taking birth according to karma, and the characteristic of the distinctions among the six destinies. There is...
The characteristics of the distinction between the form and formless realms; the characteristics of the distinction between those with perception and those without perception;

the characteristic of the sprout of future existence arising from karma as the field, moistened by the water of craving, covered by the darkness of ignorance, and having consciousness as the seed; and the characteristic of name-and-form arising together and being inseparable.

The characteristic of craving for existence through delusion and longing; the characteristic of attachment from beginningless time to the desire for experience and birth; and the characteristic of falsely claiming to have transcended the three realms while still greedily seeking them.
This seventh [section] explains the ten phrases regarding the dense forest of rebirth: first in general, then in detail. In the treatise, these are collectively treated as eight. First:

1. Diversity of the body (*kāya-vicitratā*): This refers to the multiplicity of its forms and types. 2. Diversity of karma (*karma-vicitratā*). 3. Diversity of dwelling places (*sthāna-vicitratā*). 4.

Diversity of the upper and lower realms regarding form and perception (*rūpa-saṃjñā-ūrdhvādhaḥ-vicitratā*), as expressed by the two sets of four and five [bases]. 5. Diversity of external causes of form (*bāhya-rūpa-hetu-vicitratā*):

This refers to taking external things such as fields (*kṣetra*) as common metaphors. 6. Diversity of the self-nature (*svabhāva-vicitratā*): Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise together and are mutually dependent.
[This is] distinct, because it is the very essence of the retribution. Seventh, the various types of the fundamental "conducive-to-birth cause" (*janma-hetu*):

that is, with delusion (*moha*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the basis, there is the "conducive-to-birth seeking for existence" (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*), which causes existence (*bhava*) to continue. Eighth, the two final phrases [of the verse] describe the various types of the Truth of Suffering as Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*):

that is, the three types of seeking are all causes of accumulation, yet they merely accumulate the fruit of suffering; therefore, they are called "various. The preceding phrase reveals desire (*kāma*).

There are two types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*). Seeking what one desires is "seeking through desire" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*); it refers to the incessant pursuit driven by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*). Seeking what brings about birth is "seeking through existence" (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*);
it refers to the arising of craving for the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka-bhava*) so as to obtain a superior body for oneself and further gather a retinue.

The phrase "delighting in attachment from beginningless time" reveals the faults of these two aforementioned seekings. The subsequent line refers to the "seeking of wrong holy life" (*mithyā-brahmacarya-paryeṣaṇā*), which arises from mental grasping.

Because they are attached, they do not understand the cycle of rebirth within the three realms. They greedily seek the various marks of the three realms—whether small, large, or immeasurable—and falsely claim these to be nirvana.
Some even consider slapping their bellies to be the Way, or reckon the state of non-perception or the peak of existence to be nirvana.

Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), namely: the characteristic of the distinction between practice and non-practice; the characteristic of perfuming according to the realms of existence (*gati*);

the characteristic of perfuming according to the conduct of sentient beings; the characteristic of perfuming according to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*); the characteristic of perfuming as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
the characteristic of perfuming for entry into future existence (*punarbhava*); the characteristic of sequential perfuming; and the far-reaching [practice] that does not sever the afflictions.

The characteristic of non-abandonment of perfuming; the characteristic of perfuming that is both real and unreal; and the characteristics of perfuming through seeing, hearing, associating with, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.

Among the eight explanations of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there is likewise first a general [definition] and later a specific one. The general term is "habitual tendency," which already encompasses both meanings. Therefore, it is not...

This may be restricted to the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of Arhats. Although "habit-energy" (*vāsanā*) is the term employed, within the specific [treatises] it is always referred to as "perfuming" (*bhāvanā*).
"Perfuming" (*bhāvanā*) means to imbue or infuse, like an external fragrance. "Habit" (*vāsanā*) means to practice or learn; this applies exclusively to sentient beings.

Since habit necessarily perfumes [the mind] to form a constituent part (*dhātu*), it is called "habit-energy. Thus, the *ālayavijñāna* serves as the object of perfuming (*bhāvyamāna*), because it abides constantly in a single state.

Because this [ālayavijñāna] is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is susceptible to being perfumed (*vāsya*), the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) act as the perfumers (*vāsaka*).

This is because they possess the superior power of arising and ceasing, and because they undergo increase and decrease; thus, the perfumer and the perfumed are mutually harmonized, which is termed "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
This is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. If one relies on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, even True Suchness (*tathatā*) can internally...

Regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*): the Buddha, spiritual friends, and so forth serve as external perfuming agents. Through the conjunction of internal and external factors, they form a "fragrant constituent" (*gandha-bhāga*).

Although in the preceding sections it was stated that hearing the teachings and so forth also depend on consciousness (*vijñāna*) for their reception, consciousness is therefore judged to be the "perfuming agent. Now, this applies universally;
since the text already mentions "the cause perfuming the fruit" and so forth, we know with certainty that the perfumed seeds (*bīja*) constitute the fragrant constituent.
Regarding the meaning: among the ten types of distinctions within the specific [analysis], the first is the distinction between giving fruit in the present versus not being present.

This means that when past causes of wholesome or unwholesome karma arise together with a present fruit, it is termed "active" (*carita*); when they do not so arise, it is termed "non-active" (*acarita*).
For example, when a person practices giving, it causes that person’s body to also constantly favor giving and so forth; this is the cultivation of the cause (*hetu-vāsanā*).

Second, the cultivation according to the destiny (*gati-vāsanā*) refers to the distinctions in the cultivation of the path (*mārga-vāsanā*); for instance, one who has come from the heavens remains fresh and pure even now, as is extensively explained regarding the cultivation of the path.
As stated in the *Mahātejo-ratnapradīpa-ṛṣi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, this refers to the habituation of results. The two preceding points both address the present in contrast to the past.
Third, regarding "following the conduct of sentient beings": this refers to the distinctions in associating with the conduct of sentient beings. This is the habituation of conditions;

therefore, one should distance oneself from evil, draw near to the good, and be cautious about what one cultivates. For this reason, the kings of old did not establish stables [for their own pleasure].

Regarding "established in the temple" and "at the slaughterhouse," the phrase "fourfold according to karma and so forth" refers to the distinctions in the perfuming of meritorious deeds and afflictions.

"Meritorious deeds" (karmānta) explains the term *karma* in the context of the sūtras; it refers to the performance of activities and distinguishes them from the causes of karma, such as teaching a child who is refining gold to practice counting the breaths (*ānāpāna*).
"Afflictive habits" (*kleśavāsanā*) are like a person who loves sleep, whereby sleep increases and intensifies.
"Many kinds," etc. Regarding "the five [types of] wholesome and unwholesome, etc.": this refers to the distinctions in the perfuming of wholesome karma and so forth.

This karma is itself the cause of karma, because these three natures—wholesome and so on—are designated as "karma" in relation to future fruits. For example, in one who has long practiced giving, the mind of giving becomes increasingly intense.
The aforementioned three [types of perfuming] clarify habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) solely in terms of the present life. The sixth is "entry into subsequent existence."

This refers to the differentiation of perfuming (*vāsanā*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Since the intermediate state follows immediately after the prior existence (*pūrvabhava*), just as a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) remains untainted by desire even while within the intermediate state, so too does it apply here.
Regarding the sevenfold sequence, this refers to the differentiation of perfuming according to the sequence of the ripening of fruits (*vipākaphala*).

That is to say, having cultivated wholesome or unwholesome karma, one experiences the sequence of receiving those fruits among the various realms of existence (*gati*) during the subsequent state; the habituation (*abhyāsa*) likewise [proceeds] in this manner.

The sequence of the fruits is without deviation. The preceding two [points] explain the perfuming (*vāsanā*) by referring to the present in relation to what follows. Regarding "the eight non-interruptions" and so forth:

this refers to the distinction of the causes for perfuming that transcend the world; that is to say, all untainted meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are termed "meditations transcending the world."

Cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*) is itself the cause for that. Because afflictions have not yet been severed, even though one cultivates the untainted, one is still pulled by afflictions and follows after them;
thus, the untainted is called "far-reaching" (*dūragama*). "Going" (*gati*) also carries the sense of "entering. Regarding the ninefold "real and unreal":

this refers to the distinctions between those of the same Dharma and outsiders, as well as between conduct, understanding, liberation, and cultivation. "Those of the same Dharma" explains the real; that is to say—

Because the three vehicles share the same Buddha-dharma, they differ from the non-Buddhist interpretations, which are not real because they lie outside the Buddha-dharma; thus they are called "different.
For the practitioner, the former two [vehicles] are the cause, while liberation is the fruit of the latter two; each has its own habitual cultivation (*vāsanā*).

Because one is fond of practicing the fundamental method, even if one previously cultivated the Small Vehicle and now studies the Great, one first gives rise to the Small and practices it. The rest may be inferred accordingly.

"Knowledge" (jñāna) clarifies both the deviant and the correct aspects of these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from the perspective of cultivation and realization; it also encompasses the characteristics of residual habits from the three vehicles.

The "ten vehicles of perfuming" (*daśayāna-vāsana*) pertain exclusively to the correct [path] regarding what is seen and heard. Therefore, this refers to the "Peaceful Practices" (*anuvartana-caryā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This prevents them from associating with the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*), for fear that such practice might form habitual seeds. The first seven [verses] concern time;

they clarify the mutual cultivation of the three periods and the three realms of existence, encompassing both the wholesome and the unwholesome. The eighth clarifies how evil follows upon the wholesome. The final two concern persons;
they enable one to fully comprehend all varieties of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) so as to achieve the Tathāgata’s wisdom of "habitual tendencies without habitual tendencies."

Furthermore, one knows the characteristics of sentient beings who are fixed in the right, fixed in the wrong, or not yet fixed. That is to say: the characteristic of being fixed in the right is right view;

the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong is wrong view; and the characteristic of being neither is when both are indeterminate. The five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) are the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong; the five faculties (*indriya*) are the characteristic of being fixed in the right;

and the characteristic of being neither is when both are absent. The eightfold wrong path is the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong; the right nature (*samyaktva*) is the characteristic of being fixed in the right; and the characteristic of being neither is when both are further abandoned.

The characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): the characteristic of being deeply attached to false teachings and false concentration; the characteristic of practicing the noble path and right concentration; and the characteristic of relinquishing both, which is non-concentration.

The ninth [section] explains the dense forest of the three groups (*tri-nikāya*). This also first provides a general overview and subsequently a detailed analysis. The treatise generally comprises five parts; the general overview is the first.
First, there are those with the nature for nirvāṇa and those without the nature for nirvāṇa; this is a definitive distinction among the three vehicles.

"Without" refers to the wrongly fixed (mithyātva-niyata), while "with" refers to the rightly fixed (samyaktva-niyata), as each is fixed within its own respective vehicle. Apart from these is the unfixed. This is explained in terms of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
