In the sixth [section], regarding the characteristic of being without the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), the Dharma and its meaning are distinguished by way of the ultimate and conventional truths.
First, because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is selfless, it is called "one characteristic. As for the term "indestructible," it means that selflessness is not destroyed.

If one were to say, "I know selflessness" or "I realize selflessness," then selflessness would be destroyed, because there would be a subject and an object. Second, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is... [text fragment ends].

Therefore, I speak of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. Those who are deluded regarding the aggregates cling to a self as a collection; those deluded regarding the elements (*dhātu*) cling to a self as diverse causes, because they calculate distinctions among lineages;
those deluded regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*) cling to a self as a desire, because they calculate them as gateways for birth that can receive and enter [objects];

and those deluded regarding the truths and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) cling to a self as an agent, because they clearly perceive cause and effect as involving purposeful action. All of these are the "self of phenomena" (*dharma-ātman*), and they also extend to the "person" (*pudgala*).

I now follow and observe that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of dependent origination is without intrinsic reality as an antidote, thereby attaining entry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*);
this is called skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, are the objects to be remedied by the wisdom of the Bodhisattva.
Third, the threefold teaching of the exquisite selflessness is pleasing to the mind and thus praised; it accords with principle and is therefore sublime. Fourth.
It is called "supreme selflessness" because it is superior; it is called "boundless illumination of the Dharma" because of the distinctions within its terminology.

Furthermore, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) knows the equality of the One Vehicle; the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) knows the distinct natures of the various vehicles;

the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) explains that all vehicles are without distinction; and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) explains the One [Vehicle].
The boundless Dharma of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the seventh [topic], the characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles: the principles of the Dharma are distinguished by means of the provisional and the real. Knowing the real is taken as the Dharma; knowing the provisional is taken as the meaning.
The convergence of the three vehicles into one is the expression; the opening of the gate of skillful means is the eloquence of joyful teaching. This is the single contemplation.

First, the characteristic of appearance (*lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the non-differentiation of the single contemplation, for there is but one reality. Second, the characteristic of nature (*dhātu-lakṣaṇa*):

this refers to the fact that within those root-natures (*indriya-dhātu*), there are three vehicles. Third, the characteristic of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the realization that those three vehicles equally return to the single reality, for within the characteristic of liberation there is no distinction.
The *Śāstra* says: "Based on the same liberation, they have no fear. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Now I rejoice..."
Fearlessness. Because it expounds only the unsurpassed path, it opens the gate of skillful means through the four aspects of mindfulness.

Since mental inclinations differ according to individual capacities and mental activities vary, the various vehicles of the Dharma are explained and clarified through manifold teachings; yet all are for the sake of a single purpose.
Therefore, the Treatise says they "accord with liberation."

Furthermore, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) knows all bodhisattva practices, as well as the wisdom of the practice of gnosis and the practice of phenomena, which are realized accordingly.

The unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) knows the distinctions in meaning regarding the stages and positions of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*). The unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) explains the non-differentiated characteristics of the paths and grounds.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) explains the boundless aspects of the practices of each individual ground.

Within the characteristics of the eighth bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*), the dharma-meanings are distinguished according to the essential characteristics of the stages. First is the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
This is a general designation for all bodhisattva practices. What constitutes this? It refers to the practice of the dharma that is realized and the practice of the wisdom that realizes it.
Why are these two called "bodhisattva practices"? Because wisdom accords with suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wisdom..."
This is established according to the realization. The *Śāstra* states that it is explained by means of "contemplative wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

This bodhisattva practice is the very essence of the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Second is the explanation of its characteristics: although the essence is a single wisdom, its characteristics are tenfold because they correspond to the distinct positions of the stages. However, these positions arise from the differentiation of the mind;
thus the *Śāstra* says, "The differentiation of the ten stages refers to the mind. As for what is called the "explanation of characteristics," this refers to verbal expression.

This is the explanation. Since the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states that "the meaning is immeasurable" in order to explain the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), this interpretation is thus provided.
This, then, differs from the previous [point] regarding the greatness of the meaning. Third, the characteristic of the skillful means:

this refers to skillfully explaining the ten stages and bestowing them upon sentient beings through non-perverted instruction, because there is no difference between this and the realization of the path of the stages. Fourth, entering the immeasurable...
The characteristic of the gate: because it distinguishes the entry into the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) knows that all Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment.

The unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) knows the various distinctions of different times and different places. The unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) explains the distinctions of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Distinct. Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one cannot exhaustively expound even a single phrase of the Dharma throughout immeasurable eons.
This is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata-stage. To distinguish the Dharma and its meaning according to the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*):

first is the characteristic of the Dharma-body, which is the Dharma-body in which the beginning and the origin are non-dual; thus it is said that "in a single thought-moment, one attains perfect enlightenment. Second is the characteristic of the Form-body (*rūpakāya*). [The seeds...]
Regarding the time of planting [the seeds]: it occurs within any given eon. Regarding the various locations: it pertains to the environmental rewards (*niśraya-vipāka*) in any given land.

Regarding their respective distinctions: they correspond to the marks of the threefold perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) as the superior environmental rewards of whichever Buddha-body [is concerned].

Generally speaking, because there are ten distinct types of Buddhas, and because the virtues of these Buddhas as manifesting the marks of enlightenment are inexhaustible, the explanation of them is likewise inexhaustible.

Furthermore, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) knows the speech of all Tathāgatas, their powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*),
eloquence (*pratibhāna*), skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), and the realization of the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

The unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) knows the Tathāgata’s accordance with the eighty-four thousand variations in the mental activities, faculties, and inclinations of sentient beings, as well as their voices and expressions.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence follows the conduct of all sentient beings, expounding through the various distinctions of the Tathāgata’s voice.
The unimpeded knowledge of analytical exposition follows the faith and understanding of sentient beings, expounding through the fulfillment of the pure practices of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

The tenth is the mark of acting as a presiding master (*sthiti-dhara-lakṣaṇa*). This is categorized according to the qualities of the Buddhas’ capacity to teach and the vocal teachings they expound, thereby distinguishing the Dharma and its meaning.
First is the mark of awakening (*bodha-lakṣaṇa*), which is the quality of acting as a presiding master, because one awakens to the characteristics of the *dharmatā*.

Regarding speech, there is speech that accords with one’s own intention, speech that accords with the intentions of others, and speech that accords with the intentions of both oneself and others; these constitute the capacity to expound the Dharma. Through the ten powers (*daśabala*), one destroys Māra.
With pride and fearlessness, he subdues the non-Buddhists; not shared with the two vehicles, he speaks constantly out of compassion and is able to speak through his eloquence.
"Skillful means" refers to conforming to the capacities of sentient beings; "turning the wheel of Dharma" refers to correct teaching.

All of the above are realized in accordance with the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). Second, regarding the characteristics of differentiation: knowing the Buddha’s conformity to the mental dispositions, lineages, and natures [of beings], and so forth.

Third, the characteristic of verbal expression (*vyañjana*), because it is spoken through the differentiation of the aforementioned sounds. Fourth, the characteristic of its immeasurability, because it is taught in various ways;
that is, it manifests the inexhaustible eloquence (*pratibhāna*) of the Bodhisattva according to the faith and understanding of those who hear.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," etc.: the Dharma-body of all Buddhas has the benefit of sentient beings as its activity. Because this activity accords with wisdom, it is non-dual.
It is called "pure" because it is free from defilement; it is called "perfect" because it cannot be destroyed. These terms are used here because this stage has been attained.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in the ninth stage, they attain such skillful and unimpeded wisdom, and they attain the sublime [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
The Dharma-treasury acts as a great Dharma-master.
In the third major section, "The Mastery and Accomplishment of the Dharma-master," there are two parts: first, restating the preceding [section] to introduce what follows;

second, from "attaining the meaning" onwards, the actual manifestation of accomplishment. This consists of four matters: first, accomplishment through retention, because one attains and does not lose [the teaching]; second...
First is the accomplishment of exposition, because of skillfully being able to expound [the Dharma]. Second is the accomplishment of question and answer, because of cutting through the net of doubt.

Third is the accomplishment of upholding, because of further receiving superior dharmas. Thus, the former three constitute self-perfection (*svabhāva*), while the latter one constitutes transcendence (*viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the first explains the attainment of the treasury of the sublime Dharma, while the latter three explain the role of a great Dharma-preacher. In all four of these, there is no bondage.
"Attainment" refers to the inclusion of the ninth dedication.

These are: the *dhāraṇī* of attaining meaning, the *dhāraṇī* of phenomena, the *dhāraṇī* of wisdom, the *dhāraṇī* of light-illumination, the *dhāraṇī* of excellent intelligence, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold wealth, the *dhāraṇī* of majestic power, and the *dhāraṇī* of the unobstructed gate. No...
The *paryanta-dhāraṇī*, the *nānārtha-dhāraṇī*, and so forth—
all such millions of asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇī-gates were fully perfected. He expounded the Dharma by means of millions of asaṃkhyeya gates of skillful sounds and eloquence.
The first section, "Accomplishment through the Ten Retentions," is divided into two parts. First, the ten retentions are listed as those already attained.
Second, it describes how this bodhisattva employs these aforementioned ten retentions to attain what is yet to be obtained. Regarding the first part: the ten retentions are first enumerated.

They are also named according to the activities they initiate. The first three initiate mental action (*manas-karman*); the next three initiate bodily action (*kāya-karman*); and the final four initiate verbal action (*vāk-karman*).

First is the meaning of "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*). Second is upholding the teachings of the Dharma. Third is upholding the wisdom that knows [them]. Fourth is the compassionate light that gathers in those who are gentle and kind.
Fifth is the skillful wisdom that subdues those who are fierce and stubborn; thus, various kinds of activities are performed. Sixth...
It is called "various riches" because it makes offerings to the Buddhas above and gathers in the poor below.

Seventh, for those sentient beings who are narrow-minded and inferior regarding the Mahāyāna, it demonstrates and teaches the majestic power and supreme benefits of the Mahāyāna, causing them to give rise to wholesome roots. Eighth, it is the inexhaustible eloquence.
Because wisdom is constantly expounded; ninth, because the inexhaustible eloquence is profound exposition; tenth, because the various forms of eloquence are extensive exposition.
The following passage, "In this way," concludes the section. The subsequent passage, beginning with "By means of one million," reveals the function of upholding [the teaching].
Having attained these one million *asaṃkhyeya* dharanī-doors, this bodhisattva,
in the presence of each and every one of immeasurable Buddhas, hears the True Dharma by means of these one million *asaṃkhyeya* dharanī-doors.
Having heard it, he does not forget it, and he expounds it for others through immeasurable doors of distinction.

The second is "retention," through which one shall attain the middle [stage]. Having heard [the teachings], not forgetting them clearly manifests the meaning of retention; expounding them for others is likewise the function of retention.
This bodhisattva first beholds the Buddha, prostrates at his crown, and immediately receives immeasurable dharma-gates from the Buddha.
This dharma-gate attained here cannot be received by those great śrāvakas who hear and uphold [the teachings], even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Second, regarding the explanation of accomplishment, there are three parts; first, it reveals the vastness of the Dharma received.
Having attained such dhāraṇīs and such unimpeded wisdom, this bodhisattva sits upon the Dharma-seat and expounds the Dharma.
To the sentient beings filling the great trichiliocosm, he teaches according to the differences in their inclinations and preferences;
yet, with the exception of the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have received their office, no one else in the assembly can compare to his majestic virtue and radiant light.
Second, the ability to expound extensively:
when this bodhisattva sits upon the Dharma seat, wishing to cause the entire great assembly to understand through a single voice, they immediately achieve such understanding;
or at times, wishing to cause the entire great assembly to attain awakening through various sounds, [they likewise succeed]. Or...
At times, his mind desired to emit great radiance and expound the Dharma-gates;
at other times, his mind desired that every single pore upon his body should all produce the sounds of the Dharma;

at other times, his mind desired that even all things—whether with form or without form—within the trichiliocosm should all produce the sublime sounds of the Dharma; at other times, his mind desired to...
A single word or sound pervades the entire Dharma-realm, causing all to understand and realize it.
At times, he may desire that all speech and sounds become the sound of the Dharma, abiding eternally without ceasing.

At times, he may desire that the flutes, pipes, bells, drums, and songs of all worlds, as well as all musical sounds, manifest the sound of the Dharma. At times, he may desire [to do so] within a single syllable...
He is fully endowed with all distinctions of the sounds and words of the *Dharmapada*.

At times, he may desire that from within every single atom among all the atoms of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—within unspeakably infinite worlds, there be manifested dharma-gates that cannot be expressed.
All such thoughts as these are attained according to his will, without exception.
The three types of knowledge arise as mastery in speech. The two preceding [types] have been explained as accomplished.

O Son of the Buddha, suppose all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to come before this bodhisattva, and each were to pose difficult questions using immeasurable voices and sounds; yet each and every question would not be...

The same applies to all bodhisattvas, who are able to receive and comprehend [all teachings] in a single thought-moment, and furthermore explain them universally with a single voice, causing each being to attain joy according to their own inclinations.
This extends even to all sentient beings throughout unspeakably many worlds.
In a single kṣaṇa, each [being] raises inquiries and challenges using immeasurable voices and sounds, and each inquiry is distinct from the others;
yet the Bodhisattva is able to receive them all within the span of a single thought-moment, and likewise explains them universally with a single voice,
causing each to rejoice according to their own mental inclinations, even throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds.
Throughout the world-systems filled with sentient beings, the Bodhisattvas are able to teach the Dharma according to their inclinations, faculties, and understandings.
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, they extensively perform the work of Buddhas and universally serve as a refuge for all.
The third major section consists of questions and answers regarding accomplishment. First, there is the response to the objection concerning a single realm; second, the clarification of all worlds.
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva further purifies and accomplishes the light of wisdom.

Even if, within the space of a single hair-tip, there were assemblies of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably many worlds, and within each of those assemblies, there were [unspeakably many...]"
Among the sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms of the world, each individual being possesses inclinations and dispositions numbering as many as the atoms of unspeakably many worlds.
Those Buddhas bestow upon them Dharma-gates according to their respective inclinations and dispositions.

As it is at the tip of a single hair, so it is in every location throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Regarding these immeasurable Dharma-gates thus described, the Bodhisattva, in a single thought-moment—
He is able to receive and retain all of them within his mind without any loss.
This is the fourth accomplishment of upholding [the teachings]. The practice of the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*) is now concluded. Below, the fruits of these stages are clarified.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this ninth stage, he applies himself with diligence day and night, having no other thoughts; he enters only into the Buddha-...
They draw near to the realm of the Tathāgatas, entering the profound liberations of the bodhisattvas and constantly abiding in samādhi.

They perpetually behold all Buddhas without ever being separated from them. Within each eon, they see immeasurable Buddhas—immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas, immeasurable thousands of Buddhas, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas—revering, honoring, serving, and making offerings to them.

He cultivated [these practices] and, by posing various questions and challenges before the Buddhas, attained the *dhāraṇī* of preaching the Dharma. All his roots of goodness became increasingly bright and pure.
The second major section clarifies the fruits of the stages; the three fruits are the same as those previously mentioned, but here, within the first fruit—the fruit of flexibility—one perceives...

Regarding the conditions for the Buddha: first, one perceives the Dharma-body of the Buddha based on internal realization; subsequently, one perceives the form-body of the Buddha based on samādhi. The rest may be understood accordingly.
It is like true gold: a skilled goldsmith fashions it into a precious crown, which a Cakravartin king wears upon his head as an ornament.
Within the four continents, there are no ornaments of any minor kings, ministers, or subjects that can equal them.
This second simile clarifies that the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva in this ninth stage are likewise so; they surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and...
No roots of goodness possessed by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages can equal them.
(The three points are thus combined.
O Son of the Buddha! It is, for example, like the Great Brahmā King, Lord of the Two-Thousandfold World System, whose body emits radiance throughout those two thousand worlds.
Just as it is able to illuminate and dispel the darkness in places that are deep and remote, so too are all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas in this stage;
they are able to emit light that illuminates the minds of sentient beings, causing the darkness of their afflictions to be completely extinguished.
Second is the purity of teaching and wisdom.
Among the ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva, the pāramitā of power (bala) is the most preeminent;
it is not that the other pāramitās are not practiced, but they are practiced according to one's power and capacity.
Third, the characteristics of the distinct stage.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called a brief explanation of the ninth stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable eons.
The fourth section concludes by explaining the name of the stage:
"O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell on this stage, they frequently become Great Brahmā Kings, lords of two thousand worlds.
They are skillfully able to govern with sovereignty and provide great benefit; they are able to act for the sake of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas."
Sā. He analytically expounds the practice of the pāramitās. Regarding whatever questions or challenges arise according to the minds of sentient beings, there is none who can defeat him.

Whether it be acts of giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—indeed, all such deeds he performs are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, up to and including mindfulness of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall..."
Among all sentient beings, he is the foremost, the most excellent, and even the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If this bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, in a single moment of thought, he attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds;
he even manifests as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds.
These he takes as his retinue.
Second is the fruit of the maturation of rewards:
if, by means of the bodhisattva’s extraordinary power of vows, he manifests sovereignty, it exceeds this number, even reaching hundreds of thousands.
Even in billions of nayutas of kalpas, they could not be counted or known.
This is the fruit of the wisdom of the three vows.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
With immeasurable power of wisdom, you observe with skill; Most supreme and subtle, difficult for the world to know.
Universally entering the secret realm of the Tathāgata, You benefit sentient beings and enter the ninth stage.
Mastery over dhāraṇīs and samādhis, Attaining great supernormal powers, you enter all lands.
The powers, knowledges, fearlessnesses, and unshared dharmas; the vows, powers, and compassionate mind—these enter the ninth stage.
This section of twenty-four verses from the third part, the Section of Verses, is divided into three. First, nineteen verses praise the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The next four verses concern the fruits of the stages, and the final one is a concluding eulogy. Herein, the first provides a complete verse summary of the preceding four sections.
The first two verses concern the skillful means of the Dharma-preacher:
Abiding in this stage, he upholds the treasury of the Dharma, Thoroughly understanding the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
They thoroughly understand all that is with outflows and without outflows, mundane and supramundane, as well as the conceivable and the inconceivable.
They fully observe whether phenomena are determinate or indeterminate, and the activities performed by the three vehicles.
Distinguishing between the conditioned and the unconditioned, they thus know and enter into the world.
Next, two verses concern the accomplishment of wisdom:
If one wishes to know the minds of all sentient beings, One can, through wisdom, know them as they truly are—
Their various rapid transformations, their destruction or non-destruction, And their manifold characteristics such as being without substance or being boundless.
Afflictions are boundless and ever-present as companions; their dormant and active states share a single underlying meaning.
They continue through various realms of existence, with karmic natures that are diverse and distinct.

One can thoroughly understand how causes perish and fruits accumulate, as well as the various inferior, middling, and superior faculties, along with their infinite distinctions across the limits of the past and future.
The nature of understanding, inclination, and desire are likewise so; of the eighty-four thousand [afflictions], there is none that is not known.
The delusions and views of sentient beings constantly follow and bind them;

this dense forest from time immemorial has never been cleared away, persisting together with their will and arising simultaneously with their minds, always binding them in a state of perpetual, unbroken continuity.
These are merely false imaginings and not substantial entities; they do not exist apart from the mind and have no fixed location.
Even when meditative states are attained through dhyāna, one may still regress; only upon the path of the Vajra is there ultimate cessation.
Rebirth within the six realms of existence varies according to each individual, for karma is the field, craving is the moisture, and ignorance is the covering.
Consciousness is the seed, and name-and-form is the sprout; within the three realms, there is a beginningless and constant continuity.
Through delusion, karma, and the mental habit-energies, one is born into the various destinies. If one is separated from these, one is no longer reborn.
All sentient beings exist within the three categories: some are submerged in views, while others practice the path.
The thirty-seven verses constitute the accomplishment of entering into practice.
Abiding on this stage, one observes well; according to the inclinations of the mind and the faculties and understandings, four verses and eight verses explain the accomplishment.
Among these, the first half-verse explains the accomplishment of wisdom.
With unimpeded and wondrous eloquence, he teaches according to what is appropriate for each;
seated upon the Dharma throne like a lion, like a bull king, or like the king of jewel mountains;
again, like a dragon king spreading dense clouds, he pours down the rain of nectar to fill the great ocean.

"Skillfully knowing the nature of phenomena and their profound meaning, and being able to explain them through appropriate speech"—these two subsequent verses concern the perfection of verbal action (*vākkarman*). Among these, certain metaphors are not present in the prose commentary.
Holding ten million asaṃkhyeyas in total retention, like the great ocean receiving all rains;
With total retention and samādhi both pure and clear, one can see many Buddhas in a single thought-moment;
In the presence of each and every Buddha, one hears the Dharma, And further expounds it with wondrous sounds.
The final five and a half verses praise the Dharma Master’s accomplishment of mastery. Among them, the first verse and a half praise his upholding [of the Dharma]:

“If he wishes to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, Like clouds spreading widely so that none are left untouched, He causes all to rejoice according to their faculties and inclinations.”
The next verse says:
The assemblies of Buddhas on the tips of hairs are beyond numbering, And the inclinations of sentient beings' minds are likewise infinite;
To each according to their mind, one bestows the Dharma gates— Throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it is thus.
The next verse provides a response to the question:
Through the power of diligent and vigorous effort, the Bodhisattva further attains merit that becomes ever more excellent;
he masters and retains as many Dharma-gates as there are, just as the earth can support all kinds of seeds.
Sentient beings from the ten directions, immeasurable in number, all come to approach and sit within the assembly;
in a single thought, each according to their own mind, they pose difficult questions, and with a single voice [the Buddha] answers them all, satisfying everyone.
The final two verses praise the upholding [of the teaching] and also praise the questions and answers.
Abiding in this stage, one becomes a Dharma King, Exhorting and guiding others according to their capacities without weariness;
Day and night beholding the Buddha, never forsaking him, One enters profound, tranquil wisdom and liberation.
Making offerings to all Buddhas, one’s virtuous benefit becomes ever more radiant, Like a wondrous jewel crown upon a king’s head.
Furthermore, they cause the afflictions of sentient beings to be extinguished; Like the light of Brahmā King, which shines everywhere, those who dwell here often become Great Brahmā Kings;
They transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, and the wholesome karma they practice universally benefits all, Until they shall attain the realization of All-Knowledge.
In a single thought-moment, one enters into various samādhis; likewise, one sees Buddhas preaching the Dharma in as many lands as there are atoms in an asaṃkhyeya of worlds.
What is accomplished through the power of vows exceeds even this.
These four verses in the second position describe the fruit of the stage.
This is the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), the domain traversed by Bodhisattvas of great wisdom;
it is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive. For the sake of the sons of the Buddha, I have already proclaimed it.
With this single verse, the third [section] concludes the exposition of the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence.

Volumes Thirty-eight and Thirty-nine Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, a Śramaṇa.
Commentary by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá Yán Temple;
Excerpts by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng, clarifying the meaning.
Chapter Twenty-six, Part Six: The Ten Grounds (*Daśabhūmi*).
Regarding the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*):

as for the reason for coming [to this stage], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that although one has attained great mastery in teaching the Dharma across all categories of phenomena, one has not yet attained the full realization of the perfect Dharmakāya.
Now, through diligent cultivation, this has been perfected; hence, one comes to this stage. The treatise says that within the nine stages:
Having already purified the Buddha-fields and transformed sentient beings, one practices in the tenth stage so that wisdom may reach full awakening.
Because this is superior, it is contrasted with the eighth and ninth stages, which are both characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Thus, its excellence is made manifest in relation to them.
Since [this stage] has existed from the beginning, and because it occupies the most supreme position within the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), the term "cloud" (*megha*) serves as a metaphor.

Briefly, it possesses three meanings: first, the sense of containing water; second, the sense of covering the sky; and third, the sense of pouring down rain. When applied to the Dharma according to these metaphors, there are many meanings.

Specifically, the cloud has four meanings: first, it is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); second, it is a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); third, it is a metaphor for the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and fourth...

This serves as an analogy for the cause of cultivation through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) also possesses four meanings: first, it is an analogy for *tathatā*; second, for the heavy burdensome states (*dausthulya*);
third, for the *dharmakāya*; and fourth, for the *ālayavijñāna*. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By attaining the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its universal object..."
It contains all *dhāraṇī* gates; this is a metaphor for the meaning of containing water.

The wisdom that universally takes all phenomena—such as the *sūtras*—as its object does not depart from *tathatā*, just as clouds merge with space. This *samādhi* of universal retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*) is precisely the water.
Furthermore, it says: "For example, just as a great cloud can cover the vast expanse of space because of its obstructive nature. This metaphor illustrates the meaning of covering space;

that is, the aforementioned wisdom can cover both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, it says: "Because it can push toward and fulfill the *dharmakāya*.
This has two meanings. First, it is a metaphor for the meaning of torrential rain; that is, the aforementioned wisdom gives rise to meritorious qualities that fill [the *dharmakāya*].
Because it fulfills the *dharmakāya* according to its nature, there are two types of pervasive fulfillment; this refers precisely to the aforementioned wisdom itself fulfilling the *dharmakāya*.
Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The *dharmakāya* is like space, and wisdom is like a great cloud. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
The coarse and heavy body is as vast as space, while the Dharma-body is perfectly complete like a great cloud, capable of universally covering all.
This corresponds to the second meaning in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. However, Asvabhāva’s commentary explains that wisdom covers space;
here, by "Dharma-body," it is meant that when wisdom is fulfilled, the Dharma-body is perfected. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The manifestation of the Dharma-body is the purity of wisdom."
Because it is pure. The *Mūlabhāga* states that one attains the great Dharma-body and perfect mastery; it also uses the Dharma-body as a metaphor for clouds.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), through the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, all causes consisting of the perfuming of hearing are gathered and pervade the ālayavijñāna, just as floating clouds pervade the empty sky.
By means of these clouds of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*), in a single moment, upon each mark (*lakṣaṇa*), each minor sign (*anuvyañjana*), and each pore,
they rain down immeasurable and boundless Dharma-rain, sufficing all sentient beings to be converted.
Because they are able to rain down the Dharma-rain like a cloud, yet because this [state] has not yet reached the level of a Buddha, it is established as the *dharmakāya* (the body of reality).
The term *yoga* also means "great cloud. This is because before manifesting equal enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), it is like a great cloud;
once equal enlightenment is manifested, it can rain down a great rain to bring about benefit. Thus, while the secret clouds do not yet rain, they merely contain virtue within them.
Although there are many such interpretations, they do not go beyond three meanings: namely, containing virtue through wisdom, universally severing all obstacles, and [universally bestowing benefits].

Because it is the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), that which covers the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) is the obstacle to be abandoned; namely, the obstacle consisting in the lack of mastery over all phenomena.
This obstacle pertains to the Great Dharma-Wisdom Cloud (*mahādharmanirmāṇa-jñānābhra*) of the tenth stage, as well as the activities arising from what it contains.

These constitute two types of delusion: the delusion regarding the activities arising from the obstacle, called the "delusion regarding great supernormal powers" (*mahābhijñā-moha*); and the delusion regarding the Great Wisdom Cloud itself.

One awakens to the subtle secret delusion. By severing this hindrance, one is able to realize the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for mastery over karma and so forth—meaning that one attains mastery over the performance of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), dhāraṇīs, and the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Consequently, one accomplishes the practices such as receiving the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) and fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), thereby attaining the fruits such as the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and various samādhis; this is the Cloud [Stage].
The rain falls. The ultimate *dharmakāya* of the Buddha and the *tathatā* realized therein both pervade the entirety of space; their essential meaning is one and the same.
A multitude of nayutas of gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, having heard these supreme practices within this stage, [attain realization].

Leaping in the air with hearts full of joy, they all together reverently made offerings to the Buddha and the inconceivable assembly of bodhisattvas. Also in the air, they were filled with great delight,
burning supreme and most pleasing incense that perfumed the entire assembly, making it pure.

The Sovereign King of Gods, together with a multitude of devas numbering in the hundreds of millions, stands in the void, scattering celestial robes everywhere as an offering to the Buddha; hundreds of thousands of varieties fall in profusion.
Herein begins the correct explanation of the text, which is divided into three parts. First, within the section of praise and invitation, there are sixteen verses; of these, the first thirteen...

Praise. Regarding the three subsequent requests, there are also two parts within the preceding section. The first three verses merely express offerings; these can be understood as being of three types:
The celestial maidens are immeasurable, None of whom do not joyfully make offerings to the Buddha.
The names [of the verses] are "Various Exquisite Musical Tunes" and "All Praise with These Words.
Regarding the ten subsequent verses on the offering and praise by the goddesses, there are also two parts; the first is a general heading for the offering and praise.
The Buddha’s body sits peacefully within a single land, yet manifests its form throughout all worlds;
its physical marks are majestic and beautiful, numbering in the hundreds of millions, filling the vastness of the entire Dharma-realm.
From a single pore it emits radiance, universally extinguishing the darkness of afflictions in the world.
The number of atoms in the lands may be known, but the number of these light-rays is immeasurable.
The remaining nine lines are clearly words of praise; therein there are two parts: the first eight praise the Buddha’s virtues, and the last one exhorts practice for the sake of benefit.
Within the former part, there are also two: the first five praise his sovereign great function, and the latter reveals the source of that sovereignty.
The former [part] also has two [sections]. The first two concern the universal benefit of their activities.
Either one sees the Tathāgata endowed with all marks, turning the unsurpassed wheel of the true Dharma;
or one sees him traveling through the various Buddha-fields; or one sees him remaining in silent stillness, peaceful and unmoving.
The latter three follow the [four] visions and are not equal; among them there are also two. The first one explains them collectively:

Either manifesting as dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, Or manifesting descending to enter the mother’s womb, Or showing the period of dwelling in the womb or emerging from it— Causing all to see these within immeasurable lands.

Sometimes manifesting as one who has left home to cultivate worldly paths, Or manifesting at the site of enlightenment to achieve perfect awakening, Or manifesting preaching the Dharma or entering nirvana— Universally causing all throughout the ten directions to behold them.
The latter two [verses] describe the eight marks of the final stage. The first five verses praise the sovereign mastery of the great function; the following [verse] reveals that which is mastered.
Just as a magician, knowing the art of illusion, performs many feats before a great multitude,
so too is the wisdom of the Tathāgata: it manifests its body everywhere throughout the world.
The Buddha abides in the profound and true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is quiescent, signless, and like empty space;
yet within this supreme ultimate reality, he manifests various activities,
and all deeds performed for the benefit of sentient beings are possible only by relying upon that dharmatā.

Characteristics and the absence of characteristics are without distinction; one enters the ultimate state where all are without characteristics. Regarding the subsequent section, there are also two parts.
The first part concerns the wisdom that realizes the world as an illusion; thus, the text contains both a simile and its application.

The latter two parts concern the realization of the exhaustion of nature and characteristics. Within this, half a verse establishes the essence, half a verse initiates function, and half a verse shows that function is [unimpeded].
Detachment from the essence. This half-verse shows that both essence and function are extinguished:
If one wishes to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, One should abandon all false discrimination of existence and non-existence, And realize that all things are equal;
Thus, one will swiftly become a great guide for humans and devas.
The final section is the exhortation to practice. The thirteen preceding verses are concluded; the following three verses constitute the request:

Having offered praise with various voices, the immeasurable and boundless hosts of celestial maidens, their bodies and minds tranquil, dwell together in peace and joy, gazing up at the Tathāgata in silent reverence.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, perceiving that the entire assembly was profoundly tranquil, addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Great Fearless One, true Son of the Buddha:
regarding the entry from the ninth stage into the tenth, what are the characteristics of its merits and all its practices?"
And also regarding the matters of supernormal powers and transformations—may the wise one proclaim them.
Among the three subsequent requests, the first is a silent request made through mental recitation; the latter two are verbal requests made by the leaders.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra,
saying: "O Son of the Buddha, from the first stage through to the ninth stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having observed and realized with such immeasurable wisdom,
practices through skillful reflection and cultivation, perfectly fulfills the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), and accumulates boundless factors conducive to enlightenment."
They increase great merit and wisdom; they extensively practice great compassion; they know the distinctions of worlds; they enter the dense forest of the realm of sentient beings;

they enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity; they accord with the Tathāgata’s practice of quiescence; and they constantly contemplate the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-dharmas.
This is called attaining the empowerment of the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Section Two: The Actual Exposition. This treatise is divided into eight sections: 1. The Section on the Stage of Fulfillment through Expedient Means (*upāya-pariniṣpatti-bhūmi*).

This subsumes the preceding nine stages, as the practices cultivated therein collectively serve to fulfill this stage through expedient means. 2. The Section on Attaining Samādhi. This refers to the initial dwelling in the stage (*prathama-bhūmi-vihāra*).

1. The Stage of Practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). The virtues of practice are immeasurable; this is because it universally cites the basis upon which one relies to receive the office [of Buddhahood]. 2. The Stage of Attaining the Position (*adhikāra-lābha-bhūmi*).

This refers to the practice of correctly abiding on the ground, for by relying on the power of the aforementioned meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gathers the Buddha-wisdom. 3. The Stage of Entering Great Perfection (*mahāpariniṣṭhā-praveśa-bhūmi*). This is the practice that brings this ground to completion.

In comparison to the practices of the preceding grounds, those have already been exhausted; now, as the ground is fulfilled, it represents the ultimate limit of such exhaustion. 4. The Stage of Explanation (*vyākhyāna-bhūmi*). [The text continues: Five... [explanation].
1. The Section on Names and Designations (*nāma-vibhāga*): Because at this stage, the study exhausts the qualities of eloquence and their designations become manifest.

2. The Section on Superior and Non-Superior Spiritual Powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā-vibhāga*): Once the stages are fulfilled, wondrous functions are sovereign; because the physical form is inferior to that of a Buddha, it lacks substantiality before [the Buddha]. 3. The Section on Reflected Images (*pratibimba-vibhāga*):
Using metaphors to clarify the Dharma, just as one knows the physical substance through its reflected image. 4. The Section on Manifesting Benefit (*anuśaṃsa-vibhāga*): [The eighth stage].
The latter two sections are common to all ten stages (*bhūmi*) because they encourage practice and entry; since the former encompasses the latter, it is said that this stage consists of eight parts.
If one follows the previous extended classification where the latter two sections are common to all, then this stage is divided into two:

first, the explanation of the practices of the stage (*bhūmi-caryā*), and second, the manifestation of the fruits of the stage (*bhūmi-phala*). Within the explanation of the practices of the stage, there are six sections.
As listed above, among these six, the first is the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*), while the others are the minds of abiding (*sthiti-citta*).

The mind of emergence (*niṣkramaṇa-citta*) is the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the first section, there are two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific exposition beginning with "well-fulfilled" (*suvipula*). Now, for the first:

"immeasurable wisdom" (*apramāṇajñāna*) refers to the extensiveness of the *āgama*; "observing and realizing" (*vibhāvayati pratividhyati*) refers to the profundity of realized wisdom (*adhigamajñāna*). — *Ratnagotravibhāga* (The Treatise on the Jewel Nature).

In the middle [section], Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) initiate two types of practice: first, that which is called "practice as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*), referring to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is precisely this realized wisdom (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*);
second, that which is called "partial practice" (*prādeśika-pratipatti*), referring to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is precisely this expansive wisdom (*vipula-jñāna*).

All stages fully initiate these two kinds of practice. Now, regarding the decisive discernment (*viniścaya*) of the above two, within the specific [section] of ten phrases, they are subsumed as follows:

There are seven characteristics. Because the first three, the third, the seventh, and the eighth are combined into three locations, and because one among the seven is characterized by excellent practice, these constitute the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, the first three phrases clarify the realization (*pratyakṣa*), the aids (*sahāya*), and the non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*); these are practiced identically across all stages (*bhūmi*).

The first phrase refers to the path of realization (*darśana-mārga*), as it consists of untainted pure dharmas (*anāsrava-śukla-dharma*). How is realization attained? It is through the aid of the path mentioned in the subsequent phrase. By what cause is this aid brought to completion?

By virtue of the latter phrase, "the path of non-abiding," because merit is increased, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because wisdom is increased, one does not abide in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The latter six [aspects] are specific characteristics: namely, the two extensive practices of great compassion, which constitute the characteristic of universally conforming to both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
These [six] are combined with the preceding seven stages to form a single characteristic, based on the distinctions of the seventh stage.

The characteristics have already been analyzed at the beginning of the eighth stage; therefore, they are presented here collectively. This provides a comprehensive and extensive explanation. Following this is the explanation of practice:
through great compassion and the benefiting of others, one accomplishes one's own task; thus, it is called "self-benefit. The third single phrase causes the Buddha-field to be purified.

These are the characteristics of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). The [following] three characteristics below correspond to the ninth stage; because one personally realizes them, they are frequently cited.

The fourth, the single characteristic of teaching and transforming sentient beings, corresponds to the "self-conduct" (*svacaryā*) of the ninth stage, as it involves entering the eleven "dense forests" (*gahana*).
The fifth has two phrases concerning the characteristic of skillful understanding: namely, understanding and penetrating *tathatā*, because it is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity;

and skillfully conforming to the Tathāgata, because one is able to realize the practice of *nirvāṇa*. The sixth is the characteristic of insatiability: constantly and diligently observing [the powers and so forth] with the desire to enter [them].
The former phrase refers to understanding, while this phrase refers to practice; both constitute the superior progress of the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*). As for the previous stage...
It is said that day and night one applies oneself with exclusive diligence, having no other thoughts, because one enters solely into the realm of the Buddha.

This is the culmination of the seventh stage, reaching the point of entering the marks [of realization], meaning that the realization of the ten stages has been perfected. As in the preceding stages, the conclusion of practice and entry into the position already belong to the tenth stage;
therefore, it is called "attaining the rank of receiving the position. The first section on the fulfillment of the preparatory practices is hereby concluded.

O Son of the Buddha! Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has entered the stage of receiving empowerment through such wisdom, there is the second part concerning the samādhi, which consists of two sections;
first, the summary of what precedes to introduce what follows.
He immediately attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement; the Samādhi of Entering the Distinctions of the Dharma-realm;
the Samādhi of Adorning the Site of Enlightenment; the Samādhi of the Radiance of All Kinds of Flowers; the Samādhi of the Ocean Treasury; the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal;
the Samādhi of the Vastness of the Realm of Space; the Samādhi of Contemplating the Self-nature of All Dharmas; and the Samādhi of Knowing the Mental Activities of All Sentient Beings.
The Samādhi in Which All Buddhas Appear Before One.

Next, the following section clarifies what is attained below; it consists of four parts: first, the individual listing of the ten names; second, the summary of the number of attainments starting with "In this way, etc.";
third, the manifestation of entry into fulfillment starting with "The Bodhisattva, therein..."; and fourth, the final part starting with "Its last..."

This clarifies the name of the final stage. Among the first ten [stages], the first is general and the remaining ones are specific. It is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*) in general because it is free from the stains of afflictions (*kleśa-mala*);
this name is specifically applied to this ground where all hindrances are exhausted. Within the specific [stages], the nine concentrations are each free from eight kinds of stains.
First is "entry into the stainless mystery," which means entering the profound and secret realm of the dharma-dhātu in each and every phenomenon, for it is not conjoined with delusions.
Second is "proximity to the stainless," because when the myriad practices are perfected, one is near the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Of the above, the first is understanding and the second is practice; the following three constitute the perfection of virtues, namely the mystery of the three karmas. Third is "emitting light."

1. The stainlessness of purifying the mind: this means that light opens the lotus of the mind, causing it to perceive reality, and enables one to sit upon various great jewel lotuses, for there is no place the light does not illuminate.

2. The stainlessness of the four *dhāraṇīs*: like the ocean, they contain and conceal all things. 3. The stainlessness of manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): these appear instantaneously without deliberate thought.

The above five are all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that give rise to the *dharmakāya*. 6. There are two types of concentration: [the first is the concentration of the *sambhogakāya*, and the second is the concentration of the *nirmāṇakāya*].
The pure buddha-field is stainless. The first phrase, "immeasurable," refers to the full extent of the dharma-realm;

the second phrase, "correct observation," exhausts the essential nature of the land. The first six [phrases] concern self-benefit; the seventh, "the birth of beings is stainless," concerns the benefit of others.

These two benefits both belong to the stage of one's own practice (*svabhāga-pratipatti*). The eighth, "perfect awakening is stainless," refers to the superior progress toward the higher awakening that is about to achieve *bodhi*.
"Ti. At that time, all Buddhas appear before one another and bear witness, as described in the section on the reception of office;
this is because fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) is about to manifest.
In this way, one million asaṃkhyeya samādhis all manifest before him.
The enumeration of the three fetters is likewise their retinue; that they all manifest means they have been long cultivated and perfected, appearing spontaneously without the application of effort.
The bodhisattva attains skillfulness regarding all these samādhis, whether entering them or arising from them,
and also thoroughly understands the distinctions among the functions performed by all samādhis.

Third, regarding the manifestation of entry into fulfillment: that which is able to enter encompasses both the provisional means and the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The characteristics of its arising upon entry are such that its hidden and manifest aspects are without fixed direction;
hence it is called "skillful" (*kauśalya*). To skillfully understand what is performed is to know its functional activity (*karmayoga*).
The final samādhi is named "Receiving the Supreme Position of All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñatā-viśeṣa-adhikāra-parigraha*).
The reason for manifesting this name last is that it is intended to explain the section on receiving the position. "All-knowledge" (*sarvajña*) refers to the Buddha’s non-dual wisdom.

According to the treatise, the scripture’s repetition of the word "knowledge" includes both [non-conceptual] wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). The equality of these two wisdoms is termed "receiving the position."
When this samādhi manifests before one, a great precious lotus flower suddenly appears.

This flower is vast and expansive, equal in measure to ten million trichiliocosm worlds. It is adorned with an interlacing array of various exquisite jewels, transcending all worldly realms and arising from supramundane roots of goodness.
One thereby realizes that the nature of all phenomena is like an illusion.
Accomplished through all practices, it constantly emits light that universally illumines the dharma-realm; such a thing cannot exist in any of the celestial realms.
Its stem is made of *vaiḍūrya* maṇi jewels, its pericarp of sandalwood king, its filaments of agate, and its petals of Jāmbūnada gold.
This flower always possesses immeasurable radiance; its interior is filled with various jewels, and it is completely covered by a net of precious gems. Ten...
Lotuses as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm serve as his retinue.
Third is the section on receiving the position of enlightenment; this contains four parts: first, the dharma; second, the metaphor; third, the application; and fourth, the conclusion.

Regarding the first [the dharma], there are six points: first, the seat; second, the body; third, the retinue; fourth, the marks; fifth, the place of origin; and sixth, the attainment of the position. (6)
Of the preceding five, the first four constitute the virtues of self-perfection (*svabhāva-guṇa*), while the latter one subsumes the fruit of Buddhahood.

Within the former [four], the first three positions represent the essence (*tattva*), the next one represents the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the final one represents the function (*vṛtti*). The first three correspond to the environment, the primary body, and the retinue.

Now, for the first [point]: as for what kind of seat it is, it refers to the Great Lotus King Seat. Within this, there are two parts; first, we clarify the primary lotus, which itself possesses ten characteristics.
1. The characteristic of the primary subject, which is the actual lotus flower; 2. The characteristic of the dimensions of that flower below; 3.

The characteristic of excellence through the assembly of [attributes] below, because it possesses all virtues; 4. The characteristic of transcending the lower stages, because it is the place of birth; 5. The characteristic of the mundane causes below.

Sixth, the characteristic of knowing all that is inferior as being accomplished. Seventh, the characteristic of constantly relinquishing [inferior states] for the sake of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because correct contemplation universally illuminates the manifestation of phenomena within the *dharmadhātu*;
it is like a worldly lotus flower, wherein the blooming bud (*kumuda*) is considered supreme.

Eighth, the characteristic of not being inferior to the merits of the various heavens, because the virtues of a bodhisattva attract them. Ninth, the characteristic of having a body made of *vaiḍūrya* [lapis lazuli]. Tenth, its...
The adornment of the flowers falling below. The twenty-three thousand [verses] below clarify the flowers of the retinue.
The supplementary explanation states: The one true *dharmadhātu*, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind, does not belong to either delusion or enlightenment;

therefore, the holy and the ordinary are equal, the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, and the defiled and the pure are interfused. It possesses sands-of-the-Ganges-like merits that accord with its nature (*dharmatā*). Each and every...
Pervasive, perfectly interfused, and all-encompassing, such that every phenomenon is unimpeded and equal to the *dharmadhātu*, it is therefore collectively termed the "Dharma-realm.
Yet, sentient beings are deluded regarding this single mind; because of the defiled conditions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is birth and death.
Only I, Vairocana, having awakened to this mind since time immemorial, name it the "Wisdom of Universal Radiance" (*Samantāloka-jñāna*). Relying upon—
This great wisdom serves as the foundation for practice, establishing all myriad deeds; thus, it takes the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as its basis.
By passing through the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), great wisdom attains profound realization.

When delusions are exhausted and reality is fully penetrated, the originally existing *tathāgatagarbha* mind suddenly manifests; this is called the realization of the essence of the *dharmakāya*. To repay this supreme cause, one inwardly responds to Vairocana.
That Buddha’s vast, subtle, and wondrous *saṃbhogakāya* externally manifests the *saṃbhogakṣetra* of the Flower Treasury Adornment (*Ghanavyūha*).

This is the ultimate principle of transforming the ordinary into the sacred. Now, having exhausted the causes of the ten bodhisattva stages and being about to realize the *dharmakāya*, one is capable of inheriting the lineage of the Dharma-realm; this is called the "Stage of Receiving the Position. Therefore, at this stage, the bodhi...
Sā. Having already been able to enter ten million asaṃkhyeya samādhis, his wisdom merges with principle and his practice reaches its ultimate perfection.
Therefore, he uses these samādhis to dissolve his previously differentiated practices and subsume them into the equal Dharma-realm.
Thus, when this samādhi manifests before him, a great lotus flower suddenly appears; and this flower possesses ten characteristics. And...

He serves as the embodiment of perfect virtue; he is like the image of the "Flying Dragon in Heaven" and the "Advantageous Appearance of the Great Man" from the fifth line of the Qian hexagram in the *Zhou Yi*.
Although there is textual evidence for this in the commentaries, I have not had the leisure to discuss such broad principles here.
At that time, as the Bodhisattva sat upon this flower-seat, his physical form was perfectly proportioned in size.
Second, whatever body he possessed, that exquisite body was commensurate with the seat.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas served as his retinue, each sitting upon their respective lotus flowers and surrounding him on all sides.
Each one had attained a million samādhis and gazed with single-minded devotion toward the Great Bodhisattva.
Third, regarding whichever retinue it may be:

O Son of the Buddha, when this great Bodhisattva and his retinue sit upon their lotus thrones, all their radiance and the sound of their voices pervade and fill the dharma-realm of the ten directions;
all worlds tremble, and the evil realms [are purified].
There was a restful pause. The lands were adorned and purified; all bodhisattvas who shared the same practice gathered there without exception. The music of humans and devas sounded simultaneously.
All sentient beings attained peace and happiness. With inconceivable articles of offering, they made offerings to all Buddhas.
The assemblies of all Buddhas appeared clearly before them.
Fourth, as for the characteristics:

because its characteristic is the performance of all-pervasive activity, O Son of the Buddha, when this bodhisattva sits upon that great lotus throne, he emits ten million *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light from his two feet, which universally illuminate all the great hells of the ten directions and extinguish the suffering of sentient beings. From his two knees...
He emitted millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which universally illuminated the realms of animals throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings.

From the center of his navel, he emitted millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which universally illuminated the realms of King Yama throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings.
From his left and right flanks, he emitted millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which universally illuminated the ten directions.

He extinguishes the suffering of all beings in the human realm. From his two hands, he emits millions of asaṃkhyeya rays of light that universally illuminate all the palaces of the devas and asuras throughout the ten directions.
From his two shoulders, he emits millions of asaṃkhyeya rays of light that universally illuminate all śrāvakas throughout the ten directions. From his neck and back...
He emits millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light that universally illuminate the bodies of the *pratyekabuddhas* of the ten directions.
These emerge from five locations and emerge from ten locations, causing those in the evil realms to escape; this is because the bodhisattva increases his practice.
The text is divided into four sections: first, the emission of light and its activities; second, all the sages’ collective awareness; third, the swift response of the lower classes;
and fourth, the resonance of like voices. Herein is the first section. Light is emitted from ten locations, which involves three kinds of activity. The first is the activity of benefiting others.
Second is the activity of awakening; third is the activity of subduing. Now, following their respective categories, they shall be divided into four:
first, the aforementioned seven rays consist solely of beneficial activities. Of these, the first five benefit ordinary beings, while the latter two benefit those of small capacity.

From his face, he emits millions of asaṃkhyeya rays of light that universally illuminate the bodies of all bodhisattvas from those who have first resolved upon awakening up to those on the ninth bhūmi.
Second, regarding the eighth ray, there are two and a half functions: first, the function of benefit, which benefits bodhisattvas from the ninth bhūmi downwards.
Therefore, secondly, it is for the purpose of awakening them so that they may know. As for the term "half," it signifies only gathering [them] without the sense of subduing;
it means gathering them and causing them to come.
From between his two eyebrows, he emits millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which universally illuminate the Bodhisattvas receiving their offices throughout the ten directions.
It causes the palaces of Māra to all become invisible.
The ninth single ray also has two functions and a half: first, it benefits Bodhisattvas at the stage of equality;

as the subsequent text states that since that [other] light already brings benefit here, this light must likewise benefit them there. Second, it awakens them so that they may know. It is called "one."
As for "half," it means that the palace of Māra does not appear; this is merely the subduing of karma and lacks the sense of being encompassed.

From the crown of his head, he emits light rays as numerous as the atoms in ten million asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms, universally illuminating the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Fourth, the tenth is the Light of the Summit. It merely awakens [the assembly]. The text is divided into three parts. First, the section on the extent of illumination:
[the light] circles ten times to the right and abides in the midst of space, forming a network of radiance called "Blazing Radiance.
It initiates various kinds of offerings to worship the Buddha. The other bodhisattvas, from their first generation of the mind up to the ninth...
All the offerings existing on earth do not equal even one hundredth part of this; they cannot even be approached by calculation or analogy.
That net of light pervades everywhere before the assemblies of each and every Tathāgata throughout the ten directions.
They rained down various wonderful fragrances, flower garlands, garments, banners, pennants, precious canopies, and ornaments such as mani-jewels as offerings;
all were born from supramundane roots of goodness and transcended all worldly realms.
If there are sentient beings who see such [a sight], they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Second, circumambulating to the right specifically clarifies the performance of the action, namely, the arousal of offerings and the accomplishment of benefit; the term "benefit" refers to non-retrogression from bodhi.

Regarding this, the treatise sets forth four meanings: first, because one attains certainty upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*); second, because one enters the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
third, because one is certain to be free from the evil of negligence; and fourth, because one is certain to engage in virtuous deeds.
O Son of the Buddha, when this great radiance had completed such acts of offering,

it again circled each and every assembly at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions; having performed ten circumambulations, it entered through the soles of the feet of all the Tathāgatas.

The three Buddha-sons having completed their tasks below, they withdraw the light. Regarding the statement that it "enters beneath the feet": if explained according to the characteristics of the teachings (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*), the light from the crown of the head entering the feet manifests profound reverence;

if explained according to the realization of truth (*tattva-sākṣātkriyā*), it is because the ultimate wisdom enters from below into the realm of the Buddhas, manifesting that the realization of the Buddha-realm is itself self-realization.
This concludes the first section on the initial expansion of the activity.

At that time, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that a certain Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in a certain world-system is able to practice such vast conduct and has reached the stage of receiving the position of consecration.
Second, all the noble ones know this.

O Son of the Buddha! At that time, the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the ten directions—immeasurable, boundless, and including those up to the ninth stage—all come to surround, revere, and make offerings to him.
With single-minded attention, they observe him; as they observe correctly, each of those bodhisattvas immediately...
He attained ten thousand samādhis.
In the third lower stage, *Pavana* (Wind), he extended his reverence and obtained benefit.
At that time, all the Bodhisattvas who had received their offices throughout the ten directions [manifested] upon the *vajra*-adorned chest of virtue.

From among these marks, there issues forth a great light named "Able to Destroy the Enemies of Māra," with a retinue of a million asaṃkhyeya lights that universally illumines the ten directions and manifests immeasurable supernatural transformations.
Having performed these deeds, it enters into this mark of the virtue of the adamantine-ornamented chest of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Once the light has entered, it causes—
The power of this bodhisattva’s wisdom increases a hundred-thousandfold.
This fourth stage corresponds to "Resonance with Sound," because they mutually support one another by cultivating the practice of equal causes.
As the inner virtue of auspiciousness—profound and vast—has perfected the adornment of the mind, externally, light is emitted from these marks to mutually benefit one another. Furthermore,
Previously, he illuminated this from that by emitting light from between his eyebrows, which symbolized that the Middle Way had already been illuminated. Now, he illuminates that from this;

as for the mark on his chest, it symbolizes that the mind-to-mind accord is suspended in perfect harmony. His virtues are perfected and demons are exhausted; thus he is named "Destroyer of Mara’s Enemies."
At that time, from the space between the eyebrows of all the Buddhas of the ten directions, there issued forth a pure light named "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Supernormal Powers.
With countless rays of light as its retinue, it universally illuminated all worlds throughout the ten directions.
He circumambulated it ten times, manifesting the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata; awakening immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas;
causing all buddha-fields to tremble universally; extinguishing the sufferings of all evil realms;
obscuring all the palaces of Māras; and revealing the sites where all Buddhas attain bodhi—the place of enlightenment.
The majesty and power of this assembly were magnificently adorned. Having thus universally illumined all worlds throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm,
it came to this assembly of bodhisattvas, circumambulated it to the right, and manifested various kinds of magnificent adornments.
Sixth: At that time, in the ten directions... [the following] clarifies the attainment of the respective stages. Within this, there are two parts. First, the emission of light.
Within this, there are ten activities. First, the name of the light; this is the activity of benefit, as it benefits all-knowledge so that the Buddha may attain perfection.

Second, "innumerable" and so forth refers to the light of the retinue; this is the activity of cause. Third, "manifesting" and so forth refers to the manifestation of the Buddha; this is the activity of reverence. Fourth...
1. Awakening; 2. the karma of awakening others; 3. the karma of universal pervasion; 4. the karma of causing vibration;
5. the karma of eliminating evil; 6. the karma of suppressing Māra; 7. the karma of manifestation; 8.
the karma of contraction and expansion; 9. the karma of manifesting various transformations.
Having manifested these things, [the light] entered through the crown of the Great Bodhisattva’s head. The radiance of his retinue likewise entered the crowns of those various bodhisattvas.
At that moment, this bodhisattva attained one million samādhis previously unattained;
he was said to have attained the rank of consecration, entered the realm of the Buddha, became endowed with the ten powers, and descended into the state of a Buddha.
[The stage of] Counting.

Second, having manifested these matters, one enters the "Crown" (*mūrdhan*) to achieve benefit. Regarding "entering the Crown": if considered in terms of the phenomenal aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), it means the higher [stages] encompassing the lower.
If considered in terms of the ultimate meaning, it refers to illuminating the source of the mind to its limit; this is called the "Crown of Wisdom. Herein, the fruition is realized within oneself.
This is the entry of light. The *Śāstra* states: "The lights of all Tathāgatas and those of the Bodhisattvas mutually [interpenetrate] because they are equally embraced by wisdom.
This means that when the light from the crown of the Bodhisattva enters the Buddha’s feet, it signifies the cause advancing toward the fruit.

When the Buddha’s light enters the crown of the Bodhisattva, it signifies the fruit encompassing the cause. Furthermore, when the cause encompasses the fruit, their entry leaves no trace; thus, cause and fruit are non-dual.
The simultaneous extinction of both is called "equality. At that time, the benefit attained below is termed the "stage of the lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Those who enter the realm of the Buddha share the same realization; those who possess the ten powers share the same conduct and virtue;
and those who are included among the ranks of the Buddhas are like one who, upon first leaving the household life, immediately enters the ranks of the Saṅgha.

The Supplemental Commentary states: When a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds receives their office, ten kinds of light emanate from throughout their body, universally illuminating the ten Dharma-realms and reaching the limit of all lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, above joining with the Buddhas and their retinues.

Together with the Bodhisattvas who have received empowerment, extending downward to the six paths and three realms of existence, they interpenetrate one another to form a net of light that performs all manner of deeds.
This reveals the fundamental, universal radiance-wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*) as the root of all ten dharma-realms—of both the holy and the ordinary, the defiled and the pure.
Within each and every sentient being, this is inherently and spontaneously complete; yet, for the time being, it remains unmanifest.

Because ignorance obscures its essence, the faculties and their objects remain separated, and the distinction between self and other serves as the defiled condition for birth and death, failing to manifest its great function.
Now, the Bodhisattva relies upon this fundamental wisdom to establish faith and undergoes cultivation and refinement over kalpas.
Once ignorance is shattered, the Dharma-body manifests, and the originally inherent light of wisdom suddenly bursts forth in full brilliance.
It is equal in measure to the Dharma-realm and illuminates everything without exception. This refers to the spontaneous and inconceivable activities, the various vast and great functions of karma.
This is the ultimate stage of returning from delusion to truth; one is about to ascend to Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva who receives this office sits upon a great precious lotus flower to manifest the realization of the essence. Its radiance...
The ten sites of radiance manifest the function of realization. By comprehending this radiance, one knows that it is the actual verification of the ultimate accomplishment of the causal cultivation.
