Therefore, the Bodhisattva of this stage synthesizes the causes of the three preceding stages of worthiness and the nine stages [of the Bodhisattva] to form a single, perfectly integrated ultimate fruit.
Being destined to succeed to the position of enlightenment, they are thus the crown prince of the Universal Monarch’s principal consort.
This is the symbolic representation of receiving the office through consecration. The procedure for receiving the position above is concluded. Below follows the analogy:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the crown prince born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King, whose mother is the principal queen and who is endowed with all physical marks of perfection.
That Wheel-Turning King causes this prince to sit upon a magnificent golden throne of white elephant jewels, spreads a great net-like canopy, and erects [the ceremonial banners]."
With great banners and streamers, burning incense and scattering flowers, and playing various kinds of music, he takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them within a golden vase.

The king holds this vase and pours it over the crown of the prince’s head. At that moment, he is said to have received the royal position and is counted among the number of consecrated Kṣatriya kings.
He is immediately able to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action and is also named a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).

The second analogy illustrates the aforementioned six matters; the text is slightly abbreviated and out of order. First, the analogy of "whatever body" it may be. Second, from "its turning wheel" downward, the analogy of "whatever seat" it may be.
Third, from "stretching wide" downward, the analogy of "whatever marks" it may be. Fourth, from "taking the four great elements" downward, the analogy of "whatever rank is attained.

The king represents the true body (*dharmakāya*); the hand represents the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the jar represents the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*); and the water represents [the essence].
Regarding the light of marks: there should be a third [aspect], namely, which retinue it follows, referring to the civil and military officials who serve as his assistants and counselors.
Fifth, it can clarify what kind of source it issues from.
The consecration of a bodhisattva is likewise so. Because the waters of the wisdom of all Buddhas are poured upon their crowns, it is called "receiving the office.
Because they are fully endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, they are included within the number of Buddhas.
The third [section] is the conjunction; it merely conjoins [the stages] according to the positions attained. This is the primary intent here.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the Bodhisattva’s reception of the office of great wisdom.

By means of this office of great wisdom, the Bodhisattva is able to perform immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of difficult practices and increase immeasurable merit and wisdom.
Virtue. This is called "Abiding in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.
Fourth, the summary: this concludes one section. The preceding three sections on "Attaining the Reception of the Position" are finished.
In the following text, the fourth section—beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Cloud of Dharma"—clarifies the stage of "Entering the Great Day. Regarding this:
Within this, there are five kinds of greatness: first, the greatness of wisdom; second, the greatness of liberation; third, the greatness of samādhi; fourth, the greatness of dhāraṇī;
and fifth, the greatness of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These five are based upon five meanings: first, the meaning of the true wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
1. Because of being free from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). 2. Based on the meaning of mastery over the mind, because of being free from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*). 3.
Based on the meaning of accomplishing all tasks immediately upon generating the resolve [for awakening], due to the power of concentration and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). 4.

Based on the meaning of benefiting sentient beings in accordance with all worldly needs, because the mind can universally sustain them and speech can universally comply with them. 5. Based on the capacity to deliver sentient beings.

The meaning of "arising" (*utpatti*). Because the body and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of extensive movement, the first two [powers] benefit oneself, while the latter three benefit others.
Above was the outline of the sections; below is the explanation of the text.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Dharma-Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), they know, as it truly is, the origin of the desire realm, the origin of the form realm, the origin of the formless realm;

the origin of the world-realm, the origin of the dharma-realm, the origin of the conditioned realm, the origin of the unconditioned realm, the origin of the sentient-being realm, the origin of the consciousness realm, the origin of the space realm, and the origin of the nirvāṇa realm. This Bodhisattva knows these as they truly are.

The accumulation of all views and afflictions; the knowledge of the accumulation of the formation and destruction of worlds; the knowledge of the accumulation of the practices of śrāvakas, the accumulation of the practices of pratyekabuddhas, and the accumulation of the practices of bodhisattvas;
the accumulation of the powers, fearlessnesses, form-body, and dharma-body of the Tathāgata; the accumulation of all modes of omniscience;
the demonstration of the attainment of enlightenment and the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and the entry into the discernment and resolution of all phenomena.
The Collection of Concentration and Wisdom. To state the essentials: by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one knows all collections. This section has three parts:
the first two explain individually, while the latter three provide combined illustrations. Regarding the first, the greatness of wisdom (*jñānamahātmya*), there are two divisions:

first, the individual explanation; second, the summary conclusion. Regarding the first [the individual explanation], there are seven kinds of wisdom: (1) the greatness of the wisdom of collection (*saṃgrahajñānamahātmya*); (2) the greatness of the wisdom of transformation and manifestation (*nairmāṇikajñānamahātmya*).
3. The greatness of the wisdom of the three empowerments; 4. The greatness of the wisdom that enters the subtle; 5. The greatness of the wisdom of the secret places;
6. The greatness of the wisdom that enters the kalpas; 7. The greatness of the wisdom that enters the paths. These seven arise sequentially from one another.

Now, first, the wisdom of accumulation relies on the power to sever doubt, because it realizes that phenomena are accumulated through conditions. "Accumulated through conditions" means that all phenomena depend upon the accumulation of conditions.

Because they arise [from conditions], there are two types of false causal aggregation (*mithyā-pratyaya-samudāya*): first, the aggregation of false conditions, meaning that the three realms are falsely constructed solely by the one mind, just as what is seen in a dream is understood to be nothing but the mind;
second, the aggregation of true conditions, meaning that all phenomena arise from the true mind, just as what is seen in a dream is produced by the retributive mind.
Furthermore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are three types of aggregation: first, the aggregation of objective conditions, which arises from objective conditions.
All dharmas arise from two kinds of false conditions. From those false conditions, all dharmas originate. Third is the collection of true conditions:

within the substance of true consciousness, there are inherent all the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; these mutually integrate and accumulate, and thus they are called a "collection of conditions.
In the present text, first the individual aspects are clarified, and later the essentials are raised for a concluding summary. Within the former section, there are twenty collections.
All clarify the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samudāya*). However, because this encompasses both the true and the false, as well as their synthesis, there are three divisions:
first, the defiled division; second, the pure division; and third, the cessation division. Within the text, there are six layers:

first, the purely defiled, which refers to the first four [divisions] and the collection of sentient beings, as well as the collection of various views and afflictions. Second, the purely pure, which refers to the collections of those from the śrāvakas downward. Third...
1. Cessation alone: this refers to space (*ākāśa*). 2. The four pure states combined with defilements: these refer to consciousness and the formation and destruction of the conditioned world.

3. The five pure states combined with cessation: these refer to the unconditioned and nirvāṇa. Among these, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as an unconditioned state is "pure," while non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is "cessation.
Essential purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is "cessation," while the remaining three [types of nirvāṇa] are "pure. 4. The six states encompassing both defilement and purity, and their cessation: namely—

Because of the *dharmadhātu*. The treatise states: "In accordance with whether it is correct or incorrect," because the *dharmadhātu* encompasses the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, all the phrases in the treatise contain the expression "in accordance with what is said," because [the Buddha] is able to know whatever distinctions may arise.
O Son of the Buddha! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of such supreme and superior awakening-wisdom, knows as they truly are the transformations of the karma of sentient beings,

the transformations of afflictions, the transformations of views, the transformations of worlds, the transformations of the dharma-realm, the transformations of śrāvakas, the transformations of pratyekabuddhas,
the transformations of bodhisattvas, the transformations of Tathāgatas, and all transformations of conceptualization and non-conceptualization— all such things are like [an illusion].
"Truly knowing.

Second, from "the sons of the Buddha" onwards, the wisdom of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa-jñāna*) is clarified. This section has three parts. First, the preceding is cited to introduce what follows:

because the function of transformation arises based on the previously mentioned body of accumulated wisdom (*saṃbhāra-jñāna-kāya*). Thus, the treatise says: "Based on that body, power arises. Next, "as it truly is... [The text continues].

The following section clearly elucidates [the preceding]. The subsequent "Thus" and so forth constitute the summary. Within the ten phrases of the middle section, the first three concern the sovereign transformation of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), which brings about the wholesome and unwholesome karma of sentient beings as well as their dull or sharp latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), causing sentient beings to perceive these as if they were actual acts of creation.
The phrase "in a moment" refers to the sovereign transformation of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). The subsequent five [phrases] concern the perfect awakening of wisdom.

The mastery over the world manifests as the three vehicles of perfect enlightenment; thus, there is the manifestation of the single dharma-realm, which constitutes the Dharma-practice taught for the three vehicles.
The remaining four manifestations are for the persons of the three vehicles and their fruits. The final one pervades all three worlds:
it possesses both nature and discrimination, while the vessel-world lacks discrimination. Wisdom and perfect enlightenment pervade the latter two.

Furthermore, one knows as they truly are the Buddha-holding, the Dharma-holding, the Sangha-holding, the karma-holding, the affliction-holding, the time-holding, the vow-holding, the offering-holding, the practice-holding, the eon-holding, and the wisdom-holding. All such things are known according to reality.
Third is the wisdom of empowerment according to reality as it is (*yathābhūta-adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*). The treatise states: "By the power of turning and proceeding in such and such ways.

This means that relying on those who are to be transformed, one constantly transforms them without interruption; this constitutes the practice of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-caryā*). Its manifestations are not singular;

thus the term "such" (*tathā*) is repeated. There are eleven phrases. The first three concern the non-interruption of the Three Jewels; these constitute the empowerment of the objective realm (*viṣaya-adhiṣṭhāna*). The remaining [phrases] concern other matters.

Regarding their practices: among these, the first two are practices of contrariety (*pratiloma*). Caṇḍāloka’s practice of self-immolation by fire, Anaṅgaṇa’s practice of cruelty, Vāsavadattā’s practice of lust, and Sarvārthasiddha’s practice of pervading all states are all examples of such deeds.
The latter six are practices of conformity (*anuloma*). Of these, the first four are practices that give rise to causes.
"Time" refers to the time when causes arise; "vows" and so forth constitute the essence of the cause. The latter two refer to the time when the fruit is attained; "time" here refers to long kalpas.
"Wisdom" is the essence of the fruit, meaning the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore, one knows truly the subtle wisdom with which all Buddhas and Tathāgatas enter therein, namely:

the subtle wisdom of their practice, the subtle wisdom of their passing away from life, the subtle wisdom of their taking birth, the subtle wisdom of their renunciation, and the subtle wisdom of their manifesting supernatural powers.

He knows, as they truly are, the subtle wisdom of attaining perfect enlightenment, the subtle wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma, the subtle wisdom of maintaining the lifespan, the subtle wisdom of entering parinirvāṇa, and the subtle wisdom of the endurance of the teaching; all such things he knows in accordance with reality.
The fourth clarifies subtle wisdom (*sūkṣmajñāna*). This refers to knowing the Buddha’s transformative activity (*nirmāṇaprayoga*) as being subtle and sovereign. The treatise states:

"Because it relies on that [wisdom] to perform the non-dual activity through the empowerment of the emanation and transformation. This means relying on the three aforementioned wisdoms, such as the wisdom of emanation and so forth.

These are combined into the wisdom of non-duality. Because it performs such subtle transformative functions, manifesting even a single phenomenon according to the needs of beings inherently encompasses the preceding three;
it is not merely that one of the eight phases of manifestation possesses the remaining seven.
Furthermore, one enters the secret realms of the Tathāgata, namely: the secret of body; the secret of speech; the secret of mind;
the secret of discerning the proper and improper time; the secret of bestowing predictions upon bodhisattvas; the secret of gathering sentient beings; the secret of the various vehicles;
the secret of the differences in the faculties and practices of all sentient beings; the secret of the workings of karma; and the secret of the practice for attaining awakening.
"Secret. He knows all such things as these according to reality.

Fifth, he further enters the wisdom of the lower luminous secret realm. Relying on the protection of sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature, so as not to cause them alarm or fear, he manifests the coarse while concealing the subtle;
thus, both the manifest and the secret are accomplished. The first three [lines] collectively reveal the three secrets. Next...
Third, the specific manifestation of the secret of arising and transformation has two parts: first, knowing the time for transformation through the mind;

second, bestowing predictions through speech—namely, by delaying the prediction due to indolence, or by citing those śrāvakas of actual practice to bestow predictions upon those who are merely manifested emanations. Furthermore, in the past, predictions were bestowed only upon bodhisattvas.
Thus, regarding the Śrāvakas, it is recorded as being secret; it is hidden or revealed according to their capacities. Later, there is the "secret" [aspect] of gathering sentient beings.

The *Śāstra* on the Sūtra says "gathering and subduing," which refers to both gathering (*saṃgraha*) and subduing (*nigraha*), and both pertain to body and speech. Next is the "secret" of the teaching. From the perspective of ultimate reality, there are no three, yet three are spoken of;

this very fact that three are spoken of constitutes the secret. This is solely for the purpose of transforming Bodhisattvas; from the perspective of the diverse capacities of beings, it is not a single teaching.
First, the "one" is also considered esoteric. The latter three clarify the esoteric nature in relation to that which is known:
knowing the various types of faculties, knowing the myriad differences in karma, and knowing that both adverse and favorable actions lead to bodhi; therefore, they are esoteric.
Furthermore, one knows the wisdom of all Buddhas regarding the entry into eons (*kalpa*), namely:
that one eon enters incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and incalculable eons enter one eon; that numbered eons enter unnumbered eons and unnumbered eons enter numbered eons;

that a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*) enters an eon and an eon enters a single thought-moment; that an eon enters what is not an eon and what is not an eon enters an eon; and that the eon of a Buddha enters a non-Buddha eon.
He knows as they truly are: Buddha-aeons enter non-Buddha-aeons; past and future aeons enter the present aeon, and the present aeon enters past and future aeons;
past aeons enter future aeons, and future aeons enter past aeons;
long aeons enter short aeons, and short aeons enter long aeons. All such things he knows in accordance with reality.
The sixth [knowledge] further consists of the knowledge of entering eons through lower illumination. It relies upon the mastery of sustaining life-activities and relinquishment.
That is to say, the shifting flow of eonic time is called "life-activity" (*jīva-karma*). To encompass all within one is termed "sustaining" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

To enter all within one is termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*), because it involves setting aside one's own self to identify with others. That eons revolve according to the mind is termed "mastery" (*vaśitā*).

This is also the gate of the distinct formation of phenomena separated by ten eons. Because one attains inconceivable liberation, one does not perceive length or brevity, unity or multiplicity, largeness or smallness;
rather, these mutually interpenetrate, as detailed in the "Chapter on the Arousing of the Mind."
Furthermore, one knows the various wisdoms of entry possessed by the Tathāgata. These are: the wisdom of entering the path of a single hair; the wisdom of entering atoms;

the wisdom of entering the enlightenment of the body within lands; the wisdom of entering the enlightenment of the body of sentient beings; the wisdom of entering the enlightenment of the minds of sentient beings;

the wisdom of entering the enlightenment of the conduct of sentient beings; the wisdom of entering the enlightenment that accords with all places; and the wisdom of entering the manifestation of universal activity.
Wisdom that enters into and manifests accordance with practice; wisdom that enters into and manifests contrariety to practice;

wisdom that enters into and manifests the knowledge of the conceivable and inconceivable, and the knowable and unknowable aspects of the world; and wisdom that enters into and manifests the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s conduct.

Seventh, there is also the knowledge of entering the path through the Tathāgata’s lower illumination. The treatise states that this is spoken according to the intention of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), meaning that one enters all paths;
whether proceeding in reverse or in direct order, all serve as antidotes, for there is nothing that does not constitute entry into the path. This refers to knowledge.

Regarding the path of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-mārga*): if one considers the path of ordinary beings as it pertains to the transformation through knowledge, then these very [states of] reversal and conformity are themselves the Buddha-path.

Within this, there are fourteen phrases. The first phrase generally enters into those to be transformed, namely, the "hair-path" ordinary beings (*mārga-pṛthagjana*), because they are unstable like the wind.
As the *Śāstra* on the Sūtra says: "Entering the path of ordinary beings. The *Śāstra* also says: "Relying on the stage of ordinary beings. The remaining phrases are specific.

The objects to be converted are each of three types: first, those who act out of pride (*asmimāna*), who are led to enter the wisdom of atoms (*paramāṇu-jñāna*) by contemplating the breaking down of the composite mass, because there are only atoms and no self;
second, those who rely on faith and seek birth in heaven, who enter pure lands.
Because it exceeds what is believed; as for the statement that "the rest all depend on vitarka and vicāra," therein the first phrase establishes the body of vitarka and vicāra;
the next two phrases correctly manifest the distinctions in the mental activities of vitarka and vicāra; the subsequent phrase clarifies the objects of cognition.

The aforementioned four [phrases] constitute the vitarka and vicāra of those to be transformed, while the following four phrases represent the practices of the transformer. The first [of these latter four] phrase reveals its pervasive nature.

The next two [phrases] are applied as appropriate, whether in reverse or in forward order; the final phrase concerns whether they are profound or shallow. The last four phrases transform and lead them into the fruits of the three vehicles.
O Son of the Buddha, all the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas is vast and immeasurable; Bodhisattvas on this stage are able to [comprehend it].
One attains entry.
This second section summarizes the preceding seven; all are the wisdom of the Buddha. Because Bodhisattvas are able to enter them, it is called the "Greatness of Wisdom.
The Greatness of Wisdom is concluded.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, the second is the Greatness of Illumination and Liberation, which has three parts. First is the designation of attaining the state:
that is, they attain the inconceivable liberation of a Bodhisattva, the unobstructed liberation, and the liberation of pure observation. Universally...
The liberation of illumination; the liberation of the *tathāgatagarbha*; the liberation that accords with the unimpeded wheel; the liberation of penetrating the three periods of time;
the liberation of the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*; and the liberation of the sphere of the light-wheel without remainder.

Next, there are ten brief manifestations of the lower [attainment]. Taken collectively, these are contrasted with universal wisdom (*sāmānyajñāna*). The first relies on the mastery of transformation within the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
because it cannot be reached by thought, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*), as in the attainment of Vimalakīrti.
Second, it is able to reach immeasurable worlds; because its power of wisdom through vows is without obstruction, it is called "unobstructed.
Third, it is called "pure observation" because it is liberated from hindrances. There are two aspects to being free from hindrances, both of which are known:

first, regarding their respective stages, there is a difference between what is abandoned in the mundane and supramundane realms; second, within the supramundane, there is the distinction between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Distinct. These stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) pertain equally to all three vehicles (*tri-yāna*). Among the three aforementioned [categories], the first two are explained in terms of universal application, while this one is explained in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*);

together they form a pair, elucidated by way of their general characteristics. Explaining universal application in terms of the body and manifesting wisdom in terms of the person, the next pair consists of one universal application and two types of wisdom.
The fourth is explained in terms of the mind as universal application; therefore, it is called "universal illumination," universally illuminating the capacities of sentient beings.
It transforms according to one’s will and responds universally at once, because it is like the universal gate manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.

The next two [phrases] concern the wisdom that illuminates the Dharma; the fifth is the dharma-dhāraṇī, which reveals the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the Tathāgatagarbha.
The sixth is the ability to refute the arguments of others, for it is unimpeded and perfect in refuting those arguments according to their own words; thus it is called "conformity."

Unobstructed. The next two pairs clarify the penetration of mutual inclusion through wisdom. Regarding time, penetration is explained by virtue of reaching the three periods of kalpas and being able to abide and maintain them as one wishes through mutual inclusion.
Regarding the gathering of causes and conditions, wisdom is manifested because all modes are entirely encompassed within the *dharmadhātu*;
thus it is called the "Treasury of the *Dharmadhātu*. The final two pairs clarify penetration through wisdom by way of mutual identity.
Regarding the body, it clarifies pervasiveness: because it universally illumines without departing from the single body’s wheel of light, it is the wheel of liberation-light.
Regarding time, it clarifies wisdom: because it can know the manifold within the one, it is called the "realm without remainder."
With these ten as the foremost, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gates of liberation,
all of which are attained within this tenth stage.
Hereafter, these ten are concluded with a summary of their extensive details.
In this way, they fully accomplish even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of samādhi,
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of dhāraṇī, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of supernormal powers.
Third, as stated below, this serves as a general illustration for the remaining three. The section on the Great Perfection is concluded. Below follows the section explaining the names.
O Son of the Buddha! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has mastered such wisdom and accords with immeasurable enlightenment.
One achieves skillful power of mindfulness.

Within the third section of the first major heading, "Explaining the Name," there are three parts: first, because one is able to receive the great rain-clouds of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, it is called the "Dharma-Cloud" (dharmamegha) stage;
second, the phrase "O Son of the Buddha, in this stage the Bodhisattva... and so forth, clarifies that by means of their own vows they are able to pour down rain to extinguish delusions.

Therefore, it is named the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). Thirdly, O Sons of the Buddha, because the Bodhisattvas on this stage, within a single thought-moment, clearly pour down rain that gives rise to wholesome qualities, it is named the Cloud of Dharma.
The two preceding sections were named according to what they themselves experience; now, this section is named according to its established designation.
The *Śāstra* states that it is "similar to the Cloud of Dharma" because it completely covers [all things]. Within this stage, one hears the characteristics of the Dharma.
It is "like" [the sky], because its body pervades everywhere, just as empty space does. That is to say, the cloud-like bodies of the Buddhas pervade the *dharmadhātu*;

since the rain of Dharma is vast and only this [stage] can receive it, it is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā*). The text has two parts: first, a general explanation of the virtue of being able to receive;
because the power of mindfulness is accomplished through the preceding seven wisdoms, one is able to receive many teachings. This wisdom truly accomplishes manifold virtues.
Therefore, it is called "immeasurable bodhi. This is merely a proximate explanation of the meaning of receiving and upholding.

All the immeasurable great Dharma-lights, great Dharma-illuminations, and great Dharma-rains of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions can, in a single thought-moment, be settled, received, gathered, and upheld [by this person].
It is, for example, like that of the Dragon King Sāgara.
There was a torrential downpour; except for the great ocean, all other places were unable to contain it, unable to receive it, unable to encompass it, and unable to sustain it.
In the same way, the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, the great illumination of the Dharma, the great radiance of the Dharma, and the great rain of the Dharma are likewise [incomparable];
except for Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, all other sentient beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even...
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage are all unable to settle in it, unable to receive it, unable to encompass it, and unable to maintain it.
Next, the characteristics of receiving the Dharma are specifically revealed in three parts: first, a general revelation of its abundance; second, a revelation of its abundance through enumeration;

and third, a revelation of its abundance through question and answer. Now, for the first part, there are the Dharma, the analogy, and the application. Within the Dharma, there are three sections; the first clarifies that which is received.
The Dharma is manifold. Because the Dharma received under the two great "Dharma-illuminations" (mahā-dharmāloka) is subtle, it is appropriately termed the "Secret Treasury" (guhyagarbha).
The text consists of three phrases. The first two phrases concern its nature (*svabhāva*); that is to say, the Dharma known by the three types of wisdom is the self-nature of phenomena.

"Great Dharma-illumination" is subsumed under the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), while "illumination" (*āloka*) is subsumed under the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The final phrase...
Because it is composed [for this purpose]. That is to say, it is said that he receives sentient beings like clouds and rains the rain of Dharma upon them;

thus, within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), his quality of being able to receive is revealed. A "single thought-moment" implies swiftness. Since it is both manifold and wondrous, and moreover swift, its excellence is progressively manifested.
"Able to settle" means capable of settling and receiving the text. "Receives" means to accept with faith. These two preceding [terms] regarding the reception of the text constitute the summary.
Because one contemplates and grasps the meaning; "retention" (dhāraṇī) refers to the subsequent gathering of the textual meaning, which constitutes the two types of retention.
This is explained in direct order; below, the analogy and its application will conversely demonstrate what cannot be achieved.
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the great ocean can settle, receive, gather, and sustain the torrential rains sent down by a single great nāga king;

or those of two, three, or even an infinite number of nāga kings, all falling simultaneously in a single moment—it can settle, receive, gather, and sustain them all. Why is this? Because it is immeasurably vast.
Just as a vessel is so called because it can hold, receive, contain, and sustain water, so too is it with the Bodhisattva dwelling on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
He is able to settle, receive, encompass, and maintain the light of the Dharma, the illumination of the Dharma, and the rain of the Dharma of a single Buddha;
and whether two, three, or even immeasurable Buddhas, he likewise expounds them all in a single moment of thought and at one time. For this reason, this stage is named the Cloud of Dharma.

Regarding the second section, which clarifies the many through enumeration, there is first the metaphor and then the application. The ocean is "capable of providing stability" because it receives all waters;
it is "receptive" because it does not become turbid—turbidity being like a lack of faith; it is "inclusive" because other waters enter in such numbers that they lose their original names;
and it is "sustaining" because its utility is inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said, "O Son of the Buddha, in a single thought-moment, from how many Tathāgatas can a Bodhisattva of this stage receive,
uphold, and maintain the great light of Dharma, the great illumination of Dharma, and the great rain of Dharma?"
The third question and answer clarifies the "many" through a sequence of question followed by answer.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said: "O Son of the Buddha, this cannot be known by means of calculation. I shall provide you with a simile.
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if in each of the ten directions there were ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas..."

In worlds as numerous as the atoms within other Buddha-fields, every single sentient being therein attains the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining [the teachings] and becomes an attendant to the Buddha.
Among the assembly of *śrāvakas*, they are foremost in great learning, just like the Bhikṣu Mahāvinaya under the Buddha Vajrapadmodbhava.
However, whatever Dharma one sentient being has received, others do not receive again. The Buddha...
"Son, what do you think? Are the dharmas received by these sentient beings finite or infinite?
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra replied, "Their number is extremely great, immeasurable and boundless.
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said, "O Son of the Buddha, I shall speak for you so that you may attain understanding. O Son of the Buddha, regarding this Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma..."
In the presence of a single Buddha, within the span of a single thought-moment, the great Dharma-teachings, the great illumination of the Dharma, the great rain of the Dharma,
and the treasury of the Dharma of the three periods of time that are established, received, gathered, and sustained— compared to these,
all the teachings heard and maintained by all sentient beings in as many worlds as previously mentioned do not equal even one hundredth part, nor can they be approached even by way of analogy.
The answer consists of two parts. First, it demonstrates through comparison that the Dharma received from a single Buddha is vast and manifold.
Just as it is with one Buddha, so it is with as many Buddhas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions as previously described, and even exceeding that number—immeasurable and boundless.
From each and every one of those Tathāgatas, there is the illumination of the Dharma.
Because one is able to settle, receive, gather, and uphold the Dharma-sun, the Dharma-rain, and the Dharma-treasury of the three periods of time, this stage is named "Dharma-Cloud" (Dharmameghā).

Following the example of the single Buddha cited below, the same applies to many Buddhas. As for the phrase "the Dharma-treasury of the three periods of time," it refers to the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time.
Regarding this treasury, the treatise states that within the *dharmadhātu* there are three kinds of treasuries of phenomena (*dharmatraya-dhāraṇī*).

This is intended to mean that the illumination and rain of the Dharma are stored within the *dharmadhātu*; thus, this interpretation is made because that sutra refers to it as the "Dharma-realm treasury" (*dharmadhātu-garbha*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas on this stage, by the power of their own vows, raise clouds of great compassion and thunder the great Dharma-voice.
With penetrating clarity and fearlessness as their lightning flashes, and merit and wisdom as their dense clouds, they manifest various bodies,
circulating and returning throughout the dust-motes of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions within a single thought-instant.
In that many lands, he expounds the Great Dharma and subdues the hosts of Māra.

Beyond these numbers, in lands as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds, he rains down the nectar of immortality according to the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, extinguishing the fiery dust of the karma and delusions of all beings.
For this reason, this stage is called the "Dharma" (Dharmameghā).
Clouds.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names [of the Buddhas] as "pouring rain that extinguishes delusions": herein, the clouds and so forth are explained in detail as in the "Chapter on Manifestation.

Because the cloud of compassion universally covers all, because the thunder of the Dharma awakens those in hibernation, and because it clearly manifests fearlessness, illuminates the capacities of beings, and acts with swiftness, it causes...
Because they have seen the Path, they manifest various bodies like clouds through the causes of merit and wisdom, as their forms and appearances are manifold.
Because the rain of Dharma is truly able to destroy the four māras,
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas on this stage, within a single world-system, [manifest] from descending from Tuṣita heaven down to entering Nirvāṇa, according to...
He manifests Buddha-activities according to the minds of the sentient beings to be delivered.

Whether it be two or three, or even as many lands as there are atoms in the aforementioned number of worlds, and further exceeding this, even up to as many worlds as there are atoms in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds, it is all likewise.
For this reason, this stage is named the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā).

Third, the explanation of the name "Pouring Down Rain" (*Varṣa-dhārā*) which gives rise to goodness: it may be understood through the eight aspects of gradual benefit. The fifth section, the explanation of the name, is concluded.
O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas on this stage possess clear and penetrating wisdom and mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
In the sixth major section, concerning the division of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) into those with and without superior, there are six aspects:

first, based on the internal; second, based on the external; third, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); fourth, the aspect of performing and maintaining; fifth, the aspect of causing joy; and sixth, the great excellence.
If divided according to the scriptural text, there are two parts: the first four combined form one section, which correctly reveals the supernatural powers; the latter...
Two [categories] are condensed into one: the excellence of abandonment and manifestation. Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts: first, a detailed explanation; second, a summary.

Within the detailed explanation, there are three sections. First, the explanation of the internal basis: "one whose wisdom is clear and penetrating" refers to the wisdom that gives rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which is also *dhāraṇī*.
Second, "supernormal powers" refers to the essence of the powers themselves. Third, "mastery" refers to the virtue of the powers; it also encompasses inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*).
Together with samādhi—possessing these three things, one immediately attains the unexcelled [power].
According to one's mental intention, one can transform a narrow world into a vast world, and a vast world into a narrow world.
The second [type of activity] relies on the external, meaning that its karmic function arises in dependence upon external objects.

This is also the third [point], relying on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), meaning that the activity of transformation is the characteristic of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These two scriptural passages are one in substance but divided into two in meaning.
Now, the text is explained according to specific characteristics. There are two kinds [of this]: first, the transformation of external things; within this—
Third: the mutual transformation of the concise and the extensive within the same category.
A defiled world is transformed into a pure world, and a pure world is transformed into a defiled world.
Disordered, sequential, inverted, and upright abodes—thus all immeasurable worlds can be mutually transformed into one another.
Second, the transformation of the distinction between the defiled and the pure:
either according to the mind’s intention, one may place within a single atom all the worlds, Mount Sumerus, and all mountains and rivers;
yet the characteristics of the atom remain as they were, and the worlds do not diminish. Or again, one may place two, three, or more [worlds] within a single minute atom.

Even including all the mountains, rivers, and the Sumeru mountains of unspeakably many worlds, the essential nature and characteristics of those atoms remain as they were, yet within them, all worlds appear clearly.
Or, according to his mental intention, he may manifest the adornments of two worlds within a single world, up to the adornments of unspeakably many worlds. Or, within a single world...
Within the adornment of the realms, they manifest two worlds up to unspeakably many worlds.
Or, according to their mental resolve, they place the sentient beings of unspeakably many worlds within a single world;
or, according to their mental resolve, they place the sentient beings of a single world within unspeakably many worlds, yet without causing any harm or disturbance to those sentient beings.
The containment of the three realms of dust and so forth is a manifestation of mastery;
or, according to the movement of thought, one may manifest within a single pore all the adorned phenomena of the spheres of all Buddhas.
Second, the manifestation of one’s own body should be understood. The aforementioned two [types of manifestations] rely upon external objects;
alternatively, according to the mind’s intention, within a single thought-moment, one may manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many worlds.
Each body manifests hands as numerous as those same atoms, and each hand individually holds flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
With caskets of fragrant incense, flower garlands, parasols, banners, and streamers, they made offerings to the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
Each body further manifested as many heads as there are atoms in those [lands], and each head further manifested as many tongues as there are atoms in those [lands].
In every thought-moment, they pervaded the ten directions praising the virtues of the Buddhas; or, according to their mental inclinations, they did so universally within a single thought-moment.
In the ten directions, they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment up to the entry into nirvana, as well as the adornments of their buddha-lands.
Or they manifest their bodies pervading the three periods of time, within which there are immeasurable buddhas and the adornments of their buddha-lands;
the formation and destruction of worlds are all manifested therein. Or, from a single pore of their own body, they emit...
All winds do not cause any affliction or harm to sentient beings; or, according to their mental inclinations, they may transform boundless worlds into a single great ocean.
Within the waters of this ocean, a great lotus flower appears, magnificent and adorned with radiance, completely covering immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Within it, they manifest the adornments of the great Bodhi tree, even unto the manifestation of its completion.
The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Or, within their own bodies, they manifest all the worlds of the ten directions;
the radiance of all luminous maṇi jewels, the sun, the moon, the stars, clouds, lightning, and so forth, appears without exception.

Or, by exhaling a breath from their mouths, they can shake the infinite worlds of the ten directions, yet without causing sentient beings to feel any sense of alarm or fear. Or, they manifest the winds of the ten directions.
Whether it be calamities of fire or calamities of water, or according to what sentient beings delight in their hearts, he manifests a physical body fully endowed with all ornaments;
or he manifests the body of a Buddha within his own body, or manifests his own body within the body of a Buddha;
or he manifests his own land within the body of a Buddha, or manifests the body of a Buddha within his own land.
The third is the manifestation of the sign of abiding, which means that [the activity] is constantly practiced without interruption.
Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma can manifest these and other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sovereign spiritual powers.
The second section, the summary of the supernormal powers, is concluded. Below follows the section on severing doubts and manifesting excellence.

At that time, the various bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, the four world-protecting kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā, the Śuddhāvāsa deities, Maheśvara, and all the sons of gods, all together made [these offerings].
This is the reflection: "If the power of the bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges and wisdom is such as this, what then of the Buddha?

Second, from "At that time" onwards, there is the section on severing doubts and manifesting superiority. This section has two parts: first, severing doubts; second, manifesting superiority. Now, the first part begins.
This immediately gives rise to joy because doubt has been removed. Within this, there are two parts: first, demonstrating the severance of doubt through one's own supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*);

second, severing doubt by teaching the Dharma. Regarding the first, there are two question-and-answer sequences. The first question-and-answer sequence reveals that the supernormal power is unsurpassed, causing the assembly to rejoice;
the second question-and-answer sequence reveals that the supernormal power has a superior [beyond it], causing the assembly to rejoice. The former...

In this section, the response follows the question. Within the question, first the great assembly raises a doubt: taking the Buddha as the point of comparison, they question whether the Bodhisattvas could possibly act in such a way.
They reason that while such things may be possible for the Buddha, how could it be so for a Bodhisattva?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in gold-colored speech:
"O Son of the Buddha, this great assembly has fallen into a net of doubt upon hearing of the power of the bodhisattvas' supernormal knowledge and wisdom."
"Excellent, O virtuous one! In order to sever their doubts, you should briefly manifest the deeds of a bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power.
Later, when the leaders requested him, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha immediately entered the samādhi called "The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands."

The answer consists of two parts: first, manifesting supernatural powers while in meditative concentration; second, resolving doubts through questions and answers. Now, for the first part: because he takes actual phenomena as verification, there are three sub-sections.

First, the Dharma Master enters meditative concentration. Since the essential nature of the land encompasses all without exception, he is able to contain everything within his single body without anything remaining outside.
When he entered this samādhi, all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly saw themselves within the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.

Within that space, they beheld every kind of magnificent adornment belonging to the trichiliocosm, such that even speaking for a hundred million kalpas could not exhaustively describe them. Furthermore, within that place, they saw the Bodhi tree. Its...
The circumference of its trunk spans one hundred thousand trichiliocosms, and its height reaches one million trichiliocosms;
the shade cast by its branches and leaves is likewise. Corresponding to the dimensions of the tree’s form, there is a lion throne.
Upon this throne sits a Buddha named Sarvajñābhijñārāja (King of All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers), whom the entire great assembly beholds seated beneath the Bodhi tree.
The seat of the Son was adorned with various marks and signs, such that even if one were to speak for billions of kalpas, one could not exhaustively describe them.

When the assembly below entered this state, they beheld these rare wonders, which manifested his sovereign mastery of supernatural powers; therefore, the Buddha is titled the King of Supernatural Powers (Abhijñā-rāja).
After the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had manifested such great supernormal powers, he restored the assembly so that each member returned to their original place.
At that time, the great multitude experienced what they had never known before; struck with wonder, they remained silent and gazed single-mindedly toward Vajragarbha.
The Three Vajra-Treasuries: Gathering the Functions Below and Increasing Reverence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, this samādhi is most rare and possesses great power; what is its name? Vajragarbha replied: "This samādhi is named..."
The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands. Second:
The Determination through Question and Answer. This section has three parts. First, the inquiry regarding the name;
second, the inquiry as to what the sphere of this samādhi is like. The answer states: "O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva cultivates this samādhi..."
According to what the mind contemplates, one can manifest within one's own body Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in the sands of the Ganges,
or even more than this number— immeasurable and boundless.
Second, he again asked about the scope of the lower karmic functions.
O Son of the Buddha, because a Bodhisattva dwelling on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma attains such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great samādhis,
this Bodhisattva’s physical body and physical actions, verbal speech and verbal actions, and mental mind and mental actions are unfathomable.
With sovereign mastery over supernormal powers, they observe the realm of the three periods of time, the realm of samādhi, and the realm of wisdom, sporting within all liberations.
These include the gates of transformations performed, powers of spiritual mastery performed, and radiances performed; briefly stated, even down to the lifting and lowering of a foot—
all such activities as these cannot be known even by Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of the Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī), who are like heirs to the Dharma-king.

These three categories reveal its vastness and multiplicity. Within this, there are two parts; the first merely summarizes the many concentrations, thereby demonstrating that their functional activity is inconceivable.
"O Son of the Buddha, such is the brief description of the sphere of experience of the Bodhisattva on this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma. If it were to be explained at length..."
Even if one were to spend immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one could not exhaust [the description of] them.
Later, O Son of the Buddha, when this "Cloud of Dharma" descends, it summarizes the concise and reveals the extensive; thus, the remaining virtues are inexhaustible.

This section also concerns the matters within the Great Exhaustion. Above, in the first part concerning the severing of doubts and the manifestation of excellence, the initial severing of doubts is concluded. Below—
Manifesting the supremacy of his supernormal powers,
the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha, if the sphere of a bodhisattva’s supernormal powers is such as this,
