it is the definitive name of the "Three Bonds."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom?
This is the sixth initial heading.
O Son of the Buddha, when those Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas abide in this samādhi, they are able to know all worlds of the future.
Regarding all Buddhas throughout all kalpas, this section on the two types of liberation is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the definitive activity; second, manifesting the definitive benefit. Within the first part, there are six subdivisions.
First, one comprehensively knows all Buddhas—
those already spoken of and those not yet spoken of, those already prophesied and those not yet prophesied—
with their various and distinct names, namely: innumerable names, immeasurable names, boundless names, incomparable names, and uncountable names.
He whose name is ineffable, whose name is inconceivable, whose name is immeasurable, and whose name is unspeakable—
this one of many names and epithets shall appear in the world.
He shall benefit sentient beings, act as a Dharma King, perform the Buddha-work, and preach the Dharma.
One should bring about welfare; one should praise the meaning of the wholesome; one should explain the meaning of the bright side; one should purify all evils; one should abide in merit;
one should reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); one should achieve the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*); and one should achieve omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Third, they know that they shall become Buddhas.
Those Tathāgatas have cultivated perfect conduct, made perfect vows, entered perfect wisdom, and possess a perfect assembly.
He is fully endowed with perfect adornment; he has accumulated perfect merit; he has awakened to the perfect Dharma; he has attained the perfect fruit; he possesses the perfect marks;
and he has realized perfect enlightenment.
Fourth, he fully knows that those Buddhas have perfected the causes and fulfilled the fruits;
he fully knows all such matters as the names, clans, lineages, skillful means, supernatural transformations, the ripening of sentient beings,
and the entry into parinirvāṇa of those Tathāgatas.
Fifth is the knowledge of present activities.

This bodhisattva is able, within a single thought-moment, to enter one eon, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* eons, or as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa;
he enters as many eons as there are atoms in the four continents.
Eons. Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a small thousand-world system. Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a medium thousand-world system.
Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a great thousand-world system. Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a hundred buddha-fields.
Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields. Entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* buddha-fields. Entering the infinite...
For as many eons as there are atoms in a number of Buddha-fields; entering for as many eons as there are atoms in immeasurable Buddha-fields;

entering for as many eons as there are atoms in boundless Buddha-fields; entering for as many eons as there are atoms in incomparable Buddha-fields; entering for as many eons as there are atoms in incalculable Buddha-fields;
entering for as many eons as there are atoms in inexpressible Buddha-fields; entering for as many eons as there are atoms in inconceivable Buddha-fields.
They enter eons as numerous as atoms; they enter eons as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable Buddha-fields;
they enter eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields; they enter eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
In this manner, they are able to fully comprehend with wisdom all the eons contained within all future worlds.
Sixth is the clear knowledge of the distinctions [of the factors of enlightenment]. This further manifests the functional application of meditative concentration;
because of this thorough understanding, his mind again enters ten kinds of sustaining gates (*dhāraṇīmukha*). What are these ten? They are:

by entering the sustaining gate of the Buddhas, he attains the protective mindfulness of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; by entering the sustaining gate of the Dharma, he attains...
By entering into the practice of the ten kinds of dhāraṇī-lights and inexhaustible eloquence, one gives rise to perfect and supreme vows.
By entering into the empowerment of power, one cannot be eclipsed or overcome. By entering into the empowerment of wisdom, there are no obstructions in the Buddha-dharma one practices.
By entering into the empowerment of great compassion, one turns the pure wheel of Dharma that never regresses.
By maintaining the skillful phrase of entering into distinctions, one turns the wheel of all syllables and purifies the stages of all dharma-gates.
By maintaining the entry into the dharma of the lion’s birth, one opens the locks of the Dharma and emerges from the mire of desire.
By maintaining the power of intellectual strength, one cultivates the bodhisattva practices without ever ceasing. By maintaining the power of spiritual friends, one causes boundless sentient beings—
They attain universal purity. By entering the sustaining power of non-abiding, they enter unspeakably unspeakable vast eons.
By entering the sustaining power of the Dharma, they know through unimpeded skillful wisdom that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure.
Second, the manifestation of the benefits of meditative concentration. This section has four parts: the first two concern self-benefit, and the latter two concern the benefit of others.

First, causing the mind to enter into and maintain [the teachings] brings benefit; that is, because one knows as described above, one maintains them without loss. Because one maintains them without loss, one obtains the benefit of such maintenance:

by maintaining the Buddha within a single moment of mind, one obtains the Buddha’s protective mindfulness (*ārakṣā*). Second, the mind enters into and maintains the Dharma, whereby one obtains *dhāraṇī*.

The benefit of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). The remaining phrases are to be understood by analogy. "There are twelve" refers to the increase of the number ten. "Lion-like rebirth" means not fearing the suffering of taking birth.
To demonstrate the true nature of birth and death is called "opening the lock of the Dharma.

Because one realizes that birth and death are fundamentally empty, one emerges from the mire of desire. "Sustained by the power of wisdom" refers to the simultaneous operation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Entering into the non-...
When sustained by the power of abiding, a great eon is not separate from a single thought-moment.
O Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has dwelt in this samādhi, they skillfully abide for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons;
they skillfully abide in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands; they skillfully know unspeakably unspeakable...
He speaks of the various kinds of sentient beings. He is skillfully knowledgeable regarding the distinct characteristics of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings.
He is skillfully knowledgeable regarding the common and distinct karmic retributions of unspeakably unspeakable numbers [of sentient beings].

He is skillfully knowledgeable regarding the differences in the continuities of the habitual tendencies of diligence, the faculties, and various modes of conduct among unspeakably unspeakable numbers [of sentient beings]. He is skillfully knowledgeable regarding unspeakably unspeakable...
They explain the immeasurable varieties of defiled and pure contemplations.
They are skillfully knowledgeable regarding the various meanings of unspeakably unspeakable dharmas, and the immeasurable syllables, discourses, and expressions used to expound them.

They are skillfully knowledgeable regarding the unspeakably unspeakable varieties of the appearance of Buddhas, their lineages, times, manifest signs, the teaching of the Dharma, their activities, and their entry into parinirvāṇa.
They are skillfully cognizant of unspeakably unspeakable gateways of infinite wisdom.
They are skillfully cognizant of unspeakably unspeakable, immeasurable manifestations of all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). O Son of the Buddha!

It is, for example, like when the sun rises upon the world, illuminating all villages, camps, cities, towns, palaces, houses, mountains, marshes, birds, beasts, forests, flowers, and fruits—just so [is it with these gateways].
A person with sight can clearly perceive all various kinds of objects.
O Son of the Buddha, just as the sunlight is impartial and without discrimination, yet enables the eyes to see various forms, so too is this great samādhi:
its essential nature is impartial and without discrimination, yet it enables Bodhisattvas to know unspeakably, unspeakably many hundreds of thousands [of things].
There are billions of distinct characteristics.

Second, the benefit of attaining skillfulness (*kauśalya*) consists of three parts: the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*yoga*). Now, there are two kinds of skillfulness:

first, skillfulness regarding phenomena (*vastu-kauśalya*), for which the teaching says "immeasurable and inexpressible," while the analogy says "seeing various objects. Second, skillfulness regarding reality (*yathārtha-kauśalya*)...
Because it is skillful, it is said that the sunlight is impartial. Furthermore, it is said that only when these two are unimpeded can they be called "skillful.
Therefore, it is stated together that one is able to know while remaining non-conceptual.
O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understands time in this manner, he causes all sentient beings to obtain ten kinds of non-futility.
What are these ten? First is non-futility of seeing, because it causes all sentient beings to produce roots of goodness.
Second is non-futility of hearing, because it causes all sentient beings to attain maturity. Third is non-futility of dwelling together, because it causes all...

First, because the minds of sentient beings are tamed; second, because it is non-empty in its arousal, causing all sentient beings to act according to their words and to penetrate the meaning of all dharmas;
third, because its practice is non-empty, causing infinite worlds to become completely pure;
fourth, because its proximity is non-empty, [attaining] the Tathāgatas in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
It is because they eliminate the doubts of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings.
Seventh is the non-emptiness of vows, for they cause the sentient beings they keep in mind to perform supreme offerings and fulfill all their aspirations.

Eighth is the non-emptiness of skillful means regarding the Dharma, for they cause all to abide in unimpeded liberation and pure wisdom. Ninth is the non-emptiness of raining down the rain of Dharma, for within the [unspeakably unspeakable...]
It is because they skillfully reveal the conduct of omniscience among sentient beings— whether their faculties can be described or cannot be described—
causing them to abide in the Buddha-way. Tenth is the manifestation that is not in vain, for it manifests boundless marks so that all sentient beings may receive its illumination.
One attains the non-empty benefit of the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi and attains these ten kinds of non-empty moments, the hosts of celestial kings all come to prostrate at their crown;
the hosts of nāga kings raise great clouds of incense; and the yakṣa kings prostrate before them.
The Asura Kings paid him respectful homage; the Garuḍa Kings surrounded him from front and rear;
all the Brahmā Kings came to entreat him; the Kiṃnara Kings and Mahoraga Kings all joined in praising him;
the Gandharva Kings constantly came to attend upon him; and the hosts of human kings served and made offerings to him.
Forty kings honored and sustained him.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth skillful wisdom of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Great Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom.
The definitive names of the three fetters.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of knowing the buddha-adornments of all worlds?
The seventh concentration is first introduced:
"O Son of the Buddha, for what reason is this samādhi named 'Thoroughly Knowing the Buddha-Adornments of All Worlds'?

In the second part [the explanation], there are two sections: first, clarifying the essence and function of the concentration; second, clarifying the benefits of the concentration. Within the former, there are also two parts; first—

[The author] now provides the explanation for the preceding inquiry. The reason for this repeated inquiry is that the previous one was a general inquiry regarding "certainty," whereas this is a specific inquiry regarding "adornment.
"O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they are able to enter the worlds of the eastern direction in succession;

they are able to enter the worlds of the southern direction in succession; and all the worlds of the western, northern, four intermediate directions, above, and below are likewise [entered in succession]."
In this same way, one is able to enter [the stages] in succession.
Regarding the explanation of the two [sections], first is the explanation of "all worlds. Because these are present, it simply says "the ten directions.
One sees all Buddhas appearing in the world, and also sees all the spiritual powers of those Buddhas, as well as the Buddhas themselves.
They saw all manner of playful displays; they also saw the vast majesty and power of all Buddhas,
the supreme sovereignty of all Buddhas, the great lion’s roar of all Buddhas, the various practices cultivated by all Buddhas, the diverse adornments of all Buddhas,
the miraculous transformations of the spiritual powers of all Buddhas, and the gathering of the clouds of assemblies of all Buddhas.
Second, the explanation of its adornments. This section has two parts. First, a general enumeration of ten gates, all of which constitute adornments.
Among these, the eighth—individual adornments—refers to adorning the mind with merit and wisdom, and adorning the body with physical marks and radiant light.
He clearly perceives all such things as the purity of the assembly, the vastness of the assembly, the single characteristic of the assembly, the manifold characteristics of the assembly,
the location of the assembly, the dwelling place of the assembly, the maturation of the assembly, the discipline of the assembly, and the majestic power of the assembly.
Next, the specific characteristics of the adornments are revealed in detail to expand upon the preceding two [sections]: first, the expansion of the assembly; second, the expansion of the adornments.

Regarding the first, there are three parts: first, seeing others; second, seeing oneself; third, the capacity to see. Regarding the first of these, there are also three parts: first, seeing the essential characteristics of the assembly.
He also saw assemblies whose dimensions were equal to Jambudvīpa; he also saw assemblies equal to the four continents;
he also saw assemblies equal to a small thousand-world system; he also saw assemblies equal to a medium thousand-world system;
he also saw assemblies equal in measure to a trichiliocosm; and he also saw assemblies filling hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds.
He saw buddha-fields; he also saw assemblies filling incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) buddha-fields;

he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within a hundred buddha-fields; he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within a thousand buddha-fields;
he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* buddha-fields.
He also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in countless buddha-fields;
he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable buddha-fields; he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in boundless buddha-fields;
and he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in incomparable buddha-fields.
He also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in incalculable buddha-fields;
he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in inexpressible buddha-fields;

he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in inconceivable buddha-fields; he also saw assemblies filling buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable buddha-fields.
I also see Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms of a world-system; I also see assemblies filling Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-lands;
and I also see assemblies filling Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands.
Next, the extent of what is seen is explained:
one also sees the various Buddhas within those assemblies and places of enlightenment manifesting various forms,
at various times, in various lands, with various transformations, various supernormal powers, various adornments, and various masteries.
Having witnessed various forms, dimensions, and diverse activities,
they subsequently behold the Buddha’s manifestations.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas likewise see themselves proceeding to those assemblies, and they also see themselves there, preaching the Dharma.
He also personally sees his own body upholding the Buddha’s words; he also personally sees his own body thoroughly understanding dependent origination;
he also personally sees his own body dwelling in empty space; he also personally sees his own body abiding in the Dharma-body; he also personally sees his own body free from defiled attachment;
he also personally sees his own body not dwelling in conceptual discrimination; he also personally sees his own body being without weariness; he also personally sees...
The body universally enters all wisdoms; it also perceives itself as universally knowing all meanings; it also perceives itself as universally entering all stages (*bhūmi*);
it also perceives itself as universally entering all realms of existence (*gati*); it also perceives itself as universally knowing all skillful means (*upāya*);

it also perceives itself as universally abiding before all Buddhas; it also perceives itself as universally entering all powers (*bala*); it also perceives itself as universally entering reality (*tattva*).
Likewise, they also personally see their own bodies universally entering into non-contention; they also personally see their own bodies universally entering into all dharmas.
This second illumination is the vision of oneself.
Thus, in seeing oneself, one does not discriminate between lands, one does not discriminate between sentient beings, and one does not discriminate between Buddhas. One does not...
A distinct dharma: not clinging to the body, not clinging to bodily action, not clinging to the mind, and not clinging to the intellect.
Just as all dharmas do not differentiate their own nature nor differentiate sounds, yet they do not abandon their own nature nor cease their names, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
he does not abandon his practice, following what is done in accordance with the world, yet...
Regarding these two, there is no attachment.

"Clarity" (vidyā) refers to the ability to see. This consists of the principle (*dharma*), the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis. Within the principle, it clarifies seeing without conceptualization; within the metaphor, it clarifies the signifier and the signified.
It does not say of itself, "I am the signifier and the signified," yet it does not abandon its own signified meaning, by means of the metaphor.
They know through non-conceptualization. Within this union, first they unite without abandoning; subsequently, they unite with what is below without making distinctions.
O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas behold the Buddhas’ immeasurable light and color, and their immeasurable physical forms as perfectly complete, they know them thus.
Regarding equality and purity, each is manifested before one and clearly realized.

Within the second section on the extensive adornments above, there are two parts: first, an explanation by means of the Dharma; second, an elucidation by means of a simile. Within the former, there are two further points.
First, the topical headings are set forth, briefly enumerating four kinds of adornments, all of which are clearly realized and understood.
One may see the Buddha’s body emitting various kinds of light; or see the Buddha’s body with a halo extending one fathom;
or see the Buddha’s body like the color of the blazing sun; or see the Buddha’s body with subtle and wondrous radiance; or see the Buddha’s body manifesting a pure and translucent color.
Some see the Buddha’s body as golden in color; some see the Buddha’s body as the color of vajra;
some see the Buddha’s body as deep blue; some see the Buddha’s body as infinite in color; and some see the Buddha’s body as the color of a great blue maṇi jewel.
The subsequent section provides a detailed explanation according to the specific chapters, which is divided into four parts.
First, the explanation of immeasurable light and color: some see the Buddha’s body as being seven cubits in height; some see the Buddha’s body as eight cubits;
some see it as nine cubits; some see it as ten cubits; and some see the Buddha’s body as twenty cubits in height.
Some see the Buddha’s body as thirty cubits in height; likewise, up to one hundred cubits, one thousand cubits;
or they see the Buddha’s body as one *krośa* in height, or half a *yojana*, or one *yojana*, or ten *yojanas*, or even a hundred *yojanas*.
As for their magnitude: some see the Buddha’s body as one thousand yojanas in size; some see the Buddha’s body as one hundred thousand yojanas in size;
some see the Buddha’s body as the size of Jambudvīpa; some see the Buddha’s body as the size of the four continents; some see the Buddha’s body as the size of a small thousand-world system;
some see the Buddha’s body as the size of a medium thousand-world system; some see the Buddha’s body as the size of a great thousand-world system; or they see...
The Buddha’s body is the size of a hundred great trichiliocosms; or one may see the Buddha’s body as the size of a thousand great trichiliocosms;
or one may see the Buddha’s body as the size of a hundred thousand great trichiliocosms; or one may see the Buddha’s body as the size of a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* great trichiliocosms;
or one may see the Buddha’s body as the size of countless great trichiliocosms; or one may see the Buddha’s body as the size of no...
The magnitude of the Buddha’s body is equal to the magnitude of a thousandfold world system; or one may see the Buddha’s body as being the magnitude of boundless thousandfold world systems;
or one may see the Buddha’s body as being the magnitude of incomparable thousandfold world systems; or one may see the Buddha’s body as being the magnitude of incalculable thousandfold world systems.
Some see the Buddha’s body as being the size of an incalculable trichiliocosm; some see the Buddha’s body as being the size of an inconceivable trichiliocosm;
some see the Buddha’s body as being the size of an immeasurable trichiliocosm; some see the Buddha’s body as being the size of an ineffable trichiliocosm;
or they see the Buddha’s body as being the size of an ineffable-ineffable trichiliocosm.
The measure of the world.
Second, the explanation of immeasurable forms and characteristics:
"O Son of the Buddha! In this way, the Bodhisattva perceives the Tathāgatas as having immeasurable physical marks, immeasurable forms, and immeasurable..."
They manifest immeasurable light and immeasurable nets of light, the extent of which is equal to the dharma-realm.
Within the dharma-realm, there is nowhere they do not shine, universally causing the arousal of unsurpassed wisdom.
The third explains the fulfillment of excellence above, because it reveals the fulfillment of the preceding two.
Furthermore, one sees that the Buddha’s body is free from defilement and attachment, free from obstruction, and supremely sublime and pure.
The fourth explains the aforementioned purity of equality, which simultaneously encompasses the two internal adornments.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva perceives the body of the Buddha in this way, the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases. It is like space:
it does not diminish even within the hole of a mustard seed gnawed by an insect, nor does it expand across countless worlds.
Nor does it expand. The bodies of all Buddhas are likewise thus: when seen as large, they do not increase; when seen as small, they do not decrease.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the lunar disk: to the people of Jambudvīpa, its form appears small yet it does not diminish;
to those dwelling within the moon, its form appears large yet it does not increase. So it is with the Bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva is also like this. Abiding in this samādhi, according to the inclinations of his mind, he beholds the various transformed manifestations of the bodies of all Buddhas;
he hears their words as they expound the Dharma and receives and maintains them without forgetting, yet the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
Son of the Buddha, it is, for example, like when sentient beings, after the end of their lives and as they are about to undergo rebirth, do not depart from what is seen by the mind.
Pure. It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: they do not depart from the purity seen through this profound samādhi.
Second, three metaphors are used to illustrate the middle [nature]: first, the metaphor of emptiness being without increase or decrease, which illustrates that the dharmatā-kāya cannot be increased.
Diminution. The size of emptiness ranges from the vastness of the world down to a mustard seed; it is not that the essence of emptiness itself changes.

It is like the body of the *dharmatā*, which appears differently according to the vessel of the recipient. The analogy of the second month neither increasing nor decreasing illustrates that the true, eternal form-body (*rūpakāya*) is immutable.
While there are distances in realization, the differences perceived follow the mind. The previous analogy illustrated only the Buddha’s body; this analogy [illustrates...]
This also serves as a metaphor for radiance, color, and perfect accomplishment. Third is the metaphor of objects appearing in accordance with the mind, which illustrates supreme purity:
when a Bodhisattva’s mind is pure, the Buddha appears pure; what purity or defilement could there be in the Tathāgata?
This concludes the detailed explanation of the marks of adornment.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they accomplish ten kinds of swift dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: swiftly increasing all practices to fulfill great vows; and swiftly illuminating the world with the light of the Dharma.

May you swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma through skillful means to deliver and liberate sentient beings. May you swiftly manifest the pure buddha-fields of all Buddhas in accordance with the karma of sentient beings.
May you swiftly enter the ten powers through the wisdom of equality. May you swiftly dwell together with all Tathāgatas.
May you swiftly destroy the armies of Māra through the power of great compassion. May you swiftly sever the doubts of sentient beings and cause them to give rise to joy.
They swiftly manifest miraculous transformations according to their resolute convictions; they swiftly purify all worlds through various sublime Dharma teachings and expressions.

The second major section clarifies the benefits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It briefly enumerates seven kinds of benefits, each distinguished by the term "Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*).
The first is the benefit of swiftly accomplishing practice and vows, which may be understood through its heading, inquiry, and explanation.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further attains ten kinds of Dharma-seals that seal all phenomena.
What are these ten? First, they share the same roots of goodness as all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Second, they share with all Tathāgatas the attainment of the Dharma-body of boundless wisdom. Third, they share with all Tathāgatas the dwelling in the non-dual Dharma.
Fourth, they are equal to all Tathāgatas in observing that the infinite realms of the three periods of time are entirely equal.

Fifth, they are equal to all Tathāgatas in attaining the unimpeded realm of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Sixth, they are equal to all Tathāgatas in accomplishing the ten powers (*daśabala*) so that their conduct is unimpeded.
Seventh, they are equal to all Tathāgatas in forever severing the two modes of action and abiding in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Dharma. Eighth, they are identical to all Tathāgatas in their ceaseless teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
Ninth, they are identical to all Tathāgatas in their ability to skillfully observe the skillful means of wisdom and the skillful meanings [of the teachings].
Tenth, they are identical to all Tathāgatas in being equal and non-dual with all Buddhas.
The second Dharma Seal is identical to that of the Buddha’s benefit. It consists of ten phrases in five pairs: the first two pair merit and wisdom;
the next two pair the objects and cognitions of the two truths; the next two pair essence and function; the next two pair the two benefits; and the final two pair skillful means and impartiality.

O Son of the Buddha! If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes this skillful means of the gateway to the Great Samādhi that knows the Buddha-adornments of all worlds, they are one who has no teacher, for they enter all Buddha-dharmas spontaneously without relying on the instruction of another;
they are a true man, for they are able to awaken all sentient beings; they are pure, for they know...
Because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, he is the foremost. Because he is able to deliver all the world, he is the one who brings comfort.

Because he is able to enlighten all sentient beings, he is the one who abides securely. Because he causes those not yet established in the Buddha-lineage to become so established, he is the one with true knowledge.
Because he enters the gateway to all-knowledge, he is the one free from divergent thoughts. Regarding that which is...
Because it is said that there is no duality; this is one who dwells in the treasury of the Dharma, for they have vowed to fully comprehend all Buddha-dharmas.
This is one who can rain down the rain of Dharma, for they cause all sentient beings to be fully satisfied according to their mental inclinations.
The third is the benefit of maturing others through virtue.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, who places a maṇi jewel within his topknot;

by the power of that jewel, his majestic radiance becomes even more magnificent. When that King of the Devas first obtained this jewel, he attained ten qualities that surpassed all other [thirty-three] gods.
Three days. What are these ten? First, physical appearance; second, bodily form; third, manifestation; fourth, retinue; fifth, requisites; sixth, voice;
seventh, supernormal powers; eighth, mastery; ninth, wisdom and understanding; tenth, the application of knowledge.
In these ten ways, the Bodhisattva completely surpasses all the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The Mahāsattva is also like this. When first attaining this samādhi, they obtain ten kinds of vast treasuries of wisdom.
What are these ten? First, the wisdom that illuminates all buddha-fields; second, the wisdom that knows the births of all sentient beings;
third, the wisdom that universally manifests transformations throughout the three periods of time; fourth, the wisdom that universally enters into one...
1. The wisdom of the body and mind of all Buddhas; 2. The wisdom that thoroughly penetrates all Buddha-dharmas; 3. The wisdom that universally encompasses all pure dharmas; 4.
The wisdom that causes all sentient beings everywhere to enter the Dharma-body; 5. The wisdom of the pure universal eye that directly perceives all phenomena; 6.
The wisdom of sovereign mastery that reaches the further shore in all respects; 7. The wisdom of peaceful abiding... [and so forth].
The fourth wisdom-virtue, which encompasses and benefits, consists of dwelling in the knowledge that universally exhausts all vast dharmas without remainder.
Within this, there are two parts: first the metaphor, then the application (the *yoga*), each having ten phrases.

In the application, the initial attainment is summarized and then matched; specifically, one attains ten phrases corresponding to the ten matters mentioned previously. Only the eighth and ninth [phrases] are out of order.
Although wisdom is a single entity, it is differentiated according to its objects of knowledge: first, the merging of the physical characteristics of a single Buddha-field;

second, the merging of the bodily forms of sentient beings; third, the manifestation of transformations and emanations; fourth, the merging of entry into the Buddha’s retinue, because they act as mutual leaders and companions like members of a family;
fifth, the thorough penetration of the Buddha-dharma as the requisites for the path; and sixth, the universal gathering of purity.
1. The Dharma-principle manifests the perfect sound to people. 2. All seven [faculties] cause one to enter the Dharma; this is spiritual power (*abhijñā*). 3.
The universal eye is pure, transcending and uniting with wisdom and understanding. 4. Sovereignty returns to unite with sovereignty. 5. Abiding in the Dharma unites with the function of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they further attain ten kinds of most pure and majestic bodies.
What are these ten? First, in order to illuminate unspeakably unspeakable worlds, they emit unspeakably unspeakable wheels of light.
Second, in order to cause all worlds to become completely pure, they emit...
First, [he manifests] unspeakably unspeakable wheels of light with immeasurable forms and colors.
Second, for the sake of taming sentient beings, he emits unspeakably unspeakable wheels of light.
Third, for the sake of drawing near to all Buddhas, he magically creates unspeakably unspeakable bodies. Fourth, for the sake of serving and making offerings to all Buddhas...
The Buddha therefore rains down unspeakably unspeakable clouds of various exquisite fragrant flowers.

Sixth, in order to serve and make offerings to all Buddhas and to subdue all sentient beings, he manifests within each and every pore unspeakably unspeakable varieties of musical instruments. Seventh, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity...
They manifest unspeakably, unspeakably many varieties of immeasurable sovereign spiritual transformations.
Eighth, in order to inquire about the Dharma from all Buddhas under various names throughout the ten directions, they leap over unspeakably, unspeakably many worlds in a single step.
Ninth, they act so that for all sentient beings who see or hear them, it shall not be in vain.
Therefore, he manifests an unspeakably unspeakable variety of immeasurable, pure physical forms,
the crown of whose head no one can see. Tenth, in order to reveal and teach immeasurable secret dharmas to sentient beings,
he utters unspeakably unspeakable sounds and speech.
Fifth is the benefit of the body’s majestic excellence. This consists of a heading and an explanation.
"O Son of the Buddha! Once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained these ten kinds of most pure and majestic bodies, they are able to cause sentient beings to attain ten kinds of perfection.
What are the ten? First, they are able to cause sentient beings to behold..."
First, [it causes] the Buddha; second, it enables sentient beings to have deep faith in the Buddha; third, it enables sentient beings to hear the Dharma;
fourth, it enables sentient beings to know that there are Buddha-worlds; fifth, it enables sentient beings to see the Buddha’s miraculous transformations;
sixth, it enables sentient beings to recollect the karma they have accumulated; seventh, it enables sentient beings to attain a concentrated mind.
It is perfected. Eighth, it can cause sentient beings to enter the purity of the Buddha. Ninth, it can cause sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Tenth, it can cause sentient beings to perfect the Buddha-wisdom.
The sixth is the benefit of bringing others to fulfillment. First, the preceding section is cited to introduce the subsequent one; then, the names and characteristics are inquired into:
"O Son of the Buddha, once bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have caused sentient beings to attain the ten kinds of fulfillment, they further perform ten kinds of buddha-activities for those sentient beings.
What are these ten? They are: performing buddha-activities through sound in order to bring them to maturity."
For the sake of sentient beings, they perform buddha-work through physical forms; for the sake of taming sentient beings, they perform buddha-work through mindfulness;
for the sake of purifying sentient beings, they perform buddha-work by shaking the worlds;

for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave the evil realms, they perform buddha-work through skillful means and awakening; for the sake of preventing sentient beings from losing mindfulness, they perform buddha-work through...
Manifesting signs within dreams constitutes a buddha-work for the sake of causing sentient beings to maintain constant right mindfulness.

Emitting great rays of light constitutes a buddha-work for the sake of universally gathering in all sentient beings. Cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva constitutes a buddha-work for the sake of causing sentient beings to abide in supreme vows.
Attaining perfect enlightenment constitutes a buddha-work for the sake of causing sentient beings to know...

Because of the nature of illusory dharmas; because he performs the Buddha-work of turning the sublime wheel of Dharma by preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes without missing the proper time;
because he performs the Buddha-work of manifesting a dwelling life-span in order to discipline all sentient beings;
and because he performs the Buddha-work of manifesting parinirvāṇa so that sentient beings may recognize when they have become weary and exhausted.
The seventh is the benefit of performing buddha-work through transformation.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s seventh skillful wisdom of the great samādhi that thoroughly knows the buddha-arrays of all worlds.
The Third: Conclusion of the Title.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning commented upon by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Temple;
and the essentials extracted by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Kuāngshān, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Seven, Part Three: The Ten Samādhis.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of the diverse bodies of all sentient beings?
The eighth is the Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of All Sentient Beings. First, the title is stated:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they attain ten kinds of non-attachment.
What are these ten? Namely: non-attachment to all lands, non-attachment to all directions, and non-attachment to all..."
They are non-attached to eons; they are non-attached to all assemblies; they are non-attached to all dharmas;
they are non-attached to all bodhisattvas; they are non-attached to all bodhisattva vows;
they are non-attached to all samādhis; they are non-attached to all buddhas; they are non-attached to all stages. These are the ten.
The second explanation is divided into five parts: first, clarifying the wisdom that enters; second, manifesting the characteristics of entering and emerging;
third, clarifying the benefits of entering meditative concentration; fourth, clarifying mastery over the objective sphere; and fifth, summarizing the ultimate state. Regarding the first:
by attaining ten kinds of non-attachment, one achieves mastery over subsequent entry and emergence. "All stages" refers to the Buddha-stage, the Bodhisattva-stages, and so forth.
O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter this samādhi? How does he emerge from it?

O Son of the Buddha, regarding this samādhi, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters through his internal body and emerges through his external body; he enters through his external body and emerges through his internal body.

Entering with one body, they arise in another body; entering with another body, they arise in one body. Entering with a human body, they arise in the body of a yakṣa; entering with the body of a yakṣa, they arise in the body of a nāga;
entering with the body of a nāga, they arise in the body of an asura; entering with the body of an asura, they arise in the body of a deva;
entering with the body of a deva, they arise in the body of a Brahmā king; entering with the body of a Brahmā king, they arise in the body of the desire realm.

Regarding the two aspects of entering and exiting, there are two parts: first, the raising of the inquiry; second, the explanation of the characteristics. Within this, there is first the teaching and then the analogy.

In the teaching, ten categories are briefly distinguished to represent their inexhaustibility. First, the entering and exiting are clarified through the mutual correspondence of various types of primary retributions (*vipāka*).
From among the devas, they arise entering the hells; from the hells, they arise entering the human realm; from the human realm, they arise entering other destinies.
From a thousand bodies, they arise entering a single body; from a single body, they arise entering a thousand bodies; from ten billion bodies, they arise entering a single body;
and from a single body, they arise entering ten billion bodies.

In the second heaven, the dependent retribution of the six destinies is clarified through their entering and emerging; within the three thousand bodies, the one and the many correspond to one another:
from among the multitude of beings in Jambudvīpa, they enter into the multitude of beings in Aparagoyānī and emerge from among the multitude of beings in Aparagoyānī;
they enter into the multitude of beings in Uttarakuru and emerge from among the multitude of beings in Uttarakuru. From among the multitude of beings in Uttarakuru...
From among the assembly of beings in Pūrvavideha in the east, he arises; from among the assembly of beings in Pūrvavideha, he enters the assembly of beings in the three continents and arises;
from among the assembly of beings in the three continents, he enters the assembly of beings in the four continents and arises;
from among the assembly of beings in the four continents, he enters the assembly of beings distinguished by all the oceans.
Emerging from among all the various assemblies of sentient beings in the oceans, they enter among the assemblies of ocean deities and emerge.
This clearly demonstrates the entering and emerging in relation to the great oceans of the four continents.

From within the assembly of all ocean deities, they emerge from the great element of all ocean water; from within the great element of all ocean water, they emerge from the great element of all ocean earth;
from within the great element of all ocean earth, they emerge from the great element of all ocean fire;
from within the great element of all ocean fire, they emerge from the great element of all ocean wind; from within the great element of all ocean wind...
Entering into all four great elements, he arises from within them. Entering into all four great elements, he arises from within the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Entering into the dharma of non-arising, he arises from within Mount Sumeru. Entering into Mount Sumeru, he arises from within the mountains of the seven precious jewels.
Entering into the mountains of the seven precious jewels, he arises from within all the various crops, forests, and Black Mountains upon the earth.
From within all the various crops, forests, and Black Mountains of all stages, they emerge amidst the adornments of all exquisite fragrances, flowers, and jewels.

The phenomena of the five great elements manifest through their mutual correspondence of entering and exiting; yet that which is the dharma of non-arising arises by riding upon the four great elements.
I have come for this very purpose.
From within the midst of all exquisite fragrances, flowers, and jewel adornments, I emerge from among all sentient beings taking birth throughout the four continents, below and above.
Sixth, regarding the clarity of entering and exiting through mutual correspondence with the various directions:
from among all sentient beings below and above in all four continents, he enters into the midst of the assembly of sentient beings within a small chiliocosm and arises therefrom;
from within the assembly of sentient beings in a small chiliocosm, he enters into the assembly of a medium chiliocosm.
Arising from among the assembly of beings in a medium chiliocosm, they enter the assembly of beings in a great trichiliocosm and arise from it.
From among the assembly of beings in a great trichiliocosm, they enter the assembly of beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great trichiliocosms and arise from it.
[From among the assembly of beings] in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great trichiliocosms...
From among the multitudes of sentient beings, they enter the multitudes of sentient beings in countless worlds and emerge from them;

from among the multitudes of sentient beings in countless worlds, they enter the multitudes of sentient beings in immeasurable worlds and emerge from them; from among the multitudes of sentient beings in immeasurable worlds, they enter the multitudes of sentient beings in boundless Buddha-fields and emerge from them;
from among the multitudes of sentient beings in boundless Buddha-fields, they enter the multitudes of sentient beings in the... [unspecified] worlds and emerge from them.

They arise from among the multitudes of sentient beings in immeasurable Buddha-fields; they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in immeasurable Buddha-fields and arise from among the multitudes of sentient beings in incalculable worlds;
they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in incalculable worlds and arise from among the multitudes of sentient beings in inexpressible worlds;
they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in inexpressible worlds and arise from among the multitudes of sentient beings in inconceivable worlds.
They emerge from among the multitudes of sentient beings in one world and enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in an inconceivable world;
they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in an immeasurable world and emerge from among the multitudes of sentient beings in an immeasurable world;

they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in an ineffable world and emerge from among the multitudes of sentient beings in an ineffable world; they enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in an ineffable world... [and so on].
They arise from among the multitudes of sentient beings in unspeakably many worlds.
By comparing the numbers of the seven classes of beings, their entry and emergence are clarified.
They enter among the multitudes of sentient beings in unspeakably unspeakable worlds and arise from among the multitudes of defiled sentient beings.
They enter from among the assembly of afflicted sentient beings and arise within the assembly of purified sentient beings;
they enter from among the assembly of purified sentient beings and arise within the assembly of afflicted sentient beings.
Eighth, the entry and emergence are clarified through the mutual relationship between defilement and purity:

from the eye-base one enters and emerges from the ear-base; from the ear-base one enters and emerges from the eye-base; from the nose-base one enters and emerges from the tongue-base; from the tongue-base one enters and emerges from the nose-base;
from the body-base one enters and emerges from the mind-base; from the mind-base one enters and emerges from the body-base; and from one’s own base one enters and emerges from another’s.
Arising from one place, entering another place, and arising from one’s own place.
Ninth, the relative emergence and entry of the various realms:
entering into a single atom and arising within the atoms of countless worlds; [entering] within the atoms of countless worlds...
Entering a single atom, they arise; Śrāvakas enter and Pratyekabuddhas arise. Pratyekabuddhas enter and Śrāvakas arise. One’s own body enters and the Buddha-body arises;
the Buddha-body enters and one’s own body arises. A single thought-moment enters and ten billion eons arise; ten billion eons enter and a single thought-moment arises.
Identical thoughts enter and distinct times arise; distinct times enter and identical thoughts arise. The prior limit enters and the posterior limit arises.
The future enters the past and arises; the past enters the present and arises; the present enters the past and arises.

The three periods of time enter a single moment and arise; a single moment enters the three periods of time and arises. True Suchness enters verbal expression and arises; verbal expression enters True Suchness and arises.

The tenth section, "Various Clarifications," elucidates the mutual relations among various categories and clarifies their entry and exit—namely, the coarse and the subtle, the ordinary and the sage, thought-moments and kalpas, and the real and the false.

The meaning of these entries and exits is as explained in the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (*Bhadrapāla-pṛcchā*): the former portion provides the doctrinal exposition, while the latter portion reveals it through analogies.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a person possessed by a spirit, whose body trembles and cannot find rest;
though the spirit does not manifest its own form, it causes the other's body to act thus. So too is it for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi:
his own body enters meditative absorption while another’s body emerges from it, and another’s body enters meditative absorption while his own body emerges from it.

The second section, "Illustrations," contains four metaphors that illustrate the ten preceding categories, each with its corresponding application of the Dharma (*dharmasama*). The first is the metaphor of a person supported by a ghost's power;
this illustrates the first and fourth [categories], as it primarily concerns the body.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a corpse that, through the power of a mantra, is able to rise and move; whatever task it performs is accomplished.
Although the corpse and the mantra are distinct from one another, they can harmonize to achieve that purpose.

It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi: entering meditative absorption within one sphere of objects, yet arising [in action] within another sphere of objects. Within another sphere...
Entering meditative absorption, they arise within the same objective realm.

The second [section] is the analogy of the mantra that raises a corpse; it serves as a metaphor for the second, fifth, and sixth [stages]. For the most part, this speaks of the objective realm of the dependent retribution.
"O Son of the Buddha! It is like a bhikṣu who has attained mastery over the mind, who may manifest many bodies from a single body, or [manifest a single body from] many..."
One body manifests as one body; it is not that one body perishes and many bodies arise, nor that many bodies perish and one body arises.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi: one body enters meditative concentration and many bodies emerge, while many bodies enter meditative concentration and one body emerges.
The third is the parable of the Arhat manifesting supernatural powers, which illustrates the third and seventh [stages]. This is because they primarily concern numerical categories.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the great earth, whose taste is of one kind, yet the crops it produces have various distinct tastes;
though the earth itself has no differentiation, its flavors differ. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi is also like this.

This is so; there is no conceptual discrimination. However, there is a case where one enters meditative absorption with a single mode but emerges from it in many modes, and another where one enters in many modes but emerges in a single mode.

The fourth emergence—the analogy of the single sprout from many seeds—illustrates the latter three gates. Because these various aspects are explained in combination, they are presented as a unified illustration.
The principles of the text reveal themselves through reflection.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they receive praise from ten kinds of praiseworthy qualities. What are these ten?
They are as follows: because they have entered into True Suchness (tathatā), they are called Tathāgata; because they have awakened to all phenomena...
He is called a Buddha because he is praised by all the world; he is called a Dharma-preacher because he knows all dharmas;
he is called the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) because he understands all phenomena; he is called the Place of Refuge because he is the locus of reliance for all the world;
he is called the Guide because he has thoroughly mastered the skillful means of all dharmas; and he leads all sentient beings into *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
Because he has realized the Path, he is called the Great Guide. Because he is the lamp for all the world, he is called the Radiance.

Because his resolve is perfected and his purpose accomplished, and because he has completed all that was to be done and dwells in unimpeded wisdom, discerning and understanding all phenomena, he is called the Sovereign of the Ten Powers.
Because he has thoroughly penetrated all wheels of Dharma, he is called the All-Seeing One.
These are the ten.
Within the third benefit of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there are three parts. First is the benefit of attaining praise equal to that of the Buddha’s fruition.

In all cases, the upper phrase clarifies the meaning, while the lower phrase provides the designation. Regarding the meaning of the "ten powers" (*daśabala*), the phrase "the mind's resolve is perfected" clarifies the power of self-benefit.
The meaning [of "power"] is as follows: the accomplishment of benefit and profit manifests the power of benefiting others; the completion of all tasks demonstrates the perfection of power;
abiding in unimpeded wisdom generally reveals the essence of power; and the analytical knowledge of all phenomena universally clarifies the function of power.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they further attain ten kinds of radiant illumination.
What are these ten? They are: attaining the radiance of all Buddhas, because of being equal to them;

attaining the radiance of all worlds, because of being able to universally adorn and purify them; and attaining the radiance of all sentient beings, because of going everywhere to tame and transform them.
Therefore, they attain the light of immeasurable fearlessness, for they expound the Dharma with the dharma-realm as their arena;

they attain the light of non-differentiation, for they know that all phenomena have no manifold nature; they attain the light of skillful means, for they enter into realization at the limit of detachment from all phenomena;
they attain the light of reality, for their minds are equanimous at the limit of detachment from all phenomena.
Because they are equal; because they attain the light of spiritual transformations that pervades all worlds and, being empowered by the Buddha, never ceases;
because they attain the light of skillful reflection, reaching the shore of mastery of all Buddhas;
because they attain the light of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena, skillfully expounding everything within a single pore—these are the ten.
The Illumination and Benefit of the Wisdom of the Two Bodies.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they further attain ten kinds of non-action.
What are these ten? They are: non-action in bodily karma, non-action in vocal karma, non-action in mental karma, [and non-action in] supernormal power...

These are the ten acts of non-action: the act of non-action through universal penetration; the act of non-action through realizing that phenomena have no intrinsic nature; the act of non-action through knowing that karma is indestructible;
the act of non-action through non-discriminative wisdom; the act of non-action through the wisdom of non-arising; the act of non-action through knowing that phenomena are without cessation;
and the act of non-action through conforming to the letter without violating the meaning. These are the ten.
The three types of karma function through non-action to bring benefit.

The above concludes the explanation of the benefits of entering meditative concentration. O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, there are immeasurable realms with various distinctions, namely:
entering one and arising many; entering many and arising one; entering the same and arising differently; entering differently and arising the same; and entering the subtle and arising the coarse.

Arising from the coarse, one enters the subtle; arising from the great, one enters the small; arising from the small, one enters the great. Entering in forward order, one arises in reverse order; entering in reverse order, one arises in forward order.
Entering the formless, one arises with a body; entering that which has a body, one arises formless.

Entering the signless, one arises with signs; entering that which has signs, one arises signless. Within arising, one enters; within entering, one arises. All such instances are the self-nature of this samādhi.
Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
The fourth section clarifies mastery over the objective realm. First the teaching, then the analogy. Now, for the first part:

whereas the preceding second section only explained entering and arising, this section additionally explains various objective realms such as the forward and reverse orders, existence and non-existence, and so forth. Regarding "arising within entering":

Because it is the very function of quiescence within that which is employed; because it is the very function of cessation within that which arises therein. Thus one knows that the meditative concentration of a Bodhisattva is characterized by constant entry and constant emergence.
Only when there is the constant duality of entering and emerging, yet no entering or emerging at all, does one attain mastery.
To manifest this mastery, it is elucidated through the interlacing of various objective realms.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a master of illusions who, having perfected his incantations, is able to manifest various distinct forms and appearances.
Although the incantation and the illusion are distinct, the incantation is able to produce the illusion.

The incantation is merely sound, yet it can magically create the various forms known by the eye-consciousness, the various sounds known by the ear-consciousness, the various fragrances known by the nose-consciousness, and the various [flavors] known by the tongue-consciousness.

Just as there are various tastes known by the tongue-consciousness, various tangibles known by the body-consciousness, and various objects known by the mental consciousness, so too it is for the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi:
he enters meditative absorption within the same and emerges from absorption within the different;
he enters meditative absorption within the different and emerges from absorption within the same.

The second section, "Revealing the Meaning through Similes," contains six similes, each with its own application (*yōjina*). The first is the simile of the illusory manifestation of the six sense objects, which illustrates the preceding [discussion on] similarity and difference.
"O Son of the Buddha, it is as if when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are engaged in battle with the Asuras, the gods achieve victory."
The asuras were defeated and retreated. The body of the Asura King was seven hundred yojanas tall, and he was surrounded by fourfold armies numbering in the many tens of millions.
By the power of his illusory arts, he led his host of troops and entered simultaneously into the hollow of a lotus fiber.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. Having already perfectly accomplished the stage of illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna-bhūmi*), illusory wisdom is itself the Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva is himself illusory wisdom.
Therefore, he is able to enter meditative concentration within the undifferentiated dharma and arise within differentiated dharmas;
he enters meditative concentration within differentiated dharmas and arises within the undifferentiated dharma.
Second is the parable of the two asuras hiding away. This illustrates the preceding two pairs of coarse and subtle, and large and small.
When viewed in relation to principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), non-differentiation is "subtle" and differentiation is "coarse," because principle is subtle and phenomena are coarse.

Alternatively, non-differentiation is "coarse" because the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) interpenetrate; differentiation is "subtle" because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) interpenetrate. Non-differentiation is "large" because it pervades all phenomena.

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): if there is a distinction, it is minor according to the specific case. If one were to clarify "small" and "large" solely by way of the phenomena themselves, they would both be subsumed under the category of differentiation.
Son of the Buddha, it is like a farmer sowing seeds in a field: the seed is placed below, yet the fruit grows above.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi: he enters meditative absorption within the one and arises within the many; within the many...

Emerging from one moment of meditative concentration, there is the third analogy of farmers sowing seeds. This analogy clarifies the synthesis of the upper and lower realms, as well as the unity and multiplicity.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the union of the red and white elements of a man and a woman; therein, some sentient beings may take birth. At that time...
This is called the stage of *kalala*. From this point on, it dwells in the mother’s womb in succession for ten full months.
By the power of wholesome karma, all its limbs and members are fully developed; the sense faculties are unimpaired and the mind is clear and lucid.
Although the *kalala* and those six sense faculties have distinct physical forms, it is through the power of karma that they are able to develop in succession.
Just as one achieves various karmic fruits that are similar or dissimilar to the cause, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
From the stage of the *kalala* of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), through the power of faith, understanding, and aspiration, they gradually increase; their mind becomes vast, spontaneous, and sovereign.
They enter meditative absorption within non-existence and arise within existence; they enter meditative absorption within existence and arise within non-existence.
Fourth is the analogy of conception and growth. This illustrates having a body and being without a body, because it arises from non-existence to existence.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a dragon palace that stands upon the earth and does not rely on empty space;
the dragon dwells within the palace and is likewise not in the air, yet it can raise clouds that fill the sky. When someone looks up and sees the palace, you should know this.
All these are like cities of the *gandharvas* and not the palaces of the nāgas. O Son of the Buddha, although the nāgas dwell below, their clouds spread above;
likewise, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they enter from the signless (*animitta*) into the signful (*sanimitta*), and arise from the signful into the signless.
The fifth is the parable of the dragon descending from the clouds and ascending. This illustrates that which has marks and that which is markless.
Son of the Buddha, it is like this: for example, there is the palace where the Great Brahmā King Subhakṛtsna dwells, named the "Supremely Pure Treasury of All Worlds.
Within this great palace, one can see throughout the four continents of the trichiliocosm.

The palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, the palaces of the yakṣas, the palaces of the gandharvas, the palaces of the asuras, the palaces of the garuḍas, the palaces of the kiṃnaras, and the palaces of the mahoragas;
the dwelling places of the human realm and the three evil paths; Mount Sumeru and various other mountains;
the great oceans, rivers, marshes, ponds, and springs; and cities, villages, groves, and multitudes of jewels.
All these various kinds of adornments, extending to the very limits of the Great Cakravāḍa mountains and even into the sky,
were manifested within the Brahma palace without exception, just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this Great Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of All Sentient Beings,
they know various lands, see various Buddhas, deliver various assemblies, realize various dharmas, accomplish various practices,
fulfill various understandings, enter various samādhis, manifest various supernormal powers, attain various wisdoms, and dwell in various lands.
That limit.

The metaphor of the universal manifestation of the six Brahma palaces illustrates entering the upper from within, arising from within as one arises, and the mutual correspondence of the forward and reverse sequences;
therefore, it is called "various."
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches the further shore of ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are these ten?
They are: reaching the further shore of the supernormal powers of all Buddhas that exhaustively fill empty space and pervade the Dharma-realm;

reaching the further shore of the ultimate, non-differentiated, sovereign supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas; and reaching the ability to initiate the vast practices and vows of Bodhisattvas and enter into suchness...
They have reached the perfection of spiritual powers regarding the gateways of coming and going; they have reached the perfection of spiritual powers that can shake all worlds and purify all realms;
they have reached the perfection of spiritual powers that can freely know the inconceivable karma and its fruits of all sentient beings as being like illusions and transformations;
and they have reached the perfection of spiritual powers that can freely know the coarse and subtle aspects of all samādhis.
They reach the perfection of supernatural powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) that distinguishes the characteristics of entering and departing;
they reach the perfection of supernatural powers that generates great vows within the realm of the Tathāgatas by being able to enter it with valor;

they reach the perfection of supernatural powers that can manifest emanations of Buddhas, turn the wheel of Dharma, and subdue sentient beings, causing them to produce the seeds of Buddhahood, enter the Buddha-vehicle, and swiftly attain accomplishment. They reach...
They are able to comprehend all ineffable secret phrases and turn the wheel of Dharma,

causing hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ineffably ineffable Dharma-gates to attain the purity of the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They reach the perfection of supernormal powers that,
without depending on days, nights, months, years, or kalpas, can manifest throughout the three periods of time in a single thought-moment.
These are the ten.
Fifth, the summary of the ultimate:
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the eighth great power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the differentiation of the bodies of all sentient beings.
This concludes the eighth samādhi, the "Certainty of Names," which obscures skillful wisdom.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi called "Mastery over the Dharmadhātu"?
The ninth is the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm. First, the title is stated:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters samādhi within his own sense-base of the eye, up to the sense-base of the mind;
this is called 'Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm.'"

In the second [section], the explanation, there are four parts: first, revealing the essence and function of meditative concentration; second, clarifying the benefits of accomplishing concentration; third, illustrating through metaphors; and fourth, summarizing the dual practice.
Regarding the first [part], it is divided into three sections. The first is the general revelation of the name and essence:
that is, because one attains mastery over the dharmadhātu of the eye and so forth.
The Bodhisattva enters this samādhi within each and every pore of his own body.

Second, this clarifies the locus of entry into meditative concentration; that is, he enters the concentrations of the eye and so forth within the pores, manifesting mastery over their mutual functioning.
They are naturally able to know all worlds; they know the phenomena of all worlds; they know all world-systems; they know billions of nayutas of world-systems;
they know incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) world-systems; they know world-systems as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
He saw that within all worlds, Buddhas had appeared and were surrounded by assemblies of bodhisattvas;
these were entirely filled, luminous and pure, purely wholesome and unadulterated, vast and magnificently adorned, and embellished with various kinds of precious jewels.
The third is the power of meditative mastery (*samādhi-vibhutva*). Within this, there are four aspects. The first is the thorough knowledge of the three periods of time.
Regarding these, the Bodhisattva—whether for one eon, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, ten million eons, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of eons—[remains in meditative mastery].
For incalculable eons, immeasurable eons, boundless eons, incomparable eons, uncountable eons, ineffable eons,
inconceivable eons, unfathomable eons, unspeakable eons, unspeakably unspeakable eons,
and for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without ever ceasing.
Next, they practice for many eons.
Furthermore, throughout such immeasurable eons, they abide in this samādhi, both entering and arising from it;
they also bring worlds to completion, tame sentient beings, fully comprehend the dharma-realm, universally know the three periods of time, and expound all [teachings].
The Dharma also manifests great supernormal powers and various skillful means that are unattached and unimpeded;

it possesses the three kinds of unimpeded entry and exit because it has attained mastery over the dharma-realm; it skillfully discerns the eye, skillfully discerns the ear, and skillfully discerns the nose.

He skillfully discriminates the tongue; he skillfully discriminates the body; he skillfully discriminates the mind. Thus, regarding all such various distinctions and differences, he skillfully discriminates them all, reaching their very limits.
The fourth point establishes mastery (*vaśitā*). This has two meanings: first, mastery over the principle-dharmadhātu, whereby one is able to skillfully discern the dhātus such as the eye;
second, mastery over the phenomena-dharmadhātu, which is the skillful discernment of the eighteen dhātus such as the eye.
Because these two are unimpeded, and because there is the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*dharmadharma-asaṃgatā*), all such various manifestations are horizontally exhaustive.
Reaching to its very edges and extending to its furthest limits.
Having thus skillfully known and seen this, the bodhisattva is able to give rise to ten trillion dhāraṇī-dharma-lights.
They accomplish ten trillion pure practices; they obtain ten trillion faculties; they perfect ten trillion supernormal powers;
they are able to enter ten trillion samādhis; they achieve ten trillion spiritual powers; they nurture ten trillion powers;
they fulfill ten trillion profound intentions; they exercise ten trillion supports of power; and they manifest ten...
There are a thousand billion spiritual transformations. They are fully endowed with ten thousand billion bodhisattvas' non-obstructions;
they fulfill ten thousand billion bodhisattvas' aids to the path; they accumulate ten thousand billion bodhisattva treasuries; they illuminate ten thousand billion bodhisattvas' skillful means;
they expound ten thousand billion meanings; they accomplish ten thousand billion vows; and they give rise to ten thousand billion dedications.
He thoroughly purified ten trillion bodhisattvas’ stages of right determination; he clearly understood ten trillion dharma-gates;
he revealed and taught ten trillion expositions; and he cultivated and refined the purity of ten trillion bodhisattvas.

Second, in explaining the benefits accomplished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), ten layers of benefits are distinguished. First is the benefit of generating manifold merits, which consists of twenty-one phrases, each numbering ten thousand koṭis.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further possesses innumerable merits,
immeasurable merits, boundless merits, incomparable merits, incalculable merits, ineffable merits, inconceivable merits,
unfathomable merits, unspeakable merits, and inexhaustible merits. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva...
Regarding such virtues as these, they have all been fully prepared, all accumulated, all adorned, all purified,
all rendered translucent, all embraced, all brought forth, all worthy of praise, all made firm, and all accomplished.
Second is the benefit of possessing inexhaustible virtues, because each preceding matter leads to inexhaustibility. Within these, there are twenty phrases:
the first ten concern the abundance of what is possessed, while the latter ten concern the characteristics of that which possesses them. "Pure" means the removal of defilements;
"luminously transparent" means the manifestation of the light of fundamental wisdom.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they are sustained by as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten thousand asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields, each bearing a distinct name.

Furthermore, for each individual name, there are as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten thousand asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields, each being distinct. As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, and north.
The same applies to the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Third, regarding the benefit of being sustained by all Buddhas, there are three parts. First, clarifying the sustenance:
all those Buddhas appear before him, manifesting the pure lands of the Buddhas and preaching the immeasurable [qualities] of the Buddhas.
For their bodies, he spoke of the inconceivable eyes of all Buddhas; for them, he spoke of the immeasurable ears of all Buddhas; for them, he spoke of the pure noses of all Buddhas;
for them, he spoke of the pure tongues of all Buddhas; for them, he spoke of the non-abiding minds of all Buddhas; and for them, he spoke of the unsurpassed supernormal powers of the Tathāgatas.
Next, he manifests his body and preaches the Dharma,
causing [beings] to cultivate the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata, to attain the pure voice of the Tathāgata,
to reveal the Tathāgata’s non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma, to display the Tathāgata’s boundless assemblies, and to cause them to enter the boundless secrets of the Tathāgata.
They praised all the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata, causing others to enter the impartial Dharma of the Tathāgata;

they proclaimed the lineage of the Tathāgata throughout the three periods of time, manifested the immeasurable physical forms of the Tathāgata, and expounded the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness.
They eloquently expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma-sounds of the Tathāgatas; they clearly elucidate all Buddha-worlds;
they proclaim the samādhis of all Buddhas; they manifest the successive assemblies of all Buddhas; and they protect and uphold the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas.
He taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; he clarified that the nature of all phenomena is without movement or change;
he revealed all the unsurpassed wheels of Dharma; he praised the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata; and he caused others to enter into all clouds of samādhis.
He causes them to know that their minds are like illusions and like transformations, boundless and inexhaustible;
subsequently, he causes them to cultivate and realize this.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-Dhātu, in each of the ten directions...
There are Tathāgatas with names as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields. Within each and every name,
there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields who simultaneously protect and sustain this Bodhisattva,
causing him to attain a boundless body, causing him to attain an unobstructed mind, and causing him to attain [mastery] over all phenomena.
He is without forgetfulness. He causes this bodhisattva to attain definitive wisdom regarding all phenomena;
he causes this bodhisattva to become increasingly acute and intelligent so as to be able to receive and comprehend all phenomena;

he causes this bodhisattva to understand all phenomena with complete clarity; and he causes this bodhisattva’s faculties to become sharp and keen, attaining skillfulness in all dharmas of supernatural power.
The sphere of this bodhisattva is unimpeded as they traverse the dharma-realm constantly without rest.

This causes the bodhisattva to attain unimpeded wisdom that is ultimately pure. By means of their supernormal powers, this causes the bodhisattva to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in all worlds.
