Fourth is the benefit of being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; "protected and remembered" means that the power of the Buddhas comes to empower them. O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain ten kinds of oceans.

What are these ten? They are: attaining the ocean of all Buddhas, because they behold them all; attaining the ocean of sentient beings, because they fully subdue them; attaining the ocean of all dharmas...
Because he is able to fully comprehend all things through wisdom; because he attains all oceans of lands by means of non-substantiality and effortless spiritual powers to visit them all;
because he attains an ocean of merit through the complete perfection of all practices;

because he attains an ocean of spiritual powers capable of manifesting extensively to bring beings to enlightenment; and because he thoroughly understands the various differences within the ocean of faculties.
They attain the ocean of all minds, because they know the infinite and variously differentiated minds of all sentient beings;

they attain the ocean of all practices, because they are able to fulfill them all through the power of their vows; they attain the ocean of all vows, because they cause them all to be accomplished and eternally purified.
Fifth, the benefit of attaining ten oceans of profound and vast excellence.
O Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained these ten kinds of oceans, they further attain ten kinds of supreme distinctions.
What are the ten? First, he is the foremost among all sentient beings.
Second, he is the most distinguished among all devas. Third, he is the most supremely sovereign among all Brahmā kings.
Fourth, they are unstained by and unattached to any worldly realm. Fifth, no one in any world can eclipse or obscure them.
Sixth, none of the māras can confuse or disturb them. Seventh, they enter universally into all realms of existence without any hindrance.
Eighth, knowing that taking birth in various places is not solid. Ninth, attaining mastery over all Buddha-dharmas.

Tenth, being able to manifest all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained these ten kinds of excellence, he further attains ten kinds of power with which he cultivates various practices within the realm of sentient beings. What are they?
There are ten: first is the power of valor, because it subdues the world; second is the power of diligence, because it never regresses;
third is the power of non-attachment, because it is free from all defilements; fourth is the power of tranquility, because it is without dispute regarding all phenomena;
fifth is the power of mastery over the favorable and unfavorable, because the mind is sovereign over all phenomena; sixth is...
1. The power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because it attains mastery over all meanings; 2. The power of non-obstruction, because wisdom is vast; 3.
The power of fearlessness, because it is able to expound all dharmas; 4. The power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), because it is able to uphold all dharmas;
5. The power of revelation, because wisdom is boundless.
Seventh is the benefit of attaining the various powers (*bala*). Among these, first the ten powers are enumerated:

"O Son of the Buddha, these ten kinds of powers are the vast power, the most supreme power, the power that cannot be overcome, the immeasurable power, the well-accumulated power, the immovable power, the firm power, the power of wisdom, the power of accomplishment, and the power of supreme concentration. Pure...

The power of purity; the power of extreme purification; the power of the Dharma-body; the power of the radiance of the Dharma; the power of the lamp of the Dharma; the power of the gateways of the Dharma;
the indestructible power; the power of supreme valor; the power of the Great Being; the power of the cultivation of the virtuous being;

the power of attaining perfect enlightenment; the power of the roots of goodness accumulated in the past; the power of abiding in immeasurable roots of goodness; and the power of abiding in the powers of the Tathāgata.
The power of mental reflection; the power that increases the Bodhisattva’s joy; the power that gives birth to the Bodhisattva’s pure faith;
the power that increases the Bodhisattva’s valor; the power born of the bodhicitta; the power of the Bodhisattva’s pure and profound mind; the power of the Bodhisattva’s sublime and profound mind;
the power of the Bodhisattva’s perfuming of roots of goodness; the power of the ultimate dharmas; and the power of non-obstruction.
The power of physical strength; the power of entering the dharma-gate of skillful means; the power of the pure and wondrous Dharma;
the power of abiding in great majesty such that all worlds cannot shake it; and the power that no sentient being can eclipse.
Subsequently, its preeminence is revealed. Corresponding to each of the aforementioned powers, all possess these thirty-eight powers.
O Son of the Buddha! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to produce, accomplish, fulfill, illuminate, perfect, universally perfect, expand, and consolidate such immeasurable dharmas of merit.
It can increase, it can purify, and it can thoroughly purify.
These eight knots can bring about complete fulfillment and benefit.
This is the limit of this bodhisattva’s merit, the limit of wisdom, the limit of practice, and the limit of the dharma-gates. Self-...

Regarding the limit of the extremes—the limit of asceticism, the limit of accomplishment, the limit of purification, the limit of renunciation, and the limit of mastery over phenomena—there is no one capable of describing them; yet these are what this bodhisattva has attained, accomplished, and entered.
Regarding all that is manifested before one, all objects of experience, all modes of observation, all modes of realization, all forms of purification, all forms of thorough knowledge,
and all established gateways of the Dharma— these could not be fully described even in unspeakable eons.
Ninth, because one’s own virtues are boundless, others cannot describe their benefits. Son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they are able to fully know that which is innumerable,
immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, and beyond description.
It is unspeakable that all samādhis possess infinite and vast spheres of activity for each and every one of them.
Within those spheres, there are their modes of entry, emergence, and abiding;
their characteristics, manifestations, spheres of practice, outflows, intrinsic natures, cessations, and renunciations—such as these.
There is nothing that is not clearly perceived.

These thirteen samādhis are boundless and inherently possess the benefit of complete understanding. Within the preceding ten sections, the first seven provide specific explanations, while the final three serve as a summary.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the four rivers flowing from the palace of the great nāga king Anavatapta. They are without turbidity, without admixture, and free from defilement;
their radiant color is pure like the void. On each of the four sides of that lake there is a single opening, and from each opening flows out one river.
From the mouth of the elephant flows the Gaṅgā River; from the mouth of the lion flows... [the Yamunā River].
From the mouth of the ox emerges the Śītā River; from the mouth of the horse emerges the Vakṣu River.

When these four great rivers flow forth, silver sand issues from the mouth of the Gaṅgā, diamond sand issues from the mouth of the Śītā, golden sand issues from the mouth of the Sindhu, and lapis lazuli issues from the mouth of the Vakṣu.
The mouth of the Śatadru River is the color of white silver; the mouth of the Sītā River is the color of diamond;
the mouth of the Sindhu River is the color of golden-yellow; and the mouth of the Vakṣu River is the color of lapis lazuli. Each river mouth is one yojana wide.
Once these four great rivers have flowed out, each circles the great lake seven times, following its respective direction.
The waters flow in four directions, surging and rushing toward the great ocean.
Between each of these winding rivers, there are *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses formed of celestial jewels;
their wondrous fragrances waft abroad and their exquisite colors are pure, with various petals, stalks, and filaments, all of which are [composed of the same].
The various jewels naturally reflect one another, all emitting radiance that illuminates and manifests each other.
The circumference of this Lake Anavatapta is fifty *yojanas* in breadth. Its bottom is strewn with exquisite sand made of various jewels, adorned with diverse *maṇi* gems.
Countless wonderful treasures embellish its shores, and the sublime fragrance of sandalwood is wafted throughout it. *Utpala*...
Rohita lotuses, padma lotuses, kumuda lotuses, and puṇḍarīka lotuses, as well as various other precious flowers, completely fill [the area].
A gentle breeze stirs them, and their fragrance permeates afar. Flower groves and jewel trees surround it on all sides.
When the sun rises, everything is universally illuminated; the reflections of all things within and without the ponds and rivers join their brilliance to form a radiant light.

O Minggang, all such things—whether distant or near, high or low, broad or narrow, coarse or fine, even down to the smallest single grain of sand or mote of dust—are all wondrous jewels whose radiance is transparent and penetrating.

Within them, the image of the sun’s disk appears without exception; furthermore, these images reflect one another in succession. Yet, these myriad reflections do not increase [the size of the original].
It does not diminish; it is neither conjoined nor dispersed. All are clearly perceived exactly as their original substance.

The third major section uses analogies to indirectly reveal the Middle Way, explicitly clarifying the preceding essence, function, and benefits, while also elucidating what was previously unmanifested;
therefore, it is not entirely similar to the preceding text. This section has two parts: first, a general presentation of the analogies.
O Son of the Buddha, just as the great lake Anavatapta flows from its four mouths as four rivers that enter the great ocean,
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: from the four analytical eloquences (pratisaṃvid), they flow forth all practices and ultimately enter the ocean of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Subsequently, there are thirteen sections of specific analogies with their respective applications (*pratyudāharaṇa*). In each, the analogy is presented first, followed by the application.

First, in the analogy of the confluence of sands entering the ocean, it is explained in general terms. Although four rivers are mentioned in both the analogy and the application, the intended meaning concerns the sands emerging from the four mouths;
therefore, the four rivers are explained specifically below in the ninth section.
Just as the great river Gaṅgā flows from the mouth of the silver-colored elephant with its sands of silver, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

By means of the eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*), they expound all the gateways of meaning taught by all the Tathāgatas, giving rise to all pure and white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), and ultimately entering the ocean of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna-samudra*). Just as the great river Sītā...
From the mouth of the lion of vajra-color flows vajra-sand.

In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise uses the eloquence of the Dharma to preach the vajra-words of the Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings, thereby eliciting vajra-wisdom and ultimately entering the ocean of unimpeded wisdom.
It is like the great river Sindhu, which flows from the mouth of a golden bull and carries golden sand.

Sands. It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: by means of eloquent discourse and explanations that accord with the world, they employ the skillful means of dependent origination to awaken sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice, be tamed, and reach maturity, ultimately entering the ocean of skillful means of dependent origination.
This is like the great river Vālukā, which flows from the horse-mouth [source] of lapis lazuli-colored water, carrying sands of lapis lazuli.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. With inexhaustible eloquence, he rains down hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable teachings, causing all who hear them to be thoroughly moistened and satisfied, ultimately entering the ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma.
Subsequently, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are explained separately as metaphors for the four mouths; what is spoken therein is a metaphor for the four streams.
Just as the four great rivers flow toward, encircle, and enter the ocean from the four directions after having circled Lake Anavatapta, so it is here.
The second is the simile of circling a pond to enter the ocean. In this, the simile comes first, followed by the application. This simile is as follows:
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise thus; they accomplish bodily action that is compliant, vocal action that is compliant, and mental action that is compliant.
They accomplish bodily action preceded by wisdom, vocal action preceded by wisdom, and [mental action] preceded by wisdom.
It guides the mental karma so that it flows in the four directions and ultimately enters the ocean of all-knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha, what are called the "four directions" of a bodhisattva? O Son of the Buddha, they are as follows: beholding all Buddhas and attaining awakening;
hearing all dharmas and receiving them with mindfulness so as not to forget; perfecting all practices of the pāramitās; and teaching the Dharma with great compassion to satisfy all beings.

Regarding the section on "Birth": the subsequent correspondence first matches the circumambulation of the pond. The resolve for bodhicitta is named the "pond," and the three karmas following wisdom constitute the meaning of "circumambulation.
The subsequent passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" corresponds to its four sides.
Just as four great rivers surround a large lake, and within it blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*),
and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) are found everywhere in abundance, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
within the heart of awakening (*bodhicitta*), they do not abandon sentient beings, but through teaching the Dharma and taming them, bring them all to complete fulfillment.
The *pramāṇa-samādhi* (measure-concentration). It perceives the adornment and purity of the Buddha-lands.

The metaphor of the jewel-lotus amidst the three-fold ponds carries the sense of blossoming; the preaching of the Dharma has the meaning of opening [the flowers], and samādhi possesses the power to evoke such fruits.
Adornment and purity are both specific meanings derived from "upon the flower."
Just as the Great Lake Anavatapta is surrounded by jewel trees, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise surrounded by the manifestations of the adornments of Buddha-lands,
causing all sentient beings to incline toward bodhi.
The fourth analogy is that of the jewel-tree encircling a pond.
Just as the great Anavatapta Lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, pure and free from turbidity, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Bodhicitta is immeasurable in extent; it is filled with roots of goodness and is utterly pure.
It is free from turbidity;
it is like the metaphor of the five great lakes of pure water, which constitute the body of the lake itself.
Just as the Anavatapta Great Lake has its shores adorned with immeasurable jewels and is strewn with sandalwood incense that fills them entirely.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise adorns the shore of the great vow of the bodhicitta with hundreds of thousands of billions of the ten kinds of jewels of wisdom,
universally scattering the exquisite fragrance of all manner of wholesome virtues.
The analogy of the sandalwood-fragrant shore of the six directions refers to ten kinds of jewel-like wisdom. There are two meanings:
first, the seven kinds of jewel-like wisdom within the mundane and supramundane; second, the ten kinds of wisdom beginning with the knowledge of others' minds.
Just as the bottom of the Great Lake Anavatapta is strewn with golden sand and adorned with various interspersed mani-jewels, so too is it with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
with subtle and wondrous wisdom they universally observe the inconceivable liberations of bodhisattvas;
adorned with various interspersed jewels of the Dharma, they attain the unimpeded radiance of all dharmas and abide therein.
It is the dwelling place of all Buddhas. It enters into all profound skillful means.

The analogy of spreading gold and jewels over the bottom represents this: wondrous wisdom corresponds to the gold dust, liberation corresponds to the mani-jewels, and unimpeded radiance corresponds to the two kinds of light-emitting.
Abiding in the dwelling of the Buddhas and entering into the profound is like spreading these materials across the bottom.
In each of the four preceding sections, the Anavatapta Great Lake is cited as the primary example.

Just as the Naga King Anavatapta is forever free from all the heat and afflictions inherent to the naga realm, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forever free from all worldly sorrow and affliction; though manifesting birth, he remains untainted.
[This is] the eighth analogy of the Dragon King Anavatapta; it is named after the lake because its name is derived from the dragon.
Just as the four great rivers moisten the entire land of Jambudvīpa and, having moistened it, enter the great ocean.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise. With the river of the four kinds of wisdom, he moistens and nourishes devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, causing them all to enter the great ocean of the wisdom of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He is adorned with four kinds of powers. What are these four? First is the river of the wisdom of vows, which rescues, protects, and subdues.
First, the river of wisdom for all sentient beings, which is never-ceasing;

second, the river of the wisdom of the *pāramitās*, which cultivates the practices of enlightenment to benefit sentient beings, continuing without end through the past, future, and present, until finally entering the ocean of the Buddhas' wisdom;
and third, the river of the wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s samādhis, adorned with innumerable samādhis, through which one beholds all Buddhas and enters [their realms].
The ocean of all Buddhas. Fourth is the river of great compassionate wisdom. With sovereign great kindness, they universally rescue sentient beings;
through skillful means, they gather them in without ceasing. They practice the gateway of secret merit and ultimately enter the great ocean of the ten powers.
The ninth is the simile of the four rivers providing moisture:
just as the four great rivers, once they have flowed forth from Lake Anavatapta, ultimately enter the great ocean without ever being exhausted.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise thus: through the power of great vows, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva;
their sovereign knowledge and vision are inexhaustible, and they ultimately enter the ocean of all-knowledge.
The tenth is the analogy of the four rivers being inexhaustible.
Just as the four great rivers enter the great ocean such that nothing can obstruct them from doing so, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
by constantly and diligently cultivating the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, they accomplish all the light of wisdom.
Illumination. Abiding in all the *bodhi*-dharmas of the Buddhas, one enters the wisdom of the Tathāgata without obstruction.
This is the eleventh [stage], corresponding to the analogy of entering the ocean without obstruction:
just as the four great rivers rush into the ocean and flow through it for countless eons without ever becoming weary, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

The Bodhisattva is likewise in this regard: through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, he cultivates the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout all future kalpas, entering the ocean of the Tathāgatas without ever giving rise to weariness or fatigue.
The twelfth is the parable of entering the ocean without weariness. Of the aforementioned four parables, each takes the four great rivers as its primary metaphor.
Of the aforementioned ten parables, all take the bodhisattva as the initial subject of application.

O Son of the Buddha, when the sun rises, within the Anavatapta Lake, the sands of gold, silver, diamond, and lapis lazuli, as well as all other various kinds of precious substances, all manifest the reflection of the sun.
Furthermore, each of these precious substances, such as the golden sand, likewise reflects one another; they mirror and penetrate each other without any obstruction.
Obstruction.
Thirteen: The Simile of the Interreflected Shadows of Combined Jewels. First the simile, then the application.
It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who dwells in this samādhi; within each and every pore of his own body...
Within [this state], they see all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

They also see all the lands, bodhimaṇḍas, and assemblies of those Buddhas. At each and every Buddha’s place, they listen to the Dharma, receive and uphold it, believe and understand it, and make offerings to them, doing so for unspeakably unspeakable billions of nayutas of kalpas, yet without any thought of time passing.

The length of the intervals was such that the various assemblies therein were not at all cramped. Why was this? It was because they had entered the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with a subtle and wondrous mind;
because they had entered the peerless distinctions of karmic fruits; because they had entered the inconceivable sphere of samādhi;
because they had entered the inconceivable sphere of contemplation; and because they had entered the sovereign sphere of all Buddhas. They attained...
Because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; because they have attained the great supernormal transformations of all Buddhas;

because they have attained the ten powers of the Tathāgatas, which are difficult to obtain and difficult to know; because they have entered the realm of the perfected conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
and because they have attained the power of spiritual penetrations that is free from weariness for all Buddhas.
The application consists of two parts: first, the formal application; second, from "For what reason? onwards, the investigation and explanation of the reasons for their mutual interpenetration.

"O Son of the Buddha, although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to enter and emerge from meditative concentration in a single thought-moment, they do not abandon long-term abiding in concentration, nor do they have any attachment to it.
Although they do not rely upon or dwell within objective realms, they likewise do not relinquish the single [thought-moment]."
While thoroughly engaging with all objects of focus, they enter the limit of each moment yet never grow weary of manifesting Buddha-miracles for the benefit of all sentient beings.
While equally entering the Dharma-realm, they do not perceive its boundaries.
While abiding nowhere and having no fixed location, they constantly advance upon the path to omniscience. By the power of transformation, they universally enter immeasurable assemblies.

Born among the multitudes, they fully adorn all worlds; though they are free from the inverted conceptualizations of the world and have transcended all stages of discrimination, they do not abandon the various marks [of phenomena].
Though they possess skillful means, they are ultimately pure; though they do not discriminate between the bodhisattva stages, they have already mastered them all.
"Enter, O Son of the Buddha! Just as space, though it can contain all things, is free from the notions of existence and non-existence, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
though he universally enters all worlds, he is free from the perception of a world."
Though he diligently delivers all sentient beings, he is free from the notion of "sentient beings. Though he deeply understands all phenomena (*dharma*), he is free from the notion of "phenomena.
Though he delights in beholding all Buddhas, he is free from the notion of "Buddhas.
Though he skillfully enters various samādhis, he knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like space, remaining unstained by attachment. Though he possesses boundless eloquence...
They expound inexhaustible verses of Dharma, yet their minds always abide in the dharma that is free from words and letters.

Although they delight in contemplating the ineffable Dharma, they constantly manifest pure sounds and voices. Although they dwell at the limit of all dharmas beyond speech, they constantly manifest various forms and appearances.
Although they teach and transform sentient beings, they know that all dharmas are ultimately empty by nature. Although...
Diligently cultivating great compassion to deliver sentient beings, yet knowing that the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible and undispersed;
though thoroughly realizing that the dharma-realm is eternally abiding and unchanging, one constantly and without rest employs the three wheels to subdue sentient beings;
though always dwelling securely in the abode of the Tathāgata, one’s wisdom is pure and the mind is free from fear, as one analytically expounds the various [dharmas].
Sowing all dharmas, he turns the wheel of Dharma constantly without rest.

This is the fourth major section, the general conclusion on the simultaneous practice [of means and wisdom], because there is no obstruction between the provisional and the real, or between concentration and dispersion.

Within this, there are three parts: first, the teaching; second, the analogy beginning with "O Son of the Buddha"; and third, the application beginning with "The Bodhisattva. Now, within the teaching, it is while remaining in quiescence that...
Application. To clarify through analogy that it is quiescent even while in application:
O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth skillful wisdom of the Great Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Definitive Names of the Three Bonds.
*Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra: Essential Summary*, Fascicle Forty-two;
*Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra: Essential Summary*, Fascicle Forty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning of the commentary elucidated by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dàhuá yán Monastery;
and the essential points extracted by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Monastery on Mount Kuāng, Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-seven, Part Four: The Ten Samādhis.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Unhindered Wheel Samādhi?
Regarding this tenth Unhindered Wheel Samādhi: first is the general heading, followed by the initial inquiry, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this samādhi, they abide in unimpeded physical action, unimpeded verbal action, and unimpeded mental action.
They abide in unimpeded Buddha-lands, attain unimpeded wisdom for bringing sentient beings to maturity, and acquire unimpeded wisdom for taming sentient beings.
They radiate unimpeded light and manifest unimpeded nets of light, displaying...
Obstructing vast transformations, they turn the unobstructed, pure wheel of Dharma and attain the unimpeded sovereignty of a bodhisattva.
Within these two explanations, there are three parts: first, clarifying the skillful means for entering;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha, once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi" onwards, clarifying the application of one's own wisdom upon entry; third, "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters... [and so forth].

The lower stage of Samantabhadra’s dwelling is fully accomplished for the benefit [of beings]. Herein, there are initially twenty-two phrases which also manifest the name of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The first eleven phrases concern the unimpeded application of causes; this is the meaning of "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*).

The subsequent eleven phrases, beginning with "universally entering," concern the perfection of abiding in the fruit; this is the meaning of the "wheel" (*cakra*). Within this present section, it is precisely this unimpeded...

That which is indestructible also carries the meaning of a "wheel. The first three phrases refer to the unimpeded nature of the three types of karma; the next phrase refers to the unimpeded nature of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*);
the following two phrases refer to the unimpeded nature of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*); and the remaining phrases refer to the unimpeded nature of the perfect awakening of wisdom.
They universally enter the powers of all Buddhas; they universally abide in the wisdom of all Buddhas; they perform what Buddhas do; they purify what Buddhas purify;

they manifest the spiritual powers of Buddhas; they cause the Buddhas to rejoice; they practice the conduct of Tathāgatas; they dwell in the path of Tathāgatas; they constantly draw near to immeasurable Buddhas;
they perform the works of Buddhas; and they perpetuate the lineage of Buddhas.

Subsequently, one abides within the fruition (*phala*). Because the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) penetrate both the provisional and the ultimate, it is called "abiding universally" (*puzhu*). Third, one performs deeds that bring benefit and happiness; fourth, one purifies the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*);
seventh, the seven wisdoms accord with the realm of the Buddha. The remaining seven [aspects] may be understood accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they contemplate all-knowledge; they contemplate all-knowledge collectively,
they contemplate all-knowledge individually, they accord with all-knowledge, they manifest all-knowledge, they take all-knowledge as their object of focus,
they see all-knowledge, they see all-knowledge collectively, and they see all-knowledge individually.

The second [section], on the application of wisdom that has entered into oneself, consists of four parts: first, the inclusion of the Buddha’s merits; second, the realization and entry into all dharmas;
third, the inexhaustibility of universal virtues; and fourth, the conclusion, demonstration, and exhortation to practice.

Regarding the first, it includes the twenty-one kinds of the Tathāgata’s preeminent merits, because this stage is equal to that of a Buddha. Within these, some aspects are entirely identical to those of a Buddha, while others...
Approximating the cause, they appear similar and proceed in an unerring sequence. Within this, there are three parts: first, a general clarification that wondrous realization is entirely fulfilled;

second, a specific manifestation of the twenty-one virtues; and third, a manifestation of the superior capacity of these virtues. Now, for the first part, there are ten phrases. The first phrase indicates the time of fulfillment;

the remaining nine manifest the characteristics of fulfillment. However, if *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is contrasted with *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects), it constitutes the fundamental [wisdom]. If...
To speak directly of Buddha-wisdom, it encompasses both the provisional and the real. Herein, the universal aspect is revealed. Among these, the first three phrases concern the initial contemplation.

The statement "contemplating all-knowledge" serves as the heading. How does one contemplate? There are two kinds of contemplation: first, general contemplation, which means contemplating the provisional and the real simultaneously;
second, specific contemplation, which distinguishes: "this is the real" and "this is the provisional," noting that within the provisional there are many variations.

They are distinct, for they all involve thorough and clear observation. In the subsequent three phrases, the sequence follows the same pattern: the first phrase provides the heading, while the next asks, "In what way do they accord? [The answer is:
because of the preceding general observation, one is able to manifest [the object] instantaneously; because of the preceding specific observation, one grasps each [object] individually.

The final three phrases conclude the exposition; their interpretation is the same as in the preceding contemplation. However, whereas previously it was an observation, now it is a clear realization and vision.

Regarding the vast vows, vast mind, vast conduct, vast destination, vast entry, vast radiance, vast manifestation, vast protective mindfulness, vast transformations, and vast [qualities] of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
The Path.
Second, a detailed explanation of twenty-one kinds of merit, divided into twenty sections; the final two are combined.

Now, first, the first section clarifies that the two types of activity are eternally severed, which is the merit of functioning with absolute non-obstruction regarding the objects of knowledge. However...
There are two meanings. First, it means that [the Bodhisattva] does not possess the ignorance regarding existence and non-existence as do those of the Two Vehicles.

Second, it means that he does not, like ordinary beings, manifest birth and death and give rise to various defilements; nor does he, like those of the Two Vehicles, manifest nirvana and abandon matters of benefit and happiness.

The World-Honored One does not possess them; now, the Bodhisattva likewise does not possess them. The text extensively clarifies their benefit and joy, which is thus different from that of the Two Vehicles.

They are always accompanied by wisdom, which is thus different from that of ordinary beings. Dividing the text according to its content, there are two parts: first, a general clarification of the great function’s permanence;
second, "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva has a lotus flower... and below, a specific clarification of one function. Within the former:

Second: first, an explanation by way of the principle (*dharma*); second, an elucidation by way of analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the first, the explanation by way of the principle, there are two parts: first, the actual exposition; second, the interrogation and explanation.
Now, for the first [the actual exposition], we first clarify the essence of the practice (*caryā-svabhāva*).
Uninterrupted and non-regressive; without rest or substitution; without weariness or abandonment; without distraction or confusion; constantly progressing and perpetually continuous.
Next, the nature of constancy and eternity is distinguished.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished great vows among all dharmas, set forth upon the Mahāyāna, and entered the ocean of great skillful means of the Buddha-dharma.
By the power of their supreme vows, they have attained mastery in the wisdom that clearly illuminates all the practices performed by bodhisattvas;
they are fully endowed with the supernormal powers and transformations of a bodhisattva, and are well able to protect [them].
He brings to mind all sentient beings as those who are protected and remembered by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
he constantly gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and accomplishes the unchanging Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the second section, which consists of the inquiry and the explanation: the intent of the inquiry is to ask, "How does one attain this fulfillment of wisdom and constant practice?
The intent of the explanation is that it is because the vows and practices have been well accomplished and wisdom has become skillful.
"O Son of the Buddha! It is, for example, as if someone were to place a *maṇi* jewel within a colored garment; although that *maṇi* jewel [is thus placed]..."
The color of the cloth does not abandon its own nature.
The second analogy illustrates the middle four [points]: first, the analogy; second, the application; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation. Now, for the first:

placing a mani jewel within colored cloth is a general metaphor for placing the bodhisattva’s mind-intelligence within the Buddha’s wisdom. Although it shares the same color as the cloth, [it remains distinct].
The preceding ten phrases illustrate the fulfillment of wisdom; thus, they are collectively described as "contemplating all-knowledge" and so forth, without abandoning one's own nature.
The preceding twenty phrases illustrate the constancy of practice;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, accomplishing wisdom as the jewel of the mind and contemplating all things.
Wisdom is universally and clearly manifest; yet, one does not abandon the various practices of a bodhisattva.
This is explained through a combined analogy. Why is this?
The meaning of the third inquiry is as follows: How can one, having already attained the fulfillment of wisdom, yet continue to practice without ceasing?

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes the great vow to benefit all sentient beings, to deliver all sentient beings, to serve all Buddhas, to adorn and purify all worlds, and to bring comfort to sentient beings while entering deeply into the Dharma.
O Ocean, for the sake of purifying the realm of sentient beings, you manifest great sovereignty to bestow gifts upon them;
you universally illumine the world and enter the dharma-gate of boundless illusory transformations, never retreating, never turning back, and never wearying or becoming satiated.

The fourth explanation of the intent states that because the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s unobstructed vows is naturally so, they exhaustively reach the limits of the realm of sentient beings without weariness or fatigue.
This section consists of two parts; first is the explanation by way of principle (*dharmadeśanā*).

O Son of the Buddha, it is like space, which sustains all worlds—whether they are forming or abiding—without weariness, without fatigue, without weakness, without decay, without dispersal, without destruction, without change, without alteration, and without distinction; it does not abandon its own nature. Why is this?
Because such is the natural law of the nature of space. In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise establishes the *asaṃskṛta* (unconditioned).
The capacity is vast and the vows are great; one delivers all sentient beings with a mind free from weariness or fatigue.

Subsequently, this is illustrated through metaphors. Among these, there are three metaphors, all of which illustrate tirelessness in benefiting sentient beings, each having a corresponding application to the Dharma.
First is the analogy of empty space sustaining worlds. This illustrates that because great vows are the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they are never weary.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like *nirvāṇa*: throughout the past, future, and present, immeasurable sentient beings attain liberation within it, yet it never becomes weary or exhausted.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-prakṛti*) is pure; this is called *nirvāṇa*. How could one [become weary] toward it?
If one were to become weary or disheartened midway, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva would likewise be so.
Yet, desiring to deliver all sentient beings and lead them all to transcendence, he appears in the world; how, then, could he give rise to a mind of weariness or discouragement?
Second is the analogy of universal extinction in *nirvāṇa*. This illustrates how [the Bodhisattva] never tires of purifying sentient beings. The two preceding analogies illustrate compassion.

O Son of the Buddha: just as the *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) causes all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present to be born—both already born and yet to be born—within the family of the Buddhas, and even leads them to the attainment of unsurpassed *bodhi*, without ever becoming weary or fatigued; why is this?
Therefore, because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are non-dual, and because there is no attachment to any phenomena (*dharma*),
it is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva: with a mind of equanimity abiding in omniscience, how could there be a mind of weariness or exhaustion?
The third is the analogy of the universal accomplishment of the three Buddha-wisdoms. This analogy illustrates that because the subject and object are non-dual, there is no weariness.
Since this single analogy of wisdom is neither compassion born of attachment nor views, how could there be weariness?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses a lotus flower. That flower is vast, extending to the limits of the ten directions.
It is adorned with unspeakably many petals, unspeakably many jewels, and unspeakably many fragrances.
Those unspeakably many jewels, in turn, each manifest various kinds of precious gems; they are pure, wondrous, and most excellently situated. That flower—
It constantly emits multicolored rays of light that universally illuminate all worlds in the ten directions without obstruction.
A net of pure gold covers it from above, and as precious bells sway gently, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds; these sounds expound and clarify the Dharma of omniscience.
The second section specifically reveals two aspects within a single function. First, it clarifies the excellence of the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit).

Second, it shows that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses mastery over the primary retribution beneath this flower. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections; first, it clarifies the adornment of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), which surpasses those of the ten previous stages and thus extends to the limits of the ten directions.
This great lotus is fully endowed with the pure adornments of the Tathāgata; it arises from all roots of goodness,
is manifested through the power of auspicious spiritual faculties, possesses ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* pure merits,
is accomplished through the sublime path of the bodhisattvas, flows forth from the mind of omniscience, and within it appear the reflections of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
It appears as an object of veneration for the world, like a Buddhist stūpa; among sentient beings, there are none who see it and do not pay homage.
It arises from the true Dharma that thoroughly understands illusion, and no analogy in all the worlds can equal it.
Later, when the Adornments of Virtue are manifested, viewed from within, its measure encompasses the Dharma-realm;
viewed from without, it allows sentient beings to perceive it—this is the transformation of the small into the great.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits cross-legged upon this flower; the size of his body is proportionate to the flower.
This is the second of the two [sections on] primary retribution, clarifying the size of the body.

Empowered by the spiritual authority of all Buddhas, each and every pore of the Bodhisattva’s body emits millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of light rays, as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field.
Each light ray manifests millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of mani-jewels, as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field; these jewels are all named...
The Universal Radiance Treasury is adorned with various colors and forms; it is accomplished through immeasurable merits and covered above by nets of various jewels and flowers.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of supreme, wondrous fragrances are scattered about, adorned with immeasurable colors and forms.
Furthermore, inconceivable canopies adorned with jewels appear.
These covered its top. From each and every mani-jewel, there appeared pavilions as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.

Within each and every pavilion, there appeared lion thrones of the Lotus Treasury, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields. Upon each and every lion throne, there appeared a hundred...
There were as many rays of light as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.
Each ray of light manifested as many color-forms as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.
Each color-form manifested as many circles of light as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields. Each...
A circle of light appeared, manifesting *vairocana* mani-jewel flowers as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayuta* buddha-fields.
Within each flower, there appeared terraces as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayuta* buddha-fields.
Within each terrace, there appeared [worlds] as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayuta* buddha-fields.
There were Buddhas as numerous as atoms; each Buddha manifested spiritual transformations as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands.
Each spiritual transformation purified assemblies of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands.
Within each of those assemblies of sentient beings, he manifested [Buddhas] as numerous as hundreds of billions of nayutas.
One may speak of the sovereign powers of Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field.
Each sovereign power rains down teachings of the Buddha, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
Within each teaching of the Buddha, there are sutras as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Each sutra expounds...
There are *dharmaparyāyas* as numerous as the atoms in a hundred trillion *nayutas* of unspeakable Buddha-fields.

Within each *dharmaparyāya*, there are wheels of Dharma entered by vajra-wisdom as numerous as the atoms in a hundred trillion *nayutas* of unspeakable Buddha-fields, each expounded with distinct terminology. Each wheel of Dharma brings to maturity a hundred trillion...
From among the realms of sentient beings, which are as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, within each and every realm of sentient beings,
there are millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, who attain taming within the Buddha-dharma.
The subsequent passage clarifies that the Buddha’s empowerment radiates light in twenty successive layers.

Within each succeeding layer, the light is multiplied by a factor of one hundred trillion *nayuta* times the number of atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields compared to each preceding layer; thus, its magnitude is difficult to measure.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they manifest such realms of supernatural power and immeasurable transformations;
yet, knowing them all to be like illusions, they remain unstained by attachment.
The second clarifies the realization of the signless dharma; this is identical to the merit of the Tathāgatas’ ability to enter the most pure *tathatā*.
First, it connects the preceding with the following: because one realizes the signless, one is undefiled.
It abides securely within the unobstructed limit of the Tathāgata-lineage—the reality-mark of the dharmadhātu, which is intrinsically pure, ineffable, and boundless;
it neither comes nor goes, is neither prior nor posterior, is profoundly deep and bottomless, and is attained through direct perception.
One enters by means of wisdom through one's own realization, not through awakening by another. The mind is neither deluded nor distracted, and there is no conceptual discrimination.
This subsequently clarifies abiding, which is precisely the meaning of "entering. That is to say, this *tathatā* (suchness) is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is called "boundless.
For that which is definitively existent or definitively non-existent constitutes a limit (*anta*). It cannot be described in words; it is *tathatā* beyond language.
The true mark of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the limit of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇakoṭi*) are all synonyms for *tathatā* (suchness).

Yet it is called the "lineage of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatagotra*), because all Buddhas take the *tathatā* of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their nature. The "Appearance Chapter" (*Nirmāṇakāya-parivarta*) states:

"All are of one and the same nature, namely, the nature of non-nature. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Know that dharmas are eternally without nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. There is no... [text ends].
The past, future, and so forth further clarify that true thusness (*tathatā*) is itself the Middle Way; therefore, it is profoundly bottomless.
From "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) onwards, the text specifically explains the meaning of being able to enter [this state].
It is praised by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and flows forth from the power of those Buddhas.

They enter into the essential nature of the realm of all Buddhas as it truly is; they realize it through the pure eye, see it universally with the wisdom eye, and achieve the Buddha-eye to become a bright lamp for the world.
They act within the sphere of what is known by the knowledge-eye and are extensively able to reveal subtle and wondrous Dharma gates.
The third section clarifies the virtue of abiding in the Buddha-abode. This refers to the Buddha’s effortless and perpetual abiding in the sublime, celestial, and Brahma-abodes.
In the text, the praise of the Buddhas of the three periods of time comes first; this passage applies to both preceding and following sections.

From the phrase "by the power of all Buddhas" onwards, its true meaning is explicitly revealed: that is, entering the realm of all Buddhas, which is the very realm in which the sublime, celestial, and other beings abide. Pure.
The eye directly realizes the lower luminosity that abides in its own nature, for it dwells in the perfect clarity of the ten eyes.

Thus, one accomplishes the bodhicitta and becomes a superior person (*mahāpuruṣa*). Being without obstruction regarding all objective spheres, one enters the lineage of wisdom and gives rise to all forms of knowledge.
Transcending the phenomena of worldly birth, one manifests birth through the power of supernatural transformations and skillful means to discipline beings.
In this way, all of these are nothing other than skillful means.
The fourth [section] clarifies the attainment of the Buddha’s quality of equality, meaning that there is equality when Buddhas are compared with one another.
This text consists of three parts. First, it clarifies the equality of the basis, meaning that all Buddhas rely upon purity. At the beginning of the text...
Generating the bodhicitta ultimately accomplishes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). The arising of the functions of wisdom is that upon which all depend.
Next, following "leaving behind worldly birth and phenomena," the equality of intention is clarified, because they share the same intention of taming sentient beings.
Finally, following "supernormal powers and transformations," the performance of equal activity is shown, because they equally perform the activities of enjoyment and transformation.
Their merit, understanding, and aspirations are entirely pure; they are most subtle and perfectly complete.
Their wisdom is as vast as space, and they are well able to observe the realm of the noble ones. Their power of faith, conduct, and vows is firm and unshakable.

His merit is inexhaustible and praised by the world; he is a great wise one who has gathered all manner of exquisite jewels at the ocean of omniscience—the treasury observed by all Buddhas and the locus of great enlightenment—and is naturally pure like a lotus.
All sentient beings who see it give rise to joy and all obtain benefit. Its light of wisdom shines universally, perceiving immeasurable Buddhas and purifying all phenomena.
This is the fifth virtue: reaching the state of non-obstruction through the cultivation of remedies for all obstacles. Both merit and wisdom—
"Purified" means being free from the two obstacles. In the text, the first two phrases refer to merit (*guṇa*), and the next two phrases refer to wisdom (*jñāna*);

in each case, the upper phrase indicates the purification of the obstacle and the lower phrase indicates the fulfillment of the virtue. The subsequent two phrases further clarify merit, while the remaining four phrases further clarify wisdom.

Their conduct is tranquil; they attain ultimate non-obstruction regarding all Buddha-dharmas. Constantly employing skillful means, they abide within the meritorious practices of the Buddha’s bodhi and are thereby born [into it].
Possessing the wisdom of a bodhisattva, they are the foremost among bodhisattvas. They are collectively protected and remembered by all Buddhas;

they obtain the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and accomplish the Buddha-dharma body. Their power of mindfulness is inconceivable, as they focus on a single object within their field of experience.
Yet it has no object of perception. Its practice is vast, signless, and unimpeded; it is equal to the dharma-realm, immeasurable and boundless.
The bodhi realized is like empty space, without limits and free from all bondage and attachment.
The sixth [section] clarifies the dharmas that cannot be diverted. This refers to the two types of dharma—teaching (*śāsana*) and realization (*adhigama*)—which others cannot divert.
In the text, the first two phrases briefly indicate the teaching and the realization; "tranquility" refers to realization, while "the teachings of all Buddhas" refers to the teaching.

From "constant" onwards, the teaching is specifically revealed. From "power of mindfulness" onwards, realization is further elucidated. Since it is like space, unattached, and so forth, how could others possibly divert it?
Indeed.
They universally bring benefit to all worlds. Flowing from the roots of goodness of the ocean of omniscience, they are able to penetrate all immeasurable realms.
Having perfectly accomplished the dharma of pure giving, they abide in the bodhisattva mind and purify the bodhisattva lineage.
It is able to accord with and give rise to the bodhi of all Buddhas; it attains skillfulness regarding all Buddha-dharmas;
it possesses subtle and wondrous practices and achieves steadfast power.
The seventh clarifies the virtue of unimpeded conduct: that although one performs acts of benefit and happiness for the world, the world...
The eight worldly dharmas cannot obstruct him. In this text, abiding in the bodhisattva-mind and accomplishing firm power are the causes for being unobstructed.
All Buddhas possess sovereign majestic spiritual power; though difficult for sentient beings to hear, the bodhisattvas fully know it. Thus they enter the gate of non-duality.
Abiding in the dharma of signlessness, although they have forever relinquished all signs, they are able to extensively expound upon various dharmas;
according to the inclinations, desires, and understandings of sentient beings, they bring them all to subdual and cause them all to rejoice.
The eighth clarifies the establishment of inconceivable virtues. This refers to the formal establishment of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), which ordinary fools are unable to conceive.
At the beginning of the text, it is shown in general that all teachings are established through the majestic power (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattvas are able to know this; conversely, it reveals that ordinary beings cannot conceive of it.

The section beginning with "Entering Non-duality" separately clarifies the characteristics of the inconceivable establishment, because it is extensively explained based on the signless (*animitta*). Since these are manifold according to the various inclinations of those seeking understanding, they are all inconceivable.
Taking the dharma-realm as their body, they are free from discrimination. The sphere of their wisdom is inexhaustible. Their resolve is ever courageous, and their mind is constantly equanimous.
They perceive the ultimate limit of the merits of all Buddhas and comprehend the distinct sequence of all kalpas.
The ninth clarifies the universal vision of the three periods of time. Because body and mind are equal to the dharma-realm, one’s predictions regarding the three periods are without error.
One reveals all dharmas, dwells securely in all lands, adorns and purifies all buddha-fields, and manifests [them].
The radiance of all true Dharma proclaims all the Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present;

it reveals the dwelling places of all bodhisattvas, acts as a bright lamp for the world to give rise to all roots of goodness, and ensures that one forever leaves the mundane world to be constantly born in the presence of the Buddhas.
The tenth clarifies that the body is eternally pervasive throughout all lands.
That is to say, for the sake of expounding the Dharma, he manifests the enjoyment and transformation bodies, pervading all worlds to bring about benefit and happiness.
They shall attain the Buddha’s wisdom, preeminent in clarity; they shall be collectively sustained by all Buddhas;
they shall already be numbered among the future Buddhas; they shall be born from virtuous friends; and whatever aspirations they seek shall not fail to bear fruit.
Eleventh, he possesses constant and clear wisdom that thoroughly penetrates all phenomena; that is to say, because he is skillful in discerning objects and able to sever the doubts of others,
he abides in the superior resolve endowed with great majestic power, and is able to eloquently explain whatever he has heard.
The twelfth is the illumination of the thorough knowledge of all modes of conduct.

This means that one who possesses the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is able to understand the intentions, dispositions, and behaviors of sentient beings, and manifests a body according to what is appropriate for them; such a person thus possesses majestic power (*prabhāva*).
He also reveals the wheel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) for those who abide in the roots of goodness born from hearing the Dharma;
their minds encounter no obstacles regarding all phenomena, they do not abandon any formative activities (*saṃskāra*), and they are free from all conceptual discrimination.
The thirteenth is the removal of all doubts. This refers to those who are śrāvakas, who claim to possess not even a fraction of wholesome roots;
now, by being able to reveal and show them that they shall give birth to the sublime wisdom of a Tathāgata, their minds become free from obstacles.

Regarding all phenomena, their minds are free from movement or thought. Having attained the light of wisdom, they extinguish the darkness of all delusion and are able to clearly illuminate all Buddha-dharmas.
Without destroying the various realms of existence, they are born therein; they thoroughly understand the spheres of all such existences.
From the very beginning, there has been no activity; the actions of body, speech, and mind are all entirely boundless.
The fourteenth [chapter] clarifies the unfathomable body, which contains two meanings: first, that his body does not arise from false conceptualization;
because it is free from the birth of afflictions and karma and is detached from defilement, it is unfathomable. This refers to the first line of the sutra.

This is clarified in two ways: although his body is without discrimination, like a mani jewel, it appears as golden in color and so forth through the sovereign power of the Buddha and the force of sentient beings' resolute belief (*adhimukti*), yet the Buddha remains without discrimination.
This is further clarified by the subsequent scriptural passage, which shows that he does not destroy the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
Although they expound various and immeasurable syllables in accordance with worldly conventions, they never violate the dharma that transcends syllables.
They enter deeply into the ocean of the Buddhas, knowing that all phenomena possess only provisional names, and remain unbound and unattached amidst all objective realms.
The fifteenth [topic] clarifies the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others.
This means that bodhisattvas, in order to discipline sentient beings through immeasurable syllables and characters, must first rely on the Dharma heard from the Buddha to attain sublime wisdom;
therefore, all bodhisattvas and others seek it.
One realizes that all phenomena are empty and non-existent. All practices cultivated arise from the *dharmadhātu*.
The sixteenth [stage] clarifies reaching the ultimate, non-dual shore of Buddhahood;

this means realizing that the emptiness of all phenomena and the *dharmadhātu* are equal, which is precisely the Buddha’s non-dual *dharmakāya*. Based upon this *dharmakāya*, one cultivates the practices of the *pāramitās* and so forth.
Thus they attain perfection. They arise from the *dharmadhātu*, which, like space, is signless and formless;
they penetrate deeply into the *dharmadhātu* and expound in accordance with it, giving rise to all-knowledge within a single gateway of objects.
Seventeenth, it clarifies the perfection of the Tathāgata’s impartial liberation.
This means that the bodies and lands manifested by each and every Tathāgata pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*. Like space, they are without marks and without form;

they do not obstruct one another, yet they do not intermingle, appearing as distinct entities according to the conditions for their transformation. Therefore, the text says: "He expounds in accordance [with these conditions]. Regarding this—
The gate of a single object gives rise to all wisdom, for each [wisdom] accords with its respective object.
One contemplates the stage of the Ten Powers and trains therein through wisdom; wisdom serves as a bridge to reach omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
With the eye of wisdom, one perceives phenomena without obstruction and skillfully enters the various stages.
The eighteenth is the realization of the Buddha’s level of equality, which is without center or periphery.

This means that the three bodies of the Buddha are equal and all-pervading, as there is no distinction between center and periphery. Upon reaching *sarvajñā* (omniscience), it is the self-enjoyment [body];

with wisdom serving as the bridge, one penetrates the transformation [body]. Seeing phenomena without obstruction is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Skillfully entering the various stages (*bhūmi*) is...
This is the tenth stage of the Buddha.
One knows various meanings and attains complete clarity regarding each and every dharma-gate.
The nineteenth clarifies that [this wisdom] extends to the limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); because this dharma-realm is supremely pure, it is able to give rise to equality.
The teachings of the *Sūtras* and other scriptures flow forth, reaching the furthest limits of this Dharma-realm;
all great vows to bring about the appropriate benefit and happiness of sentient beings in future ages shall be fully accomplished.
The twentieth [aspect] is that it is equal to the realm of empty space, for it is inexhaustible throughout the limits of the future; thus it is called "accomplishment.
This concludes the first section on the inclusion of all Buddha-qualities within the second entry into the function of one's own wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha! By this, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reveals the non-differentiated nature of all Tathāgatas.
This is the gateway of unimpeded skillful means. This is able to give birth to the assemblies of Bodhisattvas. This dharma is solely the realm of samādhi.
This enables one to enter courageously into sarvajñā (omniscience). This is able to open and manifest the gateways of all samādhis. This...
They are able to enter all lands universally and without obstruction; they are able to subdue all sentient beings;
they are able to abide at the limit where no sentient beings exist; they are able to reveal all Buddha-dharmas; yet within this realm, they apprehend nothing whatsoever.

The third section reveals the excellence of its virtues and powers, which consists of two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific exposition beginning with "Although all... and so forth.

Now, for the first part, there is first the formal statement: because those who reveal the Buddha’s nature of equality by means of the virtues of the events in this assembly likewise possess twenty-one kinds of merit.
This is followed by the general praise of the aforementioned virtues.
Although they expound and reveal [the Dharma] at all times, they are always far removed from conceptualization and discrimination.
Although they know that all phenomena are devoid of activity, they are able to manifest all manner of actions.

Although they know that all Buddhas have no dualistic characteristics, they are able to display all Buddhas. Although they know there is no form, they expound upon all forms. Although they know there is no...

Though knowing that there are no sensations, they experience and expound upon all sensations; though knowing there are no perceptions, they expound upon all perceptions; though knowing there are no mental formations, they expound upon all mental formations;
though knowing there is no consciousness, they expound upon all consciousness. They constantly reveal and teach all things through the Wheel of Dharma;
though knowing that dharmas are unarisen, they perpetually turn the Wheel of Dharma; though knowing that dharmas are without distinction, they speak of all [dharmas].
The Door of Differentiation: Although one knows that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, one speaks of the characteristics of all arising and ceasing.
Although one knows that all phenomena are neither coarse nor subtle, one speaks of the coarse and subtle characteristics of all phenomena.
Although one knows that all phenomena have no superior, middling, or inferior, one is able to proclaim the most supreme Dharma. Although one knows that all phenomena are ineffable...
They are able to expound pure speech. Although they know that all phenomena have neither interior nor exterior, they speak of all internal and external phenomena.
Although they know that all phenomena cannot be fully comprehended, they speak of various kinds of wisdom and observation.
Although they know that all phenomena lack any true reality, they speak of the path of true liberation. Although they know that all phenomena are ultimately...
Though they are ultimately inexhaustible, they are able to expound the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

Though they know that all phenomena are without conflict or dispute, they do not deny the distinctions between self and others. Though they know that all phenomena are ultimately without a teacher, they always revere all teachers and elders.
Though they know that all phenomena are realized without depending on another, they always revere all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Though...
Knowing that phenomena have no turning, they turn the wheel of Dharma. Although knowing that phenomena have no arising, they demonstrate various causes and conditions.
Although knowing that all phenomena have no prior limit, they extensively explain the past. Although knowing that all phenomena have no subsequent limit, they extensively explain the future.
Although knowing that all phenomena have no middle limit, they extensively explain the present. Although knowing all [phenomena]...
Although phenomena have no agent, he speaks of various actions; although he knows that all phenomena lack causes and conditions, he speaks of the causes of their accumulation;
although he knows that all phenomena lack comparison, he speaks of the paths of equality and inequality;
although he knows that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, he definitively explains the dharmas of the three periods of time; although he knows that all phenomena...

While having a basis for speech, they speak based on the wholesome dharmas to achieve transcendence. Although knowing that dharmas have no body, they extensively expound the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Although knowing that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are boundless, they can proclaim that there is but one Buddha.
Although knowing that dharmas have no form, they manifest various forms. Although knowing that dharmas are invisible, they extensively expound upon all views. Although knowing...
Although phenomena are signless, they are described with various signs; although one knows that all phenomena have no objective domain, one extensively proclaims the domain of wisdom;
and although one knows that all phenomena have no distinctions, one speaks of the various distinctions among practices and their fruits.
Although he knows that all phenomena have no departure, he teaches the pure practices of departure;
although he knows that all phenomena are primordially abiding, he speaks of all phenomena of saṃsāra;
although he knows that all phenomena have no illumination, he constantly and extensively explains the dharma of illumination.
In the second part, which specifically elucidates [the meaning], we shall first expand upon the meaning of the first "unimpeded" (an-āvaraṇa). It consists of forty-one phrases.
The first phrase states that "existence does not impede non-existence," because existence is the existence of non-existence.

The subsequent forty phrases clarify that "non-existence does not impede existence," because non-existence is the non-existence of existence. Furthermore, the former is duality yet non-duality; the latter is non-duality.
And [the two are] such that their quiescence and activity are mutually identical, and so forth.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this wheel of wisdom of the samādhi of great majestic power, they are then able to realize all Buddha-dharmas;
they are then able to enter into all Buddha-dharmas; they are then able to accomplish them; they are then able to perfect them.

When fulfilled, one is able to accumulate; when fulfilled, one is able to purify; when fulfilled, one is able to abide securely; when fulfilled, one is able to penetrate thoroughly, being in accord with the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The second major section, "Realizing the Function of All Dharmas," has four parts: first, explaining the realization; second, departing from the marks of realization;

third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation. Now, for the first part, there are ten phrases. The first phrase clarifies the meditative concentration that serves as the means of realization: the wheel of samādhi-wisdom.
It should be called the "Wisdom-Wheel Samādhi. Because its meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is most supreme, it is termed "Great Majestic Power" (*mahā-tejas*).

It is thus able to manifest downward the realized Dharma, namely, the Dharma of the realization of the Buddha-fruit. The first phrase is general; that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*), while conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) fruit is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).

The remaining phrases are specific: "entering" (*avatāra*) explains realization, and "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) explains attainment. "Perfection" (*paripūri*) applies to both, while "accumulation" (*upacaya*) refers to [the former].
The causes are fulfilled. Purity refers to the exhaustion of hindrances. Concentration enables one to abide securely, while wisdom enables thorough penetration.
When both concentration and wisdom are transcended, there is correspondence with the intrinsic nature; this constitutes realization and entry.
Yet this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such thoughts: that there are a certain number of bodhisattvas; a certain number of bodhisattva-dharmas; a certain number of bodhisattva culminations;
a certain number of culminations of illusion; a certain number of culminations of transformation; a certain number of accomplishments of supernormal powers;
a certain number of accomplishments of knowledge; a certain number of contemplations; a certain number of realizations; or a certain number of destinies.
Toward various objects.

Second, clarifying the characteristic of realization through detachment: since one realizes [the truth] precisely by means of non-thought, one cannot even attain the object of unimpeded wisdom through thought;
how much less could there be various dharmas to be realized?
Why is this? There are three points of inquiry: first, by what means is it proven that there is no conceptualization; second, why is there a single cause for multiple effects;
and third, how is it that through a fixed cause one attains the dharma of the fruit?
Because the bodhisattva samādhi has such an essential nature, is thus boundless, and is thus preeminent, there are four explanations, two of which are as follows:
first, a brief and specific explanation; second, a detailed and general explanation beginning with the words "this samādhi. Now, for the first:
A separate explanation of the three inquiries: first, because its essential nature is free from conceptual thought; second, because although the essence of samādhi is one, its functions are infinite;
third, because by means of this excellence, the causal dharma attains the resultant dharma.

Regarding these various objects, various powers, and various profound penetrations of this samādhi, the subsequent "extensive and universal explanation" means that the text is extensive and the meaning is universal, universally clarifying the three preceding phrases. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general indication.
"Objects" refers to the focal points of concentration; "profound penetration" refers to the realization and accord of concentration; and "power" refers to the [efficacy] of concentration.

As for their application: all three are fixed in essence, and all are described as "various. Therefore, it was said above that they are "boundless. Because they possess these three aspects and are manifold, they are called "extraordinary" (*viśeṣa*).
That is to say: entering the gate of ineffable wisdom; entering the various adornments free from conceptual discrimination; and entering the boundless and extraordinary.
The pāramitās. Entering into countless meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Entering into hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ineffable, vast wisdoms.
Entering into the vision of the boundless, supreme, and wondrous treasury of the Buddhas. Entering into the realms without cessation.

Entering into the pure faith, understanding, and factors conducive to the path (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Entering into the sharp faculties and great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Entering into the realms with an unobstructed mind. Entering...
They enter the eye of equality that beholds all Buddhas; they enter the accumulation of the supreme wisdom-practices of Samantabhadra;

they enter and abide in the body of the wondrous wisdom of Nārāyaṇa; they enter the exposition of the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; they enter the arousal of immeasurable kinds of sovereign spiritual transformations;
they enter the birth of the inexhaustible gates of wisdom of all Buddhas; they enter and abide in the realm of the presence of all Buddhas; they enter the purification of the universal...
The wise Bodhisattva enters the sovereign wisdom; enters the manifestation of the peerless wisdom of the universal gate;
enters the universally known subtle realms of the entire dharma-realm; enters the universally manifested subtle realms of the entire dharma-realm;
enters the light of all supreme wisdom; enters the limit of all sovereignty; enters the limit of all dharma-gates of eloquence; and enters...
The body of wisdom pervading the entire dharma realm enters the path of universal practice that accomplishes all places;
it enters the samādhi of skillfully abiding in all distinctions; and it enters the knowledge of the minds of all buddhas.

This is subsequently explained separately in twenty-eight phrases, each of which contains the three aforementioned meanings. Take the first phrase as an example: "entry" (*praveśa*) carries the meaning of "profound entry";
"ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*) carries the meaning of "boundless"; and "gate of wisdom" (*jñāna-mukha*) carries the meaning of "objective realm.
Since knowledge resides in speech, speech is termed the "gate of wisdom. Second, it is the entry into the adornment of the non-duality of merit and wisdom. Sixth, the entry into... [text truncated]
The empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the object of the sevenfold compassion and wisdom; one contemplates and delivers beings without ceasing. The rest may be understood.
Thus concludes the entry into all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the conduct of Samantabhadra, entering in every thought-moment ten billion unspeakable [realms].
Samādhi. However, one does not see the limit of the samādhi of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva nor the adornment of the Buddha’s realm in the past.
Third is "Inexhaustible Universal Virtue," which contains four parts. First, the actual manifestation of inexhaustibility:
it means that not only are the various functions listed above inexhaustible, but he can also enter many samādhis in every thought-moment, such that they too cannot be exhausted.
Why is this? The intent of the two inquiries is as follows:
since one is already able to enter the manifold [realms] in every moment, why does one not reach their end?
It is because one knows that all dharmas are ultimately inexhaustible; it is because one knows that all Buddha-fields are boundless; it is because one knows all...
Because the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable; because one knows that the prior limit is beginningless; because one knows that the future is infinite;
because one knows that the present is as boundless as empty space pervading the Dharma-realm; because one knows that the sphere of all Buddhas is inconceivable;
because one knows that the practices of all Bodhisattvas are innumerable; because one knows the eloquence of all Buddhas...
It is said that the objective sphere (*ālambana*) is ineffable because it is boundless; and one knows that all phenomena which are the objects of the illusory mind are immeasurable.
The threefold explanation of the intent states: "Because the objects of this samādhi are ultimately inexhaustible. There are ten phrases in the text:
the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
O Son of the Buddha, just as a wish-fulfilling gem grants everything that is sought,
