satisfying the intentions of those who seek it without end while the power of the gem itself never fails, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Entering this samādhi,
they know that the mind is like an illusion, giving rise to the spheres of all phenomena, which are pervasive and inexhaustible.
They do not cease. Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the unimpeded wisdom of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
they observe that immeasurable and vast illusory phenomena are like reflections, neither increasing nor decreasing.

There are four similes for illustration. Among them, there are three similes that illustrate the inexhaustibility mentioned previously; each has both the simile and its application (*yoga*). Within the first two applications, further inquiry and explanation are added.

The first is the "simile of the wish-fulfilling gem according with requests," which illustrates how the dharmas produced by a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) emerge in accordance with needs and are inexhaustible.

The intent of the inquiry is: "By what means are the dharmas produced inexhaustible, such that they do not become depleted or cease? The intent of the explanation is: "Because one realizes the manifold..."
Illusory phenomena are all like reflections; when conditions arise, they manifest—how could there be an end? Their essence neither increases nor decreases—how could there be exhaustion or cessation?
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if ordinary beings each give rise to their own thoughts: those already arisen, those currently arising, and those yet to arise, which do not [inherently exist].
It has no boundaries, is uninterrupted, and is inexhaustible; the continuous flow of its mind is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having entered this Samādhi of the Universal Door of Illusion, it is without limit and immeasurable.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized the infinite dharmas of the universal illusion of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The second is the analogy of the distinct minds of sentient beings, which illustrates the inexhaustibility of the objects of cognition.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the dragon kings Nanda, Upananda, and Manasvin, along with other great dragons, send down rain;
the drops are as large as axle-trees and have no limit, yet even as they rain thus, the clouds are never exhausted. This is...
The realm of all nāgas is one of non-action.
The analogy of the three dragon kings raining down rain illustrates entering the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. Within this, there is first the analogy and subsequently the application.
It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who dwells in this samādhi and enters the various samādhis of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The gateway of obscurity, the gateway of wisdom, the gateway of phenomena, the gateway of beholding all Buddhas, the gateway of proceeding to all directions,

the gateway of mastery over the mind, the gateway of empowerment, the gateway of spiritual transformations, the gateway of supernatural powers, the gateway of illusory manifestations, the gateway of the illusory nature of all phenomena,
and the gateway filled with unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Bodhisattvas; they draw near to as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds.
The gateway of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment; the gateway of entering the unspeakably unspeakable, vast net of illusions;

the gateway of knowing the unspeakably unspeakable distinctions of vast Buddha-fields; the gateway of knowing the unspeakably unspeakable worlds that possess intrinsic nature and those that lack intrinsic nature;
the gateway of knowing the unspeakably unspeakable perceptions of sentient beings; the gateway of knowing the...

The gateway of the distinction between times that can be described and those that cannot be described; the gateway of knowing the formation and disintegration of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds;
and the gateway of knowing unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields situated either inverted or upright.
This section is divided into three parts. First, the actual explanation of entering the Dharma. "The drops merge like axle-trees" means that one enters the vast and great Dharma.
The first phrase is general; the section beginning with "the gateways of wisdom" is specific. All are called "gateways" because they are the means by which oneself and others enter.

"The Net of Illusion" refers to how all things are illusory, mutually arising through dependent origination, and intersecting and reflecting one another. Because the nature of worlds is empty, there is no [inherent existence].

Regarding substance (*tattva*): because it is defiled or pure according to conditions, it possesses substance; furthermore, because it is the land of *dharmatā*, it possesses substance. Because the land of phenomena (*vastu*) arises from conditions, it lacks substance.
Furthermore, because the pure realm (*śuddhakṣetra*) accords with principle, it possesses substance; because the defiled realm is falsely constructed, it lacks substance.
Within a single thought-moment, he knows all things as they truly are.
Regarding the second entry into the Dharma, it coincides with the aforementioned time of the falling rain.
Thus, his entry is without limit, without end; he is neither weary nor wearying, neither ceasing nor resting.
There is no regression and no loss. Among all phenomena, one does not abide in improper places. One constantly engages in right reflection, neither sinking nor becoming agitated.

One enters the characteristics and functions of the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*). This, together with the previously mentioned boundless, inexhaustible, and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) realm, constitutes three [aspects] therein.

The first ten phrases clarify their characteristics; the subsequent section beginning with "seeking all-knowledge" clarifies their functional activity; the third section consists of an inquiry and its explanation regarding the underlying cause.
Now, for the first part: the first two phrases combine the boundless clouds and the inexhaustible rain; "without weariness" and so forth combine the realm of non-action (*anabhoga*).
Since non-action is precisely the absence of effortful application (*anābhoga*), the body does not grow weary and the mind does not become fatigued; thus, they do not cease forever.

There is no momentary rest. Because one has not yet entered [the state] that is eternally entered, one does not regress; because one has already entered that which is eternally constant, one does not lose it.

Since there is no dharma that is not the gate of entry, one does not abide in an improper place. Since there is no mind that does not accord [with reality], one always engages in correct contemplation (*samyak-manasikāra*).
Without sinking or agitation, this is precisely the characteristic of entry.
They seek omniscience with never-receding resolve; they become luminous lamps illuminating the world for all buddha-fields;
they turn the wheels of Dharma that are unspeakably unspeakable; they inquire of the Tathāgatas with wondrous eloquence without end;
they manifest the path to Buddhahood without limit; they tame sentient beings without ever ceasing; and they constantly and diligently cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
Their practices and vows never cease; they manifest immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable forms and bodies without interruption.
Regarding these two types of karmic activity, each individual gate of entry possesses such activity, and every gate is inexhaustible.

Why is this? Within the threefold inquiry and explanation, there are two points of inquiry. First: "How could it be that a bodhisattva does not attain Buddhahood through the fulfillment of their practice?
Why, then, would their karmic activity have no limit? Second: "It may be granted that the horizontal description reveals inexhaustibility; however, why [is it so] in a single..."

Within a single gateway, its function is inexhaustible. There are two further explanations for this intent: first, it is said that because the Bodhisattva’s original purpose is for the sake of sentient beings, and since those beings are inexhaustible, their function is likewise inexhaustible.

Second, regarding the subsequent intent, it is said that since both sentient beings and the world are like empty space, the function of each individual gateway is consequently inexhaustible, just as there is space within a mustard seed. For this reason, it is not...
However, from a single gate many are accomplished; likewise, in a single thought-moment, one can accomplish many matters.
It is like lighting a fire: according to the conditions present, the fire continues to burn without ceasing for as long as those conditions persist.
The commentary on the text has three parts. First, the illustration clarifies that fire follows the conditions of its fuel; when the fuel is abundant, the fire persists.
This illustrates that the Bodhisattva’s activity within the realm of sentient beings is vast in its conditions and boundless in its application.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. He observes that the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm are like empty space, without limit or boundary.

Thus, in a single moment of thought, he can travel to as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; at each and every Buddha-field, he enters into unspeakably unspeakable [realms].

By means of the various distinctions of all-knowledge, they cause unspeakably unspeakable realms of sentient beings to leave the household life for the sake of the Path and diligently cultivate roots of goodness until they reach ultimate purity.

They cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas who have not yet attained certainty regarding the practices and vows of Samantabhadra to attain such certainty, and to dwell securely within the gateway of Samantabhadra’s wisdom. By...
Through immeasurable skillful means, they enter unspeakably unspeakable eons of the vast distinctions of formation, abiding, and destruction throughout the three periods of time.
Within unspeakably unspeakable realms of the world’s distinctions of formation, abiding, and destruction,
they give rise to such great compassion and great vows as to discipline all immeasurable sentient beings, leaving none remaining.
The subsequent synthesis may be understood.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and give rise to the wisdom of Samantabhadra, thereby fulfilling all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

The subsequent section provides a critical inquiry and an explanation. The intent of the inquiry is: "For what reason does the Bodhisattva initiate such manifold karmic activities? The intent of the explanation is:
"It is for the sake of universally delivering sentient beings and fulfilling universal vows. This concludes the section on "Universal Virtues that are Inexhaustible."
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should proceed toward such types, such objects, such majestic power, such vastness, such immeasurability,
such inconceivability, such universal illumination,
such presence before all Buddhas, such being protected and remembered by all Tathāgatas, and such accomplishment.
In the *samādhi* of a mind that is thus unimpeded and immovable due to past roots of goodness, the fourth major section—concluding and exhorting toward practice—is divided into two parts:
first, the conclusion and exhortation to diligent cultivation; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "thus practicing," which is the final summary and manifestation.
Now, for the first part: it means that the Bodhisattva’s mind pervades the realm of sentient beings. It is fixed...
Because its application is boundless, it should be cultivated. This passage consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the dharmas to be cultivated;

second, from "diligently apply" onwards, the demonstration of the characteristics of diligent cultivation. Regarding the first part: the five characters "therefore, all bodhisattvas" encompass the following two sections.

The dharmas to be cultivated consist of eleven phrases; the final phrase presents the name and essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the preceding ten phrases [present its qualities].

This section separately clarifies the functional activity of the wheel of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-cakra*). Within this, it cites preceding passages as examples. First, regarding "categories" (*jāti*):

because its functional activities are manifold, the meaning of "category" is like that of the "metaphor of joining the dragon," where the multitude of those who have entered the Dharma constitutes the sense of a category.
Second, the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) refers to the focal object (*ālambana*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as in the previous analogy of the deluded thought taking an object.
Third, majestic power (*anubhāva*) refers to the manifestation of the function of concentration, as in the previous analogy of the jewel being able to produce [treasures].

Fourth, these three aforementioned aspects are all vast and expansive, each being boundless, as in the previous [analogy] of not perceiving the prior limit of samādhi. Fifth, their number is incalculable...
Sixth, they are all beyond mind and speech, because—as previously stated—they do not form such thoughts as "there are a certain number of bodhisattvas" and so forth.
Seventh, they are all accompanied by wisdom;

for although—as previously stated—they know that all phenomena are without activity, they are nonetheless able to manifest all manner of activities. This is the clarification of the provisional and the real.

8. Because of illumination, the eight aspects of essence and function are equal to the realm of the Buddhas; thus all Buddhas appear before one, as previously explained regarding the contemplation of the stage of the Ten Powers up to *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
9. Because the Tathāgatas protect and mind [the practitioner], as previously explained regarding being sustained by all Buddhas and having already entered the reckoning of future Buddhas.
10. Not only is there mastery in present application, but past roots of goodness are also perfected, as previously explained.

Because they desire that all merit and understanding be completely purified, they apply themselves with diligence to cultivation, remaining free from all feverish afflictions, without weariness or mental regression.

Establishing profound resolve and delight, they are courageous and fearless, conforming to the sphere of samādhi and entering the stage of inconceivable wisdom. They do not rely on words and letters, nor do they cling to them.
In the world, one does not grasp at phenomena, does not give rise to conceptual discrimination, is not stained by worldly affairs, and does not discriminate among objective spheres.
Within the two demonstrations of the characteristics of cultivation, there are two parts. First, a brief demonstration of transcending faults and advancing in virtue.
Following "not relying on words and letters," there is a detailed demonstration of transcending faults and advancing in virtue; therein, first, the transcending of faults.
Regarding the knowledge of all phenomena, one should simply abide therein and not engage in conceptual measurement. That is to say: to draw near to omniscience;
to awaken to and understand the Buddha’s bodhi; to achieve the light of the Dharma; to bestow roots of goodness upon all sentient beings;
to pull sentient beings out from within the realm of Māra and cause them to enter the sphere of the Buddha-Dharma; and to ensure they do not abandon their great vows while diligently contemplating.
One should enter the path. One should expand the pure realms and accomplish the various perfections (*pāramitās*). One should engender profound faith and understanding toward all Buddhas.

One should constantly observe the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and never abandon it for even a moment. One should know that one’s own self and the nature of all phenomena are universally equal.
One should clearly understand worldly activities and demonstrate to others the wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that accord with the Dharma. One should always...
One should practice diligence without rest. One should contemplate that one’s own roots of goodness are meager.
One should diligently increase the roots of goodness in others. One should personally cultivate the path to omniscience. One should diligently increase the bodhisattva realm.
One should delight in drawing near to spiritual friends. One should dwell together with those of like practice. One should not discriminate regarding the Buddha. One should...
Without abandoning mindfulness, one should always abide peacefully in the equal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). One should know that all mental consciousnesses are like illusions;

one should know that all worldly conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) are like dreams; and one should know that the manifestation of the Buddhas through the power of their vows is like reflected images.
One should know that all vast karmic activities are like magical transformations; one should know that all speech is like an echo;
one should contemplate all phenomena as being entirely like illusions; and one should know that all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are like sounds.
One should know that all Buddha-fields to which one goes are devoid of intrinsic nature. One should inquire after the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata without becoming weary or disheartened.
One should diligently provide instruction for the sake of awakening all the world, never abandoning them.
One should preach the Dharma without ceasing, knowing the proper time for the sake of subduing all sentient beings.
Thereafter, one advances in virtue; the text may be understood accordingly.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the conduct of Samantabhadra in this way, they thus fulfill the Bodhi...
The realm of the *sattva*. Thus one penetrates the path of deliverance; thus one upholds the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time;
thus one contemplates the gateway to all-knowledge; thus one reflects upon the unchanging dharma; thus one clarifies and purifies one’s superior aspiration;
thus one has faith and understanding in all Tathāgatas; thus one thoroughly understands the vast power of the Buddhas. As...
This is the resolute mind that is unimpeded. In this way, it encompasses all sentient beings.

Second, regarding the summary and demonstration: on a broad level, it serves as a general conclusion for the preceding sections; on a narrow level, it specifically concludes the preceding passage concerning the advancement of virtue.
The second major section above, clarifying the entry into one’s own intellectual function, is now complete. Below—
The fulfillment of the three concentrations brings about benefit.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this Great Wisdom Samādhi in which the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra abides, [he attains these benefits].

The third major section concerns the benefits achieved through the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This text pertains specifically to this concentration, while its intent also encompasses the preceding nine stages.

Within this, there are four parts: first, the benefit of external inspiration from the Buddha; second, the benefit of the internal perfection of virtues; third, the benefit of being subsumed within the fruit of Buddhahood;

and fourth, the benefit of being truly identical to the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the first of these, there are five points, the first of which is the identification of the basis for such inspiration, namely, that it occurs at the time of remaining in meditative concentration.
In each of the ten directions, there are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands.
In each and every land, there are names of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Before each and every one of these names, there appear Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Second, to manifest those who bestow empowerment:
they grant the power of recollection of the Tathāgata, so that one does not forget the sphere of the Tathāgata; they grant the ultimate wisdom of all dharmas, so that one enters into omniscience;
and they grant the decisive wisdom that knows the various meanings of all dharmas, so that one may receive and uphold [the teachings].
He grants unimpeded entry into all Buddha-dharmas; he bestows the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi, causing them to enter all-knowledge and awaken to the dharma-realm;
he grants the ultimate wisdom of Bodhisattvas, causing them to attain the radiance of all dharmas and be free from all darkness;

he grants the non-retrogressive knowledge of Bodhisattvas, enabling them to know the appropriate and inappropriate times through skillful means to discipline sentient beings; he grants the [unobstructed... of the Unsurpassed...
They remove obstacles to the bodhisattva’s eloquence, enabling the realization and understanding of boundless dharmas and their inexhaustible exposition.

They bestow the power of supernatural transformations, enabling the manifestation of unspeakably unspeakable varieties of distinct bodies with infinite physical forms and diverse characteristics to awaken sentient beings.
They grant the perfection of vocal resonance, enabling the manifestation of unspeakably unspeakable varieties.
Through various sounds and diverse言辞 (vāc), he awakens sentient beings, bestowing the power that is never in vain;
such that all sentient beings who either behold his form or hear his Dharma shall all achieve fulfillment, with none passing by in vain.
Third, the explicit manifestation of the characteristics of the application.
O Son of the Buddha, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has thus fulfilled the conduct of Samantabhadra, he attains the power of the Tathāgata, purifies the path of renunciation,
fulfills all-knowledge, and through unimpeded eloquence, supernormal powers, and transformations, brings beings to ultimate subdual.
All sentient beings possess the majestic power of the Buddhas, purify the conduct of Samantabhadra, and abide in the path of Samantabhadra;
until the end of the future, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, they turn the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
Fourth is the application for the fulfillment of activity.

Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, when these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such supreme great vows and bodhisattva practices, they become Dharma-teachers for all the world; they become suns of the Dharma for all the world. They...
He is the moon of wisdom for all the world; he is the king of mountains, Sumeru, for all the world—loftily rising, firm, and immovable; he is the boundless ocean of wisdom for all the world;
he is the bright lamp of the True Dharma for all the world, universally illuminating without limit, continuing in an uninterrupted succession, and revealing it to all sentient beings.
With boundless, pure merits, they cause all to dwell securely in roots of goodness and merit;

they accord with the equality of the great vows for omniscience and cultivate the vast practices of Samantabhadra. They are always able to exhort and inspire immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the samādhi of the unspeakably unspeakable vast practices and manifesting great sovereign mastery.

The fifth section provides an inquiry and explanation regarding the underlying reason. The intent of the inquiry is: "Since the universal practice has already been fulfilled, why is it necessary to continue practicing the conduct for taming sentient beings until the end of the future?
The intent of the explanation is: "Because such is the nature of unobstructed vows; having already perfected the Great Vow, one is truly capable of taming [beings]."
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained such wisdom, realized such dharmas, dwells with clear vision and firm stability in such dharmas,
acquired such supernormal powers, abides in such spheres, manifests such miraculous transformations,
and exercises such spiritual faculties. He constantly dwells in great compassion, constantly benefits sentient beings, and reveals to them peace and security.
The Right Path. He establishes the great banner of light of merit and wisdom, realizes inconceivable liberation, and dwells in the liberation of omniscience.
Having reached the further shore of the liberation of all Buddhas, he studies the skillful means of inconceivable liberation.
Having already attained accomplishment, he enters the gate of the distinctions of the Dharma-realm without error. Regarding the ineffable, ineffable [qualities] of Samantabhadra...
It speaks of samādhi: sporting with mastery, abiding in the lion-like valorous wisdom, and having unimpeded mind and intellect.
This is the second benefit, the perfection of internal virtues, which consists of four parts. First, it restates the cause for abiding in meditative concentration, summarizing the preceding text.
Their minds constantly abide in ten great treasuries of Dharma. What are these ten? They are: abiding in the recollection of all Buddhas;
abiding in the recollection of all Buddha-dharmas; abiding in the great compassion that subdues all sentient beings;
abiding in the wisdom that manifests inconceivable, pure buddha-lands; abiding in the resolute understanding that penetrates deeply into the realm of all Buddhas; and abiding in [the departure]...
They come to the bodhi characterized by the equality of all Buddhas of the past, present, and future; they abide at the limit of non-obstruction and non-attachment;
they abide in the signless nature of all phenomena; they abide in the roots of goodness shared equally by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future;

they abide in the wisdom that precedes the non-differentiated activities of body, speech, and mind within the dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future; they abide in contemplation.

The births, renunciations, journeys to the site of enlightenment, attainments of perfect awakening, turnings of the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are all contained within a single moment.
O Son of the Buddha, these ten great treasuries of Dharma are vast and immeasurable;
they are incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, and ineffable; they are inexhaustible and difficult to endure for any worldly wisdom.
It is impossible to fully describe it.
Second, to specifically indicate what has been fulfilled: the number ten signifies inexhaustibility.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already reached the further shore of all practices of Samantabhadra and has realized the pure Dharma.

The power of their resolve is vast; they reveal immeasurable roots of goodness to sentient beings, increase all the powers of bodhisattvas, fulfill all the merits of bodhisattvas in every moment of thought, and accomplish all the practices of bodhisattvas.
They attain the dhāraṇī-dharma of all Buddhas and uphold everything spoken by all Buddhas;
though they constantly abide in the reality-limit of true suchness, they conform to all worldly conventions of speech to manifest the taming of all sentient beings.
Third, the conclusion of the ultimate. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi-dharma in such a manner.
Fourth, the inquiry and explanation of the reason. The intent of the inquiry is: "How is it that a Bodhisattva is able to fulfill such a multitude of virtues? This is the explanation.
The meaning is clear.
O Son of the Buddha! By means of this samādhi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the vast wisdom of all Buddhas;
attains the eloquence of mastery in skillfully expounding all vast dharmas; and attains that which is most preeminent and pure among all worlds.
The fearless dharma of purity. Attaining entry into the wisdom of all samādhis. Attaining the skillful means of all bodhisattvas.
Attaining the gate of illumination of all dharmas. Reaching the further shore of the dharma that comforts all worlds.
Knowing the proper and improper times for all sentient beings, they illuminate every place throughout the worlds of the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to attain excellence.
Wisdom. Acting as the unsurpassed teacher of all worlds, abiding in all merits, and revealing the pure samādhi to all sentient beings, he causes them to enter the supreme knowledge.
Third, within the section on the benefit of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, there are three parts. First, the formal explanation:

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they thereby benefit sentient beings, increase their great compassion, draw near to spiritual friends, behold all Buddhas, comprehend all dharmas, and arrive at...
They enter all lands; they enter all directions; they enter all worlds; they realize the equality of all phenomena;
they know the equality of all Buddhas; and they abide in the equality of omniscience.
Next is the interrogation (*paryanuyoga*). The intent of the interrogation is as follows: "How can that which is above [the Buddha's virtues] be encompassed?

The subsequent section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva," explains the meaning: by abiding in this samādhi, one's capacity for action and what is to be accomplished is exhaustive, for one is identical to the Tathāgata.
Within this, there are three parts. First, the primary manifestation of the exhaustive activity; therefore, everything is referred to as "all."

Within this Dharma, one performs such action and no other. One dwells with a mind that is not yet satisfied, with an undistracted mind, with a concentrated mind, with a mind of diligent cultivation, with a resolute mind, and with an unchanging mind.
Thus one reflects, thus one acts, and thus one brings it to completion.
Second, the explanation of the mode of performing the activity. The first phrase generally indicates that one acts based on what preceded, performing no further insufficient activities.
The phrase "abiding in the incomplete" and so forth clarifies the meaning of this performance. The section beginning with "In this way" concludes the preceding discussion of the performance.
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not have speech that differs from action; his speech is as his action, and his action is as his speech.

This is explained through three successive difficult points, meaning that he extensively performs such karma as previously described and does not perform other karma. Within this passage, there are three sections.
This is the initial brief enumeration. Within this, it is as if one were to apply [the term] to the entire body and the mind.
Why is this? For example, just as "vajra" receives its name because it is indestructible, and there is never a time when it is apart from being indestructible, so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
he receives his name by virtue of the phenomena of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
There is never a time when one is separated from the phenomena of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Next is the interrogation. The intent of the interrogation is: "Why does one not perform other [actions]? This is followed by the extensive explanation. The intent of the explanation is:
"If one were to act differently than before, one would not be a bodhisattva. The text contains ten metaphors, which constitute ten sections, each with its own application (*yoga*). First:
The analogy of the indestructible diamond illustrates the firmness of the essence of practice.
For example, just as genuine gold receives its name because it possesses a sublime color and never at any time loses that sublime color.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he acquires his name through various wholesome karmas, and there is never a time when he is separated from those wholesome karmas.
The analogy of the exquisite color of the two kinds of true gold illustrates the external adornment of wholesome karma.
For example, the Son of the Sun Deity receives his name from the wheel of radiance; there is never a time when he is separated from that wheel of radiance.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva receives his name from the light of wisdom;
there is never a time when he is separated from the light of wisdom.
The analogy of the three wheels of light illustrates the perfect clarity of wisdom.
For example, Sumeru, the King of Mountains, stands majestically high above the great ocean with its four peaks made of precious jewels, thereby acquiring its name;
it never at any time abandons those four peaks. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise... [with]... by means of... (the four foundations of mindfulness).
The various roots of goodness remain in the world; they stand loftily elevated and thus acquire their name. There is never a time when they abandon these roots of goodness.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the four peaks of Mount Sumeru, which represent the transcendence of the roots of goodness.
For example, the great earth receives its name from supporting all things; it never at any time abandons that capacity to support.
In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives his name from delivering all beings;
he never at any time abandons his great compassion.
The analogy of the five great elements being able to sustain [all things] illustrates the bearing of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
For example, the great ocean derives its name from containing all waters; it never at any time abandons those waters.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he receives his name because of his various great vows, and he never for a moment abandons the vow to deliver sentient beings.
The sixth analogy, that of the great oceans containing water, illustrates how the great vows universally nurture all beings.
For example, just as a military general acquires his reputation through mastery in the arts of combat and never at any time abandons that skill,
so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: having acquired his name through mastery in such samādhi,
he never at any time abandons it until the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Practice.
The seventh is the analogy of the army commander’s clear battle, which illustrates practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to ward off enemies.
It is like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) who governs the four continents and constantly exerts himself to protect all sentient beings, ensuring they do not meet with untimely death.
They constantly experience happiness. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:
entering such great samādhis as these, they constantly and diligently transform and deliver all sentient beings, even leading them to ultimate purity.
The eighth is the analogy of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) protecting the world, which illustrates how objects are transformed through the power of meditative concentration.
It is like planting a seed in the earth, which eventually causes the stalks and leaves to grow;
likewise, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the conduct of Samantabhadra and thereby enables the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings to increase.
Long. Ninth is the simile of the growth of planted seeds, which illustrates the increase of wholesome things through practice.
It is like a great cloud that, during the hot summer months, pours down heavy rain, thereby causing all seeds to grow.
The simile of seeds sprouting after ten days of rain illustrates how the rain of the Dharma universally brings things to fruition.
First the simile, then the application: A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.

Entering such great samādhis as these, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and rain down the great rain of the Dharma, even unto the point of enabling all sentient beings to reach ultimate purity and ultimate nirvāṇa.
...attain parinirvāṇa. May they reach ultimate peace, the ultimate further shore, ultimate joy, and the ultimate severance of doubt.
May they become the ultimate field of merit for all sentient beings, causing their acts of giving to be entirely purified.
May they all abide in the path of non-retrogression; may they equally attain the wisdom of all-knowledge; may they all achieve liberation from the three realms; may they all...
They attain ultimate wisdom, causing all beings to obtain the ultimate Dharma of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and establishing all sentient beings in the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

This consists of two parts: first, the formal application (*yoga*), and second, the inquiry and explanation (*pṛcchā-vyākhyāna*). Within the former, the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) indicates that one transcends the initial stage of birth.
It is precisely because it culminates in completion that it descends in accordance with the opportune moment, thereby obtaining these fourteen kinds of benefits:

first, the attainment of the fruit of wisdom, because the two obstacles are purified; second, the attainment of the fruit of abandonment, because one penetrates the dharma of signlessness; third, the attainment of the fruit of grace.

Because he abides in great compassion, fourth, he attains the fruit of the ultimate perfection of the purity of his basis; these four preceding points constitute self-benefit. All subsequent points constitute benefit for others.
Fifth, by understanding the conduct of sentient beings, he causes them to rejoice; by himself being free from the ten fears, he rejoices himself.
Sixth, he attains the severance of doubt. Seventh, he becomes one worthy of offerings. All the following phrases are accomplished on this basis.

Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish these dharmas, their wisdom becomes clear and penetrating as they enter the gateway of the Dharma-realm, enabling them to purify the inconceivable and immeasurable practices of a bodhisattva.
In the subsequent section on inquiry and explanation: the intent of the inquiry is to ask by what power of practice does the Bodhisattva preach the Dharma to achieve such great benefit;

the intent of the explanation is that because they have perfected great wisdom and realized the *dharmadhātu*, they are even able to purify immeasurable practices, let alone merely accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
This section consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "That is to say."
That is to say: it can purify all wisdoms because of seeking omniscience; it can purify sentient beings because of bringing them to subdual;
it can purify buddha-lands because of constant dedication; it can purify all dharmas because of universal comprehension; it can purify fearlessness because of being free from timidity;
it can purify unimpeded eloquence because of skillful exposition; and it can purify dhāraṇīs regarding all...
Because one has attained mastery over the Dharma, one is able to purify the practice of intimacy, constantly seeing all Buddhas and bestowing [benefits] upon the world.
Within the two explanations, there are three parts; first, the listing of the virtues to be purified.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably,
unspeakably many pure merits such as these.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are vast and numerous;
because they are difficult to exhaust through individual explanation, and because one has attained mastery over such realms of samādhi, and because one is empowered by all Buddhas.
Because it flows from the power of one's own roots of goodness; because of entering the stage of wisdom with its great majesty;
because of the guiding power of spiritual friends; because of subduing all the powers of Māra; and because of the power of the purity of shared roots of goodness.
By the power of the aspiration for vast vows; by the power of the accomplishment of the roots of goodness that have been planted;
and by the peerless power of inexhaustible merit that transcends all worlds.

Third, the manifestation of the causes for purification. Regarding "roots of goodness of the same category" (*sabhāga-kuśalamūla*): each individual root of goodness is dedicated to the *dharmadhātu*, thereby forming a relationship of principal and attendant.
Regarding "transcending all worlds" and so forth: because the merit thus cultivated accords with the *dharmatā*, it transcends the world;

because the *dharmatā* does not coexist with the conventional, it has no counterpart. This concludes the third section on the fulfillment of meditative concentration and the accomplishment of benefit.
The summary of the benefit of the fruit of Buddhahood is complete.
O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain ten kinds of dharmas that are identical to those of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten? They are: attaining the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and manifold adornments, which are identical to those of all [Buddhas].
The Buddha is able to emit a great net of pure radiance, identical to all Buddhas;
he tames sentient beings through supernatural transformations, identical to all Buddhas; his boundless physical forms and pure, perfect voice are identical to all Buddhas;
he manifests pure Buddha-lands according to the karma of sentient beings, identical to all Buddhas; and he is able to encompass all the languages of all sentient beings.

Maintaining [the teachings] without forgetting or losing them, they are equal to all Buddhas. With inexhaustible eloquence, they turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, causing wisdom to arise and making them equal to all Buddhas.
Uttering the great lion’s roar without any fear, they awaken the multitudes through immeasurable dharmas, becoming equal to all Buddhas.
In a single thought-moment, through great supernormal powers, they universally enter the three...
They are equal to all Buddhas in that they are universally able to manifest for all sentient beings the adornments and the majestic power of all Buddhas;
their Buddha-realms are identical to those of all Buddhas.
The fourth major section correctly establishes the benefit of being identical to the fruit of Buddhahood. This section has two parts:
first, the actual demonstration of this identity, which includes the heading, the inquiry, and the listing of the name "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi) by which it is established.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained such dharmas as are identical to those of all Tathāgatas."

Second, the interrogation and discernment through question and answer. Within this, first the question and then the answer. In the question, first it restates the previous point of being identical to the Buddha:
Why is he not called a Buddha? Why is he not called one of the Ten Powers?
Why is he not called the Omniscient One? Why is he not called the one who has attained Bodhi within all dharmas? Why can he not be named the Universal Eye? Why...
Why is he not called one who possesses unimpeded vision regarding all objects? Why is he not called one who awakens to all dharmas?
Why is he not called one who dwells in non-duality with the Buddhas of the three periods of time? Why is he not called one who dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
Why does he still practice the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra without ceasing? Why is he unable to exhaustively realize the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and relinquish bodhi?
The Path of the Bodhisattva.
Later, he set forth his own doubts. At first, his doubt was not called a "fruit"; later, his question did not abandon the "cause.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Puyan Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha! It is as you have said."
If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is identical to all Buddhas, for what reason is he not called a Buddha, and so forth, until he is unable to abandon the bodhisattva path?
In the latter part of the answer, there are two sections: first, praising the question and restating the doubt.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already been able to cultivate all the various practices and vows of all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.
When he enters the realm of wisdom, he is called a Buddha; when he cultivates the Bodhisattva practices in the presence of the Tathāgata without cessation, he is called a Bodhisattva;
and when he has fully entered all the powers (*bala*) of the Tathāgata, he is called One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
Although they accomplish the ten powers and practice the conduct of Samantabhadra without rest, they are called Bodhisattvas;
although they know all phenomena and are able to expound them, they are called "Omniscient Ones.

Although they are able to expound all phenomena, they skillfully contemplate each and every phenomenon without ever ceasing, and thus they are called Bodhisattvas; they know that all phenomena are without dual characteristics.

This is called the realization of all phenomena. Skillfully observing the path of differentiation among all phenomena—both dual and non-dual—with ever-increasing excellence and without rest, one is called a bodhisattva.
Having been able to clearly perceive the realm of the Universal Eye, one is called the Universal Eye; although one has attained the realm of the Universal Eye, it increases with every thought-moment.
One who never rests is called a bodhisattva. One who can clearly illuminate all phenomena and is free from all obscurations of darkness is said to possess unimpeded vision.
One who constantly and diligently recollects this unimpeded vision is called a bodhisattva.
Having already attained the eye of wisdom of all Buddhas, this is called awakening to all phenomena. One contemplates the eye of the perfectly awakened wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
One who is not negligent is called a bodhisattva. One who dwells where the Buddhas dwell and is non-dual with the Buddhas is called one who dwells in non-duality with the Buddhas.
One who is sustained by the Buddhas and cultivates all forms of wisdom is called a bodhisattva.

One who constantly contemplates the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all worlds is said to be one who dwells in the reality-limit. Although they constantly observe the reality-limit of all phenomena, [they do not fall into a state of stagnation].

Neither realizing nor abandoning [this state], one is called a bodhisattva. Without coming or going, and without distinctions such as similarity or difference—all such conceptualizations are forever stilled.

This is called the one who has brought their vows to rest. When vast cultivation is perfected and non-retrogressive, yet one does not yet bring all vows to rest, this is called the one whose Samantabhadra-vows are not yet at rest. One thoroughly understands that the dharmadhātu is without limit.
All phenomena are of a single mark, which is the markless. This is called the ultimate dharma-realm that relinquishes the bodhisattva path.
Although one knows that the dharma-realm has no boundaries, one perceives all its various distinct characteristics;
thus, one gives rise to great compassion to deliver all sentient beings, never wearying until the end of the future. This is what is called Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

Next, the formal answer to the questions consists of three parts: first, the doctrinal exposition (*dharma-deśanā*); second, the illustrative analogy (*upamā*); and third, the application to the doctrine (*anusandhi*).

Herein, the first section comprises eleven sub-sections that sequentially answer the eleven preceding questions; these are easy to understand from the text, yet their underlying intent remains difficult to perceive. Specifically, one might ask:
how is it that having already entered the ten powers (*daśabala*), one can still practice universally without ceasing? This is now demonstrated collectively through an analogy: it is like a person...

Regarding "recitation and study": although one may have already attained mastery, frequent rehearsing is not equal to long-term refinement. This is illustrated by the analogy of the lower-grade elephant-fragrance (gandhahastin).

Although they appear similar, their essential natures differ; thus, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yíngluò jīng) states: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination."

This is also like the stage of perfected effort; yet it is effortless (*anābhoga*). It also demonstrates that one realizes the fruit without abandoning the cause, for throughout the limits of the future, these are all the universal [practices] (*samantabhadra*) subsequent to the stages.
O Son of the Buddha! It is, for example, like the elephant king Airāvaṇa dwelling within the seven-jeweled cave of King Suvarṇakakṣa.
The perimeter of that cave is entirely encircled by railings made of the seven jewels, with rows of precious tāla trees standing in succession and nets of pure gold covering them from above.
The elephant’s body is as pure white as jade or snow, and atop it stands a golden banner, made of gold.
Adorned with necklaces, his trunk was covered by a jeweled net from which precious bells hung down. His seven limbs were perfected and his six tusks were complete;
he was upright and full, bringing joy to all who beheld him. He was well-trained and gentle, his mind free of any contrary intent.
In the analogy, there are three parts. First, the description of the Elephant King’s excellence in both his physical form and his environment:
Airāvaṇa—here translated as "Fragrant Leaf"—constantly dwells on the slope of the foremost Golden Mountain.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was about to go forth on a journey, the Elephant King immediately discerned his intention.
He then vanished from his form within the precious cave and appeared before Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested various transformations so that his body came to have thirty-three heads. From each head, he produced six tusks; and upon each tusk—
He transformed it into seven ponds. In each pond were seven lotus flowers;
within each flower were seven celestial maidens who simultaneously performed hundreds of thousands of divine musical performances.

At that time, Śakra, riding this precious elephant, departed from the Vaijayanta Palace and proceeded to the flower garden, which was filled everywhere with *puṇḍarīka* lotuses. When Śakra had arrived at the flower garden, he...
Descending from the elephant, he entered the Palace Adorned with All Jewels. Attended by immeasurable court ladies, he enjoyed various pleasures through singing and music.
At that time, the Elephant King again used his supernormal powers to conceal his elephant form and manifest as a celestial being.
Together with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens and the court ladies, [he proceeded] to the Puṇḍarīka Flower Garden.

Their inner amusements and pleasures, the physical forms they manifest, their radiance and clothing, their coming and going, their movements, their speech, laughter, and gazes—all are identical to those of the gods, without any difference.
No one can distinguish whether this is an elephant or a god; the elephant and the god resemble each other so closely.
Second, it clarifies the sovereign spiritual transformations of the Elephant King. Regarding the "seven tusks," according to the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*, there are only six tusks;
perhaps the translator, seeing the sequence "three times seven," subsequently stated "seven. There is no one able to distinguish whether this is an elephant or a deity.
The true intention is to take this as a metaphor for the meaning of a Bodhisattva being equal to a Buddha.
O Son of the Buddha, that Elephant King Airāvaṇa, without undergoing any transformation while within the seven-jeweled cave on Mount Kāñcanaparśva, ascends to the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Desiring to make offerings to Śakra Devendra, he manifests various delightful objects;
he enjoys celestial pleasures no different from those of the gods.
The three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*) do not destroy their fundamental nature yet are able to manifest it.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:

they cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as well as various samādhis to serve as ornaments made of various jewels; the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) constitute the body of the Bodhisattva. What is manifested...
They emit radiance to form a net; they raise the great Dharma banner and ring the great Dharma bell. Great compassion is their cave, and firm great vows are their tusks.
Their wisdom and fearlessness are like those of a lion; with the Dharma silken band bound upon their heads, they reveal the secrets.
They have reached the further shore of all bodhisattva practices and vows.
Within the synthesis of these three dharmas, there are four divisions: 1. "Endowed with the adornments of all practices" synthesizes the previous [sections on] the reliance and the supported. 2.

"Desiring to establish [beings in peace]"—the subsequent explanation of cause and effect as being without attainment—synthesizes the previous [section on] mastery over spiritual transformations. 3. "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s original body...
and so forth, concludes by establishing the indestructible cause while manifesting the fruit; this synthesizes the previous [section on] the indestructibility of the fundamental nature.
It can manifest four things. Why is this? [The following] interrogative and explanatory sections are redundant. Regarding the first and second [points], they may be understood as follows:

Desiring to establish oneself upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), to achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and attain supreme perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), one increases the vast vows and practices of Samantabhadra, never retreating, never ceasing, never interrupting, and never abandoning them; with great compassion and diligence, until the end of the future.
To deliver all sentient beings from suffering and affliction.

Within these two pairs, the first clarifies the purpose for which unimpeded practice is cultivated; therein, the former serves as the fruit, while the latter, beginning with "increasing," serves as the cause.
Without abandoning the path of Samantabhadra, one manifests the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment.

This second [point] clearly reveals the aspect of unimpeded practice; therein, it is first explained in general because the causes and effects within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are without obstruction.
They manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
they manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to turning the wheel of Dharma; they manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to abiding in the profound mind;
and within unspeakably unspeakable vast lands, they manifest gateways to the transformations of nirvana.

This will be explained separately later. Within that, there are three parts; first, the manifestation of the causal gate and the resultant practice. This text contains four types of results: first, the result of wisdom;
second, the result of teaching the Dharma; third, the result of being conjoined with *prajñā*; and fourth, the result of abandonment.
In unspeakably unspeakable varieties of worlds, they manifest birth and cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra;
they manifest as unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas, attaining supreme perfect enlightenment beneath bodhi trees in unspeakably unspeakable, vast lands,
surrounded by assemblies of unspeakably unspeakable Bodhisattvas who draw near to them.
Some may attain perfect enlightenment by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra for the duration of a single thought-moment; some for a brief interval;
some at one time; some for one day; some for half a month; some for one month; some for one year; some for countless years;
or some for one kalpa—and so on, up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas—practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra.
And thus they attain perfect enlightenment.
Next, it is revealed that the fruit arises from causal practices and that the timing of its attainment differs, as these are manifested according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, they become the foremost leaders within all Buddha-fields, drawing near to the Buddhas to prostrate and make offerings.

I ask concerning the observation of the illusory realm: the pure cultivation of the bodhisattva’s immeasurable practices, immeasurable wisdoms, various miraculous transformations, various majestic powers, various forms of knowledge, various spheres of experience, and various supernormal faculties.
Various masteries, various liberations, various illuminations of the Dharma, and various methods of teaching and subduing;
subsequently, the causal practices are revealed through the gateway of the fruition.
O Son of the Buddha! The fundamental body of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perish; through the power of practice and vows, it manifests in this way in all places.

The three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) are indestructible causes from which effects manifest. Because the fundamental body in the interim does not perish, the cause itself remains indestructible. These are unified therein.
The cave does not change; it manifests transformations in all places, thereby being able to manifest results. This is included within the celestial transformations. Why is this?
It is because one wishes to subdue all sentient beings through the sovereign spiritual power of Samantabhadra;
to cause unspeakably, unspeakably many sentient beings to attain purity; and to cause them to forever sever the wheel of birth and death.
Because they purify and adorn all vast worlds; because they constantly behold all Tathāgatas; because they enter deeply into the stream of all Buddha-dharmas;
because they recollect the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they recollect all the Buddha-dharmas and the Dharma-body of the ten directions;
because they universally cultivate all bodhisattva practices to bring them to fulfillment; and because they enter the stream of Samantabhadra.
Because one is able to realize all-knowledge through mastery.
Regarding the fourth section, which consists of both the inquiry and the explanation: first, the intent of the inquiry is that cause and effect are contradictory;

how can the fruit manifest within the gate of the cause, and how can the fruit further become the cause? The intent of the explanation is that it is because the subduing of sentient beings must be conducted in this manner. Within this passage, there are two parts.
First, to explain the meaning of the effect acting as the cause:
"O Son of the Buddha, you should observe that these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not abandon the practices of Samantabhadra; they do not sever the Bodhisattva path;
they behold all Buddhas; they realize all-knowledge; and they sovereignly enjoy the dharmas of all-knowledge."
Next, the explanation of the meaning of the cause manifesting as the effect consists of four parts. First is the explanation by way of Dharma: that the effect manifests without abandoning the cause.

This is like the elephant king Airāvaṇa, who does not abandon his elephant body when he goes to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to be mounted by the gods, where he experiences celestial bliss, engages in divine play, serves the Lord of Gods, and enjoys pleasure with the celestial maidens.
It is identical to that of the devas, without any distinction.
Second, the preceding analogy is cited to clarify this point:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; they do not abandon the various practices of the Great Vehicle of Samantabhadra."
Having withdrawn from all vows, they attain the sovereign mastery of a Buddha; possessing all-knowledge, they realize the liberation of a Buddha.
Being unobstructed and unhindered, they achieve purity; they are unstained by any buddha-fields and make no conceptual distinctions within the Buddha-dharma.
Although they know that all phenomena are universally equal and devoid of dual characteristics, they constantly and clearly perceive all buddha-fields. Although...
Having already become equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva in an uninterrupted succession.
This is further integrated with the Dharma in three stages: therein, first, while not abandoning the cause, the fruit is manifested;
subsequently, although one knows that all phenomena are universally equal, the cause is manifested without destroying the fruit.
O Son of the Buddha, you should know that when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in such vast dharmas of the Samantabhadra vows and practices,
their mind attains purity.
The four desires have been explained above; this concludes the exposition of their characteristics.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s tenth Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel, the sublime mind of vast wisdom.
The names of the three fetters (saṃyojana) are to be understood. Thus concludes the detailed explanation of the ten concentrations (dhyāna).
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten great wheels of samādhi of the conduct of Samantabhadra in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells.
The subsequent section is the third major heading, which summarizes the ten numbers.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan;
the meaning commented upon by the śramaṇa Chengguan of Dàhuá yán Temple on Mount Qingliáng;
and summarized by the śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Fáyún Temple on Mount Kuāng in the Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers (*Daśābhijñā*). First, regarding the intent of its introduction:

it is for the purpose of answering the ten questions concerning the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) posed in the second assembly. Two chapters are used to clarify the vastness of their functional activity;

since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was explained previously, these powers are treated here according to the sequential order of their meaning. Second, regarding the explanation of the title: "powers" (*tong*) refers to the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). That is to say:

Sublime function that is difficult to fathom is called "spirit" (*shen*); sovereign freedom without obstruction is called "penetration" (*tong*). Sublime function is infinite; it is manifested through the ten [stages] to reveal its perfection.
That both the *Jin jing* (Jin Translation) and the *Benye jing* (Original Karma Sutra) refer to them as the "ten illuminations" (*shi ming*) is because they illuminate exhaustively without omission.

However, regarding "penetration" (*tong*) and "illumination" (*ming*), the sutras and treatises differ. Thus, the third fascicle of the *Zhidu lun* states: "Directly knowing the matters of past lives is [the first illumination]."

"Abhijñā (supernormal knowledge). If one knows the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past as "vidyā" (clear illumination) and so forth, then this sūtra now uses "abhijñā" to mean thorough illumination;
it may likewise be called "vidyā. Therefore, the subsequent sūtra states: "This is not the sphere of the abhijñās and vidyās of the various bodhisattvas.

Regarding the three essential aims (*abhiprāya*): taking mastery over the function of wisdom as the aim, and taking the fulfillment of equal enlightenment through boundless gathering and transformation [of beings] as the goal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Next, the text is correctly explained, divided into four parts: 1. Stating the number and announcing the topic; 2. Questioning the number and listing the explanations; 3. [The third part]; 4. [The fourth part].
This is a general praise of excellence. It can distinguish the fruits through four enumerations; now follows the first. Regarding the "ten": first, the knowledge of others' minds;
second, the divine eye; third, the knowledge of past abodes; fourth, [the knowledge] reaching to the end of future kalpas; fifth, the unimpeded and pure divine ear;
sixth, the ability to travel to all Buddha-fields without substance or activity; seventh, the skillful discernment of all...
1. Eloquence; 2. The eight kinds of formless bodies; 3. Knowledge of all phenomena; 4. Entry into the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena.
These ten are all called "wisdom-penetration" because they take great wisdom as their essential nature.

If explained according to their characteristics, the first eight are conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the latter two are ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*); however, in reality, they are but a single great wisdom. These ten are also...

This opens up those six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), because the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) each divide into two.
Regarding the divine eye, it divides into four based on seeing the present and the future; regarding the divine ear, it divides into seven based on distinguishing sounds and speech.

Furthermore, because one hears the holy teachings and various types of expressions, the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are divided into six and eight based on their functional application (*karmayoga*) and their physical components (*rūpakāya*).

The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is divided into nine and ten based on wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since the "one" and "three" are not further subdivided, the six become ten.

However, in the Hīnayāna, the cognitive functions of the six supernormal powers are partial; in the three vehicles, they are uniform and pervasive, yet still do not exhaustively cover all aspects. Now...
The One Vehicle possesses the ten penetrations (*daśābhijñā*); the functions of wisdom are layered and profound, pervading the entire dharma-realm like Indra’s net.

Since thought and eons are perfectly interfused, these [penetrations] already transcend that [Indra’s net]; how much more so the universal application of penetration? To manifest this perfect principle, the ten penetrations are opened and established.
What are these ten?
In the second section, which enumerates and explains the number, there is first a general inquiry, followed by a specific explanation beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha.
These ten pervasive [topics] constitute ten sections; each section consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha! Regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*):
the initial designation here as "others' minds" is because this wisdom takes the minds of others as its object (*ālambana*).

If one were to refer directly to the object itself, it should be called the "supernormal power of discerning the distinctions of mind" (*cittaviśeṣa-abhijñā*), for it is capable of knowing all various types, whether they be kings or subjects.
This is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. However, regarding the claim that cognition takes another's mind as its object, various explanations differ.

The Master Sthiramati says that while the Buddha’s wisdom takes another’s mind as its object by apprehending the actual entity (*vastu*), all others merely transform a reflected image (*pratibimba*). The Master Dharmapāla, however, maintains that even the Buddha transforms a reflected image;

for if one were to take the actual entity as the object and thereby perceive a phenomenon external to the mind, it would undermine the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Therefore, [the Buddha’s cognition] merely appears extremely similar to the actual entity.

There is another reason for this: according to the Vijñaptimātra school, Dharmapāla’s interpretation is correct. When viewed from the perspective of the present sutra in relation to the preceding one, there is no loss of consistency.
This is because, while subsuming the object within the mind, the object is not destroyed; and because, while both subject and object have vanished, their existence is not obstructed.
The ultimate mind (*paramārthacitta*) is neither identical nor different, for when it correctly takes the other as its object, that very object is itself, being none other than the Buddha-mind.
The Buddha-mind that is identical with the mind of sentient beings serves as the object of cognition;
the mind of sentient beings that is identical with the Buddha-mind serves as the subject of cognition. Thus they are fused in a state of non-duality.

Therefore, they are neither identical nor different. If sentient beings were to exist separately outside of the Buddha, it would necessitate a further transformation of reflections, which would instead lose the true meaning of "consciousness-only.
[The Buddha] knows the distinctions among the minds of sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm—namely, wholesome minds and unwholesome minds.
The expansive mind and the narrow mind; the great mind and the small mind; the mind that follows saṃsāra and the mind that turns away from saṃsāra;
the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and the mind of a bodhisattva; the mind of śrāvaka conduct, the mind of pratyekabuddha conduct, and the mind of bodhisattva conduct;
the mind of a deva, the mind of a nāga, the mind of a yakṣa, the mind of a gandharva, the mind of an asura, the mind of a garuḍa, and the mind of a kiṃnara.
The minds of mahoragas, the minds of humans, the minds of non-humans, the minds of those in the hells, the minds of animals, the minds of those in the realm of King Yama,
the minds of hungry ghosts, and the minds of sentient beings in various states of suffering—
he discerns and knows all such infinite varieties of the diverse minds of sentient beings.

In the second section, the explanation of the characteristics, there are two parts. First, knowing one *kṣetra*; second, using one as an example to categorize many. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the general;
second, the specific, beginning with "That which is called..."; and third, the conclusion, beginning with "In this way...". Within the specific section, there are twenty-eight phrases.

Among these, the first eight phrases provide a general exposition based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the subsequent twenty mental states provide a specific exposition based on persons (*pudgala*).

Within the first eight, the initial two encompass all mental states by way of their nature (*prakṛti*). The next two concern practice (*caryā*), distinguishing between those who benefit others and those who seek their own excellence. Therefore, the following two concern retribution (*vipāka*);

because the former is celestial and the latter is human, the former is great and the latter is small. The preceding four are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). The next two concern orientation (*abhimukha*) and aversion (*parāṅmukha*), and thus accord with [the distinction between] worldly and supramundane.

It pervades the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The wholesome (*kuśala*) is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*); the "adverse" is exclusively wholesome and pervades both the outflowed and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Regarding persons, the middle six are categorized by person;
among these, the first three are results and the latter three are causes—namely, the aforementioned mind that turns away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), as well as the expansive and narrow minds.
Next, the eight classes are categorized by type—namely, the aforementioned minds that accord with birth-and-death, as well as the great and small minds. [The eighth class is] hell.
This applies equally to the realms of rebirth (*gati*) and accords with the mind of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The remaining aspects of this unwholesome mind may be understood accordingly.

As it is for one world-system, so it is for a hundred world-systems, a thousand world-systems, a hundred thousand world-systems, a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* world-systems, and even for as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
He fully discerns and knows the minds of all sentient beings;
subsequently, he infers the many from a few.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s first supernormal power (abhijñā), the thorough knowledge of the minds of others.
Regarding the names of the three fetters:
O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of the unimpeded, pure divine eye,
the second divine eye is designated as "unimpeded" because its vision is sovereign, and "pure" because it is free from obstructions.

He saw beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—beings passing away here and being born there, in happy or miserable realms, with marks of merit or marks of transgression, whether handsome or ugly, defiled or pure.
Such were the immeasurable classes of beings he saw, namely: the hosts of devas, the hosts of nāgas, the hosts of yakṣas, and the hosts of gandharvas.
Among the hosts of asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans,
beings with subtle bodies, beings with vast bodies, small groups, and large groups— among all such diverse assemblies of sentient beings—
he sees them all clearly with unimpeded vision, according to the karma they have accumulated. Following...

The suffering and pleasure experienced are all seen exactly as they are, without error— following the mind, following conceptualization, following views, following verbal expression, following causes, following karma,
following objects of perception, and following their arising.

The second explanation is divided into three parts. First, a general clarification that the characteristics of the many realms are distinct, wherein the various good and evil destinies unfold successively.

Second, from the phrase "That which is called... onwards, a specific clarification that the many categories are not one, and that within each individual category there exist the preceding categories and so forth.

Third, from the phrase "In this way, these various... onwards, a detailed and clear illumination; whereas previously one merely beheld their manifest appearances, here [the nature of their arising is revealed].
The title "Ten Clarities" (*daśa-vyākaraṇa*) is established based on this illumination of causes and conditions. Among these, the first is the ability to see with clarity;
the second is to see in detail according to what is encountered, where "according to what is encountered" means that the objects of knowledge are not limited to one;
and the last is the conclusion that all [perceptions] are free from error.
This is called the second unimpeded supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the power of the divine eye.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha,
by means of the supernormal knowledge of the recollection of past abodes, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...

The third is the supernormal power of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Among the headings, the term "past abodes" (*pūrva-nivāsa*) refers to events that have already passed away.

To clearly remember these in the past is "recollection" (*anusmṛti*); thus, it is the recollection of past abodes. This is the supernormal power of the recollection of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*).
One is able to know one's own past lives, as well as those of all sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
across kalpas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—
namely, that they were born in such-and-such a place, had such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, and such-and-such food and drink.
In this way, suffering and pleasure, from beginningless time within the various realms of existence, have grown ever more through causes and conditions,
continuing in succession in an uninterrupted cycle of saṃsāra, across various categories, various lands, and various destinies of birth.
He fully understands all such matters as various physical forms, various karmic actions, various fetters and afflictions,
various mental thoughts, various causes and conditions, and the distinctions in rebirth.

Regarding the second [section], the explanation of the characteristics, there is first the knowledge of all matters. Within this, there is first the general [explanation], followed by the specific [explanation] beginning with "namely.

Furthermore, one recollects as many eons as there are atoms in that number of Buddha-fields, and within as many worlds as there are atoms in those Buddha-fields, there were as many Buddhas as there are atoms in those Buddha-fields; for each and every Buddha, such was their name and title. As...
Thus he appeared in the world; with such an assembly, such parents, such attendants, and such śrāvakas;
with such two most eminent great disciples; in such a city, having thus gone forth from home, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment beneath such a bodhi tree;
sitting upon such a seat in such a place, he proclaimed such [teachings].
Having benefited that many sentient beings through such various sūtras, remaining for such a duration of life and performing such various buddha-activities,
he entered parinirvāṇa by means of the realm of nirvana without remainder.
He is able to recollect all such things as the duration for which the Dharma will remain after the parinirvāṇa.
Next is the knowledge of the Buddha’s activities, which also consists of two parts. First, regarding the realms, it reveals their multiplicity; he knows only their results.
Furthermore, I remember the names of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Within each individual name, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

From their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, they have given rise to vows, practiced cultivation, made offerings to all Buddhas, tamed sentient beings, expounded the Dharma within their assemblies, and manifested various lifespans and spiritual powers.
He thoroughly understands their transformations and manifestations, up to their entry into nirvana without remainder;
