he fully knows the duration for which the Dharma will remain after their parinirvāṇa, as well as the construction of stūpas and temples with various adornments, and how all sentient beings plant roots of goodness therein.

Subsequently, by means of persons, the multiplicity [of dharmas] is revealed, while also knowing their causes; this is because Bodhisattvas have attained the eye of the nine periods of time, seeing them as they see the present.
Were it otherwise, if past dharmas did not fall away, they would not be called "past."

If that which has already passed away is a non-existent dharma that cannot be known, yet it is said that one "remembers and knows" because a seed-image previously experienced appears before the mind, then one is merely seeing one's own mind and not seeing that [other] mind. Furthermore, regarding matters never previously experienced, there should be no memory or knowledge of them.
Moreover, if one only sees the present and not the past, how can this be called "recollection of former abodes"?
This is called the third supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of recollecting past lives throughout kalpas of the past.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom that knows the exhaustion of all future kalpas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

The fourth is the supernormal knowledge of knowing eons (*kalpa-jñāna-abhijñā*). This, too, is named after its object. It branches out from the second [supernormal knowledge], the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), specifically regarding the future.
It knows all the eons within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields (*buddha-kṣetra-paramāṇu-rajas*), one by one.
All sentient beings within the kalpa who pass away and take rebirth, their various continuities of karmic actions and their resultant retributions—
whether wholesome or unwholesome, whether leading to transcendence or not leading to transcendence, whether determinate or indeterminate, or whether fixed in error.
Whether they are in right concentration; whether their roots of goodness are accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) or not;
whether they possess roots of goodness in their entirety or not; whether they have grasped roots of goodness or not;
whether they have accumulated roots of goodness or not; and whether they have accumulated unwholesome dharmas or not.
All such things as these can be fully known.

Within the explanation of the characteristics, there are two parts: first, knowing the ordinary; second, subsequently knowing the lower [stages] up to the Buddha. Within the former, there are also two parts:

first, clarifying the kalpas upon which it is based; this merely uses multiple world-systems to manifest multiple kalpas, rather than using names that imply a finite limit, as well as the subsequent section.

All these extend to the end of the future; this is what is known in this stage, as it is identical to that of a Buddha. Hereafter, each point will be explained in detail to reveal the phenomena upon which they depend.
However, according to the Mahāyāna school, the essence and function of dharmas in the future do not exist. How, then, can one know them?

It is by relying on the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*) that one perceives the present causal seeds and thereby knows the characteristics of the future fruit; it is not that one perceives the actual essence of future dharmas. If...
In the One Vehicle school, within the nine periods of time, both essence and function exist in the present of the future; this is known through the realization of reality.
However, because it is not the "present of the present," it is called the "future. If this existence were an existence by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [it would be untenable].
This would be identical to the Hīnayāna. If it is an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) that exists, we have not yet encountered it; how then can one say it exists?
If one examines it at the present time, the nature of the condition is entirely absent, because it is certain that the future does not exist in the present.
If one examines it by following the future time, since it is the "present" of that future, it would still exist just as it does now.

Furthermore, they know that throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, extending to the end of the future, there are eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

and in each eon, there are names of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and for each individual name, there are [inconceivable... unspeakably unspeakable numbers.
One may speak of as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field. For each and every Tathāgata— from their first generation of the mind of awakening,

through their arising of vows and establishment of practices, their making offerings to all Buddhas, their teaching and transforming of sentient beings within assemblies and their preaching of the Dharma,

the length of their lifespans, their supernormal powers and transformations, up until their entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*— and even after their *parinirvāṇa*, the duration for which the Dharma remains, [one may describe] their deeds.
They are able to fully comprehend such matters as the establishment of stupas and temples with various adornments to cause all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness;
second, they know the Buddhas.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fourth supernatural power of knowledge, which knows the kalpas extending to the end of the future.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes the unimpeded and pure divine ear.
The fifth is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*). First, the name is designated; the supernormal power of knowledge (*jñāna-abhijñā*) is omitted for brevity.

If one speaks simply of the "divine ear," it receives its name according to its essential substance. If one takes up the unimpeded, pure divine ear, it receives its designation according to its virtuous activity.
Perfectly complete, vast, profound, and free from obstructions; thoroughly penetrating and unimpeded, fully accomplished;
regarding all sounds whatsoever, he possesses sovereign mastery to hear or not to hear as he pleases.

In the explanation of the characteristics, there are three parts. First, a general manifestation of the mastery of meritorious activities. Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, a specific demonstration of the functional application in one direction.
Third, from "As in the east" onwards, citing one example to represent the rest. Now, for the first part: all nine phrases distinguish merit by way of function.
First, "perfectly complete," because they can be used interchangeably. Second, "pervasively heard," because they reach throughout the ten directions and the nine periods of time. Third...

First, it causes one to behold [reality] at once; second, because it penetrates the source; third, because it is free from the two obstacles; fourth, because it clearly understands all that is known; fifth, because conditions cannot obstruct it;
sixth, because it is not like the provisional vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which have limited scope and do not exhaustively penetrate the layers of reality;
seventh, because it has already attained realization; eighth, because it is sovereign over all things; that is to say, if one wishes to hear, it becomes subtle.
There is no escaping the distant; one who desires not to hear is near. Because there is no great disturbance, it is called "sovereign.
O Son of the Buddha, in the eastern direction, there are as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Second, the specific indication of the activity of one direction consists of two parts. First, many Buddhas are cited to demonstrate the vastness of what has been heard.
This refers to that which has been spoken, indicated, opened up, expounded, established, taught, and disciplined by all these Buddhas.
Whatever is recollected, whatever is conceptually differentiated, and all those dharmas that are profound, vast, manifoldly diverse, characterized by immeasurable skillful means,
immeasurable expertise, and purity— all of these he is able to receive and uphold.
Next, the hearing, recollecting, and upholding [of the Dharma] are revealed. This section has two parts: first, the hearing and upholding of the teachings;

and within that, regarding both the meaning and the phrasing—whether for a single person or an assembly—according to their speech, according to their wisdom, according to what they have realized, according to what is manifested, according to how they are to be disciplined, and according to their respective spheres.
As for the basis: according to the path of deliverance, he is able to retain all of it without forgetting or losing it;

without interruption or regression, and without confusion or delusion, he expounds it for others so that they may attain realization and understanding, never failing to forget even a single word or a single phrase.

The subsequent "perfection of upholding" refers to the characteristics of being able to uphold [the Dharma]. This section has two parts: first, the presentation of that which is upheld; second, the explanation of the characteristics of the upholder, which includes clarifying the process of transformation.

Regarding the former, the preceding text generally revealed the teachings spoken by the Buddha; here, we distinguish the specific differences among those teachings. Following that, the characteristics of the upholder are explained, while simultaneously clarifying the transformative activity.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir;
the same applies to the remaining three cases.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fifth supernormal power of unimpeded, pure divine ear-knowledge.
The Names of the Bonds.

O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the supernatural power of the absence of intrinsic nature, the unconditioned supernatural power, the equalizing supernatural power, the vast supernatural power, the immeasurable supernatural power, the unconditioned supernatural power, the supernatural power that accords with thought, and the arising supernatural power.

He does not give rise to supernormal powers; he does not regress from supernormal powers; he does not interrupt supernormal powers; he does not destroy supernormal powers; he increases supernormal powers;
and he possesses the supernormal power of going wherever he wishes.
The sixth is the supernormal power of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi*) among the six supernormal powers.

Within the initial designation of its name, there are fourteen aspects. The first is the general [aspect], which is the absence of intrinsic nature. The remaining specific [aspects] are: first, the functioning without effort;
second, being of the same principle and level; third, the ability to be all-pervasive; fourth, having a measure that is difficult to know; and fifth, not being said to arise as a substantial entity.
1. It arises as function; 2. its form appears through mere recollection; 3. it manifests with functional efficacy; 4. it does not move from its original location;
5. its activity is invariably consummated; 6. its function is uninterrupted; 7. it also ensures that the lineage of the Buddha is never severed; 8. it cannot be destroyed by others.
The twelfth is the ability to generate roots of goodness; the thirteenth is that which accompanies wherever one goes.

Among these thirteen, the first two, the fifth, and the eighth have the meaning of being without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*); the remainder have the meaning of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Because these two are unimpeded, they receive this name.
This bodhisattva hears the names of all Buddhas in worlds as far away as those called countless worlds,
immeasurable worlds, and even as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Having heard their names, they immediately see themselves present before those Buddhas.

Regarding the second [section], the explanation of the characteristics, there are three parts. First, the clarification of vastness: this means that upon hearing the names of the Buddhas in many lands, one immediately perceives one’s own body within those many lands.
Those various worlds—whether upright or inverted, each with its respective shape, location, and distinct characteristics—are all clearly seen.
Boundless and unimpeded, with various lands and various eons, each adorned with immeasurable and distinct merits, those respective Tathāgatas appear therein,
manifesting spiritual transformations and proclaiming their names— immeasurable, innumerable, and each different.
As soon as this Bodhisattva hears the names of those Tathāgatas, without moving from his original place, he...
He saw his own body at that Buddha’s abode, prostrating, honoring, serving, and making offerings; he questioned the Bodhisattva-dharma and entered the wisdom of the Buddhas,
fully comprehending all Buddha-lands, sites of enlightenment, assemblies, and the teachings proclaimed therein,
reaching the ultimate point without any grasping or attachment.
Second, the explanation of the meanings of immeasurability, non-arising, and so forth. This means that by again hearing the Buddha’s name from that Buddha, one proceeds to reverently serve him;
because one receives the Way without attachment.
In this manner, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, they reach everywhere throughout the ten directions without actually going anywhere.
Yet, they visit lands to behold the Buddhas, listen to the Dharma, and request the Path, without interruption and without ever ceasing.
Without rest and without weariness, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and fulfill their great vows,
bringing them all to completion without ever regressing, so that the vast lineage of the Tathāgatas shall never be severed.
The meaning of the uninterruptedness of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) refers to the fact that, over a long period of time, their essence and function are unimpeded.

This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s sixth dwelling: the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of wisdom that proceeds to all Buddha-fields while being without intrinsic nature and without activity.
Regarding the names of the three fetters:
O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s seventh supernormal power, the supernormal power of skillfully discerning the speech and sounds of all sentient beings,
is derived from the fifth [power], which is distinguished by its application to vocal sounds and linguistic expressions.

First, the title is indicated. If it is named after that which is understood, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). If it is named after that which is produced, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
[It refers to] knowing the various languages of sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Speech: namely, the speech of the noble ones and the speech that is not of the noble ones;
the speech of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
Even unto the verbal expressions of all sentient beings, numbering as many as the unspeakably unspeakable,
each representing various distinct differences— all such things he is able to fully comprehend.
Regarding the second [section], the explanation of the characteristics, there are two parts. First is the knowledge of speech:
this bodhisattva, according to whichever world they enter, is able to know all the inclinations and dispositions of the sentient beings therein.
Just as the sun, when it appears, shines universally upon all forms so that those with eyes may see them clearly, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

By means of the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all speech, they enter deeply into the clouds of all speech, such that [all beings] understand them according to their own dispositions and inclinations, without any doubt. All...
The speech is such that all those in the world who possess intelligence can fully understand it.

Next, the manifestation of speech is explained; this refers to the production of speech according to various inclinations. This consists of the three parts: the phenomenon (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis (*upanaya*).
This is called the seventh supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all speech and terminology.
O Son of the Buddha, it is called the "Three Bonds.
By means of the wisdom that produces the adornments of immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) form-bodies, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

The supernormal power of the adornment of the eighth form-body (*rūpakāya*). This is derived from the sixth [supernormal power], the power of the bases of psychic mastery (*ṛddhipāda*), by way of its functional activity and its division into the form-body;
it is designated according to what is manifested, being named after its attributes (*saviśeṣaṇa-nirdeśa*).

One knows that all phenomena are far removed from the marks of form; they possess no marks of differentiation, no marks of variety, no marks of infinity, no marks of conceptual discrimination, and no marks of blue, yellow, red, or white.
In the second section, the explanation of the characteristics, there are three parts. First, knowing that there is no form, because form is itself emptiness. Second, from "The Bodhisattva thus...
onwards, clarifying the ability to manifest form, because emptiness is itself form. Third, from "O Son of the Buddha...

onwards, explaining both the absence of form and the manifestation of form, because the purpose is not obstructed by compassion. Now, for the first part: because one realizes that the dharma-realm has no fixed, substantial form, its entire substance...
It is immediately empty, yet not an emptiness of annihilation. Within emptiness there is no form, for it does not obstruct form;

because both existence and non-existence, concealment and manifestation, are all sovereign, one is able to manifest various forms according to one's inclination. Therefore, this is explained first among the sixteen phrases.
The first [verse] generally understands that the nature of form (*rūpa*) is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because there is no dharma whatsoever that constitutes emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The remaining five [verses] specifically clarify from what kinds of characteristics it is free: 1. It is free from the characteristic of differentiation, because coarse and subtle, long and short, and so forth, are identical in their essence of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
2. It is free from various distinct characteristics, because they are empty. 3. It is free from the characteristic of immeasurable multiplicity; furthermore, it is free from the great [elements].

1. Because smallness is merely a quantitative measure. 2. Because the four [elements] are but false conceptualizations, as they cannot be found when sought. 3. Because the dual views of form and emptiness are both emotional grasping. 4.

Because whether [form] is identical to or different from [emptiness], such views are transcended. (The above applies to both shape and color. 5. Because it is independent of mutual reliance, yet exists in dependence on shape.
This encompasses the fourfold meaning within the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm and the Contemplation of True Emptiness.
In this way, the bodhisattva enters the dharma-realm and is able to manifest their body in various forms.
Regarding these two abilities to manifest form, the first summarizes what preceded and indicates what follows, because form that is itself emptiness constitutes the sublime form.
Furthermore, the non-duality of form and emptiness constitutes the aforementioned true emptiness; though non-dual, they appear as two in these wondrous forms.
The fusion and identity of form and emptiness constitute the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Within this inexhaustible dependent origination, the one manifests as the many.
That which is called boundless form, immeasurable form, pure form, adorned form, pervasive form, incomparable form, universally illuminating form,
superior form, non-opposing form, form endowed with all marks, form free from all evils, form of great majesty,
venerable form, inexhaustible form, manifold and exquisite form, and supremely magnificent form. It is un...

The color of measure; the color of excellent protection; the color capable of maturation; the color that accords with those to be transformed; the color of non-obstruction; the color of profound clarity and penetration;
the color free from defilement and turbidity; the color of extreme purity; the color of great valor and strength; and the color of inconceivable skillful means.
Indestructible color; color free from blemish and obscuration; color without obstruction or darkness; well-established color; exquisitely adorned color;
color of the perfectly dignified primary marks; color of the various secondary signs; color of great nobility; color of sublime objects; well-polished and refined color;
color of a pure and profound mind; blazing and magnificent color; most excellent and vast color; uninterrupted color.
Form; form that is without support; form that is beyond comparison; form that fills unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
increasing form; form that is firmly sustained; form of supreme merit; form that accords with the inclinations of all minds; and form of pure understanding.
The color of accumulated manifold wonders; the color of skillful certainty; the color of non-obstruction; the color of the luminous purity of space; the color of pure delight;
the color free from all dust and defilement; the color beyond measure; the color of wondrous vision; the color of universal vision; the color manifested according to the occasion;
the color of tranquility; the color free from craving; the color of the true field of merit; the color capable of bestowing peace.
The color of concealment; the color free from all fears; the color free from the conduct of ignorance; the color of courageous wisdom; the color of unimpeded bodily marks;
the color of universal wandering; the color of a mind without dependence; the color arising from great loving-kindness; the color manifested by great compassion;
the color of impartial renunciation; the color endowed with merit; the color that accords with the recollections of the mind; the color of boundless excellence.
The color of jewels; the color of the radiance of jewel-treasuries; the color that inspires faith and joy in sentient beings;

the color in which all-knowledge is manifest; the color of joyful eyes; the supreme color adorned with various jewels; the color that has no fixed location; the color manifested through sovereign power;

the color of various supernormal powers; the color of being born into the family of the Tathāgata; the color that transcends all metaphors; the color that pervades the entire Dharma-realm; and the color of the multitude...

They all proceed toward form: various forms, accomplished forms, forms of renunciation, forms of majestic deportment according to those to be converted, forms that one never tires of beholding, various luminous and pure forms, forms capable of emitting countless nets of light, forms of unspeakable radiance with various distinctions, and forms of inconceivable fragrant light that transcend the three realms. Inexpressible...
The color of the radiance illuminating the solar disc; the manifestation of the incomparable color of the lunar body;
the color of immeasurable clouds of lovely and delightful flowers; the color of the adornment of various clouds of lotus garlands;
the color of fragrant flames surpassing all worlds that universally permeate; the color from which the treasury of all Tathāgatas is produced; and the revelation through ineffable sounds.
It expounds upon the form of all phenomena and is fully endowed with the form of all Samantabhadra practices.

Hereafter, it specifically reveals their distinctions, which number one hundred and three types. Some are named according to their formal characteristics, while others receive their titles based on their virtues;

these may be sought through the power of the mind. Nevertheless, they are all forms that accord with the *dharmadhātu*, and are not like [ordinary] forms characterized by transformation and obstruction. However—
The name "form" (*rūpa*) is established according to what is manifested. O Son of the Buddha,
a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply enters such a formless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), yet is able to manifest various kinds of form-bodies (*rūpakāya*),

such as those corresponding to others, so that those to be converted may see them, so that those to be converted may remember them, and so that he may turn the wheel of Dharma for those to be converted.

According to the timing of those to be converted, and according to the characteristics of those to be converted, he causes those to be converted to draw near and causes those to be converted to attain awakening;
for the sake of those to be converted, he manifests various supernatural powers and displays various masteries.
For the sake of those to be converted, he bestows various kinds of efficacious activities.

Within the second pair that clarifies the purpose, the first part concludes the preceding section, while the subsequent part, beginning with "causing those to be converted," reveals the specific purposes;
it consists of ten phrases.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s diligent cultivation and accomplishment of the eighth incalculable [aeon] of the wisdom and supernormal powers of the form-body,
for the sake of delivering all sentient beings. This is the eighth incalculable [aeon] of the wisdom and supernormal powers of the form-body.
O Son of the Buddha! By means of the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of all phenomena, the ninth is the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-jñāna-abhijñā*).
This first provides the name; it receives its designation from the phenomena to be known, such as the ultimate and conventional truths.
One knows that all phenomena have no names, no intrinsic nature, no coming and no going;
they are neither different nor not different, neither manifold nor not manifold, neither dual nor non-dual.
In the second section, the explanation of the characteristics, there are two parts. First, the clear understanding of the Dharma, which refers to internal realization of phenomena and principle.

Second, from "this bodhisattva" onwards, the explanation of the manifestation of the Dharma, which refers to externally benefiting sentient beings. This also means that the former clarifies the constancy of principle, while the latter clarifies the constancy of phenomena within that principle;
for when activity is quiescent, there is no obstruction between quiescence and activity. Regarding the first part, there are again two sections. The first concerns the transcendence of words.

Revealing Reality. Next, from "no-self" (*anātman*) onwards, reality is revealed by means of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*). First, the initial three phrases exclusively reveal reality: first, because names lack the power to grasp objects;
second, because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); and third, because the essence is devoid of coming and going.
Below, there are three phrases that reveal reality through mutual contrast. However, in explaining these three pairs, there are three meanings. First:
1. Regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): they are different because they are empty through mutual dependence; they are said to be not different because they are mutually non-existent.

To negate difference, one says "not different," yet even this "not-difference" cannot be apprehended; thus, it is said to be "neither not-different. 2. Regarding the simultaneous manifestation of both: in essence (*tattva*), they are not different;

in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are not non-different. 3. Regarding the simultaneous negation of both: because characteristics are identical to nature (*dharmatā*), they are not different; because nature is identical to characteristics, [they are not non-different].
Therefore, they are not non-different. Furthermore, because characteristics are not characteristics, they are not different; because nature is not nature, they are not non-different.
Thus, one departs from the two extremes and does not abide in a middle way.
Without self and without peer; neither arising nor ceasing; unmoving and indestructible; without reality and without unreality;
a single mark yet markless; neither non-existent nor existent; neither dharma nor non-dharma; not conforming to the conventional, yet not non-conforming to the conventional;
neither karma nor non-karma; neither retribution nor non-retribution; neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither the ultimate truth nor not the ultimate truth.
It is a single meaning. It is neither the path nor the non-path; neither departure nor non-departure;
neither measurable nor immeasurable; neither mundane nor supramundane; neither born from causes nor not born from causes; neither determinate nor indeterminate;
neither accomplished nor unaccomplished; neither emerging nor non-emerging; neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization.
Distinct. Neither conforming to reason nor non-conforming to reason.
These two, in relation to the two emptinesses, manifest the Middle Way; they also constitute the first three pairs, which exclusively manifest the ultimate reality.

Regarding "without comparison": because there is no "mine" (mama) to serve as a counterpart to the "self" (ātman). Regarding "without reality," the following is explained for the time being by way of manifesting the ultimate reality. First, the false.
Because all [phenomena] are actually manifested through conditions; because the two natures (dharmatā) do not coexist as ultimate realities; because a single characteristic is likewise not a "one";
and because both non-existence and existence are merely dharmas that exist in relation to their opposites—therefore, there is neither "non-dharma" nor "dharma," but only conventional designations.
Seeking according to reality, both the subject that treats and the object treated are entirely quiescent.
This bodhisattva does not grasp at conventional truth, does not dwell in the ultimate truth, does not discriminate among phenomena, and does not establish verbal designations;
they accord with the nature of cessation.

Second, regarding the three aspects of external benefit through the manifestation of the Dharma: first, reiterating the preceding point to establish wisdom as the basis for the arousal of activity, one does not abandon any vows;
seeing the meaning and knowing the Dharma, one spreads the clouds of Dharma and pours down the rain of Dharma.
Second, the actual exposition of the Dharma.
Although he knows that the true nature (*dharmatā*) is ineffable, by means of skillful means and inexhaustible eloquence, he sequentially expounds it according to the phenomena and their meanings.
This is because he has attained mastery in the verbal expression and discourse regarding all phenomena, and possesses great loving-kindness and great compassion.

All are already purified; they are able to produce words from within all wordless dharmas, conforming to and not contradicting both the phenomena and their meanings, and they proclaim that all dharmas arise entirely from conditions.
Third is the unimpeded application of tranquility. Within this, there are three parts; first, tranquility does not obstruct application.

Although there is verbal expression, there is no attachment. One expounds all dharmas with inexhaustible eloquence, analyzing, establishing, opening up, and guiding the teachings, so that the nature of all dharmas is fully and clearly revealed, severing the web of doubts for all beings until they attain complete purity.
Although they gather in sentient beings, they do not abandon reality.
Next, by employing non-obstructive tranquility, they do not regress from the dharma of non-duality. They are always able to expound the unimpeded Dharma-gate through various wondrous voices.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they universally rain down the rain of Dharma without missing the proper time;
subsequently, quiescence and function are non-dual.
This is called the ninth supernormal power of the bodhisattva mahāsattva: the knowledge of all dharmas.
Regarding the names of the attainments:

O Son of the Buddha, by means of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supernormal power of wisdom regarding the samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena, and the tenth supernormal power of wisdom regarding the meditative absorption of cessation, there are ninety-two types of supernormal powers categorized by wisdom and concentration within the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). Among these:
Third: First, the title is stated: "The extinction of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-nirodha*). This means that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all quiescent in their very essence;

this is thus the extinction of principle (*li-mie*). It differs from the meditative absorption of extinction (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in other schools, which explains only the extinction of phenomena (*shi-mie*), merely extinguishing the six or seven minds and mental factors while not extinguishing the eighth consciousness and so forth. Because it is merely the extinction of phenomena, it cannot [itself] be the concentration.

Because it employs [the practice] to realize the extinction of principle, there is no obstruction between concentration and dispersion. Since principle is identical to phenomena, it does not obstruct extinction;

since phenomena are identical to principle, it does not obstruct function. Therefore, the text says: "Although entering [extinction] in every thought-moment, one does not abandon the Bodhisattva path," and so forth.
This is neither a case where the mind is fixed while the body initiates activity, nor does it merely clarify the non-obstruction of concentration and dispersion.

[This is] absolute. However, because principle and phenomena are unimpeded (*avighna*), it is as stated regarding the seven higher stages: "Although one practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not realize it;
one can enter it moment by moment and emerge from it moment by moment. Furthermore, this is the meaning of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* which states:

"Without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one manifests all dignified postures (*īryāpatha*). Because phenomena and principle are not identical, there is the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of the total extinction of all dharmas.
Because they are not distinct, the cessation (*nirodha*) itself is pervasive; this explains both interpretations.
Within every moment of thought, one enters the *nirodhasamādhi* of all dharmas.

Regarding the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts: first, clarifying that the essence and function of the samādhi itself are sovereign; second, [explaining] that "this bodhisattva dwells in samādhi."
Below: This clarifies mastery over the timing of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Within this section, there are also two parts. First, the indication of entering concentration:
one does not retreat from the bodhisattva path; one does not abandon bodhisattva activities; one does not relinquish the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
one practices the *pāramitās* without ever ceasing; one observes all buddha-fields without weariness or fatigue; and one does not abandon...
The vow to deliver sentient beings; the uninterrupted turning of the wheel of Dharma; the non-abandonment of the activity of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
the non-relinquishing of the practice of making offerings to all Buddhas; the non-relinquishing of the gate of mastery over all dharmas;

the non-relinquishing of the constant vision of all Buddhas; the non-relinquishing of the constant hearing of all dharmas; knowing that all dharmas are equal and unobstructed; and the sovereign accomplishment of everything.
In the Buddha-dharma, all supreme vows are brought to fulfillment. One thoroughly understands the distinctions between all lands, enters the lineage of the Buddhas, and reaches the further shore.
Within each and every world-system, one studies all dharmas and realizes that phenomena are signless;
one knows that all dharmas arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature, yet follows worldly conventions as an expedient means.

He expounds the teachings; although his mind abides nowhere amidst all phenomena, he skillfully preaches various dharmas in accordance with the faculties, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings.

Second is the clarification of the unobstructed function. Within this, the first two phrases provide a general overview: not retreating from what has not yet been accomplished, and not abandoning what is currently being accomplished.
This precisely distinguishes the cessation of phenomena to reveal true cessation. The remaining phrases clarify the specific aspects, which may be understood accordingly.
When this bodhisattva dwells in samādhi, according to his mental inclination, he may dwell for one kalpa,
or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or a hundred million kalpas, or ten billion kalpas, or a hundred billion kalpas, or a hundred thousand billion kalpas,
or a nayuta of billions of kalpas, or a hundred nayutas of billions of kalpas, or... he may dwell.
For a thousand nayuta-koṭī kalpas; or they may dwell for a hundred thousand nayuta-koṭī kalpas; or they may dwell for incalculable kalpas;
or they may dwell for immeasurable kalpas; and even up to dwelling for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas.
Second, the mastery over the duration of entering meditative absorption. Within this, there are three parts; first, the length of time follows the mind.

When a Bodhisattva enters this samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirodha-samādhi*), although they may remain for as many eons as there are, their body does not disintegrate, does not wither, and does not undergo transformation.
It is neither seen nor unseen; it is neither extinguished nor destroyed. It is not...
They are tireless and never weary; they can never be exhausted.
Second, their deportment is never faltering;
although they perform no action whatsoever regarding existence or non-existence, they are nonetheless able to accomplish all the deeds of bodhisattvas—namely, [to act] constantly...

Never abandoning any sentient beings, he teaches and tames them without ever missing the proper time, causing them to increase in all Buddha-dharmas and bringing them to full perfection in the practices of a bodhisattva.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, his supernormal transformations never cease; like light and shadows, they manifest everywhere, yet within samādhi he remains tranquil.
Yet it remains unmoving.

Second, its arising of function is unimpeded; concentration and distraction proceed together. Within this, first the principle and then the analogy: light and shadows appear everywhere, yet it is tranquil and without mind;
they wax and wane according to the vessel, while its essence neither comes nor goes.
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom-superknowledge for entering the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirodha*).
O Son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these ten kinds of superknowledges, all gods and humans—
It is inconceivable. It cannot be conceived by any sentient beings; it cannot be conceived by any śrāvakas, any pratyekabuddhas, or any other assembly of bodhisattvas.
This bodhisattva’s physical activity is inconceivable;
his verbal activity is inconceivable; his mental activity is inconceivable; and his mastery over samādhi is inconceivable.
Inconceivable. The realm of wisdom is inconceivable.
The third major section, which generally extols supreme capability, consists of two parts. First, manifesting superiority through inferior form; for that which is inferior cannot fathom it.
Except for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have attained this supernatural power (abhijñā), no others are able to describe,
extol, or praise the merits of such a person.
Second, it is "the superior manifesting the superior," meaning that only those such as the Buddhas can fathom them.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of supernormal powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these supernormal powers, they will fully attain the supernormal power of unimpeded knowledge regarding all three periods of time.
The fourth major section concludes the enumeration and distinguishes the fruits. The preceding "Chapter on the Tenfold Pervasion" is finished.
Regarding the introductory intent of the twenty-ninth chapter, "The Ten Patiences":

it is for the purpose of answering the ten questions posed by the Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā) regarding the Ten Summits. Of these, the first two have already clarified meditative concentration and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

[The previous section] was used for broad exposition; now, this [section] distinguishes the profound depth of its wisdom, and thus it follows next. Second, regarding the explanation of the name: "Patience" (kṣānti) refers to patient understanding and approval;
that is, the illumination and observation of wisdom that penetrates [reality], manifesting the ten stages through the perfection [of practice]. Third, regarding the essential aim:
the profound depth of the practice of wisdom is the essence (mūla), while attaining the fruit of Buddhahood—unimpeded and inexhaustible—is the goal (prayojana). Now, as for this practice of patience:

In terms of stages, this refers to the mind immediately following the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*), for the purpose of severing subtle ignorance. If considered in terms of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), it actually pervades all five stages;
it is spoken of as being at the ultimate limit. Its essence is wisdom (*jñāna*), which differs from other schools that treat patience (*kṣānti*) as the cause and wisdom as the fruit.

Although it is a single wisdom, it is described differently according to its various meanings—as the second, third, fourth, fifth, and so on—varying across different teachings. Now, regarding this Perfect [Teaching]...
Because they are taught, ten kinds are spoken of.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of patience."
Fourth, the correct explanation of the text. The text consists of prose and verse. Within the first [section], there are four parts: (1) stating the number and praising its excellence;
(2) listing the names to reveal their essentials; (3) providing a detailed explanation according to the names; and (4) summarizing their names. Now, the first [part].
If one attains this patience (*kṣānti*), one then reaches the stage of all Bodhisattvas’ unimpeded patience (*anāvaraṇa-kṣānti-bhūmi*).
All Buddha-dharmas become unimpeded and inexhaustible.

Subsequently, there is praise for its excellence: having reached the stage of non-obstruction, the causes of one’s own nature (*svabhāva-hetu*) are perfected; that the Buddha-dharmas are unimpeded constitutes superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).
The fruits are fulfilled.

What are the ten? They are: the patience of sound, the conforming patience, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the patience like an illusion, the patience like a flame, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo, the patience like a shadow, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space.
In the section "Listing the Names to Reveal the Essentials," first the number is questioned, next the names are listed, and finally the essentials of the names are revealed.
Among these, the first three concern the Dharma, while the latter seven rely on metaphors. Within the first three, the very first concerns the teaching;

that is, patience regarding the sounds of the teaching, named after its object, thus it is "patience toward sound. The next one concerns practice, for it accords with all dharmas; thus, "accordance" is itself patience. The third... [text fragment ends]
Regarding the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): if one refers to the principle of the non-arising of phenomena as "patience," it is the patience toward non-arising;
if one refers to the patience toward non-arising and the non-arising of afflictions, then non-arising itself is the patience. Thus, both explanations apply.

Furthermore, these three types of patience are explained according to their general characteristics; the first two are both preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the patience of non-arising, tending toward non-arising.

Regarding the latter seal: if one considers it according to its own stage, the three patiences (*kṣānti*) are far apart; thus, it would not be the case that the "patience conforming to non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) exists only at this stage.
Therefore, "conforming" refers only to conforming to the principle (*li*), and is not yet the "patience of conformity" (*anuloma-kṣānti*). If that is so, how does it differ from non-arising?

The patience of conformity conforms to both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle, whereas non-arising does not; therefore, they are not the same. As the Sūtra says: "One also conforms to the knowledge that dharmas exist," and so forth. Furthermore...

Based on the five patiences (*kṣānti*), one abides in the stage of quiescence (*śānta*). Now, the meaning is explained in terms of the three patiences; therefore, this corresponds to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the latter seven [patiences], they are all *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds within their metaphors, meaning "the patience that is like an illusion," and so forth.
However, there are differing interpretations of these seven metaphors by seven schools: namely, those of Guāngtǒng, Xiánshǒu, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, Yuǎngōng, Jīngāng, and Dàpǐn.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* clarifies these metaphors throughout. First, Guṇabhadra stated: "The first four metaphors refer to sound;

lightning refers to the present metaphors of shadow and transformation, corresponding to the stage of patient acceptance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). The metaphor of emptiness refers to non-arising. Furthermore, he said: 'Illusion' refers to the characteristic of arising without arising;

'a mirage' refers to the characteristic of an object without an object; 'a dream' refers to the characteristic of knowing without knowing; 'an echo' refers to the characteristic of hearing without hearing; and 'lightning'..."
Abiding in the characteristic of non-abiding. Now that it is said to be like a shadow, one should say it manifests the characteristic of non-manifestation.

That which is transformed has the characteristic of having and not having; that which is empty has the characteristic of being and not being. Thus, while the metaphor is restricted to a single characteristic, the meaning of what is illustrated extends to many dharmas.
Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, there is no error in principle. Next, Xianxiu says: "Contemplate consciousness as being like an illusion."
Feeling is like a flame; perception is like a dream; mental formations are like an echo; consciousness is like lightning; and form is like a magical illusion.

When one contemplates all aggregates, elements, and bases collectively, they are ultimately empty and thus like space. Thirdly, according to the fifth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, all eight metaphors illustrate the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
However, these are employed to dispel doubts; since the objects of doubt differ, the metaphors used likewise vary.
This is also different. There are eight modes of doubt, which, together with the subsequent four schools, mutually elucidate one another; the text is too voluminous to be recorded here.

In this present sutra, it mostly accords with the previous general [explanation], yet the metaphors used in the verses also have specific applications, as the manifestation of meaning is not restricted to a single method.
The enumeration of the names has already been explained.
These ten kinds of patience have been taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time; they are being taught now, and they shall be taught in the future.
Next, to reveal their essential nature, they are explained together because they share this same essence.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding sounds? It refers to hearing that which is spoken by all Buddhas.
Regarding the Dharma, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; they have deep faith, realization, and understanding, and they incline toward it with joyful interest.
With single-minded recollection, they cultivate, practice, and abide therein. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s first patience regarding sounds.

The third major section, the detailed explanation based on the names, consists of ten parts. In the first seven, each contains three elements: the inquiry, the explanation of the meaning, and the conclusion of the name.

Within the initial explanation of "patience" (*kṣānti*), there are eleven sentences. The first sentence generally enumerates what is heard, namely the dharmas such as the threefold absence of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The remaining [sentences] manifest the capacity for hearing and entering the dharma; that is, hearing the signless (*animitta*) without being startled, because one understands it universally.
Because they realize that all things are non-existent, they do not fear hearing of non-arising, for they understand that the dependent nature is necessarily without arising.

Because they realize that true suchness is the very nature of being without nature, they do not dread hearing of the absence of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, it is explained that when hearing the Dharma of true emptiness, they are not startled or overcome;

when contemplating it, their fear does not continue; and when practicing it, they do not remain in a state of fixed dread. Moreover, they hear that there is nothing to be grasped as existent or non-existent.
There is no alarm; because one hears that all is empty and non-existent, one does not fear. This is as explained in various Prajñāpāramitā treatises.
Those with deep faith represent the beginning of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); those who have attained realization represent the end of the wisdom of hearing.

Because initial faith leads to long-term understanding, those who focus their minds on recollection represent the commencement of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); cultivation constitutes the end. This clearly elucidates the process of practice.
Cultivation, because it reaches the root of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Abiding, because one relies on concentration to give rise to wisdom and accords with the realization of principle.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patient compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*)? It refers to the contemplation and observation of all phenomena.
It is equal and without contradiction; one understands it through compliance, purifies the mind, and correctly abides in its cultivation, entering into and accomplishing it.
This is called the second *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience of conformity) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

The second patience (*kṣānti*). Within the commentary, there are four stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: 1. Initial cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: This refers to *śamatha*, which is the concentration of thought on a single object;

and *vipaśyanā*, which is the contemplation of phenomena and their underlying principles. 2. Gradual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: This refers to *śamatha*, which is the settling of the mind upon the objective sphere of phenomena in accordance with their underlying principles.
The name "Contemplation of Equality and Non-contradiction" refers to penetrating both phenomena and principle. This is called "conforming understanding. As the verse says:

"One conforms to knowing that phenomena exist, and one also conforms to knowing that phenomena do not exist. Third is the "mastery of śamatha and vipaśyanā," which means that by ceasing delusion so it does not arise, one causes the mind to be pure;
by observing through to the preceding object, one achieves correct abiding and cultivation. Fourth is the "convergence of śamatha and vipaśyanā," which is tranquility...

Entering the realm of profound principle is called "entrance"; because wisdom is manifested within the mind, it is called "accomplishment. These four stages above all involve the concurrent practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
only in this way does one possess true conformative patience (anulomikī kṣānti).
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
The third [section on] the patience regarding non-arising is divided into three parts. First, the inquiry:
"O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising, nor does he perceive even the slightest phenomenon [as ceasing]."
Cessation.
The commentary on this consists of two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a detailed inquiry and explanation beginning with "Why?
This is the first part. Why is this so?
In the subsequent section on interrogation and explanation, there are two points of inquiry: first, how can it be known that there is no arising or ceasing?
Second, since it is called "the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), why is the cessation of dharmas not perceived?
If there is no arising, then there is no ceasing. If there is no ceasing, then there is no exhaustion. If there is no exhaustion, then there is freedom from defilement.
If there is freedom from defilement, then there is no differentiation. If there is no differentiation, then there is no location. If there is no location, then there is tranquility.
If there is tranquility, there is freedom from desire. If there is freedom from desire, there is non-action. If there is non-action, there is no aspiration.
If there is no aspiration, there is no abiding. If there is no abiding, there is neither going nor coming.
In the commentary, the explanation of the initial inquiry states: "True dharmas are fundamentally non-arising. Because dharmas arising from conditions lack intrinsic nature, they do not arise.
Since there is no arising, how could there be cessation? This, then, explains non-arising by means of the gathering of conditions.
The absence of cessation is explained by means of the absence of arising. Here, the causal collection is omitted for brevity, though it is fully present in the verse.
How does the absence of arising explain the absence of cessation? There are two points to this: first, if there were prior arising, there would necessarily be subsequent cessation.

Since the fundamental [nature] is originally unarisen, it is now without cessation. Second, because the lack of intrinsic nature within conditions is termed "unarisen," it does not mean that it becomes non-existent only after cessation has occurred;

therefore, it is subsequently stated to be "without cessation. These two [terms] serve as the general [definition]; the remainder may be understood by analogy. Regarding the intent of the second inquiry:
the forbearance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is not merely non-arising, but rather that all phenomena are entirely...
Ji (Ji) states: "Now, based on the primary sense, the designation 'non-arising' (*anutpāda*) is established; thus, 'non-extinction' and so forth are subsumed under the meaning of non-arising.
If taken from another perspective, it may also be designated as 'patience regarding non-extinction' (*anirodha-kṣānti*) and so on.

Therefore, the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* clarifies that this patience can purify the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), stating: 'First, one attains the patience regarding non-arising and causes others to abide therein as well.'"
Furthermore, it is said that "the patience of non-extinction" refers to the realization of non-arising; this text may be taken as authoritative.
Moreover, each of these phrases possesses two meanings: first, explaining the subsequent by means of the preceding and establishing the preceding by means of the subsequent;
where the preceding exists, the subsequent exists, and where the preceding is absent, the subsequent is absent. Second, all these phrases reside within non-arising.

Within these phrases, at the very moment of non-arising, all meanings are simultaneously fulfilled. This is because it is the principle inherent in phenomena (*dharmatā*), and thus not a state of annihilation;
and because it is the wisdom inherent in that principle, which is devoid of subject and object. Nevertheless, as the textual intent is comprehensive, I shall provide three brief explanations:
first, based solely on principle; second, encompassing both principle and wisdom; and third, based solely on wisdom. Regarding the first: why is it said that "each preceding [moment] exists"?

There is subsequent existence. This means that once the phenomena of birth have ceased, that cessation is an ultimate exhaustion. Exhaustion is a defiled phenomenon; being defiled, there is differentiation between the preceding and the succeeding.
Being differentiated, there is a distinction in location. When there is location, the subject and object are not quiescent.
Not being quiescent, there is desire. When there is desire, there is purposive activity. When there is activity, there is aspiration and seeking. Aspiration then—
The mind abides in its aspirational object; in the past, there was going and coming, but now, because each preceding stage is absent, each succeeding stage is thus quiescent.
Therefore, by means of each succeeding stage, non-arising is manifested and established. This accords with the prose section. Second, regarding the two aspects concerning wisdom and principle:
The first two [verses] collectively encompass both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). The subsequent four manifest that principle is unarisen; the final six manifest that wisdom is unarisen.

Therefore, the verse says, "His mind is free from attachment," and so forth. The harmonious convergence of principle and wisdom is termed "patience regarding the unarisen" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
If one considers wisdom alone: because it realizes that [dharmas] are unarisen due to dependent origination, wisdom itself does not arise; thus it is called "unarisen."
The wisdom of non-arising is limpid and immutable; therefore, it is called "non-extinction. Because it is non-extinguished, its function is never interrupted or exhausted.
Furthermore, all defiled thoughts are abandoned; it is eternally without differentiation, devoid of spatial location, and remains constantly tranquil while illuminating.

It encounters objects without being stained; though it acts, there is no agency; though it manifests compassion, there is no longing. It dwells in the world without abiding—such is the equality of dharmas.
The realms are devoid of coming and going; the former explains the latter, and the latter establishes the former. Words vanish and thoughts cease;

quiescent illumination is profoundly still—this is called the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). If one were to define the Patience of Non-arising merely by the knowledge that phenomena do not arise, it would not be sufficiently profound and mysterious.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s third patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s patience like an illusion (māyopama-kṣānti)?
The fourth section, the patience like an illusion, is divided into three parts: the inquiry, the explanation of the meaning, and the conclusion of the name. Now, for the first:
"O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are entirely like illusions, arising from causes and conditions."
Within a single phenomenon, one understands many phenomena; within many phenomena, one understands a single phenomenon.

In this commentary, there is first the brief and then the detailed explanation. Within the brief explanation, there are two parts: first, understanding the characteristics of illusory conditions; second, from the point "this bodhisattva" onwards, the accomplishment of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
Now, for the first [part], there are three sections. First, pointing out that the phenomena are identical to the analogy; second, "that which arises from causes and conditions... [and so forth].
This clarifies the origin of illusion: it arises because that which is produced by conditions is unreal. Subsequently, within the section on "one dharma," its illusory characteristics are revealed.
First, "all dharmas" serves as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the scope—whether universal or restricted—of this illustration, it has already been seen in the preceding text;

here, the intent is to clarify its universality, as it encompasses both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, I would likewise [regard it as illusory]."
It is said that they are like dreams and illusions because, although *nirvāṇa* is real, it is manifested through conditions; thus, the mind of attachment is dispelled.

In the extensive [explanation], it is stated collectively that "understanding the world as illusory" implies it resembles the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). However, the term "world of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*) also applies to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because this is obscured by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called "the world" (*loka*).
Therefore, it is said later that even *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are not seen, because one has realized their equality. Within the dharma and the metaphor, five factors are each distinguished:

for example, in the case of a single knot manifested as a single horse, there is first the cloth upon which it depends; second, the magician’s artifice; third, the [object of]... [text fragment ends].
An illusory horse appears; the very birth of the four horses is their death. (1) The first [illusion] is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

(2) The artifice is a metaphor for the causes and conditions that give rise [to phenomena], namely afflictions, karma, and so forth. (3) The third is a metaphor for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which refers to sentient beings and the like.

(4) The fourth is a metaphor for the absence of intrinsic nature in the dependent, which is itself the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Therefore, it is extensively explained that all [of these] are "not."
Furthermore, the five metaphors refer to persons and dharmas. Now, the Bodhisattva acts in reverse to this; hence it is said that he "understands and realizes.
The present sutra states: "Arising from causes and conditions. That which can give rise [to something] is the second [truth], and that which is given rise to is the third.

By taking the second as the cause, one is led to awaken to the third, thereby establishing the fourth and eliminating the fifth affliction, so as to return to the principle of the first. However, conditions likewise arise from...

Therefore, both the conditions and their fruits are illusory. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "It is like a magically conjured person who further conjures another magically conjured person"—this is precisely that meaning.
However, each of the five aforementioned meanings possesses five aspects within itself: first, the nature of the cloth exists while its appearance does not, because it is concealed by the horse;
second, the function of the artifice exists while its substance does not, because the act of making the cloth lacks substantiality; third, the appearance of the horse...

There is existence, yet it is non-existent, because that which is non-existent manifests. The four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) are thus non-existence, while death is existence, because there is no obstruction.

The five sensory faculties exist conventionally but do not exist ultimately, being merely false perceptions. Hereafter, the illusory characteristics will be revealed, briefly explained through two interpretations.
First, the interpretation by way of analogical categories: if one thing lacks substantial reality, one knows that all things are likewise so, for they all arise from conditions.

Therefore, it is said that "within one, many are understood," and so forth. Second, regarding the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), there are again three meanings. First, taking principle as the basis for phenomena, they are said to be mutually identical.
This is like the cloth on the horse's head not being different from the cloth on its feet; because it is said that the head is identical to the feet.
"One is many," and so forth. The *Avyākṛta-sūtra* states: "Lust itself is the Way" because lust is the very nature [of all phenomena].

"All phenomena are lust" because lust is the reality [of all phenomena]. Second, by means of principle, one integrates phenomena: the identity of one and many is like a horse's head having no existence apart from it;
it is the cloth itself that constitutes the head, because the substance of the cloth is perfectly interfused, such that the head is made identical [to the cloth].

This is sufficient. If one wishes to say that "one manifests many" and so forth, it is because, in terms of the power of mutual dependence within the conditions of dependent origination, the entire *dharmadhātu* is a single illusory net, causing the identity of the one and the many.
Just as the magical power of an illusionist causes many to appear as many and so on, the *Bhadramāyākāra-parivarta* states:
"Or he may manifest a moment as a hundred years," for illusory phenomena are empty and without obstruction.

Since this is so regarding their mutual identity (*lakṣaṇa-samatā*), it is likewise so regarding their mutual inclusion (*lakṣaṇa-praveśa*). Inclusion means that within one there are many, and so forth.

Since this is so for distinct entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*), it is likewise so for identical entities (*ekasvabhāva*). Since this is so for one gate, it should be understood by analogy for the remaining gates. Thus ends the explanation of how illusions arise from conditions.
Having realized that all phenomena are like illusions, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands lands, thoroughly understands sentient beings, thoroughly understands the dharma-realm,
thoroughly understands the equality of the world, thoroughly understands the equality of the appearance of Buddhas, and thoroughly understands the equality of the three periods of time.
One accomplishes various supernatural powers and transformations.

Within the second, the accomplishment of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), one accomplishes two kinds of practices by knowing that phenomena are like illusions: first, the manifestation of patient wisdom, which is called "realizing equality";

second, the unimpeded application of illusory functions, which is called "accomplishing supernatural transformations. What is meant by "equality"? First, the equality of principle and phenomenon (*tattva* and *dharma*).

1. Equality of Principle (*li-píngděng*): Because the cloth and the horse are non-dual, form is itself emptiness, and so forth. This is the equality of principle with principle; it is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 2. Equality of Phenomena (*shì-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of phenomena with phenomena. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 3. Equality of Things (*shì-shì-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of things with things. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 4. Equality of Things and Principle (*shì-lǐ-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of things and principle. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 5. Equality of Principle and Things (*lǐ-shì-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of principle and things. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 6. Equality of All Things and Principles (*yīqiè shì-lǐ-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all things and principles. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 7. Equality of All Principles and Things (*yīqiè lǐ-shì-píngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all principles and things. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 8. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the mutual equality of all things and principles. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 9. Equality of All Principles and Things with One Another (*yīqiè lǐ-shì xiāngpíngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the mutual equality of all principles and things. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 10. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè fāngmiàn*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 11. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects and Times (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè fāngmiàn shíshí*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 12. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects and Times, and the Equality of All Phenomena and Principles with One Another (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè fāngmiàn shíshí yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times, and the equality of all phenomena and principles with one another. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 13. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects and Times, and the Equality of All Phenomena and Principles with One Another, and the Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè fāngmiàn shíshí yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng*): As explained previously regarding the one and the many. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times, and the equality of all phenomena and principles with one another, and the equality of all things and principles with one another. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 14. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times, and the equality of all phenomena and principles with one another, and the equality of all things and principles with one another, and the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 15. This is the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times, and the equality of all phenomena and principles with one another, and the equality of all things and principles with one another, and the equality of all things and principles with one another in all aspects and times, and the equality of all phenomena and principles with one another. It is like the head and feet both being cloth, for there is no distinction in the cloth. It is like the Tathatā being the same for both sages and ordinary beings. 16. Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects and Times, and the Equality of All Phenomena and Principles with One Another, and the Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another, and the Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another in All Aspects and Times, and the Equality of All Phenomena and Principles with One Another, and the Equality of All Things and Principles with One Another (*yīqiè shì-lǐ xiāngpíngděng yīqiè fāngmiàn shíshí yīqiè shì-l
For example, a magical illusion is not an elephant, nor a horse; it is not a chariot, nor a pedestrian; it is not a man, nor a woman; it is not a boy, nor a girl; it is not a tree, nor a leaf;
it is not a flower, nor a fruit; it is not earth, nor water; it is not fire, nor wind; it is not day, nor night;
it is not the sun, nor the moon; it is not a half-month, nor a full month; it is not a year, nor a hundred years; it is not even an eon (*kalpa*).
It is not many eons; it is neither fixed nor chaotic; it is neither pure nor mixed; it is neither one nor different;
it is neither broad nor narrow; it is neither much nor little; it is neither measurable nor immeasurable; it is neither coarse nor subtle; it is none of these various and manifold things.

In the second [section], the "Extensive," there are three parts: first, the analogy; second, the application; third, the accomplishment of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). Within the first [of these], there are two [subdivisions].

First, it clarifies the absence of intrinsic nature, which is the meaning of the emptiness of essence (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*); therefore, the conclusion states that this is not a matter of being negated by all various kinds of things.
This may also be correlated, in sequence, with the aforementioned categories of sentient and non-sentient objects.

The various [manifestations] are not the illusion, nor is the illusion the various [manifestations]. Nevertheless, by means of illusion, the various distinct phenomena are manifested. Second, it clarifies that their characteristics exist;
this refers to the meaning of the differentiation of characteristics. Therefore, it says: "Nevertheless, by means of illusion, distinct phenomena are manifested.

Within this, the first two phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. Regarding "the various are not the illusion," this means that the elephants and so forth are not the illusion.
Therefore, the subsequent line is the reverse of this; the correspondence with the Dharma can be understood accordingly.

However, the following section correctly reveals that although phenomena are mutually negating, they nonetheless arise as effects from causes, appearing as empty yet provisional manifestations. Furthermore, it serves as a metaphor for how wisdom realizes equality while giving rise to transformative activity.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this. He contemplates all worlds as being like illusions—
namely, the world of karma, the world of afflictions, the world of lands, the world of phenomena, the world of time, the world of destinies, the world of formation,
the world of destruction, the world of movement, and the world of conditioned activity.
The two dharmas are combined. The text contains both general and specific [explanations]. Regarding the repeated mention of "the world" (*loka*), there are two meanings:

first, because it is subject to destruction, it serves as a metaphor for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, that which is concealed is called "the world," which also applies to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, these dharmas encompass all five categories.

The destinies consist of the five destinies, because their formation and destruction are described in terms of the single period of the receptacle world. Motion pertains to both sentient and insentient things, because they shift from moment to moment.
Volitional action pertains only to sentient beings, because it involves manifesting effortful activity.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all worlds as like an illusion, they do not perceive the birth of sentient beings, nor do they perceive the cessation of sentient beings.
They do not perceive the birth of lands, nor do they perceive the cessation of lands. They do not perceive the birth of phenomena, nor do they perceive the cessation of phenomena.
They do not perceive anything in the past that can be conceptually differentiated; they do not perceive any arising or activity in the future; they do not perceive the present...
