Abiding in a single thought-moment, they do not observe awakening, do not discriminate awakening, do not see the appearance of a Buddha,
do not see the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha, do not see abiding in great vows, do not see entry into the stage of certainty, and do not emerge from the nature of equality.
In the third section on the accomplishment of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), there are two parts. First is the accomplishment of the practice of true wisdom (*jñāna*).

Because one realizes that the essence is empty, it concludes by stating that one does not depart from the nature of equality (*samatā*). Furthermore, in the preceding section on phenomena (*dharma*), it clarifies the illumination within stillness, stating that one "realizes equality."
This clarifies that stillness is itself wisdom; hence it is said, "not seeing. Thus, one knows that the illusion of non-illusion is precisely the illusory dharma.
Only the vision that transcends all seeing is truly the vision of illusion.

Although this bodhisattva accomplishes buddha-fields, he knows that fields are without distinction; although he accomplishes the realm of sentient beings, he knows that sentient beings are without distinction;
although he universally contemplates the dharma-realm, he dwells peacefully in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), tranquil and unmoving;

although he realizes the equality of the three periods of time, he does not contradict the differentiation of dharmas across the three periods; although he accomplishes the aggregates and sense-bases...
Yet they have forever severed their basis [for affliction]. Although they liberate sentient beings, they understand that the dharma-realm is equal and devoid of any distinctions.
Although they know that all phenomena transcend words and are ineffable, they constantly preach the Dharma with inexhaustible eloquence.
Although they do not cling to the task of transforming sentient beings, they do not abandon great compassion in order to deliver them all.
He turns the wheel of Dharma; although he reveals past causes and conditions, he knows that the nature of causes and conditions is devoid of movement or change.

Second, it clarifies that movement and stillness are non-dual, and likewise that the provisional and the real are not two. Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom cannot apprehend existence or non-existence," and...

One arouses the mind of great compassion because, while realizing that the essence is empty, one does not destroy the distinctions of illusory appearances. Thus, it is like the birth of an elephant being identical to its death;
these two, being in opposition, should be understood through four propositions (catuṣkoṭi). That is to say, because these two are non-dual, they are not different.
Because there is no duality, it is not one. Because it is not one, it is not different. Therefore, it is not "not-one. Because it is not different, it is not one; therefore, it is not "not-different.
Furthermore, because the simultaneous illumination of both is transcended, it is not "both one and different.

If one uses the two meanings on the cloth to correspond with the two meanings regarding the object to discern non-identity and non-difference, there are briefly ten propositions. First, by means of the [cloth]...

The meaning of "forming an image" refers to the sense of differentiation within an object. To unify these into a single limit is called "non-differentiation. This is a case of taking the fundamental to follow the derivative;
it clarifies non-differentiation by way of the derivative. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharmakāya flowing through the five paths is called sentient beings;
the Tathāgatagarbha is coextensive with causes, whether arising or ceasing. Second, [it is explained] by means of a cloth remaining in its own state.
Regarding the meaning: the upper part of the "elephant" (the character for *xiàng*) signifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*). When these are combined into a single limit, it is called "non-different.

This is the process of returning the derivative to the fundamental; by relying on the fundamental, one clarifies their non-difference. As the Sūtra says: "All sentient beings are themselves suchness (*tathatā*);

they do not undergo further extinction," and so forth. Third, there is the mutual fusion of the two: the fundamental to which the derivative is returned, and the derivative from which the fundamental is derived. These two are mutually integrated without... [duality].
"Obstruction is not different. This means that the beginning and the end are equal and thus not different, because the texts of the two preceding sutras are inseparable.

Fourth, the "end" which is subsumed within and returns to the "beginning," and the "beginning" which follows the "end" as it is subsumed—these two mutually cancel each other out, and are therefore called "not different.
This is the non-difference of the simultaneous vanishing of both beginning and end, because truth and delusion are equal.

...and so forth. Because difference cannot be found [between them], the following four gates clarify that they are not one. That is to say, the fifth [gate] concerns the meaning of the cloth remaining in its own position and the meaning of its distinction from the elephant upon it.
Since these two—the root and the branch—are mutually contradictory and opposed, they are called "not one.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgatagarbha does not reside within the ālayavijñāna; therefore, the seven consciousnesses have birth."

It ceases. This refers to the fact that the *tathāgatagarbha* is neither born nor ceases. Regarding the meaning of the elephant formed upon the six pieces of cloth and the meaning of the essence of the elephant being empty:
these two are mutually contradictory and mutually destructive; therefore, they are not one. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"The seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration, do not experience suffering or pleasure, and are not the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Only the *tathāgatagarbha* experiences suffering, pleasure, and so forth."
Seventh, because the first aspect is "contrary" (*vipakṣa*) and the subsequent aspect is "harmful" (*vihiṃsā*), these two meanings are distinct; therefore, they are called "not one.

That is to say, being contrary means each turns away from the other, remaining at a vast distance from one another. Being harmful means they stand in direct opposition, even devouring and harming those close to them.
Thus, the distant and the near are not one, for the preceding scriptural passage states they are not separate. Eighth, by means of the ultimate...
Mutual harm is both extinguished and not extinguished; mutual opposition is both existent and non-existent.
This state of neither existing nor being extinguished is not a single meaning. This is the non-identity of formation and destruction, because the seven consciousnesses are empty yet existent.
Because True Suchness (tathatā) is both concealed and manifest. Ninth, the four [aspects] above are neither identical nor different;
yet they are also not identical, because their meanings do not intermingle. Tenth, nevertheless, they are not different, because the principle is universally pervasive and phenomena are non-dual.
If one takes the perspective of non-difference, all aspects are perfectly harmonized; if one takes the perspective of non-identity...
The various gates are extremely contradictory and mutually destructive; yet that which is extremely contrary and yet extremely compliant is the dharma of non-obstruction.
Just as it is with the mutual correspondence of "towel" and "elephant," the same principle applies to the interlacing of all phrases such as "skillful means" (*upāya*) and so forth.
The various passages above and below, concerning the meaning of neither identity nor difference, are all to be explained according to this.
This is called the fourth illusory-like patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Son of the Buddha, what is the flame-like patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The fifth is the "patience like a mirage. It is divided into three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Now, for the first:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all worlds are identical to a mirage."

The commentary consists of three parts: first, pointing to the dharma as being identical to the simile; second, illustrating the specific characteristics of the simile below; and third, summarizing by applying the dharma [to the meaning].
For example, a mirage has no fixed location; it is neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, and neither annihilated nor eternal.
It is not a single color, nor various colors, nor is it colorless.
Within these two [categories], if one opens up distinct thematic gates, they likewise possess five meanings: first, empty space; second, solar heat;

third, the combination of solar heat and empty space which produces a shimmering glare; fourth, the glare that resembles water but is actually without water; fifth, causing thirsty deer to perceive it as such.
There are five points: first, it is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*; second, it is a metaphor for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance;

third, it is a metaphor for the ocean of the mind stirred by habitual tendencies, giving rise to dependently originated phenomena that appear as real; fourth, it is a metaphor for the non-arising nature of the dependent (*paratantra*); and fifth, it is a metaphor for the attachment to reality held by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
It is merely displayed according to worldly convention.
Next, its characteristics are illustrated as being existent.
A bodhisattva thus observes things as they truly are, thoroughly understands all phenomena, and realizes them directly to bring them to full perfection.
Within the conjunction of these three dharmas: the first clarifies the direct realization of the dharma; the following clarifies the accomplishment of the practice of patience.
This is called the fifth patience of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which is like a flame.
The names of the three fetters.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding dreams?
Regarding the sixth patience regarding dreams, the inquiry, the explanation, and the summary of the fetters are as before.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all worlds are like dreams.
For example, a dream is neither the world nor separate from the world; it is not of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
it is neither arising nor passing away, neither defiled nor pure, yet it is manifested.

Second is the presentation of the analogies. Furthermore, there are five factors that elucidate the meaning of this dream: first, the basis, which is the awakened mind, used as an analogy for the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
second, the cause, which is the hindrance of sleep, used as an analogy for the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*);

third, that which is manifested, which is the differentiation of dream-phenomena, used as an analogy for the phenomena arising from conditions; fourth, the dream-events, which are neither existent nor non-existent, but merely...
Because the mind undergoes transformation, one does not perceive the phenomena before one's eyes. The fifth point causes the dreamer to grasp [the dream] as real.

In the text, the first part clarifies that both are non-existent, using the analogy that phenomena do not exist; the latter part states that they are nevertheless manifested as existing, using the analogy that phenomena do exist.
These are distinguished as the "both" position, while their mutual negation constitutes the "neither" position. However, these four positions all arise because it is a dream. That is to say, first—
Because this is a dream, there are dream-objects; that which appears in the dream exists [as an appearance].
Since both are said to be a dream, their nature must necessarily be empty, for one perceives what is real within that which lacks reality.

However, to speak of existence is to entirely subsume non-existence within existence, and to speak of non-existence is to entirely subsume existence within non-existence, because they do not possess dual characteristics. It is not merely that their characteristics exist.
It is simply that its nature is non-existent; reflect on this. Thirdly, because it is a dream, it must necessarily possess two meanings:

the non-existence of total existence and the existence of total non-existence. These two gates stand side by side, yet they do not accord with one another; therefore, it is neither half-existence nor half-non-existence.
The fourth [position] states that these are dreams; it must necessarily be a "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*), for form and its negation are both fused and the two characteristics are exhausted.
Yet, this "neither-nor" does not contradict the "both-yes. If existence were not negated to bring about exhaustion, there would be no basis for non-existence;

if non-existence were not negated to bring about exhaustion, there would be no basis for existence. Therefore, survival and extinction do not obstruct one another; when both are dissolved in freedom, only then is it truly so.
This is the Dharma-gate of mastery over dreams. Therefore, a sutra says: "The world is always like a dream; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence.
This is what that means.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: they know that all worlds are entirely identical to dreams, and that [in reality] there is nothing [substantial].
Because of transformation; because its intrinsic nature is like a dream; because attachment is like a dream; because its nature is free from [intrinsic reality] like a dream;

because its fundamental nature is like a dream; because what is manifested is like a dream; because there is no distinction [between waking and dreaming] like a dream; and because conceptualization is like a dream.
Because it is like awakening from a dream.
Within the three combined metaphors, there are ten phrases. The first phrase serves as the general statement; the subsequent section beginning with "there is no... provides the specific details.

Among these specific details, the first phrase corresponds closely to the preceding general statement, omitting only the two characters "like a dream" (rú mèng). Of the nine subsequent phrases, the first eight distinguish the dream, while the last...

First, regarding "clarity-awakening" (*prajñā*), these are subsumed within the preceding eight [categories] as four pairs. The first two clarify the gate of permanence and impermanence: the essence being empty and unchanging is the meaning of permanence;
its self-nature (*svabhāva*) lacking constancy is the meaning of impermanence. The next two distinguish the gate of the real and the delusive:
the delusive arises from attachment, while the real arises from the detachment of the nature. The final two concern the gate of essence and appearance: the essence is fundamentally one and such.
The manifestations appear in many forms. The latter two clarify the gateways of identity and difference:

though it is but a single mind, being one without distinction, it appears as various and different according to the differentiation of its marks. Furthermore, it is solely a single dream in which various marks manifest.

The four preceding gateways each preserve both aspects while mutually negating them to form four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); this can be seen by reflecting upon them. The final proposition clarifies awakening.
This refers to the gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). It means that one must be awake to know that it was a dream;

while actually dreaming, one does not know it is a dream because the mind is entirely obscured. Even if one were to know it is a dream while dreaming, one has not yet awakened. Only upon waking does one fully realize the dream and understand that, in reality, no dream ever existed.

Nevertheless, it is precisely because of the dream that there is awakening; thus, one distinguishes between the time of dreaming and the time of awakening. If one were apart from the dream, there would be no [awakening].
Awakening to this brings cessation. By contemplating the many gates of transcendence and ceasing to grasp at dream-like delusions, one only then achieves mastery over the dharma-gate of dreams.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s sixth patience, that of the dream-like.
The names of the three fetters.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like an echo?
The seventh patience, "like an echo," is divided into three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first [the inquiry]:

O Son of the Buddha! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and contemplated the nature of all phenomena, practices and achieves mastery, reaching the further shore.
Within these two explanations, there are three parts: first, the causes for the practice of patience; second, from "knowing all" onwards, the characteristics of achieving patience.
Third, the benefits of the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*). First:
because one is able to accomplish patience by giving rise to contemplation through hearing, one knows that all sounds are identical to echoes, manifesting as neither coming nor going.

Within these two [sections], the Dharma is presented first, followed by the analogy. Within the Dharma section, there are two parts: first, pointing to the Dharma as being identical to the analogy to briefly reveal its characteristics;
second, making it known that all sounds are like echoes—neither coming nor going—to clarify that their essence is empty, while thus manifesting that their appearance exists.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the voice of the Tathāgata as not emerging from within, not emerging from without, nor emerging from both within and without.
Although he understands that this voice is neither internal, nor external, nor emerging from both internal and external, [he perceives it thus].
Furthermore, they are able to manifest skillful mastery in the names and phrases of eloquent exposition.
Second, they understand that the Buddha’s voice is like an echo; it is not merely an analogy for worldly sounds.

Within this, first, the non-existence of that which exists is clarified: since there is no sound apart from the recipient, it is not internal; since there is no sound apart from the Buddha, it is not external. Second.
Because phenomena depend upon one another, they are neither internal nor external. If one were to speak of the union of the internal and external, there would then be two distinct sounds;

however, the mutual dependence of the internal and external reveals their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Although this is subsequently understood, the subsequent passage clarifies that this "non-existence" is itself existence.
Therefore, while it is stated that they are not three, they are nonetheless able to manifest skillfully.
For example, an echo arises from conditions;

this is illustrated by a second analogy. This consists of four parts: first, the illustration; second, the application; third, the extended illustration; and fourth, the re-application. Now, the first [the illustration]:

Directly citing that which arises from conditions: it clarifies that echoes have no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature has already been seen within the Dharma.

Nevertheless, there are five points: first, the empty valley; second, the presence of sound—these two are the conditions. Third, the sound: when the sound strikes the empty valley, an echo immediately arises;
this clarifies that which arises. Fourth, being existent yet not real: this demonstrates the absence of intrinsic nature. Fifth, the deluded person.
The "small" refers to existence (*bhava*). However, this single analogy applies universally to three dharmas: First, it illustrates all sounds:

the valley represents the throat-cavity, and the sound represents the vital breath. Second, it illustrates the voice of the Tathāgata: the valley represents the Tathāgata, and the sound represents the conditions that elicit the response.
Third, it illustrates all phenomena (*dharmas*): the valley represents the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the sound represents the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).
The breath and the nature of phenomena are not mutually contradictory, enabling all sentient beings to understand according to their respective types and thereby engage in cultivation and study.

This is the second correspondence of dharmas. It is merely the voice of each Buddha; because it originates from what is proximate, it nevertheless causes all sentient beings [to attain understanding].

Each class understands according to its own kind; the words contain both the Dharma and the simile. Regarding the Dharma, it means that the voice of the Tathāgata does not contravene the nature of dharmas, yet is able to accord with each class [of beings].

This corresponds to the aforementioned "skillful manifestation. Regarding the simile, it means that without contravening the inherent nature of the sounds and phenomena of their original voices, beings understand each according to the specific category of their own speech.
It is like Śacī, the wife of Śakra and daughter of the asuras, who produces a thousand kinds of sounds within a single utterance,
yet does not even mentally intend for them to be produced in such a way.
The three turnings are illustrated through metaphors, which have two intended meanings: first, they illustrate how the Buddha’s single voice above adapts to various types of beings;
second, they illustrate how the Bodhisattvas below universally expound the Dharma without deliberate effort.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having entered the realm of non-conceptuality, they achieve skillfulness in producing sounds that accord with the various types of beings, and they constantly turn the wheel of Dharma throughout infinite worlds.
Fourth is the convergence.
This Bodhisattva is skillfully able to observe all sentient beings and expounds the Dharma for them with the mark of the broad and long tongue.
His voice is unimpeded, pervading the lands of the ten directions, causing each to hear the Dharma differently according to what is appropriate for them.
The benefits of accomplishing the three types of patience consist of two parts. First, teaching universally according to the capacities of beings:
although one knows that sound has no arising, one manifests voices everywhere; although one knows there is nothing to be taught, one extensively expounds all dharmas.
The wondrous voice is impartial, understood differently by each according to their kind; all this is thoroughly comprehended through wisdom.
Next, it clarifies the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real, which is identical to an echo, because essence and characteristics are without obstruction.
Thus, by hearing the teaching that is like an echo, one understands sounds as being like echoes and produces speech that is like echoes, expounding the Dharma that is like an echo.
This is called the seventh patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is like an echo;
it is known by the name "the three fetters."
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like a shadow?
The eighth patience, "like a shadow," is divided into four distinct sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion; and fourth, the fruit.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is not born in the world, nor does he pass away from the world.
He is not within the world, nor is he outside the world. He does not traverse the world, nor does he not traverse the world.
He is not identical to the world, nor is he different from the world. He does not go toward the world, nor does he not go toward the world. Not...
Abiding in the world yet not non-abiding in the world; neither of this world nor of the supramundane. This explanation has three parts:
namely, the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the synthesis (*yoga*). Now, for the first: within the principle there are eleven pairs, divided into three sections.

The first seven pairs negate both extremes simultaneously to reveal the nature, thereby establishing the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), because they are like reflections that lack substantial reality.
It is neither the cultivation of bodhisattva practices nor the abandonment of great vows; it is neither real nor unreal.

By illuminating both nature and appearance through these pairs of opposites, one accomplishes contemplative practice. Just as a shadow is empty yet manifest, nature is thus not something to be cultivated, while appearance is not something to be abandoned.
Because the ultimate is identical to the conventional, it is not real; because the conventional is identical to the ultimate, it is not unreal.
Indeed,
although they constantly practice all Buddha-dharmas, they are able to accomplish all worldly affairs; they do not follow the flow of the world,
nor do they dwell in the flow of dharmas.
The three pairs of negation (*pratiṣedha*) and illumination (*āloka*) are unimpeded, forming the sovereign practice of simultaneous application (*yuganaddha*).

In the first pair, the simultaneous illumination of the ultimate and the conventional constitutes the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real. In the latter pair, the simultaneous negation of the ultimate and the conventional constitutes the simultaneous quiescence of the provisional and the real.

The simultaneity of negation and illumination is "simultaneous application," while their mutual sublation without obstruction is "sovereignty. These points conclude the preceding two sections; they are all thus.
Non-obstruction is the profound and mysterious characteristic of patience (*kṣānti*).
For example, such things as the sun and moon, men and women, houses, mountains and forests, and rivers and springs—within these two similes, five dharmas are fully contained.
First, the sun and so forth serve as the fundamental substratum (*āśraya-svabhāva*). Second, beneath the oil...

This clarifies the locus where illumination manifests. The first two [points] are the conditions (*pratyaya*); the third is the manifestation of its reflection, which is the arising of the illumination-condition;
the fourth is that the reflection and the oil below the illumination exist as non-existence; the fifth is that the ignorant and small-minded falsely claim it exists. Regarding the first:
if one employs the analogy of the reflection specifically to illustrate the Bodhisattva manifesting a body, then the sun and so forth serve as analogies for compassion, wisdom, vows, and so on.
If the analogy of the reflection is taken to apply universally to all phenomena, then the sun serves as the metaphor for the cause.
Although both the river and the spring can manifest [the reflection], they serve as the objects manifested, because the long river and the gushing spring enter into the mirror.
Regarding oil, water, the body, jewels, clear mirrors, and other such pure phenomena—among these two types of media that can manifest [images], there are both specific and general analogies.
The specific analogies represent the stimulus of the capacity (the sentient being) and the locus of the response-manifestation;
the general analogy represents the conditions, namely ignorance and so forth.
Yet its reflection appears.
Within that which arises from the three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), there are both general and specific aspects; the two results may be known.
The reflection and the oil, etc., are neither identical nor different, neither separate nor joined. Even within a flowing river, it does not drift away.
It does not sink even within the pools or wells; though it appears therein, it remains unstained by attachment.

The four clarities (*catur-vijñapti*) encompass many categories of meaning within both existence and non-existence. Among these, the concepts of identity and difference, as well as conjunction and separation, universally manifest the nature of reflections.

Here, identity and difference refer to this reflection versus that reflection, while conjunction and separation refer to the reflection in relation to the water and so forth. Next, regarding the river...

The downward flow further clarifies the meaning of the reflection; it does not apply to both types of reflections. It is like the moon reflected in the flowing waters of the Huai River: the flowing water does not carry the moon away.

When light shines upon a deep pool, though it is ten thousand fathoms deep, one does not see the light sink. This serves as a metaphor for how Bodhisattvas, while conforming to the shifting flow of the world, are not swept away by birth and death;
and while realizing true quiescence, they do not sink into *nirvāṇa*. Although they subsequently manifest descent, there is a dual conclusion regarding existence.
No. This analogy of the mutual penetration of natures includes both the mirror and the image;
yet, while sentient beings know that such a reflection appears here, they also know that no such reflection exists there.
Although distant objects and near objects both appear as reflections, the reflections themselves do not possess distance or proximity according to the objects.

Within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), one takes existence and non-existence to be truly existent or non-existent; failing to realize that these are merely reflections and utterly ungraspable, one thus forms attachments.
Among these, one first grasps at existence and non-existence as objects of attachment. Following this, the passage beginning with "distant objects" uses the reflection as an illustration.
This is the correct principle. It is revealed that [ordinary beings] grasp [at appearances] because they do not know that these reflections have neither distance nor proximity.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is able to know that both his own body and the bodies of others are entirely the domain of wisdom.
He does not form a dualistic understanding, such as distinguishing between self and other; rather, regarding his own land and the lands of others...
The lands appear simultaneously and universally, each distinct from the others.
Within the third section, "The Conjunction," there are two parts: first, the formal conjunction with the preceding text;

therein, the initial portion cites the realm of wisdom to correspond with the preceding substantial essence, while the subsequent portion, beginning with "And therein," corresponds with the preceding oil and so forth, and the final portion, beginning with "Each and every," corresponds with the preceding manifestation of reflections.
Just as within a seed there are no roots, sprouts, stalks, nodes, branches, or leaves, yet it is able to give rise to such things, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Within the non-dual dharma, they differentiate dual characteristics;
through skillful means, they penetrate them without obstruction.

The second turning uses analogies to harmonize with existence within non-existence. Within this, the analogy comes first, followed by the application. Being unimpeded regarding existence and non-existence is called "skillful means" and so forth;
this is termed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s eighth patience, "Like a Reflection."
Regarding the names of the three fetters:

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, although they do not travel to the lands of the ten directions, they are able to universally manifest in all buddha-fields without departing from here, nor do they arrive there;
like a reflection, they appear everywhere, yet their conduct is without [obstruction].
Obstruction: it causes all sentient beings to perceive their differentiated bodies as having the same solid and substantial characteristics as those of the mundane world.

Within the fourth fruit, there are three [aspects]: first, one attains a body that accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā), which reaches its destination without moving, like a shadow, because it is undivided yet pervasive.
However, this differentiation is itself non-differentiation; there is no obstruction between differentiation and non-differentiation.
Next, it is established as unimpeded because this non-differentiation is the non-differentiation of differentiation; thus, although it does not go anywhere, it is omnipresent.
This causes beings to perceive differences; yet this differentiation is the differentiation of non-differentiation. Therefore, although it is all-pervasive, it does not abide in "this" or "that.
This Bodhisattva is born from the lineage of the Tathāgata;
because his body, speech, and mind are pure and unimpeded, he is able to attain a pure body of boundless forms and marks.
The subsequent passage reveals the causes of this body; while its boundless manifestations are specifically included within the results, they also extend to the preceding dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s acceptance of [all things] as being like an illusion?

The ninth is the patience regarding the nature of transformations (*nirmāṇa-kṣānti*). The text is divided into four distinct sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion; and fourth, the fruit.
Regarding the heading, it says "transformation" because that which did not exist suddenly comes into being.
O Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all worlds are entirely like transformations (*nirmāṇa*).

This explanation has three parts: namely, the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their synthesis. Within the principle, there are two sections: first, the general indication; second, the indication that the principle is identical to the analogy, which fully comprises both the knowing subject and the known object.
Since he knows all worlds, it is not restricted merely to the categories of sentient beings who are to be transformed; thus, he briefly indicates "the world" in its entirety.
It must necessarily include the supramundane.
That is to say: the transformation of the mental karma of all sentient beings, because it arises from conceptualization;

the transformation of all worldly conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), because they arise from discrimination; and the transformation of all suffering, pleasure, and inversions, because they arise from false grasping. All...

The unreal phenomena of the world are transformations, for they are manifested through verbal expression. All afflictions and conceptual discriminations are transformations, for they arise from mental ideation.

These will be explained separately later; first, that which is known is explained, followed by that which knows. Within the former [section], there are ten phrases; the first five concern defiled transformations.
The latter five [stages] involve purification. Now, for the first [section]: it does not go beyond the three categories of karma, afflictions, and suffering.

The first four are suffering, which is the characteristic of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). 1. Consciousness arises from perception (*saṃjñā*); 2. Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise with consciousness as their cause, because discrimination is the nature of consciousness;

3. Feeling (*vedanā*) arises from perception, because perception grasps the characteristics of love and hatred; 4. Form (*rūpa*) also arises from formative forces; as for the form of neutral maturation (*avipāka*), it is like foam.
They are not real, because the permeation of names and words (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*) is itself formative action (*saṃskāra*). The fifth [member] is affliction (*kleśa*);

since affliction arises from perception (*saṃjñā*) and formative action, and mindfulness (*smṛti*) is itself formative action, karma (*karman*) pervades both [the first and fifth members]. The meaning of the first phrase is mental karma; this phrase is discrimination (*vikalpa*), as both are karma.

In this context, the mind and its associates lack intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions; they are unreal like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*). Being originally non-existent and now existing, they manifest with characteristics like a magical creation.

Thus, as the *Renwang jing* says: "Dharmas are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning; all things arise through causes and conditions. The two meanings of "purification" (*viśuddhi*) and "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) should be understood by analogy with this.

Furthermore, there is the transformation of pure subduing, because it is manifested through non-conceptualization; the transformation that does not shift across the three periods of time, because it is the equality of non-arising;
the transformation through the bodhisattva’s power of vows, because of vast cultivation; the transformation through the Tathāgata’s great compassion, because of the manifestation of skillful means;
and the transformation of skillful means for turning the wheel of Dharma, because it is what is spoken through wisdom, fearlessness, and eloquence.
The subsequent explanation of the five purities is as follows: first, the skillful means for taming sentient beings, which relies upon true wisdom;
second, the profoundly tranquil true wisdom, which is established by principle; thus the preceding text states: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time and realizes the equality of all phenomena.

Third, vows fulfilled through practice; fourth, compassion, which is likewise established based on skillful means; and fifth, possessing fearless eloquence, capable of turning the wheel of the Dharma.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva thus understands the mundane and supramundane transformations.

He realizes them through direct perception, with vast knowledge, boundless knowledge, knowledge according to reality, sovereign knowledge, and true knowledge; he cannot be shaken by false views, and he accords with the world.
The practice is likewise not lost or destroyed.
Second, this specifically reveals the capacity for knowing. Within this, the first two phrases conclude the preceding and give rise to the subsequent:

"the world" concludes the preceding defiled state, while "transcending the world" concludes the preceding purified state; it also concludes other matters not yet exhausted, namely, even down to a single dharma that transcends nirvāṇa.
Because *nirvāṇa* is also like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Alternatively, it is said that *nirvāṇa* is not like a transformation;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states this because, for newly resolved bodhisattvas, there is a fear of being startled or terrified, and thus [the teaching] distinguishes that arising and ceasing are like transformations.

The term "clearly knowing" (*parijñā*) refers to the stage subsequent to arising. Next, under the section on "direct realization," the capacity to know is explicitly revealed. Regarding the aforementioned "clearly knowing," there are six types of knowing.

The meaning [of "knowledge"] is as follows: first, because it is neither a mere matter nor a principle that is subject to inferential estimation; second, because nothing is omitted from its scope; third, because it accords with the Middle Way;
fourth, because it conforms to the conventional realm; fifth, because the ultimate and the conventional are without obstruction; and sixth, because it returns to the single ultimate truth.
The subsequent phrase, "not false or delusive," concludes the above six types of knowledge. Abiding in the true path without wavering, one practices even upon what is not the path without...
It is destroyed.
For example, a transformation (nirmāṇa) does not arise from the mind, nor does it arise from mental factors (caitta), nor does it arise from karma;
it does not undergo retribution, it is neither born in the world nor does it perish in the world; it cannot be pursued, it cannot be grasped or touched, and it does not endure for long. It is not...
It abides for a mere moment. It neither courses within the world nor is it apart from the world. It is not exclusively bound to one direction, nor is it universally attached to all directions.
It is neither finite nor infinite. It is neither weary nor does it cease; yet it is neither non-weary nor non-ceasing. It is neither ordinary nor holy.
Neither defiled nor pure; neither born nor dead; neither wise nor foolish; neither seeing nor not seeing;
neither relying on the mundane world nor entering the Dharma-realm; neither sharp-witted nor dull-witted; neither grasping nor non-grasping; neither birth-and-death nor nirvana;
neither existent nor non-existent.
In the second analogy, four meanings should be distinguished: first, the transformer serves as the metaphor for causes and conditions;

second, the manifested phenomenon serves as the metaphor for the fruit that arises; third, although it manifests functionally, it lacks substantial reality; fourth, the ignorant and small-minded take it to be real. Thus, the *Daśadṛṣṭānta-śāstra* states:
"Just as a magical creation, though empty and without reality, can cause sentient beings to experience sorrow, suffering, anger, or joy."

Delusion regarding pleasure is delusive; all phenomena are likewise so. How is it that they lack reality? Just as those conjured beings lack the sufferings of birth, old age, death, pleasure, and pain because they differ from other persons, so it is here.
Within the text there are forty phrases: the first phrase provides the heading; the subsequent thirty-seven phrases exclusively employ double negation to manifest their lack of reality;
and the final "neither existent nor non-existent" phrase has a meaning identical to these two types.
The first is also a double negation, meaning that it neither exists nor does not exist. The second is the mutual integration of nature and characteristics:
because transformations are unreal, they are not existent; because transformation-events manifest, they are not non-existent.
In this way, the Bodhisattva practices in the world through skillful means, cultivating the Bodhisattva path. Fully understanding worldly phenomena, he manifests emanations to travel among them.

This consists of two parts within the three [sections]: first, the practice of manifestation; second, the benefit of transforming others, beginning with the phrase "O Son of the Buddha. Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the arising of manifestation.

It is used because they exist as identical in their characteristics of transformation. However, the phrase "the Bodhisattva is thus" is stated simply because the various preceding negations do not individually apply to all phenomena;
therefore, "thus" refers back to those aforementioned [negations] as skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
He does not cling to the world nor grasp at his own self; he makes no conceptual distinctions regarding the world or the body.
He does not abide in the world, yet he does not depart from the world; he does not abide in dharmas, yet he does not depart from dharmas.
Second, the explanation of the wisdom of transformation (*nirmāṇajñāna*).

Because one realizes that transformations are not real, and because of one's original vow, one does not abandon even a single realm of sentient beings, nor does one fail to subdue even a few realms of sentient beings.

One does not discriminate among phenomena, yet it is not that one does not discriminate; one knows that the nature of all phenomena has neither coming nor going, and though they are non-existent, they are nonetheless fulfilled.
This completes the Buddha-dharma.
Within the clarification of the three pairs of non-manifestations,
one realizes that all phenomena are like illusions, being neither existent nor non-existent.
Fourth, the summary indicating the purport of the transformation:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus dwells in the patience regarding transformations,
they are able to fully fulfill the path to enlightenment of all Buddhas and benefit all sentient beings."
Second is the benefit through transformation;
this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s ninth patience regarding that which is like a magical creation.
Third is the concluding statement.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve this patience, whatever they do is entirely like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Just as a magically created being has no place of dependence or abiding in any Buddha-field, no grasping or attachment toward any world,
and does not give rise to discrimination regarding any Buddha-dharma, yet proceeds toward the Buddha-bodhi without weariness, so too do these Bodhisattvas cultivate [the path].
Their conduct is free from all inversions. Although they possess no body, they manifest all bodies; although they have no abode, they dwell in all lands;

although they have no form, they universally manifest all forms; and although they do not cling to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), they clearly illuminate the equality and perfection of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Within the fourth fruit, one first attains the fruit of the activity of benefiting others.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has no dependence upon any phenomena and is thus called a "liberated one."

One who has completely abandoned all faults is called "the Tamed. One who is immovable and unchanging, universally entering the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, is called "the One with Supernatural Powers.
One who has attained skillfulness regarding the dharma of non-arising is called "the Non-regressive."
One who possesses all powers such that even Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains cannot obstruct them is called "unimpeded.
Subsequently, based on self-benefit, one establishes the fruit known as the "Victorious Name.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience like space?
The tenth [perfection], as in the patience regarding space (*ākāśa-kṣānti*), also consists of four parts: the thesis, the explanation, the result, and the summary. The thesis states: "like space.

The analogy of space applies to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*). The Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*) is the metaphor for the pure dharma-realm (*viśuddha-dharmadhātu*), because it is free from differentiated characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the parables used in treatises such as the *Madhyāntavibhāga* to illustrate the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) represent only one aspect of this [topic].
However, the characteristics of those parables differ slightly from other parables. In most cases, these parables unfold their meaning through five aspects:

although they primarily employ the illusions and so forth that are produced as metaphors for phenomena (*dharma*), they also employ the conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth as metaphors for the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). In the present case, the characteristics of the parable do not unfold [in this manner].

These are distinct dharmas. They point directly to emptiness, which encompasses manifold meanings used as metaphors for phenomena. Furthermore, regarding these various metaphors, if we consider the analogies themselves:

the first five predominantly employ that which appears to exist to refute substantial existence; the "transformation" metaphor employs that which exists by not existing to refute that which merely appears to exist;
and this current metaphor employs the total transcendence of both nature and characteristics to refute everything. Moreover, the preceding six [metaphors] eliminate...

Furthermore, the emptiness [of the examples] is more extensive, while the existence established based on that emptiness is less so; this first negation of existence enters into a lesser degree of emptiness, whereas the existence established based on emptiness is greater.
Moreover, the aforementioned metaphors apply universally to all things, while the internal similes herein possess multiple meanings.

The metaphors for each object illustrate a specific category of phenomena according to their individual significance. Nevertheless, Nāgārjuna’s ten similes are explained through four successive stages.
Regarding the meaning of emptiness: first, it is near yet far-off. This means that empty space is not a visible phenomenon;
however, when one looks at it from a distance, the visual faculty turns back and perceives a pale blue color. All phenomena are likewise so: they are empty and non-existent.
Because ordinary people are distant from untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), they abandon the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and perceive [them] as male, female, and so forth.
Regarding "things": in reality, these things ultimately do not exist at all. Second, [the meaning of emptiness] is established by way of being unstained by intrinsic purity;

third, by way of having no beginning, middle, or end; fourth, by way of the fact that the substance itself is actually without any thing. These ten meanings of emptiness within the upper eight stages are all brief explanations.
However, there are differences in their specific meanings, while the common meanings and their various metaphors remain the same. As for the other meanings of non-obstruction, they are as follows:
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattvas:
"Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes that all dharma-realms are like empty space because they are without marks (*animitta*);
all worlds are like empty space because they are without arising; and all dharmas are like empty space."
Because they are non-dual: the conduct of all sentient beings is like space, for there is nothing to be conducted;
all Buddhas are like space, for they are without discrimination; and the powers of all Buddhas are like space, for they are without distinction.
All meditative concentrations are like space because they are equal throughout the three periods of time;
all dharmas that are taught are like space because they are ineffable; and all Buddha-bodies are like space because they are unattached and unimpeded.

In the second explanation, there are two parts: first, the characteristics of the understanding through patience; second, the benefits accomplished by the practice of patience. Now, for the first part: first, the specific clarifications.

Nine meanings of emptiness are used as metaphors for nine types of phenomena. Although these meanings differ according to their respective objects, they are all empty because they are dependently originated and lack intrinsic nature.

Each of the nine phrases first identifies a phenomenon and its corresponding metaphor, followed by the explanation of the underlying reason. The first identifies the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena as being like [the metaphor].
"Empty. This explains the reason for what follows: because it is signless (*animitta*). That is to say, arising from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature;

its characteristics are inherently void, for phenomena themselves are the reality-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This phrase is the general statement. Second, because the world arises from the collective karma of beings.

The threefold ritual procedure of the Dharma teachings flows from the single-flavored realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). The remaining six phrases are all to be understood according to the first phrase.
In this way, the Bodhisattva, through skillful means that are like space, realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
The final summary:
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes all phenomena through the patience and wisdom that are like space, they attain a body and bodily karma that are like space;
they attain speech and vocal karma that are like space; and they attain mind and mental karma that are like space.

Regarding the three benefits accomplished within the second stage of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), first is the general clarification of attaining the three types of action (*karman*) that are like space and the equipment of action.
For example, just as all phenomena (*dharma*) depend upon space and are neither born nor perish, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
the entire *dharmakāya* is neither born nor perishes. For example, just as space cannot be destroyed, so too the Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this. His wisdom and various powers are indestructible.
Just as space is that upon which all worlds depend, yet it itself depends on nothing, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
he is that upon which all dharmas depend, yet he himself depends on nothing. Just as space is without birth and without cessation, it can...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, sustaining the arising and ceasing of all worlds.
Without direction and without attainment, they are able to demonstrate direction and attainment, causing the world everywhere to practice with purity.
Just as space has no cardinal points and no corners, yet is able to manifest infinite directions and corners, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; without karma and without...
While abiding in retribution, they are able to manifest various karmic results.
Just as empty space neither moves nor dwells, yet can manifest various modes of deportment, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
neither moving nor dwelling, they are able to discern all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*). Just as empty space is neither form (*rūpa*) nor non-form, yet can manifest various...
Just as [the sky] produces all forms, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: neither a mundane form nor a supramundane form, yet he is able to manifest all forms.
For example, just as space is neither distant nor near, yet it abides for long and manifests all things, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: neither distant nor near, yet he is able to...

The Long-Abiding [Samādhi] reveals the various practices performed by Bodhisattvas. For example, just as space is neither pure nor defiled, yet is not separate from purity and defilement, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
he is neither an obstruction nor without obstruction, yet is not separate from obstructions and the absence of obstructions.
For example, just as space appears before all worlds, yet it does not manifest all worlds...
In the same way, for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, all dharmas appear before them, yet it is not that they appear before all dharmas.
Just as space universally enters into all things without limit, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
he universally enters into all dharmas, yet the Bodhisattva’s mind has no limit.
Second, specifically revealing that its virtues are equal to empty space. Within this, the first two lines exclusively use metaphors for that which is truly without support as being the support.
All subsequent lines reveal the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics: because they arise from conditions, and because they are empty of intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, because these two characteristics are identical, they form four propositions: (1) because it arises from conditions, it is empty; because it arises from conditions, it exists. (2) It is without... [intrinsic nature].
Because of its nature, it is empty; because it lacks intrinsic nature, it exists. Because it arises from three conditions, it exists; because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
Because it lacks the fourfold intrinsic nature, it exists; because it arises from conditions, it is empty. Since no phenomenon exists apart from emptiness, all phenomena manifest before one.
Since emptiness itself cannot be seen, it does not manifest as a phenomenon before one. The remainder of the text is self-evident.
Why is this? Because that which is performed by a bodhisattva is like space.
That is to say, all cultivation, all purification, and all accomplishment are entirely equal—of one essence, one flavor, and one measure.
Just as space is pure and pervades all places, so too does he realize and know all phenomena; regarding all phenomena, there is no differentiation.

Separate. Third, the inquiry and explanation regarding the cause for attaining benefit. As for why it is attained: it is because the contemplation of emptiness has been perfected. Within this, there are two parts.

First, because wisdom and realization are equal to emptiness. Regarding "one essence," it is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is impartial. Regarding "one flavor," it is because liberation is... [text fragment ends].
Because they are extraordinary. Regarding their single measure: both large and small, they all accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).
They adorn and purify all Buddha-lands; they perfect all bodies that have no dependence;
they understand all directions without confusion; they possess all powers that cannot be destroyed; and they fulfill all boundless merits.
They have reached the realm of all profound dharmas; they have attained mastery over the path of all pāramitās;
they sit universally upon all vajra-thrones; they universally emit voices in accordance with the various types of beings;
and for all worlds, they turn the wheel of Dharma without ever missing the proper time.
Because their subsequent virtue and function fill all of space,
this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s tenth patience, "Like Space.
This concludes the names of the three fetters.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish this patience, they attain a body that does not come, because there is no going; they attain a body that is unborn, because there is no cessation;
they attain an immovable body, because there is no decay; they attain a non-substantial body, because it is free from falsehood;
they attain a body of one mark, because it is markless; they attain an infinite body, because the powers of a Buddha are infinite; they attain a level...

Because all bodies are equal in their suchness-characteristic, one attains the body of non-differentiation; because one equally contemplates the three periods of time, one attains the body that reaches all places;
because the pure eye illuminates all without obstruction, one attains the body of the limit of desirelessness;

because one knows that all phenomena have neither conjunction nor dispersion, one attains the body of the boundless limits of space; because the treasury of merit is inexhaustible like space, one attains...

They attain a body of eloquence that is uninterrupted, inexhaustible, and equal in its dharma-nature, because they know that the characteristics of all phenomena are but a single characteristic, having non-existence as their nature, like empty space.
They attain a body of immeasurable and unimpeded sound, because it is without obstruction, like empty space.
They attain a body of the complete and pure practices of a bodhisattva, skilled in all [matters] regarding all...
Because they are unimpeded in all locations like space, they attain a body that is a continuous succession of the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas, which cannot be severed like space.
They attain a body that manifests immeasurable Buddha-fields within all Buddha-fields.
Because they are free from all attachments, like space which is boundless, they attain a body that manifests all sovereign dharmas without cessation.
Because they are like the great ocean of space, which has no limit, they attain a body of indestructible and firm power.
Because they sustain all worlds, like space, they attain faculties as sharp and keen as a vajra.
The body is firm and indestructible, for it cannot be burned by the fires of all kalpas, being like space.
It is a body that possesses the power to sustain all worlds, for its power of wisdom is like space.
Within the fourth fruit, twenty kinds of bodies are attained. The first ten resemble the ten practices and the stage of entering the supramundane.
However, their general characteristics are for the most part established based on their virtuous functions.
"O Son of the Buddha, these are called the ten kinds of patience of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
This concludes the fourth major section, which summarizes the ten patiences.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Just as there may be people in the world who, hearing that there is a place where a treasure-trove lies,
feel great joy in their hearts because it can be obtained; so too do these Bodhisattvas, the true children of the Buddha, possessing such great wisdom,
upon hearing the teachings of all Buddhas regarding the profound and quiescent nature of phenomena.

The second section, the *Geya*, consists of one hundred and seven verses. It is divided into two main parts: one hundred verses that correspond to the preceding [prose], and seven verses that serve as a concluding eulogy.
Within the first part, which merely recites the detailed explanation, there are ten sections, each consisting of ten verses. The first ten verses correspond to the "Patience toward Sounds.
Among these, the first two verses correspond to what was heard from the Buddha’s teaching.
When hearing this profound Dharma, their minds attain peace and stability; they are neither startled nor terrified, nor do they give rise to fear.
The Great Beings seeking Bodhi, upon hearing this vast sound, purify their minds and are able to endure it;
they harbor no doubt or suspicion regarding this, reflecting to themselves that they have heard it.
The profound and subtle Dharma shall bring about the attainment of all-knowledge;
Upon hearing these sounds, the Bodhisattvas, the great teachers of gods and humans, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
They gave rise to firm aspirations, seeking the teachings of all Buddhas; Because they delighted in Bodhi, their minds gradually became subdued.
Causing faith to increase further, they shall have no opposition or slander toward the Dharma;
therefore, upon hearing this sound, their minds will attain endurance, abiding therein without wavering.
For the sake of seeking bodhi, they shall practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, proceeding single-mindedly along that path with diligence and without regression.
Not abandoning the yoke of all virtues, one seeks the path to enlightenment;
with a mind free from fear, hearing the Dharma increases one’s valor, and making offerings to the Buddha brings him joy.
These two verses describe the eight qualities that can be heard. Among them, one verse describes being unstartled, and one verse describes deep faith. One...

One verse concerns awakening and understanding; two verses concern affection and delight; one verse concerns cultivation and abiding; and the final two verses praise the approach of single-minded recollection.
It is like a person of great merit who discovers a treasury of pure gold and wears whatever ornaments are appropriate for their body.
Just as one fashions and adorns ornaments, so too is the Bodhisattva. Hearing this profound meaning, they contemplate it and increase the ocean of wisdom.

By practicing in accordance with the Dharma, they know that when phenomena exist they are in accord with reality, and they know that when phenomena do not exist they are likewise in accord with reality. Following those phenomena in such a manner, they thus understand all dharmas.
Having accomplished a pure mind, clear and filled with great joy, Knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, one practices with courageous diligence;
Contemplating all phenomena with equanimity, one realizes their intrinsic nature.
Not contradicting the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, one universally awakens to all phenomena, With a resolve and delight that are ever firm and steadfast.
Purifying the Buddha’s Bodhi, immovable like Mount Sumeru, With single-minded pursuit of perfect enlightenment, they give rise to the resolve for diligence;
Furthermore, they cultivate the path of samādhi, Practicing with assiduity for immeasurable eons without ever falling back.
The Dharma entered by Bodhisattvas— This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas.
One who can thoroughly understand this, whose mind is free from weariness or indolence, and who, as taught by the Peerless One,
views all phenomena with equanimity— this is not an uneven patience, but the capacity to accomplish the wisdom of equality.
Following what the Buddha has taught, one achieves this gateway of patience and understands all things in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are ten verses that do not differentiate phenomena and accord with the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Among them, the first verse consists of three lines that praise contemplation;
the next two verses consist of one line each that praise conforming understanding which purifies the mind; and the subsequent verse praises observation.
They are equal and without contradiction. The remaining verses concern abiding correctly in cultivation:
Among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, All the sons of the gods eat from a single vessel, yet what they consume is each different;
these various kinds of food do not come from the ten directions.
Just as whatever karma one has cultivated naturally resides within its vessel, so too does the Bodhisattva observe all phenomena:
they all arise from causes and conditions; because they are unarisen, they are unceasing.

These ten verses in praise of the patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) consist of three introductory verses at the beginning, for the preceding three patiences were all [discussed in terms of] dharmas.
Thus it is said. Therefore, a metaphor is added at the beginning of each verse:

Because there is no cessation, there is no exhaustion; because there is no exhaustion, there is no defilement. One thoroughly understands that amidst the changing phenomena of the world, there is no change.
Where there is no difference, there is no location; where there is no location, there is quiescent extinction.
Their minds are free from attachment, vowing to deliver all living beings; Single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha-dharma, they never experience distraction.
With a heart of compassionate vows, they employ skillful means in the world, Diligently seeking the Ten Powers.
Abiding in the world yet not dwelling therein, They neither go nor come.
The following four verses explain the skillful means of teaching the Dharma:
"This patience is the most supreme; realizing that phenomena are inexhaustible, one enters the true realm of reality."
In reality, there is nothing entered; the Bodhisattva abiding in this patience universally beholds all Tathāgatas simultaneously bestowing upon him the prophecy.

This is called receiving the office of a Buddha. Having thoroughly realized that the phenomena of the three periods of time possess the characteristic of quiescent purity, he is able to transform sentient beings and establish them within the paths of goodness.
The final three verses offer this praise:
All the various phenomena of the world Are entirely like illusions.
If one can know them thus, the mind remains unmoved; Since all karmas arise from the mind, It is said that the mind is like an illusion.
If one is free from this conceptualization, all realms of existence are universally extinguished.
Just as a skilled illusionist manifests all manner of forms, merely causing the multitude to crave and delight in them, yet ultimately nothing is to be found—so too is the world.
All things are like illusions; they have no intrinsic nature and no arising.

The fourth verse demonstrates the various kinds of illusory-like patience (*māyopama-kṣānti*). The first six verses provide a brief exposition; among them, the first four verses point to the identity of the dharma with its metaphor and reveal the characteristics of conditions.
To deliver all sentient beings, one causes them to know that phenomena are like illusions. Sentient beings are no different from illusions;
realizing the illusion, one finds no sentient beings. Sentient beings and their lands, and all phenomena throughout the three periods of time—thus, without exception, they are all like illusions.
The final two verses establish the practice of patience:
Illusory forms of men and women, As well as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, Houses, ponds,
springs, groves, gardens, flowers, fruits, and the like— These illusory things lack sentience And have no place of abiding.
The ultimate characteristic is quiescent extinction; it merely appears according to conceptual discrimination.
The following four verses elaborate upon this. Among them, the first two verses provide a simile:
When a bodhisattva is able to perceive all worlds in this way, they see that all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are [mere appearances].
Having realized that all things are like illusions, the next verse summarizes:
Sentient beings and their worlds Are created by various karmas; They enter the limit of illusion.
Regarding that state of non-reliance and non-attachment,
the final verse describes the perfection of conduct:
"Thus attaining skillfulness, dwelling in the realm of the unobstructed, one abides in cessation free from conceptual proliferation."
The Fifth Verse on the Universal Manifestation of Great Power:
Like the Patience of the Mirage. The first [verse] follows from what preceded to generate what follows, clarifying the intent of contemplation:
"O valiant sons of the Buddhas, Following and entering the wondrous Dharma, You skillfully contemplate all perceptions."
Enmeshed within the world, manifold perceptions are like a mirage.
The Bodhisattva, skillfully understanding these perceptions, abandons all inversions.
Sentient beings differ from one another in their various forms and types, yet he realizes they are all merely perceptions; none of them possess any true reality.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions are shrouded by conceptualization. If one abandons inverted views, then the perception of a world ceases.
The world is like a mirage; through the distinctions of conceptualization, one knows that the world dwells within conceptualization.
Thus, one remains far removed from the three inversions.
The next five verses point to the dharma through a simile:
"For example, when it is hot, a mirage is seen by the world and taken for water; yet water is actually non-existent, so the wise should not seek it."
The next verse is a simile:
Sentient beings are likewise so; the realms of worldly existence do not exist at all. Like a mirage, they abide within the sphere of the unimpeded mind’s perceptions;
if one is free from all perceptions, one is also free from all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
May all those who are deluded and attached to conceptualizations attain liberation; may they distance themselves from the mind of pride,
eliminate worldly perceptions, and abide in the state where exhaustion and non-exhaustion are one— this is the final triad of verses on the skillful means of the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva realizes that all worldly phenomena are entirely like dreams; they are neither existent nor non-existent, for their essential nature is eternally quiescent.
All dharmas are without discrimination, no different from a dream and not distinct from the mind.
Thus it is with all worlds throughout the three periods of time; the very substance of a dream is without arising or ceasing.
Nor does it have any location; the three realms are all thus. The one who sees this attains liberation of mind.
A dream does not exist in the world, nor does it exist outside the world.
By not discriminating between these two, one enters the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). It is like seeing various different forms within a dream.

The world is likewise thus, no different from a dream. Those who abide in the meditative concentration on dreams understand that all worlds are like dreams—neither identical nor distinct, neither one nor manifold.
They fully comprehend that the karma of sentient beings and their lands is free from both defilement and purity. Thus they know it all.
Equal to dreams are the practices performed by Bodhisattvas, And their great vows;
all are clearly understood to be like dreams. They are no different from the world; having realized that the world is entirely empty and quiescent, they do not violate worldly conventions.
It is just as with what is seen in a dream: forms such as long and short, and so forth.
This is called the "patience like a dream"; thereby one understands worldly phenomena and swiftly accomplishes unimpeded wisdom to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
(Verse 6) Within this "patience like a dream," the verse itself corresponds to the preceding summary; it also corresponds to the introduction of the metaphor. Ten verses correspond to what preceded.
There are nine sections. First, one verse remains unaltered. Second, one verse praises the intrinsic nature; these first two verses also praise the introductory statement of the dharmas.

Third, one verse praises attachment; its reverse is liberation, which also praises the preceding metaphor. Fourth, one verse praises the nature of detachment. Fifth, one verse skips ahead to praise that which is manifested.
Sixth, one verse returns to praise the original nature. Seventh and eighth, two verses praise non-differentiation. Ninth, one verse praises conceptual discrimination.
One may understand these by reflecting upon them while awake;
practicing such conduct, one gives rise to vast understanding, skillfully knowing the nature of all phenomena,
and remains unattached to any phenomenon.
The seventh verse concerns the patience like an echo (*pratiśrutkā-sadṛśa-kṣānti*). The first stanza explains the cause for the practice of patience.

The text states that "practicing such conduct" serves to recapitulate the preceding metaphor. Since it speaks of "knowing the nature of all phenomena," its meaning is identical to the practice of patience.
All the various sounds of all the worlds, Neither internal nor external, he understands them all to be like echoes.
Just as one hears various echoes, The Bodhisattva’s mind does not give rise to discrimination when hearing sounds; His mind is likewise thus.
The next two verses praise hearing all sounds as being like echoes:
Beholding all the Tathāgatas and listening to the sound of their preaching the Dharma, Though they expound immeasurable sūtras, they hear them without attachment;
Like an echo, there is no place from which it comes, And so it is with the sounds that are heard.
Yet they are able to discern phenomena without contradicting the nature of phenomena.
[The next two verses describe how the Tathāgata’s voice is like an echo:
They thoroughly understand all sounds and voices, yet do not make conceptual distinctions regarding those sounds; they know that all sounds are entirely empty and quiescent.
Universally emitting pure sounds, they realize that phenomena do not reside in words. Skillfully entering the realm of wordlessness, they are yet able to manifest verbal teachings.
Like echoes pervading the world, they understand that the instruments of speech are complete with all vocal qualities;
knowing the nature of sound to be empty and quiescent, they speak using the conventional sounds of the world.
Just as all sounds in the world manifest according to the nature of conceptualization, so too do these sounds pervade everywhere to awaken all living beings.
When Bodhisattvas attain this patience, they purify their voices to transform the world;
with skillful means they speak of the three periods of time, yet remain unattached to the world.
The following verses describe the benefits of achieving patience; their metaphors appear throughout the stanzas.

Seeking enlightenment with single-minded intent for the sake of benefiting the world, one constantly enters the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and remains free from conceptual discrimination therein.
One universally contemplates all worlds as being quiescent and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Yet he constantly acts for the benefit [of others];

his mind remains unshakable as he practices cultivation—this is the eighth verse on "patience like a shadow. This verse explains ten pairs of dharmas; the metaphors and their applications are contained therein.
The first two stanzas concern non-arising and non-perishing in the world: because he realizes quiescence, there is no arising; because he brings about benefit, there is no perishing.
Not abiding in the world, yet not departing from the world; having nothing in the world upon which to rely, no place of dependence can be found.
The subsequent verse states that it is neither within nor without. Because it does not abide, it is not internal; because it does not depart, it is not external.
Having thoroughly understood the nature of the world, one is without attachment to that nature; though not relying on the world, one transforms the world to bring it across to liberation.
The subsequent verse praises this as neither practicing nor not practicing: because there is no defilement, it is not practicing; because one transforms the world, it is not non-practicing.
He fully knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena in the world; having realized that phenomena are non-dual, he is without attachment even to non-duality.

The subsequent verse states they are neither identical nor different: because he knows their intrinsic nature, they are not identical; because he has realized their non-duality, they are not different.
The mind does not depart from the world, nor does it dwell in the world; it does not practice for omniscience outside of the world.
Regarding the subsequent verse, "neither going nor not going": the second line refers to "not going," while the remaining three lines refer to "not not-going."
Just as a reflection in water is neither internal nor external, so too the Bodhisattva seeking awakening realizes that the world is not the mundane;
he does not abide in the world, yet he does not depart from it.
These six lines, beginning with "because the world is inexpressible," praise the state of neither abiding nor non-abiding. Among them, the first two lines specifically praise the metaphor. Thus.
"It is said to be neither internal nor external,
nor does it abide within or without. This single line, "like a shadow appearing in the world," praises that which is neither mundane nor supramundane.
Entering this profound meaning, Free from defilement and fully clear, Without abandoning the mind of the original vow,
The lamp of wisdom shines everywhere.
This subsequent verse praises neither the non-cultivation of bodhisattva practices nor the relinquishing of the great vows.
The world is boundless, yet wisdom enters it all with perfect equality; universally transforming all living beings so that they may abandon their manifold attachments.
This single verse praises how, while constantly practicing all Buddha-dharmas, one is able to accomplish all worldly affairs.
Contemplating the profound Dharma, he benefits the multitudes of sentient beings; from this, he enters into wisdom and practices all paths.
The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, clearly understanding them all to be like illusions, and thus acts with illusory conduct.
